Emergency food asssitance for the population affected by the conflict 2017: 183.000.000,00 € 2018: 102.000.000,00 € Top up financial year 2018: 51.000.000,00 € (2018 portion) Provision of general food assistance in the form of regular in-kind monthly food rations and ready-to-eat rations in the initial phase of displacement. The overall objective of the project: saving lives, sustaining lives and protecting livelihoods through the provision of emergency and regular food assistance to the most vulnerable families affected by the crisis. This contributes to SO1.
Based on the Food and Agriculture Sector 2018 sector strategy, approximately 6.5 million people are facing acute food insecurity with an additional 4 million at risk of falling into a situation of being food insecure. IDPs and people in besieged and Hard to Reach areas in addition to female headed households are between the most vulnerable groups that need food assistance to meet their minimum consumption needs. Women are increasingly becoming family breadwinners, heading more than third of the households.  Assistance to vulnerable groups with focus on female headed household will be prioritized. In addition, if the situation changed allowing a significant number of returnees among the IDPs and refugees, WFP will consider this group in the emergency general food assistance. WFP will consider various modalities as appropriate: including in-kind food assistance (Main modality for GFD) as well as cash based transfer (CBT). 
Emergency general food assistance is one of the four main activities/projects of WFP in 2018.  It will be complemented by i) nutrition project, targeting women and children to prevent and respond to undernutrition, ii) livelihood project to re build livelihood and resilience, and iii) school meals project, targeting pupils to support their learning. 

The emergency general food assistance project is aligned with the objectives 1 and 4 of the Food Security Cluster:
1. Improve the food security status of assessed food insecure people by emergency life saving and regular life sustaining food assistance
4: Strengthen the effectiveness and quality of the WoS response based on evidence, capacity building and strong coordination within the Food Security and Agriculture Sector and cross sectors.

Ukraine HRP (ECHO/UKR/BUD/2018/91009) Provision of shelter assistance to internally displaced and conflicted affected communities in Ukraine The overall aim of the project is to improve living conditions of the affected population, support returns of IDPs to the places of their previous residence and, to prevent further displacement of those who are the most affected with on going conflict. In continuity with the 2017 plan, UNHCR objectives include:

-   Urgent assistance in repairing damaged houses and apartments on both sides of the line of contact.
-   Provision of emergency shelter kits.
-   Procurement and distribution of NFIs to address individuals’ urgent needs and reduce long term vulnerability.
-   Distribution of NFI kits as a part of the response in emergency situations.
-   Winterization support – provision of winter clothes, coal, firewood or, if applicable, cash assistance for winterization purposes (fuel for heating).
-   Logistics and operational support will be provided in storage and delivery of necessary shelter and NFI assistance.

As part of its exit strategy (outside the humanitarian scope and set at 0 budget), UNHCR will be engaged in two additional activities not included in the 2017 plan: 

-   Protection guidance to state and development actors involved in the development of pilot projects on social housing.
-   Advocacy interventions for IDPs’ access to social housing.

Humanitarian Support to Protect Palestinians in the West Bank from forcible transfer Humanitarian Support to Protect Palestinians in the West Bank (including East Jerusalem) from Forcible Transfer. This Project contributes to the protection of Palestinians in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, from forcible transfer (FT) through a protection-centered approach to humanitarian responses incorporating: emergency support (cash/in-kind); provision of material assistance and essential services; legal aid; advocacy; and community empowerment.  188 communities will be specifically targeted each year for medium-term resilience-building support based on their vulnerability to FT, initially assessed using the OCHA VPP, supplemented with in-depth protection assessments taking into consideration the specific needs of women, men, children, elderly, and people with disability. Emergency and legal aid activities will be implemented across the whole West Bank, based on needs and referrals. Within the framework of the HCT, the Project supports the implementation of the Area C Policy Framework and coordinates with other actors meeting humanitarian needs of communities at risk of FT. The Project provides a mechanism to respond to OCHA triggers and ICCG coordination of response to demolitions. Shelter, WASH, Education, Health, FSS, legal responses, settler violence interventions and advocacy will be coordinated through the relevant Clusters/WGs. The Project is built on an integrated protection approach envisaged to contribute to all HRP objectives: S1:  The rights of Palestinians living under occupation are protected, respected and promoted; S2:   The basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation are met through the provision of essential services; S3:   The ability of vulnerable Palestinians to cope with the protracted crisis, including environmental threats, is supported, while solutions to violations and other root causes of threats and shocks are pursued. The Project further contributes to the three Shelter Cluster objectives (1. Support to the displaced; 2. Support to vulnerable households; 3. Increased response capacity).

(GAZA) Food Assistance to Vulnerable Food-Insecure Non- Refugee Populations In the Gaza Strip (part of ECHO/PSE/BUD/2018/91006) Country Strategic Plan for food assistance to the poor and severely food insecure population in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip WFP is committed to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and is guided by a strategic, programmatic and governance instrument to operationalize its plan and achieve its project objectives to: 
• End Hunger by protecting access to food and by improving dietary diversity;
• Support the implementation of the SDGs by enhancing the capacities of national institutions to implement food security strategies and operations;
This project directly contributes to strategic objectives two and three of the Humanitarian Response Plan 2018 2020, by meeting the basic food needs of severely vulnerable Palestinians and by improving their dietary diversity. 
WFP’s interventions focus on high food insecurity levels, including the malnutrition levels recorded by national surveys. By assisting the poor and severely food insecure Palestinian households in Gaza and Bedouin and herding communities in West Bank’s Area C, and by disseminating information on food and nutrition practices, WFP addresses the basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians and tackles one of the or root causes of some of the food insecurity levels recorded by the government institutions.
These interventions aim at improving the overall food security levels including nutrition and health status of the vulnerable Palestinians and therefore at increasing their coping abilities to sudden shocks in the market for access to food. 
The project also contributes to the Food Security Sector’s three objectives as well as to the National Policy Agenda 2017-2022 (policies on escaping poverty and strengthening social protection as well as meeting the basic needs of the communities) to ensure that the vulnerable Palestinians households basic food needs are met, by assisting households in enhancing their food security levels and by strengthening national institutions in implementing food security strategies and social security safety net programs to best identify and target food insecure and vulnerable Palestinians.

Extension of the Burundi Emergency Aid System in humanitarian emergencies for vulnerable displaced persons2018: 300.000,00 €    2019: 1.000.000,00 € (2018 portion) Emergency assistance to vulnerable people affected by natural disasters To provide comprehensive shelter to IDPs and host communities affected by natural disasters, as well as Burundian returnees from Tanzania. Activities include: i) preposition shelter and Non-Food non-food item (NFI) kits  to repair affected houses in disaster-prone areas, respond to emergencies and support affected populations; ii) provision of rental and shelter repair cash grants through bank and/or phone transfers, reaching 1,000 of the most vulnerable of the 26,000 IDP households living in urban areas throughout the country; iii) seek durable shelter solutions for the 3,000 people (600 households) living in collective sites by improving traditional construction mechanisms; iv) provision of semi-permanent shelter, repair shelter kits, cash grants and NFI kits to 15% of the most vulnerable returnees from Tanzania, targeting the provinces of Makamba, Rutana, Ruyigi and Muyinga, where the biggest returnee population is concentrated in Burundi; v) train civil servants and host communities using a shelter risk reduction approach; and vi) conduct sensitization sessions to increase awareness of safe construction mechanisms aiming to prevent landslides and the destruction of houses due to poor construction techniques and usage of low-quality materials.

Urgent support for the most vulnerable families in Gaza Strip. Enhance the resilience of vulnerable Farmers in Gaza strip Project Specific Objectives:
• 	Support the productive capacity of farmers by providing access to water through functioning water systems (irrigation, collection ponds, carrier lines)
• 	Recover and sustain the livelihoods of farmers by providing cash for work activities
The project will address Country Strategic Objective 3  and will be implemented in partnership with UAWC that have a strong presence and history of intervention in the OPTI including the Gaza Strip. Oxfam’s partnership approach is holistic and
rights-based. The project is planned to be implemented for a period of three years to achieve complementary and transitional activities aiming to enhance the productive capacities of farmers at all levels to sustain food security of farmers and bring their resilience a step forward. Humanitarian Support to Protect Palestinians in the West Bank from forcible transfer Humanitarian Support to Protect Palestinians in the West Bank (including East Jerusalem) from Forcible Transfer. This Project contributes to the protection of Palestinians in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, from forcible transfer (FT) through a protection-centered approach to humanitarian responses incorporating: emergency support (cash/in-kind); provision of material assistance and essential services; legal aid; advocacy; and community empowerment.  188 communities will be specifically targeted each year for medium-term resilience-building support based on their vulnerability to FT, initially assessed using the OCHA VPP, supplemented with in-depth protection assessments taking into consideration the specific needs of women, men, children, elderly, and people with disability. Emergency and legal aid activities will be implemented across the whole West Bank, based on needs and referrals. Within the framework of the HCT, the Project supports the implementation of the Area C Policy Framework and coordinates with other actors meeting humanitarian needs of communities at risk of FT. The Project provides a mechanism to respond to OCHA triggers and ICCG coordination of response to demolitions. Shelter, WASH, Education, Health, FSS, legal responses, settler violence interventions and advocacy will be coordinated through the relevant Clusters/WGs. The Project is built on an integrated protection approach envisaged to contribute to all HRP objectives: S1:  The rights of Palestinians living under occupation are protected, respected and promoted; S2:   The basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation are met through the provision of essential services; S3:   The ability of vulnerable Palestinians to cope with the protracted crisis, including environmental threats, is supported, while solutions to violations and other root causes of threats and shocks are pursued. The Project further contributes to the three Shelter Cluster objectives (1. Support to the displaced; 2. Support to vulnerable households; 3. Increased response capacity).

• End Hunger by protecting access to food and by improving dietary diversity;
• Support the implementation of the SDGs by enhancing the capacities of national institutions to implement food security strategies and operations;
This project directly contributes to strategic objectives two and three of the Humanitarian Response Plan 2018 2020, by meeting the basic food needs of severely vulnerable Palestinians and by improving their dietary diversity.

Multi-sector emergency and cash response for Nigerian refugees, IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host populations living in areas bordering Nigeria, Far North Cameroon Improve the access to food services to the refugees populations affected by the conflict in the Far North of region of Cameroon. In addition to the security context, the far North region of Cameroon suffers frequent droughts, floods and epidemics that usually strike the Sahel countries.  The combination of conflict and disasters together with chronic poverty have caused the gradual deterioration of the population’s livelihoods. Moreover, the fear of infiltration of Boko Haram fighters to outsource basic supplies from areas close to the Nigerian border has prompted local authorities to restrict the amount of goods to the areas which has limited the ability of the refugees and host communities to access sufficient food. There is however a noted solidarity between host communities and refugees in areas close to the border such as Makary and Fotokol, through which host community can avail pieces of land to refugees for farming but access to seeds and tools remain difficult.

This contributes to SO1.
Based on the Food and Agriculture Sector 2018 sector strategy, approximately 6.5 million people are facing acute food insecurity with an additional 4 million at risk of falling into a situation of being food insecure. IDPs and people in besieged and Hard to Reach areas in addition to female headed households are between the most vulnerable groups that need food assistance to meet their minimum consumption needs. Women are increasingly becoming family breadwinners, heading more than third of the households.  Assistance to vulnerable groups with focus on female headed household will be prioritized. In addition, if the situation changed allowing a significant number of returnees among the IDPs and refugees, WFP will consider this group in the emergency general food assistance. WFP will consider various modalities as appropriate: including in-kind food assistance (Main modality for GFD) as well as cash based transfer (CBT). 
Emergency general food assistance is one of the four main activities/projects of WFP in 2018. The emergency general food assistance project is aligned with the objectives 1 and 4 of the Food Security Cluster:
1. Improve the food security status of assessed food insecure people by emergency life saving and regular life sustaining food assistance
4: Strengthen the effectiveness and quality of the WoS response based on evidence, capacity building and strong coordination within the Food Security and Agriculture Sector and cross sectors.

To provide immediate food assistance, ACTED plans to make unconditional cash transfers, conditional cash transfers , and restricted cash vouchers. Conditional cash transfers will not only improve purchasing power of beneficiaries, but will also contribute to creation, construction and rehabilitation of key livelihood assets such as water catchments and dykes to manage floods. (GAZA) Country Strategic Plan for food assistance to the poor and severely food insecure population in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip Country Strategic Plan for food assistance to the poor and severely food insecure population in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip WFP is committed to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and is guided by a strategic, programmatic and governance instrument to operationalize its plan and achieve its project objectives to: 
• End Hunger by protecting access to food and by improving dietary diversity;
• Support the implementation of the SDGs by enhancing the capacities of national institutions to implement food security strategies and operations;
This project directly contributes to strategic objectives two and three of the Humanitarian Response Plan 2018 2020, by meeting the basic food needs of severely vulnerable Palestinians and by improving their dietary diversity. 
WFP’s interventions focus on high food insecurity levels, including the malnutrition levels recorded by national surveys. By assisting the poor and severely food insecure Palestinian households in Gaza and Bedouin and herding communities in West Bank’s Area C, and by disseminating information on food and nutrition practices, WFP addresses the basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians and tackles one of the or root causes of some of the food insecurity levels recorded by the government institutions.
These interventions aim at improving the overall food security levels including nutrition and health status of the vulnerable Palestinians and therefore at increasing their coping abilities to sudden shocks in the market for access to food. 
The project also contributes to the Food Security Sector’s three objectives as well as to the National Policy Agenda 2017-2022 (policies on escaping poverty and strengthening social protection as well as meeting the basic needs of the communities) to ensure that the vulnerable Palestinians households basic food needs are met, by assisting households in enhancing their food security levels and by strengthening national institutions in implementing food security strategies and social security safety net programs to best identify and target food insecure and vulnerable Palestinians.

Humanitarian aid Provision of general food assistance in the form of regular in-kind monthly food rations and ready-to-eat rations in the initial phase of displacement. The overall objective of the project: saving lives, sustaining lives and protecting livelihoods through the provision of emergency and regular food assistance to the most vulnerable families affected by the crisis. This contributes to SO1.
Based on the Food and Agriculture Sector 2018 sector strategy, approximately 6.5 million people are facing acute food insecurity with an additional 4 million at risk of falling into a situation of being food insecure. IDPs and people in besieged and Hard to Reach areas in addition to female headed households are between the most vulnerable groups that need food assistance to meet their minimum consumption needs. Women are increasingly becoming family breadwinners, heading more than third of the households.  Assistance to vulnerable groups with focus on female headed household will be prioritized. In addition, if the situation changed allowing a significant number of returnees among the IDPs and refugees, WFP will consider this group in the emergency general food assistance. WFP will consider various modalities as appropriate: including in-kind food assistance (Main modality for GFD) as well as cash based transfer (CBT). 
Emergency general food assistance is one of the four main activities/projects of WFP in 2018.  It will be complemented by i) nutrition project, targeting women and children to prevent and respond to undernutrition, ii) livelihood project to re build livelihood and resilience, and iii) school meals project, targeting pupils to support their learning. 

The emergency general food assistance project is aligned with the objectives 1 and 4 of the Food Security Cluster:
1. Improve the food security status of assessed food insecure people by emergency life saving and regular life sustaining food assistance
4: Strengthen the effectiveness and quality of the WoS response based on evidence, capacity building and strong coordination within the Food Security and Agriculture Sector and cross sectors.

• Support the implementation of the SDGs by enhancing the capacities of national institutions to implement food security strategies and operations;
This project directly contributes to strategic objectives two and three of the Humanitarian Response Plan 2018 2020, by meeting the basic food needs of severely vulnerable Palestinians and by improving their dietary diversity.

Iraq: Iraq Crisis -No Lost Generation (NLG) - UNICEF Multiyear (SM160522) (part of D003266 - No Lost Generation) Specialized GBV Prevention and Response Services for Conflict-affected Women and children in Iraq Overall Objectives:  To improve access to quality life-saving GBV prevention and response services for women and girls who are survivors or at risk of GBV, through age appropriate and survivor centered approaches. 

Pervasive GBV abuses against women and girls, in particular sexual violence, family violence, sexual exploitation, forced and child marriage persist.  Fears of harassment, reprisal and stigmatization, including honour killing, remain real barriers to seeking services, justice and protection for GBV survivors. The consequences of GBV require a sustained and multi-sector responses, including specialized case management services and prevention and risk mitigation strategies to ensure the safety and dignity of women and girls and reduce risks of GBV. 

This project aims to address the broad and critical needs of conflict-affected women and girls survivors or at risk of GBV and strengthen the protective environment through case management, psychosocial support and community-based prevention programmes and activities.

Specific Objectives:
1.	Provide GBV prevention and response services for highly vulnerable women and children, including community-based mitigation of GBV, in camps, non-camps settings and for those newly returning to their places of origin, to ensure their rights, safety and dignity.
2.	Provide specialized GBV case management and PSS services and protection assistance for survivors and women and girls who are at risk of GBV, including returnees, stayees, IDPs, host community and those living in mixed population areas of return.
3.	Provide emergency GBV response and protection assistance to newly displaced women and girls.
4.	Provide critical services and assistance to vulnerable women and children in areas of return to access government provided social assistance and support systems.

Emergency food asssitance for the population affected by the conflict 2017: 183.000.000,00 € 2018: 102.000.000,00 € Top up financial year 2018: 51.000.000,00 € (2018 portion) Provision of general food assistance in the form of regular in-kind monthly food rations and ready-to-eat rations in the initial phase of displacement. The overall objective of the project: saving lives, sustaining lives and protecting livelihoods through the provision of emergency and regular food assistance to the most vulnerable families affected by the crisis. This contributes to SO1.
Based on the Food and Agriculture Sector 2018 sector strategy, approximately 6.5 million people are facing acute food insecurity with an additional 4 million at risk of falling into a situation of being food insecure. IDPs and people in besieged and Hard to Reach areas in addition to female headed households are between the most vulnerable groups that need food assistance to meet their minimum consumption needs. Women are increasingly becoming family breadwinners, heading more than third of the households.  Assistance to vulnerable groups with focus on female headed household will be prioritized. In addition, if the situation changed allowing a significant number of returnees among the IDPs and refugees, WFP will consider this group in the emergency general food assistance. WFP will consider various modalities as appropriate: including in-kind food assistance (Main modality for GFD) as well as cash based transfer (CBT). 
Emergency general food assistance is one of the four main activities/projects of WFP in 2018.  It will be complemented by i) nutrition project, targeting women and children to prevent and respond to undernutrition, ii) livelihood project to re build livelihood and resilience, and iii) school meals project, targeting pupils to support their learning. 

The emergency general food assistance project is aligned with the objectives 1 and 4 of the Food Security Cluster:
1. Improve the food security status of assessed food insecure people by emergency life saving and regular life sustaining food assistance
4: Strengthen the effectiveness and quality of the WoS response based on evidence, capacity building and strong coordination within the Food Security and Agriculture Sector and cross sectors.

Provision of lifesaving emergency food security and livelihood support to the IDPs and vulnerable host communities in East Jebel Marra, South Darfur - Deribat (Envelope 1) Provision of lifesaving emergency food security and livelihood support to the IDPs and destitute vulnerable host communities’ in West and South Kordofan, and Blue Nile States (PSC sharing consortium) This proposed project builds on MC's ongoing FSL programming under the consortium arrangement in the target areas, specifically the current SHF funded consortium project, and aims to mitigate the imminent deterioration of food security and nutrition conditions among IDPs and vulnerable host communities and to protect livelihood assets of an estimated 99,000 direct beneficiaries in Abu Kershola, El Qoz and Dellami localities in South Kordofan State; Al Khowey, El Nehoud and Ghubaysh localities in West Kordofan State; Bau, El Kurmuk and El Roseires localities of Blue Nile State.

The proposed intervention follows the strategic positioning guiding the Sudan MYHS 2017-19. In particular, the outcome 1 and 3 of MYHS are emphasized throughout the project and all the interventions aimed at saving lives and reducing needs and vulnerabilities by directly increasing production and access to crops contributing to enhanced nutritional status and indirectly strengthening livestock and non-livestock based livelihoods to achieve the same objective. This intervention is shaped by the continuous process of ensuring Accountability to Affected populations and gender equality.

Integrated Protection and Education Response to Conflict Affected Iraqis (part of ECHO/IRQ/BUD/2018/91013) Protection Response to IDP communities and IDP returnees in Iraq This project aims to support vulnerable displaced families living in camps and sub-standard accommodation, and highly vulnerable people inadequately covered under the social protection network by providing them with legal counselling and legal representation services in line with all 4 Cluster Objectives of the HRP 2018. It aims to provide vulnerable families who are willing to return home but are unable to do so, the relevant information for them to take an informed decision on their return. It also aims to support people brutalized by violence, especially men and boys, as well as people with disability and their caregivers, to cope and recover through the provision of psychosocial support (PSS) activities.
In response to the ongoing humanitarian crisis in large parts of Iraq, the International Rescue Committee (IRC) will provide assistance to vulnerable conflict-affected populations through an integrated protection response program, targeting specifically IDPs and returnees in Ninewa, Anbar, Kirkuk, Baghdad and Salah al Din. This intervention will consist of protection monitoring, legal assistance (civil documentation, HLPs) and PSS for men and boys. More specifically, the project will focus on legal assistance for IDPs and returnees, through legal counselling, legal representation for civil documentation, Housing Land and Property, and GBV survivors. The legal program also includes representation for detention cases. The IRC will also ensure provision of PSS directly targeting adult men and adolescent boys to assist them to survive, recover and manage the effects of their trauma, as it impacts themselves, their families and community members. As part of the detention legal assistance, the IRC protection team will follow-up on the detainees released from detention centers through case management, linking the ex-detainees and their families to torture case management, psychosocial support, cash assistance, health provision, and any other relevant services.

Humanitarian aid Provision of general food assistance in the form of regular in-kind monthly food rations and ready-to-eat rations in the initial phase of displacement. The overall objective of the project: saving lives, sustaining lives and protecting livelihoods through the provision of emergency and regular food assistance to the most vulnerable families affected by the crisis. This contributes to SO1.
Based on the Food and Agriculture Sector 2018 sector strategy, approximately 6.5 million people are facing acute food insecurity with an additional 4 million at risk of falling into a situation of being food insecure. IDPs and people in besieged and Hard to Reach areas in addition to female headed households are between the most vulnerable groups that need food assistance to meet their minimum consumption needs. Women are increasingly becoming family breadwinners, heading more than third of the households.  Assistance to vulnerable groups with focus on female headed household will be prioritized. In addition, if the situation changed allowing a significant number of returnees among the IDPs and refugees, WFP will consider this group in the emergency general food assistance. WFP will consider various modalities as appropriate: including in-kind food assistance (Main modality for GFD) as well as cash based transfer (CBT). 
Emergency general food assistance is one of the four main activities/projects of WFP in 2018.  It will be complemented by i) nutrition project, targeting women and children to prevent and respond to undernutrition, ii) livelihood project to re build livelihood and resilience, and iii) school meals project, targeting pupils to support their learning. 

The emergency general food assistance project is aligned with the objectives 1 and 4 of the Food Security Cluster:
1. Improve the food security status of assessed food insecure people by emergency life saving and regular life sustaining food assistance
4: Strengthen the effectiveness and quality of the WoS response based on evidence, capacity building and strong coordination within the Food Security and Agriculture Sector and cross sectors.

(GAZA) Critical Food Assistance Country Strategic Plan for food assistance to the poor and severely food insecure population in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip WFP is committed to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and is guided by a strategic, programmatic and governance instrument to operationalize its plan and achieve its project objectives to: 
• End Hunger by protecting access to food and by improving dietary diversity;
• Support the implementation of the SDGs by enhancing the capacities of national institutions to implement food security strategies and operations;
This project directly contributes to strategic objectives two and three of the Humanitarian Response Plan 2018 2020, by meeting the basic food needs of severely vulnerable Palestinians and by improving their dietary diversity. 
WFP’s interventions focus on high food insecurity levels, including the malnutrition levels recorded by national surveys. By assisting the poor and severely food insecure Palestinian households in Gaza and Bedouin and herding communities in West Bank’s Area C, and by disseminating information on food and nutrition practices, WFP addresses the basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians and tackles one of the or root causes of some of the food insecurity levels recorded by the government institutions.
These interventions aim at improving the overall food security levels including nutrition and health status of the vulnerable Palestinians and therefore at increasing their coping abilities to sudden shocks in the market for access to food. 
The project also contributes to the Food Security Sector’s three objectives as well as to the National Policy Agenda 2017-2022 (policies on escaping poverty and strengthening social protection as well as meeting the basic needs of the communities) to ensure that the vulnerable Palestinians households basic food needs are met, by assisting households in enhancing their food security levels and by strengthening national institutions in implementing food security strategies and social security safety net programs to best identify and target food insecure and vulnerable Palestinians.

(Multi donor: ECHO, Denmark, France, Italy, Luxemburg, Spain) Humanitarian Support to Protect Palestinians in the West Bank (including East Jerusalem) from Forcible Transfer. This Project contributes to the protection of Palestinians in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, from forcible transfer (FT) through a protection-centered approach to humanitarian responses incorporating: emergency support (cash/in-kind); provision of material assistance and essential services; legal aid; advocacy; and community empowerment.  188 communities will be specifically targeted each year for medium-term resilience-building support based on their vulnerability to FT, initially assessed using the OCHA VPP, supplemented with in-depth protection assessments taking into consideration the specific needs of women, men, children, elderly, and people with disability. Emergency and legal aid activities will be implemented across the whole West Bank, based on needs and referrals. Within the framework of the HCT, the Project supports the implementation of the Area C Policy Framework and coordinates with other actors meeting humanitarian needs of communities at risk of FT. The Project provides a mechanism to respond to OCHA triggers and ICCG coordination of response to demolitions. Shelter, WASH, Education, Health, FSS, legal responses, settler violence interventions and advocacy will be coordinated through the relevant Clusters/WGs. The Project is built on an integrated protection approach envisaged to contribute to all HRP objectives: S1:  The rights of Palestinians living under occupation are protected, respected and promoted; S2:   The basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation are met through the provision of essential services; S3:   The ability of vulnerable Palestinians to cope with the protracted crisis, including environmental threats, is supported, while solutions to violations and other root causes of threats and shocks are pursued. The Project further contributes to the three Shelter Cluster objectives (1. Support to the displaced; 2. Support to vulnerable households; 3. Increased response capacity).

Within the framework of the HCT, the Project supports the implementation of the Area C Policy Framework and coordinates with other actors meeting humanitarian needs of communities at risk of FT. The Project provides a mechanism to respond to OCHA triggers and ICCG coordination of response to demolitions. Shelter, WASH, Education, Health, FSS, legal responses, settler violence interventions and advocacy will be coordinated through the relevant Clusters/WGs. The Project is built on an integrated protection approach envisaged to contribute to all HRP objectives: S1:  The rights of Palestinians living under occupation are protected, respected and promoted; S2:   The basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation are met through the provision of essential services; S3:   The ability of vulnerable Palestinians to cope with the protracted crisis, including environmental threats, is supported, while solutions to violations and other root causes of threats and shocks are pursued. The Project further contributes to the three Shelter Cluster objectives (1. Support to the displaced; 2. Support to vulnerable households; 3. Increased response capacity).

Cash distributions, both unconditional and CFW, are best suited to meeting the food security objectives of the proposed response especially when it comes to diversification of diet and beneficiary targeting. CFW in particular, in addition to promoting stakeholder ownership, owing to the type of works that will be selected, fit in with the broader strategy of reinforcing existing actors’ initiatives in the target area.  The same is true of DRC’s support to Community Health Clubs.

(WEST BANK/GAZA) Food Assistance (USAID/FFP) Country Strategic Plan for food assistance to the poor and severely food insecure population in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip WFP is committed to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and is guided by a strategic, programmatic and governance instrument to operationalize its plan and achieve its project objectives to: 
• End Hunger by protecting access to food and by improving dietary diversity;
• Support the implementation of the SDGs by enhancing the capacities of national institutions to implement food security strategies and operations;
This project directly contributes to strategic objectives two and three of the Humanitarian Response Plan 2018 2020, by meeting the basic food needs of severely vulnerable Palestinians and by improving their dietary diversity. 
WFP’s interventions focus on high food insecurity levels, including the malnutrition levels recorded by national surveys. By assisting the poor and severely food insecure Palestinian households in Gaza and Bedouin and herding communities in West Bank’s Area C, and by disseminating information on food and nutrition practices, WFP addresses the basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians and tackles one of the or root causes of some of the food insecurity levels recorded by the government institutions.
These interventions aim at improving the overall food security levels including nutrition and health status of the vulnerable Palestinians and therefore at increasing their coping abilities to sudden shocks in the market for access to food. 
The project also contributes to the Food Security Sector’s three objectives as well as to the National Policy Agenda 2017-2022 (policies on escaping poverty and strengthening social protection as well as meeting the basic needs of the communities) to ensure that the vulnerable Palestinians households basic food needs are met, by assisting households in enhancing their food security levels and by strengthening national institutions in implementing food security strategies and social security safety net programs to best identify and target food insecure and vulnerable Palestinians.

Contribution au PAM (WFP) pour ses activités en Syrie Provision of general food assistance in the form of regular in-kind monthly food rations and ready-to-eat rations in the initial phase of displacement. The overall objective of the project: saving lives, sustaining lives and protecting livelihoods through the provision of emergency and regular food assistance to the most vulnerable families affected by the crisis. This contributes to SO1.
Based on the Food and Agriculture Sector 2018 sector strategy, approximately 6.5 million people are facing acute food insecurity with an additional 4 million at risk of falling into a situation of being food insecure. IDPs and people in besieged and Hard to Reach areas in addition to female headed households are between the most vulnerable groups that need food assistance to meet their minimum consumption needs. Women are increasingly becoming family breadwinners, heading more than third of the households.  Assistance to vulnerable groups with focus on female headed household will be prioritized. In addition, if the situation changed allowing a significant number of returnees among the IDPs and refugees, WFP will consider this group in the emergency general food assistance. WFP will consider various modalities as appropriate: including in-kind food assistance (Main modality for GFD) as well as cash based transfer (CBT). 
Emergency general food assistance is one of the four main activities/projects of WFP in 2018.  It will be complemented by i) nutrition project, targeting women and children to prevent and respond to undernutrition, ii) livelihood project to re build livelihood and resilience, and iii) school meals project, targeting pupils to support their learning. 

The emergency general food assistance project is aligned with the objectives 1 and 4 of the Food Security Cluster:
1. Improve the food security status of assessed food insecure people by emergency life saving and regular life sustaining food assistance
4: Strengthen the effectiveness and quality of the WoS response based on evidence, capacity building and strong coordination within the Food Security and Agriculture Sector and cross sectors.

Syria Resilience Consortium (NMFA) II Strengthen socio-economic well-being and adaptive capacities of people and communities in North Syria The program’s overall objective is to strengthen resilience of communities in Northeast Syria. Mercy Corps emphasizes an integrated approach that builds households’ economic well-being as well as communities that are cohesive, inclusive and equitable. 
Mercy Corps’ Making Markets Work in Crisis approach will drive interventions to increase economic opportunities. Through this approach, Mercy Corps will target market support to key value chains, market actors, producers and local institutions. The specific implementation approach will vary according to the different contexts in Syria, taking into account market robustness, and the constraints. While some of the activities can include simple financial support to key businesses, such as micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) or smart subsidies using vouchers, other activities go deeper, analysing market systems and then providing support that enables both market actors and consumers to cope and recover through the local economy. These interventions may include better access to informal financial services and quality agricultural input supplies. For example, linking traders to bigger suppliers and providing them with better market information or short-run subsidies can reduce their operating risks. This improves traders’ ability to access key goods and sell these goods at affordable prices. Through this program Mercy Corps will address: 1) limited access to economic opportunities and financial services; and 2) the weak and insufficient, but slowly growing, body of private agricultural input suppliers in Syria.
Strengthening cohesive communities is vital to supporting the stability that is finally emerging in NES, and reinforcing post-conflict economic recovery. The combination of improving inter-communal relationships and reducing resource-based tensions will serve to prevent the escalation of some economic-based disputes into violence – for example between host and IDP communities over livelihood opportunities or social service provision – and reduce the ability of political actors to manipulate ethno-religious divisions and mobilise violence. To this end, and in close collaboration with local and neighborhood councils, Mercy Corps will implement community service projects to support local economic development and address resource-based tensions.

Food Security (USAID/FFP) Lean Season Food Assistance to the most food insecure people in rural areas Under this Flash Appeal, Food Security sector partners plan to address the most urgent food security needs of people in rural areas across the country, who are adversely affected by multiple crises, including last year’s poor harvest for many small-holder farmers, economic shocks and recent cholera and typhoid outbreaks. Building on the funding already received to reach an estimated 900,000 people as of January 2019 and the Government’s Food Deficit Mitigation Strategy, partners aim to expand the geographic coverage of assistance to reach an additional 700,000 people in food insecure rural communities through primarily cash-based assistance. Focus will be on the low-lying areas relying on rainfed agriculture disproportionately affected by last year’s erratic rain. Market-based interventions are viable despite the current economic stress, as essential food commodities remain available on rural as well as urban markets, according to the national market assessment conducted by WFP and partners in November 2018. 

The IPC analysis conducted in January 2019 projects that nearly 3.8 million people in rural areas are in need of urgent humanitarian assistance, including 2.9 million who are severely food insecure (IPC phase 3 or 4) and a further 900,000 people who are currently receiving humanitarian assistance, without which they would be in IPC phase 3 or above.

In the face of the high prevalence of food insecurity (IPC phase 4 and 3), and the high probability of another El Niño phenomena in 2019 (90% likelihood according to the most recent SARCOF analysis), partners will provide a specialised food ration in the form of CSB++ specifically targeting children 6-59 months and pregnant and lactating women to increase the nutritional value of the food basket provided as part of the general household ration/cash. 

Based on the findings of the national market assessment conducted by partners in November, partners will select the most appropriate transfer modality for each district (cash or in-kind). According to the latest price information, partners aim to cover approximately 80% of the targeted individuals’ daily food energy needs (based on a 2100 kcal diet) to supplement other available food sources, thus enabling households to meet their basic food and nutrition needs. 
 
In view of the high probability of another El Nino, food assistance at this juncture can be considered as an early action to prevent further deterioration of food insecurity amongst particularly households already in IPC 3 (Crises) and 4 (Emergency).

Improving Psychosocial Wellbeing of Children, Adolescent Girls and Young Mothers at risk of exploitation and abuse in families affected by food insecurity in Chitungwiza, Binga, Epworth and Rushinga Child Protection  for children affected by El Nino induced drought humanitarian situation The humanitarian intervention aims to ensure that girls and boys, especially the most vulnerable and those affected by humanitarian situations, are protected from all forms of violence, exploitation, abuse and harmful practices. The persistent drought and economic shocks have increased the vulnerability of children, adolescents and women to protection risks and may be exacerbated by the probable El Niño. This proposal is targeting 100,000 people, primarily children and their caregivers, adolescents especially girls including adolescent mothers, community, child protection structures as well as other humanitarian sectors responding to the effects of drought in 15 districts targeted by the child protection sub-sector. In cases of drought girls are the most affected as they suffer from family separation, child labour and child marriage. Children adopt negative coping mechanisms such as migration and this heighten increase exposure to sexual violence, exploitation and other forms of abuse. Furthermore, family tension escalate children and particularly women suffer from domestic violence. 

The implementation scale and scope of humanitarian intervention is to strengthen CPiE coordination, capacity building of Child Protection sub-sector community based mechanisms, integrate CPiE prevention and response in other intervention sectors, strengthen the resilience of children and adolescent and provide quality comprehensive child protection case management services. 

The objective is ensure that girls and boys rights to protection from violence, abuse and exploitation are sustained and promoted in humanitarian situations. Vulnerable children and those engaged in risky coping mechanisms are reached with child and social protection support to keep them safe. 

The priority intervention is support the availability and accessibility of quality comprehensive and vulnerability sensitive child protection services for all children with special needs including separated children, children with disabilities, children in contact with the law children with HIV and child survivors of violence. This is building on the National Case Management Systems which is operational in all districts. There is an existing community workforce of 10,500 Community Childcare Workers (CCWs) who have limited understanding of CPiE whose capacity requires to be strengthened. 

The expected output from this support is improved coordination of the child protection sub-sector response, strengthened capacity of child protection actors who are responsive to the needs of children and adolescents. The following target group will benefit children without appropriate care including separated and unaccompanied children, children at risk of violence, children at risk of exposure to child labour, pregnant adolescents and young mothers in need of psycho social support.

Market-based interventions are viable despite the current economic stress, as essential food commodities remain available on rural as well as urban markets, according to the national market assessment conducted by WFP and partners in November 2018. 

The IPC analysis conducted in January 2019 projects that nearly 3.8 million people in rural areas are in need of urgent humanitarian assistance, including 2.9 million who are severely food insecure (IPC phase 3 or 4) and a further 900,000 people who are currently receiving humanitarian assistance, without which they would be in IPC phase 3 or above.

In the face of the high prevalence of food insecurity (IPC phase 4 and 3), and the high probability of another El Niño phenomena in 2019 (90% likelihood according to the most recent SARCOF analysis), partners will provide a specialised food ration in the form of CSB++ specifically targeting children 6-59 months and pregnant and lactating women to increase the nutritional value of the food basket provided as part of the general household ration/cash. 

Based on the findings of the national market assessment conducted by partners in November, partners will select the most appropriate transfer modality for each district (cash or in-kind). According to the latest price information, partners aim to cover approximately 80% of the targeted individuals’ daily food energy needs (based on a 2100 kcal diet) to supplement other available food sources, thus enabling households to meet their basic food and nutrition needs. 
 
In view of the high probability of another El Nino, food assistance at this juncture can be considered as an early action to prevent further deterioration of food insecurity amongst particularly households already in IPC 3 (Crises) and 4 (Emergency).

Food Security (USAID/FFP) Food support to Refugees at Tongogara Refugee Camp WFP Zimbabwe, in partnership with UNHCR and jointly-selected partner Terre Des Hommes (TDH), is currently supporting more than 13,000 refugees in Tongogara Refugee Camp (TRC) with monthly food assistance. The refugees are mainly from DRC (72.3%), Mozambique (13.7%), Burundi (6.04%) and Rwanda (5%), with others from the Horn of Africa including Somalia, Ethiopia and South Sudan. TRC the only refugee camp in Zimbabwe, located in Chipangayi, Chipinge District in Manicaland Province, about 500 kilometres South East of the capital, Harare and approximately 80km west of Chipinge town. The camp was established in 1981 to cater for an influx of refugees from Mozambique during its civil war. The number of refugees residing at TRC has consistently increased, with a sharp rise from 5,000 in 2015 to the current 13,000. The population is expected to grow further in 2019, considering the rising tensions in DRC.
The camp measures approximately 800ha, with a possible maximum of 1,000ha available for current use and planning requirements, according to Government of Zimbabwe (GOZ).The camp is in natural region 5, characterized by temperatures that in mid-summer can average more than 40 degrees Celsius, with mean annual rainfall of less than 450mm/year and of a sporadic nature that is not suitable for growing the staple maize crop. The camp experiences cycles of floods and droughts and can go through an entire season without rain; the nearby Save River becomes an important water resource for agricultural-based livelihoods.
The GOZ and UNHCR manage the camp, and work with other partners to ensure basic needs and protection of rights of concerned population. In line with the global agreement, WFP is the main partner managing and providing food assistance for refugees at the camp since 2015; accordingly, it has built up substantial capacity to run the programme in collaboration with partners. The refugees are fully reliant on WFP’s food assistance for survival.
WFP provides monthly food assistance of the resident refugees, through cash-based transfers, sufficient to meet 100 percent of the daily energy requirements of an adult person. Chronically ill people also receive a top-up of Super Cereal through camp health facilities, enabling them to consume up to 2,380 kcal per day. The new arrivals at the camp receive an in-kind transfer for the first three months to cover the gap between their arrival at the camp and the completion of their registration, after which they are entitled to the regular cash-based assistance. 
WFP has been implementing cash transfers at the camp since 2016. The cash-based assistance has empowered the persons of concern to buy food commodities of their choice furthering their dignity and opportunity to access food, increasing diversity of food consumption and stimulating local markets. It has also empowered some of them towards pursuing other livelihoods options.
The refugee population is continuously increasing by an average of 150 persons every four weeks. This is in addition to the already existing 450 caseload of people seeking asylum. Following this trend, Zimbabwe is likely to experience a wave of new asylum seekers, with the numbers reaching 20,000 by December 2019. WFP immediately requires US$1,765,248.00, to provide the much-needed food assistance to the refugees for approximately six months, from January to June 2019. 
WFP proposes to respond through its CSP Activity 1.2 Support to Refugees, to ensure that the food-insecure refugees in TRC are enabled to meet their basic food and nutrition requirements. Support to refugees contributes to SDG target 2.1 (ending hunger and ensuring access to food) as well as SDG target 2.2 (ending all forms of malnutrition). This contribution will assist WFP to pursue the objective to improve food access to vulnerable refugees through the provision of cash-based transfers and in-kind commodities.

Coordinated Implementation of Multipurpose Cash Assistance to Support Somali Households Affected by Crisis (part of ECHO/-HF/BUD/2019/91009) Providing Durable water  solutions by increasing access to emergency and sustained water, sanitation facilities and hygiene promotion for displaced vulnerable women, girls, boys and men in IDP settlements and host communities targeting beneficiaries in South Central and Somali land The proposed project will provide durable solutions to chronic and recurrent water problems by providing adequate safe water, sanitation facilities and hygiene education targeting 66,000 beneficiaries (32,340 male and 33,660 female) - without double counting. 60,000 beneficiaries will be reached through water supply services. Specifically, 24,000 beneficiaries will benefit through water provision (18,000 in Mogadishu and 6,000 in Lower Shabelle), 21,000 will benefit through construction of mega rain water catchment pan in Bardhere, 13,800 will be reached through construction of water treatment unit in Bardhere, and 1,200 will be reached through construction of  3 berkerds in Somaliland. 
On sanitation, 21,000 beneficiaries will be reached through constriction of 700 latrines (250 Bardhere, 150 Mogadishu, 200 Baidoa and 100 Lower Shabelle). 15,000 beneficiaries will be discounted from the total since the same beneficiaries will benefit from water facilities. On hygiene promotion, 7000 AWD kits (2,500 in Bardhere, 1,500 in Mogadishu, 2000 in Baidoa and 1000 kits in Lower Shabelle) will be distributed to reach 42,000 beneficiaries. Each kit will comprise 200 sachets of aqua tabs, 2 jerry cans and 12 pieces of soap each weighing 200g to give 2400g.  All hygiene promotion beneficiaries will be discounted from the total to avoid double counting.
In Gedo region,  Bardhere, the water treatment unit is aimed at improving the water  quantity and quality will comprise the intake unit, flocculation chamber, sedimentation chamber, chlorination unit, elevated tower and distribution system. The intake unit will comprise a suction pump fitted with a flexible pipe with a floater extending to the river. Water will be delivered to the flocculation unit where aluminium sulphate is added and mixed .Water will then flow to the sedimentation unit which allows settling of large flocs. Water then flows to the chlorination unit where chlorination occurs before it is pumped to a 50 cubic elevated tower through a 2km pipe before distribution occurs through four the water kiosks constructed within the IDP camp. Water will also be pumped to existing elevated RC tank 12meters high  with a capacity of 130 cubic and distributed through and existing water distribution system to serve host communities. ; On sanitation concern plans to construct 250 latrines in the IDP camps. The latrines will be fitted with hand washing facilities aimed at promoting handwashing after use of the latrines and at critical times for AWD/Cholera prevention.  In Belet Xawa, Concern will construct a mega water pan with an improved sand filtration system. The water pan will be lined with a geotextile material to prevent seepage. The Mega Water pan will have a holding capacity of 26,965,000 liters capacity and expected to have water in all the seasons. The water pan will be fenced and provided with a drawing point and fitted with water pump. Animal troughs will also be provided for use. On hygiene, the project propose hygiene education through trained Community Health Promoters. The project will recruit and train hygiene promoters to disseminate hygiene messages during house to house visit;  mass hygiene promotion awareness using radio messaging, hygiene messages on bill-boards located in strategic locations; distribution of hygiene kits will be made to the most vulnerable members of the community; promotion of house hold water treatment through distribution of water purification tablets for rural communities
In Banadir and Bay (lower Shabelle) region, concern will provide water to 24000 IDPs through pipelines. Water will be supplied through existing pipelines and where possible extension of pipelines will be made to ensure beneficiaries get water within a minimum distance of 500 meters. Private water companies owning boreholes near the IDP locations will provide water. All the water points will be metered and payment will be made based on the actual amount of water consumed by the beneficiaries.
In Somaliland, 3 berkerds will be constructed to reach 1200 beneficiaries. The berkerds will be constructed in strategic locations to ensure maximum volume is captured during the rains. The water harvested will be utilized during the dry season.
In order to ensure sustainability of water facilities, Concern will  work with the community and local authorities to identify and train a private company managing water in Bardhere. The Private Company in Bardhere and management committee in Belet Xawa & Somaliland will be trained on management, operation and maintenance of the water supply system. The trained teams will then be issued with operation and maintenance tools for water treatment unit in Bardhere and water pan in Belet Xawa and equipment. The committee and private company will be then continue the operations after the end of the project. This will be done in close collaboration with the local authorities and leaders, the ministry of water and other stakeholders.
To ensure environmental sustainability for the water infrastructure, the operators will be trained on sludge management. Water treatment unit will be designed to have score pipes that will flush accumulated sludge from the system to a soak away pit to ensure there is no environmental pollution. Further, water point locations will be identified based on sanitary survey and absence of source contamination within 30 meters radius. 
In order to ensure the infrastructure will continue to deliver water in cases of flooding, the water treatment unit and water points will be sited on a higher ground free from flooding. Beneficiaries will access water at water points delivered through pipeline to avoid any cases of contamination. The Mega water pan will have a raised draw off well, fitted with a hand pump and linked to the Mega water pan through pipe.  This will ensure beneficiaries access water even in times of flooding and the source is not contaminated by flooding waters.
Concern recently did a pilot of a water treatment unit in Bardhere which was successful.. Bardhere town is served by private water companies providing water at a fee to residents through pipeline, The water treatment unit proposed is an upscale of the existing system and is  aimed at providing a treatment unit to major water supply companies in the town with the aim of reducing cases of AWD and water related diseases in Bardhere.

NENTAD - North East Nigeria Transition to Development	Protection Promoting Rights and Supporting Protection Needs in BAY states. The proposed intervention builds on IRC’s previous and ongoing protection programming in Borno, Yobe and Adamawa states. The intervention will target both IDPs, returnees and host community members through a well-coordinated approach that will foster access to specialized services to prevent and mitigate the harmful effects of violence on women, children and men. This will be achieved through a focus on prevention of harm by seeking to ensure that women, men, boys and girls are safe in their wider communities and receive support when they experience harm and response actions that ensure women, men, boys and girls are protected from the consequences of harm. IRC will provide or facilitate access to safe and dignified specialized services that can help women, men, boys and girls to survive, heal and recover when they experience harm.  This will be done by ensuring that:
•	Community members have information about laws, their rights and availability of services: Through protection monitoring activities, the IRC will identify and monitor protection trends/risks in order to improve contextual understanding for purposes of ensuring responsive services throughout the action; protection reporting will also be shared with relevant humanitarian actors to support improved humanitarian response and coordination, as well as evidence-driven advocacy. Monitoring teams will also actively share information on rights and service access with households and community focal points to improve access to services; cases in need of response services that are identified during protection monitoring will be supported through a safe referral process, if informed consent to do so is received. Protection monitoring will be conducted through, weekly safety audits with women and girls at the transit center, camps and surrounding communities, gender/age/ability segregated FGDs, site observation and household/community level key informant interviews.
•	Community members take individual and collective action: Through community-based protection (CBP), guided by IRC’s new guidance for CBP that sets out a 5-step chronological process to maximise impact and promote sustainability, IRC will involve IDPs and returnees in the prioritization, planning and implementation of activities. This will be primarily achieved by engaging Protection action groups and other community based structures working with other sectors in IRC. To promote a specialized focus on protection risks facing individual segments of the IDP and returnee population, new or existing community groups will each have specific objectives while at the same time working together across groups to ensure holistic and mutually reinforcing actions to advance the protection of IDPs and returnees.
•	Services and structures are safe and reduce opportunities for harm: This action will ensure that protection is mainstreamed across all sectors throughout the project period by promoting four key elements of protection mainstreaming: meaningful access to assistance and services; prioritizing safety, dignity and doing no harm; accountability and participation and empowerment of beneficiaries. IRC’s Protection Mainstreaming Monitoring and Evaluation System and global protection cluster resources will guide the projects’ protection mainstreaming interventions. Foundational capacity building activities for project staff are continuously conducted to strengthen and promote a shared understanding of protection mainstreaming, including child safe guarding principles, integrating GBV in humanitarian assistance; and prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse.  IRC draws from its client responsiveness approach which fosters the effective functioning of feedback and complaints. The approach details systematic and deliberate processes to regularly listen to and collect diverse perspectives of populations of concern, use their feedback to inform programing decisions and explain to clients what actions have been taken in response to their feedback.
Twice a year the IRC conducts protection mainstreaming beneficiary assessments for feedback on the integration safety and dignity, meaningful access, participation and empowerment of target populations into project design and implementation. IRC sensitizes the community on IRC’s accountability for quality services and on the ways they can provide confidential feedback. The IRC Child Protection team  works together with other IRC sectors to provide trainings/information on the IRC Child Safeguarding Policy during trainings for their volunteers community structures members and awareness raising sessions for community members,  protection mainstreaming is also achieved through the development of protection mainstreaming action plans which are be monitored and adjusted throughout the project. Joint monthly community dialogues are held by protection teams with Bulamas, community structures, community/opinion leaders and community members to discuss uptake of project services, key challenges, gaps including issues on protection, GBV and child protection identified. The forum is also used to provide feedback and discuss ways to mitigate risks and threats. Decisions are communicated back to the beneficiaries through community leaders, social support groups and during one on one or group sensitization sessions. 

•	Relevant stakeholders follow rules and laws to protect civilians: IRC will strengthen the knowledge, skills, capacity and accountability of duty bearers in both government institutions (e.g. SEMA, NEMA) and at the community level (e.g. religious and traditional leaders). This will be achieved through technical and material support; monitoring duty bearers’ actions and through pursuing an evidence based advocacy strategy targeting duty bearers at all levels, including where appropriate, at the national level and regional levels. Knowledge and skills will be enhanced through trainings to ensure duty bearers access information and know about protective rules and laws pertinent to the prevailing context in the North East. This will focus on protection principles; housing, land and property (HLP) rights and responsibilities; protection mainstreaming and legislative frameworks governing IDPs such as guiding principles on internal displacement and dignified returns, the Kampala Convention on IDPs, humanitarian law, human rights, the Nigerian constitution and state laws of interest.
•	Women, girls, boys and men have their urgent protection needs met: IRC protection team will strengthen referrals for specialized services for women, children and other vulnerable individuals or groups, to ensure they receive timely, appropriate and adequate services for their healing and recovery. Internal referrals will be provided for beneficiaries, including those identified through protection monitoring, by community groups, or through self-reporting to IRC’s information centers or IRC staff. Externally, IRC will also participate in updating and disseminating referral pathways developed by the protection subsector working groups (Child protection, General Protection and Gender Based Violence) and ensure that people with specific identified protection needs are referred to relevant organization for specialized services. IRC will also support access to civil documentation (in partnership with National Population Commission (NPC), National Identity Management Commission (NIMC)) and legal services (including legal counselling and case management services) and provide targeted individual assistance to address immediate needs of victims or survivors of violence (including urgent medical support. TIA which can be in form of cash or in-kind is provided to enable most vulnerable individuals in a situation where no other alternative response, assistance or support exists to meet their most urgent protection needs with dignity and reduce their vulnerability and exposure to risks and promote meaningful access for the most vulnerable. It aims to build on rather than replace existing support mechanisms, meet immediate/most urgent needs and prioritize the most vulnerable.

NENTAD - North East Nigeria Transition to Development	Protection Strengthening women and girls' safety and recovery in BAY Gender based violence remains a serious challenge within northeast Nigeria, causing more psychological imbalance for armed conflict-affected IDPs as well as returnees, especially women and girls. Displacement and continued movement of IDPs creates major protection concerns women and girls which has increased gender-based violence and access services remain a serious gap especially in hard to reach Local Governmental Areas. According to Humanitarian Response Plan, 2018, an estimated 2.4 million people have been identified to be in need of gender-based violence prevention and response across Adamawa, Borno, and Yobe states. Women and girls are often targeted while performing basic tasks such as travelling to water points, collecting firewood to cook food and going to communal latrines. They are often exposed to SEA, forced into prostitution, early marriages, and survival sex in exchange for food, their movement is restricted and basic needs are deprived. Women and girls are abducted by armed groups, are often raped and forcibly married and may be used in person borne improvised explosive device (PBIED) attacks. These women and girls, along with their children born as a result of rape, are often feared by communities and ostracized from society because they are suspected to be sympathizers of armed opposition groups. Upon their return, they require access to a full range of services to meet multiple immediate and reintegration needs as well as those of their children. Despite the consequences, families are still forcibly marrying daughters as young as 12 years old to men or members of armed opposition groups, citing poverty as the main reason. Between August 2017 and April 2018, the IRC provided case management services for over 400 gender based violence survivors in Adamawa, Borno and Yobe, indicating the high need for continued support.
 An April 2018 assessment from OCHA shows that violence against women and girls is the most widely reported protection issue (24% of all key informants). From the October 2017 OCHA assessment in Yobe, child marriage was reported to affect over a third of households in each population group in eight LGAs throughout the state, including Gujba. Additionally, according to the Nigeria HRP 2018, sexual violence, including rape, is a defining characteristic of the ongoing conflict, with 6 out of 10 women in the northeast having experienced one or more forms of GBV. Women and girls are at particular risk within the current environment, with many reports of survival sex in exchange for food, money, and freedom of movement (into and out of IDP sites). This exposes the population to increasing incidences of sexually transmitted infections including HIV, unwanted pregnancies, and obstetric fistula caused by sexual violence, leading to overall poor sexual and reproductive health outcomes. The crisis has significantly affected the dignity of women and children. This further entrenches pre-existing gender disparities. In the Global Gender Gap Index, Nigeria ranks 118th out of 144 countries.

NENTAD - North East Nigeria Transition to Development	Multisector Life-saving food assistance and livelihoods support in North-East Nigeria. WFP will provide unconditional food-assistance to the most food-insecure, crisis-affected populations. 
Life-saving general food assistance (in-kind food and cash-based transfers) will be delivered to IDPs, returnees and host populations in North-East Nigeria (Borno, Yobe and Adamawa States). 
Early recovery and resilience to shocks will be promoted through asset creation and preservation, increased livelihoods opportunities, and enhanced agricultural value chains. 
Joint multi-sectoral assessments and Emergency Food Security Analysis will be conducted regularly to monitor the nutrition, food security, and markets situation in crisis-affected states. 
A gender-transformative approach that reflects the needs of women, men, girls and boys will be adopted. WFP will mainstream protection throughout its work, supported by a solid understanding of the operational context and protection analysis. Training and capacity building of staff and partners in protection and humanitarian principles will include on-the-job coaching. WFP will ensure that affected populations (women and men) will be consulted throughout the programme cycle; beneficiary feedback mechanisms will be tailored to their preferred means of communication. Beneficiaries will continue to be empowered with knowledge on their food assistance entitlements and their rights, including WFP’s zero tolerance policy on Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA). Protection against Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) will be embedded in M&E tools, complaint feedback mechanisms and training of partners and staff. 

WFP will focus on concrete operational solutions to avoid situations in which people assisted by WFP could be exposed to SEA. Along these lines WFP will enhance its support to income generation activities targeted to women, expand their engagement in the production and use of fuel efficient stoves, deploy women as beneficiary registrars, monitors and security personnel. The referral system and monitoring system will be reviewed to maximize user friendliness and access by assisted populations as well as operational adjustments for problem solving. Particular attention will be given to supervise the retailers and operators in the distribution of cash based transfers. WFP will support milling activities for the grain commodities it provides and will implement effective solutions for the provision of condiments and cash. Deep field presence through the hubs and proximity to affected populations will be enhanced for these purposes. Three experienced international and six Nigerian protection officers will be deployed. Reporting will be done on a monthly basis through standard WFP reporting and meetings. Regular oversight and evaluations will be conducted.

WFP will continue the collection of key information on beneficiaries and assistance provided as part of its M&E activities. Monthly monitoring will include distribution and activity site management; beneficiary and entitlement verification; and ensuring adequate protection and gender measures. Lessons will be regularly drawn from monthly process and biannual outcome monitoring and reporting, and periodic reviews and evaluation to inform strategic and operational decisions.

WFP will further consolidate partnerships to enhance national and state-level emergency preparedness and response systems, including in food security and nutrition assessment and monitoring, early warning, protection, gender analysis, targeting and registration processes, safety nets, cash-based transfer capacities and supply chain. 

Where security and access to land allows, increasing livelihood activities will complement food assistance to support access to productive assets, income generating activities and self-reliance in the long-term. Assistance will be coordinated with government distributions, to ensure food assistance is complementary and fills gaps. Through an integrated approach to analyzing and addressing food and nutrition security, integrated, multi-sectoral interventions will be encouraged, for example through collaborations with the Nutrition, Health, WASH and Protection Sectors, among others. WFP will also continue to proactively engage with a wide range of federal and state actors, including the Ministries of Agriculture and Rural Development, Health, Budget and National Planning, Finance, the National Social Investment Office (NSIO), Women Affairs and Social Development, PCNI as well as other federal and state institutions. Furthermore, WFP and the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) will continue to strengthen cooperation between the two agencies. WFP will continue to partner with a number of local and international NGOs and will work with civil society organizations to continue strengthening the capacities of national actors.

The project addresses the underlying causes of the protracted crisis by further integrating humanitarian and development assistance and improving disaster risk reduction in alignment with WFP’s dual mandate and the international policy debate on bridging and operationalizing the humanitarian-development nexus, thus using a development lens in its humanitarian responses, and aligning early recovery and development interventions accordingly.
