WFP will ensure that affected populations (women and men) will be consulted throughout the programme cycle; beneficiary feedback mechanisms will be tailored to their preferred means of communication. Beneficiaries will continue to be empowered with knowledge on their food assistance entitlements and their rights, including WFP’s zero tolerance policy on Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA). Protection against Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) will be embedded in M&E tools, complaint feedback mechanisms and training of partners and staff. 

WFP will focus on concrete operational solutions to avoid situations in which people assisted by WFP could be exposed to SEA. Along these lines WFP will enhance its support to income generation activities targeted to women, expand their engagement in the production and use of fuel efficient stoves, deploy women as beneficiary registrars, monitors and security personnel. The referral system and monitoring system will be reviewed to maximize user friendliness and access by assisted populations as well as operational adjustments for problem solving. Particular attention will be given to supervise the retailers and operators in the distribution of cash based transfers. WFP will support milling activities for the grain commodities it provides and will implement effective solutions for the provision of condiments and cash. Deep field presence through the hubs and proximity to affected populations will be enhanced for these purposes. Three experienced international and six Nigerian protection officers will be deployed. Food response through IRC activities to the emergency drought that has caused food insecurity, IPC 4 and 3, through unconditional cash transfers in favour of 6120 individuals. Lean Season Food Assistance to the most food insecure people in rural areas Under this Flash Appeal, Food Security sector partners plan to address the most urgent food security needs of people in rural areas across the country, who are adversely affected by multiple crises, including last year’s poor harvest for many small-holder farmers, economic shocks and recent cholera and typhoid outbreaks. Building on the funding already received to reach an estimated 900,000 people as of January 2019 and the Government’s Food Deficit Mitigation Strategy, partners aim to expand the geographic coverage of assistance to reach an additional 700,000 people in food insecure rural communities through primarily cash-based assistance. Focus will be on the low-lying areas relying on rainfed agriculture disproportionately affected by last year’s erratic rain. Market-based interventions are viable despite the current economic stress, as essential food commodities remain available on rural as well as urban markets, according to the national market assessment conducted by WFP and partners in November 2018. 

The IPC analysis conducted in January 2019 projects that nearly 3.8 million people in rural areas are in need of urgent humanitarian assistance, including 2.9 million who are severely food insecure (IPC phase 3 or 4) and a further 900,000 people who are currently receiving humanitarian assistance, without which they would be in IPC phase 3 or above.

In the face of the high prevalence of food insecurity (IPC phase 4 and 3), and the high probability of another El Niño phenomena in 2019 (90% likelihood according to the most recent SARCOF analysis), partners will provide a specialised food ration in the form of CSB++ specifically targeting children 6-59 months and pregnant and lactating women to increase the nutritional value of the food basket provided as part of the general household ration/cash. 

Based on the findings of the national market assessment conducted by partners in November, partners will select the most appropriate transfer modality for each district (cash or in-kind). According to the latest price information, partners aim to cover approximately 80% of the targeted individuals’ daily food energy needs (based on a 2100 kcal diet) to supplement other available food sources, thus enabling households to meet their basic food and nutrition needs. 
 
In view of the high probability of another El Nino, food assistance at this juncture can be considered as an early action to prevent further deterioration of food insecurity amongst particularly households already in IPC 3 (Crises) and 4 (Emergency).

Protection and shelter for internally displaced and conflict affected persons in east Ukraine (part of 19-UF-HCR-006) Provision of shelter assistance to internally displaced and conflicted affected communities in Ukraine There is ongoing armed conflict in Ukraine, and daily violations of the ceasefire agreement. Examples of these localized flare-ups include the fighting in Avdiivka in late January 2017 and the shelling of Novoluhanskoe in December 2017. These ceasefire violations have a serious impact on civilians’ lives and property. They damage or destroy housing and infrastructure, necessitating an emergency response in terms of shelter and basic needs, especially for most vulnerable and persons with specific needs. To provide displaced and conflict-affected persons with specific needs in a timely manner UNHCR will preposition emergency NFI kits to be distributed to families at risk of displacement or newly displaced, as part of emergency response. In GCA, the emergency response is generally led by local authorities, and UNHCR’s contribution will complement their efforts. Some 1,250 kits composed of basic and domestic items will be prepositioned closed to the line of contact for households living in or returning to individual or multi-story buildings damaged during the conflict and/or newly displaced or evacuated UNHCR’s emergency response will be coordinated closely with local authorities and complementary to their efforts to respond. Winterization activities are not in UNHCR’s prioritized plan, but could be implemented if there are critical needs and pending availability of donor funds as a part of the comprehensive plan. Should funds be available, UNHCR would provide cash assistance (in GCA) or coal (in NGCA) to households who live along the contact line and have no access to the supply of fuel for heating

Life-saving general food assistance (in-kind food and cash-based transfers) will be delivered to IDPs, returnees and host populations in North-East Nigeria (Borno, Yobe and Adamawa States). 
Early recovery and resilience to shocks will be promoted through asset creation and preservation, increased livelihoods opportunities, and enhanced agricultural value chains. 
Joint multi-sectoral assessments and Emergency Food Security Analysis will be conducted regularly to monitor the nutrition, food security, and markets situation in crisis-affected states. 
A gender-transformative approach that reflects the needs of women, men, girls and boys will be adopted. WFP will mainstream protection throughout its work, supported by a solid understanding of the operational context and protection analysis. Training and capacity building of staff and partners in protection and humanitarian principles will include on-the-job coaching. WFP will ensure that affected populations (women and men) will be consulted throughout the programme cycle; beneficiary feedback mechanisms will be tailored to their preferred means of communication. Beneficiaries will continue to be empowered with knowledge on their food assistance entitlements and their rights, including WFP’s zero tolerance policy on Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA). Protection against Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) will be embedded in M&E tools, complaint feedback mechanisms and training of partners and staff. 

WFP will focus on concrete operational solutions to avoid situations in which people assisted by WFP could be exposed to SEA. Along these lines WFP will enhance its support to income generation activities targeted to women, expand their engagement in the production and use of fuel efficient stoves, deploy women as beneficiary registrars, monitors and security personnel. The referral system and monitoring system will be reviewed to maximize user friendliness and access by assisted populations as well as operational adjustments for problem solving. Particular attention will be given to supervise the retailers and operators in the distribution of cash based transfers. WFP will support milling activities for the grain commodities it provides and will implement effective solutions for the provision of condiments and cash. Deep field presence through the hubs and proximity to affected populations will be enhanced for these purposes. Three experienced international and six Nigerian protection officers will be deployed. Reporting will be done on a monthly basis through standard WFP reporting and meetings. Regular oversight and evaluations will be conducted.

WFP will continue the collection of key information on beneficiaries and assistance provided as part of its M&E activities. Monthly monitoring will include distribution and activity site management; beneficiary and entitlement verification; and ensuring adequate protection and gender measures. Lessons will be regularly drawn from monthly process and biannual outcome monitoring and reporting, and periodic reviews and evaluation to inform strategic and operational decisions.

WFP will further consolidate partnerships to enhance national and state-level emergency preparedness and response systems, including in food security and nutrition assessment and monitoring, early warning, protection, gender analysis, targeting and registration processes, safety nets, cash-based transfer capacities and supply chain. 

Where security and access to land allows, increasing livelihood activities will complement food assistance to support access to productive assets, income generating activities and self-reliance in the long-term. Assistance will be coordinated with government distributions, to ensure food assistance is complementary and fills gaps. Through an integrated approach to analyzing and addressing food and nutrition security, integrated, multi-sectoral interventions will be encouraged, for example through collaborations with the Nutrition, Health, WASH and Protection Sectors, among others. WFP will also continue to proactively engage with a wide range of federal and state actors, including the Ministries of Agriculture and Rural Development, Health, Budget and National Planning, Finance, the National Social Investment Office (NSIO), Women Affairs and Social Development, PCNI as well as other federal and state institutions. Furthermore, WFP and the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) will continue to strengthen cooperation between the two agencies. WFP will continue to partner with a number of local and international NGOs and will work with civil society organizations to continue strengthening the capacities of national actors.

WASH and Cash - Aleppo Emergency WASH Response and Building Resilience for Conflict affected Women, Men, Boys and girls in Syria  Building on experience of project interventions in Syria since 2013, Oxfam is planning to respond in the most vulnerable districts/sub-districts with high severity in Aleppo, Rural Damascus, Homs, Hama, Dar’a and Idleb based on the severity of WASH needs 

The sub-districts that will be targeted by this project have all been heavily affected by conflict and are in need of additional WASH support, based on a rapid Oxfam assessment in some of the selected villages, consultations with Syrian and international NGOs, and reliable secondary data, including the Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) 2019. The project is designed to meet specific life-saving needs around water sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and is aligned to HRP 2019 for Syria. The project focuses on WASH response with gender mainstreamed, and with a well-defined response strategy suitable to access situation and security challenges; this includes implementation through reliable and experienced site engineers, public health promotion volunteers and focal points, carefully screened private contractors, and coordination with other actors. The total estimated populated, as per UN-OCHA datasets in these sub-districts, is over 1,752,742 people.  This estimation has to be taken as a rough guide, given that many people have been displaced, with many IDP and returnee fluctuations within Governorates and Districts across Syria.

Target locations have been proposed according to severity of humanitarian needs and number of population in need. They may be altered depending on the evolution of the context on the ground, access and people's movement. 
The project aims to support life-saving WASH interventions as well as activities that focus on the maintenance and/or the light rehabilitation of existing WASH systems: a) improve the target communities' access to safe water facilities, b) appropriate capacity to maintain key health and hygiene practices; c) access to safe sanitation facilities and services and; d) WASH emergency response including the provision of WASH materials, equipment and services i.e. water taks, O&M water trucking and emergency WASH facilities 
Oxfam planned interventions will be inline with: SO1 that captures sector efforts to restore or keep Water and Sanitation infrastructure at the minimum level of operation and SO2 which describes life-saving WASH interventions such as emergency provision of water, sanitation and solid waste facilities and services as well as WASH NFI distributions. 
In the terms of the interventions above, Oxfam will target all age groups for water and sanitation interventions. For the hygiene interventions, these will be targeted women and a focus on children as a proportion of the activities will be conducted at school level.
The specific locations for activities in these sub-districts are still to be declared.  Specific WASH interventions will be assessed by Oxfam WASH teams, including full costings, and will be discussed with LWE officials, local authorities, and WASH Sector actors to ensure complementarity of interventions versus work of other actors in targeted areas.  As final interventions will require approval of both the MoWR and MoE, Oxfam will convene a project steering committee which will include both Oxfam management staff and Government representatives at Damascus level, who will discuss and agree selection of possible activities and operational challenges

The proposed project is complementary to ongoing KAALO WASH project  in Nugaal  region in Puntland and to response the existing WASH gaps to drought affected people in Puntland, KAALO proposes to provide WASH interventions and resilience strengthening to the target groups men, women and children and institutional facilities during this critical period of water shortage and Acute Water Diarrhea (AWD) risks in providing safe water through water voucher, constructing/rehabilitating WASH infrastructures for sustained access. Hygiene awareness, training on management & maintenance and Disaster Risk Reduction targeting  affected people with equal access to boys, girls, men and women., 
The committee need further training on  hygiene and sanitation as well as distribution of sanitation tools. Sensitization within members of WASH committees are needed, community education activities on hygiene and proper use of latrines etc. need more emphasis, KAALO intends to complement this with  the ongoing WASH project to cover all the existing gaps in the  targeted areas. Accountability : KAALO will develop elaborate beneficiary complain and feedback tool. implementation  plan : KAALO will recruit experienced WASH project staff that will ensure effective community participatory approach in project planning, implementation & management. Water vouchers will be provided to 20,500 people and 23 strategic water points will be constructed/rehabilitated. The water sources will be located 30m away from latrines to avoid contamination. Dewatering of 30 wells and application of shock chlorination will be done in flood-affected areas.  To strengthen community ownership and ensure sustainability of WASH assets 50 water management committee members (50% women) will be trained on operation and maintenance. The project staff and WASH committee members will also be trained on DRR and protection mainstreaming. 97 gender-sensitive latrines with hand-washing facilities, raised to avoid flooding and fitted with locks from the inside to curb GBV will be constructed in IDP camps, schools and health/nutrition centers. CLTS approach will be introduced where no latrines will be constructed. Community members particularly women and girls will be consulted in the siting and design of WASH facilities.  5000 hygiene kits will be distributed to targeted high-risk families i.e. families with malnourished children and affected by AWD. 600 hygiene promoters will be trained in the PHAST method and will carry out community hygiene campaigns. WOCCA will continuously monitor the Shabelle river and disseminate early warning and hygiene messages through radio and SMS when floods are imminent. Sensitization meetings will be held at the inception of the project with all project stakeholders including groups at risk of exclusion to inform them about the project objectives, scope, beneficiary selection criteria, and beneficiary entitlement and roles. Accountability to the affected population will be enhanced through the provision of a feedback hotline to beneficiaries where they can provide feedback and complaints. To ensure quality in the project outputs the project staff will continuously monitor and report on project indicators. WOCCA will also share GPS coordinates of all WASH structures and monthly project reports with the WASH cluster and donor. Signing off and handing over of WASH structures to beneficiaries upon completion will be done through community elders, government officials and religious leaders. WOCCA will also adhere to the principles of ""Do no harm"" through not creating any partial, nepotism, conflict-oriented and sensitive issues within the project beneficiaries.

Reduce the threat of Explosive Remnants of War (ERW) across Aleppo and Idleb and provide improved support to survivors of ERW accidents and conflict-related injuries (part of ECHO/SYR/BUD/2019/91001) Reduced threat of ERW and improved support to ERW survivors in north-west Syria. HALO with its implementing partners will deliver a comprehensive approach to Mine Action in NW Syria, involving Contamination Impact Survey (CIS), an enhanced version of CIS (ECIS), Risk Education (RE), Victim Data Collection (VDC) and Victim Assistance (VA).  Note: the key difference between ECIS and CIS is the identification, marking and reporting of ERW items. HALO will also seek to extend the scope of its activities to Explosive Remnants of War (ERW) Non-Technical Survey (NTS) and Disposal. 

To better understand the threat that ERW poses, HALO will conduct systematic CIS in 111 communities and ECIS in 692 communities across Idleb and Aleppo governorates. Under this activity, teams will visit communities, with the overall goal to identify, mark and report ERW contamination and to record its impact on the community. Data will be used to identify areas of highest priority for RE, create contamination maps, and provide essential information for future ERW clearance. The scale of this activity is unprecedented but is required to inform current and future ERW disposal/clearance, as well as immediately improving the awareness and safety of affected communities. ECIS activities will be coordinated from HALO’s operation room in Jordan, staffed by technical personnel. If the relevant authorizations are granted from the Turkish government, HALO will also establish ERW survey and disposal teams trained to complete surface-located ERW tasks (excluding IEDs) via a 6-week course derived from International Mine Action Standards (IMAS). They will be deployed under the direct control of HALO’s operations room in Jordan. At a later stage in 2019, they will complete advanced training relevant to the detection and disposal of sub-surface ERW (excluding IEDs). Extension to IED disposal requires a separate 4-week course. All disposal activities will be conducted via the use of thermite torches (T-Jets). No high explosives will be used. HALO’s ERW survey and disposal objectives for NW Syria are based on its experience in southern Syria in 2018.     

HALO will provide RE to 108,472 beneficiaries in 2019 (18,364 men, 17,692 women, 38,248 boys and 34,168 girls). A particular focus will be placed on those who are most at risk of accident (including children, young men and IDPs). Two new RE ‘Training of Trainer’ (ToT) Trainers will build on the work already underway by HALO’s existing RE ToT Trainer in NW Syria. Together, they will support NGOs currently delivering RE to vulnerable communities and IDPs, as well as NGOs willing to deliver RE along with other activities; improving the relevance, integration and reach of RE messaging across all relevant sectors. 

HALO will also collect information about ERW accidents and victims (survivors) through VDC which will be used to develop a better understanding of how and why accidents are occurring, enabling HALO, and other actors, to better tailor RE and VA activities.

In 2019, HALO and one of its implementing partners will implement a new VA initiative, where approx. 200 survivors of ERW accidents will benefit from initial basic health screening, referrals to reputable service providers and a one-off distribution of basic medical and hygiene items. The project will also support survivors (approx. 1,200) through the establishment of a rehabilitation centre and 2 x mobile outreach teams, providing physiotherapy, mental health and psycho-social support (MHPSS), peer support counselling, and referrals to a prosthetics centre. A social protection scheme providing ‘in-kind’ support to selected survivors will also be implemented. Additionally, in order to promote workplace inclusion, 5 survivors will be recruited, trained and employed by HALO’s partner.

Humanitarian Food Assistance to the the most food insecure people during the 2018/19 lean season, including urban population (ECHO/-SF/BUD/2019/91004) Lean Season Food Assistance to the most food insecure people in rural areas Under this Flash Appeal, Food Security sector partners plan to address the most urgent food security needs of people in rural areas across the country, who are adversely affected by multiple crises, including last year’s poor harvest for many small-holder farmers, economic shocks and recent cholera and typhoid outbreaks. Building on the funding already received to reach an estimated 900,000 people as of January 2019 and the Government’s Food Deficit Mitigation Strategy, partners aim to expand the geographic coverage of assistance to reach an additional 700,000 people in food insecure rural communities through primarily cash-based assistance. Focus will be on the low-lying areas relying on rainfed agriculture disproportionately affected by last year’s erratic rain. Market-based interventions are viable despite the current economic stress, as essential food commodities remain available on rural as well as urban markets, according to the national market assessment conducted by WFP and partners in November 2018. 

The IPC analysis conducted in January 2019 projects that nearly 3.8 million people in rural areas are in need of urgent humanitarian assistance, including 2.9 million who are severely food insecure (IPC phase 3 or 4) and a further 900,000 people who are currently receiving humanitarian assistance, without which they would be in IPC phase 3 or above.

In the face of the high prevalence of food insecurity (IPC phase 4 and 3), and the high probability of another El Niño phenomena in 2019 (90% likelihood according to the most recent SARCOF analysis), partners will provide a specialised food ration in the form of CSB++ specifically targeting children 6-59 months and pregnant and lactating women to increase the nutritional value of the food basket provided as part of the general household ration/cash. 

Based on the findings of the national market assessment conducted by partners in November, partners will select the most appropriate transfer modality for each district (cash or in-kind). According to the latest price information, partners aim to cover approximately 80% of the targeted individuals’ daily food energy needs (based on a 2100 kcal diet) to supplement other available food sources, thus enabling households to meet their basic food and nutrition needs. 
 
In view of the high probability of another El Nino, food assistance at this juncture can be considered as an early action to prevent further deterioration of food insecurity amongst particularly households already in IPC 3 (Crises) and 4 (Emergency).

Immediate Food Assistance for Internally Displaced Persons(IDPs) in the Far North (40,000 Beneficiaries) Immediate Food Assistance for Internally Displaced Persons(IDPs) in the Far North (40,000 Beneficiaries)  In the Far North region, the Boko Haram insurgency in Nigeria has displaced 100,504 Nigerian refugees in Cameroon as of October 2018, and 98,590 of them live in the Far North region (UNHCR, October 2018). Boko Haram attacks have also resulted in 227,581 internally displaced persons (IDPs) (UNHCR, October 2018), who are struggling to survive in strenuous conditions in villages or small towns in the area. The region is predominantly arid and regularly hit by drought and seasonal floods. Access to basic services is also more limited than in other regions of the country. The arrival of IDPs in food-insecure areas has severely affected host communities as well. This has put enormous pressure on already scarce community resources and the local economy by reducing farm productivity and access to land and food markets. Boko Haram attacks have disrupted the economic, agricultural, and pastoral activities in the Far North region, causing a depletion of livelihoods and household assets. As a consequence, the existing chronic vulnerability and structural food insecurity have been aggravated. IDPs have fleed from the bordering regions where the Boko Haram attacks have occurred but the vulnerable IDP households live without means or assets to support themselves. To address the urgent food needs of the most vulnerable IDPs, WFP plans to provide immediate food assistance with full ration to the most vulnerable 40,000 IDPs in the Far North for 12 months in 2019. 25,000 beneficiaries will be supported with the in-kind food assistance and the rest 15,000 with Cash-Based Transfer(CBT).

Chad - OCHA Office  [OCT 6570];[18/6994] Renforcement de la coordination et du plaidoyer humanitaire au Tchad Le projet vise à renforcer la mobilisation et la coordination  de la réponse humanitaire au Tchad afin de sauver des vies et protéger les personnes affectées par les crises, notamment celles affectées par la crise du lac Tchad. Une coordination humanitaire efficace et performante permet aux acteurs humanitaires de mieux identifier et répondre aux priorités humanitaires. OCHA jouera un rôle clé dans la création d'espaces d'échange et d'analyse d'informations, pour mieux guider les actions humanitaires, répondre aux besoins les plus aigus et être mieux préparé face aux urgences soudaines. Le projet permettra également d’assurer conjointement avec la communauté humanitaire le plaidoyer en faveur du respect des principes humanitaires, de la protection des civils, de l'accès humanitaire et pour la mobilisation et l'allocation efficace de ressources humanitaires. OCHA continuera de jouer  également un rôle moteur dans le renforcement du lien entre les acteurs humanitaires et de développement et la transformation de la réponse humanitaire, en lien avec les engagements pris au Sommet mondial de l'action humanitaire de 2016 et ceci à travers la nouvelle façon de travailler (NWOW).OCHA continue de mettre en oeuvre sa mission à travers ses fonctions clés (Coordination, Gestion de l' information et plaidoyer). Un accent a été mis sur l' opérationalisation de la nouvelle façon de travailler, la mise en oeuvre des plans d' action de la redevabilité envers les populations affectées (AAP) et la PSEA, la préparation aux urgences et le plaidoyer pour plus de visibilités et de mobilisation de ressources pour les différentes crises au Tchad (Bassin du Lac Tchad, insécurité alimentaire et malnutrition, épidémie sanitaires). De même, OCHA à travers sa participation dans le groupe de travail sur le CASH, continu de faire le plaidoyer pour renforcer l' utilisation du CASH pour la réponse humanitaire dans tous les secteurs et du Cash à usage multiple (Multipurpose CASH)

Promoting rights and supporting emergency protection needs in MMC, Jere and Monguno, Borno State Promoting Rights and Supporting Protection Needs in BAY states. The proposed intervention builds on IRC’s previous and ongoing protection programming in Borno, Yobe and Adamawa states. The intervention will target both IDPs, returnees and host community members through a well-coordinated approach that will foster access to specialized services to prevent and mitigate the harmful effects of violence on women, children and men. This will be achieved through a focus on prevention of harm by seeking to ensure that women, men, boys and girls are safe in their wider communities and receive support when they experience harm and response actions that ensure women, men, boys and girls are protected from the consequences of harm. IRC will provide or facilitate access to safe and dignified specialized services that can help women, men, boys and girls to survive, heal and recover when they experience harm.  This will be done by ensuring that:
•	Community members have information about laws, their rights and availability of services: Through protection monitoring activities, the IRC will identify and monitor protection trends/risks in order to improve contextual understanding for purposes of ensuring responsive services throughout the action; protection reporting will also be shared with relevant humanitarian actors to support improved humanitarian response and coordination, as well as evidence-driven advocacy. Monitoring teams will also actively share information on rights and service access with households and community focal points to improve access to services; cases in need of response services that are identified during protection monitoring will be supported through a safe referral process, if informed consent to do so is received. Protection monitoring will be conducted through, weekly safety audits with women and girls at the transit center, camps and surrounding communities, gender/age/ability segregated FGDs, site observation and household/community level key informant interviews.
•	Community members take individual and collective action: Through community-based protection (CBP), guided by IRC’s new guidance for CBP that sets out a 5-step chronological process to maximise impact and promote sustainability, IRC will involve IDPs and returnees in the prioritization, planning and implementation of activities. This will be primarily achieved by engaging Protection action groups and other community based structures working with other sectors in IRC. To promote a specialized focus on protection risks facing individual segments of the IDP and returnee population, new or existing community groups will each have specific objectives while at the same time working together across groups to ensure holistic and mutually reinforcing actions to advance the protection of IDPs and returnees.
•	Services and structures are safe and reduce opportunities for harm: This action will ensure that protection is mainstreamed across all sectors throughout the project period by promoting four key elements of protection mainstreaming: meaningful access to assistance and services; prioritizing safety, dignity and doing no harm; accountability and participation and empowerment of beneficiaries. IRC’s Protection Mainstreaming Monitoring and Evaluation System and global protection cluster resources will guide the projects’ protection mainstreaming interventions. Foundational capacity building activities for project staff are continuously conducted to strengthen and promote a shared understanding of protection mainstreaming, including child safe guarding principles, integrating GBV in humanitarian assistance; and prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse.  IRC draws from its client responsiveness approach which fosters the effective functioning of feedback and complaints. The approach details systematic and deliberate processes to regularly listen to and collect diverse perspectives of populations of concern, use their feedback to inform programing decisions and explain to clients what actions have been taken in response to their feedback.
Twice a year the IRC conducts protection mainstreaming beneficiary assessments for feedback on the integration safety and dignity, meaningful access, participation and empowerment of target populations into project design and implementation. IRC sensitizes the community on IRC’s accountability for quality services and on the ways they can provide confidential feedback. The IRC Child Protection team  works together with other IRC sectors to provide trainings/information on the IRC Child Safeguarding Policy during trainings for their volunteers community structures members and awareness raising sessions for community members,  protection mainstreaming is also achieved through the development of protection mainstreaming action plans which are be monitored and adjusted throughout the project. Joint monthly community dialogues are held by protection teams with Bulamas, community structures, community/opinion leaders and community members to discuss uptake of project services, key challenges, gaps including issues on protection, GBV and child protection identified. The forum is also used to provide feedback and discuss ways to mitigate risks and threats. Decisions are communicated back to the beneficiaries through community leaders, social support groups and during one on one or group sensitization sessions. 

•	Relevant stakeholders follow rules and laws to protect civilians: IRC will strengthen the knowledge, skills, capacity and accountability of duty bearers in both government institutions (e.g. SEMA, NEMA) and at the community level (e.g. religious and traditional leaders). This will be achieved through technical and material support; monitoring duty bearers’ actions and through pursuing an evidence based advocacy strategy targeting duty bearers at all levels, including where appropriate, at the national level and regional levels. Knowledge and skills will be enhanced through trainings to ensure duty bearers access information and know about protective rules and laws pertinent to the prevailing context in the North East. This will focus on protection principles; housing, land and property (HLP) rights and responsibilities; protection mainstreaming and legislative frameworks governing IDPs such as guiding principles on internal displacement and dignified returns, the Kampala Convention on IDPs, humanitarian law, human rights, the Nigerian constitution and state laws of interest.
•	Women, girls, boys and men have their urgent protection needs met: IRC protection team will strengthen referrals for specialized services for women, children and other vulnerable individuals or groups, to ensure they receive timely, appropriate and adequate services for their healing and recovery. Internal referrals will be provided for beneficiaries, including those identified through protection monitoring, by community groups, or through self-reporting to IRC’s information centers or IRC staff. Externally, IRC will also participate in updating and disseminating referral pathways developed by the protection subsector working groups (Child protection, General Protection and Gender Based Violence) and ensure that people with specific identified protection needs are referred to relevant organization for specialized services. IRC will also support access to civil documentation (in partnership with National Population Commission (NPC), National Identity Management Commission (NIMC)) and legal services (including legal counselling and case management services) and provide targeted individual assistance to address immediate needs of victims or survivors of violence (including urgent medical support. TIA which can be in form of cash or in-kind is provided to enable most vulnerable individuals in a situation where no other alternative response, assistance or support exists to meet their most urgent protection needs with dignity and reduce their vulnerability and exposure to risks and promote meaningful access for the most vulnerable. It aims to build on rather than replace existing support mechanisms, meet immediate/most urgent needs and prioritize the most vulnerable.

Provide sustainable access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene services and strengthen management structure for Displacement Affected Communities in Zeylac and Lughaya Districts of Awdal region, Somaliland Increased life-saving and sustainable access to water, sanitation and hygiene for Displacement Affected Communities in Somalia targeting women, men, boys and girls DRC proposes to undertake a life-saving and sustainable assistance to Disaster and Conflict Affected Communities (DACs) through provision of emergency and sustainable WASH interventions (water, sanitation and hygiene). Areas that are mostly affected by droughts, famine and floods will be targeted in the emergency interventions, some of the key areas to be targeted include the following Mogadishu, Baidoa, Baletweyne and mudug regions. proposed key activities to be implemented include water trucking through water voucher, construction of emergency latrines and other related WASH activities. DRC defines DACs as people who are internally displaced and are affected by drought and other factors  and returnees  seeking for reintegration. Therefore, DRC targets IDPs, returnees, refugees and host communities. DRC understands that the primary displacements in Somalia is as a result of natural disasters and mana-made conflict. However, secondary displacements are now a common reality due to either military offensive or forced evictions by government. These displacements are the key driver of humanitarian WASH needs in Somalia. IDPs are currently residing in urban and peri-urban informal crowded settlements, with insufficient access to WASH services that raise protection and health concerns. Therefore, DRC will ensure that, where IDPs settle they get immediate assistance of life-saving interventions. These will include water trucking where there is no safe water source, emergency latrine, sanitation ,  hygiene kits and rapid hygiene promotion. On the other hand, DRC targets Host Communities - to ensure peaceful coexistence between the local population and target groups and also because many of them are equally vulnerable and in need of humanitarian assistance. Returnees are also targeted with durable solutions in which case DRC will focus on governance and overall management of water and sanitation facilities. In this case, DRC will ensure there is a robust market system in place for continued service provision. For the case of water, DRC will encourage existing water source owners – both private and government, to extend water services to the settlements of DACs. For the case of sanitation, DRC will encourage a market-based approach – looking at creating demand for latrine construction and building capacity of the supply side to ensure enterprise-creation and therefore sustainable services beyond the project period



DRC has developed standard designs for water and sanitation facilities with detailed description scope of work. DRC also has a team of engineers and WASH staff across areas of operation. Securing the basic needs of especially vulnerable conflict-affected people in Ukraine 2018-2019 Securing of basic needs in physical and mental health of people affected by conflict in Ukraine, 2019-2020 (funded by German Federal Foreign Office) Overall context of crises in Ukraine
The human toll of the armed conflict in eastern Ukraine is critical, with 4.4 million people affected by the crisis, of whom 3.4 million require humanitarian assistance and protection. The shelling of urban areas and civilian infrastructure means that 60 per cent of 200,000 people living along the 457-kilometre ‘contact line’ in the Government-controlled area (GCA) are affected by shelling regularly, and almost 40 per cent are affected every day. There is just under a million individual crossings of the ‘contact line’ each month, which is rapidly becoming one of the most mine contaminated stretches of land in the world. Food insecurity has doubled since 2016, with 1.2 million people food insecure, and there are escalating cases of multi-drug resistant TB, HIV and even polio. HIV prevalence among pregnant women in conflict-affected oblasts is significantly higher than the national average. These impacts are aggravated by Ukraine’s extremely harsh winter, severe restrictions on humanitarian access and limited livelihood opportunities for those affected by the crisis. As hopes of a political solution have waned, so have people’s savings and their ability to cope. Four years into the crisis, millions of people, including 1.6 million internally displaced persons (IDPs), half of whom are the elderly, are being forced to make impossible choices between food, medicine, shelter, heating or their children’s education. The unique demographics of the crisis in Ukraine is that the elderly make up almost 30 per cent of people in need. Those who are most vulnerable are increasingly resorting to risky means to cope, including survival sex, trafficking and alcoholism. Today, the dire humanitarian crisis in eastern Ukraine is protracted and complex, whilst the response is severely underfunded and largely forgotten by the international community.

In-Kind:Food Security (USAID/FFP) Lean Season Food Assistance to the most food insecure people in rural areas Under this Flash Appeal, Food Security sector partners plan to address the most urgent food security needs of people in rural areas across the country, who are adversely affected by multiple crises, including last year’s poor harvest for many small-holder farmers, economic shocks and recent cholera and typhoid outbreaks. Building on the funding already received to reach an estimated 900,000 people as of January 2019 and the Government’s Food Deficit Mitigation Strategy, partners aim to expand the geographic coverage of assistance to reach an additional 700,000 people in food insecure rural communities through primarily cash-based assistance. Focus will be on the low-lying areas relying on rainfed agriculture disproportionately affected by last year’s erratic rain. Market-based interventions are viable despite the current economic stress, as essential food commodities remain available on rural as well as urban markets, according to the national market assessment conducted by WFP and partners in November 2018. 

The IPC analysis conducted in January 2019 projects that nearly 3.8 million people in rural areas are in need of urgent humanitarian assistance, including 2.9 million who are severely food insecure (IPC phase 3 or 4) and a further 900,000 people who are currently receiving humanitarian assistance, without which they would be in IPC phase 3 or above.

In the face of the high prevalence of food insecurity (IPC phase 4 and 3), and the high probability of another El Niño phenomena in 2019 (90% likelihood according to the most recent SARCOF analysis), partners will provide a specialised food ration in the form of CSB++ specifically targeting children 6-59 months and pregnant and lactating women to increase the nutritional value of the food basket provided as part of the general household ration/cash. 

Based on the findings of the national market assessment conducted by partners in November, partners will select the most appropriate transfer modality for each district (cash or in-kind). According to the latest price information, partners aim to cover approximately 80% of the targeted individuals’ daily food energy needs (based on a 2100 kcal diet) to supplement other available food sources, thus enabling households to meet their basic food and nutrition needs. 
 
In view of the high probability of another El Nino, food assistance at this juncture can be considered as an early action to prevent further deterioration of food insecurity amongst particularly households already in IPC 3 (Crises) and 4 (Emergency).

Learning For a Brighter Tomorrow: Holistic Formal and Informal Education for Children and Adolescents in Northern Syria Learning for a Brighter Tomorrow: Quality Formal and Informal Education for Children and Youth in Northern Syria From 01 January through 31 December 2019 and in partnership with Lead Partner INGO, we will continue our currently running EuropeAid-funded Education programme under which we currently supports four schools in the Ariha sub-district of Idleb governorate, assisting 1,515 students, 97 teachers/school staff (including 4 psychosocial (PSS) facilitators) over the course of this grant. 

We are proposing to support an additional six schools for a total of ten schools under a formal education component of this programme in addition to 16 Self Learning Program (SLP) temporary learning spaces in four camps under a non-formal education component, expanding it educational activities into the HNO 2019’s highly prioritized geographic areas of Saraqab and Darkosh sub-districts of Ariha, Idleb (in addition to the current coverage of Ariha sub-district); Madiq Castle in Hama and Afrin, Jandairis, Haritan and Zarbah in rural Aleppo. 

Structured around our holistic model for education during times of crisis and recovery, the proposed program has three primary objectives: (1) to improve academic teaching and learning; (2) to promote student wellbeing and protection; and (3) to strengthen educational access and resources. Comprising both formal and non-formal education components, the program will reach a total of 5920 children (3163 males, 2757 females) — of which 35 percent are adolescents and youth — as well as 291 teachers / school staff (166  males and 125 females) and 640 caretakers (256 males  and 384 females). 

Under the formal education component - via the ten schools - we aim to reach a total of 4000 children (2196 males, 1804 females) as well as 209 teachers (119 males and 90 female) and 400 caretakers (150 males and 250 females), noting that all students who receive formal education under this project will also have access to the non-formal education component. Under the non-formal education component - 16 Self-Learning Program (SLP) temporary learning spaces in 4 camps, we aim to prepare 1920 out-of-school children (967 male, 953 female) for integration into formal primary schools after one year of study, including 16 teachers (8 males and 8 females).  Note: expansion on both components’ activities can be found under the Implementation of Activities section of this proposal.

Academic teaching and learning is coupled with program components focused on student safety and wellbeing. School personnel receive training in child protection and psychosocial care, and all students participate in weekly, age-appropriate PSS sessions led by dedicated facilitators. These activities aim to promote positive social-emotional development among children, and include a youth Life Skills curriculum for older students. Further, each school has a Protection Facilitator who is responsible for monitoring protection mainstreaming measures, such as a case management and referral system for students requiring external support.  School personnel are also trained on emergency preparedness and response, and develop plans to deal with threats like attacks on or near schools. 

In light of economic barriers that require some students to work rather than attend school, the proposed intervention also includes a supplemental livelihoods pilot component. This pilot will target the most vulnerable children and families who rely on child labor as an economic coping mechanism by offering conditional cash-vouchers or food baskets to offset the financial losses incurred when transitioning children from work to school.

These ceasefire violations have a serious impact on civilians’ lives and property. Reduce the threat of Explosive Remnants of War (ERW) across Aleppo and Idleb and provide improved support to survivors of ERW. Reduced threat of ERW and improved support to ERW survivors in north-west Syria. HALO with its implementing partners will deliver a comprehensive approach to Mine Action in NW Syria, involving Contamination Impact Survey (CIS), an enhanced version of CIS (ECIS), Risk Education (RE), Victim Data Collection (VDC) and Victim Assistance (VA).  Note: the key difference between ECIS and CIS is the identification, marking and reporting of ERW items. HALO will also seek to extend the scope of its activities to Explosive Remnants of War (ERW) Non-Technical Survey (NTS) and Disposal. 

To better understand the threat that ERW poses, HALO will conduct systematic CIS in 111 communities and ECIS in 692 communities across Idleb and Aleppo governorates. Under this activity, teams will visit communities, with the overall goal to identify, mark and report ERW contamination and to record its impact on the community. Data will be used to identify areas of highest priority for RE, create contamination maps, and provide essential information for future ERW clearance. The scale of this activity is unprecedented but is required to inform current and future ERW disposal/clearance, as well as immediately improving the awareness and safety of affected communities. ECIS activities will be coordinated from HALO’s operation room in Jordan, staffed by technical personnel. If the relevant authorizations are granted from the Turkish government, HALO will also establish ERW survey and disposal teams trained to complete surface-located ERW tasks (excluding IEDs) via a 6-week course derived from International Mine Action Standards (IMAS). They will be deployed under the direct control of HALO’s operations room in Jordan. At a later stage in 2019, they will complete advanced training relevant to the detection and disposal of sub-surface ERW (excluding IEDs). Extension to IED disposal requires a separate 4-week course. All disposal activities will be conducted via the use of thermite torches (T-Jets). No high explosives will be used. HALO’s ERW survey and disposal objectives for NW Syria are based on its experience in southern Syria in 2018.     

HALO will provide RE to 108,472 beneficiaries in 2019 (18,364 men, 17,692 women, 38,248 boys and 34,168 girls). A particular focus will be placed on those who are most at risk of accident (including children, young men and IDPs). Two new RE ‘Training of Trainer’ (ToT) Trainers will build on the work already underway by HALO’s existing RE ToT Trainer in NW Syria. Together, they will support NGOs currently delivering RE to vulnerable communities and IDPs, as well as NGOs willing to deliver RE along with other activities; improving the relevance, integration and reach of RE messaging across all relevant sectors. 

HALO will also collect information about ERW accidents and victims (survivors) through VDC which will be used to develop a better understanding of how and why accidents are occurring, enabling HALO, and other actors, to better tailor RE and VA activities.

In 2019, HALO and one of its implementing partners will implement a new VA initiative, where approx. 200 survivors of ERW accidents will benefit from initial basic health screening, referrals to reputable service providers and a one-off distribution of basic medical and hygiene items. The project will also support survivors (approx. 1,200) through the establishment of a rehabilitation centre and 2 x mobile outreach teams, providing physiotherapy, mental health and psycho-social support (MHPSS), peer support counselling, and referrals to a prosthetics centre. A social protection scheme providing ‘in-kind’ support to selected survivors will also be implemented. Additionally, in order to promote workplace inclusion, 5 survivors will be recruited, trained and employed by HALO’s partner.

Lean Season Food Assistance to the most food insecure people in rural areas (USAID/FFP) Lean Season Food Assistance to the most food insecure people in rural areas Under this Flash Appeal, Food Security sector partners plan to address the most urgent food security needs of people in rural areas across the country, who are adversely affected by multiple crises, including last year’s poor harvest for many small-holder farmers, economic shocks and recent cholera and typhoid outbreaks. Building on the funding already received to reach an estimated 900,000 people as of January 2019 and the Government’s Food Deficit Mitigation Strategy, partners aim to expand the geographic coverage of assistance to reach an additional 700,000 people in food insecure rural communities through primarily cash-based assistance. Focus will be on the low-lying areas relying on rainfed agriculture disproportionately affected by last year’s erratic rain. Market-based interventions are viable despite the current economic stress, as essential food commodities remain available on rural as well as urban markets, according to the national market assessment conducted by WFP and partners in November 2018. 

The IPC analysis conducted in January 2019 projects that nearly 3.8 million people in rural areas are in need of urgent humanitarian assistance, including 2.9 million who are severely food insecure (IPC phase 3 or 4) and a further 900,000 people who are currently receiving humanitarian assistance, without which they would be in IPC phase 3 or above.

In the face of the high prevalence of food insecurity (IPC phase 4 and 3), and the high probability of another El Niño phenomena in 2019 (90% likelihood according to the most recent SARCOF analysis), partners will provide a specialised food ration in the form of CSB++ specifically targeting children 6-59 months and pregnant and lactating women to increase the nutritional value of the food basket provided as part of the general household ration/cash. 

Based on the findings of the national market assessment conducted by partners in November, partners will select the most appropriate transfer modality for each district (cash or in-kind). According to the latest price information, partners aim to cover approximately 80% of the targeted individuals’ daily food energy needs (based on a 2100 kcal diet) to supplement other available food sources, thus enabling households to meet their basic food and nutrition needs. 
 
In view of the high probability of another El Nino, food assistance at this juncture can be considered as an early action to prevent further deterioration of food insecurity amongst particularly households already in IPC 3 (Crises) and 4 (Emergency).

 (P007070) Life-saving food assistance and livelihoods support in North-East Nigeria. WFP will provide unconditional food-assistance to the most food-insecure, crisis-affected populations. 
Life-saving general food assistance (in-kind food and cash-based transfers) will be delivered to IDPs, returnees and host populations in North-East Nigeria (Borno, Yobe and Adamawa States). 
Early recovery and resilience to shocks will be promoted through asset creation and preservation, increased livelihoods opportunities, and enhanced agricultural value chains. 
Joint multi-sectoral assessments and Emergency Food Security Analysis will be conducted regularly to monitor the nutrition, food security, and markets situation in crisis-affected states. 
A gender-transformative approach that reflects the needs of women, men, girls and boys will be adopted. WFP will mainstream protection throughout its work, supported by a solid understanding of the operational context and protection analysis. Training and capacity building of staff and partners in protection and humanitarian principles will include on-the-job coaching. WFP will ensure that affected populations (women and men) will be consulted throughout the programme cycle; beneficiary feedback mechanisms will be tailored to their preferred means of communication. Beneficiaries will continue to be empowered with knowledge on their food assistance entitlements and their rights, including WFP’s zero tolerance policy on Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA). Protection against Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) will be embedded in M&E tools, complaint feedback mechanisms and training of partners and staff. 

WFP will focus on concrete operational solutions to avoid situations in which people assisted by WFP could be exposed to SEA. Along these lines WFP will enhance its support to income generation activities targeted to women, expand their engagement in the production and use of fuel efficient stoves, deploy women as beneficiary registrars, monitors and security personnel. The referral system and monitoring system will be reviewed to maximize user friendliness and access by assisted populations as well as operational adjustments for problem solving. Particular attention will be given to supervise the retailers and operators in the distribution of cash based transfers. WFP will support milling activities for the grain commodities it provides and will implement effective solutions for the provision of condiments and cash. Deep field presence through the hubs and proximity to affected populations will be enhanced for these purposes. Three experienced international and six Nigerian protection officers will be deployed. Reporting will be done on a monthly basis through standard WFP reporting and meetings. Regular oversight and evaluations will be conducted.

WFP will continue the collection of key information on beneficiaries and assistance provided as part of its M&E activities. Monthly monitoring will include distribution and activity site management; beneficiary and entitlement verification; and ensuring adequate protection and gender measures. Lessons will be regularly drawn from monthly process and biannual outcome monitoring and reporting, and periodic reviews and evaluation to inform strategic and operational decisions.

WFP will further consolidate partnerships to enhance national and state-level emergency preparedness and response systems, including in food security and nutrition assessment and monitoring, early warning, protection, gender analysis, targeting and registration processes, safety nets, cash-based transfer capacities and supply chain. 

Where security and access to land allows, increasing livelihood activities will complement food assistance to support access to productive assets, income generating activities and self-reliance in the long-term. Assistance will be coordinated with government distributions, to ensure food assistance is complementary and fills gaps. Through an integrated approach to analyzing and addressing food and nutrition security, integrated, multi-sectoral interventions will be encouraged, for example through collaborations with the Nutrition, Health, WASH and Protection Sectors, among others. WFP will also continue to proactively engage with a wide range of federal and state actors, including the Ministries of Agriculture and Rural Development, Health, Budget and National Planning, Finance, the National Social Investment Office (NSIO), Women Affairs and Social Development, PCNI as well as other federal and state institutions. Furthermore, WFP and the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) will continue to strengthen cooperation between the two agencies. WFP will continue to partner with a number of local and international NGOs and will work with civil society organizations to continue strengthening the capacities of national actors.

The project addresses the underlying causes of the protracted crisis by further integrating humanitarian and development assistance and improving disaster risk reduction in alignment with WFP’s dual mandate and the international policy debate on bridging and operationalizing the humanitarian-development nexus, thus using a development lens in its humanitarian responses, and aligning early recovery and development interventions accordingly.

Emergency response through Kapoeta East Emergency Response project (KEERP) Food Security and Livelihood Improvement Project for Drought and Conflict -Affected Population in South Sudan  The purpose of this intervention is to save lives, reduce severe food insecurity and stabilize the condition of vulnerable groups including the elderly, IDPs, persons with disabilities, child-headed households, women and children in South Sudan. The interventions will further enhance community resilience by addressing the main drivers of vulnerability in the targeted areas of Kapoeta East, Tonj North, Tonj East and Terekeka. The project will seek to enhance both food security and livelihoods of vulnerable people by improving livestock production and access to animal health care services, improving access to agricultural production units & extension services and supporting communities to develop alternative income sources / livelihoods diversification by providing financial services through Group Savings and Loan Associations (GSLAs).  Cross-cutting themes will be to promote gender equity and increased women’s participation in building resilience, peace building and conflict reduction, disaster risk reduction and sustainable natural resource management. The geographical focus of the project is Kapoeta East County (Kauto 5,064 HH; Jie-900 HH, Mogos-3,650 HH, Lotimor-1,550 HH;  and Nating'a-990 HH;  payams);  Tonj North County (Alabek-2,400 HH, Akop-2,100 HH, Rualbet- 1,900  and Marialou 1,600 payams), Tonj East (Kacuat-2,080 HH, Paweng-2,150 HH Malualchum 2, 200-HH payams) and Terekeka County (Terekeka-2,400 HH, Muni-1,800 HH, Reggo-1,750 and Nyori-1,900 payams). Proposed interventions are aligned to FSL HRP Cluster objectives as shown below:  
•	Under unconditional food assistance, IRSS proposes to provide emergency regular life sustaining and life-saving food assistance to prevent famine, improve food consumption, improve dietary diversity and improve coping strategies for the most vulnerable population. This will target the most vulnerable households including IDPs 
•	Regarding food production for the most vulnerable households, the proposed interventions will seek to increase food production by vulnerable household in order to protect the erosion of livelihoods through improved agronomic practices i.e. use of ox plough animal traction, agricultural seeds and other faming inputs. 
•	Under the transitional emergency food assistance, IRSS proposes to provide emergency targeted life sustaining food assistance to strengthen households and community coping capacities by building productive assets and reduce reliance on general food distribution transfers. Food for Asset modality will be used to enable communities produce their own food in the long-term.  
•	In order to reduce dependency on food and agricultural input support, IRSS will through livelihood & conditional cash based support for more sustainable livelihoods seek to prevent and reverse the erosion of vulnerable rural & urban households and community assets. 
The proposed interventions will therefore be aimed at providing a link between rapid humanitarian response on one hand and building community resilience on the other. This will in turn contribute to reduce community vulnerability and build their capacity to bounce back in the face of livelihood shocks resulting from drought,conflict and others.

Comprehensive health services for vulnerable and left-behind populations in Borno State (part of ECHO/-WF/BUD/2019/91045) Emergency Response for Crisis-Affected Persons in BAY States, Nigeria Provision of health care services was greatly affected by the crisis in north east and posed a huge burden on Women and children. Most of the health facilities in the rural areas were damaged and are non-functional. Women and children are the most affected in a crisis specifically those arriving from the inaccessible areas are extremely vulnerable as they have not accessed humanitarian services prior to their arrival at the reception sites.  The leading causes of morbidity and mortality linked to malnutrition has been heavily linked with diseases outbreaks such as the acute watery diarrhoea and malaria. Female headed households as well as separated and unaccompanied children face an uphill task of accessing adequate services and are exposed to sexual exploitation and abuse as well as gender based violence. Communities that have settled in the host with limited restoration of livelihood as they cannot access their fields for cultivations and are not actively engaged with economic activities, their children face the risks of repeated episodes of acute malnutrition.
Nutrition intervention targets 4M women and children in BAY states, of which 3M are children below the age of 5 and 1M are women of reproductive age with infants below 2 years.  Majority of those in need are in the host communities 2.6M while approximately 0.6M are IDPS and 0.5M returnees while 0.2M still not accessed by humanitarian workers. The prevalence of acute malnutrition in the north east is further heightened by inadequate health services coverage, poor child care practices, inadequate hygiene and sanitation conditions and food insecurity. 
Population arriving from the inaccessible areas have particularity high prevalence of acute malnutrition, a SMART survey conducted in Bama in August 2018 indicated a very high prevalence of GAM among the new arrival compared to those that have been in the camp GAM by WHZ – 37.5% (reception site) while 7.8% (rest of camp) . Similar situation is observed in all the 9 reception sites in Bama, Dikwa, Gwoza, Kalabarge, Kukawa, Mobbar and Ngala, through the screening of new arrivals. Population in host communities continue to grapple with serious nutrition situation, routine monitoring of the prevalence of acute malnutrition though the nutrition and food security surveillance Findings indicate that Borno State has a GAM rate of 9.1 per cent and a SAM rate of 0.8 percent; Adamawa State has a GAM rate of 8.2 per cent and a SAM rate of 0.4 per cent, Yobe State has a GAM rate of 12.1 per cent and a SAM rate of 2.1 per cent. North Adamawa has reported increase in GAM prevalence from 9.2 per cent reported in November to 10.1 per cent in April 2018. Yobe reported improved GAM rate in South and Northern parts while central Borno reported increased GAM from 11.6 per cent in Nov 2017 to 14.1 per cent in April (NBS, UNICEF Nutrition and Food security surveillance round 5 April 2018) .The health system is still contending with extensive damage and inadequate human resources as well as insufficient medical supplies to cater for the needs of the displaced population as well as those in the host communities to date the health system functionality is below 50%
Population movement within the northeast has been a key phenomenal with the majority arriving from the inaccessible areas has increased the burden on the existing nutrition services as this movements are associated with extreme needs as those IDPS arriving from these areas have not accessed humanitarian services. Movement have also been realized for those intending to move back to their LGA of origin to explore livelihood activities have also been reported.  This movements have been sporadic and have continued to put pressure on existing humanitarian services mostly affected including the nutrition sector as services providing SAM with medical complication have been inadequate. 
Acute malnutrition is often an outcome of poor food security, Health and poor child feeding and caring practices as well as other humanitarian services with chronic malnutrition thus the importance of involving multiple sectors in addressing malnutrition. The causes of malnutrition are complex and interconnected hence requiring intersectoral collaboration and integration with health agriculture social protection among others. An IRC Semi-Quantitative Evaluation of Access and Coverage survey (SQUEC) survey conducted by IRC between 5th to 23rd of March 2018 in 10 communities in MMC and Jere  estimated single coverage at 47.7 percent of existing needs (95 percent confidence interval between 38.7 and 56.9 percent coverage). This coverage is below the 70 percent Sphere minimum standard for urban settings
IRC has been present in North east as health and Nutrition actor since 2012 and an active member and co-lead in both sectors in the 3 north east states, As for nutrition programming IRC is currently supporting 22 OTP clinics and 1 stabilization centre in Adamawa state,22 mobile clinics in Borno state comprising of :12 mobile clinics in MMC and Jere,4 mobile clinics in Konduga, 4mobile clinics  in Monguno,10 health facility OTP in Askira Uba and also run the largest in-patient stabilization centres in Borno state(64 bed stabilization centres in MMC and Jere,10 bed capacity in Askira Uba. In addition IRC also Run 22 bed capacity stabilization centre in Gujba LGA and 12 OTP clinics in Yobe state. Each of the facilities are run by dedicated MOH and IRC staffs. IRC has expert medical Doctor who oversees all the SC’s and train SC staffs on clinical care for SAM children. The IRC expert Doctor also conducts and support WHO/UNICEF and other partners in training of staffs.In addition IRC has technical health and nutrition advisers who oversee the Quality of the CMAM and health programs. Nutrition Technical adviser visit the country after every 6 months and conduct Quality assessment and reviews the performance of the CMAM and IYCF activities

Emergency Response and durable solutions for displacement affected populations in the Far North and East regions of Cameroon Promoting civil documentation and HLP rights of displacement affected populations in the Far North region of Cameroon.				 This project aims to promote the HLP rights of internally displaced people and affected communities and prevent HLP related conflicts in displacement and return areas. The displaced population faces various kinds of HLP related issues such as lack of land for agriculture, forced eviction from housing and land, secondary occupation in return areas, etc. Women are more vulnerable and face more HLP issues as according to the customary law in the region, women do not inherit land. While their gender roles expect them to bring food home form farming, their access to secure land is very limited. Even though, they had money to buy a piece of land, they will need authorisation from their husband or family related male. Women widows are evicted form land inherit after marriage and have to struggle to meet their basic needs. This project will pay specific attention to the most vulnerable such as women, the elderly and other marginalised groups.

Promoting resilience through supporting quality education and psycho-social services to primary school students in war affected Syrian communities (Support to four schools in Ariha, Idleb, Syria) Learning for a Brighter Tomorrow: Quality Formal and Informal Education for Children and Youth in Northern Syria From 01 January through 31 December 2019 and in partnership with Lead Partner INGO, we will continue our currently running EuropeAid-funded Education programme under which we currently supports four schools in the Ariha sub-district of Idleb governorate, assisting 1,515 students, 97 teachers/school staff (including 4 psychosocial (PSS) facilitators) over the course of this grant. 

We are proposing to support an additional six schools for a total of ten schools under a formal education component of this programme in addition to 16 Self Learning Program (SLP) temporary learning spaces in four camps under a non-formal education component, expanding it educational activities into the HNO 2019’s highly prioritized geographic areas of Saraqab and Darkosh sub-districts of Ariha, Idleb (in addition to the current coverage of Ariha sub-district); Madiq Castle in Hama and Afrin, Jandairis, Haritan and Zarbah in rural Aleppo. 

Structured around our holistic model for education during times of crisis and recovery, the proposed program has three primary objectives: (1) to improve academic teaching and learning; (2) to promote student wellbeing and protection; and (3) to strengthen educational access and resources. Comprising both formal and non-formal education components, the program will reach a total of 5920 children (3163 males, 2757 females) — of which 35 percent are adolescents and youth — as well as 291 teachers / school staff (166  males and 125 females) and 640 caretakers (256 males  and 384 females). 

Under the formal education component - via the ten schools - we aim to reach a total of 4000 children (2196 males, 1804 females) as well as 209 teachers (119 males and 90 female) and 400 caretakers (150 males and 250 females), noting that all students who receive formal education under this project will also have access to the non-formal education component. Under the non-formal education component - 16 Self-Learning Program (SLP) temporary learning spaces in 4 camps, we aim to prepare 1920 out-of-school children (967 male, 953 female) for integration into formal primary schools after one year of study, including 16 teachers (8 males and 8 females).  Note: expansion on both components’ activities can be found under the Implementation of Activities section of this proposal.

Academic teaching and learning is coupled with program components focused on student safety and wellbeing. School personnel receive training in child protection and psychosocial care, and all students participate in weekly, age-appropriate PSS sessions led by dedicated facilitators. These activities aim to promote positive social-emotional development among children, and include a youth Life Skills curriculum for older students. Further, each school has a Protection Facilitator who is responsible for monitoring protection mainstreaming measures, such as a case management and referral system for students requiring external support.  School personnel are also trained on emergency preparedness and response, and develop plans to deal with threats like attacks on or near schools. 

In light of economic barriers that require some students to work rather than attend school, the proposed intervention also includes a supplemental livelihoods pilot component. This pilot will target the most vulnerable children and families who rely on child labor as an economic coping mechanism by offering conditional cash-vouchers or food baskets to offset the financial losses incurred when transitioning children from work to school.
