To save lives and alleviate suffering Supporting the Provision of Quality Community Based Nutrition Services in targeted districts of Buhera and Chipinge of Manicaland Province and Mbare District of Harare Province GOAL ZW is currently operational in Chipinge and Mbare districts implementing a Livelihoods/Nutrition intervention and a Cholera response respectively. GOAL ZW will also re-enter Buhera district for a three- year livelihoods and nutrition program as of January 2019. These districts have been identified as being amongst the most vulnerable in the country in view of the predicted El Nino in 2019. 
This action will complement GOAL’s ongoing activities in the targeted districts, by providing support to the Ministry of Health in the following areas;
-	Implementation of active screening for early identification and referral of children with acute malnutrition through community-based health workers and community volunteers.
-	Capacity building of facility-based health workers on treatment, management and reporting of acute malnutrition.
-	 Integrated refresher training for Village Health Workers (VHWs) and Community Volunteers on active screening through MUAC and odema testing, HIV prevention and treatment follow up, IYCF, ECD, child protection, micronutrients and positive parenting and Vitamin A supplementation.
The trained VHW/Community Volunteers will do the following:
-	Screen 74,896 children in 3 districts for acute malnutrition.
-	Reach 73,076 children in 3 districts with Vitamin A supplementation (VAS) and deworming
-	Reach 22,836 children with micro nutrient powders
-	Reach 58,200 caregivers in 3 districts of children < 5 years with integrated messages on nutrition, WASH, HIV, Child protection through social mobilisation activities. 
-	Establish/Support mother support groups in targeted districts continuation to the existing mother support groups in the 3 targeted districts, by reaching xxx caregivers with IYCF messages, messages on positive parenting practices and cooking demonstrations.
-	Create linkages with the Food Security Sector for provision of supplementary feeding for PLW and children under 5 in targeted districts
In coordination with the WASH and food security cluster the action will provide Community IYCF-E support and counselling specifically where cash and/or food assistance intervention are provided
Early detection of Moderate Malnutrition cases will ensure avoidance of these cases deteriorating to Severe Acute Malnutrition.

Food Security (USAID/FFP) Life-saving food assistance and livelihoods support in North-East Nigeria. WFP will provide unconditional food-assistance to the most food-insecure, crisis-affected populations. 
Life-saving general food assistance (in-kind food and cash-based transfers) will be delivered to IDPs, returnees and host populations in North-East Nigeria (Borno, Yobe and Adamawa States). 
Early recovery and resilience to shocks will be promoted through asset creation and preservation, increased livelihoods opportunities, and enhanced agricultural value chains. 
Joint multi-sectoral assessments and Emergency Food Security Analysis will be conducted regularly to monitor the nutrition, food security, and markets situation in crisis-affected states. 
A gender-transformative approach that reflects the needs of women, men, girls and boys will be adopted. WFP will mainstream protection throughout its work, supported by a solid understanding of the operational context and protection analysis. Training and capacity building of staff and partners in protection and humanitarian principles will include on-the-job coaching. WFP will ensure that affected populations (women and men) will be consulted throughout the programme cycle; beneficiary feedback mechanisms will be tailored to their preferred means of communication. Beneficiaries will continue to be empowered with knowledge on their food assistance entitlements and their rights, including WFP’s zero tolerance policy on Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA). Protection against Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) will be embedded in M&E tools, complaint feedback mechanisms and training of partners and staff. 

WFP will focus on concrete operational solutions to avoid situations in which people assisted by WFP could be exposed to SEA. Along these lines WFP will enhance its support to income generation activities targeted to women, expand their engagement in the production and use of fuel efficient stoves, deploy women as beneficiary registrars, monitors and security personnel. The referral system and monitoring system will be reviewed to maximize user friendliness and access by assisted populations as well as operational adjustments for problem solving. Particular attention will be given to supervise the retailers and operators in the distribution of cash based transfers. WFP will support milling activities for the grain commodities it provides and will implement effective solutions for the provision of condiments and cash. Deep field presence through the hubs and proximity to affected populations will be enhanced for these purposes. Three experienced international and six Nigerian protection officers will be deployed. Reporting will be done on a monthly basis through standard WFP reporting and meetings. Regular oversight and evaluations will be conducted.

WFP will continue the collection of key information on beneficiaries and assistance provided as part of its M&E activities. Monthly monitoring will include distribution and activity site management; beneficiary and entitlement verification; and ensuring adequate protection and gender measures. Lessons will be regularly drawn from monthly process and biannual outcome monitoring and reporting, and periodic reviews and evaluation to inform strategic and operational decisions.

WFP will further consolidate partnerships to enhance national and state-level emergency preparedness and response systems, including in food security and nutrition assessment and monitoring, early warning, protection, gender analysis, targeting and registration processes, safety nets, cash-based transfer capacities and supply chain. 

Where security and access to land allows, increasing livelihood activities will complement food assistance to support access to productive assets, income generating activities and self-reliance in the long-term. Assistance will be coordinated with government distributions, to ensure food assistance is complementary and fills gaps. Through an integrated approach to analyzing and addressing food and nutrition security, integrated, multi-sectoral interventions will be encouraged, for example through collaborations with the Nutrition, Health, WASH and Protection Sectors, among others. WFP will also continue to proactively engage with a wide range of federal and state actors, including the Ministries of Agriculture and Rural Development, Health, Budget and National Planning, Finance, the National Social Investment Office (NSIO), Women Affairs and Social Development, PCNI as well as other federal and state institutions. Furthermore, WFP and the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) will continue to strengthen cooperation between the two agencies. WFP will continue to partner with a number of local and international NGOs and will work with civil society organizations to continue strengthening the capacities of national actors.

The project addresses the underlying causes of the protracted crisis by further integrating humanitarian and development assistance and improving disaster risk reduction in alignment with WFP’s dual mandate and the international policy debate on bridging and operationalizing the humanitarian-development nexus, thus using a development lens in its humanitarian responses, and aligning early recovery and development interventions accordingly.

IOM has been requested by Departments of Health (DoH) to continue to support and provide lifesaving primary health services including reproductive health and emergency services, referral and health facility support, and provide mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) to conflict-affected and liberated areas across Iraq to support returnees and host communities and continue camp-based clinic responses for internally displaced persons (IDPs). IOM will support the MoH DoH through building their capacity for preparedness and response, and offering services. In line with Health Cluster objectives 1, 2 and 3 this project thus aims to increase the well-being of IDPs and highly vulnerable people and their communities. It responds to the critical health needs resulting from the extreme conflict during 2014-2018, that resulted in millions of people experiencing distressful events, disruption of social networks, loss of property and harsh living conditions. 

IOM’s support includes PHC in camp clinics, non-emergency referrals from camps to secondary/tertiary health facilities inside cities, and health facility support/capacity building training sessions. Services will be offered to two main vulnerable categories of people:
-	Displaced people in camps, temporary, formal and informal settlements: offered primary healthcare consultations, obstetrics gynecology (OB-GYN) and pediatric consultation through static clinics in camps; and non-emergency referral will be offered. MHPSS services will be offered though static community centers, and referrals supported when specialized services are not available in camp.
-	Returnees and vulnerable host communities: supported by enabling primary healthcare clinics (PHCCs) and hospitals in the areas of return to support free services to affected population, through minor revitalization and operational costs. PHCCs will also be supported to integrate MHPSS services though trained staff and revitalized MHPSS units.

Emergency shelter and NFI assistance to improve living conditions of most vulnerable families in Iraq Improve shelter conditions of most vulnerable returnee families in Heet District in Anbar Governorate, Iraq. The proposed project aims to support most vulnerable families in the Governorate of Anbar, particularly in Heet District. CCR and its partner AL MAHABA WES-SALAM (Al Mahaba) will identify and prioritize the most vulnerable families in Heet district whose houses were damaged in different levels due to the military operations. Beneficiaries will be selected based on a social and economic vulnerability assessment (recommended by the Cash Working Groups in Iraq) and the damage categories of their shelters (Based on Iraq Shelter Cluster’s Guidelines).

Partners will rehabilitate 100 damaged shelters in Heet District. Targeted houses will fall under category 2 (and 3 based on the technical assessment) of war damaged shelters. Shelter rehabilitation activities will be implemented through framework agreements with local suppliers and locally hired skilled labours. Partners will verify the local market capacity through market assessment prior to start rehabilitation. 

Partners will select 330 vulnerable families whose damaged shelter fall under damage category 1 who will be eligible to receive Sealing Off Kits (SOKs). SOKs will be designed based on the findings a community-level assessment at the beginning of the project where technical engineers will evaluate the most critical shelter repair needs and advice on selecting the components of the kits. Distribution of SOKs will follow the method of house to house/ family distribution given that selected families lack resources and capacity to manage transporting kits from central locations. Partners will ensure that targeted families will receive training on the best usage of the SOKs and distribute manuals along with the kits.

Activities aim to improve safety and privacy elements in families’ shelters which are critical to adequate shelter conditions for women, men, girls and boys. Furthermore, the proposed project will contribute to improve the substandard shelters by protecting from climate and foster healthier conditions.

CCR will coordinate with the Community Resource Centers in Anbar Governorate and HLP actors to address the needs of HLP intervention of targeted families. CCR will ensure that no harm is associated with its intervention on vulnerable families especially related to governmental compensation and lands properties and rights issues.

Lean Season Food Assistance to the most food insecure people in rural areas Lean Season Food Assistance to the most food insecure people in rural areas Under this Flash Appeal, Food Security sector partners plan to address the most urgent food security needs of people in rural areas across the country, who are adversely affected by multiple crises, including last year’s poor harvest for many small-holder farmers, economic shocks and recent cholera and typhoid outbreaks. Building on the funding already received to reach an estimated 900,000 people as of January 2019 and the Government’s Food Deficit Mitigation Strategy, partners aim to expand the geographic coverage of assistance to reach an additional 700,000 people in food insecure rural communities through primarily cash-based assistance. Focus will be on the low-lying areas relying on rainfed agriculture disproportionately affected by last year’s erratic rain. Market-based interventions are viable despite the current economic stress, as essential food commodities remain available on rural as well as urban markets, according to the national market assessment conducted by WFP and partners in November 2018. 

The IPC analysis conducted in January 2019 projects that nearly 3.8 million people in rural areas are in need of urgent humanitarian assistance, including 2.9 million who are severely food insecure (IPC phase 3 or 4) and a further 900,000 people who are currently receiving humanitarian assistance, without which they would be in IPC phase 3 or above.

In the face of the high prevalence of food insecurity (IPC phase 4 and 3), and the high probability of another El Niño phenomena in 2019 (90% likelihood according to the most recent SARCOF analysis), partners will provide a specialised food ration in the form of CSB++ specifically targeting children 6-59 months and pregnant and lactating women to increase the nutritional value of the food basket provided as part of the general household ration/cash. 

Based on the findings of the national market assessment conducted by partners in November, partners will select the most appropriate transfer modality for each district (cash or in-kind). According to the latest price information, partners aim to cover approximately 80% of the targeted individuals’ daily food energy needs (based on a 2100 kcal diet) to supplement other available food sources, thus enabling households to meet their basic food and nutrition needs. 
 
In view of the high probability of another El Nino, food assistance at this juncture can be considered as an early action to prevent further deterioration of food insecurity amongst particularly households already in IPC 3 (Crises) and 4 (Emergency).

CERF) Lean Season Food Assistance to the most food insecure people in rural areas Under this Flash Appeal, Food Security sector partners plan to address the most urgent food security needs of people in rural areas across the country, who are adversely affected by multiple crises, including last year’s poor harvest for many small-holder farmers, economic shocks and recent cholera and typhoid outbreaks. Building on the funding already received to reach an estimated 900,000 people as of January 2019 and the Government’s Food Deficit Mitigation Strategy, partners aim to expand the geographic coverage of assistance to reach an additional 700,000 people in food insecure rural communities through primarily cash-based assistance. Focus will be on the low-lying areas relying on rainfed agriculture disproportionately affected by last year’s erratic rain. Market-based interventions are viable despite the current economic stress, as essential food commodities remain available on rural as well as urban markets, according to the national market assessment conducted by WFP and partners in November 2018. 

The IPC analysis conducted in January 2019 projects that nearly 3.8 million people in rural areas are in need of urgent humanitarian assistance, including 2.9 million who are severely food insecure (IPC phase 3 or 4) and a further 900,000 people who are currently receiving humanitarian assistance, without which they would be in IPC phase 3 or above.

In the face of the high prevalence of food insecurity (IPC phase 4 and 3), and the high probability of another El Niño phenomena in 2019 (90% likelihood according to the most recent SARCOF analysis), partners will provide a specialised food ration in the form of CSB++ specifically targeting children 6-59 months and pregnant and lactating women to increase the nutritional value of the food basket provided as part of the general household ration/cash. 

Based on the findings of the national market assessment conducted by partners in November, partners will select the most appropriate transfer modality for each district (cash or in-kind). According to the latest price information, partners aim to cover approximately 80% of the targeted individuals’ daily food energy needs (based on a 2100 kcal diet) to supplement other available food sources, thus enabling households to meet their basic food and nutrition needs. 
 
In view of the high probability of another El Nino, food assistance at this juncture can be considered as an early action to prevent further deterioration of food insecurity amongst particularly households already in IPC 3 (Crises) and 4 (Emergency).

ACP-EU Natural Disaster Risk Reduction Program Agricultural productivity and food security for cyclone Idai affected population in Sofala, Manica and Zambezia provinces The Cyclone Idai weather system swept through five provinces – Sofala, Manica, Tete, Zambezia and Inhambane – decimating livelihoods and leaving a wake of death, destruction and damage. The Cyclone damaged nearly 500,000 hectares of crops, along with other livelihoods, right before the annual harvest. This number is expected to rise as the full extent of the damage becomes known. Extensive livestock losses are expected, as well as widespread damage to fisher folks’ assets. Many assets and structures, including markets in the port city of Beira, have been destroyed. Food insecurity is therefore expected to rise significantly in the months ahead as a result of the destruction and damage. Women in Mozambique play a critical role in agricultural production, providing labour to support the production of food crops and also supporting the production of cash crops. At the same time, women remain responsible for the majority of caregiving. With the caregiving burden likely to increase in the aftermath of the cyclone and floods – as illness and injury have risen – women may have to decrease their agricultural production, further heightening food insecurity.

(USAID/OFDA) Integrating Women into Disaster Preparedness and Response (Fanm yo pare) Given its international experience in disaster risk reduction, resilience and women’s empowerment, Mercy Corps seeks to implement a project that addresses women’s needs and perspectives in local contingency planning in order to pave the way for humanitarian response that will adequately address vulnerabilities and capitalize on positive gender dynamics in target communities. By partnering with women’s organizations that are involved in local humanitarian and development efforts, Mercy Corps will provide them with tools needed to better integrate women’s needs into their planning, as well as better link their planning to department-level DRR plans. 
The “Fanm yo pare” project aims to build capacity of women’s organizations to support women’s empowerment and strengthen the resilience of women to better face natural disasters. The project's activities will be developed and adapted to meet the needs of women in the west (Cabaret and Arcahaie) and the Nippes departments. The project will integrate 750 women and men into gender-focused DRR and humanitarian response trainings, workshops, and working sessions, and also integrate 1250 women and men into VSLAs, which will contribute to gender equity and social cohesion in the target communities. This multi-platform approach will build understanding of gender and protection among civil society at large, and will integrate women, girls, boys and men's needs into contingency planning, which has the potential to improve humanitarian response for the larger community, estimated at about 10,500 direct and indirect beneficiaries. 
Outcomes:
1. Women's organizations have the capacity to ensure gender-responsive disaster-risk reduction planning and action, and emergency response at the community level.

Life-saving food assistance and livelihoods support in North-East Nigeria. Life-saving food assistance and livelihoods support in North-East Nigeria. WFP will provide unconditional food-assistance to the most food-insecure, crisis-affected populations. 
Life-saving general food assistance (in-kind food and cash-based transfers) will be delivered to IDPs, returnees and host populations in North-East Nigeria (Borno, Yobe and Adamawa States). 
Early recovery and resilience to shocks will be promoted through asset creation and preservation, increased livelihoods opportunities, and enhanced agricultural value chains. 
Joint multi-sectoral assessments and Emergency Food Security Analysis will be conducted regularly to monitor the nutrition, food security, and markets situation in crisis-affected states. 
A gender-transformative approach that reflects the needs of women, men, girls and boys will be adopted. WFP will mainstream protection throughout its work, supported by a solid understanding of the operational context and protection analysis. Training and capacity building of staff and partners in protection and humanitarian principles will include on-the-job coaching. WFP will ensure that affected populations (women and men) will be consulted throughout the programme cycle; beneficiary feedback mechanisms will be tailored to their preferred means of communication. Beneficiaries will continue to be empowered with knowledge on their food assistance entitlements and their rights, including WFP’s zero tolerance policy on Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA). Protection against Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) will be embedded in M&E tools, complaint feedback mechanisms and training of partners and staff. 

WFP will focus on concrete operational solutions to avoid situations in which people assisted by WFP could be exposed to SEA. Along these lines WFP will enhance its support to income generation activities targeted to women, expand their engagement in the production and use of fuel efficient stoves, deploy women as beneficiary registrars, monitors and security personnel. The referral system and monitoring system will be reviewed to maximize user friendliness and access by assisted populations as well as operational adjustments for problem solving. Particular attention will be given to supervise the retailers and operators in the distribution of cash based transfers. WFP will support milling activities for the grain commodities it provides and will implement effective solutions for the provision of condiments and cash. Deep field presence through the hubs and proximity to affected populations will be enhanced for these purposes. Three experienced international and six Nigerian protection officers will be deployed. Reporting will be done on a monthly basis through standard WFP reporting and meetings. Regular oversight and evaluations will be conducted.

WFP will continue the collection of key information on beneficiaries and assistance provided as part of its M&E activities. Monthly monitoring will include distribution and activity site management; beneficiary and entitlement verification; and ensuring adequate protection and gender measures. Lessons will be regularly drawn from monthly process and biannual outcome monitoring and reporting, and periodic reviews and evaluation to inform strategic and operational decisions.

WFP will further consolidate partnerships to enhance national and state-level emergency preparedness and response systems, including in food security and nutrition assessment and monitoring, early warning, protection, gender analysis, targeting and registration processes, safety nets, cash-based transfer capacities and supply chain. 

Where security and access to land allows, increasing livelihood activities will complement food assistance to support access to productive assets, income generating activities and self-reliance in the long-term. Assistance will be coordinated with government distributions, to ensure food assistance is complementary and fills gaps. Through an integrated approach to analyzing and addressing food and nutrition security, integrated, multi-sectoral interventions will be encouraged, for example through collaborations with the Nutrition, Health, WASH and Protection Sectors, among others. WFP will also continue to proactively engage with a wide range of federal and state actors, including the Ministries of Agriculture and Rural Development, Health, Budget and National Planning, Finance, the National Social Investment Office (NSIO), Women Affairs and Social Development, PCNI as well as other federal and state institutions. Furthermore, WFP and the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) will continue to strengthen cooperation between the two agencies. WFP will continue to partner with a number of local and international NGOs and will work with civil society organizations to continue strengthening the capacities of national actors.

The project addresses the underlying causes of the protracted crisis by further integrating humanitarian and development assistance and improving disaster risk reduction in alignment with WFP’s dual mandate and the international policy debate on bridging and operationalizing the humanitarian-development nexus, thus using a development lens in its humanitarian responses, and aligning early recovery and development interventions accordingly.

This project aims to promote the HLP rights of internally displaced people and affected communities and prevent HLP related conflicts in displacement and return areas. The displaced population faces various kinds of HLP related issues such as lack of land for agriculture, forced eviction from housing and land, secondary occupation in return areas, etc. Women are more vulnerable and face more HLP issues as according to the customary law in the region, women do not inherit land. While their gender roles expect them to bring food home form farming, their access to secure land is very limited. Even though, they had money to buy a piece of land, they will need authorisation from their husband or family related male. Women widows are evicted form land inherit after marriage and have to struggle to meet their basic needs. This project will pay specific attention to the most vulnerable such as women, the elderly and other marginalised groups.

Community Based Protection of Water and Natural Resources on Sinjar Mountain through Cash for Assets intervention Agriculture revitalization and support to food self-sufficiency in liberated areas (Federal Iraq) The proposed intervention is in line with the 2019 HRP priority areas defined by the Food Security Cluster. Indeed the proposed project will target Tel Afar, Tilkaif, Hamdanyia.  The project complies with the 2019 HRP Strategic Objective 1: post-conflict transition towards durable solutions.

The main objective of the project is to support return and recovery processes of IDPs in Federal Iraq.

Based on TGH past and ongoing FSL actions, the present project has been designed taking into account the various local contexts and needs that strongly differ from area to another. Considering the diversity of needs calling for tailored need based responses, TGH proposes a range of solutions.
 Past actions implemented both in Federal Iraq and KRI (fodder and animal distributions in Rabia area, mobile veterinary clinics in Tilkaif and Rabia area, partnership with Dohuk Veterinary College) and recent assessments have allowed TGH to develop a strong understanding of agriculture related needs. 

Based on TGH observations in IDP camps (in which TGH implements CP activities) and field assessments, barriers to return for IDPs toward their areas of origin needs to be overcome with an adequate support to allow a durable and dignified return.  Most vulnerable population groups will be targeted by the project (farmers with a limited number of animals, matching a range of vulnerability criteria such as the level of incomes, number of children, etc.). 

Proposing a mix immediate and longer term solutions is mandatory to allow immediate and durable returns of IDPs: they need to be able to quickly restart a productive activity, while the extensive damages on productive private and public assets / infrastructure call for a longer term recovery and rehabilitation approach. To that extent, TGH aims at implementing quick impact activities (e.g.: mobile veterinary clinics, fodder and animals distribution) and working in parallel on sustainable activities such as rehabilitation of water efficient irrigation assets, training of veterinary staffs, implementation of solar powered irrigation, mapping of available irrigation resources for a more sustainable water management, rehabilitation of market chain infrastructures, etc.

Considering the damaged social fabric due to the recent events and the diversity of ethnic groups, TGH will pay a strong attention to the do no harm approach within this project. Equity and transparency in the delivered support will be crucial to avoid fueling or creating tensions. 

Since part of the present project is already funded by the French Development Agency (36 months project- starting early 2019), significant operational and means synergies are expected between the foreseen activities and funds.

The purpose of this project is to improve and sustain essential crop production and productivity through direct seed and farm tools and protect and rehabilitate the livelihoods of the most vulnerable groups in the community through essential crops, livestock, and vegetable production as per the livelihood zone capacity in the targeted counties. ACROSS will fully engage community leaders, women’s groups, the youth and others within the community throughout the life of the project. The project is designed and will be implemented with knowledge of the seasonality context and the livelihood calendar. The communities in these regions have limited productive assets, and require immediate assistance to tackle the food insecurity which is high on the cluster agenda. This project will be integrated with SSJR4 Dutch Relief Alliance (DRA) funded and Swedish PMU funded projects that ACROSS is currently implementing in Pibor and Kapoeta counties. The project will seek to diversify the household diet and address malnutrition, which is mostly a problem for children, pregnant and lactating mothers. The provision of improved inputs like seed and agricultural tools in a timely manner will significantly contribute to the restoration of agricultural inputs in remote locations enabling communities to ensure that planting is on time. The project will ensure that vulnerable people have direct access to more food through the provision of vegetable and crop seeds and tools, fishing equipment, animal health services as well as cash for work project planned. The project will integrate and augment responses to immediate needs, restoration of livelihoods, and capacity building to pave the path for long-term recovery in order to enhance communities. ACROSS proposes actions that will connect with the humanitarian response and resilience programs that will target 10,000 households (60,000 beneficiaries) in Jonglei and the Eastern Equatoria States, comprised of 29,400 males (14,406 above and 14994 below 18 years) 30,600 females (14994 above 18 years and 15606 below 18years).

Provision of equitable access to safe and adequate water, dignified sanitation, and hygiene practices to mitigate WASH related GBV and Malnutrition for the Internally displaced population (IDPs), returnee and crisis-affected communities through coordinated and integrated WASH response, reinforcing protection and enhancing resilience, communities coping mechanisms and sustainability in Pibor County, Jonglei State, South Sudan. Saving live by providing timely and appropriate access to safe and adequate water, dignified Sanitation, and enhancing safe hygiene practices for crisis affected communities through integrated WASH interventions, reinforcing protection and enhancing resilience through building capacities of communities to prepare for and cope with recurrent shocks and sustain livelihoods. In this project, CMC aims to provide timely, equitable access to safe and sufficient water as well as improving knowledge of most vulnerable population on hygiene to reduce morbidity and mortality resulting from WASH-related diseases and malnutrition.
CMC will implement integrated lifesaving WASH and nutrition activities mainstreaming protection, accountability to affected population and strengthening the capacity of affected community on copping mechanism and resilience through training of different groups of people in the community such as pump mechanics, Water management committee, women groups, community leaders among others The project will target communities affected with conflict and natural disasters with limited access to safe water supply, unsafe hygiene and sanitation practices and food insecurity with support to institutions like nutrition/health centers and schools with WASH facilities and hygiene promotion.
Under this project, CMC will implement life-saving WASH activities targeting 15000 Direct Beneficiaries and 10000 indirect beneficiaries suffering from inadequate access to safe drinking water and poor hygiene conditions. CMC intends to target vulnerable and crisis affected population with a structured, effective preparedness and response programme aimed at improving access to safe water, enhancing community awareness on safe hygiene and sanitation practices in order to prevent and mitigate WASH-related diseases. 
CMC will coordinate with nutrition, education and FSL partners to reduce malnutrition level through supporting nutrition centers and schools with WASH facilities and enhancing knowledge of mothers who are the primary care givers on safe hygiene and sanitation practices especially in areas of new displacement. This will contribute to the reduction of risk of WASH related diseases including malnutrition hence making health, nutrition and education centers safe for users. 
To enhance sustainability and resilience, CMC will implement capacity building of the community to prepare for and cope with current shocks and sustain livelihoods, linkages with development action to support resilience
Protection and accountability to affected people will be at the central point in this project, putting communities at the centre of the response. CMC will ensure that services delivered are gender-sensitive and will consider the needs of older people, children (boys and girls) and people living with disabilities. Where necessary cash programming will be incorporated through voucher for WASH NFIs like soap provided to health/nutrition centers at risk of contamination and malnutrition. Key hygiene and nutrition messaging at these institutions will be accompanied.
Before response, initial needs assessments (either IRNA or CMC’s own assessment) will be carried out in consultation with the national WASH cluster and WASH states focal persons for the targeted locations. Activities will include will include safe water supply through water point construction repair and rehabilitation, provision of sanitation facilities at institution levels especially health/nutrition centers and schools, hygiene promotion focusing on key messages  (hand washing, safe water chain and safe excreta disposal) Hygiene and sanitation campaigns in communities and institutions, capacity-building of community through trainings (pump mechanics, water user committees, community hygiene promoters, school's hygiene clubs), and distribution of WASH NFIs and Menstrual hygiene Management Materials to women and girls of reproductive age. 
To ensure accountability to affected population, indicators will be put in place to track cooperation with communities by attending to complaints and carrying out feedback sessions with the community to address GBV threats in WASH, and ensuring services provided meet the needs of the beneficiaries. Post intervention monitoring will be conducted to measure the appropriateness, coverage and effectiveness. Clear WASH NFI beneficiary selection criteria will be put in place and clearly presented to the community before and during distribution.
The continuing deteriorating access to humanitarian support services for the Internally Displaced People and Returnees contributed negatively to the affected population with serious traumatic life experiences in the sites of displacement and return, through lessons learnt by other partners in current and most recent projects, (CMC) has acknowledged the rapid increasing cases of protection and Sexual Gender Based Violence which stand as a prove that protection and Sexual Gender Based Violence is a cross cutting thematic issue that need to be addressed across all projects and this project will contribute in addressing the gaps through inter-sector response.

They have strong multi-sector capacities, with experience in: Food security, livelihoods, WASH, CP, GBV, Education, NFI, health centres, legal assistance and cash transfer.  
The Critical Needs Support Foundation (CNSF) is a rapidly growing national NGO which specializes in Shelter, WASH and cash transfer responses. CNSF conducts multiple cash transfer projects across Ninewa, for various sectors. CNSF targets marginalized communities especially in Ninewa. CNSF have a strong presence in Ninewa and Anbar, they have a country office in Erbil and Baghdad. 
This consortium will adopt a harmonized approach across two governorates, integrating six activities from two sectors in each location to deliver an integrated programme addressing some of the root causes of the vulnerability of families. This is designed to build on each organization's strengths and experience in Iraq with a specific focus on localization, following Mission East’s strategy for the coming 3 years to build the capacity of national NGO and local volunteer groups. 
In each target location a fully integrated double-sector response will be implemented in targeted, rural and per-urban, under-served returnee locations. WASH and Child Protection (CP) will be holistically addressed. The program is designed to provide synergies between the sectorial responses to support returnee needs in a rounded and comprehensive way.  This will be implemented through pre-existing community protection structures which will be trained to support child protection services including parenting skills training. In all locations mobile child protection case management teams will operate alongside outreach teams who will deliver multi-sector key messaging, covering topics on hygiene promotion, water conservation and child protection. Parenting skills packages will be delivered in each target location with the support of pre-existing community groups. This integrated package will be implemented in under-served returnee locations between Samara district, Sinjar and Telafar,. Targeting a total of 9,000 people.

Life-saving food assistance and livelihoods support in North-East Nigeria. Life-saving food assistance and livelihoods support in North-East Nigeria. WFP will provide unconditional food-assistance to the most food-insecure, crisis-affected populations. 
Life-saving general food assistance (in-kind food and cash-based transfers) will be delivered to IDPs, returnees and host populations in North-East Nigeria (Borno, Yobe and Adamawa States). 
Early recovery and resilience to shocks will be promoted through asset creation and preservation, increased livelihoods opportunities, and enhanced agricultural value chains. 
Joint multi-sectoral assessments and Emergency Food Security Analysis will be conducted regularly to monitor the nutrition, food security, and markets situation in crisis-affected states. 
A gender-transformative approach that reflects the needs of women, men, girls and boys will be adopted. WFP will mainstream protection throughout its work, supported by a solid understanding of the operational context and protection analysis. Training and capacity building of staff and partners in protection and humanitarian principles will include on-the-job coaching. WFP will ensure that affected populations (women and men) will be consulted throughout the programme cycle; beneficiary feedback mechanisms will be tailored to their preferred means of communication. Beneficiaries will continue to be empowered with knowledge on their food assistance entitlements and their rights, including WFP’s zero tolerance policy on Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA). Protection against Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) will be embedded in M&E tools, complaint feedback mechanisms and training of partners and staff. 

WFP will focus on concrete operational solutions to avoid situations in which people assisted by WFP could be exposed to SEA. Along these lines WFP will enhance its support to income generation activities targeted to women, expand their engagement in the production and use of fuel efficient stoves, deploy women as beneficiary registrars, monitors and security personnel. The referral system and monitoring system will be reviewed to maximize user friendliness and access by assisted populations as well as operational adjustments for problem solving. Particular attention will be given to supervise the retailers and operators in the distribution of cash based transfers. WFP will support milling activities for the grain commodities it provides and will implement effective solutions for the provision of condiments and cash. Deep field presence through the hubs and proximity to affected populations will be enhanced for these purposes. Three experienced international and six Nigerian protection officers will be deployed. Reporting will be done on a monthly basis through standard WFP reporting and meetings. Regular oversight and evaluations will be conducted.

WFP will continue the collection of key information on beneficiaries and assistance provided as part of its M&E activities. Monthly monitoring will include distribution and activity site management; beneficiary and entitlement verification; and ensuring adequate protection and gender measures. Lessons will be regularly drawn from monthly process and biannual outcome monitoring and reporting, and periodic reviews and evaluation to inform strategic and operational decisions.

WFP will further consolidate partnerships to enhance national and state-level emergency preparedness and response systems, including in food security and nutrition assessment and monitoring, early warning, protection, gender analysis, targeting and registration processes, safety nets, cash-based transfer capacities and supply chain. 

Where security and access to land allows, increasing livelihood activities will complement food assistance to support access to productive assets, income generating activities and self-reliance in the long-term. Assistance will be coordinated with government distributions, to ensure food assistance is complementary and fills gaps. Through an integrated approach to analyzing and addressing food and nutrition security, integrated, multi-sectoral interventions will be encouraged, for example through collaborations with the Nutrition, Health, WASH and Protection Sectors, among others. WFP will also continue to proactively engage with a wide range of federal and state actors, including the Ministries of Agriculture and Rural Development, Health, Budget and National Planning, Finance, the National Social Investment Office (NSIO), Women Affairs and Social Development, PCNI as well as other federal and state institutions. Furthermore, WFP and the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) will continue to strengthen cooperation between the two agencies. WFP will continue to partner with a number of local and international NGOs and will work with civil society organizations to continue strengthening the capacities of national actors.

The project addresses the underlying causes of the protracted crisis by further integrating humanitarian and development assistance and improving disaster risk reduction in alignment with WFP’s dual mandate and the international policy debate on bridging and operationalizing the humanitarian-development nexus, thus using a development lens in its humanitarian responses, and aligning early recovery and development interventions accordingly.

Food Assistance Programme Lean Season Food Assistance to the most food insecure people in rural areas Under this Flash Appeal, Food Security sector partners plan to address the most urgent food security needs of people in rural areas across the country, who are adversely affected by multiple crises, including last year’s poor harvest for many small-holder farmers, economic shocks and recent cholera and typhoid outbreaks. Building on the funding already received to reach an estimated 900,000 people as of January 2019 and the Government’s Food Deficit Mitigation Strategy, partners aim to expand the geographic coverage of assistance to reach an additional 700,000 people in food insecure rural communities through primarily cash-based assistance. Focus will be on the low-lying areas relying on rainfed agriculture disproportionately affected by last year’s erratic rain. Market-based interventions are viable despite the current economic stress, as essential food commodities remain available on rural as well as urban markets, according to the national market assessment conducted by WFP and partners in November 2018. 

The IPC analysis conducted in January 2019 projects that nearly 3.8 million people in rural areas are in need of urgent humanitarian assistance, including 2.9 million who are severely food insecure (IPC phase 3 or 4) and a further 900,000 people who are currently receiving humanitarian assistance, without which they would be in IPC phase 3 or above.

In the face of the high prevalence of food insecurity (IPC phase 4 and 3), and the high probability of another El Niño phenomena in 2019 (90% likelihood according to the most recent SARCOF analysis), partners will provide a specialised food ration in the form of CSB++ specifically targeting children 6-59 months and pregnant and lactating women to increase the nutritional value of the food basket provided as part of the general household ration/cash. 

Based on the findings of the national market assessment conducted by partners in November, partners will select the most appropriate transfer modality for each district (cash or in-kind). According to the latest price information, partners aim to cover approximately 80% of the targeted individuals’ daily food energy needs (based on a 2100 kcal diet) to supplement other available food sources, thus enabling households to meet their basic food and nutrition needs. 
 
In view of the high probability of another El Nino, food assistance at this juncture can be considered as an early action to prevent further deterioration of food insecurity amongst particularly households already in IPC 3 (Crises) and 4 (Emergency).

School Feeding for Local Children in the Far North (80,000 beneficiaries) School Feeding for Local Children in the Far North (80,000 beneficiaries) In the Far North region, the Boko Haram insurgency in Nigeria has resulted in 227,581 internally displaced persons (IDPs) (UNHCR, October 2018), who are struggling to survive in strenuous conditions in villages or small towns in the area. The region is predominantly arid and regularly hit by drought and seasonal floods. The arrival of IDPs in food-insecure areas has severely affected host communities as well. As a consequence, the existing chronic vulnerability and structural food insecurity have been aggravated. In addition, access to basic services is also more limited than in other regions of the country including the education.  
WFP will implement a school feeding programme in the Far North region to complement the Government’s education inputs and its work in addressing emergency needs, and to support the education of children affected by crises, particularly girls. It will provide incentives for children to enroll in schools to minimize the risk of forced recruitment into armed groups. The school feeding programme will assist 80,000 school children – of whom 50 percent will be girls – for 165 school days in 12 months with flexibility to ensure that schools in crisis areas are targeted. Home-grown school feeding has been adjusted to 5000 to be piloted in line with recommendations of the Systemic Approach for Better Education Results (SABER). School voucher procurement will incentivize purchases from men and women smallholders to create a value chain.

Emergency livelihoods support to the most vulnerable men, women, boys and girls in Rural Damascus and Dar’a Governorates Pro- Resilient Action inside Syria- Oxfam HRP EFSVL Project Oxfam aims at addressing systemic risks (agro-ecological, local governance, gender inequalities, social tensions) by enhancing socio-economic rights and capacities of 3000 conflict affected households in Qalamoun- Rural Damascus of Syria; all family members (M&F inclusive) lost the ability to enjoy equal access to livelihood opportunities then fulfill their basic rights. Women and adolescent’s girls may face particularly protection risks as a harmful coping mechanism such as child marriage, physical and sexual harassments, etc.   EFSVL team is addressing this vulnerability through immediate and sustainable solutions for start-up of micro-businesses, efficient linkages with suppliers and markets, entitlements and enhancing community resilience, including local capacities for  social cohesion. 

The results will be achieved through a range of outputs including setting-up 60 greenhouses, 1000 kitchen garden toolkits; immediate support to 1000 conflict affected vulnerable livestock breeders; strengthened productive capacity of 35 dairy, bakery and other food processors; technical and managerial skill building of 35 participants; training of 7 local veterinarian, drilling  3 new wells, powering  3 existing wells with solar system and  rehabilitation of 3 boreholes will provide income generation opportunities to conflict impacted vulnerable women, men and their families ; bring improvements in market services, soil and water conservation; provision of agricultural inputs; technical support for improved agricultural production; collaboration, networking and alliance building with a range of stakeholders and enhancing communities’ capacity to respond to shock and stresses as a result of conflict.
During the project duration, agricultural and food production will focus on two agricultural seasons of critical crops in the targeted locations. These commodities will be selected based on local seasonal calendar, farmers’ skills and their access to inputs, consultation with communities and potential for supplementing food needs and will directly support the targeted beneficiaries and indirectly their supported families (elderly, boys and girls all inclusive).Furthermore, the project design is paying attention to very specific needs of targeted women and men; distributed kits will be designed to accommodate the differences between women and men. Time and distribution locations will be gender sensitive. Special attention will be paid for impact of intervention on power dynamics in targeted communities to avoid stressing the negative social norms in roles and responsivities of women and men.
This action is based on Oxfam’s approach on developing resilient livelihoods, which integrates humanitarian relief, socioeconomic development, and empowered advocacy through improving social protection/safety nets and strengthening market system. This approach provides a coherent and gender sensitive framework to achieve the action objective, through its processes that concurrently address short-term targeted agricultural outcomes and spillover effects from strengthening of market system. 
Through this action, target households will increase capacity to cope with shocks and avoid the harmful survival mechanism such as early, forced and child marriages, child laboring, etc.  It increase the levels of agriculture production and income. Through Oxfam’s approach, this will strengthen community organizations, and enhance their ability to access services.

Providing protection and community services to IDPs, returnees and host communities in Daraa and Rural Damascus. Mitigate identified protection risks, reduce vulnerabilities and enhance the protection of displaced persons, returnees and conflict affected host communities in Syria through integrated, community based protection activities to prevent and respond to rights violations. The project aims to assist IDPs, returnees and crisis-affected communities by fostering an improved protection environment through the provision of community-based protection services. Protection interventions include 1) legal counselling and assistance 2) protection monitoring, referrals and information sharing on services 3)  social protection and support on PSS; GBV prevention and response programmes 4) child protection; 5) case management; 6) provision of in kind assistance covering basic needs and programmes of elderly and persons with disabilities; 7) non-formal education support for children at risk; 8) social protection through small-scale vocational skills training and socio-economic support specifically directed to the most vulnerable individuals, ; 9) campaigns and awareness  session including on mine risk education for communities targeting women, men, boys and girls and; 10) capacity building of first responders working in communities, volunteers, partners and government counterparts to provide better protection services. Legal aid interventions will facilitate access to civil/HLP documentation for IDPs and returnees and provide support in legal matters related to GBV, CP and other protection issues. Support to community initiatives will also be implemented engaging communities to address their own protection concerns. Intervention in the context of refugee returnees will focus on, legal aid, coordination with government counterparts and stakeholders, information management and return tracking systems and sub – district profiling to better inform return programming and interventions. In addition, the project will support coordinated protection interventions with UNHCR Syria continuing to lead Protection Sector.
Accountability to affected population in the project will be realized through participatory engagement of communities and outreach programmes conducted through community volunteers’ network. Over 2844 outreach volunteers and 112 CC were mobilized in 2018 and this project will build on this approach, to ensure a continuous link with communities, including to receive feedback on project programmes.

Through the project intervention approximately 3.35 million IDPs, returnees and crises affected individuals in host communities (70.5%, 15.5% and 14% respectively) will be reached in government and non-government controlled areas redressing their protection concerns. In addition 4,140 humanitarian workers and local authority staff will be trained and 624 communities assessed. 30% of the project beneficiaries are girls, 25% are boys, 26% are women, and 15% are men and 2% elderly women and 2% elderly men.

Addressing food insecurity for vulnerable conflict-affected populations in Syria 2019 portion Emergency food assistance and small-scale food security support to vulnerable households in Northeast Syria  The proposed intervention aims at improving the food security of vulnerable Syrian households, in both the short and the medium-long term. 

In the short-term, ACTED will reduce the food security of conflict-affected communities through the provision of rapid and flexible food assistance. This will include the following 3 modalities:  1) RTERS for vulnerable beneficiaries who do not have access to cooking facilities; 2) Food rations for households living in areas where markets are inaccessible or food is unavailable; 3) Food vouchers for families with access to functioning markets.

In the medium and long-term, ACTED food security assistance will be underpinned by the rationale of giving vulnerable households the resources and skills to obtain a self-sufficient food production. In order to achieve this, ACTED will provide targeted support to households, depending on their needs and size of land. The type of support ACTED will provide to vulnerable households will include: 1) kitchen garden kits and training; 2) polytunnel kits and training; 3) poultry kits. Overall, this project will benefit approximately 72,900 individuals. 

ACTED is coordinating with Food Security cluster members and other NGOs supporting the food security and agricultural sector to ensure that there is no duplication of assistance planned in 2019. 

While implementing its food security programming, ACTED always respects the nutrition standards of the Food Security cluster. Additionally, while targeting different locations for its programming under Food Security, ACTED also ensures that its interventions are complementary to projects under other sectors to comprehensively respond to needs in the target area. Indeed, for instance, in emergency context and whenever relevant ACTED will complement emergency food distribution with NFI distribution. In turn, ACTED often implements agricultural early-recovery activities such as the rehabilitation of agricultural assets or irrigation canals used for agricultural purposes to support further the agricultural production and availability of food products on the market.

The activities and targets proposed for this intervention reflect the current activities and targets for which ACTED has secured funding for 2019.

Improved child protection and mental health and psychosocial support service provision for children affected by the conflict in Area C and Hebron H2 Psychosocial and Child Protection for Children and Families affected by Conflict-Related Violence in Area C, H2, and East Jerusalem This project targets Palestinian children directly and indirectly exposed to violence and abuse related to the Israeli Occupation, including settler violence, unsafe school environments, home and school demolitions, and detention and/or arrests. War Child Holland (WCH) and its partner will be targeting acutely affected children and families living in Area C (Jordan Valley and Tubas), East Jerusalem (communities outside the West Bank Barrier), and Hebron H2. 

This project aims to strengthen the resilience of children, caregivers, schools, and communities in the face of chronic exposure to conflict-related violence by: (1) providing community-based child protection, psychosocial and mental health services to children and their families, (2) supporting parents, school staff, and community-based organizations with psychosocial interventions and capacity building to better take care of and respond to the needs of children in distress, (3) case management and referrals to specialized mental health, social, and educational services, including vocational and remedial education, and (4) addressing IHL and IHRL violations through advocacy initiatives targeting all duty bearers and based on documentation of grave violations. 

The outputs are designed to meet HRP 2018-2020 strategic objectives 1: “The rights of Palestinians living under occupation….are protected, respected and promoted in accordance with IHL and IHRL”; and 2: “providing support to meet the basic needs of the vulnerable population, particularly children”, and the Protection Cluster’s Objective 2 “Protection response mechanisms are in place and mitigate the effects of the occupation and conflict related violence.""

This project aims to strengthen the social safety net around children who have been exposed to conflict-related violence including killings, arrest and detention, injury, and home demolitions. Through the project, children will have access to psychosocial and mental health interventions provided by CBOs supported by WCH, as well as specialized services through case management and referrals. Children acutely affected by conflict-related violence will participate in inclusive structured recreational psychosocial support (PSS) workshops (‘TeamUp”) in and after school. TeamUp was co-developed by War Child, UNICEF and Save the Children in the Netherlands and is now used in multiple conflict-affected contexts. The group sessions are delivered on a drop-in basis, making the activity more inclusive for those children whose circumstances prevent them from regularly attending more structured interventions. Within the sessions, children and adolescents play, learn, make friends and have fun in a safe and protective setting. The activities are designed to allow emergency affected children to explore socioemotional themes in a safe and non-confrontational environment, themes including anger, fear, stress and tension, conflict, respect, bullying, assertiveness, and friendship. The modular, activity-based design of the program allows facilitators to tailor each session to the perceived needs of the particular children attending, including age, space available, physical and sensory abilities. TeamUp also acts as an entry point for children who are experiencing distress or child protection risks to be identified and referred. Children in need of more structured PSS and preventive mental health support will be referred to WCH’s most widely implemented PSS program – the DEALs - to help children and young people at high risk of occupation related violence to develop positive and alternative coping strategies, and engage in regular activities in a safe and protective environment. The DEALs  intervention  aims  to  increase  children’s  wellbeing and resilience  by  strengthening  their  social relationships; helping them cope effectively with stress and difficult emotions; and to increase their  confidence  and  sense  of  efficacy, and has specific curricula for different age groups as well as a dedicated add-on program for adolescent girls. 
 
Facilitators of the PSS activities will be trained in identification and referral of more severely affected children, who will have access to case management from War Child’s case workers. WCH’s caseworkers will have regular presence in the targeted communities, attend the Child Protection Network’s (CPN) monthly meetings in targeted governorates, and will be responsible for implementing community-based child protection activities and case management. In addition to providing timely and ongoing individualized support to the child and family, WCH’s case workers in each location will identify and refer children struggling with child protection and clinical mental health issues to specialized services, in line with the national referral pathway, including the Child Protection Network. Children and families in need of specialized mental health and/or legal services will have access to (EU-funded) individual, group and family counseling and therapy provided by WCH partners Treatment and Rehabilitation Center (TRC), and Palestinian Counseling Center (PCC), and DCIP, under its EIHDR project operating in the targeted locations of this project. Children and their families may also be referred to external mental health and other service providers, (e.g., the Ministry of Health and Palestinian Red Crescent Society), as required. There will also be a particular focus on supporting and enabling young people to re-engage with education (formal, non-formal or vocational) after conflict-related disruptions such as detention, home arrest, and injury through coordination with and referrals to protection and education cluster partners, ensuring that children receive multidisciplinary and holistic support. To ensure efficiency, timeliness, standardized vulnerability and prioritization criteria, and that minimum standards are met, a technical committee made up of WCH, CPN focal persons, and relevant service providers will be formed under this project to routinely monitor and review the referral process, including forms used, information management, feedback on the services provided and address any challenges faced in the referral process and mechanism.

To address the MHPSS needs of caregivers – who are also in need of safe, supportive places to share their worries and challenges, get support, and learn techniques for stress management - parents and school staff will be offered WCH’s caregiver wellbeing interventions designed to help caregivers manage their own stress in order to better support children, and reduce harsh parenting practices. The caregiver support intervention is research informed, and designed based on the identification of common elements of evidence-based stress management programs. It is delivered within communities by community members and para-professionals trained and supervised by War Child. The caregiver support intervention was successfully piloted in Gaza and is now undergoing randomized controlled trial in Lebanon.  Referrals for specialized legal and mental health services will also be provided to caregivers, as well as support to those in need of family counseling through WCH’s already established referral network.

Capitalizing on their cohesive network of sources including local media, health workers, CBOs, and community leaders and members throughout the West Bank, partner field workers will closely monitor, document, and rapidly report grave violations against children, including child killings and injuries; settler violence; and recruitment.  Strengthened monitoring and reporting of grave violations will yield thematic reports and advocacy initiatives to address protection violations and call for greater accountability on IHL and IHRL by duty bearers.

Réponse de sécurité alimentaire d'urgence aux populations déplacées et touchées par le conflit dans la région du nord-ouest du Cameroun Emergency Food Security Response for internally displaced population affected by the crisis in the Far North region of Cameroon				 The project aims to provide immediate food assistance to save lives and reduce suffering of households unable to access food that meets basic food and nutritional requirements. The project will be implemented in the 3 most affected departments (Logone et Chari, Mayo Sava and Mayo Tsanaga) targeting 3,100 individuals (40% male and 60% female) including IDPs (50%), returnees (30%) and vulnerable host communities (20%). NRC will pay attention to youth and women affected by displacement. Participation of all beneficiary groups will be key in ensuring ownership of the project.
To achieve the above objectives, NRC will strengthen the resilience and economic security of vulnerable households through the following activities:

1. Provision of cash/voucher to most vulnerable people to meet food needs 
Despite security concerns in Far-North, local markets are functional and accessible by both women and men, although these markets are not yet operating at the same level as before the crises. Cash approach will help ensure that households have unrestricted access to nutritious foods and additional income that would protect their remaining livelihoods assets as well as ensuring that the agricultural inputs, livestock or IGA start-up kits will not be sold and that they will be used as intended. This food assistance will also allow vulnerable individuals to build their resilience helping households not to further deplete their productive assets and avoid further use of negative coping strategies. 

2. Reestablishment of agricultural activities
NRC will negotiate with the local communities and where needed secure access to land for targeted IDPs and returnees. Once the access to land secured, NRC will provide small ruminants, seeds, inputs (agricultural tools, fertilizers, etc.) and trainings. This will improve agricultural production and provide better access to nutrient-rich food. NRC will also promote gardening, which provides households with a source of food or income during the lean season. 

3. Provision of improved stoves 
NRC will also distribute food handling kits that will allow target households to prepare food in a more effective and environment-friendly way. Improved stoves will save households money on firewood and help curb deforestation. For better community acceptance, those stoves will be made locally. They will have a more efficient use of charcoal, thus reducing the quantity needed and reduce the expenses of households for it. 

4.Provision of awareness raising on food hygiene, food diversity, food storage and food preparation  
All emergency activities will be also integrated by sessions to raise the awareness of the targeted populations on food hygiene and diversity, food preparation, and food storage. Through these trainings, beneficiaries are expected to acquire the knowledge and best practices they need to better use the food and improve the results on their nutritional status.

Reduce the threat of Explosive Remnants of War (ERW) across Aleppo and Idleb and provide improved support to survivors of ERW accidents and conflict-related injuries (part of ECHO/SYR/BUD/2019/91001) Reduced threat of ERW and improved support to ERW survivors in north-west Syria. HALO with its implementing partners will deliver a comprehensive approach to Mine Action in NW Syria, involving Contamination Impact Survey (CIS), an enhanced version of CIS (ECIS), Risk Education (RE), Victim Data Collection (VDC) and Victim Assistance (VA).  Note: the key difference between ECIS and CIS is the identification, marking and reporting of ERW items. HALO will also seek to extend the scope of its activities to Explosive Remnants of War (ERW) Non-Technical Survey (NTS) and Disposal. 

To better understand the threat that ERW poses, HALO will conduct systematic CIS in 111 communities and ECIS in 692 communities across Idleb and Aleppo governorates. Under this activity, teams will visit communities, with the overall goal to identify, mark and report ERW contamination and to record its impact on the community. Data will be used to identify areas of highest priority for RE, create contamination maps, and provide essential information for future ERW clearance. The scale of this activity is unprecedented but is required to inform current and future ERW disposal/clearance, as well as immediately improving the awareness and safety of affected communities. ECIS activities will be coordinated from HALO’s operation room in Jordan, staffed by technical personnel. If the relevant authorizations are granted from the Turkish government, HALO will also establish ERW survey and disposal teams trained to complete surface-located ERW tasks (excluding IEDs) via a 6-week course derived from International Mine Action Standards (IMAS). They will be deployed under the direct control of HALO’s operations room in Jordan. At a later stage in 2019, they will complete advanced training relevant to the detection and disposal of sub-surface ERW (excluding IEDs). Extension to IED disposal requires a separate 4-week course. All disposal activities will be conducted via the use of thermite torches (T-Jets). No high explosives will be used. HALO’s ERW survey and disposal objectives for NW Syria are based on its experience in southern Syria in 2018.     

HALO will provide RE to 108,472 beneficiaries in 2019 (18,364 men, 17,692 women, 38,248 boys and 34,168 girls). A particular focus will be placed on those who are most at risk of accident (including children, young men and IDPs). Two new RE ‘Training of Trainer’ (ToT) Trainers will build on the work already underway by HALO’s existing RE ToT Trainer in NW Syria. Together, they will support NGOs currently delivering RE to vulnerable communities and IDPs, as well as NGOs willing to deliver RE along with other activities; improving the relevance, integration and reach of RE messaging across all relevant sectors. 

HALO will also collect information about ERW accidents and victims (survivors) through VDC which will be used to develop a better understanding of how and why accidents are occurring, enabling HALO, and other actors, to better tailor RE and VA activities.

In 2019, HALO and one of its implementing partners will implement a new VA initiative, where approx. 200 survivors of ERW accidents will benefit from initial basic health screening, referrals to reputable service providers and a one-off distribution of basic medical and hygiene items. The project will also support survivors (approx. 1,200) through the establishment of a rehabilitation centre and 2 x mobile outreach teams, providing physiotherapy, mental health and psycho-social support (MHPSS), peer support counselling, and referrals to a prosthetics centre. A social protection scheme providing ‘in-kind’ support to selected survivors will also be implemented. Additionally, in order to promote workplace inclusion, 5 survivors will be recruited, trained and employed by HALO’s partner.

Mali - OCHA Office [OCT 6193];[S 09-15/Pol-10-321.50 MLI 06/18] Renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et de plaidoyer pour la protection humanitaire et l’assistance aux populations les plus vulnérables au Mali. La situation humanitaire demeure complexe et instable, principalement en raison des conflits armés et intercommunautaires dans les régions du Centre et du Nord. Le retard dans la mise en œuvre de l’Accord pour la paix et la réconciliation au Mali paraphé en juin 2015 et dans le processus de désarmement, démobilisation, réintégration (DDR) contribuent à la persistance de l’instabilité sécuritaire dans les régions de Kidal, Gao, Tombouctou, Ségou et Mopti ainsi qu’à l’aggravation des tensions sociales. La présence limitée de l’État et l’insécurité dans ces régions demeurent l’un des facteurs clés obligeant les civils à fuir leurs communautés.
Le nombre de Personnes Déplacées Internes (PDI) a atteint la barre des 199 385 en octobre 2019 en comparaison aux 80 302 enregistrés en octobre 2018. Les risques et les besoins de protection des populations fuyant leurs communautés sous la pression de la violence armée ou des tensions intercommunautaires, sont élevés. De graves abus et attaques contre les personnes, les biens et les services (écoles, centres de santé) sont régulièrement signalées alors que l’accès aux services appropriés est compromis. Comme les déplacements internes sont durables, les risques de protection et les violations des droits fondamentaux augmentent, en particulier pour les plus vulnérables (femmes, enfants, personnes âgées, personnes handicapées ou malades). De graves conséquences humanitaires ont donc été notées, telles que des taux élevés d’insécurité alimentaire et de malnutrition ainsi que le faible accès aux services sociaux de base.

En référence au Cadre Harmonisé (nov. 2019), à l'heure actuelle, 3,6 million d'hommes, de femmes, de garçons et de filles souffrent d'insécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle, dont 670 000 souffrent d'une insécurité alimentaire sévère (phase 3 à 5 du Cadre Harmonisé). La situation devrait se détériorer au cours de la période de soudure 2020, avec près de 4,9 million d'hommes, de femmes, de garçons et de filles souffrant d'insécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle, dont près de 1,2 million de personnes souffrant d'insécurité alimentaire sévère (phase 3 à 5). Les capacités de réponse existantes au Mali représentent plus de 160 organisations humanitaires, acteurs du développement ainsi que des forces militaires (MINUSMA, Forces maliennes de défense et de sécurité, Barkhane, Mission européenne de formation, G5 Sahel). Le contexte susmentionné exigera une coordination efficace et la présence d’OCHA demeure très importante. OCHA maintiendra sa présence à Bamako, Mopti, Tombouctou et Gao et ouvrira une antenne à Ségou tout en couvrant à distance les régions de Taoudénit, Ménaka, Kidal et les régions du sud.

Sept clusters actifs (Éducation, Sécurité alimentaire, Santé, Nutrition, Protection, Abris/BNA et WASH), des sous-clusters et des groupes de travail spécialisés (Accès, CM-Coord, Redevabilité, Genre et Cash) sont en place au niveau national et local. Le Bureau d’OCHA au Mali continuera ainsi à jouer un rôle central dans la mobilisation, la coordination et le soutien des acteurs humanitaires dans les domaines de la coordination, la gestion de l’information, le financement humanitaire et le plaidoyer. OCHA jouera un rôle essentiel dans la mobilisation adéquate des fonds en faveur des personnes dans le besoin, en plus de contribuer à dynamiser les efforts déployés par le gouvernement et les acteurs du développement pour s’attaquer aux causes structurelles de la vulnérabilité.

OCHA continuera à jouer son rôle central dans la mobilisation des partenaires, l’utilisation des instruments et des mécanismes de financement tout en veillant à ce que les besoins humanitaires croissants soient prises en compte. OCHA assumera son rôle clé dans la coordination militaire au niveau national et régional de concert avec les forces militaires présentes dans le pays tout en renforçant les capacités des autorités nationales en matière de coordination et de préparation des interventions d’urgence.

As part of the lockdown, national borders are closed except for formal imports of essential goods such as food and medical supplies, as well as for returning citizens. Additionally, stringent internal movement restrictions are being enforced except for essential services such as the food industry, health, and security.

Prior to the COVID 19 pandemic Zimbabwe was in the grip of widespread food insecurity caused by the poor performance of the 2019/20 agricultural season which experienced delayed onset of rain, resulting in delayed planting and limited availability of water for productive uses. The weather related shocks had a negative impact on livestock due to poor availability of grazing and limited access to water. Approximately 66 000 cattle succumbed to drought related deaths. The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) analysis conducted for  the period February to June 2020, shows the proportion of rural people facing a Crisis situation (IPC Phase 3-4) is 45 percent (4,3 million). This segment of the rural population currently requires urgent humanitarian assistance.

The project will be implemented in 4 districts targeting 10, 000 households (50,000 people) in IPC phase 3 & 4. The project aims to minimise disruptions to the food supply chain for vulnerable small holder farmers, through improved post harvest management,  provision of crop and livestock inputs, raising awareness among extension workers and farmers to minimise  the spread of COVID-19 and provision of PPE for agricultural extension officers (masks at a minimum).
