The proposed action will be implemented through existing Government-MOH system to enhance sustainability through health system strengthening (HSS) interventions thus provide quality accessible, acceptable and affordable health services to the target populations; IDPs and host community during humanitarian crisis. The action will aim at enhancing sustainable impact through HSS and therefore deliver quality health services to the target populations. Target locations are Baki and Lughaya districts of Awdal region, Burco and Odweyne districts of Togdheer region both in Somaliland, Garoowe, Burtinle and Eyl districts of Nugaal region in Puntland and Baydhaba and Qansax Dheere districts of Bay region and Dollow and Luuq districts of Gedo region in South Central Somalia. The interventions will seek to improve emergency response during crisis-driven disease and outbreaks e.g. AWD/Cholera and measles through supporting the MoH prepare emergency response plans (ERPs) at regional health authorities level and have rapid response teams (RRTs) with capacity to promptly investigate rumors, confirm outbreaks, notify WHO and MoH, mount an aggressive response, and report promptly. The action will also ensure increased access, utilization and coverage of essential health services by supporting health facilities; making them functional to provide out-patient consultations, immunization services for vaccine-preventable diseases, maternal, new-born and child health services through; capacity building to the health care workers on clinical management of rape,  BEmONC and CEmONC, EPI and cold-chain management, integrated disease surveillance and response (IDSR) and mass casualty management in order to improve their capacity to deliver quality health services; provision of essential medicines including vaccines thus avoiding stock outs and ensure availability and accessibility of supplies; strengthening emergency obstetric and new-born care through adequate staffing to provide BEmONC services in most Health Centers and CEmONC services at selected referral Health facilities, both services provided 24/7, improved case management and referral of sexual & gender-based violence survivors and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS/PFA); scale up of immunization services both routine and campaigns during disease outbreaks. Through this action also, mitigation of impact and response to shocks to the affected populations as a result of conflict and public health emergencies will be enhanced. Referral health facilities will be selected strategically and equipped to enable management of mass casualties during catastrophe and staff trained on mass casualty management. It is envisaged that through this interventions, target populations will have improved access to quality healthcare services during humanitarian crisis and therefore reduce excess mortality and morbidity.

Promotion of durable solutions in Darfur, South Kordofan and Blue Nile (part of 20-RR-IOM-003) Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM): Mobility Tracking of IDPs, Returnees and other target populations in Sudan In 2004, the International Organization for Migration began its Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) program to better support the Government of Sudan and its humanitarian partners. DTM was introduced in response to the need for accurate information on displacement and the identiﬁcation of beneﬁciaries for the delivery of humanitarian aid that arose in Sudan follow a series of crises that have affected Sudan since 2003. Following the implementation of DTM, IOM now has an established, accurate data collection system that provides displacement data in the areas most affected by conﬂict and disasters.

IOM has been working in close collaboration with the Humanitarian Aid Commission (HAC) and partners in the ﬁeld to establish a uniﬁed and systematic system to better track internally displaced populations and returnees in seven states in Sudan. Until 2018, IOM Sudan’s DTM program focused mainly on registration activities in response to requests from the Government and humanitarian partners to identify beneﬁciaries to better inform the delivery of humanitarian assistance (i.e. food vouchers by WFP). These registration activities have positioned DTM in Sudan as the key reference source of displacement data in the country.

As crisis levels within Sudan gradually reduce, and the situation broadly stabilizes the majority of the conﬂict-affected areas, there is a need to restructure the DTM program. Whilst there will continue to be a need to DTM to track displacement resulting from unpredictable events such as the ﬂooding in 2019, there are increasing  requirements in tailoring the operation to better suit the current situation of protracted displacement and return scenario. More speciﬁcally, there is the need to update displacement ﬁgures more frequently, comprehensively, systematically, and at regular intervals to ensure that data is continually collected, provides a meaningful resource and is available through IOM’s DTM system.

OCT 6293 [OCT 6293];[11630] Renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et de plaidoyer pour la protection humanitaire et l’assistance aux populations les plus vulnérables au Mali. La situation humanitaire demeure complexe et instable, principalement en raison des conflits armés et intercommunautaires dans les régions du Centre et du Nord. Le retard dans la mise en œuvre de l’Accord pour la paix et la réconciliation au Mali paraphé en juin 2015 et dans le processus de désarmement, démobilisation, réintégration (DDR) contribuent à la persistance de l’instabilité sécuritaire dans les régions de Kidal, Gao, Tombouctou, Ségou et Mopti ainsi qu’à l’aggravation des tensions sociales. La présence limitée de l’État et l’insécurité dans ces régions demeurent l’un des facteurs clés obligeant les civils à fuir leurs communautés.
Le nombre de Personnes Déplacées Internes (PDI) a atteint la barre des 199 385 en octobre 2019 en comparaison aux 80 302 enregistrés en octobre 2018. Les risques et les besoins de protection des populations fuyant leurs communautés sous la pression de la violence armée ou des tensions intercommunautaires, sont élevés. De graves abus et attaques contre les personnes, les biens et les services (écoles, centres de santé) sont régulièrement signalées alors que l’accès aux services appropriés est compromis. Comme les déplacements internes sont durables, les risques de protection et les violations des droits fondamentaux augmentent, en particulier pour les plus vulnérables (femmes, enfants, personnes âgées, personnes handicapées ou malades). De graves conséquences humanitaires ont donc été notées, telles que des taux élevés d’insécurité alimentaire et de malnutrition ainsi que le faible accès aux services sociaux de base.

En référence au Cadre Harmonisé (nov. 2019), à l'heure actuelle, 3,6 million d'hommes, de femmes, de garçons et de filles souffrent d'insécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle, dont 670 000 souffrent d'une insécurité alimentaire sévère (phase 3 à 5 du Cadre Harmonisé). La situation devrait se détériorer au cours de la période de soudure 2020, avec près de 4,9 million d'hommes, de femmes, de garçons et de filles souffrant d'insécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle, dont près de 1,2 million de personnes souffrant d'insécurité alimentaire sévère (phase 3 à 5). Les capacités de réponse existantes au Mali représentent plus de 160 organisations humanitaires, acteurs du développement ainsi que des forces militaires (MINUSMA, Forces maliennes de défense et de sécurité, Barkhane, Mission européenne de formation, G5 Sahel). Le contexte susmentionné exigera une coordination efficace et la présence d’OCHA demeure très importante. OCHA maintiendra sa présence à Bamako, Mopti, Tombouctou et Gao et ouvrira une antenne à Ségou tout en couvrant à distance les régions de Taoudénit, Ménaka, Kidal et les régions du sud.

Sept clusters actifs (Éducation, Sécurité alimentaire, Santé, Nutrition, Protection, Abris/BNA et WASH), des sous-clusters et des groupes de travail spécialisés (Accès, CM-Coord, Redevabilité, Genre et Cash) sont en place au niveau national et local. Le Bureau d’OCHA au Mali continuera ainsi à jouer un rôle central dans la mobilisation, la coordination et le soutien des acteurs humanitaires dans les domaines de la coordination, la gestion de l’information, le financement humanitaire et le plaidoyer. OCHA jouera un rôle essentiel dans la mobilisation adéquate des fonds en faveur des personnes dans le besoin, en plus de contribuer à dynamiser les efforts déployés par le gouvernement et les acteurs du développement pour s’attaquer aux causes structurelles de la vulnérabilité.

OCHA continuera à jouer son rôle central dans la mobilisation des partenaires, l’utilisation des instruments et des mécanismes de financement tout en veillant à ce que les besoins humanitaires croissants soient prises en compte. OCHA assumera son rôle clé dans la coordination militaire au niveau national et régional de concert avec les forces militaires présentes dans le pays tout en renforçant les capacités des autorités nationales en matière de coordination et de préparation des interventions d’urgence.

OCT 6293 [OCT 6293];[11630] Renforcement de la coordination et du plaidoyer humanitaire au Tchad Le projet vise à renforcer le rôle de OCHA dans la mise en œuvre sa mission à travers ses fonctions clés que sont la Coordination, Gestion de l’information et plaidoyer. Un accent a été mis sur la mise en œuvre des plans d’action de la redevabilité envers les populations affectées (AAP) et la PSEA, la préparation aux urgences et le plaidoyer pour plus de visibilités et de mobilisation de ressources pour les différentes crises au Tchad (mouvement de population – crise du Bassin du Lac Tchad, insécurité alimentaire et malnutrition, urgences sanitaires) à travers le bureau OCHA à N’Djaména et ses trois Sous bureaux à Abéché, Goré et Lac. Il sera également renforcé l’opérationnalisation du nexus humanitaire, développement et paix dans le cadre de la nouvelle façon de travailler., 

Le projet a pour but de renforcer la coordination d’une réponse humanitaire rapide afin de sauver des vies et protéger les personnes affectées par les situations de crises au Tchad. Une coordination humanitaire efficace et performante permettra aux acteurs humanitaires de mieux identifier et répondre aux besoins humanitaires, de renforcer la préparation de réponse aux urgences à travers le renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et plus spécifiquement l‘Equipe humanitaire pays, la coordination inter-clusters, la coordination civilo-militaire, les clusters et les mécanismes de coordination au niveau de terrain.
Le projet vise aussi à assurer le plaidoyer humanitaire à travers l’analyse des besoins faites par l’ensemble de la communauté humanitaire et ses partenaires en vue une compréhension commune des problématiques auxquels fait face le Tchad, ses causes profondes, l’impact sur les populations. OCHA jouera un rôle clé dans la création d'espaces de collection et d'analyse et gestion d’ informations, pour assurer une stratégie de réponse coordonnée menant à des actions humanitaires répondant aux besoins les plus aigus et être mieux préparé face aux urgences soudaines. Le projet permettra également d’assurer conjointement avec la communauté humanitaire le plaidoyer en faveur du respect des principes humanitaires, de la protection des civils, de l'accès humanitaire et pour la mobilisation et l'allocation efficace de ressources humanitaires.

OCHA continuera de jouer également un rôle moteur dans le renforcement du lien entre les acteurs humanitaires et de développement et la transformation de la réponse humanitaire, en lien avec les engagements pris au Sommet humanitaire mondial  de 2016 et ceci à travers la nouvelle façon de travailler (NWOW) et le renforcement de l’utilisation de la modalité de transfert monétaire.

Outcome 1: More out-of-school children, especially girls, marginalized groups and those in the most vulnerable situations, are enabled to access quality pre-primary, primary and alternative learning opportunities with zero tolerance to hazards

Also 1,500 school clubs will be formed and trained on upshift programme to build skills and create opportunity for the most disadvantaged young people and empowers them to identify challenges in their communities and create entrepreneurial solutions to address them. Also, the package of Unlocking literacy programme including its assessment pre- and post will be scaled up to support quality learning at 1,500 schools/ communities
Outcome 3: More communities have strengthened mechanisms to protect children from violence, abuse, and exploitation including FGM/C and child marriage for inclusive, safe and protective school environments.
The integrated approach of Education and Child Protection will be reflected in all education activities. It targets increasing awareness of 150,000 education personnel and community structures on the CP issues with signing of Code of Conduct (CoC).  Moreover, safe referral pathways and complaint mechanisms between CBCPN, PTA and Education personnel will be established with estimated 6,000 cases referred to CP agencies/networks by education staff each month from the target 1,500 schools.

REACH will be leading on the implementation of project activities. More specifically, this will be done through the following activities:
•	Producing Monthly Humanitarian Situation Overviews in Syria (HSOS)
•	Emergency assessments on the humanitarian situation situation in Syria
•	Cash and markets assessments in collaboration with CBR-TWG
•	Camps and sites profiling and mapping
•	Remote sensing to support IDP site identification and shelter counts
•	Technical advisory to the humanitarian coordination structure, among other towards the successful implementation of the 2020 Syria MSNA
•	Thematic assessments/specialised assessments to meet information gaps

REACH has designed this intervention based on feedback from humanitarian actors and seven years of experience in implementation in Syria. REACH maintains regular discussions with Whole of Syria coordination structures including the deputy regional humanitarian coordinator, OCHA, clusters/working groups, and the NES forum, and sits as well at the ICCG in Turkey and the ISWG in NES/Iraq. Additionally, REACH is part of the NGO Forum and the SIRF and also joins the SIRF Policy and Advocacy working group. These engagements enable a timely and efficient identification of information needs and gaps as well as opportunities for partnerships and collaboration. Activities included in this proposal have thus been designed based on these interactions. For example, conversations with the NES Forum, OCHA, SSWG and CCCM cluster have confirmed a general lack of information on camps and sites in northern Syria, which was flagged as of particular concern given the worsened emergency situation in both NWS and NES. REACH Camps and Sites sweeps conducted in 2019 in NWS also revealed a significant number of sites that were not yet registered by the CCCM cluster, which outlined an information gap and a need to support CCCM processes.

This project is already fully funded, but may require additional top-ups later in the year.

Faciliter l'accès aux logements, en Eau Hygiène et Assainissement aux personnes déplacés internes (PDIs) et populations hôtes affectés par le conflict au Nord et au Centre du Mali. Durant l’année 2019, le contexte sécuritaire du Centre et Nord Mali ont été marqué par la recrudescence des violences de la population. Ces violences ont occasionné de nombreux déplacés internes vivant dans des conditions précaires. Les differents rapports d’évaluation rapide et conjointe produit par les inter-agence humanitaires ressortent que 03 ménages de sur 04 n’ont pas d’abris. Le problème d'accès en eau potable dans ces sites de déplacés n’a pas été épargné. Cet accès limité à l’eau ainsi que les conditions d’hygiène et d’assainissement précaires favorisent les maladies d’origine hydrique et à potentielle épidémique dans les sites des déplacés où familles d’accueils. Ce qui explique un besoin fort en abri et de EHA.
Pour palier à ces besoins, NRC propose à travers ce projet d’apporter sa contribution afin d’améliorer les conditions des personnes touchées dans un environnement sécurisé avec un accès aux logement et aux infrastructures Wash. 
NRC construira et réhabilitera des points d’eau, forages, puits, et mettra également en place des comités EHA et Abris avec 50% de femmes accompagné d’un mécanisme de suivi. NRC mettra en place les latrines d'urgence accessibles aux handicapés avec des kits de lavage des mains en tenant de l’aspect genre et de protection avec un emplacement visibles et separées entre les femmes et les hommes. Des poupelles pour la gestion des ordures seront mise en place dans les sites. 
Le projet se focalisera sur une reponse avec la formation sur les techniques de construction des maisons/abris suivi d’une distribution de kit abri constitué de matériaux locaux adaptés aux zones. Les différentes couches d’âges de déplacés bénéficieront de cette formation. Pour le cas des déplacés vivant en location dans les zones urbaines, NRC se pensera sur une possibilité d’une assistance de Cash. Ce Cash pouvant contribuer à soulager les charges de loyer des déplacés. Au niveau des sites inappropriés et appropriés, le respect des normes de construction et de sécurité des logements seront prise en compte dans son appui technique nécessaire aux déplacés pendant l’auto construction des maisons. Il veillera au respect de la distance prevue entre abris et infrastructures. Il se convergera sur le renforcement au respect du genre par les communautés à travers des sensibilisations sur l’égalité des sexes. NRC mettra en place plusieurs activités en commençant d’abord par une évaluation de base, des enquêtes CAP permettant d’avoir des informations de référence, les prises de contacts avec les partenaires et les leaders communautaires des déplacés. Cela dans le but de définir les approches à mettre places et les critères de ciblage. NRC ciblera la population extrêmement vulnérables avec un accent sur le genre et les personnes a besoins spécifiques. Ces groupes de personnes représentent un risque de protection plus élévé Lorsqu’elles sont dans une situation de deplacement. NRC s’assurera que son assistance ne nuira pas à la sécurité de ces personnes y compris l’environnement dans lequel ils vivent. 
NRC optera à une méthodologie de sélection des bénéficiaires en tenant compte des orientations des partenaires externes. Les aspects protection et sécuritaire ne seront pas négligés. Ces partenaires, bénéficiaires seront impliqués dans le processus de ciblage. Pour éviter toute exclusion lors du processus de ciblage, une analyse des risques de protection liée à la réponse de NRC sera entreprise. Des mecasnismes des plaintes sera mise en place.
Pour maintenir la collaboration et les efforts entre les acteurs dans le secteur Abri et Wash, NRC participera activement aux réunions de coordination et forums humanitaire au niveau national et régional organiser par OCHA, les 2 Clusters, des instances gouvernementales et niveau des sites des déplacés pour discuter des questions problématiques liées aux déplacés. Il participera à la conception des outils d’évaluation, aux évaluation des besoins, au rapportage, à l’harmonisation des kits.

The Teknaf area suffers each year from water scarcity during the dry season and, because the Master Water Network planning process will not begin before 2020, therefore the proposed project will include contingency capacity for water trucking to cover drinking-water needs. NGO Forum/NCA/AAR will maintain and improve water and sanitation infrastructures and services to support rights holders in coping with natural disasters. The project will continue with hygiene promotion activities and distribute Menstrual Hygiene Management (MHM) items based on latest REACH survey identified women preferences, and explore the use of the voucher system in conducive market environment. As an integrated programming approach, NGO Forum/NCA/AAR will train and sensitise the WASH team, especially the community volunteers, on SGBV topics enabling them to identify cases and do referrals.  Specific gender concern in the WASH program: Within the humanitarian community itself, site planning and WASH infrastructure planning/design processes have mainly been dominated by male architects and engineers, often with gendered assumptions about the user. In general, latrine provision in the initial stages of the response was largely determined through an engineering lens or from the perspective of quantitively reaching minimum standards, and did not always incorporate women and girls’ needs, gender disparities and socio-cultural constructs. The proposed project will aim to strongly focus on the consultation aspect during the initial deisgn phase of a gender segregated latrine construction, to address the major issues identified in prior WASH and gender specific research, namely the sharing facilities, lack of sex-segregation, distance, privacy, dignity, and difficulties to manage menstruation. The expected impact of the gender focused WASH activities will be the improved qualitative WASH indicators and a reduction in the percentage of households (women and men) facing problems accessing latrines and bathing facilities, and a reduction of percentage of women and men reporting feeling unsafe while accessing latrine facilities, as well as an overall increase in the percentage satisfaction of WASH services provided.

Improving Emergency Shelter and Non-food Items interventions to communities affected by conflict to access support and lifesaving assistance in Ayod and Fangak of Jonglei State in South Sudan. Improving emergency Shelter and Non-food items response to newly displaced IDPs and Returnees in Fangak, Ayod County of Jonglei State;  Koch and Mayendit Counties of Unity State of South Sudan. Fangak, Ayod (in Jonglei State); Koch and Mayendit Counties (in Unity State) – all bordering The Sudan - have been identified as cantonment sites. Thousands of returnees are expected back home in these counties in 2020, based on high prospects of a revitalized peace in South Sudan. The presence of these cantonment sites in the mentioned counties is a source of vulnerability to the returnee population. Civil population will be exposed to protection risks such as forced and voluntary recruitments into the army; exposure to GBV risks; interference during access to civilian humanitarian services; occupation of civilian infrastructure; availability, exposure and spread of weapon; misuse of humanitarian aid (including deviation, looting and exploitation); violation of housing, land and property right; lack of political will and support - targeted mocks on civilians. As flood-prone areas, the locations almost always experience floods, resulting in human displacements. Besides, man-made disasters are recurrent: tribal attacks and escalation of conflict between warring parties. Historically, the mentioned States have been experiencing massive displacement of people, killing of children, women, the elderly and loss of livestock and property, including burning of houses. In 2019, an estimated 35,000 Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) were quarterly displaced in these States. 75,000 people returned from PoCs in Bor, Malakal , Juba, Ethiopia and Sudan . In 2020, thousands more are expected back home in the mentioned States.This project aims to ensure provision of S/NFIs to the most affected population of conflict and disaster, vulnerable categories in the mentioned counties, especially the IDPs and the most affected vulnerable host communities. These are based on the Humanitarian Needs overview (HNO) and Humanitarian Response Plans (HRP) for South Sudan. The project will target a population of 30,000 individuals in Fangak, Ayod Counties of Jonglei State; Koch and Mayendit Counties of Unity State. It targets populations in four locations:  Fangak (12, 000); Ayod (6,000); Koch (6,000) and Mayendit (6,000) individuals respectively. Due to the magnitude of the displacement, about 70% of households are expected to be women-headed, with no less than one third widows, plus the housewives whose husbands will be relocating to cantonment sites, seeking for military service or promotions within the army with an intention of earning more money for their households left behind in home villages. IDPs and returnees are (as of 2019) settled in Old Fangak, New Fangak, Ayod, Koch and Mayendit. Several joint assessment and responses conducted from 20th July to 5th Sept 2019 reported IDPs lacking essential NFIs services. Other IDPs had health related issues, especially diarrhea, vomiting, skin diseases, and fever, especially amongst children. IDPs were reportedly sleeping in Kangas and shawls, with about ten or more individuals sharing with one host household. Many children who were attending school were out of school in the locations where IDPs have settled. Children are also at risk of neglect, child labour, gender based violence (GBV), recruitment into armed groups, forced marriage (for girls) and family separation especially after going through the violence when fighting broke out. Over 60% of the most-at-risk IDP populations in these areas will mainly be women and children, with family shelter and NFI needs. The humanitarian imperative is: provide S/NFI to these IDPs and host populations, the basis of this proposal. Upon project approval, ADA will send pipeline requests for the S/NFI supplies to the Logistics Cluster who will share the request with the S/NFI Cluster. The latter will approve or seek clarifications from ADA who will respond to the queries. Once approved, the Logistics Cluster will update the items to be sent to the field and notify ADA accordingly. ADA will liaise with field teams/bases to ensure supplies are received and distributed.

Mali - OCHA Office [OCT 5493];[PARTNERSHIP AGREEMENT 2017-2020] Renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et de plaidoyer pour la protection humanitaire et l’assistance aux populations les plus vulnérables au Mali. La situation humanitaire demeure complexe et instable, principalement en raison des conflits armés et intercommunautaires dans les régions du Centre et du Nord. Le retard dans la mise en œuvre de l’Accord pour la paix et la réconciliation au Mali paraphé en juin 2015 et dans le processus de désarmement, démobilisation, réintégration (DDR) contribuent à la persistance de l’instabilité sécuritaire dans les régions de Kidal, Gao, Tombouctou, Ségou et Mopti ainsi qu’à l’aggravation des tensions sociales. La présence limitée de l’État et l’insécurité dans ces régions demeurent l’un des facteurs clés obligeant les civils à fuir leurs communautés.
Le nombre de Personnes Déplacées Internes (PDI) a atteint la barre des 199 385 en octobre 2019 en comparaison aux 80 302 enregistrés en octobre 2018. Les risques et les besoins de protection des populations fuyant leurs communautés sous la pression de la violence armée ou des tensions intercommunautaires, sont élevés. De graves abus et attaques contre les personnes, les biens et les services (écoles, centres de santé) sont régulièrement signalées alors que l’accès aux services appropriés est compromis. Comme les déplacements internes sont durables, les risques de protection et les violations des droits fondamentaux augmentent, en particulier pour les plus vulnérables (femmes, enfants, personnes âgées, personnes handicapées ou malades). De graves conséquences humanitaires ont donc été notées, telles que des taux élevés d’insécurité alimentaire et de malnutrition ainsi que le faible accès aux services sociaux de base.

En référence au Cadre Harmonisé (nov. 2019), à l'heure actuelle, 3,6 million d'hommes, de femmes, de garçons et de filles souffrent d'insécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle, dont 670 000 souffrent d'une insécurité alimentaire sévère (phase 3 à 5 du Cadre Harmonisé). La situation devrait se détériorer au cours de la période de soudure 2020, avec près de 4,9 million d'hommes, de femmes, de garçons et de filles souffrant d'insécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle, dont près de 1,2 million de personnes souffrant d'insécurité alimentaire sévère (phase 3 à 5). Les capacités de réponse existantes au Mali représentent plus de 160 organisations humanitaires, acteurs du développement ainsi que des forces militaires (MINUSMA, Forces maliennes de défense et de sécurité, Barkhane, Mission européenne de formation, G5 Sahel). Le contexte susmentionné exigera une coordination efficace et la présence d’OCHA demeure très importante. OCHA maintiendra sa présence à Bamako, Mopti, Tombouctou et Gao et ouvrira une antenne à Ségou tout en couvrant à distance les régions de Taoudénit, Ménaka, Kidal et les régions du sud.

Sept clusters actifs (Éducation, Sécurité alimentaire, Santé, Nutrition, Protection, Abris/BNA et WASH), des sous-clusters et des groupes de travail spécialisés (Accès, CM-Coord, Redevabilité, Genre et Cash) sont en place au niveau national et local. Le Bureau d’OCHA au Mali continuera ainsi à jouer un rôle central dans la mobilisation, la coordination et le soutien des acteurs humanitaires dans les domaines de la coordination, la gestion de l’information, le financement humanitaire et le plaidoyer. OCHA jouera un rôle essentiel dans la mobilisation adéquate des fonds en faveur des personnes dans le besoin, en plus de contribuer à dynamiser les efforts déployés par le gouvernement et les acteurs du développement pour s’attaquer aux causes structurelles de la vulnérabilité.

OCHA continuera à jouer son rôle central dans la mobilisation des partenaires, l’utilisation des instruments et des mécanismes de financement tout en veillant à ce que les besoins humanitaires croissants soient prises en compte. OCHA assumera son rôle clé dans la coordination militaire au niveau national et régional de concert avec les forces militaires présentes dans le pays tout en renforçant les capacités des autorités nationales en matière de coordination et de préparation des interventions d’urgence.

HSYR19-PRO-CPN;PRO-GBV;PRO-MIN;PRO-156394-1 Enhancement of protection of displaced persons, returnees and conflict affected host communities in Syria through integrated, community-based protection activities. The project aims to strengthen protection and resilience of Syrian IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host communities to enjoy rights, legal and physical protection and access to services through advocacy, identification of risks and response, coordination and provision of community-based protection services.  It will capitalize on UNHCR’s community- centers network in Syria to help identify protection needs and facilitate response to people in need of protection and access to services to enhance their legal and physical protection. As such protection interventions including legal counselling and assistance, protection monitoring, referrals and information sharing, social protection through livelihoods support to most vulnerable people, psychosocial support, GBV prevention and response, child protection, case management, in- kind assistance covering basic needs of elderly and persons with disabilities, education support to vulnerable children, campaigns and awareness including on mine education for communities targeting women, men, boys and girls and capacity building of first responders working in communities, volunteers, partners and government counterparts will be provided through the project. Outreach to communities will be convened through static and mobile facilities including outreach volunteers, through which people in need of protection services in areas of SGBV, CP, civil documentation, psychosocial support and community empowerment will be provided and enhanced. Activities on community initiatives will also be implemented engaging communities to address own protection concerns and enhance participation, inclusion, ownership and social cohesion.  Legal aid interventions will enhance access to civil/HLP documentation of IDPs and refugee returnees and provide support in legal matters related to GBV, CP and other protection risks. Accountability to affected people will be realized through meaningful participation of communities, structured focus group discussions and enhancement of community- based complaints mechanism to receive feedback with regards to programmes delivered through the project and complains including regarding sexual exploitation and abuse (SEA) and the redressal of incidents.  

Intervention to refugee returnees will focus on humanitarian assistance, legal aid, coordination with government counterparts and UN and NGO stakeholders, information management and return tracking systems and sub – district profiling to better inform return programming and interventions. In addition, the project will support coordination fora between protection actors ensuring coordinated protection interventions as well as providing technical training to local stakeholders and HLP Technical Working Group. UNHCR Syria will continue to lead Protection Sector in coordination of response plans of IDPs and affected people as well it will execute leadership roles in refugee return programmes in collaboration with the Government. In North West Syria, it will lead Protection Monitoring Task Force (PMTF). 

Through the project intervention approximately 3 million IDPs, returnees and affected host communities (60 %, 25 % and 15% respectively) will be reached in government and non-government-controlled areas redressing their protection concerns.  3,000 humanitarian workers and local authority staff will be trained, and 2,700 communities consulted through FGDs and 2,310 communities through protection monitoring. 30% of the project beneficiaries are girls, 25% are boys, 24% are women, and 15% are men and 3% elderly women and 3% elderly men. 840 humanitarian workers and local authority staff are to be trained and 120 communities will be assessed through protection monitoring activities. 

The project will ensure GBV prevention through community-based mechanisms, such as women committees.

Lebanon: WFP - Multisector Beirut Explosion  (USAID/FFP) Food assistance for vulnerable populations affected by the Beirut port explosion.  WFP will provide immediate, life-saving in-kind food and cash assistance for to up to 420,000 vulnerable beneficiaries in order to: a) protect the food security of the vulnerable blast-affected population through the provision of in-kind assistance; and b) to meet food needs of the most vulnerable populations whose livelihoods have been affected by the triple shock of the blast, COVID-19, and economic crisis. 

In the immediate response to explosion-affected populations who lost their homes in the blast, WFP will provide hot meals through support to communal kitchens, and take-home rations to up to 5,000 families, who will reive a 60kg food parcel, which includes rice, pasta, bulgur, chickpeas, vegetable oil, sugar, and salt, enough to feed a family of five for one month. 

WFP will target up to 150,000 explosion-affected vulnerable, food in-secure individuals with a cash-based transfer to cover food needs, plus a multi-purpose cash top-up to meet the essential needs.

In addition, WFP will target up to 270,000 food-insecure individuals affected by the triple shock of the blast, COVID-19, and economic crisis, with a cash-based transfer to cover food needs.

Beirut Explosion Response - Health, Shelter and Settlements Affected Areas Caritas Lebanon - Beirut Blast (shelter) The overarching aim of this project is to ensure the protection of vulnerable populations, to provide access of vulnerable households, for both displaced and host communities, IN ADDITION TO MIGRANT WORKER POPULATIONS, to physically adequate and safe shelters with security of tenure. This is accomplished through the provision of protection-focused shelter assistance that addresses the inadequacies in terms of the safety of vulnerable households.
This project will apply the standards set through technical guidelines on selected shelter activities drafted by the sector working group, UN partners and LRC to maximize impact, complement services and avoid duplication.

In response to the crisis, Caritas Lebanon (CL) will provide cash for shelter activities and minor renovation direct interventions to enable vulnerable households whose shelters were damaged to carry out essential repairs to ensure protection from the elements. The assistance will be provided as direct renovation interventions through a preset renovation methodology and quality assurance guidelines.

The intervention will ensure that rehabilitation of shelters will not lead to evictions or rent increases (do no harm) for the tenants. Finally, this intervention will be accompanied by services provided by other projects that fall under other sectors such as psychological first aid and psychosocial support.

Caritas Lebanon (CL) will organize trainings and ongoing technical capacity building through direct mentoring all along the project’s implementation. 

The emergency response will assist 2180 AFFECTED HOUSEHOLDS (approx. 10,900 INDIVIDUALS) in the economically vulnerable neighborhoods of Beirut and Metn. Eligible households will be selected impartially strengthening social cohesion in the affected areas.

The selection criteria will include
-	Inclusion: This sector will primarily target the general need of shelter of the vulnerable population affected by the blast while ensuring the inclusion of different age groups, gender and diversity, ESPECIALLY THE DISPLACED AND MIGRANT WORKER POPULATIONS.
-	Targeted assistance to the most vulnerable households: Caritas will determine eligibility based on the needs assessment reports set out by UN Habitat and LRC. Special attention will be given to
o	Female headed households
o	Elderlies
o	Household with PWD
o	Household with dead family member
o	Household with heavily injured member
-	Coordination with local actors: Understanding the holistic needs of affected communities requires inter-sectoral collaboration. Shelter assistance will be coordinated between partners within the sector and with activities of other sectors for improved impact and complementarity of interventions where applicable, including but not limited to protection and health concerns.
-	Safeguarding social stability and livelihood: Coordination with the above mentioned partners to ensure adequate housing conditions

Emergency Cash Assistance (ECA) for vulnerable population affected by the explosion in Beirut Cash Emergency for Disaster Affected Residents and Nutrition (CEDAR & NUT) The project aims to expand cash based assistance for individuals affected by the Beirut blast through a 3 months-cycle of MPCA (food portion and basic needs) based on nutrition-sensitive vulnerability criteria as entry point for targeting, coupled with guidance to safeguard nutrition security for vulnerable HHs (special focus to infants and proper use of breastmilk subsitutes). Responding to the Health Needs of the Host and Rohingya Communities through the Production of Hygiene Materials Responding to the Health Needs of the Host and Rohingya Communities through the Production of Hygiene Materials In addition to the health impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic in Bangladesh, there are long-term effects on socioeconomic factors as a result of the health crisis. While needed to save lives, restrictions on movement and trade have crushing effects on local and national economies. Incomes of vulnerable people are disrupted; businesses shrink or close; supply chains are impeded, and hundreds of millions of people are losing their jobs in the informal and formal sector, resulting in loss of access to the cash or credit needed to buy life essentials. Highly vulnerable individuals who already live in poverty and rely on daily or wage labor are struggling to buy food, maintain access to safe housing, purchase health and hygiene supplies, or meet other basic needs as they lose crucial income. The project will focus on the health response through utilizing local capacity in the production of hygiene materials such as cloth-masks, hand sanitizer and PPE. In line with the Food Security Sector (FSS) Strategic Response, IOM will ensure host communities, front line health responders, local government authorities and government law enforcement are equipped with preventive hygiene materials to mitigate the spread of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Countering the Economic Impact of Covid-19 In Refugee Camps in White Nile State (CEIRC) (part of ECHO/-AF/BUD/2020/91029) Integrated Response for Refugees in Khartoum and White Nile ADRA will prioritize the access of refugees to basic services in Khartoum State, and enhance cohesion through engagement and awareness of host communities. The project will enhance the protection environment through the establishment of inter dialogue Community Circles. The Circles will include both host community and refugee members, within the circles the members will be trained in various topics, mainly conflict resolution and community protection. As part of its global strategy in Education, ADRA also aims at enhancing education for vulnerable refugee children, through a comprehensive and efficient voucher based response, that ensures that children are able to continue their education in safe environments.

The project will aim at strengthening community based self-protection structures such as Inter Communal Dialogue Groups (ICDGs), Women’s Groups (WGs) and forming Youth Groups by doing so the groups accountability will be strengthened towards decision makers and other actors’ partners. The aim is to institutionalize the groups to be part of the former camp governance system. This action will build the capacity of the SSR and host community (HC) to improve social protection systems and increase the groups’ awareness of and linkage to referral mechanisms.
This action will reduce protection risks associated with negative coping mechanisms by implementing cash for work and distributing charcoal vouchers which will reduce exposure to GBV during firewood collection, supported by production and distribution of Fuel Efficient Stoves (FES). Particular attention will be given to trainings on stove usage and environmental issues and cash for work will include targeted reforestation as well as FES production, thereby strengthening the linkage between activities, aligning interests of SSR and HC and creating space for the SSR and HC to jointly address protection issues.

Emergency GBV service provision to SGBV survivors and women and girls at risk Emergency GBV service provision to SGBV survivors and women and girls at risk The project focuses on ensuring the emergency GBV service provision to SGBV survivors and women and girls at risk, with special attention to vulnerable populations (adolescent girls, heads of household, people with disabilities, migrant workers, older people, LGBTQI+ people) in affected areas by the Beirut explosion. The project will provide women and girls with psychosocial support services including GBV case management, and refer them to specialized legal, health, mental health and other required services through static and mobile facilities. The project also aims at addressing vulnerability of women and girls by distribution of Dignity Kits as well as information materials on GBV risk mitigation and available services as well as on COVID-19 specific mitigation measures. Building on the findings of study on Integrating   for cash and voucher assistance (CVA) into GBV program conducted by UNFPA Lebanon (August 2020), UNFPA with its partners will ensure the provision of CVA targeting women and girls at high risk of GBV or GBV survivors with an aim to reduce household tensions by contributing to household needs, to pay for safe alternative accommodation and for GBV survivors to meet urgent needs. Outreach activities will be conducted to facilitate access to the GBV services for women and girls as well as to increase awareness of men and boys on GBV risks and mitigation to have them as allies based on ""do no harm"" approach. UNFPA will support its partners to establish and scale up existing hotlines for provision of remote specialized services. Support to existing Women and Girls Safe Spaces (WGSS) managed by UNFPA partners will be further strengthened and linkages with sexual and reproductive services will be reinforced. UNFPA and its partners will continue to conduct GBV safety audits to ensure that programmes are accountable to the needs of people in a way that promotes their safe and dignified participation and engagement in decisions affecting them. UNFPA IPs will conduct site-/location-based advocacy on GBV risk mitigation with other sectors, namely shelter, health, and protection; Specific focus will be given to GBV risk mitigation within the newly established shelters through the schools.
UNFPA will enhance partner capacity on Prevention from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA). Based on the PSEA protocol developed for Lebanon, feedback and complaints mechanisms are in place and UNFPA will ensure response to unethical behavior by humanitarian workers as per agreed code of conduct. UNFPA will ensure that staff and partners are aware of PSEA standards and will keep raising awareness on SEA risks.  The social workers and mobile team members at the WGSS will be deployed only after going through training and having relevant/required skills on survivor-centered approach for GBV case management and emergency psychosocial support. Mobile teams are also oriented on Psychological First Aid (PFA), community outreach, and both have critical tenets of ‘do no harm’ approach. All partners and staff working on the projects, including frontline workers, will be further capacitated through supervision and mentoring on survivor-centered approach; basic protection skills, whose main tenet is ensuring a ""do no harm"" principle.

Multi-Sector Integrated Approach to Improve Access to Basic Services and Resilience of the Vulnerable Population to the Recurrent Shocks in North Delta Locality, Kassala Improving food security and livelihoods of vulnerable households affected by conﬂict and natural disaster in Blue Nile, North Darfur and Kassala states The project interventions are intended to lead to increased food security & strengthen community resilience to climate shocks &conflict through enabling sustainable increases in agricultural and livestock productivity & adopting alternative livelihoods which will decrease competition over natural resource. The ultimate beneﬁciaries of the project are mainly the farmers and pastoralist, IDPs, returnees & poor residents in Blue Nile, North Darfur and Kassala states (around 580790 people). Agricultural tools, drought resistant seeds & seedlings, vegetables and horticulture will be provided to increase household food production. Promotion of climate smart & resilient crops & livestock production systems, protection of livestock based livelihoods in pastoral & agro pastoral community through provision of emergency livestock assistance, livestock watering, restocking with goat & poultry; awareness raising on the important of healthy diet in addition to women training on food processing for malnutrition, these inputs will build the capacity of the targeted communities to achieve their own food security & improve their livelihoods by increasing their production & income to better able them to withstand future shocks, droughts & other natural disasters. Solar powered women farms will enable produce quality diversified food items for household consumption and income & will reduce work load compared to currently practiced irrigation methods. Establish women saving & loan groups & support it with clean fuel (LPG cylinders & stoves) to establish revolving funds thus reducing wood collection work load & negative health impacts of indoor pollution. Process of women farms will be supported by nurseries, business management & agro processing trainings, linkage to markets & solar lights for safe gathering and mobile charging. The project will support assets protection and increase the ability of the target communities to decrease post-harvest losses & increase their resilience to shocks through provision of cash for work & cash for assets. The project will facilitate regeneration of ecosystem through a range of activities that aims to increase access to water, pasture and forestry which in the past directly contributed to conﬂict between farmers and pastoralists. Training will be provided on the management of these resources and environmental conservation techniques. The project will support the formation & reinforcement of farmers’ groups & community based associations strengthen their institutional capacity and consolidate their links to government service providers & other actors; to facilitate delivery of other project activities. For example, the training & technical support will be provided through these groups. The Project will apply participatory approaches for prioritizing & planning community needs to ensure that community planning & service delivery is tailored to local needs. More over the project will arrange to raise community awareness on themes other than production of the value chain products, including gender, protection & environment. As with elsewhere in the three targeted states men & women have different and unequal access to agriculture and livestock production inputs and technology (women represent about 49% of the total population yet are responsible for more than 65% of agriculture and livestock livelihood activities); therefore the project will ensure that everyone in the affected community women, girls, boys and men have a voice in the development & implementation of the project & have access to opportunities that the project gives. Restocking with livelihoods kits, vegetable growing & marketing will enable women and youth to better engage in income generating activities and production process. The project will be run in environment friendly pattern, saving natural resources & increase target population awareness about environment issues through discussion & orientation sessions.

Agriculture recovery and cash-based intervention to strengthen resilience and food security among most vulnerable households in Southern Syria Escaping poverty through increasing self-resilience in access to food for the most vulnerable households in Dara’, Hama and Rural Damascus The aim of the project is to support self-resilience of HHs in Rural Damascus, Hama and Dar'a through distribution of agro-kits and poultry kits. The Action will strengthen resilience of the affected HHs and reduce the dependency on aid of the most vulnerable Syrian population living in these areas. The Project will contribute to the Sector Objective 2 “Support self-reliance of affected households by protecting and building productive assets and restoring or creating income generating opportunities to save and sustain lives” in order to reach 1.2 million people in 2020. 
To decrease the dependency on food assistance and to promote the self-resilience and consequently the dignity of beneficiaries, the Project will provide agro inputs (seeds) and poultry for family consumption to a total of 10,000 HHs. Agro-inputs will be delivered to those families who have an access to their land, ensuring that lands are free of UXOs, while in the areas still UXOs affected or for the families who do not possess land, poultry kits will be delivered. 
In the process of beneficiary’s selection specific focus will be on returnees and local population (host communities). Special attention will be given to female headed HHs, elderly, HHs with People with Disabilities, unaccompanied children and to those groups who have only limited access to income to cover the family food needs and are forced to adopt negative copying mechanisms, unskilled or seasonal workers for instance. 
The most common negative coping mechanism detected by COOPI during the implementation of the current projects and through last post harvesting assessment (September 2019) are: not buying clothes, not buying uniforms for children attending school, taking loans, requested support from relatives, waiting for aid coming from INGOs and SARC, families sent their children to work.
 During the preparation and implementation of the activities, COOPI will ensure the coordination with local authorities and robust participation of the communities giving them a voice to express desired modalities of implementation (the design of similar projects have been already successfully tested by COOPI in Dar’a and Nashabiyeh). Coordination will be ensured with the FSA Sector and its members but also with international and national actors active in the same villages in order to harmonized the response, avoid overlapping and to promote synergies. Synergies will also be promoted by COOPI through other projects submitted to HRP 2020 taking place in the governorates of this Action. 
Additionally, the same approach will be implemented in NES and NW if access is granted to INGOs.

Providing protection through community-based services to high priority areas in three governorates: Homs, Idlib, and Deir-ez-Zor Enhancement of protection of displaced persons, returnees and conflict affected host communities in Syria through integrated, community-based protection activities. The project aims to strengthen protection and resilience of Syrian IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host communities to enjoy rights, legal and physical protection and access to services through advocacy, identification of risks and response, coordination and provision of community-based protection services.  It will capitalize on UNHCR’s community- centers network in Syria to help identify protection needs and facilitate response to people in need of protection and access to services to enhance their legal and physical protection. As such protection interventions including legal counselling and assistance, protection monitoring, referrals and information sharing, social protection through livelihoods support to most vulnerable people, psychosocial support, GBV prevention and response, child protection, case management, in- kind assistance covering basic needs of elderly and persons with disabilities, education support to vulnerable children, campaigns and awareness including on mine education for communities targeting women, men, boys and girls and capacity building of first responders working in communities, volunteers, partners and government counterparts will be provided through the project. Outreach to communities will be convened through static and mobile facilities including outreach volunteers, through which people in need of protection services in areas of SGBV, CP, civil documentation, psychosocial support and community empowerment will be provided and enhanced. Activities on community initiatives will also be implemented engaging communities to address own protection concerns and enhance participation, inclusion, ownership and social cohesion.  Legal aid interventions will enhance access to civil/HLP documentation of IDPs and refugee returnees and provide support in legal matters related to GBV, CP and other protection risks. Accountability to affected people will be realized through meaningful participation of communities, structured focus group discussions and enhancement of community- based complaints mechanism to receive feedback with regards to programmes delivered through the project and complains including regarding sexual exploitation and abuse (SEA) and the redressal of incidents.  

Intervention to refugee returnees will focus on humanitarian assistance, legal aid, coordination with government counterparts and UN and NGO stakeholders, information management and return tracking systems and sub – district profiling to better inform return programming and interventions. In addition, the project will support coordination fora between protection actors ensuring coordinated protection interventions as well as providing technical training to local stakeholders and HLP Technical Working Group. UNHCR Syria will continue to lead Protection Sector in coordination of response plans of IDPs and affected people as well it will execute leadership roles in refugee return programmes in collaboration with the Government. In North West Syria, it will lead Protection Monitoring Task Force (PMTF). 

Through the project intervention approximately 3 million IDPs, returnees and affected host communities (60 %, 25 % and 15% respectively) will be reached in government and non-government-controlled areas redressing their protection concerns.  3,000 humanitarian workers and local authority staff will be trained, and 2,700 communities consulted through FGDs and 2,310 communities through protection monitoring. 30% of the project beneficiaries are girls, 25% are boys, 24% are women, and 15% are men and 3% elderly women and 3% elderly men. 840 humanitarian workers and local authority staff are to be trained and 120 communities will be assessed through protection monitoring activities. 

The project will ensure GBV prevention through community-based mechanisms, such as women committees.

Infrastructure rehabilitation in Aleppo and Hama governorates Fostering Resilience through Early Recovery response for the Most Crisis-impacted Communities in Syria The Integrated Response for Resilience Programme aims at providing a comprehensive response through Early Recovery support in 80 communities  impacted by the crisis. 
Communities, particularly those most dramatically affected – and under additional stress because of IDPs returns and other displacements - need assistance in reinforcing their resilience to address these shocks as well as the consequences of the protracted crisis, and to address their needs on seriously depleted infrastructures and service capacities.
The essence of the Programme is about providing Syrian communities with – still limited - support to regain control over their basic needs (livelihoods, access to essential services) and reduce their dependency on humanitarian assistance. Prioritization of locations, is the outcome of a context analysis and needs assessment conducted on more than 5,000 Syrian communities, based on the following three criteria:
1) Hard to Reach Areas
2) Areas of major IDPs presence and IDPs returns
3) Highest scoring in the Severity Scale

The integrated response consists of the following components: strengthening of social services-related capacities (access and coverage), livelihoods creation and rural recovery, PWDs support, social cohesion/community safety, reducing gender inequality and youth marginality, women empowerment, tensions reduction and rehabilitation of basic infrastructure and public services.
The program is built in a modular manner both in terms of geographical and sectoral/thematic interventions and foresees the allotment of average 1 Million US$ per community. Hence, donors willing to support this approach will be able to pre-select certain location(s) and/or area(s) of intervention of their preference, within the 200 prioritized communities.
The programme relates directly to the sector objectives:
1. Living conditions
2. Livelihoods
3. Access to social services
4. Access to productive and market infrastructure
5. Social protection
6. Strengthening of local public services delivery capacity
7. Reinforcing opportunities and capacities for civic engagement

Area-based response to the emergency shelter and protection needs in Lebanon following the Beirut Port Explosion (ECHO/SYR/BUD/2020/91039) Provision of tailored are-based shelter assistance to the vulnerable individuals most heavily impacted by the Beirut Port Explosions The proposed response aims to tackle the immediate shelter needs emerged as a result of the explosion, providing access to safe and liveable residential units to the affected communities of the Beirut Lebanese, migrant and refugee population, while also contributing to the multi-sectoral longer term rehabilitation of areas affected, in close coordination with national and local actors. 
Tapping into the overall coordination mechanisms of the shelter sector and Lebanese institutions, as well as initiatives on the ground, this programme proposes area-based and punctual assistance to estimated 21,190 individuals (10,172 men and 11,018 women; of which 5,297 are elderly; 10,595 between 18-65; and 5,298 under 18) need via:
a)	Emergency weatherproofing assistance to an estimated 300 target HH beneficiaries 
b)	Provision of conditional cash for rent to 1000 individuals 
c)	Minor repair of 1200 residential / non-residential units 
d)	Rehabilitation of 500 residential shelters. 
e)	Rehabilitation of 100 common areas within residential units
f)	Rehabilitation of structural damages within 20 residential buildings
g)	Implementation of 5 community support projects in affected areas
h)	Capacity building of 30 national institutions and organizations on shelter response
i)	Production of 10 assessment studies that are made accessible and widely disseminated
This program aims to complement other ACTED implemented/planned intervention across other sectors (such as Food Security, WASH, Protection and Health) and will target zones 71-74 and 104-110 in Bourj Hammoud, zones 66-69 in Basta el-Tahta and zones 6-8 and 10-12 in Karantina where ACTED’s historical presence and long term programming in the target areas (since 2013) made it one of the first and key responders to provide immediate relief to the Beirut Port Explosion. Within the first days of the response and in coordination with the Shelter sector, ACTED supported the implementation of the LRC MSNA assessment, jointly with the distribution of emergency weatherproofing kits. To date, ACTED has distributed 1064 core relief items (including 217 sealing off kits, dignity and baby kits) and removing over 1232 tons of debris from the streets and HHs of Beirut. 
Through its shelter programs ACTED will enhance its ongoing coordination with Lebanese institutions and initiatives who have played an integral role in the immediate shelter response. In the aftermath of the disaster, ACTED provided GIS support to the Beirut Municipality through the provision of an expert to improve their efficiency of building safety checks; and a solid waste management expert was deployed to support the Beirut Municipality and their contractor to improve management of the waste dumps. Moreover, ACTED has engaged with Beirut Urban Labs, the Order of Engineers and other prominent urban planners and initiatives in Lebanon to ensure the response is people centred. ACTED has supported many local initiatives in the response (such as Arcenciel, Bassma, Migrant Community Center), through provision of resources to expand the shelter response and/or recycling efforts. 
As a shelter sector actor part of the immediate response, and member of the Cash for Rent and Rehabilitation Task Forces, ACTED will ensure each form of shelter programming will align with sector harmonized packages and adhere to sector guidance to prevent generating conflict due to lack of harmonization of assistance. Beirut Explosion Response - Multi-Sector Assistance (State/PRM) Beirut Blast Shelter Response and Recovery Programme According to the Shelter Sector, the 4 August blast impacted an estimated 72,265 apartments in 9,700 buildings located within three kilometres of the epicenter. It is believed that 29,771 apartments (89,313 individuals) fall within level 1 damages - minor damages, 17,100 apartments (51,300 ind.) fall within level 2 - moderate - and 1,144 apartments (30,660 ind.) fall within level 3 - heavy damage. The explosion also affected communal areas, shared open-spaces and minor infrastructure, further impacting community self-recovery capacity. 

With shelter needs at the core of the crisis, UNHCR will support men, women, girls and boys, both Lebanese and other nationalities, who were affected by the blast. UNHCR's response includes immediate weatherproofing temporary solutions, followed by a phased approach to support individuals and families to repair or rehabilitate houses and to sustain rental payments for those displaced. In addition, through community support projects and common area rehabilitation, UNHCR will enhance the safety, security, dignity and resilience of communities.

Speed and appropriateness of interventions, maximizing flexibility through rapid utilization of cash as a key modality for implementation, combined with ongoing response monitoring, will help ensure nimble and flexible interventions that are built on evolving needs. Community engagement will be at the centre of the response, ensuring effective participation. Beneficiary selections will also be based on the LRC emergency needs assessment in addition to UNHCR shelter partner assessments within allocated areas of intervention. According to CAS/ILO (LFHLC Survey), Beirut residents are comprised of about 7% children below 5 years of age, 13% between 5 and 14 years old, 15% between 15 and 24, 43% between 25 and 59, and 22% above 60 years old. In addition, 54% are female and 46% male. Age and gender considerations will thus guide the response, including with special considerations on the selection of beneficiaries and implementation modalities to address specific needs of particular groups. The response adopts a whole-population approach, targeting the most affected and most vulnerable households and individuals – including Lebanese, refugees and migrant workers – as well as their communities in the hardest hit and vulnerable areas affected by the blast. Do no harm, conflict-sensitivity and PSEA will be integrated throughout the response.

Partially Against Syria HRP Enhancement of protection of displaced persons, returnees and conflict affected host communities in Syria through integrated, community-based protection activities. The project aims to strengthen protection and resilience of Syrian IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host communities to enjoy rights, legal and physical protection and access to services through advocacy, identification of risks and response, coordination and provision of community-based protection services.  It will capitalize on UNHCR’s community- centers network in Syria to help identify protection needs and facilitate response to people in need of protection and access to services to enhance their legal and physical protection. As such protection interventions including legal counselling and assistance, protection monitoring, referrals and information sharing, social protection through livelihoods support to most vulnerable people, psychosocial support, GBV prevention and response, child protection, case management, in- kind assistance covering basic needs of elderly and persons with disabilities, education support to vulnerable children, campaigns and awareness including on mine education for communities targeting women, men, boys and girls and capacity building of first responders working in communities, volunteers, partners and government counterparts will be provided through the project. Outreach to communities will be convened through static and mobile facilities including outreach volunteers, through which people in need of protection services in areas of SGBV, CP, civil documentation, psychosocial support and community empowerment will be provided and enhanced. Activities on community initiatives will also be implemented engaging communities to address own protection concerns and enhance participation, inclusion, ownership and social cohesion.  Legal aid interventions will enhance access to civil/HLP documentation of IDPs and refugee returnees and provide support in legal matters related to GBV, CP and other protection risks. Accountability to affected people will be realized through meaningful participation of communities, structured focus group discussions and enhancement of community- based complaints mechanism to receive feedback with regards to programmes delivered through the project and complains including regarding sexual exploitation and abuse (SEA) and the redressal of incidents.  

Intervention to refugee returnees will focus on humanitarian assistance, legal aid, coordination with government counterparts and UN and NGO stakeholders, information management and return tracking systems and sub – district profiling to better inform return programming and interventions. In addition, the project will support coordination fora between protection actors ensuring coordinated protection interventions as well as providing technical training to local stakeholders and HLP Technical Working Group. UNHCR Syria will continue to lead Protection Sector in coordination of response plans of IDPs and affected people as well it will execute leadership roles in refugee return programmes in collaboration with the Government. In North West Syria, it will lead Protection Monitoring Task Force (PMTF). 

Through the project intervention approximately 3 million IDPs, returnees and affected host communities (60 %, 25 % and 15% respectively) will be reached in government and non-government-controlled areas redressing their protection concerns.  3,000 humanitarian workers and local authority staff will be trained, and 2,700 communities consulted through FGDs and 2,310 communities through protection monitoring. 30% of the project beneficiaries are girls, 25% are boys, 24% are women, and 15% are men and 3% elderly women and 3% elderly men. 840 humanitarian workers and local authority staff are to be trained and 120 communities will be assessed through protection monitoring activities. 

The project will ensure GBV prevention through community-based mechanisms, such as women committees.

Support of the OCHA country offices in Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger Renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et de plaidoyer pour la protection humanitaire et l’assistance aux populations les plus vulnérables au Mali. La situation humanitaire demeure complexe et instable, principalement en raison des conflits armés et intercommunautaires dans les régions du Centre et du Nord. Le retard dans la mise en œuvre de l’Accord pour la paix et la réconciliation au Mali paraphé en juin 2015 et dans le processus de désarmement, démobilisation, réintégration (DDR) contribuent à la persistance de l’instabilité sécuritaire dans les régions de Kidal, Gao, Tombouctou, Ségou et Mopti ainsi qu’à l’aggravation des tensions sociales. La présence limitée de l’État et l’insécurité dans ces régions demeurent l’un des facteurs clés obligeant les civils à fuir leurs communautés.
Le nombre de Personnes Déplacées Internes (PDI) a atteint la barre des 199 385 en octobre 2019 en comparaison aux 80 302 enregistrés en octobre 2018. Les risques et les besoins de protection des populations fuyant leurs communautés sous la pression de la violence armée ou des tensions intercommunautaires, sont élevés. De graves abus et attaques contre les personnes, les biens et les services (écoles, centres de santé) sont régulièrement signalées alors que l’accès aux services appropriés est compromis. Comme les déplacements internes sont durables, les risques de protection et les violations des droits fondamentaux augmentent, en particulier pour les plus vulnérables (femmes, enfants, personnes âgées, personnes handicapées ou malades). De graves conséquences humanitaires ont donc été notées, telles que des taux élevés d’insécurité alimentaire et de malnutrition ainsi que le faible accès aux services sociaux de base.

En référence au Cadre Harmonisé (nov. 2019), à l'heure actuelle, 3,6 million d'hommes, de femmes, de garçons et de filles souffrent d'insécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle, dont 670 000 souffrent d'une insécurité alimentaire sévère (phase 3 à 5 du Cadre Harmonisé). La situation devrait se détériorer au cours de la période de soudure 2020, avec près de 4,9 million d'hommes, de femmes, de garçons et de filles souffrant d'insécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle, dont près de 1,2 million de personnes souffrant d'insécurité alimentaire sévère (phase 3 à 5). Les capacités de réponse existantes au Mali représentent plus de 160 organisations humanitaires, acteurs du développement ainsi que des forces militaires (MINUSMA, Forces maliennes de défense et de sécurité, Barkhane, Mission européenne de formation, G5 Sahel). Le contexte susmentionné exigera une coordination efficace et la présence d’OCHA demeure très importante. OCHA maintiendra sa présence à Bamako, Mopti, Tombouctou et Gao et ouvrira une antenne à Ségou tout en couvrant à distance les régions de Taoudénit, Ménaka, Kidal et les régions du sud.

Sept clusters actifs (Éducation, Sécurité alimentaire, Santé, Nutrition, Protection, Abris/BNA et WASH), des sous-clusters et des groupes de travail spécialisés (Accès, CM-Coord, Redevabilité, Genre et Cash) sont en place au niveau national et local. Le Bureau d’OCHA au Mali continuera ainsi à jouer un rôle central dans la mobilisation, la coordination et le soutien des acteurs humanitaires dans les domaines de la coordination, la gestion de l’information, le financement humanitaire et le plaidoyer. OCHA jouera un rôle essentiel dans la mobilisation adéquate des fonds en faveur des personnes dans le besoin, en plus de contribuer à dynamiser les efforts déployés par le gouvernement et les acteurs du développement pour s’attaquer aux causes structurelles de la vulnérabilité.

OCHA continuera à jouer son rôle central dans la mobilisation des partenaires, l’utilisation des instruments et des mécanismes de financement tout en veillant à ce que les besoins humanitaires croissants soient prises en compte. OCHA assumera son rôle clé dans la coordination militaire au niveau national et régional de concert avec les forces militaires présentes dans le pays tout en renforçant les capacités des autorités nationales en matière de coordination et de préparation des interventions d’urgence.

IRC Centrality of Protection . 2020/2021. 2020 portion amount CHF 100,000 (7F-10666.01) Ensuring safety, dignity, and access to Multi-Purpose Cash Interventions for conflict-affected individuals in the Mezam Division in North West, Cameroon Cameroon’s South West (SW) and North West (NW) regions began to experience social instability and unrest following protests against the government’s treatment of the Anglophone population and the government’s response to this unrest in 2016. The resulting socio-political crisis gradually turned into insecurity and armed violence as early as October 2017, which has only escalated. Since 2018, civilians have had to endure heightened tensions and erupting conflict between the area’s separatist militias and the country’s national security forces. Since the SW/NW conflict began, over 500,000 people have been internally displaced, and more than 1.3 million people are in need of humanitarian assistance . The continuous offensive by Government forces against non-state armed groups (NSAGs) has also pushed almost 40,000 Cameroonians to seek refuge in Nigeria.  By the end of 2018, UN agencies had declared a Level 2 emergency owing to the worsening humanitarian situation in the SW and NW. 
In a context of insecurity, the protection of civilians is particularly at risk. Between January and July 2019, protection actors identified and reported over 3,700 protection incidents through protection monitoring and assessments conducted in two thirds (seven) of the NW/SW divisions. Among these incidents 2,300 were recorded in the SW and 1,400 in the NW. In both regions, Mezam, Fako, Meme, Lebialem and Manyu were the most affected divisions, with 84% of incidents; 55% of the victims were females and 13% were children. The most frequent incidents were violations of the right to property through house destruction, which constitutes about 50% of the incidents.

To respect the Do-No-Harm principles and to achieve the objective stated above the proposed project will partner with and work within the framework of the WFP’s Multi-Purpose Cash assistance activities to provide a complementary protection component, which will be carried out through the following activities:

Activity 1. Conduct Do No Harm risk assessments and support  Protection Mainstreaming Action Plan implementation 
The IRC will undertake an initial protection risk assessment and do-no-harm assessment at the beginning of the project to identify main protection risks faced by people in their daily life and issues related to the cash assistance transfer cycle. After identifying risks faced by populations, IRC and WFP will develop an Action Plan proposing mitigation measures, to address risks and the barriers as well as ensure meaningful access to assistance. This assessment will also include the validation and/or review of WFP vulnerability targeting criteria with affected communities. 

Activity 2: Conduct protection mainstreaming training and ToTs for beneficiary sensitisation
To ensure implementation of a ‘Do-No-Harm’ (DNH) approach and protection mainstreaming plan, the IRC will develop training modules and conduct a joint training with WFP at the beginning of the project for relevant staff and local partner, on their own code of conduct, protection principles, and specific measures to ensure implementation of a DNH approach and specific measures for protection mainstreaming during project implementation (including protection-sensitive management of complaints and feedback mechanisms). The pre-test and post-tests are part of the training component. All participants to IRC training organized with partners will undergo these tests before and at the end of the training in order to verify that they have achieved the learning objectives. 

Activity 3: Supporting and reinforcing feedback mechanisms for clients and accountability mechanism
The IRC's protection staff and accountability and feedback mechanism staff will support the strengthening of WFP’s existing complaints and feedback mechanism (CFM).

The multipurpose cash component of the project is implemented by WFP.

Multi-purpose cash assistance (MPCA) enables the most vulnerable families to meet their basic needs with dignity, and prepares them with financial stability and increased choices to access decent work. This activity is essential both in terms of economic stability while Lebanon continues to address COVID-19 pandemic and aftermath of the Beirut blast, and as a response to ongoing economic distress. Social assistance is a right for the most vulnerable, and for those with labor capacity it is also an essential stepping stone for families to pursue future livelihoods and decent work. For families directly affected by the explosion, a separate cash envelope will also be available as an immediate protection need, in line with sector guidance.
