Addressing urgent protection and psychosocial needs of children and adolescents through mobile response in Northeast Nigeria Plan International’s mobile programming has been effectively used in its German Federal Foreign Office (GFFO) funded project in 6 LGAs of Borno State. Plan proposes using the mobile unit approach in the four targeted LGAs of Borno. The mobile response ensures the deployment of the mobile team within 72 hours of a specific request, or of a report from relevant humanitarian clusters groups of acute needs. In cases of first response, the mobile unit will be deployed for a period of 6 and up to 12 weeks to provide urgent lifesaving assistance including provision of cash transfer. The mobile team currently is based in Maiduguri and serves LGAs within Borno state. They are being deployed in Kaga, Damboa, Bama, and four different locations of Maiduguri Metropolitan City-Jere, Madinatu, Bolori and Teachers village camp. The team can also be stationed in other field locations like Mubi, Dikwa, Pulka or Gwoza and be deployed from there. The mobile protection team will conduct a participatory rapid needs assessment, engaging the affected population to identify immediate needs. The outcome of the rapid assessment will be used to determine the line of response and also to identify existing community based services. Based on the findings of the assessment a rapid referral pathway will be developed to guide the provision of protection services to the children and adolescents. The referral pathway will be disseminated among stakeholders and will be used to coordinate actors providing services on the ground especially during the first line of response which will include provision of direct case management services. 
In addition, the mobile team will set up rapid complaints and feedback response mechanism to address issues of protection of sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA) as well as advocate for services that are needed and not available. Communities will be engaged to identify the most suitable and safe mechanisms to raise complaints and provide feedback on both services and operations of the mobile team and other available community services. Improving access of vulnerable children in the Gaza Strip to protection and education services Responding to the Protection Needs of Vulnerable Children Victims of Child  Labour and School drop out in the Gaza Strip  In a context characterized by prolonged strain and economic isolation-de-development-, vulnerable families, including those with a large number of children, female-headed households and families with people with disabilities, have adopted different coping mechanisms to deal with the high level of poverty and vulnerabilities. According to OCHA (2019), the deteriorating socio-economic condition in Gaza has a negative consequence on children’s rights and their ability to access education and protection services as manifested in an increase of school drop-outs and child labour (OCHA, 2019, UNICEF 2018, and Tdh 2019). This Action involves multi-sectoral interventions that are consistent with the strategic objectives of Protection, Education, and Food Security Sector. The project aims to eliminate child labour in the Gaza Strip and to increase children's access to formal education system and other vocational training opportunities through provision of child protection services, psychosocial services, educational reintegration, family support and increased community mobilization toward the issue of child Labour and dropout of schools. Along with protecting children's rights to access to education, this project focuses on the right of the child to be protected from economic exploitation and from performing any work that is likely to be hazardous and could negatively affect their overall wellbeing and development. The project will target 8985 beneficiaries, including 700 working and or dropped out of school children (450 boys and 250 girls).
The proposed activities will include responsive and remedial protection activities. The security context in the target area has recently deteriorated, with increasing tensions between host communities and refugees, exacerbated by environmental disasters, lack of access to income-generating activities and pressure on local resources, such as water and agricultural land. NGO Forum/NCA will consult with the refugees and host communities in order to prioritise activities that will integrate the needs of the communities. The Teknaf area suffers each year from water scarcity during the dry season and, because the Master Water Network planning process will not begin before 2020, therefore the proposed project will include contingency capacity for water trucking to cover drinking-water needs. NGO Forum/NCA/AAR will maintain and improve water and sanitation infrastructures and services to support rights holders in coping with natural disasters. The project will continue with hygiene promotion activities and distribute Menstrual Hygiene Management (MHM) items based on latest REACH survey identified women preferences, and explore the use of the voucher system in conducive market environment. As an integrated programming approach, NGO Forum/NCA/AAR will train and sensitise the WASH team, especially the community volunteers, on SGBV topics enabling them to identify cases and do referrals.  Specific gender concern in the WASH program: Within the humanitarian community itself, site planning and WASH infrastructure planning/design processes have mainly been dominated by male architects and engineers, often with gendered assumptions about the user. In general, latrine provision in the initial stages of the response was largely determined through an engineering lens or from the perspective of quantitively reaching minimum standards, and did not always incorporate women and girls’ needs, gender disparities and socio-cultural constructs. The proposed project will aim to strongly focus on the consultation aspect during the initial deisgn phase of a gender segregated latrine construction, to address the major issues identified in prior WASH and gender specific research, namely the sharing facilities, lack of sex-segregation, distance, privacy, dignity, and difficulties to manage menstruation. The expected impact of the gender focused WASH activities will be the improved qualitative WASH indicators and a reduction in the percentage of households (women and men) facing problems accessing latrines and bathing facilities, and a reduction of percentage of women and men reporting feeling unsafe while accessing latrine facilities, as well as an overall increase in the percentage satisfaction of WASH services provided.

The overall purpose of this thematic component is to further strengthen all NRC country teams' ability to use gender-sensitive Cash and Voucher Assistance impact fully, and every time they are appropriate.  (QZA-20/0048-37)

Raise awareness and hygiene kits for Covid 19 and a single cash transfer to HH Integrated COVID-19 WASH Response to the Rohingya  and Host population in Cox’s Bazar ""WaSH project is continuing to ensure inclusive and equitable provision of life saving water and sanitation services building on infrastructure already constructed in the previous phase in 2019 (in the Camp no,14 and 15 and host community) and strengthening behaviour change communication (BCC) by encouraging community-based collective measures. 
 There are two main routes of transmission of COVID-19: respiratory droplets and direct contact. Respiratory droplets are generated when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Droplets may also land on surfaces where the virus could remain viable and thus, the immediate environment of an infected individual can serve as a source of transmission (contact transmission). The provision of safe water, sanitation, hygienic living and environmental conditions are essential to protect human health during all infectious disease outbreaks, including the COVID-19outbreak. Hand hygiene, personal and social hygiene are key elements in preventing this disease to spread. As of today, a lot of aspects of COVID-19 prevention and control are still unclear, including implications related to WASH interventions (like virus persistence on surfaces or sewage). 

  The previous phase of the intervention has contributed to an increase in the appropriate usage of handwashing. Almost 79% of the respondents from the end of project evaluation reported that handwashing points installed under the project were utilized for hygiene maintenance. In terms of safe and inclusive access to water, the water point accessibility for PWD, pregnant women, adolescent girls and aged persons has been enhanced. The increase in ease of accessibility for pregnant women rose from 6% in baseline to 48%, similarly, for adolescent girls, it improved from 24% to 83%. So, maintenance of these essential WaSH facilities and services are vital to reduce the risk of disease outbreak.
Bear in mind the gravity of the issue, CAID will continue to ensure lifesaving water and sanitation services to the Rohingya and host communities in 2020. Focus will be provided to address the key challenges facing WaSH service such as congestion at water points, unequal distribution, inclusive access and protection concerns in bathing cubicles and latrines.""

To save lives and alleviate suffering Food Security and Livelihoods Project  In North Darfur,  GOAL works closely with the Ministries of Agriculture and Animal Resources in Khartoum and in North Darfur as well as FAO on identifying needs, gaps in coverage, and on programme implementation. In addition, GOAL remains an active participant in the FSL Cluster at both national and state levels  where FSL programming is implemented, including North Darfur. GOAL’s FSL programming is closely integrated with other sectors, especially nutrition, health, and protection through targeting vulnerable households (including affected by malnutrition, people living with disabilities, and women-headed households) in catchment areas of supported clinics. GOAL will also incorporate protection and women’s empowerment approaches. With OFDA funding, GOAL proposes to focus on the IDP populations in Kutum Town as well as Kassab and Fata Borno Camps near Kutum, and complementary funding (SHF) will be used to reach vulnerable host communities in Kutum and Al Waha localities to ensure all relevant communities have their needs addressed. Activities are closely coordinated with other FSL actors in North Darfur to eliminate any duplication of effort. Through the FSL Cluster and Cash Working Groups, GOAL incorporates and shares lessons learned and harmonized approaches to livelihoods activities in order to maintain high technical standards in its work.
In South Kordofan, GOAL will work with Village Development Committee (VDC) in areas where they are already established and functional. If the VDC are not available, GOAL will work community leaders to form a VDC consisting of community leaders, influential community members (such as teachers, health workers, religious leaders etc.) as selected by community members. A close effort will be made to ensure that gender representation is observed in the composition of VDC members. And then, GOAL will work with the VDC to identify 200 households in each locality (400 total) to benefit from the first and second phase distribution. The first 100 households will receive 3 local species female goats per family directly from GOAL in the first phase of distribution and this group will make commitment with the VDC to pass on the first generation to the remaining 100 households. The commitment will be between among the first phase beneficiaries, VDC and the second phase beneficiary. This means each beneficiary from the second phase is tied with specific households from the first phase. Male goats will be distributed to the VDC and managed by them to ensure that they are accessed equally by all recipients of female goats. 

GOAL will identify and support existing Community Animal Health Workers (CAHWs) in the targeted areas to provide training and ongoing monitoring and care for the distributed animals. GOAL will provide refresher training to CAHWs and facilitate their work, in particular by supporting their transportation to rural and IDPs areas, as the lack of vehicles or resources for transport has been identified as a major challenge to effective support for animal welfare services across South Kordofan.

Emergency response to the Ethiopian refugee crisis in Gadarif state in Sudan Improving the conditions of refugees in WK and Gadaref States through multi sector interventions covering WASH, Education, and Livelihood, Health and Nutrition in Energy and Environment   IRW intends to intervene in East Sudan and WK addressing urgent needs of refugees and host communities through multi sector projects that includes: Education, WASH, Livelihood, Health, Nutrition and Environment mainstreamed by protection activities. The plan will target a total of 47,644 persons including 15% host communities (17,587 (13,182 refugees, and 4,407 host community) in East Sudan and 30055 in WK)
Education sector intervention will contribute in increasing refugee children enrollment in primary school and secondary school. In WK the intervention will focus on construction/rehabilitation of primary classrooms in WK and secondary classes in Gadaref equipped with essential student and teacher seating, construction/rehabilitation of gender sensitive latrines with water facilities and hygiene promotion in school/ learning spaces, where as in East Sudan the intervention will also focus on school retention and provision of refugee teachers’ incentives. In both East Sudan and WK the sector will form and train student clubs, support them with recreation materials and promote their skills to enhance awareness in schools and community on hygiene issues. Trainings will conducted for teachers and PTAs in schools.
WASH intervention will contribute to improving access to safe sufficient water supply, promote and enhance access to hygiene services and support improving access to safe dignified sanitation and clean environment free from open defecation in WK. In East Sudan the response will focus on health promotion.
Livelihood sector intervention will consider strengthening the refugees and host community self-reliance. IN WK the intervention will focus on improving livelihood opportunities through provision of agricultural inputs, building their capacity on climate-smart crop production and vocational trainings. Refugees will be supported with income generating activities/business opportunities or employment and support with cash or in kind. In Sudan the intervention will focus vocational training for both men and women y, business skills training such as entrepreneurship, business management and simple book keeping. In kind supports will be provided to the trained targets to enable them start small business in their community. 
Health and Nutrition sector intervention will be carried out in WK only and will contribute to provision of standard primary health care and nutrition services through construction/rehabilitation of health facilities, conduct trainings to health staff to ensure delivery of standard services. Nutrition staff will be trained on CMAM, community outreach volunteers will identified and trained on CMAM to carry out regular MUAC screening, mother to mother groups will be established and train on IYCF promotion. Nutrition supplies will be availed and distributed on monthly basis.
Energy and Environment this sector intervention will be carried out in East Sudan only and will focus on providing fuel efficient cooking stove to 2197 HH.

------ Coordination Evidence-based planning and programming for humanitarian actors in Syria  REACH, a joint initiative of IMPACT, ACTED and the United Nations Operational Satellite Applications Programme (UNOSAT), aims to facilitate evidence-based planning, technical advisory and coordination support for humanitarian actors in Syria by providing information management, technical advisory and coordination support to at least 225 humanitarian organizations. REACH will be leading on the implementation of project activities. More specifically, this will be done through the following activities:
•	Producing Monthly Humanitarian Situation Overviews in Syria (HSOS)
•	Emergency assessments on the humanitarian situation situation in Syria
•	Cash and markets assessments in collaboration with CBR-TWG
•	Camps and sites profiling and mapping
•	Remote sensing to support IDP site identification and shelter counts
•	Technical advisory to the humanitarian coordination structure, among other towards the successful implementation of the 2020 Syria MSNA
•	Thematic assessments/specialised assessments to meet information gaps

REACH has designed this intervention based on feedback from humanitarian actors and seven years of experience in implementation in Syria. REACH maintains regular discussions with Whole of Syria coordination structures including the deputy regional humanitarian coordinator, OCHA, clusters/working groups, and the NES forum, and sits as well at the ICCG in Turkey and the ISWG in NES/Iraq. Additionally, REACH is part of the NGO Forum and the SIRF and also joins the SIRF Policy and Advocacy working group. These engagements enable a timely and efficient identification of information needs and gaps as well as opportunities for partnerships and collaboration. Activities included in this proposal have thus been designed based on these interactions. For example, conversations with the NES Forum, OCHA, SSWG and CCCM cluster have confirmed a general lack of information on camps and sites in northern Syria, which was flagged as of particular concern given the worsened emergency situation in both NWS and NES. REACH Camps and Sites sweeps conducted in 2019 in NWS also revealed a significant number of sites that were not yet registered by the CCCM cluster, which outlined an information gap and a need to support CCCM processes.

This project is already fully funded, but may require additional top-ups later in the year.

IMPACT is a leading Geneva based think-and-do-tank, created in Switzerland in 2010 on the initiative of ACTED and firstly operationalised in 2012. While autonomous organizations, IMPACT and ACTED operate together thanks to a formalised global partnership. Together, IMPACT, ACTED and UNOSAT set up the REACH program in order to promote and facilitate the development of information products that enhance the humanitarian community’s decision making and planning capacity. IMPACT is the lead-organization in REACH and hosts the REACH global team in its Geneva HQ. As sister organizations, IMPACT and ACTED coordinate on field implementation. In all field operations of the REACH program, ACTED provides operational support (security management, office space, cars, national HR recruitment, etc.), while IMPACT provides strategic and programmatic oversight through its global team and is in charge of the validation and dissemination of reports, and external relations

Humanitarian assistance	Food Security	Syria HRP 2021 Restoring livelihoods of crisis affected population in Syria through light rehabilitation of irrigation infrastructure at community level The United Nations (UN) estimates that the number of crisis-affected people in need of humanitarian assistance in Syria is 14.2 million, of which 6 million are in acute need. The above figure of people in need includes 6.7 million protracted internally displaced persons (IDPs); estimated 320,000 spontaneous IDPs return; 75,000 refugees return; 438,000 Palestine refugees and the rest overburdened host communities.  

More than 75% of the number of people in need of humanitarian assistance are accessible from within Syria. Overall, 12.4 million of people are estimated to be food insecure (including 1.27 million severely food insecure) and 1.9 million people at risk of food insecurity. 

In this context, FAO has designed a project to assist 120,000 vulnerable crisis-affected food insecure farming households (equivalent to 750,000 people) in Syria. About 15% of the targeted householders will be selected from those who receive food support to help them shift from depending on food assistance to producing their own food and enhancing their self-sufficiency. The objective of the proposed action is to protect and enhance the livelihoods of vulnerable farmers and IDPs through the restoration of critical irrigation infrastructures to increase household food production and security. The project outputs include:

•	Output 1: Local small-scale irrigation infrastructures in the targeted governorates are assessed and light rehabilitation undertaken. 
•	Output 2: Capacity of technical staff and relevant stakeholders strengthened.

FOOD SECURITY AND AGRICULTURE (USAID/BHA) Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP camps, and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity.

WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying  mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan. 

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities, or other solution. 

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19 have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). Food & Cash-based Assistance for Vulnerable Populations in Somalia for 2021 (2021 portion) Food & Cash-based Assistance for Vulnerable Populations in Somalia for 2021 Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas.  As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation.  The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of a La Niña that is currently developing (75 percent chance through Feb 2021). Potential drought conditions will likely develop as a result of below average 2020 Deyr (Oct-Dec), a harsh 2021 dry Jilaal (Jan-Mar) season and a possible delay and/or poor performance of the 2021 Gu (Apr-Jun). 

Continued emergency relief alongside a further scale up of support to increase resilience is required in order to avert the hardship situation. WFP is therefore seeking resources in 2021 to sustain the on-going efforts and enable households meet immediate food needs and help build resilience against shocks. WFP is planning to implement unconditional and conditional transfers to improve access to food under integrated multi sectoral assistance to meet needs of vulnerable girls and women, pregnant and lactating women, boys and men and leverage resources with other partners to meet the level of humanitarian assistance required. WFP will continue to participate in cluster, joint planning, assessments and regular meetings with other humanitarian actors in Somalia. WFP employs gender sensitive beneficiary targeting in all its projects and prioritizes female and single headed households. Community consultations are carried out with men and women to ensure that their voices are heard. Accountability to affected populations ensured through information sharing, surveys and beneficiary feedback mechanisms. Beneficiaries are targeted and registered through biometric SCOPE system that provides real time data.

Increased access to education for out of school IDP and rural children in Puntland and South Central Somalia According to education cluster need analysis note 2021, an estimated three-million school-aged children and youth (six-18 years) are out‐of‐school. Enrolment rates are lowest for the most vulnerable children such as girls, rural and internally displaced children (IDP). Middle Shabelle and Mudug are part of the regions with the lowest attendance rates. Other locations with high out of school children includes areas that host Internally Displaced Persons including Galkayo and Bosasso and hard to reach rural areas such as Callula, Qandala among others. Children with disability are cut off from mainstream education system. The project will target rural/hard to reach areas and IDP locations to address this gap. Girls are disproportionally being negatively affected, due to increased chores and responsibilities, as well as GBV risks including FGM, early marriage, sexual and physical violence. In Somalia’s patriarchal society where gender inequality shapes gender roles and responsibilities, girls’ education is barely prioritized by caregivers. Girls consistently face greater challenges to accessing education. While the gender parity for enrollment at primary school level is 0.91 (1 is equal enrolment) it drops to 0.83 at the secondary level. In times of crisis such as the current economic crisis due to COVID 19, girls are the first victims of family’s economic stress, experiencing school dropout and early marriage. Other barriers that affect girls’ access and retention in school include; lack of sanitary kits, unfriendly school latrine for use during menstrual periods, harassment from boys among others. The project intends to work at school, family and community level to mitigate barriers faced by girls to continue their education. At the school level, the project will work with teachers to promote gender responsive and inclusive teaching practices and with CECs to promote a conducive learning environment for all children. In particular the provision of education materials and food rations will directly address economic barriers to girls’ education. The rehabilitation of WASH facilities at school will be done with a gender and disability lens to ensure that girls, including those with disabilities, are safe and feel comfortable to go to school, including when they are menstruated. The provision of sanitary kits will contribute to address to prevent adolescent girls’ absenteeism during their periods.   The strong focus on protection will ensure that girls are safe when going to school. COVID-19 school closure had affected 1.1M children enrolled in the schools across the country from March to August 2020. This impacted not only their learning but also their wellbeing as schools also contribute to psychosocial wellbeing and protection of learners. When families cannot afford to pay tuition or other expenses associated with education, children drop out of school. These repercussions can lead to child labor, child marriage and other negative outcomes, RI will use Cash assistance to address the economic barriers to education. Barriers to access for children with disabilities are considerable and includes negative attitudes towards children with disabilities, unfavorable learning environments compounded by teachers lacking training on inclusive education, bullying by peers among others. An estimated 216,004 school aged children in need of humanitarian assistance are living with some form of disability though there is insufficient data on children with disability. The project will train teachers on inclusive education and create positive learning environment for children with disability and work with school management to ensure school facilities are disability friendly. Schools will be supported to serve as a critical entry point for critical lifesaving services, including access to safe drinking water, food, AWD/cholera prevention, protection mechanisms and psychosocial support which is critical for learners to recover from crisis.

The project seeks to improve Agricultural production and household incomes of beneficiaries in affected areas : Conflict-affected IDP, returnee and host community farming households have improved access to agricultural inputs / nutritious food, livelihoods and safe access to fuel and energy (SAFE). Critical agricultural livelihoods support to conflict- and pandemic-affected households in northeast Nigeria In 2021, FAO will improve food security, nutritional status and incomes among vulnerable, conflict- and pandemic-affected households in Borno, Adamawa and Yobe states in Northeast Nigeria. The now more than decade-long insurgency has decimated agricultural livelihoods upon which more than 80 percent of the population relies as a primary source of household income. The COVID-19 pandemic has further compounded this already highly vulnerable humanitarian context, generating interconnected vulnerabilities that negatively affect availability and access to food, agriculture inputs, finance, farming land, extension services, markets and the fundamental viability of agricultural livelihoods. 
Support to crop production and the rebuilding of a robust crop value chain have been identified by FAO as key to the restoration of livelihoods and to improving the food and nutrition security of vulnerable populations in the BAY states. FAO will support vulnerable households with critical inputs for rainy and dry season cultivation as well as for micro-/backyard gardening and seed production.   
Prior to the insurgency, close to 80 percent of households in northeast Nigeria reared livestock and/or poultry as a vital source of food and household income. The conflict has caused the wide-scale loss of these assets either through looting, property destruction, disease, or abandonment when fleeing attacks by armed insurgents. In addition to being a source of income generation through breeding for sale, livestock and poultry restocking increases the availability of meat, milk and eggs at the household level. FAO will increase support to livestock and poultry production in 2021 in support of affected households.
Prior to the crisis, the fisheries sector had significant economic importance and fish from the northeast were supplied to the rest of Nigeria. With increased land and areas retaken by the military, the return of IDPs to their communities of origin is ongoing, thereby enabling some to access fishing grounds and resume their traditional livelihood. However, the lack of quality inputs remains a limiting factor for the majority of fishers who continue to rely on humanitarian assistance to meet their food and livelihood needs. By leveraging FAO’s extensive experience and capacity, conflict-affected fisherfolk households will be supported to resume their livelihoods and meet their food and nutritional needs. 
The ongoing crisis is also termed a ‘protection crisis’ with vulnerable social groups – particularly children, women and the elderly – disproportionately affected by the impact of the ongoing conflict and the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic and are at heightened risk of adopting negative coping strategies such as child labour, borrowing, street begging, basic needs deprivation, transactional sex, early and forced marriage as their families seek to reduce the number of mouths to feed in their homes, and collection of fuelwood in insecure areas, which remains a high-risk livelihood. FAO will support vulnerable households by way of fuel-efficient stoves to reduce exposure to potential protection risks, and stove production and briquette production centres for income generation. 
Access to credit is a particular challenge for vulnerable groups in Northeast Nigeria, particularly women. Through the establishment of Group Savings and Loans Associations (GSLA), in 2021 FAO will extend its GSLA programme and will identify vulnerable groups to enhance their access to credit and financial services as an important social safety net.  
FAO is the co-lead of the Food Security Sector (FSS) which plays a critical role in coordinating food security programming in the BAY states. Food security data collection and analysis are also key and upon which food security actors base their intervention. In 2021, FAO will continue to support and host the Food Security Sector to facilitate the required coordination and analyses required to reach people most in need.

Providing integrated and timely humanitarian aid to the displaced population in Burkina Faso and Niger (2021 portion) Apporter une assistance WASH aux réfugiés, retournés, PDI et famille d’accueil dans les régions de Maradi, Tillabéry et Diffa Dans ce projet, NRC vise de contribuer au renforcement de l’accès aux services d’eau d’hygiène et d’assainissement en vue de réduire le risque et l'exposition aux maladies diarrhéiques auprès de 56 000 personnes dont des femmes, hommes, refugiées, retournes et famille d’accueil touchés par les déplacements, les inondations et les épidémies grâce à un meilleur accès à l'eau potable en qualité et quantité, à des installations sanitaires appropriées et aux pratiques d'hygiène. Les interventions WASH de NRC se feront dans les village d’accueil, les sites d’accueil des déplacés et les écoles.  La cible souhaitée est d’attendre 20% refugies, 25% déplacés internet et 5% retournes et 45% population hôtes. La réponse intègrera la réponse COVID-19. La réponse visera les ménages refugiés, PDI, retournes et population hôte.  Le plan de réponse prévoit de réhabiliter et de construire des nouveaux systèmes d’approvisionnement en eau potable utilisant les technologies à énergie renouvelable comme le solaire, et là où cela sera nécessaire l’approvisionnement en eau par du water-trucking, le traitement d'eau en situation d’urgence sur les sites temporaires, des infrastructures d’assainissement et des campagnes de sensibilisation de masse seront organisées pour le changement de comportement. Pour améliorer la gestion de l’eau, NRC créera et ou renforcera des comités de gestion des points d'eau avec une participation active des femmes visant d’atteindre 50% de participations des femmes dans les comités de gestion. Ces comités comprendront au moins sept membres, hommes et femmes, choisis par une assemblée villageoise.  NRC construira des blocs de latrines et douches dotées chacun d’un dispositif de lavage des mains dans les sites temporaires, dans les familles d’accueil vulnérables et dans les écoles ciblées par ce projet. Des kits d’entretien des latrines seront distribués aux ménage pour le nettoyage et l’entretien des latrines. Les latrines et les douches seront séparées par sexe pour atténuer les problèmes de protection, garantir la dignité des femmes et des jeunes filles et améliorer l'accès gratuit et sûr aux installations.
Pour améliorer l’hygiène en milieu scolaire, NRC mettra en place du paquet d'infrastructure minimum WASH dans les écoles et centres de santé le cas échéant. Des campagnes de sensibilisation pour la promotion de l'hygiène seront organisées afin de promouvoir le changement de comportement et d'encourager les meilleures pratiques d'hygiène personnelle. Pour ce faire, NRC va identifier, former et équiper des relais communautaires d’hygiène en collaboration avec les structures sanitaires avec au moins 50% de femmes. Des kits d'hygiène comprenant des kits d'hygiène familiale et des kits de dignité pour les femmes seront distribués aux ménages ciblés. NRC métra en place des comités d'hygiène et d’assainissement dans les sites temporaires pour une bonne gestion des structures d’assainissement. Les relais communautaires et les comité d’assainissement vont conduire des campagnes de sensibilisation dans les communautés, les écoles et dans les camps. Les matériels d'IEC et les kits d’hygiène seront conçus par le biais d'une consultation communautaire et après une enquête initiale sur les connaissances, attitudes et pratiques (CAP) menée par le NRC en coordination avec la DRHA, les districts sanitaires afin de se concentrer sur les problèmes les plus pertinents mis en évidence par les communautés et où les résultats de l'enquête montrent les plus grandes faiblesses des pratiques. NRC veillera à ce que les relais d'hygiène communautaires soient formés sur les méthode de communication/sensibilisation au niveau communautaire et équipés avec des matériels IEC. Cela inclura des démonstrations sur les pratiques de lavage des mains, le nettoyage des latrines et des douches, la chaîne de collecte de l'eau salubre (y compris le nettoyage des bidons) afin de conduire vers le changement de comportement parmi les communautés ciblées;

Mali - OCHA Office  [OCT 8533];[FCDO for CMCoord training in the Sahel] Renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et de plaidoyer pour la protection humanitaire et l’assistance aux populations les plus vulnérables au Mali. 
La situation humanitaire demeure complexe et instable, principalement en raison des conflits armés et intercommunautaires dans les régions du Centre et du Nord. Le retard dans la mise en œuvre de l’Accord pour la paix et la réconciliation au Mali paraphé en juin 2015 et dans le processus de désarmement, démobilisation, réintégration (DDR) contribuent à la persistance de l’instabilité sécuritaire dans les régions de Kidal, Gao, Ménaka, Tombouctou, Ségou et Mopti ainsi qu’à l’aggravation des tensions sociales. A cause des activités des acteurs armés, l’accès humanitaire demeure difficile mais fluide dans certaines zones. 

La présence limitée de l’État et l’insécurité dans ces régions demeurent l’un des facteurs clés obligeant les civils à fuir leurs communautés. La grogne sociale qui a conduit au changement de régime en août 2021 prouve l’inaccessibilité des populations maliennes aux services sociaux de base et l’aggravation de leur vulnérabilité à laquelle s’ajoute le poids de la pandémie de COVID-19. 

Le nombre de Personnes Déplacées Internes (PDI) a atteint la barre des 311,191 en octobre 2020 en comparaison aux 199 385 enregistrés à la même période en 2019 et 80 302 en 2018.  Les risques et les besoins de protection des populations fuyant leurs communautés sous la pression de la violence armée ou des tensions intercommunautaires, sont élevés. De graves abus et attaques contre les personnes, les biens et les services (écoles, centres de santé) sont régulièrement signalées alors que l’accès aux services appropriés est compromis. Comme les déplacements internes sont de longue durée, les risques de protection et les violations des droits fondamentaux augmentent, en particulier pour les plus vulnérables (femmes, enfants, personnes âgées, personnes handicapées ou malades). De graves conséquences humanitaires ont donc été notées, telles que des taux élevés d’insécurité alimentaire et de malnutrition ainsi que le faible accès aux services sociaux de base.

Avec près de 4,7 millions de personnes affectées par l’insécurité alimentaire, dont 2,3 millions personnes avec des besoins d’assistance d’urgence, l’année 2020 a été, selon les résultats des exercices du Cadre Harmonisé (CH), l’année la plus fortement marquée par l’insécurité alimentaire depuis 2014. Les conséquences de cette détérioration resteront perceptibles sur le niveau de vie de populations en 2021. Les capacités de réponse existantes au Mali représentent environ 200 organisations humanitaires, acteurs du développement ainsi que des forces militaires (MINUSMA, Forces maliennes de défense et de sécurité, Barkhane, Mission européenne de formation, G5 Sahel). Le contexte susmentionné exigera une coordination efficace et la présence d’OCHA demeure très importante. OCHA maintiendra sa présence à Bamako, Mopti, Tombouctou et Gao ainsi que son antenne de Ségou tout en couvrant à distance les régions de Taoudénit, Ménaka, Kidal et les régions du sud.

Sept clusters actifs (Éducation, Sécurité alimentaire, Santé, Nutrition, Protection, Abris/BNA et WASH), des sous-clusters et des groupes de travail spécialisés (Accès, CMCoord, Redevabilité, Genre et Cash) sont en place au niveau national et local. Le Bureau d’OCHA au Mali continuera ainsi à jouer un rôle central dans la mobilisation, la coordination et le soutien des acteurs humanitaires dans les domaines de la coordination, la gestion de l’information, le financement humanitaire et le plaidoyer avec un accent accru dans le domaine de Civilo-Militaire et d’accès humanitaire afin de garantir la conservation et la consolidation de l’espace humanitaire. OCHA jouera un rôle essentiel dans la mobilisation adéquate des fonds en faveur des personnes dans le besoin, en plus de contribuer à dynamiser les efforts déployés par le Gouvernement et les acteurs du développement pour s’attaquer aux causes structurelles de la vulnérabilité.

Cash assistance in response to rising food insecurity Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP camps, and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity.

WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying  mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan. 

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities, or other solution. 

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19 have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

part of PQ21S13 - Provision of in-kind food assistance to Palestine Refugees in Rural Damascus Provision of in-kind food assistance to Vulnerable Palestine refugees in Syria  UNRWA estimates that 418,000 Palestine refugees in Syria will continue to require humanitarian assistance in 2021. In a context of rising inflation and additional economic hardship caused by COVID-19, Palestine refugees are more and more affected by food insecurity and therefore increasingly depend on UNRWA assistance to meet their minimum food needs. Due to the vulnerability of Palestine refugees in the current socio-economic crisis, compounded by COVID-19, in 2021 UNRWA will expand its food programming and provide all 418,000 Palestine refugees with in-kind food assistance  through three distribution rounds. The Agency will continue to monitor the availability of food on the markets and will retain operational flexibility to adjust to a changing context as appropriate.

The composition of the food basket was developed based on WFP guidelines and in view of meeting ~ 50% of daily nutritional needs for 4 months.

UNRWA's original plan is to distribute 3 rounds of in-kind food assistance, each round covering a period of 4 months. However, this depends on the availability of funds. Until May 2021, UNRWA received or confirmed pledges are only sufficient to cover the first two rounds of 2021. The Agency will continue to mobilize resources to ensure funding for the third round is also secured.

In 2021, the number of people estimated to be in need of humanitarian assistance including for food needs is 418,000 Palestine refugees to strengthen their resilience and prevent further deterioration into acute food insecurity. As per its emergency planning, UNRWA aims to provide food assistance as well as multipurpose cash assistance, and protection interventions at both household and community levels, as well as the coordination of these activities across the different Sectors framework.

UNRWA has been providing life-saving humanitarian aid to Palestine refugees since the start of the crisis in Syria. The in-kind food assistance program remains one of the most important forms of UNRWA emergency support to stabilize the food security status for Palestine refugees in Syria, as it helps them meet part of their basic nutritional and survival requirements (~50% of kcal/person/day) which will increase resilience, and reduce humanitarian needs and the spiraling food insecurity levels.

Food & Cash-based Assistance for Vulnerable Populations in Somalia for 2021 Food & Cash-based Assistance for Vulnerable Populations in Somalia for 2021 Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas.  As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation.  The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of a La Niña that is currently developing (75 percent chance through Feb 2021). Potential drought conditions will likely develop as a result of below average 2020 Deyr (Oct-Dec), a harsh 2021 dry Jilaal (Jan-Mar) season and a possible delay and/or poor performance of the 2021 Gu (Apr-Jun). 

Continued emergency relief alongside a further scale up of support to increase resilience is required in order to avert the hardship situation. WFP is therefore seeking resources in 2021 to sustain the on-going efforts and enable households meet immediate food needs and help build resilience against shocks. WFP is planning to implement unconditional and conditional transfers to improve access to food under integrated multi sectoral assistance to meet needs of vulnerable girls and women, pregnant and lactating women, boys and men and leverage resources with other partners to meet the level of humanitarian assistance required. WFP will continue to participate in cluster, joint planning, assessments and regular meetings with other humanitarian actors in Somalia. WFP employs gender sensitive beneficiary targeting in all its projects and prioritizes female and single headed households. Community consultations are carried out with men and women to ensure that their voices are heard. Accountability to affected populations ensured through information sharing, surveys and beneficiary feedback mechanisms. Beneficiaries are targeted and registered through biometric SCOPE system that provides real time data.

Assistance to address food insecurity of vulnerable households and enhance resilience of local communities in Jonglei State of South Sudan Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP camps, and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity.

WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying  mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan. 

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities, or other solution. 

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19 have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). Increase access to quality education for refugee returnees, poor host community and IDPs Access to education continues to be inadequate, with only 30 % of children aged six-13 years are enrolled in primary education and only 26 % of children aged 14-17 years are enrolled in secondary education. According to education cluster needs analysis 2021 an estimated 1.4 million school-aged children (45% girls) need humanitarian assistance, out of these children,1,139,632 are children from non-displaced families and 300,398 are children from displaced families.  According to UNHCR PRMN, an estimated 893,000 people have been displaced in Somalia between January and August 2020, of which 357,200 (40%) are school-aged children. According to Education Management Information System (EMIS) 2018/2019 systems across the country (FGS, Puntland & Somaliland), one million children are enrolled in schools which is 21% of school age children.

In addition, Somalia is also home to 35,884 refugee returnees’ school-aged children who need education support in 2021. This number excludes another 9,927 refugee returnees projected to return to Somalia in 2021. Due to limited livelihood opportunities for families of these children, parents cannot afford to meet the education cost; hence concerned children miss the opportunity to access quality primary and secondary education. There is a need to explore approaches to expand the reintegration of refugee returnees into the public schools.  There are limited intermediate/ secondary education opportunities for IDPs and returnees. Tradition, culture and religion make it difficult to reach the grass-root level, and females are constrained from expressing their ideas and needs.

In addressing the key gaps and needs identified in the Cluster Needs Analysis and other assessments outlined above, UNHCR will assist IDPs, poor host community and returnees in accessing education through provision of education grants and scholastic materials to the parents of each returnee child enrolled in school, parents will receive a cash grant for the school going child through mobile money transfer, The support shall be based on school term modality, whereby parents received cash grant of $ 30 per child. This will be paid in one or two installments.
 
In addition, UNHCR will support existing schools in areas of return to increase their absorption capacity, including; provision of scholastic materials, teaching and learning materials, and rehabilitation of school infrastructure (classrooms, construction of gender specific latrines, playgrounds and provision of sporting facilities/items, water points/hand washing sinks, etc.). UNHCR will also conduct teachers' training and awareness raising for Community Education Committees on child protection and mitigation of COVID-19 impacts. In coordination with the Ministry of Education and other relevant actors, UNHCR will also support interventions aimed at greater school attendance and retention of students, in particular of girls, including through providing sanitary and hygiene items to girls attending school.
Inclusion will be key to UNHCR’s approach; as such, UNHCR will support the Ministry of Education in integrating returnee children into the national public-school system in order to prevent the continuation of NGO-managed parallel systems.  Overall, UNHCR will work closely with the Ministry of Education and the Education Cluster, adopting a local area-based approach, where the emphasis is placed on supporting existing systems to increase capacities. UNHCR will support 46,034 students of returnees ( 25,319 boys,20,715 girls ) of which 4,603 (2,531 boys, 2,072 girls) are verified as living with various disability and they have difficulties in accessing education including lack of disability-friendly services in the schools, lack of qualified teachers and infrastructural challenges like ramps, UNHCR will work with partners to provide friendly services to children who are living with specials needs like training teachers on brails and providing assistive devices.

Mitigating negative impact of COVID-19 pandemic on  human trafficking, exploitation and abuse among the most vulnerable communities in Eastern Conflict Area  The project aims to mitigate the exacerbating impact of COVID-19 on human trafficking  exploitation and abuse among vulnerable population in Eastern Conflict Area of Ukraine (ECA) by providing holistic and tailored social protection assistance to community members (including men, women and children) and though carrying out prevention activities.  

The severe decrease of economic opportunities in Ukraine and ECA specifically due to COVID-19 pandemic in addition to the protracted conflict, compounded by ramping unemployment rates, scarcely efficient social services and precarious social safety-nets, had already increased the strain on the most vulnerable groups within displaced and host communities, who were often left with no choice but resort to negative coping mechanisms. As a result, the most fragile social segments are left vulnerable to drivers of instability and to protection risks including vulnerability to trafficking in persons, exploitation and abuse – as well as more prone to resort to undesired migration and/or other negative coping strategies. Furthermore, not all types of protection and assistance needed by VoTs returning to Ukraine or (potentially) exploited in the country are available from the State.

IOM’s activities include legal aid, medical care, mental health and psychosocial support, financial support, vocational training, and other types of assistance to (potential) victims of trafficking, exploitation and abuse. Concurrently, IOM will carry out preventive measures raising awareness about risks of trafficking and exploitation and providing contacts of the currently operating hotlines , which provide information on safe migration and employment as well as providing further referrals to protection assistance for vulnerable population. Furthermore IOM share information on regular/safe migration and employment, prevention of trafficking and exploitation within youth, unemployed, newly graduates from vocational and technical schools etc.

Based on latest projections, 2.1 million Somalis are in IPC Phases 3 and above through December 2020. Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of the La Nina developing, which tends to trigger dry conditions in Somalia. If the forecast below-average Deyr rains (Oct-Dec 2020) is followed by below-average or delayed 2021 Gu rains (Apr-Jun), this could lead to a rapid and substantial worsening of the humanitarian situation. 

Rural populations are at a high risk of further deteriorating food security, given the direct and indirect impacts of these threats on rural livelihoods, related assets, food production and income. FAO’s proposal responds both to the lifesaving and life-sustaining needs of rural populations in IPC Phases 3 and above, against a Population in Need (PiN) of 3.1 million people prioritized for Food Security Cluster (FSC) assistance under the 2021 HRP. Also under SO2, in anticipation of drought conditions in early 2021, FAO will also strategically position water bladder tanks and provide nutritive animal feed blocks to protect the small milking animals of up to 20,000 pastoral households impacted by scarce pasture from dry conditions and/or locust damage. Countrywide livestock vaccination and supportive treatment campaigns will further protect livestock assets belonging to at least 2.2 million men, women and children. Preparedness for animal health emergencies will be enhanced through strategic stocking of vaccines and related supplies (PPR), and training to local partners in Livestock Emergency Guidelines and Standards (LEGS), antimicrobial resistance, disease surveillance and reporting, among others.

OCT 6294 [OCT 6294];[52040482 Amendment 4] Renforcement de la coordination et du plaidoyer humanitaire au Tchad Le projet vise à renforcer le rôle de OCHA dans la mise en œuvre de son mandat et son rôle auprès des partenaires humanitaires et gouvernementaux au niveau des fonctions coordination, gestion de l’information et plaidoyer. Le bureau national d’OCHA à N’Djaména et ses trois sous-bureaux régionaux à l’Est (Abéché) au Sud (Goré) et la province du Lac (Baga Sola) mettent l’accent sur l’opérationnalisation de ses fonctions y compris en assurant une lien entre les activités humanitaires et de développement (nexus) en vue de promouvoir une solution durable visant à ne pas perpétuer une situation de dépendance humanitaire. Dans le cadre de cette nouvelle façon de travailler outre l’opérationnalisation du nexus, le lien avec les objectifs commun des programmes développement, paix et sécurité sera mis en avant. L’accent est aussi mis sur le renforcement de la coordination civilo-militaire afin de faciliter l’accès et la protection des civils.

Le projet a pour but de renforcer la coordination d’une réponse humanitaire rapide et efficace afin de sauver des vies et protéger les personnes affectées par les situations de crises au Tchad. Une coordination humanitaire rapide et correctement évaluée au niveau des besoins de la population affectée permettra aux acteurs humanitaires de mieux identifier et répondre aux besoins humanitaires, de renforcer la préparation de réponse aux urgences à travers le renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et plus spécifiquement l‘Equipe humanitaire pays, la coordination inter-clusters, la coordination civilo-militaire, les clusters et les mécanismes de coordination au niveau de terrain.
Le projet vise aussi à assurer le plaidoyer humanitaire à travers l’analyse des besoins faites par l’ensemble de la communauté humanitaire et ses partenaires en vue une compréhension commune des problématiques auxquels fait face le Tchad, ses causes profondes, l’impact sur les populations. OCHA jouera un rôle clé dans la création d'espaces de collection et d'analyse et gestion d’informations, pour assurer une stratégie de réponse coordonnée menant à des actions humanitaires répondant aux besoins les plus aigus et être mieux préparé face aux urgences soudaines. Le projet permettra également d’assurer conjointement avec la communauté humanitaire le plaidoyer en faveur du respect des principes humanitaires, de la protection des civils, de l'accès humanitaire et pour la mobilisation et l'allocation efficace de ressources humanitaires.

Un accent a été mis sur la mise en œuvre des plans d’action de la redevabilité envers les populations affectées (AAP), la PSEA et la préparation aux urgences en plus d'intégrer une attention au genre et de renforcer la centralité de la protection.
Un plaidoyer pour plus de visibilité des résultats tangibles au niveau de la réponse facilitant la mobilisation de ressources pour les différentes crises au Tchad (mouvement de population – crise du Bassin du Lac Tchad, insécurité alimentaire et malnutrition, urgences sanitaires) est aussi défini comme une priorité dans ce projet 

OCHA continuera de jouer également un rôle moteur dans le renforcement du lien entre les acteurs humanitaires et de développement et la transformation de la réponse humanitaire, en lien avec les engagements pris au Sommet humanitaire mondial de 2016 et ceci à travers la nouvelle façon de travailler (NWOW) et le renforcement de l’utilisation de la modalité de transfert monétaire.

Mali - OCHA Office. OCT 6294 [OCT 6294];[52040482 Amendment 4] Renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et de plaidoyer pour la protection humanitaire et l’assistance aux populations les plus vulnérables au Mali. 
La situation humanitaire demeure complexe et instable, principalement en raison des conflits armés et intercommunautaires dans les régions du Centre et du Nord. Le retard dans la mise en œuvre de l’Accord pour la paix et la réconciliation au Mali paraphé en juin 2015 et dans le processus de désarmement, démobilisation, réintégration (DDR) contribuent à la persistance de l’instabilité sécuritaire dans les régions de Kidal, Gao, Ménaka, Tombouctou, Ségou et Mopti ainsi qu’à l’aggravation des tensions sociales. A cause des activités des acteurs armés, l’accès humanitaire demeure difficile mais fluide dans certaines zones. 

La présence limitée de l’État et l’insécurité dans ces régions demeurent l’un des facteurs clés obligeant les civils à fuir leurs communautés. La grogne sociale qui a conduit au changement de régime en août 2021 prouve l’inaccessibilité des populations maliennes aux services sociaux de base et l’aggravation de leur vulnérabilité à laquelle s’ajoute le poids de la pandémie de COVID-19. 

Le nombre de Personnes Déplacées Internes (PDI) a atteint la barre des 311,191 en octobre 2020 en comparaison aux 199 385 enregistrés à la même période en 2019 et 80 302 en 2018.  Les risques et les besoins de protection des populations fuyant leurs communautés sous la pression de la violence armée ou des tensions intercommunautaires, sont élevés. De graves abus et attaques contre les personnes, les biens et les services (écoles, centres de santé) sont régulièrement signalées alors que l’accès aux services appropriés est compromis. Comme les déplacements internes sont de longue durée, les risques de protection et les violations des droits fondamentaux augmentent, en particulier pour les plus vulnérables (femmes, enfants, personnes âgées, personnes handicapées ou malades). De graves conséquences humanitaires ont donc été notées, telles que des taux élevés d’insécurité alimentaire et de malnutrition ainsi que le faible accès aux services sociaux de base.

Avec près de 4,7 millions de personnes affectées par l’insécurité alimentaire, dont 2,3 millions personnes avec des besoins d’assistance d’urgence, l’année 2020 a été, selon les résultats des exercices du Cadre Harmonisé (CH), l’année la plus fortement marquée par l’insécurité alimentaire depuis 2014. Les conséquences de cette détérioration resteront perceptibles sur le niveau de vie de populations en 2021. Les capacités de réponse existantes au Mali représentent environ 200 organisations humanitaires, acteurs du développement ainsi que des forces militaires (MINUSMA, Forces maliennes de défense et de sécurité, Barkhane, Mission européenne de formation, G5 Sahel). Le contexte susmentionné exigera une coordination efficace et la présence d’OCHA demeure très importante. OCHA maintiendra sa présence à Bamako, Mopti, Tombouctou et Gao ainsi que son antenne de Ségou tout en couvrant à distance les régions de Taoudénit, Ménaka, Kidal et les régions du sud.

Sept clusters actifs (Éducation, Sécurité alimentaire, Santé, Nutrition, Protection, Abris/BNA et WASH), des sous-clusters et des groupes de travail spécialisés (Accès, CMCoord, Redevabilité, Genre et Cash) sont en place au niveau national et local. Le Bureau d’OCHA au Mali continuera ainsi à jouer un rôle central dans la mobilisation, la coordination et le soutien des acteurs humanitaires dans les domaines de la coordination, la gestion de l’information, le financement humanitaire et le plaidoyer avec un accent accru dans le domaine de Civilo-Militaire et d’accès humanitaire afin de garantir la conservation et la consolidation de l’espace humanitaire. OCT 6294 [OCT 6294];[52040482 Amendment 4] Fortalecer a nivel operativo y estratégico la coordinación humanitaria y abogacía en Venezuela En 2021, OCHA en Venezuela continuará reforzando las estructuras de coordinación (Equipo Humanitario de País –EHP-, Grupo Inter cluster, cuatro centros de coordinación de terreno y grupos de trabajo temáticos, incluyendo CASH, gestión de la información –GTMI-, Comunicación Humanitaria, rendición de cuentas ante las poblaciones afectadas –AAP- y la red de puntos focales de protección contra la explotación y abusos sexuales -PEAS). -	Fortalecer los foros de coordinación para alcanzar una respuesta humanitaria oportuna, efectiva y basada en los principios humanitarios.
-	Desarrollar la capacidad de los socios humanitarios para participar de manera efectiva en el HPC y proporcionar una respuesta más efectiva.
-	Fortalecer la comunicación humanitaria, para mejorar la comprensión de los principios humanitarios, los logros de la respuesta y la aceptación de las organizaciones humanitarias.
-	Fortalecer los centros de coordinación en terreno, para asegurar que cubran efectivamente su área geográfica, mejorando las capacidades de evaluación, respuesta y monitoreo y la coordinación con los socios y partes interesadas.
-	Acoger al clúster de Logistica, para fortalecer la coordinación entre los socios, el intercambio de informaciones puntuales sobre temas logísticos, apoyar la abogacía con las contrapartes institucionales, y promover soluciones conjuntas para mejorar la capacitad operacional y de respuesta.
-	Contribuir al aumento del nivel de apoyo financiero proporcionado por los donantes.
-	Mejorar el diálogo con todas las partes interesadas, incluyendo autoridades civiles y militares, para facilitar la aceptación y el acceso.

BURKINA FASO - Emergency food security and nutrition, WASH, and cash benefits to vulnerable populations affected by the humanitarian crisis in the Sahel (2021 portion) Assistance aux populations vulnérables affectées par la crise humanitaire dans les provinces du Bam et du Gourma Welthungerhilfe, propose une intervention ciblée ayant pour objectif principal de contirbuer à l'amélioration des conditions de vie des populations les plus vulnérables avec une réponse intégrant trois secteurs d'intervention : La sécurité alimentaire, la nutrition, et l'eau, hygiène et assainissement.
OS1 : La relance des moyens de d'existence adapté au climat est assurée.
OS2 : Prévenir, en colaboration avec les districts sanitaire, l'augmentation des taux de malnutrition des FEFA et enfants<5ans ainsi que la mortalité et la morbidité associés
OS3 : Prévenir, avec des interventions en eau, hygiène et assainisement, les risques de malnutritions et des maladies associées.
WHH porte une attention particulière aux groupes nécessistant un appui spécifique ou de protection : filles / femmes soumises à des pressions familiales et sociales fortes, voient leur études réduites et devant faire face à une charge de travail plus importante, auquel vient s'ajouter le risque plus élevé de perte de vie ou d'être victime de violence et d'exploitation sexuelle, les garçons / hommes dont les attentes sociales sotn également fortes, pouvant avoir des comportements plus à risque pour subvenir aux besoins de leur famille et se voient assumer de nouveaux rôles en temps de crise, ils bénéficient généralement de très peu de soutien en cas d'abus sexuel, les personnes âgés pouvant souffrir d'isolement, de problème de santé et voient leur stratégie de subsistance perturbées, les personnes vivants avec un handicap, ont plus de difficultés à accèder à l'assistance et aux infrastructures de base, ont moins d'accès à l'information et ont une grande dépendance, ils sont souvent stigmatisés, risquent d'isolement et manque d'inclusion.
WHH intègre la protection transversale en consultant les différents groupes de personnes, en répondant à leur besoins spécifiques, en mettant ces populations au centre dela réponse et en les impliquant dans les différentes activités en fonction de leurs capacités ainsi qu'en tenant compte des rôles et dynamiques de pouvoir en cherchant à réduire les barrières sociales liées au genre et à la discrimination.
WHH intègre également la participation et la redevabilité dans les différentes phases du cycle de projet. Les représentants des communautés feront partie du mécanisme de redevabilité en collectant les feedbacks et les plaintes. Des comités au niveau de chauque commune d'intervention seront directement en liaison avec le responsable de la redevabilité auprès du bureau pays de WHH. Des réunions périodiques seront instaurées avec les autorités locales, les services techniques décentralisés et les représentants des bénéficiares pour la restitution des réalisations du projet et les avancements relatifs aux différentes plaintes et recommendations reçues de la part des communautés.
Ces stratégies de cohésion sociale, de protection transversales et de participation des acteurs permettrons de réduire les risques et d'améliorer la qualité de la réponse humanitaire en tenant compte du principe de Do No Arm.
Dans le cadre du Nexus, WHH se coordonne tant avec les acteurs d'urgence que de Développement.
