To save lives and alleviate suffering Improved food security and dietary diversity of vulnerable conflict affected and food insecure populations Although the formation of transitional government of national unity in February 2020 resulted in improved security however the subsequent shocks including COVID-19, flooding, inter-communal violence and political conflict in part of country continue to exacerbate the already fragile humanitarian context in South Sudan. The livelihood and food insecurity was prompted by years of conflict, climate shocks, wrecked economy and extreme poverty. According to the IPC situation analysis released on 18, December 2020, an estimated 6.35 million people (52.6% of the population) faced Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worst acute food insecurity, over two million faced Emergency (IPC Phase 4) acute food insecurity and 24,000 people were likely in Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5). The projection for the lean session estimate that over 60% of population will likely to be in IPC Phase 3 or worse.

The proposed FSL interventions aim to improve food production, strengthen the household’s ability to enhance their productive assets, create livelihood opportunities, build resilience and contribute toward overall improved nutrition status of the affected communities. Concern will support vulnerable IDP, returnee and host community households with emergency access to agricultural and fishing inputs to improve food production and access to nutritious foods. In Aweil West and Aweil North, NBeG, Concern will continue to provide access to seeds, agriculture tools and crop production through block farming as well as technical support and training on seed multiplication and seed saving. Community Agricultural Extension Workers and lead farmers will be supported to train vulnerable farmers on Climate Smart Agriculture, bio-pesticide production and post-harvest handling. Concern will support dry season vegetable production to support income generation opportunities and access to nutritious foods. In Juba IDP camp and Bentiu PoC, Concern will build on its approach of nutrition gardens to support improving dietary diversity through training lead mothers on sack gardening where space is limited in IDP/PoC sites and they will train Mother-to-Mother Support Groups. Focus will be on households with members in OTP and TSFP. In Rubkona and Guit, Concern having supported vegetable gardens to improve access to nutritious foods will expand its FSL interventions considering the gaps in FSL support and most of the population being dependent on food assistance. Vegetable production and fishing will be supported to provide income generation opportunities and increase dietary diversity. Considering asset depletion, crop losses due to flooding, inflation and limited access to livelihood, hunger  is expected to deepen due mainly to depleted food stocks and high food prices therefore Concern in partnership with WFP in NBeG continue to provide emergency food assistance through General Food Distribution, School Feeding Program and Cash/Food for Asset program.

To save lives and alleviate suffering Improving access to inclusive and quality primary education in protective and inclusive learning environments for children in the Far North region, Cameroon. The project “Improving access to inclusive and quality primary education in protective and inclusive learning environments for children in the Far North region, Cameroon” is proposed to support children out of school and those at risk of dropping out as a direct result of the attacks on education (children, teachers, parents, school infrastructure, etc.) and insecurity. The actions will focus on creating and maintaining the protective learning environment for children and teachers, as well as strengthening their knowledge and skills cope with threats and attacks; special focus will also be put on developing and expanding relevant non-formal and informal education opportunities for the adolescents. Cash transfer as a modality will also be applied to support parents and communities in enrolling and retaining their children in school and learning centers. 
The project will target children, girls and boys (3-18 years) affected by the crisis in the Far-North Region, particularly in Mayo-Sava, Mayo-Tsanaga and Logone-and-Chari divisions.
This project is designed to carry out activities in collaboration with the Ministry of Basic Education aimed at ameliorating the situation of children with focus on education in emergencies.  
Equitable access to safe and protective learning environments shall be facilitated through the Construction (classrooms, latrines and water points), school facilities built and used by all students, girls and boys, including children living with disabilities.
Access to quality alternative education adapted to the needs of girls and boys (3-18 years old) who are out of school because of the crisis shall be reinforced through learning or training activities.
Rights of girls and boys shall be protected from immediate and future threats through access to conflict-sensitive education, disaster and conflict risk reduction, strengthening psychosocial coping and protecting schools from attack.

To save lives and alleviate suffering Emergency lifesaving interventions for most vulnerable affected populations in IPC phase 4 and 5 to meet food and livelihoods needs The proposed HRP 2021 intervention will target locations with IPC 4 and 5 with emergency food security and livelihoods assistance for the most vulnerable populations affected by shocks including floods and conflict, which has contributed to the elevation of food security outcomes to include Famine Likely. The convergence of shocks including floods, conflict and hyperinflation of prices for basic commodities compounded with the social and economic impacts of COVID-19 have increased the population's vulnerability deepening the humanitarian situation. The proposed interventions are aligned to cluster objectives 1: Provide food assistance to prevent famine and improve food consumption, dietary diversity and coping strategies for vulnerable populations (in IPC 5, 4 & some 3 and 2), and 2: Enhance and sustain emergency food production through complementary vegetable and crop livelihood inputs, fishing and livestock support. The delivery of the assistance will be via two modalities (IRRM and static operations) in the proposed locations: Jonglei (Akobo, Nyirol) and Greater Pibor Administrative areas (Pibor). 

With the impact of interwoven shocks, the population of South Sudan is in dire support of humanitarian assistance. Years of conflict have ravaged the country and the population's resilience capacity to withstand shocks without humanitarian assistance has been depleted. As a consequence of the conflict, there are multi-dimensional outcomes which have aggravated the suffering of the most vulnerable households and communities, who have been exposed to recurrent inter-communal violence due to a security vacuum, limited access to food due to reduced farming capacity as a result of displacement and depleted households farming inputs (seeds). The prices of commodities have skyrocketed due to devaluation of the local currency and limited flow of supplies due to insecurity as well as physical inaccessibility resulting from poor road networks. The proposed HRP project is designed to ensure the most vulnerable households have access to immediate food and livelihood assistance to avert the worsening food security outcomes in IPC phase 4 and 5. The proposed interventions will focus on livelihoods assistance and access to food. Livelihood assistance will be implemented for the main season and dry season to ensure continuous production of food at household level, to enable vulnerable households and communities meet their dietary needs. The proposed activities are designed to achieve the objectives of the HRP 2021. The interventions will integrate safe programming principles of Do No Harm, COVID-19 SOPs, and ensure Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP). 

The project will be implemented by Oxfam directly but in close coordination with key Clusters, including FSL cluster, TWGs AAP and partners operational in targeted project locations. At field level, the coordination will be with county line departments of agriculture and fisheries and other stakeholders. This coordination will be of essential importance to ensure that the project delivery consistent with AAP principles, avoidance of duplication of exclusion of vulnerable communities. The project will pay attentions to other cross cutting issues in delivery of the assistance such as safe programming with Do No Harm lenses, Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse, inclusion of other groups such as disability and conflict sensitive programming.

To save lives and alleviate suffering Amelioration de  l'acces  a l'education et a  la formation professionnelle des enfants, jeunes et des femmes  vulnerables  des regions de Tahoua et Maradi Ce projet vise d'une part,  a améliorer l’Environnement d’apprentissage sûrs et protecteur pour  15 360  enfants  dont  7680 filles et garçons, 645 handicapes  affectés par les crises humanitaires  pour leur bien-être physique et psychosocial  et d'autre part a renforcer la  résilience des écoles, enfants, et des communautés à travers le développement des plans de préparation et de réponses aux risques conjointement élaborés par la communauté éducatives (élèves, enseignants, CGDES) dans les regions de Maradi et Tahoua.  il s'agira aussi de promouvoir l’accès à des offres innovantes  d’éducation inclusive et de qualité pour les garçons et filles de 4 à 17 ans affectés par les crises avec un accent particulier sur le développement professionnel de 307 enseignants retournés, déplacés et réfugiés dans les 51 ecoles ou  centres de regroupement des ecoles.
La reponse aux besoins de ces   15 360  enfants filles et garcons, 307 enseignantes et enseignants,  familles  touchees par les  differentes crises securiatires et sanitaires se  fera en terme  d'appui en infrastrures d'acces,  mobiles ou fixes,  par l'amelioration de l'environnement d'apprentissage sur, invclusif, securisant et portecteur qui favorise la protection et le bien-être congnitif, emotionnel et psychosocial des apprenants, particulierement les filles,  des enseignants et des autres personnels de l'education. Une place de choix sera accordee a la formation des eneignants, la  gestion des risques et de catastrophe par la mise en place des plans de prévention, de préparation et de réponse aux risques de catastrophes et de conflits armés et de la COVID 19, soutien  aux familles vunerables surtout les femmes.  Parallement,  la reponse  sera axee sur  des offres éducatives formelle et non formelle innovantes  de qualité  et des opportunités de formation professionnelle pour les enfants retournés, déplacés, réfugiés et des communautés d’accueil vulnérables.   Enfin, le projet appuyera les centres de regoupement des ecoles pour leur assurer les minmums de conditions d'ensEIgnement et d'apprntissage et leur  suivi par les encadreurs pedagogiaues.

Food and nutrition assitance to crisis-affected local populations and refugees (part of ECHO/-AF/BUD/2020/91001) Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP camps, and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity.

WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying  mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan. 

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities, or other solution. 

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19 have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

Chad - OCHA Office Renforcement de la coordination et du plaidoyer humanitaire au Tchad Le projet vise à renforcer le rôle de OCHA dans la mise en œuvre de son mandat et son rôle auprès des partenaires humanitaires et gouvernementaux au niveau des fonctions coordination, gestion de l’information et plaidoyer. Le bureau national d’OCHA à N’Djaména et ses trois sous-bureaux régionaux à l’Est (Abéché) au Sud (Goré) et la province du Lac (Baga Sola) mettent l’accent sur l’opérationnalisation de ses fonctions y compris en assurant une lien entre les activités humanitaires et de développement (nexus) en vue de promouvoir une solution durable visant à ne pas perpétuer une situation de dépendance humanitaire. Dans le cadre de cette nouvelle façon de travailler outre l’opérationnalisation du nexus, le lien avec les objectifs commun des programmes développement, paix et sécurité sera mis en avant. L’accent est aussi mis sur le renforcement de la coordination civilo-militaire afin de faciliter l’accès et la protection des civils.

Le projet a pour but de renforcer la coordination d’une réponse humanitaire rapide et efficace afin de sauver des vies et protéger les personnes affectées par les situations de crises au Tchad. Une coordination humanitaire rapide et correctement évaluée au niveau des besoins de la population affectée permettra aux acteurs humanitaires de mieux identifier et répondre aux besoins humanitaires, de renforcer la préparation de réponse aux urgences à travers le renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et plus spécifiquement l‘Equipe humanitaire pays, la coordination inter-clusters, la coordination civilo-militaire, les clusters et les mécanismes de coordination au niveau de terrain.
Le projet vise aussi à assurer le plaidoyer humanitaire à travers l’analyse des besoins faites par l’ensemble de la communauté humanitaire et ses partenaires en vue une compréhension commune des problématiques auxquels fait face le Tchad, ses causes profondes, l’impact sur les populations. OCHA jouera un rôle clé dans la création d'espaces de collection et d'analyse et gestion d’informations, pour assurer une stratégie de réponse coordonnée menant à des actions humanitaires répondant aux besoins les plus aigus et être mieux préparé face aux urgences soudaines. Le projet permettra également d’assurer conjointement avec la communauté humanitaire le plaidoyer en faveur du respect des principes humanitaires, de la protection des civils, de l'accès humanitaire et pour la mobilisation et l'allocation efficace de ressources humanitaires.

Un accent a été mis sur la mise en œuvre des plans d’action de la redevabilité envers les populations affectées (AAP), la PSEA et la préparation aux urgences en plus d'intégrer une attention au genre et de renforcer la centralité de la protection.
Un plaidoyer pour plus de visibilité des résultats tangibles au niveau de la réponse facilitant la mobilisation de ressources pour les différentes crises au Tchad (mouvement de population – crise du Bassin du Lac Tchad, insécurité alimentaire et malnutrition, urgences sanitaires) est aussi défini comme une priorité dans ce projet 

OCHA continuera de jouer également un rôle moteur dans le renforcement du lien entre les acteurs humanitaires et de développement et la transformation de la réponse humanitaire, en lien avec les engagements pris au Sommet humanitaire mondial de 2016 et ceci à travers la nouvelle façon de travailler (NWOW) et le renforcement de l’utilisation de la modalité de transfert monétaire.

Mali - OCHA Office Renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et de plaidoyer pour la protection humanitaire et l’assistance aux populations les plus vulnérables au Mali. 
La situation humanitaire demeure complexe et instable, principalement en raison des conflits armés et intercommunautaires dans les régions du Centre et du Nord. Le retard dans la mise en œuvre de l’Accord pour la paix et la réconciliation au Mali paraphé en juin 2015 et dans le processus de désarmement, démobilisation, réintégration (DDR) contribuent à la persistance de l’instabilité sécuritaire dans les régions de Kidal, Gao, Ménaka, Tombouctou, Ségou et Mopti ainsi qu’à l’aggravation des tensions sociales. A cause des activités des acteurs armés, l’accès humanitaire demeure difficile mais fluide dans certaines zones. 

La présence limitée de l’État et l’insécurité dans ces régions demeurent l’un des facteurs clés obligeant les civils à fuir leurs communautés. La grogne sociale qui a conduit au changement de régime en août 2021 prouve l’inaccessibilité des populations maliennes aux services sociaux de base et l’aggravation de leur vulnérabilité à laquelle s’ajoute le poids de la pandémie de COVID-19. 

Le nombre de Personnes Déplacées Internes (PDI) a atteint la barre des 311,191 en octobre 2020 en comparaison aux 199 385 enregistrés à la même période en 2019 et 80 302 en 2018.  Les risques et les besoins de protection des populations fuyant leurs communautés sous la pression de la violence armée ou des tensions intercommunautaires, sont élevés. De graves abus et attaques contre les personnes, les biens et les services (écoles, centres de santé) sont régulièrement signalées alors que l’accès aux services appropriés est compromis. Comme les déplacements internes sont de longue durée, les risques de protection et les violations des droits fondamentaux augmentent, en particulier pour les plus vulnérables (femmes, enfants, personnes âgées, personnes handicapées ou malades). De graves conséquences humanitaires ont donc été notées, telles que des taux élevés d’insécurité alimentaire et de malnutrition ainsi que le faible accès aux services sociaux de base.

Avec près de 4,7 millions de personnes affectées par l’insécurité alimentaire, dont 2,3 millions personnes avec des besoins d’assistance d’urgence, l’année 2020 a été, selon les résultats des exercices du Cadre Harmonisé (CH), l’année la plus fortement marquée par l’insécurité alimentaire depuis 2014. Les conséquences de cette détérioration resteront perceptibles sur le niveau de vie de populations en 2021. Les capacités de réponse existantes au Mali représentent environ 200 organisations humanitaires, acteurs du développement ainsi que des forces militaires (MINUSMA, Forces maliennes de défense et de sécurité, Barkhane, Mission européenne de formation, G5 Sahel). Le contexte susmentionné exigera une coordination efficace et la présence d’OCHA demeure très importante. OCHA maintiendra sa présence à Bamako, Mopti, Tombouctou et Gao ainsi que son antenne de Ségou tout en couvrant à distance les régions de Taoudénit, Ménaka, Kidal et les régions du sud.

Sept clusters actifs (Éducation, Sécurité alimentaire, Santé, Nutrition, Protection, Abris/BNA et WASH), des sous-clusters et des groupes de travail spécialisés (Accès, CMCoord, Redevabilité, Genre et Cash) sont en place au niveau national et local. Aid to victims of conflict in Somalia Cash and livelihoods assistance to households facing crisis and emergency Save the Children (SC) aims to provide support in line with the spectrum of the Somalia food security cluster strategic objectives of:
1.	Improved Access to Food and Safety Nets (IASN): SC will provide unconditional unrestricted cash assistance and food vouchers where appropriate to improve access to immediate food needs for the most vulnerable and marginalized households with emphasis on pregnant and lactating women (PLW), HHs with U2 and U5 children and households with disability. The cash transfer will be delivered through mobile money platform to minimize protection risks. 
2.	Protecting and restoring livelihoods related to food security and income sources. SC will provide livelihood inputs to the two main sources of livelihoods in Somalia i.e. crop and livestock agriculture. In the crop agriculture sector; seed inputs, tools, agriculture trainings, tillage hours, rehabilitating main agriculture related infrastructure e.g. canals will be done while in livestock agriculture, livestock treatment, provision of water and restocking where and when is possible. 
    
Save the Children adopted mobile money transfer back in 2014 and in Somalia context Mobile money is a feasible transfer mechanism for a number of reasons, including wide community acceptance and strong private entities (eg Hormuud, Golis and Somtel), efficient and timely and fast set up, and safe and secure means for HHs to receive and manage cash transfers. Across Somalia in general, and in proposed program areas specifically, mobile money is a mechanism widely accepted for payments with a broad array of vendors operating as mobile money agents. According to findings from SC post distribution monitoring, shops and cash-out agents are generally available within a 30 minute to 1-hour walk for most HHs, with the exception of pastoralists who might take longer pending their location. Beneficiaries are able to both cash-out their accounts, or but make direct purchases through mobile money without cashing out, depending on their preferences.
Mobile money enables a timely and efficient transfer for cash to target as it restricts the shop/vendor and food commodities to be transferred to beneficiaries. It also offers improved safety and security compared to in-kind or cash transfers, which can expose HHs and women, as primary beneficiaries, to greater risk. It also minimizes unnecessary beneficiary movement and profiling at the point of payment. 

SC will mobilize and sensitize mothers through IYCF sessions on how to utilize cash received to purchase quality and variety of foods for better nutrition outcomes for children, particularly in the first 1,000 days, as the primary cash recipients. SC will also carry out other bulk messaging on Fraud awareness creation, cash diversion and COVID-19 awareness messages to take advantage of the larger reach of cash transfer beneficiaries.
Cash programing will enable HHs to purchase preferred foods (rice, sorghum and wheat) from a wide number of shops and markets while also strengthening local drought-affected shops and markets, with a potential broader impact on markets than voucher programming, which typically works with only a few commodities and or vendors. In addition, cash is most appropriate to address reduced purchasing power through improved food access, while also increasing demand in local markets with resultant stimulation of market growth and increase of trading opportunities. 
SC has been monitoring the market situation at key markets (both intervention and supply markets) in all target regions since June 2018.

To save lives and alleviate suffering Improving access to emergency life-saving  and  sustainable WASH services to vulnerable IDPs and host communities in Gedo, Somalia The proposed project will improve access to sustainable WASH services namely safe water, sanitation facilities and promote good hygiene practices for 7,846 female and 7,539 male beneficiaries in underserved and hard-to-reach villages and IDP camps in Belet Xawa, Dollow, Garbaharey and Luuq districts in Gedo. Among the target beneficiaries will be 2,308 persons with disabilities (1177 male, 1131 female).
The below-average rainfall forecast for the upcoming Deyr season (Oct to Dec) which may be compounded by a harsh Jilaal dry season in 2021 calls for a greater focus on WASH and a re-prioritization of life-saving approaches in Gedo. Access to improved water sources remains low in Gedo with a significant portion of the population relying on the rivers and other seasonal streams as their primary water sources. A joint multi-sectoral assessment led by Trócaire in Dollow riverine communities in December 2019 indicated that 90% of households consume untreated water from the Juba river. The same assessment identified poor latrine coverage as a challenge, with 80% of the population lacking access to latrines. This results in wider open defecation, which is suspected to be one of the factors contributing to the frequent occurrence of diarrheal diseases in the area. A detailed site assessment by REACH in February 2020 further reported widespread open defecation at 64 and 100 percent respectively in assessed sites in Luuq and Dollow. The most severely affected community members are women and girls, who are often forced to use nearby bushes, putting them at a greater risk of SGBV. The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has further compounded WASH needs in communities, with Trocaire noting serious gaps in knowledge, skills and resources to prevent and control the pandemic especially in IDP and rural communities. 
The project aims to contribute to the achievement of specific objectives of the WASH cluster: delivering life-saving WASH assistance to reduce acute needs, and restoring access to safe and equitable basic WASH services in target locations. This will be done through the construction of one (1) solar powered shallow well with piping to communities in Dollow, rehabilitation of one flood-damaged water system in Dollow and provision of Genset, construction of 110 permanent gender-sensitive latrines with handwashing stations, desludging of 85 latrines, hygiene promotion sessions with distribution of hygiene kits, and environmental cleanup campaigns. In addition, Trocaire will conduct water testing and treatment of water facilities in target locations, and conduct trainings and refresher trainings for representative Water Management Committees while equipping them with tools necessary for effective management of water points. Trocaire will collaborate with Somali Humanitarian Relief Action (SHRA) and Active in Development Aid (ADA), national NGOs with strong experience in implementing WASH projects in Gedo, in delivery of this project in the four target districts.
Trocaire shall work closely with local partners identified to promote protection of beneficiaries and ensure access to services especially for people living with disabilities. The Water Management Committees will particularly be sensitized on inclusivity in water access for people with disabilities and their families. Hygiene promotion outreach teams will be trained to identify and deliver services in homes with people living with disabilities. Gender inclusivity will be ensured through creation or support to adequately representative community structures, as well as working closely with women groups in target location. All data collected will be dis aggregated by gender, age and disability, to inform adaptive programming in meeting the different needs of the different social groups reached.

Ce projet compte apporter une réponse à 5600 bénéficiaires à travers les axes suivants :

Le premier axe de la réponse se focalisera sur la réalisation/Réhabilitation des points d’eau avec la mise en place (ou redynamisera) des comités de gestion des points d’eau (avec 50% de femmes). NRC formera des artisans réparateurs pour assurer la maintenance des ouvrages et l’octroi de kits de maintenance pour la gestion durable de ces ouvrages. Food Assistance (USAID/BHA) Food & Cash-based Assistance for Vulnerable Populations in Somalia for 2021 Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas.  As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation.  The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of a La Niña that is currently developing (75 percent chance through Feb 2021). Potential drought conditions will likely develop as a result of below average 2020 Deyr (Oct-Dec), a harsh 2021 dry Jilaal (Jan-Mar) season and a possible delay and/or poor performance of the 2021 Gu (Apr-Jun). 

Continued emergency relief alongside a further scale up of support to increase resilience is required in order to avert the hardship situation. WFP is therefore seeking resources in 2021 to sustain the on-going efforts and enable households meet immediate food needs and help build resilience against shocks. WFP is planning to implement unconditional and conditional transfers to improve access to food under integrated multi sectoral assistance to meet needs of vulnerable girls and women, pregnant and lactating women, boys and men and leverage resources with other partners to meet the level of humanitarian assistance required. WFP will continue to participate in cluster, joint planning, assessments and regular meetings with other humanitarian actors in Somalia. WFP employs gender sensitive beneficiary targeting in all its projects and prioritizes female and single headed households. Community consultations are carried out with men and women to ensure that their voices are heard. Accountability to affected populations ensured through information sharing, surveys and beneficiary feedback mechanisms. Beneficiaries are targeted and registered through biometric SCOPE system that provides real time data.

South Sudan 2021 HRP Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2021, there are more than 314,000 refugees from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, as well as the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, including from Sudan, Democratic Republic of Congo and Central African Republic.

At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for long-term stability, some 357,500 South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since November 2017, 122,000 of those in 2020 alone. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan at this stage, the increase in numbers warrants a scaling-up of support following an area-based approach, including strengthening linkages with development actors, to help returnees and the communities they settle in live in safety and dignity, with greater security and services.

Refugees largely reside in conﬂict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction of basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.

Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will beneﬁt from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Speciﬁc protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identiﬁed at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with speciﬁc protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as veriﬁcation exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the eﬃciency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to beneﬁt from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

Mali - OCHA Office. OCT 8624 [OCT 8624];[P010182 / 7429111 OCHA programme] Renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et de plaidoyer pour la protection humanitaire et l’assistance aux populations les plus vulnérables au Mali. 
La situation humanitaire demeure complexe et instable, principalement en raison des conflits armés et intercommunautaires dans les régions du Centre et du Nord. Le retard dans la mise en œuvre de l’Accord pour la paix et la réconciliation au Mali paraphé en juin 2015 et dans le processus de désarmement, démobilisation, réintégration (DDR) contribuent à la persistance de l’instabilité sécuritaire dans les régions de Kidal, Gao, Ménaka, Tombouctou, Ségou et Mopti ainsi qu’à l’aggravation des tensions sociales. A cause des activités des acteurs armés, l’accès humanitaire demeure difficile mais fluide dans certaines zones. 

La présence limitée de l’État et l’insécurité dans ces régions demeurent l’un des facteurs clés obligeant les civils à fuir leurs communautés. La grogne sociale qui a conduit au changement de régime en août 2021 prouve l’inaccessibilité des populations maliennes aux services sociaux de base et l’aggravation de leur vulnérabilité à laquelle s’ajoute le poids de la pandémie de COVID-19. 

Le nombre de Personnes Déplacées Internes (PDI) a atteint la barre des 311,191 en octobre 2020 en comparaison aux 199 385 enregistrés à la même période en 2019 et 80 302 en 2018.  Les risques et les besoins de protection des populations fuyant leurs communautés sous la pression de la violence armée ou des tensions intercommunautaires, sont élevés. De graves abus et attaques contre les personnes, les biens et les services (écoles, centres de santé) sont régulièrement signalées alors que l’accès aux services appropriés est compromis. Comme les déplacements internes sont de longue durée, les risques de protection et les violations des droits fondamentaux augmentent, en particulier pour les plus vulnérables (femmes, enfants, personnes âgées, personnes handicapées ou malades). De graves conséquences humanitaires ont donc été notées, telles que des taux élevés d’insécurité alimentaire et de malnutrition ainsi que le faible accès aux services sociaux de base.

Humanitarian support 2021 Saving Lives and Livelihoods in Rural Somalia  Somalia faced a growing number of threats to its food security in 2020, starting with the ongoing Desert Locust crisis, followed by COVID-19 first reported in March, severe flooding between April and September and poor rains forecast for the Deyr 2020 season. Based on latest projections, 2.1 million Somalis are in IPC Phases 3 and above through December 2020. Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of the La Nina developing, which tends to trigger dry conditions in Somalia. If the forecast below-average Deyr rains (Oct-Dec 2020) is followed by below-average or delayed 2021 Gu rains (Apr-Jun), this could lead to a rapid and substantial worsening of the humanitarian situation. 

Rural populations are at a high risk of further deteriorating food security, given the direct and indirect impacts of these threats on rural livelihoods, related assets, food production and income. FAO’s proposal responds both to the lifesaving and life-sustaining needs of rural populations in IPC Phases 3 and above, against a Population in Need (PiN) of 3.1 million people prioritized for Food Security Cluster (FSC) assistance under the 2021 HRP. FAO’s planned activities will directly support 103,850 households in IPC 3-4 under both FSC Strategic Objectives (SOs), while further delivering support to protect food security in Somalia at a wider scale through countrywide animal health campaigns, among other activities. 

Under SO1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 76,300 rural households, including IDPs, in the form of Cash+, UCT and CFW activities delivered through FAO’s e-Platform for Mobile Money and Livelihood Assistance. All cash-based programmes include trainings on good nutrition practices, covering infancy to old age.

Under SO2, to protect livelihoods, FAO will provide in-kind and technical support to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security threats across Somalia’s rural livelihood zones, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to 53,500 households targeted for Cash+ interventions under SO1 (while supporting an additional 7,550 households with agricultural inputs only). FAO’s planned Cash+ activities combine cash transfers with tailored livelihood support packages to assist rural families out of hunger sooner. Alongside cash transfers, the assistance packages will protect and restore the livelihoods of households in IPC Phases 3-4 by providing: (i) farmers with quality inputs to produce a nutritious variety of food crop (cereal, pulse and vegetable seeds, storage bags, fertilizer and irrigation/tractor services, where appropriate; (ii) pastoralists with nutrient-rich feed blocks and deworming to improve livestock productivity especially milk supply; and (iii) coastal communities with a variety of basic fishing gear and processing equipment to improve catch and consumption.  

Also under SO2, in anticipation of drought conditions in early 2021, FAO will also strategically position water bladder tanks and provide nutritive animal feed blocks to protect the small milking animals of up to 20,000 pastoral households impacted by scarce pasture from dry conditions and/or locust damage. Countrywide livestock vaccination and supportive treatment campaigns will further protect livestock assets belonging to at least 2.2 million men, women and children. Preparedness for animal health emergencies will be enhanced through strategic stocking of vaccines and related supplies (PPR), and training to local partners in Livestock Emergency Guidelines and Standards (LEGS), antimicrobial resistance, disease surveillance and reporting, among others.

Humanitarian support 2021 Critical agricultural livelihoods support to conflict- and pandemic-affected households in northeast Nigeria In 2021, FAO will improve food security, nutritional status and incomes among vulnerable, conflict- and pandemic-affected households in Borno, Adamawa and Yobe states in Northeast Nigeria. The now more than decade-long insurgency has decimated agricultural livelihoods upon which more than 80 percent of the population relies as a primary source of household income. The COVID-19 pandemic has further compounded this already highly vulnerable humanitarian context, generating interconnected vulnerabilities that negatively affect availability and access to food, agriculture inputs, finance, farming land, extension services, markets and the fundamental viability of agricultural livelihoods. 
Support to crop production and the rebuilding of a robust crop value chain have been identified by FAO as key to the restoration of livelihoods and to improving the food and nutrition security of vulnerable populations in the BAY states. FAO will support vulnerable households with critical inputs for rainy and dry season cultivation as well as for micro-/backyard gardening and seed production.   
Prior to the insurgency, close to 80 percent of households in northeast Nigeria reared livestock and/or poultry as a vital source of food and household income. The conflict has caused the wide-scale loss of these assets either through looting, property destruction, disease, or abandonment when fleeing attacks by armed insurgents. In addition to being a source of income generation through breeding for sale, livestock and poultry restocking increases the availability of meat, milk and eggs at the household level. FAO will increase support to livestock and poultry production in 2021 in support of affected households.
Prior to the crisis, the fisheries sector had significant economic importance and fish from the northeast were supplied to the rest of Nigeria. With increased land and areas retaken by the military, the return of IDPs to their communities of origin is ongoing, thereby enabling some to access fishing grounds and resume their traditional livelihood. However, the lack of quality inputs remains a limiting factor for the majority of fishers who continue to rely on humanitarian assistance to meet their food and livelihood needs. By leveraging FAO’s extensive experience and capacity, conflict-affected fisherfolk households will be supported to resume their livelihoods and meet their food and nutritional needs. 
The ongoing crisis is also termed a ‘protection crisis’ with vulnerable social groups – particularly children, women and the elderly – disproportionately affected by the impact of the ongoing conflict and the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic and are at heightened risk of adopting negative coping strategies such as child labour, borrowing, street begging, basic needs deprivation, transactional sex, early and forced marriage as their families seek to reduce the number of mouths to feed in their homes, and collection of fuelwood in insecure areas, which remains a high-risk livelihood. FAO will support vulnerable households by way of fuel-efficient stoves to reduce exposure to potential protection risks, and stove production and briquette production centres for income generation. 
Access to credit is a particular challenge for vulnerable groups in Northeast Nigeria, particularly women. Through the establishment of Group Savings and Loans Associations (GSLA), in 2021 FAO will extend its GSLA programme and will identify vulnerable groups to enhance their access to credit and financial services as an important social safety net.  
FAO is the co-lead of the Food Security Sector (FSS) which plays a critical role in coordinating food security programming in the BAY states. Food security data collection and analysis are also key and upon which food security actors base their intervention. In 2021, FAO will continue to support and host the Food Security Sector to facilitate the required coordination and analyses required to reach people most in need.

Ensuring the Support for the Rohingya Refugees Affected by the Fire in March 2021 (part of 21-RR-IOM-004) Health-related vulnerabilities of Rohingya and Host Communities are reduced through increased quality access to comprehensive health services The aims of IOMs’ health interventions aim to respond to the lifesaving needs and improve the resilience of affected populations, with special attention to gender and age considerations, and vulnerable groups. In the camps,34% Rohingya refugee populations, have reported going into debt to pay for health expenses, and 27% seeking lower-quality care or medication, due to a lack of money (Joint Multi-Sector Needs Assessment J-MSNA 2020). This demonstrates some challenges in the already strained health service system in Cox’s Bazar. To address this, this intervention aims to contribute  to  i) increased safe, dignified and meaningful access and utilization of quality comprehensive healthcare services, focusing on sexual, reproductive, maternal, neonatal, child and adolescent health; mental health and psychosocial support; and non-communicable diseases (NCD); ii) improved health seeking behavior, encouragement of  healthy living and promotion of the  utilization of essential service package and community engagement, with special attention to vulnerable groups iii) measures to prepare and (timely) respond  to health emergencies, during disaster (including monsoon and cyclone) and outbreaks of communicable disease (e.g.  COVID-19 and AWD). IOM also aims to contribute to the improvement of quality of services through performance monitoring, evaluation, coordination and capacity building.

Humanitarian response in Libya -   Health (P010166001) Increase access to lifesaving sexual and reproductive health services to vulnerable population affected by Conflict and COVID19 pandemic in Libya. In 2020, 3.5 million population lacks consistent access to primary and secondary health care services. This is due to the reason that more than half of the functional health facilities in 2019 are closed due to the intensification of conflict and the onset of COVID19 in 2020. Lifesaving health services such as reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent Health (RMNCAH) and mental health services have been severely disrupted, neglected and underfunded in the past many years. The situation amid COVID19 pandemic is further compounded by lack of personal protective equipment (PPEs), delays in payment of salaries to the health care providers, and closer of many health facilities or the suspension of operations especially in maternity hospitals in urban areas. The supply chain management for medical supplies, equipment and pharmaceuticals are globally and locally disrupted and it has closed many public health facilities. Due to this situation, majority of the patients are now referring to private health care facilities, which is making out of pocket expenditure more catastrophic for the people, especially for IDPs, migrants and people living in conflict zones or along the migration routes in Libya.

This project is designed to maintain and provide emergency reproductive and sexual health services amid covid19 pandemic to 53,800 women of child bearing age, among conflict affected, IDPs and migrant population and host communities. The services are planned to be provided in severely affected municipalities / geographical areas ranked above 3 on the severity scale with a focus on un(der)served population. The project intends to provide EmONC services to an estimated population of 9,157 pregnant women. Services will mainly target migrants, refugees, returnees and IDPs and host communities in Tripoli, Benghazi, Sebha, Misurata and Sirt and people in need among none-displaced and migrants are more specifically targeted in affected municipalities or hard to reach areas of Ghat, Sirt, Murzuq, Alkufra and Aljufra.
Considering the humanitarian situation in the country, scarcity of midwives and OBGYN specialists, low capacity level and limited availability of female healthcare providers (especially specialized nurses and midwifes) to provide quality SRH services and unavailability of SRH supplies in the health facilities, there is clearly the need for a humanitarian complementary service package. The services that will be provided through this project are in line with minimum initial services package (MISP) for life saving sexual and reproductive health services of UNFPA and Essential Health Service (EHS) package of WHO issued for the context of COVID19 pandemic. UNFPA will work with its partner agencies, stakeholders, communities and local authorities for the following:

1.	Provision of Lifesaving Essential Maternal, sexual and reproductive health services to prevent excess neonatal and maternal mortality and morbidity among affected population.
2.	Coordinate Sexual and Reproductive Health Services to ensure continuous provision of essential SRH services 
3.	Provision of Essential medicine, medical supplies and equipment to sustain health SRH services
4.	Increase access to SRH services through the deployment of mobile medical teams and enhance the performance of existing primary healthcare facilities and community health workers in targeted areas of vulnerable population.
5.	Strengthen health sector and community resilience to ensure social protection and sustainable and equitable access to quality SRH services.

Humanitarian response in South Sudan -   Multisector (P010168001) Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2021, there are more than 314,000 refugees from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, as well as the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, including from Sudan, Democratic Republic of Congo and Central African Republic.

At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for long-term stability, some 357,500 South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since November 2017, 122,000 of those in 2020 alone. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan at this stage, the increase in numbers warrants a scaling-up of support following an area-based approach, including strengthening linkages with development actors, to help returnees and the communities they settle in live in safety and dignity, with greater security and services.

Refugees largely reside in conﬂict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction of basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.

Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will beneﬁt from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Speciﬁc protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identiﬁed at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with speciﬁc protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as veriﬁcation exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the eﬃciency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to beneﬁt from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

Mali - OCHA Office. OCT 9552 [OCT 9552];[QZA-18/0177, Addendum 24] Renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et de plaidoyer pour la protection humanitaire et l’assistance aux populations les plus vulnérables au Mali. 
La situation humanitaire demeure complexe et instable, principalement en raison des conflits armés et intercommunautaires dans les régions du Centre et du Nord. Le retard dans la mise en œuvre de l’Accord pour la paix et la réconciliation au Mali paraphé en juin 2015 et dans le processus de désarmement, démobilisation, réintégration (DDR) contribuent à la persistance de l’instabilité sécuritaire dans les régions de Kidal, Gao, Ménaka, Tombouctou, Ségou et Mopti ainsi qu’à l’aggravation des tensions sociales. A cause des activités des acteurs armés, l’accès humanitaire demeure difficile mais fluide dans certaines zones. 

La présence limitée de l’État et l’insécurité dans ces régions demeurent l’un des facteurs clés obligeant les civils à fuir leurs communautés. La grogne sociale qui a conduit au changement de régime en août 2021 prouve l’inaccessibilité des populations maliennes aux services sociaux de base et l’aggravation de leur vulnérabilité à laquelle s’ajoute le poids de la pandémie de COVID-19. 

Le nombre de Personnes Déplacées Internes (PDI) a atteint la barre des 311,191 en octobre 2020 en comparaison aux 199 385 enregistrés à la même période en 2019 et 80 302 en 2018.  Les risques et les besoins de protection des populations fuyant leurs communautés sous la pression de la violence armée ou des tensions intercommunautaires, sont élevés. De graves abus et attaques contre les personnes, les biens et les services (écoles, centres de santé) sont régulièrement signalées alors que l’accès aux services appropriés est compromis. Comme les déplacements internes sont de longue durée, les risques de protection et les violations des droits fondamentaux augmentent, en particulier pour les plus vulnérables (femmes, enfants, personnes âgées, personnes handicapées ou malades). De graves conséquences humanitaires ont donc été notées, telles que des taux élevés d’insécurité alimentaire et de malnutrition ainsi que le faible accès aux services sociaux de base.

Avec près de 4,7 millions de personnes affectées par l’insécurité alimentaire, dont 2,3 millions personnes avec des besoins d’assistance d’urgence, l’année 2020 a été, selon les résultats des exercices du Cadre Harmonisé (CH), l’année la plus fortement marquée par l’insécurité alimentaire depuis 2014. Les conséquences de cette détérioration resteront perceptibles sur le niveau de vie de populations en 2021. Les capacités de réponse existantes au Mali représentent environ 200 organisations humanitaires, acteurs du développement ainsi que des forces militaires (MINUSMA, Forces maliennes de défense et de sécurité, Barkhane, Mission européenne de formation, G5 Sahel). Le contexte susmentionné exigera une coordination efficace et la présence d’OCHA demeure très importante. Humanitarian response in Somalia - Multisector (P010181002) Food & Cash-based Assistance for Vulnerable Populations in Somalia for 2021 Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas.  As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation.  The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of a La Niña that is currently developing (75 percent chance through Feb 2021). Potential drought conditions will likely develop as a result of below average 2020 Deyr (Oct-Dec), a harsh 2021 dry Jilaal (Jan-Mar) season and a possible delay and/or poor performance of the 2021 Gu (Apr-Jun). 

Continued emergency relief alongside a further scale up of support to increase resilience is required in order to avert the hardship situation. WFP is therefore seeking resources in 2021 to sustain the on-going efforts and enable households meet immediate food needs and help build resilience against shocks. WFP is planning to implement unconditional and conditional transfers to improve access to food under integrated multi sectoral assistance to meet needs of vulnerable girls and women, pregnant and lactating women, boys and men and leverage resources with other partners to meet the level of humanitarian assistance required. WFP will continue to participate in cluster, joint planning, assessments and regular meetings with other humanitarian actors in Somalia. WFP employs gender sensitive beneficiary targeting in all its projects and prioritizes female and single headed households. Community consultations are carried out with men and women to ensure that their voices are heard. Accountability to affected populations ensured through information sharing, surveys and beneficiary feedback mechanisms. Beneficiaries are targeted and registered through biometric SCOPE system that provides real time data.

Unconditional in-kind food assistance to 61,200 vulnerable CAR refugees in East, Adamaoua and North Region (P010179001) Unconditional in-kind food assistance to 61,200 vulnerable CAR refugees in East, Adamaoua and North Region Through this project WFP will providing unconditional food support to 61,200 Central African refugees in the East regions. In line with WFP Cameroon Country Strategic Plan (CSP 2018-2020 extended to 2021), life-saving assistance will be provided CAR refugees in East. The transfer modality of food assistance to the beneficiaries will be a mix of in-kind distribution and cash-based transfers through unconditional monthly food distributions to support CAR refugees’ households’ access to adequate and nutritious food, therefore prevent them from adopting negative coping practices. The daily food rations will comprise 350g cereals, 100g pulses, 35g vegetable, and 5g salt to cover their needs of 2,100 kcal energy per day per person for the beneficiaries who entirely rely on humanitarian food assistance.

Food assistance to vulnerable refugees outside Detention Centres UN Other Funds and Agencies (excl. CERF) Food assistance to vulnerable refugees outside Detention Centres As of November 2020, Libya hosts over 45,000 registered refugees and asylum-seekers from Eritrea, Ethiopia, Iraq, Palestine, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Syria and Yemen. Some 2,000 migrants and refugees/asylum-seekers are being held in government-run detention centres in Libya. Of these, 666 are persons of concern to UNHCR. Libya faces multiple challenges, including low cash liquidity and fuel shortages, further compounded by lockdown restrictions due to COVID-19 earlier in 2020. The 2021 Humanitarian Needs Overview estimates that 604,307 individuals people 7,213 refugees are in needs for food assistance. 

Due to a lack of access, transparency, the impossibility to monitor, and given that, according to international law, individuals under detention in a country must be provided with the means to live with dignity by the government of this country, WFP, along with the partners of the Food Security Sector took the decision not to intervene in detention in order not to legitimize detention and provide assistance blindly where access and monitoring are impossible.

Consequently, alternative forms of assistance to vulnerable refugees have been developed and this project, targeting food insecure migrants outside detention centres, has been designed to support the food security and nutrition status of refugees and asylum-seekers while preserving them from any form of exposure, stigmatization and discriminations, ensuring their protection and promoting their inclusion within the local communities.

WFP and UNHCR have built its functioning partnership since June 2020 to provide food assistance to vulnerable refugees and asylum-seekers in Libya based on analyzed data. As of November 2020, over 17,000 food boxes have distributed since June 2020. The most food-insecure non-detained refugees were identified in close partnership with UNHCR. WFP mobilized its full capacities to provide its ready-to-eat food assistance to some 1,000 urgent cases who were freshly released from detention centres. 

Based on the built success, under the 2021 HRP - Food Security Sector, WFP will work with UNHCR and local NGO partners to maximize the impacts, outputs and outcomes for people in need, while targeting the monthly life-saving assistance to a monthly average of 7,213 vulnerable and non-detained refugee/asylum-seekers in urban settings.

Through its distribution cycles in June-November 2020 and under the separate partnership with IOM in April - May 2020, WFP experienced in reaching vulnerable non-Libyan under situations having the COVID-19 restrictions. Adaptation measures such as masks, disinfection, social distancing, temperature checks were systematically applied. These experience will be applied to this proposed project in 2021. 

The experience in WFP's food assistance to vulnerable Libyan in the past years indicates that the ratio of beneficiaries is 69% men / 31% women. For comparison, non-Libyan population in Libya ratio is 89% men / 11% women. Women-headed households are proven to be more food insecure. Consequently, the proportion of supported women is higher in this programme.

On the basis of nutrition screening, WFP will provide specialized nutritious foods for refugee children aged 6–59 months and pregnant and lactating women and girls with moderate acute malnutrition to prevent acute malnutrition. It will ensure that nutrition-sensitive messaging accompanies general distributions and is disseminated by cooperating partners, and that persons with disabilities and other vulnerable people are accommodated in dignified, safe ways.

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities, or other solution. 

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19 have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

Humanitarian response in Pakistan- Multisector (P010171001) Food Security, Livelihood, and Agriculture Support to Communities Affected by Multiple Shocks Overall, around 5.82 million people are in need of food security and livelihood assistance across 39 districts in three provinces (Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) in Pakistan, of which around one million people (17% of the overall people in need) will be targeted through food/cash and agriculture-based livelihoods assistance packages in 2021. The PIN has been determined by undertaking a severity analysis of the population in each vulnerable districts experiencing multiple shocks recently such as (drought, monsoon rains/flooding, winterized emergency, locust infestation and  COVID) which has affected their food security security situation. Based on available information, two indicators have been used to estimate the people in need: IPC acute food insecurity  phase classification, and percentage of households who have inadequate resources to buy food. The severity analysis classified the proportion of the population in each district into minimal, stress, severe, extreme and catastrophic categories, and 39 districts with up to 4 natural hazards/ shocks and pre-existing vulnerabilities are prioritized across three provinces (Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) in Pakistan. Thus, the final PIN is estimated based on the proportion of the people in JIAF severity level 3 and above and considering the experience of recent multiple natural hazards/shocks and pre-existing vulnerabilities.
Of the 5.82 million people in need, most of them are in 12 districts in Sindh province (2.75 million), primarily because of their exposure to multiple shocks ( monsoon rains/floods 2020, locust 2019-2020, drought 2018-2019), and being in JIAF severity level three and above. Similarly, in Balochistan, around 1.9 million people are in need in 14 districts, because of experience of multiple emergencies such as drought 2018-19, monsoon rains/floods 2020, flash floods/snow 2020, and locust 2019-20). In KP  province, 1.17 million people are in need in 13 newly merged areas and they experienced conflict, displacement, instability in the past and recently locust infestation. The most-affected population groups are refugees, Temporary Displaced Persons (TDPs), and Returnees, people living in districts with a high risk of recurrent natural disasters, migrants (Afghan Citizen Card Holders, Undocumented Afghans), poor and food-insecure households, small farmers and livestock holders, daily wage-earners and small businesses, under-five malnourished children, malnourished pregnant and lactating women, persons with disabilities, and elderly population. The combined effects of multiple shocks and food insecurity vulnerabilities are adverse on the most vulnerable groups owing to their inability to meet their food consumption and other basic needs and over-reliance on negative coping strategies.

Emergency assistance to food insecurity affected communities in South Sudan (part of 21-RR-CEF-010) Emergency WASH Response in South Sudan UNICEF will provide women, men, girls, and boys affected by multiple shocks and hazards in South Sudan with critical water, sanitation, and hygiene services, items, and facilities.  The objective of this project is to provide lifesaving emergency water supply, sanitation and hygiene promotion services for conflict affected people, vulnerable host communities and people in disease prone (high GAM famine and outbreak related) areas including protection related actions to mitigate GBV, strengthening of communities’ resilience to cope with the impact of emergencies and recurrent shocks. This emergency WASH project will comprise of situation assessments, preparedness, transitional programs, frontline emergency WASH response, strengthening of partners’ capacity, and cluster coordination including sector information management. UNICEF will deliver emergency lifesaving support by providing access to WASH services as per Sphere and WASH Cluster standards.

The project will focus on addressing the following:
- Effective Cluster coordination mechanism in the country
- Provide timely equitable access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene for IDPs/host communities and returnees, including transitional programming
- WASH in Nutrition for famine prevention with a minimum package of interventions.
- WASH in Health for outbreak control at wider community level (i.e. Ebola, Cholera, etc.)
- While implementing projects a special attention will be given to mitigate WASH-related GBV.

The project will also support expansion of partnerships with local and international NGOs and CBOs in highly affected areas to ensure basic services are provided and long-term capacity built. The activities will be implemented in complementarity with other sectors such as Health, Nutrition, Protection and where possible Education projects including disaster risk reduction (DRR) focusing on strengthening community coping mechanisms.
