Life-saving activities to protect the nutrition and food security situation of vulnerable people in anticipation of a severe drought shock. Food & Cash-based Assistance for Vulnerable Populations in Somalia for 2021 Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas.  As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation.  The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of a La Niña that is currently developing (75 percent chance through Feb 2021). Potential drought conditions will likely develop as a result of below average 2020 Deyr (Oct-Dec), a harsh 2021 dry Jilaal (Jan-Mar) season and a possible delay and/or poor performance of the 2021 Gu (Apr-Jun). 

Continued emergency relief alongside a further scale up of support to increase resilience is required in order to avert the hardship situation. WFP is therefore seeking resources in 2021 to sustain the on-going efforts and enable households meet immediate food needs and help build resilience against shocks. WFP is planning to implement unconditional and conditional transfers to improve access to food under integrated multi sectoral assistance to meet needs of vulnerable girls and women, pregnant and lactating women, boys and men and leverage resources with other partners to meet the level of humanitarian assistance required. WFP will continue to participate in cluster, joint planning, assessments and regular meetings with other humanitarian actors in Somalia. WFP employs gender sensitive beneficiary targeting in all its projects and prioritizes female and single headed households. Community consultations are carried out with men and women to ensure that their voices are heard. Accountability to affected populations ensured through information sharing, surveys and beneficiary feedback mechanisms. Beneficiaries are targeted and registered through biometric SCOPE system that provides real time data.

South Sudan Concept Note: Addressing the protection needs of persons with specific needs - Protection - Gender-Based Violence (part of 21-RR-HCR-006) Internally Displaced Population in South Sudan supported through provision of protection and targeted assistance to promote resilience, protection advocacy and achievement of solutions. The project aims to strengthen community and rights-based protection response for IDPs, IDP returnees and vulnerable persons within their host communities. The project will focus on providing physical and legal protection through advocacy, timely protection monitoring, life-saving protection response based on identified needs and solutions. The project will address Housing, Land and Property (HLP) rights issues through the provision of legal assistance, facilitate issuance of property and identity documents, and work with mediation mechanisms to support HLP related dispute resolution. Community-based networks will be utilized as part of the protection response to foster community buy in and ownership of protection. The project will use evidence-based planning to expand outreach and develop the capacity of displaced communities to cope, recover, contribute to and ultimately achieve solutions. Out of 1.6 million IDPs, 475,000 IDPs and IDP returnees will be supported with protection interventions and assistance in seven (7) states and an administrative areas. Recognising the protection concerns linked to food insecurity, the Agency activities also include a scaling-up of activities in South Sudan’s highly food insecure and prioritised locations, i.e. Pibor County, Akobo, Aweil South, Tonj East, Tonj North, Tonj South. There will be continuous advocacy and support in the area of law and policy with relevant government bodies such as the   Ministries of Justice Home Affairs, Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management, and the Relief and Rehabilitation Commission (RRC) to ensure the centrality of protection, enact the “Protection and Assistance to Internally Displaced Persons Act 2018” (IDP) Bill, National Framework on Returns, and various HLP initiatives. The relevant line ministries will also receive capacity building and technical assistance. Building on UNHCR’s existing operational presence in Bentiu Bor, Juba, Malakal, Wau, Yambio, Yei, the Agency will continue to advance on the 2020 geographic expansion of IDP activities by leveraging both static and mobile presence through 15 partners to Central Equatoria, Unity, Upper Nile, Joinglei, Western Bahr El Ghazal, Northern Bahr El Ghazal, Lakes, Western Equatoira, Eastern Equatoris and Warrap. Response and monitoring will cover 19 identified priority counties and Pibor Administrative Area, including remote or hard to-reach areas, in full support to the Protection Cluster Strategy for mobile assessments and response. Partners comprise of both national and international organizations, with selection undertaken on the basis of their pre-existing presence, access to populations of concern and capacity to carry out static and remote protection monitoring and response. While not all proposed activity locations fall under the severity 3, 4 or 5 in terms of food insecurity, recognizing the fluidly and unpredictable nature of sub-national violence in South Sudan, UNHCR’s protection by presence approach requires presence in areas affected by conflict as well as areas of potential return in light of increased momentum in terms of solutions 
Resources and advocacy will focus primarily on protection response and solutions, either durable or transitional (where the former is not yet possible), including assessments on needs, risks, and intentions and feasibility of durable solutions, while also strengthening community-based structures, supporting HLP initiatives, promotion of livelihoods and peaceful coexistence. Improving coordination and quality of assessments and monitoring will be a key component. A mobile tool was introduced in late 2019 that has enhanced data collection and triangulation of information through timely collection and analysis capabilities, which will further improve information products, leading to a more fitting risk-mitigation approach, reduced response time; while underpinning protection mainstreaming across other operational interventions, including of other Clusters.

South Sudan Concept Note: Addressing the protection needs of persons with specific needs (part of 21-RR-HCR-006) Targeted support to displaced persons with specific needs with lifesaving non-food items and emergency shelter in hard to reach areas and areas of IDP returns The UNHCR ES/NFI project for 2021 is focused on responding to the humanitarian needs of internally displaced persons (IDPs) and ensure humanitarian standards are maintained. IDPs continue to be exposed dire living conditions with limited livelihood options, the lack of access to markets and often more than one displacement.  The need for provision of basic and domestic items remains a priority. Families are often displaced without substantial household items, fleeing with little more than they can carry. Inadequate shelter may also lead to increased protection risks and susceptibility to diseases. In addition, populations in situations of protracted displacement require replenishment of assistance to ensure basic humanitarian needs are met. With COVID-19 preventive measures mainstreamed, considerations for decongestion of sites and number of persons per shelter shall be taken into account in consultation with the CCCM cluster and other stakeholders. Emergency stocks need to be replenished and prepositioned on a regular basis in order to allow rapid response to the identified protection and assistance needs. UNHCR’s material assistance will continue to be targeted and protection focused, to ensure that the most vulnerable displaced households are not left without basic material support, including the specific needs of women and girls are catered for. In 2021, UNHCR will continue to identify the most vulnerable IDPs (up to 30% of the priority target) through protection monitoring, community-based mechanisms, and outreach efforts, to implement targeted interventions aimed at reducing the burden on communities. UNHCR both directly and through partners, will leverage their expanded operational coverage to ensure protection monitoring and participation of populations of concern in RPAs, IRNA and RRM. These assessments, ES/NFI analysis tools, and inter-cluster discussions will reinforce the centrality of affected persons to decision-making, and help determine the most appropriate methodology of distribution, taking each unique context into consideration. The project will focus on delivery of timely life-saving activities, streamlining prevention-oriented initiatives including COVID-19 preventive measures, evidence-based planning, and strengthening community-based protection for capacity development of displaced communities to cope, recover, contribute to and achieve solutions. In efforts to minimize risks including SGBV, prevention/response activities will continue with a focus on community engagement, strengthening referrals and prevention with awareness raising. At the same time, there is an increasing trend and willingness of IDPs to return to their homes. It is anticipated that more development-oriented programming will be implemented in South Sudan considering the R-ARCSS, 2019-2020 UN Cooperation Framework, and the 2018-2022 National Development Strategy for South Sudan. In order to increase the absorption capacity of receiving communities, UNHCR will focus support at the community level, maintaining targeted assistance at the individual level to persons with specific needs (PSNs) and the most vulnerable. UNHCR will use its age, gender and diversity policy and ES/NFI analysis tools, to ensure the entire population is reached, the voices of marginalised members of the community are taken into consideration and the response does not place any person at heightened risk. In 2021, UNHCR aims to reach 50% of the projected IDP population equal to 800,000 persons with targeted assistance to 200,000 persons. IDP and refugee returnees often face additional challenges of finding their houses damaged, destroyed and/or occupied. The need for decent shelter in areas of return is critical to realizing transitional and durable solutions. UNHCR will work with the Protection Cluster and HLP working group to address HLP rights issues through the provision of legal assistance, issuance of property and identity documents, and mediation mechanisms.

Protection Monitoring for corrective response management Provision of multi-sectoral protection, assistance and solutions to refugees, asylum seekers and refugee returnees and stateless population and those at risk of statelessness in Somalia. In 2021 UNHCR will continue to focus its intervention on providing protection and assistance and working towards the attainment of durable solutions for refugees, asylum-seekers and returnees working in close partnership with the Government, international and national actors. In addition to 28,002 refugees and asylum seekers and 109,989 refugee returnees (of these 18,050 are expected to be assisted with return to Somalia in the course of 2021) that are estimated to be in need of variety of protection, assistance and solutions support in 2021, UNHCR will also focus its efforts on working closely with the Government of Somalia for identification and protection of stateless people, as well as prevention and reduction of statelessness. The study on statelessness is yet to be conducted, thus the scope of the statelessness is not yet known for Somalia. UNHCR will continue to provide technical support to the Government of Somalia in that endeavor.

Emergency drought response through provision of temporary clean safe water, hygiene promotion, sanitation and health care services Provision of lifesaving assistance and sustainable solutions through safe Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) services, for people in crises and their host communities in multiple regions in Somalia. IOM WASH is proposing to contribute to the continuation and restoration of access to safe and equitable basic WASH services to overall 380,000 beneficiaries from vulnerable IDP and host-communities in multiple regions in Somalia. 

Specifically, the project will target 228,000 Nondisplaced people (children 107,160; men 41,040; women 36,480; elderly 9,120 and disabled 34,200) and 152,000 displaced populations (children 71,440; men 27,360; women 24,320; elderly 6,080 and disabled 22,800). 

IOM will rehabilitate 50 strategic water sources for multi-use that will provide continued, equitable, safe, sufficient and sustainable water to regions, targeted by the cluster, prone to natural disasters. 

IOM further proposes to construct 3,000 new emergency sanitation facilities (following cluster specifications) targeting populations without access to basic sanitation and hygiene.

The project will also strengthen the capacity of the Federal Government of Somalia and Federal Members States, community leaders and water committees/technicians for better coordination with government authorities and communities and sustainability of the constructed/ rehabilitated WASH infrastructures. In addition, the project will nurture community participation in good hygiene practices through training and community sensitization campaigns.  All trainings, awareness raising and capacity building activities will follow national guidelines on COVID-19 preventive measures, e.g. on physical distancing, to avoid mass gatherings and minimize risks of exposure.

The project is aligned with protection mainstreaming to ensure safety and dignity of affected populations without causing harm. Affected populations and all relevant stakeholders including men, women, boys, girls, elderly and people with disability will be involved in decision making throughout the project activities/cycle. 

Furthermore, the project will be a part of an IOM integrated emergency response program and resilience building, where possible, efforts will be made to integrate IOM health, nutrition, shelter, CCCM and protection activities.

Facilitate and strengthen the effective coordination of humanitarian action in Venezuela (ECHO/-AM/BUD/2021/91018) Fortalecer a nivel operativo y estratégico la coordinación humanitaria y abogacía en Venezuela En 2021, OCHA en Venezuela continuará reforzando las estructuras de coordinación (Equipo Humanitario de País –EHP-, Grupo Inter cluster, cuatro centros de coordinación de terreno y grupos de trabajo temáticos, incluyendo CASH, gestión de la información –GTMI-, Comunicación Humanitaria, rendición de cuentas ante las poblaciones afectadas –AAP- y la red de puntos focales de protección contra la explotación y abusos sexuales -PEAS). Para la implementación del Ciclo de Programa Humanitario 2021 (HPC), OCHA apoyará las evaluaciones y el monitoreo de las necesidades en el terreno; facilitará la identificación conjunta de las prioridades de respuesta y el monitoreo regular de la respuesta; y contribuirá a mejorar la comunicación conjunta sobre la situación general, incluyendo avances y retos en la respuesta humanitaria. OCHA planea expandir aún más su abogacía para facilitar el acceso a las áreas más vulnerables y movilizar más fondos para la respuesta.

Para apoyar las capacidades operativas de los diferentes actores humanitarios y promover el respeto por los principios humanitarios, OCHA con el apoyo de otras organizaciones, ofrecerá formaciones e iniciativas de desarrollo de capacidades sobre los principios humanitarios, la coordinación humanitaria, la coordinación civil-militar, herramientas de gestión de la información, metodologías para la evaluación de necesidades, el HPC y temas transversales como AAP, PEAS y género.

Las prioridades dentro de la estrategia de OCHA Venezuela para 2021 son:
-	Mejorar el panorama conjunto de la comunidad humanitaria sobre las necesidades humanitarias, mediante el monitoreo de necesidades y evaluaciones periódicas, que facilite la priorización de las actividades humanitarias.
-	Fortalecer el sistema de monitoreo del HRP y publicar productos regulares sobre los avances y retos de la respuesta.
-	Fortalecer los foros de coordinación para alcanzar una respuesta humanitaria oportuna, efectiva y basada en los principios humanitarios.
-	Desarrollar la capacidad de los socios humanitarios para participar de manera efectiva en el HPC y proporcionar una respuesta más efectiva.
-	Fortalecer la comunicación humanitaria, para mejorar la comprensión de los principios humanitarios, los logros de la respuesta y la aceptación de las organizaciones humanitarias.
-	Fortalecer los centros de coordinación en terreno, para asegurar que cubran efectivamente su área geográfica, mejorando las capacidades de evaluación, respuesta y monitoreo y la coordinación con los socios y partes interesadas.
-	Acoger al clúster de Logistica, para fortalecer la coordinación entre los socios, el intercambio de informaciones puntuales sobre temas logísticos, apoyar la abogacía con las contrapartes institucionales, y promover soluciones conjuntas para mejorar la capacitad operacional y de respuesta.
-	Contribuir al aumento del nivel de apoyo financiero proporcionado por los donantes.
-	Mejorar el diálogo con todas las partes interesadas, incluyendo autoridades civiles y militares, para facilitar la aceptación y el acceso.

Provision of Emergency Shelter and NFIs in Belet Xaawo District, Gedo Region Provision of life-saving ESKs and NFIs to IDPs in Lower Juba and Gedo. The project is a response to increasing shelter and NFI needs of newly arrived IDPs and those whose shelter and NFIs were damaged by prolonged flooding, displacements due to conflict, drought, forced eviction and inability to repair/ replace them owing to their poor economic situation.

The project targets 2,600 households with lifesaving assistance in Lower Juba and Gedo. In the target sites, newly arrived IDPs continue to construct shelter using cardboard, clothes, plastic sheets and wooden stick that does not provide privacy and protection against weather elements. Women and girls feel unsafe in such shelters while IDPs living in protracted displacement situations in IDP sites, live in makeshift shelters and need emergency shelter and NFI assistance. The small makeshift structures not only compromise physical security but also privacy and leave women, girls, men, boys, elderly and people with disabilities exposed to rain, temperature fluctuations from cold to extremely hot and diseases. 
 
Under the proposed project, HAPEN will distribute 2,600 ESKs and 2,600 NFIs to newly arrived IDPs, protracted IDPs and in the spirit of inclusion and Do No Harm, to affected hosts who have been affected by drought and floods and have not received any support for the last 1 to 2 years. This will benefit 15,600 people including 5,304 boys, 4,992 girls, 2,496 men and 2,808 women. 

The project will also carry out basic site planning to reduce congestion and increase adherence to Shelter Cluster and SPHERE Standards relating to provision of essential services, access, drainage, site planning, fire safety, common areas, etc.
 
The proposed target IDP sites are located in Kismayo and Afmadow (Lower Juba), Dollow, Garbahaarey, Luuq and Belet Hawo (Gedo).

The selection criteria will include newly arrived IDPs, pregnant and lactating women, women headed HHs, physical and mental disability, child headed households, elderly and households with a large number of children under 5 years. People living with disabilities and hosts may constitute up to 10% and 8% of the beneficiaries respectively. 

A participatory process of beneficiary selection will be employed. Supporting Displacement Affected Communities through holistic and integrated Housing, Land and Property solutions in Kismayo, Jubaland. Facilitating recovery and durable solutions through protection and HLP interventions Recovery and the pursuit of durable solutions remain a daunting prospect as local communities across Somalia continue to grapple with the legacy of decades of war. The challenges confronting displaced communities in Somalia are entrenched and cumulative. While meaningful strides are being made by the government and international partners to address the displacement situation, these efforts are being continually reversed and/or undermined by generalized inadequate protection of HLP rights, including widespread evictions. A little over 200,000 individuals have been evicted across Somalia in 2019 alone (HLP Subcluster). Forced or otherwise, evictions have an enormous impact on the victims’ dignity, physical security, livelihoods, and most importantly, their search for durable solutions to displacement. In addition to the enormous cost in humanitarian investments, the consequences range from secondary displacements and total destruction of livelihood strategies and assets to the disruption of established life routines and social networks. 

Widespread tenure insecurity and general inadequate legal and policy frameworks remain the primary underpinning factors. Still, development-induced evictions, inability to pay rent and dispute over ownership between competing landowners are among the reasons most cited for evictions. Eviction as a problematic
phenomenon remains a foundational imperative to addressing the issue of displacement in Somalia in a realistic, comprehensive, and sustainable way. It suffices to conclude that efforts to strengthen protection and contribute to durable solutions to displacement in Somalia will be incomplete and/or undermined without addressing the issue of eviction concurrently and systematically.

It is within this broader strategic framework that the current project, which seeks to facilitate enhanced protection of displaced communities from evictions, has been conceptualized. Project services and customized assistance packages will benefit 196,100 individuals in 21 districts across 15 regions. In terms of delivery modalities and outputs, the overarching objectives of the project will be achieved through a combination of complementarily reinforcing set of actions that are framed around the following eight core pillars.

1.	Strengthening ongoing eviction monitoring systems to enhance analysis, data availability, and usability.
2.	Scaling up and consolidating eviction risk mapping to inform advocacy and response.
3.	Supporting proactive engagements to negotiate improved tenure arrangements and/or facilitating dignified relocations for populations of concern.
4.	Mitigating protection risks exacerbated by evictions by providing different forms of tenure security support to displaced populations, including facilitating the issuance of documentation at both household and group levels. Documentation will also seek to reduce risks to HLP assets on which local livelihood initiatives are dependent.
5.	Supporting extremely vulnerable victims of evictions cope with post-eviction stress (PES) through the provision of multi-sectoral cash assistance, specialized counseling, and legal assistance services.
6.	Mobilizing and supporting the government’s effort to address evictions, including robust engagement with landlords, gatekeepers, and community leaders.
7.	Facilitating access to information designed to assist IDPs access services, navigate complex procedures, and utilize existing remedies in areas of displacement to enhance their protection.
8.	Strengthen coordination, as well as the functional and operational capacity of the HLP sub-cluster.

Somalia’s population is currently experiencing multiple shocks including desert locust upsurge that started in late 2019 in many parts of the country; riverine and flash floods that affect the food security, livelihoods and safety of farmers and people living in flood-prone, populated areas and the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic that is having severe health and socio-economic impacts. Based on the cumulative, combined impacts of multiple shocks, FSNAU and FEWS NET projected in May 2020 that around 3.5 million Somalis would be in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) through at least September 2020. An additional 3 million Somalis were anticipated to be Stressed (IPC Phase 2) and engaging in negative coping strategies to meet their food and non-food needs. Analysis of household food security survey data collected in the July/August 2020 post-Gu assessment resulted in reduced estimates through December 2020. However, anticipated La Niña conditions are associated with an elevated likelihood of consecutive below-average rainfall seasons, and Somalia faces a high risk that drought conditions will develop by early 2021 while desert locusts could exacerbate crop and pasture losses. As a result, a high proportion of the population that is projected to be Stressed (IPC Phase 2) in October-December 2020 could deteriorate to Crisis (IPC Phase 3) in early 2021. The Food Security Cluster projects an average of 3.5 million Somalis to be in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) through 2021.

Against the above background, the purpose of the proposed project is that the food security situation of vulnerable and affected households in Somaliland is stabilized and households are more resilient towards drought, desert locusts scourge and other shocks. Specifically, the proposed project will contribute to two objectives including; 1: Improving access  to food through conditional and unconditional transfers and 2: Provide seasonal livelihood inputs support (agriculture and livestock). These will be achieved through conditional and unconditional cash transfers, rehabilitation of communal assets and agricultural inputs support. 

Target beneficiaries 
The project will target at risk and affected populations in rural areas including farmers, agro pastoralists, pastoralists and rural IDPs and host communities to whom humanitarian assistance is key to prevent them from further deterioration of their food security and nutrition situation. In total the project will target 1,450 households  (10,150 individuals) in the districts of  Owdweyne in Togdheer region and Talex and Xudun in Sool regions of Eastern Somaliland and Zeylac district in Awdal region of Western Somaliland. Priority will be given to households headed by disabled persons or elderly persons without support, poor female-headed households, poor households with malnourished children under 5 years and poor pregnant and lactating women, who are at increased risk of malnutrition. The project will be implemented between January to December 2021. 

The criteria for selection of the beneficiaries will be guided by food insecurity levels (IPC 3 and 4, based on latest FEWSNET and FSNAU analysis), Structural vulnerability or social status including minority groups, IDPs, women or child headed households, elderly or persons with disability, and families with malnourished children under 5 years

Provision of Integrated Support Through Protection, WASH, Shelter and CCCM Interventions in Beletxawa IDP Settlements. To improve the living conditions and protection of IDPs at site level in Banadir, Lower Shebelle, Lower Jubba, and Gedo Region to ensure equitable access to services and assistance of all persons in need, with a clear focus on moving toward attaining durable solutions. According to HNO 2020, an estimated 709,000 new displacements were reported from January to December 2019, mostly to urban areas, where displaced people move to private IDP sites with poor living conditions and little access to basic services. There are over 2,000 recorded IDP sites across Somalia. Approximately 85 percent of the sites are informal settlements on private land and about 74 percent of them are in urban areas according to the Detailed Site Assessment (DSA). According to the DSA, over 70 percent of IDPs in informal sites lack access to information about their rights and available services. Displaced communities, especially new arrivals, people with disabilities and women need access to information and representation in the community governance structure to make informed decisions about how to receive services and potential solutions to displacement. This year (2020), Somalia has seen serious flooding which have forced hundreds of thousands of people to flee their homes amid risks of COVID-19. According to UNHCR more than 150,000 Somalis have been forced to flee their homes since late June, including some 23,000 in the last week of July, due to flash and riverine flooding in the Southern regions of Somalia. As of 19 May (OCHA), ongoing flash and riverine flooding in Somalia has affected about 919,000 people, of whom 412,000 have been displaced and 24 killed, in 29 districts. 

The displaced people in informal sites in Banadir, Lower Shebelle, Lower Jubba, and Gedo Region are in greatest need of CCCM services to improve the living conditions and protection of IDPs at the site level. The target areas have been through successive years of drought and conflict, leaving the population vulnerable to shocks and inhibiting a sustainable return to places of origin. The displaced population in these areas are living in precarious conditions with their basic needs not met due to inconsistent service provision and exclusion with all existing coordination and management mechanisms at site level being informal, with most sites managed by landlords and gatekeepers limiting accountability and adherence to minimum standards. While ensuring equitable access to services and assistance of all persons in need, NoFYL will ensure to enhance the accountability of affected populations through community participation and consistent engagement with a focus on moving toward attaining durable solutions. 

NoFYL intends to scale up its CCCM program to contribute towards strengthening camp coordination and camp management to improve the living conditions and protection of IDPs at the site level by ensuring equitable access to services and assistance of all persons in need. All the project activities will be carried out to maximize community participation and enhance the accountability of humanitarian actors to the affected population. NoFYL will coordinate with relevant responders and mobilized towards providing sectorial assistance to those identified as very vulnerable at the site level. Together with the established site governance, NoFYL will carry out service monitoring activities aimed at highlighting service gaps, and ensuring that minimum standards are being adhered to at the site-level. To ensure that sites are safe and hygiene conditions are ensured NoFYL will provide training on-site maintenance and site planning to camp committees to strengthen their capacity, Support community-led site maintenance activities to ensure the upkeep of sites through cash for work activities, distribution of tools to site maintenance committees. The project will also support maintaining inter-sector complaints feedback mechanisms (CFMs) at the IDP site-level.

The project will be implemented in 4 regions, including Banaadir, Gedo region covering Beletxaawo and Ceelwaaq districts, and Lower Juba covering Kismayo. The project will target 60 sites in total targeting an estimated IDP population of 64,000 to be verified through the detailed site assessments.

Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan - WFP Multi-Bi Allocation 2021 - (7F-09777.52) Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP camps, and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity.

WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying  mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan. 

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities, or other solution. 

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19 have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

In response to the current water and food shortages caused by the ‘triple threat’ of drought, locust and COVID-19 in Eastern Somaliland, Oxfam and local partner Taakulo will support 43,800 rural IDPs and host communities (pastoralists) with integrated WASH and Food Security interventions in the Sool, Sanaag and Togdheer regions Life-saving integrated food security and livelihoods support for Somaliland and Puntland communities   The project is responding to humanitarian needs of drought, covid 19 and locust affected community in target locations of Puntland and Somaliland through cash injection to address the immediate food needs of the people. Cash transfer programming will be used to reach households that are in IPC 3 and above. While focusing on life-saving interventions, the project will also support recovery and resilience building of the people where possible. 
Findings from FSNAU  2020 post-Gu seasonal food security and nutrition assessment conducted across Somalia during July and August 2020 indicate that Due to the combined effects of widespread and severe flooding, Desert Locust infestation, socioeconomic impacts of COVID-19 and the cumulative impacts of previous shocks, up to 2.1 million people across Somalia are expected to face food consumption gaps or depletion of assets indicative of Crisis (IPC Phase 3)1 or worse outcomes through December 2020 in the absence of humanitarian assistance. In addition, 849 900 children under the age of five are likely to be acutely malnourished through August 2021. 
Desert Locust continues to pose a serious risk of damage to both pasture and crops at least until the end of 2020. The 2020 Deyr (October-December) rainfall season is likely to be below average to average across the country, which could lead to drought and trigger a worsening of the humanitarian situation if the 2021 Gu (April-June) season rainfall is also delayed or performs poorly.

The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the Somalis’s economy is significant impacting on poor urban and IDP households, as well as pastoralists in northern Somalia, namely Puntland and Somaliland.  External remittance flows from the Somali diaspora constitutes 1.4-2 billion USD every year and contribute 23-32 percent of Gross Domestic Product, according to the World Bank. However, after the onset of COVID-19, money vendors report that the volume of cash transactions declined approximately 30-40 percent from March to June 2020
Improving food availability through support to agricultural production in Awdal and Nugal  and introducing it in Sool and Sanag regions of Somalia is seen as an entry point to diversify pastoral livelihoods of those two regions. This plan involves also supporting communities’ recovery and livelihoods diversification interventions through livestock support with vaccination and treatment and Improving Agricultural Production/Food Security. 

Livestock production was severely affected by the drought leading to substantially reduced herds; which is the country’s prime investment especially in rural communities. The mains reasons leading to the death were water shortages and lack of pasture.  In view of this situation the project will explore fodder production combined with campaigns on livestock treatment. These include promotion of carrying capacity for sustained production. These actions will be coupled with Cash for Work activities which will be used for communal asset development linked to crop and animal husbandry. 

In times of shock and more critical food insecurity, Oxfam will utilize cash and voucher assistance to reach to the most affected households impacted by triple threats of drought, covid or locust  to meet the immediate emergency needs of at risk communities. cash is the preferred option for Oxfam to reach to people in remote areas, it is faster, sacure and easy to cover at scale. cash and voucher assistance also helps people to have flexibility on their needs and decision, choice and have multiplier effect on the economy

The worsening humanitarian context in Tigray Region resulting from the conflict between the Federal Government and Tigray Regional Administration needs an urgent, coordinated, and integrated response to save lives, contain the humanitarian crisis, and ensure people are protected. The response will focus on providing life-saving assistance, through the distribution of food commodity vouchers/cash for displacement affected population in Tigray region. The response will pay specific attention to vulnerable groups like children, women, and people with disabilities. The project aims to reach 1700 HHs (8500 individuals) with food voucher assistance.

This project will target the most vulnerable communities in rural villages of Afmadow districts that are not currently supported by other humanitarian actors with water supply and hygiene kits, through vouchers. A total of 1,398 HH (8,388 individuals) will be reached with an emergency water supply of 10 litres per person per day for 45 days. The most vulnerable 500 households from the same communities will receive hygiene kits through voucher as a one-time intervention, in addition to hygiene promotion awareness.For purposes of completeness of response and given that no rains have fallen to date, this action will be sequenced and aligned to other actions in particular those to be supported by FCDO, ECHO, UNHCR and the EU to ensure that the target population does not fall back into deep vulnerability and destituation after this Sida funded response. Coordinated consultation with multiple donors and INGOs are ongoing. Providing life-saving WASH assistance to the most vulnerable disaster affected populations and increasing access to sustainable WASH services for the chronically under-served host and displaced populations in Somalia. Project aims to provide live-saving WASH assistance to disaster affected displaced and
non- displaced population in order to reduce the excess morbidity and mortality rate from
preventable crisis-driven diseases and public health outbreaks among most vulnerable
people. The project will continue to restore access to safe and equitable basic WASH
services in targeted locations in a dignified manner. Lack of adequate WASH services to
the population is a main cause of spread of Acute Diarrheal Diseases (ADD), leading to
malnutrition in the country and contributing to increasing the existing stunting rate of
25.3% in children below 5 years of age.
Access to safe water will be increased through construction and or rehabilitation of water
sources including 8 boreholes (2 new), 20 shallow wells, 2 river water intake system with
water treatment. New borehole construction will be preceded by hydrogeological survey
and safe pumping regime will be designed. River water intakes will be preceded
hydrological study. In all cases, an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) will be
undertaken for new water sources and mitigation measures put in place for negative
impacts. All water systems will be equipped with distribution infrastructure and hybrid
energization systems. Pipeline extensions will also be made. Taps stand will be located
within a radius of at least 500m to reduce distance and enhance security of women and
girls. Project will also construct 2 major improved water dams in locations that lack other
options. All well heads will be raised at a minimum 0.5m to reduce risk flooding and
contamination. Water committees comprising men and women from all community

Emergency food aid for refugees, internally displaced persons and host communities in accordance with Strategic Objective 1 of the WFP country program (excluding UNHAS flights) Food & Cash-based Assistance for Vulnerable Populations in Somalia for 2021 Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas.  As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation.  The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of a La Niña that is currently developing (75 percent chance through Feb 2021). Potential drought conditions will likely develop as a result of below average 2020 Deyr (Oct-Dec), a harsh 2021 dry Jilaal (Jan-Mar) season and a possible delay and/or poor performance of the 2021 Gu (Apr-Jun). 

Continued emergency relief alongside a further scale up of support to increase resilience is required in order to avert the hardship situation. WFP is therefore seeking resources in 2021 to sustain the on-going efforts and enable households meet immediate food needs and help build resilience against shocks. WFP is planning to implement unconditional and conditional transfers to improve access to food under integrated multi sectoral assistance to meet needs of vulnerable girls and women, pregnant and lactating women, boys and men and leverage resources with other partners to meet the level of humanitarian assistance required. WFP will continue to participate in cluster, joint planning, assessments and regular meetings with other humanitarian actors in Somalia. WFP employs gender sensitive beneficiary targeting in all its projects and prioritizes female and single headed households. Community consultations are carried out with men and women to ensure that their voices are heard. Accountability to affected populations ensured through information sharing, surveys and beneficiary feedback mechanisms. Beneficiaries are targeted and registered through biometric SCOPE system that provides real time data.

Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP camps, and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity.

WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying  mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan. 

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities, or other solution. 

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19 have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

Increased Access to Sustainable Education Services for IDPs and Children from Vulnerable Host Communities in Gedo Region Program on Increased Access to Education Services for Vulnerable Girls and Boys in Lower Juba and Gedo Regions This project is designed to ensure that most vulnerable crisis-affected children and youth - including children living with disabilities - have access to safe, protective, inclusive and continuous learning opportunities in Gedo and Lower Juba Regions of Somalia. In achieving this, the intervention will implement a set of integrated actions aimed at increasing access and retaining these vulnerable learners in school whilst ensuring they are able to access lifesaving learning within a protective environment. The 10,000 learners (5,000 girls, 5,000 boys) will primarily be targeted from IDPs and vulnerable host communities. Of these targeted beneficiaries, the project will deliberately target 1,000 children living with disabilities, 50% of whom will be girls. The project proposes a set of integrated activities consisting of: construction/rehabilitation of learning spaces with child friendly and inclusive WASH facilities, provision of 5,000 litre water tank to schools, Enrollment awareness campaign, cash voucher assistance for vulnerable learners, provision of teaching and learning materials, incentive payment for teachers, emergency school feeding and provision of sanitary kits for female learners. Disability mainstreaming will also be targeted, to ensure CwDs are able to access inclusive education. In order to strengthen the capacity of education actors to deliver effective and coordinated EiE preparedness and response in Lower Juba and Gedo regions, the action will train teachers on inclusive, protective and socio-emotional teaching and learning and psychosocial support; CECs on school management, child protection and school safety. MoE staff at State and District level will be trained on emergency preparedness and response planning and coordination. In Gedo and Lower Juba, protection related issues have been identified as one of the hindrances to safe access to protective learning environments. These include the presence of armed personnel at checkpoints on the road to school, as well as at the school premises. GBV on the way to school and back is also another concern, in addition to lack of fences and gender sensitive WASH facilities, which particularly impacts girls’ access to education. Cultural practices e.g. FGM, early marriage and child labor also causes children to not enroll in schools or drop out prematurely. Marginalization and discrimination of children is prevalent and access to education for children from marginalized groups, CWDs and girls is being hampered. To respond to these challenges, the project will establish referral system in schools and community-based Child Protection Mechanisms for quick and efficient referrals of children with protection needs. This will include training, mapping of services and focal points within community and school (community child protection committees, School Management Committees, school Child Protection focal points); Provision of community and school based PSS to the affected children and their families through CFS, school clubs, community groups activities, procurement of recreational and dignity kits.; Case management – for Unaccompanied and Separated Children through documentation, immediate care, referrals and family tracing and response to GBV survivors & capacity building and life-saving messaging on prevention of family separation, child recruitment Risk Education, and other protection concerns- for teachers, community members, CP committees. The action will provide and support safe and free education that will help mitigate the impact of conflict and disasters by giving children and families a sense of normalcy, stability, structure and hope for the future, especially post-COVID. Disability mainstreaming will also be ensured in the action, by deliberately increasing efforts to identify barriers, risks and enablers for CwDs, and will disaggregate data by disability; consult closely with CWDs and address the additional risk they face in accessing education.

Without sustained large scale humanitarian assistance worse food security outcomes

Strengthening the Protection of vulnerable girls, women, boys and men affected by conflict and climatic shocks in Somalia Women and children are disproportionately affected by violence, emergencies and displacement, which exacerbates the protection risks faced, especially those in IDP populations who are at grave risk of exploitation, violence and abuse and are vulnerable to a range of protection concerns and bear the brunt of these vulnerabilities resulting in negative coping strategies. Groups such as women-headed households, unaccompanied children, socially marginalized and discriminated communities are at particular risk and face further protection concerns.  Many children are exposed to risks adopt negative coping strategies including enlisting into armed groups/forces and other harmful activities like criminal gangs and substance abuse among many. According to the GBV AOR, 95% of all incident reported in 2019 were women and girls while 76% of these were from displaced communities. Further, due to cultural barriers and weak protection institutions, inequality and disrespect of women and children’s rights continue with dire results such as separation of families, unwanted pregnancies, transmission of STI’s and mental disorders among others. The objective of the project is to strengthen the protection of most vulnerable girls, boys, women and men including people with special needs affected by conflict and climatic shocks by reducing risks and vulnerabilities and increasing community capacities. It will employ participatory and right based approaches, survivor- centre approach, AGD approach and community-based approach which will involve, inclusion of the target population; refugees/asylum seekers, migrants, IDPs and most vulnerable host communities in addition to local authorities in the project cycle. The project aims to build and strengthen local capacities within the community and support them to establish a protection framework to prevent and respond to violations. It will focus on improving capacity for immediate response to violations and remedial action as well as strengthening the protective environment in Somalia.On immediate response, the action will aim to address acute protection needs of girls, boys, women and men, stemming from violence, including GBV, child rights violations, as well as coercion, and abuse. Using a survivor centered multi-sectoral approach DRC, vulnerable women and girls will receive GBV services through Women and girls safe spaces, psychosocial support (PSS) and case management. To enable recovery and restore dignity of individual and community victims of violence, neglect, abuse and exploitation and to improve positive coping strategies and prevent further violations, DRC will establish child friendly spaces through which psychological first aid support will be provided. In addition, material assistance and livelihood skills training for GBV survivors will also be provided. On environment building, DRC will reinforce formal and community institutions for better legal and community-based protection of vulnerable groups from violence, coercion and abuse. Key to achieve this objective, activities will include awareness-raising and outreach among communities on protection issues, capacity building and training for stakeholders on GBV, CP and HLP. In addition, DRC will map out civil identification documentation required in Somalia to obtain/access government services such as ID's, passports, title deeds as well as birth and death certificates. The information will be disseminated to strengthen governance structures and to support service delivery to affected populations. On advocacy, DRC will strengthen coordination of protection services and enhance advocacy on protection with relevant stakeholders. Key activities will include strengthening of referral pathways, mapping of service providers and Protection Monitoring of rights violations. DRC will further identify and provide protection-oriented support to people with disabilities. The proposed action will reach 55,700persons (3500G, 3500B, 24000M & 24700W).

OCT 8682 [OCT 8682];[N/A] Renforcement de la coordination et du plaidoyer humanitaire au Tchad Le projet vise à renforcer le rôle de OCHA dans la mise en œuvre de son mandat et son rôle auprès des partenaires humanitaires et gouvernementaux au niveau des fonctions coordination, gestion de l’information et plaidoyer. Le bureau national d’OCHA à N’Djaména et ses trois sous-bureaux régionaux à l’Est (Abéché) au Sud (Goré) et la province du Lac (Baga Sola) mettent l’accent sur l’opérationnalisation de ses fonctions y compris en assurant une lien entre les activités humanitaires et de développement (nexus) en vue de promouvoir une solution durable visant à ne pas perpétuer une situation de dépendance humanitaire. Dans le cadre de cette nouvelle façon de travailler outre l’opérationnalisation du nexus, le lien avec les objectifs commun des programmes développement, paix et sécurité sera mis en avant. L’accent est aussi mis sur le renforcement de la coordination civilo-militaire afin de faciliter l’accès et la protection des civils.

Le projet a pour but de renforcer la coordination d’une réponse humanitaire rapide et efficace afin de sauver des vies et protéger les personnes affectées par les situations de crises au Tchad. Une coordination humanitaire rapide et correctement évaluée au niveau des besoins de la population affectée permettra aux acteurs humanitaires de mieux identifier et répondre aux besoins humanitaires, de renforcer la préparation de réponse aux urgences à travers le renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et plus spécifiquement l‘Equipe humanitaire pays, la coordination inter-clusters, la coordination civilo-militaire, les clusters et les mécanismes de coordination au niveau de terrain.
Le projet vise aussi à assurer le plaidoyer humanitaire à travers l’analyse des besoins faites par l’ensemble de la communauté humanitaire et ses partenaires en vue une compréhension commune des problématiques auxquels fait face le Tchad, ses causes profondes, l’impact sur les populations. OCHA jouera un rôle clé dans la création d'espaces de collection et d'analyse et gestion d’informations, pour assurer une stratégie de réponse coordonnée menant à des actions humanitaires répondant aux besoins les plus aigus et être mieux préparé face aux urgences soudaines. Le projet permettra également d’assurer conjointement avec la communauté humanitaire le plaidoyer en faveur du respect des principes humanitaires, de la protection des civils, de l'accès humanitaire et pour la mobilisation et l'allocation efficace de ressources humanitaires.

Un accent a été mis sur la mise en œuvre des plans d’action de la redevabilité envers les populations affectées (AAP), la PSEA et la préparation aux urgences en plus d'intégrer une attention au genre et de renforcer la centralité de la protection.
Un plaidoyer pour plus de visibilité des résultats tangibles au niveau de la réponse facilitant la mobilisation de ressources pour les différentes crises au Tchad (mouvement de population – crise du Bassin du Lac Tchad, insécurité alimentaire et malnutrition, urgences sanitaires) est aussi défini comme une priorité dans ce projet 

OCHA continuera de jouer également un rôle moteur dans le renforcement du lien entre les acteurs humanitaires et de développement et la transformation de la réponse humanitaire, en lien avec les engagements pris au Sommet humanitaire mondial de 2016 et ceci à travers la nouvelle façon de travailler (NWOW) et le renforcement de l’utilisation de la modalité de transfert monétaire.

Provision of Emergency Shelter Kits, NFIs and Transitional Shelters in Baidoa Providing Shelter assistance to displacement effected population including IDPs, refugee returnees and vulnerable host communities across Somalia The project will focus on improving the physical protection and dignity of IDPs, refugee returnees and poor host communities across Somalia through provision of locally purchased Non Food Items (NFIs), Emergency Shelter Kits (ESKs) and construction of Transitional Shelters through cash/voucher/in-kind modalities, through community driven or owner driven approaches, settlement (re)planning training, conducting Post Construction Monitoring (PCM) exercises for Shelters and Post Distribution Monitoring (PDM) exercises for NFIs & ESKs and participation in infrastructure mapping exercises led by Shelter cluster or any other partner.
For the beneficiaries’ selection and registration, NRC will use an electronic mobile data collection tool called Kobo tool box, which provides an accurate and real time data. The data received through Kobo is easily manageable and transferable. 20% to 30% Poor host community members will be selected to ensure 'DO NO HARM' and other humanitarian principles including humanity, neutrality, impartiality and independence. Similarly, 15% Persons With Disabilities (PWDs) will also be condisered in each project. For the provision of NFIs, each HH will be provided with a cash of $100 as per cluster agreed standard NFI kit while for the provision of ESKs, each HH will be provided with a cash of either USD247 (for ESK Type-1 with a size of 380 cm x 550 cm) or USD213 (for ESK Type-2 with a size of 360 cm x 440 cm) depending upon the area of land available. If the area available is less, ESK Type-2 will be selected esle ESK Type-1 will be proiratized.  The cash for ESKs will be distributed in two subsequent installments (50% as first installment and remaining 50% as second installment). NRC will acquire the services of local telecom companies (viz. Hurmuud telecom in South and Central Somalia and Somtel & Golis in Puntland and Somaliland) for the cash transfers. NRC will provide a complete list of selected beneficiaries to respective telecom companies for their cross checking purposes. This list will include all details of selected beneficiaries including their telephone numbers and token numbers. After reviewing and cross checking, respective telecom company will transfer specified amount of money to selected beneficiaries through mobile transfer facility.
Beneficiaries will be selected through predetermined beneficiary selection criteria prioritizing the Extremely Vulnerable Individuals (EVIs) including female and single headed HHs, orphans, chronically ill, aged and child headed households. Gender will be mainstreamed into the project through the specific consideration of the different needs of women, men, boys and girls during the design of activities. The project will ensure that all participants have equal access to resources. Monitoring and evaluation will be based on gender, age and diversity dis-segregated data. NRC will target total 75,900 individuals (50% females) consisting of 43,200 in South and Central Somalia, 18,000 in Puntland and 14,700 in Somaliland through Shelter interventions throughout the year 2021. Based on the ground requirements and assessments conducted, NRC will target same beneficiaries with provision of both NFIs and ESKs but in locations where only NFIs or ESKs are needed, only respective assistance will be provided.
NRC staff will ensure that the provided cash is to be utilized for intended purpose by coordinating with the beneficiaries and conduct follow up visits with the support of the community leaders, local authorities and the relevant cluster partners. A Post Distribution Monitoring (PDM) exercises for NFIs and ESKs and Post Construction Monitoring (PCM) exercises for Tranisitional Shelters will be conducted to analyse outcomes, the beneficiaries’ level of satisfaction and draw lessons learnt for future programming.

Mali - OCHA Office [OCT 8267];[720BHA21IO00078] Renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et de plaidoyer pour la protection humanitaire et l’assistance aux populations les plus vulnérables au Mali. 
La situation humanitaire demeure complexe et instable, principalement en raison des conflits armés et intercommunautaires dans les régions du Centre et du Nord. Le retard dans la mise en œuvre de l’Accord pour la paix et la réconciliation au Mali paraphé en juin 2015 et dans le processus de désarmement, démobilisation, réintégration (DDR) contribuent à la persistance de l’instabilité sécuritaire dans les régions de Kidal, Gao, Ménaka, Tombouctou, Ségou et Mopti ainsi qu’à l’aggravation des tensions sociales. A cause des activités des acteurs armés, l’accès humanitaire demeure difficile mais fluide dans certaines zones. 

La présence limitée de l’État et l’insécurité dans ces régions demeurent l’un des facteurs clés obligeant les civils à fuir leurs communautés. La grogne sociale qui a conduit au changement de régime en août 2021 prouve l’inaccessibilité des populations maliennes aux services sociaux de base et l’aggravation de leur vulnérabilité à laquelle s’ajoute le poids de la pandémie de COVID-19. 

Le nombre de Personnes Déplacées Internes (PDI) a atteint la barre des 311,191 en octobre 2020 en comparaison aux 199 385 enregistrés à la même période en 2019 et 80 302 en 2018.  Les risques et les besoins de protection des populations fuyant leurs communautés sous la pression de la violence armée ou des tensions intercommunautaires, sont élevés. De graves abus et attaques contre les personnes, les biens et les services (écoles, centres de santé) sont régulièrement signalées alors que l’accès aux services appropriés est compromis. Comme les déplacements internes sont de longue durée, les risques de protection et les violations des droits fondamentaux augmentent, en particulier pour les plus vulnérables (femmes, enfants, personnes âgées, personnes handicapées ou malades). De graves conséquences humanitaires ont donc été notées, telles que des taux élevés d’insécurité alimentaire et de malnutrition ainsi que le faible accès aux services sociaux de base.

Avec près de 4,7 millions de personnes affectées par l’insécurité alimentaire, dont 2,3 millions personnes avec des besoins d’assistance d’urgence, l’année 2020 a été, selon les résultats des exercices du Cadre Harmonisé (CH), l’année la plus fortement marquée par l’insécurité alimentaire depuis 2014. Les conséquences de cette détérioration resteront perceptibles sur le niveau de vie de populations en 2021. Les capacités de réponse existantes au Mali représentent environ 200 organisations humanitaires, acteurs du développement ainsi que des forces militaires (MINUSMA, Forces maliennes de défense et de sécurité, Barkhane, Mission européenne de formation, G5 Sahel). Le contexte susmentionné exigera une coordination efficace et la présence d’OCHA demeure très importante. OCHA maintiendra sa présence à Bamako, Mopti, Tombouctou et Gao ainsi que son antenne de Ségou tout en couvrant à distance les régions de Taoudénit, Ménaka, Kidal et les régions du sud.

Sept clusters actifs (Éducation, Sécurité alimentaire, Santé, Nutrition, Protection, Abris/BNA et WASH), des sous-clusters et des groupes de travail spécialisés (Accès, CMCoord, Redevabilité, Genre et Cash) sont en place au niveau national et local. Le Bureau d’OCHA au Mali continuera ainsi à jouer un rôle central dans la mobilisation, la coordination et le soutien des acteurs humanitaires dans les domaines de la coordination, la gestion de l’information, le financement humanitaire et le plaidoyer avec un accent accru dans le domaine de Civilo-Militaire et d’accès humanitaire afin de garantir la conservation et la consolidation de l’espace humanitaire. OCHA jouera un rôle essentiel dans la mobilisation adéquate des fonds en faveur des personnes dans le besoin, en plus de contribuer à dynamiser les efforts déployés par le Gouvernement et les acteurs du développement pour s’attaquer aux causes structurelles de la vulnérabilité.

Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP camps, and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity.

WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying  mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan. 

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities, or other solution. 

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19 have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.
