Soutien psychosocial (ligne téléphonique gratuite) d'écoute et de renseignement) Increase access to lifesaving sexual and reproductive health services to vulnerable population affected by Conflict and COVID19 pandemic in Libya. In 2020, 3.5 million population lacks consistent access to primary and secondary health care services. This is due to the reason that more than half of the functional health facilities in 2019 are closed due to the intensification of conflict and the onset of COVID19 in 2020. Lifesaving health services such as reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent Health (RMNCAH) and mental health services have been severely disrupted, neglected and underfunded in the past many years. The situation amid COVID19 pandemic is further compounded by lack of personal protective equipment (PPEs), delays in payment of salaries to the health care providers, and closer of many health facilities or the suspension of operations especially in maternity hospitals in urban areas. The supply chain management for medical supplies, equipment and pharmaceuticals are globally and locally disrupted and it has closed many public health facilities. Due to this situation, majority of the patients are now referring to private health care facilities, which is making out of pocket expenditure more catastrophic for the people, especially for IDPs, migrants and people living in conflict zones or along the migration routes in Libya.

This project is designed to maintain and provide emergency reproductive and sexual health services amid covid19 pandemic to 53,800 women of child bearing age, among conflict affected, IDPs and migrant population and host communities. The services are planned to be provided in severely affected municipalities / geographical areas ranked above 3 on the severity scale with a focus on un(der)served population. The project intends to provide EmONC services to an estimated population of 9,157 pregnant women. Services will mainly target migrants, refugees, returnees and IDPs and host communities in Tripoli, Benghazi, Sebha, Misurata and Sirt and people in need among none-displaced and migrants are more specifically targeted in affected municipalities or hard to reach areas of Ghat, Sirt, Murzuq, Alkufra and Aljufra.
Considering the humanitarian situation in the country, scarcity of midwives and OBGYN specialists, low capacity level and limited availability of female healthcare providers (especially specialized nurses and midwifes) to provide quality SRH services and unavailability of SRH supplies in the health facilities, there is clearly the need for a humanitarian complementary service package. The services that will be provided through this project are in line with minimum initial services package (MISP) for life saving sexual and reproductive health services of UNFPA and Essential Health Service (EHS) package of WHO issued for the context of COVID19 pandemic. UNFPA will work with its partner agencies, stakeholders, communities and local authorities for the following:

1.	Provision of Lifesaving Essential Maternal, sexual and reproductive health services to prevent excess neonatal and maternal mortality and morbidity among affected population.
2.	Coordinate Sexual and Reproductive Health Services to ensure continuous provision of essential SRH services 
3.	Provision of Essential medicine, medical supplies and equipment to sustain health SRH services
4.	Increase access to SRH services through the deployment of mobile medical teams and enhance the performance of existing primary healthcare facilities and community health workers in targeted areas of vulnerable population.
5.	Strengthen health sector and community resilience to ensure social protection and sustainable and equitable access to quality SRH services.

Emergency aid for internally displaced persons and host communities in Somalia (2021 portion) Provision of lifesaving assistance and sustainable solutions through safe Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) services, for people in crises and their host communities in multiple regions in Somalia. IOM WASH is proposing to contribute to the continuation and restoration of access to safe and equitable basic WASH services to overall 380,000 beneficiaries from vulnerable IDP and host-communities in multiple regions in Somalia. 

Specifically, the project will target 228,000 Nondisplaced people (children 107,160; men 41,040; women 36,480; elderly 9,120 and disabled 34,200) and 152,000 displaced populations (children 71,440; men 27,360; women 24,320; elderly 6,080 and disabled 22,800). 

IOM will rehabilitate 50 strategic water sources for multi-use that will provide continued, equitable, safe, sufficient and sustainable water to regions, targeted by the cluster, prone to natural disasters. 

IOM further proposes to construct 3,000 new emergency sanitation facilities (following cluster specifications) targeting populations without access to basic sanitation and hygiene.

The project will also strengthen the capacity of the Federal Government of Somalia and Federal Members States, community leaders and water committees/technicians for better coordination with government authorities and communities and sustainability of the constructed/ rehabilitated WASH infrastructures. In addition, the project will nurture community participation in good hygiene practices through training and community sensitization campaigns.  All trainings, awareness raising and capacity building activities will follow national guidelines on COVID-19 preventive measures, e.g. on physical distancing, to avoid mass gatherings and minimize risks of exposure.

The project is aligned with protection mainstreaming to ensure safety and dignity of affected populations without causing harm. Affected populations and all relevant stakeholders including men, women, boys, girls, elderly and people with disability will be involved in decision making throughout the project activities/cycle. 

Furthermore, the project will be a part of an IOM integrated emergency response program and resilience building, where possible, efforts will be made to integrate IOM health, nutrition, shelter, CCCM and protection activities.

Integrated Health Support to Vulnerable Populations in the Mudug Region of Somalia (2021 portion) Water, Sanitation and Hygiene Response for Drought and Flood-affected communities in Bari, Nugaal, Sanaag, Mudug, Galgaduud and Hiraan regions of Somalia. The proposed intervention seeks to improve access to safe water and sanitation facilities and promote good hygiene practices in an effort to improve the health status of 24,100 people in Puntland, Galmudug and Hiraan regions. This will be done through the rehabilitation of solar boreholes, the extension of pipelines and water tank construction for communities and health facilities to improve access and storage, installation of desalination machines to purify water, rehabilitation of shallow wells, and provision of temporary access to water through voucher. The intervention will also promote household water treatment and safe storage (HWTs) to improve the quality of drinking water and reduce water-borne diseases (using cost-effective and context-appropriate treatment technologies such as filters and disinfectants). 
The IRC also proposes to construct/rehabilitate latrines with handwashing stations in IDPs and health facilities to improve safe excreta disposal, hygiene and sanitation promotion, distribution of basic hygiene kits including menstrual management materials, promoting solid waste disposal, and training hygiene promotion volunteers to support the effective implementation of hygiene promotion activities and best use of WASH facilities. 
WASH services are at risk of being disrupted by the COVID-19 outbreak; the proposed intervention will address the immediate need to mitigate the spread of COVID-19 and the public health consequences of the pandemic in target locations including Infection Prevention and Control (IPC), and focus on opportunities to strengthen recovery especially supporting local communities/actors with the tools and resources needed to maintain critical WASH services in the longer term
The proposed intervention will also take into consideration gender concerns by ensuring implementation of activities are delivered in non- discriminatory ways that promote the safety, dignity and integrity of affected men, women, boys , girls and people with disabilities. The project will be designed in such a way that the water points and latrines are constructed close to settlement areas thus reducing the distance travelled by women and children (especially girls). The project will consult marginalized groups including women and people with disabilities on site selection, establishing water management structures and will prioritize inclusion of women (60%) in water- user committees to strengthen their participation in water related decision-making. The project will ensure all the latrines to be constructed in IDP camps and settlements are gender- segregated, lockable from inside and have adequate lighting. The latrines will be equipped with assistive devices such as toilet chairs and ramp to increase access for people with disability to ensure the WASH programming contribute to greater coverage and gender equality in terms of access and use of WASH facilities and services.

Fostering Resilience through Early Recovery response for the Most Crisis-impacted Communities in Syria The Integrated Response for Resilience Programme aims at providing a comprehensive response through Early Recovery support in 80 communities impacted by the crisis. Communities, particularly those most dramatically affected – and under additional stress because of IDPs returns and other displacements - need assistance in reinforcing their resilience to address these shocks as well as the consequences of the protracted crisis, and to address their needs on seriously depleted infrastructures and service capacities.
The essence of the Programme is about providing Syrian communities with – still limited - support to regain control over their basic needs (livelihoods, access to essential services) and reduce their dependency on humanitarian assistance. Prioritization of locations, is the outcome of a context analysis and needs assessment conducted on more than 5,000 Syrian communities, based on the following three criteria:
1) Hard to Reach Areas
2) Areas of major IDPs presence and IDPs returns
3) Highest scoring in the Severity Scale


The integrated response consists of the following components: strengthening of social services-related capacities (access and coverage), livelihoods creation and rural recovery, PWDs support, social cohesion/community safety, reducing gender inequality and youth marginality, women empowerment, tensions reduction and rehabilitation of basic infrastructure and public services.
The program is built in a modular manner both in terms of geographical and sectoral/thematic interventions and foresees the allotment of average 1 Million US$ per community. Hence, donors willing to support this approach will be able to pre-select certain location(s) and/or area(s) of intervention of their preference, within the 200 prioritized communities.
The programme relates directly to the sector objectives:
1. Living conditions
2. Livelihoods
3. Access to social services
4. Access to productive and market infrastructure
5. Social protection
6. Strengthening of local public services delivery capacity
7. Reinforcing opportunities and capacities for civic engagement

Enhanced access to quality formal education and psychosocial-support services in high-need areas of Northwest Syria Access to quality education and child protection services for conflict-affected children in Northern Syria  The proposed action seeks to increase the access and quality of education and PSS services in target areas by implementing a combination of formal (non-accredited) and non-formal education activities that complement each other where possible. PIN takes an integrated and holistic approach to address the Education in Emergencies (EiE), and Child Protection needs. PIN will employ a dual approach to supporting  education, including through establishing temporary learning centres (TLCs) for provision of PSS and non-formal education using the cluster-approved Self-Learning Programme (SLP) curriculum in areas with acute concentrations of OOSC – including in IDP camps and informal settlements; and assistance to non-accredited schools where education has been disrupted through providing light repairs, equipment, teaching and learning materials, support for running costs, and provision of after-school catch-up and remedial classes to support pathways into education and reduce drop-out. Specific consideration will be given to particularly vulnerable households with Out of School Children or children at risk of education disruption, who will be provided with psychosocial support and pathways for (re)integration into education. PIN takes an evidence-based approach to programming based on rigorous feedback loops to promote accountability and enhance impact. All activities will be implemented in line with relevant Education cluster tools, materials, and approaches, in addition to core INEE and Sphere standards, with a focus upon promoting safe learning spaces and essential WASH facilities and maximizing accessibility for those at risk of education disruption, including girls and children living with disabilities. Teaching and student kits will be provided to facilitate quality learning opportunities and minimise education barriers for children from low-income HH. PIN also provides ECCD classes for adult TVET students’ children from 3 to 5 years old to help caregivers overcome barriers in attending the TVET courses while providing essential support during the developmental phase of pre-school-aged children. Geographical targeting will occur through further in-depth needs assessments in areas pre-identified in cooperation with the Education Cluster. These will determine schools and communities most in need of educational and child protection support. The process will ensure the participation of relevant stakeholders to consider local priorities while also ensuring that transparency is at the forefront and that PIN is accountable to the populations in its areas of intervention. Assessments will be conducted by PIN staff and engineers in collaboration with local authorities, where relevant. PIN will target communities where education services have been disrupted due to conflict, where there is no, or limited, access to education. Experience highlights that in such areas, significant gaps also exist to meeting teachers’ and students’ needs for safe and quality learning. Throughout the entire cycle, there will be a strong focus on community outreach and engagement, including caregivers. Right to Education for All for Displaced Children in Hard to Reach Areas of Southwest State of Somalia – READ Project Integrated Education in Emergencies Response for Crises Affected Children in Bay and Bakool regions of Somalia Bay and Bakool regions are among the most affected regions in Somalia by protracted droughts, flash floods and locust swarms, causing high displacement and acute humanitarian needs. Baydhaba hosts high number of IDP (392,274 IDP) and has 110,905 primary school aged children. About 91,259 children (36,504F; 54,756M) are estimated to be in schools, while 162,239 are out of school children (OOSC) and 1,381 are IDP children with disability (CWD). In Diinsoor, 14,112 are primary school aged children, among those only 3,135 (1,163F; 1,972M) are enrolled in 8 primary schools, with 10,977 being OOSC and 226 CWD. In Ceel-barde there are 1,720 primary school aged children, with only 698 (414M;312F) enrolled in 3 public and IDP schools, while 1,032 (568M; 464F) are OOSC and 50 children are CWD. In Xudur, only 4,384 children (2,436M;1,948F) are currently enrolled in the 16 public and IDP schools, while 10,692 children (5,988M; 4,705F) remain out of schools and 151 are CWD (FCA needs assessment 09-10/20).

Major findings of FCA assessments in the four districts showed enormous shortage of accessible and gender friendly infrastructure such as latrines, handwashing facilities and classrooms, lack of learning and teaching materials, and inadequate number of qualified teachers especially female teachers. Girls face tremendous barriers in accessing to education due social norms that restrict their enrolment, retention and movement. The existing education system also reflects the persistence of these norms and does little to promote change in perception, attitude and behaviours. Children with disabilities met significant challenges such as strong stigma, discrimination and misconceptions, limited disability friendly infrastructure, poor learning environment and lack of specialised teachers trained in special education needs. Caregivers also faced with challenges in covering foods, school fees, uniforms and scholastic materials. Many of IDP children face significant health risks and psychological distress. Child protection and safeguarding mechanisms in schools are weak, due to lack of protection knowledge and relevant trainings among key education personnel. This has compromised the safety and well-being of the children, especially for girls and CWD in accessing education. 

Aligning with the 2021 Somalia Humanitarian Response Plan, Education Sector Strategic Plan and Covid-19 Emergency Response Plan for Education, the initiative aims to restore and maintain access to safe, protective, inclusive and continuous learning opportunities for crises and emergency affected primary school boys and girls in Bay and Bakool regions of South West State of Somalia. The project will put a strong emphasis on an integrated approach to education focusing on access, quality of education, protection, child safeguarding, gender equality, conflict sensitivity, and disaster risk reduction (DRR) in the design, approach and activities. 

The project will remove barriers to primary education for 7,365 affected children (3,314F;4,051M), prioritising children from the most vulnerable groups such as IDPs, girls, CWD and destitute host community children. About 736 children with disability (331F;405M) will also be targeted (10%). Particularly, 40% IDP children, 60% destitute host community children and 45% of girls will benefit from the support.
 
FCA will partner with GREDO to implement some components of the project, particularly in relation to rehabilitation and construction of infrastructure, community mobilisation and protection mechanisms in schools. FCA will engage Somalia Institute for Special Education Needs and Disability (SISEN) for capacity building on inclusion and SEN for teachers, MoE and other education personnel. 

FCA has excellent capacity to scale up the approach and apply best practice in the four target locations built on its ongoing EiE response in Bay and Bakool regions and solid expertise as a well-known and trusted Finnish education actor.

Relief Assistance to vulnerable people in Somalia and Shock Response Urban and Rural Safety Nets (ECHO/-HF/BUD/2021/91024) Food & Cash-based Assistance for Vulnerable Populations in Somalia for 2021 Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas.  As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation.  The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of a La Niña that is currently developing (75 percent chance through Feb 2021). Potential drought conditions will likely develop as a result of below average 2020 Deyr (Oct-Dec), a harsh 2021 dry Jilaal (Jan-Mar) season and a possible delay and/or poor performance of the 2021 Gu (Apr-Jun). 

Continued emergency relief alongside a further scale up of support to increase resilience is required in order to avert the hardship situation. WFP is therefore seeking resources in 2021 to sustain the on-going efforts and enable households meet immediate food needs and help build resilience against shocks. WFP is planning to implement unconditional and conditional transfers to improve access to food under integrated multi sectoral assistance to meet needs of vulnerable girls and women, pregnant and lactating women, boys and men and leverage resources with other partners to meet the level of humanitarian assistance required. WFP will continue to participate in cluster, joint planning, assessments and regular meetings with other humanitarian actors in Somalia. WFP employs gender sensitive beneficiary targeting in all its projects and prioritizes female and single headed households. Community consultations are carried out with men and women to ensure that their voices are heard. Accountability to affected populations ensured through information sharing, surveys and beneficiary feedback mechanisms. Beneficiaries are targeted and registered through biometric SCOPE system that provides real time data.

Critical livelihood support to vulnerable IDPs, host communities and returnee households and strengthening Protection, Food security analysis and coordination. Critical agricultural livelihoods support to conflict- and pandemic-affected households in northeast Nigeria In 2021, FAO will improve food security, nutritional status and incomes among vulnerable, conflict- and pandemic-affected households in Borno, Adamawa and Yobe states in Northeast Nigeria. The now more than decade-long insurgency has decimated agricultural livelihoods upon which more than 80 percent of the population relies as a primary source of household income. The COVID-19 pandemic has further compounded this already highly vulnerable humanitarian context, generating interconnected vulnerabilities that negatively affect availability and access to food, agriculture inputs, finance, farming land, extension services, markets and the fundamental viability of agricultural livelihoods. 
Support to crop production and the rebuilding of a robust crop value chain have been identified by FAO as key to the restoration of livelihoods and to improving the food and nutrition security of vulnerable populations in the BAY states. FAO will support vulnerable households with critical inputs for rainy and dry season cultivation as well as for micro-/backyard gardening and seed production.   
Prior to the insurgency, close to 80 percent of households in northeast Nigeria reared livestock and/or poultry as a vital source of food and household income. The conflict has caused the wide-scale loss of these assets either through looting, property destruction, disease, or abandonment when fleeing attacks by armed insurgents. In addition to being a source of income generation through breeding for sale, livestock and poultry restocking increases the availability of meat, milk and eggs at the household level. FAO will increase support to livestock and poultry production in 2021 in support of affected households.
Prior to the crisis, the fisheries sector had significant economic importance and fish from the northeast were supplied to the rest of Nigeria. With increased land and areas retaken by the military, the return of IDPs to their communities of origin is ongoing, thereby enabling some to access fishing grounds and resume their traditional livelihood. However, the lack of quality inputs remains a limiting factor for the majority of fishers who continue to rely on humanitarian assistance to meet their food and livelihood needs. By leveraging FAO’s extensive experience and capacity, conflict-affected fisherfolk households will be supported to resume their livelihoods and meet their food and nutritional needs. 
The ongoing crisis is also termed a ‘protection crisis’ with vulnerable social groups – particularly children, women and the elderly – disproportionately affected by the impact of the ongoing conflict and the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic and are at heightened risk of adopting negative coping strategies such as child labour, borrowing, street begging, basic needs deprivation, transactional sex, early and forced marriage as their families seek to reduce the number of mouths to feed in their homes, and collection of fuelwood in insecure areas, which remains a high-risk livelihood. FAO will support vulnerable households by way of fuel-efficient stoves to reduce exposure to potential protection risks, and stove production and briquette production centres for income generation. 
Access to credit is a particular challenge for vulnerable groups in Northeast Nigeria, particularly women. Through the establishment of Group Savings and Loans Associations (GSLA), in 2021 FAO will extend its GSLA programme and will identify vulnerable groups to enhance their access to credit and financial services as an important social safety net.  
FAO is the co-lead of the Food Security Sector (FSS) which plays a critical role in coordinating food security programming in the BAY states. Food security data collection and analysis are also key and upon which food security actors base their intervention. In 2021, FAO will continue to support and host the Food Security Sector to facilitate the required coordination and analyses required to reach people most in need.

Humanitarian Coordination and Advocacy in Mali (ECHO/-AF/BUD/2021/92074) Renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et de plaidoyer pour la protection humanitaire et l’assistance aux populations les plus vulnérables au Mali. 
La situation humanitaire demeure complexe et instable, principalement en raison des conflits armés et intercommunautaires dans les régions du Centre et du Nord. Le retard dans la mise en œuvre de l’Accord pour la paix et la réconciliation au Mali paraphé en juin 2015 et dans le processus de désarmement, démobilisation, réintégration (DDR) contribuent à la persistance de l’instabilité sécuritaire dans les régions de Kidal, Gao, Ménaka, Tombouctou, Ségou et Mopti ainsi qu’à l’aggravation des tensions sociales. A cause des activités des acteurs armés, l’accès humanitaire demeure difficile mais fluide dans certaines zones. 

La présence limitée de l’État et l’insécurité dans ces régions demeurent l’un des facteurs clés obligeant les civils à fuir leurs communautés. La grogne sociale qui a conduit au changement de régime en août 2021 prouve l’inaccessibilité des populations maliennes aux services sociaux de base et l’aggravation de leur vulnérabilité à laquelle s’ajoute le poids de la pandémie de COVID-19. 

Le nombre de Personnes Déplacées Internes (PDI) a atteint la barre des 311,191 en octobre 2020 en comparaison aux 199 385 enregistrés à la même période en 2019 et 80 302 en 2018.  Les risques et les besoins de protection des populations fuyant leurs communautés sous la pression de la violence armée ou des tensions intercommunautaires, sont élevés. De graves abus et attaques contre les personnes, les biens et les services (écoles, centres de santé) sont régulièrement signalées alors que l’accès aux services appropriés est compromis. Comme les déplacements internes sont de longue durée, les risques de protection et les violations des droits fondamentaux augmentent, en particulier pour les plus vulnérables (femmes, enfants, personnes âgées, personnes handicapées ou malades). De graves conséquences humanitaires ont donc été notées, telles que des taux élevés d’insécurité alimentaire et de malnutrition ainsi que le faible accès aux services sociaux de base.

Avec près de 4,7 millions de personnes affectées par l’insécurité alimentaire, dont 2,3 millions personnes avec des besoins d’assistance d’urgence, l’année 2020 a été, selon les résultats des exercices du Cadre Harmonisé (CH), l’année la plus fortement marquée par l’insécurité alimentaire depuis 2014. Les conséquences de cette détérioration resteront perceptibles sur le niveau de vie de populations en 2021. Les capacités de réponse existantes au Mali représentent environ 200 organisations humanitaires, acteurs du développement ainsi que des forces militaires (MINUSMA, Forces maliennes de défense et de sécurité, Barkhane, Mission européenne de formation, G5 Sahel). Le contexte susmentionné exigera une coordination efficace et la présence d’OCHA demeure très importante. OCHA maintiendra sa présence à Bamako, Mopti, Tombouctou et Gao ainsi que son antenne de Ségou tout en couvrant à distance les régions de Taoudénit, Ménaka, Kidal et les régions du sud.

Sept clusters actifs (Éducation, Sécurité alimentaire, Santé, Nutrition, Protection, Abris/BNA et WASH), des sous-clusters et des groupes de travail spécialisés (Accès, CMCoord, Redevabilité, Genre et Cash) sont en place au niveau national et local. Le Bureau d’OCHA au Mali continuera ainsi à jouer un rôle central dans la mobilisation, la coordination et le soutien des acteurs humanitaires dans les domaines de la coordination, la gestion de l’information, le financement humanitaire et le plaidoyer avec un accent accru dans le domaine de Civilo-Militaire et d’accès humanitaire afin de garantir la conservation et la consolidation de l’espace humanitaire. OCHA jouera un rôle essentiel dans la mobilisation adéquate des fonds en faveur des personnes dans le besoin, en plus de contribuer à dynamiser les efforts déployés par le Gouvernement et les acteurs du développement pour s’attaquer aux causes structurelles de la vulnérabilité.

Renforcement de la coordination humanitaire et du plaidoyer au Tchad (ECHO/-AF/BUD/2021/92011) Renforcement de la coordination et du plaidoyer humanitaire au Tchad Le projet vise à renforcer le rôle de OCHA dans la mise en œuvre de son mandat et son rôle auprès des partenaires humanitaires et gouvernementaux au niveau des fonctions coordination, gestion de l’information et plaidoyer. Le bureau national d’OCHA à N’Djaména et ses trois sous-bureaux régionaux à l’Est (Abéché) au Sud (Goré) et la province du Lac (Baga Sola) mettent l’accent sur l’opérationnalisation de ses fonctions y compris en assurant une lien entre les activités humanitaires et de développement (nexus) en vue de promouvoir une solution durable visant à ne pas perpétuer une situation de dépendance humanitaire. Dans le cadre de cette nouvelle façon de travailler outre l’opérationnalisation du nexus, le lien avec les objectifs commun des programmes développement, paix et sécurité sera mis en avant. L’accent est aussi mis sur le renforcement de la coordination civilo-militaire afin de faciliter l’accès et la protection des civils.

Le projet a pour but de renforcer la coordination d’une réponse humanitaire rapide et efficace afin de sauver des vies et protéger les personnes affectées par les situations de crises au Tchad. Une coordination humanitaire rapide et correctement évaluée au niveau des besoins de la population affectée permettra aux acteurs humanitaires de mieux identifier et répondre aux besoins humanitaires, de renforcer la préparation de réponse aux urgences à travers le renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et plus spécifiquement l‘Equipe humanitaire pays, la coordination inter-clusters, la coordination civilo-militaire, les clusters et les mécanismes de coordination au niveau de terrain.
Le projet vise aussi à assurer le plaidoyer humanitaire à travers l’analyse des besoins faites par l’ensemble de la communauté humanitaire et ses partenaires en vue une compréhension commune des problématiques auxquels fait face le Tchad, ses causes profondes, l’impact sur les populations. OCHA jouera un rôle clé dans la création d'espaces de collection et d'analyse et gestion d’informations, pour assurer une stratégie de réponse coordonnée menant à des actions humanitaires répondant aux besoins les plus aigus et être mieux préparé face aux urgences soudaines. Le projet permettra également d’assurer conjointement avec la communauté humanitaire le plaidoyer en faveur du respect des principes humanitaires, de la protection des civils, de l'accès humanitaire et pour la mobilisation et l'allocation efficace de ressources humanitaires.

Un accent a été mis sur la mise en œuvre des plans d’action de la redevabilité envers les populations affectées (AAP), la PSEA et la préparation aux urgences en plus d'intégrer une attention au genre et de renforcer la centralité de la protection.
Un plaidoyer pour plus de visibilité des résultats tangibles au niveau de la réponse facilitant la mobilisation de ressources pour les différentes crises au Tchad (mouvement de population – crise du Bassin du Lac Tchad, insécurité alimentaire et malnutrition, urgences sanitaires) est aussi défini comme une priorité dans ce projet 

OCHA continuera de jouer également un rôle moteur dans le renforcement du lien entre les acteurs humanitaires et de développement et la transformation de la réponse humanitaire, en lien avec les engagements pris au Sommet humanitaire mondial de 2016 et ceci à travers la nouvelle façon de travailler (NWOW) et le renforcement de l’utilisation de la modalité de transfert monétaire.

Documentation Renewal and Information Verification Exercise (DRIVE) of Registered Afghan Refugees in Pakistan (ECHO/-AS/BUD/2021/91020) Multi-sectoral Response for the provision of protection and assistance to the refugee and asylum seeker populations living in Pakistan Approximately 1,436,521 million Persons of Concern to UNHCR, including over 1.4 million Afghan refugees holding a Proof of Registration (PoR) Card and asylum seekers and refugees of various nationalities in Pakistan, continue to require some humanitarian assistance and solutions. 

The voluntary repatriation of over 1.4m Afghan refugees continues but has been limited due to the ongoing insecurity and instability in their country of origin and is further influenced by the peace process. They are still in need of international protection and multi-sectoral assistance with projects that consider their age, gender and diversity, to enable them to lead lives in dignity, in a protective environment.

In partnership with the GoP, Ministry of SAFRON and the Commissionerate for Afghan Refugees; UNHCR works to ensure the overall protection, security, assistance, management and administration of the Afghan refugee population residing in the refugee villages and urban areas. This includes voluntary repatriation activities and activities related to health, education, livelihoods, water and sanitation, community-based protection (CBP) and other services.

Food Security, Livelihood, and Agriculture Support to Communities Affected by Multiple Shocks (In kind) Food Security, Livelihood, and Agriculture Support to Communities Affected by Multiple Shocks Overall, around 5.82 million people are in need of food security and livelihood assistance across 39 districts in three provinces (Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) in Pakistan, of which around one million people (17% of the overall people in need) will be targeted through food/cash and agriculture-based livelihoods assistance packages in 2021. The PIN has been determined by undertaking a severity analysis of the population in each vulnerable districts experiencing multiple shocks recently such as (drought, monsoon rains/flooding, winterized emergency, locust infestation and  COVID) which has affected their food security security situation. Based on available information, two indicators have been used to estimate the people in need: IPC acute food insecurity  phase classification, and percentage of households who have inadequate resources to buy food. The severity analysis classified the proportion of the population in each district into minimal, stress, severe, extreme and catastrophic categories, and 39 districts with up to 4 natural hazards/ shocks and pre-existing vulnerabilities are prioritized across three provinces (Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) in Pakistan. Thus, the final PIN is estimated based on the proportion of the people in JIAF severity level 3 and above and considering the experience of recent multiple natural hazards/shocks and pre-existing vulnerabilities.
Of the 5.82 million people in need, most of them are in 12 districts in Sindh province (2.75 million), primarily because of their exposure to multiple shocks ( monsoon rains/floods 2020, locust 2019-2020, drought 2018-2019), and being in JIAF severity level three and above. Similarly, in Balochistan, around 1.9 million people are in need in 14 districts, because of experience of multiple emergencies such as drought 2018-19, monsoon rains/floods 2020, flash floods/snow 2020, and locust 2019-20). In KP  province, 1.17 million people are in need in 13 newly merged areas and they experienced conflict, displacement, instability in the past and recently locust infestation. The most-affected population groups are refugees, Temporary Displaced Persons (TDPs), and Returnees, people living in districts with a high risk of recurrent natural disasters, migrants (Afghan Citizen Card Holders, Undocumented Afghans), poor and food-insecure households, small farmers and livestock holders, daily wage-earners and small businesses, under-five malnourished children, malnourished pregnant and lactating women, persons with disabilities, and elderly population. The combined effects of multiple shocks and food insecurity vulnerabilities are adverse on the most vulnerable groups owing to their inability to meet their food consumption and other basic needs and over-reliance on negative coping strategies.

OCT 8579 [OCT 8579];[PARTNERSHIP AGREEMENT 2017-2020/2021] Renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et de plaidoyer pour la protection humanitaire et l’assistance aux populations les plus vulnérables au Mali. 
La situation humanitaire demeure complexe et instable, principalement en raison des conflits armés et intercommunautaires dans les régions du Centre et du Nord. Le retard dans la mise en œuvre de l’Accord pour la paix et la réconciliation au Mali paraphé en juin 2015 et dans le processus de désarmement, démobilisation, réintégration (DDR) contribuent à la persistance de l’instabilité sécuritaire dans les régions de Kidal, Gao, Ménaka, Tombouctou, Ségou et Mopti ainsi qu’à l’aggravation des tensions sociales. A cause des activités des acteurs armés, l’accès humanitaire demeure difficile mais fluide dans certaines zones. 

La présence limitée de l’État et l’insécurité dans ces régions demeurent l’un des facteurs clés obligeant les civils à fuir leurs communautés. La grogne sociale qui a conduit au changement de régime en août 2021 prouve l’inaccessibilité des populations maliennes aux services sociaux de base et l’aggravation de leur vulnérabilité à laquelle s’ajoute le poids de la pandémie de COVID-19. 

Le nombre de Personnes Déplacées Internes (PDI) a atteint la barre des 311,191 en octobre 2020 en comparaison aux 199 385 enregistrés à la même période en 2019 et 80 302 en 2018.  Les risques et les besoins de protection des populations fuyant leurs communautés sous la pression de la violence armée ou des tensions intercommunautaires, sont élevés. De graves abus et attaques contre les personnes, les biens et les services (écoles, centres de santé) sont régulièrement signalées alors que l’accès aux services appropriés est compromis. Comme les déplacements internes sont de longue durée, les risques de protection et les violations des droits fondamentaux augmentent, en particulier pour les plus vulnérables (femmes, enfants, personnes âgées, personnes handicapées ou malades). De graves conséquences humanitaires ont donc été notées, telles que des taux élevés d’insécurité alimentaire et de malnutrition ainsi que le faible accès aux services sociaux de base.

Avec près de 4,7 millions de personnes affectées par l’insécurité alimentaire, dont 2,3 millions personnes avec des besoins d’assistance d’urgence, l’année 2020 a été, selon les résultats des exercices du Cadre Harmonisé (CH), l’année la plus fortement marquée par l’insécurité alimentaire depuis 2014. Les conséquences de cette détérioration resteront perceptibles sur le niveau de vie de populations en 2021. Les capacités de réponse existantes au Mali représentent environ 200 organisations humanitaires, acteurs du développement ainsi que des forces militaires (MINUSMA, Forces maliennes de défense et de sécurité, Barkhane, Mission européenne de formation, G5 Sahel). Le contexte susmentionné exigera une coordination efficace et la présence d’OCHA demeure très importante. OCHA maintiendra sa présence à Bamako, Mopti, Tombouctou et Gao ainsi que son antenne de Ségou tout en couvrant à distance les régions de Taoudénit, Ménaka, Kidal et les régions du sud.

Sept clusters actifs (Éducation, Sécurité alimentaire, Santé, Nutrition, Protection, Abris/BNA et WASH), des sous-clusters et des groupes de travail spécialisés (Accès, CMCoord, Redevabilité, Genre et Cash) sont en place au niveau national et local. Le Bureau d’OCHA au Mali continuera ainsi à jouer un rôle central dans la mobilisation, la coordination et le soutien des acteurs humanitaires dans les domaines de la coordination, la gestion de l’information, le financement humanitaire et le plaidoyer avec un accent accru dans le domaine de Civilo-Militaire et d’accès humanitaire afin de garantir la conservation et la consolidation de l’espace humanitaire. OCHA jouera un rôle essentiel dans la mobilisation adéquate des fonds en faveur des personnes dans le besoin, en plus de contribuer à dynamiser les efforts déployés par le Gouvernement et les acteurs du développement pour s’attaquer aux causes structurelles de la vulnérabilité.

Against Nigeria HRP Improvement of the Protection of People of Concern in North East Nigeria Through the Provision of Shelter and NFI Assistance. This project will target IDPs and returnees in three affected states, Yobe, Adamawa and Borno with provision of emergency shelters, Non-food Items (NFIs), transitional and shelter repair kits as protection live-saving assistance aligned with Shelter/ NFI/ CCCM Sector strategic objectives for the HRP 2019. In 2019 UNHCR continued to effectively respond to shelter needs and aims to target a total of 69,569 households, 347,846 individuals in formal and informal camps and newly accessible areas by the end of the year. As the number of returns and displacement increases due to military operations, there is need to provide shelter related assistance for returnees who are residing in their plots and as well as for host families whose resources have been overstretched. Subsequently acknowledging that the humanitarian situation is still unpredictable; there is need to provide shelters and NFIs for life-saving emergency assistance to promote the protection, safety and dignity of affected Persons of Concern (PoCs). Despite the achievements in the past, the continuous needs for IDPs, though shaped by very different dynamics, revealed that quite a significant majority of people are living in congested camps. The needs assessment conducted in 2019 by Shelter/ NFI/ CCCM sector indicated that as of end of June 2019, 3809 IDP households were living without shelter and NFI assistance since their arrival. In addition to that, 7593 households living in partitioned communal shelters needed NFIs and dignified emergency shelters. The ongoing and protracted displacement leaves the affected people in need of other humanitarian assistance such as Food, WASH, and Health among others. In 2020, UNHCR shall build upon progress being made in 2019 and proposes to respond to unmet needs in Adamawa (Mubi North, Mubi South, Madagali, Michika, Yola South and Yola north); Borno (Bama, Banki, Damasak, Damboa, Dikwa, Jere, konduga, Gwoza, Pulka, Maiduguri, Mobbar, Monguno, Rann and Ngala) and Yobe State (Damaturu and Gujba,) through provision of; - (1) 7,000 Emergency shelters (2) 52,129 NFIs kits to IDPs in both formal and informal camps (3) 10,440 Shelter repair kits to returnees with the provision of conditional CASH component of NGN 30,000 Naira adequate to cover for the cost labor and molding of mud bricks among other unforeseen needs. All the shelters are designed to cater for Women, Men, Girls and boys, persons with specific needs and partitioned to mitigate SGBV cases. The selection of beneficiaries will be based on needs assessment and vulnerability screening in the locations at the time of implementation. Identification and verification of beneficiaries are guided by UNHCR’s Protection principles, and endorsed by community leaders, NEMA, and SEMA officials at LGA areas. UNHCR will reinforce a transparent process of beneficiary selection and the prioritization of needs of vulnerable groups. The project targets the IDPs and Returnees households suffering from protracted displacement and returning home. UNHCR will work to ensure that potential beneficiaries are aware of their responsibilities during the project and of options available to them. It is important to recognize that not everyone can manage the construction/ repair of their own house and that their time might be better used to generate income. The families’ decision to participate in this programme will be achieved through sensitization meetings, detailed assessments, participatory planning and prioritizing the provision of technical training and capacity building. A community-based feedback mechanism through regular mass meetings and focus group discussions will be established to enable IDPs express their opinions on issues affecting their assistance need. The discussions will also provide beneficiaries the opportunity to understand the shelter selection and allocation process.

Food security, Emergency food assistance. Multi year 2021 to 2024. 2021, portion total amount CHF450,000  (7F-10736.01) Améliorer la sécurité alimentaire et restaurer les moyens de subsistance agro-pastoraux des populations vulnérables hôtes et déplacées dans les régions de Tahoua et Diffa touchées par les crises sécuritaire et climatique L’objectif général du projet est d’améliorer la sécurité alimentaire et de renforcer les moyens d’existence et la résilience des populations déplacées et hôtes, affectées par les crises sécuritaires dans les régions de Tahoua et de Diffa, en fournissant une assistance humanitaire et un support pour le renforcement des moyens d’existence aux communautés les plus touchées par les crises sécuritaires, les déficits pluviométriques et les faibles productions agricoles et pastorales en 2021. 
L’Action répondra aux besoins alimentaires immédiats des ménages vulnérables pendant les périodes critiques (pré soudure et soudure pastorale et agricole) et soutiendra les principaux moyens d’existence des ménages les plus vulnérables. Elle ciblera les localités agro-pastorales et pastorales des départements de Diffa, Nguigmi, dans la région de Diffa, et le département de Tilia, région de Tahoua, les plus affectées par les crises sécuritaires (nombre de déplacés, taux d’insécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle) et climatiques (déficit agricoles et pastoraux). Les activités bénéficieront directement à 5 600 ménages (39 200 personnes) déplacés, hôtes, identifiés comme les plus vulnérables selon une approche de ciblage participative (Household Economy Approach) impliquant les communautés, les services techniques, les autorités locales, les partenaires locaux, et les organisations paysannes.

Dans le cadre de cette intervention, le premier axe d'intervention sera la réponse aux besoins urgents de sécurité alimentaire des ménages les plus vulnérables des départements de Diffa, Nguigmi (Diffa) et Tillia (Tahoua) par une assistance alimentaire sous forme de Cash for Work. Les transferts d'argent liquide permettront aux bénéficiaires d'avoir accès à une nourriture de qualité et ainsi de faire face à l'insécurité alimentaire aiguë. En effet, selon tous les acteurs rencontrés (services techniques, autorités locales, partenaires locaux et communautés) lors de l'évaluation interne des interventions FSLH de Diffa réalisée par ACF, le changement le plus significatif apporté par les activités CFW a été l'amélioration de la situation alimentaire des ménages grâce à l'augmentation du nombre de repas (jusqu'à 3 repas par jour), et l'augmentation de la durée des stocks alimentaires des ménages. Au niveau de Tillia, l'évaluation des besoins menée par ACF a montré que le besoin d'assistance alimentaire était l'un des besoins prioritaires cités par les communautés, en particulier parmi les personnes déplacées.
Le deuxième domaine d'intervention consistera à protéger et à renforcer les moyens de subsistance des populations les plus touchées dans les zones ciblées.  Les activités prévues sont basées sur les principaux moyens de subsistance des populations. L'agriculture (32,5% des ménages bénéficiaires), le petit commerce (31,7%) et l'élevage (19,9%) constituent les trois (3) principales activités des bénéficiaires (source : ACF, précédents projets).  Au niveau de Tillia, l'activité principale reste l'élevage et la zone a une vocation pastorale selon la classification du gouvernement du Niger. Ainsi, les activités s'articuleront autour de la restauration et du renforcement du patrimoine pastoral des communautés du département. Afin de renforcer les activités agricoles des bénéficiaires à Diffa, un soutien sera apporté à la culture maraîchère et à l'agriculture pluviale.

IADB02-G5 Sahel-COVID19-Jul20 Protection and assistance to Nigerian refugees in the Diffa region  (Situation Lake Chad) L’intervention en faveur des réfugiés présents à Diffa va se décliner autour de 3 objectifs suivants : 1- Maintenir et renforcer un environnement de protection favorable (protection monitoring et réponse de protection, dont child protection, SGBV, PBS, apatridie, enregistrement/documentation), améliorer les capacités d’intervention des autorités nationales pour délivrer des services de protection conformes aux standards internationaux et maintenir ouvert l’accès au territoire nigérien et aux procédures d’asile.2 – Assurer une assistance d’urgence et une capacité adéquate au niveau du camp de Sayam Forage et améliorer l’accès aux services sociaux de base. 3 - Renforcer la recherche des solutions durables et l’intégration socio-économique des réfugiés installés au Niger notamment via le programme urbanisation et la construction de logements pour les plus vulnérables. .
La stratégie de réponse est conforme avec les orientations du Gouvernement du Niger en termes d’alternatives aux camps et avec le Pacte Mondial pour les Réfugiés. Le nexus humanitaire – développement est au cœur des réflexions qui accompagnent la mise en œuvre de la réponse. Cela suppose le renforcement de la capacité d’absorption des services de base pour alléger les pressions, et l’accompagnement de la coexistence pacifique, en parallèle d’une réponse multisectorielle urgente. Alors qu’une assistance de type communautaire est développée pour l’accès aux services de base tels que l’eau ou la santé, c’est le niveau de vulnérabilité et non le statut qui régit l’assistance individuelle.

Aid and protection measures for refugees and internally displaced persons in the East Africa / Great Lakes region Protection and Assistance to Persons of Concern UNHCR will provide protection and seek solutions for IDPs and IDP-returnees, while working with partners at inter-agency level for provision of additional support, as follows:
-	IDP response will be characterized by enhanced protection monitoring (at community and household levels) and analysis, support to community-based protection networks and community reconciliation committees, tangible support to persons with specific needs (e.g. legal aid, civil documentation, or referral to psycho-social support, or cash-based interventions), youth programming, quick impact community support projects in IDP hosting and returnee receiving areas, and will contribute to durable solutions profiling and planning.
-	Coordination leadership of the Protection Sector will be reinforced, through working with partners and authorities to bolster preparedness including early warning, as well as protection assessment, analysis and response capacities. 
-	The Centrality of Protection will be championed within the UN/HCT, including through UNHCR serving as secretariat for the HCT Protection Task Force (HCT PTF), which oversees the implementation of the HCT Protection Strategy. UNHCR will work with the HCT PTF, and any new protection coordination forums established under UNITAMS, on advocacy related to protection of civilians, peacebuilding and durable solutions, particularly during the UNAMID drawdown and transition to an integrated mission. UNHCR will also bolster its advocacy with GoS on ensuring that laws and policies conform with international standards, and will support implementation of GoS’ National Plan on Protection of Civilians, at national and state-levels. These advocacy efforts will be buttressed by analysis of protection needs, threats and trends. 
-	The UNHCR/UNDP co-led Durable Solutions Working Group will prioritize the collection of relevant data to inform the inter-agency and governmental drive toward durable solutions, complemented by monitoring of returns by UNHCR to ensure they adhere to minimum standards of voluntariness, safety and dignity.  
-	UNHCR will strengthen the integration of PSEA actions, and maintain its active contributions to the RC/HC’s PSEA Network, and actively contribute to Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) approaches through co-leadership of the newly established AAP/Community Engagement WG under the ISCG.

Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan (USAID/BHA) Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP camps, and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity.

WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying  mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan. 

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities, or other solution. 

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19 have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

Against South Sudan HRP Internally Displaced Population in South Sudan supported through provision of protection and targeted assistance to promote resilience, protection advocacy and achievement of solutions. The project aims to strengthen community and rights-based protection response for IDPs, IDP returnees and vulnerable persons within their host communities. The project will focus on providing physical and legal protection through advocacy, timely protection monitoring, life-saving protection response based on identified needs and solutions. The project will address Housing, Land and Property (HLP) rights issues through the provision of legal assistance, facilitate issuance of property and identity documents, and work with mediation mechanisms to support HLP related dispute resolution. Community-based networks will be utilized as part of the protection response to foster community buy in and ownership of protection. The project will use evidence-based planning to expand outreach and develop the capacity of displaced communities to cope, recover, contribute to and ultimately achieve solutions. Out of 1.6 million IDPs, 475,000 IDPs and IDP returnees will be supported with protection interventions and assistance in seven (7) states and an administrative areas. Recognising the protection concerns linked to food insecurity, the Agency activities also include a scaling-up of activities in South Sudan’s highly food insecure and prioritised locations, i.e. Pibor County, Akobo, Aweil South, Tonj East, Tonj North, Tonj South. There will be continuous advocacy and support in the area of law and policy with relevant government bodies such as the   Ministries of Justice Home Affairs, Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management, and the Relief and Rehabilitation Commission (RRC) to ensure the centrality of protection, enact the “Protection and Assistance to Internally Displaced Persons Act 2018” (IDP) Bill, National Framework on Returns, and various HLP initiatives. The relevant line ministries will also receive capacity building and technical assistance. Building on UNHCR’s existing operational presence in Bentiu Bor, Juba, Malakal, Wau, Yambio, Yei, the Agency will continue to advance on the 2020 geographic expansion of IDP activities by leveraging both static and mobile presence through 15 partners to Central Equatoria, Unity, Upper Nile, Joinglei, Western Bahr El Ghazal, Northern Bahr El Ghazal, Lakes, Western Equatoira, Eastern Equatoris and Warrap. Response and monitoring will cover 19 identified priority counties and Pibor Administrative Area, including remote or hard to-reach areas, in full support to the Protection Cluster Strategy for mobile assessments and response. Partners comprise of both national and international organizations, with selection undertaken on the basis of their pre-existing presence, access to populations of concern and capacity to carry out static and remote protection monitoring and response. While not all proposed activity locations fall under the severity 3, 4 or 5 in terms of food insecurity, recognizing the fluidly and unpredictable nature of sub-national violence in South Sudan, UNHCR’s protection by presence approach requires presence in areas affected by conflict as well as areas of potential return in light of increased momentum in terms of solutions 
Resources and advocacy will focus primarily on protection response and solutions, either durable or transitional (where the former is not yet possible), including assessments on needs, risks, and intentions and feasibility of durable solutions, while also strengthening community-based structures, supporting HLP initiatives, promotion of livelihoods and peaceful coexistence. Improving coordination and quality of assessments and monitoring will be a key component. A mobile tool was introduced in late 2019 that has enhanced data collection and triangulation of information through timely collection and analysis capabilities, which will further improve information products, leading to a more fitting risk-mitigation approach, reduced response time; while underpinning protection mainstreaming across other operational interventions, including of other Clusters.

Against South Sudan 2021 HRP Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2021, there are more than 314,000 refugees from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, as well as the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, including from Sudan, Democratic Republic of Congo and Central African Republic.

At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for long-term stability, some 357,500 South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since November 2017, 122,000 of those in 2020 alone. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan at this stage, the increase in numbers warrants a scaling-up of support following an area-based approach, including strengthening linkages with development actors, to help returnees and the communities they settle in live in safety and dignity, with greater security and services.

Refugees largely reside in conﬂict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction of basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.

Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will beneﬁt from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Speciﬁc protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identiﬁed at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with speciﬁc protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as veriﬁcation exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the eﬃciency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to beneﬁt from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

Supporting Survivors and Addressing Risks and Root Causes of GBV in Conflict-Affected Areas of South Sudan The impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic, particularly the increased economic instability and school closures, along with expected high levels of food insecurity in 2021, flooding, and conflict-related displacements, continue to exacerbate the already existing high levels of gender-based violence (GBV). IOM's programmatic assessments  indicate that the COVID-19 prevention measures and economic contraction have had a significant impact, particularly on adolescent girls and young women, especially related to increased use of harmful coping mechanisms, such as sexual exploitation and forced marriage, resulting in increased adolescent pregnancies. 

The current humanitarian context is exacerbated by a high prevalence of violence against women and girls, particularly conflict-related sexual violence (CRSV), intimate partner violence (IPV), and forced marriage, including child marriage. This violence is structurally underpinned by a patriarchal social system, connected to the political economy of bridewealth (Luedke, 2019), with harmful gender norms underpinning cycles of violence within and between communities, particularly affecting the rights of women and girls. 

Furthermore, the needs for GBV services are high, yet the availability of multi-sectoral GBV services across the country is low, and access remains a challenge for women, especially in rural communities. Key barriers for survivors include distance to services, availability of qualified service providers, social restrictions over the women and girls movement, and high levels of social stigma and possible harmful repercussions for disclosure (including the threat of divorce and marriage to perpetrators). 

IOM aims to contribute to strengthening the humanitarian response to GBV contributing to HRP objective 2.4. IOM’s approach is to work closely to build national capacities to implement GBV prevention and response programming based on the Interagency GBV minimum standards. This includes strengthening community-based referral mechanisms to improve access for GBV survivors, establishing women and girl friendly spaces with tailored and age-appropriate activities for awareness, skills-building and psychosocial support, provision of GBV case management, psychosocial and legal counselling. For outreach and GBV prevention, IOM utilizes messaging developed with communities based on key issues identified and primary prevention approaches including Engaging Men through Accountable Practices and with school-age children, with significant capacity building and supervision requirement to ensure real behaviour change is created on these issues. Finally, IOM builds capacity among IOM outreach teams and partners on PSEA, community-based complaints and feedback mechanisms as well as working with organisations of persons with disabilities and elderly persons to improve inclusivity of GBV programming.

ECHO/-AF/BUD/2019/91019           IOM Project ID: DP.2081 Building Resilience and Strengthening Protection (BRSP) Project This IOM Protection project aims to contribute towards the achievement of Strategic Objectives 1 and 3 of the Protection Cluster. SO2: Ensure safe, equitable and dignified access to critical cross-sectoral basic services to enable populations to meet their basic needs in locations of severity level 4 and 5 and S.O.3 requests to enable vulnerable people to recover from crisis, seek solutions to displacement, and build resilience to acute shocks and chronic stresses through targeted programming to support coping capacities and livelihoods in prioritized areas.

The project seeks to provide protection assistance to the most vulnerable focusing on IDPs, host communities and returnees in Warrap, Unity, Western Bahr El Ghazal, and Central Equatoria states. The project focus will be on continuing the current support to community-based protection, provision of access to justice, protection assistance to victims of trafficking, and housing, land, and property assistance. The components to be implemented at each project site will be based on assessments and community consultations in order to address specific needs. Aside from supporting the Protection Cluster Objectives, the project is also a part of IOM’s Protection Strategy. The counties to be targeted include in Warrap State: Twic, Tonj North, Tonj South; in Western Bahr el Ghazal State: Wau, Jur River; and in Unity State: Leer. These locations have been prioritized by the cluster and have also been confirmed by needs assessments.

Objective 2: CO 1: IOM will ensure the provision of critical protection related assistance and specialized services through an integrated approach to address the priority needs of targeted people among vulnerable women, men, girls and boys in hard-to-reach and priority geographical areas.

IOM Protection will specifically undertake to support vulnerable  girls, boys, women, men, older persons, persons with disabilities, and other persons with specific needs at risk of, or who have experienced violence, abuse, exploitation, and neglect, including gender-based violence and are in hard-to- reach geographical areas, through the provision of specialized protection and multi-sectoral services by the following:

(a) Provision of protection assistance including targeted assistance to victims of trafficking, persons with disabilities and other vulnerable groups through of case management services, access to justice for survivors of gender-based violence and other vulnerable persons as determined by joint needs assessments with other partners. This will be achieved through static as well as through mobile interventions integrated with GBV as well as with other sectors such as WASH and S-NFI.

(b) Awareness raising on protection, rights and entitlements, disability inclusion, protection from sexual exploitation and abuse including sensitization of community structures on protection risks and mitigation and working with community protection committees on referrals.

In regard to SO 3 IOM will facilitate conflict- and gender-sensitive access to safe housing, land, and property for women, men, girls, and boys, with a sufficient security of tenure. IOM will do this through:

(i) Provision of legal awareness raising including on Housing, Land, and Property rights and responsibilities;

(ii) Provision of legal counselling;

(iii) Legal capacity building to dispute resolution mechanisms at the community level; and 

(iv) Use of cash-based assistance to ensure individuals will not have rights denied due to lack of funds.

The project is intended to assist the beneficiaries to claim their rights and to build the capacity of the authorities to protect and provide access to rights of the affected populations.

Overall the project will target 28,925 individual beneficiaries, of these 15,665 will benefit from the HLP component of the project and 13,260 from the GP component of the project. The overall budget for this project is USD 867,750 - which averages 30USD/beneficiary.

40098297/40098937          IOM Project ID: DP.2204 Supporting Survivors and Addressing Risks and Root Causes of GBV in Conflict-Affected Areas of South Sudan The impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic, particularly the increased economic instability and school closures, along with expected high levels of food insecurity in 2021, flooding, and conflict-related displacements, continue to exacerbate the already existing high levels of gender-based violence (GBV). IOM's programmatic assessments  indicate that the COVID-19 prevention measures and economic contraction have had a significant impact, particularly on adolescent girls and young women, especially related to increased use of harmful coping mechanisms, such as sexual exploitation and forced marriage, resulting in increased adolescent pregnancies. 

The current humanitarian context is exacerbated by a high prevalence of violence against women and girls, particularly conflict-related sexual violence (CRSV), intimate partner violence (IPV), and forced marriage, including child marriage. This violence is structurally underpinned by a patriarchal social system, connected to the political economy of bridewealth (Luedke, 2019), with harmful gender norms underpinning cycles of violence within and between communities, particularly affecting the rights of women and girls. 

Furthermore, the needs for GBV services are high, yet the availability of multi-sectoral GBV services across the country is low, and access remains a challenge for women, especially in rural communities. Key barriers for survivors include distance to services, availability of qualified service providers, social restrictions over the women and girls movement, and high levels of social stigma and possible harmful repercussions for disclosure (including the threat of divorce and marriage to perpetrators). 

IOM aims to contribute to strengthening the humanitarian response to GBV contributing to HRP objective 2.4. IOM’s approach is to work closely to build national capacities to implement GBV prevention and response programming based on the Interagency GBV minimum standards. This includes strengthening community-based referral mechanisms to improve access for GBV survivors, establishing women and girl friendly spaces with tailored and age-appropriate activities for awareness, skills-building and psychosocial support, provision of GBV case management, psychosocial and legal counselling. For outreach and GBV prevention, IOM utilizes messaging developed with communities based on key issues identified and primary prevention approaches including Engaging Men through Accountable Practices and with school-age children, with significant capacity building and supervision requirement to ensure real behaviour change is created on these issues. Finally, IOM builds capacity among IOM outreach teams and partners on PSEA, community-based complaints and feedback mechanisms as well as working with organisations of persons with disabilities and elderly persons to improve inclusivity of GBV programming.

Communities, particularly those most dramatically affected – and under additional stress because of IDPs returns and other displacements - need assistance in reinforcing their resilience to address these shocks as well as the consequences of the protracted crisis, and to address their needs on seriously depleted infrastructures and service capacities.
The essence of the Programme is about providing Syrian communities with – still limited - support to regain control over their basic needs (livelihoods, access to essential services) and reduce their dependency on humanitarian assistance. Prioritization of locations, is the outcome of a context analysis and needs assessment conducted on more than 5,000 Syrian communities, based on the following three criteria:
1) Hard to Reach Areas
2) Areas of major IDPs presence and IDPs returns
3) Highest scoring in the Severity Scale

Hence, donors willing to support this approach will be able to pre-select certain location(s) and/or area(s) of intervention of their preference, within the 200 prioritized communities.

1. Living conditions
2. Livelihoods
3. Access to social services
4. Access to productive and market infrastructure
5. Social protection
6. Strengthening of local public services delivery capacity
7. Reinforcing opportunities and capacities for civic engagement
