Rehabilitation of Water Intake Pumping Station and Lifting Station in Irrigation Secor 7 in Deir Ezzor Restoring livelihoods of crisis affected population in Syria through light rehabilitation of irrigation infrastructure at community level The United Nations (UN) estimates that the number of crisis-affected people in need of humanitarian assistance in Syria is 14.2 million, of which 6 million are in acute need. The above figure of people in need includes 6.7 million protracted internally displaced persons (IDPs); estimated 320,000 spontaneous IDPs return; 75,000 refugees return; 438,000 Palestine refugees and the rest overburdened host communities.  

More than 75% of the number of people in need of humanitarian assistance are accessible from within Syria. Overall, 12.4 million of people are estimated to be food insecure (including 1.27 million severely food insecure) and 1.9 million people at risk of food insecurity. 

In this context, FAO has designed a project to assist 120,000 vulnerable crisis-affected food insecure farming households (equivalent to 750,000 people) in Syria. About 15% of the targeted householders will be selected from those who receive food support to help them shift from depending on food assistance to producing their own food and enhancing their self-sufficiency. The objective of the proposed action is to protect and enhance the livelihoods of vulnerable farmers and IDPs through the restoration of critical irrigation infrastructures to increase household food production and security. The project outputs include:

•	Output 1: Local small-scale irrigation infrastructures in the targeted governorates are assessed and light rehabilitation undertaken. 
•	Output 2: Capacity of technical staff and relevant stakeholders strengthened.

A training programme on enhancing irrigation management, water use efficiency in small-scale irrigation, agricultural land management will be based on FAO standards and approaches. It is expected that stakeholders and farmers (water user association) will join this training. 

This project is expected to contribute to increasing access to irrigation water for crisis-affected farmers and their families in the targeted areas through the light rehabilitation of local small scale irrigation infrastructure. Cultivation and other agricultural practices, including livestock and animal feed production, will consequently benefit from the water supply plans as an emergency response to crisis. The proposed intervention will strengthen household food production capacities and knowledge and address immediate food security and nutrition needs through increasing local availability and supply of food.  This may in turn promote flourishing of agricultural based livelihoods in the rural community, which would contribute to social cohesion, peace and stability. The project seeks to utilize intensive labour in order to maximize community participation and inject cash into the local community.  
FAO as part of the CWG will discuss at project level with the group to identify the rate, modality, etc. of the cash intervention to be in line with the CWG and to achieve the purpose of the intervention

Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2021, there are more than 314,000 refugees from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, as well as the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, including from Sudan, Democratic Republic of Congo and Central African Republic.

At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for long-term stability, some 357,500 South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since November 2017, 122,000 of those in 2020 alone. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan at this stage, the increase in numbers warrants a scaling-up of support following an area-based approach, including strengthening linkages with development actors, to help returnees and the communities they settle in live in safety and dignity, with greater security and services.

Refugees largely reside in conﬂict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction of basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.

Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will beneﬁt from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Speciﬁc protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identiﬁed at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with speciﬁc protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as veriﬁcation exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the eﬃciency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to beneﬁt from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

SOMALIA - Combating the locust plague (2021 portion) Saving Lives and Livelihoods in Rural Somalia  Somalia faced a growing number of threats to its food security in 2020, starting with the ongoing Desert Locust crisis, followed by COVID-19 first reported in March, severe flooding between April and September and poor rains forecast for the Deyr 2020 season. Based on latest projections, 2.1 million Somalis are in IPC Phases 3 and above through December 2020. Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of the La Nina developing, which tends to trigger dry conditions in Somalia. If the forecast below-average Deyr rains (Oct-Dec 2020) is followed by below-average or delayed 2021 Gu rains (Apr-Jun), this could lead to a rapid and substantial worsening of the humanitarian situation. 

Rural populations are at a high risk of further deteriorating food security, given the direct and indirect impacts of these threats on rural livelihoods, related assets, food production and income. FAO’s proposal responds both to the lifesaving and life-sustaining needs of rural populations in IPC Phases 3 and above, against a Population in Need (PiN) of 3.1 million people prioritized for Food Security Cluster (FSC) assistance under the 2021 HRP. FAO’s planned activities will directly support 103,850 households in IPC 3-4 under both FSC Strategic Objectives (SOs), while further delivering support to protect food security in Somalia at a wider scale through countrywide animal health campaigns, among other activities. 

Under SO1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 76,300 rural households, including IDPs, in the form of Cash+, UCT and CFW activities delivered through FAO’s e-Platform for Mobile Money and Livelihood Assistance. All cash-based programmes include trainings on good nutrition practices, covering infancy to old age.

Under SO2, to protect livelihoods, FAO will provide in-kind and technical support to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security threats across Somalia’s rural livelihood zones, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to 53,500 households targeted for Cash+ interventions under SO1 (while supporting an additional 7,550 households with agricultural inputs only). FAO’s planned Cash+ activities combine cash transfers with tailored livelihood support packages to assist rural families out of hunger sooner. Alongside cash transfers, the assistance packages will protect and restore the livelihoods of households in IPC Phases 3-4 by providing: (i) farmers with quality inputs to produce a nutritious variety of food crop (cereal, pulse and vegetable seeds, storage bags, fertilizer and irrigation/tractor services, where appropriate; (ii) pastoralists with nutrient-rich feed blocks and deworming to improve livestock productivity especially milk supply; and (iii) coastal communities with a variety of basic fishing gear and processing equipment to improve catch and consumption.  

Also under SO2, in anticipation of drought conditions in early 2021, FAO will also strategically position water bladder tanks and provide nutritive animal feed blocks to protect the small milking animals of up to 20,000 pastoral households impacted by scarce pasture from dry conditions and/or locust damage. Countrywide livestock vaccination and supportive treatment campaigns will further protect livestock assets belonging to at least 2.2 million men, women and children. Preparedness for animal health emergencies will be enhanced through strategic stocking of vaccines and related supplies (PPR), and training to local partners in Livestock Emergency Guidelines and Standards (LEGS), antimicrobial resistance, disease surveillance and reporting, among others.

OCHA planea expandir aún más su abogacía para facilitar el acceso a las áreas más vulnerables y movilizar más fondos para la respuesta.

Para apoyar las capacidades operativas de los diferentes actores humanitarios y promover el respeto por los principios humanitarios, OCHA con el apoyo de otras organizaciones, ofrecerá formaciones e iniciativas de desarrollo de capacidades sobre los principios humanitarios, la coordinación humanitaria, la coordinación civil-militar, herramientas de gestión de la información, metodologías para la evaluación de necesidades, el HPC y temas transversales como AAP, PEAS y género.

Las prioridades dentro de la estrategia de OCHA Venezuela para 2021 son:
-	Mejorar el panorama conjunto de la comunidad humanitaria sobre las necesidades humanitarias, mediante el monitoreo de necesidades y evaluaciones periódicas, que facilite la priorización de las actividades humanitarias.
-	Fortalecer el sistema de monitoreo del HRP y publicar productos regulares sobre los avances y retos de la respuesta.
-	Fortalecer los foros de coordinación para alcanzar una respuesta humanitaria oportuna, efectiva y basada en los principios humanitarios.
-	Desarrollar la capacidad de los socios humanitarios para participar de manera efectiva en el HPC y proporcionar una respuesta más efectiva.

-	Acoger al clúster de Logistica, para fortalecer la coordinación entre los socios, el intercambio de informaciones puntuales sobre temas logísticos, apoyar la abogacía con las contrapartes institucionales, y promover soluciones conjuntas para mejorar la capacitad operacional y de respuesta.

Disaster Preparedness in Niger: Humanitarian Assistance for affected populations after the 2021 rainy season Assistance humanitaire en Abris et en Biens non-alimentaires (BNA) pour les sinistrés d'inondation au Niger. Dans le cadre de HRP 2021 au travers de ce projet, l'OIM vise à apporter un appui au gouvernement du Niger dans le cadre de la réponse d'urgence aux personnes sinistrées des inondations. Ce projet propose de répondre aux besoins des ménages sinistrés à travers les requêtes qui seront exprimées par le Gouvernement au travers du Ministère de l’Action Humanitaire et de la Gestion des Catastrophes (MAH/GC). Cette réponse s’adressera uniquement aux ménages vulnérables victimes d’inondations dont les abris ou cases auront été endommagés et/ou ceux dont les Biens non-alimentaires (BNA) auront été emportés par les eaux. Le présent projet poursuit comme objectif d’atteindre 8 000 ménages soit 56 000 personnes à travers tout le Niger prioritairement dans les régions de Niamey, Dosso et Diffa. En coordination avec le MAH/GC et la Direction Générale de la Protection Civile (DGPC), l’OIM mettra à disposition 8 000 kits abris et 8 000 kits de Biens non-alimentaires qui seront distribués aux ménages sinistrés. En plus des kits, l’OIM couvrira les coûts liés à la logistique et à la distribution des kits. Ce projet ne couvrira pas une zone ou région donnée mais permettra d’intervenir là où les besoins se présentent et aussi de pouvoir compléter les activités des autres acteurs en cas de besoin en tant que prestataire de dernier recours pour la réponse humanitaire en abri d'urgence et BNA. L’OIM en tant que Co-Lead du Groupe de Travail Abri et Bien non-alimentaire (GTABNA) avec le MAH/GC s'assurera que les activités sont menées en étroite coordination avec les autres partenaires humanitaires membres du GTABNA pour la réponse en abri et Biens non-alimentaires pour les ménages sinistrés des inondations au Niger. Conformément à la logique de la stratégie du Secteur abris/BNA et en fonction de la faisabilité, les interventions pourront se faire en transferts monétaires conditionnels. Cela réduirait considérablement les coûts logistiques qui sont très élevés en période hivernale à cause du mauvais état des routes mais aussi et permettrait aussi de résoudre en partie le problème d’accès lié à l'insécurité qui souvent retarde les interventions. Enfin, la mise en œuvre du présent projet fera l’objet d’un suivi régulier de la qualité des interventions réalisées mais aussi de l’implication des bénéficiaires et autorités locales. Pour cela, les feedbacks de la communauté cible seront collectés à travers des évaluations post-distribution et des séances de discussion de groupe séparées par genre et âge avant et après l'assistance. Aussi, en tant qu’acteur humanitaire, l'OIM et ses partenaires de mise en œuvre s’assureront que ses actions n’induisent aucune tension ou problème dans la zone et n’exposent pas les bénéficiaires. A cet effet la phase d'évaluation de besoins sera réalisée de commun accord avec les populations dans les communes ciblées, les sessions d'information sur le projet seront organisées à l'attention de communauté bénéficiaires, le mecanisme de ciblage de bénéficiaires sera réalisé en etroite collabation avec les autorités au niveau local (do no harm). Une collaboration étroite faite avec les acteurs de protection pour un suivi de pret de toutes questions de protection. Le cout total du projet sera de 4.650.000 USD.

Protection Cluster:Niger HRP 2021 Contribuer à l’amélioration des conditions de vie des populations vulnérables au Niger - RRM Le mécanisme RRM est financé par ECHO (le RRM est une priorité dans le HIP 2020 et dans la version préliminaire du HIP 2021) et USAID, avec le soutien de l’UNICEF pour la fourniture de kits Abri et BNA supplémentaire. Les secteurs d'intervention RRM sont les ABNA, l'EHA, la protection et la sécurité alimentaire. Le projet proposé pour 2021 vise à répondre aux besoins urgents des populations les plus vulnérables déplacées à la suite d'un choc depuis moins de 3mois (et/ou accessibles depuis moins de 3 mois). La réponse du Consortium RRM commence par une veille humanitaire et une série d'évaluations multisectorielles (MSA) afin d'identifier les secteurs dans lesquels des intervention d'urgence sont nécessaires pour chaque site accueillant des déplacés. Un réseau de points focaux est mis en place par chaque partenaire. Une MSA (évaluation multisectorielle) ou une évaluation flash sont ensuite déclenchées dans les 24h suivant la confirmation de l'alerte, et les rapports d'évaluation sont transmis à la communauté humanitaire à travers OCHA dans les 72h pour assurer une coordination avec les partenaires et permettre leur positionnement afin couvrir des besoins complémentaires ou quand l'intervention n'est pas du ressort du RRM, le cas échéant. Si les seuils de déclenchement sont atteints, une intervention RRM est lancée, et des consultations avec les communautés et leaders communautaires prennent place pour prioriser les besoins. Le ciblage des bénéficiaires se fait sur des critères de vulnérabilité établis, en prenant en compte les ménages hôtes affectés par l'arrivée des nouveaux ménages et de manière participative pour faire en sorte de réduire les risques de tensions communautaires. Dans les 30 jours qui suivent l'intervention, une évaluation post intervention prend place pour mesure l'impact et la satisfaction des populations supportées. La stratégie protection du Consortium RRM repose sur une approche transversale qui vise à renforcer les extrants de l'intervention en termes de réduction des risques et des vulnérabilités. Cela se base sur des évaluations rapides de protection (ERP) qui ont lieu en même temps ou juste après la réalisation d’une MSA. L’objectif des ERP est d'identifier les problématiques prioritaires de protection et donc de guider la réponse.
En fonction des cas, le Consortium assurera le référencement ou/et la prise en charge des cas de protection. L’assistance de protection consiste en une assistance individuelle (API) composée d’un appui matériel ou en transfert monétaire (BNA selon les besoins de la personne, ou prise en charge de frais nécessaires pour la personne mais ne pouvant être couverts par le ménage, comme les frais médicaux, les frais de transport vers un CSI etc.) et d’un référencement vers des services de prise en charge médicale, juridique, et de santé mentale.
Les acteurs humanitaires et étatiques qui ne travaillent pas dans les secteurs de la protection verront leurs capacités renforcées, afin qu’ils puissent bien/mieux prendre en compte les aspects de protection dans leur travail avec les populations déplacées suite à un conflit ou une catastrophe naturelle.
Les interventions du Consortium se font avec une prise en compte du COVID-19 pour préserver les agents et les bénéficiaires des risques de transmission du virus. Des SOP ont été mises en place pour le Consortium afin d’harmoniser les pratiques, en ligne avec les recommandations des autorités nigériennes et de l’OMS. Des séances de sensibilisation ont lieu. En cas de besoin, les activités de groupe sont reportées et/ou adaptées pour réduire les risques. Les partenaire font aussi en sorte d’adapter leur réponse à l’évolution de la situation grâce à un suivi de la progression du COVID au Niger.

Provision of integrated sustainable livelihoods and WaSH services to the most vulnerable Internally Displaced People, refugees, host communities and returnees of Greater Upper Nile, South Sudan Provision of timely, equitable and integrated food security and livelihoods services to the conflict, epidemic and natural disaster affected populations in South Sudan South Sudan protracted crises have left 7.5 million people in dire need of humanitarian assistance in 2020 despite the signature of the Revitalized peace agreement, and continues to face conflict, natural disasters and climate instability, food insecurity, and lack of basic services. According to the latest IPC analysis for South Sudan published in December 2020, an estimated 7.7 million people are expected to experience acute food insecurity and worse (IPC 3, 4 and 5) in 2021. 
SI has started to implement its humanitarian response in South Sudan in 2006. Its long lasting presence has contributed to building a wealth of experience in Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) and Food, Security and Livelihoods (FSL). This allowed SI to pilot large-scale unconditional cash transfers, seeds distribution amongst IDPs and host communities in Western Bahr El Ghazal, Upper Nile, Jonglei and Central Equatoria states. SI aims at supporting the most vulnerable households, who are struggling to restore their livelihoods, in order to help them to improve their food security situation. Currently, SI is running five operational bases: Raja town and Wau town (Western Bahr el-Ghazal), Aburoc/Malakal (Upper Nile), Lankien (Jonglei) and Juba (Central Equatoria). For 2021, SI will focus on linking its first line response, through its EPR and static teams, with activities having longer-term impact in WASH and FSL sectors. In FSL specifically, this will mean emergency livelihood response to quickly replenish the destroyed assets. In second step SI will complement the response, wherever possible, with capacity building to allow for income generation and longer-term food preservation. SI will therefore aim at providing timely, equitable and integrated food security and livelihoods services to the conflict, epidemic and natural disaster affected populations of South Sudan.

Integrated Life-saving Assistance for disaster affected populations in Somalia (part of ECHO/-HF/BUD/2021/91021) Life-saving integrated food security and livelihoods support for Somaliland and Puntland communities   The project is responding to humanitarian needs of drought, covid 19 and locust affected community in target locations of Puntland and Somaliland through cash injection to address the immediate food needs of the people. Cash transfer programming will be used to reach households that are in IPC 3 and above. While focusing on life-saving interventions, the project will also support recovery and resilience building of the people where possible. 
Findings from FSNAU  2020 post-Gu seasonal food security and nutrition assessment conducted across Somalia during July and August 2020 indicate that Due to the combined effects of widespread and severe flooding, Desert Locust infestation, socioeconomic impacts of COVID-19 and the cumulative impacts of previous shocks, up to 2.1 million people across Somalia are expected to face food consumption gaps or depletion of assets indicative of Crisis (IPC Phase 3)1 or worse outcomes through December 2020 in the absence of humanitarian assistance. In addition, 849 900 children under the age of five are likely to be acutely malnourished through August 2021. 
Desert Locust continues to pose a serious risk of damage to both pasture and crops at least until the end of 2020. The 2020 Deyr (October-December) rainfall season is likely to be below average to average across the country, which could lead to drought and trigger a worsening of the humanitarian situation if the 2021 Gu (April-June) season rainfall is also delayed or performs poorly.

The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the Somalis’s economy is significant impacting on poor urban and IDP households, as well as pastoralists in northern Somalia, namely Puntland and Somaliland.  External remittance flows from the Somali diaspora constitutes 1.4-2 billion USD every year and contribute 23-32 percent of Gross Domestic Product, according to the World Bank. However, after the onset of COVID-19, money vendors report that the volume of cash transactions declined approximately 30-40 percent from March to June 2020
Improving food availability through support to agricultural production in Awdal and Nugal  and introducing it in Sool and Sanag regions of Somalia is seen as an entry point to diversify pastoral livelihoods of those two regions. This plan involves also supporting communities’ recovery and livelihoods diversification interventions through livestock support with vaccination and treatment and Improving Agricultural Production/Food Security. 

Livestock production was severely affected by the drought leading to substantially reduced herds; which is the country’s prime investment especially in rural communities. The mains reasons leading to the death were water shortages and lack of pasture.  In view of this situation the project will explore fodder production combined with campaigns on livestock treatment. These include promotion of carrying capacity for sustained production. These actions will be coupled with Cash for Work activities which will be used for communal asset development linked to crop and animal husbandry. 

In times of shock and more critical food insecurity, Oxfam will utilize cash and voucher assistance to reach to the most affected households impacted by triple threats of drought, covid or locust  to meet the immediate emergency needs of at risk communities. cash is the preferred option for Oxfam to reach to people in remote areas, it is faster, sacure and easy to cover at scale. cash and voucher assistance also helps people to have flexibility on their needs and decision, choice and have multiplier effect on the economy

Provision of protection and humanitarian assistance to vulnerable internally displaced, returnees and host communities across Syria. In addition to over 100 community centres providing integrated protection services, outreach to communities will be convened through over 2,800 outreach volunteers. 
Accountability to affected people will be realized through meaningful participation of communities, structured focus group discussions and enhancement of community-based complaint mechanisms. UNHCR will continue its capacity building efforts to ensure services are delivered according to the standards and that accountability to affected population and do no harm principles are respected.

Dans le même temps ACF maintiendra un appui technique et matériel minimal aux 5 aires santé qui abritent les déplacés et les populations d’accès difficile afin d’améliorer pour renforcer leurs capacités de réponses de réponse aux urgences. ACF intégrera aussi dans son intervention une composante Santé mentale et pratiques de soins, un mécanisme de référence et de contre-référence d’urgence, un système de surveillance épidémiologique et des déplacements de populations et l’approche de PB/Œdèmes par les mères.
L’objectif de l’intervention étant d’améliorer la couverture et l'accès aux soins en nutrition/santé/santé mentale, pratiques de soins et WASH in Nut des populations affectées par des chocs récurrents grâce à une intervention d'urgence au renforcement des capacités techniques des centres de santé accueillant régulièrement les personnes déplacées (IDPS et refugiés) suite à ces chocs avec la participation active des communautés bénéficiaires  
Les cibles de l'intervention sont les populations vivant dans les communautés du département de Logone et Chari frontalières du Nigéria et vulnérabilisées par chocs récurrents liés aux incidents sécuritaires. Les communautés qui accueillent les déplacés suite à ces incidents, seront également ciblées afin de répondre aux besoins urgents en Santé/Nut aussi bien pour les déplacés internes/réfugiés que les populations hôtes. Les centres de santé ciblés pour la préparation et la réponse aux urgences sont ceux qui accueillent le plus de déplacés (IDPs, Refugiés, retournés) en cas de chocs.
Au sein de ces populations déplacées et hôtes, les cibles prioritaires sont d'une part les enfants de moins de 5 ans qui de par leurs morphologies, en pleine croissance, restent une couche sensible aux maladies et aux déficits alimentaires et d'autre part les femmes enceintes et allaitantes. Integrated program aiming at ensuring the food security and access to livelihood for the local communities, displaced and returnees Provision of timely, equitable and integrated food security and livelihoods services to the conflict, epidemic and natural disaster affected populations in South Sudan South Sudan protracted crises have left 7.5 million people in dire need of humanitarian assistance in 2020 despite the signature of the Revitalized peace agreement, and continues to face conflict, natural disasters and climate instability, food insecurity, and lack of basic services. According to the latest IPC analysis for South Sudan published in December 2020, an estimated 7.7 million people are expected to experience acute food insecurity and worse (IPC 3, 4 and 5) in 2021. 
SI has started to implement its humanitarian response in South Sudan in 2006. Its long lasting presence has contributed to building a wealth of experience in Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) and Food, Security and Livelihoods (FSL). This allowed SI to pilot large-scale unconditional cash transfers, seeds distribution amongst IDPs and host communities in Western Bahr El Ghazal, Upper Nile, Jonglei and Central Equatoria states. SI aims at supporting the most vulnerable households, who are struggling to restore their livelihoods, in order to help them to improve their food security situation. Currently, SI is running five operational bases: Raja town and Wau town (Western Bahr el-Ghazal), Aburoc/Malakal (Upper Nile), Lankien (Jonglei) and Juba (Central Equatoria). For 2021, SI will focus on linking its first line response, through its EPR and static teams, with activities having longer-term impact in WASH and FSL sectors. In FSL specifically, this will mean emergency livelihood response to quickly replenish the destroyed assets. In second step SI will complement the response, wherever possible, with capacity building to allow for income generation and longer-term food preservation. SI will therefore aim at providing timely, equitable and integrated food security and livelihoods services to the conflict, epidemic and natural disaster affected populations of South Sudan.

Appui à la résilience : renforcement de capacités, cash for work, distributions d’intrants agricoles Improving access and availability of food while building resilient systems to improve living conditions of Somali Households affected by crisis.   Through implementation, ACTED intends to save lives and improve the ability of Somali households to meet their basic needs through multi-purpose cash transfers for severely disaster-affected populations and to show progress towards the long-term goal of a Somali safety net. Through this project, the Somalia Cash Consortium, of which ACTED is a member, intends to address the needs of the most vulnerable disaster-affected households by providing multi-purpose unrestricted cash transfer. ACTED’s involvement in this project aims at supporting vulnerable households in Baidoa IDP sites of bay region, El-Afweyn and Erigavo districts of Sanaag region, through unconditional cash transfers through six months of mobile money transfers. The Consortium will target the most vulnerable households with life-saving multi-purpose unconditional cash transfers. The Action will specifically target populations in IPC 3, 4 and 5, especially newly displaced and worst-affected Pastoralist and agro-pastoralist communities. In addition, this Action seeks to provide life-saving assistance to food insecure communities in Bay, Gedo and Lower Juba regions while implementing recovery and resilience activities to
restore livelihoods and respond to the needs of IDPs and rural communities in Baidoa, Kismayo, El-Afwayne, Badhan, Diinsoor and Buurhakaba districts who are impacted by floods and drought, lack sustainable livelihoods, at risk of displacement and with limited access to adequate WASH and shelter services.

Appui à la résilience : renforcement de capacités, cash for work, distributions d’intrants agricoles Food security and livelihoods support to host and IDPs populations affected by recurrent shocks in Somalia Action Against Hunger provide Food Security and Livelihoods (FSL) support to pastoralist, agro-pastoralist, peri-urban/urban and internally displaced (IDP) populations affected by persistent periods of armed conflict, political instability as well as environmental and economic shocks in Somalia. The 2021 FSL project target 81,873 individuals (21,615 male, 32,729 female, 16,047 boys and 16,702 girls) living in Bakool (Xudur, Elbarde, Wajid, Rabdhure), Sool (Xudun), Lower Shebelle ( Afgooye), Banadir (Khada), Hiraan (Beletweyne) and Nugaal (Eyl, Garowe) regions. The project plan to reach 65,304 individuals (displaced and non-displaced)  in integrated phase classification (IPC) 3, 4 and beyond with immediate lifesaving interventions including unconditional, conditional cash assistance and fresh food voucher to meet their immediate acute food needs to mitigate shocks/stress. Further 16,570 individuals’ (IPC 2) will be supported with seasonal livelihood inputs support for agriculture and livestock activities to build and strengthen their resilience capacities  to meet their immediate recovery needs, leverage on existing assets to withstand the effects of a shock and lay the foundation for future economic growth activities. In order to foster more sustainable stress mitigation mechanisms, ACF activities will focus on creating greater resilience for the beneficiary population by promoting economic growth activities. These activities capitalize on the foundation laid under strategies designed to enhance absorptive and adaptive capacity and promote a pathway to income generating opportunities while ensuring that the systems that support economic growth are appropriately developed and protected for future sustainability.

Appui à la résilience : renforcement de capacités, cash for work, distributions d’intrants agricoles Emergency Relief for Vulnerable IDP, Returnees and Host Communities in Kismayo, Somalia Somalia has been affected by a combination of climatic and non-climatic shocks: conflicts, droughts, floods, protracted displacement, inequality, marginalization and poverty. For instance, heavy and erratic Gu’ rainfall that started in April 2020,  caused flush floods which contributed to displacement of an estimated 893,000 people across Somalia  while in  Kisimayo District  alone had 9,560 families affected by flash floods of which about 370 families were displaced, leaving their original settlement area for higher grounds. Some 2.6 million internally displaced persons (IDP) living in 2,000 sites in Somalia face serious risks of evictions, marginalization and exclusion; and lack access to essential services such as shelter, water and sanitation  (OCHA Somalia, 2020). IDPs comprise 30% of Somalis in IPC 3 and 4 requiring lifesaving assistance in 2021 (FSC HNO page). Kismayo District hosts over 7,000 IDPs spread over 139 IDP camps. It is the third largest city in Somalia and the capital of both the Lower Juba region and the Jubaland State. Many IDPs and returnees have ended up settling in Kismayo where they can get assistance from international organizations as well as get open spaces where they can set up temporary shelters – albeit as squatters with no defined tenure. The dire humanitarian situation in Somalia has been exacerbated by the Covid-19 global pandemic which has caused suffering and death in virtually all corners of the globe. Somalia has not been spared and has so far suffered 3,847 confirmed infections and 99 Covid19-related deaths as at beginning of October, 2020. The pandemic has also had a devastating effect on food security and livelihood for the millions of Somalis who are not able to go about their life normally. Prior to the floods in the early part of the year, the population in Kismayo District were affected by impact of the COVID-19 directives that led to increase of prices of food and Non-Food Items (NFIs). According to market assessment done by CARE International in April, prices of food items increased by an average 17 percent while those of Non-Food Items (NFIs) increased by 12 percent following COVID-19 related restrictions.
SIF has planned an integrated response to the on-going humanitarian crises in Kismayo, Lower Juba through contributing to improvement of livelihood and food security among the IDPs, poor host communities and returnees in the area. The project will focus on addressing their weakened capacity to recover from effects of conflict and cyclical climatic shocks by implementing activities that will improve immediate access to food and non-food items and to promote activities that ensure that the vulnerable households being supported are able to have sustainable livelihoods beyond the emergency support. Currently, the basic foodstuffs are available from the local markets which are well supplied by both local producers as well as from outside Kismayo area. 
The overall objective of the project is to contribute to the improvement of food security and livelihood of the most vulnerable Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs), poor host communities (HC) and returnees in Kismayo. The project has two specific objectives: (i) Improve access to food through provision of UCT to 900 vulnerable IPD and poor host community households (7,200 individuals); and, (ii) improve livelihood opportunities and resilience for 600 vulnerable IDP and host community households (4,800 individuals).
Beneficiaries will be assessed using the following criteria: They must (i)be from the geographically targeted areas; (ii)be considered poor or very poor; (iii) come from households with large family size (7 persons or more); (iv)hail from a vulnerable HH headed by woman, elderly, PWDs, child, or chronically ill persons; (vi) newly arrived/displaced IDPs; and/or (vi) households that are living in temporary shelters due to lack of means.

Appui à la résilience Provision of timely, equitable and integrated WASH services to the conflict, epidemic and natural disaster affected populations in South Sudan South Sudan protracted crises have left 7.5 million people in dire need of humanitarian assistance in 2020 despite the signature of the Revitalized peace agreement, and continues to face conflict, natural disasters and climate instability, food insecurity, and lack of basic services. As per the Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) 2021, lack of or inadequate access to clean water and improved sanitation and hygiene practices in South Sudan will negatively impact an estimated 5.6 million people in 2021.
Since 2006, SI has become a key WASH actor in South Sudan, implementing emergency lifesaving response and providing integrated WASH services to crisis-affected populations in the areas thanks to its static presence in Juba County, Nyirol County, Fashoda County, Raja and Wau Counties. Since 2012 SI has played a key role in the Emergency Preparedness and Response (EPR) strategy in South Sudan, implementing multi-sectoral assessments and delivering emergency responses to crisis-affected populations all over the country. In 2021, SI will aim at improving timely, equitable and integrated access to WASH services to the conflict, epidemic and natural disaster affected populations in South Sudan.

Assistance alimentaire d'urgence Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP camps, and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity.

WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying  mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan. 

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities, or other solution. 

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19 have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

Renforcement de la résilience des communautés de la région de Tillabéri face à l'insécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle et aux chocs (phase 2) Niger Country Strategy Plan  This CSP aims to contribute all year-round to: Crisis-affected populations to meet their basic food and nutrition needs during and after the crises; Food insecure school-age children, to access adequate and nutritious food; Vulnerable groups (children, pregnant women and adolescent girls) to have enhanced nutritional status; Food insecure populations and communities to have more resilient livelihoods and sustainable food systems; Capacity strengthening of National institutions; Humanitarian and development partners to access common services unti appropriate an sustainable alternative are available.

Coordinated humanitarian assistance to climate and conflict affected populations in Somalia Provision of Life-Saving Shelter and Life Sustaining NFI to Vulnerable Populations in Somalia Due to the ongoing humanitarian crisis, Shelter and Non-Food Items (SNFI) needs remain consistently high, with an estimated 3.1 million Somalis with SNFI needs according to the Humanitarian Needs Overview 2021, especially in Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) sites where many households (HHs) live in makeshift shelters. Oftentimes, these makeshift shelters do not provide adequate privacy and protection against weather elements, whilst a lack of tenure security, random evictions and vulnerability to fires further exacerbate the shelter needs of IDPs. It is therefore estimated that around one-third of the Somali population lack essential NFIs. 

Therefore, SNFI needs are the subject of much collaborative efforts; Collective Outcome 2 of the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) aims ‘to reduce the risks and vulnerabilities, and build resilience of displaced and host communities to reach durable solutions’, whilst Specific Objective 2.2 aims to scale-up and provide CCCM, WASH, education, health, nutrition, shelter and NFI services for 1.6 million people in established IDP sites across 68 districts by the end of 2021.

For the 2021 HRP, 75,000 individuals (12,500 households with an average of 6 individuals per household) will receive NFI support through a mixed-methods strategy of in-kind contingency stocks provision to be undertaken with contingency stock partners and direct implementation of Cash-Based Intervention (CBI) for NFI needs. A further 75,000 individuals will receive shelter support through emergency shelter, in-kind shelter kits, and CBI for shelter needs. Finally, 15,000 individuals will receive infrastructure support, both in-kind and through CBI. The transfer mechanism for CBI   will be evidence-based and linked to market assessment and needs analysis. The breakdown of the planned intervention is as follows: (1) the provision of contingency stock with in-kind NFI and shelter kits for 10,000 households (NFI: 7,500, Shelter: 2,500), available for distribution nationwide by shelter cluster partners where need arises; (2) emergency/transitional shelter (Emergency: 7,500; Transitional: 2,500) and NFI (5,000) support to newly displaced IDPs in the Gedo and Bay region targeting 15,000 households; (3) infrastructure support to 2,500 households in Gedo and Bay region.

Coordinated humanitarian assistance to climate and conflict affected populations in Somalia Provision of lifesaving assistance and sustainable solutions through safe Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) services, for people in crises and their host communities in multiple regions in Somalia. IOM WASH is proposing to contribute to the continuation and restoration of access to safe and equitable basic WASH services to overall 380,000 beneficiaries from vulnerable IDP and host-communities in multiple regions in Somalia. 

Specifically, the project will target 228,000 Nondisplaced people (children 107,160; men 41,040; women 36,480; elderly 9,120 and disabled 34,200) and 152,000 displaced populations (children 71,440; men 27,360; women 24,320; elderly 6,080 and disabled 22,800). 

IOM will rehabilitate 50 strategic water sources for multi-use that will provide continued, equitable, safe, sufficient and sustainable water to regions, targeted by the cluster, prone to natural disasters. 

IOM further proposes to construct 3,000 new emergency sanitation facilities (following cluster specifications) targeting populations without access to basic sanitation and hygiene.

The project will also strengthen the capacity of the Federal Government of Somalia and Federal Members States, community leaders and water committees/technicians for better coordination with government authorities and communities and sustainability of the constructed/ rehabilitated WASH infrastructures. In addition, the project will nurture community participation in good hygiene practices through training and community sensitization campaigns.  All trainings, awareness raising and capacity building activities will follow national guidelines on COVID-19 preventive measures, e.g. on physical distancing, to avoid mass gatherings and minimize risks of exposure.

The project is aligned with protection mainstreaming to ensure safety and dignity of affected populations without causing harm. Affected populations and all relevant stakeholders including men, women, boys, girls, elderly and people with disability will be involved in decision making throughout the project activities/cycle. 

Furthermore, the project will be a part of an IOM integrated emergency response program and resilience building, where possible, efforts will be made to integrate IOM health, nutrition, shelter, CCCM and protection activities.

Aide alimentaire d'urgence : aide en nature Provision of in-kind food assistance to Vulnerable Palestine refugees in Syria  UNRWA estimates that 418,000 Palestine refugees in Syria will continue to require humanitarian assistance in 2021. In a context of rising inflation and additional economic hardship caused by COVID-19, Palestine refugees are more and more affected by food insecurity and therefore increasingly depend on UNRWA assistance to meet their minimum food needs. Due to the vulnerability of Palestine refugees in the current socio-economic crisis, compounded by COVID-19, in 2021 UNRWA will expand its food programming and provide all 418,000 Palestine refugees with in-kind food assistance  through three distribution rounds. The Agency will continue to monitor the availability of food on the markets and will retain operational flexibility to adjust to a changing context as appropriate.

The composition of the food basket was developed based on WFP guidelines and in view of meeting ~ 50% of daily nutritional needs for 4 months.

UNRWA's original plan is to distribute 3 rounds of in-kind food assistance, each round covering a period of 4 months. However, this depends on the availability of funds. Until May 2021, UNRWA received or confirmed pledges are only sufficient to cover the first two rounds of 2021. The Agency will continue to mobilize resources to ensure funding for the third round is also secured.

In 2021, the number of people estimated to be in need of humanitarian assistance including for food needs is 418,000 Palestine refugees to strengthen their resilience and prevent further deterioration into acute food insecurity. As per its emergency planning, UNRWA aims to provide food assistance as well as multipurpose cash assistance, and protection interventions at both household and community levels, as well as the coordination of these activities across the different Sectors framework.

UNRWA has been providing life-saving humanitarian aid to Palestine refugees since the start of the crisis in Syria. The in-kind food assistance program remains one of the most important forms of UNRWA emergency support to stabilize the food security status for Palestine refugees in Syria, as it helps them meet part of their basic nutritional and survival requirements (~50% of kcal/person/day) which will increase resilience, and reduce humanitarian needs and the spiraling food insecurity levels.

Against South Sudan 2021 HRP Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2021, there are more than 314,000 refugees from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, as well as the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, including from Sudan, Democratic Republic of Congo and Central African Republic.

At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for long-term stability, some 357,500 South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since November 2017, 122,000 of those in 2020 alone. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan at this stage, the increase in numbers warrants a scaling-up of support following an area-based approach, including strengthening linkages with development actors, to help returnees and the communities they settle in live in safety and dignity, with greater security and services.

Refugees largely reside in conﬂict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction of basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.

Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will beneﬁt from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Speciﬁc protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identiﬁed at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with speciﬁc protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as veriﬁcation exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the eﬃciency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to beneﬁt from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

Against South Sudan 2021 HRP Internally Displaced Population in South Sudan supported through provision of protection and targeted assistance to promote resilience, protection advocacy and achievement of solutions. The project aims to strengthen community and rights-based protection response for IDPs, IDP returnees and vulnerable persons within their host communities. The project will focus on providing physical and legal protection through advocacy, timely protection monitoring, life-saving protection response based on identified needs and solutions. The project will address Housing, Land and Property (HLP) rights issues through the provision of legal assistance, facilitate issuance of property and identity documents, and work with mediation mechanisms to support HLP related dispute resolution. Community-based networks will be utilized as part of the protection response to foster community buy in and ownership of protection. The project will use evidence-based planning to expand outreach and develop the capacity of displaced communities to cope, recover, contribute to and ultimately achieve solutions. Out of 1.6 million IDPs, 475,000 IDPs and IDP returnees will be supported with protection interventions and assistance in seven (7) states and an administrative areas. Recognising the protection concerns linked to food insecurity, the Agency activities also include a scaling-up of activities in South Sudan’s highly food insecure and prioritised locations, i.e. Pibor County, Akobo, Aweil South, Tonj East, Tonj North, Tonj South. There will be continuous advocacy and support in the area of law and policy with relevant government bodies such as the   Ministries of Justice Home Affairs, Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management, and the Relief and Rehabilitation Commission (RRC) to ensure the centrality of protection, enact the “Protection and Assistance to Internally Displaced Persons Act 2018” (IDP) Bill, National Framework on Returns, and various HLP initiatives. The relevant line ministries will also receive capacity building and technical assistance. Building on UNHCR’s existing operational presence in Bentiu Bor, Juba, Malakal, Wau, Yambio, Yei, the Agency will continue to advance on the 2020 geographic expansion of IDP activities by leveraging both static and mobile presence through 15 partners to Central Equatoria, Unity, Upper Nile, Joinglei, Western Bahr El Ghazal, Northern Bahr El Ghazal, Lakes, Western Equatoira, Eastern Equatoris and Warrap. Response and monitoring will cover 19 identified priority counties and Pibor Administrative Area, including remote or hard to-reach areas, in full support to the Protection Cluster Strategy for mobile assessments and response. Partners comprise of both national and international organizations, with selection undertaken on the basis of their pre-existing presence, access to populations of concern and capacity to carry out static and remote protection monitoring and response. While not all proposed activity locations fall under the severity 3, 4 or 5 in terms of food insecurity, recognizing the fluidly and unpredictable nature of sub-national violence in South Sudan, UNHCR’s protection by presence approach requires presence in areas affected by conflict as well as areas of potential return in light of increased momentum in terms of solutions 
Resources and advocacy will focus primarily on protection response and solutions, either durable or transitional (where the former is not yet possible), including assessments on needs, risks, and intentions and feasibility of durable solutions, while also strengthening community-based structures, supporting HLP initiatives, promotion of livelihoods and peaceful coexistence. Improving coordination and quality of assessments and monitoring will be a key component. A mobile tool was introduced in late 2019 that has enhanced data collection and triangulation of information through timely collection and analysis capabilities, which will further improve information products, leading to a more fitting risk-mitigation approach, reduced response time; while underpinning protection mainstreaming across other operational interventions, including of other Clusters.

Against South Sudan 2021 HRP Targeted support to displaced persons with specific needs with lifesaving non-food items and emergency shelter in hard to reach areas and areas of IDP returns The UNHCR ES/NFI project for 2021 is focused on responding to the humanitarian needs of internally displaced persons (IDPs) and ensure humanitarian standards are maintained. IDPs continue to be exposed dire living conditions with limited livelihood options, the lack of access to markets and often more than one displacement.  The need for provision of basic and domestic items remains a priority. Families are often displaced without substantial household items, fleeing with little more than they can carry. Inadequate shelter may also lead to increased protection risks and susceptibility to diseases. In addition, populations in situations of protracted displacement require replenishment of assistance to ensure basic humanitarian needs are met. With COVID-19 preventive measures mainstreamed, considerations for decongestion of sites and number of persons per shelter shall be taken into account in consultation with the CCCM cluster and other stakeholders. SOMALIA - Multisectoral humanitarian aid in western, central and eastern Africa (2021 portion) Humanitarian WASH Response in Somaliland and Puntland Regions, Somalia  Unreliable access to a temporary and/or inadequate WASH facility remains an important feature of the humanitarian landscape in Somalia. This dire situation is even worsened by the COVID19 pandemic which require more water for frequent handwashing for prevention and containment. Schools in Somalia are reopening and due to COVID19, a number of schools are requesting urgent water supply for both students consumption and to support frequent handwashing. 

The water supply coverage in Somalia is strongly dependent on rainfall performance. In the last two rainy seasons namely 2019 Dayr and 2020 Gu, the performance of rains has improved slightly (SWALIM/FAO). From 2017 onwards, the water coverage has shown slight improvement due to improved rain performance. The National WASH Cluster estimates 59% as having sufficient drinking water with 66% of those with access walk less than 15 minutes for a water point and 20% having challenges to access the minimum quantity of safe water. (JMCNA ). 48% access their own improved latrines, while 52% use either unimproved latrines or practicing open defecation (22%) posing a huge public health risk. Furthermore, 2% used soap with water at latrines, 52% use soap at household level while 40% use other substitute for handwashing. 45% of women/girls access MHM materials. 
On the other hand, Oxfam needs assessment conducted late 2019 in Sool, Sanaag and Togdheer regions indicates that over 40% of both IDP and host communities rely on purchasing water from commercial trucks. There is no well-organized and reliable government data that shows the coverage of water, sanitation, and hygiene in Somalia. In December 2019 and January 2020, Oxfam and FAO/SWALIM conducted a WASH inventory in all regions of Somaliland. The inventory focused on sustainable and strategic water sources in the country including boreholes, springs, and protected shallow wells. The functionality of these sources is critical. However, the current functionality rate is estimated to be much below 70% and decreases as the stress level goes up during the drought period. The analysis of the final report is not yet finalized but expected to inform the sector on ways to increase functionality and reduce interruption of services. Until the end of May 2020, over 412,000 people are displaced by the floods (UNOCHA, Flood Bulletin). The capacity of regional states and the federal government is limited only to response instead of constructing large scale flood protection structures.

In order to address malnutrition prevention, prioritizing pregnant and lactating women and caregivers of young children with nutrition, Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) and hygiene promotion and counseling is a priority in modalities that meet the needs and concerns of the communities supported, whether individually or in groups, in health facilities or in the community, all while mobilizing the community. To complement these interventions, ensuring that caregivers are empowered to assess and follow-up on their U5 children's malnutrition status is as crucial. Support for critical Desert Locust control operations in Ethiopia 56% Somalia 44% - (SOMALIA) (part of ECHO/-HF/BUD/2021/91003) Saving Lives and Livelihoods in Rural Somalia  Somalia faced a growing number of threats to its food security in 2020, starting with the ongoing Desert Locust crisis, followed by COVID-19 first reported in March, severe flooding between April and September and poor rains forecast for the Deyr 2020 season. Based on latest projections, 2.1 million Somalis are in IPC Phases 3 and above through December 2020. Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of the La Nina developing, which tends to trigger dry conditions in Somalia. If the forecast below-average Deyr rains (Oct-Dec 2020) is followed by below-average or delayed 2021 Gu rains (Apr-Jun), this could lead to a rapid and substantial worsening of the humanitarian situation. 

Rural populations are at a high risk of further deteriorating food security, given the direct and indirect impacts of these threats on rural livelihoods, related assets, food production and income. FAO’s proposal responds both to the lifesaving and life-sustaining needs of rural populations in IPC Phases 3 and above, against a Population in Need (PiN) of 3.1 million people prioritized for Food Security Cluster (FSC) assistance under the 2021 HRP. FAO’s planned activities will directly support 103,850 households in IPC 3-4 under both FSC Strategic Objectives (SOs), while further delivering support to protect food security in Somalia at a wider scale through countrywide animal health campaigns, among other activities. 

Under SO1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 76,300 rural households, including IDPs, in the form of Cash+, UCT and CFW activities delivered through FAO’s e-Platform for Mobile Money and Livelihood Assistance. All cash-based programmes include trainings on good nutrition practices, covering infancy to old age.

Under SO2, to protect livelihoods, FAO will provide in-kind and technical support to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security threats across Somalia’s rural livelihood zones, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to 53,500 households targeted for Cash+ interventions under SO1 (while supporting an additional 7,550 households with agricultural inputs only). FAO’s planned Cash+ activities combine cash transfers with tailored livelihood support packages to assist rural families out of hunger sooner. Alongside cash transfers, the assistance packages will protect and restore the livelihoods of households in IPC Phases 3-4 by providing: (i) farmers with quality inputs to produce a nutritious variety of food crop (cereal, pulse and vegetable seeds, storage bags, fertilizer and irrigation/tractor services, where appropriate; (ii) pastoralists with nutrient-rich feed blocks and deworming to improve livestock productivity especially milk supply; and (iii) coastal communities with a variety of basic fishing gear and processing equipment to improve catch and consumption.  

Also under SO2, in anticipation of drought conditions in early 2021, FAO will also strategically position water bladder tanks and provide nutritive animal feed blocks to protect the small milking animals of up to 20,000 pastoral households impacted by scarce pasture from dry conditions and/or locust damage. Countrywide livestock vaccination and supportive treatment campaigns will further protect livestock assets belonging to at least 2.2 million men, women and children. Preparedness for animal health emergencies will be enhanced through strategic stocking of vaccines and related supplies (PPR), and training to local partners in Livestock Emergency Guidelines and Standards (LEGS), antimicrobial resistance, disease surveillance and reporting, among others.

Food Assistance Programme Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP camps, and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity.

WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying  mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan. 

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities, or other solution. 

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19 have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

Food Security Emergency Food Security and Livelihoods for flood affected Households in Upper Nile Heavy rain and flooding created historical overflow of the Nile and Sobat Rivers since July 2020, creating the worst flooding in 60 years. The flood destroyed homes and livelihoods of people - damaged settlements, agriculture (crops and cattle), horticulture, and market access which are crucial for peoples’ livelihoods. 40% of the crops and vegetable gardens in GOAL operational areas have been affected and no yield has been harvested during harvesting in 2020. People are also displaced and feared to turn to negative coping mechanisms such as informal borrowing, selling productive assets, and depletion of working capital which might be used to protect from the impact of the disaster. The  flooding crisis came at the back drop of very grim hunger situation in these areas, where already 163,000 were suffering from acute and severe hunger (about 70% of population in Baliet, and 85% in Ulang) (IPC Phases 3, and 4). And 59,462 in IPC4. This situation was further impacted by the current economic downturn and higher inflation rates, in addition to food price hikes exacerbated by the impact of COVID-19 pandemic. The floods severely affected the opportunities for income generating schemes leading to loss of household income and inability to afford food and meet basic needs. Negative coping mechanisms of poor and most affected households have been reported, such as taking fewer meals per day (mostly amongst women and girls), selling assets or borrowing money at high rates to purchase food items, causing unmanageable debt. The flooding also resulted in increased incidences of human diseases such as malaria and acute watery diarrhoea that will affect productivity and deplete savings in the form of increased medical expenses – this will further contribute to household vulnerability and reduce resources available for purchasing food.
GOAL is requesting access to the HRP to cover the immediate needs of 25,800 vulnerable individuals severely  affected by the current flooding of the Sobat river. The individuals targeted will be from existing GOAL beneficiaries who have been flood affected. The flooding affected 68,502 people in Baliet  and Ulang counties. Under the GOAL programme, GOAL has been providing support to build the resilience of 160,000 people in Melut, Baliet, Ulang, Rubkona, and Panyinjar counties since 2016. Prior to the current flooding GOAL program has been implementing various flood risk preparedness and mitigation activities including: dissemination of Early Warning Information, and  development of an early response strategy to mitigate the impact of flooding, stakeholders coordination, formation of flood response committees, identification of most vulnerable people and high-risk areas; distribution of empty sacks to aid dyke construction, dyke construction and monitoring implementation of flood response actions. This request for HRP is sought as the scale and magnitude of the current flooding and livelihood crisis it has compounded requires additional interventions to help vulnerable households meet their immediate needs, reducing the hunger gap and mitigating negative coping mechanisms. This intervention will also provide support to host communities that had to cope with people displaced. 
There is a significant gap in the response to these needs. WFP food distribution covers only 50% of the monthly  households’ food needs. This presents an urgent need for emergency livelihood interventions. The HRP will support households through Cash for Assets to address their immediate food needs, while building assets, such as constructing flood control dikes that will improve their livelihoods, reduce risks and impact of shocks, increase food productivity, and strengthen resilience to natural disasters. The cash for assets will be conditional cash transfer with two components of conditionality – engagement on Cash for Asset, to rebuild community assets, for able bodied households; and mandatory attendance on trainings.

BURKINA FASO - Emergency food security and nutrition, WASH, and cash benefits to vulnerable populations affected by the humanitarian crisis in the Sahel (2021 portion) Assistance aux populations vulnérables affectées par la crise humanitaire dans les provinces du Bam et du Gourma Welthungerhilfe, propose une intervention ciblée ayant pour objectif principal de contirbuer à l'amélioration des conditions de vie des populations les plus vulnérables avec une réponse intégrant trois secteurs d'intervention : La sécurité alimentaire, la nutrition, et l'eau, hygiène et assainissement.
OS1 : La relance des moyens de d'existence adapté au climat est assurée.
OS2 : Prévenir, en colaboration avec les districts sanitaire, l'augmentation des taux de malnutrition des FEFA et enfants<5ans ainsi que la mortalité et la morbidité associés
OS3 : Prévenir, avec des interventions en eau, hygiène et assainisement, les risques de malnutritions et des maladies associées.
WHH porte une attention particulière aux groupes nécessistant un appui spécifique ou de protection : filles / femmes soumises à des pressions familiales et sociales fortes, voient leur études réduites et devant faire face à une charge de travail plus importante, auquel vient s'ajouter le risque plus élevé de perte de vie ou d'être victime de violence et d'exploitation sexuelle, les garçons / hommes dont les attentes sociales sotn également fortes, pouvant avoir des comportements plus à risque pour subvenir aux besoins de leur famille et se voient assumer de nouveaux rôles en temps de crise, ils bénéficient généralement de très peu de soutien en cas d'abus sexuel, les personnes âgés pouvant souffrir d'isolement, de problème de santé et voient leur stratégie de subsistance perturbées, les personnes vivants avec un handicap, ont plus de difficultés à accèder à l'assistance et aux infrastructures de base, ont moins d'accès à l'information et ont une grande dépendance, ils sont souvent stigmatisés, risquent d'isolement et manque d'inclusion.
WHH intègre la protection transversale en consultant les différents groupes de personnes, en répondant à leur besoins spécifiques, en mettant ces populations au centre dela réponse et en les impliquant dans les différentes activités en fonction de leurs capacités ainsi qu'en tenant compte des rôles et dynamiques de pouvoir en cherchant à réduire les barrières sociales liées au genre et à la discrimination.
WHH intègre également la participation et la redevabilité dans les différentes phases du cycle de projet. Les représentants des communautés feront partie du mécanisme de redevabilité en collectant les feedbacks et les plaintes. Des comités au niveau de chauque commune d'intervention seront directement en liaison avec le responsable de la redevabilité auprès du bureau pays de WHH. Des réunions périodiques seront instaurées avec les autorités locales, les services techniques décentralisés et les représentants des bénéficiares pour la restitution des réalisations du projet et les avancements relatifs aux différentes plaintes et recommendations reçues de la part des communautés.
Ces stratégies de cohésion sociale, de protection transversales et de participation des acteurs permettrons de réduire les risques et d'améliorer la qualité de la réponse humanitaire en tenant compte du principe de Do No Arm.
Dans le cadre du Nexus, WHH se coordonne tant avec les acteurs d'urgence que de Développement.
