Provision of in-kind food assistance to Palestine Refugees in Syria Provision of in-kind food assistance to Vulnerable Palestine refugees in Syria  UNRWA estimates that 418,000 Palestine refugees in Syria will continue to require humanitarian assistance in 2021. In a context of rising inflation and additional economic hardship caused by COVID-19, Palestine refugees are more and more affected by food insecurity and therefore increasingly depend on UNRWA assistance to meet their minimum food needs. Due to the vulnerability of Palestine refugees in the current socio-economic crisis, compounded by COVID-19, in 2021 UNRWA will expand its food programming and provide all 418,000 Palestine refugees with in-kind food assistance  through three distribution rounds. The Agency will continue to monitor the availability of food on the markets and will retain operational flexibility to adjust to a changing context as appropriate.

The composition of the food basket was developed based on WFP guidelines and in view of meeting ~ 50% of daily nutritional needs for 4 months.

UNRWA's original plan is to distribute 3 rounds of in-kind food assistance, each round covering a period of 4 months. However, this depends on the availability of funds. Until May 2021, UNRWA received or confirmed pledges are only sufficient to cover the first two rounds of 2021. The Agency will continue to mobilize resources to ensure funding for the third round is also secured.

In 2021, the number of people estimated to be in need of humanitarian assistance including for food needs is 418,000 Palestine refugees to strengthen their resilience and prevent further deterioration into acute food insecurity. As per its emergency planning, UNRWA aims to provide food assistance as well as multipurpose cash assistance, and protection interventions at both household and community levels, as well as the coordination of these activities across the different Sectors framework.

UNRWA has been providing life-saving humanitarian aid to Palestine refugees since the start of the crisis in Syria. The in-kind food assistance program remains one of the most important forms of UNRWA emergency support to stabilize the food security status for Palestine refugees in Syria, as it helps them meet part of their basic nutritional and survival requirements (~50% of kcal/person/day) which will increase resilience, and reduce humanitarian needs and the spiraling food insecurity levels.

Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP camps, and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity.

WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying  mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan. 

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities, or other solution. 

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19 have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

Emergency Food Assistance for underserved communities in Aweil South , Aweil East and Panijiar Counties of South Sudan   The purpose of the project is to enhance emergency food production, diversify food consumption and strengthen the resilience of targeted communities. The project aims to achieve this purpose by distributing crop and vegetable seed kits, agricultural tool kits, fishing kits, provide agronomic training for 8,400 households, approximately 50,400 individuals. Food production trainings will be through provision of farmer extension services, establishment of farmer field schools and vegetable gardens in schools and nutrition centers. Diet diversity will be achieved by increased consumption of vegetables, increased availability of fish at household level and local markets as well as through targeted sensitization on food preparation (cooking demonstrations), IYCF and basic household hygiene. Further, the resilience of the target communities will be strengthened by encouraging them to participate in construction or rehabilitation of community assets through cash for asset approach. This approach is supplementary expected to provide an alternative source of income to targeted individuals. Additional measures of addressing underlying causes of food insecurity shall include capacity building in disaster risk reduction, natural resources management and establishment of referral pathways to other services including nutrition health care, education, protection, and WASH.

Improve the most vulnerable crisis-affected people’s access to timely and appropriate food assistance, including fuel and energy related support, to meet their immediate food needs. Critical agricultural livelihoods support to conflict- and pandemic-affected households in northeast Nigeria In 2021, FAO will improve food security, nutritional status and incomes among vulnerable, conflict- and pandemic-affected households in Borno, Adamawa and Yobe states in Northeast Nigeria. The now more than decade-long insurgency has decimated agricultural livelihoods upon which more than 80 percent of the population relies as a primary source of household income. The COVID-19 pandemic has further compounded this already highly vulnerable humanitarian context, generating interconnected vulnerabilities that negatively affect availability and access to food, agriculture inputs, finance, farming land, extension services, markets and the fundamental viability of agricultural livelihoods. 
Support to crop production and the rebuilding of a robust crop value chain have been identified by FAO as key to the restoration of livelihoods and to improving the food and nutrition security of vulnerable populations in the BAY states. FAO will support vulnerable households with critical inputs for rainy and dry season cultivation as well as for micro-/backyard gardening and seed production.   
Prior to the insurgency, close to 80 percent of households in northeast Nigeria reared livestock and/or poultry as a vital source of food and household income. The conflict has caused the wide-scale loss of these assets either through looting, property destruction, disease, or abandonment when fleeing attacks by armed insurgents. In addition to being a source of income generation through breeding for sale, livestock and poultry restocking increases the availability of meat, milk and eggs at the household level. FAO will increase support to livestock and poultry production in 2021 in support of affected households.
Prior to the crisis, the fisheries sector had significant economic importance and fish from the northeast were supplied to the rest of Nigeria. With increased land and areas retaken by the military, the return of IDPs to their communities of origin is ongoing, thereby enabling some to access fishing grounds and resume their traditional livelihood. However, the lack of quality inputs remains a limiting factor for the majority of fishers who continue to rely on humanitarian assistance to meet their food and livelihood needs. By leveraging FAO’s extensive experience and capacity, conflict-affected fisherfolk households will be supported to resume their livelihoods and meet their food and nutritional needs. 
The ongoing crisis is also termed a ‘protection crisis’ with vulnerable social groups – particularly children, women and the elderly – disproportionately affected by the impact of the ongoing conflict and the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic and are at heightened risk of adopting negative coping strategies such as child labour, borrowing, street begging, basic needs deprivation, transactional sex, early and forced marriage as their families seek to reduce the number of mouths to feed in their homes, and collection of fuelwood in insecure areas, which remains a high-risk livelihood. FAO will support vulnerable households by way of fuel-efficient stoves to reduce exposure to potential protection risks, and stove production and briquette production centres for income generation. 
Access to credit is a particular challenge for vulnerable groups in Northeast Nigeria, particularly women. Through the establishment of Group Savings and Loans Associations (GSLA), in 2021 FAO will extend its GSLA programme and will identify vulnerable groups to enhance their access to credit and financial services as an important social safety net.  
FAO is the co-lead of the Food Security Sector (FSS) which plays a critical role in coordinating food security programming in the BAY states. Food security data collection and analysis are also key and upon which food security actors base their intervention. In 2021, FAO will continue to support and host the Food Security Sector to facilitate the required coordination and analyses required to reach people most in need.

Mali - OCHA Office  [OCT 9842];[ONU04512] Renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et de plaidoyer pour la protection humanitaire et l’assistance aux populations les plus vulnérables au Mali. 
La situation humanitaire demeure complexe et instable, principalement en raison des conflits armés et intercommunautaires dans les régions du Centre et du Nord. Le retard dans la mise en œuvre de l’Accord pour la paix et la réconciliation au Mali paraphé en juin 2015 et dans le processus de désarmement, démobilisation, réintégration (DDR) contribuent à la persistance de l’instabilité sécuritaire dans les régions de Kidal, Gao, Ménaka, Tombouctou, Ségou et Mopti ainsi qu’à l’aggravation des tensions sociales. A cause des activités des acteurs armés, l’accès humanitaire demeure difficile mais fluide dans certaines zones. 

La présence limitée de l’État et l’insécurité dans ces régions demeurent l’un des facteurs clés obligeant les civils à fuir leurs communautés. La grogne sociale qui a conduit au changement de régime en août 2021 prouve l’inaccessibilité des populations maliennes aux services sociaux de base et l’aggravation de leur vulnérabilité à laquelle s’ajoute le poids de la pandémie de COVID-19. 

Le nombre de Personnes Déplacées Internes (PDI) a atteint la barre des 311,191 en octobre 2020 en comparaison aux 199 385 enregistrés à la même période en 2019 et 80 302 en 2018.  Les risques et les besoins de protection des populations fuyant leurs communautés sous la pression de la violence armée ou des tensions intercommunautaires, sont élevés. De graves abus et attaques contre les personnes, les biens et les services (écoles, centres de santé) sont régulièrement signalées alors que l’accès aux services appropriés est compromis. Comme les déplacements internes sont de longue durée, les risques de protection et les violations des droits fondamentaux augmentent, en particulier pour les plus vulnérables (femmes, enfants, personnes âgées, personnes handicapées ou malades). De graves conséquences humanitaires ont donc été notées, telles que des taux élevés d’insécurité alimentaire et de malnutrition ainsi que le faible accès aux services sociaux de base.

Avec près de 4,7 millions de personnes affectées par l’insécurité alimentaire, dont 2,3 millions personnes avec des besoins d’assistance d’urgence, l’année 2020 a été, selon les résultats des exercices du Cadre Harmonisé (CH), l’année la plus fortement marquée par l’insécurité alimentaire depuis 2014. Les conséquences de cette détérioration resteront perceptibles sur le niveau de vie de populations en 2021. Les capacités de réponse existantes au Mali représentent environ 200 organisations humanitaires, acteurs du développement ainsi que des forces militaires (MINUSMA, Forces maliennes de défense et de sécurité, Barkhane, Mission européenne de formation, G5 Sahel). Le contexte susmentionné exigera une coordination efficace et la présence d’OCHA demeure très importante. OCHA maintiendra sa présence à Bamako, Mopti, Tombouctou et Gao ainsi que son antenne de Ségou tout en couvrant à distance les régions de Taoudénit, Ménaka, Kidal et les régions du sud.

Sept clusters actifs (Éducation, Sécurité alimentaire, Santé, Nutrition, Protection, Abris/BNA et WASH), des sous-clusters et des groupes de travail spécialisés (Accès, CMCoord, Redevabilité, Genre et Cash) sont en place au niveau national et local. Le Bureau d’OCHA au Mali continuera ainsi à jouer un rôle central dans la mobilisation, la coordination et le soutien des acteurs humanitaires dans les domaines de la coordination, la gestion de l’information, le financement humanitaire et le plaidoyer avec un accent accru dans le domaine de Civilo-Militaire et d’accès humanitaire afin de garantir la conservation et la consolidation de l’espace humanitaire. OCHA jouera un rôle essentiel dans la mobilisation adéquate des fonds en faveur des personnes dans le besoin, en plus de contribuer à dynamiser les efforts déployés par le Gouvernement et les acteurs du développement pour s’attaquer aux causes structurelles de la vulnérabilité.

Addressing the protection needs of women and girls in South Sudan through an integrated protection response for female education and empowerment Internally Displaced Population in South Sudan supported through provision of protection and targeted assistance to promote resilience, protection advocacy and achievement of solutions. The project aims to strengthen community and rights-based protection response for IDPs, IDP returnees and vulnerable persons within their host communities. The project will focus on providing physical and legal protection through advocacy, timely protection monitoring, life-saving protection response based on identified needs and solutions. The project will address Housing, Land and Property (HLP) rights issues through the provision of legal assistance, facilitate issuance of property and identity documents, and work with mediation mechanisms to support HLP related dispute resolution. Community-based networks will be utilized as part of the protection response to foster community buy in and ownership of protection. The project will use evidence-based planning to expand outreach and develop the capacity of displaced communities to cope, recover, contribute to and ultimately achieve solutions. Out of 1.6 million IDPs, 475,000 IDPs and IDP returnees will be supported with protection interventions and assistance in seven (7) states and an administrative areas. Recognising the protection concerns linked to food insecurity, the Agency activities also include a scaling-up of activities in South Sudan’s highly food insecure and prioritised locations, i.e. Pibor County, Akobo, Aweil South, Tonj East, Tonj North, Tonj South. There will be continuous advocacy and support in the area of law and policy with relevant government bodies such as the   Ministries of Justice Home Affairs, Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management, and the Relief and Rehabilitation Commission (RRC) to ensure the centrality of protection, enact the “Protection and Assistance to Internally Displaced Persons Act 2018” (IDP) Bill, National Framework on Returns, and various HLP initiatives. The relevant line ministries will also receive capacity building and technical assistance. Building on UNHCR’s existing operational presence in Bentiu Bor, Juba, Malakal, Wau, Yambio, Yei, the Agency will continue to advance on the 2020 geographic expansion of IDP activities by leveraging both static and mobile presence through 15 partners to Central Equatoria, Unity, Upper Nile, Joinglei, Western Bahr El Ghazal, Northern Bahr El Ghazal, Lakes, Western Equatoira, Eastern Equatoris and Warrap. Response and monitoring will cover 19 identified priority counties and Pibor Administrative Area, including remote or hard to-reach areas, in full support to the Protection Cluster Strategy for mobile assessments and response. Partners comprise of both national and international organizations, with selection undertaken on the basis of their pre-existing presence, access to populations of concern and capacity to carry out static and remote protection monitoring and response. While not all proposed activity locations fall under the severity 3, 4 or 5 in terms of food insecurity, recognizing the fluidly and unpredictable nature of sub-national violence in South Sudan, UNHCR’s protection by presence approach requires presence in areas affected by conflict as well as areas of potential return in light of increased momentum in terms of solutions 
Resources and advocacy will focus primarily on protection response and solutions, either durable or transitional (where the former is not yet possible), including assessments on needs, risks, and intentions and feasibility of durable solutions, while also strengthening community-based structures, supporting HLP initiatives, promotion of livelihoods and peaceful coexistence. Improving coordination and quality of assessments and monitoring will be a key component. A mobile tool was introduced in late 2019 that has enhanced data collection and triangulation of information through timely collection and analysis capabilities, which will further improve information products, leading to a more fitting risk-mitigation approach, reduced response time; while underpinning protection mainstreaming across other operational interventions, including of other Clusters.

La respuesta se enfocará en 5 municipios de 2 departamentos del corredor seco de Guatemala donde los sistemas de agua fueron dañados por eventos naturales o ampliaciones para el mejoramiento de los mismos.
La implementación será a través de socios nacionales o locales que coordinarán y fortalecerán a las municipalidades y comunidades buscando que mejoren sus capacidades de respuesta a emergencia, vincularse al desarrollo con sistemas de información pertinentes y oportunos en cuanto a WASH se refiere.
Se realizarán sistemas de agua y saneamiento sostenibles con participación activa de las partes, que incluyan el enfoque de resiliencia, vinculado con actividades de cambio de comportamiento de manera inclusiva y participativa. La orientación del proyecto es a personas con mayor vulnerabilidad como población rural, mujeres, niñas y personas con discapacidad.
Además, se coordinará con los clústeres de nutrición, salud, educación y protección para generar una respuesta cohesiva e integral y generar sinergia con las otras acciones que se integran dentro de este proyecto, las principales acciones se realizarán en conjunto con UNICEF y ONU Mujeres.
Las acciones más relevantes son:
- Fortalecimiento de capacidades para la sostenibilidad de los sistemas a funcionarios municipales de WASH, responsables de AOM de sistemas comunitarios e integrantes del hogar en sistemas unifamiliares.
- Rehabilitación, mejora y construcción de sistemas de agua a escala familiar y comunitaria.
- Mejora de la calidad de agua en sistemas en hogar, comunidad, escuelas y establecimientos de salud.
- Promoción y vinculación del triple nexo en acciones WASH relacionados con captación de agua lluvia, uso de recursos hídricos, tratamiento de aguas para consumo y residuales para reciclado.
- WASH en escuelas y establecimientos de salud abordando las necesidades de higiene menstrual.
- Campañas de comunicación para promover la práctica de hábitos de higiene, desinfección, uso y manipulación del agua.

Somalia/CE: Food Assistance, Agriculture and Food Security, Natural and Technological Risks, Economic Recovery and Market Systems, Humanitarian Coordination and Info Management  (USAID/BHA) Saving Lives and Livelihoods in Rural Somalia  Somalia faced a growing number of threats to its food security in 2020, starting with the ongoing Desert Locust crisis, followed by COVID-19 first reported in March, severe flooding between April and September and poor rains forecast for the Deyr 2020 season. Based on latest projections, 2.1 million Somalis are in IPC Phases 3 and above through December 2020. Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of the La Nina developing, which tends to trigger dry conditions in Somalia. If the forecast below-average Deyr rains (Oct-Dec 2020) is followed by below-average or delayed 2021 Gu rains (Apr-Jun), this could lead to a rapid and substantial worsening of the humanitarian situation. 

Rural populations are at a high risk of further deteriorating food security, given the direct and indirect impacts of these threats on rural livelihoods, related assets, food production and income. FAO’s proposal responds both to the lifesaving and life-sustaining needs of rural populations in IPC Phases 3 and above, against a Population in Need (PiN) of 3.1 million people prioritized for Food Security Cluster (FSC) assistance under the 2021 HRP. FAO’s planned activities will directly support 103,850 households in IPC 3-4 under both FSC Strategic Objectives (SOs), while further delivering support to protect food security in Somalia at a wider scale through countrywide animal health campaigns, among other activities. 

Under SO1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 76,300 rural households, including IDPs, in the form of Cash+, UCT and CFW activities delivered through FAO’s e-Platform for Mobile Money and Livelihood Assistance. All cash-based programmes include trainings on good nutrition practices, covering infancy to old age.

Under SO2, to protect livelihoods, FAO will provide in-kind and technical support to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security threats across Somalia’s rural livelihood zones, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to 53,500 households targeted for Cash+ interventions under SO1 (while supporting an additional 7,550 households with agricultural inputs only). FAO’s planned Cash+ activities combine cash transfers with tailored livelihood support packages to assist rural families out of hunger sooner. Alongside cash transfers, the assistance packages will protect and restore the livelihoods of households in IPC Phases 3-4 by providing: (i) farmers with quality inputs to produce a nutritious variety of food crop (cereal, pulse and vegetable seeds, storage bags, fertilizer and irrigation/tractor services, where appropriate; (ii) pastoralists with nutrient-rich feed blocks and deworming to improve livestock productivity especially milk supply; and (iii) coastal communities with a variety of basic fishing gear and processing equipment to improve catch and consumption.  

Also under SO2, in anticipation of drought conditions in early 2021, FAO will also strategically position water bladder tanks and provide nutritive animal feed blocks to protect the small milking animals of up to 20,000 pastoral households impacted by scarce pasture from dry conditions and/or locust damage. Countrywide livestock vaccination and supportive treatment campaigns will further protect livestock assets belonging to at least 2.2 million men, women and children. Preparedness for animal health emergencies will be enhanced through strategic stocking of vaccines and related supplies (PPR), and training to local partners in Livestock Emergency Guidelines and Standards (LEGS), antimicrobial resistance, disease surveillance and reporting, among others.

provision of emergency life saving support to drought affected poor and vulnerable IDPS and host community in IPC 3 and 4 in Garbaharey district through food voucher support to vulnerable food insecure holds in Somalia through provision of essential livelihoods packages  According to FSNAU/ FEWSNET September 2020, acute food insecurity and malnutrition conditions exist in Somalia at alarming levels due to multiple shocks that negatively affected livelihood assets of the most vulnerable households. GU seasonal flooding and Desert locust upsurge contributed to loss and damage to property, housing, farmland and infrastructure. Also, social economic impacts occasioned by COVID 19 pandemic significantly contributed to food insecurity in Somalia. Social unrest in some parts of the country led to unprecedented levels of population displacement and disruption of livelihoods forcing hundreds of thousands to adopt negative coping mechanisms. Although livestock holding and milk availability is improving generally in Somalia, however, protracted droughts over the years combined with desert locust manifestation resulted drastic decline of livestock herd size holding among pastoral and agro pastoral households in Somalia leading to increased destitution and displacement in rural setups. 
401, 136 people are in emergency (IPC 4) of which 31% are rural population, 8% urban, 61 IDPs and urban population, while 3,048,080 people are in crisis (IPC 3) of which 24% are non-displaced rural population, 51% urban population while 26% are IDPs/ urban/ rural population (FSNAU/FEWSNET December 2020). Without sustained large scale humanitarian assistance worse food security outcomes 
The proposed intervention seeks to respond to the food needs of the affected households in Galgaduud and Lower Juba regions of Somalia with essential livelihood packages such as cash, voucher, livestock treatment and feed in order to strengthen and protect the livelihood assets of the poor and most vulnerable households.HOD currently implementing livestock activities with FAO Galgaduud. HOD seeks to use integrated food security packages which will respond to both immediate and the long term needs of the affected population. The intervention will support 2,100 households with total population of 12,600 persons (Women 3110, men 1285, boys 3765, and girls 4340). The transfer value will be based on the current regional MEB. Providing Agro inputs and Restore Livelihood for Drought affected agro-pastoral Communities in Rural Bardhere, Gedo Region of Somalia. Addressing Acute Food Insecurity in Gedo and Galgaduud regions in Southern Somalia 6.3 million Somalis are acutely food insecure through June 2020, a 36% increase since late 2019. This includes 2.1 million Somalis in IPC 3-4 (double an average year) and 4.2 million in IPC 2 (the highest on record). The situation deteriorated most significantly in rural areas, where the population in IPC 2-4 doubled and IPC 3-4 tripled. Since 2016, six out of seven rainy seasons have been poor, including Gu 2019 which yielded Somalia’s lowest cereal harvest in decades in southern Somalia. Pastoralists also struggle to recover from significant livestock losses and debt incurred from the protracted drought. ADA’s project is expected to directly assist 20,549 households (123,294 people) spread across the two regions of Gedo and Galgaguud, Somalia hence contributing across FSC’s three strategic objectives (SOs).

To improve immediate access to food (SO1),ADA will deliver cash assistance to 7800 households through cash-for-work (CFW) to repair community infrastructures and 8200 households through integrated cash and livelihood Programmes (Cash+). Beneficiaries will receive 3-6 monthly cash transfers, based on duration of the lean season and their vulnerability. To support transition out of emergency cash programmes, ADA will offer lighter and longer-term cash and livelihood assistance to the most chronically vulnerable households in the target districts with high recurrence of IPC 3-4. ADA’s cash programme assists severely food insecure people to meet their food immediate needs, while giving them choice and re-injecting cash into the local economy. ADA delivers cash through mobile money operators and money vendors, adopts rates recommended by the Cash Working Group and regularly monitors the availability and prices of selected food and non-food commodities in local markets through the support of FSNAU.

To protect and restore livelihoods (SO2), ADA will provide quality production inputs and training to Cash+ beneficiaries and an additional 2460 vulnerable households. Tailored livelihood support packages will enable farmers to secure a Gu/ Deyr harvest, pastoralists to enhance milk production and coastal communities to improve fish catch and processing. The project will further enhance production and promote climate smart practices through field school approaches, targeting 1044 farming and pastoral households that will pass on the knowledge to their wider communities. To protect livestock assets, ADA together with FAO and the Somali Ministry of Livestock and Veterinary Services will conduct region-wide livestock treatment and vaccination campaigns to protect thousands of animals; and deliver emergency water supply and animal feed in the case of severe drought (1045 vulnerable households).

To build resilience and mitigate new shocks (SO3) at a community level, the project will improve water management and related infrastructure to protect rural populations and livelihoods against flooding (repaired river embankments) and cope with drought (fenced water catchments, animal troughs, canal sluice gates).

Improved Immediate Access to Food for Vulnerable IDPs in Dayniile District, Mogadishu in Banadir Region Support for Life Saving and Restoration of livelihoods for Vulnerable Populations in Benadir, Lower Shabelle and Galmudug Regions. Somalia continues to face a dire humanitarian situation, with an estimated 5.2 million people in need of humanitarian assistance. This is attributed to cumulative shocks, including erratic 2020 Gu season, widespread and severe seasonal flooding, desert locust infestation, socio-economic impacts of COVID-19 and protracted conflict and flood-related displacements.

According to the 2020 Post Gu Seasonal Food Security and Nutrition Analysis for September (FAO/FSNAU), an estimated 1.3 million people are facing Crisis or worse (IPC Phase 3 or higher) outcomes through September 2020. This number is expected to increase to 2.1 million people through December 2020, in the absence of humanitarian assistance. An additional 2.5 million people are Stressed (IPC Phase 2), bringing the total number of people experiencing acute food insecurity to 3.8 million. In addition, 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition over the next 12 months (September 2020 to August 2021), including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

The ongoing Deyr rains in parts of central regions of Galmudug pose a high risk of flash flooding especially in low-lying areas. In Baxda village, Caddado district, Mudug region, one person died following heavy rains that collapsed their house. According to a multi-agency assessment in Adado district in May 2020, about 1,350 IDP households and 350 households from vulnerable host community need food security intervention. Seasonal Hagaa flooding since July has resulted in the displacement of nearly 342,000 people, inundated 294 villages and destroyed property and about 15,000 to 20,000 hectares of assorted crops, mainly in rural areas along the Shabelle river valley according to the UNHCR-led Protection and Return Monitoring Network (PRMN) in Somalia. 

Desert locusts continue to cause havoc in different parts of Somalia. In Galmudug, adult locusts continue to spread in rural villages in Galkacyo, Hobyo, Cabudwaaq, Cadaado, and Dhuusamarreeb. The locust problem has a wide range of impacts that worry Galmudug pastoralist as the region’s economic mainstay is livestock rearing. The locust will have a long-term impact on grazing lands and the poor performance of the rainy seasons may lead to depletion of pasture and acceleration of the dry season. 

CPD plans to reach 23,400 people facing severe acute food insecurity in Galmudug, Benadir and Lower Shabelle regions, mainly IDPs and host communities affected by the impacts of floods, desert locusts, conflicts and socio-economic impacts of the Covid-19 pandemic by improving access to food through unconditional and conditional transfers. Weak, vulnerable members of the IDPs and the host communities such as women and child-headed households, people with disability and the elderly will receive unconditional support through mobile cash transfers as per the CWG recommended transfer values per region (Benadir $70, Galgadud $110, Lower Shabelle $60, Mudug $80).  The men and the youth will be engaged in conditional transfers e.g. cash/food-for-work for livelihood interventions that will support community recover their livelihood and meet their immediate needs. Activities include rehabilitation and establishment of community infrastructure such as water catchments i.e. water pans.

CPD will protect and restore livelihoods related to food and income sources for the target communities through skills training to increase household income; rehabilitation and support for productive capacities of communities through agricultural inputs (e.g. quality seed, farm tools, training, land preparation and irrigation support) and livelihood strengthening and diversification (e.g. fishing).

Project will be inclusive by incorporating people with disability, women, youth and marginalized groups in all project phases in the target areas. Covid-19 measures and guidelines will be incorporated in project implementation.

Emergency Water, Sanitation and Hygiene Intervention for Vulnerable and Displaced Communities in Adado District Provision of basic and life-saving WASH services in Galmudug, South West, Hirshabelle States and Benadir region of South-Central Somalia The continuation of protracted crises in Somalia, now compounded by the effects of Covid-19, Floods and droughts has resulted in massive challenges pertaining to Water, Sanitation and Hygiene. Approximately, 4.6 million Somalis are still in need due to insufficient access to portable water and inadequate sanitation services of the affected population in many districts, thus negatively affecting the country’s public health and the dignity of highly vulnerable and displaced communities. Lack of access to water and adequate sanitation in schools is also a factor contributing to poor school attendance. In historically drought-affected districts, lack of access to water for humans and for livestock remain one of the leading causes of displacement, conflict and diseases. 

According to JMCNA, approximately 8.9 million people are affected by the prevalent poor WASH conditions in Somalia. The population in need of adequate WASH services in 2021 includes approximately 1.16 million IDPs 3.36 million host communities, 53,906 Returnees and 28,002 Refugees. 

According to a Joint Rapid Assessment carried out in Galmudug State in May 2020 by the government and humanitarian partners including CPD, five IDP settlements hosting 2,000 households (12,000 people) have partially or completely lost their shelters following a heavy storm in Adado. The affected IDPs settlements include: Badbaado, Kulmiye, Karama, Daryeel and Xeeb. Moreover, 700 vulnerable households (4,200 people) from the host community also lost their shelters and household items. The multi-agency assessment indicates an estimated 68,000 internally displaced people (IDPs) who are in urban and peri urban areas in Galgaduud region have WASH needs. Most of the IDP’s do not have access to safe drinking water with the only option being unprotected berkads, putting women and children at risk as they are mostly the handlers of water in the household. New IDP’s lack sanitation facilities leading to open defecation, compromising the security and privacy of women and girls. 

The proposed interventions will include piping of water from the strategic boreholes to IDPs and vulnerable host communities in the rural areas through cash for work for digging trenches and laying pipes. It will also include rehabilitation of 12 water pans through cash for work across the target areas, provision of water bladders in IDP camps, construction of strategic boreholes, shallow wells, gender-segregated latrines for under-served public primary schools and public health facilities and hygiene promotion activities.

Persons with disabilities face additional challenges and barriers. Barriers include environmental barriers, which inhibit access to WASH facilities, as well as social barriers, leading to discrimination within communities and further aggravating the risk of exclusion to WASH services. Water and sanitation facilities such as latrines will be accessible to people with disability and this will be done through design and construction of disability-friendly facilities. Considering the figures above, there are correlations between districts that have a limited access to water and sanitation and account for a high proportion of total incidence of AWD across Somalia.

CPD is targeting 29,580 people and train management committees in order to avoid over reliance on unsustainable means of accessing clean water by using long term high yielding well managed community boreholes. Committees will also be established to maintain clean sanitation facilities, as well as scale up hygiene promotion initiatives to help minimize AWD/cholera outbreaks during the rainy seasons when there is flooding. Management committees will be inclusive by ensuring representation of women, youth and persons living with disabilities. These marginalized groups will also be consulted in all project phases including design and implementation. Covid-19 regulations and guidelines will be adopted in the project implementation.

Food Security, Livelihood, and Agriculture Support to Communities Affected by Multiple Shocks Food Security, Livelihood, and Agriculture Support to Communities Affected by Multiple Shocks Overall, around 5.82 million people are in need of food security and livelihood assistance across 39 districts in three provinces (Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) in Pakistan, of which around one million people (17% of the overall people in need) will be targeted through food/cash and agriculture-based livelihoods assistance packages in 2021. The PIN has been determined by undertaking a severity analysis of the population in each vulnerable districts experiencing multiple shocks recently such as (drought, monsoon rains/flooding, winterized emergency, locust infestation and  COVID) which has affected their food security security situation. Based on available information, two indicators have been used to estimate the people in need: IPC acute food insecurity  phase classification, and percentage of households who have inadequate resources to buy food. The severity analysis classified the proportion of the population in each district into minimal, stress, severe, extreme and catastrophic categories, and 39 districts with up to 4 natural hazards/ shocks and pre-existing vulnerabilities are prioritized across three provinces (Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) in Pakistan. Thus, the final PIN is estimated based on the proportion of the people in JIAF severity level 3 and above and considering the experience of recent multiple natural hazards/shocks and pre-existing vulnerabilities.
Of the 5.82 million people in need, most of them are in 12 districts in Sindh province (2.75 million), primarily because of their exposure to multiple shocks ( monsoon rains/floods 2020, locust 2019-2020, drought 2018-2019), and being in JIAF severity level three and above. Similarly, in Balochistan, around 1.9 million people are in need in 14 districts, because of experience of multiple emergencies such as drought 2018-19, monsoon rains/floods 2020, flash floods/snow 2020, and locust 2019-20). In KP  province, 1.17 million people are in need in 13 newly merged areas and they experienced conflict, displacement, instability in the past and recently locust infestation. The most-affected population groups are refugees, Temporary Displaced Persons (TDPs), and Returnees, people living in districts with a high risk of recurrent natural disasters, migrants (Afghan Citizen Card Holders, Undocumented Afghans), poor and food-insecure households, small farmers and livestock holders, daily wage-earners and small businesses, under-five malnourished children, malnourished pregnant and lactating women, persons with disabilities, and elderly population. The combined effects of multiple shocks and food insecurity vulnerabilities are adverse on the most vulnerable groups owing to their inability to meet their food consumption and other basic needs and over-reliance on negative coping strategies.

Provision of life-saving integrated emergency CCCM, Shelter/NFI, WASH and general protection assistance to flood-affected communities in Beletweyne and Jowhar districts of Middle Shabelle Somalia Provision of CCCM services to displacement affected communities in Bay, Bakool & Lower Shabelle regions, Somalia. For almost 3 decades, Somalia has been faced by political instability, power vacuums, recurrent and devastating droughts and armed conﬂicts that has exacerbated the situation especially for IDPs and made the environment for returning of refugees unpredictable. Latest estimations of displacement conditions in Somalia indicate that around 2.3 million people have settled in around 2,400 IDP sites, most of which are informal, small and scattered settlements in urban or peri-urban areas. Living in private land often means that IDPs are at constant risk of eviction, which further stresses their already vulnerable situation. Protracted conﬂict-driven displacement aggravated by natural disasters, limited livelihood opportunities, limited availability of public services and limited access to durable solutions all contribute to the continued increase in the number and vulnerability of IDPs.
The main objective of the proposed action is to strengthen camp coordination and camp management at the site level, improve information management, and empower community engagement in order to improve access to life-saving services for displaced persons. Through the delivery of comprehensive CCCM assistance, CESDO aims to facilitate better living conditions and protection of IDPs, while facilitating clear focus on moving towards durable solutions with full community participation. CESDO will continue to strengthen its existing site coordination and management in Baidoa, Berdale, Bay region to provide life-saving services to flood and drought affected IDPs.
This project will target Baidoa/Berdale, Waajid, Wanlawayn and Afgoye districts, Somalia and the objectives are to support the improvement of conditions in IDP sites through strengthening the predictability and effectiveness of service provision and protection for displaced populations, to enhance community self-management and information sharing between all stakeholders. CESDO will ensure that all displaced persons are enabled to partake meaningfully in the governance structures and management of the sites by facilitating sites maintenance through cash-for-work and establishment or strengthening of an inclusive community governance structures and support on Camp Coordination and Camp management capacity buildings. Through this project CESDO will reach more than 4,000 HHs - 50 % female, ensure disability inclusion at all stages of the project, Gender will be mainstreamed into the project through the speciﬁc consideration of the different needs of women, men, boys and girls during the design of activities. The project will ensure that all participants have equal access to resources and training. Monitoring and evaluation will be based on gender, age and diversity dis-segregated data.

Support disaster affected populations in Hirshabelle, and Puntland states to protect their livelihoods and food security In June, Crisis (IPC 3) or Stressed (IPC 2) outcomes persist across the country. Nearly 20 percent of the total 2.7 million people in need of food assistance did not access it, including in riverine and rural areas of the South, where humanitarian access is low. The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the Somali economy is significant. Poor urban and IDP households, as well as pastoralists in northern Somalia, are likely to be most affected by an estimated 30-50 percent decline in annual external remittances, anticipated 25-35 percent decline in annual livestock exports, lower labor demand, and above-average imported staple food prices. In most IDP settlements and urban areas, at least 20 percent of the population still face food consumption gaps or are engaged in negative livelihoods coping strategies indicative of Crisis (IPC Phase 3) even after food assistance distributions. Additionally, Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected from June to September in parts of central Somalia, where livestock holdings are lowest, and in northeastern Somalia, where the economy is more dependent on livestock, seafood, and frankincense exports. The erratic distribution of rainfall during the April to June gu season has worsened Gu cereal production prospects in south-central Somalia. During the July to September dry season, up to 3.5 million people are anticipated to be unable to meet their minimum food needs and in need of urgent humanitarian food assistance. Further, the NOAA/CPC NMME forecast predicts an increased likelihood of a below-average deyr rainfall season from October to December 2020. FEWS NET’S research shows the NMME forecast has a strong capability to predict below-average rainfall during the October to December rainfall season in eastern East Africa. Combined with the persistent threat of desert locust, the impact of below-average rains on crop and livestock production is expected to lead to widespread deterioration to Crisis (IPC Phase 3) in northern and central pastoral areas and southern agropastoral areas in the absence of sustained food assistance. The conflict between insurgents and the FGS – supported by AMISOM and other forces – and conflict between clans over the control of land and resource management is expected to continue to periodically restrict humanitarian access, cause loss of life and assets, cause displacement, and disrupt trade and population movements. Conflict is most likely to affect Bakool, Bay, Galgaduud, Gedo, Hiiraan, the Jubas, and the Shabelles regions. Thus, AADSOM will support disaster-affected populations in Hirshabelle, and Puntland to protect their livelihoods, support local food production, and prevent the adoption of crisis strategies. AADSOM will carry out the following activities to reach the above objectives:
1. AADSOM will increase access to food and improve nutrition through Unconditional Cash Transfer to crisis-affected and underserved 1,000 IDPs and host communities HHs in Bari, and Hiran regions, benefiting around 6,000 women, men, boys, and girls including disabled people and marginalized communities. The supporting period will be 3 months and the rate is 60% Minimum Expenditure Basket (MEB) which corresponding to 60 USD. 
2. Supporting 2000 farmers in Hiran and Bari regions with land preparation and input distribution; 
3. To keep the sustainability of the project and increase the production of the beneficiaries, AADSOM will train 100 selected lead farmers on Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) to increase their livelihoods production and adapt the new technologies. 
4. Rehabilitation of  5 primary canals in Hiran region through CFW, benefiting 500 workers for a period of three months, benefiting around 3,000 (450 men, 600 women, 900 girls, 900 boys and 150 disabilities). 
During the project implementation, women, men, children, disabled, marginalized communities, and IDPs will be heard their voices and consulted.

Improving access to WASH services for drought affected and displaced populations in Garbaharey Improving access to emergency life-saving  and  sustainable WASH services to vulnerable IDPs and host communities in Gedo, Somalia The proposed project will improve access to sustainable WASH services namely safe water, sanitation facilities and promote good hygiene practices for 7,846 female and 7,539 male beneficiaries in underserved and hard-to-reach villages and IDP camps in Belet Xawa, Dollow, Garbaharey and Luuq districts in Gedo. Among the target beneficiaries will be 2,308 persons with disabilities (1177 male, 1131 female).
The below-average rainfall forecast for the upcoming Deyr season (Oct to Dec) which may be compounded by a harsh Jilaal dry season in 2021 calls for a greater focus on WASH and a re-prioritization of life-saving approaches in Gedo. Access to improved water sources remains low in Gedo with a significant portion of the population relying on the rivers and other seasonal streams as their primary water sources. A joint multi-sectoral assessment led by Trócaire in Dollow riverine communities in December 2019 indicated that 90% of households consume untreated water from the Juba river. The same assessment identified poor latrine coverage as a challenge, with 80% of the population lacking access to latrines. This results in wider open defecation, which is suspected to be one of the factors contributing to the frequent occurrence of diarrheal diseases in the area. A detailed site assessment by REACH in February 2020 further reported widespread open defecation at 64 and 100 percent respectively in assessed sites in Luuq and Dollow. The most severely affected community members are women and girls, who are often forced to use nearby bushes, putting them at a greater risk of SGBV. The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has further compounded WASH needs in communities, with Trocaire noting serious gaps in knowledge, skills and resources to prevent and control the pandemic especially in IDP and rural communities. 
The project aims to contribute to the achievement of specific objectives of the WASH cluster: delivering life-saving WASH assistance to reduce acute needs, and restoring access to safe and equitable basic WASH services in target locations. This will be done through the construction of one (1) solar powered shallow well with piping to communities in Dollow, rehabilitation of one flood-damaged water system in Dollow and provision of Genset, construction of 110 permanent gender-sensitive latrines with handwashing stations, desludging of 85 latrines, hygiene promotion sessions with distribution of hygiene kits, and environmental cleanup campaigns. In addition, Trocaire will conduct water testing and treatment of water facilities in target locations, and conduct trainings and refresher trainings for representative Water Management Committees while equipping them with tools necessary for effective management of water points. Trocaire will collaborate with Somali Humanitarian Relief Action (SHRA) and Active in Development Aid (ADA), national NGOs with strong experience in implementing WASH projects in Gedo, in delivery of this project in the four target districts.
Trocaire shall work closely with local partners identified to promote protection of beneficiaries and ensure access to services especially for people living with disabilities. The Water Management Committees will particularly be sensitized on inclusivity in water access for people with disabilities and their families. Hygiene promotion outreach teams will be trained to identify and deliver services in homes with people living with disabilities. Gender inclusivity will be ensured through creation or support to adequately representative community structures, as well as working closely with women groups in target location. All data collected will be dis aggregated by gender, age and disability, to inform adaptive programming in meeting the different needs of the different social groups reached.

Restoring livelihoods of vulnerable populations to catastrophic food and nutrition insecurity in Borno, Adamawa and Yobe States Critical agricultural livelihoods support to conflict- and pandemic-affected households in northeast Nigeria In 2021, FAO will improve food security, nutritional status and incomes among vulnerable, conflict- and pandemic-affected households in Borno, Adamawa and Yobe states in Northeast Nigeria. The now more than decade-long insurgency has decimated agricultural livelihoods upon which more than 80 percent of the population relies as a primary source of household income. The COVID-19 pandemic has further compounded this already highly vulnerable humanitarian context, generating interconnected vulnerabilities that negatively affect availability and access to food, agriculture inputs, finance, farming land, extension services, markets and the fundamental viability of agricultural livelihoods. 
Support to crop production and the rebuilding of a robust crop value chain have been identified by FAO as key to the restoration of livelihoods and to improving the food and nutrition security of vulnerable populations in the BAY states. FAO will support vulnerable households with critical inputs for rainy and dry season cultivation as well as for micro-/backyard gardening and seed production.   
Prior to the insurgency, close to 80 percent of households in northeast Nigeria reared livestock and/or poultry as a vital source of food and household income. The conflict has caused the wide-scale loss of these assets either through looting, property destruction, disease, or abandonment when fleeing attacks by armed insurgents. In addition to being a source of income generation through breeding for sale, livestock and poultry restocking increases the availability of meat, milk and eggs at the household level. FAO will increase support to livestock and poultry production in 2021 in support of affected households.
Prior to the crisis, the fisheries sector had significant economic importance and fish from the northeast were supplied to the rest of Nigeria. With increased land and areas retaken by the military, the return of IDPs to their communities of origin is ongoing, thereby enabling some to access fishing grounds and resume their traditional livelihood. However, the lack of quality inputs remains a limiting factor for the majority of fishers who continue to rely on humanitarian assistance to meet their food and livelihood needs. By leveraging FAO’s extensive experience and capacity, conflict-affected fisherfolk households will be supported to resume their livelihoods and meet their food and nutritional needs. 
The ongoing crisis is also termed a ‘protection crisis’ with vulnerable social groups – particularly children, women and the elderly – disproportionately affected by the impact of the ongoing conflict and the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic and are at heightened risk of adopting negative coping strategies such as child labour, borrowing, street begging, basic needs deprivation, transactional sex, early and forced marriage as their families seek to reduce the number of mouths to feed in their homes, and collection of fuelwood in insecure areas, which remains a high-risk livelihood. FAO will support vulnerable households by way of fuel-efficient stoves to reduce exposure to potential protection risks, and stove production and briquette production centres for income generation. 
Access to credit is a particular challenge for vulnerable groups in Northeast Nigeria, particularly women. Through the establishment of Group Savings and Loans Associations (GSLA), in 2021 FAO will extend its GSLA programme and will identify vulnerable groups to enhance their access to credit and financial services as an important social safety net.  
FAO is the co-lead of the Food Security Sector (FSS) which plays a critical role in coordinating food security programming in the BAY states. Food security data collection and analysis are also key and upon which food security actors base their intervention. In 2021, FAO will continue to support and host the Food Security Sector to facilitate the required coordination and analyses required to reach people most in need.

Improved access to adequate housing and community infrastructure in Libya NRC’s shelter program in Libya seeks to improve the living conditions and physical protection and well-being of conflict affected populations and internally displaced persons through the maintenance and rehabilitation of houses for vulnerable families residing in or intending to return to damaged or substandard houses in urban settings, the rehabilitation works will focus in improving protection from the elements, physical security and safety as well as improving access to functioning sanitation facilities and water. The intervention will aim at supporting a total of 160 households divided between Benghazi and Tripoli. 

The program will also promote improved access to basic services through the investment in rehabilitating and upgrading community infrastructure such as health facilities, power utilities, roads, or communal buildings providing essential services to the public. This component of the program will be mainly focused in Tripoli in areas that have been heavily affected and damaged by the conflict during the past year. The Program will aim at providing infrastructure solutions in three neighborhoods benefiting an estimated 1,500 individuals.

In Tripoli the program will also promote safe and dignified returns of IDP’s that remain unable to return due to the physical conditions of their shelters or due to the lack of adequate community infrastructure.

Enhancing emergency humanitarian response in Tonj North. The intervention will target 12 642 (3100 men, 5242 women, 1900 boys and 2400 girls) individuals who are facing catastrophic levels of hunger but whom are not currently receiving any funding or humanitarian support. 2107 households will receive emergency food packs, 1950 households will receive WASH NFI, 500 women and girls will receive dignity kits, 3000 individuals will benefit from the rehabilitation of 6 water boreholes, and 10 000 people will be sensitized on GBV/PSEA. Emergency FSL intervention to Vulnerable Populations (IDPs, Returnees and Host Communities) in South Sudan In South Sudan 6.35 Million people (52.6% of the population), 5.82 million (48.3% of the population) and 7.24 million people (60% of the population) were projected in October to November 2020, December 2020 to March 2021 and April to July 2021 respectively to faced crisis (IPC phase 3) or worse acute food insecurity. An estimated 24,000 people were classified in Catastrophe (IPC phase 5) acute food insecurity, of which 89,820 people in Tonj North County of Warrap state are in IPC phase 5 (IPC South Sudan Oct 2020 - July 2021). Almost half of Tonj North County have a convergence of high needs related to food insecurity, protection and WASH due to inter-communal conflicts.  Livelihood needs in Kajo-Keji, Terekeka and Kapoeta East are dire given that they are classified as IPC 4. The proposed intervention aims to saves lives, enhance early recoveries and build community resilience by addressing the main drivers of vulnerabilities because apparently unresolved conflicts leaves these areas extremely fragile. With the advent of COVID-19 with lockdown the already ailing economy drastically went down making the already vulnerable population lose their livelihoods and ability to feed their families. It is widely appealed that in order to save lives and avert total collapse of livelihoods in the affected counties, particularly those with the populations in catastrophe IPC Phase 5 and Emergency IPC Phase 4, there is an urgent need for immediate scale-up humanitarian assistance. 
The intervention will seek to support 41,850 vulnerable people with emphasis on access to food emergency livelihoods deprived during conflict and floods. IRW will provide food items, unconditional and conditional cash transfers in all areas of intervention except Tonj North where delivery of food items to the beneficiaries will be through Voucher. To further strengthen resilient livelihoods income diversification the project will provide pathways for communities to recover and adapt to climate variability. Activities will provision of inputs for crop and vegetable production, distribution of livelihood kits with farming tools (hoes, moloda, rakes) crop seeds (groundnut, maize, sorghum, cowpeas), and vegetable seeds (tomatoes, onion, eggplant, Okra, kale, kudra, Amaranth). IRW will also conduct basic training in agronomic- and post-harvest practices, and emerging threats such as trans-boundary crop diseases.
Enhancing household resilience will be through capacity building including trainings on modern livestock management and milk handling and processing to increase production, Community Animal health Workers (CAHWs) will be trained and provided start up kits for management of livestock diseases. The CAHWs are specifically work on livestock and poultry.  Trainings will be done by facilitators contracted from the department of Livestock at state level because they use local languages understandable by beneficiaries.  Some households will benefit from Re-stocking of livestock program to replace the animals which were killed or died during the crisis as registered and confirmed by the local beneficiary community themselves during open meetings; Distribution of fishing kits and training on fish preservation and marketing during fishing seasons in river areas. Training of Community Agricultural Extension Workers (CAEW) who specifically deal with crops by providing extension services to farmers benefiting from the in order to increase agriculture production.
The intervention is expected to reinforce and strengthen protection of the various groups affected by the conflict. Livelihood roles are expected to change to include women as decision makers in household income generation hence reducing the risks of SEA accosted with poverty. IRSS will conduct FSL based protection risk analysis to mitigate all risks to various groups women, girls and children and the marginalized of the affected group. Awareness on GBV, sexual exploitation and child abuse and exploitation.
