Lifesaving emergency support to displaced families due to flooding in the Middle Shebelle region of Somalia. Providing life-saving WASH assistance to the most vulnerable disaster affected populations and increasing access to sustainable WASH services for the chronically under-served host and displaced populations in Somalia. Project aims to provide live-saving WASH assistance to disaster affected displaced and
non- displaced population in order to reduce the excess morbidity and mortality rate from
preventable crisis-driven diseases and public health outbreaks among most vulnerable
people. The project will continue to restore access to safe and equitable basic WASH
services in targeted locations in a dignified manner. Lack of adequate WASH services to
the population is a main cause of spread of Acute Diarrheal Diseases (ADD), leading to
malnutrition in the country and contributing to increasing the existing stunting rate of
25.3% in children below 5 years of age.
Access to safe water will be increased through construction and or rehabilitation of water
sources including 8 boreholes (2 new), 20 shallow wells, 2 river water intake system with
water treatment. New borehole construction will be preceded by hydrogeological survey
and safe pumping regime will be designed. River water intakes will be preceded
hydrological study. In all cases, an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) will be
undertaken for new water sources and mitigation measures put in place for negative
impacts. All water systems will be equipped with distribution infrastructure and hybrid
energization systems. Pipeline extensions will also be made. Taps stand will be located
within a radius of at least 500m to reduce distance and enhance security of women and
girls. Project will also construct 2 major improved water dams in locations that lack other
options. All well heads will be raised at a minimum 0.5m to reduce risk flooding and
contamination. Water committees comprising men and women from all community
groups including the minority and the marginalized will be trained on management,
operation and maintenance. Local technicians will be trained and provided with O&M
tools to undertake repairs whereas consumers will pay for the technician’s services. For
major water supply in urban areas, Private Public Parternship (PPP) management system
will be adopted. Where possible NRC will partner will local private investors to establish
sustainable water sources and equip them with SmartTAPs to enhance revenue collection
and accountability. Project will construct 400 latrines for families reintegrated through the
durable solutions. NRC undertakes sanitary surveys periodically to identify contamination
risks for timely mitigation. All latrine will be installed with handwashing equipment and
community sensitized to use soap for handwashing. Design of infrastructure will take into
consideration the needs of special groups in the community including the disabled, old,
children to ensure they have equitable access to the services. Life-saving WASH
interventions will be implemented in case of sudden disaster to reduce the related
mortality and morbidity especially among children. This will be through temporary
provision of safe water through direct delivery or restricted cash depending on context and
market functionality, provision of hygiene kits through cash (3000 HH), construction of
550 simple design emergency latrines, latrine emptying (450 latrines) and safe fecal
sludge disposal and hygiene promotion. Schools and health facilities will be provided with
latrines offering private space for menstrual hygiene (200 institutional latrines). All
latrines will be raised above ground level to reduce the risk of flooding during rains.
Women and girls will be involved in identification of sites for facilities to ensure their
safety and security is taken into account. Latrines will be gender separated, provided with
lockable doors and handwashing equipment. Solar street lights (35 posts) will be provided
near water points and latrines to improve the security and safety of women and girls
especially in crowded IDP settlements. Throughout the implementation period the
beneficiaries will be provided with adequate information on NRC’s complaints, response
and feedback (CRFM) mechanisms.

Provisions of life-saving WASH assistance to drought-affected most vulnerable communities, displaced populations in under-served and hard-to-reach areas of Badhade district, lower Juba region of Somalia Providing life-saving WASH assistance and restoration of access to safe and equitable basic WASH services to most vulnerable communities displaced by conflicts, drought, floods, and diseases , living  in Lower juba, Middle Shebele, Banadir, Sool and Sanaag  region of Somalia/Somaliland  In the context of the current multi-faceted emergencies (increased risks of flooding, protracted conflict, droughts, Covid 19, Cholera/AWD Outbreaks and the projected La Nina phenomena expected in Somalia, ARC proposes this emergency WASH project to target IDPs and most vulnerable host communities living in Kismayo, Benadir, lascanod,Xudun, Telex,  Afmadow, Balcad, Badade , and El-Afweyne district with aim of saving lives and reducing morbidities associated with WASH-related diseases. ARC understands that internal displacements are the key driver of humanitarian needs in Somalia. Many IDPs and Poor vulnerable Host communities are currently residing in Urban and pre-urban informal crowded areas with insufficient access to water and Sanitation. According to JMCNA assessment done in August by REACH, 53% of the IDPs face challenges in terms of access to WASH services in Somalia. The situation of IDPs and non- IDPs vulnerable host community members are complicated by frequent forced evictions meted on them leading to disruptions of access to critical  WASH services and  loss of gains made on access to these essentials services. According to an assessment done by ARC in Mogadishu in September 2020, more than 7000 IDPs households were forcefully evicted from their homes in Kaxda district, Benadir in the past three months. Ongoing conflicts and riverine flooding along Juba and Shebelle will continue to displace more people to major towns. In Sanaag and Sool regions, persistent clan conflicts, insecurity and recurring droughts are the major cause of displacement of people in the region.
Cognizant of these contexts,  ARC will provide emergency water trucking to  12000 (2000HH) Drought- affected IDPs and vulnerable pastoral communities living in drought-prone areas of lascanod, xudun, telex and Celf-Afweyn districts for a period of two months as the agency will find and  rehabilitate alternative water sources for the affected people. 20 critical shallow wells will be rehabilitated and protected targeting IDPs and Non- IDPs vulnerable communities and settlements from Kismayo, Kaxda &Darkenley (Banadir), lascanod, Cel-Afweyne and Telex. ARC will also conduct Disinfections and chlorination of floods affected wells.
ARC will Provide 10 Strategic boreholes in drought-prone locations in lascanood, telex and Cel- Afweyen district with Generators, submersible pumps, cable wires and control panels to ensure drought affected peoples have access to safe, adequate and reliable water.ARC will establish  6 Pipeline water extensions to identified IDPs Camps and non- IDPs camps including construction of elevated water storage tanks, installation of solar powered systems  and water kiosk with a minimum of 6 taps  to ensure increased access to adequate water by the IDPs and Non-IDPs.
ARC will construct/rehabilitate 2000 gender-segregated, disability-friendly communal latrines for IDPs and vulnerable host community members who have no access to any sanitation facilities.
ARC will construct for the targeted sex-Disaggregated, Disability Inclusive 40 Institutional latrines with water and Handwashing facilities for 24 target schools and 15 health centers.
Hygiene promotion will remain a key component of the intervention to prevent the spread of Covid 19 and others WASH-related diseases through risk communications and community engagement promoting behavior changes. Hygiene kits and basic MHM kits will be provided to adolescent girls in schools and villages/camps. ARC will target approximately 71, 800 beneficiaries from North and south-central Somalia (11488 women, 7180 men, 22165 boys, 23069 girls, 5744 disabled, and 2154 elderly people).
ARC will consult men, boys, girls, elderly, and people with disabilities on their needs and preference regarding the type, Design and location of the water and sanitation facilities to address barriers relating to access. ARC will involve women, boys, girls and disabled people in the project monitoring and feedback sought.

Strengthening emergency GBV services for the most vulnerable internally displaced populations through gender-based violence response in Daynile and Kahda districts in Banadir region Provision of protection services to the most vulnerable IDP in Middle Shabelle, Lower Shabelle and Bay Regions, Somalia Covid-19 pandemic, coupled by Gu 2020 seasonal flooding and sustained conflict in Middle and Lower Shabelle and Bay Regions has impacted to increased numbers displaced populations in  IDP camps  where they live in informal and unplanned settlements under very deplorable living conditions. Women and Young Girls' condition are worsened by increased exposure to violence, exploitation and discrimination and other forms of abuse worsened by very serious risks and threats to their safety and security.  Of particular focus are persons with disabilities face increased risks of exploitation, abuse and discrimination while accessing assistance meant for them hence strong need for their inclusion in the project right from the beginning of the project throughout the implementing period including monitoring, till completion. Its against this background that the project intends to provide timely and  appropriate protection services to increase protection of boys and girls and vulnerable displaced  and marginalized women as well as those with disabilities. The project targets total of 9190 women including GBV survivors  those those with disabilities.

Protection monitoring services provided in Kahda and Daynile districts of Banadir to identify protection risks, human rights violations and gaps in available services.. Scaling up of protection services to vulnerable Internally Displaced Persons in Banadir region. Most of the 2.6 million IDPs in Somalia live in informal and unplanned settlements where living conditions are poor and forced eviction is a common threat. Safety and security concerns remain a high priority for all affected populations, with displacement contributing to immediate and heightened exposure to violence, exploitation and other forms of abuse. Serious risks and threats to safety and security. The protection needs in Somalia changed and evolved over time. The current crisis affects individuals of all ages and genders, as well as from diverse social backgrounds, in different ways and scale. The most vulnerable groups include people with physical, sensorial, intellectual and mental disabilities, adolescent girls and boys, pregnant and lactating women and girls, female and child-headed households, unaccompanied and separated children, persons from minority clans, older persons without caregivers, persons missing documentation, persons facing eviction, persons living in areas with armed conflict and violence. Women and adolescent girls from 18 – 50 years old (including those living with disabilities) are subjected to Intimate Partner Violence, rape, sexual exploitation, sexual harassment and abuse. Low reporting of GBV cases persist due to stigmatization, victim blaming, shame and interference by clan and religious leaders, slow access to justice and weak or lack of legal framework for the protection of women and girls from GBV. Persons with disabilities face various physical, attitudinal and institutional barriers to access food, health, shelter and protection on an equal basis with others. Persons with disabilities are estimated to be at least 15% of the population and  the majority are among the poorest part of the population. They also face disability-based discrimination, which is exacerbated in situations of crisis, and when it intersects with other factors, such as poverty, gender or age. To mitigate the above mentioned challenge, SSWC will conduct  meetings and consult with people living with disabilities throughout the project phases.  Transportation plans for people living with disabilities will be made for easy access to our centres and our field monitors will ensure that they target households with people living with disabilities in their daily visits within the target areas. Up to 66 per cent of the population in need in Somalia are children who continue to be exposed to threats of recruitment, abuse, neglect, abduction, exploitation and violence. Hence, 1.88 million children including 10% of children with disabilities need immediate child protection services. Boys and girls of all ages in Somalia continue to endure multiple protection risks and violations of their rights including family separation, sexual and physical violence, killing and maiming, psycho social distress, worst forms of child labor, widespread recruitment and use of children, forced and protracted. SSWC wants to address GBV and child protection programming due to high number of Incidents of GBV this is as a result of reported cases, predominantly in IDP sites throughout the country. The objective of the project is to fill up  the existing critical gaps in protection targeting 50,000 beneﬁciaries in Banadir district. The purpose of the intervention is to significantly reduce the incidents of GBV, promote awareness on prevention and response to GBV and provide child protection services to the community living in Banadir. Protection activities include provision of psychosocial support, Medical referrals, legal aid counselling, distribution of emergency social assistance (dignity kits), awareness and sensitization on GBV prevention and response, Capacity building for community structures on GBV prevention and response and comprehensive case management services at the Women Wellness centers and Safe houses.Establishment of Child friendly spaces, facilitation of psycho-social support for children including play therapy, art work and drawing.

Strengthening the Protection and Lifesaving of 9,420 people (1,570hhs) in IDP sites through Shelter & NFIs assistance in Daynile and Kaxda districts, Banadir region. Shelter and NFIs Assistance for Crisis-Affected Populations including IDPs, Returnees and Poor host communities in Banadir, Lower shabelle, Bay and Hiiraan regions- Somalia. According to draft 2021 HNO that revealed that 3.15 million people are in need of shelter and NFIs assistance due to prolonged humanitarian issues caused by recurrent drought, conflict, and floods and due to inadequate shelter conditions, overcrowding, economic, hardship, and lack of security of tenure. 

In consideration of severity factors, this project is to strengthen the protection and address life-saving needs of IDP families and poor host communities through Shelter and NFIs response in Kaxda and Daynile districts of Banadir region, Lower Afgoye and Marka districts of Lower Shabelle region, Baidoa district of Bay region, and Beledeweyne of Hiiraan region in South and Central Somalia including women-headed household families, extended families, families with disabled and elderly persons who are most in need of humanitarian assistance to mitigate risk and its consequences on crisis-affected populations at the target areas. The main objective is to improve the living conditions and safe access to services of IDP families including refugee returnees and poor host communities in the targeted locations. HINNA aims at providing 4800 ESKs and NFI kits to 4800 HHs (28,800 beneficiaries/Individuals) while 2,880 (10%) people of them will be poor host communities through in-kind distribution to improve the living conditions of the target beneficiaries who faced inadequate shelter/NFIs conditions. The reason we can't use cash transfer programming for this project is that we have had several meetings with the communities in some of the project target areas and most of them have told us that this type of program can cause insecurity, family violence that can lead to family breakdown and other things including missing kits or rising market prices.
Through this project disaggregation of gender will be promoted in full consideration with protection mainstreaming. The total beneficiaries of the project (28,800 people) of the drought, floods, and conflict-affected populations in Banadir region (Daynile and Kaxda districts), Lower Shabelle region (Afgoye and Marka districts), Bay region (Baidoa district) including (4320 women, 4320 men, 9504 boys, and 9504 girls) including 1152 elderly people (4%) will directly be receiving any benefits of the project based on their need of shelter and NFIs assistance through selection criteria set by the shelter cluster.

Enhanced Emergency WASH Services for Vulnerable Tafta Tag and Hashiwer IDPs and Suriyo Village Non-IDPs in Garbaharey District. Increased Access to WASH Services by Vulnerable IDP and Host Communities in Jubaland, Banadir and Galgadud The project aims to increase WASH services to the over 4.6M people in need in Somalia targeting districts that are categorized as stressed or severe in the severity scale, those that are hard to reach and those that have reported AWD/cholera cases. The project targets approximately   7,164 vulnerable IDPs 16,716 host communities with a special focus on vulnerable segments of the community including 5, 383women, 12, 895children 3582 PLWD and 1194 elderly people. 
In line with HRP strategic objective 1, specific objective 1.2, this project will contribute to the WASH cluster objective of delivering life-saving WASH assistance to reduce acute needs among most vulnerable settlements and communities through emergency water tracking, water vouchers, provision of hygiene kits and hygiene promotion activities. Lifesaving Wash assistance will target hard to reach communities in Garbaharey and Elwak districts and IDPs households in Banadir, Kismayo, Dolow Belet Hawa.  This project is also aligned to HRP strategic objective 2, specific objective 2.1, contributing to WASH cluster objective of restoring access to safe and equitable basic WASH services to vulnerable communities and in schools. This will be achieved through rehabilitation of water infrastructures including shallow wells, water pipe network, elevated tanks and water kiosks. Solar pumping systems will be installed in boreholes and shallow wells to reduce the O&M of community water systems. Community mobilizations and capacity building in management of water projects and O&M of solar system will be done to ensure active community participation in the implementation and management of the water facilities. This project will also contribute to the WASH cluster objective of restoring access to basic sanitation and hygiene in schools in Abudwak and Dussammarreeb, through rehabilitation of gender segregated latrines with lockable doors from inside with hand washing facilities.  
All the WASH infrastructures proposed in this project are designed with consideration of the safety, equity and easy accessibility by vulnerable groups such as women, girls, PLWD and the elderly. The target beneficiaries will actively participate in the selection of the sites for water facilities in their locations that will be strategic to serve households within approximately 500m distance that will be in open and clear places to ensure safety of users. Additionally water kiosks will be designed to ensure easy water collection by girls, women, elderly and those with disabilities. For water trucking water collection points will be selected by the beneficiaries and will be at about 500m from the households and in open places for safety purposes. The water collection will be planned such that the elderly and PLWD will have separate times to collect their water. The latrines constructed in schools will be strategically located to ensure safety of users and dignity of users. Hygiene kits will be collected from reasonable distances from the beneficiary households for safety of the beneficiaries as they carry them home. Use of water and hygiene kits vouchers will further enhance safety and equity of vulnerable groups targeted in this project. Mainstreaming of protection and gender in this project will contribute to HRP strategic objective 3, specific objective 3.1 as well as the WASH cluster objective of maintaining safety, equity and accessibility of the vulnerable groups (including women, boys, girls, elderly and people with disabilities) when accessing WASH services. This project will build on WASH and COVID 19 interventions implemented by NAPAD (2019 and 2020) in Galgadud, Jubaland and Banadir regions that includes rehabilitation of water infrastructures such as water tanks, water pipe networks, installation of solar water pumping systems, installation of hand washing facilities, provision of hygiene kits and mass hygiene promotion using the mass media and door to door promotion by community hygiene

Provision of Integrated Emergency Support Through Protection, CCCM, and Shelter Interventions in IDP Settlements in Deynille and Kaxda Districts. To improve the living conditions and protection of IDPs at site level in Banadir, Lower Shebelle, Lower Jubba, and Gedo Region to ensure equitable access to services and assistance of all persons in need, with a clear focus on moving toward attaining durable solutions. According to HNO 2020, an estimated 709,000 new displacements were reported from January to December 2019, mostly to urban areas, where displaced people move to private IDP sites with poor living conditions and little access to basic services. There are over 2,000 recorded IDP sites across Somalia. Approximately 85 percent of the sites are informal settlements on private land and about 74 percent of them are in urban areas according to the Detailed Site Assessment (DSA). According to the DSA, over 70 percent of IDPs in informal sites lack access to information about their rights and available services. Displaced communities, especially new arrivals, people with disabilities and women need access to information and representation in the community governance structure to make informed decisions about how to receive services and potential solutions to displacement. This year (2020), Somalia has seen serious flooding which have forced hundreds of thousands of people to flee their homes amid risks of COVID-19. According to UNHCR more than 150,000 Somalis have been forced to flee their homes since late June, including some 23,000 in the last week of July, due to flash and riverine flooding in the Southern regions of Somalia. As of 19 May (OCHA), ongoing flash and riverine flooding in Somalia has affected about 919,000 people, of whom 412,000 have been displaced and 24 killed, in 29 districts. 

The displaced people in informal sites in Banadir, Lower Shebelle, Lower Jubba, and Gedo Region are in greatest need of CCCM services to improve the living conditions and protection of IDPs at the site level. The target areas have been through successive years of drought and conflict, leaving the population vulnerable to shocks and inhibiting a sustainable return to places of origin. The displaced population in these areas are living in precarious conditions with their basic needs not met due to inconsistent service provision and exclusion with all existing coordination and management mechanisms at site level being informal, with most sites managed by landlords and gatekeepers limiting accountability and adherence to minimum standards. While ensuring equitable access to services and assistance of all persons in need, NoFYL will ensure to enhance the accountability of affected populations through community participation and consistent engagement with a focus on moving toward attaining durable solutions. 

NoFYL intends to scale up its CCCM program to contribute towards strengthening camp coordination and camp management to improve the living conditions and protection of IDPs at the site level by ensuring equitable access to services and assistance of all persons in need. All the project activities will be carried out to maximize community participation and enhance the accountability of humanitarian actors to the affected population. NoFYL will coordinate with relevant responders and mobilized towards providing sectorial assistance to those identified as very vulnerable at the site level. Together with the established site governance, NoFYL will carry out service monitoring activities aimed at highlighting service gaps, and ensuring that minimum standards are being adhered to at the site-level. To ensure that sites are safe and hygiene conditions are ensured NoFYL will provide training on-site maintenance and site planning to camp committees to strengthen their capacity, Support community-led site maintenance activities to ensure the upkeep of sites through cash for work activities, distribution of tools to site maintenance committees. The project will also support maintaining inter-sector complaints feedback mechanisms (CFMs) at the IDP site-level.

The project will be implemented in 4 regions, including Banaadir, Gedo region covering Beletxaawo and Ceelwaaq districts, and Lower Juba covering Kismayo. The project will target 60 sites in total targeting an estimated IDP population of 64,000 to be verified through the detailed site assessments.

Provision of Life-saving Integrated Emergency Shelter/NFI and Housing Land & Property (HLP) assistance to flood-affected communities in Jowhar District of Middle Shabelle & Beletweyne district of Hiran Region Providing NFI and shelter assistance to the displaced and affected population in Bay, Bakol, lower juba & Lower Shabelle in south central Somalia. Climate shocks including drought and flooding as well as ongoing conflict contributes to internal displacement in Somalia, with an estimated 2.6M men, women, girls and boys who are currently displaced. This people/ IDPs are now living in IDP camps with lack of enough basic services including shelter, The 2020 Gu’ Season flooding has caused several displacement, damage of properties, housing, farmland and social amenities and also Massive displacement especially in the river rine areas of Middle Lower Shabelle areas. 
This areas are also prone to conflict crises particularly in South Central Somalia where part of it is under al-shabaab control hence contributes to more displacement and increase the need of the IDPs who were already in need 0f basic services, this also contributes to the protection concerns of vulnerable groups e.g. women, girls and  people with specific needs and also people with disabilities.
 Through this project, Juba Foundation aims to address the humanitarian needs of the displaced IDPs and poor host communities in poor shelter conditions in south central Somalia.
The project will focus on improving the lives & dignity of IDPs and poor host communities across Somalia through the provision of locally purchased Non food items (NFIs) Emergency shelter kits (Esks) through in-kind distribution where feasible and if there is functional market with shelter and NFI materials cash or voucher can be an option. But at the moment Juba Foundation is Flexible to use either cash or in-kind Distribution. 
For the beneficiaries’ selection and registration, juba foundation will give consideration to the female headed Household. People with specific needs among other households. The host communities will also be given consideration with selection of 20 – 30 %, similarly 15% will be selected from persons with disabilities in each project.
Juba Foundation will ensure the affected population will have full protection and improve their dignity and living conditions through the provision of appropriate emergency shelter kits (Esks) for each household will receive ESK( type 2 with a size of 4.4m x 3.6m)  depending on land availability. For the provision of NFIs each household will be provided with one NFI kit as per the cluster guidelines along with the Esks. 
The proposed intervention will focus on providing of Esks (1,500) and NFIs (1,500) that consist of 1 plastic sheet, 3 blankets, 2 sleeping mats, 1 kitchen set, 1 solar lamp, 1 mosquito net and 2 jerricans. That will total up to 9,000 Individuals.
Juba foundation will train the camp leaders and camp committees on selection of beneficiaries, HLP issues, site planning to ensure all shelter and NFI projects meet the required cluster standard.

Provision of Life-saving Integrated Emergency Shelter/NFI and Housing Land & Property (HLP) assistance to flood-affected communities in Jowhar District of Middle Shabelle & Beletweyne district of Hiran Region Strengthen safe access to multi sectorial services at site level through improved site management and coordination through Improvement of living conditions of displaced people through site development, care and maintenance and self-management within selected districts of Lower Juba, Gedo, Bay, Bakool, and Lower Shabelle Region of south central Somalia In the midst of increasing IDP caseload in Somalia, Juba Foundation is submitting this proposal with the aim of enhancing the living conditions of the Internally Displaced People (IDPs) through enhanced coordination, access to information and multi-sectoral services at site level, site maintenance, and durable solutions. Proposed interventions will covers IDPs in need in Bakol, Bay, Lower Shabelle, Lower Juba, and Gedo . Combined, these regions host 1,337,000 IDPs, or 51% of the entire IDP population in Somalia (OCHA HNO 2020). This project aim is to focus on Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM) activities undertaken in selected districts of Bay, Bakool, Gedo, Lower Juba and Lower Shabelle by enhancing the overall protective environment for flood affected population, increasing access to basic services linked to different sectors, reducing the risk thereof, and availing specialized support assistance to beneficiaries to help them address other interconnected protection concerns. 

To achieve cluster objectives, Juba Foundation will undertake a number of interrelated and complementary activities including setting up and strengthening of camp governance structures where necessary to enhance information-sharing and foster system-wide coordination among service providers. Besides, we will support community-led site maintenance activities through cash for work schemes to ensure upkeep of sites, enhance hygiene and sanitation levels and contribute to overall reduction in communicable diseases. Where necessary, JF will implement emergency site improvement projects to minimize protection risks and ensure safety. Key program activities will also include service mapping and site monitoring processes that will be carried out in close coordination with the CCCM cluster and other partners to effectively address existing gaps and maximize eﬃciency of the humanitarian response. Compiling of a master list of sites and mapping of both accessible infrastructure and partners operating in sites will be prioritized to enhance service delivery and coordination. In the selection of beneficiaries to participate in program activities. We will adapt a systematic approach with a clear criterion to prioritize most vulnerable households including the marginalized, single headed-households, large families and/or families with children under the age of 5, women at risk as identified by protection oﬃcers and those with special needs. Data collected to inform beneficiary selection will be segregated by gender to ensure that no group is left-out. The effectiveness of the aid package will be evaluated through monitoring of activities thus ensuring that beneficiaries access their services safely and in a dignified manner. Protection will be mainstreamed throughout project duration by closely coordinating with other partners operating Sexual and Gender Based Violence (SGBV) crisis centers and facilitating principled referrals where necessary. An elaborate feedback and complain mechanism will be setup to ensure accountability to the affected population.
JF with the presence in the targeted regions/ districts will ensure that there is proper coordination to ensure quality service delivery to the beneficiaries. Increased access to safe water, sanitation facilities and improved hygiene practices for drought affected populations in Baidoa District in Somalia Provide lifesaving WASH support for crises affected IDP and host communities in Somalia The 2021 WASH response aims to provide continuity of life-saving support for the most vulnerable host and internally displaced persons (IDP) communities affected by undernutrition, WASH related disease outbreaks, COVID-19 and climate/human induced disasters but will be adapted to shift the focus on activities addressing the direct consequences of COVID-19 and floods. Somalia will therefore most likely be faced with rising water scarcity, which requires greater investments in emergency water services and restoration of basic water supply services. The WASH response will contribute to prevention of a further increase in AWD, as well as raise awareness to prevent the spread of COVID19 through risk communication and community engagement, and support compliance to recommended measures through hygiene promotion, hygiene kits distribution and increased access to water and soap. To further improve the contribution of WASH to the achievement of health outcomes, the proposed WASH response will invest in improvements in hand hygiene behaviour and access to WASH facilities in health care facilities and other public institutions. Provision of Emergency WASH services to communities in Akobo east and west affected by food insecurity Stabilizing the food access and livelihoods of conflict and disasters affected returnees, internally displaced persons and the host communities in South Sudan through integrated emergency and static Food Security and Livelihood response. This project aims to meet the immediate, medium and long-term food security needs of the target communities of IPC level 3,4 and 5, also having the focus on restoring livelihood, enhancing food production, building resilience and strengthening capacity of the targeted population.

Access to fishing kits and learning of fishery practices is another means to improve food security and livelihood. Fishing has the potential to immediately address food security needs. It enables people to immediately harvest fish from the rivers and swamps in the areas.

Climate-Resilient and Shock Informed Aniticipatory Action in Somalia Saving Lives and Livelihoods in Rural Somalia  Somalia faced a growing number of threats to its food security in 2020, starting with the ongoing Desert Locust crisis, followed by COVID-19 first reported in March, severe flooding between April and September and poor rains forecast for the Deyr 2020 season. Based on latest projections, 2.1 million Somalis are in IPC Phases 3 and above through December 2020. Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of the La Nina developing, which tends to trigger dry conditions in Somalia. If the forecast below-average Deyr rains (Oct-Dec 2020) is followed by below-average or delayed 2021 Gu rains (Apr-Jun), this could lead to a rapid and substantial worsening of the humanitarian situation. 

Rural populations are at a high risk of further deteriorating food security, given the direct and indirect impacts of these threats on rural livelihoods, related assets, food production and income. FAO’s proposal responds both to the lifesaving and life-sustaining needs of rural populations in IPC Phases 3 and above, against a Population in Need (PiN) of 3.1 million people prioritized for Food Security Cluster (FSC) assistance under the 2021 HRP. FAO’s planned activities will directly support 103,850 households in IPC 3-4 under both FSC Strategic Objectives (SOs), while further delivering support to protect food security in Somalia at a wider scale through countrywide animal health campaigns, among other activities. 

Under SO1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 76,300 rural households, including IDPs, in the form of Cash+, UCT and CFW activities delivered through FAO’s e-Platform for Mobile Money and Livelihood Assistance. All cash-based programmes include trainings on good nutrition practices, covering infancy to old age.

Under SO2, to protect livelihoods, FAO will provide in-kind and technical support to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security threats across Somalia’s rural livelihood zones, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to 53,500 households targeted for Cash+ interventions under SO1 (while supporting an additional 7,550 households with agricultural inputs only). FAO’s planned Cash+ activities combine cash transfers with tailored livelihood support packages to assist rural families out of hunger sooner. Alongside cash transfers, the assistance packages will protect and restore the livelihoods of households in IPC Phases 3-4 by providing: (i) farmers with quality inputs to produce a nutritious variety of food crop (cereal, pulse and vegetable seeds, storage bags, fertilizer and irrigation/tractor services, where appropriate; (ii) pastoralists with nutrient-rich feed blocks and deworming to improve livestock productivity especially milk supply; and (iii) coastal communities with a variety of basic fishing gear and processing equipment to improve catch and consumption.  

Also under SO2, in anticipation of drought conditions in early 2021, FAO will also strategically position water bladder tanks and provide nutritive animal feed blocks to protect the small milking animals of up to 20,000 pastoral households impacted by scarce pasture from dry conditions and/or locust damage. Countrywide livestock vaccination and supportive treatment campaigns will further protect livestock assets belonging to at least 2.2 million men, women and children. Preparedness for animal health emergencies will be enhanced through strategic stocking of vaccines and related supplies (PPR), and training to local partners in Livestock Emergency Guidelines and Standards (LEGS), antimicrobial resistance, disease surveillance and reporting, among others.

rengthening agricultural water use efficiency and productivity in Ein AlQusair & Al Houla villages Restoring livelihoods of crisis affected population in Syria through light rehabilitation of irrigation infrastructure at community level The United Nations (UN) estimates that the number of crisis-affected people in need of humanitarian assistance in Syria is 14.2 million, of which 6 million are in acute need. The above figure of people in need includes 6.7 million protracted internally displaced persons (IDPs); estimated 320,000 spontaneous IDPs return; 75,000 refugees return; 438,000 Palestine refugees and the rest overburdened host communities.  

More than 75% of the number of people in need of humanitarian assistance are accessible from within Syria. Overall, 12.4 million of people are estimated to be food insecure (including 1.27 million severely food insecure) and 1.9 million people at risk of food insecurity. 

In this context, FAO has designed a project to assist 120,000 vulnerable crisis-affected food insecure farming households (equivalent to 750,000 people) in Syria. About 15% of the targeted householders will be selected from those who receive food support to help them shift from depending on food assistance to producing their own food and enhancing their self-sufficiency. The objective of the proposed action is to protect and enhance the livelihoods of vulnerable farmers and IDPs through the restoration of critical irrigation infrastructures to increase household food production and security. The project outputs include:

•	Output 1: Local small-scale irrigation infrastructures in the targeted governorates are assessed and light rehabilitation undertaken. 
•	Output 2: Capacity of technical staff and relevant stakeholders strengthened.

A training programme on enhancing irrigation management, water use efficiency in small-scale irrigation, agricultural land management will be based on FAO standards and approaches. It is expected that stakeholders and farmers (water user association) will join this training. 

This project is expected to contribute to increasing access to irrigation water for crisis-affected farmers and their families in the targeted areas through the light rehabilitation of local small scale irrigation infrastructure. Cultivation and other agricultural practices, including livestock and animal feed production, will consequently benefit from the water supply plans as an emergency response to crisis. The proposed intervention will strengthen household food production capacities and knowledge and address immediate food security and nutrition needs through increasing local availability and supply of food.  This may in turn promote flourishing of agricultural based livelihoods in the rural community, which would contribute to social cohesion, peace and stability. The project seeks to utilize intensive labour in order to maximize community participation and inject cash into the local community.  
FAO as part of the CWG will discuss at project level with the group to identify the rate, modality, etc. of the cash intervention to be in line with the CWG and to achieve the purpose of the intervention

Protection Monitoring for corrective response management GBV portion Protection and targeted assistance to promote resilience and solutions for IDPs and non-IDP communities and refugee returnees.   The project aims to strengthen a rights-based protection response for IDPs and non-IDP communities, as well as refugee returnees, in particular those most vulnerable through stronger advocacy, life-saving protection and assistance activities, evidence-based programming with the focus on developing and building the capacity of affected communities to cope and recover and better position them for the attainment of durable solutions. Improving coordination and quality of assessments and monitoring will also be key components of the project. The project also foresees benefiting the entire displaced population through continuous advocacy and support in the area of Law and Policy, fostering the successful engagement with relevant authorities and partners with a focus on the approval and implementation of the new IDP Law. This activity will be built upon efforts by UNHCR that in 2020 culminated in the Somalia accession to Kampala Convention and development of draft IDP Law that is aimed to domesticate it.   
UNHCR will continue to make the best of its key membership of the protection cluster and ensure regular reporting to the clusters’ 5Ws and strong participation and contribution in the different clusters’ working groups to ensure coordination and complementarity of interventions, avoiding duplication with other members and ensuring regular sharing of protection reports with the cluster. 
Many IDPs in protracted displacement remain in situations with no progress towards durable solutions and suffer from systemic marginalization. Access to life-saving assistance and basic services, such as education and health, exclusion from services provided by government are other factors that contribute to heightened protection risks faced by displaced and other conflict-affected populations. Sexual and gender-based violence also remains a critical protection concern for IDPs. A significant proportion of IDPs are members of minority groups lacking the protection of major clans. COVID-19 pandemic has further exacerbated pre-existing risks and vulnerabilities. In Somalia internally displaced persons (IDPs) have been facing despicable acts of man-made violence including forced evictions and natural hazards which have led to multiple displacement and limited access to durable solution opportunities. Many newly displaced IDPs still remain in need of assistance. Many of the IDPs reside in overcrowded areas with poor living conditions and limited security provision. The basic needs of IDPs are often not met due to inconsistent service provision, exclusion from accessing services, or from the sheer absence of services due to poor targeting of settlements. Forced evictions remain one of the most severe and prevalent protection threats, particularly for IDPs and poor households, due to an underdeveloped regulatory framework, hampered access to justice, low awareness of and respect for HLP rights, and a weak protective environment. It is anticipated that opening of the borders and lifting some of the COVID-19 travel restrictions can lead to an increase of number of returns as compared to 2020 that will bring overall number of returnees in the Somalia that will be in need of variety of protection services to 109,989. Many returnees choose not to return to their areas of origin, preferring to settle in urban areas. Many of these contribute to and suffer the results of pressure on basic services, further compounded by recurrent influxes of IDPs. Any intervention will be vulnerability and needs based.  While there is increased effort to promote sustainable return and re-integration, a substantial number of returnees have limited access to basic services, precarious or no physical security and are constantly exposed to myriad protection risks that proposed project will seek to address. The project includes a sustainability/handover component where feasible, particularly in the areas of Law and Policy, as well as community mobilization and NNGOs engagement.

Increase resilience of affected communities, focusing on sustainable initiatives that support equitable access of targeted communities to WASH needs and help protect livelihoods through the provision of needed energy and rehabilitation of basic infrastru Fostering Resilience through Early Recovery response for the Most Crisis-impacted Communities in Syria The Integrated Response for Resilience Programme aims at providing a comprehensive response through Early Recovery support in 80 communities impacted by the crisis. Communities, particularly those most dramatically affected – and under additional stress because of IDPs returns and other displacements - need assistance in reinforcing their resilience to address these shocks as well as the consequences of the protracted crisis, and to address their needs on seriously depleted infrastructures and service capacities.
The essence of the Programme is about providing Syrian communities with – still limited - support to regain control over their basic needs (livelihoods, access to essential services) and reduce their dependency on humanitarian assistance. Prioritization of locations, is the outcome of a context analysis and needs assessment conducted on more than 5,000 Syrian communities, based on the following three criteria:

The programme relates directly to the sector objectives:

Against South Sudan HRP - Assisting persons of concern affected in East and Horn of Africa and Great Lakes Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2021, there are more than 314,000 refugees from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, as well as the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, including from Sudan, Democratic Republic of Congo and Central African Republic.

At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for long-term stability, some 357,500 South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since November 2017, 122,000 of those in 2020 alone. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan at this stage, the increase in numbers warrants a scaling-up of support following an area-based approach, including strengthening linkages with development actors, to help returnees and the communities they settle in live in safety and dignity, with greater security and services.

Refugees largely reside in conﬂict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction of basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.

Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will beneﬁt from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Speciﬁc protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identiﬁed at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with speciﬁc protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as veriﬁcation exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the eﬃciency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to beneﬁt from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

Emergency COVID Health intervention for vulnerable populations in Lebanon Emergency Health support for vulnerable Lebanese and Migrants Medair’s health work has been operating since 2014, supporting both refugees and vulnerable Lebanese through health centres and community outreach. Whilst originally focussed within health centres within Social Development Centres as part of the Ministry of Social Affairs, since the beginning of 2021, Medair has expanded operations to the South / Nabatiye and working with an additional 15 health centres within the Ministry of Public Health network, particularly for routine vaccinations. Medair opened a COVID mass vaccination centre in Saida in June 2021. There is a growing focus on nutrition activities such as IYCF, which are detailed under the Nutrition sector of the ERP.
Health activities that are aligned under the health sector of the ERP include the provision of medication, PPE provision and IPC training for health centres, and integrated messaging through community health volunteers (CHVs). 54 CHVs focused on reaching Lebanese populations will be mobilised from pre-existing Medair networks, and while the remaining number 46+ (additional figures contingent on anticipated future funding) will be newly recruited (with additional CHVs as part of the LCRP). These Community Health Volunteers will reach all populations within their geographic areas of intervention (around the supported health centres).
Medair has seen a four-fold increase in the usage of medication in recent months as more Lebanese are dependent on medication in the public sector due to shortages within pharmacies. Medair therefore aims to provide more medication through supplying pharmacies in supported health centres – expanding the number of centres supported. Medication will be provided free of charge to all those accessing the centres. Medair acknowledges the challenges with procuring medicines in the current context given we do not hold an importation license, yet is actively participating in coordination conversations with other agencies to explore alternative options for procurement of imports as well as engaging with advocacy efforts at the humanitarian and governmental levels. Medair will also include a small cash-for-health component for vulnerable people needing to access medication from other locations, which has been piloted through a blockchain modality in the Bekaa over the past six months. Medair also has experience in cash-for-health programming within the Middle East region, in addition to cash programming within Lebanon.

INTEGRATED FOOD, HEALTH AND NUTRITION SECURITY FOR VULNERABLE HOUSEHOLDS IN NASSIR, MAIWUT, PANYIKANG AND ULANG COUNTIES OF UPPER NILE STATE Emergency Food Security and Livelihoods for flood affected Households in Upper Nile Heavy rain and flooding created historical overflow of the Nile and Sobat Rivers since July 2020, creating the worst flooding in 60 years. The flood destroyed homes and livelihoods of people - damaged settlements, agriculture (crops and cattle), horticulture, and market access which are crucial for peoples’ livelihoods. 40% of the crops and vegetable gardens in GOAL operational areas have been affected and no yield has been harvested during harvesting in 2020. People are also displaced and feared to turn to negative coping mechanisms such as informal borrowing, selling productive assets, and depletion of working capital which might be used to protect from the impact of the disaster. The  flooding crisis came at the back drop of very grim hunger situation in these areas, where already 163,000 were suffering from acute and severe hunger (about 70% of population in Baliet, and 85% in Ulang) (IPC Phases 3, and 4). And 59,462 in IPC4. This situation was further impacted by the current economic downturn and higher inflation rates, in addition to food price hikes exacerbated by the impact of COVID-19 pandemic. The floods severely affected the opportunities for income generating schemes leading to loss of household income and inability to afford food and meet basic needs. Negative coping mechanisms of poor and most affected households have been reported, such as taking fewer meals per day (mostly amongst women and girls), selling assets or borrowing money at high rates to purchase food items, causing unmanageable debt. The flooding also resulted in increased incidences of human diseases such as malaria and acute watery diarrhoea that will affect productivity and deplete savings in the form of increased medical expenses – this will further contribute to household vulnerability and reduce resources available for purchasing food.
GOAL is requesting access to the HRP to cover the immediate needs of 25,800 vulnerable individuals severely  affected by the current flooding of the Sobat river. The individuals targeted will be from existing GOAL beneficiaries who have been flood affected. The flooding affected 68,502 people in Baliet  and Ulang counties. Under the GOAL programme, GOAL has been providing support to build the resilience of 160,000 people in Melut, Baliet, Ulang, Rubkona, and Panyinjar counties since 2016. Prior to the current flooding GOAL program has been implementing various flood risk preparedness and mitigation activities including: dissemination of Early Warning Information, and  development of an early response strategy to mitigate the impact of flooding, stakeholders coordination, formation of flood response committees, identification of most vulnerable people and high-risk areas; distribution of empty sacks to aid dyke construction, dyke construction and monitoring implementation of flood response actions. This request for HRP is sought as the scale and magnitude of the current flooding and livelihood crisis it has compounded requires additional interventions to help vulnerable households meet their immediate needs, reducing the hunger gap and mitigating negative coping mechanisms. This intervention will also provide support to host communities that had to cope with people displaced. 
There is a significant gap in the response to these needs. WFP food distribution covers only 50% of the monthly  households’ food needs. This presents an urgent need for emergency livelihood interventions. The HRP will support households through Cash for Assets to address their immediate food needs, while building assets, such as constructing flood control dikes that will improve their livelihoods, reduce risks and impact of shocks, increase food productivity, and strengthen resilience to natural disasters. The cash for assets will be conditional cash transfer with two components of conditionality – engagement on Cash for Asset, to rebuild community assets, for able bodied households; and mandatory attendance on trainings.

Assistance humanitaire en abris et biens non-alimentaires pour les populations sinistrées des inondations dans les zones à fort risque de Choléra au Niger Assistance humanitaire en Abris et en Biens non-alimentaires (BNA) pour les sinistrés d'inondation au Niger. Dans le cadre de HRP 2021 au travers de ce projet, l'OIM vise à apporter un appui au gouvernement du Niger dans le cadre de la réponse d'urgence aux personnes sinistrées des inondations. Ce projet propose de répondre aux besoins des ménages sinistrés à travers les requêtes qui seront exprimées par le Gouvernement au travers du Ministère de l’Action Humanitaire et de la Gestion des Catastrophes (MAH/GC). Cette réponse s’adressera uniquement aux ménages vulnérables victimes d’inondations dont les abris ou cases auront été endommagés et/ou ceux dont les Biens non-alimentaires (BNA) auront été emportés par les eaux. Le présent projet poursuit comme objectif d’atteindre 8 000 ménages soit 56 000 personnes à travers tout le Niger prioritairement dans les régions de Niamey, Dosso et Diffa. En coordination avec le MAH/GC et la Direction Générale de la Protection Civile (DGPC), l’OIM mettra à disposition 8 000 kits abris et 8 000 kits de Biens non-alimentaires qui seront distribués aux ménages sinistrés. En plus des kits, l’OIM couvrira les coûts liés à la logistique et à la distribution des kits. Ce projet ne couvrira pas une zone ou région donnée mais permettra d’intervenir là où les besoins se présentent et aussi de pouvoir compléter les activités des autres acteurs en cas de besoin en tant que prestataire de dernier recours pour la réponse humanitaire en abri d'urgence et BNA. L’OIM en tant que Co-Lead du Groupe de Travail Abri et Bien non-alimentaire (GTABNA) avec le MAH/GC s'assurera que les activités sont menées en étroite coordination avec les autres partenaires humanitaires membres du GTABNA pour la réponse en abri et Biens non-alimentaires pour les ménages sinistrés des inondations au Niger. Conformément à la logique de la stratégie du Secteur abris/BNA et en fonction de la faisabilité, les interventions pourront se faire en transferts monétaires conditionnels. Cela réduirait considérablement les coûts logistiques qui sont très élevés en période hivernale à cause du mauvais état des routes mais aussi et permettrait aussi de résoudre en partie le problème d’accès lié à l'insécurité qui souvent retarde les interventions. Enfin, la mise en œuvre du présent projet fera l’objet d’un suivi régulier de la qualité des interventions réalisées mais aussi de l’implication des bénéficiaires et autorités locales. Pour cela, les feedbacks de la communauté cible seront collectés à travers des évaluations post-distribution et des séances de discussion de groupe séparées par genre et âge avant et après l'assistance. Aussi, en tant qu’acteur humanitaire, l'OIM et ses partenaires de mise en œuvre s’assureront que ses actions n’induisent aucune tension ou problème dans la zone et n’exposent pas les bénéficiaires. A cet effet la phase d'évaluation de besoins sera réalisée de commun accord avec les populations dans les communes ciblées, les sessions d'information sur le projet seront organisées à l'attention de communauté bénéficiaires, le mecanisme de ciblage de bénéficiaires sera réalisé en etroite collabation avec les autorités au niveau local (do no harm). Une collaboration étroite faite avec les acteurs de protection pour un suivi de pret de toutes questions de protection. Le cout total du projet sera de 4.650.000 USD.

Humanitarian support and shelter of internally displaced persons and refugees in the region suffering from the Afghanistan situation Support for voluntary repatriation of Undocumented Afghans The presence of over 1.4 million registered Afghan refugees, and approximately 1.24 million Undocumented (840,000 Afghan Citizenship Card holders and 400,000 Undocumented Afghans), Pakistan hosts one of the largest protracted refugee situations globally. IOM supports the Government of Pakistan in the implementation of cross-border programming, with voluntary repatriation as one of the key elements, together with integration support, which aims at preserving space for Undocumented Afghans and promoting peaceful co-existence with host communities. 

More specifically, IOM activities have focused on (i) support to the Government during the Documentation Exercise; (ii) advocacy for inclusion of ACC holders and Undocumented Afghans to inform and plan aid assistance; (iii) support for ACC and Undocumented Afghans through livelihood and skills trainings; (iv) facilitation of voluntary and safe returns; (v) access to healthcare; and (vi) protection and assistance to the most vulnerable. 

To respond more effectively to the joint vision between Afghanistan and Pakistan for return of Afghan migrants, including anticipated multifaceted challenges posed by the complexity of large-scale cross border flows in 2021, IOM Pakistan aims to facilitate safe, dignified and voluntary returns of Undocumented Afghans from Pakistan to Afghanistan through a cohesive cross-border programming approach. In addition to creating an environment conducive for voluntary repatriation, IOM will also introduce them to skills development opportunities during their stay in Pakistan, to ensure access to livelihood opportunities in host communities as well as for sustainable reintegration in Afghanistan. 

IOM requires $40 million to address the immediate needs of 1,240,000 Undocumented Afghans in 2021 and beyond. Of this amount, $29 million included in this appeal is urgently needed for the provision of cash grants to returnees to ensure repatriation is made more sustainable.

Protection, Assistance and Durable Solutions for People with Disabilities in North-East Nigeria (part of 21-UF-HCR-027) Improvement of the Protection of People of Concern in North East Nigeria Through the Provision of Shelter and NFI Assistance. This project will target IDPs and returnees in three affected states, Yobe, Adamawa and Borno with provision of emergency shelters, Non-food Items (NFIs), transitional and shelter repair kits as protection live-saving assistance aligned with Shelter/ NFI/ CCCM Sector strategic objectives for the HRP 2019. In 2019 UNHCR continued to effectively respond to shelter needs and aims to target a total of 69,569 households, 347,846 individuals in formal and informal camps and newly accessible areas by the end of the year. As the number of returns and displacement increases due to military operations, there is need to provide shelter related assistance for returnees who are residing in their plots and as well as for host families whose resources have been overstretched. Subsequently acknowledging that the humanitarian situation is still unpredictable; there is need to provide shelters and NFIs for life-saving emergency assistance to promote the protection, safety and dignity of affected Persons of Concern (PoCs). Despite the achievements in the past, the continuous needs for IDPs, though shaped by very different dynamics, revealed that quite a significant majority of people are living in congested camps. The needs assessment conducted in 2019 by Shelter/ NFI/ CCCM sector indicated that as of end of June 2019, 3809 IDP households were living without shelter and NFI assistance since their arrival. In addition to that, 7593 households living in partitioned communal shelters needed NFIs and dignified emergency shelters. The ongoing and protracted displacement leaves the affected people in need of other humanitarian assistance such as Food, WASH, and Health among others. In 2020, UNHCR shall build upon progress being made in 2019 and proposes to respond to unmet needs in Adamawa (Mubi North, Mubi South, Madagali, Michika, Yola South and Yola north); Borno (Bama, Banki, Damasak, Damboa, Dikwa, Jere, konduga, Gwoza, Pulka, Maiduguri, Mobbar, Monguno, Rann and Ngala) and Yobe State (Damaturu and Gujba,) through provision of; - (1) 7,000 Emergency shelters (2) 52,129 NFIs kits to IDPs in both formal and informal camps (3) 10,440 Shelter repair kits to returnees with the provision of conditional CASH component of NGN 30,000 Naira adequate to cover for the cost labor and molding of mud bricks among other unforeseen needs. All the shelters are designed to cater for Women, Men, Girls and boys, persons with specific needs and partitioned to mitigate SGBV cases. The selection of beneficiaries will be based on needs assessment and vulnerability screening in the locations at the time of implementation. Identification and verification of beneficiaries are guided by UNHCR’s Protection principles, and endorsed by community leaders, NEMA, and SEMA officials at LGA areas. UNHCR will reinforce a transparent process of beneficiary selection and the prioritization of needs of vulnerable groups. The project targets the IDPs and Returnees households suffering from protracted displacement and returning home. UNHCR will work to ensure that potential beneficiaries are aware of their responsibilities during the project and of options available to them. It is important to recognize that not everyone can manage the construction/ repair of their own house and that their time might be better used to generate income. The families’ decision to participate in this programme will be achieved through sensitization meetings, detailed assessments, participatory planning and prioritizing the provision of technical training and capacity building. A community-based feedback mechanism through regular mass meetings and focus group discussions will be established to enable IDPs express their opinions on issues affecting their assistance need. The discussions will also provide beneficiaries the opportunity to understand the shelter selection and allocation process.

Supporting contact-line Hromadas and vulnerable population through distribution of hygiene kits, improving WASH facilities and capacitating local authorities in remote provision of social and administrative services Most vulnerable communities and residents have improved access to safe and affordable water, sanitation and hygiene, prevention and reduction of risks of COVID-19 proliferation The WASH project aims to improve access to sufficient safe water and enable adequate sanitation and hygiene practices for the most vulnerable women, girls, boys and men in conflict-affected areas and put at greater risks in the face of COVID-19. Through enhanced targeting of particularly underserved communities and enhanced community-based approach, the project covers both actions of immediate relief and longer-term resilience and self-sufficiency, and will invest special attention and efforts to support both transition in GCA and responding to enduring humanitarian needs in NGCA.
The project first aims to improve access to sufficient safe water to the most vulnerable left with chronically unmet water needs in conflict-affected areas, through a dual approach. The project will first focus on improving the water system infrastructure (including repair/maintain centralized, decentralized and private water supply in public infrastructure and social institutions and/or organizing new access to sustainable/alternative water source). It will do so through the facilitation of partnerships among communities, authorities and water utilities for an inclusive and accountable implementation. The project will then keep an agile approach to respond to the life-saving needs for safe drinking and technical water of the most underserved and vulnerable communities and individuals through water trucking, installation of water tanks, and in case of shocks and emergencies, distributions of water bottles. To help transitioning the response to ensuring the sustainable provision of access to safe water, the project will include to foster community-based and multi-stakeholder engagement on water governance, as well as to amplify advocacy with local, regional, national and international stakeholders on water quality.
The project also aims to improve access to adequate sanitation by initiating support for community-driven waste management. This will include to facilitate and support partnerships between communities, CSOs, the local administrations and other local stakeholders on improving solid waste management in selected communities. This will also include to test community-based waste management activities in the most vulnerable, underserved locations where over-accumulated solid waste is presenting a serious public health threat. 
The project finally aims to enable adequate hygiene awareness and practices, especially in the face of COVID-19 risks, to the most vulnerable women, girls, boys and men. It will do so by keeping here as well an agile approach enabling different modalities of assistance, through the provision of hygiene kits, vouchers and promotion through risk communication and community engagement actions.
Throughout these actions, PIN will maintain a robust Community Feedback and Accountability Mechanism though its community-based approach and engagement with women, girls, boys, men, elderly and people with disabilities to raise their voices; enhanced consultations and testing of participation and social accountability mechanisms; feedback and complaints hotline, response, referrals and analysis for further adjustment of the assistance.

Supporting contact-line Hromadas and vulnerable population through distribution of hygiene kits, improving WASH facilities and capacitating local authorities in remote provision of social and administrative services Comprehensive humanitarian assistance to vulnerable populations affected by the military conflict in eastern Ukraine and / or COVID-19 with a focus on access to food and income opportunities The FSL project aims to improve the food security for the most vulnerable women, girls, boys and men in conflict-affected areas and put at greater risks in the face of COVID-19, and support women and men engage in sustainable livelihoods, in the agriculture and in other sectors alike. Through enhanced targeting of particularly underserved communities and enhanced community-based approach, the project covers three levels of actions, from immediate relief, through self-sufficiency, and longer-term resilience. It will invest special attention and efforts to support both transition in GCA and responding to enduring humanitarian needs in NGCA, and integrate the age, gender and diversity factors influencing food security and livelihoods, including factors of feminised poverty and care dependency.
At a first level the project aims to ‘ensure immediate access to food’ for the most vulnerable women, girls, boys and men living along the ‘line of contact’ in both Luhansk and Donetsk NGCA. The assistance will take the form of food vouchers, and be organised through quarterly rounds to take account of seasonal variations. In addition, PIN will provide short-term, immediate assistance in the form of food kits for those most at risk in the face of COVID-19. Through this modality, those individuals with greater health risks and no direct support system will have access to food items while minimising their exposure to COVID-19 infection risks.
At a second level, in GCA the project will then aim to improve longer-term, sustainable food security for women and men and their households with access to small landplots near the LoC. Such assistance will take the form of seasonal activities, with distribution of vouchers for seeds, of drip irrigation kits, and delivery of trainings. As such the project will directly contribute to the cluster objective to ‘Improve food security through the provision of emergency and time-critical agriculture assistance’.

Trainings will be held, not only on employment, vocational and business-related topics, but also to foster individual empowerment. Special attention will be paid to support women- and youth-led entreprises for equal access to opportunities and as vectors of development for their entire communities. On short-term and seasonable basis, cash-for-work opportunities will be created around community needs, whether to rehabilitate priority infrastructure or realise other community-based initiatives, account taken of age, gender and diversity. As such the project will directly contribute to the cluster objective to ‘Enhance resilience of vulnerable people affected by conflict and/or COVID-19 through restoring of non-agriculture livelihood and promote resilience to shocks (including wildfire, unemployment, higher prices, and other hazard) at community level’.

Protection services and interventions for Palestine Refugees in Syria In 2021, UNRWA will continue to provide critical protection assistance to Palestine refugees. It is anticipated that the vulnerabilities of Palestine refugee will further increase due to COVID-19 and the current economic situation.  
The Agency will seek to improve the protection of Palestine refugees in Syria through various interventions:
-	Mainstreaming protection within UNRWA services will remain a priority. Corresponding to needs, protection training, including on disability inclusion, GBV, PSEA, addressing violence against children, will be delivered to a wide range of staff and volunteers. 
-	Dedicated programmatic responses will be implemented through regular service-delivery and stand-alone initiatives to support the needs of vulnerable populations including those related to psychosocial distress. Areas most affected by conflict-related violence as well as displaced and returning populations will be prioritized.
-	Legal support services will be offered while prioritising women and children experiencing GBV by assisting them in obtaining civil documentation and referrals to external partners. 
-	Mine risk awareness campaigns will continue throughout the country targeting students and other community members, with a specific focus on areas of spontaneous returns. 
-	Protection monitoring, reporting and advocacy will continue to be prioritised through the participation of UNRWA in global protection mechanisms and the international human rights system (IHRS). This will be done through the interaction with relevant stakeholders, including the protection sector of the Humanitarian Country Team (HCT) in Syria. In parallel, UNRWA will focus specifically on monitoring the return of Palestine refugees displaced within and outside Syria.
In a cross-cutting approach, UNRWA will continue to strengthen Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) by systematically increasing the participation of Palestine refugees in programme identification, design, delivery and lesson learning. Feedback will be sought on programme quality and to assess Palestine refugees’ satisfaction with the services provided. This will help UNRWA to implement programmes that are of higher quality, with greater and more sustainable impact.

Food Security Provision of timely, equitable and integrated food security and livelihoods services to the conflict, epidemic and natural disaster affected populations in South Sudan South Sudan protracted crises have left 7.5 million people in dire need of humanitarian assistance in 2020 despite the signature of the Revitalized peace agreement, and continues to face conflict, natural disasters and climate instability, food insecurity, and lack of basic services. According to the latest IPC analysis for South Sudan published in December 2020, an estimated 7.7 million people are expected to experience acute food insecurity and worse (IPC 3, 4 and 5) in 2021. 
SI has started to implement its humanitarian response in South Sudan in 2006. Its long lasting presence has contributed to building a wealth of experience in Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) and Food, Security and Livelihoods (FSL). This allowed SI to pilot large-scale unconditional cash transfers, seeds distribution amongst IDPs and host communities in Western Bahr El Ghazal, Upper Nile, Jonglei and Central Equatoria states. SI aims at supporting the most vulnerable households, who are struggling to restore their livelihoods, in order to help them to improve their food security situation. Currently, SI is running five operational bases: Raja town and Wau town (Western Bahr el-Ghazal), Aburoc/Malakal (Upper Nile), Lankien (Jonglei) and Juba (Central Equatoria). For 2021, SI will focus on linking its first line response, through its EPR and static teams, with activities having longer-term impact in WASH and FSL sectors. In FSL specifically, this will mean emergency livelihood response to quickly replenish the destroyed assets. In second step SI will complement the response, wherever possible, with capacity building to allow for income generation and longer-term food preservation. SI will therefore aim at providing timely, equitable and integrated food security and livelihoods services to the conflict, epidemic and natural disaster affected populations of South Sudan.
