Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan (USAID/BHA) Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP camps, and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity.

WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying  mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan. 

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities, or other solution. 

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19 have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

part of AUB01/SRH/Pakistan Humanitarian Response Plan 2021/Provision and scale up of life-saving Sexual and Reproductive Health services and prevention and response to Gender Based Violence in Cross Border Areas in Pakistan(part of EOL No. 74399) Lifesaving SRH-GBV integrated response with COVID-19 prevention and protection to ensure continuity of SRH services 4,7 million women are estimated as currently pregnant in Pakistan. 66% deliveries occur at health facilities, 22% of them are at government facilities.  3,5 million births expected by end of December, 2020. 
10%-20% decline in service coverage of essential maternal health care (ANC and post-natal care) may result in increasing of maternal deaths up to 2,056 -3,135 cases respectively.
There was not a tangible decline in institutional deliveries observed in the provinces where UNFPA mobile units are functional.  However, the number of ANC and Postnatal visits decreased by 30% due to lockdown and accessibility of the services. 
Distribution of COVID 19 positive cases among male and female population is unequal in different age groups. Most prevalent cases observed among male population in middle age group (65%). The impact of pandemic is frequently discussed by the government but more in economic terms and yet there is negligible mention of women or the gendered effects of the coronavirus. ‘The government’s approach towards women has always been paternalistic, and it is no different now; women are viewed as passive victims of a socio-economic and healthcare disaster’. 

Assessment conducted by OCHA in 2020 in collaboration with other UN organizations/agencies has unfold a gloomy picture of the health systems which also comes with some noticeable geographic disparities;  for instance; 
- Only 26.9% of the health facilities in Sajawal were having medicine available and on the other hand 88.9% of the health facilities in TM Khan were having medicine available in the health facility.
- Only 32.9% of deliveries take place in health facilities and 27.7% of post-natal care is provided by trained health staff. Recent estimates reveal that over 2.2 million people have limited or no access to essential health care services including women at reproductive age (15-49 years) 
- Access to health facilities by pregnant women is poor. For instance, only 52% in TM Khan and 28.2% in Sajawal have access to a health facility that assisting with birth 24/7, (Joint UN assessment 2020). 

Overall, 27% of the health facilities were reported as nonfunctional in the flood affected communities. Out of the functional health facilities only 27% providing 24/7 health care services. Overall, 52% of the respondents reported medicine available at the nearest health facilities, while 48% reported medicine were not available at the health facility.
The above situation is aggravated by:
- The ongoing outbreak of COVID-19 pandemic in Pakistan has increased burden on the already weak health system. Many of the existing resources (human, equipment, infrastructure, funds etc) have been diverted to support COVID-19 response. This and the additional financial resources allocated from routine health programmes have impacted negatively on the delivery of health services particularly those entrapped in protracted crises, such as, Afghan Refugees and Temporary displaced persons.   
- The non-pharmaceutical response to COVID-19 especially restriction to movements have adversely  affected  access to health services by the disaster affected population because repeated lockdowns with resultant supply chain breakdowns not only hampered services availability but also restricted population access to these services - Since, Health sector workforce including doctors from public and private sector, nurses, paramedics staff and pharmaceutical experts, lab technicians are at the forefront of Coronavirus. The workforce is facing disruptions and closure of the health care system for non-COVID related illnesses like routine immunization, maternal and childcare in many locations. Therefore, using national level PDHS 2017-18 Data, UN (2020) Socio-economic Impact assessment of COVID-19 on the Most Vulnerable Population has drawn two kinds of scenarios for the impact of COVID 19 on SRH services. According to the assessment report, if there is 10% reduction in the continuity of current services

part of IEA24/GBV/Zimbabwe - HRP 2021/UNFPA	GBV response in Humanitarian Settings (part of PZIM/2021) Ensuring access to life-saving, essential GBV risk mitigation and response services for women and girls, men and boys  in remote and hard to reach areas in 26 drought affected districts         The protracted drought, compounded by the economic crisis and socio-economic Impact of COVID19, will continue to expose most vulnerable women and girls, men and boys, to exacerbated risks of GBV and harmful practices in 2021.

Between March and October 2020, the National GBV hotline has recorded an average increase in GBV calls of 60%, with 94% being females and 90% of cases being IPV. As a result of the multi-hazard crisis and its socio-economic impact, more than 1,700,000 women and girls and 560,000 men and boys will face increased risks of exposure to GBV in 2021.

GBV vulnerability assessments conducted between March and October 2020 reported that drought is contributing to modify daily routine patterns (e.g. water fetching and firewood collecting) which forces women and girls to walk long distance and spend long hours away from home, generating tension on the homestead, and leading to increased IPV. In the eastern provinces, where Apostolic faith sectarianism is predominant, girls are increasingly exposed to early marriage, as lobola (bride price) is often the only alternative household income source. SRHR consequences include      increased teenage pregnancy rates, and increased risks of ante and post-natal complications, which can be  fatal. 

Bordering towns also represent hotspots for GBV, as women and girls are exposed to trafficking and illegal migration, while female headed households become the most frequent target for SEA. IDPs in the eastern provinces that were affected by Cyclone Idai in 2019 continue to face increased GBV risks as they continue to be hosted at temporary camps with limited GBV risk mitigation measures. Women and girls with disabilities are also among the most vulnerable to GBV risks, and face further challenges of mobility to reach essential services.

The protracted drought, compounded by the economic hardship, hyperinflation and related basic goods price Increase, and the constrained access to cash, further contributes to reducing the capacity of survivors to sustain transport fees to reach services. The gradually decreasing availability of basic health services further contributes to the pre-existing critically low access to life-saving essential GBV services. According to the ZIMVAC rural livelihood assessment (October 2020), 68% of Individuals have no access to GBV services. When available, GBV multi-sectoral services remain fragmented, and mostly available at provincial and district level, often resulting out of reach for those living in most remote areas. De-prioritization of GBV services Is a documented result of unavailability of services, especially in remote areas. The proliferation of traditional healing systems deriving from the health system constraints, also results in an increased SEA risks.

In order to respond to the heightened GBV concerns, UNFPA with support from
international and local NGOs will scale up GBV mitigation and response interventions
targeting a total of 337,472 individuals (74% women and girls, 26% men and boys, 7% PWDs) in 26 districts.

The proposed interventions aim at:

1) Enhancing effectiveness of community-based GBV risk mitigation mechanisms;
2) Strengthening the availability and accessibility of life saving multi-sectoral survivor-centered
GBV services for GBV survivors in the most hard to reach areas
3) Improving the capacity of GBV specialized and non-specialized humanitarian actors to
integrate GBV and PSEA interventions across programs, to avoid unintended GBV
consequences and ensure DO-NO Harm.

Integrated life-saving Child Protection, GBV, and Education Response for disaster affected communities in Tawila, Melit, Kebkabiya, and Saraf Omra localities in North Darfur State Access to Humanitarian life-saving child protection and GBV response services in North Darfur, North / South Kordofan and White Nile states The project objective is to protect people from violence, neglect, and exploitation by providing access to life-saving child protection and GBV response services to targeted communities in White Nile, North Kordofan, and North Darfur. In order to accomplish this, Plan will provide high quality protection services and contribute to community stabilization and resilience. Protection services and capacity building activities will include: CP and GBV case management, distribution of dignity kits to vulnerable girls, multi-purpose cash transfer to vulnerable households and hosting UASC, and referrals mechanisms including to Family and Child Protection Units, training of social workers and partner staff on GBV, CP, and referral pathways, and psychosocial support to conflict affected children and youth. The provision of protection services must be paired with activities to increase knowledge of and access to those services. Therefore, Plan will also establish/strengthen and equip Community Based Child Protection Networks (CBCPNs), conduct community awareness session of CP, FGM, SEA and child marriage risks, and conduct sensitization on GBV prevention and response. Plan will foster communal stability and resilience by providing life skills training, parenting sessions, conducting community awareness sessions on peacebuilding and conflict transformation, and training duty bearers and community leaders on peacebuilding.  Additionally, Plan will establish child-friendly community feedback and response mechanisms so that all project beneficiaries are able to provide feedback and file complaints.

WASH & S/NFI assistance for IDPs, returnees, PINs and host community This project aims to achieve sustainable improvement in access to quality water supply, sanitation condition, hygiene practices and distribution of essential life-saving NFI and emergency shelters among IDPs and host communities in East and South Darfur states as well Khartoum State, the project will focus on subsectors of water supply, sanitation, hygiene promotion, environmental health and NFI and emergency shelters. ARC will continue to provide access to safe water in communities suffering from malnutrition above emergency thresholds for IDPs as well as the vulnerable host communities impacted by the presence of IDPs through context specific technologies such as surface water treatment systems and sustainable Point of Use water treatment solutions appropriate for a highly mobile population. Food & Cash-based Assistance for Vulnerable Populations in Somalia for 2021 Food & Cash-based Assistance for Vulnerable Populations in Somalia for 2021 Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas.  As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation.  The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of a La Niña that is currently developing (75 percent chance through Feb 2021). Potential drought conditions will likely develop as a result of below average 2020 Deyr (Oct-Dec), a harsh 2021 dry Jilaal (Jan-Mar) season and a possible delay and/or poor performance of the 2021 Gu (Apr-Jun). 

Continued emergency relief alongside a further scale up of support to increase resilience is required in order to avert the hardship situation. WFP is therefore seeking resources in 2021 to sustain the on-going efforts and enable households meet immediate food needs and help build resilience against shocks. WFP is planning to implement unconditional and conditional transfers to improve access to food under integrated multi sectoral assistance to meet needs of vulnerable girls and women, pregnant and lactating women, boys and men and leverage resources with other partners to meet the level of humanitarian assistance required. WFP will continue to participate in cluster, joint planning, assessments and regular meetings with other humanitarian actors in Somalia. WFP employs gender sensitive beneficiary targeting in all its projects and prioritizes female and single headed households. Community consultations are carried out with men and women to ensure that their voices are heard. Accountability to affected populations ensured through information sharing, surveys and beneficiary feedback mechanisms. Beneficiaries are targeted and registered through biometric SCOPE system that provides real time data.

EUB15/SRH/Libya Humanitarian Response Plan 2021/Advancing midwifery and specialized nursing in Libya (ENI/2018/399-480) Increase access to lifesaving sexual and reproductive health services to vulnerable population affected by Conflict and COVID19 pandemic in Libya. In 2020, 3.5 million population lacks consistent access to primary and secondary health care services. This is due to the reason that more than half of the functional health facilities in 2019 are closed due to the intensification of conflict and the onset of COVID19 in 2020. Lifesaving health services such as reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent Health (RMNCAH) and mental health services have been severely disrupted, neglected and underfunded in the past many years. The situation amid COVID19 pandemic is further compounded by lack of personal protective equipment (PPEs), delays in payment of salaries to the health care providers, and closer of many health facilities or the suspension of operations especially in maternity hospitals in urban areas. The supply chain management for medical supplies, equipment and pharmaceuticals are globally and locally disrupted and it has closed many public health facilities. Due to this situation, majority of the patients are now referring to private health care facilities, which is making out of pocket expenditure more catastrophic for the people, especially for IDPs, migrants and people living in conflict zones or along the migration routes in Libya.

This project is designed to maintain and provide emergency reproductive and sexual health services amid covid19 pandemic to 53,800 women of child bearing age, among conflict affected, IDPs and migrant population and host communities. The services are planned to be provided in severely affected municipalities / geographical areas ranked above 3 on the severity scale with a focus on un(der)served population. The project intends to provide EmONC services to an estimated population of 9,157 pregnant women. Services will mainly target migrants, refugees, returnees and IDPs and host communities in Tripoli, Benghazi, Sebha, Misurata and Sirt and people in need among none-displaced and migrants are more specifically targeted in affected municipalities or hard to reach areas of Ghat, Sirt, Murzuq, Alkufra and Aljufra.
Considering the humanitarian situation in the country, scarcity of midwives and OBGYN specialists, low capacity level and limited availability of female healthcare providers (especially specialized nurses and midwifes) to provide quality SRH services and unavailability of SRH supplies in the health facilities, there is clearly the need for a humanitarian complementary service package. The services that will be provided through this project are in line with minimum initial services package (MISP) for life saving sexual and reproductive health services of UNFPA and Essential Health Service (EHS) package of WHO issued for the context of COVID19 pandemic. UNFPA will work with its partner agencies, stakeholders, communities and local authorities for the following:

1.	Provision of Lifesaving Essential Maternal, sexual and reproductive health services to prevent excess neonatal and maternal mortality and morbidity among affected population.
2.	Coordinate Sexual and Reproductive Health Services to ensure continuous provision of essential SRH services 
3.	Provision of Essential medicine, medical supplies and equipment to sustain health SRH services
4.	Increase access to SRH services through the deployment of mobile medical teams and enhance the performance of existing primary healthcare facilities and community health workers in targeted areas of vulnerable population.
5.	Strengthen health sector and community resilience to ensure social protection and sustainable and equitable access to quality SRH services.

Promoting Inclusive Action in Peacebuilding (PIAP Initiative) Saving Lives and Livelihoods in Rural Somalia  Somalia faced a growing number of threats to its food security in 2020, starting with the ongoing Desert Locust crisis, followed by COVID-19 first reported in March, severe flooding between April and September and poor rains forecast for the Deyr 2020 season. Based on latest projections, 2.1 million Somalis are in IPC Phases 3 and above through December 2020. Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of the La Nina developing, which tends to trigger dry conditions in Somalia. If the forecast below-average Deyr rains (Oct-Dec 2020) is followed by below-average or delayed 2021 Gu rains (Apr-Jun), this could lead to a rapid and substantial worsening of the humanitarian situation. 

Rural populations are at a high risk of further deteriorating food security, given the direct and indirect impacts of these threats on rural livelihoods, related assets, food production and income. FAO’s proposal responds both to the lifesaving and life-sustaining needs of rural populations in IPC Phases 3 and above, against a Population in Need (PiN) of 3.1 million people prioritized for Food Security Cluster (FSC) assistance under the 2021 HRP. FAO’s planned activities will directly support 103,850 households in IPC 3-4 under both FSC Strategic Objectives (SOs), while further delivering support to protect food security in Somalia at a wider scale through countrywide animal health campaigns, among other activities. 

Under SO1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 76,300 rural households, including IDPs, in the form of Cash+, UCT and CFW activities delivered through FAO’s e-Platform for Mobile Money and Livelihood Assistance. All cash-based programmes include trainings on good nutrition practices, covering infancy to old age.

Under SO2, to protect livelihoods, FAO will provide in-kind and technical support to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security threats across Somalia’s rural livelihood zones, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to 53,500 households targeted for Cash+ interventions under SO1 (while supporting an additional 7,550 households with agricultural inputs only). FAO’s planned Cash+ activities combine cash transfers with tailored livelihood support packages to assist rural families out of hunger sooner. Alongside cash transfers, the assistance packages will protect and restore the livelihoods of households in IPC Phases 3-4 by providing: (i) farmers with quality inputs to produce a nutritious variety of food crop (cereal, pulse and vegetable seeds, storage bags, fertilizer and irrigation/tractor services, where appropriate; (ii) pastoralists with nutrient-rich feed blocks and deworming to improve livestock productivity especially milk supply; and (iii) coastal communities with a variety of basic fishing gear and processing equipment to improve catch and consumption.  

Also under SO2, in anticipation of drought conditions in early 2021, FAO will also strategically position water bladder tanks and provide nutritive animal feed blocks to protect the small milking animals of up to 20,000 pastoral households impacted by scarce pasture from dry conditions and/or locust damage. Countrywide livestock vaccination and supportive treatment campaigns will further protect livestock assets belonging to at least 2.2 million men, women and children. Preparedness for animal health emergencies will be enhanced through strategic stocking of vaccines and related supplies (PPR), and training to local partners in Livestock Emergency Guidelines and Standards (LEGS), antimicrobial resistance, disease surveillance and reporting, among others.

Against Nigeria HRP -various donors- private Improvement of the Protection of People of Concern in North East Nigeria Through the Provision of Shelter and NFI Assistance. This project will target IDPs and returnees in three affected states, Yobe, Adamawa and Borno with provision of emergency shelters, Non-food Items (NFIs), transitional and shelter repair kits as protection live-saving assistance aligned with Shelter/ NFI/ CCCM Sector strategic objectives for the HRP 2019. In 2019 UNHCR continued to effectively respond to shelter needs and aims to target a total of 69,569 households, 347,846 individuals in formal and informal camps and newly accessible areas by the end of the year. As the number of returns and displacement increases due to military operations, there is need to provide shelter related assistance for returnees who are residing in their plots and as well as for host families whose resources have been overstretched. Subsequently acknowledging that the humanitarian situation is still unpredictable; there is need to provide shelters and NFIs for life-saving emergency assistance to promote the protection, safety and dignity of affected Persons of Concern (PoCs). Despite the achievements in the past, the continuous needs for IDPs, though shaped by very different dynamics, revealed that quite a significant majority of people are living in congested camps. The needs assessment conducted in 2019 by Shelter/ NFI/ CCCM sector indicated that as of end of June 2019, 3809 IDP households were living without shelter and NFI assistance since their arrival. In addition to that, 7593 households living in partitioned communal shelters needed NFIs and dignified emergency shelters. The ongoing and protracted displacement leaves the affected people in need of other humanitarian assistance such as Food, WASH, and Health among others. In 2020, UNHCR shall build upon progress being made in 2019 and proposes to respond to unmet needs in Adamawa (Mubi North, Mubi South, Madagali, Michika, Yola South and Yola north); Borno (Bama, Banki, Damasak, Damboa, Dikwa, Jere, konduga, Gwoza, Pulka, Maiduguri, Mobbar, Monguno, Rann and Ngala) and Yobe State (Damaturu and Gujba,) through provision of; - (1) 7,000 Emergency shelters (2) 52,129 NFIs kits to IDPs in both formal and informal camps (3) 10,440 Shelter repair kits to returnees with the provision of conditional CASH component of NGN 30,000 Naira adequate to cover for the cost labor and molding of mud bricks among other unforeseen needs. All the shelters are designed to cater for Women, Men, Girls and boys, persons with specific needs and partitioned to mitigate SGBV cases. The selection of beneficiaries will be based on needs assessment and vulnerability screening in the locations at the time of implementation. Identification and verification of beneficiaries are guided by UNHCR’s Protection principles, and endorsed by community leaders, NEMA, and SEMA officials at LGA areas. UNHCR will reinforce a transparent process of beneficiary selection and the prioritization of needs of vulnerable groups. The project targets the IDPs and Returnees households suffering from protracted displacement and returning home. UNHCR will work to ensure that potential beneficiaries are aware of their responsibilities during the project and of options available to them. It is important to recognize that not everyone can manage the construction/ repair of their own house and that their time might be better used to generate income. The families’ decision to participate in this programme will be achieved through sensitization meetings, detailed assessments, participatory planning and prioritizing the provision of technical training and capacity building. A community-based feedback mechanism through regular mass meetings and focus group discussions will be established to enable IDPs express their opinions on issues affecting their assistance need. The discussions will also provide beneficiaries the opportunity to understand the shelter selection and allocation process.

Multi-sectoral project for community resilience Comprehensive humanitarian assistance to vulnerable populations affected by the military conflict in eastern Ukraine and / or COVID-19 with a focus on access to food and income opportunities The FSL project aims to improve the food security for the most vulnerable women, girls, boys and men in conflict-affected areas and put at greater risks in the face of COVID-19, and support women and men engage in sustainable livelihoods, in the agriculture and in other sectors alike. Through enhanced targeting of particularly underserved communities and enhanced community-based approach, the project covers three levels of actions, from immediate relief, through self-sufficiency, and longer-term resilience. It will invest special attention and efforts to support both transition in GCA and responding to enduring humanitarian needs in NGCA, and integrate the age, gender and diversity factors influencing food security and livelihoods, including factors of feminised poverty and care dependency.
At a first level the project aims to ‘ensure immediate access to food’ for the most vulnerable women, girls, boys and men living along the ‘line of contact’ in both Luhansk and Donetsk NGCA. The assistance will take the form of food vouchers, and be organised through quarterly rounds to take account of seasonal variations. In addition, PIN will provide short-term, immediate assistance in the form of food kits for those most at risk in the face of COVID-19. Through this modality, those individuals with greater health risks and no direct support system will have access to food items while minimising their exposure to COVID-19 infection risks.
At a second level, in GCA the project will then aim to improve longer-term, sustainable food security for women and men and their households with access to small landplots near the LoC. Such assistance will take the form of seasonal activities, with distribution of vouchers for seeds, of drip irrigation kits, and delivery of trainings. It will enable smallholder farmers in underserved communities to increase their self-sufficiency throughout the year. As such the project will directly contribute to the cluster objective to ‘Improve food security through the provision of emergency and time-critical agriculture assistance’.
At a third level, in GCA the project will eventually aim to support access to employment and micro-, small businesses for women and men in communities near the LoC. Trainings will be held, not only on employment, vocational and business-related topics, but also to foster individual empowerment. Special attention will be paid to support women- and youth-led entreprises for equal access to opportunities and as vectors of development for their entire communities. On short-term and seasonable basis, cash-for-work opportunities will be created around community needs, whether to rehabilitate priority infrastructure or realise other community-based initiatives, account taken of age, gender and diversity. This will serve both poverty reduction, community social cohesion and living conditions in the communities. As such the project will directly contribute to the cluster objective to ‘Enhance resilience of vulnerable people affected by conflict and/or COVID-19 through restoring of non-agriculture livelihood and promote resilience to shocks (including wildfire, unemployment, higher prices, and other hazard) at community level’. 
Throughout these actions, PIN will maintain a robust Community Feedback and Accountability Mechanism though its community-based approach and engagement with women, girls, boys, men, elderly and people with disabilities to raise their voices; enhanced consultations and testing of participation and social accountability mechanisms; feedback and complaints hotline, response, referrals and analysis for further adjustment of the assistance.

Health (STATE/PRM) Improved access to and utilization of integrated emergency lifesaving primary health services in Upper Nile State This intervention is aimed at improving access to and utilization of health services through five fixed primary health care facilities including Rirnyang PHCU in Ulang County, Kiechkuon PHCC, Makak PHCU, and Wandeng PHCU in Nasir and Jekow PHCU in Maiwut. To scale-up health care services in Nasir, Longechuk, Maiwut, and Ulang Counties. RI will also establish eight MMUs and ICCMs to serve the hard-to-reach population with lifesaving health care services. In total the project will target 99,094 vulnerable individuals.
RI will recruit and deploy qualified health workers including clinical officers, nurses, midwives, community health workers, and vaccinators to all supported fixed facilities and mobile medical units. Alongside this, Boma Health Workers will be selected within the targeted communities to implement ICCM activities. 
The intervention will further focus on continuous screening and treatment of communicable and non-communicable diseases through patient consultations. Additional services provided will include antenatal care, skilled deliveries, postnatal care, and clinical management of rape (SGBV services) in the health facilities and mobile medical units. The intervention will also integrate and strengthen mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) and services for people with disabilities.  
The project will continue streamlining and strengthening the referral pathways for mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), sexual and gender-based violence survivors and, maternal and child health emergencies. RI’s health team through this response will conduct routine and outreach immunization services to children under 59months of age. 
This project will engage all communities in the targeted counties throughout the implementation stages to ensure the sustainability of the program. Beneficiary exit satisfaction interviews will be conducted at fixed facilities and MMUs and community feedback mechanism meetings will be conducted to facilitate feedback from the communities. This project builds on RI's existing static and mobile health interventions, are locations and static facilities not services by other actors - serving the most vulnerable, and hard to reach IDP, host and returnee community in Upper Nile State.

Child protection, GBViE and PSEA Children (girls and boys) and their families affected by disaster are protected against violence, abuse, exploitation, discrimination and other violations of their rights. Child protection issues are exacerbated during disaster, requiring immediate protection services to bring normalcy back in the lives of girls, boys and women. Measures to prevent abuse and violence and respond to cases of survivors of violence and exploitation need to be strengthened by providing safe access to protective services. Likewise, psychosocial distress experienced by people at the onset of any emergency requires professional care and support. Hence, the project provides mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) and coordination as a core area of response. An increase of CP risks is being observed in the current COVID-19 pandemic as well. Some of these may include: Physical and emotional maltreatment, Gender-based violence (GBV), mental health and psychosocial distress, child labour, unaccompanied and separated children and social exclusion. Following are some of the interventions:

1.	Establishment of protective spaces to cater the needs of vulnerable girls, boys and women including disable. The protective spaces will be run by trained facilitators and provided with recreational and learning materials. It will offer opportunities for girls and boys to build resilience and recover from their experiences, provide a daily routine and a sense of normalcy.
2.	Provision of Psychosocial Support (PSS) is primarily aimed at those individuals or group of people who require care and support including those in isolation or quarantine in case of the current COVID-19 situation. Digital platforms will be used for delivering PSS while there are movement restrictions in place. The PSS will be provided at three levels tailored to the needs of target population:
•	Within facilities receiving suspected/infected people for care and support including isolation and quarantine facilities.
•	Community based support in areas identified with suspected/infected people or receiving people exiting isolation/quarantine facilities and going through the social reintegration phase. Families, relatives and caregivers of such people will also be able to avail such services and support.
•	Referral pathways in collaboration of case management for accessing social protection services/packages.
3.	People demonstrating exacerbated distress and signs of mental health concerns or adverse reactions, would be referred to specialized mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS). Digital platforms will be used for delivery of MHPSS while movement restrictions are in place. 
4.	Provide CP monitoring and outreach social mobilization through dedicated and trained CP monitors and facilitators in coordination with community-based CP structures and CP Working Groups and Govt. counterparts;
5.	Establish and strengthen coordination amongst key stakeholders and community-based CP structures for the identification of vulnerable girls, boys and women, including missing, unaccompanied, separated and disabled children, and promote their access to protection, social and psychosocial services through an effective and efficient case management and referral system;
6.	Capacity building of relevant service providers, Govt. officials including DMAs, CSOs, rights-holders and duty-bearers in Child Protection in Emergency (CPiE), psychosocial support and strengthening advocacy and support for girls, boys and women affected by disaster to achieve enhanced protection for them;
7.	Dissemination of critical information for prevention of violence against children (VAC) using different communication channels. In the current context, service provision will prioritize prevention of stigma, labelling and discrimination of people who are perceived to be infected or affected by COVID-19. The promotion of correct information and addressing emerging myths and rumors including positive understanding and behaviours about ‘social distancing’ should therefore include actions that support people to adopt and maintain healthy and rationale lifestyles.

South Sudan Acute food insecurity Joint Response (SSACJR) Improving food security in Jonglei and Unity South Sudan In line with the South Sudan HRP and cluster objectives 1 and 2, the project will save lives by addressing the acute severe food insecurity of 57,000 conflict and natural disaster affected people in IPC3+ in Jonglei (Pigi/Canal, Bor) and Unity State (Rubkona and Guit) through distribution of food vouchers to 2,500 HH and enhanced and sustained food production through distribution of seeds, crop and fishing kits, training and cash for work to 9,500 HH. In support of nutrition centres, kitchen gardens will be established to improve the nutritional status of people. This will allow severe and acute food insecure people in IPC3+ to meet their immediate food needs whilst allowing them to rebuild their assets. In addition, by improving people's food security, acute malnutrition will be reduced. All the selected locations are affected by different natural and man-made disaster, showing high and multiple vulnerabilities and are priority areas as they are in IPC3 or worse, confirmed by Cordaid assessments. Assessments also showed that women (incl. PLW), children (incl. children under 5), PWD, elderly and chronically ill are impacted differently and are bearing the brunt of conflict, droughts/ floods and COVID-19. The project will therefore target these most vulnerable groups through inclusive assistance, and will ensure that protection, gender and COVID-19 is mainstreamed in the proposed activities. 
Protection will be mainstreamed throughout the project cycle to ensure beneficiary safety & dignity, avoiding doing harm as result of the intervention, providing meaningful access to all sets of beneficiaries and ensuring all groups are actively involved and participate in the project in an inclusive manner. Additionally, the project will ensure all necessary Covid-19 measures and protocols will be adhered to; for example, during distributions, beneficiaries will be encouraged to maintain safe social distance, always wash their hands and wear face masks.
Cordaid has been responding to the increasing humanitarian needs in all 4 areas providing WASH, FSL and ES&NFI assistance and is fully operational in the 4 areas with offices in Malakal, Bor and Bentiu.

Protection and assistance to people of concern in Syrian Arab Republic, Niger, Mali and Uganda Enhancement of protection of displaced persons, returnees and conflict affected host communities in Syria through integrated, community based protection activities.  The project aims to strengthen protection and resilience of Syrian IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host communities through advocacy, coordination and provision of community-based protection services. 
UNHCR Syria will continue to lead the Protection Sector/Cluster to ensure coordinated protection interventions programming for safe refugees return.
UNHCR’s protection interventions include legal counselling and assistance, protection monitoring, referrals and information sharing, social protection through livelihoods support to most vulnerable people, GBV prevention and response, child protection, psychosocial support and in-kind assistance for persons with specific needs, non-formal education, and awareness activities on various subjects targeting women, men, boys and girls. In addition to over 100 community centres providing integrated protection services, outreach to communities will be convened through over 2,800 outreach volunteers. 
Accountability to affected people will be realized through meaningful participation of communities, structured focus group discussions and enhancement of community-based complaint mechanisms. UNHCR will continue its capacity building efforts to ensure services are delivered according to the standards and that accountability to affected population and do no harm principles are respected. 
UNHCR Syria will continue to lead Protection Sector in coordination of response plans of IDPs and affected people as well it will execute leadership roles in refugee return programmes in collaboration with the Government. In North West Syria, it will lead Protection Monitoring Task Force (PMTF).

WASH Emergency WASH Response in South Sudan UNICEF will provide women, men, girls, and boys affected by multiple shocks and hazards in South Sudan with critical water, sanitation, and hygiene services, items, and facilities.  The objective of this project is to provide lifesaving emergency water supply, sanitation and hygiene promotion services for conflict affected people, vulnerable host communities and people in disease prone (high GAM famine and outbreak related) areas including protection related actions to mitigate GBV, strengthening of communities’ resilience to cope with the impact of emergencies and recurrent shocks. This emergency WASH project will comprise of situation assessments, preparedness, transitional programs, frontline emergency WASH response, strengthening of partners’ capacity, and cluster coordination including sector information management. UNICEF will deliver emergency lifesaving support by providing access to WASH services as per Sphere and WASH Cluster standards.

The project will focus on addressing the following:
- Effective Cluster coordination mechanism in the country
- Provide timely equitable access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene for IDPs/host communities and returnees, including transitional programming
- WASH in Nutrition for famine prevention with a minimum package of interventions.
- WASH in Health for outbreak control at wider community level (i.e. Ebola, Cholera, etc.)
- While implementing projects a special attention will be given to mitigate WASH-related GBV.

The project will also support expansion of partnerships with local and international NGOs and CBOs in highly affected areas to ensure basic services are provided and long-term capacity built. The activities will be implemented in complementarity with other sectors such as Health, Nutrition, Protection and where possible Education projects including disaster risk reduction (DRR) focusing on strengthening community coping mechanisms.

part of UOH70/GBV/Life-saving multisectoral GBV response services are accessible to women and girls and delivered through a survivor centred approach (part of 20-RR-FPA-042) Ensuring access to quality, timely and confidential services for GBV survivors and strengthening coordination for GBV mitigation and prevention in Somalia  Needs:
GBV continues to be an issue of great concern in Federal members States Galmudug, South West State, Jubaland, Hirashebelle Puntland and Somaliland with the event of the COVID19.  Recent spikes in the increase of Intimate Partner Violence, rape, sexual exploitation, sexual harassment and abuse have multiplied GBV risks for women and girls with worsening impact on women and girls living with disabilities. In IDP camps and host communities – inadequate physical infrastructure, distance to water points, markets, health facilities and schools, poor lightening, lack of doors on toilets and lack of disaggregation of sanitary facilities are some of major factors that increase GBV exposure. In addition, distance to distribution centers and lack of specific measures to ensure women’s inclusion and participation in food distributions, continue to worsen levels of exposure of women and girls to GBV risks. In the July 2020 “GBV/FGM assessment during the COVID19”, 38 percent responders indicated that there has been an increase in GBV incidents; 35 percent indicated GBV incidents are the same.  The number of GBV survivors call in to hotlines for help also increased by 283% in FMS and 767% in Somaliland despite the inactivation of some of the hotlines in the states. 

In addition, GBVIMS 2020 data reports a trend indicating an increase of GBV noting that over half (61%) of reported GBV incidents were Physical Assault, 13% Rape, 12% Sexual Assault, 6% Psychological/Emotional Abuse, 5% experienced Denial of Resources, and the remaining 3% percent Forced/Early marriage.       Furthermore, Anecdotal media and programming report has indicated a spike in rape of women and girls including a specific targeting of recent on boys. Majority of Women and girls fleeing violence in Somalia do not have options for safety and protection. In 2020, there has been significant efforts to broaden women and girls’ safe spaces, however, this has been severely impacted by funding limitations and also due to COVID. 

GBV service provision remains low as compared to the need and geographical landscape. Recently, worsening relations between communities and service providers exacerbated by the heightened political atmosphere impacted provision of GBV services or coordination. GBV service provision in Somalia has historically been characterized by limited specialized services such as rape treatment for rape survivors, psycho-social support and higher levels of mental health care for traumatized women and girls are major hindrances to expanding provision of timely, confidential and quality GBV services. Also, lack of actors to provide specialized services undermines efforts invested to assure access to GBV services by survivors. At present, the GBV AoR in Somalia has 58 partners that reports on the 5Ws.

B) Enhance the capacity/and mobilize 200 PSS counsellors; 150 health workers to provide timely, quality and confidential PSS and rape treatment. C) Promote mobilization of women and girls to access services through the establishment of 15 safe spaces for women and girls (WGSS) to reach 3000 women and girls. D) Support the operationalization of integrate referral pathways for dissemination and access to services reach 2000 women, girls, boys and men. E) Provide 2,000 dignity kits and 36 post rape kits dignity protection for women and girls and treatment of rape. ZZT07/GBV/Somalia Humanitarian Response Plan 2021/TTF POOL RHCS II/TTF - MULTI DONOR Ensuring access to quality, timely and confidential services for GBV survivors and strengthening coordination for GBV mitigation and prevention in Somalia  Needs:
GBV continues to be an issue of great concern in Federal members States Galmudug, South West State, Jubaland, Hirashebelle Puntland and Somaliland with the event of the COVID19.  Recent spikes in the increase of Intimate Partner Violence, rape, sexual exploitation, sexual harassment and abuse have multiplied GBV risks for women and girls with worsening impact on women and girls living with disabilities. In IDP camps and host communities – inadequate physical infrastructure, distance to water points, markets, health facilities and schools, poor lightening, lack of doors on toilets and lack of disaggregation of sanitary facilities are some of major factors that increase GBV exposure. In addition, distance to distribution centers and lack of specific measures to ensure women’s inclusion and participation in food distributions, continue to worsen levels of exposure of women and girls to GBV risks. In the July 2020 “GBV/FGM assessment during the COVID19”, 38 percent responders indicated that there has been an increase in GBV incidents; 35 percent indicated GBV incidents are the same.  The number of GBV survivors call in to hotlines for help also increased by 283% in FMS and 767% in Somaliland despite the inactivation of some of the hotlines in the states. 

In addition, GBVIMS 2020 data reports a trend indicating an increase of GBV noting that over half (61%) of reported GBV incidents were Physical Assault, 13% Rape, 12% Sexual Assault, 6% Psychological/Emotional Abuse, 5% experienced Denial of Resources, and the remaining 3% percent Forced/Early marriage.       Furthermore, Anecdotal media and programming report has indicated a spike in rape of women and girls including a specific targeting of recent on boys. Majority of Women and girls fleeing violence in Somalia do not have options for safety and protection. In 2020, there has been significant efforts to broaden women and girls’ safe spaces, however, this has been severely impacted by funding limitations and also due to COVID. 

GBV service provision remains low as compared to the need and geographical landscape. Recently, worsening relations between communities and service providers exacerbated by the heightened political atmosphere impacted provision of GBV services or coordination. GBV service provision in Somalia has historically been characterized by limited specialized services such as rape treatment for rape survivors, psycho-social support and higher levels of mental health care for traumatized women and girls are major hindrances to expanding provision of timely, confidential and quality GBV services. Also, lack of actors to provide specialized services undermines efforts invested to assure access to GBV services by survivors. At present, the GBV AoR in Somalia has 58 partners that reports on the 5Ws.

UNFPA interventions will target the displaced and non-displaced communities including all age groups and persons with disabilities, and with the following specific objectives: a) Facilitate access to comprehensive multi sectoral GBV services (medical, legal, psychosocial) for 6000 women and girls. B) Enhance the capacity/and mobilize 200 PSS counsellors; 150 health workers to provide timely, quality and confidential PSS and rape treatment. C) Promote mobilization of women and girls to access services through the establishment of 15 safe spaces for women and girls (WGSS) to reach 3000 women and girls. D) Support the operationalization of integrate referral pathways for dissemination and access to services reach 2000 women, girls, boys and men. E) Provide 2,000 dignity kits and 36 post rape kits dignity protection for women and girls and treatment of rape. F) Support 200 women and girls’ survivors of GBV with cash voucher assistance and grants for livelihood. G) Support the mainstreaming initiatives on IASC Guidelines for cluster programming on GBV for 300 cluster-coordinators at national and sub national levels.

Améliorer l'accès à l’eau potable, l’assainissement et l’hygiène et à des abris d’urgence dans les sites des déplacés et communautés hôtes des régions de Tillabéri et Diffa Appui à l'amélioration de l'accès à l’eau potable, l’assainissement et l’hygiène dans les sites des déplacés et communautés hôtes dans les régions de Tillabéri et Diffa Ce projet proposé a pour objectif de protéger les personnes contre les maladies liées à l’eau, l'assainissement et à l'hygiène, au bénéfice des populations déplacées et des communautés hôtes résidant dans les zones ciblées. Le nombre des bénéficiaires de ce projet est estimé à 15 000 personnes dont 55% seront les filles et femmes  et 10% de refugiés (1000 ). Le projet sera mis en oeuvre à travers les activités clés ci-après:                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  
-  Construction/ réabilitation des points d'eau(forages , PEA, mini-AEP...)
- Contruction des latrines d'urgences et durables incluant les kits d'entretiens
- Promotion de l'hygiène incluant la distribution  des kits d'hygiène...
La mise en oeuvre du projet prendra en compte  les aspects de genre et redevabilité  de manière à assurer un accès équitable et sécurisé au profit des bénéficiaires. il faut noter que ce projet tiendra également  en compte de l'approche cash transfert.
 
Le suivi et évaluation sera assuré par l’Officier en charge avec l’appui du conseiller national de suivi-évaluation en étroite collaboration avec le coordonnateur WASH. Sur le terrain, un suivi de contrôle qualité sera assuré conjointement avec les services techniques déconcentrés de l’Etat et les différents membres des structures de gestion communautaires. IRC soucieux de la qualité de son travail, mettra à la disposition des équipes des applications spécialisées dans la collecte des données et de leur traitement. (Kobocollect, CommCARE...).

En vue  d'assurer la durabilité/perennisation  des infrastructures WASH , IRC se propose d'impliquer fortement les membres des comités de gestion des infrastructures (CGPE, AUSPE, relais communautaires...) , les services techniques de l'Etat (DRHA) et les communes ainsi que les leaders communautaires des zones ciblées. IRC  prevoit également des mises en place/ renforcement de capacité / recyclage des comités de gestion des points (pour l'accès durable aux infrastrucures) en accord avec la DRHA et les communes concernées.

Améliorer l'accès à l’eau potable, l’assainissement et l’hygiène et à des abris d’urgence dans les sites des déplacés et communautés hôtes des régions de Tillabéri et Diffa Assistance d'urgence aux ménages déplacés et populations hôtes affectés par les conflits et les catastrophes naturelles dans les régions de Diffa, Maradi et Tillabéri au Niger. Le présent projet envisage de contribuer au bien-être et à la restauration de la dignité des populations affectées par les conflits via l’assistance en abris et BNA. Les populations ciblés sont les déplacés, les réfugiés et les communautés hôtes des régions de Diffa, Maradi et Tillabéri. Afin d'identifier les besoins, des évaluations sectorielles seront réalisées dans les localités affectées accueillant les populations. Une coordination sera faite avec les autres acteurs sur le terrain notamment l'UHNCR pour assurer une réponse intégrée et multisectorielle aux besoins de ces populations. L’assistance se fera sur la base de la vulnérabilité. 9 000 ménages vulnérables (63 000 personnes) seront assistés en biens non alimentaires et en abris transitionnels et d’urgences. Les modalités de réponse seront définis en fonction du contexte dans les zones du projet.  Le projet assurera la participation effective des populations dans la mise en œuvre des activités. Ceci passera notamment par leur consultation et leur implication lors de l'identification des bénéficiaires, la mise en place de comité de plaintes et des monitorings post-distributions afin de recueillir leur retour sur l'assistance. Les leaders locaux et les représentants des communautés affectées seront fortement impliqués dans l’ensemble du processus partant des évaluations des besoins jusqu’à la réponse. Aussi, IRC s’appuiera fortement sur son équipe protection qui fera des analyses des risques chaque fois que cela s’avèrera nécessaire afin de réduire les impacts négatifs que pourraient engendrer les interventions de l'organisation. Les interventions réalisées contribueront à renforcer la protection des bénéficiaires notamment à travers la fourniture des abris dignes et sûrs conformes aux standards du GT ABNA au Niger. De plus, les abris transitionnels vont contribuer à la résilience des communautés cibles. Les personnes à besoin spécifique (femmes cheffes de ménage, personnes âgées, personnes en situation d’handicap) seront prioritairement ciblées au cours de la mise en œuvre du projet. Ces personnes seront appuyées dans la construction de leurs abris. Une attention particulière leur sera portée lors des opérations de distribution afin d'éviter qu'elles n'attendent longtemps dans les rangs. Les abris distribués seront équipés de porte pour renforcer la sécurité des ménages bénéficiaires. L'IRC veillera à ce que les espaces entre les abris construits respectent les standards mais aussi que les sites d'installation des personnes ciblées ne soient pas inondables. Aussi, compte tenu de la pandémie de la COVID-19 qui touche aussi le Niger, IRC s’assurera de mettre en place des mesures de prévention et de réduction des risques au cours de la mise en œuvre des activités du projet. Ces mesures comprendront entre autres : le port du masque pour les staffs, la mise en place des dispositifs de lavages de mains avec du savon lors des assistances, la sensibilisation des bénéficiaires sur les gestes barrières.

Response to food insecurity needs in South Sudan identified as per World Food Programme's 2021 operational response plan. Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP camps, and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity.

WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying  mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan. 

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities, or other solution. 

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19 have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

Provision of lifesaving emergency S-NFI for protection and dignity of Internally Displaced Persons in Yambio, Ezo and Nzara Counties Access to emergency SNFI and durable solutions for displaced populations of Greater Equatoria and Jonglei State YEDA will target 26,600 indivuduals with cash and in-kind modalities in Morobo, Yei and Mundri East Counties, and only in-kind in Terekeka, Pibor and Nagero, due to lack of functional markets and access constraints.
The response modality is informed by YEDA’s previous experience, and the need to scale-up CVA as an avenue to recovery&resilience. All interventions will be carried out following Covid-19 preventive measures; social distancing, use of PPE and preventive messaging through IEC. YEDA will maintain static presence in Mundri East, Pibor and Yei Counties, which will also allow delivering assistance to the other targeted areas through mobile response within two weeks from alert.
Beneficiary targeting will be guided by the SNFI Cluster criteria; PLWs, children <5, the elderly, PWN/PWDs (30%), high number of dependents, multiple displacement, lack of ties with the local community/purchasing power, GBV and COVID-19 risks associated with SNFI needs. 
The response will improve access to safe and appropriate S/NFIs to 12,000 new displacements/people with new vulnerabilities, improve the living conditions of 4,800 vulnerable individuals in protracted displacement/host populations through ES upgrade and NFI replacement and 2000 through CVA, support vulnerable 5,400 returnees and affected host community with ES upgrade and NFI replacement and 1,800 with CVA, and assist the 600 most vulnerable returnees/host communities with durable solutions through construction of 100 transitional shelters, and increase the ability of  people to respond to new shocks through CBIs, including CFW and multipurpose cash vouchers.
For in-kind response, pipeline items will be requested upon approval of SNFI analysis report by the SNFI Cluster coordinators, and delivered in areas without access to local market/shelter material. The CVA will include the creation of a multi-purpose cash fund for procurement of shelter materia/NFIs from the local market, allowing vulnerable families to repair their homes, and ensuring appropriate shelter, protection and dignity. Since in remote areas framing material is not accessible due to protection concerns, hence the project will include a small CFW component targeting 200 individuals for training in shelter construction by the YEDA local shelter expert, with secondary benefits for host communities (financial empowerment and conflict risk reduction). Risk of conflict over land will be mitigate by identifying land ownership/tenure arrangements and local mechanisms for settling land disputes, involving all relevant local authorities and local stakeholders to handle eventual cases of disputes, and training staff, volunteers and communities in HLP access rights.
Multi-purpose cash vouchers will be distributed in two istallments of $70 and $30, allowing households to purchase SNFIs as per their priority. FSPs will be mapped out in the project sites, and distribution facilitated by YEDA staff. Female heads of household and PWDs will be prioritized, to ensure financial empowerment of intended people and GBV risk reduction.
To measure the project success and take evidence-based decision on the course of action, continuous monitoring and end evaluation will be conducted jointly with community members/local leaders as part of a Response, Feedback and Complaint Mechanism, on weekly and monthly basis.
Coordination with the SNFI cluster through the SFPs on by-monthly basis, and with other humanitarian partners utilizing humanitarian hubs in Mundri, Pibor, Yambio and Yei on monthly basis in order to take part to joint responses, will minimize duplication, and promote integrated response, gender and protection mainstreaming, GBV referrals, risk mitigation, and incorporation of HIV/AID and COVID-19 prevention messages. As alternate WES SFP, Greater Mundri SiFP and DFC focal point for UN OCHA, YEDA will lead humanitarian interventions through the cluster methodology, lead humanitarian coordination and refer need/gaps to ICWG.

IOM:  Protection, Emergency Shelter and Non-Food Items . Diffa, Maradi, Tahoua (STATE/PRM) Assistance humanitaire en Abris et en Biens non-alimentaires (BNA) pour les sinistrés d'inondation au Niger. Dans le cadre de HRP 2021 au travers de ce projet, l'OIM vise à apporter un appui au gouvernement du Niger dans le cadre de la réponse d'urgence aux personnes sinistrées des inondations. Ce projet propose de répondre aux besoins des ménages sinistrés à travers les requêtes qui seront exprimées par le Gouvernement au travers du Ministère de l’Action Humanitaire et de la Gestion des Catastrophes (MAH/GC). Cette réponse s’adressera uniquement aux ménages vulnérables victimes d’inondations dont les abris ou cases auront été endommagés et/ou ceux dont les Biens non-alimentaires (BNA) auront été emportés par les eaux. Le présent projet poursuit comme objectif d’atteindre 8 000 ménages soit 56 000 personnes à travers tout le Niger prioritairement dans les régions de Niamey, Dosso et Diffa. En coordination avec le MAH/GC et la Direction Générale de la Protection Civile (DGPC), l’OIM mettra à disposition 8 000 kits abris et 8 000 kits de Biens non-alimentaires qui seront distribués aux ménages sinistrés. En plus des kits, l’OIM couvrira les coûts liés à la logistique et à la distribution des kits. Ce projet ne couvrira pas une zone ou région donnée mais permettra d’intervenir là où les besoins se présentent et aussi de pouvoir compléter les activités des autres acteurs en cas de besoin en tant que prestataire de dernier recours pour la réponse humanitaire en abri d'urgence et BNA. L’OIM en tant que Co-Lead du Groupe de Travail Abri et Bien non-alimentaire (GTABNA) avec le MAH/GC s'assurera que les activités sont menées en étroite coordination avec les autres partenaires humanitaires membres du GTABNA pour la réponse en abri et Biens non-alimentaires pour les ménages sinistrés des inondations au Niger. Conformément à la logique de la stratégie du Secteur abris/BNA et en fonction de la faisabilité, les interventions pourront se faire en transferts monétaires conditionnels. Cela réduirait considérablement les coûts logistiques qui sont très élevés en période hivernale à cause du mauvais état des routes mais aussi et permettrait aussi de résoudre en partie le problème d’accès lié à l'insécurité qui souvent retarde les interventions. Enfin, la mise en œuvre du présent projet fera l’objet d’un suivi régulier de la qualité des interventions réalisées mais aussi de l’implication des bénéficiaires et autorités locales. Pour cela, les feedbacks de la communauté cible seront collectés à travers des évaluations post-distribution et des séances de discussion de groupe séparées par genre et âge avant et après l'assistance. Aussi, en tant qu’acteur humanitaire, l'OIM et ses partenaires de mise en œuvre s’assureront que ses actions n’induisent aucune tension ou problème dans la zone et n’exposent pas les bénéficiaires. A cet effet la phase d'évaluation de besoins sera réalisée de commun accord avec les populations dans les communes ciblées, les sessions d'information sur le projet seront organisées à l'attention de communauté bénéficiaires, le mecanisme de ciblage de bénéficiaires sera réalisé en etroite collabation avec les autorités au niveau local (do no harm). Une collaboration étroite faite avec les acteurs de protection pour un suivi de pret de toutes questions de protection. Le cout total du projet sera de 4.650.000 USD.

Food Security (Multi year) 2021 portion Provision of emergency food security and livelihoods support for vulnerable Agro-pastoralists households in Terekeka and Bor South Counties in Central Equatoria & Jonglei States. The proposed project will provide training to the vulnerable households to enhance fishing, crop and vegetable production mainly for consumption at the household level and sale of surplus at local markets in selected payams of (Bor town, Kolnyang, Anyidi, Makuach, Jalle and Baidit) in Bor South County of Jonglei state and (Nyikabur, Tukoro, Yokara, Bori, Bokana and Lojora) payams in Terekeka County of Central Equatoria state which will create extra income for these vulnerable households. These payams are chosen due to their suitability for fishing, crop and vegetable production.
SAADO will target 9,000 households in Bor South County and 7,000 households in Terekeka County in this proposed response with emergency fishing, crop and vegetable kits support. The 2 locations have been selected because of the needs prevalent in these counties according to the Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) January 2021 which shows both Counties in IPC 4 extreme levels of food insecurity and the existence of ongoing food security and livelihoods supported by FAO-ELRP, Cash for Seeds, Livestock vaccination and treatment and WFP supported Food for Assets programming by SAADO in the proposed areas. The emergency livelihood kits will be obtained from the FSL cluster recommended FAO core pipeline.
 SAADO will put in place a mechanism for effective and participatory community vulnerability mapping in the selected payams and bomas and will use a comprehensive beneficiary selection criteria developed, discussed and agreed upon with the communities to include Men, Women, Boys and Girls. 
During community consultations at various levels, men, women boys and girls will be consulted to fully understand and appreciate the impact of the current crisis on vulnerable men, women and children that would further inform our proposed response. “Do no harm” and AAP principles will be applied throughout the duration of the project, so that any possible negative implications of the project at community level are addressed before they occur. This will be done through integrating a strong Communicating with Communities and Engagement (CCE) feedback mechanisms. 
The proposed project will build upon and complement SAADO's 11-year experience in implementing food security and livelihoods programmes in the proposed counties of Terekeka and Bor South Counties including; Terekeka County:  General food distribution (GFD), School Feeding Programme (SF), Food for Assets Project-2020 to 2022 (FFA) supported by WFP, Emergency Livelihoods Response Programme (ELRP) 2020 to 2023; Cash for Seeds project 2020 to 2023; Livestock vaccination and treatment supported by FAO 2018 to 2021. In Bor South County: Emergency Livelihoods Response Programme (ELRP) 2020 to 2023; Cash for Seeds project 2020 to 2023; Livestock vaccination and treatment supported by FAO 2018 to 2021.
SAADO’s proposed emergency response will also complement the lifesaving, livelihoods and nutrition activities carried out by other FSL partners in the two counties such as ADRA in Terekeka County and VSF-Germany in Bor South County of Jonglei state. The proposed activities are necessary and sufficient to achieve the stated cluster objectives for these interventions based on the relevance of each activity in increasing access to emergency food security and livelihoods support for the most vulnerable households in the targeted communities. The indicators selected are SMART and SAADO has in place a strong monitoring and evaluation system and mechanisms to measure these indicators and to ensure the intended results are achieved. The means of verification, such as monthly reports, distribution lists and regular field visits are strongly credible and are currently used by the organization in its MEAL processes across its field offices in the country.

Integrated CCCM and Protection response for communities affected by the sub-national violence in Tambura County Comprehensive, safe and dignified SGBV prevention and response services for conflict and displacement affected individuals and communities in South Sudan In response to identified priority needs of protection risk mitigation and protection service provision, DRC will deliver Sexual and Gender Based Violence (SGBV) prevention and response services for conflict and displacement affected communities. DRC will implement SGBV prevention and response activities in a variety of locations including hard to reach locations through both static and mobile modalities. In doing so DRC aims to contribute to the overarching intersectoral strategic objectives for the 2021 HRP through contributing to the four-protection cluster strategic objectives:
-	Ensure the provision of critical protection related assistance and specialized services through an integrated approach to address the priority needs of targeted people among vulnerable women, men, girls and boys in hard-to-reach and priority geographical areas 
-	Prevent and mitigate protection risks through enhanced preparedness and resilience 
-	Enable durable solutions for IDPs and other population 
-	Enhance protection assessment and monitoring to inform protection and overall humanitarian response 

DRC GBV program activities will ensure GBV prevention and response services are available to women and girls, boys and men, those who are survivors or at risk of GBV. DRC prevention activities will include risk mitigation through protection awareness raising and information dissemination, distribution of dignity kits, capacity building for duty bearers and strengthening of community-based protection capacities. Gender-responsive action will include mobilising communities in the prevention of violence against women and girls through the SASA! community mobilization program, working with both men and women to challenge the negative consequences of gender inequality and harmful power dynamics. SGBV response activities will include case management for survivors of SGBV and focused non-specialized individual and group-based counselling for women and girls. DRC will also support where appropriate the establishment of community based safe shelters and/or safe homes. DRC will strengthen or support the establishment of safe referral pathways in areas of both static and mobile operation. Many IDPs in protracted displacement remain in situations with no progress towards durable solutions and suffer from systemic marginalization.
