Emergency life-saving support to Pastoral and Agro-pastoral households at risk of drought. Saving Lives and Livelihoods in Rural Somalia  Somalia faced a growing number of threats to its food security in 2020, starting with the ongoing Desert Locust crisis, followed by COVID-19 first reported in March, severe flooding between April and September and poor rains forecast for the Deyr 2020 season. Based on latest projections, 2.1 million Somalis are in IPC Phases 3 and above through December 2020. Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of the La Nina developing, which tends to trigger dry conditions in Somalia. If the forecast below-average Deyr rains (Oct-Dec 2020) is followed by below-average or delayed 2021 Gu rains (Apr-Jun), this could lead to a rapid and substantial worsening of the humanitarian situation. 

Rural populations are at a high risk of further deteriorating food security, given the direct and indirect impacts of these threats on rural livelihoods, related assets, food production and income. FAO’s proposal responds both to the lifesaving and life-sustaining needs of rural populations in IPC Phases 3 and above, against a Population in Need (PiN) of 3.1 million people prioritized for Food Security Cluster (FSC) assistance under the 2021 HRP. FAO’s planned activities will directly support 103,850 households in IPC 3-4 under both FSC Strategic Objectives (SOs), while further delivering support to protect food security in Somalia at a wider scale through countrywide animal health campaigns, among other activities. 

Under SO1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 76,300 rural households, including IDPs, in the form of Cash+, UCT and CFW activities delivered through FAO’s e-Platform for Mobile Money and Livelihood Assistance. All cash-based programmes include trainings on good nutrition practices, covering infancy to old age.

Under SO2, to protect livelihoods, FAO will provide in-kind and technical support to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security threats across Somalia’s rural livelihood zones, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to 53,500 households targeted for Cash+ interventions under SO1 (while supporting an additional 7,550 households with agricultural inputs only). FAO’s planned Cash+ activities combine cash transfers with tailored livelihood support packages to assist rural families out of hunger sooner. Alongside cash transfers, the assistance packages will protect and restore the livelihoods of households in IPC Phases 3-4 by providing: (i) farmers with quality inputs to produce a nutritious variety of food crop (cereal, pulse and vegetable seeds, storage bags, fertilizer and irrigation/tractor services, where appropriate; (ii) pastoralists with nutrient-rich feed blocks and deworming to improve livestock productivity especially milk supply; and (iii) coastal communities with a variety of basic fishing gear and processing equipment to improve catch and consumption.  

Also under SO2, in anticipation of drought conditions in early 2021, FAO will also strategically position water bladder tanks and provide nutritive animal feed blocks to protect the small milking animals of up to 20,000 pastoral households impacted by scarce pasture from dry conditions and/or locust damage. Countrywide livestock vaccination and supportive treatment campaigns will further protect livestock assets belonging to at least 2.2 million men, women and children. Preparedness for animal health emergencies will be enhanced through strategic stocking of vaccines and related supplies (PPR), and training to local partners in Livestock Emergency Guidelines and Standards (LEGS), antimicrobial resistance, disease surveillance and reporting, among others.

WFP Relief Response to Drought Affected Population Food & Cash-based Assistance for Vulnerable Populations in Somalia for 2021 Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas.  As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation.  The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of a La Niña that is currently developing (75 percent chance through Feb 2021). Potential drought conditions will likely develop as a result of below average 2020 Deyr (Oct-Dec), a harsh 2021 dry Jilaal (Jan-Mar) season and a possible delay and/or poor performance of the 2021 Gu (Apr-Jun). 

Continued emergency relief alongside a further scale up of support to increase resilience is required in order to avert the hardship situation. WFP is therefore seeking resources in 2021 to sustain the on-going efforts and enable households meet immediate food needs and help build resilience against shocks. WFP is planning to implement unconditional and conditional transfers to improve access to food under integrated multi sectoral assistance to meet needs of vulnerable girls and women, pregnant and lactating women, boys and men and leverage resources with other partners to meet the level of humanitarian assistance required. WFP will continue to participate in cluster, joint planning, assessments and regular meetings with other humanitarian actors in Somalia. WFP employs gender sensitive beneficiary targeting in all its projects and prioritizes female and single headed households. Community consultations are carried out with men and women to ensure that their voices are heard. Accountability to affected populations ensured through information sharing, surveys and beneficiary feedback mechanisms. Beneficiaries are targeted and registered through biometric SCOPE system that provides real time data.

Improving Child Protection for vulnerable populations in Somaliland, particuarly IDPs in Hargeisa and Togdheer  In 2021 humanitarian response, Plan International will improve protection environment and promote child rights in Somaliland for IDP and vulnerable populations, particularly at-risk children. The country has one of the lowest child and gender indicators in the world with only one-quarter of girls – 24% aged 15-24 considered as literate, 45% married before 18 years and 98% subjected to female genital mutilation/cutting (FGM/C). The COVID19 quarantine measures to prevent and control the spread of COVID-19 exposed children and women to increased protection risks, particularly within the home, owing to increased stress caused by the outbreak, exacerbating existing gender inequalities and violence. Child Protection Areas of Responsibility in collaboration with UNICEF conducted a child protection survey in April 2020 showed more than half of the CP agencies (57%) reported an increase in physical violence particular on girls. There has also been increased exposure to violence especially to girls through FGM/C. According to the United Nations Population Fund, COVID-19 could have far reaching impacts on the effort to end FGM/C, with a potential 2 million FGM/C cases occurring over the next decade that could have otherwise been averted.  Plan will work with CSOs and other partners to effectively promote and support improving community-based child protection mechanisms. Key interventions will target young girls and boys, their parents and other decision-makers to raise awareness on child protection and GBV, establish and strengthen referral mechanisms for case management and other services including MHPSS and financial support, and capacity building and advocacy with local authorities and for national agenda on centrality of protection  (e.g. importance of child protection and campaigns on GBV, adoption of the positive discipline techniques, inclusion of children with disability) and distribution dignity kits. Plan and partners will also promote PSS for children and adolescents affected by crisis, support youth-led DRR initiatives, and establish girls groups to prioritize creating safe spaces for dialogue and peer friendships. Plan and partners will provide age-appropriate, gender-sensitive, and disability inclusive services that address the different impacts of emergencies on adolescents and young children, boys and girls and promote the potential for positive transformation of gender norms. Plan and partners will maintain child-friendly feedback and complaint mechanism and promote transparency across all activities.

The project will address Housing, Land and Property (HLP) rights issues through the provision of legal assistance, facilitate issuance of property and identity documents, and work with mediation mechanisms to support HLP related dispute resolution. Community-based networks will be utilized as part of the protection response to foster community buy in and ownership of protection. The project will use evidence-based planning to expand outreach and develop the capacity of displaced communities to cope, recover, contribute to and ultimately achieve solutions. Out of 1.6 million IDPs, 475,000 IDPs and IDP returnees will be supported with protection interventions and assistance in seven (7) states and an administrative areas. Recognising the protection concerns linked to food insecurity, the Agency activities also include a scaling-up of activities in South Sudan’s highly food insecure and prioritised locations, i.e. Pibor County, Akobo, Aweil South, Tonj East, Tonj North, Tonj South. There will be continuous advocacy and support in the area of law and policy with relevant government bodies such as the   Ministries of Justice Home Affairs, Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management, and the Relief and Rehabilitation Commission (RRC) to ensure the centrality of protection, enact the “Protection and Assistance to Internally Displaced Persons Act 2018” (IDP) Bill, National Framework on Returns, and various HLP initiatives. The relevant line ministries will also receive capacity building and technical assistance. Building on UNHCR’s existing operational presence in Bentiu Bor, Juba, Malakal, Wau, Yambio, Yei, the Agency will continue to advance on the 2020 geographic expansion of IDP activities by leveraging both static and mobile presence through 15 partners to Central Equatoria, Unity, Upper Nile, Joinglei, Western Bahr El Ghazal, Northern Bahr El Ghazal, Lakes, Western Equatoira, Eastern Equatoris and Warrap. Response and monitoring will cover 19 identified priority counties and Pibor Administrative Area, including remote or hard to-reach areas, in full support to the Protection Cluster Strategy for mobile assessments and response. Partners comprise of both national and international organizations, with selection undertaken on the basis of their pre-existing presence, access to populations of concern and capacity to carry out static and remote protection monitoring and response. While not all proposed activity locations fall under the severity 3, 4 or 5 in terms of food insecurity, recognizing the fluidly and unpredictable nature of sub-national violence in South Sudan, UNHCR’s protection by presence approach requires presence in areas affected by conflict as well as areas of potential return in light of increased momentum in terms of solutions 
Resources and advocacy will focus primarily on protection response and solutions, either durable or transitional (where the former is not yet possible), including assessments on needs, risks, and intentions and feasibility of durable solutions, while also strengthening community-based structures, supporting HLP initiatives, promotion of livelihoods and peaceful coexistence. The activities will be implemented in complementarity with other sectors such as Health, Nutrition, Protection and where possible Education projects including disaster risk reduction (DRR) focusing on strengthening community coping mechanisms.

WFP Response to Humanitarian Needs of Flood Affected People in South Sudan (part of 21-RR-WFP-039) Food Assistance for conflict affected populations in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP camps, and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity.

WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying  mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan. 

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities, or other solution. 

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19 have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

Accès inclusif et durable à une éducation de qualité pour les enfants et jeunes déplacés et de la communauté hôte affectés par la crise sécuritaire dans les régions de Maradi et de Tillaberi ette proposition de NRC s’aligne sur les principales priorités de la Stratégie nationale de réponse aux vulnérabilités du système éducatif 2020 en apportant une contribution spécifique aux populations les plus vulnérables dans le cadre des crises identifiées dans la Stratégie en termes d’Accès, de Qualité et d’amélioration de la Gouvernance dans le secteur de l’éducation dans les régions de Maradi et de Tillabéry. L’action vise à soutenir l'éducation de 25 000 enfants et jeunes âgés de 6 à 17 ans touchés par la crise et le déplacement, tout en atténuant la propagation de COVID-19. Le NRC privilégie l'utilisation des normes minimales de l'INEE pour assurer une programmation de qualité dans tous les résultats.
NRC facilitera la réouverture des écoles au sein des communautés d'accueil et à fournir l’accès à un environnement d’apprentissage de qualité à tous les enfants touchés, y compris les enfants des communautés d'accueil et les enfants déplacés/réfugiés. L'intervention du NRC pour soutenir l'éducation formelle comprend des actions relatives au renforcement de la résilience des parties prenantes, à la sécurisation de structures éducatives fonctionnelles et à la construction et l'adaptation des infrastructures éducatives existantes et de l'environnement scolaire afin de se préparer aux multiples risques qui peuvent affecter le système éducatif, y compris le risque de catastrophes naturelles et les risques sanitaires, par exemple par la construction/réhabilitation de systèmes WASH (eau, hygiène et assainissement). Afin de répondre aux besoins des enfants qui ont manqué l'école à cause du conflit et du déplacement, le NRC introduira des cours de rattrapage ou de soutien scolaire de courte durée ainsi que des PEA pour les élèves réfugiés, déplacés et vulnérables afin d'assurer leur réintégration, leur maintien et leur progression dans le système officiel, tout en étant en accord avec les directives du gouvernement d'accueil. L’intervention de NRC visera aussi à offrir des possibilités de formation professionnelle aux jeunes déplacés internes et aux jeunes vulnérables non scolarisés dans notre zone d'intervention ciblée au Burkina Faso. Afin de garantir le respect et la dignité des personnes assistées et surtout de nous rassurer que nos interventions ne nuisent pas à leur bien-être (Do Not Harm), NRC veillera à consulter systématiquement les communautés bénéficiaires avant toute intervention et activités sur le terrain. Des mécanismes déjà mis en place dans certaines de nos communes d’interventions (Ligne téléphoniques, boites à suggestions…) seront d’avantage renforcée en 2021 au sein des écoles et des communautés afin que les communautés puissent signaler et reporter toutes formes de nuisances du fait de NRC ou de ses partenaires de mise en œuvre.
Notre intervention prend également en compte les questions de Nexus Humanitaire – Développement à travers le renforcement des structures de gouvernance et de dialogue scolaire, ou encore la mise en place des solutions durables dans nos interventions.

Réponse d'urgence aux populations affectées par les déplacements pour un accès effectif aux services d'eau, hygiène, assainissement et abris et biens non alimentaires, dans la région de Tillabéry Contribuer à l’amélioration des conditions de vie des populations vulnérables au Niger - RRM Depuis sa mise en place 2015 par IRC, puis avec DRC, ACTED et ACF, le RRM a démontré son efficacité dans la réponse de première intention aux besoins des populations nouvellement déplacées dans les régions de Maradi, Diffa, Tahoua et Tillabéri. Le mécanisme est financé par ECHO (le RRM est une priorité dans le HIP 2020 et dans la version préliminaire du HIP 2021) et USAID, avec le soutien de l’UNICEF pour la fourniture de kits Abri et BNA supplémentaire. Les secteurs d'intervention RRM sont les ABNA, l'EHA, la protection et la sécurité alimentaire et la réponse du Consortium s'inscrit en lien direct avec les différentes stratégies de réponses sectorielles développées par les organes de coordination humanitaire au Niger. Le projet est aussi en lien direct avec la stratégie de réponse des autorités nigériennes, et en particulier le Ministère de l'Action Humanitaire et de la Gestion des Catastrophes (MAH), qui est le ministère de tutelle pour les partenaires du RRM. Le projet proposé pour 2021 vise à répondre aux besoins urgents en ABNA des populations les plus vulnérables déplacées depuis moins de 3mois (et/ou accessibles depuis moins de 3 mois). Au total, le consortium RRM vise a distribuer 4612 kits Abri, 14400 kits BNA et a lancer un pilote cash pour 850 bénéficiaires, pilote qui permettrait de renforcer la liberté de choix des bénéficiaires, et qui est aussi influencé par les préférences des bénéficiaires. Le projet soumis par ACTED a été élaboré en coordination directe avec le GT ABNA et avec UNICEF, qui fournit en in-kind une partie des kits BNA listé ci dessus. Les kits Abri sont couverts par UNICEF. La réponse proposée par ACTED et les ONG partenaires du RRM, complémentaire de celle d'UNICEF couvrira 3 512 ménages, soit environ 24 584 personnes pour le secteur des BNA.
La réponse du Consortium RRM commence par une veille humanitaire et une série d'évaluations multisectorielles (MSA) afin d'identifier les secteurs dans lesquels des intervention d'urgence sont nécessaires pour chaque site accueillant des déplacés. Un réseau de points focaux est mis en place par chaque partenaire dans ses zones prioritaires d'intervention pour relayer les alertes de déplacements de populations. Les alertes sont triangulées par les partenaires RRM qui s'appuient sur leur réseau d'informateurs clés, au premier rang desquelles se trouvent les autorités locales et nationales, dont le MAH. Une MSA (évaluation multisectorielle) ou une évaluation flash sont ensuite déclenchées dans les 24h suivant la confirmation de l'alerte, et les rapports d'évaluation sont transmis à la communauté humanitaire à travers OCHA et les GT/Clusters dans les 72h. Ce partage des informations permet d'assurer la bonne coordination avec les partenaires et leur positionnement afin couvrir des besoins complémentaires. Cela permet aussi, le cas échéant, de couvrir les besoins quand l'intervention n'est pas du ressort du RRM. Si les seuils de déclenchement sectoriels calculés à travers la MSA sont atteints, une intervention RRM est lancée (toutes les activités se font suivant le principe ""do no harm"" en respectant les SOP relatives au COVID pour préserver les bénéficiaires et les agents) et des consultations avec les communautés et leaders communautaires prennent place pour prioriser les besoins. Le ciblage des bénéficiaires se fait de manière participative pour réduire les risques de tensions communautaires, et sur des critères de vulnérabilité établis, en prenant en compte les ménages hôtes affectés. Le prépositionnement d'intrants et la disponibilité des équipes et des ressources financières garantissent une mobilisation dans les 7 jours suivant l'alerte. Dans les 30 jours qui suivent l'intervention, une évaluation post intervention mesure l'impact et la satisfaction des populations supportées (respect de la sécurité et dignité lors de l'intervention) ces évaluations participent à améliorer les interventions et assurer la redevabilité vis à vis des personnes affectées.

The IRC Child Protection (CP) program will provide life-saving immediate support to the extremely vulnerable and conflict-affected children in South Sudan who are exposed to abuse, exploitation, neglect, and violence to support them heal, recover and feel safe again when they do experience harm. The IRC CP program will reach 40,000 (17,903G, 15,106 B, 4,894 W, 2,097 M) people through an integrated response in the priority locations (severity three and four) of Panyijar, Koch, Aweil East, Aweil South and Pariang Counties of Unity State, Northern Bahr el Ghazal State and Ruweng Administrative Area respectively. The proposed CP responses are linked with the strategic objectives one and two of the HRP, the cluster objective one and two and the three priority areas of the CP sub-cluster for the HRP period in 2021. The comprehensive case management service will be provided to children with protection concerns, family tracing and reunification (FTR) services, and alternative care arrangements for unaccompanied and separated children (UASC) and cash assistance to meet the basic need of children. The mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) service will be provided for children and caregivers with psychological distress using a combination of approaches such as safe healing and learning space (SHLS) and schools for social and emotional learning, families make the difference curriculum for parenting skills of caregivers, supporting adolescents and their families in emergencies curriculum (SAFE) for life skills of adolescents, and IRC’s brighter futures model for malnourishment and children with protection concerns. Finally, the community-based child protection (CBCP) structures will establish/strengthen the lower structure of the community, community outreach on CP awareness and COVID-19 prevention messages and capacity building of the frontline staff and community volunteers.

Multi-sectoral Response in Kassala State Access to Humanitarian life-saving child protection and GBV response services in North Darfur, North / South Kordofan and White Nile states The project objective is to protect people from violence, neglect, and exploitation by providing access to life-saving child protection and GBV response services to targeted communities in White Nile, North Kordofan, and North Darfur. In order to accomplish this, Plan will provide high quality protection services and contribute to community stabilization and resilience. Protection services and capacity building activities will include: CP and GBV case management, distribution of dignity kits to vulnerable girls, multi-purpose cash transfer to vulnerable households and hosting UASC, and referrals mechanisms including to Family and Child Protection Units, training of social workers and partner staff on GBV, CP, and referral pathways, and psychosocial support to conflict affected children and youth. The provision of protection services must be paired with activities to increase knowledge of and access to those services. Therefore, Plan will also establish/strengthen and equip Community Based Child Protection Networks (CBCPNs), conduct community awareness session of CP, FGM, SEA and child marriage risks, and conduct sensitization on GBV prevention and response. Plan will foster communal stability and resilience by providing life skills training, parenting sessions, conducting community awareness sessions on peacebuilding and conflict transformation, and training duty bearers and community leaders on peacebuilding.  Additionally, Plan will establish child-friendly community feedback and response mechanisms so that all project beneficiaries are able to provide feedback and file complaints.

Mali - OCHA Office[OCT 10165];[UN-G-28335] Renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et de plaidoyer pour la protection humanitaire et l’assistance aux populations les plus vulnérables au Mali. 
La situation humanitaire demeure complexe et instable, principalement en raison des conflits armés et intercommunautaires dans les régions du Centre et du Nord. Le retard dans la mise en œuvre de l’Accord pour la paix et la réconciliation au Mali paraphé en juin 2015 et dans le processus de désarmement, démobilisation, réintégration (DDR) contribuent à la persistance de l’instabilité sécuritaire dans les régions de Kidal, Gao, Ménaka, Tombouctou, Ségou et Mopti ainsi qu’à l’aggravation des tensions sociales. A cause des activités des acteurs armés, l’accès humanitaire demeure difficile mais fluide dans certaines zones. 

La présence limitée de l’État et l’insécurité dans ces régions demeurent l’un des facteurs clés obligeant les civils à fuir leurs communautés. La grogne sociale qui a conduit au changement de régime en août 2021 prouve l’inaccessibilité des populations maliennes aux services sociaux de base et l’aggravation de leur vulnérabilité à laquelle s’ajoute le poids de la pandémie de COVID-19. 

Le nombre de Personnes Déplacées Internes (PDI) a atteint la barre des 311,191 en octobre 2020 en comparaison aux 199 385 enregistrés à la même période en 2019 et 80 302 en 2018.  Les risques et les besoins de protection des populations fuyant leurs communautés sous la pression de la violence armée ou des tensions intercommunautaires, sont élevés. De graves abus et attaques contre les personnes, les biens et les services (écoles, centres de santé) sont régulièrement signalées alors que l’accès aux services appropriés est compromis. Comme les déplacements internes sont de longue durée, les risques de protection et les violations des droits fondamentaux augmentent, en particulier pour les plus vulnérables (femmes, enfants, personnes âgées, personnes handicapées ou malades). De graves conséquences humanitaires ont donc été notées, telles que des taux élevés d’insécurité alimentaire et de malnutrition ainsi que le faible accès aux services sociaux de base.

Avec près de 4,7 millions de personnes affectées par l’insécurité alimentaire, dont 2,3 millions personnes avec des besoins d’assistance d’urgence, l’année 2020 a été, selon les résultats des exercices du Cadre Harmonisé (CH), l’année la plus fortement marquée par l’insécurité alimentaire depuis 2014. Les conséquences de cette détérioration resteront perceptibles sur le niveau de vie de populations en 2021. Les capacités de réponse existantes au Mali représentent environ 200 organisations humanitaires, acteurs du développement ainsi que des forces militaires (MINUSMA, Forces maliennes de défense et de sécurité, Barkhane, Mission européenne de formation, G5 Sahel). Le contexte susmentionné exigera une coordination efficace et la présence d’OCHA demeure très importante. OCHA maintiendra sa présence à Bamako, Mopti, Tombouctou et Gao ainsi que son antenne de Ségou tout en couvrant à distance les régions de Taoudénit, Ménaka, Kidal et les régions du sud.

Sept clusters actifs (Éducation, Sécurité alimentaire, Santé, Nutrition, Protection, Abris/BNA et WASH), des sous-clusters et des groupes de travail spécialisés (Accès, CMCoord, Redevabilité, Genre et Cash) sont en place au niveau national et local. Le Bureau d’OCHA au Mali continuera ainsi à jouer un rôle central dans la mobilisation, la coordination et le soutien des acteurs humanitaires dans les domaines de la coordination, la gestion de l’information, le financement humanitaire et le plaidoyer avec un accent accru dans le domaine de Civilo-Militaire et d’accès humanitaire afin de garantir la conservation et la consolidation de l’espace humanitaire. OCHA jouera un rôle essentiel dans la mobilisation adéquate des fonds en faveur des personnes dans le besoin, en plus de contribuer à dynamiser les efforts déployés par le Gouvernement et les acteurs du développement pour s’attaquer aux causes structurelles de la vulnérabilité.

Food assistance to newly displaced persons from Afghanistan, and highly food insecure host communities in Pakistan Food Security, Livelihood, and Agriculture Support to Communities Affected by Multiple Shocks Overall, around 5.82 million people are in need of food security and livelihood assistance across 39 districts in three provinces (Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) in Pakistan, of which around one million people (17% of the overall people in need) will be targeted through food/cash and agriculture-based livelihoods assistance packages in 2021. The PIN has been determined by undertaking a severity analysis of the population in each vulnerable districts experiencing multiple shocks recently such as (drought, monsoon rains/flooding, winterized emergency, locust infestation and  COVID) which has affected their food security security situation. Based on available information, two indicators have been used to estimate the people in need: IPC acute food insecurity  phase classification, and percentage of households who have inadequate resources to buy food. The severity analysis classified the proportion of the population in each district into minimal, stress, severe, extreme and catastrophic categories, and 39 districts with up to 4 natural hazards/ shocks and pre-existing vulnerabilities are prioritized across three provinces (Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) in Pakistan. Thus, the final PIN is estimated based on the proportion of the people in JIAF severity level 3 and above and considering the experience of recent multiple natural hazards/shocks and pre-existing vulnerabilities.
Of the 5.82 million people in need, most of them are in 12 districts in Sindh province (2.75 million), primarily because of their exposure to multiple shocks ( monsoon rains/floods 2020, locust 2019-2020, drought 2018-2019), and being in JIAF severity level three and above. Similarly, in Balochistan, around 1.9 million people are in need in 14 districts, because of experience of multiple emergencies such as drought 2018-19, monsoon rains/floods 2020, flash floods/snow 2020, and locust 2019-20). In KP  province, 1.17 million people are in need in 13 newly merged areas and they experienced conflict, displacement, instability in the past and recently locust infestation. The most-affected population groups are refugees, Temporary Displaced Persons (TDPs), and Returnees, people living in districts with a high risk of recurrent natural disasters, migrants (Afghan Citizen Card Holders, Undocumented Afghans), poor and food-insecure households, small farmers and livestock holders, daily wage-earners and small businesses, under-five malnourished children, malnourished pregnant and lactating women, persons with disabilities, and elderly population. The combined effects of multiple shocks and food insecurity vulnerabilities are adverse on the most vulnerable groups owing to their inability to meet their food consumption and other basic needs and over-reliance on negative coping strategies.

1. The cash transfer will be delivered through mobile money platform to minimize protection risks. 
2.	Protecting and restoring livelihoods related to food security and income sources. SC will provide livelihood inputs to the two main sources of livelihoods in Somalia i.e. crop and livestock agriculture. In the crop agriculture sector; seed inputs, tools, agriculture trainings, tillage hours, rehabilitating main agriculture related infrastructure e.g. canals will be done while in livestock agriculture, livestock treatment, provision of water and restocking where and when is possible. 
    
Save the Children adopted mobile money transfer back in 2014 and in Somalia context Mobile money is a feasible transfer mechanism for a number of reasons, including wide community acceptance and strong private entities (eg Hormuud, Golis and Somtel), efficient and timely and fast set up, and safe and secure means for HHs to receive and manage cash transfers. Across Somalia in general, and in proposed program areas specifically, mobile money is a mechanism widely accepted for payments with a broad array of vendors operating as mobile money agents. According to findings from SC post distribution monitoring, shops and cash-out agents are generally available within a 30 minute to 1-hour walk for most HHs, with the exception of pastoralists who might take longer pending their location. Beneficiaries are able to both cash-out their accounts, or but make direct purchases through mobile money without cashing out, depending on their preferences.
Mobile money enables a timely and efficient transfer for cash to target as it restricts the shop/vendor and food commodities to be transferred to beneficiaries. It also offers improved safety and security compared to in-kind or cash transfers, which can expose HHs and women, as primary beneficiaries, to greater risk. It also minimizes unnecessary beneficiary movement and profiling at the point of payment. 

SC will mobilize and sensitize mothers through IYCF sessions on how to utilize cash received to purchase quality and variety of foods for better nutrition outcomes for children, particularly in the first 1,000 days, as the primary cash recipients. SC will also carry out other bulk messaging on Fraud awareness creation, cash diversion and COVID-19 awareness messages to take advantage of the larger reach of cash transfer beneficiaries.

In addition, cash is most appropriate to address reduced purchasing power through improved food access, while also increasing demand in local markets with resultant stimulation of market growth and increase of trading opportunities.

Support to the Food Security and Nutrition Analysis Unit (FSNAU) for Somalia Saving Lives and Livelihoods in Rural Somalia  Somalia faced a growing number of threats to its food security in 2020, starting with the ongoing Desert Locust crisis, followed by COVID-19 first reported in March, severe flooding between April and September and poor rains forecast for the Deyr 2020 season. Based on latest projections, 2.1 million Somalis are in IPC Phases 3 and above through December 2020. Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of the La Nina developing, which tends to trigger dry conditions in Somalia. If the forecast below-average Deyr rains (Oct-Dec 2020) is followed by below-average or delayed 2021 Gu rains (Apr-Jun), this could lead to a rapid and substantial worsening of the humanitarian situation. 

Rural populations are at a high risk of further deteriorating food security, given the direct and indirect impacts of these threats on rural livelihoods, related assets, food production and income. FAO’s proposal responds both to the lifesaving and life-sustaining needs of rural populations in IPC Phases 3 and above, against a Population in Need (PiN) of 3.1 million people prioritized for Food Security Cluster (FSC) assistance under the 2021 HRP. FAO’s planned activities will directly support 103,850 households in IPC 3-4 under both FSC Strategic Objectives (SOs), while further delivering support to protect food security in Somalia at a wider scale through countrywide animal health campaigns, among other activities. 

Under SO1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 76,300 rural households, including IDPs, in the form of Cash+, UCT and CFW activities delivered through FAO’s e-Platform for Mobile Money and Livelihood Assistance. All cash-based programmes include trainings on good nutrition practices, covering infancy to old age.

Under SO2, to protect livelihoods, FAO will provide in-kind and technical support to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security threats across Somalia’s rural livelihood zones, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to 53,500 households targeted for Cash+ interventions under SO1 (while supporting an additional 7,550 households with agricultural inputs only). FAO’s planned Cash+ activities combine cash transfers with tailored livelihood support packages to assist rural families out of hunger sooner. Alongside cash transfers, the assistance packages will protect and restore the livelihoods of households in IPC Phases 3-4 by providing: (i) farmers with quality inputs to produce a nutritious variety of food crop (cereal, pulse and vegetable seeds, storage bags, fertilizer and irrigation/tractor services, where appropriate; (ii) pastoralists with nutrient-rich feed blocks and deworming to improve livestock productivity especially milk supply; and (iii) coastal communities with a variety of basic fishing gear and processing equipment to improve catch and consumption.  

Also under SO2, in anticipation of drought conditions in early 2021, FAO will also strategically position water bladder tanks and provide nutritive animal feed blocks to protect the small milking animals of up to 20,000 pastoral households impacted by scarce pasture from dry conditions and/or locust damage. Countrywide livestock vaccination and supportive treatment campaigns will further protect livestock assets belonging to at least 2.2 million men, women and children. Preparedness for animal health emergencies will be enhanced through strategic stocking of vaccines and related supplies (PPR), and training to local partners in Livestock Emergency Guidelines and Standards (LEGS), antimicrobial resistance, disease surveillance and reporting, among others.

Protection and assistance to people of concern in Niger Protection and assistance to Nigerian refugees in the Maradi region (Situation north-west Nigeria) L’intervention se concentre sur 3 composantes. La première vise le renforcement de l’environnement de protection. En vue de prévenir les risques de protection et d’apporter une réponse de qualité, les actions prioritaires visent : l’accès à l’asile ; le maintien du caractère civil de l’asile; la relocalisation des réfugiés; la collecte systématique des informations sur l’environnement sécuritaire, les incidents de protection et les mouvements des populations; la réponse de protection avec une attention particulière sur les volets GBV, Child Protection et PBS, ainsi que la réponse psycho-sociale ; le renforcement de la protection à base communautaire et la coordination des acteurs pour garantir la transversalité de la  protection. Du fait de l’éparpillement des réfugiés, ce dernier axe est fondamental pour le monitoring des incidents de protection, la prévention et la réponse. Les sensibilisations et le renforcement des capacités des autorités (administratives, civiles, judiciaires), des forces de défense et de sécurité, des acteurs humanitaires et des communautés sur les thématiques autour la protection internationale permettront d’assurer une compréhension commune du contexte et de faciliter la collaboration. 
La seconde composante vise à assurer une réponse d’urgence au niveau des villages d’accueil. La réponse multisectorielle d’urgence continuera de se réaliser en complémentarité avec les autres acteurs. Le focus du HCR se fera sur les volets abris d’urgence et biens non alimentaires ainsi que sur la réponse en santé au niveau des villages d’accueil (stock de médicaments, appui en ressources humaine). 
La troisième composante concerne le processus de relocalisation et les villages d’opportunités. L’objectif ici est d’une part de consolider les villages d’opportunités existants (Chadakori, Dan Dadji Makaw et Garin Kaka) notamment en termes de renforcement des services et infrastructures de base (EHA, éducation, santé) répondant aux normes nationales, d’accès aux opportunités économiques et a l’énergie domestique, ainsi que l’appui en abris durables. Des villages d’opportunités additionnels seront également aménagés pour accompagner le processus de relocalisation. Une réponse d’urgence sera fournie à chaque ménage relocalisé et aux ménages les plus vulnérables déjà relocalisés. La stratégie de réponse est conforme avec les orientations du Gouvernement du Niger en termes d’alternatives aux camps et avec le Pacte Mondial pour les Réfugiés. Le nexus humanitaire – développement est au cœur des réflexions qui accompagnent la mise en œuvre de la réponse.

Protection and assistance to people of concern in Niger Protection and assistance to Nigerian refugees in the Diffa region  (Situation Lake Chad) L’intervention en faveur des réfugiés présents à Diffa va se décliner autour de 3 objectifs suivants : 1- Maintenir et renforcer un environnement de protection favorable (protection monitoring et réponse de protection, dont child protection, SGBV, PBS, apatridie, enregistrement/documentation), améliorer les capacités d’intervention des autorités nationales pour délivrer des services de protection conformes aux standards internationaux et maintenir ouvert l’accès au territoire nigérien et aux procédures d’asile.2 – Assurer une assistance d’urgence et une capacité adéquate au niveau du camp de Sayam Forage et améliorer l’accès aux services sociaux de base. 3 - Renforcer la recherche des solutions durables et l’intégration socio-économique des réfugiés installés au Niger notamment via le programme urbanisation et la construction de logements pour les plus vulnérables. .
La stratégie de réponse est conforme avec les orientations du Gouvernement du Niger en termes d’alternatives aux camps et avec le Pacte Mondial pour les Réfugiés. Le nexus humanitaire – développement est au cœur des réflexions qui accompagnent la mise en œuvre de la réponse. Cela suppose le renforcement de la capacité d’absorption des services de base pour alléger les pressions, et l’accompagnement de la coexistence pacifique, en parallèle d’une réponse multisectorielle urgente. Alors qu’une assistance de type communautaire est développée pour l’accès aux services de base tels que l’eau ou la santé, c’est le niveau de vulnérabilité et non le statut qui régit l’assistance individuelle.

Assistance rapide en AME aux populations nouvellement affectées par les conflits dans les régions du Centre Nord, Est, Nord, Sahel, Centre-est, Boucle du Mouhoun La situation sécuritaire continue de se dégrader en 2020. Depuis janvier au 12 novembre 2020; 442 incidents ont été enregistrés causant le décès de 651 personnes, dont 31 enfants . La crise sécuritaire, couplée à l’impact de la COVID-19, ont créé une situation humanitaire sans précédent particulièrement dans 6 régions prioritaires du HRP/HNO . Ces crises viennent exacerber les vulnérabilités déjà existantes dans ces régions, causant le déplacement de 1,049,767 personnes , dont plus de 60% d’enfants. Les ménages affectés ont en majorité perdus leurs AME (Articles Ménagers Essentiels), leurs réserves alimentaires et autres moyens de subsistance affectant la survie des enfants et des familles. De nombreux ménages sont actuellement sans abris et ont intégré des familles d’accueil en attendant la remise en état de leurs abris. La majorité (80%) vivent dans des conditions de logement très précaires, avec l’incapacité financière et matérielle pour faire face aux multiples besoins notamment logement, nourriture les frais de scolarité et l’accès aux soins. La fragilité du contexte actuel exacerbe une vulnérabilité aigüe qu'une partie importante de la population locale vit déjà, et contribue à générer une pression accrue sur l'accès aux ressources d’une manière générale. Il apparait donc urgent d’apporter une réponse à cette situation. La présente action s’inscrit dans cette perspective et vise à « fournir une assistance humanitaire d'urgence en articles ménagers essentiels et en apport monétaire aux populations déplacées affectées par les conflits dans les régions du Centre Nord, Est, Nord, Sahel, Centre-est, Boucle du Mouhoun». Il s’agira de : (i) cibler environ 70,000 personnes dans le besoin en leur fournissant assistance rapide en kits AME de première nécessité alignes sur les standards du cluster et en apport monétaire multisectorielle inconditionnel. Le ciblage géographique selon le nombre des enfants déplacés sera combiné avec des enquêtes ménages de base. On utilisera les infrastructures communautaires pour allouer l'aide à des ménages ayant des enfants avec vulnérabilités aigues. (ii) de veiller à ce que cette assistance soit fournie dans un environnement de protection tout en respectant le principe de « Do no harm ». Les femmes seront les principaux récipiendaires des AME.

Provision of Integrated Multi-sectoral Assistance to Vulnerable Displaced Population in Somalia	WASH Provision of lifesaving assistance and sustainable solutions through safe Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) services, for people in crises and their host communities in multiple regions in Somalia. IOM WASH is proposing to contribute to the continuation and restoration of access to safe and equitable basic WASH services to overall 380,000 beneficiaries from vulnerable IDP and host-communities in multiple regions in Somalia. 

Specifically, the project will target 228,000 Nondisplaced people (children 107,160; men 41,040; women 36,480; elderly 9,120 and disabled 34,200) and 152,000 displaced populations (children 71,440; men 27,360; women 24,320; elderly 6,080 and disabled 22,800). 

IOM will rehabilitate 50 strategic water sources for multi-use that will provide continued, equitable, safe, sufficient and sustainable water to regions, targeted by the cluster, prone to natural disasters. 

IOM further proposes to construct 3,000 new emergency sanitation facilities (following cluster specifications) targeting populations without access to basic sanitation and hygiene.

The project will also strengthen the capacity of the Federal Government of Somalia and Federal Members States, community leaders and water committees/technicians for better coordination with government authorities and communities and sustainability of the constructed/ rehabilitated WASH infrastructures. In addition, the project will nurture community participation in good hygiene practices through training and community sensitization campaigns.  All trainings, awareness raising and capacity building activities will follow national guidelines on COVID-19 preventive measures, e.g. on physical distancing, to avoid mass gatherings and minimize risks of exposure.

The project is aligned with protection mainstreaming to ensure safety and dignity of affected populations without causing harm. Affected populations and all relevant stakeholders including men, women, boys, girls, elderly and people with disability will be involved in decision making throughout the project activities/cycle. 

Furthermore, the project will be a part of an IOM integrated emergency response program and resilience building, where possible, efforts will be made to integrate IOM health, nutrition, shelter, CCCM and protection activities.

Provision of Integrated Multi-sectoral Assistance to Vulnerable Displaced Population in Somalia	SNFI Provision of Life-Saving Shelter and Life Sustaining NFI to Vulnerable Populations in Somalia Due to the ongoing humanitarian crisis, Shelter and Non-Food Items (SNFI) needs remain consistently high, with an estimated 3.1 million Somalis with SNFI needs according to the Humanitarian Needs Overview 2021, especially in Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) sites where many households (HHs) live in makeshift shelters. Oftentimes, these makeshift shelters do not provide adequate privacy and protection against weather elements, whilst a lack of tenure security, random evictions and vulnerability to fires further exacerbate the shelter needs of IDPs. It is therefore estimated that around one-third of the Somali population lack essential NFIs. 

Therefore, SNFI needs are the subject of much collaborative efforts; Collective Outcome 2 of the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) aims ‘to reduce the risks and vulnerabilities, and build resilience of displaced and host communities to reach durable solutions’, whilst Specific Objective 2.2 aims to scale-up and provide CCCM, WASH, education, health, nutrition, shelter and NFI services for 1.6 million people in established IDP sites across 68 districts by the end of 2021.

For the 2021 HRP, 75,000 individuals (12,500 households with an average of 6 individuals per household) will receive NFI support through a mixed-methods strategy of in-kind contingency stocks provision to be undertaken with contingency stock partners and direct implementation of Cash-Based Intervention (CBI) for NFI needs. A further 75,000 individuals will receive shelter support through emergency shelter, in-kind shelter kits, and CBI for shelter needs. Finally, 15,000 individuals will receive infrastructure support, both in-kind and through CBI. The transfer mechanism for CBI   will be evidence-based and linked to market assessment and needs analysis. The breakdown of the planned intervention is as follows: (1) the provision of contingency stock with in-kind NFI and shelter kits for 10,000 households (NFI: 7,500, Shelter: 2,500), available for distribution nationwide by shelter cluster partners where need arises; (2) emergency/transitional shelter (Emergency: 7,500; Transitional: 2,500) and NFI (5,000) support to newly displaced IDPs in the Gedo and Bay region targeting 15,000 households; (3) infrastructure support to 2,500 households in Gedo and Bay region.

Child Protection Children (girls and boys) and their families affected by disaster are protected against violence, abuse, exploitation, discrimination and other violations of their rights. Child protection issues are exacerbated during disaster, requiring immediate protection services to bring normalcy back in the lives of girls, boys and women. Measures to prevent abuse and violence and respond to cases of survivors of violence and exploitation need to be strengthened by providing safe access to protective services. Likewise, psychosocial distress experienced by people at the onset of any emergency requires professional care and support. Hence, the project provides mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) and coordination as a core area of response. An increase of CP risks is being observed in the current COVID-19 pandemic as well. Some of these may include: Physical and emotional maltreatment, Gender-based violence (GBV), mental health and psychosocial distress, child labour, unaccompanied and separated children and social exclusion. Following are some of the interventions:

1.	Establishment of protective spaces to cater the needs of vulnerable girls, boys and women including disable. The protective spaces will be run by trained facilitators and provided with recreational and learning materials. It will offer opportunities for girls and boys to build resilience and recover from their experiences, provide a daily routine and a sense of normalcy.
2.	Provision of Psychosocial Support (PSS) is primarily aimed at those individuals or group of people who require care and support including those in isolation or quarantine in case of the current COVID-19 situation. Digital platforms will be used for delivering PSS while there are movement restrictions in place. The PSS will be provided at three levels tailored to the needs of target population:
•	Within facilities receiving suspected/infected people for care and support including isolation and quarantine facilities.
•	Community based support in areas identified with suspected/infected people or receiving people exiting isolation/quarantine facilities and going through the social reintegration phase. Families, relatives and caregivers of such people will also be able to avail such services and support.
•	Referral pathways in collaboration of case management for accessing social protection services/packages.
3.	People demonstrating exacerbated distress and signs of mental health concerns or adverse reactions, would be referred to specialized mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS). Digital platforms will be used for delivery of MHPSS while movement restrictions are in place. 
4.	Provide CP monitoring and outreach social mobilization through dedicated and trained CP monitors and facilitators in coordination with community-based CP structures and CP Working Groups and Govt. counterparts;
5.	Establish and strengthen coordination amongst key stakeholders and community-based CP structures for the identification of vulnerable girls, boys and women, including missing, unaccompanied, separated and disabled children, and promote their access to protection, social and psychosocial services through an effective and efficient case management and referral system;
6.	Capacity building of relevant service providers, Govt. officials including DMAs, CSOs, rights-holders and duty-bearers in Child Protection in Emergency (CPiE), psychosocial support and strengthening advocacy and support for girls, boys and women affected by disaster to achieve enhanced protection for them;
7.	Dissemination of critical information for prevention of violence against children (VAC) using different communication channels. In the current context, service provision will prioritize prevention of stigma, labelling and discrimination of people who are perceived to be infected or affected by COVID-19. The promotion of correct information and addressing emerging myths and rumors including positive understanding and behaviours about ‘social distancing’ should therefore include actions that support people to adopt and maintain healthy and rationale lifestyles.

services Health-related vulnerabilities of Rohingya and Host Communities are reduced through increased quality access to comprehensive health services The aims of IOMs’ health interventions aim to respond to the lifesaving needs and improve the resilience of affected populations, with special attention to gender and age considerations, and vulnerable groups. In the camps,34% Rohingya refugee populations, have reported going into debt to pay for health expenses, and 27% seeking lower-quality care or medication, due to a lack of money (Joint Multi-Sector Needs Assessment J-MSNA 2020). This demonstrates some challenges in the already strained health service system in Cox’s Bazar. To address this, this intervention aims to contribute  to  i) increased safe, dignified and meaningful access and utilization of quality comprehensive healthcare services, focusing on sexual, reproductive, maternal, neonatal, child and adolescent health; mental health and psychosocial support; and non-communicable diseases (NCD); ii) improved health seeking behavior, encouragement of  healthy living and promotion of the  utilization of essential service package and community engagement, with special attention to vulnerable groups iii) measures to prepare and (timely) respond  to health emergencies, during disaster (including monsoon and cyclone) and outbreaks of communicable disease (e.g.  COVID-19 and AWD). IOM also aims to contribute to the improvement of quality of services through performance monitoring, evaluation, coordination and capacity building.

Humanitarian response in Pakistan- Multisector (P010171001) Food Security, Livelihood, and Agriculture Support to Communities Affected by Multiple Shocks Overall, around 5.82 million people are in need of food security and livelihood assistance across 39 districts in three provinces (Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) in Pakistan, of which around one million people (17% of the overall people in need) will be targeted through food/cash and agriculture-based livelihoods assistance packages in 2021. The PIN has been determined by undertaking a severity analysis of the population in each vulnerable districts experiencing multiple shocks recently such as (drought, monsoon rains/flooding, winterized emergency, locust infestation and  COVID) which has affected their food security security situation. Based on available information, two indicators have been used to estimate the people in need: IPC acute food insecurity  phase classification, and percentage of households who have inadequate resources to buy food. The severity analysis classified the proportion of the population in each district into minimal, stress, severe, extreme and catastrophic categories, and 39 districts with up to 4 natural hazards/ shocks and pre-existing vulnerabilities are prioritized across three provinces (Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) in Pakistan. Thus, the final PIN is estimated based on the proportion of the people in JIAF severity level 3 and above and considering the experience of recent multiple natural hazards/shocks and pre-existing vulnerabilities.
Of the 5.82 million people in need, most of them are in 12 districts in Sindh province (2.75 million), primarily because of their exposure to multiple shocks ( monsoon rains/floods 2020, locust 2019-2020, drought 2018-2019), and being in JIAF severity level three and above. Similarly, in Balochistan, around 1.9 million people are in need in 14 districts, because of experience of multiple emergencies such as drought 2018-19, monsoon rains/floods 2020, flash floods/snow 2020, and locust 2019-20). In KP  province, 1.17 million people are in need in 13 newly merged areas and they experienced conflict, displacement, instability in the past and recently locust infestation. The most-affected population groups are refugees, Temporary Displaced Persons (TDPs), and Returnees, people living in districts with a high risk of recurrent natural disasters, migrants (Afghan Citizen Card Holders, Undocumented Afghans), poor and food-insecure households, small farmers and livestock holders, daily wage-earners and small businesses, under-five malnourished children, malnourished pregnant and lactating women, persons with disabilities, and elderly population. The combined effects of multiple shocks and food insecurity vulnerabilities are adverse on the most vulnerable groups owing to their inability to meet their food consumption and other basic needs and over-reliance on negative coping strategies.

Back to school campaign Back to school Campaign in Flood Affected Areas of Sindh The Back to School Campaign through provision of food aims to encourage return and resumption to education in areas affected by natural disasters, with the aim of reducing barriers in access to  primary school  for boys and girls while supporting their families to meet their basic food needs at home. Targeted beneficiaries  will receive fortified wheat flour of 25 kg (bimonthly) as take-home ration, conditional upon enrolment and regular attendance at schools or temporary learning centers notified by the Government. The project will be implemented in collaboration with Education and Literacy Department, Government of Sindh and target 71,480 children (35,740 boys & 35,740 girls) enrolled in primary boys’ and girls’ schools with 3,574 MT of Wheat Flour in affected areas of districts Badin and Sajawal, Sindh. The project is in alignment with the objectives of Sindh Education Sector Plan and CM’s forthcoming Bokh Mitao Programme and will implemented in areas where WFP’s other interventions (nutrition, food assistance, DRR and social protection) are ongoing. 
 
Justification:
 According to UNDP’s latest Report on Multi-dimensional Poverty in Pakistan the incidence and severity of multi-dimensional poverty is high in the southern part of the province. For instance, approximately 84% of peoples live in multi-dimensional poverty in Badin while it is 68% for Sajawal district. Similarly, according to RNA 2020, 72% of assessed population in Badin and 63% in Sajawal reported inability to buy food and in the case of any emergency the average food stock for their own consumption may last for 5 days only. These districts also host many out of schoolboys and girls of age 5-16 years, and school completion rates are drastically low. Displacement, school damages and discontinuity of educational activities resulting from floods and other disasters further deteriorates education situation in the affected areas.

Disasters’ negative impact on lives, livelihoods, livestock, agriculture, infrastructure, access to social and life-saving services and income generation opportunities is significantly high on the children, women, disabled and elderly peoples. Among others, the incidences of less availability of food for children and women at home, engagement in labor and income generation activities, children dropout from school and early marriages of girls are common in most of the cases. 

WFP’s experience of emergency response in Pakistan suggests that school feeding programmes can play an instrumental role in bringing children back to school while reducing their chances of drop out, engagement in child labor or early marriages. Provision of take-home rations- a means to transfer resources to vulnerable households and subsidize families’ food basket, motivate families to send and retain their children in schools and hence, contribute to increase enrolment, retention and attendance at schools. 

Effectiveness of school feeding is evident from flood response in 2011-12. WFP field monitoring reports of school feeding under indicated that almost 97 percent of students were retained in schools in Sindh. Similarly, analysis of education indicators in WFP assisted vs non-assisted schools in Erstwhile FATA showed that enrolment rates increased at 15% in WFP assisted schools as compared to 3% in non-assisted schools. Moreover, the retention rate in WFP-assisted primary schools in 2016-2017 was as high as 80.1 %, against WFP’s target of 70 % (compared to 24% in all primary schools in erstwhile FATA).

ACT 1 RELIEF Food & Cash-based Assistance for Vulnerable Populations in Somalia for 2021 Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas.  As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation.  The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of a La Niña that is currently developing (75 percent chance through Feb 2021). Potential drought conditions will likely develop as a result of below average 2020 Deyr (Oct-Dec), a harsh 2021 dry Jilaal (Jan-Mar) season and a possible delay and/or poor performance of the 2021 Gu (Apr-Jun). 

Continued emergency relief alongside a further scale up of support to increase resilience is required in order to avert the hardship situation. WFP is therefore seeking resources in 2021 to sustain the on-going efforts and enable households meet immediate food needs and help build resilience against shocks. WFP is planning to implement unconditional and conditional transfers to improve access to food under integrated multi sectoral assistance to meet needs of vulnerable girls and women, pregnant and lactating women, boys and men and leverage resources with other partners to meet the level of humanitarian assistance required. WFP will continue to participate in cluster, joint planning, assessments and regular meetings with other humanitarian actors in Somalia. WFP employs gender sensitive beneficiary targeting in all its projects and prioritizes female and single headed households. Community consultations are carried out with men and women to ensure that their voices are heard. Accountability to affected populations ensured through information sharing, surveys and beneficiary feedback mechanisms. Beneficiaries are targeted and registered through biometric SCOPE system that provides real time data.

Somalia HRP Shelter and NFIs Assistance to Crisis affected population in Somalia The project will target affected population groups (newly displaced populations, IDPs living in a protracted situation, refugee returnees and affected host communities) with shelter and NFI interventions. The interventions include provision of NFI kit, emergency shelter and transitional shelter. 

According to JMCNA 2020, Shelter is the first priority need of more than half of the population. 3.15 million people are in need of shelter and NFI assistance mainly due to inadequate shelter conditions, overcrowding, economic hardship and lack of security of tenure. Those in need of shelter and NFI assistance include IDPs, poor host communities, refugees and asylum seekers and refugee returnees.  Factors that have been considered for calculating the severity and people in need include shelter conditions, type of shelter, overcrowding, availability of NFIs at household level and security of tenure.

UNHCR plans to distribute NFI kits to 90,000 households (HH) in kind/cash, provision of emergency shelters to 25,000 HH and transitional shelters to 500 HH. The project will target 540,000 individuals with NFI kits, 150,000 individuals with emergency shelters and 3,000 individuals with transitional shelters. NFI, emergency shelters and transitional shelters assistance will be provided in cash or in kind and the response modality will depend on the availability of items in the local market, user preference and associated protection risks.

UNHCR will carry out Post Distribution Monitoring and will establish Complaints, Response and Feedback Mechanism for each project. The Post Distribution Monitoring (PDM) exercise will be conducted 4-6 weeks after NFIs and ESKs distribution to analyze the impact of the project, the beneficiaries’ level of satisfaction and establish the lessons learnt for future programming

UNHCR will target vulnerable HH including women headed households, child headed households, households with persons with disabilities and households with the elderly. 

UNHCR will undertake infrastructure support targeting 8,250 vulnerable households (49,500 individuals). Site decongestion through expanding the site using available adjacent land and through basic site planning will be a priority and will be implemented where feasible under infrastructure support. Most of the IDPs live in the sites that are overcrowded and are not planned, leading to the increased risk of fire outbreak, spread of diseases including COVID 19, GBV related incidences and flooding due to the absence of or poor drainage system. 

UNHCR will target a total of 543,000 individuals of the 2.5 million individuals targeted by the Shelter Cluster with assistance. Of the targeted individuals, 83,803 women, 81,616 men, 170,927 girls, 184,794 boys, 21,860 elderly and 81,450 disabled individuals. The project targets 108,600 vulnerable individuals from the host community and 434,400 vulnerable IDPs. The targeting will occur based on UNHCR and Shelter Cluster assessments for those most in need and highly vulnerable. The project will target Bari, Banadir, Bay, Lower Juba, Gedo, Mudug, Hiraan, Nugaal, Middle Shabelle, Lower Shabelle and Woqooyi Galbeed regions. 

The activities will be implemented through partners. UNHCR will monitor the activities through the Implementing Partners. Settlement leaders and local authorities will participate in different phases of the interventions. Monthly project tracking will be carried out and 4W matrix inputs shared on monthly basis with Somalia National Shelter Cluster.

To provide Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) to support COVID-19 Response for Refugees and Host Communities in Kenya, Tanzania and South Sudan Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2021, there are more than 314,000 refugees from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, as well as the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, including from Sudan, Democratic Republic of Congo and Central African Republic.

At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for long-term stability, some 357,500 South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since November 2017, 122,000 of those in 2020 alone. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan at this stage, the increase in numbers warrants a scaling-up of support following an area-based approach, including strengthening linkages with development actors, to help returnees and the communities they settle in live in safety and dignity, with greater security and services.

Refugees largely reside in conﬂict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction of basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.

Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will beneﬁt from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Speciﬁc protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identiﬁed at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with speciﬁc protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as veriﬁcation exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the eﬃciency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to beneﬁt from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.
