Humanitarian Assistance for Middle East, African and European Countries Internally Displaced Population in South Sudan supported through provision of protection and targeted assistance to promote resilience, protection advocacy and achievement of solutions. The project aims to strengthen community and rights-based protection response for IDPs, IDP returnees and vulnerable persons within their host communities. The project will focus on providing physical and legal protection through advocacy, timely protection monitoring, life-saving protection response based on identified needs and solutions. The project will address Housing, Land and Property (HLP) rights issues through the provision of legal assistance, facilitate issuance of property and identity documents, and work with mediation mechanisms to support HLP related dispute resolution. Community-based networks will be utilized as part of the protection response to foster community buy in and ownership of protection. The project will use evidence-based planning to expand outreach and develop the capacity of displaced communities to cope, recover, contribute to and ultimately achieve solutions. Out of 1.6 million IDPs, 475,000 IDPs and IDP returnees will be supported with protection interventions and assistance in seven (7) states and an administrative areas. Recognising the protection concerns linked to food insecurity, the Agency activities also include a scaling-up of activities in South Sudan’s highly food insecure and prioritised locations, i.e. Pibor County, Akobo, Aweil South, Tonj East, Tonj North, Tonj South. There will be continuous advocacy and support in the area of law and policy with relevant government bodies such as the   Ministries of Justice Home Affairs, Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management, and the Relief and Rehabilitation Commission (RRC) to ensure the centrality of protection, enact the “Protection and Assistance to Internally Displaced Persons Act 2018” (IDP) Bill, National Framework on Returns, and various HLP initiatives. The relevant line ministries will also receive capacity building and technical assistance. Building on UNHCR’s existing operational presence in Bentiu Bor, Juba, Malakal, Wau, Yambio, Yei, the Agency will continue to advance on the 2020 geographic expansion of IDP activities by leveraging both static and mobile presence through 15 partners to Central Equatoria, Unity, Upper Nile, Joinglei, Western Bahr El Ghazal, Northern Bahr El Ghazal, Lakes, Western Equatoira, Eastern Equatoris and Warrap. Response and monitoring will cover 19 identified priority counties and Pibor Administrative Area, including remote or hard to-reach areas, in full support to the Protection Cluster Strategy for mobile assessments and response. Partners comprise of both national and international organizations, with selection undertaken on the basis of their pre-existing presence, access to populations of concern and capacity to carry out static and remote protection monitoring and response. While not all proposed activity locations fall under the severity 3, 4 or 5 in terms of food insecurity, recognizing the fluidly and unpredictable nature of sub-national violence in South Sudan, UNHCR’s protection by presence approach requires presence in areas affected by conflict as well as areas of potential return in light of increased momentum in terms of solutions 
Resources and advocacy will focus primarily on protection response and solutions, either durable or transitional (where the former is not yet possible), including assessments on needs, risks, and intentions and feasibility of durable solutions, while also strengthening community-based structures, supporting HLP initiatives, promotion of livelihoods and peaceful coexistence. Improving coordination and quality of assessments and monitoring will be a key component. A mobile tool was introduced in late 2019 that has enhanced data collection and triangulation of information through timely collection and analysis capabilities, which will further improve information products, leading to a more fitting risk-mitigation approach, reduced response time; while underpinning protection mainstreaming across other operational interventions, including of other Clusters.

Communities, particularly those most dramatically affected – and under additional stress because of IDPs returns and other displacements - need assistance in reinforcing their resilience to address these shocks as well as the consequences of the protracted crisis, and to address their needs on seriously depleted infrastructures and service capacities.
The essence of the Programme is about providing Syrian communities with – still limited - support to regain control over their basic needs (livelihoods, access to essential services) and reduce their dependency on humanitarian assistance. Prioritization of locations, is the outcome of a context analysis and needs assessment conducted on more than 5,000 Syrian communities, based on the following three criteria:
1) Hard to Reach Areas
2) Areas of major IDPs presence and IDPs returns
3) Highest scoring in the Severity Scale


The integrated response consists of the following components: strengthening of social services-related capacities (access and coverage), livelihoods creation and rural recovery, PWDs support, social cohesion/community safety, reducing gender inequality and youth marginality, women empowerment, tensions reduction and rehabilitation of basic infrastructure and public services.
The program is built in a modular manner both in terms of geographical and sectoral/thematic interventions and foresees the allotment of average 1 Million US$ per community. Hence, donors willing to support this approach will be able to pre-select certain location(s) and/or area(s) of intervention of their preference, within the 200 prioritized communities.
The programme relates directly to the sector objectives:
1. Living conditions
2. Livelihoods
3. Access to social services
4. Access to productive and market infrastructure
5. Social protection
6. Strengthening of local public services delivery capacity
7. Reinforcing opportunities and capacities for civic engagement

Cash Assistance in Re-Emerging Markets in Syria – phase 2 (CARMA2) Integrated Multi-AoR protection services for high at risk groups in Jebel Saman, Aleppo The intervention is part of a project aiming at securing the basic needs and providing integrated community-based protection activities in Karm Jazmati, Seken Shebebi, Karm al Tarrab, and Dahret Awwad. The project is held by Caritas Germany (CS), back-funded by the German Federal Foreign Ministry (GFO) and implemented from 01.04.2019 -31.12.2022 by Caritas Syria (CS). It was initially designed based on the results of a needs assessment conducted in Karm Jazmati in January 2019, and has been, upon extension and top-up in 2021, adjusted to changing needs as per M/E results. In course of the project phase two, which started on 01.04.2021, the project locations have shifted: While Jazmati is still the main project location where the Community Center is based, Jabal Badro has been taken out of the intervention since there have been other actors providing basic assistance and CS has, under another project, started implementing Livelihood and Early Recovery activities. Coordination meetings with other (I)NGOs as well as the sub-sectors FSL, and protection, three new neighborhoods bordering Jazmati, have been included in the project. In direct and continuous contact with the FSL and protection sector, CS has started to implement BA and protection activities in the new areas as of April 2021 and is considered the main actor for these sectors in Jazmati, Seken Shebebi, Karm al Tarrab, and Dahret Awwad.
Following a participatory approach, the needs have been regularly assessed, i.e., via PDMs applying a proportional piling method, and FDGs. Furthermore, a robust FCM has contributed to ensure the engagement and thus self-identification of the needs in the community. Hence, throughout the project lifetime, the engagement of all community members has been promoted, establishing a two-way communication with the community. This has ensured a timely incorporation of community feedback. 
The regular coordination with the Aleppo-based sub-sectors Protection, CP, GBV, and FSL as well as the application of a protection scoring system,CS ensures the inclusion of high at-risk groups in protection activities while avoiding duplication of efforts. The community center in Jazmati has been well received by the residents of Jazmati since its opening in 2019 and continues to be the central point for the provision of integrated community-based protection services, to women, adolescent girls, children and elderly. 
The center follows an open-door policy, ensuring the active engagement of the community, allowing real-time evaluations and timely adjustments of activities as per beneficiaries’ feedback.  In response to the feedback collected from beneficiaries, i.e. via PDMs, satisfaction surveys, and FGDs, and following the strategy of the protection sector, the activities are adjusted in 2021-22. Following an inclusive approach, non-specialized PSS, and awareness sessions for women, children, elderly, and men are planned. Contributing to the reduction of GBV risks, literacy courses for women will be provided. Applying interactive learning approaches, informal education activities (Maths, Arabic, and English) for school-aged children will contribute to reducing child protection risk factors. Further, capacity strengthening activities for the CS team will be offered to further increase the responding capacity of CS.

Projet de protection des personnes à Besoins spécifiques et personnes vivant avec le handicap dans la Région de Diffa  Dans le contexte humanitaire de Diffa, les PBS sont soumises à plusieurs barrières dans leur accès aux services sociaux de base adaptés à leurs besoins spécifiques.
Il s’agit des barrières physiques pour les personnes handicapées et les personnes âgées (inaccessibilité des infrastructures publiques comme les points d’eau, les toilettes, les abris), des barrières socio-culturelles liées à la stigmatisation des personnes vivant avec handicap souvent par la communauté (violences basées sur le handicap), absence des aides techniques (aide à la mobilité, à la vue, à l’audition, abris adaptés,), absence de services spécialisés répondant à leurs besoins spécifiques.
En réponse à cette problématique, la première phase du projet ACTIPH mise en œuvre par HI en 2019 avec l’appui du HCR, a permis de réaliser plusieurs actions en faveur de la levée des barrières physique et socio-économique vers l’accès plein et équitable des groupes de personnes handicapées aux services sociaux de base à travers les réponses humanitaires et leur inclusion dans la communauté. 
En dépit de ces actions développées en 2019, le contexte humanitaire de Diffa reste encore difficile, dans les prévisions et analyse de la réponse humanitaire, les intentions ou possibilité de retour pour les déplacés reste très faibles voir marginale en raison du contexte sécuritaire. L 'appui du HR en 2020 avec le projet ""Protection des Personnes à Besoins Spécifiques et personnes vivant avec handicap dans la Région de Diffa "" a permis d'avoir les résultats en termes de :  Formation des cadres techniques étatiques d’infrastructures, des comités de protection, de personnes sensibilisées, de rencontre de plaidoyer, d’aménagement d’accessibilité physique des personnes à besoin spécifiques, de formation de groupement de PBS en AGR et de distribution de cash. Les activités d’autonomisation telle que les AGR et le cash transfert a eu des effets sur les moyens de production et les sources de revenus des PBS plus précisément des personnes handicapées. 
Objectif du Projet : Contribuer à une meilleure prise en charge des personnes à besoins spécifiques, dont les personnes handicapées (femmes et enfants handicapés en particulier), en favorisant leur inclusion et leur autonomie.

Internal flexible funding from the Humanitarian Fund Nutrition Emergency nutrition response The humanitarian situation in Zimbabwe has been further worsened by the current COVID19 pandemic. Approximately, 56.2% or around 5.5 million rural people are likely to be food insecure at the peak of the hunger season from January to March 2021.  The prospect of significant deterioration in the health and nutritional status of the communities cannot be ruled out unless support to these communities is strengthened and maintained.

In response to this humanitarian situation, Save the Children proposes to implement lifesaving nutrition interventions in 5 Districts across the 5 provinces thus Binga, Beitbridge, Kariba, Mbire, and Matabo districts. The project will target the most vulnerable population thus the children under the age of five, pregnant and lactating women. The key area of focus includes strengthening the capacity of health workers and community volunteers (VHWs) to provide timely community based nutrition response. These includes supporting caregivers to screen their children and improve the referral, reporting and treatment of children with acute malnutrition. The project will also support the formulation and proper implementation of community based IYCF activities that includes counselling of caregivers of children 6-23 on IYCF by VHW
The project aims to save the lives of under-five children with acute malnutrition through improved multi-sectoral coordination and integrated emergency response in 5 drought affected districts of Zimbabwe. This will be realized through strengthening mass screening for early case identification of moderate and severe acute malnutrition, and behaviour change communication for improved infant feeding and child caring practices. In addition, this nutrition emergency response will build capacity of health workers and community volunteers on life saving nutrition interventions like IMAM and cIYCF as well as strengthening counselling of caregivers of children 6-23 on IYCF. The project will also strengthen linkages with health, HIV care and treatment, WASH and Social protection.

Préparation et réponse humanitaire multi-secteurs aux vulnérabilités aigues des populations affectées par les conflits, catastrophes naturelles et épidémies au Niger (Rapid Response Mechanism - RRM)
---- Food Security Améliorer la sécurité alimentaire et restaurer les moyens de subsistance agro-pastoraux des populations vulnérables hôtes et déplacées dans les régions de Tahoua et Diffa touchées par les crises sécuritaire et climatique L’objectif général du projet est d’améliorer la sécurité alimentaire et de renforcer les moyens d’existence et la résilience des populations déplacées et hôtes, affectées par les crises sécuritaires dans les régions de Tahoua et de Diffa, en fournissant une assistance humanitaire et un support pour le renforcement des moyens d’existence aux communautés les plus touchées par les crises sécuritaires, les déficits pluviométriques et les faibles productions agricoles et pastorales en 2021. 
L’Action répondra aux besoins alimentaires immédiats des ménages vulnérables pendant les périodes critiques (pré soudure et soudure pastorale et agricole) et soutiendra les principaux moyens d’existence des ménages les plus vulnérables. Elle ciblera les localités agro-pastorales et pastorales des départements de Diffa, Nguigmi, dans la région de Diffa, et le département de Tilia, région de Tahoua, les plus affectées par les crises sécuritaires (nombre de déplacés, taux d’insécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle) et climatiques (déficit agricoles et pastoraux). Les activités bénéficieront directement à 5 600 ménages (39 200 personnes) déplacés, hôtes, identifiés comme les plus vulnérables selon une approche de ciblage participative (Household Economy Approach) impliquant les communautés, les services techniques, les autorités locales, les partenaires locaux, et les organisations paysannes.

Dans le cadre de cette intervention, le premier axe d'intervention sera la réponse aux besoins urgents de sécurité alimentaire des ménages les plus vulnérables des départements de Diffa, Nguigmi (Diffa) et Tillia (Tahoua) par une assistance alimentaire sous forme de Cash for Work. Les transferts d'argent liquide permettront aux bénéficiaires d'avoir accès à une nourriture de qualité et ainsi de faire face à l'insécurité alimentaire aiguë. En effet, selon tous les acteurs rencontrés (services techniques, autorités locales, partenaires locaux et communautés) lors de l'évaluation interne des interventions FSLH de Diffa réalisée par ACF, le changement le plus significatif apporté par les activités CFW a été l'amélioration de la situation alimentaire des ménages grâce à l'augmentation du nombre de repas (jusqu'à 3 repas par jour), et l'augmentation de la durée des stocks alimentaires des ménages. Au niveau de Tillia, l'évaluation des besoins menée par ACF a montré que le besoin d'assistance alimentaire était l'un des besoins prioritaires cités par les communautés, en particulier parmi les personnes déplacées.
Le deuxième domaine d'intervention consistera à protéger et à renforcer les moyens de subsistance des populations les plus touchées dans les zones ciblées.  Les activités prévues sont basées sur les principaux moyens de subsistance des populations. L'agriculture (32,5% des ménages bénéficiaires), le petit commerce (31,7%) et l'élevage (19,9%) constituent les trois (3) principales activités des bénéficiaires (source : ACF, précédents projets).  Au niveau de Tillia, l'activité principale reste l'élevage et la zone a une vocation pastorale selon la classification du gouvernement du Niger. Ainsi, les activités s'articuleront autour de la restauration et du renforcement du patrimoine pastoral des communautés du département. Afin de renforcer les activités agricoles des bénéficiaires à Diffa, un soutien sera apporté à la culture maraîchère et à l'agriculture pluviale.

Support to the Food Security and Nutrition Analysis Unit (FSNAU) for Somalia Saving Lives and Livelihoods in Rural Somalia  Somalia faced a growing number of threats to its food security in 2020, starting with the ongoing Desert Locust crisis, followed by COVID-19 first reported in March, severe flooding between April and September and poor rains forecast for the Deyr 2020 season. Based on latest projections, 2.1 million Somalis are in IPC Phases 3 and above through December 2020. Humanitarian needs could increase further in 2021 due to the influence of the La Nina developing, which tends to trigger dry conditions in Somalia. If the forecast below-average Deyr rains (Oct-Dec 2020) is followed by below-average or delayed 2021 Gu rains (Apr-Jun), this could lead to a rapid and substantial worsening of the humanitarian situation. 

Rural populations are at a high risk of further deteriorating food security, given the direct and indirect impacts of these threats on rural livelihoods, related assets, food production and income. FAO’s proposal responds both to the lifesaving and life-sustaining needs of rural populations in IPC Phases 3 and above, against a Population in Need (PiN) of 3.1 million people prioritized for Food Security Cluster (FSC) assistance under the 2021 HRP. FAO’s planned activities will directly support 103,850 households in IPC 3-4 under both FSC Strategic Objectives (SOs), while further delivering support to protect food security in Somalia at a wider scale through countrywide animal health campaigns, among other activities. 

Under SO1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 76,300 rural households, including IDPs, in the form of Cash+, UCT and CFW activities delivered through FAO’s e-Platform for Mobile Money and Livelihood Assistance. All cash-based programmes include trainings on good nutrition practices, covering infancy to old age.

Under SO2, to protect livelihoods, FAO will provide in-kind and technical support to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security threats across Somalia’s rural livelihood zones, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to 53,500 households targeted for Cash+ interventions under SO1 (while supporting an additional 7,550 households with agricultural inputs only). FAO’s planned Cash+ activities combine cash transfers with tailored livelihood support packages to assist rural families out of hunger sooner. Alongside cash transfers, the assistance packages will protect and restore the livelihoods of households in IPC Phases 3-4 by providing: (i) farmers with quality inputs to produce a nutritious variety of food crop (cereal, pulse and vegetable seeds, storage bags, fertilizer and irrigation/tractor services, where appropriate; (ii) pastoralists with nutrient-rich feed blocks and deworming to improve livestock productivity especially milk supply; and (iii) coastal communities with a variety of basic fishing gear and processing equipment to improve catch and consumption.  

Also under SO2, in anticipation of drought conditions in early 2021, FAO will also strategically position water bladder tanks and provide nutritive animal feed blocks to protect the small milking animals of up to 20,000 pastoral households impacted by scarce pasture from dry conditions and/or locust damage. Countrywide livestock vaccination and supportive treatment campaigns will further protect livestock assets belonging to at least 2.2 million men, women and children. Preparedness for animal health emergencies will be enhanced through strategic stocking of vaccines and related supplies (PPR), and training to local partners in Livestock Emergency Guidelines and Standards (LEGS), antimicrobial resistance, disease surveillance and reporting, among others.

Integrated Health Support to Vulnerable Populations in the Mudug Region of Somalia WASH Response to Drought and conflict - Affected Population in Mudug, Nugaal, Sanaag, Bari, Galgaduud and Hiraan regions in Somalia  In Somalia, Only 52% of the  population has access to basic water supply, with limited regulation of private water supplies frequently resulting in high prices, forcing families to fetch water from distant and unsafe open wells. In conflict-affected areas and camps for displaced people, access to safe water is frequently hampered due to damaged water infrastructure, which increases the risk of disease and malnutrition among people living in overcrowded conditions. In March 2021 alone, over 70 boreholes were reported to have broken in Puntland and Galmudug regional states due to over-use, weak management, and high operation and maintenance costs, forcing IDPs and host communities to buy water at prohibitive costs. According to a UNICEF report published in 2020, sanitation and hygiene coverage in Somalia is low, with only 38% of the population having access to basic sanitation facilities and services, posing a high rate of open defecation that leads to contamination of water sources and increases the risk of disease outbreaks. Hand washing with soap at critical moments is practiced by only one-third of the population due to a lack of soap and access to a functional handwashing point Coupled by poor knowledge of good hygiene and sanitation practices. WASH in health care institutions has been a source of concern for many years. A significant proportion of Somalia's health facilities lack on-site water connections and rely on water trucks from long distances. This severely jeopardizes service delivery and undermines safe WASH practices, which are critical in controlling and preventing disease outbreaks. This proposed project will increase access to safe and clean water, promote sanitation and hygiene conditions, and contribute to a reduction in infant and under-5 mortality rates as well as WASH-related diseases in general. The project will address the needs of 28,000 vulnerable population in Somalia's Mudug, Nugaal, Sanaag, Galmudug, and Hiraan regions. This will be done through the rehabilitation of boreholes with solar installations, extension of pipelines and water tank construction for communities and health facilities to improve access and storage, provision of water vouchers, rehabilitation of shallow wells, and training of community structures (committees) to increase their capacity to manage and maintain rehabilitated water systems. In addition, the IRC will construct/rehabilitate sanitation facilities (latrines and solid waste management infrastructure) with a focus on IDPs, as well as ensure access to essential WASH services in health facilities to improve health and nutritional outcomes. In addition, IRC will promote hygiene and sanitation and distribute basic hygiene kits to households, including materials for menstrual management. (Applying market –based programming approach where feasible as a complement to in-kind distribution).  The IRC will target communities in hard-to-reach areas with limited access to WASH services, as well as those in cholera/AWD hotspots and crowded IDP settlements, with particular focus on the COVID-19 situation, risk management, and infection prevention and control measures. The proposed response will be delivered through a strong protection lens, which will include efforts to ensure that latrines are gender separated, have lockable doors, adequate lighting, and that the distance to water points is kept within the agreed-upon standards. The IRC will adopt a universal design to ensure water and sanitation facilities are accessible to all, including persons with disabilities.  The project will also consider the impact of conflict on women and children in terms of access to WASH services, as well as the unique needs of menstruating women and girls. The proposed actions will address and prevent gender-based violence risks, thereby improving and contributing to greater gender equality.

Mali - OCHA Office [OCT 8359];[S 09-45/Pol-10-321.50 MLI 06/20] (2022 portion) Renforcement des mécanismes de Coordination et de Plaidoyer pour la protection humanitaire et l’assistance aux populations les plus vulnérables au Mali En 2021, la crise humanitaire au Mali s'est aggravée en raison de l'augmentation et de l'expansion des de la violence intercommunautaire et des attaques des groupes armés non étatiques (GANE) dans les régions du centre, du sud et de l'ouest. Cette crise a été aggravée par les bouleversements politiques marqués par deux coups d'état en août 2020 et mai 2021, et l'incertitude persistante de la transition politique laisse l'État dans l'incapacité de répondre aux services sociaux de base des populations. 
Les déplacements internes de personnes ont augmenté de 100 000 en 2021, atteignant plus de 401 000 personnes soit quatre fois plus qu'il y a deux ans. Au total, 156 000 réfugiés maliens résident dans les pays voisins tandis que le Mali accueille 48 000 réfugiés et leur fournit protection et assistance. Les gains économiques du Mali se sont érodés, avec 900 000 personnes (0,04% de la population) qui sont retombées dans la pauvreté en raison de la crise socioéconomique de la COVID-19. la capacité des ménages est fragilisée à cause de la perte de revenus, de la réduction des transferts de fonds et à l'augmentation du coût de la vie. 
La Banque mondiale prévoit une augmentation du taux de pauvreté à 4,8 % en 2022. La crise de protection est également aggravée avec une augmentation des incidents de sécurité.  Les acteurs de la violence basée sur le genre (VBG) ont signalé 5 486 incidents de VBG, soit une augmentation de 41 % comparativement à la même période en 2020. Plus de 1 640 écoles sont fermées en raison de l'insécurité, affectant plus de 2,9 millions d'enfants dont 40 % se trouvent dans la région centrale de Mopti. Quatre districts centraux ont signalé que 40 % des écoles étaient fermées. Dans les régions du sud, 10 pour cent des écoles sont fermées à Koulikoro, Koutiala et Sikasso, privant 30 000 enfants de leur éducation. A ce jour, le Mali a rapporté plus de 15 800 cas de COVID-19.
En 2021, 1,3 million de personnes ont connu un niveau élevé d'insécurité alimentaire aiguë. le niveau le plus élevé depuis 2015, et 3 055 253 personnes ont été touchées par les mauvaises pluies et une saison de soudure prolongée. La situation humanitaire reste entravée par l'augmentation des besoins et la faiblesse des financements, avec 32 % des fonds mobilisés au 31 octobre 2021. Malgré les contraintes opérationnelles, les partenaires humanitaires ont aidé plus de 2,45 millions des 4,7 millions de personnes ciblées au 30 septembre 2021. 
Les capacités de réponse existantes au Mali représentent plus de 160 organisations humanitaires, acteurs du développement ainsi que des forces militaires (MINUSMA, Forces maliennes de défense et de sécurité, Barkhane, Mission européenne de formation, G5 Sahel). Le contexte susmentionné exigera une coordination efficace et la présence d’OCHA demeure très importante. Multi year 2020/2021/2022. 2022 portion total amount CHF 50,000 (7F-10525.01) Improved food security and livelihoods of IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host communities in South Sudan In line with the South Sudan 2022 Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) and the FSL Cluster priorities, NPA will support vulnerable and food-insecure Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs), returnees and vulnerable host communities in IPC 4 locations in Canal/Pigi, Fangak, Pochalla & Bor South Counties of Jonglei State, Rumbek East, Rumbek Center, Cueibet, Yirol East, Yirol West and Awerial Counties of Lakes State, Terekeka County of Central Equatoria State and Kapoeta North County of Eastern Equatoria State. The targeted communities in the identified counties will be supported to improve their food security and livelihoods through provision of timely and appropriate main season and dry season inputs/kits (Crop, vegetable and fishing), training in improved agronomic and fishing practices. In addition, NPA will support food-insecure with cash transfers in Rumbek East and Rumbek Center Counties in Lakes State with cash transfers to address their food needs. NPA’s emergency assistance and livelihoods support aims at saving lives and averting total collapse of livelihoods in the target Counties. The provision of agricultural and fishing inputs/kits, training in agricultural production and fishing is expected to improve the food production and in turn the food security of the target households (HHs) thus supporting them to recover from crisis and placing them on an accelerated path to early recovery and resilience to acute shocks. NPA’s response will address the food security and livelihoods needs and priorities identified in the South Sudan 2022 Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO).

NPA seeks to support 105,056 HHs (630,338 individuals) in the targeted Counties with livelihood kits and cash transfers to address food insecurity. Some of the kits will be provided by FAO and some procured by NPA. Training on improved agronomic and fishing practices, marketing and group dynamics will be done through model farmers and fisher folk who will undergo a Training of Trainers (ToT) and subsequently cascade the knowledge and skills to the farmers and fisher folk in their communities. Gender-Based Violence (GBV) risk mitigation and strengthening of women’s and girls’ access to GBV services and Menstrual Hygiene Management (MHM) Enhance access to quality, timely and confidential services for GBV survivors and strengthening coordination for GBV mitigation and prevention in Somalia GBV incidence continues to worsen in due to multiple displacements, forced evictions, loss of livelihoods, disruption of social and community protection systems due to floods, droughts, sacking of communities by Alshabab with significant impact on the lives and well-being of women and adolescent girls. GBV risks and exposure includes distance to water points, Schools, markets and GBV service sites. Lack of lockable latrines, poor lighting in IDPs camps and overcrowded shelters/lack of privacy.  Media and programme reports of gang rapes, homicide, forced abortion of young pregnant adolescents, attempted suicide of rape survivors and increasing levels of FGM are common place. The recent displacement in Lasánod aggravated the situation for women and girls.  More women and girls including elderly have been left without food and shelter. The displacement is coming at a time when Somali authorities are facing difficulties in containing the spread of COVID19 virus. 

Women and girls living in IDP Camps are more prone to sexual violence and abuse than those living in host communities with a better housing infrastructure and service sites and markets. The JMCNA 2021 informs that 13 percent of households were concerned that girls in host communities and 17 per cent in IDP camps were exposed to sexual violence and harassment, while 16 per cent (host community) and 18 per cent (IDP) households were concerned that girls were to be forcibly married. In addition, it was indicated that 29 percent of respondents lacked proper bathing facilities, 26 per cent poor lighting, and 14 per cent privacy in shelter; 31 per cent lacked lockable latrines; 93 per cent use common latrines that are far or not in proximity. Similarly, the GBVIMS report from January – June 2021 indicates 62 per cent of the reported GBV incidents were physical assault, 11 per cent rape, 10 per cent sexual assault, 8 per cent denial of resources, while 6 per cent psychological/emotional abuse, and the remaining 4 per cent percent forced and early marriage.

Safety concerns of adolescent for adolescent boys and men continue to worsen with severe food insecurity and prevailing armed and communal conflicts. They are subject to kidnap, forceful recruitment by armed groups. Women and adolescent girls are relying on direct cash and voucher assistance to meet basic survival and material needs to improve their resilience to mitigate/escape GBV. Given the widespread food insecurity in Somalia, there may be a possibility of vulnerable women and adolescent girls exchanging sex for food. Reliance on cash support is providing a buffer for poor families but may also contribute to rising intimate partner violence with divergent priorities for families on where to invest the cash support. Increasing population in need for GBV services, limited services provision to cover the landscape of needs is a major concern for the GBV humanitarian response in Somalia. 

UNFPA interventions will target the displaced and non-displaced communities including all age groups, women and girls living with disabilities, widowed and divorced women, married adolescents and women and adolescent girls from minority clans. Some of the key interventions will include: 1) Support access to comprehensive multi sectoral GBV services (medical, legal, psychosocial) for 6000 women and girls. 2) Strengthen the capacity/and mobilize 200 PSS counsellors; 150 health workers to provide timely, quality, and confidential PSS and rape treatment. 3)  Support the establishment 6 GBV one-stop centers in South West State, Banadir and Lasanod. 4) Provide 2,000 dignity kits and 36 post rape kits dignity protection for women and girls and treatment of rape. 5) Support 600 women and girls’ survivors of GBV with cash voucher assistance and grants for livelihood.

Emergency food aid for refugees, internally displaced persons and host communities in accordance with Strategic Objective 1 of the WFP country program (excluding UNHAS flights) WFP SOMALIA 2022 HRP - FSC Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas. As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation. The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

South Sudan/CE: Agriculture; Health; Humanitarian Coordination, Information Management and Assessments (HCIMA); Nutrition; Protection; WASH (USAID/BHA) Increased access to nutrition sensitive food security and livelihood support to strengthen the resilience of crisis-affected vulnerable communities in Jonglei and Warrap States. The proposed 2022 FSL cluster HRP highlights the gaps identified among vulnerable communities affected by crisis and in IPC 4 to 5, particularly limited access to improved high yielding vegetable and crop seeds, limited tools for farming, limited access to cash for essential food and HHs needs and inadequate fishing equipment. The project aim to provide immediate lifesaving intervention for crisis affected vulnerable communities by targeting  58,973 Fangak,15,683Tonj East and 42,609 Pibor which are  117,264(56,521m, 60743f) people (Host 50%, IDPs 30% and Returnees 20%) and 10% disable people which are in crisis due to insecurity, yearly flooding, drought and were the farming practices among the predominantly peasantry communities are very poor culminating in to problems of food insecurity, poverty and environmental degradation.
The action will provide conditional cash assistance for most vulnerable households during the 6 months lean season to enable HHs community asset creation however enabling continues access to diversified food and HHs needs. Targeted HHs provided with vegetable and crop kits for cultivation ensuring continuous access to food for a long period of time, fishing kit to complement household food needs during floods times since most flooding in this areas comes with fish mean while supporting continues fishing in areas close to rivers as fish is a rich nutritious protein source for consumption and surplus sold for income generation by the community. The project will ensure year round production of vegetable crops through recession irrigation practices during dry season and diversification of the livelihood activity options among the vulnerable communities, increasing dietary diversity for the farming community and the fishing groups. The project aimed at complimenting the current interventions in an effort to prevent an even more severe food shortage as well as strengthening the coping capacities of the vulnerable communities with special focus given to people with disabilities and chronically sick to make sure they are not left out including pregnant and lactating mothers. The project inputs will be procured and transported to the field to the field with timeliness of delivery of these inputs  very critical. Capacity building support will be conducted for selected beneficiaries and continuous practical sessions through the central demonstration gardens learning sites within the communities including health/nutrition centres. The cash beneficiaries will be trained on creation of community dykes to prevent flooding within their gardens. The project seeks to create synergies with other thematic areas such as Wash, health and nutrition of AAH and other implementing partners on ground through integrated approach. The program will also integrate with nutrition project focusing on areas of food preparation, utilization and cooking demonstration and technically supporting rolling out of training by establishment of kitchen gardens for the targeted groups. 
The project will benefit the most vulnerable households (IDPs, disable, Child-headed, chronically sick, PLW, Elderly and Female-headed households) which account for the 27.9 % households under IPC 4 and 5 suffering crisis and acute food insecurity and at high risk of malnutrition as food insecurity is likely to continue affecting these counties negatively.
The project will ensured continuous collaboration with key stakeholders including the government ministries at both county and state level to be part to support ongoing activities.
The project will target at least 60% women for support, as women are the most vulnerable group mostly involved in farming activities. The project considers Do No Harm principles by encouraging environmentally friendly activities including strategies to improve soil fertility, water tolerant crops such as rice and drought tolerant crops such as sorghum/millet will be promoted and awareness on protection against GBV provided.

SOMALIA - Combating the locust plague (2022 portion) Emergency Lifesaving Cash and Livelihood Support to IDP and Non- IDP Communities in Somalia Somalia is facing a severe and deteriorating humanitarian crisis as we enter 2022 as a result of the compounding effects of conflict, recurrent climate shocks, diseases and pests outbreaks with increased levels of vulnerability and substantial increase in the humanitarian caseload (Somalia HNO, 2022). There is a serious risk that the impact of consecutive below average to poor rainfall in most parts of the country will develop into a severe drought by early to mid- 2022 with the number of people facing acute food insecurity on the rise. It is likely that minority groups, women, children, people with disabilities, will experience heightened protection risks as a result, unless they are intentionally targeted to receive tailored assistance.

With approximately 3.5 million individuals in IPC 3 and 4 through at least December 2021, FAO proposes to target 160,300 households (961,800 individuals- 91,500 IDPs and 870,300 non- IDPs) in IPC 3 and IPC 4 caseloads respectively. This will include 216,790 women, 254,492 girls, 264,880 boys and 225,638 men and 144,270 people living with disabilities (PWD) across 59 districts in Somalia through its flagship Cash+ approach combining short-term cash transfers with tailored livelihood support in accordance with technical and humanitarian standards. Vulnerable households will identified from at-risk pastoral, agro-pastoral, fishing, riverine farmers, IDPs and Non- IDP communities in IPC 3 and 4 areas. This intervention will integrate short-term cash transfers aimed at enabling the most vulnerable households to meet their immediate needs, with livelihood support to allow crisis-affected households to get back into production. FAO will employ community- led beneficiary selection processes and ensure adequate targeting and representation of extremely vulnerable and minority groups in community committees. Interventions proposed will employ a Do No Harm approach with a gender lens that ensures conflict- sensitivity to reduce protection risks for all individuals, and to mitigate the risk of conflict or community tensions. 

Under Food Security Cluster (FSC) Objective 1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 160,300 households through a blend of conditional (Cash-for-Work) and unconditional (UCT) transfers. Under UCT, FAO will prioritize Cash+ interventions including Cash+ Agriculture, Cash+ livestock and Cash+ fisheries. These modalities will increase households’ immediate access to food by providing sufficient cash to access the minimum expenditure basket (MEB), while supporting the rehabilitation of critical productive and community infrastructure. It will also boost household food production, increase household incomes and create employment opportunities. Cash transfer values will be informed by the Cash Working Group and are expected to differ per district/ region of intervention. They, however, will be valued at 80 percent of the food MEB, which can range from USD 50- 100 per month. All cash-based programmes will include training on good nutrition practices. 

Under FSC Objective 2, to protect livelihoods and related food sources, FAO will provide in-kind, technical support and tailored trainings to 112,500 HHs to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security and nutrition threats, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to targeted HHs. In addition, FAO shall provide transitional cash support to 13,100 HHs across agro pastoral, pastoral and fishing livelihood zones to augment the adaptive capacity of HHs, strengthen and foster resilience to future shocks, cushioning them from food insecurity and malnutrition. Trainings shall be delivered alongside input provision to build skills in sustainable use of resources provided, build skills in livelihoods management including harvest, post- harvest management, linking beneficiaries to long- term interventions that provide them opportunities to enhance their livelihoods and skills.

Multi-sectoral humanitarian assistance (WASH, EFSVL, Protection) in the Western, Eastern and Central Africa Improving access to protection services for vulnerable women men boys and girls through community based protection. Somalia’s protracted humanitarian crisis is characterized by ongoing conflicts, climate-related shocks, communicable disease outbreaks and weak social protection mechanisms. The 2022 Humanitarian Needs overview highlights that 7.7Million people in need (5.5M non- internally displaced people, 2.2 Million Internally displaced people, and 0.16M refugees and asylum seekers) an increase from the 5.9 Million recorded in 2021. 
The 2022 HNO people in need for the General Protection is 2.7 million, of whom 63 per cent are children, and 49 per cent are women and girls. From January to August of 2021, the Protection Return Monitoring Network (PRMN) reported conflict as the main driver of displacement. Insecurity and conflict contribute to protection challenges such as physical attacks and threat to life, arbitrary arrest and detention, kidnapping, sexual assault, child recruitment, amongst others. This situation is exacerbated by the limited availability of basic services, and support for the victims of abuse. 
Oxfam will make direct implementation and at the same time will work local NGO partners in the implementation of the response. 
The proposed Protection package aims to increase the resilience, capacities and protective environment of the targeted communities by strengthening community-based protection mechanisms through capacity building, improving access to information and available services, awareness raising, service mapping, and referrals toward mitigating risks (including SGBV), especially for women and girls. Community-based structures, including Community Protection Volunteers, Women’s Forum, Community Committees and duty bearers will play a key role in the project. A protection analysis will be conducted in the target locations to identify existing (strategic and practical) needs and dynamics, vulnerabilities, and threats faced by women, men, boys, and girls. 
Though the community based protection approach a community lighting initiatives will be implemented during the action to improve community safety and dignity and reduce protection threats faced by crises affected communities speciﬁcally women and girls in IDPs settlement and vulnerable host communities. Other materials including wheelbarrows will be provided to most vulnerable households to reduce work burden resulted by changing gender roles due to the crises which make the work of women and girls more demanding, e.g fetching water and ﬁrewood collection which in most cases they travel in long distances. In addition this material provision will reduce the frequency of risk exposure and will contribute community cohesion to strengthen community self- protection mechanisms.
Mapping existing services will improve access to information, establishing protection reporting mechanisms, a referral system, and training community volunteers to reduce protection vulnerabilities while increasing the capacities of the target population, who will be able to make informed decisions. Further the action will establish women forums to balance traditional male dominated structures and create safe space for women and girls discuss protection issues. The  issues identiﬁed by women groups will then be incorporated systematically into Community Action Plans for further actions and advocacies aiming to strength women’s engagement in community decision making process to address speciﬁc issues affecting them.Oxfam is fundamentally committed to ensuring accountability to affected people. Women, men, girls, and boys within target beneficiaries will be directly involved at all stages of the project cycle in order to encourage community ownership and participation in project activities. Gender protection analysis will be carried out to inform program implementation. Separate consultations will be conducted for different gender groups including persons with disabilities , clan affiliated minorities and other marginalized groups including women and girls.

Integrated Humanitarian Response Focused on Food Security, Legal Assistance and Education Seguridad alimentaria y medios de vida para la población afectada por la situación humanitaria en Venezuela  El proyecto está conformado por cuatro ejes principales, basado en las necesidades identificadas, población vulnerable y la experiencia de intervenciones actualmente implementándose. NRC tiene la capacidad de adaptar y ampliar sus proyectos, aportando y proponiendo: 

A) Proveer de insumos, herramientas y asistencia técnica que ayude a mejorar la producción y construcción de capacidades en centros educativos que tienen componente técnico agropecuario, con niños, niñas y adolescentes, así como las comunidades aledañas. Esto conlleva el fortalecimiento del modelo productivo orgánico, auto-suficiente y sostenible que sirva de modelo para replicar a nivel de pequeños productores. Entre otras cosas se contempla la entrega de ganado vacuno, ovino, porcino, pollos y gallinas, sistemas de producción de queso; ordeños mecánicos; restauración y rehabilitación de espacios para pasto, siembra, gallineros, jardines, semilleros, viveros, dotación de semillas, tanques de agua y sistemas de riego; alimentos para ganado y animales de granja. Así como todo tipo de apoyo en el área técnica agropecuaria, emprendimiento y capacidad técnica para jóvenes, en sinergia y de forma complementaria con otros proyectos sectoriales ASH, educación, protección, bajo el modelo integral de intervención de NRC. 

B) Concienciación en hábitos de vida saludables y apoyo técnico a hogares en riesgo de inseguridad alimentaria (réplica de modelos productivos exitosos, construyendo capacidades, sostenibilidad y auto-producción ecológica). Se promueve un cambio cultural respecto a hábitos saludables a través de una intervención integral y complementaria, para ayudar en la toma de conciencia sobre la importancia de una buena alimentación, preparación y cocinado, huertos familiares y comunitarios, comedores y ollas comunitarias para personas en tránsito, personas de la tercera edad y/o niños, entrega de semillas, mejora de riego, cultivos y métodos alternativos. 

C) Apoyo a las escuelas y familias de los alumnos: niños y adolescentes. Trabajo conjunto y complementario con proyectos de educación (comedores escolares) en la que se alcanza la mejora de la asistencia escolar, unido a la mejora en las condiciones de seguridad alimentaria de las familias y comunidad. Integral y articulado con proyectos de protección y ASH. 

D) Distribuciones de bolsas de alimentos. Dirigidas a grupos más vulnerables identificados, NRC distribuye una canasta de alimento para atender los gastos calóricos necesarios para 2 o 3 meses de una familia con 4 personas en promedio. Particularmente, las modalidades de asistencia se adaptarán según las necesidades de la población y respetando cualquier riesgo sanitario que pueda afectar a los beneficiarios.

La respuesta ASH de NRC pretenden ser Integradas a otros programas como el de Educación que apunta a una mejora de la calidad de la educación, inclusivas e integradas con el programa ASH centrándose en la mejora de la infraestructura ASH, para garantizar las instalaciones satisfagan las necesidades de todos los grupos de NNAs, profesores y personas con discapacidad.

Assistance humanitaire en abris et biens non-alimentaires pour les populations sinistrées des inondations dans les zones à fort risque de Choléra au Niger Assistance d'urgence aux personnes déplacées dans les régions de Tahoua et Tillabéry Dans le cadre du HRP 2021, partant de la stratégie du GTABNA et en étroite collaboration avec le Ministère de l’Action Humanitaire, l'OIM poursuit l'objectif général de contribuer à l'amélioration les conditions de vie des populations. En particulier des populations déplacées vulnérables victimes des crises armées et l'activisme de GANEs spécialement dans les zones frontalières, dans les régions de Tahoua et de Tillabéry, par la fourniture d'abris d'urgence et de Biens Non Alimentaires. En tant que Co-Lead du Cluster,  l'OIM va contribuer au  renforcement de la coordination du Groupe de travail Abris et Biens Non Alimentaires, renforcer la collecte des informations, d'informer les intervenants sur la localisation, la nature et l'ampleur des besoins exprimés, sensibiliser les partenaires et membres du secteur à mener les activités dans le respect de la stratégie du secteur et les principes humanitaires et d'appuyer les services étatiques locaux dans leurs rôles de coordination et suivi des activités du secteur. La situation sécuritaire dans les régions de Tahoua et Tillabéry étant toujours volatile, le GTABNA reste attentif à tout mouvement de population et suit la situation au travers des annonces de sécurité, les MSA de RRM et le monitoring de protection du cluster protection fournissant les informations indicatives à la réponse en abris d’urgence et Biens Non Alimentaires.  Partant de la cible du HRP 2022, le secteur abris et bien non alimentaire mettra à disposition 7 000 kits abris d’urgence et 7 000 kits BNA en vue de répondre aux nouveaux mouvements de population, aux mouvements secondaires ainsi qu'au renouvèlement des abris détériorés des ménages. L’assistance basée sur la vulnérabilité ciblera également les familles hôtes vulnérables. Sur base de la stratégie du Secteur abris/BNA et dépendamment de la faisabilité, les interventions pourront se faire en transfert monétaires conditionnels. Cette modalité offrira la réduction considérable des coûts logistiques qui sont très élevés en période hivernale à cause du mauvais état des routes et permettra de résoudre le problème d’accès lié à l'insécurité qui retarde les interventions. Les activités de la réponse d'urgence se conformeront aux Principes de Protection transversales et au Cadre institutionnel de l'OIM de lutte contre les violences basées sur le genre en situation de crise (GBV), intégrera des mesures visant à assurer la sécurité, la dignité et le bien-être de la population touchée. Ce projet s'inscrira dans le respect des principes humanitaires et portera une attention particulière au principe ne pas nuire, de sécurité et non-discrimination. Les activités du projet seront mises en œuvre dans le respect soutenu des règles de lutte contre la COVID-19 par l'observation de mesures barrières telles que le port du masque, le lavage des mains, le respect de la distanciation sociale afin d'endiguer tout risque de contamination et de propagation de la maladie auprès des bénéficiaires. Dans le cadre de la redevabilité des sessions d'information sur le projet seront organisées avec les bénéficiaires, la phase d'évaluation des besoins sera réalisée de commun accord avec les populations dans les communes ciblées, la communication avec les communautés et les autorités locales sur les critères de ciblage seront organisées et après intervention, les feedbacks de la communauté cible seront collectés à travers des évaluations post-distribution et des séances de discussion de groupe séparées par genre et âge avant et après l'assistance. Aussi, en tant qu’acteur humanitaire, l'OIM et ses partenaires de mise en œuvre s’assureront que les actions n’induisent aucune tension ou problème dans la zone et n’exposent pas les bénéficiaires en affichant les compositions de kits BNA et Abris. A cet effet, une collaboration étroite sera faite avec les acteurs de protection pour un suivi de prêt de toute question de protection. Le coût total du projet sera de 4 161 500 USD.

Emergency life- saving support to the most drought- affected pastoral and agro-pastoral households in Southwest State of Somalia Emergency Lifesaving Cash and Livelihood Support to IDP and Non- IDP Communities in Somalia Somalia is facing a severe and deteriorating humanitarian crisis as we enter 2022 as a result of the compounding effects of conflict, recurrent climate shocks, diseases and pests outbreaks with increased levels of vulnerability and substantial increase in the humanitarian caseload (Somalia HNO, 2022). There is a serious risk that the impact of consecutive below average to poor rainfall in most parts of the country will develop into a severe drought by early to mid- 2022 with the number of people facing acute food insecurity on the rise. It is likely that minority groups, women, children, people with disabilities, will experience heightened protection risks as a result, unless they are intentionally targeted to receive tailored assistance.

With approximately 3.5 million individuals in IPC 3 and 4 through at least December 2021, FAO proposes to target 160,300 households (961,800 individuals- 91,500 IDPs and 870,300 non- IDPs) in IPC 3 and IPC 4 caseloads respectively. This will include 216,790 women, 254,492 girls, 264,880 boys and 225,638 men and 144,270 people living with disabilities (PWD) across 59 districts in Somalia through its flagship Cash+ approach combining short-term cash transfers with tailored livelihood support in accordance with technical and humanitarian standards. Vulnerable households will identified from at-risk pastoral, agro-pastoral, fishing, riverine farmers, IDPs and Non- IDP communities in IPC 3 and 4 areas. This intervention will integrate short-term cash transfers aimed at enabling the most vulnerable households to meet their immediate needs, with livelihood support to allow crisis-affected households to get back into production. FAO will employ community- led beneficiary selection processes and ensure adequate targeting and representation of extremely vulnerable and minority groups in community committees. Interventions proposed will employ a Do No Harm approach with a gender lens that ensures conflict- sensitivity to reduce protection risks for all individuals, and to mitigate the risk of conflict or community tensions. 

Under Food Security Cluster (FSC) Objective 1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 160,300 households through a blend of conditional (Cash-for-Work) and unconditional (UCT) transfers. Under UCT, FAO will prioritize Cash+ interventions including Cash+ Agriculture, Cash+ livestock and Cash+ fisheries. These modalities will increase households’ immediate access to food by providing sufficient cash to access the minimum expenditure basket (MEB), while supporting the rehabilitation of critical productive and community infrastructure. It will also boost household food production, increase household incomes and create employment opportunities. Cash transfer values will be informed by the Cash Working Group and are expected to differ per district/ region of intervention. They, however, will be valued at 80 percent of the food MEB, which can range from USD 50- 100 per month. All cash-based programmes will include training on good nutrition practices. 

Under FSC Objective 2, to protect livelihoods and related food sources, FAO will provide in-kind, technical support and tailored trainings to 112,500 HHs to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security and nutrition threats, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to targeted HHs. In addition, FAO shall provide transitional cash support to 13,100 HHs across agro pastoral, pastoral and fishing livelihood zones to augment the adaptive capacity of HHs, strengthen and foster resilience to future shocks, cushioning them from food insecurity and malnutrition. Trainings shall be delivered alongside input provision to build skills in sustainable use of resources provided, build skills in livelihoods management including harvest, post- harvest management, linking beneficiaries to long- term interventions that provide them opportunities to enhance their livelihoods and skills.

Emergency drought response through provision of integrated water, sanitation and hygiene promotion (WASH) services. Provision of lifesaving assistance and sustainable solutions through safe Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) services, for people in crises and their host communities in multiple regions in Somalia. IOM WASH is proposing to contribute to lifesaving of access to safe and equitable basic WASH services to overall 281,400 beneficiaries from vulnerable Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) and host-communities in multiple regions in Somalia. 

Specifically, the project will target 168,840 Non displaced people (children 104,681; women 27,014; Disabled 25,326; and elderly 11,819) and 112,560 displaced populations (children 69,787; Women 18,010; Disabled 16,884; and elderly 7,879)
IOM will rehabilitate 60 strategic water sources for multi-use (human and animals) and further 55 community berkads (water reservoirs) that will provide continued, equitable, safe, sufficient and sustainable water to regions, targeted by the cluster, prone to natural disasters.
IOM further proposes to construct 3,300 new emergency sanitation facilities (following cluster specifications) targeting populations without access to basic sanitation and hygiene.

The project will also strengthen the capacity of the Federal Government of Somalia and Federal Members States, community leaders and water committees/technicians for better coordination with government authorities and communities and sustainability of the constructed/ rehabilitated WASH infrastructures. In addition, the project will nurture community participation in good hygiene practices through training and community sensitization campaigns.

Affected populations and all relevant stakeholders including men, women, boys, girls, elderly and people with disability will be involved in decision making throughout the project activities/cycle. Provision of lifesaving integrated Sexual and Reproductive Health (SRH) services and information including clinical management of rape for GBV survivors -drought affected women and adolescent girls. Enhance access to quality, timely and confidential services for GBV survivors and strengthening coordination for GBV mitigation and prevention in Somalia GBV incidence continues to worsen in due to multiple displacements, forced evictions, loss of livelihoods, disruption of social and community protection systems due to floods, droughts, sacking of communities by Alshabab with significant impact on the lives and well-being of women and adolescent girls. GBV risks and exposure includes distance to water points, Schools, markets and GBV service sites. Lack of lockable latrines, poor lighting in IDPs camps and overcrowded shelters/lack of privacy.  Media and programme reports of gang rapes, homicide, forced abortion of young pregnant adolescents, attempted suicide of rape survivors and increasing levels of FGM are common place. The recent displacement in Lasánod aggravated the situation for women and girls.  More women and girls including elderly have been left without food and shelter. The displacement is coming at a time when Somali authorities are facing difficulties in containing the spread of COVID19 virus. 

Women and girls living in IDP Camps are more prone to sexual violence and abuse than those living in host communities with a better housing infrastructure and service sites and markets. The JMCNA 2021 informs that 13 percent of households were concerned that girls in host communities and 17 per cent in IDP camps were exposed to sexual violence and harassment, while 16 per cent (host community) and 18 per cent (IDP) households were concerned that girls were to be forcibly married. In addition, it was indicated that 29 percent of respondents lacked proper bathing facilities, 26 per cent poor lighting, and 14 per cent privacy in shelter; 31 per cent lacked lockable latrines; 93 per cent use common latrines that are far or not in proximity. Similarly, the GBVIMS report from January – June 2021 indicates 62 per cent of the reported GBV incidents were physical assault, 11 per cent rape, 10 per cent sexual assault, 8 per cent denial of resources, while 6 per cent psychological/emotional abuse, and the remaining 4 per cent percent forced and early marriage.

Safety concerns of adolescent for adolescent boys and men continue to worsen with severe food insecurity and prevailing armed and communal conflicts. They are subject to kidnap, forceful recruitment by armed groups. Women and adolescent girls are relying on direct cash and voucher assistance to meet basic survival and material needs to improve their resilience to mitigate/escape GBV. Given the widespread food insecurity in Somalia, there may be a possibility of vulnerable women and adolescent girls exchanging sex for food. Reliance on cash support is providing a buffer for poor families but may also contribute to rising intimate partner violence with divergent priorities for families on where to invest the cash support. Increasing population in need for GBV services, limited services provision to cover the landscape of needs is a major concern for the GBV humanitarian response in Somalia. 

UNFPA interventions will target the displaced and non-displaced communities including all age groups, women and girls living with disabilities, widowed and divorced women, married adolescents and women and adolescent girls from minority clans. Some of the key interventions will include: 1) Support access to comprehensive multi sectoral GBV services (medical, legal, psychosocial) for 6000 women and girls. 2) Strengthen the capacity/and mobilize 200 PSS counsellors; 150 health workers to provide timely, quality, and confidential PSS and rape treatment. 3)  Support the establishment 6 GBV one-stop centers in South West State, Banadir and Lasanod. 4) Provide 2,000 dignity kits and 36 post rape kits dignity protection for women and girls and treatment of rape. 5) Support 600 women and girls’ survivors of GBV with cash voucher assistance and grants for livelihood.

Provision of Protection, Emergency Shelter and Non-Food Items interventions benefiting drought affected populations (IDPs and vulnerable host communities) in Galmudug and South West States Protection and targeted assistance targeting IDPs and vulnerable non-IDP communities and refugee returnees The project aims to strengthen a rights-based protection response for IDPs and non-IDP communities, as well as refugee returnees, in particular those most vulnerable through stronger advocacy, life-saving protection and assistance activities, evidence-based programming with the focus on developing and building the capacity of affected communities to cope and recover and better position them for the attainment of durable solutions. Improving coordination and quality of assessments and monitoring will also be key components of the project. The project also foresees benefiting the entire displaced population through continuous advocacy and support in the area of law and policy, fostering the successful engagement with relevant authorities and partners with a focus on the approval and implementation of the new IDP Law. 
UNHCR will continue to make the best of its key membership of the protection cluster and ensure regular reporting to the clusters’ 5Ws and strong participation and contribution in the different clusters’ working groups to ensure coordination and complementarity of interventions, avoiding duplication with other members and ensuring regular sharing of protection reports with the cluster.

Provision of Protection, Emergency Shelter and Non-Food Items interventions benefiting drought affected populations (IDPs and vulnerable host communities) in Galmudug and South West States Shelter and NFIs Assistance to Crisis Affected Populations in Somalia In 2022, UNHCR will target affected populations including; newly displaced populations, IDPs currently living in protracted situations, refugee returnees, and affected host communities with adequate shelter and basic household items. This will be done through the provision of Non-Food Items (NFI kits), Emergency Shelters, and where feasible transitional and durable shelter solutions through different modalities including in-kind and through cash.
The Somalia Joint Multi-Cluster Needs Assessment (JMCNA) 2021, reports the living standard gap of Shelter and NFIs to be at 84%. According to the same assessment, the most commonly reported priority need of more than half of the affected population is still shelter or housing due to poor shelter conditions, lack of space, poverty and lack of security of tenure. The critical indicators that were considered in the calculation of the severity of the POCs in the sector were access to safety of enclosures, technical performance of shelters and the access to vital household NFIs. In addition to these indicators, others that were also considered were living conditions including overcrowding, functional domestic living space, occupancy status, and security of tenure.
In response to the identified needs in the HNO 2022, UNHCR plans to distribute NFI Kits to 56,800 households in kind/cash, provide emergency shelters to 20,000 households, transitional shelters to 800 households and permanent shelters to 600 households. The project will target 340,800 individuals with NFI kits, 120,000 individuals with emergency shelters, 4,800 individuals with transitional shelters and 3,600 individuals with permanent shelters. NFI, emergency shelters and transitional shelter assistance will be provided in cash or in kind and the response modality will depend on the availability of items in the local market, access to the locations, user preference and associated protection risks. Permanent shelters will be provided in kind through implementing partners.
As per the HNO, it is reported that a total of 237 IDP sites hosting 593,058 individuals were congested with associated health risks and fire outbreaks. These overcrowded sites are not planned, leading to the increased risk of fire outbreaks, spread of diseases including COVID 19, relatively higher GBV related incidences and flooding due to the absence of adequate drainage systems. In response to this, through an ongoing inter-cluster initiative between the Shelter Cluster and the CCCM Cluster, UNHCR will provide settlement planning and infrastructure support in 49,500 individuals in sites to be identified by the shelter cluster basing on the level of risk and feasibility of the project. This infrastructure support will be done to ensure site decongestion through settlement extensions and implementation of basic site planning principles where feasible. 
UNHCR will carry out Post Distribution Monitoring (PDM) and ensure the utilization of the Complaints, Response and Feedback Mechanism for each project. The PDM exercise will be conducted 4-6 weeks after NFI and ESK distribution to analyze the impact of the projects, level of beneficiary satisfaction and establish the lessons learnt for future programming.
UNHCR will target a total of 469,200 vulnerable individuals of the 3.6 million persons identified as in need of shelter assistance. Of the targeted individuals, 84,456 women, 65,688 men, 218,849 children, 18,768 elderly and 93,840 disabled individuals. UNHCR will also incorporate 93,840 vulnerable individuals from the host community and 375,360  vulnerable POCs as part of its target group. The targeting will occur based on UNHCR and Shelter Cluster assessments for those most in need and highly vulnerable. Activities will be implemented in Bari, Banadir, Bay, Lower Juba, Gedo, Mudug, Hiraan, Nugaal, Middle Shabelle, Lower Shabelle and Woqooyi Galbeed regions.
UNHCR will implement and monitor the activities through the support of Implementing Partners.

WFP Relief Response to Drought Affected Population in Bay, Bakool, Galgaduud and Mudug regions of Somalia. WFP SOMALIA 2022 HRP - FSC Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas. As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation. The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

La production céréalière brute 2021 est estimée à 3 562 549 tonnes (contre 5 576 371 tonnes en 2020) soit une baisse de 36% par rapport à l’année 2020. A l'heure, c'est environ 2 554 833 personnes (364,976 ménages) qui sont en insécurité alimentaire sévère et qui nécessitent une aide humanitaire d'urgence.Pour répondre à cette crise alimentaire, le gouvernement a élaboré un plan d'urgence estimé à plus de  280 Milliards de Dollars USD pour la période de novembre 2021 à Mars 2022 en attendant l'élaboration du plan de soutien . Cette réponse s’inscrit dans la Stratégie de Prévention et de Gestion des Crises Alimentaires 2021 – 2025 du Dispositif National de Prévention et de Gestion de Crises Alimentaires (DNPGCA). Rappelons que l’Activité 1, relative aux urgences s’inscrit dans l’effet direct stratégique 1 du CSP (2020-2024) du PAM Niger « Les populations affectées, y compris les réfugiés, les personnes déplacées internes, les communautés hôtes et les retournés dans les zones ciblées sont en mesure de répondre aux besoins alimentaires minimums pendant et après la crise ». •	La réponse aux crises prolongées.
•	La réponse à la soudure agricole et pastorale.
Par ailleurs la prévention de la malnutrition aux enfants 6-23 mois est combinée aux trois composantes ci-dessus.
