OCT 10186 [OCT 10186];[52040482 Amendment 5] Renforcement de la coordination et du plaidoyer humanitaire au Tchad Le projet vise à renforcer le rôle de OCHA dans la mise en œuvre de son mandat et son rôle auprès des partenaires humanitaires et gouvernementaux au niveau des fonctions coordination, gestion de l’information et plaidoyer. Le bureau national d’OCHA à N’Djaména et ses trois sous-bureaux régionaux à l’Est (Abéché) au Sud (Goré) et la province du Lac (Baga Sola) mettent l’accent sur l’opérationnalisation de ses fonctions y compris en assurant un lien entre les activités humanitaires et de développement (nexus) en vue de promouvoir une solution durable visant à ne pas perpétuer une situation de dépendance humanitaire. Dans le cadre de cette nouvelle façon de travailler outre l’opérationnalisation du nexus, le lien avec les objectifs commun des programmes développement, paix et sécurité sera mis en avant. L’accent est aussi mis sur le renforcement de la coordination civilo-militaire afin de faciliter l’accès et la protection des civils.

Le projet a pour but de renforcer la coordination d’une réponse humanitaire rapide et efficace afin de sauver des vies et protéger les personnes affectées par les situations de crises au Tchad. Une coordination humanitaire rapide et correctement évaluée au niveau des besoins de la population affectée permettra aux acteurs humanitaires de mieux identifier et répondre aux besoins humanitaires, de renforcer la préparation de réponse aux urgences à travers le renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et plus spécifiquement l‘Equipe humanitaire pays, la coordination inter-clusters, la coordination civilo-militaire, les clusters et les mécanismes de coordination au niveau de terrain.
Le projet vise aussi à assurer le plaidoyer humanitaire à travers l’analyse des besoins faites par l’ensemble de la communauté humanitaire et ses partenaires en vue une compréhension commune des problématiques auxquels fait face le Tchad, ses causes profondes, l’impact sur les populations. OCHA jouera un rôle clé dans la création d'espaces de collection et d'analyse et gestion d’informations, pour assurer une stratégie de réponse coordonnée menant à des actions humanitaires répondant aux besoins les plus aigus et être mieux préparé face aux urgences soudaines. Le projet permettra également d’assurer conjointement avec la communauté humanitaire le plaidoyer en faveur du respect des principes humanitaires, de la protection des civils, de l'accès humanitaire et pour la mobilisation et l'allocation efficace de ressources humanitaires.

Un accent a été mis sur la mise en œuvre des plans d’action de la redevabilité envers les populations affectées (AAP), la PSEA et la préparation aux urgences en plus d'intégrer une attention au genre et de renforcer la centralité de la protection.
Un plaidoyer pour plus de visibilité des résultats tangibles au niveau de la réponse facilitant la mobilisation de ressources pour les différentes crises au Tchad (mouvement de population – crise du Bassin du Lac Tchad, insécurité alimentaire et malnutrition, urgences sanitaires) est aussi défini comme une priorité dans ce projet

OCHA continuera de jouer également un rôle moteur dans le renforcement du lien entre les acteurs humanitaires et de développement et la transformation de la réponse humanitaire, en lien avec les engagements pris au Sommet humanitaire mondial de 2016 et ceci à travers la nouvelle façon de travailler (NWOW) et le renforcement de l’utilisation de la modalité de transfert monétaire.

Provision of integrated sustainable livelihoods and WaSH services to the most vulnerable Internally Displaced People, refugees, host communities and returnees of Greater Upper Nile, South Sudan Provision of integrated, equitable, and timely WASH services to emergency affected populations in South Sudan Protracted crises in South Sudan, including climactic shocks and continued conflict, have resulted in 8.9 million people projected to be in need of humanitarian assistance in 2022. As a result of the shocks, such as flooding, inter-communal violence (ICV) and ongoing armed clashes, the majority of the population are facing increased food insecurity, lack of access to basic services, and protection risks. As per the Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) 2022, lack of or inadequate access to clean water and improved sanitation and hygiene practices in South Sudan will negatively impact an estimated 6.1 million people in 2022. 

Since 2006, Solidarites International has become a key WASH actor in South Sudan, implementing emergency lifesaving responses across the country and providing integrated WASH services to crisis-affected populations in areas of static presence in Upper Nile, Jonglei, and Western Bahr el Ghazal. Since 2012 SI has played a key role in the Emergency Preparedness and Response (EPR) strategy in South Sudan, implementing multi-sectoral assessments and delivering emergency responses to crisis-affected populations all over the country. 

In 2022, SI will continue to provide emergency live-saving  WASH responses across the South Sudan to restore basic access to safe water, hygiene, and sanitation while ensuring equitable access, safety, and accountability to supported populations. Through its roving Emergency Preparedness and Response (EPR) team, SI will deploy to emergency-affected locations to provide first phase and second phase responses including distribution of household water treatment items and soap, emergency provision of safe water, and rapid repair of emergency-affected infrastructure.

At the same time, SI will expand its static presence in Upper Nile and Jonglei to provide basic integrated WASH services that target the most vulnerable, including those suffering malnutrition, food insecurity and protection threats. Static programs will focus on providing community-based solutions for sustainable WASH services that ensure that improvements in access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene are durable and can be maintained independently by communities. Engagement and joint programming with Protection and Nutrition actors will ensure that WASH services can be accessed by the most vulnerable and will have a tangible impact on reducing overall priority humanitarian needs. The increased integration of protection, inclusion, and conflict sensitivity analysis in all programming will ensure that WASH services and resources can be safely accessed by all in the community. Greater engagement of communities and local markets will support the design of long term and flood resistant WASH infrastructure and supply chains to ensure that interventions produce durable results for communities.

OCT 10186 [OCT 10186];[52040482 Amendment 5] Renforcement des mécanismes de Coordination et de Plaidoyer pour la protection humanitaire et l’assistance aux populations les plus vulnérables au Mali En 2021, la crise humanitaire au Mali s'est aggravée en raison de l'augmentation et de l'expansion des de la violence intercommunautaire et des attaques des groupes armés non étatiques (GANE) dans les régions du centre, du sud et de l'ouest. Cette crise a été aggravée par les bouleversements politiques marqués par deux coups d'état en août 2020 et mai 2021, et l'incertitude persistante de la transition politique laisse l'État dans l'incapacité de répondre aux services sociaux de base des populations. 
Les déplacements internes de personnes ont augmenté de 100 000 en 2021, atteignant plus de 401 000 personnes soit quatre fois plus qu'il y a deux ans. Au total, 156 000 réfugiés maliens résident dans les pays voisins tandis que le Mali accueille 48 000 réfugiés et leur fournit protection et assistance. Les gains économiques du Mali se sont érodés, avec 900 000 personnes (0,04% de la population) qui sont retombées dans la pauvreté en raison de la crise socioéconomique de la COVID-19. la capacité des ménages est fragilisée à cause de la perte de revenus, de la réduction des transferts de fonds et à l'augmentation du coût de la vie. 
La Banque mondiale prévoit une augmentation du taux de pauvreté à 4,8 % en 2022. La crise de protection est également aggravée avec une augmentation des incidents de sécurité.  Les acteurs de la violence basée sur le genre (VBG) ont signalé 5 486 incidents de VBG, soit une augmentation de 41 % comparativement à la même période en 2020. Plus de 1 640 écoles sont fermées en raison de l'insécurité, affectant plus de 2,9 millions d'enfants dont 40 % se trouvent dans la région centrale de Mopti. Quatre districts centraux ont signalé que 40 % des écoles étaient fermées. Dans les régions du sud, 10 pour cent des écoles sont fermées à Koulikoro, Koutiala et Sikasso, privant 30 000 enfants de leur éducation. A ce jour, le Mali a rapporté plus de 15 800 cas de COVID-19.
En 2021, 1,3 million de personnes ont connu un niveau élevé d'insécurité alimentaire aiguë. le niveau le plus élevé depuis 2015, et 3 055 253 personnes ont été touchées par les mauvaises pluies et une saison de soudure prolongée. La situation humanitaire reste entravée par l'augmentation des besoins et la faiblesse des financements, avec 32 % des fonds mobilisés au 31 octobre 2021. Providing life-saving protection and health-care support to migrants and other populations in vulnerable situations in Lebanon ​PROVISION OF PROTECTION AND HUMANITARIAN ASSISTANCE SERVICES TO MIGRANTS IN VULNERABLE SITUATIONS  The project’s aim is to provide a range of protection services to migrants in need, strengthen links between targeted community groups and partners, improve the quality of services available, and enhance knowledge on migrant population groups in Lebanon. Services will target both male and female migrants, with a higher caseload of the latter group due to their increased number in country. Beneficiaries will typically be working age, between 18 and 40 years old. The services that IOM will deliver, either directly or through partners, include legal assistance, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), safe and temporary shelters for vulnerable migrants, provision of non-food items, multipurpose cash assistance (MPCA), and voluntary humanitarian return. These services will be made accessible to migrants by scaling up IOM’s pre-existing case management services, supporting enhanced capacity of, and referral with partners, strengthening culturally appropriate outreach to large migrant groups, including translation and interpretation,, and expanding community-level networks to strengthen targeted communities’ awareness of and access to IOM and partner services, as well as wider issues of concern. Additionally, IOM will provide training to partner organizations in case management, identification of vulnerable migrants and victims of trafficking, and Psychological First Aid, as well as other important thematic areas such as migrants with diverse SOGIESC and rights of migrants with regards to detention. Finally, enhancing knowledge of migrant populations will involve nationwide data-collection efforts via key informant interviews. The project will be implemented by the IOM in partnership with civil society organizations (CSO) and community-based initiatives. Provision of or onward referral to multisector assistance such as food or health support will be mainstreamed across the project.

Support for refugees and host communities affected by COVID-19 to prevent the spread of infection in South Sudan. Multi Sector Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2022, there are some 335,000 refugees and asylum seekers from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, primarily from Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic.
At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for longer term stability, hundreds of thousands of South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since the signing of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan, this spontaneous movement has prompted the development of an area-based approach, to support refugees, returnees and host communities, through enhanced engagement with development actors, to support greater access to services where possible.
Refugees largely reside in conflict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction in basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.
Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will benefit from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Specific protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identified at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with specific protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as verification exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the efficiency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to benefit from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

Right to Education for All for Displaced Children in Hard to Reach Areas of Southwest State of Somalia – READ Project Education in Emergencies Response for Crises Affected Children in Bay region of Somalia 
Conflict and environmental shocks have been the primary drivers of humanitarian needs in Somalia, leaving girls and boys out of school. According to the Protection Return Monitoring Network (PRMN), 593,000 people were displaced in Somalia between January and September 2021, of which 420,000 were displaced due to conflict and 98,000 due to drought1. Of the people displaced this year, an estimated 237,200 (40%) are school-aged children. In total, there is about 2.9 million displaced people in Somalia and an estimated 1 million of these are school-aged children.

FCA rapid needs assessment (10/21) highlighted the challenges faced by the assessed schools in baidoa and Dinsoor  which include  lack of accessible and gender friendly structures such as chairs,  desks, classrooms, latrines and handwashing facilities, accompanied by shortage of learning and teaching materials such as books, pens and chalks. Lack of qualified and inadequate number of teachers, especially female teachers as well as teachers who are trained in special education needs to handle children with CWDs and negative cultural norms have contributed to the low enrolment, attendance and retention of girls and CwD in schools. The barriers faced by CwD are not limited to those faced by girls, but their enrolment, retention and movement to education are hindered by additional stigma, discrimination and misconceptions. Lack of adequate fencing of the school compound to promote protection and safety and long distances to school cause safety concerns particularly for girls. EiE actors require capacity to provide quality education to CwD. Caregivers also faced with challenges in covering school fees, uniforms and scholastic materials. Strengthening the involvement of community in school management activities and mainstreaming child protection and child safeguarding mechanisms into education will improve access to education for girls and CwD.
Aligning with the 2022 Somalia Humanitarian Response Plan, the proposed initiative aims to restore and maintain access to and retention of crisis-affected school children to safe, protective, inclusive and continuous learning opportunities in Bay region of South West State of Somalia. The project will put a strong emphasis on an integrated approach to education focusing on access, quality of education, protection, child safeguarding, gender equality, conflict sensitivity, and disaster risk reduction (DRR) in the design, approach and activities. 
The proposed project will benefit 7100, crisis-affected children (4,400 children in Baidoa and 2,700 children in Dinsor) with at least 45% of girls. The vulnerable poor host community children (40%) will also be targeted since they are also affected by the crisis and have limited access to quality education. Protection and psychosocial well-being of the affected boys and girls as well as teachers is central to the project. FCA will closely work with Somalia Institute for Special Education Needs and Disability (SISEND), the only disability NGO in Somalia that specializes in special education needs, to provide capacity building to teachers, MoE and other education personnel. 
FCA has excellent capacity to scale up, applying best practices and lessons learned from its EiE experiences in other districts of South West State (Baidoa, El-berde and Hudur) to Dinsoor.. Utilizing FCA integrated and innovative approach based on well-known Finnish education system, FCA will take into account the potential impact of Covid-19 pandemic and develop innovative solutions to ensure uninterrupted access to education by the target children.

The proposed project will be implemented in Baidoa and Dinsoor where there are high number of IDP and are in IPC 3. The implementation will be done in close partnership with GREDO; a local NGO that is currently partnering with FCA on the ECHO funded EiE Projects. The project will also be implemented in close collaboration with MoE of Southwest State.

These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. ACT 3 NUTRITION Providing Life Saving Treatment and Prevention Nutrition Services to the Vulnerable Communities in Somalia Food and Nutrition context in Somalia
Decades of conflict and natural disasters including repeated droughts and seasonal flooding followed by limited government and institutional support have had a profound negative effect on the food security situation and social service sector in Somalia. Nearly seven in ten Somalis live on less than USD 1.90 per day,  the sixth-highest poverty rate in sub-Saharan Africa. Poverty is both widespread and deep, particularly for households in rural areas and internally displaced person (IDP) settlements. The number of food-insecure people experiencing long-term stress is trending upwards, indicating that chronic food insecurity persists, requiring sustainable solutions. Recurrent climate-related shocks and political instability are key drivers of food insecurity and pose continuing risks to crop production and food access. Malnutrition in Somalia is driven by a combination of factors such as recurrent food insecurity, child illnesses, high morbidity, micronutrient deficiencies, low immunization levels, poor access to clean water and sanitation, poor hygiene practice, gender inequality and discriminatory sociocultural attitudes leading to poor care practices. Based on the latest Post Gu FSNAU assessment (September 2021), it is estimated that a total of 3.5 million out of the 15.8m people face acute food insecurity (IPC 3 and above – crisis or worse)  until December 2021. At the national level the median prevalence of Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) has remained at a serious level of 11.1%. Approximately 1.2 million children under the age of five are likely to be acutely malnourished, including 295,515 who are likely to be severely malnourished. In addition to this, around 245,909 Pregnant & Lactating Women (PLWs) will be at risk of acute malnutrition. 

Acute malnutrition is a major public health problem in Somalia. It affects disproportionately children under the age of five, as well as Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLWs), especially among IDPs, vulnerable (agro) pastoralist communities and those living in areas affected by flooding. Morbidity among children is high (≥ 20%). Out of a total of 40 surveyed population groups 18 recorded high morbidity presence of above 20%. 
Vitamin A supplementation and Measles vaccination remains low <40% in several population groups. 

TB prevalence remains one of the highest globally with Somalia in the top 10 countries with high TB burden (262 per 100,000 population) while the HIV prevalence remains <1% however with high stigma and discrimination levels at 94%.

Project activities
The World Food Program is the leading UN agency in Somalia in fighting hunger. In Somalia, WFP together with the Ministry of Health (MoH), nutrition cluster and the partners, supports nutrition service delivery and prevention. WFP collaborates with the MoH and UNICEF to offer an integrated package of nutrition and health, following the revised MoH IMAM guidelines for treating acute malnutrition in Somalia.

WFP will cover both treatment and preventive nutrition services including:
•	Targeted Supplementary Feeding Program for 665,846 moderately acute malnourished children 6-59 months; 173,746 malnourished Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLW), 10,794 malnourished People Living with HIV on ART treatment and malnourished TB patients.
•	Preventive Nutrition services for 386,102 children 6-23 months and 173,746 PLW enrolled in Maternal Child Health and Nutrition services and blanket Supplementary Feeding Program for children 6-23 months and PLW in districts where GAM (Global Acute Malnutrition) rate is above 15%.
•	Monthly cash vouchers of USD 15 for 24,104 PLWs in selected target districts.
•	24,206 caregivers with SAM children admitted to the Stabilisation  will receive food while staying at the Stabilisation Center 
•	A total of 96,150 pregnant women will receive food rations for their families when delivering their baby at a health facility

Humanitarian support 2022 - Food security and nutrition Programa de seguridad alimentaria basado en la escuela  Con el objetivo de contribuir a la seguridad alimentaria de la población con mayores necesidades, el Programa Mundial de Alimentos de Naciones Unidas (WFP, por sus siglas en inglés) en Venezuela desarrolla un programa de asistencia humanitaria basado en la escuela para garantizar el acceso de los más vulnerables a una alimentación adecuada y nutritiva en el entorno escolar, familiar y comunitario. 
Este programa inició en 2021 con comidas escolares en emergencias priorizando escuelas iniciales y de educación especial.

WFP proporciona comidas escolares acompañado de un paquete integrado de intervenciones para mejorar el acceso a alimentos nutritivos y diversificados a través de las escuelas, contribuyendo al mismo tiempo a mejorar la salud y la nutrición de los niños en edad escolar, los estudiantes con discapacidad y el personal escolar, y apoyando a las comunidades a reducir la dependencia en estrategias de afrontamiento. De manera gradual, el WFP está realizando compras locales de alimentos, e incluyendo acciones para apoyar los mercados locales con compras a pequeños productores y apoyo técnico para acceso a mercados.

En este sentido, el programa de comidas escolares en emergencias tiene los siguientes componentes, para asegurar un enfoque integral que apoye al estudiante en el entorno escolar y familiar:

1. Entrega de comidas escolares nutritivas para estudiantes y personal escolar, promoviendo las compras locales y a pequeños productores.
2. Apoyo a la seguridad alimentaria del hogar a través de comida en especie o transferencias monetarias.
3. Rehabilitación de cocinas escolares para garantizar condiciones adecuadas de preparación de alimentos.
4. Comunicación para sensibilizar acerca de los principios humanitarios, la adecuada preparación de alimentos, nutrición, higiene y mantenimiento de cocinas escolares.
5. Fortalecimiento de capacidades de socios implementadores y personal escolar.
6. Acciones sensibles a la nutrición, que incluyen, tamizaje en las escuelas, educación nutricional, referencia a servicios especializados y entrega de alimento complementario fortificado (Supercereal Plus).

Humanitarian support 2022 - Food security and nutrition Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace.

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

Provision of life-saving, inclusive and sustainable WASH services to the conflict and climate-affected communities in Banadir, Middle Shabelle, and Hiraan Regions and emergency WASH assistance in Hirshabelle and Galmudug States of Somalia
COVID-19 Provision of Emergency and sustainable  WASH Services for Vulnerable IDPs and communities in Banadir (Kaxda and Deynile), Middle Shabelle (Balcad and Jowhar) and Galgadud region of Somalia (Adado, dusmareb and Guricel district). The continuation of protracted crises in Somalia, now compounded by the effects of Covid-19, Floods and droughts has resulted in massive challenges pertaining to Water, Sanitation and Hygiene. 
An estimated 6.4 million people, 40 per cent of the Somali population need emergency life-saving WASH assistance of which 3.5 million will need safe drinking water, 5.1 million sanitation services, and 6.4 million hygiene supplies. 16 per cent of these are females, children for 64 per cent and the elderly for 4 per cent. This presents an increase of 39 per cent from 2021, in which 4.6 million were estimated to be in need of WASH services across Somalia. This increase is due to adjusted population figures of Somalia, in combination with continuous failed rainy seasons, which are expected to further strain existing limited WASH services, especially in rural areas424. The population in need of WASH services in 2022 includes approximately 1,619,415 IDPs and 4,818,944 vulnerable host communities. Estimated that 6,058,603 people (38 per cent) in the Severe category” lack access to safe water and proper sanitation services and are highly vulnerable to AWD and cholera and around 379,757 people (2 percent) are in “extreme condition as they access water directly from rivers and surface bonds, practice open defecation and lack access to soap and other essential hygiene materials and are susceptible to communicable diseases.
The proposed project is designed to boost the ongoing lifesaving assistance and will target the most vulnerable displaced, floods, and drought-affected communities in Banadir, Galgadud, and Middle Shabelle regions of Somalia. At the moment, IDPs and urban poor and rural communities are among the most vulnerable groups in the society. Since the capacity of the local community to address their needs is very weak it is clear that the increasing number of IDPs and urban poor in crisis requires an urgent comprehensive action to support the target populations. The project responds to urgent humanitarian needs including (1) Deliver life-saving WASH assistance to reduce acute needs among the most vulnerable settlements and communities (2) Reduce the risk of violence against women, children, and vulnerable groups when accessing WASH services, and (3) Provide or restore sustainable access to safe water and adequate sanitation services in targeted communities and institutions.
Further, the target population will be involved in activities planning, implementation, and monitoring. Special attention will be given to women, children, and the elderly, and people with disabilities during the designing and construction WASH activities (i.e. 15% of all latrines will have disability-friendly features and will be constructed close to their shelters to ease access). Moreover, women will be part of WASH committees and will be represented in all community structures to empower them. Minority groups and femaleheaded households likely to face exclusion will be part of community-based committees to represent the voice of the minorities. Distribution sites will be pre-selected by target population and hygiene kits contents shared with beneficiaries allowing them to understand their rights and entitlements. Different distribution modalities will be used where protection concerns are mitigated and reported if they occur. The household-level distribution will be employed if people with disabilities and the elderly cannot access distribution sites.

Humanitarian support 2022 Provision of in-kind food assistance to Vulnerable Palestine refugees in Syria UNRWA estimates that 420,000 Palestine refugees in Syria will continue to require humanitarian assistance in 2022. In a context of rising inflation and additional economic hardship caused by COVID-19, Palestine refugees are more and more affected by food insecurity and therefore increasingly depend on UNRWA assistance to meet their minimum food needs. The Agency will continue to monitor the availability of food on the markets and will retain operational flexibility to adjust to a changing context as appropriate. The composition of the food basket was developed based on WFP guidelines and in view of meeting  50% of daily nutritional needs for 4 months. 
UNRWA's original plan is to distribute 3 rounds of in-kind food assistance, each round covering a period of 4 months. However, this depends on the availability of funds. Until January 2022, UNRWA received or confirmed pledges are only sufficient to cover the first two rounds of 2022. The Agency will continue to mobilize resources to ensure funding for the third round is also secured. In 2022, the number of people estimated to be in need of humanitarian assistance including for food needs is 420,000 Palestine refugees to strengthen their resilience and prevent further deterioration into acute food insecurity. As per its emergency planning, UNRWA aims to provide food assistance as well as multipurpose cash assistance, and protection interventions at both household and community levels, as well as the coordination of these activities across the different Sectors framework. The in-kind food assistance program remains one of the most important forms of UNRWA emergency support to stabilize the food security status for Palestine refugees in Syria with the MPC based on complementarity approach considering that MPC transfer value will not cover the full needs of the beneficiaries and the potential unavailability of fund.  , as it helps them meet part of their basic nutritional and survival requirements (~50% of kcal/person/day) which will increase resilience, and reduce humanitarian needs and the spiraling food insecurity levels.

Assistance alimentaire et nutritionnelle aux personnes déplacées internes dans les régions de Tahoua et Tillabéry Niger Country Strategic Plan  La vision de la réponse aux urgences dans le cadre du Plan Stratégique Pays (PSP) 2020-2024 du PAM Niger est la réduction de l’empreinte humanitaire dans la mise en œuvre de l’Activité 1, relative aux urgences du PSP à travers la promotion de l’approche NEXUS. Cette réponse s’inscrit dans la Stratégie de Prévention et de Gestion des Crises Alimentaires 2021 – 2025 du Dispositif National de Prévention et de Gestion de Crises Alimentaires (DNPGCA). Ce plan s’inscrit aussi dans le Plan d’Action 2021-2023 du Comité Technique Tripartite sur le Nexus Urgence-Développement (CTTNUD), en vue d’une mobilisation des ressources financières pour une planification et une mise en œuvre concertée des activités relatives à la promotion du NEXUS.  Dans le cas spécifique de l’assistance aux retournés dans leurs villages d’origine, qui est envisagée en 2022, la Loi 2018-74, relative à la protection et à l’assistance aux Personnes Déplacées Internes (PDI) cadrera le processus. Rappelons que l’Activité 1, relative aux urgences s’inscrit dans l’effet direct stratégique 1 du CSP (2020-2024) du PAM Niger « Les populations affectées, y compris les réfugiés, les personnes déplacées internes, les communautés hôtes et les retournés dans les zones ciblées sont en mesure de répondre aux besoins alimentaires minimums pendant et après la crise ».  La réponse aux urgences du PAM concernant la SECAL, basée sur une approche flexible, concernera toutes les trois (3) composantes de cette réponse en 2022 :
•	Le Mécanisme de Réponse Rapide (RRM)
•	La réponse aux crises prolongées.
•	La réponse à la soudure agricole et pastorale.
Par ailleurs la prévention de la malnutrition aux enfants 6-23 mois est combinée aux trois composantes ci-dessus.

Emergency flood-response through provision of Emergency Shelter in Gedo region Provision of life-saving Shelter and Non-Food Item (NFI) support to vulnerable populations in Somalia For HRP 2022, IOM will contribute to the cluster objectives namely: CO#1: Ensure that persons affected by conflict and natural disasters have protection from the weather and privacy through provision of shelter and NFIs; and CO#2: Vulnerable displacement and disasters affected populations have access to transitional or durable shelter, enabling safer and more dignified living standards and preventing recovering communities from slipping back into humanitarian need; through provision of: (1) NFI support to 10,000 newly displaced households through in-kind (through contingency stocks – 5,000 kits) and Cash-Based Interventions (CBI)); (2) Emergency (3,000 households (HH)), transitional (1,000) and permanent shelter (250) support through mix methods of in-kind and CBI; (3) Mainstream risk and resilience into project activities through infrastructural support and site de-congestion activities (500 HH). Interventions will focus on Baidoa, Dollow and Kismayo.

Somalia is at the crossroads of mixed and complex migration flows, often resulting in internal and external displacement due to ongoing conflicts, climate-related shocks, communicable disease outbreaks and weak social protection mechanisms. It is estimated that the pressing need for shelter has persisted and worsened into 2021; the 2022 Humanitarian Needs Overview for Somalia estimates that 3.6 million people are in need of shelter and NFI assistance with 2.7 million of these categorised as displaced population with 573,000 being newly displaced with an increasing trend of migration to urban centres related to climatic shocks, insecurity and better livelihood opportunities.

For the 2022 HRP, IOM will focus on providing 60,000 individuals with NFI support through a mixed method of in-kind and CBI support through contingency stocks and direct implementation respectively. A further 24,000 individuals will receive shelter support either emergency, transitional or permanent shelter using in-kind or CBIs. The unit cost for durable shelters is 3,000 USD. Finally, 3,000 individuals will receive infrastructure support under umbrella of risk reduction activities or site decongestion.

Humanitarian support 2022, emergency support to livelihoods. Amélioration de la qualité et de la coordination de la réponse aux situations d’urgence Le Mali comme la majeure partie des pays de la zone Sahélienne, est confronté à une crise humanitaire depuis plusieurs années qui tend à s’aggraver au lieu de diminuer. Parmi les principales causes, il peut être citer les conséquences des changements climatiques qui frappent durement les pays de la zone avec des phénomènes comme l’irrégularité des pluies, les inondations, les sécheresses localisées ou généralisées. A ces phénomènes, il faut ajouter les épidémies comme le cholera ou encore la COVID 19. En effet, Afin de lutter efficacement comme la pandémie de la COVID 19, les pays de la zone sahélienne dont restreint les mouvements des populations, fermer des marchés ou encore instaurer des couvres feu. Ces mesures ont négativement impacté les revenus des ménages les plus vulnérables. De même, du fait des mesures de restriction liées à la COVID 19, les transferts monétaires des Maliens de l’étranger vers leurs familles restées au pays ont diminué de manière significative augmentant par la même occasion la vulnérabilité des populations. Mais c’est la situation d’insécurité qui prévaut dans le nord et le centre du pays qui est à la base de la plus grande crise humanitaire actuelle. En effet, un grand nombre de ménages ne sont pas en mesure de se rendre dans leurs champs pour cultiver du fait de l’insécurité qui règne. De même, du fait de la fermeture de nombreux marchés itinérants de fait de l’insécurité, les ménages ne sont plus en mesure vendre leurs surplus de récoltes ou de se ravitailler. Mais la conséquence la plus visible de cette situation d’insécurité est le déplacement d’un grand nombre de ménages principalement issus du milieu rural. Selon le DTM de septembre 2022, ce sont 401.736 personnes déplacées internes soit (69.696 ménages) qui ont été enregistrés sur l’ensemble du territoire malien. Les zones d’installation de ces personnes déplacées internes sont les suivantes, Bamako, Gao, Kayes, Kidal, Koulikoro, Ménaka, Mopti, Ségou, Sikasso. 
Afin de répondre à ces différentes situations d’urgence, plusieurs organisations développent des projets qu’ils mettent en œuvre au profit des ménages affectés. Cependant, force est reconnaitre qu’il y a souvent un manque de préparation et un déficit de coordination sur le terrain. 
Le présent projet vise à répondre à cette faiblesse de la réponse aux situations d’urgence en renforçant les capacités des organisations sur la préparation et la réponse mais également en renforçant la coordination entre les acteurs de la réponse humanitaire.

Humanitarian support 2022 - emergency support to livelihoods. Assistance aux populations victimes du déficit céréalier de 2021 des Régions de Tahoua, Tillabéri, Dosso, Diffa, Maradi et Agadez A l’issue de la campagne agricole 2021, il a été enregistré 6430 villages déficitaires à plus de 50% pour une population estimée à 8 762 358 personnes.Ce déficite résulte du changement climatique (dont l'impact a été des sécheresses prolongées, des inondations, un arrêt précoce de la saison pluvieuse), une détérioration de la situation sécuritaire qui continue d’impacter négativement l'éffort de production des populations et leurs moyens d’existence dans certaines zones localisées des régions de Diffa, Tillabéri, le  nord Tahoua et le sud-ouest de Maradi. La production céréalière brute 2021 est estimée à 3 562 549 tonnes (contre 5 576 371 tonnes en 2020) soit une baisse de 36% par rapport à l’année 2020. A l'heure, c'est environ 2 554 833 personnes (364,976 ménages) qui sont en insécurité alimentaire sévère et qui nécessitent une aide humanitaire d'urgence.Pour répondre à cette crise alimentaire, le gouvernement a élaboré un plan d'urgence estimé à plus de  280 Milliards de Dollars USD pour la période de novembre 2021 à Mars 2022 en attendant l'élaboration du plan de soutien . Selon les résultats de cadre harmonisé de novembre 3.6 millions de personnes seraient en insécurité alimentaire en période de soudure s'y les réponses adaquates ne sont pas apportées. L’objectif global du Plan d’urgence est de contribuer à la sécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle des populations vulnérables affectées par cette crise humanitaire à travers des actions harmonisées d’assistance alimentaire et de protection de leurs moyens d’existence. Le plan vise à améliorer l’accès aux aliments pour les ménages vulnérables, protéger et renforcer les moyens d’existence des ménages vulnérables, faciliter l’accès aux intrants agricoles, vétérinaires et zootechniques des ménages vulnérables.Ainsi en soutien au plan de d'urgence, de soutien et du plan de réponse humanitaire  en lien avec la stratégie du ccluster sécurité alimentaire la FAO apportera un appui au volet agricole par un soutien à la production agricole à 91144 ménages vulnérables et des appuis AGR.

Humanitarian support 2022 - emergency support to livelihoods Emergency Lifesaving Cash and Livelihood Support to IDP and Non- IDP Communities in Somalia Somalia is facing a severe and deteriorating humanitarian crisis as we enter 2022 as a result of the compounding effects of conflict, recurrent climate shocks, diseases and pests outbreaks with increased levels of vulnerability and substantial increase in the humanitarian caseload (Somalia HNO, 2022). There is a serious risk that the impact of consecutive below average to poor rainfall in most parts of the country will develop into a severe drought by early to mid- 2022 with the number of people facing acute food insecurity on the rise. It is likely that minority groups, women, children, people with disabilities, will experience heightened protection risks as a result, unless they are intentionally targeted to receive tailored assistance.

With approximately 3.5 million individuals in IPC 3 and 4 through at least December 2021, FAO proposes to target 160,300 households (961,800 individuals- 91,500 IDPs and 870,300 non- IDPs) in IPC 3 and IPC 4 caseloads respectively. This will include 216,790 women, 254,492 girls, 264,880 boys and 225,638 men and 144,270 people living with disabilities (PWD) across 59 districts in Somalia through its flagship Cash+ approach combining short-term cash transfers with tailored livelihood support in accordance with technical and humanitarian standards. Vulnerable households will identified from at-risk pastoral, agro-pastoral, fishing, riverine farmers, IDPs and Non- IDP communities in IPC 3 and 4 areas. This intervention will integrate short-term cash transfers aimed at enabling the most vulnerable households to meet their immediate needs, with livelihood support to allow crisis-affected households to get back into production. FAO will employ community- led beneficiary selection processes and ensure adequate targeting and representation of extremely vulnerable and minority groups in community committees. Interventions proposed will employ a Do No Harm approach with a gender lens that ensures conflict- sensitivity to reduce protection risks for all individuals, and to mitigate the risk of conflict or community tensions. 

Under Food Security Cluster (FSC) Objective 1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 160,300 households through a blend of conditional (Cash-for-Work) and unconditional (UCT) transfers. Under UCT, FAO will prioritize Cash+ interventions including Cash+ Agriculture, Cash+ livestock and Cash+ fisheries. These modalities will increase households’ immediate access to food by providing sufficient cash to access the minimum expenditure basket (MEB), while supporting the rehabilitation of critical productive and community infrastructure. It will also boost household food production, increase household incomes and create employment opportunities. Cash transfer values will be informed by the Cash Working Group and are expected to differ per district/ region of intervention. They, however, will be valued at 80 percent of the food MEB, which can range from USD 50- 100 per month. All cash-based programmes will include training on good nutrition practices. 

Under FSC Objective 2, to protect livelihoods and related food sources, FAO will provide in-kind, technical support and tailored trainings to 112,500 HHs to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security and nutrition threats, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to targeted HHs. In addition, FAO shall provide transitional cash support to 13,100 HHs across agro pastoral, pastoral and fishing livelihood zones to augment the adaptive capacity of HHs, strengthen and foster resilience to future shocks, cushioning them from food insecurity and malnutrition. Trainings shall be delivered alongside input provision to build skills in sustainable use of resources provided, build skills in livelihoods management including harvest, post- harvest management, linking beneficiaries to long- term interventions that provide them opportunities to enhance their livelihoods and skills.

Provision of lifesaving and emergency livelihoods support to the most vulnerable agro-pastoral affected by drought in Rural Bardhere districts of Gedo region, Somalia. Providing Food Security and Livelihood Assistance to the most vulnerable communities in Gedo, Lower Juba and Galgadud regions According to FSNAU Post-Gu Technical Report released September 2021, indicates that from Oct–Dec 2021, food insecurity is expected to further deteriorate among poor rural, urban, and displaced populations including Galgadud, Gedo and Lower Juba regions due to the impacts of anticipated, below-average 2021 Deyr (Oct-Dec) season rainfall, continued insecurity and other food security related risk factors, including rising food prices and cost of living, declining availability of milk for both consumption and sale, and a likely reduction in agricultural employment opportunities during the forthcoming Deyr season.
Furthermore, FSNAU Post-Gu Technical Report –September 2021, points out that estimated 55,290  people in Galgadud region including Abudwak district are experiencing food crisis/or IPC 3 and estimated 3,900 people in the rural parts are in IPC 4, translating to about 13% of total in Crisis and Emergency as percentage of total population. In Gedo region a significant number of people (66,080) are in IPC 3 and 6,430 people are in the IPC 4, translating to about 15% of total in Crisis and Emergency as proportion of total population. As for Lower Juba region, encompassing Badhadhe district, an estimated 93,830 people are in IPC 3 and 8,840 of the population are in IPC 4, representing about 12% of the total population. 

Cluster Objective 1: Improve access to food for 3.1 million of people facing severe acute food insecurity including million IDPs, 2 million non-displaced people and persons with disabilities in 64 districts. ADA will aim to improve immediate access to food to at least 5,250 households. 

Cluster Objective 2:  Protect livelihoods and related food sources for 830 000 farmers, pastoralists, agro pastoralist and 163 000 rural IDPs across Somalia through emergency agriculture, livestock, and other livelihoods support. ADA will ensure to  protect  and  restore  livelihoods  related  to  food  and  income  sources at least 3,500 households will be reached.

The planned project activities are;
Activity 1: Community mobilization, identification of 10 water catchments and household that are vulnerable but can provide labour for deepening and expansion of productive facilities. 
Activity 2 Procurement and provision of seeds to agro-pastoralist farmers (12kg sorghum, 10kg cowpea and 10 Kg maize) for 3,500 farmers at least 30% women.
Activity 3 Training of farmers on good agronomic practices including conservation agriculture reaching 10% of the target farmers.
Activity 4: 5,250 agro-pastoralist households have increased access to productive assets through rehabilitation of water catchments.
Activity 5: Desilt community water catchments through Cash for Work to increase water storage by 4,200,000lts seasonally in each pan in respective village. The water catchments will provide water for human and livestock and enable the local population to concentrate on crop production.

The livestock will have enough water for drinking, having enough water available to livestock allows for optimal animal performance and health. High water in-take, and the more an animal drinks, the more the milk production and better animal performance. The availability of milk and meat obtained from the livestock, will mean that the household's income will be better, since the households have substitutes to either trade the livestock or sell the direct consumption outputs such as milk or meat, thus the household will utilise the money obtained from such action in many ways, which will consequently enhance the food security situation of the households. 
Activity 6: Conduct post distribution monitoring in each cycle of CFW payments to beneficiaries and food distribution, where at least 5% of the target beneficiaries will be interviewed.
Activity 7: Conduct crop yield assessments for the planted crop stages.
Activity 8: At least 3,000 animals comprising of goats and cows will be supported in animal interventions including support in treatment.

Integrated Shelter/(HLP) and CCCM response to the displaced persons by providing shelter and NFIs and HLP services in Afmadow and Dobley districts in Lower Juba Provision of Emergency shelter Kits and Non Food Items to the most Vulnerable IDPs and the Host community in South and Central Regions of Somalia According to the JMCNA 2021, shelter is one of the top three priority need of more than half of the entire population and of 58 percent of IDPs. An estimated 3.7 million people need shelter and NFI assistance mainly due to poor shelter conditions, overcrowding and lack of space, poverty, and lack of security of tenure. Those in need of shelter and NFI assistance include displaced and non-displaced populations. Conflict, drought, flooding, evictions and cyclones are the key drivers of displacement, which in turn exacerbates humanitarian shelter and NFI needs. Natural disasters are one of the main causes of displacement and therefore accelerate migration from rural to urban and peri-urban centers that started decades ago. Urbanization is rarely organized through urban planning and multiyear plans. Women and girls living in sub-standard and overcrowded shelters are particularly vulnerable. They tend not to feel safe in makeshift shelters which do not offer privacy and sufficient protection from weather elements and increase the risk of gender based violence. Juba Foundation conducted a quick assessment that aimed to ascertain the needs of over 50,000 beneficiaries in the targeted regions, it was noted from the assessment that women and girls are at risk of disaeses as most of them live in makeshift shelter and face the risk of eviction, there is no land tenure security. It is with this in mind that Juba foundation proposes to intervene and provide emergency shelter kits to 3000 HHs  (18000 individuals both women, men, boys and girls) 4000 HHs with Non Food Items (24,000 women, men, boys and girls) and also construction of 400 transitional shelter) in Lower Shabelle, Lower Juba, Galgaduud, Hiraan, Bay and Bakool Regions. Juba foundation will conduct a market assessment in the target areas to establish the functionality of the markets and the availability of the commodities, this will be done to ascertain the modality that will be used for delivery of the Non Food items and ESK. Where feasible vouchers will be used.

Emergency livelihoods support to the most vulnerable drought affected populations (farmers, pastoralists, agro pastoralists and rural IDPs) Provision of Livelihood Support and Farm Inputs to Crisis-Affected IDPs in Banadir and Farmers in Middle Shabelle of Somalia. Protracted political instability, continued population’s displacements, ongoing armed conflict, and enduring environmental stress have rendered many of the country’s estimated 15.7 million people to be acutely food insecure. It is projected that drought will be one of one of the primary drivers of food insecurity in the country in 2022. This is largely attributed to the La Nina condition experienced in the greater Horn of Africa region.

2021 witnessed a delayed start, early end, and erratic rainfall distribution of the Gu rainfall season as a result, cumulative rainfall was below the 40-year average across much of the country, especially in central and southern Somalia. Forecasted La Niña conditions are associated with an elevated likelihood of consecutive below-average rainfall seasons, and Somalia faces a high risk that drought conditions will develop by early 2022.

According to Post- Gu assessment done by FSNAU and FEWS NET in September 2021, 3.5 million persons would be in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) through to December 2021, if urgent humanitarian assistance is not provided. Of this, 1.1 are Internally Displaced Persons who are likely to face moderate to severe food consumption gap. 640,000 persons of the 3.5M people in need of urgent food assistance are facing significant food gap, this is envisaged to continue until late in 2021. Further 3.7M people in IPC Phase 3 (stressed) that engaged in negative coping strategies to meet their food and non-food needs may push the total of acute food insecure population to 7.2M by December, 2021.

Cyclic climatic shocks and perennial conflicts are negatively impacting on traditional rural livelihoods resulting influx to urban centers. This is expected to continue in 2022 further exacerbating food insecurity that already biting in the country. It is projected that girls and women will be disproportionately impacted if urgent and deliberate interventions are not put in place. Girls and women are likely to take on opportunities to place food on their families’ tables, fetch water and other duties that would not only burden them but also put them at risks of violations and exploitations. 

Other drivers of food insecurity include lack of information by minority and marginalized groups stemming from lack of consultation and participation in decision making, pushing the included groups to the brink of starvation.

Impact of COVID-19, crippling poverty levels, and protection concerns; particularly among
vulnerable groups like Internally Displaced Persons, women headed households, girls, elderly and minority communities and persons with disabilities are likely to exacerbate food consumption gaps among urban communities.

Aid Vision proposed project is aimed at providing access to lifesaving and sustaining food security and livelihood interventions to 9,000 crisis affected population in Banadir and Middle Shabelle Regions, Aid Vision has presence in the two regions for over two decades and established networks of community structures and local authorities. The project will provide Cash Based interventions, rehabilitation of farming infrastructure, provision farm inputs, irrigation support, training of farmers on contemporary farming techniques and provision of agricultural extension services. It is envisioned that the interventions will go a long way in not only improving food security in the target regions but also enhance community resilience to shocks in future.

Emergency livelihoods support to drought affected rural communities in Belet_Xaawo district, Gedo region Provision of Life Saving assistance to the disaster affected communities in Somalia Recurrent drought has severely and directly affected communities whose sources of food, income and water are diminishing and increasingly at risk. This has led to HH food insecurity, sharp increase in debt levels among poor HHs and poor animal health and produce. 
A delayed and poor Deyr season, worsened drought conditions in the target regions resulting in majority of HHs having inadequate access to food and water while staple food and commodity prices have risen at an average of 8.5% in Gedo and 24% in Bay regions over the past year (COOPI PNA, Oct 2021). From October to December 2021, food insecurity is expected to further deteriorate among poor rural, urban, and displaced populations due to the impacts of anticipated, below-average 2021 Deyr (October-December) season rainfall, continued insecurity and other food security related risk factors, including rising food prices and cost of living, declining availability of milk for both consumption and sale, and a likely reduction in agricultural employment opportunities during the forthcoming Deyr season.
The project focuses on the delivery of basic lifesaving and protection/restoration of livelihoods of the target population with a special focus on all locations with FSC prioritized persons in need, including IDPs and host communities that are classified in IPC Phase 3 & 4 in terms of response. 
The project is aimed at improving the ability of vulnerable HHs to meet their basic needs, supports protection and recovery of livelihood assets through life-saving UCT, animal treatment services, provision of locally preferred high quality seeds kits and trainings, and rehabilitation of community productive assets through CFW to support the resilience of vulnerable populations against shocks and prevent them from slipping into acute food insecurity. The proposed project aims to target at least 6,600 HHs (39,600) pastoral, agro-pastoral and IDP HHs in Bay, Banadir, Gedo and Togdheer regions in crisis and emergency with delivery of life saving interventions in line with the strategic objectives of the HRP and FSC response plan.
The project is informed by the centrality of protection and a gender, age and diversity-sensitive approach which is mainstreamed throughout the project cycle. Moreover, the project reflects the principles of COOPI Protection Policy and is built consistently with COOPI Protection SOPs and Protection Mainstreaming guidelines. The project will be guided by the principles of DO NO HARM, ensuring safety and dignity of target population is upheld and at the same time providing for accountability, participation and empowerment. COOPI prioritizes respect for the rights, dignity and safety of the people affected by crisis and is committed to taking account of, giving account to, and being held to account by the populations benefiting from the intervention. During implementation, the beneficiary women, girls and the disabled will be included in decision making processes and in monitoring so as ensure that the most marginalized and vulnerable are represented and have influence.
In summary the following activities will be carried out:
1.	Provide UCT to 3,100 HHs that are faced with severe levels of food insecurity (crisis and emergency) with the aim of improving immediate access to food for 3 months.
2.	Rehabilitation of community productive assets through CFW targeting 1,000 vulnerable HHs.
3.	Provision of locally preferred high quality seed kits, trainings and fuel for irrigation for 500 flood affected female and male headed vulnerable riverine farmers in Bele-Hawa Gedo region.
4.	Provision of locally preferred high quality seeds kit (drought tolerant) and trainings for 1,000 female and male headed vulnerable agro-pastoral farmers in Burhakaba district, Bay region.
5.	Emergency livestock treatment (treatment and deworming) campaigns for animals belonging to 1,000 HHs will be dewormed and treated against endemic &prevalent diseases.

Provision of life saving WASH services and ensure dignity for drought affected communities in Luuq District, Gedo region Somalia Response to immediate and sustainable access to safe and equitable basic WASH services in Somalia  The high humanitarian needs in Somalia are driven by seasonal floods, severe drought conditions, acute water diarrhoea/ cholera outbreaks exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. According to 2022 HNO, The population in need of WASH services in 2022 is estimated at 1,619,415 IDPs and 4,818,944 vulnerable host communities. Access to basic water supply in Somalia is 37% in rural and 79 % in urban areas. The JMCNA assessment report 2021 approximates that 39% of the vulnerable people in Somalia do not have access to sustained, improved and safe water source for drinking and other domestic uses, while 25 per cent still walk for more than 15 minutes to collect water from a nearest water source. In addition, 16% of households do not have access to enough drinking water while 45% reported having no access to soap, while more than half of HHs reported lacking access to improved latrines and menstrual hygiene materials. CCCM cluster reports indicate that the majority of those most acutely affected are vulnerable groups; women, elderly, refugee returnees, minority groups and people living with disability (PLWD), putting further stressing affected families and limiting their ability to cope. In October 2021, Ministry of Water and Energy-Jubaland (Gedo Regional Office) and Regional WASH Cluster (Gedo Region) needs assessment report indicates that the drought situation in Gedo region is continually deteriorating. This has worsened in Doolow where estimated 5,244 household have no access to clean and adequate water Doolow due to displacements during recent inter clan conflicts in 17 riverine villages. The same scenario exists in Luuq District where more than 7, 120, HHs living in northern and south rural villages are also in need of basic WASH services including specific appeal for hygiene kits and sanitation tools. The inadequate access to water and sanitation services are particularly prevalent across the majority of congested IDP sites compared to host communities, which in turn leads to higher rates of acute diarrheal and other water-borne diseases, increasing the risk of malnutrition and disability. Further, aggravating the recurrent drought situation in Somalia, the Somalia Water and Land Information Management SWALIM reports that around 40% of existing water supply systems are non-functional mainly due to weak water supply management resulting to affected populations to depend on water trucking. For the year 2022, COOPI proposes to address the immediate Water, Sanitation and Hygiene needs of the severely affected people while sustaining ongoing response in Doolow, Luuq, Owdweyne, Baidoa and Banadir through activities aligned with the Humanitarian Programme Cycle for 2022. As part of the intervention, COOPI will purposefully target PLWD during identification of beneficiaries, design and build facilities to ensure accessibility to all, ensure Water Management Committees include at least one member with disability and that WASH campaigns are all inclusive.

Integrating CCCM response by strengthening safe access to multi sectorial services including emergency responses at site level in Dhobley and Afmadow IDP Camps Improve living conditions of Internally Displaced People (IDPs) through site development, care and maintenance and decongestion initiatives in Afgoye, Wanla Weyne and Marka (lower Shabelle region), Dhusaamareeb (Galgaduud region) and Mogadishu (Kahda, Daynile, Dharkeenley) Banadir region Conflict, drought, COVID-19, and flooding are only a few of the major shocks that have uprooted at least 2.9 million Somalis. In urban, semi-urban, and rural locations around the country, the bulk of displaced persons have self-settled in over 2,400 substandard and unplanned IDP settlements. Persons who have been displaced to these locations are living in dangerous situations, with the majority of them not being able to meet their basic needs due to inconsistencies in service delivery or being denied access to humanitarian aid. More than 80% of sites are informal settlements situated on private land, with the bulk of sites located in metropolitan areas, according to the CCCM cluster's comprehensive site assessment findings (DSA) and site verification assessments.
In Somalia, internally displaced persons (IDPs) are the most vulnerable population group: Somalia's IDP population continues to exhibit traits that make them more vulnerable than people living in host communities, whether they are urban or rural. Factors like as deplorable living conditions in settlements, inclusion challenges, and overall disenfranchisement in obtaining key services continue to be common among IDPs, making it even more challenging for these populations to achieve substantive change. Persons with disabilities (PWDs), members of minority clans, women, and youth are among the populations in IDP camps with the most pressing needs, and they face significant challenges to receiving humanitarian aid, preventing them from living in dignified conditions.
Therefore, the overall goal of the proposed initiative is to improve the living conditions and general security of IDP population in the camps, as well as provide fair access to services and assistance for all those in need. Through this, the initiative is anticipated to strengthen safe access to multi sectorial services at site level through improved site management and coordination. Secondly, the project will improve living conditions of displaced people through site development, care and maintenance and decongestion initiatives. Lastly, the project is anticipated to strengthen community self-management and access to information for displaced populations.
The outcome of the initiative is to have site- level information available and shared with stakeholders.  The activities that will generate this outcome include; conducting site verifications on bi-annual basis, establishing or updating service mapping of partners operating in various sites at the target districts.  Carry out service monitoring activities on monthly basis aimed at highlighting service gaps at the site-level and ensuring that minimum standards are being adhered to.
The second outcome is to have activities aimed at improving site-level living conditions administered across the regions targeted by the project. This will include; providing trainings on-site maintenance and site planning to camp committees; supporting community-led site maintenance activities to ensure upkeep of sites (cash for work, site maintenance committees, distribution of tools); implementing emergency sites improvement activities to minimize protection risks and ensure safety in sites (flood mitigation, fire prevention). Administer joint stakeholder site decongestion activities allowing for short-term improvements in settlement standards, minimizing protection threats and ameliorating COVID-19 transmission. Conduct safety audits annually to inform site improvement activities and to illustrate targeted initiatives that sector agencies should administered
Lastly, the project aims at ensuring that all sites in the target districts have a governance structure in place that serves to fulfil the needs of the displaced population. This will be achieved by undertaking mapping of existing community structures; providing core trainings (CMC Training Package) to community governance structures; identifying and supporting governance structures, encouraging participation.

Lifesaving Response to Worsening Drought in Hotspot Locations within Puntland WASH Response to Drought and conflict - Affected Population in Mudug, Nugaal, Sanaag, Bari, Galgaduud and Hiraan regions in Somalia  In Somalia, Only 52% of the  population has access to basic water supply, with limited regulation of private water supplies frequently resulting in high prices, forcing families to fetch water from distant and unsafe open wells. In conflict-affected areas and camps for displaced people, access to safe water is frequently hampered due to damaged water infrastructure, which increases the risk of disease and malnutrition among people living in overcrowded conditions. In March 2021 alone, over 70 boreholes were reported to have broken in Puntland and Galmudug regional states due to over-use, weak management, and high operation and maintenance costs, forcing IDPs and host communities to buy water at prohibitive costs. According to a UNICEF report published in 2020, sanitation and hygiene coverage in Somalia is low, with only 38% of the population having access to basic sanitation facilities and services, posing a high rate of open defecation that leads to contamination of water sources and increases the risk of disease outbreaks. Hand washing with soap at critical moments is practiced by only one-third of the population due to a lack of soap and access to a functional handwashing point Coupled by poor knowledge of good hygiene and sanitation practices. WASH in health care institutions has been a source of concern for many years. A significant proportion of Somalia's health facilities lack on-site water connections and rely on water trucks from long distances. This severely jeopardizes service delivery and undermines safe WASH practices, which are critical in controlling and preventing disease outbreaks. This proposed project will increase access to safe and clean water, promote sanitation and hygiene conditions, and contribute to a reduction in infant and under-5 mortality rates as well as WASH-related diseases in general. The project will address the needs of 28,000 vulnerable population in Somalia's Mudug, Nugaal, Sanaag, Galmudug, and Hiraan regions. This will be done through the rehabilitation of boreholes with solar installations, extension of pipelines and water tank construction for communities and health facilities to improve access and storage, provision of water vouchers, rehabilitation of shallow wells, and training of community structures (committees) to increase their capacity to manage and maintain rehabilitated water systems. In addition, the IRC will construct/rehabilitate sanitation facilities (latrines and solid waste management infrastructure) with a focus on IDPs, as well as ensure access to essential WASH services in health facilities to improve health and nutritional outcomes. In addition, IRC will promote hygiene and sanitation and distribute basic hygiene kits to households, including materials for menstrual management. (Applying market –based programming approach where feasible as a complement to in-kind distribution).  The IRC will target communities in hard-to-reach areas with limited access to WASH services, as well as those in cholera/AWD hotspots and crowded IDP settlements, with particular focus on the COVID-19 situation, risk management, and infection prevention and control measures. The proposed response will be delivered through a strong protection lens, which will include efforts to ensure that latrines are gender separated, have lockable doors, adequate lighting, and that the distance to water points is kept within the agreed-upon standards. The IRC will adopt a universal design to ensure water and sanitation facilities are accessible to all, including persons with disabilities.  The project will also consider the impact of conflict on women and children in terms of access to WASH services, as well as the unique needs of menstruating women and girls. The proposed actions will address and prevent gender-based violence risks, thereby improving and contributing to greater gender equality.

Emergency Food Security and Livelihood support to the most vulnerable drought affected groups (pastoralists, agro-pastoralists, farmers and rural IDPs) in Luuq and Dollow Districts – Gedo Region Livelihood Support for vulnerable IDPs and poor Host Communities in Mudug and Galgadud Regions-Galmudug State of Somalia. Mercy Corps proposes a project on Livelihood Support targeting vulnerable IDPs and poor host communities in Mudug and Galgadud Regions of Galmudug State of Somalia, with the aim to contribute to the achievement of FSC strategies and objectives aligned to the HRP 2022. The project will benefit a total of 4,120vulnerable and marginalized households (1,100 Men, 1,500 women, 600 boys, 920 girls) in IDPs and host communities in Galkayo, Hobyo, Caabudwaq and Caadado Districts. The proposed intervention will improve immediate access to food, provide livelihood inputs (Livestock), and skills training for new livelihoods for the communities. Access to immediate food assistance will be provided through Conditional and Unconditional Cash transfers in forms of the multipurpose cash assistance and food vouchers to meet their basic needs and to protect and restore livelihoods, related food, and income sources. Communities will also participate in the rehabilitation and establishment of community infrastructure such as water catchments, and feeder roads, whereby they will receive cash-for-work and pastoral households will receive livelihood assets in form of livestock restocking for restoration. Technical vocational skills training will also be provided as a form of building new livelihoods.  The project targets the most vulnerable populations categorized as facing IPC Phases 3 and 4.
The proposed project is cognizant of the current food security context of Galmudug region of Somalia. According to FSNAU and FEWS NET, Post-Gu Assessment in September 2021 projected that nearly 3.5 million Somalis would be in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) through at least December 2021, in the absence of humanitarian assistance. That includes 1.1 million internally displaced persons who will face moderate to large food consumption gaps through late 2021. Out of the total 3.5 million people in need of urgent food assistance, 640,000 people face significant food consumption gaps. In addition, 3.7 million people are classified in IPC phase 2 (Stressed), engaging in negative coping strategies to meet their food and non-food needs, bringing the total number of Somalis experiencing acute food insecurity to 7.2 million by late 2021. In addition to, majority of the estimated 2.9 million IDPs across Somalia are poor with limited livelihood assets, few income earning opportunities, low communal support, and rely heavily on external humanitarian assistance. As a result, one-third of internally displaced persons (in both rural and urban settlements) face moderate to large food consumption gaps through late 2021. The COVID-19 pandemic and related containment measures seem to affect the urban poor population more than rural poor population. As a result, the urban poor face moderate to large food consumption gaps, partly due to a slowdown in economic activities in urban areas and the rising costs of food and other essential non-food items. 
Mercy Corps field assessments in target regions revealed the deepening effect of frequent droughts and conflicts, which have led to high food consumption gaps and loss of livelihood assets. There is urgent need to address the food insecurity and livelihood threats for the IDPs and communities in the region. As the food security situation in Galmudug state remains tenuous, Mercy Corps sees an urgent need to respond and save lives, alleviate human suffering, and reduce the social and economic impact of the humanitarian crisis. This will reduce acute humanitarian needs and excess mortality among the most vulnerable by providing lifesaving and sustaining integrated assistance. The project will consider all gender groups and disability needs in implementation and will maintain accountability to the population through ensuring community feedback mechanisms and adherence to policies.

For the beneficiaries’ selection and registration, NRC will use an electronic mobile data collection tool called Kobo tool box, which provides an accurate and real time data.
