Integrated shelter, HLP and CCCM assistance to displacement affected community in Bossaso Strengthening protection and durable solutions in Somalia through an integrated and holistic Housing Land and Property (HLP) response  The Housing, Land and Property (HLP) challenges confronting displaced communities in Somalia are protracted and multifaceted limiting access to and impacting the enjoyment of HLP rights. The centrality of Housing, Land and Property (HLP) is a key component of achieving sustainable durable solutions to displacement. Despite increased prevention efforts, over 100,000 individuals have been forcefully evicted across Somalia in 2021 alone and 1,054,306 persons in a span of five years (HLP Sub cluster 2021). The HLP challenges are created by repeated and protracted displacement in urban areas that are exacerbated by the high demand (in the context of rapid urbanisation, investment and development) and rocketing land prices. This has been compounded by competing claims on land coupled with limited legal and policy frameworks around HLP rights, inadequate technical and functional land registries or departments.  And yet, evictions, forced or otherwise result in widespread protection risks, impact victims’ dignity, livelihoods, physical safety and reverses incremental gains made in attaining sustainable durable solutions. 
Further to this, the shelter situation in Somalia is critical, coupled with limited public land available to establish new settlements. 85% of informal settlements are constructed on private land (CCCM Cluster, 2020). Moreover, tenure insecurity remains widespread, leading to an alarming rate of forced evictions countrywide. Most informal settlements are either without formal documents or written land tenure agreements or have in place some form of short-term arrangements (Shelter Cluster, 2020). In addition to this, IDPs who lack legal identity documents, specifically nationality documents and civil registration such as birth certificates are disproportionately affected. There is increasing evidence that legal identity is linked to HLP rights. Land owners are increasingly demanding for proof of identity as a prerequisite for accessing HLP. The project seeks to facilitate enhanced protection of displaced communities from Housing Land and Property violations including but not limited to forced evictions. 
Through holistic and integrated assistance packages, this Project will benefit 500,000 individuals (women, girls, boys and men, including persons with disabilities) in 21 districts across 15 regions around the following seven complementing actions. 
1. Strengthening access to documentation for displaced persons including women, girls and persons with disability through a comprehensive analysis and response to documentation needs.
2. Strengthening of ongoing eviction monitoring systems and expanding eviction risk mapping to collect, review and analyze data.
3. Supporting proactive engagements to negotiate improved tenure arrangements and/or facilitating dignified relocations for populations of concern. 
4. Mitigating protection risks exacerbated by HLP violations such as inadequate access to housing, and forced evictions.
5. Supporting extremely vulnerable victims of evictions cope with post-eviction stress (PES) through the provision of multi-purpose cash assistance, specialized counselling and legal assistance services. 
6. Strengthening Eviction taskforce members, and supporting government’s effort to address evictions, including robust engagement with landlords, gatekeepers and community leaders.
 7. Facilitating access to HLP and legal identity information, legal services, awareness campaigns and, communication materials.
8. Strengthen coordination as well as the functional and operational capacity of the HLP sub cluster.
9. Invest in research, studies, analyses and assessments related to HLP, legal identity and other protection specific issues identified through this response 
10. Conduct evidence based advocacy and policy influence on thematic areas identified through data and evidence generated during the course of implementation. 
11. Ensuring access to justice for IDPs is a priority, in line with the HLP AoR

Provision of lifesaving Water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) assistance to the most vulnerable drought-affected/displaced populations in Qandala and Bosasso of the Bari region, Somalia's Puntland state Provision of life-saving WASH assistance to drought and conflict affected communities and improvement of health standards for the IDPs, and Host Communities in Mudug and Nugaal in puntland state of Somalia. To increase access to life-saving sustained safe drinking Water, Gender-sensitive sanitation facilities, and promotion of good hygiene practices to support 8,500 people including PWDs in Galkacyo, Burtinle, Garowe, Galdogob, IDPs, and Host Communities in crisis and/or emergency affected Women, Girls, Boys, and Men. These groups shall be involved at the various project stages from planning to actual implementation to ensure their views and needs are fully captured. The project's cluster objective 1 will require 65% financial requirements while Cluster objective 2 will require 35% project finances for efficient and successful implementation.
This will be achieved through increased access to adequate, safe, and sustainable water following the rehabilitation and construction of flood-proof water infrastructure proposed under this project, improvement of access to gender-sensitive sanitation food-prone prone settlements, and promoting a culture of good hygiene practices in order to reduce the related protection and disease risks especially among women, girls and children in the targeted locations. As an initial lifesaving intervention, PMWDO will prioritize the provision of vouchers for hygiene kits to 2000 extremely vulnerable households to increase their household water storage capacity thereby reducing the frequent trips to water points, which will as a result reduce congestion at the existing facilities. Within the first 5 months of the project, PMWDO will establish and capacity build water committees and rehabilitate 10 strategic water infrastructures whose combined water supply will benefit 8,000 individuals. To ensure improved quality of the water both at households and supported water points, PMWDO will undertake initial tests and regular water treatment at the source (bucket and batch chlorination). Further, PMWDO will provide water treatment tablets to 2000 vulnerable households who will be sensitized about household water treatment and safe storage. PMWDO will utilize the capacity of the local market by promoting market-based programming in WASH through the use of vouchers (for NFIs) and contracting suitable construction services from the local market following extensive market assessments and monitoring. In order to improve the hygiene knowledge and practices among the target populations, PMWDO will determine the hygiene knowledge and practice gaps through KAP surveys, one (baseline survey) at project inception to inform approaches to awareness-raising and composition of emergency hygiene kits to be distributed to the most vulnerable households. An online KAP survey will be conducted towards the end of the intervention to gauge the impact made in water, latrine, environmental and personal hygiene, and in general, behavior change. To ensure community ownership and sustainability, PMWDO will help establish 10 water resource management committees 50 members (30 women and 20 men) water source management committees. Where possible, a technician from each village and a representative from the local administration will be incorporated into the committee. All the members will be trained in basic operation, maintenance, troubleshooting, and orderly access to the source. The training will be conducted jointly by PMWDO staff, Ministry of Energy, Water and Natural Resources staff, and the private sector (suppliers of spare parts). To instill a sustained culture of good hygiene practice, the project will train and effectively engage the existing 24 community health volunteers recruited from the targeted villages to enable mainstream hygiene promotion activities into the communities. The hygiene promotion intervention is expected to benefit 8500 individuals.
PMWDO seeks to improve access to safe and affordable water and clean sanitation facilities in rural communities and sites where the internally displaced have settled.

Provision of emergency Food assistance, Seasonally appropriate livelihood inputs and Restoration of productive communal asset in Badhadhe district of Lower Juba region of Somalia. With 2.9 million people estimated to be internally displaced throughout the country, of these, 2.2 million require urgent humanitarian assistance. IDPs are chronically more food insecure and vulnerable than host communities. Somalia continues to grapple with multiple shocks that exacerbate existing acute food insecurity and acute malnutrition. The failure of the 2021 GU rains put the pastoral and the agro-pastoral livelihoods in one of the worst crisis. The COVID-19 pandemic and associated socioeconomic impacts also contributed to the food insecurity situation in Somalia. As a result, the FNSAU post GU assessment projected 3.5 million Somalis would be in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) through at least December 2021, in the absence of humanitarian assistance. That includes 1.1 million internally displaced persons who will face moderate to large food consumption gaps through late 2021.
Lower juba is one of the worst affected region by the protracted drought. The ministry of Humanitarian and disaster management of Juballand estimated over 60% of the animals in Juballand have perished due to lack of water and pasture. With no alternative livelihood or coping strategy left, over 11 cases of suicide were also reported in Jubaland. 1. Provide unconditional cash grant to 500 most vulnerable households in Kismayo @75 dollar for 5 round; 
2. Provide seasonally appropriate livelihood inputs (Crop and vegetable) to 500 riverine and small-scale poor farmers along river juba in Kismayo district. 
3.Provide assorted agricultural hand tools to 500 poor farmers to enhance their farming and production ability.
4. 500 pastoral households will be provided with livestock treatment and fodder vouchers 
5. 200HH supported through conditional cash transfer for restoration of communal assets

Lifesaving and life-sustaining emergency food security and livelihood support to drought-affected communities in Galdogob District, Mudug region Improved Access to Food and Livelihood Options for Vulnerable Households in Somalia Ongoing armed conflicts and insecurity, with recurring climate shocks, has resulted in a protracted economic vulnerability and internal displacements across Somalia.Somalis are vulnerable to various shocks such as drought and flood that contribute to poverty and displacement. The Center for Global Development  places Somalia at the top of the list of 167 countries for overall vulnerability to climate change adjusted for coping capacity.
The Cyclical climatic shocks and ongoing conflict are challenging traditional rural livelihoods and causing 
growing number of urban poor and internally displaced people in Somalia. Displacements due to armed 
conflict and political tensions, drought, and lack of livelihoods are expected to continue in 2022, further 
exacerbating food insecurity in many areas.
According to FSNAU,out of the total 3.5 million people in need of urgent food assistance, 640,000 people face significant food consumption gaps. In addition, 3.7 million people are classified in IPC phase 2 (Stressed), engaging in negative coping strategies to meet their food and non-food needs, bringing the total number of Somalis experiencing acute food insecurity to 7.2 million by late 2021.

Furthermore,COVID-19 pandemic and related containment measures seem to have affected the urban poor population more than rural poor population. As a result, the urban poor face moderate to large food consumption gaps, partly due to a slowdown in economic activities in urban areas and the rising costs of food and other essential non-food items.
World Vision proposes a multi pronged interventions  to reverse the current trajectory at which Somalia is going.The interventions would include immediate access to food needs by vulnerable households facing hunger and starvation, improving livelihoods and creating opportunities for diversified livelihoods by protecting key livelihood assets .
The proposed project intends to address the food insecurity situation, loss of livelihood strategies, poor HH and community livelihood assets, as well as minimum interventions integrated to address the environmental degradation on which most livelihoods hinge upon. 
These activities will target IDPs, pastoral and agro-pastoral communities across Somalia, in districts where World Vision operates in.

Provision of emergency lifesaving livelihood support to the most vulnerable drought affected populations (pastoral communities and rural IDPs) in Banderbayla District, Puntland State, Somalia Sustainable Livelihood support and strengthening resilience of drought, floods and conflict affected IDPs, returnees and vulnerable communities in Galgadud, Hiraan, Bay, Middle Shabelle and Lower Shabelle Regions, Somalia Severe food insecurity continues to worsen owing to current depleted livelihoods and diminishing coping mechanisms that has significantly impacted into the lives of the most vulnerable host communities and marginalized IDPs and returnees including the elderly and persons with living with disabilities in  Galgadud, Hiraan, Bay, Middle Shabelle and Lower Shabelle Regions, Somalia. The situation is attributed to combined effects of poor and erratic Gu 2021 rainfall against the  background of previous successive erratic and below average Gu and Deyr 2020 rains compounded by previous successive drought seasons as well as floods along riverine areas of Hiiraan, Middle Shabelle regions hence below-average Gu crop production. The situation is further exacerbated by impacts of desert locust that continue to pose a serious threat to both crop availability and crop production. The project will be implemented through the following activities: Provision of food vouchers for most vulnerable and displaced women and children headed households and those with chronic illnesses and the disabled, rehabilitation of water catchments, farming lands, irrigation canals and feeder roads on CFW scheme, Provision of hay/fodder to the most vulnerable and drought affected, pastoral families, distribution of farm inputs (seed package including seeds and fertilizers) targeted to farming households as well as provision of tractor hours to the targeted farming households.

According to FSNAU-FEWS NET 2021 Post Gu Technical Report of  September 9, 2021, approximately 3.5 million people in Somalia face acute food insecurity Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse outcomes in late 2021 whereas reports of current weather forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of below-average rainfall during the 2021 Deyr (October-December) season across most parts of the country which will seriously affect food security and nutrition outcomes thus food insecurity is expected to deteriorate further to 2022. South Sudan Regional Refugee Response Plan 2022 Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2022, there are some 335,000 refugees and asylum seekers from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, primarily from Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic.
At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for longer term stability, hundreds of thousands of South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since the signing of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan, this spontaneous movement has prompted the development of an area-based approach, to support refugees, returnees and host communities, through enhanced engagement with development actors, to support greater access to services where possible.
Refugees largely reside in conflict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction in basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.
Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will benefit from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Specific protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identified at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with specific protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as verification exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the efficiency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to benefit from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

response through Early Recovery support in 80 communities impacted by the crisis.
Communities, particularly those most dramatically affected – and under additional stress
because of IDPs returns and other displacements - need assistance in reinforcing their
resilience to address these shocks as well as the consequences of the protracted crisis,
and to address their needs on seriously depleted infrastructures and service capacities.
The essence of the Programme is about providing Syrian communities with – still limited -
support to regain control over their basic needs (livelihoods, access to essential services)
and reduce their dependency on humanitarian assistance. Prioritization of locations, is the
outcome of a context analysis and needs assessment conducted on more than 5,000
Syrian communities, based on the following three criteria:
1) Hard to Reach Areas
2) Areas of major IDPs presence and IDPs returns
3) Highest scoring in the Severity Scale

services-related capacities (access and coverage), livelihoods creation and rural recovery,
PWDs support, social cohesion/community safety, reducing gender inequality and youth
marginality, women empowerment, tensions reduction and rehabilitation of basic
infrastructure and public services.
The program is built in a modular manner both in terms of geographical and
sectoral/thematic interventions and foresees the allotment of average 1 Million US$ per
community. Hence, donors willing to support this approach will be able to pre-select
certain location(s) and/or area(s) of intervention of their preference, within the 200
prioritized communities.
The programme relates directly to the sector objectives:
1. Living conditions
2. Livelihoods
3. Access to social services
4. Access to productive and market infrastructure
5. Social protection
6. Strengthening of local public services delivery capacity
7. Reinforcing opportunities and capacities for civic engagement

Support to IDP/host community in Abyei and Twic through provision of protection and promotion of solutions Targeted support to persons with specific needs with lifesaving non-food items and emergency shelter to displaced population in hard-to-reach areas and IDP returnee families  In 2022, Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) continue to face multi-faceted crises which are worsened by conflict, floods, impacts of COVID – 19 pandemic, and protracted displacement from locations of their habitual residence. Displaced families often have inadequate shelter and household goods which expose them to heightened protection risks. Increased mobility, continued insecurity and protracted displacement has over the years eroded household coping mechanisms and livelihood options especially considering the poor nature of local markets without stocks for household goods and shelter materials. 

UNHCR’s project will focus on responding to the humanitarian needs of IDPs and IDP and refugee returnees with targeted and protection focused core relief items (emergency shelter and non-food items – S/NFIs) prioritizing the most vulnerable households and persons with specific needs especially women and girls.

The project will contribute to the following sectoral objectives:
SO 1 – percentage of the targeted population that is able to access shelter material and non-food items in situations of emergency and transition.
The project will identify the most vulnerable IDPs and returnees through protection monitoring and assessments including through IRNAs and RRMs. The assessments and inter cluster discussions will inform the decisions regarding the specific response modalities between in kind and cash assistance. Unique contextual factors including market conditions will be considered. 

SO 2 - Enhance community dignity and engagement in the provision of S/NFI services.
The project will deliver timely lifesaving activities while streamlining protection-oriented initiatives including COVID – 19 preventive measures. The project will strengthen community-based protection through the involvement of community based structures for self-management in response delivery, ensuring that their capacities to cope, recover, contribute to and achieve solutions are enhanced.

SO 3 - Community members’ exposure to environmental hazards is reduced through the construction of disaster-resistant structures.
In 2022, UNHCR will increase its active participation in humanitarian coordination forums including the ES/NFI cluster both at national level and in the field, strongly advocating for protection mainstreaming and joint vulnerability assessments, the results of which will be very useful in the optimization of the limited resources. Emergency food and nutrition assistance to vulnerable people affected by the recent outbreak of violence in the Abyei Region Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace.

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

Acción Contra el Hambre (ACH) en Venezuela atiende las necesidades humanitarias de los grupos más vulnerables en riesgo de desnutrición aguda: < de 5 años, 5 – 14 años, mujeres embarazadas y lactantes (MEL), personas con discapacidades o con problemas de salud, en particular adultos mayores. Son agravantes las situaciones de pobreza y necesidades básicas no satisfechas como la falta de acceso a: alimentos, condiciones higiénico-sanitarias adecuadas, servicios de salud, y medios de vida. La desnutrición y el deterioro de la salud repercuten en una mayor exposición a factores agravantes como la violencia de género, embarazos adolescentes y criminalidad. Agriculture Oromiya, Somali    (USAID/BHA) Agricultural Seed Activity Project (ASAP) II Over the past three years, intercommunal conflict and extreme climate variability and shocks have displaced tens of millions of people in Ethiopia. In the Oromia, Somali and Southern Nations, Nationalities and People’s (SNNP) Regions there are over 1.1 million people in need . As the conflict subsides, the government continues to force IDP’s to return to their former homes, but in the haste of this operation, most return to their communities with few belongings and no productive assets. The provision of seed vouchers alongside basic agricultural advice, for major staple crops (e.g., wheat, tef, OPV maize, sorghum), pulses (e.g., haricot beans) and cash for nutritious vegetable seeds and/or other needed agricultural inputs are essential for the IDP returnees to provide a rapid restart to food production, diversify production for improved consumption and strengthen livelihoods for income generation. 

To support both vulnerable farmers and IDP returnees  Catholic Relief Services (CRS) and our local partners built on the effective response of the first phase of this project funded by USAID/BHA, the Agricultural Seed Activity Project (ASAP) in Oromia Somali, and SNNP by scaling up the cash and voucher-based seed response to benefit farming households who are vulnerable to acute seed insecurity caused by conflict and acute environmental shocks. The purpose of the project is to improve agricultural production through the provision of agricultural inputs (seeds), training in good agricultural practices and links to input suppliers by reaching out to 97,392 beneficiary households.

In the second half of 2021, armed conflict significantly increased the number of internally displaced persons (IDPs) in the Amhara region with high displacement figures especially in South Wello and North Wello.  The IOM Displacement Tracking Matrix published on 31 December 2021 indicates that displacement in Amhara region reached 1.4 million IDPs in early December 2021. Per the regional cluster assessment, large scale return movements starting in mid-December 2021 on wards have resulted in the return of an estimated 480,401 IDPs in South Wello and North Shewa zones. According to the preliminary assessment conducted by ESNFI sub cluster members and CRS emergency in the mid-week of March 2022, new IDPs are arriving in the Amhara region's border areas as a result of the ongoing conflict, and the Ethiopian government has relocated more than 10,000 IDPs to the Jara site as of March 22, 2022. Over 58,000 IDPs are expected to be  relocated to the same place by the government as per the Amhara sub-national cluster.  

In response CRS is proposing to address needs of of conflict-affected HHs through ESNFI and repair kit at Legambo and Harbu town in South Wollo and and Harbu/Jara in North Wello, Amhara Region. Legambo and Habru/Jara will be targeted for IDP/returnee responses and Harbu town will be targeted for IDP responses only. For returnee CRS will consider cash for labor while distributing shelter repair kits based on findings of a market assessment. 

CRS is targeting a total of 35,440 individuals (7,876 HH) across the three woredas with the following support: 
- 19,318 IDP individual (4,293HHs) will receive ESNFI V2 kits budgeted at $140. 
- 5,316 non-displaced individuals (1,181HHs) will receive ESNFI V2 kits budgeted at $140. 
- 5,316 disabled individuals (1,181 HHs) will receive ESNFI V2-Disable kits budgeted at $182. 
- 5,490 returnee individuals (1,220 HHs) will receive shelter repair kits.

Emergency Holistic Protection Services for Migrant Women facing Exploitation, Trauma and Abuse Women migrant domestic workers (WMDWs) – an already marginalized group, continue to be disproportionately impacted by Lebanon’s manifold humanitarian crisis. Due to the Kafala system, WMDWs live with almost no legal and social protection, facing high levels of exploitation and different types of abuse while facing huge obstacles to access justice. They rarely resort to the authorities to seek redress, often due to isolation in their place of work, fear from the authorities, lack of awareness about legal procedures and their rights, the absence of financial means, and language barriers.
In light of this situation, UN Women in partnership with Kafa (enough) Violence & Exploitation and GIZ are partnering to address the emergency protection needs of WMDWs in Lebanon. This project works towards the achievement of the ERP Objective 3: to enhance timely, unhindered, and equitable access to protection assistance for migrants. Under this project, migrant women will have access to a 24/7 helpline, increased access to legal and protection services, better access to quality MHPSS services, and basic and humanitarian return assistance. Socioeconomically marginalized migrant women will be targeted across all regions in Lebanon. UN Women will oversee and monitor the overall project implementation. Services will be provided directly by KAFA, with support on Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) technical assistance provided by GIZ. 

Under 1.1, UN Women and Kafa will conduct mass awareness raising of legal information as a first step to increase their access to protection and obtainment of their legal rights. The campaign will utilize both social media platforms and traditional communication materials, including fliers and leaflets in high traffic areas. Given the fuel and electricity crisis, expanding outreach interventions to migrant women who are not online or have access to internet and mobile phones, is essential. All materials will be translated in the languages of migrant workers. Legal aid will also be provided via individual and group legal counseling, and legal representation for specific cases. 

Under 2.1, Kafa will continue the operation of an established 24/7 helpline dedicated to MDWs. The helpline provides information counseling and provide referrals to specialized legal actors and service providers. Victims of physical and sexual abuse, they will be provided with immediate socio-legal protection information and/or measures. MHPSS will be implemented through different modalities. Social workers operating the helpline will provide immediate psycho-social counseling for WMDWs in psychological distress and make specialized refers. KAFA will also provide direct PSS interventions, including targeting the mental health of migrant community leaders in order to help them manage stress and prevent burnout. GIZ has been a key actor in the MHPSS response for migrants in Lebanon, and will provide quality assurance, and advise on technical referrals to specialized services, as well as coordination with the MHPSS task-force for migrant domestic workers.  
Under 3.1, While protection data will be collected and monitored across all project activity implementation, UN Women will specifically collect and analyze data on female migrant population in North Lebanon (Tripoli and Akkar), with a focus on gender and protection in order to respond to data gaps in that region and improve it service provision outreach. 
Under 6.1, UN Women and Kafa will provide multi-purpose cash assistance to address urgent needs of WMDWs. The cash assistance will be provided to the most vulnerable WMDWs to cover rent, and other basic needs. 
Under 7.1, UN Women and Kafa will facilitate voluntary humanitarian return assistance for WMDWs facing high-risk protection issues. A specific focus will be given to scaling up voluntary return support to migrant women who are in detention, and arbitrary detention – a violation of human rights.

Enhancement of protection of displaced persons, returnees and conflict affected host communities in Syria through integrated, community-based protection activities. Relief Assistance to vulnerable people in Somalia and Shock Response Urban and Rural Safety Nets (ECHO/-HF/BUD/2021/91024) WFP SOMALIA 2022 HRP - FSC Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas. As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation. The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

Nutrition Providing Life Saving Treatment and Prevention Nutrition Services to the Vulnerable Communities in Somalia Food and Nutrition context in Somalia
Decades of conflict and natural disasters including repeated droughts and seasonal flooding followed by limited government and institutional support have had a profound negative effect on the food security situation and social service sector in Somalia. Nearly seven in ten Somalis live on less than USD 1.90 per day,  the sixth-highest poverty rate in sub-Saharan Africa. Poverty is both widespread and deep, particularly for households in rural areas and internally displaced person (IDP) settlements. The number of food-insecure people experiencing long-term stress is trending upwards, indicating that chronic food insecurity persists, requiring sustainable solutions. Recurrent climate-related shocks and political instability are key drivers of food insecurity and pose continuing risks to crop production and food access. Malnutrition in Somalia is driven by a combination of factors such as recurrent food insecurity, child illnesses, high morbidity, micronutrient deficiencies, low immunization levels, poor access to clean water and sanitation, poor hygiene practice, gender inequality and discriminatory sociocultural attitudes leading to poor care practices. Based on the latest Post Gu FSNAU assessment (September 2021), it is estimated that a total of 3.5 million out of the 15.8m people face acute food insecurity (IPC 3 and above – crisis or worse)  until December 2021. At the national level the median prevalence of Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) has remained at a serious level of 11.1%. Approximately 1.2 million children under the age of five are likely to be acutely malnourished, including 295,515 who are likely to be severely malnourished. In addition to this, around 245,909 Pregnant & Lactating Women (PLWs) will be at risk of acute malnutrition. 

Acute malnutrition is a major public health problem in Somalia. It affects disproportionately children under the age of five, as well as Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLWs), especially among IDPs, vulnerable (agro) pastoralist communities and those living in areas affected by flooding. Morbidity among children is high (≥ 20%). Out of a total of 40 surveyed population groups 18 recorded high morbidity presence of above 20%. 
Vitamin A supplementation and Measles vaccination remains low <40% in several population groups. 

TB prevalence remains one of the highest globally with Somalia in the top 10 countries with high TB burden (262 per 100,000 population) while the HIV prevalence remains <1% however with high stigma and discrimination levels at 94%.

Project activities
The World Food Program is the leading UN agency in Somalia in fighting hunger. In Somalia, WFP together with the Ministry of Health (MoH), nutrition cluster and the partners, supports nutrition service delivery and prevention. WFP collaborates with the MoH and UNICEF to offer an integrated package of nutrition and health, following the revised MoH IMAM guidelines for treating acute malnutrition in Somalia.

WFP will cover both treatment and preventive nutrition services including:
•	Targeted Supplementary Feeding Program for 665,846 moderately acute malnourished children 6-59 months; 173,746 malnourished Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLW), 10,794 malnourished People Living with HIV on ART treatment and malnourished TB patients.
•	Preventive Nutrition services for 386,102 children 6-23 months and 173,746 PLW enrolled in Maternal Child Health and Nutrition services and blanket Supplementary Feeding Program for children 6-23 months and PLW in districts where GAM (Global Acute Malnutrition) rate is above 15%.
•	Monthly cash vouchers of USD 15 for 24,104 PLWs in selected target districts.
•	24,206 caregivers with SAM children admitted to the Stabilisation  will receive food while staying at the Stabilisation Center 
•	A total of 96,150 pregnant women will receive food rations for their families when delivering their baby at a health facility

Provision of Multisectoral Lifesaving Assistance for Flood-Affected population in Bentiu and Rubkona CCCM Assistance to conflict and disaster-induced displaced persons in South Sudan According to Round 11 of IOM DTM’s monitoring of displacement and return movement, 2,017,236 people remain displaced in South Sudan, 78% of which are sheltering with already crisis-affected host communities. In a number of displacement sites and collective centers, including current and former PoCs, more than 440,000 individuals continue to live in situations of protracted displacement. Displacement figures have continued to increase despite the signing of the R-ARCSS in 2018 due to an increase of displacement-inducing incidents such as sub-national conflict and unprecedented climate-related disasters.

IOM CCCM aims to target 523,000 people of the total 1.4 million people targeted under the CCCM Cluster Response Plan. IOM will continue to provide displaced communities with basic and emergency camp management services, ensuring that the provision of protection and cross-sectoral humanitarian assistance is equitable, coordinated, monitored and adhering to standards. Of critical relevance to the current displacement environment in the country, IOM CCCM’s interventions will also integrate a robust, community-led disaster-mitigation lens in all care & maintenance interventions and capacity building exercises to enhance protective environments to increase resilience of infrastructure and communities to climate shocks. Further, fully committed to ensuring that AAP is streamlined in any and all activities, IOM will continue to develop and improve AAP mechanisms to ensure that the organization is accountable to the people that it serves and that programmes are informed by the voices of the displaced communities.

IOM intends to contribute to the sectoral objectives through the following interventions:

1)	Continued and adapted provision of critical CCCM activities to IDPs living in Bentiu, Naivasha and Hai Masna IDP Sites as well as critical care & maintenance activities in Malakal PoC.
2)	Deployment of emergency CCCM teams to deliver sustainable mobile responses promoting self-governance, community ownership and resilience in hard-to-reach locations following triggers at the ICCG-level.
3)	Co-lead the CCCM Cluster at national level and continue acting as SFP in WBeG, Jonglei and Upper Nile States in order to support national and state-level partner agencies in accountable CCCM responses and systems.
4)	Continue chairing the CCEWG in order to provide technical CCE support to partner organizations and to operationalize outputs under the 2021 South Sudan AAP Framework.

Multisectoral Rapid Response to the people affected by the lean season Northeast Nigeria Nutrition Response 2022 The Nutrition response in 2022 will prioritise implementation of the nutrition lifesaving activities (inpatient, outpatient, and targeted supplemental feeding programmes) and targeting of LGAs with high rates of GAM (above 10%) such as MMC/Jere, Nganzai, Bama, Machina. Hard-to-reach areas (such as Gubio, Rann, Magumeri), areas with large IDP  and returnee populations (like Monguno) and high-risk/inaccessible locations such as Marte LGA will also be prioritised for nutrition assistance. 
UNICEF will primarily target acutely malnourished children and PLW who are at a significantly high risk of death. The nutrition response will also target the total under-five and PLW with preventive nutrition services e.g. micronutrient supplementation to ensure levels of acute malnutrition are not above average thresholds, and to also reduce morbidity and mortality. The response will prioritise households with persons living with disabilities, who face barriers in accessing health, nutrition and WASH services and are disproportionately food insecure due to high levels of exclusion. 
The nutrition status of the targeted population in the BAY states significantly deteriorates during the period from May-August every year, which is the lean season and coincides with the rainy season. The season is characterised by very high rates of acute malnutrition with medical complications due to poor food access and a high prevalence of diarrhoea and malaria. UNICEF will need to adequately prepare for the lean season period by prepositioning supplies, increasing the overall sector capacity to treat acute malnutrition with a focus on inpatient care and IYCF-E
The nutrition response in BAY states will be contextualised in 2022 based on the following categorisation: 
1. Protracted crisis e.g north and central Borno LGAs where the rates of acute malnutrition are high, worsened by poor access to food and health systems. The approach in these areas will include INGO/NNGO direct support to the affected population, and prioritisation of lifesaving nutrition activities. 
3. New emergencies – locations of new crisis and fluctuations such as relocations, displacements and spike in acute malnutrition. The approach will focus on the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) with a focus on lifesaving activities. 
4. Hard-to-reach / inaccessible areas – locations with limited humanitarian footprints and access e.g Gubio and Magumeri. The approach will include RRM and remote management strategy (where feasible) with a focus on life-saving interventions. UNICEF will also strengthen the implementation of nutrition interventions through local organizations or community-based structures to implement nutrition services in hard-to-reach/inaccessible areas. 
UNICEF response is primarily through services and in-kind deliveries. UNICEF will employ the use of cash and voucher assistance (CVA) to fill the nutrient gap in the Nutrition/Food Minimum Expenditure Basket to ensure that populations have access to a varied diet e.g CVA for meats and vegetables. 
The nutrition status of the affected population is an outcome of various underlying issues including access to health, WASH, food security, child protection, and gender issues. The main cause of acute malnutrition among children and women in BAY states is the high morbidity rates. High diarrhoea prevalence is the major cause of acute malnutrition among the IDPs and urban poor population due to the prevailing poor hygiene and sanitation conditions worsened by congested living conditions. The response will strengthen the integration of nutrition-sensitive interventions including WASH, food security, health, livelihoods and child protection, and gender-based violence risk mitigation.
UNICEF will prioritise projects that include basic nutrition packages such as integrated treatment of acute malnutrition (SAM and MAM) and prevention services including integration with WASH, food security, health and protections services.

Food assistance to the most vulnerable conflict affected people in the northeast Nigeria Life-saving food assistance in North-East Nigeria WFP will provide unconditional food assistance to the most food-insecure, crisis-affected populations. Life-saving general food assistance (in-kind food and cash-based transfers) will be delivered to IDPs, returnees, and host populations in North-East Nigeria (Borno, Yobe, and Adamawa States). Early recovery and resilience to shocks will be promoted through asset creation and preservation, increased livelihoods opportunities, and enhanced agricultural value chains. Joint multi-sectoral assessments and Emergency Food Security Analysis will be conducted regularly to monitor the food security, and markets situation in crisis-affected states. 
A gender-transformative approach that meets the needs of women, men, girls, and boys will be adopted. WFP will mainstream protection throughout its work, supported by a solid understanding of the operational context and protection analysis. Training and capacity building of staff and partners in the protection and humanitarian principles will include on-the-job coaching. WFP will ensure that affected populations (women and men) will be consulted throughout the programme cycle; beneficiary feedback mechanisms will be tailored to their preferred means of communication. Beneficiaries will continue to be empowered with knowledge on their food assistance entitlements and their rights, including WFP’s zero-tolerance policy on Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA). Protection against Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) will be embedded in M&E tools, complaint feedback mechanisms, and training of partners and staff.
WFP will continue the collection of key information on beneficiaries and assistance provided as part of its M&E activities. Monthly monitoring will include distribution and activity site management; beneficiary and entitlement verification; and ensuring adequate protection and gender measures. Lessons will be regularly drawn from monthly process and biannual outcome monitoring and reporting, and periodic reviews and evaluation to inform strategic and operational decisions.
WFP will further consolidate partnerships to enhance national and state-level emergency preparedness and response systems, including food security and nutrition assessment and monitoring, early warning, protection, gender analysis, targeting and registration processes, safety nets, cash-based transfer capacities, and supply chain.
Where security and access to land allow, increasing livelihood activities will complement food assistance to support access to productive assets, income-generating activities, and self-reliance in the long term. Assistance will be coordinated with government distributions, ensure food assistance is complimentary and no gaps. self-reliance in the long term. Integrated Nutrition response in South Sudan Enhancing capacities of women, men, girls, and boys in IPC 3, 4 and 5 in South Sudan to withstand and recover from food insecurity Project Summary The proposed HRP 2022 interventions will target locations with IPC 4 and 5 with emergency food security and livelihoods assistance to the most vulnerable populations affected by shocks including floods, conflicts which has contributed to the elevation of food insecurity outcomes with 31 counties of extreme or severe concern and 36 very high or high concern. The convergence of shocks such as floods, conflicts, hyperinflation of prices for basic commodities and now compounded with social and economic impact of Covid 19 at glance have made the population vulnerable deepening the humanitarian situation. The proposed interventions are aligned to the HRP 2022 cluster objectives; CO1: Provide food assistance to prevent famine and improve food consumption, dietary diversity and coping strategies for vulnerable populations, CO2: Enhance and sustain emergency food production through complementary vegetable and crop livelihood inputs, fishing and livestock support and CO3: Reduce dependency on food and agricultural inputs to support and strengthen households’ ability to absorb shocks. The project is planned to be implemented in Kajo Keji, Yirol east, Akobo, Pibor, Uror, Nyirol, Rumbek centre, Pochalla.
This HRP project will complement Oxfam ongoing resilient programming to provide immediate quick impact activities while protecting the gains of resilience programming. Protection and Gender will be mainstreamed throughout the project lifetime, a Do No Harm approach as enshrined in Oxfam safe programming approach will be mainstreamed by ensuring participation and accountability to affected population. This project will be implemented by Oxfam and its local partners.

Multisector humanitarian response in South Sudan Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace.

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

FAOs drought response aims to immediately increase urgent access to food, water, and basic necessities and protect livelihoods for 61,200  severely drought-affected individuals in south and central Somalia. Emergency Lifesaving Cash and Livelihood Support to IDP and Non- IDP Communities in Somalia Somalia is facing a severe and deteriorating humanitarian crisis as we enter 2022 as a result of the compounding effects of conflict, recurrent climate shocks, diseases and pests outbreaks with increased levels of vulnerability and substantial increase in the humanitarian caseload (Somalia HNO, 2022). There is a serious risk that the impact of consecutive below average to poor rainfall in most parts of the country will develop into a severe drought by early to mid- 2022 with the number of people facing acute food insecurity on the rise. It is likely that minority groups, women, children, people with disabilities, will experience heightened protection risks as a result, unless they are intentionally targeted to receive tailored assistance.

With approximately 3.5 million individuals in IPC 3 and 4 through at least December 2021, FAO proposes to target 160,300 households (961,800 individuals- 91,500 IDPs and 870,300 non- IDPs) in IPC 3 and IPC 4 caseloads respectively. This will include 216,790 women, 254,492 girls, 264,880 boys and 225,638 men and 144,270 people living with disabilities (PWD) across 59 districts in Somalia through its flagship Cash+ approach combining short-term cash transfers with tailored livelihood support in accordance with technical and humanitarian standards. Vulnerable households will identified from at-risk pastoral, agro-pastoral, fishing, riverine farmers, IDPs and Non- IDP communities in IPC 3 and 4 areas. This intervention will integrate short-term cash transfers aimed at enabling the most vulnerable households to meet their immediate needs, with livelihood support to allow crisis-affected households to get back into production. FAO will employ community- led beneficiary selection processes and ensure adequate targeting and representation of extremely vulnerable and minority groups in community committees. Interventions proposed will employ a Do No Harm approach with a gender lens that ensures conflict- sensitivity to reduce protection risks for all individuals, and to mitigate the risk of conflict or community tensions. 

Under Food Security Cluster (FSC) Objective 1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 160,300 households through a blend of conditional (Cash-for-Work) and unconditional (UCT) transfers. Under UCT, FAO will prioritize Cash+ interventions including Cash+ Agriculture, Cash+ livestock and Cash+ fisheries. These modalities will increase households’ immediate access to food by providing sufficient cash to access the minimum expenditure basket (MEB), while supporting the rehabilitation of critical productive and community infrastructure. It will also boost household food production, increase household incomes and create employment opportunities. Cash transfer values will be informed by the Cash Working Group and are expected to differ per district/ region of intervention. They, however, will be valued at 80 percent of the food MEB, which can range from USD 50- 100 per month. All cash-based programmes will include training on good nutrition practices. 

Under FSC Objective 2, to protect livelihoods and related food sources, FAO will provide in-kind, technical support and tailored trainings to 112,500 HHs to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security and nutrition threats, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to targeted HHs. In addition, FAO shall provide transitional cash support to 13,100 HHs across agro pastoral, pastoral and fishing livelihood zones to augment the adaptive capacity of HHs, strengthen and foster resilience to future shocks, cushioning them from food insecurity and malnutrition. Trainings shall be delivered alongside input provision to build skills in sustainable use of resources provided, build skills in livelihoods management including harvest, post- harvest management, linking beneficiaries to long- term interventions that provide them opportunities to enhance their livelihoods and skills.

The funding will provide life-saving relief food assistance through cash-based transfers (CBT) to 90,000 drought-affected newly displaced individuals in Banadir Region (Mogadishu) and Bay Region (Baidoa).

Syria HRP for UNICEF Strengthening Child Protection interventions for girls and boys most at risk of violence, abuse, neglect and exploitation across whole of Syria In line with the CP Area of Responsibility (AOR) Strategy and the “No Lost Generation” framework, UNICEF will enhance equitable access to quality CP services with a resilience focus, including for Survivors of abuse, violence, neglect and exploitation as well as children with disabilities, targeting 117 high severity sub-districts (3 to 5) and 38 low severity ones.

UNICEF’s CP Strategy in 2022-2023 includes:
• Addressing behavioural, social, cultural and economic determinants of CP violations as a prevention approach.  
• Improving the reach and quality of specialized CP services
• Capacity development of CP responders
•  Monitoring, evidence generation and advocacy 

UNICEF will support the delivery of integrated programming that will encourage social transformation, prioritizing:
• Structured and sustained CP MHPSS and EORE programmes
• Specialized integrated CP services including case management for survivors of violence, exploitation, neglect and abuse (child labour, CAFAAG, child survivors of GBV, child marriages, justice for children, birth registration and unaccompanied or separated children amongst others) 
• Parenting programmes to promote positive child rearing skills and experience for caregivers
• Elimination of violence against children, including GBV prevention and empowerment for girls, boys and women, prevention of violence in schools, homes and communities.
• Awareness-raising on CP risks
• Capacity development of CP responders and social workers

UNICEF will generate evidence to inform the humanitarian response and advocacy including setting up an information management system for case management. UNICEF will embrace new delivery modalities and implement cash transfers aimed at child protection outcomes for vulnerable families. UNICEF will also continue to support the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism on grave violations against children.

CP services will be delivered by partners based on minimum standards and IASC guidelines. 7,200 CP and social workers will be trained on case management, MHPSS, EORE, advocacy, evidence generation and coordination across sectors for a comprehensive CP response.
 
UNICEF will support MHPSS for 364,000 children to benefit from improved mental health and social wellbeing. UNICEF will equip 61,500 parents and caregivers with skills to provide a stimulating and safe environment at home, including reduced violence.  

Violence prevention is a key priority. Family violence prevalence is high for girls 12-17 years (47%), boys 12-17 years (44%), boys below 12 (45%) and girls below 12 (44%) (UNICEF 2018). UNICEF will work to protect children from violence and abuse through prevention activities in schools, homes and communities and providing survivors of violence with child-friendly and gender sensitive services. Support will be provided for PSEA mechanisms to protect beneficiaries and build the capacity of humanitarian actors. PSEA programming will be implemented with the Protection Sector AORs.

Based on HNO 2021, one in three communities in Syria is reportedly contaminated by explosive ordnance. One in four victims is a child (Joint MA & CP Analysis, 2020). EORE messages will be provided to 1,460,000 children and adults through humanitarian actors and public service providers using static facilities and mobile teams. UNICEF will build the capacity of partners to provide quality EORE that is age, gender and disability appropriate and to provide child victims with assistance.
 
UNICEF will strengthen the justice system to ensure that children in contact with the law victims, offenders or witnesses are protected through child-friendly, gender-sensitive services, that are community-based and family focused.

As Lead Agency for the CP AOR, UNICEF will ensure coordination needs at Hub and WOS levels. Two UN-led and one INGO-led coordination hubs in Damascus, Gaziantep and NES, as well as a WOS overall coordination system, to ensure coherence across the CP response.

UNICEF will work to protect children from violence and abuse through prevention activities in schools, homes and communities and providing survivors of violence with child-friendly and gender sensitive services. Support will be provided for PSEA mechanisms to protect beneficiaries and build the capacity of humanitarian actors. PSEA programming will be implemented with the Protection Sector AORs.

Based on HNO 2021, one in three communities in Syria is reportedly contaminated by explosive ordnance. One in four victims is a child (Joint MA & CP Analysis, 2020). EORE messages will be provided to 1,460,000 children and adults through humanitarian actors and public service providers using static facilities and mobile teams. UNICEF will build the capacity of partners to provide quality EORE that is age, gender and disability appropriate and to provide child victims with assistance.
 
UNICEF will strengthen the justice system to ensure that children in contact with the law victims, offenders or witnesses are protected through child-friendly, gender-sensitive services, that are community-based and family focused.

Réponse d'urgence à l'épidémie de choléra dans les régions du Sud-Ouest et du Littoral Reduced excess morbidity and mortality among affected populations of the North West region and South West region of Cameroon The North West region and South West region of Cameroon are affected by a complex humanitarian crisis that has resulted in system wide breakdown of infrastructure and services especially in the health sector. This crisis has resulted in the displacement of over 1.1 Million people, especially women and children1.  Data from the MSNA conducted in February 2021, revealed that 199 (22%) out of 893 health centers were no longer functional2.  Attacks on healthcare is a common feature of this crisis and remains a major threat to the availability of healthcare in the North West region and the South West region.  There are limited specialized services to take care of victims of physical and mental trauma in these regions as the number of cases have been on the rise because of the crisis. This situation has been worsened by the COVID-19 Pandemic which has increased the burden on a health system that has already been fragilized by the humanitarian crisis. Three health districts (Ekondo Titi, Mbongue, Bakassi) have had cholera epidemics this year with case fatality rates sometimes reaching 40%. In the most of affected areas, health services are not available while less affected areas have health services of poor quality. This project aims to reduce excess morbidity and mortality of internal displaced populations (IDP) and affected host communities in the North West and South West regions of Cameroon affected by the humanitarian crisis by ensuring a timely and equitable access to health care services. The project will target 373,069 IDPs persons (51% of this target are women, 16% are children under 5, and 11% are people over 60 years old). The areas of intervention will be Fako, Meme, Lebialem, Ndian and Kupe - Muanenguba divisions in the South-West region and Mezam, Momo, Bui, Ngo-ketunjia, Mechum and Boyo in the North-West region. The project will emphasize on timely access to equitable health care through mobile clinics in areas with no functional health facilities and the use of vouchers in areas where health facilities are operational.

Emergency drought response through provision of integrated water, sanitation and hygiene promotion (WASH) services in Somalia Provision of lifesaving assistance and sustainable solutions through safe Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) services, for people in crises and their host communities in multiple regions in Somalia. IOM WASH is proposing to contribute to lifesaving of access to safe and equitable basic WASH services to overall 281,400 beneficiaries from vulnerable Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) and host-communities in multiple regions in Somalia. 

Specifically, the project will target 168,840 Non displaced people (children 104,681; women 27,014; Disabled 25,326; and elderly 11,819) and 112,560 displaced populations (children 69,787; Women 18,010; Disabled 16,884; and elderly 7,879)
IOM will rehabilitate 60 strategic water sources for multi-use (human and animals) and further 55 community berkads (water reservoirs) that will provide continued, equitable, safe, sufficient and sustainable water to regions, targeted by the cluster, prone to natural disasters.
IOM further proposes to construct 3,300 new emergency sanitation facilities (following cluster specifications) targeting populations without access to basic sanitation and hygiene.

The project will also strengthen the capacity of the Federal Government of Somalia and Federal Members States, community leaders and water committees/technicians for better coordination with government authorities and communities and sustainability of the constructed/ rehabilitated WASH infrastructures. In addition, the project will nurture community participation in good hygiene practices through training and community sensitization campaigns.

The project is aligned with protection mainstreaming to ensure safety and dignity of affected populations without causing harm. Affected populations and all relevant stakeholders including men, women, boys, girls, elderly and people with disability will be involved in decision making throughout the project activities/cycle. Furthermore, the project will be a part of an IOM integrated emergency response program and resilience building, where possible, efforts will be made to integrate IOM health, nutrition, shelter, CCCM and protection activities.

WFP Integrated Response to Prevent Famine in Bay, Banadir and Mudug regions of Somalia. WFP SOMALIA 2022 HRP - FSC Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas. As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation. The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

WFP Integrated Response to Prevent Famine in Bay, Banadir and Mudug regions of Somalia. Providing Life Saving Treatment and Prevention Nutrition Services to the Vulnerable Communities in Somalia Food and Nutrition context in Somalia
Decades of conflict and natural disasters including repeated droughts and seasonal flooding followed by limited government and institutional support have had a profound negative effect on the food security situation and social service sector in Somalia. Nearly seven in ten Somalis live on less than USD 1.90 per day,  the sixth-highest poverty rate in sub-Saharan Africa. Poverty is both widespread and deep, particularly for households in rural areas and internally displaced person (IDP) settlements. The number of food-insecure people experiencing long-term stress is trending upwards, indicating that chronic food insecurity persists, requiring sustainable solutions. Recurrent climate-related shocks and political instability are key drivers of food insecurity and pose continuing risks to crop production and food access. Malnutrition in Somalia is driven by a combination of factors such as recurrent food insecurity, child illnesses, high morbidity, micronutrient deficiencies, low immunization levels, poor access to clean water and sanitation, poor hygiene practice, gender inequality and discriminatory sociocultural attitudes leading to poor care practices. Based on the latest Post Gu FSNAU assessment (September 2021), it is estimated that a total of 3.5 million out of the 15.8m people face acute food insecurity (IPC 3 and above – crisis or worse)  until December 2021. At the national level the median prevalence of Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) has remained at a serious level of 11.1%. Approximately 1.2 million children under the age of five are likely to be acutely malnourished, including 295,515 who are likely to be severely malnourished. In addition to this, around 245,909 Pregnant & Lactating Women (PLWs) will be at risk of acute malnutrition. 

Acute malnutrition is a major public health problem in Somalia. It affects disproportionately children under the age of five, as well as Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLWs), especially among IDPs, vulnerable (agro) pastoralist communities and those living in areas affected by flooding. Morbidity among children is high (≥ 20%). Out of a total of 40 surveyed population groups 18 recorded high morbidity presence of above 20%. 
Vitamin A supplementation and Measles vaccination remains low <40% in several population groups. 

TB prevalence remains one of the highest globally with Somalia in the top 10 countries with high TB burden (262 per 100,000 population) while the HIV prevalence remains <1% however with high stigma and discrimination levels at 94%.

Project activities
The World Food Program is the leading UN agency in Somalia in fighting hunger. In Somalia, WFP together with the Ministry of Health (MoH), nutrition cluster and the partners, supports nutrition service delivery and prevention. WFP collaborates with the MoH and UNICEF to offer an integrated package of nutrition and health, following the revised MoH IMAM guidelines for treating acute malnutrition in Somalia.

WFP will cover both treatment and preventive nutrition services including:
•	Targeted Supplementary Feeding Program for 665,846 moderately acute malnourished children 6-59 months; 173,746 malnourished Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLW), 10,794 malnourished People Living with HIV on ART treatment and malnourished TB patients.
•	Preventive Nutrition services for 386,102 children 6-23 months and 173,746 PLW enrolled in Maternal Child Health and Nutrition services and blanket Supplementary Feeding Program for children 6-23 months and PLW in districts where GAM (Global Acute Malnutrition) rate is above 15%.
•	Monthly cash vouchers of USD 15 for 24,104 PLWs in selected target districts.
•	24,206 caregivers with SAM children admitted to the Stabilisation  will receive food while staying at the Stabilisation Center 
•	A total of 96,150 pregnant women will receive food rations for their families when delivering their baby at a health facility
