Emergency food assistance and nutrition support to vulnerable populations in Pibor and Fangak Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace.

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

State of Palestine 	 Global - Thematic Humanitarian Response Integrated psychosocial support and child protection services for the most affected boys and girls in Gaza Strip This project will support the delivery of quality, integrated child protection and psychosocial support (PSS) services to the most vulnerable boys and girls aged 4-18 in Gaza Strip, especially those affected by the May 2021 escalation, as well as COVID-19. The escalation has affected all aspects of life in the Gaza Strip, including child protection needs and services. 

The project will ensure that 12 family centres and 30 outreach sites in Gaza are fully operational, responding to the pressing mental health and psychosocial and child protection needs of 23,440 children (55% girls) and 5,480 caregivers (77% women).
Service delivery will be directed to the most affected locations and the most vulnerable children through a coordinated continuum of services in Gaza. Each family centre will be connected to a community-based child protection committee that informs the family centre of community child protection needs and acts as a focal point for identifying vulnerable children for referral. Family centres will operate through established Community-Based Organisations (CBOs) and outreach sites and will assess/screen and refer children for further services through:
1) a case management approach for the worst affected;
2) referral of complex child protection cases to child protection services (relevant stakeholders and Civil Society Organizations (CSOs); and 
3) referral of children with further psychosocial support needs to more specialized psychological support services. 

Services will also strengthen outreach capacities to detect and link up children in need with service providers while providing mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) through the family centres. Mali - OCHA Office [Donor:O540, Recipient:O514] Renforcement des mécanismes de Coordination et de Plaidoyer pour la protection humanitaire et l’assistance aux populations les plus vulnérables au Mali En 2021, la crise humanitaire au Mali s'est aggravée en raison de l'augmentation et de l'expansion des de la violence intercommunautaire et des attaques des groupes armés non étatiques (GANE) dans les régions du centre, du sud et de l'ouest. Cette crise a été aggravée par les bouleversements politiques marqués par deux coups d'état en août 2020 et mai 2021, et l'incertitude persistante de la transition politique laisse l'État dans l'incapacité de répondre aux services sociaux de base des populations. 
Les déplacements internes de personnes ont augmenté de 100 000 en 2021, atteignant plus de 401 000 personnes soit quatre fois plus qu'il y a deux ans. Au total, 156 000 réfugiés maliens résident dans les pays voisins tandis que le Mali accueille 48 000 réfugiés et leur fournit protection et assistance. Les gains économiques du Mali se sont érodés, avec 900 000 personnes (0,04% de la population) qui sont retombées dans la pauvreté en raison de la crise socioéconomique de la COVID-19. la capacité des ménages est fragilisée à cause de la perte de revenus, de la réduction des transferts de fonds et à l'augmentation du coût de la vie. 
La Banque mondiale prévoit une augmentation du taux de pauvreté à 4,8 % en 2022. La crise de protection est également aggravée avec une augmentation des incidents de sécurité.  Les acteurs de la violence basée sur le genre (VBG) ont signalé 5 486 incidents de VBG, soit une augmentation de 41 % comparativement à la même période en 2020. Plus de 1 640 écoles sont fermées en raison de l'insécurité, affectant plus de 2,9 millions d'enfants dont 40 % se trouvent dans la région centrale de Mopti. Quatre districts centraux ont signalé que 40 % des écoles étaient fermées. Dans les régions du sud, 10 pour cent des écoles sont fermées à Koulikoro, Koutiala et Sikasso, privant 30 000 enfants de leur éducation. A ce jour, le Mali a rapporté plus de 15 800 cas de COVID-19.
En 2021, 1,3 million de personnes ont connu un niveau élevé d'insécurité alimentaire aiguë. le niveau le plus élevé depuis 2015, et 3 055 253 personnes ont été touchées par les mauvaises pluies et une saison de soudure prolongée. La situation humanitaire reste entravée par l'augmentation des besoins et la faiblesse des financements, avec 32 % des fonds mobilisés au 31 octobre 2021. Malgré les contraintes opérationnelles, les partenaires humanitaires ont aidé plus de 2,45 millions des 4,7 millions de personnes ciblées au 30 septembre 2021. 
Les capacités de réponse existantes au Mali représentent plus de 160 organisations humanitaires, acteurs du développement ainsi que des forces militaires (MINUSMA, Forces maliennes de défense et de sécurité, Barkhane, Mission européenne de formation, G5 Sahel). Le contexte susmentionné exigera une coordination efficace et la présence d’OCHA demeure très importante. OCHA maintiendra sa présence à Bamako, Mopti, Tombouctou, Gao et ouvrira une antenne à Ségou tout en couvrant à distance les régions de Taoudénit, Ménaka, Kidal et les régions du sud Est et Ouest. 

Sept clusters actifs (Éducation, Sécurité alimentaire, Santé, Nutrition, Protection, Abris/BNA et WASH), des sous-clusters et des groupes de travail spécialisés (Accès, CM-Coord, Redevabilité, Genre et Cash) sont en place au niveau national et local. Le Bureau d’OCHA au Mali continuera ainsi à jouer un rôle central dans la mobilisation, la coordination et le soutien des acteurs humanitaires dans les domaines de la coordination, la gestion de l’information, le financement humanitaire et le plaidoyer.

Coordinated Action for Multi-Sector Programming in Camp and Out-of-Camp Settings Provision of shelter and NFI support to communities affected by displacement and environmental shocks in Somalia and Somaliland. As conflicts and recurrent environmental shocks continue to drive people out of their places of origin, resulting in unpredictable and sudden displacements, requiring a quick response from humanitarian actors to deliver essential relief.  According to the CCCM cluster, 2,241,328 people will need humanitarian assistance in 2022 due to the lack of durable solutions, continued conflicts, and recurrent shocks. 
As such, shelter and non-food item needs remain significant across displacement-affected communities in Somalia, with recurrent displacement trends underpinning protracted needs for shelter and NFI assistance in the proposed locations. Therefore, the proposed action will target locations in Kismayo, Hargeysa, Ceel Afweyn, Laasqoray and Baidoa districts. The project will benefit 16,446 individuals (2,741 HHs without double counting). Under this, ACTED proposes an in-kind distribution methodology instead of a voucher system to allow for prepositioning and rapid emergency response when the need arises. The storage and transportation of the materials to the distribution points and related costs are managed by the selected competent and qualified suppliers, a requirement in the contract signed between ACTED and the suppliers.  In parallel with the provision of emergency shelter and NFI support, and in line with the primary objective of working towards facilitating recovery and access to durable solutions, ACTED will provide transitional shelters to IDP households living on land protected by land tenure agreements in IDP sites that have stable land tenure agreements. Significant rates of eviction render durable shelter solutions appropriate only in cases where land tenure agreements exist and provide a critical foundation for persons facing protracted displacement in the assertion of pathways to recovery. 
In order to assess the efficiency of the assistance provided, level of satisfaction of the beneficiaries with the items received and the overall impact, ACTED will conduct post distribution monitoring 6 weeks after the distribution of ESK/NFI and post construction monitoring 3 months after the handover of transitional shelters to analyze the impact and draw lessons learnt for future programming.

Accès à une Education de qualité, sûre et inclusive des enfants affectés par la crise sécuritaire dans la région de Tillabéri au Niger (AccED) Assurer la continuité de l'éducation des enfants affectés par la crise sécuritaire dans la région de Tillaberi au Niger L’escalade de l’insécurité dans les zones frontalières durant continue d’impacter tous les secteurs, mais encore plus durablement le secteur de l’Education.  En effet, selon les résultats de l’analyse de l’impact de l’insécurité sur l’éducation, 579 écoles sont fermées dans la région de Tillaberi avec une situation très critique dans les départements frontaliers, tels que Torodi avec plus 50% d’écoles fermées, Téra, 45% et Ayorou avec 37%. Cette fermeture a affecté plus de 53 562 enfants dont 48% de filles. Les efforts de l’Etat et ses partenaires, ont permis le retour à l’école et l’inscription de certains enfants, soit 18% des enfants (19% chez les filles) issus des écoles fermées (DREN Tillaberi, Novembre 2021). Au cours de l’année académique 2021/2022, plus de 82% des élèves issus des écoles fermées, sans compter les enfants qui devraient s’inscrire cette année en cours d’initiation (CI) sont en dehors de l’école. Selon qu’on soit dans les zones de conflits ou dans les zones d’accueil des populations déplacés, les problèmatiques en matière d’éducation ne sont pas les mêmes.
Il est plus que nécessaire de développer des alternatives éducatives adaptées au contexte sécuritaire de chaque zone (zone de conflit et zone d’accueil) pour favoriser le retour à l’école des enfants affectés par cette crise sécuritaire. C’est ainsi qu’un consortium composé de la Fundacion Education Y Cooperacion ( Educo) et l’ Association Nigérienne pour le Traitement de la Délinquance et la prévention du crime (ANTD) ont initié ce projet dont l’objectif global est de contribuer à la réinsertion et à la continuité de l’accès à une éducation inclusive, sure et de qualité des filles et garçons affectés par les crises humanitaires dans la région de Tillaberi au Niger. De manière spécifique, cette initiative vise à réduire les obstacles à l’éducation des filles et des garçons de 6 à 17 ans hors du système éducatif affectés par la crise sécuritaire et sanitaire dans les départements de Tera, Bankilaré et Ouallam, de la région de Tillaberi. Pour concrétiser ces objectifs, le projet prévoit les strategies éducatives suivante : 1)   le transfert de 734 élèves de 12 à 17 ans en particulier les filles et porteurs de handicap, issus des zones de conflits, vers les écoles des zones les plus sécurisées , 2) la mise en place d’Espaces communautaire d’apprentissage ouvert au profit de 1101 enfants de 6 à 12 ans dans les zones à conflits modéré, 3) la promotion de l’éducation à distance (radio) au profit de 1468 enfants de 9 à 12ans dans les zones à conflits modéré, 4) la réinsertion scolaire par la Stratégie de scolarisation accélérée/passerelle (SSAP) au profit de 734 enfants de 9 à 14 ans en dehors de l’écoles dans les zones d’accueil des PDI et des Réfugiés, 5) l’inscription, réinscription de 2568 enfants de 6 à 17 ans en dehors de l’écoles dans les zones d’accueil des PDI et des Réfugiés et 6) le maintien scolaire de 734 enfants non accompagnés de 13 à 17 ans issus des zones de conflits réinscrit dans les écoles sécurisé. Le projet touchera un total de 7338 enfants, y compris les enfants porteurs d’handicap de 6 à 17 ans dont 60% de filles.

Livestock are suffering from lack of pasture and water. Estimates from regional Governments indicated more than 1.46 million livestock deaths (67 % in Somali, 31 % in Oromia, and 7 % in Southwest and SNNP regions). Surviving animals have a significantly deteriorated body condition which has decreased their market value which has led to decrease of the purchasing power of households. According to the most recent seasonal forecast by ICPAC, a below average belg season is expected. The situation seems not expected to improve rapidly.Thus, the affected pastoral communities require continuous support. According to the humanitarian response plan, Humanitarian partners are targeting 12.8 million people for food assistance (out of which 8.0 million people also receive other types of assistance). To response to the situation CARE proposed three major intervention that include Livestock feed provisions, Animal health provision and restocking with shoat to Liben of Somali region and Borena of Oromia region.
East Hararge DRM office Early warning department report showed the rain delayed by 48days this show in FY22 no longer expect of belg crop (short season) planting and delays may happen on Meher crop planting.  Zonal Agriculture office noted to partners the need to support the farmers on provision of short season maturing seed. Similarly, the shortage of seeds noted in West Hararge Zone.  In response to this CARE proposed the provision of agriculture inputs such as improved seeds and /or vegetables to both Eastern and Western Hararge zones.
The political dynamics have changed dramatically in Ethiopia's Tigray Region following the unilateral ceasefire declaration by the Ethiopian Government on 28 June 2021.  However, the breakdown of essential services such as the blackout of electricity, telecommunications, and internet throughout Tigray region will only exacerbate the already dire humanitarian situation.  According to the UNOCHA the shortages of cash and fuel in the region can compromise the duty of care of aid workers on the ground. Several locations remained hard to reach for partners’ humanitarian operations due to security concerns, including Abergele and Tsagibji kebeles, parts of Zequala kebeles in Wag Hamra Zone, large sections of Kobo in North Wello Zone, and in Addi Arekay in the North Gondar Zone. However, the livelihoods of the people in the above zones are highly affected by the conflict that leaves many affected people for need of agriculture input support. CARE proposes the agriculture input provisions which includes improved seeds and /or vegetables, provision of hand tools, and the provision of Draught power for the Amhara and Tigray region affected woredas. The recent UNOCHA updates shows in Afar, the humanitarian situation continued to be dire with a high number of IDPs in need of support while the response is still insufficient to compare with needs in the region. Because of the conflict the main livelihood and income source from livestock highly affected. To respond the situation CARE proposed Animal feed provision, animal health and restocking interventions

USAID / BHA Northeast Nigeria Nutrition Response 2022 The Nutrition response in 2022 will prioritise implementation of the nutrition lifesaving activities (inpatient, outpatient, and targeted supplemental feeding programmes) and targeting of LGAs with high rates of GAM (above 10%) such as MMC/Jere, Nganzai, Bama, Machina. Hard-to-reach areas (such as Gubio, Rann, Magumeri), areas with large IDP  and returnee populations (like Monguno) and high-risk/inaccessible locations such as Marte LGA will also be prioritised for nutrition assistance. 
UNICEF will primarily target acutely malnourished children and PLW who are at a significantly high risk of death. The nutrition response will also target the total under-five and PLW with preventive nutrition services e.g. micronutrient supplementation to ensure levels of acute malnutrition are not above average thresholds, and to also reduce morbidity and mortality. The response will prioritise households with persons living with disabilities, who face barriers in accessing health, nutrition and WASH services and are disproportionately food insecure due to high levels of exclusion. 
The nutrition status of the targeted population in the BAY states significantly deteriorates during the period from May-August every year, which is the lean season and coincides with the rainy season. The season is characterised by very high rates of acute malnutrition with medical complications due to poor food access and a high prevalence of diarrhoea and malaria. UNICEF will need to adequately prepare for the lean season period by prepositioning supplies, increasing the overall sector capacity to treat acute malnutrition with a focus on inpatient care and IYCF-E
The nutrition response in BAY states will be contextualised in 2022 based on the following categorisation: 
1. Protracted crisis e.g north and central Borno LGAs where the rates of acute malnutrition are high, worsened by poor access to food and health systems. The approach in these areas will include INGO/NNGO direct support to the affected population, and prioritisation of lifesaving nutrition activities. 
3. New emergencies – locations of new crisis and fluctuations such as relocations, displacements and spike in acute malnutrition. The approach will focus on the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) with a focus on lifesaving activities. 
4. Hard-to-reach / inaccessible areas – locations with limited humanitarian footprints and access e.g Gubio and Magumeri. (USAID/BHA) Emergency WASH assistance to Conflict and drought-affected vulnerable IDPs and poor host community members from affected Woredas in Tigray,  Amharic and Somali region of Ethiopia  Ethiopia just like other Horn African countries has been hit by an exceptionally severe drought that was occasioned by the failure of the last three consecutive rains. Poor rains in October-December 2020 and March-May 2021 have been followed by an extremely dry October- December 2021. Current forecasts point to a fourth below-normal rainfall season during March-May 2022, a sequence that was never seen since 1981 in the region, which if it happens as predicted could further exacerbate the current humanitarian challenges in the region. The Somali region of Ethiopia is one of the regions hard–hit by the ongoing drought. The Post- deyr rains assessment and regional drought response plan, prepared in December 2021, confirmed that the whole Somali region is affected by the current drought and 2,279.606 people in the region are reported to be in need of water trucking, at 657 sites across 85 Woredas.  Water resources are increasingly being strained as a result of the drought conditions while most surface water sources have largely dried up in the region. The humanitarian situation in Northern Ethiopia has been worsening since the onset of the war in November 2020 in the region which has affected more than 6 million people, displaced more than 2.2 million people displaced from their homes including almost one million women and girls as the fighting crossed into the Neighboring Amhara and Afar region. In Tigray and Amhara region particularly in the war-affected areas, the conflict has rendered a large number of water points dysfunctional due to damage to water supplies systems, looting of water points, the collapse of water governing structures, disruptions in the Supply chains of Essential WASH equipment in the region. A recent OCHA update reported that there are about 418,000 IDPs in 131 sites in Tigray that require water trucking supports and that about 9300 water points (more than 54%) are not functional in Tigray affecting access of more than 3.5 million people to safe drinking water.
 According to the WASH cluster situation update from the Amhara region (issued 1st march 2022). There are over 256, 491 IDPs in the region, of which the majority are newly displaced. - IDPs are mainly found in North Shewa, North Wollo, Waghemra, and North Gondar zones - There are sheltered in 20 Collective sites across the Amhara region.  In view of the above, Alight proposes emergency WASH Services provisions to the conflict and drought-affected IDPs and vulnerable host communities including Schools and health facilities that are also in need of basic WASH services from affected Woredas in Tigray, Amhara and the Somali region with the aim of saving lives and reducing morbidities associated with WASH-related diseases. In this proposal Alight will:
•	Prioritize emergency Water trucking supports to IDPs and vulnerable host community members for 2 months benefiting approximately 30,000 beneficiaries. 
•	Restore the functionality of 10 strategic boreholes and shallow wells by rehabilitating and providing critical pumping and power systems installations to support durable access to water for the targeted beneficiaries
•	Construct  400 communal emergency latrines and bathing cubicles for IDPs populations
•	Distribute environmental sanitation kits to IDPs especially newly arrived IDPs to help them manage waste.
•	Provide WASH Supports to 14 Institutions (8 schools and 6 Health facilities.
•	Hygiene promotion will remain a key component of the intervention to prevent the spread of Covid 19 and other WASH-related diseases through risk communications and community engagement promoting behaviour changes. 
•	Where feasible, Alight will use Market based programming approach in the delivery of the planned WASH Interventions ( e.g use of commodity and cash vouchers). The project plans to reach a total of 90,000 beneficiaries ( 20700 men, 24300 women,19800 boys and 25200 girls).

Renforcement de la protection pour lespersonnes vulnérables, en particulier lesenfants, les survivants de violencebasée sur le genre (VBG) et victimes detraite dans les régions de Diffa,Tillabéry, Maradi et Tahoua Renforcement de la protection pour les personnes vulnérables, en particulier les enfants, les survivants de violence basée sur le genre (VBG) et victimes de traite dans les régions de Diffa, Tillabéry, Maradi et Tahoua Les risques de violations des droits des hommes et femmes, y compris les risques de traite et de VBG, seront amoindris à travers la promotion d’un environnement communautaire protecteur et d’un accès renforcé aux services de protection, y compris aux services Santé mentale soutien psychosocial (SMSPS), dans les régions de Tillabéri, Diffa, Maradi et Tahoua.
Les activités cibleront les retournés, déplacés et membres des populations hôtes. Le projet prévoit 4 axes d’intervention.
1. Renforcement des capacités étatiques et des services sociaux de base dans les départements cibles pour une meilleure prise en charge des personnes en mobilité et notamment des enfants, y compris des survivant-e-s VBG et des victimes de traite : Un cycle de formation sur la protection des victimes de traite en situation de crise, permettant aussi de vulgariser le mécanisme national de référencement des victimes de traite, sera organisé pour tout acteur de la chaine de protection dans les communes cibles, dont les travailleurs sociaux de la protection de l’enfance et des organisations de la société civile (OSC). Il comprendra également des sessions sur la spécificité de la prise en charge des enfants non accompagnés en contexte humanitaire, et les besoins spécifiques des survivantes de VBG. 
2. Prévention des violences notamment envers les enfants, les femmes et les personnes en situation d'handicap, y compris de survivants de  VBG et diverses exploitations, à travers le renforcement des mécanismes communautaires de protection, l’appui aux leaders communautaires et la mobilisation des filles et garçons : En collaboration avec les DDPFPE, les mairies et les OSC, une cartographie et évaluation des besoins des structures communautaires, y compris les comités de protection, les espaces amis des enfants, les espaces surs et les écoles coraniques accueillant des enfants déplacés, seront réalisées. Suite à cette analyse, l’OIM les appuiera en matériel, afin que ces dernières puissent jouer leur rôle de protection. Leurs compétences seront renforcées afin qu’ils puissent signaler et référer les cas de protection, mais aussi qu’ils développent des actions de prévention qui encouragent des normes et comportements positifs favorisant des communautés respectueuses, égalitaires, et non violentes à l'égard des femmes et des filles. Des appuis aux initiatives des jeunes pour qu’ils sensibilisent leurs pairs seront réalisés.

Assistance humanitaire en abris et biens non-alimentaires pour les populations déplacées en situation de vulnérabilité dans les régions de Tahoua et Tillabéri au Niger Assistance d'urgence aux personnes déplacées dans les régions de Tahoua et Tillabéry Dans le cadre du HRP 2021, partant de la stratégie du GTABNA et en étroite collaboration avec le Ministère de l’Action Humanitaire, l'OIM poursuit l'objectif général de contribuer à l'amélioration les conditions de vie des populations. En particulier des populations déplacées vulnérables victimes des crises armées et l'activisme de GANEs spécialement dans les zones frontalières, dans les régions de Tahoua et de Tillabéry, par la fourniture d'abris d'urgence et de Biens Non Alimentaires. En tant que Co-Lead du Cluster,  l'OIM va contribuer au  renforcement de la coordination du Groupe de travail Abris et Biens Non Alimentaires, renforcer la collecte des informations, d'informer les intervenants sur la localisation, la nature et l'ampleur des besoins exprimés, sensibiliser les partenaires et membres du secteur à mener les activités dans le respect de la stratégie du secteur et les principes humanitaires et d'appuyer les services étatiques locaux dans leurs rôles de coordination et suivi des activités du secteur. La situation sécuritaire dans les régions de Tahoua et Tillabéry étant toujours volatile, le GTABNA reste attentif à tout mouvement de population et suit la situation au travers des annonces de sécurité, les MSA de RRM et le monitoring de protection du cluster protection fournissant les informations indicatives à la réponse en abris d’urgence et Biens Non Alimentaires.  Partant de la cible du HRP 2022, le secteur abris et bien non alimentaire mettra à disposition 7 000 kits abris d’urgence et 7 000 kits BNA en vue de répondre aux nouveaux mouvements de population, aux mouvements secondaires ainsi qu'au renouvèlement des abris détériorés des ménages. L’assistance basée sur la vulnérabilité ciblera également les familles hôtes vulnérables. Sur base de la stratégie du Secteur abris/BNA et dépendamment de la faisabilité, les interventions pourront se faire en transfert monétaires conditionnels. Cette modalité offrira la réduction considérable des coûts logistiques qui sont très élevés en période hivernale à cause du mauvais état des routes et permettra de résoudre le problème d’accès lié à l'insécurité qui retarde les interventions. Les activités de la réponse d'urgence se conformeront aux Principes de Protection transversales et au Cadre institutionnel de l'OIM de lutte contre les violences basées sur le genre en situation de crise (GBV), intégrera des mesures visant à assurer la sécurité, la dignité et le bien-être de la population touchée. Ce projet s'inscrira dans le respect des principes humanitaires et portera une attention particulière au principe ne pas nuire, de sécurité et non-discrimination. Les activités du projet seront mises en œuvre dans le respect soutenu des règles de lutte contre la COVID-19 par l'observation de mesures barrières telles que le port du masque, le lavage des mains, le respect de la distanciation sociale afin d'endiguer tout risque de contamination et de propagation de la maladie auprès des bénéficiaires. Dans le cadre de la redevabilité des sessions d'information sur le projet seront organisées avec les bénéficiaires, la phase d'évaluation des besoins sera réalisée de commun accord avec les populations dans les communes ciblées, la communication avec les communautés et les autorités locales sur les critères de ciblage seront organisées et après intervention, les feedbacks de la communauté cible seront collectés à travers des évaluations post-distribution et des séances de discussion de groupe séparées par genre et âge avant et après l'assistance. Aussi, en tant qu’acteur humanitaire, l'OIM et ses partenaires de mise en œuvre s’assureront que les actions n’induisent aucune tension ou problème dans la zone et n’exposent pas les bénéficiaires en affichant les compositions de kits BNA et Abris. A cet effet, une collaboration étroite sera faite avec les acteurs de protection pour un suivi de prêt de toute question de protection. Le coût total du projet sera de 4 161 500 USD.

Mise en œuvre des services intégrés SR/VBG dans les 4 régions affectées par les mouvements des populations consécutifs à l’insécurité Assurer une prise en charge holistique, adaptée et opportune aux survivantes de VGB  pour les déplacées internes, populations hotes des regions de Diffa, Tillaberi, Tahoua, et Maradi et Niamey Le projet vise à assurer dans un cadre bien coordonné, une prise en charge holistique qualitative de proximité adaptée au sexe, à l’âge, au handicap et au statut de déplacement pour les personnes survivant(e)s de VBG et réduire les risques de Violences Sexuelles et Basées sur le Genre, les exploitations et abus sexuels chez les personnes à risque. Il cible les populations, non déplacées /hôtes , les déplacées internes, les  retournées incluant les femmes, les hommes, les filles , y compris  les adolescentes et les personnes handicapées dans les régions de Tillaberi (départements de:  Téra, Torodi, Banibangou, Oullam, Say , Tillaberi , Ayerou, Bankilaré, Abala , Flingué,  Balleyara, Gotheye) ;  Tahoua( départements de : Abalak, Bagaroua, Birnin Koni, Illela, Madaoua , Tahoua, Tchintabaraden, Tillia, Tassara ), Maradi (départements de : Guidan Roundji , Madarounfa, Maradi ville ), et Diffa( départements de Bosso, Diffa, Goudoumaria, Maine-soroa, Ngourti, N'Nguigmi)  et Niamey affectées par les crises sécuritaires et transfrontalières. Le projet mobilisera les autres acteurs humanitaires des secteurs clés, les services déconcentrés de l’Etat, les communautés incluant les femmes, les hommes, les filles, les garçons et les personnes handicapées, pour assurer une participation inclusive dans la mise en œuvre des activités de façon intégrée en veillant au caractère adaptés et opportun pour survivantes de VBG. Ainsi tout en renforçant (formation équipements, suivi) les services de prise en charge, les outils (cartographie, SOP et chemin de référencement ; messages et module de formation à jours et compréhensifs) seront développés et mis à disposition des acteurs. Les acteurs communautaires (para juristes, comités de vigilances, chefs traditionnels, radio communautaires) seront formés et dotés de supports adaptés pour mener les activités de prévention et réduction des risques de VBG et assurer l'orientation des cas selon la stratégie communautaire (information et sensibilisation et orientation vers les services disponibles de qualités sur la base de des cartographie et chemin de référencement). Un mécanisme de gestion de l'information VBG (collecte analyse et partage) basé sur le GBVIMS garantira la qualité des données des cas et des évaluations périodiques renforceront le suivi de la situation pour une réponse adaptée et opportune. Des mécanismes de feed-back et de plaintes à la portée des communautés seront mis en place et opérationnalisés afin de mieux garantir la participation des communautés tout le long du cycle du projet et renforcer la qualité des interventions. Dans ce cadre chaque trimestre des rencontres inter acteurs et bénéficiaires seront organisées au niveau de chaque département où il sera partagé les résultats les insuffisances constatées et dégager les besoins d'amélioration pour la suite. Pour la redevabilité envers les mécanismes de coordination et les partenaires (bailleurs) des réunions mensuelles de coordination au niveau national et sous nationale de l'ensemble des acteurs membres du sous cluster renforcées par des missions de suivi et appui technique de la coordination nationale du sous cluster sur le terrain permettront de faire le suivi de la qualité, la veille de la situation, des rapports et des fac-sheet seront produits et partagés chaque trimestre..

Assistance alimentaire et nutritionnelle aux personnes vulnérables au Niger en soutien au plan d'urgence du gouvernement Niger Country Strategic Plan  La vision de la réponse aux urgences dans le cadre du Plan Stratégique Pays (PSP) 2020-2024 du PAM Niger est la réduction de l’empreinte humanitaire dans la mise en œuvre de l’Activité 1, relative aux urgences du PSP à travers la promotion de l’approche NEXUS. Cette réponse s’inscrit dans la Stratégie de Prévention et de Gestion des Crises Alimentaires 2021 – 2025 du Dispositif National de Prévention et de Gestion de Crises Alimentaires (DNPGCA). Ce plan s’inscrit aussi dans le Plan d’Action 2021-2023 du Comité Technique Tripartite sur le Nexus Urgence-Développement (CTTNUD), en vue d’une mobilisation des ressources financières pour une planification et une mise en œuvre concertée des activités relatives à la promotion du NEXUS.  Dans le cas spécifique de l’assistance aux retournés dans leurs villages d’origine, qui est envisagée en 2022, la Loi 2018-74, relative à la protection et à l’assistance aux Personnes Déplacées Internes (PDI) cadrera le processus. Rappelons que l’Activité 1, relative aux urgences s’inscrit dans l’effet direct stratégique 1 du CSP (2020-2024) du PAM Niger « Les populations affectées, y compris les réfugiés, les personnes déplacées internes, les communautés hôtes et les retournés dans les zones ciblées sont en mesure de répondre aux besoins alimentaires minimums pendant et après la crise ».  La réponse aux urgences du PAM concernant la SECAL, basée sur une approche flexible, concernera toutes les trois (3) composantes de cette réponse en 2022 :
•	Le Mécanisme de Réponse Rapide (RRM)
•	La réponse aux crises prolongées.
•	La réponse à la soudure agricole et pastorale.
Par ailleurs la prévention de la malnutrition aux enfants 6-23 mois est combinée aux trois composantes ci-dessus.

Emergency WASH services for drought affected displaced communities in Adado District Provision of basic and life-saving WASH services in South West, Hirshabelle States, Benadir and Galmudug region of South-Central Somalia Somalia continued to be under crisis in 2021 with continued conflict, political instability, economic decline, increasing food insecurity, climatic shocks, disease outbreaks including COVID-19, and the worst desert locust infestation in years.. Some 5.9 million people are in need of humanitarian assistance across 74 districts in Somalia in 2021. 
The 2022 Humanitarian Needs Overview states that the high humanitarian needs in Somalia are driven by seasonal floods, severe drought conditions, acute water diarrhea/ cholera outbreaks and protracted crises, exacerbated by the COVID-19 outbreak. Drought remains the main driver of WASH needs in Somalia leading to displacement and communal conflict over water points. 
According to the WHO-UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) 2020, only 39 per cent of people in rural areas have access to water supply. 39 per cent of vulnerable people in Somalia do not have access to sustained, improved and safe water source for drinking and other domestic uses, while 84 per cent still walk for more than 15 minutes to the nearest water source. Due to these constraints, one in five Somalis do not have enough water per day to cover their basic needs for both drinking and domestic use. 92 per cent of the households don’t have water collection and storage containers further impacting their regular access to water. It is estimated that 1.3 million people in 24 drought hotspot locations hugely depend on water trucking during drought due to frequent breakdown or and dry-up of strategic water sources. This is quite unsustainable.
Access to improved sanitation facilities in Somalia is very low. JMCNA 2021 noted that 57 percent of households do not have access to improved sanitation facilities. Additionally, 23 per cent of people across Somalia still defecate in the open, 49 per cent of which are in rural areas. There are 1,507 IDP sites which still have less than 1 latrine per 50 individuals as per the recommended WASH Cluster minimum standards. 
Over half of all IDPs reportedly still faced challenges in terms of access to soap and hand washing facilities according to JMCNA 2021. Only 53 per cent of households across Somalia practise proper hand washing with soap and water while (39 percent) reported that they wash their hands but without soap and only 45 per cent of households have access to Menstrual Hygiene Management (MHM) material at home or can access it through their local market. 
According to the HNO 2022, the population in need of WASH services in 2022 includes approximately 1,619,415 IDPs and 4,818,944 vulnerable host communities. It's estimated that 6,058,603 people (38 per cent) in the 'Severe' category lack access to safe water and proper sanitation services and are highly vulnerable to AWD and cholera and around 379,757 people (2 percent) are in extreme condition as they access water directly from rivers and surface bonds, practice open defecation and lack access to soap and other essential hygiene materials and are susceptible to communicable diseases
Women and girls are exposed to protection risks including gender-based violence (GBV) when collecting water from too distant water sources or using unimproved overcrowded sanitation facilities which lack safety and protection features. 
CPD is targeting 24,900 people and will train gender-balanced management committees in order to avoid over reliance on unsustainable means of accessing clean water by rehabilitating strategic reliable water points. Committees will also be established to maintain clean sanitation facilities, as well as scale up hygiene promotion initiatives to help minimize AWD/cholera outbreaks during the rainy seasons. Marginalized groups will be consulted in all project phases including design and implementation and ensuring that the location, distance and access routes to the water points, latrines and distribution sites are accessible to all members of the community, including the disabled.

Improved access to food and other urgent basic needs through multipurpose cash assistance for drought affected displaced households and families with malnourished children in Baidoa. Strengthening food and livelihood security of conflict and disaster affected vulnerable IDPs and host communities through support to agricultural production and cash assistance to meet their immediate basic needs. In the face of increasing food insecurity and the need to meet other basic urgent needs, initiatives to  address immediate food needs of the most vulnerable and food insecure population are paramount in saving lives and protecting assets of the most vulnerable. The proposed project is in-line with Humanitarian Needs Overview 2022, Food Security Cluster (FSC) priorities and objectives. The project aims at improving the ability of 66,610 vulnerable people including 41,280 IDPs and 9,991 people with disability to meet their food and basic needs and reduce consumption gaps through life-saving cash assistance and agriculture inputs. Of these 52,965 people under FSC CO1 and 13,645 people under FSC CO2. 
These households are affected by multiple shocks – including conflicts and facing wide consumption gaps, due to successive below-average agricultural and pastoral yields, and a lack of casual labour income opportunities in urban and IDP communities. Unconditional cash transfer (UCT) and agriculture input assistance will improve beneficiary household’s access to food and other basic needs, while preventing households from resorting to negative coping mechanisms which erode long-term resilience. Community and stakeholder engagement, gender sensitive vulnerability and eligibility criteria for beneficiary selection and emphasis on participation of men, women, boys and girls of different ages and other at-risk groups will improve gender equality and women’s empowerment and inclusion of marginalized population. Target population will be provided with six months of UCT totaling 3,675,965$ - based on the monthly transfer value recommended by Cash Working Group (CWG). In addition, 2,047 farmers households will be supported with agricultural inputs including seeds and tractor services through in kind and voucher and consumption support of 30$/month for 4 months. Cash for work will generate employment of 22,742 person days to create community assets.
Settlement and beneficiary targeting will follow a participatory and community-based process. To target the settlements, Concern will conduct stakeholder consultations and key informants interview at regional and district level. Village Relief Committees (VRC) with average 8 to 10 members in each comprising both men and women, including representatives from marginalized population groups will be established (or existing ones mobilized) and receive information on the project and the beneficiary selection process. VRCs will lead community based participatory beneficiary selection process, this will also help project to empower participating communities – including women in decision making. A key component in the beneficiary selection criteria will be gender, age and disability considerations. 
In line with Concern’s approach and quality standard for Cash and Voucher based assistance and Accountability to Affected Populations, Concern will disseminate information on its Complaints Response Mechanism (CRM) channels during sensitization to ensure that beneficiaries, target communities and project stakeholders are fully aware of and are able to raise any feedback or issues of concern for timely action. Concern’s independent Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability and Learning (MEAL) unit will regularly monitor the project and will conduct Post Distribution Monitoring (PDM).
Concern with its local NGO partners is implementing both emergency response and longer term programmes in proposed districts in this project. The proposed project will further leverage upon Concern’s efforts and strengthen envisaged resilience outcomes in the target districts, while providing the project with opportunity to ensure convergence and integration while addressing the underlying causes of vulnerability – including gender inequalities and poverty.

Emergency support for IDPs and drought affected rural communities in IPC3&4 in Baidoa district, Bay region Provision of Life Saving assistance to the disaster affected communities in Somalia Recurrent drought has severely and directly affected communities whose sources of food, income and water are diminishing and increasingly at risk. This has led to HH food insecurity, sharp increase in debt levels among poor HHs and poor animal health and produce. 
A delayed and poor Deyr season, worsened drought conditions in the target regions resulting in majority of HHs having inadequate access to food and water while staple food and commodity prices have risen at an average of 8.5% in Gedo and 24% in Bay regions over the past year (COOPI PNA, Oct 2021). From October to December 2021, food insecurity is expected to further deteriorate among poor rural, urban, and displaced populations due to the impacts of anticipated, below-average 2021 Deyr (October-December) season rainfall, continued insecurity and other food security related risk factors, including rising food prices and cost of living, declining availability of milk for both consumption and sale, and a likely reduction in agricultural employment opportunities during the forthcoming Deyr season.
The project focuses on the delivery of basic lifesaving and protection/restoration of livelihoods of the target population with a special focus on all locations with FSC prioritized persons in need, including IDPs and host communities that are classified in IPC Phase 3 & 4 in terms of response. 
The project is aimed at improving the ability of vulnerable HHs to meet their basic needs, supports protection and recovery of livelihood assets through life-saving UCT, animal treatment services, provision of locally preferred high quality seeds kits and trainings, and rehabilitation of community productive assets through CFW to support the resilience of vulnerable populations against shocks and prevent them from slipping into acute food insecurity. The proposed project aims to target at least 6,600 HHs (39,600) pastoral, agro-pastoral and IDP HHs in Bay, Banadir, Gedo and Togdheer regions in crisis and emergency with delivery of life saving interventions in line with the strategic objectives of the HRP and FSC response plan.
The project is informed by the centrality of protection and a gender, age and diversity-sensitive approach which is mainstreamed throughout the project cycle. Moreover, the project reflects the principles of COOPI Protection Policy and is built consistently with COOPI Protection SOPs and Protection Mainstreaming guidelines. The project will be guided by the principles of DO NO HARM, ensuring safety and dignity of target population is upheld and at the same time providing for accountability, participation and empowerment. COOPI prioritizes respect for the rights, dignity and safety of the people affected by crisis and is committed to taking account of, giving account to, and being held to account by the populations benefiting from the intervention. During implementation, the beneficiary women, girls and the disabled will be included in decision making processes and in monitoring so as ensure that the most marginalized and vulnerable are represented and have influence.
In summary the following activities will be carried out:
1.	Provide UCT to 3,100 HHs that are faced with severe levels of food insecurity (crisis and emergency) with the aim of improving immediate access to food for 3 months.
2.	Rehabilitation of community productive assets through CFW targeting 1,000 vulnerable HHs.
3.	Provision of locally preferred high quality seed kits, trainings and fuel for irrigation for 500 flood affected female and male headed vulnerable riverine farmers in Bele-Hawa Gedo region.
4.	Provision of locally preferred high quality seeds kit (drought tolerant) and trainings for 1,000 female and male headed vulnerable agro-pastoral farmers in Burhakaba district, Bay region.
5.	Emergency livestock treatment (treatment and deworming) campaigns for animals belonging to 1,000 HHs will be dewormed and treated against endemic &prevalent diseases.

""""Emergency Food Security and Livelihood support to the most vulnerable drought-affected groups in Baidoa and Bardale Districts"""" Livelihood Support for vulnerable IDPs and poor Host Communities in Mudug and Galgadud Regions-Galmudug State of Somalia. Mercy Corps proposes a project on Livelihood Support targeting vulnerable IDPs and poor host communities in Mudug and Galgadud Regions of Galmudug State of Somalia, with the aim to contribute to the achievement of FSC strategies and objectives aligned to the HRP 2022. The project will benefit a total of 4,120vulnerable and marginalized households (1,100 Men, 1,500 women, 600 boys, 920 girls) in IDPs and host communities in Galkayo, Hobyo, Caabudwaq and Caadado Districts. The proposed intervention will improve immediate access to food, provide livelihood inputs (Livestock), and skills training for new livelihoods for the communities. Access to immediate food assistance will be provided through Conditional and Unconditional Cash transfers in forms of the multipurpose cash assistance and food vouchers to meet their basic needs and to protect and restore livelihoods, related food, and income sources. Communities will also participate in the rehabilitation and establishment of community infrastructure such as water catchments, and feeder roads, whereby they will receive cash-for-work and pastoral households will receive livelihood assets in form of livestock restocking for restoration. Technical vocational skills training will also be provided as a form of building new livelihoods.  The project targets the most vulnerable populations categorized as facing IPC Phases 3 and 4.
The proposed project is cognizant of the current food security context of Galmudug region of Somalia. According to FSNAU and FEWS NET, Post-Gu Assessment in September 2021 projected that nearly 3.5 million Somalis would be in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) through at least December 2021, in the absence of humanitarian assistance. That includes 1.1 million internally displaced persons who will face moderate to large food consumption gaps through late 2021. Out of the total 3.5 million people in need of urgent food assistance, 640,000 people face significant food consumption gaps. In addition, 3.7 million people are classified in IPC phase 2 (Stressed), engaging in negative coping strategies to meet their food and non-food needs, bringing the total number of Somalis experiencing acute food insecurity to 7.2 million by late 2021. In addition to, majority of the estimated 2.9 million IDPs across Somalia are poor with limited livelihood assets, few income earning opportunities, low communal support, and rely heavily on external humanitarian assistance. As a result, one-third of internally displaced persons (in both rural and urban settlements) face moderate to large food consumption gaps through late 2021. The COVID-19 pandemic and related containment measures seem to affect the urban poor population more than rural poor population. As a result, the urban poor face moderate to large food consumption gaps, partly due to a slowdown in economic activities in urban areas and the rising costs of food and other essential non-food items. 
Mercy Corps field assessments in target regions revealed the deepening effect of frequent droughts and conflicts, which have led to high food consumption gaps and loss of livelihood assets. There is urgent need to address the food insecurity and livelihood threats for the IDPs and communities in the region. As the food security situation in Galmudug state remains tenuous, Mercy Corps sees an urgent need to respond and save lives, alleviate human suffering, and reduce the social and economic impact of the humanitarian crisis. This will reduce acute humanitarian needs and excess mortality among the most vulnerable by providing lifesaving and sustaining integrated assistance. The project will consider all gender groups and disability needs in implementation and will maintain accountability to the population through ensuring community feedback mechanisms and adherence to policies.

Life-saving health and WASH program to crisis-affected populations in Beletweyne and Bulaburte districts, Hiraan region, Somalia. Emergency Inclusive WASH Program in Galagaduud, Mudug and Hiraan regions, South Central Somalia Mercy-USA for Aid and Development (Mercy-USA) aims to improve the quality of life and protect vulnerable communities from morbidity and mortality associated with water-related diseases through water, sanitation and hygiene activities. This 12 month WASH project will target vulnerable people affected by drought, floods and conflict in Hiiraan, Galgadud, and Mudug regions by improving access to safe water and sanitation facilities and facilitating the uptake of acceptable hygiene practices. The project activities are in line with relevant strategic plans, including the Somalia National Development Plan, UN Strategic Framework and WASH Cluster priorities and guidance. 
The target populations in Hiraan, Galgadud and Mudug regions have been facing simultaneously multiple barriers and inequalities in accessing WASH services. These barriers include, geographical barriers, where some of the target communities live in rural settings, physical barriers, where persons with disabilities, children, older persons, pregnant women and others vulnerable groups are unable to access WASH services due to inappropriate design, and economic barriers.
Lack of access to safe water and sanitation increases the prevalence of preventable, water-borne diseases such as diarrhoea and dysentery, caused mainly by ingesting unclean water and contaminated food due to poor hygiene and poor human waste disposal. 
Mercy-USA thus seeks to increase access to sustainable and inclusive WASH services for disadvantaged individuals and groups, including IDPs, people living in rural and remote areas, as well as people with disabilities and increase their resilience to emergencies, including current COVID-19 pandemic.
Mercy-USA's proposed inclusive WASH response is immediate and designed to control the spread of water-borne diseases and preserve the health of the target populations, focusing on the severely affected and hard-to-reach. Proposed interventions include the provision of free, safe and sustainable drinking water, routine chlorination of existing water sources, testing of communal water sources for chemical and microbiological hazards by use of a portable water testing kit, construction of gender-segregated VIP latrines for underserved public primary schools and public health facilities and hygiene promotion. Mercy-USA will directly implement project activities. 
Mercy-USA will ensure stakeholder involvement in the implementation of project activities by first carrying out a stakeholder analysis to identify who has an interest or influence over WASH outcomes, at regional level, district level, institutional levels, community level, and private sector level. Mercy-USA will seek to incorporate their needs and ideas to implement inclusive, sustainable and climate-resilient WASH activities. Mercy-USA will ensure synergy with other Clusters to ensure adequate coordination of the activities through regular coordination with Health, Education, Shelter/NFIs, Protection, Nutrition, CWG and FSL Clusters to add value to the overall response through integrated response.

Decades of conflict, recurrent climate shocks, disease outbreaks and increasing poverty are devastating the people of Somalia. Without humanitarian assistance, nearly 3.5 million are expected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse outcomes through the end of 2021.

Provision of sustained access to emergency WASH services for the drought-affected IDP and Non-IDP households in Abudwak District Vulnerable IDP and Host Communities in Jubaland, Banadir and Galgadud have  Increased Access to WASH Services  The project aims to increase WASH services to the over 6.4 M people in need in Somalia targeting districts that are categorized as stressed or severe in the severity scale, those that are hard to reach and those that have reported AWD/cholera cases. The project targets approximately  6,552 vulnerable IDPs  11,448 host communities with a special focus on vulnerable segments of the community including  7 803 women  9,900 children 1,800 PLWD and 875 elderly people. In line with HRP strategic objective 1, specific objective 1.2, this project will contribute to the WASH cluster objective of delivering life-saving WASH assistance to reduce acute needs among most vulnerable settlements and communities through emergency water tracking, water vouchers, provision of hygiene kits and hygiene promotion activities. Lifesaving Wash assistance will target hard to reach communities in Garbaharey and Dolow districts and IDPs households in Banadir and Dolow. This project is also aligned to HRP strategic objective 2, specific objective 2.1, contributing to WASH cluster objective of restoring access to safe and equitable basic WASH services to vulnerable communities and in schools. This will be achieved through rehabilitation of water infrastructures including shallow wells, water pipe network, elevated tanks and water kiosks. Solar pumping systems will be installed in boreholes and shallow wells to reduce the O&M of community water systems. Community mobilizations and capacity building in management of water projects and O&M of solar system will be done to ensure active community participation in the implementation and management of the water facilities. This project will also contribute to the WASH cluster objective of restoring access to basic sanitation and hygiene in schools in Abudwak and Dollow, through rehabilitation of gender segregated latrines with lockable doors from inside with hand washing facilities. All the WASH infrastructures proposed in this project are designed with consideration of the safety, equity and easy accessibility by vulnerable groups such as women, girls, PLWD and the elderly. The target beneficiaries will actively participate in the selection of the sites for water facilities in their locations that will be strategic to serve households within approximately 500m distance that will be in open and clear places to ensure safety of users. Additionally water kiosks will be designed to ensure easy water collection by girls, women, elderly and those with disabilities. For water trucking water collection points will be selected by the beneficiaries and will be at about 500m from the households and in open places for safety purposes. The water collection will be planned such that the elderly and PLWD will have separate times to collect their water. The latrines constructed in schools will be strategically located to ensure safety of users and dignity of users. Hygiene kits will be collected from reasonable distances from the beneficiary households for safety of the beneficiaries as they carry them home. Use of water and hygiene kits vouchers will further enhance safety and equity of vulnerable groups targeted in this project. Mainstreaming of protection and gender in this project will contribute to HRP strategic objective 3, specific objective 3.1 as well as the WASH cluster objective of maintaining safety, equity and accessibility of the vulnerable groups (including women, boys, girls, elderly and people with disabilities) when accessing WASH services. This project will build on WASH and COVID 19 interventions implemented by NAPAD (2019, 2020 and 2021) in Galgadud, Jubaland and Banadir regions that includes rehabilitation of water infrastructures such as water tanks, water pipe networks, installation of solar water pumping systems, installation of handwashing facilities, provision of hygiene kits and mass hygiene promotion using the mass media and door to door promotion by community hygiene

""""Strengthen CCCM services to improve the living conditions and enhancing access to HLP rights of drought-affected IDPs in Bardheere, Ceelwaq, Luuq Gedo Region"""" Strengthening protective environment for displacement affected populations In Banadir, Galmudug, Lower Jubba and Gedo Regions through HLP interventions to improve tenure security situation and address post-eviction complications. The intervention is geared toward preventing and responding to eviction, monitoring of threats to evictions by assessing potential eviction sites, monitoring, documentation and reporting to relevant authorities and relevant clusters to mobilize support for advocacy. The advocacy and campaigns will aim to ensure actors facilitate lawful eviction processes. Capacity development targeting settlement managers, local authorities on Housing, Land and proper protection monitoring through ensuring collection of information based on the methodology of the Somalia Protection Monitoring System (SPMS).
Protection, monitoring and response mechanisms with regards to land, housing and property is lacking in most of protection programming. Most often legal Aid services, land, houses and property rights are not prioritized hence leaving big gaps in the protection response mechanism. There is poor coordination among protection and response service providers especially on land, housing and property rights. Furthermore, the protection response mechanisms have limited or no provision of free legal aid services to IDPs, survivors of GBV and HLP.
Therefore, this project seeks to improve and strengthen coordination among service providers and to enhance legal protection and response mechanism for IDPs on land, housing and property rights. Improved access to water for drought-affected communities in Las Anod Emergency WASH Response for people affected by emergency in Somaliland/Somalia  The humanitarian situation in Somalia remains critical due to the ongoing impacts of drought, conflict, locust infestation, and the COVID 19 pandemic. An estimated 6.61 million people, about 42 per cent of the Somali population are in need of emergency life-saving WASH assistance of which 4.2 million will need safe drinking water, 3.2 million sanitation services, and 5.2 million hygiene supplies. According to FAO/SWALIM draught analysis from 2000 to July 2021, the trend shows that Somalia has been experiencing cyclic drought every five to six years: 2000/2001, 2004/2005, 2010/2011, 2016/2017, and currently in 2020/2021. These drought conditions were triggered by consecutive seasons of below-average rainfall including the below-average Gu rains (April to July 2021) and delay of short Dayr rains (October to December 2021). The Somalia Food Security Cluster as of 18th October 2021 confirms that half of Somalia is still experiencing serious drought conditions (moderate to severe drought with water shortages and livestock losses), with the worst impacts being felt in Jubaland, South West State, Galmudug, and areas of Puntland. The Deyr seasonal rainfall is expected to be below average, with depressed rains not going to be effective in mitigating drought conditions. A devastating drought is likely to continue into 2022 given the 1) La Nina conditions, 2) poor rainfall forecast for October and November and 3) existing drought conditions.
Access to water is mainly dependent on rainfall in the majority of the country. Barkads in nonriverine areas are the major water sources while others depend on shallow/deep groundwater sources. Thus, failure in rains triggers massive shortages as currently being reported from Jubaland, Part of Somaliland, Galmudug, and many other areas. 50 of the 74 districts in Somalia faced severe water shortages and water prices increased by 66 per cent7 in Gedo, Galgadud, Mudug, Sool, and Sanaag regions (JMCNA 2021). The Non-functionality of few strategic boreholes also increases as the operation hours increase. Many shallow-water sources are drying while others are having increased brackish water intrusions. Over 39% of Somalis don’t have access to sustained, improved and safe water. As result, over 84% are walking more than 15minuts to access water while over 92% don’t have water collection and storage facilities. Due to limited access and poor quality of existing water sources, over 1.3 million people in 24 drought-affected locations are dependent on water trucking – the majority of them are private water trucking. Oxfam PDMs and HNO results confirm the majority of Somalis use two jerry cans per day during drought conditions. 39% of people assessed confirm they wash their hands but have reported having no access to soap. 45% of girls assessed have reported having access to Menstruation hygiene management (MHM) materials at or can access from local markets.
Oxfam has been working in Somalia for over 40 years and will continue to provide life-saving humanitarian support and build the capacity of both private and public institutions. Oxfam is working with over 10 national NGOs in a different part of Somalia. In response to the continued emergency, Oxfam will continue supporting efforts to nation/local government in containment and prevention of COVID-19, will monitor and rehabilitate non-function strategic boreholes, will conduct expansion of existing water sources in order to reduce the walking time, will drill boreholes in chronically water insecure areas, will provide cash and voucher assistant for people to access live-saving water, hygiene and MHM kits from local markets or access point established by Oxfam, will work with community health volunteers to increase awareness and handwashing practice during critical times and will construct shared household latrines for communities practicing open defecations.

Providing Life Saving Treatment Nutrition Services to Somali Vulnerable Communities most severely affected by the drought Providing Life Saving Treatment and Prevention Nutrition Services to the Vulnerable Communities in Somalia Food and Nutrition context in Somalia
Decades of conflict and natural disasters including repeated droughts and seasonal flooding followed by limited government and institutional support have had a profound negative effect on the food security situation and social service sector in Somalia. Nearly seven in ten Somalis live on less than USD 1.90 per day,  the sixth-highest poverty rate in sub-Saharan Africa. Poverty is both widespread and deep, particularly for households in rural areas and internally displaced person (IDP) settlements. The number of food-insecure people experiencing long-term stress is trending upwards, indicating that chronic food insecurity persists, requiring sustainable solutions. Recurrent climate-related shocks and political instability are key drivers of food insecurity and pose continuing risks to crop production and food access. Malnutrition in Somalia is driven by a combination of factors such as recurrent food insecurity, child illnesses, high morbidity, micronutrient deficiencies, low immunization levels, poor access to clean water and sanitation, poor hygiene practice, gender inequality and discriminatory sociocultural attitudes leading to poor care practices. Based on the latest Post Gu FSNAU assessment (September 2021), it is estimated that a total of 3.5 million out of the 15.8m people face acute food insecurity (IPC 3 and above – crisis or worse)  until December 2021. At the national level the median prevalence of Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) has remained at a serious level of 11.1%. Approximately 1.2 million children under the age of five are likely to be acutely malnourished, including 295,515 who are likely to be severely malnourished. In addition to this, around 245,909 Pregnant & Lactating Women (PLWs) will be at risk of acute malnutrition. 

Acute malnutrition is a major public health problem in Somalia. It affects disproportionately children under the age of five, as well as Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLWs), especially among IDPs, vulnerable (agro) pastoralist communities and those living in areas affected by flooding. Morbidity among children is high (≥ 20%). Out of a total of 40 surveyed population groups 18 recorded high morbidity presence of above 20%. 
Vitamin A supplementation and Measles vaccination remains low <40% in several population groups. 

TB prevalence remains one of the highest globally with Somalia in the top 10 countries with high TB burden (262 per 100,000 population) while the HIV prevalence remains <1% however with high stigma and discrimination levels at 94%.

Project activities
The World Food Program is the leading UN agency in Somalia in fighting hunger. In Somalia, WFP together with the Ministry of Health (MoH), nutrition cluster and the partners, supports nutrition service delivery and prevention. WFP collaborates with the MoH and UNICEF to offer an integrated package of nutrition and health, following the revised MoH IMAM guidelines for treating acute malnutrition in Somalia.

WFP will cover both treatment and preventive nutrition services including:
•	Targeted Supplementary Feeding Program for 665,846 moderately acute malnourished children 6-59 months; 173,746 malnourished Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLW), 10,794 malnourished People Living with HIV on ART treatment and malnourished TB patients.
•	Preventive Nutrition services for 386,102 children 6-23 months and 173,746 PLW enrolled in Maternal Child Health and Nutrition services and blanket Supplementary Feeding Program for children 6-23 months and PLW in districts where GAM (Global Acute Malnutrition) rate is above 15%.
•	Monthly cash vouchers of USD 15 for 24,104 PLWs in selected target districts.
•	24,206 caregivers with SAM children admitted to the Stabilisation  will receive food while staying at the Stabilisation Center 
•	A total of 96,150 pregnant women will receive food rations for their families when delivering their baby at a health facility

Emergency Food Security Response to drought affected communities in Odweyne District in the Togdheer region. Enhancing Food Security and Livelihoods among Vulnerable Communities  
In Somalia, nearly 3.5 million people are expected to face food consumption gaps or depletion of livelihood assets indicative of Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse outcomes through the end of the year 2021, in the absence of humanitarian assistance (FSNAU/ FEWSNET, Sept. 2021). Furthermore, approximately 1.2 million children under the age of five are likely to be malnourished. 

From October to December 2021, food insecurity is expected to further deteriorate among poor and displaced populations due to the impacts of anticipated, below-average 2021 Deyr (October-December) season rainfall, continued insecurity and other food security related risk factors, including rising food prices and declining availability of milk, and a likely reduction in agricultural employment opportunities. Without sustained humanitarian food assistance, 3.5 million people across Somalia are expected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse outcomes between October and December 2021 and probably into the following year 2022. Out the 3.5 million people in need of urgent food assistance, 640,000 people face significant food consumption gaps and engaging in negative coping strategies to meet their food and non-food needs. 

According to FSNAU (October – December 2021) projections, out of a total population of 464,487 in Sool, 119,340 will be in IPC 2, 81,690 in IPC 3 and 22,260 in IPC 4. In Sanaag, out of 362,723 people, 84,270 will be in IPC 2, 94,640 in IPC 3 and 22,570 in IPC 4. Candlelight assessments and consultations from other cluster partners further confirm the severity of food insecurity in the 2 proposed target districts of LaasCanod and Laasqoray. These require interventions aimed at reducing food consumption gaps, eradicating acute malnutrition, saving lives, and protecting and saving livelihoods. 

Response 
In respect of the above, the proposed project seeks to contribute to Food Security Cluster Objectives 1 and 2; which focus on improving immediate access to food and protecting livelihoods and related food sources respectively. The project will have positive impacts on food security, agricultural productivity, household incomes and resilience of smallholders particularly women in Sool and Sanag. Component 1: Cash transfers: Vulnerable families will receive and utilize unconditional and conditional cash transfers to improve their access to food and to stabilize their family’s food security. 200 households (HH) will receive UCTs, while 247 households will receive conditional cash.

HRP FOOD SECURITY - REFUGEE Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace.

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.
