Cette crise a été aggravée par les bouleversements politiques marqués par deux coups d'état en août 2020 et mai 2021, et l'incertitude persistante de la transition politique laisse l'État dans l'incapacité de répondre aux services sociaux de base des populations. 
Les déplacements internes de personnes ont augmenté de 100 000 en 2021, atteignant plus de 401 000 personnes soit quatre fois plus qu'il y a deux ans. Au total, 156 000 réfugiés maliens résident dans les pays voisins tandis que le Mali accueille 48 000 réfugiés et leur fournit protection et assistance. Les gains économiques du Mali se sont érodés, avec 900 000 personnes (0,04% de la population) qui sont retombées dans la pauvreté en raison de la crise socioéconomique de la COVID-19. la capacité des ménages est fragilisée à cause de la perte de revenus, de la réduction des transferts de fonds et à l'augmentation du coût de la vie. 
La Banque mondiale prévoit une augmentation du taux de pauvreté à 4,8 % en 2022. La crise de protection est également aggravée avec une augmentation des incidents de sécurité.  Les acteurs de la violence basée sur le genre (VBG) ont signalé 5 486 incidents de VBG, soit une augmentation de 41 % comparativement à la même période en 2020. Plus de 1 640 écoles sont fermées en raison de l'insécurité, affectant plus de 2,9 millions d'enfants dont 40 % se trouvent dans la région centrale de Mopti. Quatre districts centraux ont signalé que 40 % des écoles étaient fermées. Dans les régions du sud, 10 pour cent des écoles sont fermées à Koulikoro, Koutiala et Sikasso, privant 30 000 enfants de leur éducation. A ce jour, le Mali a rapporté plus de 15 800 cas de COVID-19.
En 2021, 1,3 million de personnes ont connu un niveau élevé d'insécurité alimentaire aiguë. le niveau le plus élevé depuis 2015, et 3 055 253 personnes ont été touchées par les mauvaises pluies et une saison de soudure prolongée. La situation humanitaire reste entravée par l'augmentation des besoins et la faiblesse des financements, avec 32 % des fonds mobilisés au 31 octobre 2021. Malgré les contraintes opérationnelles, les partenaires humanitaires ont aidé plus de 2,45 millions des 4,7 millions de personnes ciblées au 30 septembre 2021. 
Les capacités de réponse existantes au Mali représentent plus de 160 organisations humanitaires, acteurs du développement ainsi que des forces militaires (MINUSMA, Forces maliennes de défense et de sécurité, Barkhane, Mission européenne de formation, G5 Sahel). Le contexte susmentionné exigera une coordination efficace et la présence d’OCHA demeure très importante. OCHA maintiendra sa présence à Bamako, Mopti, Tombouctou, Gao et ouvrira une antenne à Ségou tout en couvrant à distance les régions de Taoudénit, Ménaka, Kidal et les régions du sud Est et Ouest. 

Sept clusters actifs (Éducation, Sécurité alimentaire, Santé, Nutrition, Protection, Abris/BNA et WASH), des sous-clusters et des groupes de travail spécialisés (Accès, CM-Coord, Redevabilité, Genre et Cash) sont en place au niveau national et local. Le Bureau d’OCHA au Mali continuera ainsi à jouer un rôle central dans la mobilisation, la coordination et le soutien des acteurs humanitaires dans les domaines de la coordination, la gestion de l’information, le financement humanitaire et le plaidoyer.

JEOP targets transitory or acute food insecure households through a participant targeting process led by the Government of Ethiopia’s (GoE) National Disaster Risk Management Commission (NDRMC). JEOP complements emergency needs outlined in the GoE’s Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP). Over the last decade, JEOP has served as a food pipeline for up to 33% of the emergency-affected woredas in five regions and one city administration, flexing to meet evolving need.

Currently targeting over seven million people nationwide, JEOP is one of the largest food operators in Ethiopia, working with the GoE alongside the World Food Program (WFP). JEOP’s principal objective is to ensure that targeted communities in need of emergency food assistance have access to sufficient, appropriate, food in a timely manner. This is done primarily through round-based distributions of commodities to targeted project participants (15kg. wheat, 1.5kg pulses and 0.45kg oil).  Since 2018, JEOP expanded its modalities to include cash transfers in two forms; a) cash in lieu of wheat in line with seasonal availability of grains on local markets, and b) transfers to offset cost of transportation for families living far from final distribution points. Modality decisions are based on market and cash feasibility assessments looking at market conditions, access, preference, risk analysis, cost efficiency and effectiveness, with attention to intra-household and community conflict dynamics.
Led by Catholic Relief Services (CRS), the JEOP consortium includes CARE, Food for the Hungry Ethiopia (FHE), Organization for Rehabilitation and Development in Amhara (ORDA), Relief Society of Tigray (REST), and World Vision Ethiopia (WV). CRS implements through its local Catholic Church partners, the Hararghe Catholic Secretariat (HCS) and Meki Catholic Secretariat (MCS). CRS is responsible for overall consortium management.

Subsequent modifications extended JEOP through July 2022, the current end date of the program. Meanwhile, CRS is the Apparent Successful Applicant (ASA) for follow on funding for JEOP under another 5-year award and has applied for additional funding under another BHA Emergency mechanism to cover 18 months of the current caseload in Northern Ethiopia Response (implemented in Tigray and Amhara).

Este programa inició en 2021 con comidas escolares en emergencias priorizando escuelas iniciales y de educación especial.

WFP proporciona comidas escolares acompañado de un paquete integrado de intervenciones para mejorar el acceso a alimentos nutritivos y diversificados a través de las escuelas, contribuyendo al mismo tiempo a mejorar la salud y la nutrición de los niños en edad escolar, los estudiantes con discapacidad y el personal escolar, y apoyando a las comunidades a reducir la dependencia en estrategias de afrontamiento. De manera gradual, el WFP está realizando compras locales de alimentos, e incluyendo acciones para apoyar los mercados locales con compras a pequeños productores y apoyo técnico para acceso a mercados.

En este sentido, el programa de comidas escolares en emergencias tiene los siguientes componentes, para asegurar un enfoque integral que apoye al estudiante en el entorno escolar y familiar:

1. Entrega de comidas escolares nutritivas para estudiantes y personal escolar, promoviendo las compras locales y a pequeños productores.

States, Improved food security and livelihoods of IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host communities in South Sudan In line with the South Sudan 2022 Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) and the FSL Cluster priorities, NPA will support vulnerable and food-insecure Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs), returnees and vulnerable host communities in IPC 4 locations in Canal/Pigi, Fangak, Pochalla & Bor South Counties of Jonglei State, Rumbek East, Rumbek Center, Cueibet, Yirol East, Yirol West and Awerial Counties of Lakes State, Terekeka County of Central Equatoria State and Kapoeta North County of Eastern Equatoria State. NPA’s emergency assistance and livelihoods support aims at saving lives and averting total collapse of livelihoods in the target Counties. The provision of agricultural and fishing inputs/kits, training in agricultural production and fishing is expected to improve the food production and in turn the food security of the target households (HHs) thus supporting them to recover from crisis and placing them on an accelerated path to early recovery and resilience to acute shocks. NPA’s response will address the food security and livelihoods needs and priorities identified in the South Sudan 2022 Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO).

NPA seeks to support 105,056 HHs (630,338 individuals) in the targeted Counties with livelihood kits and cash transfers to address food insecurity. Some of the kits will be provided by FAO and some procured by NPA. Training on improved agronomic and fishing practices, marketing and group dynamics will be done through model farmers and fisher folk who will undergo a Training of Trainers (ToT) and subsequently cascade the knowledge and skills to the farmers and fisher folk in their communities. NPA will employ a community-based beneficiary selection approach which will entail establishing Project Management Committees (PMC’s) to lead the selection of eligible beneficiaries based on the beneficiary selection criteria. Vulnerable HHs with severe food insecurity including female, child, disabled/chronically ill headed HHs; persons living with or at risk of HIV/AIDS and survivors of Gender-Based Violence (GBV) will be targeted in this project.

The target communities will be the prime movers of the implementation process through engagement in the project. Through various means, NPA will gather feedback from the target communities and stakeholders to improve project implementation.

This has led to HH food insecurity, sharp increase in debt levels among poor HHs and poor animal health and produce. 
A delayed and poor Deyr season, worsened drought conditions in the target regions resulting in majority of HHs having inadequate access to food and water while staple food and commodity prices have risen at an average of 8.5% in Gedo and 24% in Bay regions over the past year (COOPI PNA, Oct 2021). From October to December 2021, food insecurity is expected to further deteriorate among poor rural, urban, and displaced populations due to the impacts of anticipated, below-average 2021 Deyr (October-December) season rainfall, continued insecurity and other food security related risk factors, including rising food prices and cost of living, declining availability of milk for both consumption and sale, and a likely reduction in agricultural employment opportunities during the forthcoming Deyr season.
The project focuses on the delivery of basic lifesaving and protection/restoration of livelihoods of the target population with a special focus on all locations with FSC prioritized persons in need, including IDPs and host communities that are classified in IPC Phase 3 & 4 in terms of response. 
The project is aimed at improving the ability of vulnerable HHs to meet their basic needs, supports protection and recovery of livelihood assets through life-saving UCT, animal treatment services, provision of locally preferred high quality seeds kits and trainings, and rehabilitation of community productive assets through CFW to support the resilience of vulnerable populations against shocks and prevent them from slipping into acute food insecurity. The proposed project aims to target at least 6,600 HHs (39,600) pastoral, agro-pastoral and IDP HHs in Bay, Banadir, Gedo and Togdheer regions in crisis and emergency with delivery of life saving interventions in line with the strategic objectives of the HRP and FSC response plan.
The project is informed by the centrality of protection and a gender, age and diversity-sensitive approach which is mainstreamed throughout the project cycle. Moreover, the project reflects the principles of COOPI Protection Policy and is built consistently with COOPI Protection SOPs and Protection Mainstreaming guidelines. The project will be guided by the principles of DO NO HARM, ensuring safety and dignity of target population is upheld and at the same time providing for accountability, participation and empowerment. COOPI prioritizes respect for the rights, dignity and safety of the people affected by crisis and is committed to taking account of, giving account to, and being held to account by the populations benefiting from the intervention. During implementation, the beneficiary women, girls and the disabled will be included in decision making processes and in monitoring so as ensure that the most marginalized and vulnerable are represented and have influence.
In summary the following activities will be carried out:
1.	Provide UCT to 3,100 HHs that are faced with severe levels of food insecurity (crisis and emergency) with the aim of improving immediate access to food for 3 months.
2.	Rehabilitation of community productive assets through CFW targeting 1,000 vulnerable HHs.
3.	Provision of locally preferred high quality seed kits, trainings and fuel for irrigation for 500 flood affected female and male headed vulnerable riverine farmers in Bele-Hawa Gedo region.
4.	Provision of locally preferred high quality seeds kit (drought tolerant) and trainings for 1,000 female and male headed vulnerable agro-pastoral farmers in Burhakaba district, Bay region.
5.	Emergency livestock treatment (treatment and deworming) campaigns for animals belonging to 1,000 HHs will be dewormed and treated against endemic &prevalent diseases.

Experts Enhance protection environment through provision of specialized protection and gender-based violence (GBV) response services to internally displaced persons (IDPs) in Ethiopia  Ongoing armed conflict, intercommunal violence and climate change (drought and flood) continue to be the key driver of humanitarian needs in Ethiopia and increased displacements across the country. Specifically, humanitarian situation in Northern Ethiopia remains challenging due to the conflict in regions of Tigray, Amhara and Afar. In Tigray, 5.2 million people are reported to need urgent humanitarian assistance according to the OCHA Tigray region Humanitarian Update from early September 2021. IOM’s draft Site Assessment (SA) Round 28 identified a total of 4,509,081 internally displaced people (IDPs) displaced across different sites in the country. From this, 2,452,077 are found in Tigray, Amhara and Afar regions. 

Affected populations face longer term protection concerns arising from shocks such as conflict, climate change, and disasters. Systemic, long-standing protection concerns such as gender-based violence (GBV) – including harmful practices, lack of access to specialized services, as well as other basic needs are exacerbated due to conflict or climatic shocks. 

Often in emergencies, women and children with and without disabilities, constitute majority of affected population with heightened risk to different rights abuse including GBV. With limited access to services such as health and MHPSS, food, WASH, shelter, psychosocial support, education and livelihoods coupled with weak social support system, IDPs are living under undignified and distressed conditions. These factors entail increased vulnerability to engage in negative coping mechanisms such as forced marriages, child labour abuse and transactional sex.   Additionally, lack of awareness of the right to assistance and limited coverage of response services, complicated by deep-rooted social norms related to gender make accessing services ever more challenging.
Despite the high number of IDPs, there has been inconsistent humanitarian assistance to the affected population due to limited resource and ongoing security concerns in the regions. Poorly coordinated relocations and returns which fall short of meeting standards also negatively affected the service delivery rendering affected population to secondary displacement and ending up living in collective centres or within host community. 
With the goal of contributing to enhancing protection environment of affected populations through prevention, risk mitigation and response efforts.  Following the Protection Cluster priorities, IOM will target primarily IDPs and returnees affected by conflict and drought through general protection and GBV prevention and response integrating Mental Health and Psychosocial support (MHPSS) interventions in Amhara, Tigray, Somali, SNNP, Diredawa, Afar and Oromia regions. 
The response and activities will be in line with the three overarching protection objectives in the HRP.

Experts Enhance protection environment through provision of specialized protection and gender-based violence (GBV) response services to internally displaced persons (IDPs) in Ethiopia  Ongoing armed conflict, intercommunal violence and climate change (drought and flood) continue to be the key driver of humanitarian needs in Ethiopia and increased displacements across the country. Specifically, humanitarian situation in Northern Ethiopia remains challenging due to the conflict in regions of Tigray, Amhara and Afar. In Tigray, 5.2 million people are reported to need urgent humanitarian assistance according to the OCHA Tigray region Humanitarian Update from early September 2021. IOM’s draft Site Assessment (SA) Round 28 identified a total of 4,509,081 internally displaced people (IDPs) displaced across different sites in the country. From this, 2,452,077 are found in Tigray, Amhara and Afar regions. 

Affected populations face longer term protection concerns arising from shocks such as conflict, climate change, and disasters. Systemic, long-standing protection concerns such as gender-based violence (GBV) – including harmful practices, lack of access to specialized services, as well as other basic needs are exacerbated due to conflict or climatic shocks. 

Often in emergencies, women and children with and without disabilities, constitute majority of affected population with heightened risk to different rights abuse including GBV. With limited access to services such as health and MHPSS, food, WASH, shelter, psychosocial support, education and livelihoods coupled with weak social support system, IDPs are living under undignified and distressed conditions. These factors entail increased vulnerability to engage in negative coping mechanisms such as forced marriages, child labour abuse and transactional sex.   Additionally, lack of awareness of the right to assistance and limited coverage of response services, complicated by deep-rooted social norms related to gender make accessing services ever more challenging.
Despite the high number of IDPs, there has been inconsistent humanitarian assistance to the affected population due to limited resource and ongoing security concerns in the regions. Poorly coordinated relocations and returns which fall short of meeting standards also negatively affected the service delivery rendering affected population to secondary displacement and ending up living in collective centres or within host community. 
With the goal of contributing to enhancing protection environment of affected populations through prevention, risk mitigation and response efforts. Ethiopia Humanitarian Response Plan 2022-Emergency Shelter and NFI Provision of life saving shelter and Non - food items assistance to IDPs, returnees and non- displaced population in Amhara and Afar Region.   The spread of the conflict in Tigray into neighboring regions of Afar and Amhara during 2021, has left millions of people, displaced and non-displaced, in need of assistance and protection in these two regions of Northern Ethiopia. In response to this, UNHCR harmonizes its IDP response with the Cluster system, the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP), the Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO), the Sustainable Development Goals, the Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement (1999) and the Kampala Convention (2009) to support PoCs.
Recognizing that contexts across the region is volatile with unique needs per location, UNHCR Shelter and Non- food item response is planned to address the needs of people in all phases of displacement, with a focus on the emergency phase, care, and maintenance of shelter for people in protracted displacements and supporting sustainable returns and recovery where the context allows. The planned interventions include consideration of shelter preparedness, response, and shelter recovery support to account for both returns and secondary displacement and will be conducted in close coordination with multi-sectoral stakeholders to ensure that approaches are integrated, and that broader needs are addressed. Holding the protection of affected populations at its core: Do no harm incl. accountability, participation and empowerment of affected people, enhancing resilience, coordination, and context-driven responses, principles will be mainstreamed throughout our responses as per the ESNFI cluster strategy.  Through this interventions, including provision of in-kind assistance and cash when feasible, UNHCR planes to reach 80,533 HH (402,664 Individuals) across the Amhara and Afar regions through the below responses.
Emergency Shelters (Communal, family shelters or Emergency Shelter kits) provision Non Food Items and ESNFI provision. For the displaced who have returned to their original homes, support such as Shelter Repair kits either through Cash or In-kind with technical guidance on building better and addressing Housing Land and Property (HLP) will be the focus. Shelter Repair is also planned for displaced populations who are unable to return to their place of origin due to protracted displacement, where government allow to settle in a secondary location. Capacity building of staff, authorities, affected populations and advocacy for those with shelter and household needs is also considered. All the ES/NFIs component will be undertaken in consultation with the IDPs and host communities to ensure it meets their most urgent needs. The IDP hosting communities will also benefit from the responses. As per the cluster guideline 10-15% of the vulnerable host communities hosting IDPs will be targeted. Acknowledging any responses that exclude groups and individuals, increase violence and SGBV risks and increase risk of exploitation, UNHCR will undertake essential actions to reduce risks and mitigate Sexual and Gender-Based Violence (SGBV) associated with shelter and NFI responses. Awareness-raising sessions will be delivered to ensure that the communities are made aware of the protection risks in shelter and NFI response and how best to mitigate them. UNHCR will continue to use IASC GBV guidelines & related tools for SEA risk assessment and mitigation, including its newly developed GBV policy guidelines, National action plan and Victim centered approach for addressing sexual misconduct to make programmes safe and accessible to all women, girls and other at risk group. Most often persons with disabilities are disproportionately affected by disasters and conflict and they face multi-layered barriers to accessing humanitarian services. As an effort to enhance inclusive humanitarian action principles, UNHCR will provide awareness-raising and training of those at the forefront of service delivery and from the overall target reserving a minimum of 15% of kits (tailor made for disables).

Food Security	Development of resilient local food systems through a school-based feeding social protection programme approach Fortalecimiento de la SAN y la resiliencia de las comunidades vulnerables, a través de un modelo de Alimentación Escolar saludable proveniente de la Agricultura Familiar local. La persistencia de la crisis económica y política en Venezuela durante los últimos años ha colocado a una parte importante de su población en situación de extrema precariedad. Las interrupciones de las actividades educativas y la cadena de suministro de alimentos locales debido a la pandemia COVID-19, ha afectado profundamente la oportunidad de la población vulnerable, incluidos niños en edad escolar y familias productoras, de acceder a alimentos esenciales y a insumos productivos que fortalezcan su SAN, respectivamente. 
En este sentido, durante el periodo 2020-2021, la cobertura del Programa de Alimentación Escolar (PAE) ha tenido deficiencia en frecuencia, ingesta nutricional y dieta equilibrada para no menos de 4.5 millones de niños y se estima que alrededor de 1.1 millones corren el riego de abandonar la Escuela. Al mismo tiempo, la disminución continua de la producción local de alimentos se agrava por el limitado acceso a insumos agrícolas esenciales -como semillas con calidad- por parte de los pequeños productores, agravando la inseguridad alimentaria y financiera preexistente en las comunidades.
Por lo anterior expuesto, la presente acción tiene como propósito principal el de mejorar la SAN de niños y niñas en edad escolar, además de los hogares rurales en situación de vulnerabilidad, esto, mediante el desarrollo de modelos de Alimentación Escolar basados en la producción local que FAO y UNICEF han pilotado y validad en cuatro estados del país. Complementariamente, la acción promoverá esquemas comunitarios de producción variada de semillas de forma artesanal, adaptadas climáticamente y que respetan la cultura y saberes locales productivos. 
Bajo este objetivo, se propone el desarrollo de los siguientes componentes:
PRODUCTO 1: Fortalecido el modelo de Alimentación Escolar basado en la producción local de la Agricultura Familiar (AF): A través de rehabilitar y/o mejorar las capacidades productivas de las Escuelas Técnicas Agrícolas (ETA) y Asociación Local de Productores (ALP) incrementando su productividad aplicando prácticas agroecológicas para producción de alimentos, huevos y semillas, además desarrollando acciones de asistencia técnica. Se espera que, con la disponibilidad de una producción local de huevos, hortalizas y frutas, se logre fomentar modelos alimentarios de circuito corto, saludables y sostenibles, en donde los niños y niñas de edad escolar en situación de vulnerabilidad - y de manera indirecta el de familias vulnerables de agricultores de pequeña escala - mejoran el consumo de alimentos diversificados, frescos y nutritivos.
PRODUCTO 2: Mejorado el acceso a semillas con calidad, por parte de los pequeños productores familiares locales; a través de una implementación de un modelo de producción de semillas comunitario, sostenibles y resilientes. En este modelo, las ETA jugarán un rol de motor de producción y difusión de conocimiento y los productores a través de las ALP, serán el factor de escalamiento de la capacidad de producción y accesibilidad de la semillas para los demás productores
Para la implementación del proyecto se han priorizado estados con población indígena y, cuando sea posible, se dará la prioridad de participación a agricultoras y agricultores indígenas y a mujeres líderes de hogar, en los estados Amazonas, Sucre, Monagas, Falcon, Zulia, Delta Amacuro, Bolívar y Apure. La acción espera dar cobertura a alrededor de 13 750 hogares de pequeños productores y productoras, aglutinando alrededor de 450 grupos productivos y/o Bancos de Semillas Comunitarios, que contribuyan a la protección y acumulación de sus medios de vida productivos esenciales y en conjunto con 50 ETAs y 25 escuelas de educación básica y primaria, puedan abastecer complementos alimentarios frescos y sanos para alrededor 27 000 niños y niñas en edad escolar.

Livelihood assets rehabilitated through small scale labor and cash for-assets; Critical livelihood inputs are made available to small-scale agropastoralists in drought-affected districts; Critical livestock support provided to nomadic pastoralists to prevent animal deaths and minimize animal sickness in drought-affected districts Emergency Lifesaving Cash and Livelihood Support to IDP and Non- IDP Communities in Somalia Somalia is facing a severe and deteriorating humanitarian crisis as we enter 2022 as a result of the compounding effects of conflict, recurrent climate shocks, diseases and pests outbreaks with increased levels of vulnerability and substantial increase in the humanitarian caseload (Somalia HNO, 2022). There is a serious risk that the impact of consecutive below average to poor rainfall in most parts of the country will develop into a severe drought by early to mid- 2022 with the number of people facing acute food insecurity on the rise. It is likely that minority groups, women, children, people with disabilities, will experience heightened protection risks as a result, unless they are intentionally targeted to receive tailored assistance.

With approximately 3.5 million individuals in IPC 3 and 4 through at least December 2021, FAO proposes to target 160,300 households (961,800 individuals- 91,500 IDPs and 870,300 non- IDPs) in IPC 3 and IPC 4 caseloads respectively. This will include 216,790 women, 254,492 girls, 264,880 boys and 225,638 men and 144,270 people living with disabilities (PWD) across 59 districts in Somalia through its flagship Cash+ approach combining short-term cash transfers with tailored livelihood support in accordance with technical and humanitarian standards. Vulnerable households will identified from at-risk pastoral, agro-pastoral, fishing, riverine farmers, IDPs and Non- IDP communities in IPC 3 and 4 areas. This intervention will integrate short-term cash transfers aimed at enabling the most vulnerable households to meet their immediate needs, with livelihood support to allow crisis-affected households to get back into production. FAO will employ community- led beneficiary selection processes and ensure adequate targeting and representation of extremely vulnerable and minority groups in community committees. Interventions proposed will employ a Do No Harm approach with a gender lens that ensures conflict- sensitivity to reduce protection risks for all individuals, and to mitigate the risk of conflict or community tensions. 

Under Food Security Cluster (FSC) Objective 1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 160,300 households through a blend of conditional (Cash-for-Work) and unconditional (UCT) transfers. Under UCT, FAO will prioritize Cash+ interventions including Cash+ Agriculture, Cash+ livestock and Cash+ fisheries. These modalities will increase households’ immediate access to food by providing sufficient cash to access the minimum expenditure basket (MEB), while supporting the rehabilitation of critical productive and community infrastructure. It will also boost household food production, increase household incomes and create employment opportunities. Cash transfer values will be informed by the Cash Working Group and are expected to differ per district/ region of intervention. They, however, will be valued at 80 percent of the food MEB, which can range from USD 50- 100 per month. All cash-based programmes will include training on good nutrition practices. 

Under FSC Objective 2, to protect livelihoods and related food sources, FAO will provide in-kind, technical support and tailored trainings to 112,500 HHs to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security and nutrition threats, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to targeted HHs. In addition, FAO shall provide transitional cash support to 13,100 HHs across agro pastoral, pastoral and fishing livelihood zones to augment the adaptive capacity of HHs, strengthen and foster resilience to future shocks, cushioning them from food insecurity and malnutrition. Trainings shall be delivered alongside input provision to build skills in sustainable use of resources provided, build skills in livelihoods management including harvest, post- harvest management, linking beneficiaries to long- term interventions that provide them opportunities to enhance their livelihoods and skills.

Emergency cash transfers to drought affected populations 	Programmed under So1 WFP SOMALIA 2022 HRP - FSC Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas. As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation. The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

(BPRM) Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2022, there are some 335,000 refugees and asylum seekers from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, primarily from Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic.
At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for longer term stability, hundreds of thousands of South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since the signing of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan, this spontaneous movement has prompted the development of an area-based approach, to support refugees, returnees and host communities, through enhanced engagement with development actors, to support greater access to services where possible.
Refugees largely reside in conflict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction in basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.
Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will benefit from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Specific protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identified at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with specific protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as verification exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the efficiency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to benefit from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

South Sudan Regional Refugee Response Plan 2022 Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2022, there are some 335,000 refugees and asylum seekers from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, primarily from Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic.
At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for longer term stability, hundreds of thousands of South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since the signing of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan, this spontaneous movement has prompted the development of an area-based approach, to support refugees, returnees and host communities, through enhanced engagement with development actors, to support greater access to services where possible.
Refugees largely reside in conflict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction in basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.
Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will benefit from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Specific protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identified at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with specific protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as verification exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the efficiency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to benefit from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

The project will target where ADRA has a permanent presence implementing Humanitarian Livelihoods long term programs while responding to the recurrently arising humanitarian emergencies in the target area. This is in line with the recent document of the HRP 2022 location and activities prioritization Guide for the Clusters. 

To achieve this objective, ADRA will focus lifesaving interventions for 7 months with possible Cluster decision of flexibility to adjust in case of new life threatening crises occurs. To ensure smooth implementation and complementarity ADRA will closely coordinate with the DRM-ATF Cluster, Federal, Regional and zonal authorities, and other operational partners in the targeted communities as the needs are massive and will require concerted efforts. Continuous monitoring will be undertaken in the implementation period to ensure all emerging trends are captured and reported to stakeholders. Community participation will be incorporated during the project design with women and children needs emphasis who mostly form a great percentage of the displaced populations. This approach will continue in the project implementation and lessons learnt incorporated in future responses.

In addition, ADRA will establish a protection committees involving men, women, a community leader, Religious leaders, a representative from the local authority and the police aimed to raise awareness on sexual violence and its impacts in the community; connect GBV and HIV; denounce any abuses of human rights; and share knowledge on how people could protect themselves. 
Humanitarian crises increase the risk that GBV will occur—compounding the challenges already faced by people. Girls and women are disproportionally affected by Livelihoods and Food security issues that arise during humanitarian emergencies. Forced to travel long distances to Aid Items distribution points with existing sanitation facilities often lacking privacy, lighting, or locks—they are at increased risk of sexual assault and harassment. Livelihoods and Food security scarcity can create tension in the home and heighten the possibility of domestic violence. And a shortage of culturally appropriate and accessible NFIs/Dignity Kits supplies, services and other support materials can increase all of these risks. ADRA’s proposed emergency Livelihoods and Food security NFI/Dignity Kits intervention will be integrated with gender-based violence (GBV) protection, mitigation and reduction activities, that will play a critical role in enhancing the safety and well-being of those most vulnerable people affected by humanitarian crises.

Humanitarian support 2022 Respuesta integral en seguridad alimentaria y nutricional de emergencia para la población más vulnerable afectada por la crisis en Venezuela.  Acción Contra el Hambre (ACH) en Venezuela atiende las necesidades humanitarias de los grupos más vulnerables en riesgo de desnutrición aguda: < de 5 años, 5 – 14 años, mujeres embarazadas y lactantes (MEL), personas con discapacidades o con problemas de salud, en particular adultos mayores. Son agravantes las situaciones de pobreza y necesidades básicas no satisfechas como la falta de acceso a: alimentos, condiciones higiénico-sanitarias adecuadas, servicios de salud, y medios de vida. La desnutrición y el deterioro de la salud repercuten en una mayor exposición a factores agravantes como la violencia de género, embarazos adolescentes y criminalidad. A través del HRP, ACH brindará una respuesta humanitaria para la reducción del sufrimiento y ayudar a salvar vidas, identificando casos de desnutrición aguda y severa en las familias más a riesgo. Humanitarian assistance Venezuela. Lifesaving food and necessary non-food items assistance, protection and WASH in line with humanitarian principles.   (QZA-20/0053-5) ASISTENCIA Y PROTECCIÓN HUMANITARIA A FAMILIAS AFECTADAS POR LOS IMPACTOS DE LA CRISIS PROLONGADA DE VENEZUELA El programa está dirigido a las poblaciones las más vulnerables en Venezuela, es decir, que se seleccionaron las parroquias de intervención de acuerdo con los siguientes criterios de vulnerabilidad, operatividad y estrategia de inclusión política y social:
•	Altos niveles de pobreza
•	Altos niveles de desnutrición crónica y alta prevalencia de enfermedades infecciosas.
•	Estados fronterizos que han manejado regularmente la presión adicional del intercambio con poblaciones muy pobres y desplazados del territorio colombiano.
•	Exposición a amenazas naturales
•	Alto nivel de conflictividad y violencia social en los últimos meses, debido a la escasez.
•	Capacidad organizativa comunitaria y capacidad operativa de Cáritas consolidadas.
Los beneficiarios serán involucrados en la identificación de las necesidades para ciertas actividades, como es el caso de la selección de medicamentos a dispensar, el contenido de las bolsas complementarias de alimentos para las familias con niños/as desnutridos y la compra de filtros artesanales de agua. En otras actividades, como la detección de la desnutrición, los niños/niñas son sujetos pasivos, beneficiarios de una acción para diagnosticar y tratar la desnutrición detectada durante la primera fase del proyecto, motivada por la escasez de alimentos en el país a causa de la crisis económica. Durante la ejecución del proyecto, los beneficiarios serán implicados a través de los promotores comunitarios, quienes serán el enlace con el resto de los actores del proyecto. 
El presente proyecto se centrará en cuatro (4) resultados entre sí, que al tiempo que contribuyen a mejorar las condiciones de vida, refuerzan la resiliencia de las poblaciones más afectadas por la crisis. Ellos son: 1) Monitoreo de la situación nutricional y las condiciones de vida en las comunidades en riesgo de desnutrición en niños y mujeres embarazadas. 2) Suplementación nutricional de las comunidades vulnerables asociada a la desnutrición, con entrega de insumos terapéuticos, de insumos alimenticios y de transferencias en efectivo; 3) Atención a la salud y saneamiento, fundamentalmente a la familia de los niños menores de 5 años en situación de riesgo nutricional y de las mujeres embarazadas atendidas. Este enfoque ejecuta dos actividades que brindan respuesta a dos necesidades apremiantes, la salud y la higiene; 4) Fortalecimiento de capacidades de la Red de Cáritas de Venezuela que le permita poder adherirse a los protocolos de Cáritas Internacionalis (CI) y alcanzar un Plan de mejoras que permita incrementar la eficacia en la operatividad de los proyectos

VEN, ACH: Multisectorial Emergency Response. 2021/2023 (7F-10336.02) Respuesta integral en seguridad alimentaria y nutricional de emergencia para la población más vulnerable afectada por la crisis en Venezuela.  Acción Contra el Hambre (ACH) en Venezuela atiende las necesidades humanitarias de los grupos más vulnerables en riesgo de desnutrición aguda: < de 5 años, 5 – 14 años, mujeres embarazadas y lactantes (MEL), personas con discapacidades o con problemas de salud, en particular adultos mayores. Son agravantes las situaciones de pobreza y necesidades básicas no satisfechas como la falta de acceso a: alimentos, condiciones higiénico-sanitarias adecuadas, servicios de salud, y medios de vida. La desnutrición y el deterioro de la salud repercuten en una mayor exposición a factores agravantes como la violencia de género, embarazos adolescentes y criminalidad. A través del HRP, ACH brindará una respuesta humanitaria para la reducción del sufrimiento y ayudar a salvar vidas, identificando casos de desnutrición aguda y severa en las familias más a riesgo. Se trabajará a nivel comunitario y se coordinará con instituciones locales, en particular con escuelas y centros de salud. ACH trabaja con un enfoque de programa país y dentro de una estrategia regional, con intervenciones complementarias e integrales en: 1) Nutrición: sensibilización y consejerías; detección, tratamiento de la desnutrición aguda, y derivación de los casos con complicaciones médicas; capacitación en el manejo preventivo de la desnutrición aguda; 2) Salud: atención primaria, equipos, insumos, medicamentos, métodos anticonceptivos; 3) Seguridad Alimentaria y medios de vida: distribución de alimentos y apoyo para la producción de alimentos; 4) ASH: acceso a servicios de agua, saneamiento, e higiene, en escuelas y centros comunitarios; distribución de kits de higiene, y rehabilitación/reparación de sistemas de abastecimiento de agua y de saneamiento en comunidades. El sector de Protección y género, de manera transversal, trabajará en prevención de VBG, nuevas masculinidades y DSSR; establecimiento y/o fortalecimiento de espacios seguros para mujeres y niñas; atención psico-social, distribución de kits de higiene menstrual y protección para mujeres en riesgo. La respuesta actual de ACH se concentra en Caracas DC, Guárico, Carabobo, Miranda, Zulia, Bolívar, y próximamente en Falcón, Amazonas y Sucre.

Deliver of integrated life-saving health, nutrition and WASH interventions to vulnerable children and their fami-lies affected by the humanitarian crisis in Venezuela (2022 portion) Fortalecer el sistema de protección de NNA con servicios de prevención y respuesta con enfoque en edad, genero y diversidad.  UNICEF mantendrá su enfoque en apoyar a los diferentes integrantes del sistema de Protección para que brinden servicios de prevención y respuestas de calidad con un enfoque en edad, género y diversidad para los NNA y familias más vulnerables y en riesgo. UNICEF mantendrá los esfuerzos en el desarrollo de los objetivos e indicadores sectoriales del Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria 2022-2023, a través de planes de trabajo con socios implementadores nacionales e internacionales. La Protección de la Infancia es la prevención y respuesta a la explotación, abuso, negligencia, prácticas nocivas y la violencia contra los niños, niñas y adolescentes (NNA). Está incorporada en la Convención sobre los Derechos del Niño y las Metas de Desarrollo Sostenible. Con un abordaje socio-ecológico, UNICEF y sus socios trabajaran con un enfoque en los NNA, las familias, las comunidades y el sistema de protección formal e informal para que acciones preventivas y de respuestas para temas de protección de NNA sean implementadas en los estados priorizados del país.  El enfoque principal de esta propuesta es la prevención que se realiza no solamente a través de los socios de protección, pero también con el apoyo de otros sectores como nutrición y educación para cumplir resultados de protección infantil. Los principales temas cubiertos incluyen: VbG, separación familiar, violencia en general incluyendo la de género y crianza positiva. Además de nuestro enfoque central en la prevención, UNICEF Venezuela se enfoca en que ningún NNA se quede atrás: trabajaremos con socios para alcanzar a los NNA con mayor riesgo de protección que incluyen NNA con discapacidades, NNA separados y no acompañados, de poblaciones indígenas y afro-descendientes y NNA que sufren otras formas de discriminación y exclusión. 
Donde los NNA están sufriendo violaciones, UNICEF trabajará con socios gubernamentales y no-gubernamentales para fortalecer el acceso a los servicios de respuesta para prevenir reincidencia y brindar atención, apoyo y justicia. Los principales servicios brindados incluyen: apoyo en acceder a registro de nacimiento, salud mental y apoyo psicosocial, gestión de caso incluyendo a NNA sobreviviente de VbG. Una modalidad diferente para alcanzar objetivos de protección será la de las transferencias monetarias, otra componente importante de todas las intervenciones es el enfoque en la calidad y en temas transversales como lo de género, AAP, PEAS y discapacidad. El numero total de NNA alcanzado (sin calcular el apoyo al Ministerio de Salud con EV25) será de 628,536.

Además de nuestro enfoque central en la prevención, UNICEF Venezuela se enfoca en que ningún NNA se quede atrás: trabajaremos con socios para alcanzar a los NNA con mayor riesgo de protección que incluyen NNA con discapacidades, NNA separados y no acompañados, de poblaciones indígenas y afro-descendientes y NNA que sufren otras formas de discriminación y exclusión. 
Donde los NNA están sufriendo violaciones, UNICEF trabajará con socios gubernamentales y no-gubernamentales para fortalecer el acceso a los servicios de respuesta para prevenir reincidencia y brindar atención, apoyo y justicia. Los principales servicios brindados incluyen: apoyo en acceder a registro de nacimiento, salud mental y apoyo psicosocial, gestión de caso incluyendo a NNA sobreviviente de VbG. Una modalidad diferente para alcanzar objetivos de protección será la de las transferencias monetarias, otra componente importante de todas las intervenciones es el enfoque en la calidad y en temas transversales como lo de género, AAP, PEAS y discapacidad. El numero total de NNA alcanzado (sin calcular el apoyo al Ministerio de Salud con EV25) será de 628,536.

Deliver of integrated life-saving health, nutrition and WASH interventions to vulnerable children and their fami-lies affected by the humanitarian crisis in Venezuela (2022 portion) Apoyo a los servicios básicos de salud materno-infantil y de adolescentes en los estados priorizados y fortalecimiento del programa nacional de inmunización. 
Con el objetivo principal de contribuir a poner fin a las muertes prevenibles de madres, recién nacidos y niños, al tiempo que se promueve la salud y el desarrollo de todos los niños, en el sector de la salud UNICEF aplicará dos enfoques: abordar las desigualdades en los resultados sanitarios y fortalecer los sistemas de salud, incluida la prevención y la respuesta al COVID-19. Para abordar las desigualdades en los resultados sanitarios, UNICEF, junto con las ONG asociadas, contribuirá a reforzar los sistemas de información y a promover el uso de datos cualitativos y cuantitativos desglosados para identificar a los grupos marginados y ajustar los programas a sus necesidades; esto incluye la mejora de los sistemas de estadísticas vitales en 10 hospitales de referencia, ya que las actividades no supervisadas tienden a carecer de calidad. Simultáneamente, UNICEF apoyará acciones que establezcan mejoras sostenidas en la provisión, utilización y calidad de los servicios, apoyando 150,000 consultas de atención prenatal y las atenciones de parto seguro para 150.000 mujeres embarazadas y sus recién nacidos en hospitales y ambulatorios; proporcionando cuidados intensivos a 7.500 recién nacidos gravemente enfermos, y atenciones pediátricas para 483.820 niños y niñas menores de cinco años. En particular, UNICEF tratará de mejorar y retener la capacidad del personal sanitario a través de la formación en cuidados prenatales, neonatales, pediátricos y de emergencia, incluidos los cuidados de casos complicados del COVID-19, para 14.364 profesionales sanitarios, e incentivos para 500 miembros del personal sanitario de áreas críticas, al tiempo que se refuerza la cadena de suministros para 189 centros de salud, incluidos 114 ambulatorios y 75 hospitales de referencia, con el fin de mejorar el acceso  a los servicios y productos sanitarios neonatales e infantiles de calidad, para reducir la tasa de mortalidad neonatal y materna y dignificar la atención sanitaria. Se proporcionará tratamiento antirretroviral pediátrico ininterrumpido para 1,022 niños menores de 15 años que viven con el VIH y tratamiento para enfermedades oportunistas para 4.970 niños registrados en el programa nacional de VIH, suministros para el diagnóstico precoz del VIH en mujeres embarazadas y niños expuestos, y tratamiento para la prevención de la transmisión materno-infantil del VIH. UNICEF proporcionará ocho vacunas y equipos auxiliares al Programa Ampliado de Inmunización para 1.832.601 niños y niñas de hasta 10 años y 450.681 mujeres embarazadas, y seguirá reforzando la cadena de frío en 24 almacenes regionales y proveyendo refrigeradores para 800 puestos de vacunación para mejorar la capacidad de almacenamiento de vacunas de rutina y las vacunas contra el COVID-19, 24 vehículos para actividades en la comunidad, 7 vehículos refrigerados, 3 botes para áreas remotas fluviales, 25 incineradores para desechos de vacunación y 23 cuartos fríos para mejorar la capacidad del programa ampliado de vacunación. 
•	UNICEF apoyará la rehabilitación de 08 consultorios para el programa de Salud Escolar y de 08 consultas especializadas para adolescentes, para contribuir a reducir las desigualdades en el acceso a los servicios de salud de los niños más vulnerables en zonas remotas o zonas urbanas empobrecidas. Para contribuir a la protección del personal de salud, 60.000 trabajadores de primera línea recibirán EPP. A través de la capacitación del personal de salud y el preposicionamiento de insumos de emergencia, se apoyará al MMPS y  Protección Civil en la gestión de desastres a nivel nacional, con capacidad para atender hasta 960.000 personas, y se rehabilitarán 21 centros de salud que prestan servicios maternos y neonatales para aumentar el acceso de la población más vulnerable a servicios de salud funcionales y dignos. - Solicitar información sobre las actividades humanitarias de cada una de las organizaciones que participan en la Línea de Contacto.
- Presentar quejas sobre la asistencia humanitaria recibida.
- Dejarnos sugerencias sobre las actividades realizadas por las agencias y/o sus socios implementadores.
- Reportar posibles casos de explotación y abuso sexual, maltrato o uso indebido de servicios y/o actividades humanitarias por parte de personal humanitario.

Después de una fase piloto en los municipios Mara y Maracaibo en el estado Zulia de julio a diciembre de 2021, el Comité Ejecutivo de la LdCI decidió su ampliación a los 4 estados del CCT Maracaibo (Zulia, Lara, Falcón y Trujillo) a partir de enero de 2022, con una ampliación a nivel nacional para recibir posibles casos de explotación y abuso sexual. A partir de julio de 2022, se prevé la expansión a nivel nacional de la LdCI. 

La implementación de la LdCI forma parte de los compromisos incluidos en el Marco Colectivo de AAP en Venezuela, aprobado por el Equipo Humanitario de País en septiembre de 2020. Provision of WASH support to populations affected by the Northern Ethiopian Crisis
(2022 portion) Emergency Water Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) support to population affected by conflict and climate induced crises in Ethiopia  IOM is leading WASH activities in many IDP sites and host communities across Ethiopia, including distribution of hygiene kits, water trucking, construction and rehabilitation of water points, emergency latrines, and handwashing stations, establishment of community-based water or sanitation management committees, and hygiene promotion activities through contextualized campaigns and mobilization of gender-balanced hygiene promoters. 

In Ethiopia currently the internal displacement and humanitarian needs are mainly derived by the ongoing conflicts and droughts in some parts of the country. The displacement level in Ethiopia doubled in 2021, with over 2 million additional people displaced during 2021. According to IOM’s latest Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) National Displacement Report released in December 2021, a total of 4.2 million people were internally displaced across Ethiopia. This includes around 2.11 million IDPs identified in Tigray and neighbouring zones in Afar and Amhara regions as a result of the Northern Ethiopia Crisis. The ongoing displacements continue to pose serious protection concerns for the affected population. The majority of the displaced population live-in collective sites or in spontaneous settlements where they have limited access to essential services, dignified and safe living conditions to sustain their families and communities. A large number of the displaced population are women and children under 18.
 
IOM works under the framework of the 2021 HRP and 2022 draft HRP to enhance understanding of the crisis and assist joint, strategic response planning. This is particularly relevant to address new shocks and the confluence of needs. All interventions occur based on assessed needs, inter-cluster Initial Rapid Needs Assessments (IRNA) and cluster-specific assessments. All assessments integrate specific gender analyses. IOM further considers key protection needs including the risk of exposure to harm, exploitation, harassment, deprivation and abuse, including forms of violence that are gender-based; the ability to meet basic needs; access to basic services; and coping mechanisms. IOM uses both qualitative and quantitative assessment methodologies, including IOM's DTM; questionnaires; household and key informant interviews (including with local authorities and key community leaders); focus group discussions with women and youth; direct observation and review of secondary information. 

IOM has existing WASH programming in Tigray, Amhara, Afar, Oromia (East Hararghe and Borena), Somali (Dawa and Fafan zone), and SNNP regions (Konso zone) covering IDPs, returnees and host communities. Limited access to WASH NFIs, inadequate sources of safe water, inadequate sanitation facilities and prevalence of poor hygiene practices can render the populations living in collective centers/sites at risk of preventable diseases and overcrowded and congested IDP sites also pose a high level of risk to waterborne diseases, such as cholera. Assessments indicated that integrated WASH services are critical to ensure that facilities are maintained at a good standard and can be scaled up in case of population influxes, both in terms of the provision of safe water and increased hygiene promotion to prevent disease outbreaks.

In 2022, IOM appeals for USD 23,5 million to reach 1,6 million individuals through its WASH activities in IDP sites and host communities across Ethiopia. Interventions will comprise water trucking, construction and rehabilitation of water points, emergency latrines including distribution of hygiene kits, and handwashing stations, establishment of community-based water or sanitation management committees, and hygiene promotion activities through contextualized campaigns and mobilization of gender-balanced hygiene promoters. IOM will also support implementing partners, particularly national NGOs to provide access to safe water, WASH NFIs and hygiene promotion.

NENTAD - North East Nigeria Transition to Development Integrated Emergency, Recovery and Resilience Response for Crisis-affected Persons in MMC and Jere The aim of this intervention is: conflict-affected communities in MMC and Jere LGAs are sustainably protected from, and treated for, the main causes of morbidity and mortality; supported to meet immediate and long-term Shelter and Settlement, WASH and Protection needs, while being protected and provided with the legal assistance they need. To achieve this, the proposed project will be implemented by a consortium led by the International Rescue Committee (IRC), in partnership with the Danish Refugee Council (DRC) and Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC). The consortium will leverage the expertise of each partner to deliver a multi-sectoral, area-based response, providing integrated services across the following sectors: Health, WASH, Nutrition, Food Assistance, Multi-purpose Cash Assistance (MPCA), Nutrition, Economic Recovery and Market Systems (ERMS), Protection and Shelter and Settlements. The consortium aims to meet the most immediate and life-saving needs of IDPs, host communities and returnees in MMC and Jere, which will translate into reduced mortality and improved living conditions. The consortium will also address the ongoing, protracted needs, and supporting early recovery through capacity-building, the strengthening of existing health systems and community-based structures, and increasing the ownership of life-saving, life-sustaining, and life-building services by local authorities, service providers, and local communities to ensure sustainability. In order to build the resilience of individuals and communities, the unique humanitarian and development challenges in MMC and Jere LGAs (presence of service delivery actors against an ongoing flux of IDPs in and out of camps and host communities throughout the city) must be addressed simultaneously by increasing access to quality, sustainable basic services, building sustainable livelihoods, and strengthening local systems and structures.

PROVISIONOF LIFE-SAVING NUTRITION COMMODITIES TO CHILDREN UNDER-5 Northeast Nigeria Nutrition Response 2022 The Nutrition response in 2022 will prioritise implementation of the nutrition lifesaving activities (inpatient, outpatient, and targeted supplemental feeding programmes) and targeting of LGAs with high rates of GAM (above 10%) such as MMC/Jere, Nganzai, Bama, Machina. Hard-to-reach areas (such as Gubio, Rann, Magumeri), areas with large IDP  and returnee populations (like Monguno) and high-risk/inaccessible locations such as Marte LGA will also be prioritised for nutrition assistance. 
UNICEF will primarily target acutely malnourished children and PLW who are at a significantly high risk of death. The nutrition response will also target the total under-five and PLW with preventive nutrition services e.g. micronutrient supplementation to ensure levels of acute malnutrition are not above average thresholds, and to also reduce morbidity and mortality. The response will prioritise households with persons living with disabilities, who face barriers in accessing health, nutrition and WASH services and are disproportionately food insecure due to high levels of exclusion. 
The nutrition status of the targeted population in the BAY states significantly deteriorates during the period from May-August every year, which is the lean season and coincides with the rainy season. The season is characterised by very high rates of acute malnutrition with medical complications due to poor food access and a high prevalence of diarrhoea and malaria. UNICEF will need to adequately prepare for the lean season period by prepositioning supplies, increasing the overall sector capacity to treat acute malnutrition with a focus on inpatient care and IYCF-E
The nutrition response in BAY states will be contextualised in 2022 based on the following categorisation: 
1. Protracted crisis e.g north and central Borno LGAs where the rates of acute malnutrition are high, worsened by poor access to food and health systems. The approach in these areas will include INGO/NNGO direct support to the affected population, and prioritisation of lifesaving nutrition activities. 
3. New emergencies – locations of new crisis and fluctuations such as relocations, displacements and spike in acute malnutrition. The approach will focus on the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) with a focus on lifesaving activities. 
4. Hard-to-reach / inaccessible areas – locations with limited humanitarian footprints and access e.g Gubio and Magumeri. The approach will include RRM and remote management strategy (where feasible) with a focus on life-saving interventions. UNICEF will also strengthen the implementation of nutrition interventions through local organizations or community-based structures to implement nutrition services in hard-to-reach/inaccessible areas. 
UNICEF response is primarily through services and in-kind deliveries. UNICEF will employ the use of cash and voucher assistance (CVA) to fill the nutrient gap in the Nutrition/Food Minimum Expenditure Basket to ensure that populations have access to a varied diet e.g CVA for meats and vegetables. 
The nutrition status of the affected population is an outcome of various underlying issues including access to health, WASH, food security, child protection, and gender issues. The main cause of acute malnutrition among children and women in BAY states is the high morbidity rates. High diarrhoea prevalence is the major cause of acute malnutrition among the IDPs and urban poor population due to the prevailing poor hygiene and sanitation conditions worsened by congested living conditions. The response will strengthen the integration of nutrition-sensitive interventions including WASH, food security, health, livelihoods and child protection, and gender-based violence risk mitigation.
UNICEF will prioritise projects that include basic nutrition packages such as integrated treatment of acute malnutrition (SAM and MAM) and prevention services including integration with WASH, food security, health and protections services.

FOOD SECURITY AND AGRICULTURE (USAID/BHA) Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace.

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

Provision of life-saving nutrition and livelihood support to vulnerable
populations in Caabudwaaq District, Galgadud Region, Somalia Lifesaving preventive nutrition services to IDP and Non- IDP populations in Somalia  This project will contribute to the Nutrition Cluster’s strategic objective two, strengthening lifesaving preventive nutrition services, by improving nutritious food acquisition, knowledge, practices, consumption and ultimately nutrition outcomes for rural and IDP populations within IPC 3 and 4.
In Somalia, the high cost of a nutritious diet does not support the creation of an enabling food environment for a healthy population.  In addition to the issue of low affordability, poor and vulnerable people face physical access constraints related to the lack of availability of nutritious diets. These constraints, coupled with poor knowledge and skills in food choices and preparation, contribute significantly to sustained high numbers of malnourished individuals. Children Under-5 and lactating women are consistently the most vulnerable to malnutrition in Somalia. 
FAO plans to support 2,000 rural and IDP households with children between 6 to 59 months with a blended approach prioritizing unconditional cash transfers (UCTs) valued at 80 percent of the Food Minimum Expenditure Basket (MEB) to improve immediate access to nutritious foods. To enhance the impact of cash, this intervention will be complemented by Behavior Change Communication (BCC) and nutrition education adapted to the local context. This activity will engage primary caregivers in cooking demonstrations, role-play and individual counselling to increase the chances of retention and adoption of new healthy habits. The aim is to improve complementary feeding for children 6-59 months to prevent recurrent cases of malnutrition.
 FAO shall also provide 800 pregnant and lactating women (PLW) enrolled in nutrition treatment with conditional cash transfers (CCT), valued at 80 percent of the food MEB by region, on the condition that they attend maternal and child care support groups within their communities. Through these peer support groups, they will receive knowledge and peer support during pregnancy and lactation period. Through the cash assistance, they will have access to nutritious foods to meet their nutritional needs. Under this activity, FAO shall consider approximately 200 PLW to receive UCTs to accommodate participants that would be willing, but are not able to attend trainings. FAO shall work closely with partners to provide flexible ways of receiving the content of trainings for this smaller group.
FAO will also support the creation of mother-to-mother support groups reaching an additional 1,000 women between 15 to 49 years. Each group will be made up of 10-15 mothers from vulnerable households in rural areas. These groups will receive kitchen gardening kits and simple tools to promote the establishment of kitchen gardens that can provide a source of nutritious foods especially during dry seasons.
Nutrition education, awareness and training sessions will be conducted by locally recruited and trained members of the community called Nutrition Champions (one male and one female in every village). These champions will be trained to disseminate information and knowledge on nutrition and services available across their villages.

In total, FAO shall support 4,000 households/ 24,000 individuals with life-saving nutrition assistance. FAO will employ community- led beneficiary selection processes and ensure adequate targeting and representation of extremely vulnerable and minority groups in community committees including women, youth and people living with disabilities (PWD). Interventions proposed will employ a DoNoHarm, a gender lens, and conflict- sensitive approach to reduce protection risks for all individuals, and to reduce the risk of conflict or community tensions.

FOOD ASSISTANCE - SCHOOL MEALS Programa de seguridad alimentaria basado en la escuela  Con el objetivo de contribuir a la seguridad alimentaria de la población con mayores necesidades, el Programa Mundial de Alimentos de Naciones Unidas (WFP, por sus siglas en inglés) en Venezuela desarrolla un programa de asistencia humanitaria basado en la escuela para garantizar el acceso de los más vulnerables a una alimentación adecuada y nutritiva en el entorno escolar, familiar y comunitario. 
Este programa inició en 2021 con comidas escolares en emergencias priorizando escuelas iniciales y de educación especial.

WFP proporciona comidas escolares acompañado de un paquete integrado de intervenciones para mejorar el acceso a alimentos nutritivos y diversificados a través de las escuelas, contribuyendo al mismo tiempo a mejorar la salud y la nutrición de los niños en edad escolar, los estudiantes con discapacidad y el personal escolar, y apoyando a las comunidades a reducir la dependencia en estrategias de afrontamiento. De manera gradual, el WFP está realizando compras locales de alimentos, e incluyendo acciones para apoyar los mercados locales con compras a pequeños productores y apoyo técnico para acceso a mercados.

En este sentido, el programa de comidas escolares en emergencias tiene los siguientes componentes, para asegurar un enfoque integral que apoye al estudiante en el entorno escolar y familiar:

1. Entrega de comidas escolares nutritivas para estudiantes y personal escolar, promoviendo las compras locales y a pequeños productores.
2. Apoyo a la seguridad alimentaria del hogar a través de comida en especie o transferencias monetarias.
3. Rehabilitación de cocinas escolares para garantizar condiciones adecuadas de preparación de alimentos.
4. Comunicación para sensibilizar acerca de los principios humanitarios, la adecuada preparación de alimentos, nutrición, higiene y mantenimiento de cocinas escolares.
5. Fortalecimiento de capacidades de socios implementadores y personal escolar.
6. Acciones sensibles a la nutrición, que incluyen, tamizaje en las escuelas, educación nutricional, referencia a servicios especializados y entrega de alimento complementario fortificado (Supercereal Plus).
