South Sudan Humanitarian Response Plan 
Total private sector contributions from June 2022 Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2022, there are some 335,000 refugees and asylum seekers from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, primarily from Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic.
At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for longer term stability, hundreds of thousands of South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since the signing of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan, this spontaneous movement has prompted the development of an area-based approach, to support refugees, returnees and host communities, through enhanced engagement with development actors, to support greater access to services where possible.
Refugees largely reside in conflict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction in basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.
Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will benefit from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Specific protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identified at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with specific protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as verification exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the efficiency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to benefit from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

Emergency drought response through provision of integrated water, sanitation and hygiene promotion (WASH) services Provision of lifesaving assistance and sustainable solutions through safe Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) services, for people in crises and their host communities in multiple regions in Somalia. IOM WASH is proposing to contribute to lifesaving of access to safe and equitable basic WASH services to overall 281,400 beneficiaries from vulnerable Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) and host-communities in multiple regions in Somalia. 

Specifically, the project will target 168,840 Non displaced people (children 104,681; women 27,014; Disabled 25,326; and elderly 11,819) and 112,560 displaced populations (children 69,787; Women 18,010; Disabled 16,884; and elderly 7,879)
IOM will rehabilitate 60 strategic water sources for multi-use (human and animals) and further 55 community berkads (water reservoirs) that will provide continued, equitable, safe, sufficient and sustainable water to regions, targeted by the cluster, prone to natural disasters.
IOM further proposes to construct 3,300 new emergency sanitation facilities (following cluster specifications) targeting populations without access to basic sanitation and hygiene.

The project will also strengthen the capacity of the Federal Government of Somalia and Federal Members States, community leaders and water committees/technicians for better coordination with government authorities and communities and sustainability of the constructed/ rehabilitated WASH infrastructures. In addition, the project will nurture community participation in good hygiene practices through training and community sensitization campaigns.

The Republic of South Sudan	the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace.

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

IRC Food Assistance, Protection Unity $1,900,000 Integrated Food Security and Livelihoods Protection in Mayendit and Panyijiar Counties, Unity State, South Sudan  The project objective(s) is to enhance and sustain emergency food production through complementary vegetable and crop livelihood inputs, fishing, and livestock; reduce dependency on food and agricultural inputs to support and strengthen households’ ability to absorb shocks in a way that prevents the spread and transmission of COVID-19 for households affected by floods and conflict in Panyijiar and Mayendit counties, Unity state of South Sudan. The IRC proposes to provide a sequence of food production to support to most severe food-insecure and malnourished households in the main season farming of May to July and dry season of Nov to March. To strengthen households’ resilience, the project will mainstream gender, conflict sensitivity, disaster risks reduction, and COVID-19 risk mitigation measures to support at-risk households focused on improving vegetable, crop, livestock, and fisheries production and bolstering resilience towards recurrent shocks and stresses. In pursuit of the project objective(s), the following activities will be implemented: 
(a) The IRC together with the complaint and feedback mechanism (CFM/AAP) committee will mobilize, engage community members to inform the needs of the most vulnerable households and selection criteria for registration together with Nutrition partners. 
(b) Preposition and distribute emergency (short-term maturing) agricultural inputs (Cereal & Vegetable seeds, and tools) and fishing kits to 53,760 people. The IRC anticipates FAO will provide complimentary in-kind inputs to support the project. During distribution, community health volunteers will be engaged to disseminate COVID-19 messages, provide personal protective kits including facemasks, hand washing station, hand sanitizers, and limit the crowd at distribution points following COVID-19 protocol. 
(c) To improve nutritional practices for pregnant women and caregivers of children under 5 years with MAM and SAM. Nutrient-dense vegetable seeds will be provided, establish demonstration gardens at nutrition facilities close to water points, provide basic training on vegetable production, harvest, and conservation techniques. The IRC Nutrition team will conduct nutrition-sensitive awareness, food cooking demonstrations showing how to enrich households’ meals with locally available foods.
(d) The IRC will identify 400 potential seed producers, provide foundation seeds, establish seeds multiplication centers and plots. The seed producers will receive at least 200 USD cash grants, training on quality seeds selection, quality seeds production techniques, and crop management practices. Seed producers will be supported to form VSLA to increase access to finance for seeds production and access to markets will be facilitated.  
(e) The IRC with the County Agriculture Department, State Ministry of Agriculture, and FAO will contribute to livestock disease surveillance and monitoring, facilitate vaccination campaigns, mass vaccination exercises and treatments to livestock to be led by CAHW.
(f) Facilitate capacity building to community-based extension agents (CAHWs, AEA’s), crop producers, pastoralists, and fisherfolks on sustainable production skills and provision of proximate extension services on production, post-harvest handling through demonstration gardens. Also, fisherfolks to receive basic training on fish preservation and kit repairs to enhance household nutrition and income.
Overall, the project will reach 6% most vulnerable households in need (HNO, 2022) in Panyijiar (33,000 People) and Mayendit (20,160 People) equivalent to a total of 53,760 people (5,376 Male children, 8,064 Female children, 12,902 Adult male, 19,354 Adult Female, 3,225 elderly Male, 4,839 elder Female) people. After a sudden shock, IDPs often gather in informal displacement sites in extremely precarious conditions, most of the time without access to basic services and information, and with limited decision-making power on issues that affect their daily lives and their future. These gathering places are often characterized by an increased exposure to security risks and protection needs, particularly for the most vulnerable groups. Poor living conditions; lack of financial resources and limited access to basic services can lead to outbreaks of disease, increased prevalence of GBV or domestic violence, and tensions between population groups within the informal camps. Likewise, overcrowding could led to challenges in maintaining safe levels of hygiene and sanitation. Continued political uncertainty, coupled with the increased risks of climate change has also largely resulted in the inability of the international community to return these IDP’s to more suitable locations and an unwillingness from the camps inhabitants to leave. Regarding Bor and Juba former PoC camps, as of February 2022, 2,745 IDPs resided in Bor IDPs Camp, 7,299 in Juba IDPs Camp 1 and 24,255 in Juba IDPs Camp 3. Since the transition from former PoCs sites under UNMISS management to conventional IDPs site under the South Sudanese government responsibility in November 2020, the 2,745 residents of Bor IDPs camp have continued benefitting from essential services provision. The RRC offices of Jonglei at State and County levels have taken up the camp administration responsibility after the transition and are well involved, present and committed in the camp activities. However, the state and county authorities are facing limited resources to fully take over the camp administration responsibility. ACTED will aim at reinforcing the local authorities’ resources and abilities in Jonglei, while continuing to build capacity of camp leadership representatives, leading to the full handover of the Camp management responsibilities to the Community Members Committees and Camp administration role to RRC office in Jonglei by the last quarter of 2022. On the other hand, the 31,554 residents of Juba IDPs Camp 1 and 3 have faced a drastic decrease of essential service provision since the transition from former PoC sites under UNMISS management to conventional IDPs camps under the leadership of the South Sudan Government. Since the transition and re-designation of roles over to the government of South Sudan the RRC office has not yet taken over the responsibility of the camps.
ACTED is aiming to continue to work to design a road map for RRC’s take over and to work closely with Juba IDP camps service providers. ACTED would continue to engage in discussions with key actors and communities impacted to take active role in several fora including the Durable Solutions Working Group. During the semi-static phase, ACTED is planning to provide in-kind support to local authorities, including RRC, that are facing a lack of resources to take over the camp administration role, while enhancing the camp leadership skills. Therefore, ACTED will continue implementing CCCM interventions in line with the following cluster objectives: CO1: Improve living condition of IDPs by facilitating safe, equitable and dignified access to cross-sectoral humanitarian services, including CCCM CO2: Enhance the protective environment, respond to vulnerable population with priority on addressing protection gaps and strengthen the predictability and effectiveness of multi sectorial interventions at site level CO3: Support vulnerable IDPs to recover from the crisis by strengthening community self-management, build resilience to promote solutions for displaced people in sites.

WFP somalia response WFP SOMALIA 2022 HRP - FSC Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas. As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation. The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

Nutrition Providing Life Saving Treatment and Prevention Nutrition Services to the Vulnerable Communities in Somalia Food and Nutrition context in Somalia
Decades of conflict and natural disasters including repeated droughts and seasonal flooding followed by limited government and institutional support have had a profound negative effect on the food security situation and social service sector in Somalia. Nearly seven in ten Somalis live on less than USD 1.90 per day,  the sixth-highest poverty rate in sub-Saharan Africa. Poverty is both widespread and deep, particularly for households in rural areas and internally displaced person (IDP) settlements. The number of food-insecure people experiencing long-term stress is trending upwards, indicating that chronic food insecurity persists, requiring sustainable solutions. Recurrent climate-related shocks and political instability are key drivers of food insecurity and pose continuing risks to crop production and food access. Malnutrition in Somalia is driven by a combination of factors such as recurrent food insecurity, child illnesses, high morbidity, micronutrient deficiencies, low immunization levels, poor access to clean water and sanitation, poor hygiene practice, gender inequality and discriminatory sociocultural attitudes leading to poor care practices. Based on the latest Post Gu FSNAU assessment (September 2021), it is estimated that a total of 3.5 million out of the 15.8m people face acute food insecurity (IPC 3 and above – crisis or worse)  until December 2021. At the national level the median prevalence of Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) has remained at a serious level of 11.1%. Approximately 1.2 million children under the age of five are likely to be acutely malnourished, including 295,515 who are likely to be severely malnourished. In addition to this, around 245,909 Pregnant & Lactating Women (PLWs) will be at risk of acute malnutrition. 

Acute malnutrition is a major public health problem in Somalia. It affects disproportionately children under the age of five, as well as Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLWs), especially among IDPs, vulnerable (agro) pastoralist communities and those living in areas affected by flooding. Morbidity among children is high (≥ 20%). Out of a total of 40 surveyed population groups 18 recorded high morbidity presence of above 20%. 
Vitamin A supplementation and Measles vaccination remains low <40% in several population groups. 

TB prevalence remains one of the highest globally with Somalia in the top 10 countries with high TB burden (262 per 100,000 population) while the HIV prevalence remains <1% however with high stigma and discrimination levels at 94%.

Project activities
The World Food Program is the leading UN agency in Somalia in fighting hunger. In Somalia, WFP together with the Ministry of Health (MoH), nutrition cluster and the partners, supports nutrition service delivery and prevention. WFP collaborates with the MoH and UNICEF to offer an integrated package of nutrition and health, following the revised MoH IMAM guidelines for treating acute malnutrition in Somalia.

WFP will cover both treatment and preventive nutrition services including:
•	Targeted Supplementary Feeding Program for 665,846 moderately acute malnourished children 6-59 months; 173,746 malnourished Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLW), 10,794 malnourished People Living with HIV on ART treatment and malnourished TB patients.
•	Preventive Nutrition services for 386,102 children 6-23 months and 173,746 PLW enrolled in Maternal Child Health and Nutrition services and blanket Supplementary Feeding Program for children 6-23 months and PLW in districts where GAM (Global Acute Malnutrition) rate is above 15%.
•	Monthly cash vouchers of USD 15 for 24,104 PLWs in selected target districts.
•	24,206 caregivers with SAM children admitted to the Stabilisation  will receive food while staying at the Stabilisation Center 
•	A total of 96,150 pregnant women will receive food rations for their families when delivering their baby at a health facility

The number of food-insecure people experiencing long-term stress is trending upwards, indicating that chronic food insecurity persists, requiring sustainable solutions. Recurrent climate-related shocks and political instability are key drivers of food insecurity and pose continuing risks to crop production and food access. Malnutrition in Somalia is driven by a combination of factors such as recurrent food insecurity, child illnesses, high morbidity, micronutrient deficiencies, low immunization levels, poor access to clean water and sanitation, poor hygiene practice, gender inequality and discriminatory sociocultural attitudes leading to poor care practices. Based on the latest Post Gu FSNAU assessment (September 2021), it is estimated that a total of 3.5 million out of the 15.8m people face acute food insecurity (IPC 3 and above – crisis or worse)  until December 2021. In addition to this, around 245,909 Pregnant & Lactating Women (PLWs) will be at risk of acute malnutrition. 

Acute malnutrition is a major public health problem in Somalia. It affects disproportionately children under the age of five, as well as Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLWs), especially among IDPs, vulnerable (agro) pastoralist communities and those living in areas affected by flooding. Morbidity among children is high (≥ 20%). Out of a total of 40 surveyed population groups 18 recorded high morbidity presence of above 20%. 
Vitamin A supplementation and Measles vaccination remains low <40% in several population groups. 

TB prevalence remains one of the highest globally with Somalia in the top 10 countries with high TB burden (262 per 100,000 population) while the HIV prevalence remains <1% however with high stigma and discrimination levels at 94%.

The World Food Program is the leading UN agency in Somalia in fighting hunger. To save lives and alleviate suffering. Strengthening food and livelihood security of conflict and disaster affected vulnerable IDPs and host communities through support to agricultural production and cash assistance to meet their immediate basic needs. In the face of increasing food insecurity and the need to meet other basic urgent needs, initiatives to  address immediate food needs of the most vulnerable and food insecure population are paramount in saving lives and protecting assets of the most vulnerable. The proposed project is in-line with Humanitarian Needs Overview 2022, Food Security Cluster (FSC) priorities and objectives. The project aims at improving the ability of 66,610 vulnerable people including 41,280 IDPs and 9,991 people with disability to meet their food and basic needs and reduce consumption gaps through life-saving cash assistance and agriculture inputs. Of these 52,965 people under FSC CO1 and 13,645 people under FSC CO2. 
These households are affected by multiple shocks – including conflicts and facing wide consumption gaps, due to successive below-average agricultural and pastoral yields, and a lack of casual labour income opportunities in urban and IDP communities. Unconditional cash transfer (UCT) and agriculture input assistance will improve beneficiary household’s access to food and other basic needs, while preventing households from resorting to negative coping mechanisms which erode long-term resilience. Community and stakeholder engagement, gender sensitive vulnerability and eligibility criteria for beneficiary selection and emphasis on participation of men, women, boys and girls of different ages and other at-risk groups will improve gender equality and women’s empowerment and inclusion of marginalized population. Target population will be provided with six months of UCT totaling 3,675,965$ - based on the monthly transfer value recommended by Cash Working Group (CWG). In addition, 2,047 farmers households will be supported with agricultural inputs including seeds and tractor services through in kind and voucher and consumption support of 30$/month for 4 months. Cash for work will generate employment of 22,742 person days to create community assets.
Settlement and beneficiary targeting will follow a participatory and community-based process. To target the settlements, Concern will conduct stakeholder consultations and key informants interview at regional and district level. Village Relief Committees (VRC) with average 8 to 10 members in each comprising both men and women, including representatives from marginalized population groups will be established (or existing ones mobilized) and receive information on the project and the beneficiary selection process. VRCs will lead community based participatory beneficiary selection process, this will also help project to empower participating communities – including women in decision making. A key component in the beneficiary selection criteria will be gender, age and disability considerations. 
In line with Concern’s approach and quality standard for Cash and Voucher based assistance and Accountability to Affected Populations, Concern will disseminate information on its Complaints Response Mechanism (CRM) channels during sensitization to ensure that beneficiaries, target communities and project stakeholders are fully aware of and are able to raise any feedback or issues of concern for timely action. Concern’s independent Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability and Learning (MEAL) unit will regularly monitor the project and will conduct Post Distribution Monitoring (PDM).
Concern with its local NGO partners is implementing both emergency response and longer term programmes in proposed districts in this project. The proposed project will further leverage upon Concern’s efforts and strengthen envisaged resilience outcomes in the target districts, while providing the project with opportunity to ensure convergence and integration while addressing the underlying causes of vulnerability – including gender inequalities and poverty.

To save lives and alleviate suffering. Improved Access to Food and Livelihood Options for Vulnerable Households in Somalia Ongoing armed conflicts and insecurity, with recurring climate shocks, has resulted in a protracted economic vulnerability and internal displacements across Somalia.Somalis are vulnerable to various shocks such as drought and flood that contribute to poverty and displacement. The Center for Global Development  places Somalia at the top of the list of 167 countries for overall vulnerability to climate change adjusted for coping capacity.
The Cyclical climatic shocks and ongoing conflict are challenging traditional rural livelihoods and causing 
growing number of urban poor and internally displaced people in Somalia. Displacements due to armed 
conflict and political tensions, drought, and lack of livelihoods are expected to continue in 2022, further 
exacerbating food insecurity in many areas.
According to FSNAU,out of the total 3.5 million people in need of urgent food assistance, 640,000 people face significant food consumption gaps. In addition, 3.7 million people are classified in IPC phase 2 (Stressed), engaging in negative coping strategies to meet their food and non-food needs, bringing the total number of Somalis experiencing acute food insecurity to 7.2 million by late 2021.

Furthermore,COVID-19 pandemic and related containment measures seem to have affected the urban poor population more than rural poor population. As a result, the urban poor face moderate to large food consumption gaps, partly due to a slowdown in economic activities in urban areas and the rising costs of food and other essential non-food items.
World Vision proposes a multi pronged interventions  to reverse the current trajectory at which Somalia is going.The interventions would include immediate access to food needs by vulnerable households facing hunger and starvation, improving livelihoods and creating opportunities for diversified livelihoods by protecting key livelihood assets .
The proposed project intends to address the food insecurity situation, loss of livelihood strategies, poor HH and community livelihood assets, as well as minimum interventions integrated to address the environmental degradation on which most livelihoods hinge upon. 
These activities will target IDPs, pastoral and agro-pastoral communities across Somalia, in districts where World Vision operates in.

To save lives and alleviate suffering Improving Food security for vulnerable populations in Somaliland, particularly  IDPs in Hargeisa, Togdheer, and Sool Somalia is facing a growing number of threats to its food security. The ongoing desert locust invasion, socio-economic effects of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic and recurrent climate shocks, including frequent flooding and drought, continue to severely impact the lives and livelihoods of the vulnerable population. With this multifaceted crises, 7.7 Million people across Somalia need in emergency food assistance. With humanitarian needs expected to further increase in 2022, it is critical to enhance immediate food access, protect and restore livelihoods and strengthen the resilience of vulnerable households. Sustained humanitarian assistance is required to prevent the further deterioration of food security and nutrition.
Through this project, Plan International and Partners will effectively provide emergency assistance for food and promote dignity and choices among project participants by increasing purchasing power with short term injection of unconditional cash transfers for 1182 HH (7092 beneficiaries; 3546F, 3546M) for six months. Through field monitoring, government reports, and sector coordination, Plan and Partners will target households in areas identified as IPC3 or worse, risk of drought, and/or IDP communities, including those recently evicted by Somaliland government. These families have insufficient income to cover rising cost of food particularly during periods of drought and other shocks due to COVID19, instability and climate change, and will qualify per criteria, e.g. female headed household, household with person with disability, etc. Partners will ensure the crises affected families receive messages on Infant, Young Child Feeding and Hygiene and have access to sufficient, safe and nutritious foods to meet their dietary needs and food preferences for an active and healthy life. Partners have complementary programs running in these areas to enable consultant and selection within communities. By targeting vulnerable families particularly with children and delivering this intervention in a gender sensitive manner, Plan strives for secondary outcomes of improved the protection environment with reduced risks to women and girls.

Multisectoral Response to the communities affected by malnutrition Northeast Nigeria Nutrition Response 2022 The Nutrition response in 2022 will prioritise implementation of the nutrition lifesaving activities (inpatient, outpatient, and targeted supplemental feeding programmes) and targeting of LGAs with high rates of GAM (above 10%) such as MMC/Jere, Nganzai, Bama, Machina. Hard-to-reach areas (such as Gubio, Rann, Magumeri), areas with large IDP  and returnee populations (like Monguno) and high-risk/inaccessible locations such as Marte LGA will also be prioritised for nutrition assistance. 
UNICEF will primarily target acutely malnourished children and PLW who are at a significantly high risk of death. The nutrition response will also target the total under-five and PLW with preventive nutrition services e.g. micronutrient supplementation to ensure levels of acute malnutrition are not above average thresholds, and to also reduce morbidity and mortality. The response will prioritise households with persons living with disabilities, who face barriers in accessing health, nutrition and WASH services and are disproportionately food insecure due to high levels of exclusion. 
The nutrition status of the targeted population in the BAY states significantly deteriorates during the period from May-August every year, which is the lean season and coincides with the rainy season. The season is characterised by very high rates of acute malnutrition with medical complications due to poor food access and a high prevalence of diarrhoea and malaria. UNICEF will need to adequately prepare for the lean season period by prepositioning supplies, increasing the overall sector capacity to treat acute malnutrition with a focus on inpatient care and IYCF-E
The nutrition response in BAY states will be contextualised in 2022 based on the following categorisation: 
1. Protracted crisis e.g north and central Borno LGAs where the rates of acute malnutrition are high, worsened by poor access to food and health systems. The approach in these areas will include INGO/NNGO direct support to the affected population, and prioritisation of lifesaving nutrition activities. 
3. New emergencies – locations of new crisis and fluctuations such as relocations, displacements and spike in acute malnutrition. The approach will focus on the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) with a focus on lifesaving activities. 
4. Hard-to-reach / inaccessible areas – locations with limited humanitarian footprints and access e.g Gubio and Magumeri. The approach will include RRM and remote management strategy (where feasible) with a focus on life-saving interventions. UNICEF will also strengthen the implementation of nutrition interventions through local organizations or community-based structures to implement nutrition services in hard-to-reach/inaccessible areas. 
UNICEF response is primarily through services and in-kind deliveries. UNICEF will employ the use of cash and voucher assistance (CVA) to fill the nutrient gap in the Nutrition/Food Minimum Expenditure Basket to ensure that populations have access to a varied diet e.g CVA for meats and vegetables. 
The nutrition status of the affected population is an outcome of various underlying issues including access to health, WASH, food security, child protection, and gender issues. The main cause of acute malnutrition among children and women in BAY states is the high morbidity rates. High diarrhoea prevalence is the major cause of acute malnutrition among the IDPs and urban poor population due to the prevailing poor hygiene and sanitation conditions worsened by congested living conditions. The response will strengthen the integration of nutrition-sensitive interventions including WASH, food security, health, livelihoods and child protection, and gender-based violence risk mitigation.
UNICEF will prioritise projects that include basic nutrition packages such as integrated treatment of acute malnutrition (SAM and MAM) and prevention services including integration with WASH, food security, health and protections services.

To save lives and alleviate suffering Providing Access to Emergency WASH Services in Gedo, Somalia The project proposes to improve access to safe water, sanitation facilities and promote good hygiene practices in an effort to improve the health conditions of 16,000 ( 8,759F, 6,600M and 640 elderly) drought affected individuals including internally displaced, marginalized riverine and vulnerable host women, men, boys and girls in Belet Xawa, Ceel Waaq, Dollow, Garbaharey and Luuq districts in Gedo region. Among the target beneficiaries will be 2,400 persons with disabilities.				 
The recurrent drought in Gedo has largely contributed to inadequate population access to potable water and resulted in frequent disease outbreaks, mainly AWD/cholera. WASH conditions are particularly poor (inadequate access to water to meet basic needs, lack of access to latrines, reliance on poor quality water sources). An assessment by REACH in June 2020 shows 93% of the households in Gedo have a WASH Living Standards Gap (LSG), with access to improved water sources below 41%. The region is served by small, seasonal, open water sources which are rapidly depleted with the recurrent droughts, leaving communities vulnerable to new outbreaks as they lack access to water for consumption and personal hygiene. Further, the assessment shows that 36% of the households have no access to a functional and improved sanitation facility. Serious protection concerns, and rights violations persist, where persons with disabilities, children and women are among the most affected social groups due to compounded vulnerabilities. The REACH DSA in March 2021 further shows that people with disabilities (100%), children (50%) and women (50%) are the top 3 groups reportedly facing impediments in accessing latrines. 
As part of the WASH cluster’s efforts to address the critical WASH needs in priority populations, this intervention will respond to the WASH gaps in the five target districts through the construction of two (2) solar powered water systems with piping to communities, rehabilitation of two existing shallow wells and training of 4 five-member water management committee. In addition, 8 existing high volume water points will be provided with fuel subsidies for three months during the hot and dry Jilaal season while water trucking will be done for 2,000 persons in rural villages for three months. The project will also construct150 universally design emergency latrines  with handwashing stations and distribute 150 latrine cleaning kits as well as 3,000 hygiene kits through Cash Vouchers. Hygiene promotion messaging will also be conducted in all the five districts. 
Trócaire will collaborate with Somali Humanitarian Relief Action (SHRA) and Active in Development Aid (ADA), national NGOs with strong experience in implementing WASH projects in Gedo, in the implementation of this project in the five target districts.

Health,Water, Sanitation and Hygiene,Protection,Multipurpose Cash Assistance,Nutrition (BHA/USAID) Réduction de la morbidité et de la mortalité liées à la malnutrition dans les régions du Sahel et du Nord du Burkina Faso Les régions du Sahel et du Nord connaissent depuis 2016 des violences armées avec des exactions sur la population. Cette spirale de violence s’est exacerbée depuis 2018. Ce qui a entrainé des déplacements massifs sans cesse croissants des populations dans le pays. Le CONASUR  estime à 1481701 le nombre de PDIs à travers le pays en Octobre 2021. Les régions les plus touchées sont celles du Sahel, Nord, Centre Nord, Est et Boucle du Mouhoun mais depuis quelques mois, les PDIs sont enregistrés dans l’ensemble du territoire national. La région du Sahel enregistre 510279 PDIs soit environ 34% des PDIs du pays, suivi de celle du Centre Nord (510110 PDIs). Dans ces régions, les mouvements des populations compliquent l’accès des populations aux soins de santé, aux ressources clés telles que l’eau et les denrées alimentaires. Cette crise touche de plein fouet le système de santé avec des centres de santé fermés ou fonctionnant à minima, rendant difficile l’accès des populations aux soins de santé et le dépistage et prise en charge de la malnutrition. En Novembre 2021, 48 formations sanitaires étaient fermées dans la région du Sahel sur 89 structures fermées dans le pays. Dans la région du Nord, 7 FS étaient fermées et majoritairement dans le DS de Titao. La situation sécuritaire et humanitaire s’est dégradée à Titao à la suite d’une vague de violence enregistrée entre au cours du dernier trimestre de 2021. L’enquête SMART de 2020 a révélé des prévalences MAG de 15,1% (IC : 11,7% - 19,3%) dans la région du Sahel et 8,2% (IC : 6,1% - 10,4%) dans la région du Nord. Les prévisions du cadre harmonisé placent la plupart des provinces du Sahel et du Nord en phase 3 et plus. 
Le Burkina Faso a enregistré en Mars 2020 ses premiers cas de COVID 19. La pandémie a touché à la date du 25 Novembre plus de 15000 personnes causant la mort de plus de 280 personnes.
Plusieurs ONG apportent une assistance humanitaire dans ces régions notamment la Croix Rouge Belge et Médecins du Monde France dans le DS de Djibo ainsi que MSF France à Titao pour une réponse nutritionnelle. Cependant en raison de l’inaccessibilité de certaines zones, il existe des poches où les besoins ne sont pas couverts.
IRC qui intervient déjà dans ces zones avec des activités de santé communautaires est à la recherche de fonds pour compléter son action et offrir des soins holistiques aux enfants de moins de 5 ans et aux femmes enceintes et allaitantes.
IRC propose cette intervention pour i) renforcer la prévention de la sous nutrition parmi les populations cibles ii) renforcer le dépistage et la surveillance nutritionnelle dans les zones en insécurité, iii) garantir l’accès aux soins nutritionnels pour les enfants de moins de 5 ans et les femmes enceintes et allaitantes y compris par l’approche simplifiée et communautaire.

Health,Water, Sanitation and Hygiene,Protection,Multipurpose Cash Assistance,Nutrition (BHA/USAID) Protection et soins améliorés pour les garçons et les filles déplacés de moins de 18 ans dans les régions du Nord et du Sahel au Burkina Faso  Depuis 2015, le Burkina Faso est confronté à un climat d’insécurité, traduit par des pertes en vies humaines, de déplacements internes, les attaques et affrontements armés répétés dans certaines régions du Burkina Faso ont conduit une partie non négligeable de la population à fuir leur localité. Alors que 38 000 burkinabè ont été contraints de se réfugier dans les pays voisins, selon les données statistique CONASUR au 30 septembre 2021, 1 407 685 est le nombre de personnes déplacées internes (PDI) dans le pays dont 618 301 enfants de 5ans et plus.  Sur le nombre total de déplacés en septembre 2021 les deux régions concernées ont accueillies 621 870 déplacés dont 493 708 au Sahel et 128 162 au Nord.  264 521 de 621 870 sont des enfants de 5ans et plus.  À la suite des incidents sécuritaires, ces PDIs cherchent majoritairement à trouver refuge dans les centres urbains les plus proches. Leurs conditions de vie, déjà précaires, dégradent d’autant plus aux sentiments de discriminations auxquelles elles font face de la part des populations hôtes.
IRC à travers ce projet va apporter une réponse intégrée pour la protection des enfants dans les régions du Nord et du Sahel.  Les réponses seront apportées aux besoins identifiés à travers l’interaction de l’IRC avec les communautés dans les zones d’intervention en général et il s’inspire aussi et surtout des différentes évaluations rapides conduites par les autres acteurs humanitaires et les données du CONASUR sur les déplacées internes.   Tout au long de ce projet l’IRC conduira des évaluations sur une base régulière pour informer d’une manière continuelle la réponse et s’assurer que les services fournis répondent aux besoins réels des populations affectes. Ainsi, la réponse offrira la protection aux enfants affectés par le conflit en leur apportant une assistance psychosociale et en les réintégrant dans la vie socioéconomique et scolaire. L’IRC assurera que tout enfant victime d’abus ou exploitations puisse accéder aux services de qualité. Un accent sera mis sur la coordination pour s’assurer que des mécanismes de référencement sont fonctionnels entre les acteurs, et dans le respect des principes directeurs. Vu les risques élevés, l’IRC va également renforcer les efforts de réduction des risques à travers le renforcement des mécanismes communautaire de prévention des cas d’abus sont protégés contre la violence à la maison et dans la communauté.

Ethiopia Humanitarian Response Plan 2022
--- Protection Provision of Integrated Protection and Site Management Services to Internally displaced people, Returnees, Host Community  and Other Persons With Specific Needs in Ethiopia UNHCR’s 2022 protection programme builds on the scale up of 2021 response and will be implemented in nine regions. The programme, builds on evidence gathered from ongoing protection monitoring using the revamped Ethiopia Protection Monitoring Tool (E-PMT) in the operational areas to ensure the ongoing identification of protection and specific needs and changes in the protection landscape for IDPs, IDP returnees, host communities and other persons with specific needs requiring protection services. 
As the Protection Cluster-lead agency, UNHCR ensures the coordination of its activities, implemented directly or through partnerships, through the Protection Cluster at national and sub-national level as appropriate.
Based on the protection monitoring, UNHCR will implement an integrated set of protection services and interventions tailored to the needs and priorities of the affected, which include:
•	the provision of information, counselling, identification of protection and specific needs, referrals to services/assistance, 
•	direct provision of services and assistance to persons at risk or with specific needs; 
•	GBV awareness, prevention and response activities;
•	child protection awareness raising and case management;
•	strengthening of MHPSS, 
•	emergency EORE as required by the Mine Action AOR,
•	provision of legal awareness and legal aid for GBV case management, HLP, legal identity and civil document restoration, 
•	and strengthen social cohesion and community-based peacebuilding.

Through its CCCM intervention, UNHCR will provide care and maintenance service of site infrastructure for IDPs living in 63 sites in Tigray, 4 sites in Afar and 11 sites in Amhara for at least 230,000 vulnerable IDP children of under 18 (120,000 girls, 110,000 boys) and assisting more than 230,000 adult IDP population (103,000 Adult Men, 107,000 Adult Women(18-59 years), 11,000 Elderly Men and 10,000 Elderly Women (60 and above) which include 32,000 people with disabilities to ensure protection and assistance while striving for durable solutions.

winterization assistance for crisis-affected IPDs in Northeast Syria - 2022 FSA support to the most vulnerable IDPs, host and refugees residing in NES CARE NES proposed strategy is in line with 2021 Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) and specifically aligns with Strategic Objective 3 (Increase the resilience of affected communities by improving access to livelihood opportunities and basic services, especially among the most vulnerable households and communities). CARE’s proposed intervention will target Hasakah and Deir-ez-Zor (DEZ) governorate in NES, one of the most impoverished areas in the country. CARE proposes to implement the project in this governorates due to the scale of unmet needs. 
The multi sectoral approach integrated with an innovative methodology grounding resilience in socio-economic wellbeing linking increased household economic capacities and opportunities with access to functioning basic infrastructure at community level and inclusive decision making at household and community levels, promoting more inclusive environment and improved ability of copying with stress. Based on that CARE is shifting towards a more integrated cross-cutting approach, allowing for a holistic understanding of the needs of communities and households. CARE has a strong programmatic focus around  value chains since they link producers and buyers from different communities and purposefully integrate women, older persons, people with disabilities, IDPs and/or returnees. CARE’s proposed value chain approach in the short, medium and long term is expected to help Syrian families and communities affected by conflict to achieve a greater level of resilience, mitigate protection risks and participate in economic life.
Under FS & Agriculture, CARE will support the most vulnerable population of NorthEast Syria for economic recovery and the restoration of livelihoods and functioning markets related to wheat and sheep value chains as well as increasing community well-being and social cohesion: more specifically provision of agricultural and livestock inputs (seeds, fertilizers, Drip irrigation systems, sheep, fodder), establishment of veterinary services (vaccinations, trainings of doctors), establishment of vocational training centers. CARE NES team strongly coordinate with NES active clusters including Food Security & Livelihood Cluster, Agriculture working group, Cash Working Group, early Recovery & Livelihood Working Group to avoid any duplication and to be inline with cluster guidelines.

IGAD TB Grant and C19RM   QPA-T-IGAD   TB Care & Prevention, TB/HIV, MDR-TB, RSSH Grant Management and COVID-19 Response Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2022, there are some 335,000 refugees and asylum seekers from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, primarily from Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic.
At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for longer term stability, hundreds of thousands of South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since the signing of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan, this spontaneous movement has prompted the development of an area-based approach, to support refugees, returnees and host communities, through enhanced engagement with development actors, to support greater access to services where possible.
Refugees largely reside in conflict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction in basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.
Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will benefit from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Specific protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identified at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with specific protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as verification exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the efficiency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to benefit from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

FOOD SECURITY AND AGRICULTURE (USAID/BHA) Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace.

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

Education in Emergency support in Duk County	Provision of Inclusive Quality Education for Out-of-School Children in Duk County - Jonglei  State Provision of Inclusive, Protective & Effective Education Services to Conflict-affected Children & Youth in Ayod, Uror, Duk, Ulang, Nasir and Longechuk Counties of Jonglei & Upper Nile States. This CMD’s Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) for 2022 seeks to provide inclusive, protective and effective education services to accelerate learning recovery and make schools more equitable, efficient and resilient for 7, 339 (3, 302 girls) school-aged children, 250 (50 female) teachers, 275 (82 female) PTA members and 60 (10 female) local education officials in 6 Counties of Jonglei & Upper Nile States by building on investments made during the Pandemic and previous years of EiE programming in South Sudan.

The expected results are equalised participation and improved learning outcomes across gender and disability for 7, 339 (45% female) children and youth through provision of essential school facilities and supplies, psychosocial support, gender-sensitive delivery of curriculum, classroom management, teacher conduct and schoolyard dynamics in 25 target schools (5 ECD centers, 15 primary schools, and 5 secondary schools) in Ayod, Uror & Duk Counties of Jonglei State and Ulang, Nasir and Longechuk Counties of Upper Nile State respectively. These 7, 339 children (5-17) and 250 teachers will be provided with teaching and learning materials in the form of 10 ECD learner kits, 250 learner kits for primary and 10 learner kits for secondary schools. 250 recreational kits will be provided to enhance learning and play and psychosocial wellbeing during schooling.

For their protective and safe school environment, 30 temporary learning spaces will be established in line with Inter-INEE's Minimum Standards for Education in Emergencies and Standards in Education Cluster Strategy 2019; and 30 gender segregated latrines and 30 water points in line with INEE and sphere standards. (unit of measurement: 1:60 for boys, 1:30 for girls). CMD will distribute 95 (500-litre) plastic water tanks with taps, 95 (50-litre) hand-washing tanks with taps and on their metal stands; 285 (1-litre) liquid sanitisers, 190 cartons of toilet soap, 95 bags (20 kgs) of detergent/powder soap, 95, 000 face masks, and 375 pairs of gumboots to provide sanitation and PPE for students and teachers. 2, 000 adolescent girls will receive dignity kits and undergo MHM sessions to better enhance their self-esteem and school attendance.

The plan targets 2, 339 (935 girls & 1, 404 boys) children in Ayod; 1, 000 (400 girls & 600 boys) in Uror; 1, 000 (400 girls & 600 boys) in Duk; 1, 000(400 girls & 600 boys) in Ulang; 1, 000 (400 girls & 600 boys) in Nasir; and 1, 000 (400 girls & 600 boys) in Longechuk. 50 (10 female) teachers in Ayod; 40 (10 female) in Uror; 40 (10 female) in Duk; 40 (10 female) in Ulang; 40 (5 female) in Nasir; and 40 (5 female) in Longechuk will benefit from active EiE pedagogy that is centered on children and adolescents and their full development, and that responds to school needs and favours the equitable achievement of learning goals. These teachers will Improve the quality of gender and disability-inclusive education services and teachers' capacity to protect the wellbeing of all children and prevent the negative impact of the emergencies on learning environments.

Equally important, 75 (27 female) PTA members in Ayod; 40 (11 female) in Uror; 40 (11 female) in Duk; 40(11female) in Ulang; 40(11 female) in Nasir; and 40 (11 female) in Longechuk and 10 (1 female) education officials in Ayod, 10 (1) in Uror; 10 (1) in Duk; 10(1) in Ulang; 10(1) in Nassir; and 10 (1 female) in Longechuk will be trained in School Management, Psychosocial Support (PSS) and Disaster Risk Reduction in Education (DRR).

CMD will also conduct 12 Back to Learning (BTL) campaigns through public information campaigns intended for the entire affected population and/or awareness raising activities aimed at specific segments of the out-of-schoolchildren (OOSC) as well as current learners identified as most at-risk.

Improving access to health, nutrition, WASH, education, child protection and cash benefits for vulnerable children and their families in Somalia (program-based project funding), The Covid share is recorded separately AA-S09-321.50 SOM 01/20-COV Integrated access to quality basic education in a protective and inclusive environment for crisis affected children and youth According to the 2021 Humanitarian needs overview report, it is estimated that 3 million school aged children need sustained equitable access to quality education in a protective learning environment. Out of these children, 2,419,059 are from non-displaced families and 667,891 are from displaced families. Despite the low caseload of IDPs, children living in IDP camps are particularly vulnerable to protection risks due to limited provision of services and poor living conditions. REACH 2021 site assessment shows low education service provision in IDP camps. This is the result of a lack of government support, and inadequate and short-term funding to support affected IDP school-aged children. 

It is estimated that 463,042 of the 3 million children in need of education are school aged children living with disabilities. Children with disabilities are significantly affected and face challenges to access an inclusive learning environment. Recent school screening identified prevalent negative attitudes towards children with disabilities by teachers and parents, and structural challenges that hinder these children to access an inclusive learning environment. According to rapid assessment conducted by Ministry of Education in Somaliland in September 2021 in drought affected areas shows 42 schools were closed due to drought. Findings from the assessment reveals 80% of the schools closed are in the rural areas (Sool, Sanag and Togdheer regions are among the regions where most of the schools closed are located). The findings from the assessment highlights that the main reasons for the school closure is due to the movement of the families as a result of the prevailing drought and lack of or inadequate number of school teachers. The HRP project will target areas with most marginalized and deprived communities (displaced and extremely poor host communities) in Southern states, Puntland and Somaliland. 

The project will provide safe and protective learning environments and access to life-saving services for children through an integrated approach targeting 95,600 children in the worst emergency affected areas and drought displaced children in South Central Somalia (47,800 (50% girls) Puntland (18,032; 50% girls) and Somaliland (29,636; 50% girls) 1,000 schools per area will be targeted in South Central Somalia, Puntland and Somaliland respectively (40:25:35).

SC will ensure school going children are retained in their current schools while those dropped out are re-enrolled. Children will be provided with access to safe drinking water, emergency school feeding, hygiene promotion and provision of teaching and learning materials. This is expected to mitigate and prevent children from dropping out from school as a result of the drought. The response will provide a protective learning environment through the construction of temporary learning spaces, distribution of teaching and learning materials, and support to teachers with emergency teacher incentives. 
The project will target 95,600 (50% girls) learners who are either dropped out or at risk of dropping out from school due to the impact of the drought. Psychosocial support services (PSS) will be provided for teachers, Community Education Committees (CECs), Child Welfare Committee (CWC), education officials in terms of case management, referral services for learners, especially in response to the drought impact and enhance their wellbeing. Community-led back-to-school campaigns will also be conducted to ensure that progress made on access to education is not lost.  SC will work with MoE to promote alternative education pathways for children who lost time out of school and will provided catch up and remedial classes to cope with their classmate. Emphasis will be given to IDP children, poor host community children, including children with disabilities and those marginalized children to ensure they are also reached with education services.

Integrated Assistance to Vulnerable Populations in Northeast Nigeria The proposal is aligned with the overall Food Security, Nutrition, and WASH sectors strategies as defined in the Humanitarian Response Plan 2021. The action is designed to run for 12 months
To deliver on the food security component of this muli-sectoral proposed interventions, Caritas Nigeira will provide wet-feeding to newly arrived refugee returnees and IDPs across border communities/camps in Banki, Bama and Gwoza; and provide energy energy for cooking to vulnerable households not yet reached across Banki, Bama, Gwoza and Konduga LGAs of Borno State. 
The nutrition component will contribute to a reduction of morbidity and mortality caused by malnutrition amongst children under 5 years of age through treatment of SAM with medical complications at stabilisation centers in Hong and Gombi LGAs of Adamawa State: and the prevention of acute malnutrition through screening, identification, referral to the OTP centers, and Targeted Supplementary Feeding Programme (TSFP) across Kaga, Konduga, Bama LGAs in Borno State and Mubi North, Gombi and Hong LGAs in Adamawa State. It will also ensure promotion of infant and young child feeding practices amongst pregnant and lactating women (PLW) to prevent malnutrition in the target LGAs. We will form support groups (MTMSG and FTFSG) where they do not exist and strengthen already formed ones where they are weak. Caregivers will be reached with health talk and IYCF Counselling in addition to food demonstration sessions. The programme will also support caregivers of children with SAM who have medical complications to receive a one-off cash transfer for immediate food needs. We will ensure enhanced needs analysis of the nutrition situation and enhanced monitoring and coordination of response. The nutrition programme will also focus on capacity building for staff in government health facilities through on-the-job training, as well as through participation in formal training and courses. Our primary focus is to provide training on Integrated Management of Severe Acute Malnutrition, which promotes the identification and treatment of SAM in line with the Government of Nigeria ministry of health (MoH) guidelines and SPHERE standards.
The WASH component will target host communities, IDP camps, schools, and health facilities, in order to reach the most vulnerable populations in need of WASH across Mubi North, Mubi South, Girei LGAs in Adamawa State and Kaga, Konduga,and Gwoza LGAs in Borno State; through the provision of solar boreholes powered by climate smart energy sources, construction of new ventilated improved pit (VIP) latrine and renovation of damaged ones, construction of new bath showers, distribution of menstrual hygiene management (MHM) and Dignity kits that are reusable to young girls and women of reproductive age, regular Hygiene promotion messaging, distribution of water treatment tablets (Aquatabs), distribution of Cholera Preparedness Kits, procurement of hand wash stations to be placed in strategic public places, including VIP latrines, and training of the beneficiaries on solid waste management. The intervention will complement other ongoing emergency/recovery programmes in the target locations using the SPHERE standards. 
For sustainability, various groups within target communities will be trained on the use locally available food items to prepare nutritious meals as well as on nutrition sensitive agriculture (home gardening). These will help to stem future malnutrition among infants, young children; WASHCOMMS will be formed, trained and strengthened to handle minor repairs and linked to Local Area Mechanics (LAMs) and technicians of solar panels and boreholes. The action is designed to run for 12 months
To deliver on the food security component of this muli-sectoral proposed interventions, Caritas Nigeira will provide wet-feeding to newly arrived refugee returnees and IDPs across border communities/camps in Banki, Bama and Gwoza; and provide energy energy for cooking to vulnerable households not yet reached across Banki, Bama, Gwoza and Konduga LGAs of Borno State. 
The nutrition component will contribute to a reduction of morbidity and mortality caused by malnutrition amongst children under 5 years of age through treatment of SAM with medical complications at stabilisation centers in Hong and Gombi LGAs of Adamawa State: and the prevention of acute malnutrition through screening, identification, referral to the OTP centers, and Targeted Supplementary Feeding Programme (TSFP) across Kaga, Konduga, Bama LGAs in Borno State and Mubi North, Gombi and Hong LGAs in Adamawa State. It will also ensure promotion of infant and young child feeding practices amongst pregnant and lactating women (PLW) to prevent malnutrition in the target LGAs. We will form support groups (MTMSG and FTFSG) where they do not exist and strengthen already formed ones where they are weak. Caregivers will be reached with health talk and IYCF Counselling in addition to food demonstration sessions. We will ensure enhanced needs analysis of the nutrition situation and enhanced monitoring and coordination of response. Our primary focus is to provide training on Integrated Management of Severe Acute Malnutrition, which promotes the identification and treatment of SAM in line with the Government of Nigeria ministry of health (MoH) guidelines and SPHERE standards.

Lifesaving food and necessary non-food items assistance, protection and WASH in line with humanitarian principles. ASISTENCIA Y PROTECCIÓN HUMANITARIA A FAMILIAS AFECTADAS POR LOS IMPACTOS DE LA CRISIS PROLONGADA DE VENEZUELA El programa está dirigido a las poblaciones las más vulnerables en Venezuela, es decir, que se seleccionaron las parroquias de intervención de acuerdo con los siguientes criterios de vulnerabilidad, operatividad y estrategia de inclusión política y social:
•	Altos niveles de pobreza
•	Altos niveles de desnutrición crónica y alta prevalencia de enfermedades infecciosas.
•	Estados fronterizos que han manejado regularmente la presión adicional del intercambio con poblaciones muy pobres y desplazados del territorio colombiano.
•	Exposición a amenazas naturales
•	Alto nivel de conflictividad y violencia social en los últimos meses, debido a la escasez.
•	Capacidad organizativa comunitaria y capacidad operativa de Cáritas consolidadas.
Los beneficiarios serán involucrados en la identificación de las necesidades para ciertas actividades, como es el caso de la selección de medicamentos a dispensar, el contenido de las bolsas complementarias de alimentos para las familias con niños/as desnutridos y la compra de filtros artesanales de agua. En otras actividades, como la detección de la desnutrición, los niños/niñas son sujetos pasivos, beneficiarios de una acción para diagnosticar y tratar la desnutrición detectada durante la primera fase del proyecto, motivada por la escasez de alimentos en el país a causa de la crisis económica. Durante la ejecución del proyecto, los beneficiarios serán implicados a través de los promotores comunitarios, quienes serán el enlace con el resto de los actores del proyecto. 
El presente proyecto se centrará en cuatro (4) resultados entre sí, que al tiempo que contribuyen a mejorar las condiciones de vida, refuerzan la resiliencia de las poblaciones más afectadas por la crisis. Ellos son: 1) Monitoreo de la situación nutricional y las condiciones de vida en las comunidades en riesgo de desnutrición en niños y mujeres embarazadas. 2) Suplementación nutricional de las comunidades vulnerables asociada a la desnutrición, con entrega de insumos terapéuticos, de insumos alimenticios y de transferencias en efectivo; 3) Atención a la salud y saneamiento, fundamentalmente a la familia de los niños menores de 5 años en situación de riesgo nutricional y de las mujeres embarazadas atendidas. Este enfoque ejecuta dos actividades que brindan respuesta a dos necesidades apremiantes, la salud y la higiene; 4) Fortalecimiento de capacidades de la Red de Cáritas de Venezuela que le permita poder adherirse a los protocolos de Cáritas Internacionalis (CI) y alcanzar un Plan de mejoras que permita incrementar la eficacia en la operatividad de los proyectos

Multisectoral and coordinated emergency response directed to the most vulnerable population affected by the complex crisis in Venezuela Respuesta integral en seguridad alimentaria y nutricional de emergencia para la población más vulnerable afectada por la crisis en Venezuela.  Acción Contra el Hambre (ACH) en Venezuela atiende las necesidades humanitarias de los grupos más vulnerables en riesgo de desnutrición aguda: < de 5 años, 5 – 14 años, mujeres embarazadas y lactantes (MEL), personas con discapacidades o con problemas de salud, en particular adultos mayores. Son agravantes las situaciones de pobreza y necesidades básicas no satisfechas como la falta de acceso a: alimentos, condiciones higiénico-sanitarias adecuadas, servicios de salud, y medios de vida. La desnutrición y el deterioro de la salud repercuten en una mayor exposición a factores agravantes como la violencia de género, embarazos adolescentes y criminalidad. A través del HRP, ACH brindará una respuesta humanitaria para la reducción del sufrimiento y ayudar a salvar vidas, identificando casos de desnutrición aguda y severa en las familias más a riesgo. Se trabajará a nivel comunitario y se coordinará con instituciones locales, en particular con escuelas y centros de salud. ACH trabaja con un enfoque de programa país y dentro de una estrategia regional, con intervenciones complementarias e integrales en: 1) Nutrición: sensibilización y consejerías; detección, tratamiento de la desnutrición aguda, y derivación de los casos con complicaciones médicas; capacitación en el manejo preventivo de la desnutrición aguda; 2) Salud: atención primaria, equipos, insumos, medicamentos, métodos anticonceptivos; 3) Seguridad Alimentaria y medios de vida: distribución de alimentos y apoyo para la producción de alimentos; 4) ASH: acceso a servicios de agua, saneamiento, e higiene, en escuelas y centros comunitarios; distribución de kits de higiene, y rehabilitación/reparación de sistemas de abastecimiento de agua y de saneamiento en comunidades. El sector de Protección y género, de manera transversal, trabajará en prevención de VBG, nuevas masculinidades y DSSR; establecimiento y/o fortalecimiento de espacios seguros para mujeres y niñas; atención psico-social, distribución de kits de higiene menstrual y protección para mujeres en riesgo. La respuesta actual de ACH se concentra en Caracas DC, Guárico, Carabobo, Miranda, Zulia, Bolívar, y próximamente en Falcón, Amazonas y Sucre.

Acción Contra el Hambre (ACH) en Venezuela atiende las necesidades humanitarias de los grupos más vulnerables en riesgo de desnutrición aguda: < de 5 años, 5 – 14 años, mujeres embarazadas y lactantes (MEL), personas con discapacidades o con problemas de salud, en particular adultos mayores. Son agravantes las situaciones de pobreza y necesidades básicas no satisfechas como la falta de acceso a: alimentos, condiciones higiénico-sanitarias adecuadas, servicios de salud, y medios de vida. La desnutrición y el deterioro de la salud repercuten en una mayor exposición a factores agravantes como la violencia de género, embarazos adolescentes y criminalidad. A través del HRP, ACH brindará una respuesta humanitaria para la reducción del sufrimiento y ayudar a salvar vidas, identificando casos de desnutrición aguda y severa en las familias más a riesgo. Se trabajará a nivel comunitario y se coordinará con instituciones locales, en particular con escuelas y centros de salud. ACH trabaja con un enfoque de programa país y dentro de una estrategia regional, con intervenciones complementarias e integrales en: 1) Nutrición: sensibilización y consejerías; detección, tratamiento de la desnutrición aguda, y derivación de los casos con complicaciones médicas; capacitación en el manejo preventivo de la desnutrición aguda; 2) Salud: atención primaria, equipos, insumos, medicamentos, métodos anticonceptivos; 3) Seguridad Alimentaria y medios de vida: distribución de alimentos y apoyo para la producción de alimentos; 4) ASH: acceso a servicios de agua, saneamiento, e higiene, en escuelas y centros comunitarios; distribución de kits de higiene, y rehabilitación/reparación de sistemas de abastecimiento de agua y de saneamiento en comunidades. El sector de Protección y género, de manera transversal, trabajará en prevención de VBG, nuevas masculinidades y DSSR; establecimiento y/o fortalecimiento de espacios seguros para mujeres y niñas; atención psico-social, distribución de kits de higiene menstrual y protección para mujeres en riesgo. La respuesta actual de ACH se concentra en Caracas DC, Guárico, Carabobo, Miranda, Zulia, Bolívar, y próximamente en Falcón, Amazonas y Sucre.
