Support of UNRWA's COVID measures in the Palestinian territories (food aid, hygiene measures and cash benefits) Ensuring safe access to emergency education for UNRWA vulnerable refugee students. The proposed intervention aims at ensuring continuity of learning and safe and equitable access to inclusive and quality education for 20,991 students (9,919 boys and 11,081 girls) and 951 school staff (319 men and 632 women) in a context of increased violence as a result of protracted crisis and continued military occupation, as well as increased vulnerability  due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The project targets 26 schools that are affected by frequent military incursions, clashes and settler violence and are located at risk areas namely East Jerusalem, Hebron H2, Area C, and inside refugee camps.

The first aim of the project is to ensure that students affected by education-related violations or the COVID-19 pandemic benefit from a protective environment and that school-aged children are able to complete  their basic education. This is achieved through the provision of safe transportation to vulnerable children while commuting to and from school, and protective presence in two schools particularly affected by ISF incursions, use of live ammunition and tear gas and settlers' violence.  Emphasis is also given in supporting the psychosocial well-being and enhancing resilience of students and teachers. This is achieved through the deployment of ten school counsellors at high-risk schools; provision of recreational activities through school-based summer camps, enhancement of recreational spaces, and stress management workshops aiming to strengthen teachers’ resilience.  
The second objective of the project is to ensure inclusivity of all vulnerable students. Learning support through catch-up classes will be provided to help children with learning difficulties.  In addition, 1,852 children with disabilities (767 boys and 1,085 girls) and special needs will be supported through assistive devices and referrals. 

In the context of COVID-19, the third aim of the project is to guarantee that schools prevent the spread of COVID-19 and protect the health of the students and teacher.  UNRWA will provide hygiene kits and Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) to all targeted students and teachers. 

Finally, the intervention also aims to improve the confidentiality, safety and accessibility of complaints mechanisms, including complaints of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA). The project intervention provides  multiple child-friendly channels to receive and respond to complaints which are adapted to the target population. UNRWA has developed ad hoc SoPs on the management of cases of SEA which abide to CBCM SoPs.   Complaints of SEA will be handled by PSEA focal points who will ensure a survivor centered approach in how the complaint is handled and support is offered to the survivor. UNRWA West Bank Field Office works closely with the PSEA Network and will undertake compulsory reporting and external referrals. 

This action contributes to the achievement of two of the strategic objectives under the HRP: 

STRATEGIC OBJECTIVE 2: The basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians living under occupation are met through the provision of quality basic services and improved access to resources, in accordance with the rights of protected persons under IHL. 

STRATEGIC OBJECTIVE 3: Safe, accessible mechanisms are in place for reporting complaints and feedback, including complaints of SEA, particularly in high-risk areas.

Supporting the sustainable increase of fish for consumption in Somali coastal fishing communities through improved post-harvest management Emergency Lifesaving Cash and Livelihood Support to IDP and Non- IDP Communities in Somalia Somalia is facing a severe and deteriorating humanitarian crisis as we enter 2022 as a result of the compounding effects of conflict, recurrent climate shocks, diseases and pests outbreaks with increased levels of vulnerability and substantial increase in the humanitarian caseload (Somalia HNO, 2022). There is a serious risk that the impact of consecutive below average to poor rainfall in most parts of the country will develop into a severe drought by early to mid- 2022 with the number of people facing acute food insecurity on the rise. It is likely that minority groups, women, children, people with disabilities, will experience heightened protection risks as a result, unless they are intentionally targeted to receive tailored assistance.

With approximately 3.5 million individuals in IPC 3 and 4 through at least December 2021, FAO proposes to target 160,300 households (961,800 individuals- 91,500 IDPs and 870,300 non- IDPs) in IPC 3 and IPC 4 caseloads respectively. This will include 216,790 women, 254,492 girls, 264,880 boys and 225,638 men and 144,270 people living with disabilities (PWD) across 59 districts in Somalia through its flagship Cash+ approach combining short-term cash transfers with tailored livelihood support in accordance with technical and humanitarian standards. Vulnerable households will identified from at-risk pastoral, agro-pastoral, fishing, riverine farmers, IDPs and Non- IDP communities in IPC 3 and 4 areas. This intervention will integrate short-term cash transfers aimed at enabling the most vulnerable households to meet their immediate needs, with livelihood support to allow crisis-affected households to get back into production. FAO will employ community- led beneficiary selection processes and ensure adequate targeting and representation of extremely vulnerable and minority groups in community committees. Interventions proposed will employ a Do No Harm approach with a gender lens that ensures conflict- sensitivity to reduce protection risks for all individuals, and to mitigate the risk of conflict or community tensions. 

Under Food Security Cluster (FSC) Objective 1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 160,300 households through a blend of conditional (Cash-for-Work) and unconditional (UCT) transfers. Under UCT, FAO will prioritize Cash+ interventions including Cash+ Agriculture, Cash+ livestock and Cash+ fisheries. These modalities will increase households’ immediate access to food by providing sufficient cash to access the minimum expenditure basket (MEB), while supporting the rehabilitation of critical productive and community infrastructure. It will also boost household food production, increase household incomes and create employment opportunities. Cash transfer values will be informed by the Cash Working Group and are expected to differ per district/ region of intervention. They, however, will be valued at 80 percent of the food MEB, which can range from USD 50- 100 per month. All cash-based programmes will include training on good nutrition practices. 

Under FSC Objective 2, to protect livelihoods and related food sources, FAO will provide in-kind, technical support and tailored trainings to 112,500 HHs to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security and nutrition threats, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to targeted HHs. In addition, FAO shall provide transitional cash support to 13,100 HHs across agro pastoral, pastoral and fishing livelihood zones to augment the adaptive capacity of HHs, strengthen and foster resilience to future shocks, cushioning them from food insecurity and malnutrition. Trainings shall be delivered alongside input provision to build skills in sustainable use of resources provided, build skills in livelihoods management including harvest, post- harvest management, linking beneficiaries to long- term interventions that provide them opportunities to enhance their livelihoods and skills.

his project will provide GBV protection services for the most critically vulnerable Lebanese, refugee and migrant populations women, and girls, including persons with disabilities and older persons, living in Baabda, and El Metn districts. 
It will address GBV needs through provision of GBV risk mitigation and prevention services including case management, protection cash, PSS, life skills trainings, in addition to legal services. 
GBV survivors will receive based on individual assessment protection cash assistance and dignity kits. Comprehensive Protection Services in Bekaa, Aley, Batroun, and greater Beirut  This project will provide protection services for the most critically vulnerable Lebanese population, including women, men, girls, and boys, working both to prevent protection violations as well as respond to needs. It will address GBV needs through provision of services including psychosocial support and case management. It will also address child protection needs through protection case management, focused and non-focused psychosocial support, and recreational activities. The project will address legal needs for GBV and CP cases through provision of legal services, including legal counselling and payment of legal fees, for individuals both in and out of detention through partner organization, MSD. 

The project will operate through Tabitha-run community centers in Batroun, North Gov.; Aley, Mount Lebanon (3 centers in Aley city, Choueifat and Bayssour) in addition Chouf through the intervention in the SDC of Chehime; Achrafieh, Beirut ; and through the mobile unit in the Bekaa Valley in addition to greater Beirut area (Metn and Baabda) that Tabitha is planning to target through the proposal submitted to OCHA lately. These centers and mobile unit contain Tabitha’s community outreach workers, a psychologist, and social workers who maintain a presence within targeted communities. Cases taken up by these social workers may come from multiple sources- referrals from other NGOs and CSOs, cases identified by community outreach workers, cases identified through individuals or family members already participating in Tabitha’s community center protection services, etc. Tabitha also partners with another Lebanese NGO, Migration Services and Development (MSD), that specializes in legal services and has access to individuals in detention facilities. MSD lawyers also maintain designated offices within Tabitha community centers. 
Tabitha will also coordinate its work with the stakeholders of each area, for Achrafieh and Greater Beirut, Tabitha will coordinate with Makhzoumi & TDH Lausanne following the recommendation of the sector.
Case Management will be implemented through the use of the social work methodology including individual vulnerability/needs assessments (through interviews and home visits when possible), a network of outreach workers (selected and trained among vulnerable refugees/host communities) to facilitate trust and access to isolated groups on a timely and safe manner. Tabitha follows the national protection working groups, all the team is trained on the usage of the national SOP for GBV and CP, using the recognized referrals pathways to ensure cases that require specialized follow-up are referred to be assessed, specialized service providers. MHPSS services will be made available for those attending programs at the community centers in all the locations- this includes the elderly, children, and those who have experienced severe trauma and abuse. A licensed psychologist is present in all locations and animators/facilitators are trained to facilitate group PSS sessions, especially for children. The legal assistance program operates using a holistic approach, whereas both lawyers & social workers provide services to those in need of assistance. Beneficiaries are referred to or approach Tabitha community centers for issues related to civil documentation or access to justice. Services provided include: support with employer or family issues such as divorce; child registration and birth registration; marriage certificates; documentation for the continuity of education; renewal of documentation to stay in Lebanon; or organization of documentation to return to Syria. As the beneficiaries for the legal program are vulnerable conflict affected households, often cases of GBV and CP, cases are referred from social workers either within Tabitha, or from the referral pathway system established in country.  With homelessness rising, legal support is also needed for rental and eviction, another service of MSD.

Water, Sanitation and Hygiene,Protection,Economic Recovery and Market Systems,Multipurpose Cash Assistance Sécurité alimentaire et autonomisation des populations vulnérables de la région de l’Extrême-Nord victimes des exactions des bandes armées et des inondations Le présent projet se propose de renforcer les moyens de subsistance de 2 000 ménages vulnérables (60 femmes et 40% hommes)  de la population cible des départements du Mayo Sava (Arrondissement de Kolofata, Mora), du Mayo Danay (Arrondissement de Vellé), du Mayo Tsanaga (Arrondissements de Mokolo et Mozogo) et du Logone-et-Chari (Arrondissements de Makary, Goulfey et Logone birni) de la région de l’Extrême-Nord du Cameroun à travers la distribution des intrants agricoles pour les cultures maraîchères et vivrières et leur capacitation pour le développement des AGR sur la période Avril-Décembre 2022, ceci afin de les permettre d’améliorer la sécurité alimentaire et de renforcer leur résilience aux chocs divers. 
Plus spécifiquement, il s’agira :
De contribuer à la formation sur des thématiques diverses de 2 000 ménages vulnérables, cible du projet. Il sera question de former les bénéficiaires sur les meilleures techniques de culture maraîchères, vulgariser les bonnes pratiques de récoltes, de conservation et de transformations des produits locaux.
D’inciter à la création des activités génératrices de revenus (AGR) afin de réduire la pression sur les moyens d’existence en période de soudure.
Les activités principales suivantes sont envisagées :
Ciblage de 2 000 ménages (14 000 individus, une taille moyenne de 7 personnes)
Le ciblage des 2 000 ménages soit en moyenne 14 000 personnes bénéficiaires intégrera l’ensemble des parties prenantes y compris l’autorité administrative et celle traditionnelle. Les critères prendront leur source des 14 critères généralement reconnus dans la sphère. Un exercice de priorisation sera organisé avec les représentants des cibles et les autorités des sites arrêtés. Le projet ciblera les populations déplacées (40%), les retournées (20%) et les communautés hôtes vulnérables (40%). Un ratio de 60% de femmes cheffe de ménage contre 40% d’hommes sera respecté. Les femmes étant celles victimes de pratiques indécentes des hommes et culturellement, plus actives dans les activités agricoles. Par ailleurs, elles sont celles qui veillent sur la santé alimentaire et sécuritaire de la famille.
Formation des bénéficiaires sur les thématiques diverses liées à la production agropastorale, la récolte, la conservation et la transformation des produits locaux
2 000 ménages recevront des formations théoriques et pratiques au cours de 02 séances sur les itinéraires techniques agropastorales, les meilleures techniques de récoltes, conservation et transformation des produits locaux, la production des biopesticides et des engrais organiques. Un conseil agricole sera offert aux bénéficiaires pendant la durée du projet. Les orientations et cadrages seront assurés par les techniciens du terrain en collaboration avec l’administration camerounaise en charge des questions agricoles et élevages (le MINADER et le MINEPIA) pour une meilleure appropriation et de durabilité des acquis. 
Développement des activités génératrices de revenu (AGR)
L’ensemble des ménages recevront des conseils pratiques sur le développement et la gestion des AGR en donnant une valeur ajoutée aux produits récoltés de la session vivrière notamment à travers la conservation et la transformation des produits locaux.
Les résultats attendus sont les suivants :
R1 : Les ménages bénéficiaires des départements du Mayo Sava, du Mayo Danay, du Mayo Tsanaga et Logone-Et-Chari, ont accès aux meilleures pratiques de production et à des intrants et équipements agricoles afin d’améliorer leur résilience durant la période de soudure et de moins agresser les moyens de subsistance.

Agriculture and Food Security,Water, Sanitation and Hygiene,Shelter and Settlements Community-based Protection response to conflict affected communities in North West and South West regions of Cameroon INTERSOS proposes to promote a protective environment for conflict-affected people, in particular IDPs with a focus on Child Protection and GBV. Four main elements will be addressed: 1) Prevention of child abuse, neglect, and exploitation; 2) Prevention by addressing the risks of sexual and gender-based violence and responding to the immediate needs of survivors of GBV, 3) Material support for the most vulnerable IDPs with NFI; and 4) identifying and strengthening existing positive community protection mechanism.
Outputs to prevent and respond to Child Protection needs and GBV: Creation of 175 Child Friendly Spaces (Fako, Meme, Manyu, Kupe, Mezam, Momo, Boyo) where children and caregivers would be able to improve their protection environment and theirs capacities through the active participation in the existing Protection structures that INTERSOS supported during the year 2021, Integrated GBV Case management for boys girls and their caregivers, share INTERSOS’ Hotline, provision of psychological first aid (PFA), referral and accompaniment to specialized services, individual follow up, Psychosocial Support (PSS) inside and outside CFS facilities though individual & group counselling, community based recreational and PSS activities, basic skills acquisition and informal education, MH support for children and caregivers through individual case management and referrals to specialized services, Targeted material assistance for identified protection needs: Auto-referral for dignity kits to vulnerable women and girls including PwSN of reproductive age; Auto-referral for Mama kits for vulnerable pregnant and lactating women and girls, Auto-referral for cash for protection: Community capacity building on Child Protection and GBV principles & personal/relational accountability, Material support for the most vulnerable IDP household through the distribution of contextualized NFI case by case.
The overall objective of the project is to improve the protection environment of children and caregivers affected by the crisis and foster a community-based approach for the protection of the most vulnerable IDPs by contributing to the reduction of child abuse and gender-based violence (GBV) through promoting socio-cultural norms that respect age/gender equality, through holistic care of children and caregivers affected by the crisis, and GBV survivors by promoting their recovery and resilience. Also, the empowerment of community members and groups in identifying, referring and responding to protection concerns. 
The project aims at initiating key changes in behaviors and socio-cultural norms in order to sustainably reduce child abuse and GBV.
Through awareness-raising campaigns, capacity building of caregivers and the active involvement of community leaders, communities are called upon to adopt attitudes that are protective for children and respectful of gender equality.
CFS are key avenues to providing confidential medium for disclosure of psychosocial distress and GBV without the fear of stigmatization, they also provide caregivers and survivors an opportunity to build support networks through peer-to-peer activities and build on their recovery and resilience through activities that foster social interactions.
Though this project, INTERSOS will integrate the CP response to his spectrum of protection activities in a systematic approach, based on the Community based strategy that INTERSOS is implementing and the Protection monitoring mechanisms already in place covering 10 divisions of NWSW, INTERSOS will be able to early identify cases of child abuse and to promptly address the protection needs of children affected by the crisis. The complementarity of this project with the ongoing protection program, and the recognition that INTERSOS gained in NWSW regions which greatly facilitate humanitarian access in hard-to-reach areas, are valuable assets that will impact the quality and the promptness of the assistance

Top-up Syria 2022 - Annual programme 2022 Supporting most vulnerable Lebanese children to access and continue learning through quality and inclusive education programing The purposed intervention takes a holistic approach responding to the economic crisis affecting the learning of children all over Lebanon. Plan will collaborate with LOST to address the educational needs of children by targeting the most vulnerable Leb children in North Beqaa with a focus on out of school, children that dropped out or shifted to public schools to access or remain in formal education. The intervention will be adapted in line with covid-19 measures to ensure children are safe and protected. Caregivers will be supported by addressing both their financial and emotional burden. Also Plan and LOST will be working on supporting the formal education system, to ensure that students are provided with an inclusive and quality education while ensuring schools have the needed basic conditions and resources to adhere to the influx of students transitioning from private education. The project two main objectives are: Obj 1: Direct community support to support the most vulnerable children to ensure continued learning. Plan’s programs are based on a needs bases with a strong emphasis on learning component to ensure that the most vulnerable children educational needs are met.  Plan will coordinate with all educational stakeholders in the area to fully map out the most vulnerable areas in North Beqaa. Plan and LOST will be working on addressing both financial and social emotional burden. Plan has already a strong cash component under its programming and has all the developed guidelines and SOPs established to support families in need. Also, awareness sessions will be provided for caregivers to increase their soft skills while also focusing on decreasing their social emotional burdens using an internally developed curriculum “Parenting skills for protection”. In addition to that, Plan and LOST will support in addressing other educational challenges through a strong referral pathway internally and externally to other service providers such as Basic Assistance and FSS, Protection, WaSH and Health. The Second Obj 2: Improving Formal Education of most vulnerable Lebanese and migrant children through schools. This objective will be focusing on schools and ensuring that all aspects such human and operational resources are fully functional to ensure a protective and inclusive environment for all children. Plan under the Beirut blast response was able to distribute close to 1000 education kits and 735 Laptops to children affected by the Beirut blast. Distribution of emergency shelter NFI kits with a specific focus on women’s hygiene/dignity Emergency WASH and ESNFI Response to Conflict Affected People in Tigray Region As of February 2022, a total of 4.51 million IDPs have been identified thus far across the country. Of the total displaced population, the main causes of displacement were conflict which displaced 3.63 million IDPs (81%). Tigray has remained to be the priority region and continues to have significant IDPs and affected host population that remains vulnerable under the current circumstances- conflict. According to the Emergency Site Assessment (ESA) round 8, 386,741 households comprising 1,814,284 IDPs were identified in 581 accessible sites in Tigray region due to the Northern Ethiopia Crisis. 
Humanitarian needs remain significantly high as the current response is not meeting the increasing needs of those in need as the resources available are not matching the requirements to ensure that minimum lifesaving humanitarian standards are maintained for the targeted population. According to the northern Ethiopia humanitarian update shared (OCHA, 14 April 2022), between 1 January and 4 April 2022, only 42.11% of the targeted people were reached with ESNFI response in Tigray region. Critical needs prioritized include, provision of adequate shelters and NFIs for IDPs living in highly congested and substandard living conditions, provision of shelter and NFI assistance to IDPs willing to return to their areas of origin, and to IDPs currently living within host communities, and rental assistance schemes or other arrangements for IDPs living in host communities. 
Inadequate provision of WASH services poses a risk of disease outbreaks at IDP sites. About 9,300 water points or more than 54 per cent of the 17,080 water points in Tigray are not functional affecting the access of more than 3.5 million people to safe drinking water. About 418,000 IDPs in 131 sites require 295 trips of water trucking every day which requires 1,990 liters of fuel daily. Construction of more than 17,000 latrines at IDP sites are required to mitigate the risks of disease transmission. Low stock of key WASH NFIs, including water treatment chemical, water containers and hygiene supplies have also been reported in Tigray. Priority WASH needs include, emergency water trucking, rehabilitation of  water schemes, rehabilitation of sanitation facilities, distribution of WASH NFIs, and hygiene promotion activities.
The locations and activities considered for the WASH and ES/NFI interventions under this project plan are identified in the HRP 2022 prioritization list to address the immediate and life-saving needs of crisis-affected communities in line with the respective clusters' priority activities. The actions will be WASH and ESNFI services and carried out in line with cluster objectives CLWSH/CO1 (Deliver conflict-sensitive essential life-saving WASH services to affected people), CLWSH/CO3 (To enhance vulnerable households’ ability to withstand recurrent and future shocks in Ethiopia through early recovery and resilience interventions), and CLSHL/CO1, (Ensure contextualized access to lifesaving shelter and NFIs for displacement affected population with a focus on the most vulnerable and at-risk population group to safeguard their health security, privacy, and dignity  )and CLSHL/CO2 (Contribute to improving protection outcomes by ensuring the conflict/displacement affected people have adequate safety, dignity, well-being, and equitable access to shelter solutions).
The projects aim to enhance the protection, health, and well-being of the conflict affected IDPs and host communities, and will directly reach 43,765 people through WASH and 40,055 people through ES/NFI prioritizing the most vulnerable, including women, girls, children, elderly, and people with disabilities in particular.
The project will ensure the active participation of the targeted beneficiaries and stakeholders throughout the project cycle. Protection and safety concerns will be given priority and DRC will ensure providing safe, easy, and dignified access to the facilities by the most vulnerable.

Agriculture and Food Security,Water, Sanitation and Hygiene,Multipurpose Cash Assistance  (USAID/BHA) Livelihood Response to Conflict and Drought induced Emergencies (LRCDE) in Afar region  In the Afar region, the humanitarian situation deteriorated by multifaceted natural and man-made hazards such as erratic rainfall patterns and dry spells, ethnic conflict as well as Tigray war which spills over to Afar , degradation of rangeland (due to invasive species of Prosopis juliflora, outbreaks of human (including COVID-19 pandemic) and livestock diseases, invasion by various pests (Fall Armyworm and Desert Locusts) which all contributed towards to poor crop harvests and loss of plant and pastures, which then lead to low crop and livestock production as well as livelihood losses. VSF G collected and analyzed at ground level information with beneficiary communities and then the prioritization of these locations also informed by the currently IPC 3 & 4 priority locations based on the January IPC projections, IDP numbers, experienced droughts and areas with emergency needs as the lean season deepens. To contribute to the achievements of agriculture cluster objective one “protect and sustain core-agricultural livelihoods of climate and conflict affected households in Ethiopia through humanitarian interventions in 2022” and to enhance vulnerable households’ ability to withstand recurrent and future shocks in Ethiopia through early recovery and resilience interventions”, VSF Germany designed this project with key activities which includes: provision of veterinary services (voucher based treatment and vaccination); provision of supplementary animal feed to milking goats and provision of emergency seed pack (cereals, legumes, vegetables) and fodder seeds including farm tools. Moreover, this project has proposed restocking of assets for those lost their asset due to drought and multipurpose cash assistance to improve household income through unconditional cash transfer. Different Capacity building training to communities and government experts including awareness creation on COVID-19 control and prevention measures and mainstreaming of accountability to affected population and GBV. The project will give emphasis to beneficiaries such as female-headed households, people with disabilities, child-headed households, as well as IDPs. As indicated above the identified and proposed activities by the cluster and planned by VSF G are in line with the draft 2022 HRP which aims to address the needs of the most at risk and vulnerable populations by focusing on priority needs. The proposed action will ensure synergies/integration with ongoing project or resources being implemented internally and with other partners’ projects in the target woredas. In order to augment the impact of the projects, VSF-Germany links the proposed activities with nutrition, WASH and other livelihood interventions specifically during the targeting of beneficiary HHs. The integration/synergies will have positive impact on the quick recovery of HHs from the shock specifically HHs with cases of malnutrition and other related shocks.  The project will contribute to protection of the environmental by training VSF G staffs, CAHWs, government and community where proper collection and disposal of all packing materials of drugs such as bottles, feeds and seeds after use. This action will be implemented for a period of nine months starting in Mid-April to May in the five woredas (Aba’ala, Erebeti, Berhale, Dalol and Kuneba of zone 2 (Kilbati rasu) of Afar region.

Cette réponse s’inscrit dans la Stratégie de Prévention et de Gestion des Crises Alimentaires 2021 – 2025 du Dispositif National de Prévention et de Gestion de Crises Alimentaires (DNPGCA). Ce plan s’inscrit aussi dans le Plan d’Action 2021-2023 du Comité Technique Tripartite sur le Nexus Urgence-Développement (CTTNUD), en vue d’une mobilisation des ressources financières pour une planification et une mise en œuvre concertée des activités relatives à la promotion du NEXUS.  Dans le cas spécifique de l’assistance aux retournés dans leurs villages d’origine, qui est envisagée en 2022, la Loi 2018-74, relative à la protection et à l’assistance aux Personnes Déplacées Internes (PDI) cadrera le processus. Rappelons que l’Activité 1, relative aux urgences s’inscrit dans l’effet direct stratégique 1 du CSP (2020-2024) du PAM Niger « Les populations affectées, y compris les réfugiés, les personnes déplacées internes, les communautés hôtes et les retournés dans les zones ciblées sont en mesure de répondre aux besoins alimentaires minimums pendant et après la crise ».  La réponse aux urgences du PAM concernant la SECAL, basée sur une approche flexible, concernera toutes les trois (3) composantes de cette réponse en 2022 :
•	Le Mécanisme de Réponse Rapide (RRM)
•	La réponse aux crises prolongées.
•	La réponse à la soudure agricole et pastorale.
Par ailleurs la prévention de la malnutrition aux enfants 6-23 mois est combinée aux trois composantes ci-dessus.

WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.

GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. Strengthening the humanitarian response to mitigate protection risks associated with mixed migration flows and displacement situations in Latin America. Respuesta multisectorial humanitaria en Venezuela En Venezuela, DRC busca proporcionar asistencia humanitaria a poblaciones vulnerables y afectadas por la crisis actual como son las consecuencias socioeconómicas de la pandemia del COVID-19, de los flujos migratorios mixtos hacia fuera de Venezuela y de las problemáticas fronterizas relacionados a actividades ilícitas y conflictos de grupos armados que vive la población que reside en Venezuela, tales como desplazamientos y/o confinamientos masivos. Por medio de una intervención multisectorial, DRC brindará asistencia de emergencia con un enfoque de protección tanto para refugiados en Venezuela, venezolanos con la intención de migrar, venezolanos retornados, desplazados internos y a población de acogida afectada, aplicando de manera transversal un enfoque sensible a la edad, el género y la discapacidad para llegar a un total de 21,288 personas vulnerables. Los perfiles priorizados por DRC serán aquellos que presenten altos niveles de vulnerabilidad como lo son las personas con necesidades específicas de protección (NNA, mujeres, LGBTI, ancianos, etc.), personas con discapacidad, sobrevivientes o personas en riesgo de violencia basada en género, víctimas de desplazamiento masivo o confinamiento, grupos indígenas entre otros. Este proyecto será implementado en todas las regiones en las cuales DRC trabaja en Venezuela, que, al mismo tiempo, son zonas de mayor proporción de necesidades humanitarias severas de acuerdo con el HRP 2022/23: Zulia, Sucre y Apure. Esta acción tiene como objetivo ofrecer una intervención de protección integrada que combina la protección y asistencia de emergencia para mejorar las condiciones de las poblaciones vulnerables antes mencionadas. 
La acción propuesta incluye los siguientes sectores/actividades: Coordinación, Protección, Seguridad Alimentaria, Salud, Agua, saneamiento e higiene y Educación. El presente proyecto tendrá como línea de intervención principal, el abordaje de las necesidades de protección encontradas en una evaluación de campo llevada a cabo en noviembre del 2021 en los estados de Sucre (municipios de Arismendi, Cajigal, Mariño y Valdés), Zulia (municipios de Maracaibo, Rosario de Perijá, Machiques de Perijá, Páez) y Apure (municipio Páez) y como líneas complementarias a los sectores de salud, WASH, educación y seguridad alimentaria. Es por ello que DRC plantea una respuesta integral no solo a necesidades de  protección como son, el acceso a información, asistencia legal y acceso a documentación para población vulnerable, incluidas las personas sobrevivientes y en riesgo de VbG,  el acceso a asistencia individualizada y especifica de protección y prevención de trata sino también a cubrir necesidades básicas de seguridad alimentaria;  mediante distribuciones mensuales de kits familiares alimenticios por 10 meses en las zonas de intervención, salud; con la rehabilitación de centros médicos seleccionados y educación; proveyendo suministros escolares y de higiene personal y familiar, a través de una intervención multisectorial y previamente coordinada con autoridades y comunidades locales. Uno de los hallazgos de la evaluación de campo fue la falta de data relacionada a protección para poder producir análisis confiables, es por esto por lo que DRC plantea implementar un análisis de protección basado en evidencia a través de un monitoreo continuo de protección en las localidades de intervención, con la finalidad de tener información a tiempo para poder identificar riesgos y priorizar necesidades.

Esta acción tiene como objetivo ofrecer una intervención de protección integrada que combina la protección y asistencia de emergencia para mejorar las condiciones de las poblaciones vulnerables antes mencionadas.

Es por ello que DRC plantea una respuesta integral no solo a necesidades de  protección como son, el acceso a información, asistencia legal y acceso a documentación para población vulnerable, incluidas las personas sobrevivientes y en riesgo de VbG,  el acceso a asistencia individualizada y especifica de protección y prevención de trata sino también a cubrir necesidades básicas de seguridad alimentaria;  mediante distribuciones mensuales de kits familiares alimenticios por 10 meses en las zonas de intervención, salud; con la rehabilitación de centros médicos seleccionados y educación; proveyendo suministros escolares y de higiene personal y familiar, a través de una intervención multisectorial y previamente coordinada con autoridades y comunidades locales. Uno de los hallazgos de la evaluación de campo fue la falta de data relacionada a protección para poder producir análisis confiables, es por esto por lo que DRC plantea implementar un análisis de protección basado en evidencia a través de un monitoreo continuo de protección en las localidades de intervención, con la finalidad de tener información a tiempo para poder identificar riesgos y priorizar necesidades.

Support vulnerable individuals through health tailored activities designed to strengthen the resilience of households with vulnerable pregnant/lactating women and access the EmOC services for hospital care support Strengthening the resilience of households with vulnerable pregnant/lactating women through a comprehensive and integrated life saving intervention Throughout this project, PUI will support vulnerable individuals through health tailored activities designed to strengthen the resilience of households with vulnerable pregnant/lactating women. This project was designed based on PUI’s technical expertise and long-term presence and acceptance in the area of intervention.

Monitoring activities will be carried out throughout the life of the project in order to guarantee the compliance of the activities with agreed objectives and targets. A detailed monitoring and evaluation plan (M&E) will be developed at the beginning of the project by PUI’s Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability and Learning (MEAL) unit together with the technical teams and programme staff, in line with the proposed indicators defined in the intervention logical framework. Tools and monitoring activities detailed in the M&E plan will provide regular feedback on the progress towards the proposed results and allow for swift adjustment if needed. A dedicated MEAL Activities Schedule will also be prepared and followed up by the MEAL Manager.
Data collection and storage tools will grant the highest level of data protection and confidentiality, allowing a systematic disaggregation per sex, age and disability and providing automatic reporting features. While PUI MEAL team will ensure the design, development and maintenance of internal Indicator Tracking Tables and Databases, a wider integration with the MoPH Health Information System (Phenix) will also be pursued, allowing an additional layer of data triangulation between different sources and thus enhancing the overall data quality and accuracy.
 
Programme monitoring will combine different methodologies, based on qualitative and quantitative approaches, including field visits and surveys occurring on a regular basis. Their roll out will be ensured under the supervision of the MEAL Manger, which will be in charge of the design of the tools, the management of the MEAL Officers in the bases, and of the data analysis and report writing and dissemination. In particular:
Patient Satisfaction and Post Intervention Surveys will be conducted at least twice during the project implementation period in order to gather feedback from pregnant women on their perceptions about the quality and the outcomes of the services received, their feeling about topics such safety and accessibility as well as the patient centred approach supported by PUI. While based on a quantitative approach, these surveys might also include qualitative data collection methodologies such as Focus Groups Discussion and in-depth interviews, depending on the context.
Post Distribution Monitoring exercises will be regularly carried out in order to monitor cash and NFIs distribution, focusing on outcome and process related research questions, including direct feedback from beneficiaries about the items distributed and, potentially, complaints to be addressed.
In specific circumstances preventing direct access to the project areas, such as COVID 19 related movements restrictions decided by the GOL or civil unrest, measures will be taken to shift these activities to remote modalities (phone calls, reduced sample sizes, online FGDs, etc.)
 
Dedicated capitalisation activities, to be conducted at least every six months, will include Lessons Learnt workshops and/or project reviews, to be facilitated by the MEAL unit and involving technical and field teams. Such activities will be carried out against specific ToRs and will focus on detailed learning agendas and evaluation questions; best practices, implementation challenges and ways forward will be identified and discussed; capitalisation reports will be issued and disseminated to all relevant stakeholders.

Food Assistance,Nutrition WFP Emergency relief response The World Food Programme (WFP) is United Nations frontline agency in the fight against hunger and working closely with the Government of Ethiopia (GoE) and humanitarian partners to save lives as well as strengthen and support the resilience of the most vulnerable population.
Ethiopia CO (WFP) continues to provide emergency and lifesaving food assistance in conflict, post-conflict or disaster situations based on government request. WFP has been supporting the Government of Ethiopia in its effort to tackle the country’s food insecurity problems through providing humanitarian food assistance and addressing underlying causes. The majority of GFD is provided through in-kind (food assistance) with an increasing portion in cash-based transfers (CBT).

Water, Sanitation and Hygiene Emergency Water Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) support to population affected by conflict and climate induced crises in Ethiopia  IOM is leading WASH activities in many IDP sites and host communities across Ethiopia, including distribution of hygiene kits, water trucking, construction and rehabilitation of water points, emergency latrines, and handwashing stations, establishment of community-based water or sanitation management committees, and hygiene promotion activities through contextualized campaigns and mobilization of gender-balanced hygiene promoters. 

In Ethiopia currently the internal displacement and humanitarian needs are mainly derived by the ongoing conflicts and droughts in some parts of the country. The displacement level in Ethiopia doubled in 2021, with over 2 million additional people displaced during 2021. According to IOM’s latest Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) National Displacement Report released in December 2021, a total of 4.2 million people were internally displaced across Ethiopia. This includes around 2.11 million IDPs identified in Tigray and neighbouring zones in Afar and Amhara regions as a result of the Northern Ethiopia Crisis. The ongoing displacements continue to pose serious protection concerns for the affected population. The majority of the displaced population live-in collective sites or in spontaneous settlements where they have limited access to essential services, dignified and safe living conditions to sustain their families and communities. A large number of the displaced population are women and children under 18.
 
IOM works under the framework of the 2021 HRP and 2022 draft HRP to enhance understanding of the crisis and assist joint, strategic response planning. This is particularly relevant to address new shocks and the confluence of needs. All interventions occur based on assessed needs, inter-cluster Initial Rapid Needs Assessments (IRNA) and cluster-specific assessments. All assessments integrate specific gender analyses. IOM further considers key protection needs including the risk of exposure to harm, exploitation, harassment, deprivation and abuse, including forms of violence that are gender-based; the ability to meet basic needs; access to basic services; and coping mechanisms. IOM uses both qualitative and quantitative assessment methodologies, including IOM's DTM; questionnaires; household and key informant interviews (including with local authorities and key community leaders); focus group discussions with women and youth; direct observation and review of secondary information. 

IOM has existing WASH programming in Tigray, Amhara, Afar, Oromia (East Hararghe and Borena), Somali (Dawa and Fafan zone), and SNNP regions (Konso zone) covering IDPs, returnees and host communities. Limited access to WASH NFIs, inadequate sources of safe water, inadequate sanitation facilities and prevalence of poor hygiene practices can render the populations living in collective centers/sites at risk of preventable diseases and overcrowded and congested IDP sites also pose a high level of risk to waterborne diseases, such as cholera. Assessments indicated that integrated WASH services are critical to ensure that facilities are maintained at a good standard and can be scaled up in case of population influxes, both in terms of the provision of safe water and increased hygiene promotion to prevent disease outbreaks.

In 2022, IOM appeals for USD 23,5 million to reach 1,6 million individuals through its WASH activities in IDP sites and host communities across Ethiopia. Interventions will comprise water trucking, construction and rehabilitation of water points, emergency latrines including distribution of hygiene kits, and handwashing stations, establishment of community-based water or sanitation management committees, and hygiene promotion activities through contextualized campaigns and mobilization of gender-balanced hygiene promoters. IOM will also support implementing partners, particularly national NGOs to provide access to safe water, WASH NFIs and hygiene promotion.

Protection Enhance protection environment through provision of specialized protection and gender-based violence (GBV) response services to internally displaced persons (IDPs) in Ethiopia  Ongoing armed conflict, intercommunal violence and climate change (drought and flood) continue to be the key driver of humanitarian needs in Ethiopia and increased displacements across the country. Specifically, humanitarian situation in Northern Ethiopia remains challenging due to the conflict in regions of Tigray, Amhara and Afar. In Tigray, 5.2 million people are reported to need urgent humanitarian assistance according to the OCHA Tigray region Humanitarian Update from early September 2021. IOM’s draft Site Assessment (SA) Round 28 identified a total of 4,509,081 internally displaced people (IDPs) displaced across different sites in the country. From this, 2,452,077 are found in Tigray, Amhara and Afar regions. 

Affected populations face longer term protection concerns arising from shocks such as conflict, climate change, and disasters. Systemic, long-standing protection concerns such as gender-based violence (GBV) – including harmful practices, lack of access to specialized services, as well as other basic needs are exacerbated due to conflict or climatic shocks. 

Often in emergencies, women and children with and without disabilities, constitute majority of affected population with heightened risk to different rights abuse including GBV. With limited access to services such as health and MHPSS, food, WASH, shelter, psychosocial support, education and livelihoods coupled with weak social support system, IDPs are living under undignified and distressed conditions. These factors entail increased vulnerability to engage in negative coping mechanisms such as forced marriages, child labour abuse and transactional sex.   Additionally, lack of awareness of the right to assistance and limited coverage of response services, complicated by deep-rooted social norms related to gender make accessing services ever more challenging.
Despite the high number of IDPs, there has been inconsistent humanitarian assistance to the affected population due to limited resource and ongoing security concerns in the regions. Poorly coordinated relocations and returns which fall short of meeting standards also negatively affected the service delivery rendering affected population to secondary displacement and ending up living in collective centres or within host community. 
With the goal of contributing to enhancing protection environment of affected populations through prevention, risk mitigation and response efforts.  Following the Protection Cluster priorities, IOM will target primarily IDPs and returnees affected by conflict and drought through general protection and GBV prevention and response integrating Mental Health and Psychosocial support (MHPSS) interventions in Amhara, Tigray, Somali, SNNP, Diredawa, Afar and Oromia regions. 
The response and activities will be in line with the three overarching protection objectives in the HRP. 

1.	Mitigate and respond to violence, abuse or neglect and restore capacities: through protection monitoring, individual protection assistance (IPA), including multi-purpose cash assistance (MPCA) and/or in-kind assistance and community based Mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS). 
2.	GBV response and prevention services: including case management, Psychosocial assistance, set-up of women and girls friendly spaces (WGFS) providing safe entry points for women and girls to access GBV services, and skill-building and awareness and knowledge on GBV and Protection issues. 
3.	Strengthening capacities of government counterparts, partners, and IOM staff on Protection and GBV service provision

address the critical needs for strengthened child protection (CP) and sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV) prevention and response services in Saida, South Governorate and Wadi Khaled, Akkar Governorate. Protection Response for Vulnerable Lebanese and Other Resident Populations According to the LCRP (2017-2020), child mothers, early married girls, unaccompanied and separated boys and girls, women and girls with disabilities, older women, and female heads of households continue to be the most at risk. The most commonly reported type of GBV as reported in the GBVIMS and IMC data from its work across Lebanon involves physical violence, mainly linked to violence within the family, sexual violence (rape and sexual assault), as well as forced and early marriage. Protection risks for all targeted populations remains high, with women and girls facing significant risks of multiple forms of GBV. The economic insecurity combined with different levels of crisis affecting the country as well as risks related to legal status, add to these vulnerabilities.

GBV is a pervasive public health and human rights issue, affecting the physical and psychological health of survivors, as well as the health and well-being of families and communities. Throughout the health and economic crisis that Lebanon is going through, the frequency, severity and risk of GBV, especially affecting young women and girls is increasing. Preventing, mitigating, and responding to GBV in emergencies is a lifesaving priority and an essential component of humanitarian action, especially in a country with extreme structural gender inequalities. Lebanon ranks 145 out of 153 countries in the World Economic Forum Global Gender Gap Report.

The below proposed activities focus on survivor-centered care with case management teams working with local actors in order to meet the immediate, lifesaving needs of women and girls while laying the groundwork for survivors of GBV, their families and their communities to recover. Under Indicator 1.1, the project will be providing non-focused PSS for 375 participants, dignity kits to 3000 beneficiaries and awareness sessions to 1725 non-unique beneficiaries. There will be an overlap of beneficiaries for this activity where beneficiaries that attend non-focused PSS activities will also be attending awareness sessions (this also applies for the recipients of the dignity kits).  Under Indicator 4.1, IMC will be providing case management and focused PSS for 260 beneficiaries. As part of GBV case management, emergency cash assistance will also be offered. IMC will provide the services in four safe spaces, 2 in Akkar, 1 in Beirut and 1 in the South. GBV department is well established in these areas with well-trained Case managers and Social workers.

Based on IMC’s safety audits previously conducted, focus group discussions implemented in the area and PDM reports, the objectives of the ERP directly address the needs of the communities especially vulnerable women and girls. IMC will organize empowerment activities for women and adolescent girls and will also reach men and boys in awareness raising activities. IMC will coordinate with local actors, authorities, and other sectors to strengthen GBV prevention and response and will continue working with communities to shift social norms that contribute to GBV and threaten the protection and wellbeing of women, girls and individuals at risk.

Ethiopia/CE: Health, Agriculture and Food Security, Water, Sanitation and Hygiene, Nutrition		(USAID/BHA) Livelihoods based emergency response for conflict and drought affected households in Tigray Amhara, Afar, Oromia and Somali regional States of Ethiopia The prolonged drought in southeastern and southern Ethiopia is the result of three consecutive failed rainy seasons since late 2020. The impact of the drought is deepening and according to April 2022, UNOCHA update at least 81 million people in Oromia, Somali, SNNP and Southwest regions are affected.  Livestock are suffering from lack of pasture and water. Estimates from regional Governments indicated more than 1.46 million livestock deaths (67 % in Somali, 31 % in Oromia, and 7 % in Southwest and SNNP regions). Surviving animals have a significantly deteriorated body condition which has decreased their market value which has led to decrease of the purchasing power of households. According to the most recent seasonal forecast by ICPAC, a below average belg season is expected. The situation seems not expected to improve rapidly.Thus, the affected pastoral communities require continuous support. According to the humanitarian response plan, Humanitarian partners are targeting 12.8 million people for food assistance (out of which 8.0 million people also receive other types of assistance). To response to the situation CARE proposed three major intervention that include Livestock feed provisions, Animal health provision and restocking with shoat to Liben of Somali region and Borena of Oromia region.
East Hararge DRM office Early warning department report showed the rain delayed by 48days this show in FY22 no longer expect of belg crop (short season) planting and delays may happen on Meher crop planting.  Zonal Agriculture office noted to partners the need to support the farmers on provision of short season maturing seed. Similarly, the shortage of seeds noted in West Hararge Zone.  In response to this CARE proposed the provision of agriculture inputs such as improved seeds and /or vegetables to both Eastern and Western Hararge zones.
The political dynamics have changed dramatically in Ethiopia's Tigray Region following the unilateral ceasefire declaration by the Ethiopian Government on 28 June 2021.  However, the breakdown of essential services such as the blackout of electricity, telecommunications, and internet throughout Tigray region will only exacerbate the already dire humanitarian situation.  According to the UNOCHA the shortages of cash and fuel in the region can compromise the duty of care of aid workers on the ground. Despite the dynamic and uncertain situation, it has been reported the security situation in Tigray has been generally calm over the past few days, with limited humanitarian activities being implemented around Mekelle and Shire.  If the situation improves there will be a possibility of accessing the affected woreda.  
According to UNOCHA recent updates, in Amhara region areas bordering Tigray, namely in Wag Hamra, North Wollo and North Gondar zones, situations remained unpredictable but relatively calm during the reporting period. Several locations remained hard to reach for partners’ humanitarian operations due to security concerns, including Abergele and Tsagibji kebeles, parts of Zequala kebeles in Wag Hamra Zone, large sections of Kobo in North Wello Zone, and in Addi Arekay in the North Gondar Zone. However, the livelihoods of the people in the above zones are highly affected by the conflict that leaves many affected people for need of agriculture input support. CARE proposes the agriculture input provisions which includes improved seeds and /or vegetables, provision of hand tools, and the provision of Draught power for the Amhara and Tigray region affected woredas. The recent UNOCHA updates shows in Afar, the humanitarian situation continued to be dire with a high number of IDPs in need of support while the response is still insufficient to compare with needs in the region. Because of the conflict the main livelihood and income source from livestock highly affected. To respond the situation CARE proposed Animal feed provision, animal health and restocking interventions

Water, Sanitation and Hygiene Emergency WASH and ERD assistance for host and IDP. East Bale is one of the Zones found in Oromia Region that newly established a year ago.  Out of seven Rural woredas five woredas   are in lowland, desert, semi-desert weather conditions. In these woredas More than 80% of population are pastoralist that depends on livestock as main economic source and livelihoods. East Bale Zone experiences two rainy seasons, Gena   and Arfasa. Gena lasts from fourth week of August to November while the Arfasa season extends from March to May. Dawe Sarar and Lagahidha are some of the lowland Woredas extremely hard hit by the drought. Following the extreme drought in the Zone, IRC has approached a donor and secured fund from Ireland Government to intervene this drought through deploying relevant and experienced staff. The expected output of this project is Reduced mortality and morbidity and increased recovery and resilience of drought affected people in Dawe Serer and Lagahidha Woreda of East Bale Zone, This will be achieved through provision of multi-sectoral humanitarian response, such as disbursement of unconditional and unrestricted cash transfer which enables the community to purchase basic need as per their choose and provision of safe water supply to targeted drought affected community in order that reduce school dropout rate cased due to drought. The IRC will implement the proposed intervention through close coordination with government and non-government partners in the region to effectively implement the lifesaving interventions across the Two targeted woredas where drought highly affect the community.
The duration of the project is for six months (March 01, 2022, to Aug 31, 2022) and 28140 (Male 13849& Female 14291) individuals will be benefited.

Post Distribution Monitoring"""" Emergency WASH and ESNFI Response to Conflict Affected People in Tigray Region As of February 2022, a total of 4.51 million IDPs have been identified thus far across the country. Of the total displaced population, the main causes of displacement were conflict which displaced 3.63 million IDPs (81%). Tigray has remained to be the priority region and continues to have significant IDPs and affected host population that remains vulnerable under the current circumstances- conflict. According to the Emergency Site Assessment (ESA) round 8, 386,741 households comprising 1,814,284 IDPs were identified in 581 accessible sites in Tigray region due to the Northern Ethiopia Crisis. 
Humanitarian needs remain significantly high as the current response is not meeting the increasing needs of those in need as the resources available are not matching the requirements to ensure that minimum lifesaving humanitarian standards are maintained for the targeted population. According to the northern Ethiopia humanitarian update shared (OCHA, 14 April 2022), between 1 January and 4 April 2022, only 42.11% of the targeted people were reached with ESNFI response in Tigray region. Critical needs prioritized include, provision of adequate shelters and NFIs for IDPs living in highly congested and substandard living conditions, provision of shelter and NFI assistance to IDPs willing to return to their areas of origin, and to IDPs currently living within host communities, and rental assistance schemes or other arrangements for IDPs living in host communities. 
Inadequate provision of WASH services poses a risk of disease outbreaks at IDP sites. About 9,300 water points or more than 54 per cent of the 17,080 water points in Tigray are not functional affecting the access of more than 3.5 million people to safe drinking water. About 418,000 IDPs in 131 sites require 295 trips of water trucking every day which requires 1,990 liters of fuel daily. Construction of more than 17,000 latrines at IDP sites are required to mitigate the risks of disease transmission. Low stock of key WASH NFIs, including water treatment chemical, water containers and hygiene supplies have also been reported in Tigray. Priority WASH needs include, emergency water trucking, rehabilitation of  water schemes, rehabilitation of sanitation facilities, distribution of WASH NFIs, and hygiene promotion activities.
The locations and activities considered for the WASH and ES/NFI interventions under this project plan are identified in the HRP 2022 prioritization list to address the immediate and life-saving needs of crisis-affected communities in line with the respective clusters' priority activities. The actions will be WASH and ESNFI services and carried out in line with cluster objectives CLWSH/CO1 (Deliver conflict-sensitive essential life-saving WASH services to affected people), CLWSH/CO3 (To enhance vulnerable households’ ability to withstand recurrent and future shocks in Ethiopia through early recovery and resilience interventions), and CLSHL/CO1, (Ensure contextualized access to lifesaving shelter and NFIs for displacement affected population with a focus on the most vulnerable and at-risk population group to safeguard their health security, privacy, and dignity  )and CLSHL/CO2 (Contribute to improving protection outcomes by ensuring the conflict/displacement affected people have adequate safety, dignity, well-being, and equitable access to shelter solutions).
The projects aim to enhance the protection, health, and well-being of the conflict affected IDPs and host communities, and will directly reach 43,765 people through WASH and 40,055 people through ES/NFI prioritizing the most vulnerable, including women, girls, children, elderly, and people with disabilities in particular.
The project will ensure the active participation of the targeted beneficiaries and stakeholders throughout the project cycle. Protection and safety concerns will be given priority and DRC will ensure providing safe, easy, and dignified access to the facilities by the most vulnerable.

Agriculture and Food Security Drought Response in Borana Zone (Oromia Region), Dawa and Liben Zones (Somali Region) and South Omo Zone (SNNPR) Communities in Southern Ethiopia are facing the worst drought in decades. The failure of two consecutive rainy seasons has pushed pastoralist and agro-pastoralist communities towards severe food and livelihood insecurity. Loss of crops and livestock means that an estimated 1.8 million people are in urgent need of humanitarian support.
The drought has adversely affected livestock production and productivity resulting in occurrence of livestock diseases, poor livestock body condition and death of animals. Viable pastures within local rangelands are highly depleted, leading to a sharp decline in animal productivity. Cattle with poor body condition cannot be sold in the local markets, severely affecting income opportunities and purchasing power of local communities. Household cash availability levels have been negatively affected by declining livestock prices and extremely low agricultural production.
18,000 households (117,000 individuals) will directly benefit from the drought response project. The response aims to enhance the resilience-building capacity and support the livelihood restoration efforts of drought-affected pastoral communities. The project will last for six months and will benefit 3,000 drought affected Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) households and 15,000 host community households. The beneficiary breakdown is as follows: 750 IDP households and 5,250 host community households in Dawa, 750 IDP households and 5,250 host community households in Liben, 750 IDP households and 2,250 host community households in Borana and 750 IDP households and 2,250 host community households in South Omo.
The project will focus on access to supplementary animal feed and cash transfer assistance. The activities are informed and aligned with the Agriculture Cluster objectives and framework priorities, including protection of core productive assets and access to livelihoods of crises affected households, and the Ethiopian Cash Working Group (ECWG) guide on cash transfer programming.
The project is planned to be implemented in four zones of three Regions in Southern Ethiopia. The reasons for the geographic focus are: 1) severity of the drought and needs of the target population; 2) HEKS’s presence on the ground – where the organization has logistics set-up, staff that know the context and culture, institutional relationships – and capacity to respond to the drought; 3) regular engagement of HEKS in local coordination platforms; and 4) sound relationship with the local government. The project will promote localization by working together with local partner Agri-Service Ethiopia building on previous joint interventions and thus developing the capacity of the local partner to deliver emergency responses. The project will also work with Dorcas building on existing partnerships and expertise.
The project will be implemented in locations that do not increase vulnerabilities, do not facilitate forced return, and will be implemented with careful planning to ensure that all targeted groups are consulted, engaged and involved for assistance. The project will ensure the engagement of women, people with disabilities, elderly people and other vulnerable groups in the planning, implementation and monitoring of the projects inputs, outputs and results.

Water, Sanitation and Hygiene Emergency WASH response Borana and Guji Zone, Oromiya Region The project will be implemented in Dilo, Miyo and Moyale woreda, Borana Zone and Liben Woreda Guji Zone, Oromiya Region, where due to conflict 35,311 persons are displaced and in urgent need of humanitarian assistance, especially in the area of access to water, sanitation and hygiene services. The project will last for six months and will benefit all the 29,228 internally displaced persons (IDPs) in the target area and 18,033 host community members. The project activities will focus, construction of 10 semi-permanent latrines benefitting 2,000 IDPs, hygiene promotion and delivery of 500 essential WASH Non-Food Item (NFI) packages, including provision of 1,000 Menstrual Hygiene Management (MHM) kits for adolescent girls, benefitting 3,250 people, rehabilitation and maintenance of 4 water schemes (motorized scheme) and training of WASHCOs, providing access to safe water to 23,000 people. The proposed project will also promote the practice of adequate hand washing and environmental sanitation to mitigate potential outbreaks of water-borne diseases, including cholera, and curb the spread of the COVID-19 pandemic.
To further promote equity, the project will ensure regular consultation of women, PWD (17.6% of the total beneficiaries), elderly people and other vulnerable groups. Staff will follow the Core Commitments for Children in Humanitarian Action framework to uphold the rights of children. Project events on WASH will include sessions on gender, children rights, and equity to create long-lasting awareness. The project will promote equitable access to humanitarian assistance regardless of beneficiaries’ sex for example through accessibility of project sites to pregnant women, elders and people with disabilities. The project will also identify potential negative effect on different gender and age groups and put preventive measures in place. As a standard, HEKS follows strict Protection from Sexual Exploitation, Abuse and Harassment (PSEAH) rules when interacting with beneficiaries. Participation of women was key during pre-project consultations and project design and will continue playing a central role during implementation and evaluation. HEKS has been implementing in the target areas for several years in different thematic areas like WASH, Cash transfer, Market system Development, Agriculture and climate and environmental projects both emergency and development programs which have an office in Yabelo. Mixed humanitarian teams including male and female members will carry out activities following a gender-sensitive approach.
The project will be implemented from the HEKS Office in Yabelo town in Borena Zone of Oromiya region. HEKS has qualified staff at field level and equipped facilities to carry out the intervention. HEKS is participating in the local Government-NGO Forum and has been very active in other forums and platforms, including the humanitarian coordination platform since late 2019, and the WASH Cluster SAG. The organization is closely engaged with other key humanitarian actors in the zone including implementing partners GPDI. The zonal and woreda offices, the DRR office and WASH Cluster have been providing information, data and advice in the process of developing this project for coordinated efforts. HEKS will further engage with locally active stakeholders to avoid duplication of effort and maximize efficiency. HEKS will work with relevant government offices/agencies and community leaders that have roles and responsibilities in humanitarian crisis preparedness and response. Coordination will occur through regular information sharing at both local (woreda, zonal and regional) level and at national level for example through 5W reports to different clusters as well as through participation in inter-agency reviews of needs and priorities.

Building a Pathway Out of Poverty for Ultra-poor IDP’s and Vulnerable Host Communities in Baidoa Improving food availability and supporting resilience for Somali households affected by crisis ACTED is acutely aware of the ongoing food insecurity situation facing households in many parts of Somalia. In late 2021, this serious situation has been exacerbated by conflict, forced evictions of IDPs, and ongoing drought. ACTED will save lives and improve the ability of Somali households to meet their basic needs through conditional and unconditional cash transfers to affected households. Through this project, ACTED will address food insecurity through providing unconditional cash transfers based on values from the Somalia Cash Working Group and through providing temporary employment opportunities (cash-for-work) for residents of IDP settlements. Cash-for-work provides an excellent opportunity for efficiently using funds, as funds will provide cash support to families suffering food insecurity while also funding basic improvements to local infrastructure (feeder roads, paths, local market infrastructure, fencing of water points). ACTED’s involvement in this project aims at supporting vulnerable households in Baidoa IDP sites of Bay region, El-Afweyn and Erigavo districts of Sanaag region, through unconditional cash transfers through six months of mobile money transfers. The Consortium will target the most vulnerable households with life-saving multi-purpose unconditional cash transfers. The project will specifically target populations in IPC 3, 4 and 5, especially newly displaced and worst-affected pastoralist and agro-pastoralist communities. In addition, this Action seeks to provide life-saving assistance to food insecure communities in the target locations while implementing recovery and resilience activities to restore livelihoods and respond to the needs of IDPs and rural communities in Baidoa, El-Afwayne, Badhan, Diinsoor and Buurhakaba districts. 

Gender and intersecting issues (e.g, disability, pregnancy, age) are key determining factors in how displacement in Somalia is impacting populations across multiple domains. Gender norms relating to men’s and women’s societal roles and responsibilities have resulted in women and girls being disproportionately affected by displacement – and in men representing the majority of victims of intercommunal violence.  Gender is also a key factor in determining IDP’s needs and priorities, and this is particularly notable with regard to SGBV concerns highlighted earlier in this concept note and SHRH and menstrual hygiene concerns. A common challenge that IDP girls and women face is managing menstruation safely and with dignity, and a present lack of access to basic materials such as sanitary pads and underwear can lead to stigmatization (stemming from societal beliefs regarding menstruation) and further associated challenges. Insufficient resources for management of menstrual hygiene can also entail more frequent visits to public sanitation/WASH facilities, increasing risk of SGBV and disease. With regard to institutions and governance, informal governance in Somali IDP sites tends to be male-dominated unless CCCM initiatives have explicitly undertaken gender-mainstreaming interventions to improve community-led site management. In a context such as Somali IDP sites, where gender-based threats and challenges are ever-present, humanitarian programming needs to be gender-responsive – not only through targeting gender-based needs, but by ensuring that programming is thoughtfully and consultatively designed to be maximally accessible to all genders and persons.

FOOD ASSISTANCE Emergency Lifesaving Cash and Livelihood Support to IDP and Non- IDP Communities in Somalia Somalia is facing a severe and deteriorating humanitarian crisis as we enter 2022 as a result of the compounding effects of conflict, recurrent climate shocks, diseases and pests outbreaks with increased levels of vulnerability and substantial increase in the humanitarian caseload (Somalia HNO, 2022). There is a serious risk that the impact of consecutive below average to poor rainfall in most parts of the country will develop into a severe drought by early to mid- 2022 with the number of people facing acute food insecurity on the rise. It is likely that minority groups, women, children, people with disabilities, will experience heightened protection risks as a result, unless they are intentionally targeted to receive tailored assistance.

With approximately 3.5 million individuals in IPC 3 and 4 through at least December 2021, FAO proposes to target 160,300 households (961,800 individuals- 91,500 IDPs and 870,300 non- IDPs) in IPC 3 and IPC 4 caseloads respectively. This will include 216,790 women, 254,492 girls, 264,880 boys and 225,638 men and 144,270 people living with disabilities (PWD) across 59 districts in Somalia through its flagship Cash+ approach combining short-term cash transfers with tailored livelihood support in accordance with technical and humanitarian standards. Vulnerable households will identified from at-risk pastoral, agro-pastoral, fishing, riverine farmers, IDPs and Non- IDP communities in IPC 3 and 4 areas. This intervention will integrate short-term cash transfers aimed at enabling the most vulnerable households to meet their immediate needs, with livelihood support to allow crisis-affected households to get back into production. FAO will employ community- led beneficiary selection processes and ensure adequate targeting and representation of extremely vulnerable and minority groups in community committees. Interventions proposed will employ a Do No Harm approach with a gender lens that ensures conflict- sensitivity to reduce protection risks for all individuals, and to mitigate the risk of conflict or community tensions. 

Under Food Security Cluster (FSC) Objective 1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 160,300 households through a blend of conditional (Cash-for-Work) and unconditional (UCT) transfers. Under UCT, FAO will prioritize Cash+ interventions including Cash+ Agriculture, Cash+ livestock and Cash+ fisheries. These modalities will increase households’ immediate access to food by providing sufficient cash to access the minimum expenditure basket (MEB), while supporting the rehabilitation of critical productive and community infrastructure. It will also boost household food production, increase household incomes and create employment opportunities. Cash transfer values will be informed by the Cash Working Group and are expected to differ per district/ region of intervention. They, however, will be valued at 80 percent of the food MEB, which can range from USD 50- 100 per month. All cash-based programmes will include training on good nutrition practices. 

Under FSC Objective 2, to protect livelihoods and related food sources, FAO will provide in-kind, technical support and tailored trainings to 112,500 HHs to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security and nutrition threats, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to targeted HHs. In addition, FAO shall provide transitional cash support to 13,100 HHs across agro pastoral, pastoral and fishing livelihood zones to augment the adaptive capacity of HHs, strengthen and foster resilience to future shocks, cushioning them from food insecurity and malnutrition. Trainings shall be delivered alongside input provision to build skills in sustainable use of resources provided, build skills in livelihoods management including harvest, post- harvest management, linking beneficiaries to long- term interventions that provide them opportunities to enhance their livelihoods and skills.
