According to the school damage assessment reports, many schools at southern east Tigray have the following problems. The majority of the schools has lost their facilities/ supplies like; black board, Desks, Books, Chalk, Science kits, teaching aids, etc. They also run out of WASH facilities and they have poor access to clean water and even some of them have lost their classrooms either fully or partially which needs renovation. In addition to this, the teachers and the students are highly traumatized where they are in a high need of PSS and SEL trainings. As the teachers were away from reading, they need to be capacitated with different trainings like; pedagogical trainings, Conflict sensitive education, teaching methodologies, and so on. In this regard, the unreleased school damage assessment report also shows that 83% of schools are either damaged or looted (Education Bureau, 2022). Besides, more than 1,000 schools were damaged or looted in Tigray affecting an estimated 160,000 students. 79 Schools in Tigray, are still occupied by IDPs limiting access to education for 40,518 children, including 20,120 girls. (OCHA 2022). According to the Southeast Zone, 96,687 children (48,134 girls) were planned to attend at the six Woredas that WV has intervening on grades 0-6. Whereas the number of children who are now attending in school are 17,013 (8,662 girls) which is only 17.6%. This shows that, 79,674 (39,472), i.e. 82.4% of the children are still left out of school. The reason behand the children’s low attendances is lack of scholastic materials and lack of food which can be mitigated by scholastic material support and cash injection as motivation for attendance of school feeding if possible. In this regard, WV has best experience to accomplish this for the reason that, World Vision aspires “educated for life” for all girls and boys with strategies; Enhanced Early Readiness of Children, Enhanced Literacy Environment and Conducive School Atmosphere. To realize those expected results, WVE has been employed various appropriate working models to each result. The models include Learning Root (LR), which goes with Early Childhood Development (ECD); Unlock Literacy (UL) it goes with reading, & Basic Education Programme - Safe school and Life skills (BEP) which is for conducive schools. Those models are selected, for each model is directly associated to each immediate outcomes of the Technical Program. In turn, each model has its own well-structured pillars, which indicate how to reach to their results in a synergic manner. P
Protection interventions are also highly needed in Tigray Amhara and Afar. Across the three regions, the top three reported risks affecting boys and girls were, in order, being killed or maimed, mental health/psychosocial problems, and sexual violence. Nearly 95% of respondents in all three regions stated that there is either partial or no access to the following services: safe spaces (56%), case management (47%), and medical care for SGBV survivors (43%), and MPHSS (54%). When asked why, nearly all HHs responded that they have either no awareness/knowledge about the service or that current service providers do not prioritize these services because they are providing for more immediate needs. These facts and field realities require a critical need for protection, SGBV services, mental and psycho-social support for the affected people in general and for children and women who suffered traumatic experiences in particular. In addition, there is critical need to other basic humanitarian assistance.

Shelter and Settlements Afar, Amhara, Tigray (USAID/BHA) Emergency Shelter& NFI response for IDPs and host communities living in Kiremu Woreda, East Wolega zone, Oromia Region. (Funded by UNOCHA/WVE) The existing humanitarian crises related to the persistent displacement of people in to West and East Wellega Zone of Oromia region has resulted recurrent displacements, which leads to insecurity, access constraints, and socio-economic downturns in West and East Wellega Zone. Currently, 20,809 HH or 127,787 individuals in both East and West Wellega remain displaced in different Woredas, towns and kebeles dispersed in the host community hosting with the relatives, renting houses or living in temporary substandard local material built shelters with the support of the host community. According to Inter agency multi sectoral assessment conducted in West and East Wollega as well as Kamashi zone in August 2021, Shelter and NFI was one of the priorities reported among both the secondary and the new crisis-driven displaced persons, IDPs are living in a congested situation with 4 to 6 HH in one shelter. Rental houses are not affordable for many of them since they do not have means of income. Moreover, the impact of COVID-19 has become an additional burden for families in their struggle for survival.

This project proposal is developed with an objective of providing life-saving emergency shelter services to the conflict affected peoples in Kiremu Woreda of East wollega zone through provision of timely and appropriate cash for rent assistance and ensure that conflict affected peoples have adequate protection, safety, dignity, well-being and equitable access to the shelter solution. Hence, World Vision Ethiopia (WVE) in partnership with Action for the Needy in Ethiopia (ANE) will respond to the emergency shelter and NFI need of the IDP in Kiremu Woreda of East wollega Zone.

Accordingly, the proposed emergency shelter and NFI intervention is aimed at addressing conflict-induced displaced community in Kiremu Woreda of East wollega Zone. The project will be implemented for 6 month with a total budget of $ 280,000.

Water, Sanitation and Hygiene,Shelter and Settlements,Agriculture Integrated Emergency Shelter and NFI, WASH and Agriculture Support for conflict-affected populations in Eastern Zone of Tigray Regions In 2021, conflict was the primary cause of displacement in the country. Particularly, the conflict that started in December 2020 in Tigray region with a spillover effect in the neighboring regions of Afar and Amhara in mid-2021 caused strife, limited access to basic services and displacement of a total of 2.11 million IDPs with 1.8 million in Tigray according to DTM Overview 2021. Following the conflict, despite the tremendous efforts by humanitarian partners to assist the most affected population limited humanitarian access, cash deficient, lack of electricity and telecommunications, inflation, hike of price of basic goods and services, inadequate fuel access, and movement and entry restriction to Tigray exacerbated the crisis. 
At the moment, there are 259,000 displacement affected populations in Tigray regions Eastern Zone. To fill the gaps identified in Eastern Zone, through this intervention, ZOA will address the immediate shelter and NFI needs of 8,721 IDP and Returnee households or 47,963 individuals (with the assumption of 5.5 household size) throughout the intervention Woredas selected in the Zone. Overall, a total of 2,616 (14,389) men, 3488 (19,185) women, 1221 (6,715) boys and 1,395 (7,674) girls will be reached. In Freweyni town 1,309 households (HHs) beneficiaries will receive NFI V1 kits and 145 households will receive NFI V1 disable kits for highland. In Gulo Mekeda, 3,223 HHs beneficiaries will receive NFI V1 kits, 50 households will receive Repair Kit for Returnees and 364 households will receive NFI V1 disable kits for highland.  In Saesie, 1,145 households will receive NFI V1 kits and 127 will receive NFI V1 disable kits for highland. In Erob, 2,071 HHs will receive NFI V1 kits, 50 HHs will benefit from Repair kits for Returnees and 236 HHs will receive NFI V1 disable kits for highland. 

This intervention is in line with the shelter cluster’s strategic objective of provision of safe, appropriate, and critical lifesaving Emergency Shelter and non-food items to displacement affected; improving the living conditions, physical protection, and safety of the displaced population and provision of safe, appropriate lifesaving Emergency Shelter Repair Kits to returnees. The proposed intervention will address cross-cutting themes through activities such as awareness raising on protection and gender mainstreaming and the Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) in collaboration with organizations to reinforce referral systems in the project sites. Moreover, through the establishment of strong Complaint and feedback mechanisms beneficiaries will concerns and issues will be addressed in time and in a safe manner. Our beneficiary targeting approach will encourage the active participation of women, girls and other marginalized groups. 

Furthermore, this intervention will be complemented with WASH and Food security and livelihoods activities to address the most urgent needs of the conflict-affected returnee and IDP communities in Tigray region. The intervention also includes a capacity strengthening element in both the WASH and Food Security and Livelihoods sectors. ZOA will provide some resources, as well as training to relevant government stakeholders, to capacitate them to fulfill their roles as duty bearers and service providers towards their constituencies.

Shelter and Settlements Emergency Shelter and Nonfood Items responses to conflict affected households in Tigray Region Recent armed conflict in the Tigray region of Ethiopia between federal forces and regional security forces has led to extreme humanitarian need, with refugees fleeing to Sudan and widespread displacement throughout northern Ethiopia. In the first quarter of 2022, new displacements continue to take place from multiple corners of Tigray region and bordering woredas due to conflict, as well as from bordering Regions. IDPs from Western Zone, Amhara and Afar are currently living across all accessible zones in Tigray. Congestion is still an issue in the IDP collective sites, resulting in increasing cases of scabies with over 8,000 cases reported in Northwestern Zone sites only since the beginning of the year, that calls for NFI distribution and replenishment. Relocation sites are being prepared in Shire and Sheraro for IDPs from Western Zone, but progress has been slow due to material and cash scarcity. Efforts are ongoing from Cluster partners to airlift ES/NFI stock from Addis Ababa to Mekelle as well as use road transportation.
According to April report of ES/NFI Cluster, partners continued providing life-saving emergency shelter and NFI assistance to IDPs, returnees, and affected non-displaced population with 47K beneficiaries receiving NFI kits, 0.5K ES/NFI kits, 34K ES kits, 4K constructed emergency shelters, 7K shelter repair kits, to the displacement affected people in Tigray. Overall, the Cluster has been able to reach 79K individuals with completed activities which amounts to 9% of the targeted 1.3M people targeted. According to recent assessments from partners in the region, Shelter and NFI is a critical need next to food and health in the IDPs. 
UNOCHA’s displacement scenario stated that there will be as many as 1.8 million IDPs because of ongoing conflict. IDPs are currently sheltering in collective centers, open areas, damaged shelters & with host communities and most of the displaced population are women, girls, and youth. Many IDPs are living in overcrowded settlement sites and collective centers, there are protection concerns for the most vulnerable, including for women and girls at risk of gender-based violence (GBV). According to the ESNFI cluster, peoples in need in the proposed locations such as Adet woreda (1,665 HH), Enticho town (3,290 HH) and Mekelle (7,735 HH) are residing in extremely poor conditions who need urgent emergency shelter and NFI assistance. All the three woredas have IDPs whereas Mekele includes returnees.
GE assumes the project activities addresses the strategic objectives with significant positive impact on the identified needs of the respective clusters. The project activities are all a priority to the respective sectors. GE aims an in-kind or cash for non-food items assistance for IDPs and shelter repair kit assistance for returnees. To maximize the impact on the intervention, GOAL proposed this ESNFI standalone applications whereby the other GOAL Ethiopia projects are implemented with the same sectors with BHA, ECHO, UNICEF, and IA funding sources and/or proposed for standalone allocation with other sector applications in this EHF/HPC. 
The ESNFI proposed interventions for this HPC will be:
- Emergency shelter repair kits distribution for 90 HHs returnees in Mekele town.
- Emergency Non-Food Items Kits (NFI V1 highland) distribution for 8,125 HHs (1,415 in Adet, 2,650 in Enticho town and 4,060 in Mekele) IDPs.
- Emergency Non-Food Items Kits (NFI V1 disable highland) distribution for 1,259 HHs (250 in Adet, 400 in Enticho town and 609 in Mekele) IDPs.
- Conduct independent beneficiary identification and verification process based on revised SOPs considering national/regional cluster standards.
- Information sessions, establishment and roll-out of community response & feedback mechanisms.
- Conduct HLP assessment.
- Conduct regular joint and independent monitoring. 
- Conduct post distribution monitoring

Ethiopia/CE: Water, Sanitation and Hygiene	(USAID/BHA) Emergency shelter and NFI support for conflict affected IDPs in Amahar and Afar Region  The northern conflict started in November 2020, and the tension spilled over to Amhara and Afar regions. As a result, hundreds of thousands of people are displaced and lose their assets. The situation in these regions remains volatile and unpredictable despite reported limited improvements in the security situation in some areas where fighting has recently erupted in the border areas between Afar and Amhara regions. According to the UNOCHA report, on March 31, 2022, in Amhara, the situation along areas bordering Tigray, namely in Wag Hamra, North Wollo, and North Gondar zones, remains volatile. Several locations remain hard to reach for humanitarian operations including Abergele, Tsagibji kebeles as well as some parts of Zequala kebeles in Wag Hamra Zone, large parts of Kobo in North Wollo Zone, and Addi Arkay in North Gondar. In Amhara, the regional Government authorities continued with the relocation of IDPs.Since the 14th of March 2022, it has relocated at least 12,000 people out of an estimated 58,000 registered IDPs planned for relocation from Kobo in North Wollo Zone to Jara, near Woldiya, the zonal capital. Hence, CARE proposed an emergency in-kind or cash for shelter and NFI and shelter repairing response for the conflict-affected peoples in Amhara and Afar regions. The objectives of the project are to improve the protection risks by ensuring the conflict-affected people have adequate safety, dignity, well-being, and equitable access to shelter solutions; and to strengthen access to appropriate live-saving Emergency Shelter and Non-food Items (NFI) to safeguard the health and protection of the displacement affected population. Through this project, 49,471 people will be targeted in Afar, and Amhara, and assisted with Emergency shelter, ESNFI and NFI and Shelter repairing kits.

Food Security and Protection Improved food security and livelihoods of IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host communities in South Sudan In line with the South Sudan 2022 Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) and the FSL Cluster priorities, NPA will support vulnerable and food-insecure Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs), returnees and vulnerable host communities in IPC 4 locations in Canal/Pigi, Fangak, Pochalla & Bor South Counties of Jonglei State, Rumbek East, Rumbek Center, Cueibet, Yirol East, Yirol West and Awerial Counties of Lakes State, Terekeka County of Central Equatoria State and Kapoeta North County of Eastern Equatoria State. The targeted communities in the identified counties will be supported to improve their food security and livelihoods through provision of timely and appropriate main season and dry season inputs/kits (Crop, vegetable and fishing), training in improved agronomic and fishing practices. In addition, NPA will support food-insecure with cash transfers in Rumbek East and Rumbek Center Counties in Lakes State with cash transfers to address their food needs. NPA’s emergency assistance and livelihoods support aims at saving lives and averting total collapse of livelihoods in the target Counties. The provision of agricultural and fishing inputs/kits, training in agricultural production and fishing is expected to improve the food production and in turn the food security of the target households (HHs) thus supporting them to recover from crisis and placing them on an accelerated path to early recovery and resilience to acute shocks. NPA’s response will address the food security and livelihoods needs and priorities identified in the South Sudan 2022 Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO).

NPA seeks to support 105,056 HHs (630,338 individuals) in the targeted Counties with livelihood kits and cash transfers to address food insecurity. Some of the kits will be provided by FAO and some procured by NPA. Training on improved agronomic and fishing practices, marketing and group dynamics will be done through model farmers and fisher folk who will undergo a Training of Trainers (ToT) and subsequently cascade the knowledge and skills to the farmers and fisher folk in their communities. The knowledge gained from these trainings will improve the agricultural and fishing practices of the target HHs thus improving food production, addressing their immediate food security needs and building their resilience to future shocks. The provision of cash transfers and agricultural inputs and fishing kits and subsequent enhancement of food production and fishing is expected to contribute to improvement of the Household Diversity Score (HDDS) and Food Consumption Score (FCS) of the target HHs. COVID-19 preventive and mitigation measures will be mainstreamed throughout all activities to prevent spread and transmission of the virus. The proposed interventions are aligned to the FSL cluster objective 1: CO1: Provide food assistance to prevent famine and improve food consumption, dietary diversity and coping strategies for vulnerable populations (in IPC 5, 4 & some 3) in a way that prevents the spread & transmission of COVID 19 and Objective 2: Enhance and sustain emergency food production through complementary vegetable and crop livelihood inputs, fishing and livestock support in a way that prevents the spread & transmission of COVID 19.

NPA will employ a community-based beneficiary selection approach which will entail establishing Project Management Committees (PMC’s) to lead the selection of eligible beneficiaries based on the beneficiary selection criteria. Vulnerable HHs with severe food insecurity including female, child, disabled/chronically ill headed HHs; persons living with or at risk of HIV/AIDS and survivors of Gender-Based Violence (GBV) will be targeted in this project.

The target communities will be the prime movers of the implementation process through engagement in the project. Through various means, NPA will gather feedback from the target communities and stakeholders to improve project implementation.

affected by shocks in 2 priority locations in Unity state Provision of integrated, equitable, and timely WASH services to emergency affected populations in South Sudan Protracted crises in South Sudan, including climactic shocks and continued conflict, have resulted in 8.9 million people projected to be in need of humanitarian assistance in 2022. As a result of the shocks, such as flooding, inter-communal violence (ICV) and ongoing armed clashes, the majority of the population are facing increased food insecurity, lack of access to basic services, and protection risks. As per the Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) 2022, lack of or inadequate access to clean water and improved sanitation and hygiene practices in South Sudan will negatively impact an estimated 6.1 million people in 2022. 

Since 2006, Solidarites International has become a key WASH actor in South Sudan, implementing emergency lifesaving responses across the country and providing integrated WASH services to crisis-affected populations in areas of static presence in Upper Nile, Jonglei, and Western Bahr el Ghazal. Since 2012 SI has played a key role in the Emergency Preparedness and Response (EPR) strategy in South Sudan, implementing multi-sectoral assessments and delivering emergency responses to crisis-affected populations all over the country. 

In 2022, SI will continue to provide emergency live-saving  WASH responses across the South Sudan to restore basic access to safe water, hygiene, and sanitation while ensuring equitable access, safety, and accountability to supported populations. Through its roving Emergency Preparedness and Response (EPR) team, SI will deploy to emergency-affected locations to provide first phase and second phase responses including distribution of household water treatment items and soap, emergency provision of safe water, and rapid repair of emergency-affected infrastructure.

At the same time, SI will expand its static presence in Upper Nile and Jonglei to provide basic integrated WASH services that target the most vulnerable, including those suffering malnutrition, food insecurity and protection threats. Static programs will focus on providing community-based solutions for sustainable WASH services that ensure that improvements in access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene are durable and can be maintained independently by communities. Engagement and joint programming with Protection and Nutrition actors will ensure that WASH services can be accessed by the most vulnerable and will have a tangible impact on reducing overall priority humanitarian needs. The increased integration of protection, inclusion, and conflict sensitivity analysis in all programming will ensure that WASH services and resources can be safely accessed by all in the community. Greater engagement of communities and local markets will support the design of long term and flood resistant WASH infrastructure and supply chains to ensure that interventions produce durable results for communities.

Food Security WFP SOMALIA 2022 HRP - FSC Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas. As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation. The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

The project aims People affected by drought have increased access to safe drinking water and improved their awareness on sanitation and hygiene and have improved access to food and meet other basic needs and minimize negative coping strategies through provision of unconditional multipurpose cash response in Dawe Serer, Legehidha and Sewena woredas of East Bale Zone. the project will be implemented in the coming Six months and 20901 individuals will be benefited.

Multiple clusters/sectors	Protection Enhancement of protection of displaced persons, returnees and conflict affected host communities in Syria through integrated, community-based protection activities. The project aims to strengthen protection and resilience of Syrian IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host communities through advocacy, coordination, provision of community-based protection services and legal services UNHCR Syria will continue to lead the Protection Sector/Cluster to ensure coordinated protection interventions programming for safe refugees return. UNHCR’s protection interventions include legal counselling and assistance, protection monitoring, referrals and information sharing, social protection through livelihoods support to most vulnerable people, GBV prevention and response, child protection, psychosocial support and in-kind assistance for persons with specific needs including persons with disabilities, non-formal education, and awareness activities on various subjects targeting women, men, boys and girls. In addition to over 125 community centres providing integrated protection services, outreach to communities will be convened through over 2,800 outreach volunteers. Accountability to affected people will be realized through meaningful participation of communities based on age, gender and diversity approach, structured focus group discussions and enhancement of the community-based feedback and complaint mechanisms. UNHCR will continue its capacity building efforts to ensure services are delivered according to the standards and that accountability to affected population and do no harm principles are respected. UNHCR Syria will continue to lead Protection Sector in coordination of response plans of IDPs and affected people as well it will execute leadership roles in refugee return programmes in collaboration with the Government. Monitoring and evaluation of the planned interventions is based on the reports and observations by the partners and on regular direct observation and ongoing assessment by UNHCR and the comparison of achievements and related financial expenditures with objectives. Evaluation is conducted through different channels including the post distribution monitoring to determine the effectiveness of/measure the satisfaction of POCs with the service and the distribution process in addition to multiple satisfaction surveys and tracking tools related to different protection interventions. Monitoring and evaluation activities are carried out at various levels by partners and agencies implementing subprojects, UNHCR Branch Office, Sub Office and Field Offices. Situation reports are submitted by all UNHCR Field Offices to their respective Supervising Office and Branch Offices submit a corresponding report to Headquarters.

The project seeks to build resilience among the most vulnerable i.e. women, children, persons with disabilities and the elderly among others. South Sudan/CE:  Protection, Humanitarian Coordination and Info Management	 (USAID/BHA) Protection and Legal Assistance for Displacement affected populations in South Sudan The NRC seeks to improve the overall protective environment in South Sudan by not only responding to people's most immediate material needs during a crisis, but also by promoting their safety and dignity, as well as preventing, reducing, or mitigating the protection risks they face. It is also to address the root causes of displacement and to contribute to the creation of conditions conducive to long-term solutions for displaced people. To achieve the project objective, NRC will focus on three key components i.e. 1) General Protection; Housing, Land and Property; 3) Gender Based Violence. 

NRC proposes a community-based approach to displaced and conflict-affected populations protection, including static, mobile, and emergency responses.  Protection context assessments will be done in all locations, as well as, where possible, community-based protection monitoring, in which community focal points will be trained to report on protection needs and risks. Protection incidents will be documented and analyzed in order to better understand trends and evolution in the protection context, and the findings will be disseminated to communities and relevant stakeholders. 

NRC will provide at-risk populations with both awareness-raising sessions and individualized assistance in obtaining national identity documentation. Foster improved ability to exercise HLP rights for individuals and groups affected by displacement with priority given to the most vulnerable, including female and child headed households, the elderly, individuals with physical and mental disabilities, and those who are extremely poor. NRC will target conflict-affected areas and areas of potential return.

NRC will also carry out GBV prevention and risk mitigation activities in 6 counties located in hard to reach areas. Activities will include awareness raising, referrals to response services, cash assistance to GBV survivors, distribution of dignity kits and training on GBV basic concepts among others.

To achieve the main objective, the will focus on the below key activities
1) Carrying out of information and awareness raising activities; awareness will focus on GBV (GBV risks, available response services, GBV referral pathways, timely reporting), HLP (social cohesion and collaborative dispute resolution mechanisms, land rights issues) and general protection (protection risks, available services)
2) Provision of cash assistance (individual protection assistance) to persons at GBV survivors and other persons at heightened risks including referral of GBV survivors for response services
3) Training frontline workers and community focal points on basic GBV concepts, GBV guiding principles and responses services.
4) Training of state-level authorities, community leaders and representative on HLP, alternative dispute resolution
5) Facilitating peaceful coexistence and inclusive resolutions of local conflict through training and mentoring the local community in collaborative dispute resolution (CDR) mechanisms
6) Distribute dignity kits to women and adolescent girls.
7) Provision of legal aid and counselling

HRP FOOD SECURITY Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace.

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

Health,Agriculture and Food Security,Water, Sanitation and Hygiene,Protection,Nutrition,Humanitarian Coordination and Info Management (USAID/BHA) Food and livelihood assistance to the most vulnerable and crisis affected population in South Sudan  The proposed project aims to provide food assistance, livelihood and resilience support to 1,105,380 vulnerable populations in Upper Nile, Western Equatoria, Central Equatoria and Greater Bahr el Ghazal. The project will implement activities that will prevent famine and improve food consumption, dietary diversity and coping strategies of target beneficiaries in IPC 5, 4 and 3. The project will also seek to enhance emergency food production and contribute to the reduction of dependency to food and agricultural inputs. World Vision will adopt a mix of intervention approaches including but not limited to unconditional and General Food Distribution, cash transfers, complementary livelihood support, capacity building (e.g., modern agronomic practices, Integrated Pest Management, Natural Resource Management, etc.), and resilience building at the household level. The proposed project will also be implemented in synergy with other sectors implemented by World Vision in the targeted locations such as health, nutrition, WASH, gender and protection related programming while maintaining coordinating and complementarity with the efforts of other humanitarian actors and line ministries. In order to reach the target beneficiaries with prioritized cluster objectives, World Vision South Sudan proposed a total of $4,512,952 US project budget for 2022.

Health,Agriculture and Food Security,Water, Sanitation and Hygiene,Protection,Nutrition,Humanitarian Coordination and Info Management (USAID/BHA) Emergency Child Protection, GBV & Mine Action: Prevention, Mitigation & Response to assist IDPs, Returnees and Host Communities in conflict-affected & high risk areas of Warrap, Upper Nile, Western Equatoria and Central Equatoria States, South Sudan  The already high needs of critical child protection services in South Sudan has been exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic, protracted displacement, and limited access to basic services which continues to significantly affect the physical, mental, and social well-being of children, adolescents and caregivers. This situation has been worsened by the limited availability of mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services and the low level of core child protection services, including family tracing and reunification, case management, and reintegration services for children affected by armed forces and groups, leaving many children untreated and unable to access the needed services. Climate shocks, severe drought, massive flooding, and conflicts have contributed to the increase in GBV risks in the country which requires to strengthen GBV case management, psychosocial support, legal service, livelihood, economic support, GBV referral pathways and to integrate GBV into other sectoral responses. The high contamination with landmines and explosive remnants of war (ERW), especially in the Greater Equatoria region, along major supply routes and areas for returnees from Uganda, and the increase in expected returns require to prevent, mitigate and respond to mine risk issues through enhanced preparedness and resilience.
This proposed integrated CP, GBV and EORE project is in line with the Protection Cluster Objectives and will ensure the provision of critical protection-related assistance and specialized services and the prevention and mitigation of Protection risks through enhanced preparedness. The project targets to reach an average of 60,000 (20,000 women, 20,000 men, 10,000 girls, 10,000 men) (CP), 50,000 (20,000 women, 10,000 men, 10,000 girls, 10,000 boys) (GBV) and 20,000 (5000 men, 5000 women, 5000 girls, 5000 boys) (MA) including people with disabilities.
Using the 2022 Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP), World Vision International South Sudan (WVI-SS) aims to reach the most vulnerable populations in 11 counties in Warrap, Upper Nile, Western Equatoria and Central Equatoria States with improved access to quality lifesaving child protection for vulnerable girls, boys, men and women including children with disabilities who are at risk of mortality and morbidity and protection incidents/threats. Through the provision of specialized / lifesaving child protection and multi sectoral services WVI-SS seeks to reduce the suffering of boys, girls, women and men including children with disabilities who are at risk or experience violence, abuse, exploitation and neglect including GBV.
The proposed project will reduce the suffering of GBV survivors including women, men, girls, boys and people with disabilities by providing multi-sectoral specialized GBV response services. Furthermore, WVI-SS seeks to ensure that vulnerable women, men, girls, boys including people with disabilities have improved access to the provision of GBV prevention and risk mitigation interventions. Through protection monitoring, advocacy, awareness-raising and prevention and response services the project aims to reduce the vulnerability of women, men, girls and boys including people with disabilities at increased risk of mortality and morbidity and protection incidents/threats in priority areas.
In line with the Core Humanitarian Standards, WVI-SS will maintain its commitment to engage with affected communities at all phases of the project cycle, through focus group discussions with women, men, boys and girls. Establishing/strengthening local structures such as Project Management Committee is one example of how WVI-SS engages the community in a sustainable and accountable manner to determine and support appropriate need-based responses. WVI's Quality Assurance framework ensures that each project implemented is carried out effectively and continually reviewed in line with community needs and in line with other humanitarian frameworks.

The aim of this is to reduce suffering, morbidity, and mortality related to malnutrition among vulnerable populations, SCI's proposed response will focus both treatment and preventative approaches, using community-based management of acute malnutrition (CMAM) and infant and young child feeding (IYCF) approaches. SCI Emergency nutrition programs will include. i) Community mobilization to increase access and coverage of CMAM services, ii) Treatment of children and PWLs with acute malnutrition through inpatient and Outpatient therapeutic programs. iii) blanket Supplementary feeding program. iv) Institutional feeding program (IFP), v) Maternal dietary supplementation, vi) Promotion of optimal IYCF through mother-to-mother support groups. vii) Improving Dietary Diversity through household kitchen gardening, viii) Strengthen nutrition information systems and operations research to ensure an evidence-based response, ix) Building capacity for frontline nutrition workers and institutions at all levels. SCI will work through communities to promote, protect and support recommended IYCF practices through one-on-one counselling and group message and counselling. Besides the CMAM and behaviour change interventions, SCI will implement cash transfer intervention in selected areas targeting families of severely malnourished children and SAM PLW to maximize the program's nutrition outcomes and reduce the relapse of acute malnutrition among under-five children and PLW. Through this response, SCI will support 104 static OTP/TSFPs and eight stabilization centres integrated with health facilities. The service will be delivered through static and outreach/mobile facilities for remote and hard-to-reach areas in the targeted project locations. SCI will work with MOH, UNICEF and WFP to secure timely provision of Nutrition supplies necessary for Nutrition Service Delivery. SCI will reach 73,683 under-five Children and 66,992 PLW. 
SCI will make deliberate efforts to enhance coordination and integration with the Health, WASH, FSL, Protection and Education clusters to address the causes of malnutrition through a multi-sectoral approach that aims to reduce vulnerabilities, prevent malnutrition and build resilience among the vulnerable people. Specific multi-sectoral activities are to increase access to safe water and sanitation, promote critical WASH messages, and integrate early childhood development strategies in nutrition treatment sites. Kitchen gardening, screening and treating of malaria, managing diarrhea, and mainstreaming child protection and gender-based violence risk mitigation will also be promoted at the nutrition sites.y. SCI will also support hygiene interventions to improve nutrition outcomes and reduce risk of hygiene-related morbidities

Spot checks, supportive supervision and monitoring visits will monitor service delivery and engage with the community and other stakeholders to gauge evolving needs. Community nutrition volunteers will be supported to undertake household visits, conduct regular screening of malnourished children and women to ensure timely detection and treatment, and report on a monthly basis. Data collection tools and analysis will be strengthened to enhance monitoring of integrated services

Health,Protection,Economic Recovery and Market Systems,Nutrition  (USAID/BHA) Integrated Food Security and Livelihoods Protection in Mayendit and Panyijiar Counties, Unity State, South Sudan  The project objective(s) is to enhance and sustain emergency food production through complementary vegetable and crop livelihood inputs, fishing, and livestock; reduce dependency on food and agricultural inputs to support and strengthen households’ ability to absorb shocks in a way that prevents the spread and transmission of COVID-19 for households affected by floods and conflict in Panyijiar and Mayendit counties, Unity state of South Sudan. The IRC proposes to provide a sequence of food production to support to most severe food-insecure and malnourished households in the main season farming of May to July and dry season of Nov to March. To strengthen households’ resilience, the project will mainstream gender, conflict sensitivity, disaster risks reduction, and COVID-19 risk mitigation measures to support at-risk households focused on improving vegetable, crop, livestock, and fisheries production and bolstering resilience towards recurrent shocks and stresses. In pursuit of the project objective(s), the following activities will be implemented: 
(a) The IRC together with the complaint and feedback mechanism (CFM/AAP) committee will mobilize, engage community members to inform the needs of the most vulnerable households and selection criteria for registration together with Nutrition partners. 
(b) Preposition and distribute emergency (short-term maturing) agricultural inputs (Cereal & Vegetable seeds, and tools) and fishing kits to 53,760 people. The IRC anticipates FAO will provide complimentary in-kind inputs to support the project. During distribution, community health volunteers will be engaged to disseminate COVID-19 messages, provide personal protective kits including facemasks, hand washing station, hand sanitizers, and limit the crowd at distribution points following COVID-19 protocol. 
(c) To improve nutritional practices for pregnant women and caregivers of children under 5 years with MAM and SAM. Nutrient-dense vegetable seeds will be provided, establish demonstration gardens at nutrition facilities close to water points, provide basic training on vegetable production, harvest, and conservation techniques. The IRC Nutrition team will conduct nutrition-sensitive awareness, food cooking demonstrations showing how to enrich households’ meals with locally available foods.
(d) The IRC will identify 400 potential seed producers, provide foundation seeds, establish seeds multiplication centers and plots. The seed producers will receive at least 200 USD cash grants, training on quality seeds selection, quality seeds production techniques, and crop management practices. Seed producers will be supported to form VSLA to increase access to finance for seeds production and access to markets will be facilitated.  
(e) The IRC with the County Agriculture Department, State Ministry of Agriculture, and FAO will contribute to livestock disease surveillance and monitoring, facilitate vaccination campaigns, mass vaccination exercises and treatments to livestock to be led by CAHW.
(f) Facilitate capacity building to community-based extension agents (CAHWs, AEA’s), crop producers, pastoralists, and fisherfolks on sustainable production skills and provision of proximate extension services on production, post-harvest handling through demonstration gardens. Also, fisherfolks to receive basic training on fish preservation and kit repairs to enhance household nutrition and income.
Overall, the project will reach 6% most vulnerable households in need (HNO, 2022) in Panyijiar (33,000 People) and Mayendit (20,160 People) equivalent to a total of 53,760 people (5,376 Male children, 8,064 Female children, 12,902 Adult male, 19,354 Adult Female, 3,225 elderly Male, 4,839 elder Female) people. By program type: 53,760 livelihoods inputs distribution (Crop, Vegetable, Tools & fishing Kits), 5,376 people production skills (Crop, Vegetables, fisheries skills (Fishing kits repairs, fish preservation etc) training and 400 seeds growers/producers

Health,Protection,Nutrition Gender-based Violence (GBV) Prevention and Response for Conflict-Affected Population in South Sudan 
The GBV prevention and response program of International Medical Corps (IMC) in South Sudan aims to empower communities and build resilience through promoting social and behavioral change to address the root causes of GBV in the country. The project targets key population to create a sustainable change in attitude and practices through male engagement, working with community leaders and building capacity of local stakeholders. Leveraging on the vast experiences, gains, and successes of IMC in implementing GBV prevention and response interventions through the FCDO-HARISS program, this project will be continued to implement in the states of Western Bahr el Ghazal (Wau IDP Camp and County), Upper Nile and Malakal PoC and County), Unity (Nyal County), and in Canal/Pigi County. It will directly benefit about 27495 vulnerable women and girls across the target locations. One of the project’s key priorities is to further strengthen core services to survivors of GBV and other vulnerable women and girls in the aforesaid intervention sites. These services include quality case management using a survivor-centered approach, along with psychosocial support to enhance healing and recovery. IMC UK works to ensure that survivors’ holistic needs are met by providing multi-sectoral services, referring to health centers for clinical management of rape, to legal justice services and to other kinds of support based on the needs of survivors. In addition to individual PSS for survivors, IMC UK will continue with PSS group activities for all vulnerable women and girls in the women girls’ safe spaces (WGSS). To ensure sustainability of the project and ownership by the community, especially of the WGSSs, in Wau, Nyal and Malakal, IMC already established, leadership committee comprise of 8 members from the community selected by their fellow women with the responsibility to give support, information, feedback, and suggestions that will foster empowerment and ownership of the space and the overall wellbeing of their members. The women committee members will be further empowered with knowledge and skills through hands-on management of the spaces and co-leading with them on the daily functioning of the WGSS. The women committee will be continuously mentored and trained on GBV basic concepts, safe referral, and referral pathways, and on leadership and conflict management and facilitation techniques and on various psychosocial support activities using IMC’s and IRC’s global WGSS toolkit. IMC UK will implement holistic community engagement strategies on the promotion of long-term positive change in the targeted communities. IMC will use the GBV community mobilization tool called SASA! - Phase-based strategy to help communities rethink about “power” and the positive use of power. “Preventing Violence against Women and Girls: Engaging Men in Accountable Practice (EMAP)” is also another tool that will be used to ensure men engagement with accountability to prevent GBV in the targeted community in Nyal, Wau and Malakal. In addition, IMC trains and collaborates with GBV Taskforce members in Wau, Malakal and Nyal. These will be supported by staff IMC UK staff to do awareness raising, and safe confidential referral of any survivors who disclose to them. IMC UK will provide emergency cash assistance for case management to the vulnerable women and girls. Cash assistance is one of the interagency minimum standards in GBV programming in emergency (Standard 11: Dignity Kits, Cash Assistance). In addition to this, IMC UK opts to implement cash assistance based on lesson learnt and feedback from women and girls on importance of cash assistance as lifesaving; for example, it can help a survivor meet the costs associated with fleeing an abusive relationship (e.g., rent, temporary shelter, transportation, food, clothing, etc).

(2022 & Coordination portion of EUR 4 mio) Capacity Development support for northwest Syrian response community IOM aims to contribute to effective coordination and the UN's localization efforts by building the capacity of implementing partners. As the humanitarian situation in northwest Syria remains grave with increasing hostilities, a deteriorating humanitarian situation, and new displacements, the capacity of humanitarian actors in northwest Syria is stretched thin after 10 years of conflict. It is also possible that in  the event of non-renewal of the UNSCR, some UN agencies may be forced to scale down or adapt their cross-border activities. INGOs and NGOs would then be required to significantly scale up their operations in order to continue supporting affected communities. INGOs and NGOs will be expected to maintain the delivery of quality humanitarian response activities and ensure effective coordination. As such, it is paramount to continue building the capacity of INGO and NGO partners across technical and cross-cutting topics.

In 2021, IOM supported the capacity development of its partners and cluster partners through trainings, coaching, mentoring, learning exchange workshops, and improving the partner’s institutional process and procedures through reviewing, and developing guidance documents, SoPs and checklists. Topics varied from project cycle management, finance, procurement, humanitarian access negotiation, and Cash-Based Intervention (CBI). In addition to those training, IOM published COVID-19 AAP videos and COVID-19 vaccination videos to support the information sharing, awareness-raising effort towards COVID-19 by the COVID-19 task force and the Health cluster. 

The need for building the organizational capacity of implementing partners remains critical. This has been reflected in the different joint capacity need assessments IOM regularly conducts with its partners.  IPs consistently highlighted the need for more capacity-building sessions on administrative areas such as Governance, Human Resources, Compliance, Programme Development and Reporting to improve their institutional process and procedures in resource mobilization and management. Furthermore, IOM aims to build the capacity of implementing partners and Cluster partners on sector-specific topics and cross-cutting topics such as community engagement, humanitarian principle, access negotiation and disability inclusion. 

Building on its capacity development activities in 2021, IOM will organize around 64 trainings, consultation and coaching sessions on humanitarian access negotiation, human resource management, governance, compliance, and trainings on WASH-related topics in 2022 and 2023. IOM will facilitate a Training of facilitators (ToF) and Advance Certificate training on humanitarian access negotiation under the auspices of Access Working Group and OCHA for the sake of reaching in a wider group. Based on a clear workplan, the participants from the ToF will conduct peer workshops on humanitarian access and negotiation in northwest Syria reaching field humanitarian staff. In addition to the above trainings, IOM will also support the partners’ development of organizational and operational policy and procedures. All activities will be coordinated with relevant Clusters, Technical Working Groups, and other coordination fora.

Integrated Emergency Preparedness and Response to address critical humanitarian needs in South Sudan Quality Education for Emergency Affected Children and Youth in South Sudan. The overall objective of the intervention is to ensure that emergency affected girls and boys as well as youth continually access quality learning opportunities relevant for their psycho-social well-being, physical and cognitive development.  The project targets children and youth aged between 6 - 17  from IDP, returnees and host community families with age appropriate interventions that respond to their education needs. Primary focus for this project is displacement affected out-of-school children and youth affected by conflict and climate emergencies. NRC anticipates to reach 38,873 children (52% girls); 875 adults (400 men ; 475 women [375 teachers & 500 parents/caregivers and other non-teaching professionals) as direct beneficiaries. The project will focus on strengthening and improving quality and delivery of education in four strategic response areas which are 1) First Phase response - through NRC's mobile response operations and targeting newly displaced families, with short term education activities lasting from 6-9 months. 2) Formal education - conducted through NRC's static program operations across the country in prioritized counties where NRC has existing physical presence; 3) Non Formal education through ALP classes for over-aged children who missed years of schooling due to conflict and displacement and 4) Youth Education and training with an emphasis on vocational skills training, peace-building and life-skills training.  In close collaboration with parents, caregivers and local actors, NRC will construct and repair learning spaces/classrooms and gender segregated school WASH facilities; provide school hardware assets (desks/benches), essential learning materials, teacher aids, recreational & hygiene kits; girls dignity kits for MHM; support mgt of schools through teacher selection, recruitment, motivation, training on child centered pedagogical methods, curriculum planning, classroom mgt & conflict sensitive education; support teacher learning cycles (TLCs) for continuous professional dvpt; facilitate community engagement in education through establishment/strengthening of PTAs & SMCs through training in roles and responsibilities, school development planning and awarding school improvement grants; conduct awareness raising community dialogue sessions to mobilize enrollment, promote attendance and support retention especially for girls who face multiple barriers to education including harmful and social practices such as forced early marriages and boys who also face protection risks that include child labour and forced recruitment into armed groups; conduct life skills training & support structured recreational activities for physical and psycho-social development; provide technical and material support non-teaching professionals (county education directors,  supervisors) to effectively conduct their school supervision and support duties; training of teachers, facilitators, on Mental Health and psycho-social support (MHPSS), Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR), child protection, child safeguarding and PSEA; provide cash and vouchers assistance to the most vulnerable for examination registration. 
Key approaches that NRC will adopt in this project include integration, partnerships and community based programming.  NRC will collaborate local structures as well as with other clusters including protection, WASH, shelter, LFS, Nutrition and Health to deliver comprehensive package that addresses the holistic needs of targeted population. Furthermore, for durable solutions, NRC will work with local actors, parents and care-givers building their capacity for self reliance and also to increase coverage in hard to reach areas  with periodic access challenges and bureaucratic impediments. For effective and efficient use of resources and for learning purposes, NRC will continue to participate in coordination mechanisms at both the national and sub-national levels to avoid overlaps and duplication with other education players.

Integrated Emergency Preparedness and Response to address critical humanitarian needs in South Sudan Emergency S/NFIs response to IDPs, Returnees and Host Community affected by disasters in South Sudan The project aims to provide Survival Kits /Emergency shelter/Non Food items both in-kind and in cash modalities to the most vulnerable persons, newly displaced/host communities and returnees. The project will focus on the life saving shelter/NFIs needs, as identified through assessment to protect the affected displaced people from harsh weather conditions and protection risks targeting all states of South Sudan. The intervention will be implemented through mobile response as well as using its static teams based in Kajo Keji, Juba, Koch, Mayom, Leer, Bor, Duk, Twic East, Akobo, Aweil, Wau and Alek. However the major focus areas will be Jonglei, Unity, Northern Bahrel Ghazal, Central, Western and Eastern Equatoria states. Cash programming will also be considered in areas where markets are fully or semi-functional and shelter/NFI items are available and accessible by the community. When blanket targeting is not applicable, the intervention will target mainly lactating and pregnant women, households with malnourished children, and households with members who have certain health complications. Besides unaccompanied children, unaccompanied elderly and persons with no community linkages will also be targeted.
The project will promote timely delivery of assistance through deployment of rapid response teams in line with humanitarian priorities for 2022 HRP's. NRC’s mobile response teams will be ready for deployment within 8 days to conduct assessments and within 22 days for full-fledged delivery of NFIs and emergency shelters and other activities per location. The project will also support returnees in settlement as part of the local integration or as they settle into their areas of origin. The project will benefit 120,000 individuals directly.

Integrated Emergency Preparedness and Response to address critical humanitarian needs in South Sudan Protection and Legal Assistance for Displacement affected populations in South Sudan The NRC seeks to improve the overall protective environment in South Sudan by not only responding to people's most immediate material needs during a crisis, but also by promoting their safety and dignity, as well as preventing, reducing, or mitigating the protection risks they face. It is also to address the root causes of displacement and to contribute to the creation of conditions conducive to long-term solutions for displaced people. To achieve the project objective, NRC will focus on three key components i.e. 1) General Protection; Housing, Land and Property; 3) Gender Based Violence. 

NRC proposes a community-based approach to displaced and conflict-affected populations protection, including static, mobile, and emergency responses.  Protection context assessments will be done in all locations, as well as, where possible, community-based protection monitoring, in which community focal points will be trained to report on protection needs and risks. Protection incidents will be documented and analyzed in order to better understand trends and evolution in the protection context, and the findings will be disseminated to communities and relevant stakeholders. 

NRC will provide at-risk populations with both awareness-raising sessions and individualized assistance in obtaining national identity documentation. Foster improved ability to exercise HLP rights for individuals and groups affected by displacement with priority given to the most vulnerable, including female and child headed households, the elderly, individuals with physical and mental disabilities, and those who are extremely poor. NRC will target conflict-affected areas and areas of potential return.

NRC will also carry out GBV prevention and risk mitigation activities in 6 counties located in hard to reach areas. Activities will include awareness raising, referrals to response services, cash assistance to GBV survivors, distribution of dignity kits and training on GBV basic concepts among others.

To achieve the main objective, the will focus on the below key activities
1) Carrying out of information and awareness raising activities; awareness will focus on GBV (GBV risks, available response services, GBV referral pathways, timely reporting), HLP (social cohesion and collaborative dispute resolution mechanisms, land rights issues) and general protection (protection risks, available services)
2) Provision of cash assistance (individual protection assistance) to persons at GBV survivors and other persons at heightened risks including referral of GBV survivors for response services
3) Training frontline workers and community focal points on basic GBV concepts, GBV guiding principles and responses services.
4) Training of state-level authorities, community leaders and representative on HLP, alternative dispute resolution
5) Facilitating peaceful coexistence and inclusive resolutions of local conflict through training and mentoring the local community in collaborative dispute resolution (CDR) mechanisms
6) Distribute dignity kits to women and adolescent girls.
7) Provision of legal aid and counselling

Integrated Emergency Preparedness and Response to address critical humanitarian needs in South Sudan Food Security and Livelihoods Support to disaster affected populations in Northern Bahr el Ghazal, Unity, Western Bahr Warrap, Central Equatoria and Jonglei States of South Sudan The project will utilize the humanitarian pipe line for crops, vegetables and fisheries kits from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). Where markets are functional market based interventions such as direct purchases and or seed and tool fairs will be sought as informed by respective market assessments. These activities will be complimented by capacity building/training modules in the specific livelihoods so as to improve the targeted farmer production, productivity capacities and improve yields and returns. The fisheries training will enable target beneficiaries utilize their kits in the proper way and also improve their knowledge and skills in fish processing, preservation and marketing. The crops and vegetable production training will be based on the crop production seasonal calendar which includes land preparation, planting weeding, pest and disease management, harvesting, post-harvest management and marketing. Using the training of trainers (ToT) approach, the project will target 7,500 crop/vegetable farmers and 4,500 fisher folk for assorted livelihoods inputs support as well as training and engaging community based extension workers to provide the technical support to these farmers while they replicate the training to the other beneficiaries. The proposed interventions will also train targeted households with trainings on approved agronomic practices, pests and disease control, post-harvest handling and value addition and linkages to markets and other value chain actors In addition, 1,500 HHs will be supported through unconditional/conditional cash transfer programming especially in flood and conflicted affected areas. The action will also target 1250 HHs with small ruminant (goat/sheep) or poultry restocking through livestock voucher modality, 750 women, youth and men will be engaged in VSLAs/IGAs while 450 HHs will be engaged in natural resource management and climate adaptation activities.
To ensure integration the intervention will target nutrition & health centers, schools and mother garden’s locations conveniently with/without of access and proximity of a water source. Additional community gardens will be promoted at locations such as schools, health facilities where they will be jointly tended by students and community volunteers. The FSL interventions will be designed taking into consideration and incorporating mainstreaming of protection, safety, GBV prevention, Prevention of Sexual Abuse & Exploitation and conflict sensitivity analysis.  The project teams will work closely with local authorities to identify persons with disabilities both men and women so that they are supported. This number is not expected to exceed 5% of the 10,500 HH targeted. This ensures participants are selected based on needs alone, a rigorous community-based targeting process with participation and inclusion of vulnerable groups such as female and child headed households, disabled and the elderly.  The proposed project will also take into consideration cross-cutting issues like environmental protection, HIV/AIDS, community-based participatory planning, gender, nutrition will be considered during project implementation.
All agricultural and fisheries activities will be implemented in collaboration with the State Ministry of Agriculture in order to ensure that government extension workers benefit from and also contribute to the technical components that will be offered by the project by so doing building capacities that will continue to be utilized after project closure. Community based extension workers such as lead farmers will be trained to continue supporting other farmers during and after project closure.

Coordinated Action for Multi-Sector Programming in Camp and Out-of-Camp Settings
----- Shelter Shelter and NFI Assistance for IDPs and host community members in Northern Syria The proposed project aims at addressing emergency and more sustainable shelter and NFI needs of vulnerable households with acute needs (both IDPs and host community members) in Northeast and Northwest Syria.  

The intervention will target a total of 123,625 beneficiaries under shelter activities, and 153,004 beneficiaries under NFI activities across Northwest and Northeast Syria for a total budget of 5,472,963$ including 4,209,680$ of program budget. To note, some beneficiaries will receive more than one type of assistance. As a result, some of them if will double-counted under the activities in section 4. 

In Northwest Syria, ACTED will provide fuel for heaters to better equip the residents for winter in A’zaz and Idleb sub-districts for 111,095 individuals for 1,148,474$ (program budget). Under this intervention, the same number of camp residents will also receive emergency NFI kits -composed of, for example, tarpaulin, jerry can, mattresses/sleeping mats, blankets, solar lamps, floor mat, stove, cooking pot, bowl for food, and cutlery - as well as winterization kits, to guarantee shelter and dignified living conditions to newly displaced household, for 196,296$ (program budget). Through contractors, ACTED will rehabilitate private off-camp shelter units to 600 individuals in A’zaz sub-district for 131,046$ (program budget). In addition, ACTED will rehabilitate shelters in-camp to 500 individuals in Jarablus sub-district for 135,061$ (program budget). In addition, 750 individuals out-of-camp will benefit from shelter repairs for 255,409$ (program budget) and ACTED will provide multi-purpose cash Assistance for winterization to 15,000 individuals in Aleppo governorate, for a total amount of 266,051$ (program budget). 

In Northeast Syria, ACTED will provide fuel and heaters to 14,433 camp residents across Areesheh camp, Al-Hasake governorate, to better equip the residents for winter for a total amount of 829,868$ (program budget).  In Serekaniye camp, Al-Hasake governorate, ACTED will distribute fuel and heaters to 12,476 camp residents for a total of 291,840$ (program budget). 
These camp residents will also benefit from installation and maintenance of fire safety points, for 11,333$ (program budget). In Ar-Raqqa governorate, ACTED will rehabilitate household shelters for dignified living conditions to 10,680 beneficiaries in out-of-camp areas for a total of 1,365,650$ (program budget). 

ACTED will take into account the different risks and concerns affecting women, men, girls and boys and people with disabilities when designing this intervention. With regards to the latter, ACTED will ensure that the distributions are conducted respectfully of the needs of the most vulnerable, with specific distribution lines dedicated to women and elderlies. ACTED will also conduct the distributions directly at the HH level when needed. As for the shelter rehabilitation activity, ACTED will ensure to select the HHs also based on vulnerability, with consideration for income and/or demographics. ACTED will develop BoQs for each shelter based on technical shelter assessments. The assessment of the shelter will take into consideration privacy needs, as well as specific needs for people with disabilities when relevant and particular works will be incorporated as necessary. This will ensure safe and dignified living conditions to the targeted HHs in the area of intervention.

Multi-sectoral humanitarian assistance to vulnerable displacement-affected people and communities in Venezuela Respuesta multi-sectorial para mejorar el acceso a una educación de calidad y segura para NNA afectados por la situación humanitaria  La intervención educativa forma parte de la respuesta integrada de NRC Venezuela. El equipo de Educación continuará trabajando en colaboración con los programas Información, Orientación y Asistencia legal (ICLA), Agua Higiene y Saneamiento (ASH) y Medios de vida y seguridad alimentaria (LFS) para permitir que las poblaciones afectadas por la situación humanitaria y desplazamientos satisfagan sus necesidades básicas, disfruten de sus derechos y se beneficien de los caminos hacia soluciones duraderas. La acción propuesta por el NRC tiene como objetivo garantizar la permanencia y los caminos de regreso al aprendizaje y la integración en la educación formal, particularmente luego del cierre de las escuelas por dos años durante la pandemia COVID-19 y su reciente reapertura. NRC responderá a los diversos problemas y necesidades que enfrentan los niños, niñas y adolescentes vulnerables en cuatro estados en Venezuela (Delta Amacuro, Bolívar, Táchira y Zulia) a través de una estrategia de respuesta basada en el Programa de Educación infantil (CEP), Programa Puente (PP) y Programa de Nivelación, así como una versión contextualizada del Better Learning Program (BLP) de NRC. Todos estos programas están adaptados al contexto venezolano.

Multi-sectoral humanitarian assistance to vulnerable displacement-affected people and communities in Venezuela Protección y asistencia humanitaria a personas en movilidad y en riesgo, así como comunidades de acogida vulnerables afectadas por el desplazamiento  El objetivo principal de la intervención busca brindar protección legal a personas afectadas con necesidades específicas y vulnerables, la mitigación de riesgos asociados a la movilidad tanto interna como externa y el fortalecimiento de la resiliencia de la población venezolana afectada, incluyendo a las comunidades de acogida. Dentro de los objetivos específicos se encuentran promover el empoderamiento de las personas en movilidad o en riesgos de movilidad, así como identificar, derivar y atender a personas con necesidades de alta vulnerabilidad y riesgos de protección.  Las actividades de información y orientación a personas en tránsito y desplazadas, retornados, comunidades de acogida y otras personas de interés se realizarán por medio de la atención personal y confidencial en los puntos de información como el centro comunitario y activación de equipos móviles en las comunidades meta de los estados prioritarios (Bolívar, Delta Amacuro, Táchira, Zulia). Las mesas de información y los equipos móviles brindarán información sobre derechos, riesgos, documentación civil y rutas para la migración segura, y asegurarán una atención inmediata y derivaciones pertinentes a las personas con necesidades específicas. La derivación de los casos se hará en base a las rutas de atención existentes, ya sea para la Red de Espacios Seguros para la atención de supervivientes de violencia sexual o de género y niñez en riesgo, como a miembros de las Redes de Protección. NRC también hará derivaciones a organizaciones prestadoras de servicios de respuesta multisectorial a sobrevivientes de VBG. Temáticas como el acceso a la documentación civil será parte de la asistencia humanitaria con enfoque de derechos a implementar. Además, se priorizarán los servicios de información, asesoría y asistencia legal que puedan necesitar la población retornada por causa de la pandemia COVID-19. De esta forma se asegura un mejor proceso de integración de poblaciones retornadas. Por último, ICLA pondrá en marcha su componente Digital ICLA como parte de sus modalidades de prestación de servicios, a fin de mejorar su capacidad para brindar soporte remoto y llegar a las personas en el área de difícil acceso (H2R). Nuestra población meta recibirá información sobre rutas migratorias seguras. NRC utilizará las alianzas y el apoyo brindado a otras ONG, agencias o autoridades que gestionan puntos de atención y explorarán colaboraciones para ampliar aún más el alcance de Digital ICLA. Se explorará el uso de chatbots u otras herramientas tecnológicas.
