Humanitarian Assistance and Resilience Programme (HARP)	Nutrition
(MINA Project) for Children Northeast Nigeria Nutrition Response 2022 The Nutrition response in 2022 will prioritise implementation of the nutrition lifesaving activities (inpatient, outpatient, and targeted supplemental feeding programmes) and targeting of LGAs with high rates of GAM (above 10%) such as MMC/Jere, Nganzai, Bama, Machina. Hard-to-reach areas (such as Gubio, Rann, Magumeri), areas with large IDP  and returnee populations (like Monguno) and high-risk/inaccessible locations such as Marte LGA will also be prioritised for nutrition assistance. 
UNICEF will primarily target acutely malnourished children and PLW who are at a significantly high risk of death. The nutrition response will also target the total under-five and PLW with preventive nutrition services e.g. micronutrient supplementation to ensure levels of acute malnutrition are not above average thresholds, and to also reduce morbidity and mortality. The response will prioritise households with persons living with disabilities, who face barriers in accessing health, nutrition and WASH services and are disproportionately food insecure due to high levels of exclusion. 
The nutrition status of the targeted population in the BAY states significantly deteriorates during the period from May-August every year, which is the lean season and coincides with the rainy season. The season is characterised by very high rates of acute malnutrition with medical complications due to poor food access and a high prevalence of diarrhoea and malaria. UNICEF will need to adequately prepare for the lean season period by prepositioning supplies, increasing the overall sector capacity to treat acute malnutrition with a focus on inpatient care and IYCF-E
The nutrition response in BAY states will be contextualised in 2022 based on the following categorisation: 
1. Protracted crisis e.g north and central Borno LGAs where the rates of acute malnutrition are high, worsened by poor access to food and health systems. The approach in these areas will include INGO/NNGO direct support to the affected population, and prioritisation of lifesaving nutrition activities. 
3. New emergencies – locations of new crisis and fluctuations such as relocations, displacements and spike in acute malnutrition. The approach will focus on the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) with a focus on lifesaving activities. 
4. Hard-to-reach / inaccessible areas – locations with limited humanitarian footprints and access e.g Gubio and Magumeri. The approach will include RRM and remote management strategy (where feasible) with a focus on life-saving interventions. UNICEF will also strengthen the implementation of nutrition interventions through local organizations or community-based structures to implement nutrition services in hard-to-reach/inaccessible areas. 
UNICEF response is primarily through services and in-kind deliveries. UNICEF will employ the use of cash and voucher assistance (CVA) to fill the nutrient gap in the Nutrition/Food Minimum Expenditure Basket to ensure that populations have access to a varied diet e.g CVA for meats and vegetables. 
The nutrition status of the affected population is an outcome of various underlying issues including access to health, WASH, food security, child protection, and gender issues. The main cause of acute malnutrition among children and women in BAY states is the high morbidity rates. High diarrhoea prevalence is the major cause of acute malnutrition among the IDPs and urban poor population due to the prevailing poor hygiene and sanitation conditions worsened by congested living conditions. The response will strengthen the integration of nutrition-sensitive interventions including WASH, food security, health, livelihoods and child protection, and gender-based violence risk mitigation.
UNICEF will prioritise projects that include basic nutrition packages such as integrated treatment of acute malnutrition (SAM and MAM) and prevention services including integration with WASH, food security, health and protections services.

Drought Response Scale up in Somalia - continuation of critical services to drought-affected rural communities Provision of  Shelter assistance to displacement affected communities including poor host communities in Somalia This project will focus on improving the physical protection and dignity of IDPs, refugee returnees and poor host communities across all parts of Somalia through distribution and provision of locally purchased Non Food Items (NFIs) and Emergency Shelter Kits (ESKs) through cash/voucher/in-kind modalities and construction of Transitional and/or Permanent Shelters through community driven or owner driven approaches (where appropriate). To avoid decongestion, settlement (re)planning training will also be conducted and Post Construction Monitoring (PCM) exercises for Shelters and Post Distribution Monitoring (PDM) exercises for NFIs & ESKs will also be conducted. NRC will also ensure participation in infrastructure mapping exercises led by Shelter cluster or any other partner.
For the beneficiaries’ selection and registration, NRC will use an electronic mobile data collection tool called Kobo tool box, which provides an accurate and real time data. The data received through Kobo is easily manageable and transferable. 20% to 30% Poor host community members will be selected to ensure 'DO NO HARM' and other humanitarian principles including humanity, neutrality, impartiality and independence. Similarly, 5 to 15% Persons With Disabilities (PWDs) will also be condisered in each project.
For the provision of NFIs, each HH will be provided with a cash of $100 as per cluster agreed standard NFI kit while for the provision of ESKs, each HH will be provided with a cash of either USD 247 (for ESK Type-1 with a size of 380 cm x 550 cm) or USD 213 (for ESK Type-2 with a size of 360 cm x 440 cm) depending upon the area of land available. If the area available is less, ESK Type-2 will be selected esle ESK Type-1 will be proiratized. The cash for ESKs will be distributed in two subsequent installments (50% as first installment and remaining 50% as second installment). NRC will acquire the services of local telecom companies (viz. Food Security Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace.

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

Life-saving food assistance in North-East Nigeria Life-saving food assistance in North-East Nigeria WFP will provide unconditional food assistance to the most food-insecure, crisis-affected populations. Life-saving general food assistance (in-kind food and cash-based transfers) will be delivered to IDPs, returnees, and host populations in North-East Nigeria (Borno, Yobe, and Adamawa States). Early recovery and resilience to shocks will be promoted through asset creation and preservation, increased livelihoods opportunities, and enhanced agricultural value chains. Joint multi-sectoral assessments and Emergency Food Security Analysis will be conducted regularly to monitor the food security, and markets situation in crisis-affected states. 
A gender-transformative approach that meets the needs of women, men, girls, and boys will be adopted. WFP will mainstream protection throughout its work, supported by a solid understanding of the operational context and protection analysis. Training and capacity building of staff and partners in the protection and humanitarian principles will include on-the-job coaching. WFP will ensure that affected populations (women and men) will be consulted throughout the programme cycle; beneficiary feedback mechanisms will be tailored to their preferred means of communication. Beneficiaries will continue to be empowered with knowledge on their food assistance entitlements and their rights, including WFP’s zero-tolerance policy on Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA). Protection against Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) will be embedded in M&E tools, complaint feedback mechanisms, and training of partners and staff.
WFP will continue the collection of key information on beneficiaries and assistance provided as part of its M&E activities. Monthly monitoring will include distribution and activity site management; beneficiary and entitlement verification; and ensuring adequate protection and gender measures. Lessons will be regularly drawn from monthly process and biannual outcome monitoring and reporting, and periodic reviews and evaluation to inform strategic and operational decisions.
WFP will further consolidate partnerships to enhance national and state-level emergency preparedness and response systems, including food security and nutrition assessment and monitoring, early warning, protection, gender analysis, targeting and registration processes, safety nets, cash-based transfer capacities, and supply chain.
Where security and access to land allow, increasing livelihood activities will complement food assistance to support access to productive assets, income-generating activities, and self-reliance in the long term. Assistance will be coordinated with government distributions, ensure food assistance is complimentary and no gaps. self-reliance in the long term. Strengthening humanitarian coordination and advocacy to respond to humanitarian crisis Renforcement de la coordination et du plaidoyer humanitaire au Tchad Le projet vise à renforcer le rôle de OCHA dans la mise en œuvre de son mandat et son rôle auprès des partenaires humanitaires et gouvernementaux au niveau des fonctions coordination, gestion de l’information et plaidoyer. Le bureau national d’OCHA à N’Djaména et ses trois sous-bureaux régionaux à l’Est (Abéché) au Sud (Goré) et la province du Lac (Baga Sola) mettent l’accent sur l’opérationnalisation de ses fonctions y compris en assurant un lien entre les activités humanitaires et de développement (nexus) en vue de promouvoir une solution durable visant à ne pas perpétuer une situation de dépendance humanitaire. Dans le cadre de cette nouvelle façon de travailler outre l’opérationnalisation du nexus, le lien avec les objectifs commun des programmes développement, paix et sécurité sera mis en avant. L’accent est aussi mis sur le renforcement de la coordination civilo-militaire afin de faciliter l’accès et la protection des civils.

Le projet a pour but de renforcer la coordination d’une réponse humanitaire rapide et efficace afin de sauver des vies et protéger les personnes affectées par les situations de crises au Tchad. Une coordination humanitaire rapide et correctement évaluée au niveau des besoins de la population affectée permettra aux acteurs humanitaires de mieux identifier et répondre aux besoins humanitaires, de renforcer la préparation de réponse aux urgences à travers le renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et plus spécifiquement l‘Equipe humanitaire pays, la coordination inter-clusters, la coordination civilo-militaire, les clusters et les mécanismes de coordination au niveau de terrain.
Le projet vise aussi à assurer le plaidoyer humanitaire à travers l’analyse des besoins faites par l’ensemble de la communauté humanitaire et ses partenaires en vue une compréhension commune des problématiques auxquels fait face le Tchad, ses causes profondes, l’impact sur les populations. OCHA jouera un rôle clé dans la création d'espaces de collection et d'analyse et gestion d’informations, pour assurer une stratégie de réponse coordonnée menant à des actions humanitaires répondant aux besoins les plus aigus et être mieux préparé face aux urgences soudaines. Le projet permettra également d’assurer conjointement avec la communauté humanitaire le plaidoyer en faveur du respect des principes humanitaires, de la protection des civils, de l'accès humanitaire et pour la mobilisation et l'allocation efficace de ressources humanitaires.

Un accent a été mis sur la mise en œuvre des plans d’action de la redevabilité envers les populations affectées (AAP), la PSEA et la préparation aux urgences en plus d'intégrer une attention au genre et de renforcer la centralité de la protection.
Un plaidoyer pour plus de visibilité des résultats tangibles au niveau de la réponse facilitant la mobilisation de ressources pour les différentes crises au Tchad (mouvement de population – crise du Bassin du Lac Tchad, insécurité alimentaire et malnutrition, urgences sanitaires) est aussi défini comme une priorité dans ce projet

WASH - Lul/Kodok (Fashoda county)	Provision of life-saving water, sanitation and hygiene response to the most vulnerable population affected by Tonga Crisis in Kodok and Lul Payam in Fashoda County Upper Nile State Provision of integrated, equitable, and timely WASH services to emergency affected populations in South Sudan Protracted crises in South Sudan, including climactic shocks and continued conflict, have resulted in 8.9 million people projected to be in need of humanitarian assistance in 2022. As a result of the shocks, such as flooding, inter-communal violence (ICV) and ongoing armed clashes, the majority of the population are facing increased food insecurity, lack of access to basic services, and protection risks. As per the Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) 2022, lack of or inadequate access to clean water and improved sanitation and hygiene practices in South Sudan will negatively impact an estimated 6.1 million people in 2022. 

Since 2006, Solidarites International has become a key WASH actor in South Sudan, implementing emergency lifesaving responses across the country and providing integrated WASH services to crisis-affected populations in areas of static presence in Upper Nile, Jonglei, and Western Bahr el Ghazal. Since 2012 SI has played a key role in the Emergency Preparedness and Response (EPR) strategy in South Sudan, implementing multi-sectoral assessments and delivering emergency responses to crisis-affected populations all over the country. 

In 2022, SI will continue to provide emergency live-saving  WASH responses across the South Sudan to restore basic access to safe water, hygiene, and sanitation while ensuring equitable access, safety, and accountability to supported populations. Through its roving Emergency Preparedness and Response (EPR) team, SI will deploy to emergency-affected locations to provide first phase and second phase responses including distribution of household water treatment items and soap, emergency provision of safe water, and rapid repair of emergency-affected infrastructure.

At the same time, SI will expand its static presence in Upper Nile and Jonglei to provide basic integrated WASH services that target the most vulnerable, including those suffering malnutrition, food insecurity and protection threats. Static programs will focus on providing community-based solutions for sustainable WASH services that ensure that improvements in access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene are durable and can be maintained independently by communities. Engagement and joint programming with Protection and Nutrition actors will ensure that WASH services can be accessed by the most vulnerable and will have a tangible impact on reducing overall priority humanitarian needs. The increased integration of protection, inclusion, and conflict sensitivity analysis in all programming will ensure that WASH services and resources can be safely accessed by all in the community. Greater engagement of communities and local markets will support the design of long term and flood resistant WASH infrastructure and supply chains to ensure that interventions produce durable results for communities.

Provision of Protection and ESN/NFI Support to IDPs in Oromia, Jijiga and Assosa, Ethiopia Provision of life saving shelter and Non - food items assistance to IDPs and non- displaced drought affected population in Oromia and Somalia Regions.  Natural hazards such as flood and drought remain the main factors impacting people’s lives and livelihoods. The prolonged drought resulting from three consecutive failed rainy reasons since late 2020 has affected the lives of millions people living in Oromia, SNNP, Somali and Southwest regions. Natural hazards such as floods but most notably the drought in the southern part of the country makes the main drivers of needs. UNHCR, through harmonizing  its IDP response with the Cluster system, the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP), the Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO), the Sustainable Development Goals, the Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement (1999) and the Kampala Convention (2009) planes to respond to need of drought affected population in Somali, Oromia and SNNP regions. 
Recognizing that contexts across the region is volatile with unique needs per location, UNHCR Shelter and Non- food item response is planned to address the needs of people in all phases of displacement, with a focus on the emergency phase, care, and maintenance of shelter for people in protracted displacements and supporting sustainable returns and recovery where the context allows. The planned interventions include consideration of shelter preparedness, response, and shelter recovery support to account for both returns and secondary displacement and will be conducted in close coordination with multi-sectoral stakeholders to ensure that approaches are integrated, and that broader needs are addressed. Holding the protection of affected populations at its core: Do no harm principles incl. prioritizing health, privacy, safety, and dignity, accountability, management of expectations, adequate targeting, ensuring meaningful access to affected populations, participation and empowerment of affected people, enhancing resilience, coordination, and context-driven responses will be mainstreamed throughout our responses as per the ESNFI cluster strategy.  Through this interventions, including provision of in-kind assistance and cash when feasible, UNHCR planes to reach 50,048 HH (250,241 Individuals) across the three regions through the below responses.

•	Emergency Shelters (Communal, family shelters or Emergency Shelter kits) provision 
•	Non Food Items and ESNFI provision

In addition, capacity building of staff, authorities, affected populations and advocacy for those with shelter and household needs will also be considered. All the ES/NFIs component will be undertaken in consultation with the IDPs and host communities to ensure it meets their most urgent needs. The IDP hosting communities will also benefit from the responses. As per the cluster guideline 10-15% of the vulnerable communities hosting IDPs will be targeted.

To reduce risk and mitigate Sexual and Gender-Based Violence (SGBV) associated with shelter and NFI responses, UNHCR will conduct awareness-raising sessions to ensure that the communities are made aware of the protection risks in shelter and NFI response and how best to mitigate them. UNHCR will continue to use IASC GBV guidelines & related tools for SEA risk assessment and mitigation, including its newly developed GBV policy guidelines, National Action Plan and victim centered approach for addressing sexual misconduct to ensure accessibility to all women, girls and other at risk group.

As an effort to enhance inclusive humanitarian action principles, UNHCR will also provide awareness-raising and training of those at the forefront of service delivery and from the overall target reserving a minimum 15% of kits (tailor made for disables) to be allocated to households with family members with disabilities

South Sudan	South Sudan Humanitarian Response Plan 2022 Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2022, there are some 335,000 refugees and asylum seekers from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, primarily from Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic.
At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for longer term stability, hundreds of thousands of South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since the signing of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan, this spontaneous movement has prompted the development of an area-based approach, to support refugees, returnees and host communities, through enhanced engagement with development actors, to support greater access to services where possible.
Refugees largely reside in conflict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction in basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.
Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will benefit from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Specific protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identified at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with specific protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as verification exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the efficiency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to benefit from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

Mali - OCHA Office [Donor:O539, Recipient:O514] Renforcement des mécanismes de Coordination et de Plaidoyer pour la protection humanitaire et l’assistance aux populations les plus vulnérables au Mali En 2021, la crise humanitaire au Mali s'est aggravée en raison de l'augmentation et de l'expansion des de la violence intercommunautaire et des attaques des groupes armés non étatiques (GANE) dans les régions du centre, du sud et de l'ouest. Cette crise a été aggravée par les bouleversements politiques marqués par deux coups d'état en août 2020 et mai 2021, et l'incertitude persistante de la transition politique laisse l'État dans l'incapacité de répondre aux services sociaux de base des populations. 
Les déplacements internes de personnes ont augmenté de 100 000 en 2021, atteignant plus de 401 000 personnes soit quatre fois plus qu'il y a deux ans. Au total, 156 000 réfugiés maliens résident dans les pays voisins tandis que le Mali accueille 48 000 réfugiés et leur fournit protection et assistance. Les gains économiques du Mali se sont érodés, avec 900 000 personnes (0,04% de la population) qui sont retombées dans la pauvreté en raison de la crise socioéconomique de la COVID-19. la capacité des ménages est fragilisée à cause de la perte de revenus, de la réduction des transferts de fonds et à l'augmentation du coût de la vie. 
La Banque mondiale prévoit une augmentation du taux de pauvreté à 4,8 % en 2022. La crise de protection est également aggravée avec une augmentation des incidents de sécurité.  Les acteurs de la violence basée sur le genre (VBG) ont signalé 5 486 incidents de VBG, soit une augmentation de 41 % comparativement à la même période en 2020. Plus de 1 640 écoles sont fermées en raison de l'insécurité, affectant plus de 2,9 millions d'enfants dont 40 % se trouvent dans la région centrale de Mopti. Quatre districts centraux ont signalé que 40 % des écoles étaient fermées. Dans les régions du sud, 10 pour cent des écoles sont fermées à Koulikoro, Koutiala et Sikasso, privant 30 000 enfants de leur éducation. A ce jour, le Mali a rapporté plus de 15 800 cas de COVID-19.
En 2021, 1,3 million de personnes ont connu un niveau élevé d'insécurité alimentaire aiguë. le niveau le plus élevé depuis 2015, et 3 055 253 personnes ont été touchées par les mauvaises pluies et une saison de soudure prolongée. La situation humanitaire reste entravée par l'augmentation des besoins et la faiblesse des financements, avec 32 % des fonds mobilisés au 31 octobre 2021. Malgré les contraintes opérationnelles, les partenaires humanitaires ont aidé plus de 2,45 millions des 4,7 millions de personnes ciblées au 30 septembre 2021. 
Les capacités de réponse existantes au Mali représentent plus de 160 organisations humanitaires, acteurs du développement ainsi que des forces militaires (MINUSMA, Forces maliennes de défense et de sécurité, Barkhane, Mission européenne de formation, G5 Sahel). Le contexte susmentionné exigera une coordination efficace et la présence d’OCHA demeure très importante. OCHA maintiendra sa présence à Bamako, Mopti, Tombouctou, Gao et ouvrira une antenne à Ségou tout en couvrant à distance les régions de Taoudénit, Ménaka, Kidal et les régions du sud Est et Ouest. 

Sept clusters actifs (Éducation, Sécurité alimentaire, Santé, Nutrition, Protection, Abris/BNA et WASH), des sous-clusters et des groupes de travail spécialisés (Accès, CM-Coord, Redevabilité, Genre et Cash) sont en place au niveau national et local. Le Bureau d’OCHA au Mali continuera ainsi à jouer un rôle central dans la mobilisation, la coordination et le soutien des acteurs humanitaires dans les domaines de la coordination, la gestion de l’information, le financement humanitaire et le plaidoyer. 

OCHA continuera à jouer son rôle central dans la mobilisation des partenaires, l’utilisation des instruments et des mécanismes de financement tout en veillant à ce que les besoins humanitaires croissants soient prises en compte. OCHA assumera son rôle clé dans la coordination militaire au niveau national et régional de concert avec les forces militaires présentes dans le pays tout en renforçant les capacités des autorités nationales en matière de coordination

Cash Assistance in Re-Emerging Markets in Syria – phase 2 (CARMA2) Integrated Multi-AoR protection services for high at risk groups in Jebel Saman, Aleppo The intervention is part of a project aiming at securing the basic needs and providing integrated community-based protection activities in Karm Jazmati, Seken Shebebi, Karm al Tarrab, and Dahret Awwad. The project is held by Caritas Germany (CG), back-funded by the German Federal Foreign Ministry (GFO) and implemented from 01.04.2019 -31.12.2022 by Caritas Syria (CS). 
The protection activities carried out under this project have been regularly aligned to the protection sector strategy. In the 2019 established community center in Karm al Jazmati, integrated community-based protection services are offered to residents in Jazmati, Seken Shebebi, Karm al Tarrab, and Dahret Awwad. 
The center follows an open-door policy, ensuring the active engagement of the community, allowing real-time evaluations and timely adjustments of activities as per beneficiaries’ feedback. In response to the feedback collected from beneficiaries, i.e. via PDMs, satisfaction surveys, and FGDs, and following the strategy of the protection sector, the activities are regularly adjusted to the actual needs, or new activities are included.
In 2022, women are provided with courses aiming to prevent GBV, such as literacy. Boys and girls in school age are provided PSS and interactive learning courses accompanying them throughout the school year. Women, men, and children receive a consecutive and tailored package of protection-related awareness sessions. Boys and girls 14-17 years old will participate in community initiatives. Further, socially isolated elderly are visited in their homes by the trained CS elderly team at least once a month, following up on their psychosocial needs as well as aiming to re(establish) relationships in the community. Women are invited to participate in PSS group sessions. In case mothers of young children are participating, the CS team has established a CFS in the center to take care of the children while the mothers are attending courses. In addition, capacity strengthening activities for the CS team will be offered to further increase the responding capacity of CS.
The target groups are selected interconnectedly, aiming for greater impact within the families and, in turns, the entire community: For example, the husbands or adult sons of women participating in the awareness, PSS or GBV prevention sessions, are invited to FDGs to assess their interest and needs in men’s awareness sessions. The parents of children coming to the center are actively addressed and invited either to participate in one of the protection services or for regular follow-up regarding their children. With a newly established safe referral policy, CS aims to enhance their assistance to cases that need other or more specialized support. 
Following a participatory approach, the needs have been regularly assessed, i.e., via PDMs applying a proportional piling method, and FDGs. Furthermore, a robust FCM has contributed to ensure the engagement and thus self-identification of the needs in the community. Hence, throughout the project lifetime, the engagement of all community members has been promoted, establishing a two-way communication with the community. This has ensured a timely incorporation of community feedback.
The regular coordination with the Aleppo-based sub-sectors Protection, CP, GBV, and FSL, CS ensures alignment of its protection activities while avoiding duplication of efforts. The community center in Jazmati has been well received by the residents of Jazmati since its opening in 2019 and continues to be the central point for the provision of integrated community-based protection services, to women, adolescent girls, children, men and elderly.

PREVENTION OF MALNUTRITION Life-saving food assistance in North-East Nigeria WFP will provide unconditional food assistance to the most food-insecure, crisis-affected populations. Life-saving general food assistance (in-kind food and cash-based transfers) will be delivered to IDPs, returnees, and host populations in North-East Nigeria (Borno, Yobe, and Adamawa States). Early recovery and resilience to shocks will be promoted through asset creation and preservation, increased livelihoods opportunities, and enhanced agricultural value chains. Joint multi-sectoral assessments and Emergency Food Security Analysis will be conducted regularly to monitor the food security, and markets situation in crisis-affected states. 
A gender-transformative approach that meets the needs of women, men, girls, and boys will be adopted. WFP will mainstream protection throughout its work, supported by a solid understanding of the operational context and protection analysis. Training and capacity building of staff and partners in the protection and humanitarian principles will include on-the-job coaching. WFP will ensure that affected populations (women and men) will be consulted throughout the programme cycle; beneficiary feedback mechanisms will be tailored to their preferred means of communication. Beneficiaries will continue to be empowered with knowledge on their food assistance entitlements and their rights, including WFP’s zero-tolerance policy on Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA). Protection against Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) will be embedded in M&E tools, complaint feedback mechanisms, and training of partners and staff.
WFP will continue the collection of key information on beneficiaries and assistance provided as part of its M&E activities. Monthly monitoring will include distribution and activity site management; beneficiary and entitlement verification; and ensuring adequate protection and gender measures. Lessons will be regularly drawn from monthly process and biannual outcome monitoring and reporting, and periodic reviews and evaluation to inform strategic and operational decisions.
WFP will further consolidate partnerships to enhance national and state-level emergency preparedness and response systems, including food security and nutrition assessment and monitoring, early warning, protection, gender analysis, targeting and registration processes, safety nets, cash-based transfer capacities, and supply chain.
Where security and access to land allow, increasing livelihood activities will complement food assistance to support access to productive assets, income-generating activities, and self-reliance in the long term. Assistance will be coordinated with government distributions, ensure food assistance is complimentary and no gaps. self-reliance in the long term. PREVENTION OF MALNUTRITION WFP SOMALIA 2022 HRP - FSC Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas. As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation. The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

PREVENTION AND TREATMENT OF MALNUTRITION Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. Canada to Venezuela HRP 2022 Programa de seguridad alimentaria basado en la escuela  Con el objetivo de contribuir a la seguridad alimentaria de la población con mayores necesidades, el Programa Mundial de Alimentos de Naciones Unidas (WFP, por sus siglas en inglés) en Venezuela desarrolla un programa de asistencia humanitaria basado en la escuela para garantizar el acceso de los más vulnerables a una alimentación adecuada y nutritiva en el entorno escolar, familiar y comunitario. 
Este programa inició en 2021 con comidas escolares en emergencias priorizando escuelas iniciales y de educación especial.

WFP proporciona comidas escolares acompañado de un paquete integrado de intervenciones para mejorar el acceso a alimentos nutritivos y diversificados a través de las escuelas, contribuyendo al mismo tiempo a mejorar la salud y la nutrición de los niños en edad escolar, los estudiantes con discapacidad y el personal escolar, y apoyando a las comunidades a reducir la dependencia en estrategias de afrontamiento. De manera gradual, el WFP está realizando compras locales de alimentos, e incluyendo acciones para apoyar los mercados locales con compras a pequeños productores y apoyo técnico para acceso a mercados.

En este sentido, el programa de comidas escolares en emergencias tiene los siguientes componentes, para asegurar un enfoque integral que apoye al estudiante en el entorno escolar y familiar:

1. Entrega de comidas escolares nutritivas para estudiantes y personal escolar, promoviendo las compras locales y a pequeños productores.
2. Apoyo a la seguridad alimentaria del hogar a través de comida en especie o transferencias monetarias.
3. Rehabilitación de cocinas escolares para garantizar condiciones adecuadas de preparación de alimentos.
4. Comunicación para sensibilizar acerca de los principios humanitarios, la adecuada preparación de alimentos, nutrición, higiene y mantenimiento de cocinas escolares.
5. Fortalecimiento de capacidades de socios implementadores y personal escolar.
6. Acciones sensibles a la nutrición, que incluyen, tamizaje en las escuelas, educación nutricional, referencia a servicios especializados y entrega de alimento complementario fortificado (Supercereal Plus).

Response to the appeal of the United Nations Secretary General on the serious food crisis in Somalia and in favor of the World Food World Food Program (WFP); WFP SOMALIA 2022 HRP - FSC Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas. As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation. The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

Contribution to rehabilitation of irrigation systems in Al Raqqa Light infrastructure rehabilitation and efficient use of water (irrigation canals, wells and irrigation systems). Overall, the Food Security Sector (FSS) estimates that 12 million people in Syria are facing acute food insecurity, which is at least 55.3% of Syria population. While the food insecure figures have slightly declined by at least 4% compared to last year’s record increase, the number of people facing acute food insecurity remains extremely high and 51% higher than in 2019, pre-Lebanese financial crisis period and before the COVID-19 outbreak. Moreover, drought-like conditions in Syria are affecting agriculture production capacity, thus affecting farmer’s livelihoods and local food production.  In this context, FAO has designed a project to assist 240, 000 small-scale farming households (equivalent to 1,440,000 people) in Syria, with the objective of protecting and enhancing the livelihoods of vulnerable farmers and IDPs through the restoration of critical irrigation infrastructures and improve water use efficiency to increase household food production and food security. 
. The project outputs include:
•	Output 1: Critical small-scale irrigation infrastructures in the targeted governorates are assessed and light rehabilitation undertaken. 
•	Output 2: Capacity of technical staff and relevant stakeholders including farmers strengthened to increase water use efficiency and establishment of Water Users Associations (WUAs)
A training programme on enhancing irrigation management, water use efficiency in small-scale irrigation, agricultural land management will be based on FAO standards and approaches. It is expected that stakeholders and farmers will participate in the proposed trainings. 
This project is expected to contribute to increasing access to irrigation water for crisis-affected farmers and their families in the targeted areas through the light rehabilitation of critical small scale irrigation infrastructure. Crop cultivation and other agricultural practices, including livestock and animal feed production, will consequently benefit from the improved water supply plans as an emergency response to the prevailing crisis and drought-like conditions. The proposed intervention will strengthen household food production capacities, skills and knowledge and address immediate food security and nutrition needs, through increasing local availability and supply of food. This may in turn promote flourishing of agricultural based livelihoods in the targeted rural communities, which would contribute to social cohesion, peace and stability. The project seeks to utilize intensive labour in order to maximize community participation and inject cash into the local community.

(2022 portion of EUR 700,000) Enhancing smallholder farmers’ livelihood through market linkage and watershed management with social cohesion approach in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh The project will provide support to the targeted population which is identified by addressing the needs of the Rohingya and host communities through a recent study of FAO (FAO, 2021)  as:
1.	Develop portable skills for Rohingya refugees and improve farm productivity for host communities 
The project will provide technical support to refugees in developing portable skills on homestead gardening that will capacitate and equip them with relevant transferable technological competencies for sustainable integration into the economy upon their return to Myanmar. The project will also provide inputs support to the host communities in practicing climate-smart homestead vegetable gardening production methods for year-round households’ consumption and improved nutrition. 
In addition, the Digital Village initiative will be introduced to connect the farming families to agricultural information, ICT-based extension services, and financial inclusion. This will also promote a decentralized digital knowledge-sharing platform among rural farmers.
2.	Strengthening market linkage and social cohesion
Livelihood activities in the host community will mainly focus on marketing system approaches to ensure sustainability and adaptation of methodologies of the smallholders. In this regard, the project will provide technical support to improve the operational capacities of six Aggregation Centers (ACs) to establish vertical integration of the smallholder farmers with the traders and retailers in accessing the WFP led camp market/outlets. The farmers will be linked with the WFP’s ongoing activities including Fresh Food Corners in Rohingya camps to localize the supply of agricultural goods. This will support the income resilience of local farmers and enhance the social cohesion activity between the Rohingya and host communities.
FAO will work to strengthen functioning of the aggregation centers and provide transports, tools and other infrastructural facilities to them in improving efficacy.
The project will also conduct an assessment in identifying barriers to social cohesion and mapping the dynamics including driving factors within and between host communities and Rohingya people. 
3.	   Watershed and natural resource management
The intervention related to natural resource management will be implemented through a number of activities, such as land stabilization and reforestation which will contribute to the strengthen resilience capacities of communities by reducing climate-related risks, such as floods and landslides. The assessment under this output will provide guidance to project implementation and pave the way for future planning of interventions. 
The project will also contribute to applying climate-smart agricultural practices and diversified income-generating activities for the local farmers and forest-dependent vulnerable communities. This intervention will help the project stakeholders in the adaptive planning and decision-making process for sustainable natural resource management, while simultaneously contributing to the conservation of biodiversity and better functionality of the ecosystem.
Gender, age, and disability Inclusion: Project interventions will be identified considering the needs of men and women with an account of concerns, choice, and extra workload of women. The identified trades will also ensure equal access to men and women based on intersectionality analysis including SADDD (Sex, Age, and Disability Disaggregated Data).

Con el objetivo principal de contribuir a poner fin a las muertes prevenibles de madres, recién nacidos y niños, al tiempo que se promueve la salud y el desarrollo de todos los niños, en el sector de la salud UNICEF aplicará dos enfoques: abordar las desigualdades en los resultados sanitarios y fortalecer los sistemas de salud, incluida la prevención y la respuesta al COVID-19. Simultáneamente, UNICEF apoyará acciones que establezcan mejoras sostenidas en la provisión, utilización y calidad de los servicios, apoyando 150,000 consultas de atención prenatal y las atenciones de parto seguro para 150.000 mujeres embarazadas y sus recién nacidos en hospitales y ambulatorios; proporcionando cuidados intensivos a 7.500 recién nacidos gravemente enfermos, y atenciones pediátricas para 483.820 niños y niñas menores de cinco años. Se proporcionará tratamiento antirretroviral pediátrico ininterrumpido para 1,022 niños menores de 15 años que viven con el VIH y tratamiento para enfermedades oportunistas para 4.970 niños registrados en el programa nacional de VIH, suministros para el diagnóstico precoz del VIH en mujeres embarazadas y niños expuestos, y tratamiento para la prevención de la transmisión materno-infantil del VIH. UNICEF proporcionará ocho vacunas y equipos auxiliares al Programa Ampliado de Inmunización para 1.832.601 niños y niñas de hasta 10 años y 450.681 mujeres embarazadas, y seguirá reforzando la cadena de frío en 24 almacenes regionales y proveyendo refrigeradores para 800 puestos de vacunación para mejorar la capacidad de almacenamiento de vacunas de rutina y las vacunas contra el COVID-19, 24 vehículos para actividades en la comunidad, 7 vehículos refrigerados, 3 botes para áreas remotas fluviales, 25 incineradores para desechos de vacunación y 23 cuartos fríos para mejorar la capacidad del programa ampliado de vacunación.

Para contribuir a la protección del personal de salud, 60.000 trabajadores de primera línea recibirán EPP. UNICEF mantendrá su enfoque en apoyar a los diferentes integrantes del sistema de Protección para que brinden servicios de prevención y respuestas de calidad con un enfoque en edad, género y diversidad para los NNA y familias más vulnerables y en riesgo. UNICEF mantendrá los esfuerzos en el desarrollo de los objetivos e indicadores sectoriales del Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria 2022-2023, a través de planes de trabajo con socios implementadores nacionales e internacionales. La Protección de la Infancia es la prevención y respuesta a la explotación, abuso, negligencia, prácticas nocivas y la violencia contra los niños, niñas y adolescentes (NNA). Está incorporada en la Convención sobre los Derechos del Niño y las Metas de Desarrollo Sostenible. Con un abordaje socio-ecológico, UNICEF y sus socios trabajaran con un enfoque en los NNA, las familias, las comunidades y el sistema de protección formal e informal para que acciones preventivas y de respuestas para temas de protección de NNA sean implementadas en los estados priorizados del país.  El enfoque principal de esta propuesta es la prevención que se realiza no solamente a través de los socios de protección, pero también con el apoyo de otros sectores como nutrición y educación para cumplir resultados de protección infantil. Los principales temas cubiertos incluyen: VbG, separación familiar, violencia en general incluyendo la de género y crianza positiva. Además de nuestro enfoque central en la prevención, UNICEF Venezuela se enfoca en que ningún NNA se quede atrás: trabajaremos con socios para alcanzar a los NNA con mayor riesgo de protección que incluyen NNA con discapacidades, NNA separados y no acompañados, de poblaciones indígenas y afro-descendientes y NNA que sufren otras formas de discriminación y exclusión. 
Donde los NNA están sufriendo violaciones, UNICEF trabajará con socios gubernamentales y no-gubernamentales para fortalecer el acceso a los servicios de respuesta para prevenir reincidencia y brindar atención, apoyo y justicia. Los principales servicios brindados incluyen: apoyo en acceder a registro de nacimiento, salud mental y apoyo psicosocial, gestión de caso incluyendo a NNA sobreviviente de VbG. Una modalidad diferente para alcanzar objetivos de protección será la de las transferencias monetarias, otra componente importante de todas las intervenciones es el enfoque en la calidad y en temas transversales como lo de género, AAP, PEAS y discapacidad. El numero total de NNA alcanzado (sin calcular el apoyo al Ministerio de Salud con EV25) será de 628,536.

Humanitarian crisis in Somalia WFP SOMALIA 2022 HRP - FSC Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas. As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation. The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

South Sudan	South Sudan Humanitarian Response Plan 2022 Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2022, there are some 335,000 refugees and asylum seekers from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, primarily from Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic.
At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for longer term stability, hundreds of thousands of South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since the signing of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan, this spontaneous movement has prompted the development of an area-based approach, to support refugees, returnees and host communities, through enhanced engagement with development actors, to support greater access to services where possible.
Refugees largely reside in conflict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction in basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.
Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will benefit from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Specific protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identified at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with specific protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as verification exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the efficiency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to benefit from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

Multi-sectoral assistance to populations affected by humanitarian crises in Somalia
---- Protection Strengthening the Protection of Crisis Affected Communities through Timely and Effective Humanitarian Interventions in Somalia and Somaliland. The Humanitarian Crisis in Somalia continues to further aggravate with over 7.7 million people projected to require urgent and life-saving assistance in 2022, a significant increase from 2019 (4.9 million) and 2020 (5.2 million). The principle drivers being the deepened armed conflict in many parts of South-Central Somalia and erratic climatic conditions with flooding and drought happening simultaneously in different parts of the Country. 
This coupled with COVID 19 pandemic, not only hampers access to basic services but also leads to increased marginalization of minority groups, displaced persons and persons with special needs, heightened protection risks, loss of livelihoods and income, and limited freedom of movement. In addition, communities have reduced coping capacities and resilience, with women and girls, minority clan members, and people living with disabilities being disproportionately affected. With the country gearing for state and federal elections, there is the likelihood of displacements and disruptions of lives amid intensified attacks from non-state actors. Recent conflicts and violence in mid-2021 displaced 250,000 people in Banaadir, Bardaale and Badweyn, including nearly 207,000 people who were temporally displaced in Mogadishu owing to election-related violence in April 2021. This against a backdrop of limited and constrained humanitarian assistance will not only result in loss of lives, affected livelihoods and destroyed property, but also increased vulnerabilities and heightened protection risks for vulnerable groups.
Data from the PRMN, SPMS and MRM systems designates heightened protection risks in the country with over 4 million people projected to need lifesaving protection assistance (HNO, 2021).  The GBV AOR reported a spike in Intimate Partner Violence, rape, sexual exploitation, sexual harassment and abuse against women and girls in 2021 most of which are from displacement affected communities. Furthermore, accruing to the MRM data, Somalia is now the most dangerous conflict on earth for children, where over 23,000 grave violations were recorded in the last 5 year, and of concern is the number of child recruitment and abductions far exceeding any other country in the world. 
Thus, DRC will design and implement interventions targeting the most vulnerable persons in the communities including DACs, girls, women, boys, and men at risk of/ survivors of GBVs, minority groups/clans, persons with disabilities, children and adults affected by armed violence including explosive remnants of wars (ERWs) and other explosive devices, people at risk of forced evictions and most vulnerable host communities to strengthening capacity and the commitment of families and communities to protect communities especially children and women from violence, exploitation and harmful practices, through elimination of harmful practices and all forms of gender-based violence, provision of timely holistic and quality age and gender appropriate services to survivors, persons at risks and vulnerable persons including PSNs in addition to strengthened community-based protection systems.
The proposed interventions thus align with the general protection, GBV, Explosive Hazards (EH) and Housing, Land and Property (HLP) cluster objectives and indicators and the Strategic objectives 1, 2 and 3 of 2022 Humanitarian Response Plan.  The interventions will employ participatory and right based approaches, age, gender and diversity (AGD) approach and community-based child protection approaches which will involve, inclusion of children and caregivers from refugee’s/asylum seeker communities, migrants, IDPs, persons with disability and most vulnerable host communities in addition to local authorities in the project management cycle. 
DRC targets to reach 58,500 persons (10,000girls,2,500B,30,000W,16,000M) in selected districts in Somalia.

Improving Food security for vulnerable populations in Somaliland, particularly  IDPs in Hargeisa, Togdheer, and Sool Somalia is facing a growing number of threats to its food security. The ongoing desert locust invasion, socio-economic effects of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic and recurrent climate shocks, including frequent flooding and drought, continue to severely impact the lives and livelihoods of the vulnerable population. With this multifaceted crises, 7.7 Million people across Somalia need in emergency food assistance. With humanitarian needs expected to further increase in 2022, it is critical to enhance immediate food access, protect and restore livelihoods and strengthen the resilience of vulnerable households. Sustained humanitarian assistance is required to prevent the further deterioration of food security and nutrition.
Through this project, Plan International and Partners will effectively provide emergency assistance for food and promote dignity and choices among project participants by increasing purchasing power with short term injection of unconditional cash transfers for 1182 HH (7092 beneficiaries; 3546F, 3546M) for six months. Through field monitoring, government reports, and sector coordination, Plan and Partners will target households in areas identified as IPC3 or worse, risk of drought, and/or IDP communities, including those recently evicted by Somaliland government. These families have insufficient income to cover rising cost of food particularly during periods of drought and other shocks due to COVID19, instability and climate change, and will qualify per criteria, e.g. female headed household, household with person with disability, etc. Partners will ensure the crises affected families receive messages on Infant, Young Child Feeding and Hygiene and have access to sufficient, safe and nutritious foods to meet their dietary needs and food preferences for an active and healthy life. Partners have complementary programs running in these areas to enable consultant and selection within communities. By targeting vulnerable families particularly with children and delivering this intervention in a gender sensitive manner, Plan strives for secondary outcomes of improved the protection environment with reduced risks to women and girls.

This allocation contributes to meeting the objectives of UNHCR’s response plan for Syria. UNHCR supports refugees, internally displaced people (IDPs) and returnees (refugees and internally displaced people who have returned to their home areas) by providing assistance to those most in need using a community-based and area-based approach. Enhancement of protection of displaced persons, returnees and conflict affected host communities in Syria through integrated, community-based protection activities. The project aims to strengthen protection and resilience of Syrian IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host communities through advocacy, coordination, provision of community-based protection services and legal services UNHCR Syria will continue to lead the Protection Sector/Cluster to ensure coordinated protection interventions programming for safe refugees return. UNHCR’s protection interventions include legal counselling and assistance, protection monitoring, referrals and information sharing, social protection through livelihoods support to most vulnerable people, GBV prevention and response, child protection, psychosocial support and in-kind assistance for persons with specific needs including persons with disabilities, non-formal education, and awareness activities on various subjects targeting women, men, boys and girls. In addition to over 125 community centres providing integrated protection services, outreach to communities will be convened through over 2,800 outreach volunteers. Accountability to affected people will be realized through meaningful participation of communities based on age, gender and diversity approach, structured focus group discussions and enhancement of the community-based feedback and complaint mechanisms. UNHCR will continue its capacity building efforts to ensure services are delivered according to the standards and that accountability to affected population and do no harm principles are respected. UNHCR Syria will continue to lead Protection Sector in coordination of response plans of IDPs and affected people as well it will execute leadership roles in refugee return programmes in collaboration with the Government. Monitoring and evaluation of the planned interventions is based on the reports and observations by the partners and on regular direct observation and ongoing assessment by UNHCR and the comparison of achievements and related financial expenditures with objectives. Evaluation is conducted through different channels including the post distribution monitoring to determine the effectiveness of/measure the satisfaction of POCs with the service and the distribution process in addition to multiple satisfaction surveys and tracking tools related to different protection interventions. Monitoring and evaluation activities are carried out at various levels by partners and agencies implementing subprojects, UNHCR Branch Office, Sub Office and Field Offices. Situation reports are submitted by all UNHCR Field Offices to their respective Supervising Office and Branch Offices submit a corresponding report to Headquarters.

Supplies in kind (CIK) of RUTF Northeast Nigeria Nutrition Response 2022 The Nutrition response in 2022 will prioritise implementation of the nutrition lifesaving activities (inpatient, outpatient, and targeted supplemental feeding programmes) and targeting of LGAs with high rates of GAM (above 10%) such as MMC/Jere, Nganzai, Bama, Machina. Hard-to-reach areas (such as Gubio, Rann, Magumeri), areas with large IDP  and returnee populations (like Monguno) and high-risk/inaccessible locations such as Marte LGA will also be prioritised for nutrition assistance. 
UNICEF will primarily target acutely malnourished children and PLW who are at a significantly high risk of death. The nutrition response will also target the total under-five and PLW with preventive nutrition services e.g. micronutrient supplementation to ensure levels of acute malnutrition are not above average thresholds, and to also reduce morbidity and mortality. The response will prioritise households with persons living with disabilities, who face barriers in accessing health, nutrition and WASH services and are disproportionately food insecure due to high levels of exclusion. 
The nutrition status of the targeted population in the BAY states significantly deteriorates during the period from May-August every year, which is the lean season and coincides with the rainy season. The season is characterised by very high rates of acute malnutrition with medical complications due to poor food access and a high prevalence of diarrhoea and malaria. UNICEF will need to adequately prepare for the lean season period by prepositioning supplies, increasing the overall sector capacity to treat acute malnutrition with a focus on inpatient care and IYCF-E
The nutrition response in BAY states will be contextualised in 2022 based on the following categorisation: 
1. Protracted crisis e.g north and central Borno LGAs where the rates of acute malnutrition are high, worsened by poor access to food and health systems. The approach in these areas will include INGO/NNGO direct support to the affected population, and prioritisation of lifesaving nutrition activities. 
3. New emergencies – locations of new crisis and fluctuations such as relocations, displacements and spike in acute malnutrition. The approach will focus on the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) with a focus on lifesaving activities. 
4. Hard-to-reach / inaccessible areas – locations with limited humanitarian footprints and access e.g Gubio and Magumeri. The approach will include RRM and remote management strategy (where feasible) with a focus on life-saving interventions. UNICEF will also strengthen the implementation of nutrition interventions through local organizations or community-based structures to implement nutrition services in hard-to-reach/inaccessible areas. 
UNICEF response is primarily through services and in-kind deliveries. UNICEF will employ the use of cash and voucher assistance (CVA) to fill the nutrient gap in the Nutrition/Food Minimum Expenditure Basket to ensure that populations have access to a varied diet e.g CVA for meats and vegetables. 
The nutrition status of the affected population is an outcome of various underlying issues including access to health, WASH, food security, child protection, and gender issues. The main cause of acute malnutrition among children and women in BAY states is the high morbidity rates. High diarrhoea prevalence is the major cause of acute malnutrition among the IDPs and urban poor population due to the prevailing poor hygiene and sanitation conditions worsened by congested living conditions. The response will strengthen the integration of nutrition-sensitive interventions including WASH, food security, health, livelihoods and child protection, and gender-based violence risk mitigation.
UNICEF will prioritise projects that include basic nutrition packages such as integrated treatment of acute malnutrition (SAM and MAM) and prevention services including integration with WASH, food security, health and protections services.
