Somalia/CE	Somalia Food Assistance,Nutritione Providing Life Saving Treatment and Prevention Nutrition Services to the Vulnerable Communities in Somalia Food and Nutrition context in Somalia
Decades of conflict and natural disasters including repeated droughts and seasonal flooding followed by limited government and institutional support have had a profound negative effect on the food security situation and social service sector in Somalia. Nearly seven in ten Somalis live on less than USD 1.90 per day,  the sixth-highest poverty rate in sub-Saharan Africa. Poverty is both widespread and deep, particularly for households in rural areas and internally displaced person (IDP) settlements. The number of food-insecure people experiencing long-term stress is trending upwards, indicating that chronic food insecurity persists, requiring sustainable solutions. Recurrent climate-related shocks and political instability are key drivers of food insecurity and pose continuing risks to crop production and food access. Malnutrition in Somalia is driven by a combination of factors such as recurrent food insecurity, child illnesses, high morbidity, micronutrient deficiencies, low immunization levels, poor access to clean water and sanitation, poor hygiene practice, gender inequality and discriminatory sociocultural attitudes leading to poor care practices. Based on the latest Post Gu FSNAU assessment (September 2021), it is estimated that a total of 3.5 million out of the 15.8m people face acute food insecurity (IPC 3 and above – crisis or worse)  until December 2021. At the national level the median prevalence of Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) has remained at a serious level of 11.1%. Approximately 1.2 million children under the age of five are likely to be acutely malnourished, including 295,515 who are likely to be severely malnourished. In addition to this, around 245,909 Pregnant & Lactating Women (PLWs) will be at risk of acute malnutrition. 

Acute malnutrition is a major public health problem in Somalia. It affects disproportionately children under the age of five, as well as Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLWs), especially among IDPs, vulnerable (agro) pastoralist communities and those living in areas affected by flooding. Morbidity among children is high (≥ 20%). Out of a total of 40 surveyed population groups 18 recorded high morbidity presence of above 20%. 
Vitamin A supplementation and Measles vaccination remains low <40% in several population groups. 

TB prevalence remains one of the highest globally with Somalia in the top 10 countries with high TB burden (262 per 100,000 population) while the HIV prevalence remains <1% however with high stigma and discrimination levels at 94%.

Project activities
The World Food Program is the leading UN agency in Somalia in fighting hunger. In Somalia, WFP together with the Ministry of Health (MoH), nutrition cluster and the partners, supports nutrition service delivery and prevention. WFP collaborates with the MoH and UNICEF to offer an integrated package of nutrition and health, following the revised MoH IMAM guidelines for treating acute malnutrition in Somalia.

WFP will cover both treatment and preventive nutrition services including:
•	Targeted Supplementary Feeding Program for 665,846 moderately acute malnourished children 6-59 months; 173,746 malnourished Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLW), 10,794 malnourished People Living with HIV on ART treatment and malnourished TB patients.
•	Preventive Nutrition services for 386,102 children 6-23 months and 173,746 PLW enrolled in Maternal Child Health and Nutrition services and blanket Supplementary Feeding Program for children 6-23 months and PLW in districts where GAM (Global Acute Malnutrition) rate is above 15%.
•	Monthly cash vouchers of USD 15 for 24,104 PLWs in selected target districts.
•	24,206 caregivers with SAM children admitted to the Stabilisation  will receive food while staying at the Stabilisation Center 
•	A total of 96,150 pregnant women will receive food rations for their families when delivering their baby at a health facility

Syria: Protecting children and supporting the future of Syria and the region
Cross-Sectoral (two or more outcome areas) Strengthening Child Protection interventions for girls and boys most at risk of violence, abuse, neglect and exploitation across whole of Syria In line with the CP Area of Responsibility (AOR) Strategy and the “No Lost Generation” framework, UNICEF will enhance equitable access to quality CP services with a resilience focus, including for Survivors of abuse, violence, neglect and exploitation as well as children with disabilities, targeting 117 high severity sub-districts (3 to 5) and 38 low severity ones.

UNICEF’s CP Strategy in 2022-2023 includes:
• Addressing behavioural, social, cultural and economic determinants of CP violations as a prevention approach.  
• Improving the reach and quality of specialized CP services
• Capacity development of CP responders
•  Monitoring, evidence generation and advocacy 

UNICEF will support the delivery of integrated programming that will encourage social transformation, prioritizing:
• Structured and sustained CP MHPSS and EORE programmes
• Specialized integrated CP services including case management for survivors of violence, exploitation, neglect and abuse (child labour, CAFAAG, child survivors of GBV, child marriages, justice for children, birth registration and unaccompanied or separated children amongst others) 
• Parenting programmes to promote positive child rearing skills and experience for caregivers
• Elimination of violence against children, including GBV prevention and empowerment for girls, boys and women, prevention of violence in schools, homes and communities.
• Awareness-raising on CP risks
• Capacity development of CP responders and social workers

UNICEF will generate evidence to inform the humanitarian response and advocacy including setting up an information management system for case management. UNICEF will embrace new delivery modalities and implement cash transfers aimed at child protection outcomes for vulnerable families. UNICEF will also continue to support the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism on grave violations against children.

CP services will be delivered by partners based on minimum standards and IASC guidelines. 7,200 CP and social workers will be trained on case management, MHPSS, EORE, advocacy, evidence generation and coordination across sectors for a comprehensive CP response.
 
UNICEF will support MHPSS for 364,000 children to benefit from improved mental health and social wellbeing. UNICEF will equip 61,500 parents and caregivers with skills to provide a stimulating and safe environment at home, including reduced violence.  

Violence prevention is a key priority. Family violence prevalence is high for girls 12-17 years (47%), boys 12-17 years (44%), boys below 12 (45%) and girls below 12 (44%) (UNICEF 2018). UNICEF will work to protect children from violence and abuse through prevention activities in schools, homes and communities and providing survivors of violence with child-friendly and gender sensitive services. Support will be provided for PSEA mechanisms to protect beneficiaries and build the capacity of humanitarian actors. PSEA programming will be implemented with the Protection Sector AORs.

Based on HNO 2021, one in three communities in Syria is reportedly contaminated by explosive ordnance. One in four victims is a child (Joint MA & CP Analysis, 2020). EORE messages will be provided to 1,460,000 children and adults through humanitarian actors and public service providers using static facilities and mobile teams. Food assistance WFP SOMALIA 2022 HRP - FSC Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas. As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation. The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

Multi-Sector Assistance for Sudanese Refugees in Ajuong Thok and Pamir Refugee Camps, and Child Protection  Intervention for the Host Community in Pariang County Integrated Food Security and Livelihoods Protection in Mayendit and Panyijiar Counties, Unity State, South Sudan  The project objective(s) is to enhance and sustain emergency food production through complementary vegetable and crop livelihood inputs, fishing, and livestock; reduce dependency on food and agricultural inputs to support and strengthen households’ ability to absorb shocks in a way that prevents the spread and transmission of COVID-19 for households affected by floods and conflict in Panyijiar and Mayendit counties, Unity state of South Sudan. The IRC proposes to provide a sequence of food production to support to most severe food-insecure and malnourished households in the main season farming of May to July and dry season of Nov to March. To strengthen households’ resilience, the project will mainstream gender, conflict sensitivity, disaster risks reduction, and COVID-19 risk mitigation measures to support at-risk households focused on improving vegetable, crop, livestock, and fisheries production and bolstering resilience towards recurrent shocks and stresses. In pursuit of the project objective(s), the following activities will be implemented: 
(a) The IRC together with the complaint and feedback mechanism (CFM/AAP) committee will mobilize, engage community members to inform the needs of the most vulnerable households and selection criteria for registration together with Nutrition partners. 
(b) Preposition and distribute emergency (short-term maturing) agricultural inputs (Cereal & Vegetable seeds, and tools) and fishing kits to 53,760 people. The IRC anticipates FAO will provide complimentary in-kind inputs to support the project. During distribution, community health volunteers will be engaged to disseminate COVID-19 messages, provide personal protective kits including facemasks, hand washing station, hand sanitizers, and limit the crowd at distribution points following COVID-19 protocol. 
(c) To improve nutritional practices for pregnant women and caregivers of children under 5 years with MAM and SAM. Nutrient-dense vegetable seeds will be provided, establish demonstration gardens at nutrition facilities close to water points, provide basic training on vegetable production, harvest, and conservation techniques. The IRC Nutrition team will conduct nutrition-sensitive awareness, food cooking demonstrations showing how to enrich households’ meals with locally available foods.
(d) The IRC will identify 400 potential seed producers, provide foundation seeds, establish seeds multiplication centers and plots. The seed producers will receive at least 200 USD cash grants, training on quality seeds selection, quality seeds production techniques, and crop management practices. Seed producers will be supported to form VSLA to increase access to finance for seeds production and access to markets will be facilitated.  
(e) The IRC with the County Agriculture Department, State Ministry of Agriculture, and FAO will contribute to livestock disease surveillance and monitoring, facilitate vaccination campaigns, mass vaccination exercises and treatments to livestock to be led by CAHW.
(f) Facilitate capacity building to community-based extension agents (CAHWs, AEA’s), crop producers, pastoralists, and fisherfolks on sustainable production skills and provision of proximate extension services on production, post-harvest handling through demonstration gardens. Also, fisherfolks to receive basic training on fish preservation and kit repairs to enhance household nutrition and income.
Overall, the project will reach 6% most vulnerable households in need (HNO, 2022) in Panyijiar (33,000 People) and Mayendit (20,160 People) equivalent to a total of 53,760 people (5,376 Male children, 8,064 Female children, 12,902 Adult male, 19,354 Adult Female, 3,225 elderly Male, 4,839 elder Female) people. By program type: 53,760 livelihoods inputs distribution (Crop, Vegetable, Tools & fishing Kits), 5,376 people production skills (Crop, Vegetables, fisheries skills (Fishing kits repairs, fish preservation etc) training and 400 seeds growers/producers

Multi-Sector Assistance for Sudanese Refugees in Ajuong Thok and Pamir Refugee Camps, and Child Protection  Intervention for the Host Community in Pariang County Facilitating access to protection and justice services, and information services on protection and HLP for recovery of at-risk displacement and conflict-affected  people in Mayendit, Panyijiar and Juba Rejaf in South Sudan The proposed project in Unity State and Juba is designed to provide protection services through strengthening the protection capacity and resilience of the most vulnerable individuals in targeted communities of Mayendit, Panyijiar and Juba (Rejaf) of South Sudan. The project will have a 60% protection mitigation and response component and a 40% access to justice and HLP rights component. The protection concerns of the communities across South Sudan and specifically in areas where there is little to no permanent protection actors remain high. Communal violence, including cyclical revenge killing, tribal conflict, and cattle-related violence, have continued across the country, fueled by negative coping mechanisms resulting from multi-generational trauma and militarized community response structures. Repeated shocks have weakened individual and household capacity and community-based structures plus consistent services. Government continue to exhibit and perpetuate a weak system that compels the civil society to fill that gap so as to address protection and HLP needs of people in need. In light of that, durable remains a pipe dream for displaced and conflict affected people in Mayendit, Panyijiar and Juba Rejaf. Through an integrated protection and lifesaving support mechanisms (collaborating with IRC WPE, CP, ERD, Health and Nutrition actions coupled with interventions by other actors plus linking with service provider alliances from the government), this action intends to provide protection mitigation and response activities including responsive protection, return/ post return and HLP monitoring, comprehensive protection case management, targetted individual assistance including emergency cash assistance to the most vulnerable groups of people, legal counseling and assistance (coining a fine nexus with HLP support activities and referrals from WPE and CP), two-way communication and information system (linking with and integrating risk communication services), incident profiling and reporting, and provide a platform for discourse on HLP and durable solutions. This activity will be complemented through the strengthening of community-based protection networks plus establishing a community of paralegals that will assist in the identification of vulnerable beneficiaries and the provision of support provided to individuals with protection, legal and HLP concerns in their communities. Housing, Land and Property (HLP) rights is becoming one of the most critical issues for IDPs, and returnees in Panyijiar, Mayendit and Juba (including host of displaced communities). As such this action will promote community-based monitoring of HLP issues, establish HLP trends to inform response and advocacy, raise awareness on HLPs and build the capacity of duty bearers at county level and community level on their role and need to prioritize HLP concerns as human rights issues. IRC will deploy a roving legal protection team to support access to justice and HLP programming. In Panyijiar and Juba, IRC will scale up its protection and rule of law activities that empower communities to influence their recovery and protection - placing the centrality of protection across all the activities, and taking into account conflict sensitivity aspects. Protection activities will be conducted through static and mobile teams in Mayendit and Panyijiar. The action will also endeavor to create links between protection actors and peace committees in the target locations to implement peace building activities.

Nigeria/CE-NE 	Nigeria	(USAID/BHA) Life-saving food assistance in North-East Nigeria WFP will provide unconditional food assistance to the most food-insecure, crisis-affected populations. Life-saving general food assistance (in-kind food and cash-based transfers) will be delivered to IDPs, returnees, and host populations in North-East Nigeria (Borno, Yobe, and Adamawa States). Early recovery and resilience to shocks will be promoted through asset creation and preservation, increased livelihoods opportunities, and enhanced agricultural value chains. Joint multi-sectoral assessments and Emergency Food Security Analysis will be conducted regularly to monitor the food security, and markets situation in crisis-affected states. 
A gender-transformative approach that meets the needs of women, men, girls, and boys will be adopted. WFP will mainstream protection throughout its work, supported by a solid understanding of the operational context and protection analysis. Training and capacity building of staff and partners in the protection and humanitarian principles will include on-the-job coaching. WFP will ensure that affected populations (women and men) will be consulted throughout the programme cycle; beneficiary feedback mechanisms will be tailored to their preferred means of communication. Beneficiaries will continue to be empowered with knowledge on their food assistance entitlements and their rights, including WFP’s zero-tolerance policy on Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA). Protection against Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) will be embedded in M&E tools, complaint feedback mechanisms, and training of partners and staff.

Lessons will be regularly drawn from monthly process and biannual outcome monitoring and reporting, and periodic reviews and evaluation to inform strategic and operational decisions.

Where security and access to land allow, increasing livelihood activities will complement food assistance to support access to productive assets, income-generating activities, and self-reliance in the long term. Improving Malian refugees, IDP and host communitiesliving conditions in Ouallam, Abala and Ayerou (Tillabery region) Assurer l'accès à l'eau potable et à un assainissement viable aux IDPs et communautés hôtes de Ouallam, région de Tillaberi Par le présent projet, GOAL Niger vise à apporter une assistance WASH aux personnes déplacés internes ainsi que leur communauté d’accueil dans le département de Ouallam, région de Tillabéry. Cette assistance concernera l'accès à l'eau potable, la promotion des latrines et la sensibilisation sur l'hygiène et la Covid-19,  tout en garantissant la protection des plus vulnérables.
Ainsi, notre action dans le sous-secteur de l'eau visera à :
- Renforcer la disponibilité de l'eau à Tondikiwindi: réaliser, grâce à ce financement, une extension de la mini-AEP vers le site des déplacés avec une borne fontaines d'au moins  4 robinets de puisage. Ce qui permet la disponibilité de l'eau sécurisée pour au moins 1 000 personnes conformément aux normes nationales ou 2 000 déplacés conformément aux normes SPHERE.  
- Garantir l'accès sécurisé à l'eau potable à  1 470 ménages soit 10 290 déplaces 5 sur les 4 sites d'accueil:  Cet accès sera garanti auprès des gérants en subventionnant une moyenne de 10 litres par jour par personnes pendant 10 mois pour les ménages les plus vulnérables. Une enquête HEA sera conduite afin de mener un ciblage qui prendra en compte de manière intentionnelle les besoins des personnes et/ou des groupes les plus vulnérables à savoir les ménages des personnes vivant avec handicap, ceux dirigés par des femmes ou des enfants, ceux accueillant des enfants non accompagnés, les ménages avec les personnes âgées. 
- promouvoir la purification de l'eau dans les 4 localités à travers un appui à la vulgarisation des purifiants par des opérateurs économiques privés. l'objectif étant de disposer d'au moins un revendeur de purifiants d'eau dans chacune des localités.
Pour l'assainissement:
Vu que les latrines d’urgence ne rencontrent pas l’assentiment des bénéficiaires, GOAL se propose d'initier un dialogue communautaire autour de la défécation a l’aire libre et convenir d’un plan d’action basé sur le renforcement du système en faveur des latrines améliorées au niveau des sites et des communautés hôtes. Ceci tournera notamment autour de la mise en place de kits d’EHA classiques, d'un réseau de maçons privés et de structures communautaires d’EHA pour encourager la bonne pratique, une stratégie favorisant la demande des latrines et la gestion des déchets solides.
 Pour susciter davantage la demande, des concours inter quartiers d'hygiène et assainissement seront lancés sur chaque sites avec l'adhésion des bénéficiaires. les critères établis par les bénéficiaires, seront évalués par des jurys locaux et les lauréats récompensés par des kits WASH. Nous envisageons de former une vingtaine de maçons privés, équipés pour la construction des latrines améliorées dans les 4 localités. Ces maçons seront utilisés pour la construction de 500 latrines familiales améliorées principalement à Mangaizé, mais également sur les autres sites.
1 000 kits NFI WASH constitués de 2 bidons, 1 seau, 15 savons et 3 serviettes hygiéniques seront également partagés aux bénéficiaires. 48 relais communautaires seront formés pour la promotion de l'hygiène sur les 4 sites.
Enfin, une campagne de sensibilisation radiophonique sera entreprise à travers les 2 radios communautaires de Ouallam et Tondikiwindi, sur les thématiques de l'hygiène assainissement et de la COVID-19.

Improving Malian refugees, IDP and host communitiesliving conditions in Ouallam, Abala and Ayerou (Tillabery region) Promouvoir la protection et la cohésion sociale entre les populations déplacées et les communautés hôtes de Ouallam,Tillaberi GOAL est présente sur les 4 sites des déplacés de Ouallam à savoir Ouallam, Tondikiwindi, Diney et Mangaizé, sur financement de OCHA (FRHAOC) dans les secteurs de la santé (Cliniques mobiles), nutrition, Abris et biens non alimentaires.
GOAL vise à travers ce nouveau projet à donner une réponse aux gaps en contribuant aux Objectifs Spécifiques 1 et 3 du cluster protection, en renforçant la cohésion sociale par une sensibilisation sur les thématiques de la protection et de la redevabilité ainsi que des actions d’accompagnement et de réhabilitation (AGR) pour certains vulnérables, dans les sites IDPs des communes rurales de Tondikiwindi et Ouallam, dudit département.
Le projet ciblera intentionnellement parmi les populations déplacées et les communautés hôtes les veuves, les ménages dirigés par les femmes ou les enfants, les personnes vivant avec handicap, les vieillards, les familles accueillant les enfants non accompagnés, les jeunes filles, les élèves déplacés.
L’éveil des consciences général et le renforcement de l’autonomisation financière se feront à travers des formations, des sensibilisations sur les thématiques de protections et des remises des kits de protection ou de réhabilitation.
Ainsi le projet contribuera en:
•	Formant les personnels sur la sécurité, l'équipe genre et inclusion sociale, les droits des enfants et leurs protections, la protection transversale, la redevabilité, PSEA et le plaidoyer lobbying, Do No Harm.
•	Mettant en place un cadre d'écoute et d'échange favorables aux plus vulnérables notamment les PVH, les femmes. Ainsi, des points focaux genre sensible seront identifiés avec les communautés suivant le zonage existant sur chaque site (ou ajuste au besoin). Ces points focaux et les mobilisateurs communautaires seront formes et accompagnes sur l'équité genre et inclusion sociale, les droits des enfants et leurs protections, la protection transversale, la redevabilité, PSEA et le plaidoyer lobbying) pour mieux prendre en compte les intérêts des plus vulnérables. GN s'appuiera sur l'existant en termes de structuration tout en le renforçant.
•	mettant en relation les points focaux protection avec les autres acteurs clés de la protection de leurs zones pour le référencement au besoin.
•	collaborant avec les autres partenaires intervenant dans les programmes pour une meilleure prise en compte des plus vulnérables dans leurs ciblages. 
•	Organisant des conférences débats sur la cohésion sociale et/ou Organisation d'émissions radios sur la paix et la réconciliation.
•	Créant et diffuser des messages de sensibilisation via la plateforme de service Viamo.
•	Organisant des séances de sensibilisation sur la prévention au COVID-19.
•	Mettant en place un mécanisme d’Ecoute & de Gestion des Plaintes.
•	Renforçant et promouvant les activités génératrices de revenus comme le maraichage, VSLA, la savonnerie, la teinturerie, tricotage etc au profit de vulnérables (veuves, enfant chef de ménage) pour renforcer leur autonomisation.
Compte tenu du contexte sécuritaire, toutes les formations se feront à Ouallam. GOAL intervient toujours en collaboration avec les autorités locales, les services techniques déconcentrés, les bénéficiaires, les partenaires présents.

2022 UNHCR Global Appeal  (STATE/PRM) Enhancement of protection of displaced persons, returnees and conflict affected host communities in Syria through integrated, community-based protection activities. The project aims to strengthen protection and resilience of Syrian IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host communities through advocacy, coordination, provision of community-based protection services and legal services UNHCR Syria will continue to lead the Protection Sector/Cluster to ensure coordinated protection interventions programming for safe refugees return. UNHCR’s protection interventions include legal counselling and assistance, protection monitoring, referrals and information sharing, social protection through livelihoods support to most vulnerable people, GBV prevention and response, child protection, psychosocial support and in-kind assistance for persons with specific needs including persons with disabilities, non-formal education, and awareness activities on various subjects targeting women, men, boys and girls. In addition to over 125 community centres providing integrated protection services, outreach to communities will be convened through over 2,800 outreach volunteers. Accountability to affected people will be realized through meaningful participation of communities based on age, gender and diversity approach, structured focus group discussions and enhancement of the community-based feedback and complaint mechanisms. UNHCR will continue its capacity building efforts to ensure services are delivered according to the standards and that accountability to affected population and do no harm principles are respected. UNHCR Syria will continue to lead Protection Sector in coordination of response plans of IDPs and affected people as well it will execute leadership roles in refugee return programmes in collaboration with the Government. Monitoring and evaluation of the planned interventions is based on the reports and observations by the partners and on regular direct observation and ongoing assessment by UNHCR and the comparison of achievements and related financial expenditures with objectives. Evaluation is conducted through different channels including the post distribution monitoring to determine the effectiveness of/measure the satisfaction of POCs with the service and the distribution process in addition to multiple satisfaction surveys and tracking tools related to different protection interventions. Monitoring and evaluation activities are carried out at various levels by partners and agencies implementing subprojects, UNHCR Branch Office, Sub Office and Field Offices. Situation reports are submitted by all UNHCR Field Offices to their respective Supervising Office and Branch Offices submit a corresponding report to Headquarters.

SUPPORT TO VULNERABLE MALIAN REFUGEES AND SELECTED HOST AND IDP COMMUNITIES THROUGH LIVELIHOODS AND PROTECTION ACTIVITIES IN THE NORTH AND SAHEL REGIONS OF BURKINA FASO - PHASE III Renforcement des moyens d’existence des Personnes Déplacées Internes (PDI), des communautés hôtes et des populations affectées par la crise humanitaire dans les régions du Nord, du Centre Nord, du Sahel, de l’Est et du Centre-Est L’OIM prévoit de fournir une réponse en renforcement des moyens d’existence pour les ménages affectés, déplacés et hôtes à travers la distribution de kits agricoles et d’élevage, la construction/réhabilitation de structures communautaires et la réalisation des petites entreprises.

Forte de sa présence de longue date au Burkina Faso avec plus de 80 staff, un bureau principal à Ouagadougou et cinq sous-bureaux répartis dans les régions, notamment à Kaya (Centre-Nord), Dori (Sahel), Ouahigouya (Nord), Fada (Est) et Tenkodogo (Centre-Est), l’OIM est engagée dans la réponse collective afin d’aider le Gouvernement du Burkina Faso à faire face aux besoins multisectoriels générés par la situation humanitaire. l’OIM a une équipe d’urgence en place depuis 2019, qui comprend notamment un Coordinateur d’Urgences, une chargée de projets d’urgence, deux assistants experts en abris, et cinq assistants de projet repartis dans les cinq sous-bureaux sur le terrain. 

L’OIM est un membre actif et contribuant du Cluster Sécurité Alimentaire et Renforcements de Moyens d’Existence depuis ses débuts et est engagée dans toutes les discussions récentes.

En 2019, 2020 et 2021, l’OIM a reçu des financements pour le renforcement de moyens d’existence dans le Nord, la région du Centre-Nord et le Sahel, et a achevé tous les résultats. En complément des programmes d’urgence de l’OIM déjà existants principalement centrés sur les abris, la protection, et la santé mentale et le soutien psychosocial, y compris sur des financements du CERF, la réponse de l'OIM dans le secteur de l’accès aux moyens d’existence sera axée sur la fourniture d’une assistance en nature mais aussi sous forme de transferts monétaires, lesquels permettront à chaque bénéficiaire d’être responsable de l’acquisition de leurs propre kit d’actifs (productifs et non productifs) et d’en apprécier la valeur marchande.

DIRECT HUMANITARIAN ASSISTANCE TO VULNERABLE POPULATIONS AFFECTED BY FORCED DISPLACEMENT IN NIGER Renforcement de la protection pour les personnes vulnérables, en particulier les enfants, les survivants de violence basée sur le genre (VBG) et victimes de traite dans les régions de Diffa, Tillabéry, Maradi et Tahoua Les risques de violations des droits des hommes et femmes, y compris les risques de traite et de VBG, seront amoindris à travers la promotion d’un environnement communautaire protecteur et d’un accès renforcé aux services de protection, y compris aux services Santé mentale soutien psychosocial (SMSPS), dans les régions de Tillabéri, Diffa, Maradi et Tahoua.
Les activités cibleront les retournés, déplacés et membres des populations hôtes. Le projet prévoit 4 axes d’intervention.
1. Renforcement des capacités étatiques et des services sociaux de base dans les départements cibles pour une meilleure prise en charge des personnes en mobilité et notamment des enfants, y compris des survivant-e-s VBG et des victimes de traite : Un cycle de formation sur la protection des victimes de traite en situation de crise, permettant aussi de vulgariser le mécanisme national de référencement des victimes de traite, sera organisé pour tout acteur de la chaine de protection dans les communes cibles, dont les travailleurs sociaux de la protection de l’enfance et des organisations de la société civile (OSC). Il comprendra également des sessions sur la spécificité de la prise en charge des enfants non accompagnés en contexte humanitaire, et les besoins spécifiques des survivantes de VBG. 
2. Prévention des violences notamment envers les enfants, les femmes et les personnes en situation d'handicap, y compris de survivants de  VBG et diverses exploitations, à travers le renforcement des mécanismes communautaires de protection, l’appui aux leaders communautaires et la mobilisation des filles et garçons : En collaboration avec les DDPFPE, les mairies et les OSC, une cartographie et évaluation des besoins des structures communautaires, y compris les comités de protection, les espaces amis des enfants, les espaces surs et les écoles coraniques accueillant des enfants déplacés, seront réalisées. Suite à cette analyse, l’OIM les appuiera en matériel, afin que ces dernières puissent jouer leur rôle de protection. Leurs compétences seront renforcées afin qu’ils puissent signaler et référer les cas de protection, mais aussi qu’ils développent des actions de prévention qui encouragent des normes et comportements positifs favorisant des communautés respectueuses, égalitaires, et non violentes à l'égard des femmes et des filles. Des appuis aux initiatives des jeunes pour qu’ils sensibilisent leurs pairs seront réalisés. 
3. Atténuation des risques de protection dans les zones ciblées : En vue de prévenir l’adoption de stratégies de survie négatives des populations et de promouvoir leur dignité, l’OIM poursuivra la distribution des kits de protection adaptés aux besoins,  identifiés avec les populations. Enfin, l'organisation continuera le renforcement de la sécurité sur les sites d'intervention de l'équipe Abris et BNA & WASH afin de contribuer à la réduction des risques de protection. 
4. Offre de services de soutien psychosocial et de santé mentale (SMSPS) aux personnes déplacées, notamment les enfants, aux survivants de VBG et aux communautés hôtes : La stratégie de services de SMSPS de l’OIM est basée sur son expertise acquise auprès des migrants vulnérables et conformément aux principes développés par le « manuel de santé mentale et soutien psychosocial communautaire en situations d’urgence et de déplacement » (OIM, 2021). Des activités de sensibilisation et de formations des leaders communautaires et d’agents de santé sont organisées au préalable. Des équipes mobiles composées notamment d’un-e travailleur-se social-e, d’un-e infirmier-ère, d’un-e pyschologue, d’un-e mobilisateur-trice communautaire, se déplaceront pour offrir des activités psychosociales aux populations hôtes et déplacées, notamment là où les structures communautaires sont inexistantes. Tout au long du projet, l’OIM s’engagera avec les partenaires dans la Protection contre l’exploitation et les abus sexuels et le renforcement de la redevabilité envers les personnes affectées.

DIRECT HUMANITARIAN ASSISTANCE TO VULNERABLE POPULATIONS AFFECTED BY FORCED DISPLACEMENT IN NIGER Assistance en abris et Biens non-alimentaires (BNA) aux personnes déplacées vulnérables dans les régions de Diffa et Maradi Le projet proposé par l'OIM vise la poursuite d'une réponse coordonnée pour couvrir de façon adéquate aux besoins en abris et en Biens non-alimentaires (BNA) aux populations affectées par la crise du basin du lac Tchad qui affecte les régions de Diffa et Maradi. L'objectif est de contribuer à l'amélioration des conditions de vies des populations déplacées à travers la fourniture d'abris d'urgences, kits NFI, abris transitionnel et l'intervention en cash. 
L'assistance contiendra un total de 11 000 ménages et reparti comme suit : 
i) la fourniture d'abris aux ménages vulnérable, la distribution de kits BNA, dont  3 000 kits d'abris d'urgence et 3 000 kits de BNA à Diffa puis 1 000 kits d'abris d'urgence et 1 000 kits de BNA à Maradi, dans le cadre du HRP 2022. 
ii) Mettant à disposition 2 000 kits de BNA  et 2 000 kits d'abris  à titre de renouvellement des abris endommagé et Kits NFI n'existant plus, respectivement à Diffa et Maradi à travers l'option transferts monétaires conditionnel. 
iii)  La mise à disposition de 5 000  abris transitionnels et 5 000 qui seront  fournis  à Diffa pour améliorer les conditions de vie des ménages retournés, après plus de 5 ans de déplacement, considérant le retour amorcés par le Gouvernement dans cette région. En tant que Co-Lead du Secteur abris et BNA  l'OIM va continuer d'assurer la coordination du Groupe de travail abris et Biens non-alimentaires en étroite collaboration avec le Ministère de l'Action Humanitaire, en  renforçant la collecte des informations de façon régulière dans le souci d'informer les intervenants sur la localisation, la nature et l'ampleur des besoins exprimés et des activités de réponse, de continuer à appuyer les partenaires et membres du secteur pour mener les activités dans le respect de la stratégie du Groupe de Travail et des principes humanitaires et d'appuyer les services étatiques dans leurs rôles de coordination et suivi des activités du secteur. Les activité de la réponse d'urgence se conformeront aux Principes de Protection transversale et au Cadre institutionnel de l'OIM de lutte contre les violences basées sur le genre en situation de crise (VBV) , intégrera des mesures visant à assurer la sécurité, la dignité et le bien-être de la population touchée, et intégrera le respect strict de principe tolérance zéro pour toute exploitation et abus sexuels. Ce projet s'inscrira dans le respect des principes humanitaires et portera une attention particulière au principe ne pas nuire, de sécurité et non-discrimination. Les activités du projet seront mises en œuvre  respectant les règles de lutte contre COVID 19 par l'observation de mesures barrières telles que le port du masque, le lavage des mains, le respect de la distanciation sociale afin d'endiguer tout risque de contamination et de propagation de la maladie auprès des bénéficiaires. Un système de gestion de mécanisme de plaintes sera mis en place afin que les plaintes sensibles soient traitées conséquemment dans le but d'apporter une assistance respectant l'égalité et la dignité des communautés bénéficiaire.  Dans le cadre de la redevabilité de sessions d'information sur le projet seront organisées avec les bénéficiaires, la phase d'évaluation de besoins sera réalisée de commun accord avec les populations dans les communes ciblées, la communication avec les communautés et les autorités locales sur les critères de ciblage seront organisées et après intervention, les feedbacks de la communauté cible seront collectés à travers des évaluations post-distribution et des séances de discussion de groupe séparées par genre et âge avant et après l'assistance. Aussi, en tant qu’acteur humanitaire, l'OIM et ses partenaires de mise en œuvre s’assureront que les actions n’induisent aucune tension ou problème dans la zone et n’exposent pas les bénéficiaires en affichant les compositions de kits BNA et Abris. Une collaboration étroite sera faite avec les acteurs de protection. Le cout total du projet sera de 7.453.000 USD.

Africa Regional Migration Program (ARMP) Renforcement de la protection pour les personnes vulnérables, en particulier les enfants, les survivants de violence basée sur le genre (VBG) et victimes de traite dans les régions de Diffa, Tillabéry, Maradi et Tahoua Les risques de violations des droits des hommes et femmes, y compris les risques de traite et de VBG, seront amoindris à travers la promotion d’un environnement communautaire protecteur et d’un accès renforcé aux services de protection, y compris aux services Santé mentale soutien psychosocial (SMSPS), dans les régions de Tillabéri, Diffa, Maradi et Tahoua.
Les activités cibleront les retournés, déplacés et membres des populations hôtes. Le projet prévoit 4 axes d’intervention.
1. Renforcement des capacités étatiques et des services sociaux de base dans les départements cibles pour une meilleure prise en charge des personnes en mobilité et notamment des enfants, y compris des survivant-e-s VBG et des victimes de traite : Un cycle de formation sur la protection des victimes de traite en situation de crise, permettant aussi de vulgariser le mécanisme national de référencement des victimes de traite, sera organisé pour tout acteur de la chaine de protection dans les communes cibles, dont les travailleurs sociaux de la protection de l’enfance et des organisations de la société civile (OSC). Il comprendra également des sessions sur la spécificité de la prise en charge des enfants non accompagnés en contexte humanitaire, et les besoins spécifiques des survivantes de VBG. 
2. Prévention des violences notamment envers les enfants, les femmes et les personnes en situation d'handicap, y compris de survivants de  VBG et diverses exploitations, à travers le renforcement des mécanismes communautaires de protection, l’appui aux leaders communautaires et la mobilisation des filles et garçons : En collaboration avec les DDPFPE, les mairies et les OSC, une cartographie et évaluation des besoins des structures communautaires, y compris les comités de protection, les espaces amis des enfants, les espaces surs et les écoles coraniques accueillant des enfants déplacés, seront réalisées. Suite à cette analyse, l’OIM les appuiera en matériel, afin que ces dernières puissent jouer leur rôle de protection. Leurs compétences seront renforcées afin qu’ils puissent signaler et référer les cas de protection, mais aussi qu’ils développent des actions de prévention qui encouragent des normes et comportements positifs favorisant des communautés respectueuses, égalitaires, et non violentes à l'égard des femmes et des filles. Des appuis aux initiatives des jeunes pour qu’ils sensibilisent leurs pairs seront réalisés. 
3. Atténuation des risques de protection dans les zones ciblées : En vue de prévenir l’adoption de stratégies de survie négatives des populations et de promouvoir leur dignité, l’OIM poursuivra la distribution des kits de protection adaptés aux besoins,  identifiés avec les populations. Enfin, l'organisation continuera le renforcement de la sécurité sur les sites d'intervention de l'équipe Abris et BNA & WASH afin de contribuer à la réduction des risques de protection. 
4. Offre de services de soutien psychosocial et de santé mentale (SMSPS) aux personnes déplacées, notamment les enfants, aux survivants de VBG et aux communautés hôtes : La stratégie de services de SMSPS de l’OIM est basée sur son expertise acquise auprès des migrants vulnérables et conformément aux principes développés par le « manuel de santé mentale et soutien psychosocial communautaire en situations d’urgence et de déplacement » (OIM, 2021). Africa Regional Migration Program (ARMP) Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM): Mobility Tracking of IDPs, Returnees and Other Mobile Populations in Sudan Following the crises that has affected Sudan since February 2003 and, in response to the need for accurate information on displacement and the identification of beneficiaries for the delivery of humanitarian aid, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) began its Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) program in 2004 to support the Government of Sudan (GoS) and its humanitarian partners in establishing an accurate data collection system and providing data on displacement in areas most affected by the conflict and natural disaster. DTM is a system to track and monitor displacement and population mobility. It is designed to regularly and systematically capture, process and disseminate information to provide a better understanding of the movements and evolving needs of displaced populations, whether on site or en route.
Data collection strategies and tools are based on the DTM global methodology but have been adapted to reflect context and population movements specific to Sudan. IOM has been working in close collaboration with the Humanitarian Aid Commission (HAC) and partners in the field to establish a unified and systematic method to collect individual data on internally displaced persons (IDPs) and returnees in seven states. Up until 2018, the DTM program in Sudan focused on registration, including biometric registration (since 2010), of IDPs and returning IDPs. Registration was mostly carried out in response to requests from the government and humanitarian partners for the identification of beneficiaries and the delivery of humanitarian assistance (i.e. food vouchers by WFP), positioning DTM Sudan as the reference source of displacement data in the country.
While the emergency levels of the crisis in the country reduces and the situation stabilizes in most of the conflict affected areas, there remains a strong need to restructure the program and tailor the operation to better suit the current protracted displacement and return scenario, to in turn inform evidence-based programming by IOM and the wider humanitarian community in Sudan. Specifically, there is the need to further update displacement figures more frequently, comprehensively, systematically, and in regular intervals to ensure that data is continually collected, provides a meaningful resource and is available through IOM’s DTM system.

South Sudan Humanitarian Response Plan 2022
Total private sector contributions from December 2022 Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2022, there are some 335,000 refugees and asylum seekers from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, primarily from Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic.
At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for longer term stability, hundreds of thousands of South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since the signing of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan, this spontaneous movement has prompted the development of an area-based approach, to support refugees, returnees and host communities, through enhanced engagement with development actors, to support greater access to services where possible.
Refugees largely reside in conflict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction in basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.
Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will benefit from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Specific protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identified at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with specific protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as verification exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the efficiency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to benefit from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

Chad - OCHA Office [Donor:O538, Recipient:O270] Renforcement de la coordination et du plaidoyer humanitaire au Tchad Le projet vise à renforcer le rôle de OCHA dans la mise en œuvre de son mandat et son rôle auprès des partenaires humanitaires et gouvernementaux au niveau des fonctions coordination, gestion de l’information et plaidoyer. Le bureau national d’OCHA à N’Djaména et ses trois sous-bureaux régionaux à l’Est (Abéché) au Sud (Goré) et la province du Lac (Baga Sola) mettent l’accent sur l’opérationnalisation de ses fonctions y compris en assurant un lien entre les activités humanitaires et de développement (nexus) en vue de promouvoir une solution durable visant à ne pas perpétuer une situation de dépendance humanitaire. Dans le cadre de cette nouvelle façon de travailler outre l’opérationnalisation du nexus, le lien avec les objectifs commun des programmes développement, paix et sécurité sera mis en avant. L’accent est aussi mis sur le renforcement de la coordination civilo-militaire afin de faciliter l’accès et la protection des civils.

Le projet a pour but de renforcer la coordination d’une réponse humanitaire rapide et efficace afin de sauver des vies et protéger les personnes affectées par les situations de crises au Tchad. Une coordination humanitaire rapide et correctement évaluée au niveau des besoins de la population affectée permettra aux acteurs humanitaires de mieux identifier et répondre aux besoins humanitaires, de renforcer la préparation de réponse aux urgences à travers le renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et plus spécifiquement l‘Equipe humanitaire pays, la coordination inter-clusters, la coordination civilo-militaire, les clusters et les mécanismes de coordination au niveau de terrain.
Le projet vise aussi à assurer le plaidoyer humanitaire à travers l’analyse des besoins faites par l’ensemble de la communauté humanitaire et ses partenaires en vue une compréhension commune des problématiques auxquels fait face le Tchad, ses causes profondes, l’impact sur les populations. OCHA jouera un rôle clé dans la création d'espaces de collection et d'analyse et gestion d’informations, pour assurer une stratégie de réponse coordonnée menant à des actions humanitaires répondant aux besoins les plus aigus et être mieux préparé face aux urgences soudaines. Le projet permettra également d’assurer conjointement avec la communauté humanitaire le plaidoyer en faveur du respect des principes humanitaires, de la protection des civils, de l'accès humanitaire et pour la mobilisation et l'allocation efficace de ressources humanitaires.

Un accent a été mis sur la mise en œuvre des plans d’action de la redevabilité envers les populations affectées (AAP), la PSEA et la préparation aux urgences en plus d'intégrer une attention au genre et de renforcer la centralité de la protection.
Un plaidoyer pour plus de visibilité des résultats tangibles au niveau de la réponse facilitant la mobilisation de ressources pour les différentes crises au Tchad (mouvement de population – crise du Bassin du Lac Tchad, insécurité alimentaire et malnutrition, urgences sanitaires) est aussi défini comme une priorité dans ce projet

OCHA continuera de jouer également un rôle moteur dans le renforcement du lien entre les acteurs humanitaires et de développement et la transformation de la réponse humanitaire, en lien avec les engagements pris au Sommet humanitaire mondial de 2016 et ceci à travers la nouvelle façon de travailler (NWOW) et le renforcement de l’utilisation de la modalité de transfert monétaire.

Mali - OCHA Office [Donor:QATU, Recipient:O514] Renforcement des mécanismes de Coordination et de Plaidoyer pour la protection humanitaire et l’assistance aux populations les plus vulnérables au Mali En 2021, la crise humanitaire au Mali s'est aggravée en raison de l'augmentation et de l'expansion des de la violence intercommunautaire et des attaques des groupes armés non étatiques (GANE) dans les régions du centre, du sud et de l'ouest. Cette crise a été aggravée par les bouleversements politiques marqués par deux coups d'état en août 2020 et mai 2021, et l'incertitude persistante de la transition politique laisse l'État dans l'incapacité de répondre aux services sociaux de base des populations. 
Les déplacements internes de personnes ont augmenté de 100 000 en 2021, atteignant plus de 401 000 personnes soit quatre fois plus qu'il y a deux ans. Au total, 156 000 réfugiés maliens résident dans les pays voisins tandis que le Mali accueille 48 000 réfugiés et leur fournit protection et assistance. Les gains économiques du Mali se sont érodés, avec 900 000 personnes (0,04% de la population) qui sont retombées dans la pauvreté en raison de la crise socioéconomique de la COVID-19. la capacité des ménages est fragilisée à cause de la perte de revenus, de la réduction des transferts de fonds et à l'augmentation du coût de la vie. 
La Banque mondiale prévoit une augmentation du taux de pauvreté à 4,8 % en 2022. La crise de protection est également aggravée avec une augmentation des incidents de sécurité.  Les acteurs de la violence basée sur le genre (VBG) ont signalé 5 486 incidents de VBG, soit une augmentation de 41 % comparativement à la même période en 2020. Plus de 1 640 écoles sont fermées en raison de l'insécurité, affectant plus de 2,9 millions d'enfants dont 40 % se trouvent dans la région centrale de Mopti. Quatre districts centraux ont signalé que 40 % des écoles étaient fermées. Dans les régions du sud, 10 pour cent des écoles sont fermées à Koulikoro, Koutiala et Sikasso, privant 30 000 enfants de leur éducation. A ce jour, le Mali a rapporté plus de 15 800 cas de COVID-19.
En 2021, 1,3 million de personnes ont connu un niveau élevé d'insécurité alimentaire aiguë. le niveau le plus élevé depuis 2015, et 3 055 253 personnes ont été touchées par les mauvaises pluies et une saison de soudure prolongée. La situation humanitaire reste entravée par l'augmentation des besoins et la faiblesse des financements, avec 32 % des fonds mobilisés au 31 octobre 2021. Malgré les contraintes opérationnelles, les partenaires humanitaires ont aidé plus de 2,45 millions des 4,7 millions de personnes ciblées au 30 septembre 2021. 
Les capacités de réponse existantes au Mali représentent plus de 160 organisations humanitaires, acteurs du développement ainsi que des forces militaires (MINUSMA, Forces maliennes de défense et de sécurité, Barkhane, Mission européenne de formation, G5 Sahel). Le contexte susmentionné exigera une coordination efficace et la présence d’OCHA demeure très importante. OCHA maintiendra sa présence à Bamako, Mopti, Tombouctou, Gao et ouvrira une antenne à Ségou tout en couvrant à distance les régions de Taoudénit, Ménaka, Kidal et les régions du sud Est et Ouest. 

Sept clusters actifs (Éducation, Sécurité alimentaire, Santé, Nutrition, Protection, Abris/BNA et WASH), des sous-clusters et des groupes de travail spécialisés (Accès, CM-Coord, Redevabilité, Genre et Cash) sont en place au niveau national et local. Le Bureau d’OCHA au Mali continuera ainsi à jouer un rôle central dans la mobilisation, la coordination et le soutien des acteurs humanitaires dans les domaines de la coordination, la gestion de l’information, le financement humanitaire et le plaidoyer. 

OCHA continuera à jouer son rôle central dans la mobilisation des partenaires, l’utilisation des instruments et des mécanismes de financement tout en veillant à ce que les besoins humanitaires croissants soient prises en compte. OCHA assumera son rôle clé dans la coordination militaire au niveau national et régional de concert avec les forces militaires présentes dans le pays tout en renforçant les capacités des autorités nationales en matière de coordination

Emergency Life saving and Livelihoods Project (ELLPP) Protecting lives and restoring livelihoods of vulnerable agro-pastoral and riverine- men, women, boys and girls in Baardhere District, Gedo, Somalia. This proposed intervention in Bardheere district (Gedo Region, Somalia) targets 8,130 vulnerable men, women, boys and girls in 1,355 Non-IDPs (agro-pastoralists & riverine farmers in the rural areas) and IDP households for 12 months (January 2022- December 2022). The project will prioritize the most vulnerable HHs/population including: women (women headed households, single women, pregnant and lactating women-PLW, children, persons with disabilities, persons with minority clan affiliations, older persons, persons with chronic illness, large families and/ or those with babies or with children attending school. The project will select the target vulnerable beneficiaries from 38,960 individuals (in approx. 6,493 HHs) currently under IPC 3&4 in Bardhere district (as per the FSC 2021 Overall targets of People in Need-IPC 3&4 in Bardhere). Project activities are aligned with the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP)/Food Security Cluster (FSC) Objectives prioritizing lifesaving and life-sustaining assistance, as detailed in the UN OCHA (HRP-Somalia. Humanitarian Programme Cycle 2021-Issued in February 2021). The FSC Objective 1 of improving immediate access to food will be achieved through: (i) 600 men, women, boys and girls from 100 vulnerable HHs benefiting from Unconditional cash transfer (UCT) for 3 months ($ 70 per month per HH) and (ii) 4,350 men, women, boys and girls from 725 vulnerable HHs benefiting from conditional transfers-Cash For Work-CFW (rehabilitation of community infrastructure- Irrigation canals)about 70 Kms for 30 days @ $8 per HH per day.  These will improve immediate access to food, prevent selling of assets, bridge the food gap for beneficiary farmers as well as increase skills and ultimately improve food production, soil and water conservation and HH income. The FSC objective 2 of protecting and restoring livelihoods related to food and income sources will be achieved through: (i) 520 vulnerable agro-pastoralists and riverine farmers HHs (3,120 men, women, boys, girls) supported with seasonally appropriate agricultural inputs (e.g quality fodder seeds, farm tools, training on fodder production, conservation and utilization, seed bulking, group dynamics, business skills, DRR; land preparation and irrigation support).  This will ultimately protect and restore livelihoods as well as enhance HH feed security, food security, nutrition, income generation and resilience. The main approaches that will be used will include: Needs/market assessments/baseline survey; community based targeting; adult learning techniques; use of lead farmers as ToTs; conflict sensitive programing; protection mainstreaming; Gender sensitive and human rights based approaches. The main common project activities will include: (i) Conducting internal planning meeting for project staff to acquaint on project objectives, targets and outcome.(ii) Introduction of the project to local authorities and launch .(iii)Conducting community mobilization, sensitization, selection of beneficiaries- in the targeted 5 sites (Mardha, Hureena, Sarinleey, Bender and Shimbiroole); verification and registration (iv)Conducting a baseline survey to determine the benchmark and (v) M&E of project activities. VSF-Suisse has vast experience in  UCT and CFW activities and for over 6 years (2015-2020-through USAID/OFDA(BHA funding): supported 1,700 male & female fodder farmers and 1,270 Irrigation farmers in Gedo Region (including Bardhere district) practicing fodder activities, EWS and DRR; distribution of agricultural inputs and promoted linkages. VSF-Suisse supported rehabilitation of 74 Kms of Irrigation canals through CFW approaches and water supply infrastructure (13 water pans & 12 shallow wells) in Gedo. VSF-Suisse will work closely with stakeholders including communities, local authority/leaders, relevant technical ministries, NGOs and adhere to the FSC cluster & CWG guidelines, LEGS, Sphere standards, while observing CDC, WHO and government COVID-19 health measures.

Emergency health response to prevent cholera-related morbidity and mortality in Lebanon Emergency Health support for vulnerable Lebanese and Migrants Medair’s health work has been operating since 2014, supporting both refugees and vulnerable Lebanese through health centres and community outreach. Whilst originally focussed within health centres within Social Development Centres as part of the Ministry of Social Affairs, since the beginning of 2021, Medair has expanded operations to the South / Nabatiye and working with an additional 15 health centres within the Ministry of Public Health network, particularly for routine vaccinations. Medair opened a COVID mass vaccination centre in Saida in June 2021. There is a growing focus on nutrition activities such as IYCF, which are detailed under the Nutrition sector of the ERP.
Health activities that are aligned under the health sector of the ERP include the provision of medication, PPE provision and IPC training for health centres, and integrated messaging through community health volunteers (CHVs). 54 CHVs focused on reaching Lebanese populations will be mobilised from pre-existing Medair networks, and while the remaining number 46+ (additional figures contingent on anticipated future funding) will be newly recruited (with additional CHVs as part of the LCRP). These Community Health Volunteers will reach all populations within their geographic areas of intervention (around the supported health centres).
Medair has seen a four-fold increase in the usage of medication in recent months as more Lebanese are dependent on medication in the public sector due to shortages within pharmacies. Medair therefore aims to provide more medication through supplying pharmacies in supported health centres – expanding the number of centres supported. Medication will be provided free of charge to all those accessing the centres. Medair acknowledges the challenges with procuring medicines in the current context given we do not hold an importation license, yet is actively participating in coordination conversations with other agencies to explore alternative options for procurement of imports as well as engaging with advocacy efforts at the humanitarian and governmental levels. Medair will also include a small cash-for-health component for vulnerable people needing to access medication from other locations, which has been piloted through a blockchain modality in the Bekaa over the past six months. Medair also has experience in cash-for-health programming within the Middle East region, in addition to cash programming within Lebanon. 
Medair’s existing COVID programming already supports health centres with the provision of PPE and IPC training for staff and will be expanding this to a further 10 health centres. For more information on the centres, please see the list sent to the Health Sector. 
Medair also has an active shelter team who cover water and sanitation components, in addition to expanding into alternative energy options. The health and shelter teams have recently been jointly assessing the health facilities to consider how to ensure the continuation of health services, including WASH and solar options – both fridges for cold chain, and for the whole centre to enable lights, equipment and the internet (to access PHENICS) to function. Medair is therefore well placed to provide integrated health, shelter and WASH solutions.
Medair is an active part of the health sector, and has close working relationships with both the Ministry of Public Health, the Ministry of Social Affairs and other key stakeholders listed in the ERP. Medair has programming operating across Lebanon, including in BML and the North/Akkar, although the majority of health programming under this ERP is anticipating to take place in Bekaa/Baalbek and the South/Nabatiye.

Food Security 	Villages of Hope Emergency Lifesaving Cash and Livelihood Support to IDP and Non- IDP Communities in Somalia Somalia is facing a severe and deteriorating humanitarian crisis as we enter 2022 as a result of the compounding effects of conflict, recurrent climate shocks, diseases and pests outbreaks with increased levels of vulnerability and substantial increase in the humanitarian caseload (Somalia HNO, 2022). There is a serious risk that the impact of consecutive below average to poor rainfall in most parts of the country will develop into a severe drought by early to mid- 2022 with the number of people facing acute food insecurity on the rise. It is likely that minority groups, women, children, people with disabilities, will experience heightened protection risks as a result, unless they are intentionally targeted to receive tailored assistance.

With approximately 3.5 million individuals in IPC 3 and 4 through at least December 2021, FAO proposes to target 160,300 households (961,800 individuals- 91,500 IDPs and 870,300 non- IDPs) in IPC 3 and IPC 4 caseloads respectively. This will include 216,790 women, 254,492 girls, 264,880 boys and 225,638 men and 144,270 people living with disabilities (PWD) across 59 districts in Somalia through its flagship Cash+ approach combining short-term cash transfers with tailored livelihood support in accordance with technical and humanitarian standards. Vulnerable households will identified from at-risk pastoral, agro-pastoral, fishing, riverine farmers, IDPs and Non- IDP communities in IPC 3 and 4 areas. This intervention will integrate short-term cash transfers aimed at enabling the most vulnerable households to meet their immediate needs, with livelihood support to allow crisis-affected households to get back into production. FAO will employ community- led beneficiary selection processes and ensure adequate targeting and representation of extremely vulnerable and minority groups in community committees. Interventions proposed will employ a Do No Harm approach with a gender lens that ensures conflict- sensitivity to reduce protection risks for all individuals, and to mitigate the risk of conflict or community tensions. 

Under Food Security Cluster (FSC) Objective 1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 160,300 households through a blend of conditional (Cash-for-Work) and unconditional (UCT) transfers. Under UCT, FAO will prioritize Cash+ interventions including Cash+ Agriculture, Cash+ livestock and Cash+ fisheries. These modalities will increase households’ immediate access to food by providing sufficient cash to access the minimum expenditure basket (MEB), while supporting the rehabilitation of critical productive and community infrastructure. It will also boost household food production, increase household incomes and create employment opportunities. Cash transfer values will be informed by the Cash Working Group and are expected to differ per district/ region of intervention. They, however, will be valued at 80 percent of the food MEB, which can range from USD 50- 100 per month. All cash-based programmes will include training on good nutrition practices. 

Under FSC Objective 2, to protect livelihoods and related food sources, FAO will provide in-kind, technical support and tailored trainings to 112,500 HHs to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security and nutrition threats, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to targeted HHs. In addition, FAO shall provide transitional cash support to 13,100 HHs across agro pastoral, pastoral and fishing livelihood zones to augment the adaptive capacity of HHs, strengthen and foster resilience to future shocks, cushioning them from food insecurity and malnutrition. Trainings shall be delivered alongside input provision to build skills in sustainable use of resources provided, build skills in livelihoods management including harvest, post- harvest management, linking beneficiaries to long- term interventions that provide them opportunities to enhance their livelihoods and skills.

Cash Based Transfer Assistance for the Syrian Arab Republic for Vulnerable Food Insecure Syrian Population
-- Nutrition General Food Assistance (GFA) As highlighted in the 2022 HNO, Syria continues to suffer from multiple and complex socioeconomic difficulties - continued effects of the Lebanese economic crisis, tightening of unilateral coercive measures and consequences of the Covid-19 pandemic. The protracted crisis, now in its 11th year, is exacerbating food security and livelihood needs for many families across the country, further eroding the resilience and recovery prospects. These factors have triggered unprecedented inflation rates of basic commodities, including basic food items, pushing additional people into food insecurity. The Syria Food Security and Agriculture sector has identified the overall people in need for 2022 – of food insecure and those at risk of food insecurity – to be estimated at 13.9 million, with 12 million facing acute food insecurity and 1.9 million at risk of sliding into food insecurity. The acute food insecure include 1.9 million people living in camps and deemed to be 100% food insecure. WFP’s GFA covers the critical food needs of Syrian families across all 14 governorates. Subject to availability of funds, WFP’s GFA will ensure that food needs are being met through a food basket planned to have a minimum basic caloric value, across modalities from 2,100 kcal per person per day for the most food-insecure, like the IDP in camps in Northeast Syria, 1,700 kcal per person per day for beneficiaries assessed as severely food insecure or living in camps in Northwest Syria, to 1,300 kcal per person per day for beneficiaries assessed as moderately food-insecure. Target beneficiaries include the most vulnerable crisis-affected population groups. These include the need based IDPs settled in camps or host communities, IDP returnees, host communities, and poor rural and urban households. In total, WFP Interim Country Strategic Plan aims to target 7.75 million food-insecure people each month in 2022 and 2023, including the severely food-insecure (1.3 million); 50 percent moderately food-insecure (4.7 million); and all need based IDPs living in camps and informal settlements across the north-western and north-eastern governorates (1.7 million). This plan to target 7.75 million food-insecure people each month in 2022 is costed at US$985,564,157.

WFP is completing the nationwide Vulnerability Needs Assessment (VNR) exercise, to allow effective prioritization of assistance to households identified as most vulnerable. The VNR exercise will enhance the currently used ""Beneficiary Selection Tool"" by applying indicators that more accurately capture vulnerability status compared to relying only on demographic characteristics.

The operational context in Syria continues to present a complex risk climate. WFP applies the organization's enterprise risk management policy and internal control framework that enables WFP to address and monitor risk and opportunities proactively. Some examples of risks that WFP continues to address cover deteriorating economic and security conditions, inconsistent access to affected population, increasing number of people in need of assistance and impact of COVID-19 pandemic. These risks challenge the safety and security of staff, personnel and beneficiaries, and compromise efficient programme implementation. To address these challenges, WFP continuously reviews its internal and external operating environment, update its risk register, and actively identifies solutions to address current and emerging risks to enable the programme to deliver on its objectives.

With large population unable to cover basic needs and dependent on humanitarian agencies for assistance, PSEA risks resulting from power dynamics between affected population and responding agencies are also at risk of increasing. WFP will continue its work with UN agencies participating in the PSEA network and its partners to ensure that in-place PSEA policies and protocols are fully adopted, implemented, including capacity building, and establishing mechanisms.

HRP FOOD SECURITY Programa de seguridad alimentaria basado en la escuela  Con el objetivo de contribuir a la seguridad alimentaria de la población con mayores necesidades, el Programa Mundial de Alimentos de Naciones Unidas (WFP, por sus siglas en inglés) en Venezuela desarrolla un programa de asistencia humanitaria basado en la escuela para garantizar el acceso de los más vulnerables a una alimentación adecuada y nutritiva en el entorno escolar, familiar y comunitario. 
Este programa inició en 2021 con comidas escolares en emergencias priorizando escuelas iniciales y de educación especial.

WFP proporciona comidas escolares acompañado de un paquete integrado de intervenciones para mejorar el acceso a alimentos nutritivos y diversificados a través de las escuelas, contribuyendo al mismo tiempo a mejorar la salud y la nutrición de los niños en edad escolar, los estudiantes con discapacidad y el personal escolar, y apoyando a las comunidades a reducir la dependencia en estrategias de afrontamiento. Support to WFP's ICSP 1&2 food and nutrition for 3m people Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace.

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.
