Winterization response - distribution of shelter and non food items Sustain the lives of 40,440 persons requiring emergency food assistance across Banadir region with particular focus on IDPs and people with disability.  The proposed project is emergency in nature and is going to deliver immediate humanitarian food assistance to address the food insecurity gap of the severely drought affected IDP populations living across Benadir region. The project will address the acute food insecurity among the targeted households with particular focus on recently displaced families who are at the borderline and have no means of survival, people with disability and vulnerable groups including women who are unable to engage livelihood means for earning and will support 6,740 H.H under IPC#4 phase living in Benadir IDP camps for a period of 4 months with unconditional food assistant through voucher system. The interventions are expected to enhance the vulnerable household’s food consumption score and improve nutrition status among children and also reduce the negative coping mechanism they apply when such nature of crisis strike. 
The project will give an early relief to the crisis affected people enabling them to quickly access food and improve food consumption score among children, women and elderly people living in the IDP camps. At the end, food security status of 6,740 vulnerable H.H living in Benadir will be improved through monthly food voucher assistants thus contributing to the overall cluster strategy of minimizing the number of people in crises (IPC4 and above). QC in collaboration with the target recipient groups, QC will identify food vendors/suppliers in the target zone with particular attention given to the protection concerns in the process of food collection. People will be given the chance to demonstrate their willingness and choice regarding vendor selection process.  Once vendor suppliers identified, Beneficiaries will be given voucher to enable visit the vendor and collect the food ration on monthly basis. QC MEAL staff will conduct continues monitoring exercise on the process of distribution and they will be present at the distribution points to ensure process are smooth and people are receiving their entitlement accordingly. In addition to this, food quality will be inspected before and during distribution exercise to ensure food quality. 
Community based targeting will be used for beneficiary selection process. Gender will be given special role as project will work to improve gender equity and participation in all project planning and implementation processes. Local authorities and camp relief committees will be engaged during the selection process. Community will take the process ownership and identify beneficiary based on vulnerability criteria set. Camp relief committees will be trained on selection process especially vulnerability criteria. Post selection verification will be conducted by QC team to verify the lists with the participation of the whole community. The final and verified list will be jointly approved by the camp relief committee, local authorities and QC.  
Project will engage broader stakeholders in the ground including government officials, local authorities, members from local community and other humanitarian partners for coordination and collaboration reasons. Further on this, QC will work to build exist strategy through linking the supported beneficiaries with other resilience programs going on in the areas. This will be achieved through continued networking and engagement with all including federal ministries officials, local authorities and partners that work resilience programming.

Support to International Medical Corps (IMC) for the Gender Based Violence Prevention and Response for conflict- affected population in South Sudan
-- FCDO Gender-based Violence (GBV) Prevention and Response for Conflict-Affected Population in South Sudan 
The GBV prevention and response program of International Medical Corps (IMC) in South Sudan aims to empower communities and build resilience through promoting social and behavioral change to address the root causes of GBV in the country. The project targets key population to create a sustainable change in attitude and practices through male engagement, working with community leaders and building capacity of local stakeholders. Leveraging on the vast experiences, gains, and successes of IMC in implementing GBV prevention and response interventions through the FCDO-HARISS program, this project will be continued to implement in the states of Western Bahr el Ghazal (Wau IDP Camp and County), Upper Nile and Malakal PoC and County), Unity (Nyal County), and in Canal/Pigi County. It will directly benefit about 27495 vulnerable women and girls across the target locations. One of the project’s key priorities is to further strengthen core services to survivors of GBV and other vulnerable women and girls in the aforesaid intervention sites. These services include quality case management using a survivor-centered approach, along with psychosocial support to enhance healing and recovery. IMC UK works to ensure that survivors’ holistic needs are met by providing multi-sectoral services, referring to health centers for clinical management of rape, to legal justice services and to other kinds of support based on the needs of survivors. In addition to individual PSS for survivors, IMC UK will continue with PSS group activities for all vulnerable women and girls in the women girls’ safe spaces (WGSS). To ensure sustainability of the project and ownership by the community, especially of the WGSSs, in Wau, Nyal and Malakal, IMC already established, leadership committee comprise of 8 members from the community selected by their fellow women with the responsibility to give support, information, feedback, and suggestions that will foster empowerment and ownership of the space and the overall wellbeing of their members. The women committee members will be further empowered with knowledge and skills through hands-on management of the spaces and co-leading with them on the daily functioning of the WGSS. The women committee will be continuously mentored and trained on GBV basic concepts, safe referral, and referral pathways, and on leadership and conflict management and facilitation techniques and on various psychosocial support activities using IMC’s and IRC’s global WGSS toolkit. IMC UK will implement holistic community engagement strategies on the promotion of long-term positive change in the targeted communities. IMC will use the GBV community mobilization tool called SASA! - Phase-based strategy to help communities rethink about “power” and the positive use of power. “Preventing Violence against Women and Girls: Engaging Men in Accountable Practice (EMAP)” is also another tool that will be used to ensure men engagement with accountability to prevent GBV in the targeted community in Nyal, Wau and Malakal. In addition, IMC trains and collaborates with GBV Taskforce members in Wau, Malakal and Nyal. These will be supported by staff IMC UK staff to do awareness raising, and safe confidential referral of any survivors who disclose to them. IMC UK will provide emergency cash assistance for case management to the vulnerable women and girls. Cash assistance is one of the interagency minimum standards in GBV programming in emergency (Standard 11: Dignity Kits, Cash Assistance). In addition to this, IMC UK opts to implement cash assistance based on lesson learnt and feedback from women and girls on importance of cash assistance as lifesaving; for example, it can help a survivor meet the costs associated with fleeing an abusive relationship (e.g., rent, temporary shelter, transportation, food, clothing, etc).

-- FCDO Food and livelihood assistance to the most vulnerable and crisis affected population in South Sudan  The proposed project aims to provide food assistance, livelihood and resilience support to 1,105,380 vulnerable populations in Upper Nile, Western Equatoria, Central Equatoria and Greater Bahr el Ghazal. The project will implement activities that will prevent famine and improve food consumption, dietary diversity and coping strategies of target beneficiaries in IPC 5, 4 and 3. The project will also seek to enhance emergency food production and contribute to the reduction of dependency to food and agricultural inputs. World Vision will adopt a mix of intervention approaches including but not limited to unconditional and General Food Distribution, cash transfers, complementary livelihood support, capacity building (e.g., modern agronomic practices, Integrated Pest Management, Natural Resource Management, etc.), and resilience building at the household level. The proposed project will also be implemented in synergy with other sectors implemented by World Vision in the targeted locations such as health, nutrition, WASH, gender and protection related programming while maintaining coordinating and complementarity with the efforts of other humanitarian actors and line ministries. In order to reach the target beneficiaries with prioritized cluster objectives, World Vision South Sudan proposed a total of $4,512,952 US project budget for 2022.

Durable Solutions Phase II Emergency Shelter, NFI and Protection Assistance to Vulnerable Households in Afar and Amhara IOM as Shelter and NFI (S-NFI) Cluster Lead Agency (CLA), plans to reach up to 439,021 vulnerable individuals (79,822 households) whose capacity to anticipate, cope with and recover from conflict stresses have been eroded. To respond to the lifesaving humanitarian needs faced by an estimated 8.9 million persons across the country where as SNFI cluster plans to targets around 5 million persons (1.3 million in Afar and Amhara region (360,260 in Afar and 955,230 in Amhara region). These most vulnerable individuals are the one who are unable to support themselves with lifesaving shelter and non-food items. The targeted communities include newly displaced persons, IDPs in protracted displacement in camps and collective centers, IDPs living with host communities, and affected non-displaced host communities.  The proposed activities are designed in line with HRP strategic objectives 2022, as well as the S-NFI Cluster objectives and key activities.
Output: Improve access to life saving shelter and life sustaining non-food items and enhance resilience of most vulnerable population through area-based programming. (HRP CO1 and CO2; S- NFI Cluster Objectives).
IOM has extensive experience in Shelter and NFI responses in both emergency and post-crisis environments. IOM has static presence across Afar and Amhara and currently responds to humanitarian needs. IOM is the ES/NFI Cluster lead agency which conducts assessments and training for local authorities and Cluster Partners on ES, NFI, cash assistance. IOM supports SNFI Cluster partners through the provision of in-kind ES and NFI kits as well as supportive supervision. 
IOM provides integrated programing alongside health, CCCM, MHPSS, Protection and WASH responses. Delivering Shelter assistance, Housing, Land and Property (HLP) support including ES/NFI assistance to vulnerable communities maximizes the impact of the project in these locations. 
•	Improve access to ES and lifesaving NFIs through in-kind and Cash-Based Interventions. Breaking the Silence Against SGBV in Torit and Ikwotos, Eastern Equatoria State Creating a Safe Environment for and Providing Life-Saving GBV Response Services as well as integrating child protection components to the Crisis-Affected Women, Girls and Children in South Sudan In line with the identified needs and gaps, CARE International in South Sudan aims to provide a comprehensive package of GBV response services, which will be complemented with the prevention activities that address the root causes of the GBV in Juba, Magwi, Ikotos, Torit, Kapoeta North, Budi, Wau, Jur River, Koch, Rubkona, Pariang, Bor South, Pibor, Twic East, Duk and Akobo.  The interventions will be provided through static centers and through mobile and outreach teams. Static Women Girls Safe Spaces (WGFS) will be used as entry points to reach out to the communities, while outreach sessions by mobile teams will also be used as means of engaging with communities. The WGFSs will serve as the centers where women and girls can come together and socialize while also improving their psychosocial wellbeing. In order to do that CARE will provide structured and unstructured PSS activities. The unstructured activities will take the form of recreational activities which will be determined in consultation with the women and girls, i.e.. knitting, baking, sewing, painting or handicrafts. The structured activities on the other hand will aim to promote overall life skills of women and girls. Similarly, CARE will train women and girls on usage and set up of Fuel Efficient Stoves as part of GBV risk mitigation measures. These efforts will be supported with experience sharing sessions among women on cooking or sharing recipes to promote cohesion and communication among women groups. CARE will also offer income generation activities to the women and girls who fit into the activity criteria, which will include vulnerable individuals, survivors, female-headed households and so on.

Through the WGFSs, CARE will provide GBV case management services to the survivors, while ensuring updating (or creating referral pathways) referral pathways and service mappings for these locations to provide safe referrals to the services. As part of the individual case management plans, CARE will also provide one-time cash assistance to support the GBV survivors, when deemed necessary according to the developed SOPs. Community members who need legal advice and/or need to attend legal information sessions will also be provided with legal support at the WGFSs. Women and girls of reproductive age, who fit into vulnerability criteria set up in line with UNFPA's guidance will also be provided with dignity kits to ensure they can maintain their dignity and mobility in a crisis context.

CARE will also additionally provide awareness raising sessions to raise awareness on key gender and protection topics, as well as gender equality through mobile teams and at the WGFSs. This will help to engage men and boys in the discussions. Similarly, CARE will lead on the primary prevention activities by engaging men and boys through structured curriculums such as EMAP and Program RA.

In order to ensure that the staff are well equipped to provide support to the communities, all frontline staff and community mobilizers will be trained in various topics including case management, PSS, GBV risk mitigation and GBV core concepts. CARE's previous and existing presence in the aforementioned locations, as well as GBV programming experience in these locations will help to ensure community buy-in and prevent backlash from the communities. 

CARE will partner with UNIDOR to implement CP activities to provide case management, PSS, referrals to support child GBV survivors.

Emergency aid in the areas of protection and health as well as cash transfers for those in particular need of protection Lifesaving and sustaining protection response services for vulnerable individuals in Khartoum, Gedaref, and Blue Nile Specialized Women’s Protection and Empowerment (WPE) prevention and response services will be delivered to support women and girls at risk, such as elderly women, pregnant women, breastfeeding women, women and girls with disabilities, and female headed households (HHs) with minors in charge and without resources. The project will support the integration of reproductive health and WPE services so that gender-based violence (GBV) survivors can access safe and timely clinical care for the harmful health consequences - both physical and emotional. WPE staff integrated into health facilities will provide lifesaving GBV response services, including GBV case management and non-focused psycho-social support (PSS) to at-risk women and girls. At the same time, focused PSS sessions, recreational activities, and awareness-raising will be delivered through a Women and Girls Safe Space (WGSS). The IRC will also bolster protection services by providing general and specialized GBV training sessions to internal and external actors, including GBV core concepts, referral pathways, disclosure and safe referrals and other and GBV trainings required to provide services for women and girls. 

The project will also deliver Child Protection (CP) services through the implementation of CP activities. The IRC will ensure that children are safe in their homes when they experience harm. This will be achieved by supporting children facing protection concerns to have access to quality services and a robust Child Protection response inclusive of case management and a Safe Healing and Learning Spaces (SHLS) where the IRC's Social and Emotional Learning (SEL) curriculum will be implemented. The IRC will also engage community members  to further mitigate potential risks for children and adolescents. At the core of the SHLS model is the SEL intervention, which follows a curriculum designed to strengthen five SEL competencies through lessons and games. The SHLS also serves as an entry point to identify children at risk and to refer them for specialized services, as well as supporting children receiving case management services. Case management services will be central to the child protection services provided. Through child-, family- and community focused strategies and coordinated case management service delivery mechanisms, the IRC will identify children at-risk of harm or who have experienced harm and will provide immediate support, ensuring the individual needs of children are assessed and addressed. Targeted children for case management include boys and girls who show signs of psychological distress, children who have experienced abuse and exploitation, unaccompanied and separated children (UASC) and children engaged in the worst forms of child labour.

Enhancing IDP Protection Services in South Sudan to facilitate and scale up protection monitoring, targeted  Protection Assistance (including GBV and CP), as well as HLP support to the most vulnerable IDPs and Returnees The projects seek to ensure that the most vulnerable people in need and Persons with Specific Needs (PSNs) including IDPs, retunes and the host community will benefit from scaled up protection services with a focus on critical lifesaving and resilience targeted assistance through comprehensive structured protection monitoring, allowing to improve efficient targeting for overall protection, , as well as GBV, CP and HLP. The activities will be implemented in Juba, Wau, Bentiu, Bor, Malakal, Yei, Yambio and Torit and prioritized respective counties   

The project will facilitate the use of the Protection Monitoring tool piloted in 2021 and used at household H/H level. This will offer standardized methodology of collecting data, which will be used by protection actors across the country for informed planning in  support to vulnerable men, women, boys and girls of all ages and diversity components. Protection concerns identified will be dealt both on individual protection services/case management basis and through community-based approaches (by ensuring referrals to the respective actor or through provision of various types of direct assistance by UNHCR. Community based protection will involve quick impact projects to address infrastructure and livelihood challenges faced by communities. 

Protection challenges will be addressed through awareness raising protection risk, targeting communities and their leaders. Support will be provided through child friendly spaces, outreach to reduce incidence of teenage pregnancy and child labor; support for psychosocial support affecting children.
SGBV issues will be addressed through outreach to ensure communities understand the benefits of reporting of incidence, addressing taboos linked to SGBV enhancing psychosocial support,  case management (including cash-based interventions), legal assistance, renovation and construction of safe houses. 

The project will address House Land and Policy issues by ensuring displaced populations benefit from outreach, legal aid/representation, counselling, support to replacement of ownership documentation through working with the Nationality, Civil Registry, Passports and Immigration. 

Overall the project will seek to empower communities affected by displacement through supporting gaps, outreach and awareness, material and cash assistance to support their resilience and ensure sustainability of assistance provided.

The Luxembourgish Government has Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the UNHCR. The UNHCR guarantees the rights of displaced people and refugees. Provision of Integrated Protection and Site Management Services to Internally displaced people, Returnees, Host Community  and Other Persons With Specific Needs in Ethiopia UNHCR’s 2022 protection programme builds on the scale up of 2021 response and will be implemented in nine regions. The programme, builds on evidence gathered from ongoing protection monitoring using the revamped Ethiopia Protection Monitoring Tool (E-PMT) in the operational areas to ensure the ongoing identification of protection and specific needs and changes in the protection landscape for IDPs, IDP returnees, host communities and other persons with specific needs requiring protection services. 
As the Protection Cluster-lead agency, UNHCR ensures the coordination of its activities, implemented directly or through partnerships, through the Protection Cluster at national and sub-national level as appropriate.
Based on the protection monitoring, UNHCR will implement an integrated set of protection services and interventions tailored to the needs and priorities of the affected, which include:
•	the provision of information, counselling, identification of protection and specific needs, referrals to services/assistance, 
•	direct provision of services and assistance to persons at risk or with specific needs; 
•	GBV awareness, prevention and response activities;
•	child protection awareness raising and case management;
•	strengthening of MHPSS, 
•	emergency EORE as required by the Mine Action AOR,
•	provision of legal awareness and legal aid for GBV case management, HLP, legal identity and civil document restoration, 
•	and strengthen social cohesion and community-based peacebuilding.

Through its CCCM intervention, UNHCR will provide care and maintenance service of site infrastructure for IDPs living in 63 sites in Tigray, 4 sites in Afar and 11 sites in Amhara for at least 230,000 vulnerable IDP children of under 18 (120,000 girls, 110,000 boys) and assisting more than 230,000 adult IDP population (103,000 Adult Men, 107,000 Adult Women(18-59 years), 11,000 Elderly Men and 10,000 Elderly Women (60 and above) which include 32,000 people with disabilities to ensure protection and assistance while striving for durable solutions.

--- 2022 - Health Apoyo a los servicios básicos de salud materno-infantil y de adolescentes en los estados priorizados y fortalecimiento del programa nacional de inmunización. 
Con el objetivo principal de contribuir a poner fin a las muertes prevenibles de madres, recién nacidos y niños, al tiempo que se promueve la salud y el desarrollo de todos los niños, en el sector de la salud UNICEF aplicará dos enfoques: abordar las desigualdades en los resultados sanitarios y fortalecer los sistemas de salud, incluida la prevención y la respuesta al COVID-19. Para abordar las desigualdades en los resultados sanitarios, UNICEF, junto con las ONG asociadas, contribuirá a reforzar los sistemas de información y a promover el uso de datos cualitativos y cuantitativos desglosados para identificar a los grupos marginados y ajustar los programas a sus necesidades; esto incluye la mejora de los sistemas de estadísticas vitales en 10 hospitales de referencia, ya que las actividades no supervisadas tienden a carecer de calidad. Simultáneamente, UNICEF apoyará acciones que establezcan mejoras sostenidas en la provisión, utilización y calidad de los servicios, apoyando 150,000 consultas de atención prenatal y las atenciones de parto seguro para 150.000 mujeres embarazadas y sus recién nacidos en hospitales y ambulatorios; proporcionando cuidados intensivos a 7.500 recién nacidos gravemente enfermos, y atenciones pediátricas para 483.820 niños y niñas menores de cinco años. En particular, UNICEF tratará de mejorar y retener la capacidad del personal sanitario a través de la formación en cuidados prenatales, neonatales, pediátricos y de emergencia, incluidos los cuidados de casos complicados del COVID-19, para 14.364 profesionales sanitarios, e incentivos para 500 miembros del personal sanitario de áreas críticas, al tiempo que se refuerza la cadena de suministros para 189 centros de salud, incluidos 114 ambulatorios y 75 hospitales de referencia, con el fin de mejorar el acceso  a los servicios y productos sanitarios neonatales e infantiles de calidad, para reducir la tasa de mortalidad neonatal y materna y dignificar la atención sanitaria. Se proporcionará tratamiento antirretroviral pediátrico ininterrumpido para 1,022 niños menores de 15 años que viven con el VIH y tratamiento para enfermedades oportunistas para 4.970 niños registrados en el programa nacional de VIH, suministros para el diagnóstico precoz del VIH en mujeres embarazadas y niños expuestos, y tratamiento para la prevención de la transmisión materno-infantil del VIH. UNICEF proporcionará ocho vacunas y equipos auxiliares al Programa Ampliado de Inmunización para 1.832.601 niños y niñas de hasta 10 años y 450.681 mujeres embarazadas, y seguirá reforzando la cadena de frío en 24 almacenes regionales y proveyendo refrigeradores para 800 puestos de vacunación para mejorar la capacidad de almacenamiento de vacunas de rutina y las vacunas contra el COVID-19, 24 vehículos para actividades en la comunidad, 7 vehículos refrigerados, 3 botes para áreas remotas fluviales, 25 incineradores para desechos de vacunación y 23 cuartos fríos para mejorar la capacidad del programa ampliado de vacunación. 
•	UNICEF apoyará la rehabilitación de 08 consultorios para el programa de Salud Escolar y de 08 consultas especializadas para adolescentes, para contribuir a reducir las desigualdades en el acceso a los servicios de salud de los niños más vulnerables en zonas remotas o zonas urbanas empobrecidas. Para contribuir a la protección del personal de salud, 60.000 trabajadores de primera línea recibirán EPP. A través de la capacitación del personal de salud y el preposicionamiento de insumos de emergencia, se apoyará al MMPS y  Protección Civil en la gestión de desastres a nivel nacional, con capacidad para atender hasta 960.000 personas, y se rehabilitarán 21 centros de salud que prestan servicios maternos y neonatales para aumentar el acceso de la población más vulnerable a servicios de salud funcionales y dignos. La capacitación y empoderamiento de las comunidades en salud materno infantil y de adolescentes y en preparación y respuesta a desastres será transversalizada en 2022

Food Security WFP SOMALIA 2022 HRP - FSC Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas. As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation. The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

Nutrition Providing Life Saving Treatment and Prevention Nutrition Services to the Vulnerable Communities in Somalia Food and Nutrition context in Somalia
Decades of conflict and natural disasters including repeated droughts and seasonal flooding followed by limited government and institutional support have had a profound negative effect on the food security situation and social service sector in Somalia. Nearly seven in ten Somalis live on less than USD 1.90 per day,  the sixth-highest poverty rate in sub-Saharan Africa. Poverty is both widespread and deep, particularly for households in rural areas and internally displaced person (IDP) settlements. The number of food-insecure people experiencing long-term stress is trending upwards, indicating that chronic food insecurity persists, requiring sustainable solutions. Recurrent climate-related shocks and political instability are key drivers of food insecurity and pose continuing risks to crop production and food access. Malnutrition in Somalia is driven by a combination of factors such as recurrent food insecurity, child illnesses, high morbidity, micronutrient deficiencies, low immunization levels, poor access to clean water and sanitation, poor hygiene practice, gender inequality and discriminatory sociocultural attitudes leading to poor care practices. Based on the latest Post Gu FSNAU assessment (September 2021), it is estimated that a total of 3.5 million out of the 15.8m people face acute food insecurity (IPC 3 and above – crisis or worse)  until December 2021. At the national level the median prevalence of Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) has remained at a serious level of 11.1%. Approximately 1.2 million children under the age of five are likely to be acutely malnourished, including 295,515 who are likely to be severely malnourished. In addition to this, around 245,909 Pregnant & Lactating Women (PLWs) will be at risk of acute malnutrition. 

Acute malnutrition is a major public health problem in Somalia. It affects disproportionately children under the age of five, as well as Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLWs), especially among IDPs, vulnerable (agro) pastoralist communities and those living in areas affected by flooding. Morbidity among children is high (≥ 20%). Out of a total of 40 surveyed population groups 18 recorded high morbidity presence of above 20%. 
Vitamin A supplementation and Measles vaccination remains low <40% in several population groups. 

TB prevalence remains one of the highest globally with Somalia in the top 10 countries with high TB burden (262 per 100,000 population) while the HIV prevalence remains <1% however with high stigma and discrimination levels at 94%.

Project activities
The World Food Program is the leading UN agency in Somalia in fighting hunger. In Somalia, WFP together with the Ministry of Health (MoH), nutrition cluster and the partners, supports nutrition service delivery and prevention. WFP collaborates with the MoH and UNICEF to offer an integrated package of nutrition and health, following the revised MoH IMAM guidelines for treating acute malnutrition in Somalia.

WFP will cover both treatment and preventive nutrition services including:
•	Targeted Supplementary Feeding Program for 665,846 moderately acute malnourished children 6-59 months; 173,746 malnourished Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLW), 10,794 malnourished People Living with HIV on ART treatment and malnourished TB patients.
•	Preventive Nutrition services for 386,102 children 6-23 months and 173,746 PLW enrolled in Maternal Child Health and Nutrition services and blanket Supplementary Feeding Program for children 6-23 months and PLW in districts where GAM (Global Acute Malnutrition) rate is above 15%.
•	Monthly cash vouchers of USD 15 for 24,104 PLWs in selected target districts.
•	24,206 caregivers with SAM children admitted to the Stabilisation  will receive food while staying at the Stabilisation Center 
•	A total of 96,150 pregnant women will receive food rations for their families when delivering their baby at a health facility

•	La réponse à la soudure agricole et pastorale.

Assurer l'accès à l'eau potable et à un assainissement viable aux IDPs et communautés hôtes de Ouallam, région de Tillaberi Par le présent projet, GOAL Niger vise à apporter une assistance WASH aux personnes déplacés internes ainsi que leur communauté d’accueil dans le département de Ouallam, région de Tillabéry. Cette assistance concernera l'accès à l'eau potable, la promotion des latrines et la sensibilisation sur l'hygiène et la Covid-19,  tout en garantissant la protection des plus vulnérables.
Ainsi, notre action dans le sous-secteur de l'eau visera à :
- Renforcer la disponibilité de l'eau à Tondikiwindi: réaliser, grâce à ce financement, une extension de la mini-AEP vers le site des déplacés avec une borne fontaines d'au moins  4 robinets de puisage. Ce qui permet la disponibilité de l'eau sécurisée pour au moins 1 000 personnes conformément aux normes nationales ou 2 000 déplacés conformément aux normes SPHERE.  
- Garantir l'accès sécurisé à l'eau potable à  1 470 ménages soit 10 290 déplaces 5 sur les 4 sites d'accueil:  Cet accès sera garanti auprès des gérants en subventionnant une moyenne de 10 litres par jour par personnes pendant 10 mois pour les ménages les plus vulnérables. Une enquête HEA sera conduite afin de mener un ciblage qui prendra en compte de manière intentionnelle les besoins des personnes et/ou des groupes les plus vulnérables à savoir les ménages des personnes vivant avec handicap, ceux dirigés par des femmes ou des enfants, ceux accueillant des enfants non accompagnés, les ménages avec les personnes âgées. 
- promouvoir la purification de l'eau dans les 4 localités à travers un appui à la vulgarisation des purifiants par des opérateurs économiques privés. l'objectif étant de disposer d'au moins un revendeur de purifiants d'eau dans chacune des localités.
Pour l'assainissement:
Vu que les latrines d’urgence ne rencontrent pas l’assentiment des bénéficiaires, GOAL se propose d'initier un dialogue communautaire autour de la défécation a l’aire libre et convenir d’un plan d’action basé sur le renforcement du système en faveur des latrines améliorées au niveau des sites et des communautés hôtes. Ceci tournera notamment autour de la mise en place de kits d’EHA classiques, d'un réseau de maçons privés et de structures communautaires d’EHA pour encourager la bonne pratique, une stratégie favorisant la demande des latrines et la gestion des déchets solides.
 Pour susciter davantage la demande, des concours inter quartiers d'hygiène et assainissement seront lancés sur chaque sites avec l'adhésion des bénéficiaires. les critères établis par les bénéficiaires, seront évalués par des jurys locaux et les lauréats récompensés par des kits WASH. Nous envisageons de former une vingtaine de maçons privés, équipés pour la construction des latrines améliorées dans les 4 localités. Enfin, une campagne de sensibilisation radiophonique sera entreprise à travers les 2 radios communautaires de Ouallam et Tondikiwindi, sur les thématiques de l'hygiène assainissement et de la COVID-19.

(USAID / BHA) Northeast Nigeria Nutrition Response 2022 The Nutrition response in 2022 will prioritise implementation of the nutrition lifesaving activities (inpatient, outpatient, and targeted supplemental feeding programmes) and targeting of LGAs with high rates of GAM (above 10%) such as MMC/Jere, Nganzai, Bama, Machina. Hard-to-reach areas (such as Gubio, Rann, Magumeri), areas with large IDP  and returnee populations (like Monguno) and high-risk/inaccessible locations such as Marte LGA will also be prioritised for nutrition assistance. 
UNICEF will primarily target acutely malnourished children and PLW who are at a significantly high risk of death. The nutrition response will also target the total under-five and PLW with preventive nutrition services e.g. micronutrient supplementation to ensure levels of acute malnutrition are not above average thresholds, and to also reduce morbidity and mortality. The response will prioritise households with persons living with disabilities, who face barriers in accessing health, nutrition and WASH services and are disproportionately food insecure due to high levels of exclusion. 
The nutrition status of the targeted population in the BAY states significantly deteriorates during the period from May-August every year, which is the lean season and coincides with the rainy season. The season is characterised by very high rates of acute malnutrition with medical complications due to poor food access and a high prevalence of diarrhoea and malaria. UNICEF will need to adequately prepare for the lean season period by prepositioning supplies, increasing the overall sector capacity to treat acute malnutrition with a focus on inpatient care and IYCF-E
The nutrition response in BAY states will be contextualised in 2022 based on the following categorisation: 
1. Protracted crisis e.g north and central Borno LGAs where the rates of acute malnutrition are high, worsened by poor access to food and health systems. The approach in these areas will include INGO/NNGO direct support to the affected population, and prioritisation of lifesaving nutrition activities. 
3. New emergencies – locations of new crisis and fluctuations such as relocations, displacements and spike in acute malnutrition. The approach will focus on the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) with a focus on lifesaving activities. 
4. Hard-to-reach / inaccessible areas – locations with limited humanitarian footprints and access e.g Gubio and Magumeri. The approach will include RRM and remote management strategy (where feasible) with a focus on life-saving interventions. UNICEF will also strengthen the implementation of nutrition interventions through local organizations or community-based structures to implement nutrition services in hard-to-reach/inaccessible areas. 
UNICEF response is primarily through services and in-kind deliveries. UNICEF will employ the use of cash and voucher assistance (CVA) to fill the nutrient gap in the Nutrition/Food Minimum Expenditure Basket to ensure that populations have access to a varied diet e.g CVA for meats and vegetables. 
The nutrition status of the affected population is an outcome of various underlying issues including access to health, WASH, food security, child protection, and gender issues. The main cause of acute malnutrition among children and women in BAY states is the high morbidity rates. High diarrhoea prevalence is the major cause of acute malnutrition among the IDPs and urban poor population due to the prevailing poor hygiene and sanitation conditions worsened by congested living conditions. The response will strengthen the integration of nutrition-sensitive interventions including WASH, food security, health, livelihoods and child protection, and gender-based violence risk mitigation.
UNICEF will prioritise projects that include basic nutrition packages such as integrated treatment of acute malnutrition (SAM and MAM) and prevention services including integration with WASH, food security, health and protections services.

Multi-sectoral assistance to populations affected by humanitarian crises in Somalia
---- Shelter & NFI Provision of emergency and durable shelters and NFIs to displacement affected communities in Somalia The Humanitarian Needs Overview estimates that 3.6 million people will be in need of Shelter support in 2022. This includes both IDPs and non-IDPs and remains a concern for 58% of the entire IDP population in Somalia. Key concerns under shelter include overcrowding, lack of security, and poor shelter conditions with majority of those living in IDP sites lacking permanent tenure to land thus increasing their risk for forced evictions. Lack of access to income is also a key concern for the most vulnerable as they often lack the necessary finances to put up adequate shelters thus necessitating the need to provide emergency shelter and non-food items. This remains particularly crucial especially in hard to reach areas of Somalia. 
The ongoing conflict and floods in parts of Somalia has resulted in damages to shelter among other critical infrastructure, and with the resulting displacement, populations often find themselves living in dangerous and unsustainable shelters. Those that are displaced for a shorter period with the intention and capability of returning to regions of origin often need emergency shelter kits while those that have been displaced for a longer period of time would require more durable shelters. Although access to shelter and housing is an issue that cuts across the different groups, IDPs remain particularly vulnerable due to their lack of tenure and displacement status. 
As such, DRC will target a total of 103,800 displacement affected communities (DACs) through provision of emergency shelter kits (ESK), non-food items (NFIs), transitional shelter and durable shelter solutions. DRC defines DACs as people affected by displacement internally and those that are returning seeking for reintegration. Therefore, DRC targets new IDPs, the IDPs in protracted situation, returnees and host communities. DRC understands that the primary displacements in Somalia is as a result of natural disasters and man-made conflict; but also, secondary displacements are now a common reality due to military offensive. These displacements are the key driver of humanitarian shelter needs in Somalia. IDPs remain in need of Shelter and NFIs support for protection from harsh climatic conditions, overall improvements to their living conditions and improvement to their chances to access livelihoods and durable solutions. On the other hand, DRC targets Host Communities – to ensure peaceful coexistence between the local population and target groups and also because many of them are equally vulnerable and in need of humanitarian assistance. For IDPs in protracted situation, DRC offers transitional shelter assistance. This also includes negotiating for extension of land lease/tenure to allow for a longer stay until full re-integration is sought. Returnees are also targeted with durable housing solutions in which case DRC proposes permanent shelter. For permanent shelter, DRC will ensure an integrated approach where other needs - WASH, shelter, livelihood, and protection are included in the settlement planning. Therefore, DRC will target newly displaced populations with emergency shelter and NFIs. For IDPs in protracted situation and returnees, DRC will seek transitional shelter and durable solutions respectively. Where cash based intervention or voucher is sought, DRC will undertake registration based on AGD and vulnerability criteria through an electronic system. Then DRC will undertake a verification exercise whereby beneficiaries will be screened to see if they meet set criteria. The list of beneficiaries selected shall be shared with a mobile money transfer company operated by telephone service providers. The cash shall be released in two tranches of 70% and 30% respectively for both NFIs and ESKs. This shall minimize risk of cash being used for other activities not related with shelter but also to make sure the cash goes to the right beneficiaries.

Strengthening essential WASH and protection services in Maban camps and surrounding host communities Humanitarian coordination and provision of CCCM-integrated responses to displacement-affected populations in Juba and Bor former PoC sites (semi-static) in hard-to-reach areas (mobile) According to the South Sudan CCCM Cluster HNO 2022, 1.64 million people are currently IDPs in need of CCCM assistance across South Sudan. After a sudden shock, IDPs often gather in informal displacement sites in extremely precarious conditions, most of the time without access to basic services and information, and with limited decision-making power on issues that affect their daily lives and their future. These gathering places are often characterized by an increased exposure to security risks and protection needs, particularly for the most vulnerable groups. Poor living conditions; lack of financial resources and limited access to basic services can lead to outbreaks of disease, increased prevalence of GBV or domestic violence, and tensions between population groups within the informal camps. Likewise, overcrowding could led to challenges in maintaining safe levels of hygiene and sanitation. Continued political uncertainty, coupled with the increased risks of climate change has also largely resulted in the inability of the international community to return these IDP’s to more suitable locations and an unwillingness from the camps inhabitants to leave. Regarding Bor and Juba former PoC camps, as of February 2022, 2,745 IDPs resided in Bor IDPs Camp, 7,299 in Juba IDPs Camp 1 and 24,255 in Juba IDPs Camp 3. Since the transition from former PoCs sites under UNMISS management to conventional IDPs site under the South Sudanese government responsibility in November 2020, the 2,745 residents of Bor IDPs camp have continued benefitting from essential services provision. Food Security Assistance inconditionnelle en cash et kits AGRs pour renforcer la résilience des ménages PDIs et communautés hôtes du département de Ouallam, région de Tillabery L'objectif dudit projet vise à améliorer la sécurité alimentaire et renforcer la résilience des ménages vulnérables à travers le cash reçu et les Kits AGRs de protection sociale. Les activités de ce projet seront mises en œuvre au niveau des communes de Ouallam et de Tondikiwindi (Mangaizé, Tondikiwindi et Diney) au profit des ménages vulnérables PDIs et communautés hôtes. Au total, 1 600 ménages seront identifiés à travers l'enquête d'Analyse de l'Economie des Ménages/Household Economic Analysis (HEA).  Cette identification tiendra compte du genre (chefs de ménages hommes et chefs de ménages femmes), de l'inclusion sociale : personnes vivant avec handicap, vieilles personnes, ménage avec enfant non accompagné, femmes enceintes ou allaitantes, etc…). Le présent projet touchera 11 200 personnes (soient 4,72% de la cible présentée dans le document « PIN & Cibles SECAL 2022"") pendant six (6) mois allant de Mars 2022 à Aout 2022 afin de satisfaire leurs besoins alimentaires au cours des périodes de pré-soudure et soudure surtout qu’il y’a risque d’épuisement précoce des stocks céréaliers cette année (décembre/janvier) et des disponibilités fourragères aggravées par l’inaccessibilité dans les zones de conflits et les pertes dues aux feux de brousse. Chaque ménage bénéficiaire recevra une somme de 32 500 F CFA par mois pour lui permettre de se procurer de vivres pour le besoin du ménage. Le paiement des bénéficiaires sera facilité par une Institution de Microfinance. En plus, ces ménages recevront de kits AGRs de protection sociale (les femmes des 1 600 ménages bénéficiaires seront organisés en groupe de 20 femmes, ce qui donne 80 groupes de femmes et chaque groupe recevra un kit AGRs), des séances de sensibilisation communautaire sur les Engins Explosifs Improvisées (EEI) seront conduites par les agents de GOAL et des actions de plaidoyer à l’échelle locale et communautaire seront menées afin d’avoir un meilleur impact national. Le projet sera mis en œuvre avec la participation de tous les acteurs concernés (les autorités : administratives, Communales, Coutumières ; les services techniques et les communautés concernés).

Based on HNO 2021, one in three communities in Syria is reportedly contaminated by explosive ordnance. One in four victims is a child (Joint MA & CP Analysis, 2020). EORE messages will be provided to 1,460,000 children and adults through humanitarian actors and public service providers using static facilities and mobile teams. UNICEF will build the capacity of partners to provide quality EORE that is age, gender and disability appropriate and to provide child victims with assistance.
 
UNICEF will strengthen the justice system to ensure that children in contact with the law victims, offenders or witnesses are protected through child-friendly, gender-sensitive services, that are community-based and family focused.

Multi-Sector Needs Assessment (MSNA) in oPt - Phase I Informing the humanitarian response in the occupied Palestinian territories through multi-sector, evidence-based monitoring, assessments, and analysis Through this proposed action, REACH (a joint initiative of ACTED, IMPACT Initiatives and UNOSAT) will support the coordination and technical implementation of two initiatives: a Multi-Sector Needs Assessment (MSNA) and a Joint Market Monitoring initiative, to provide evidence on vulnerabilities and market dynamics throughout the West Bank and Gaza. 

The MSNA will consist of a multi-sectoral household survey employed among a representative sample of the affected population in both the West Bank and Gaza. The MSNA will be conducted in partnership with OCHA oPt and within the framework of the wider development and humanitarian architecture. As in 2021, household data for the MSNA will be collected in partnership with the Palestinian Central Bureau for Statistics (PCBS). Central to this collaborative data partnership are strategies and protection measures, including specific channels to ensure accountability to affected populations, the most vital of which is a dedicated strategy and platform to ensure complaint mechanisms are accessible, properly communicated, and relevant to all population groups according to CBCM SOPs.

The proposed MSNA and JMMI will aim to achieve the following objectives:

1. Directly inform joint humanitarian-development response planning based on the nexus approach that the United Nations Country Team (UNCT) has adopted beginning in 2022, through the provision of comprehensive, multi-sectoral household data as well as monitoring and reporting of market prices and availability dynamics. Data from both the MSNA and JMMI will therefore aim to inform the development of both the 2023 HNO/HRP and further support the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework planned for 2023-27;

2. Provide a detailed inter-sectoral analysis of the magnitude and severity of humanitarian needs among crisis-affected populations in oPt, to support the calculation of sectoral and overall People in Need (PiN) and severity calculations.

3. Provide a detailed vulnerability analysis to identify at-risk and ‘furthest left behind’ population groups, as well as geographic areas with the most acute needs and vulnerabilities, to subsequently inform assistance targeting and response planning efforts; 

4. Support inclusive and people-centred assistance provision based on the principles of Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP), through the collection of information regarding preferred communication, information sharing, and assistance modalities. 

5. To improve access to timely and accurate regional and nationwide data through the harmonized joint market monitoring framework that will provide evolutions in prices, market functionality/access, and household expenditure to inform cash transfer programming, development programmes and identify contextual factors (both historically and on a monthly basis) that might affect market dynamics to support cash-based interventions for programmatic actors.  

REACH will produce the following key outputs: 
1 clean, anonymized multi-sectoral needs household dataset; 
1 static summary findings dashboard; series of presentations to key stakeholders; 
1 package of six sectoral factsheets; 
1 final analytical report (MSNA Bulletin)
1 Interactive/dynamic Market Monitoring dashboard
2 Static infographics on Survival Minimum Expenditure Basket (SMEB)/Cash Transfer Value (CTV) and price indexes
2 Static infographics on market functionality and goods availability.
1 final JMMI report/findings summary

Solidarités International est déterminée à prévenir tout acte d’exploitation ou d’abus sexuel allant à 
l’encontre de nos bénéficiaires de la part des travailleurs humanitaires et veut réaffirmer son objectif 
de mettre en place les 6 principes adoptés en 2012 (et revu en 2019) par l’Inter Agency Standing 
Committee Task Force à propos la prévention et la réponse à l’exploitation et aux abus sexuels. 
Cette politique est complémentaire de notre Code de Conduite et de notre Politique de Protection 
qui stipulent qu’il est strictement interdit pour tout employé i) d’utiliser sa position pour obtenir une 
quelconque faveur, y compris sexuelle, et ii) d’avoir des relations sexuelles avec des mineurs. Une 
politique d’Alerte professionnelle ainsi qu’un document cadre sur les mécanismes de réponse aux 
plaintes sont les piliers du pack de procédures de Solidarités International. 

SI s’engage à : 
 Diffuser et déployer cette Politique de protection en matière d’exploitation et d’abus sexuels 
sur toutes ses missions, 
 Sensibiliser ses employés à l’obligation de respecter les 6 principes IASC, 
 Veiller à la mise en place effective et au respect de cette politique, 
 Agir si jamais une violation de cette règle devait être observée. 
Chaque employé signe obligatoirement le Code d’éthique et de conduite qui inclue les 6 piliers de 
Politique de protection en matière d’exploitation et d’abus sexuels (PSEA) de SI. 

Solidarités International mentionne ces responsabilités dans les descriptions des postes de 
management concernés (comme la formation du staff ou la mise en place de mécanismes de plaintes 
et les réponses à mettre en place) pour appuyer et s’assurer d’une mise en place efficace du PSEA. 
Solidarités International met en place un mécanisme de plaintes qui permet aux bénéficiaires de ses 
actions de reporter une exploitation ou un abus sexuel, ainsi qu’un mécanisme d’alerte profesionnelle 
pour dénoncer tout comportement abusif. 

Solidarités International s’engage à investiguer dans les temps et de manière professionnelle sur toute 
allegation d’abus ou d’exploitation sexuelles impliquant des employés de SI. SI prendra des mesures 
rapides et appropriées, en ayant recours à des mesures légales si nécessaires contre les salariés ou le 
personnel associé à SI ayant commis un abus ou une exploitation sexuelle.

Multi-sectoral humanitarian response to Complex Emergencies in Venezuela and Colombia
---- Education Fortalecimiento de capacidades de respuesta comunitaria e institucional ante la ocurrencia de desastres naturales y de origen antrópico en los estados Trujillo y Mérida El proyecto tiene por objeto disminuir la vulnerabilidad y fortalecer las capacidades de recuperación y la resiliencia de las personas afectadas por grupo de edad, género y diversidad en comunidades vulnerables ante eventos adversos de origen natural y antrópico en los estados Trujillo (municipio Urdaneta) y  Mérida (municipios Tovar y Pinto Salinas). 
Las zonas objeto de intervención son frecuentemente impactadas con inundaciones, crecidas torrenciales y  movimientos en masa producto de las características topográficas de la región, la inestabilidad geológica,  las frecuentes  lluvias y el impacto del cambio climático en la zona, el periodo de retorno de eventos con importantes consecuencias parece reducirse según investigaciones recientes de la Universidad de Los Andes y análisis hechos por los organismos de seguridad del estado, como protección civil. 
El último evento ocurrió en agosto del año 2021 y aún  se encuentran en  espacios de alojamiento temporal 80 familias afectadas para quienes, en el corto plazo, no se vislumbran alternativas de reubicación, según datos aportados por las autoridades locales.  Estas personas requieren de un apoyo inmediato con enfoque intersectorial, que incluya atención psicosocial, jornadas de salud (adultos, pediátrica y ginecobstétrica), entrega de kits de enseres e higiene que incluyan insumos para la higiene menstrual y   la implementación de un programa de formación  para el emprendimiento  que facilite  el empoderamiento económico de las mujeres cabeza de familia que han sido afectadas. 
Tomando en cuenta el nexo entre actividades humanitarias y de desarrollo, dadas las características de las zonas de intervención y sus  antecedentes, en función de mitigar el impacto en vidas humanas  y contribuir a  mejorar el restablecimiento de medios de vida, mantenimiento y protección de los hogares,  se prevé la capacitación para la gestión del riesgo y el fortalecimiento de la capacidad de respuesta de los habitantes de  5 comunidades vulnerables de los referidos municipios, así como la transversalización  del conocimiento de la gestión del riesgo mediante la formación  a docentes en tres escuelas. 
Asimismo, se hará  la identificación del riesgo y preparación para la respuesta en emergencia de los hospitales de Tovar y  Santa Cruz de Mora y el ambulatorio de Quebrada de Cueva en el municipio Urdaneta de Trujillo, con la capacitación del talento humano y la instalación de sistemas fotovoltaicos que  garanticen la atención en áreas vitales de estos centros de salud en momentos de emergencia.
Se prioriza también la necesidad de atender debilidades en cuanto a la preparación de respuesta por parte de las instituciones del Estado y la creación de planes de gestión de la emergencia.
La iniciativa comprende actividades de sensibilización y formación para fortalecer las capacidades comunitarias, institucionales y de organizaciones de la sociedad civil para identificar el riesgo,  adaptarse, prevenir, mitigar y responder a eventos adversos.
Este fortalecimiento de capacidades pasa por acciones educativas y de comunicación; la identificación y evaluación de zonas vulnerables, la zonificación de susceptibilidad y escenarios de amenazas hidrogeomorfológicas por parte de las propias comunidades, la conformación de brigadas de emergencia comunitarias y la implementación de medidas adaptativas (sistemas de alerta temprana) que ayuden a la gestión preventiva y  correctiva del riesgo de desastres; actividades orientadas a brindar atención diferenciada para personas con discapacidad en medio de la emergencia,  así como la preparación para la gestión del agua en situaciones de emergencia y el fortalecimiento y capacitación de los organismos de primera respuesta.
Se trata de un proyecto con acciones replicables en otras zonas del país con características similares. Al término de la implementación contaremos con comunidades conscientes del riesgo y preparadas para gestionar de forma efectiva la emergencia.

Global Food Crisis – Humanitarian Assistance to People Affected by the Severe Food Insecurity Crisis in East and Southern Africa. Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Integrated Rapid Response Mechanism (IRRM). IRRM is a Delivering as One approach, in which UNICEF supports WASH and nutrition activities, FAO provides emergency seeds and livelihood kits, and WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.

Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness and mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace.

Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities and are part of the ‘new way of working’.

Global Food Crisis – Humanitarian Assistance to People Affected by the Severe Food Insecurity Crisis in East and Southern Africa. WFP SOMALIA 2022 HRP - FSC Somalia has been impacted by multiple shocks in 2020, including desert locust invasion, flash floods and COVID-19. This has negatively affected the ability of vulnerable households to meet their food security needs. The urban poor, including IDP households, have been disproportionally affected due to the socio-economic effects from COVID-19 due their heavy reliance on food purchases from the market and casual labor as the main sources of income. These households are likely to face food consumption gaps due to declines in employment and income-earning opportunities. The desert locust caused significant damage to cereal crops, fruits, vegetables and pasture in the northern and central regions. Control efforts of the government and partners in Somaliland and Puntland made progress, but an increasing number of adult locust groups was reported in central regions. In addition, in the northeast, remained swarms have matured, and some have moved towards central areas. As per FAO, the hatching and band formation is occurring now and more swarms are likely to move to other areas in central Somalia and at later stages are expected to move towards crop producing areas in the south; which can have some negative impact to the crops and pasture up to early next year.

The impact of localized flooding particularly in riverine areas destroyed farmland and crops and caused population displacement, leading to significant crop losses and the loss of income from agricultural employment.

Jointly with the Government and other humanitarian actors, WFP Somalia has supported communities and vulnerable houses impacted by the multiple shocks. The high levels of sustained humanitarian assistance in 2020 have played a critical role in stabilizing the situation. The immediate food security outlook for Somalia however looks bleak despite the efforts sustained in 2020. According to the latest Post-Gu Assessment, 2.1 million people are expected to be food insecure (IPC 3 and 4) across Somalia through December 2020. An additional 3 million people are expected to be Stressed (IPC 2), bringing the total number of people facing cute food insecurity to 5.1 million until the end of this year. Based on results of the 2020 Post Gu assessment, an estimated 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition between September 2020 and August 2021, including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

Integrated Protection Assistance Program for Venezuelan mixed migration flows in South America and vulnerable population living in Venezuela and Colombia. Respuesta multisectorial humanitaria en Venezuela En Venezuela, DRC busca proporcionar asistencia humanitaria a poblaciones vulnerables y afectadas por la crisis actual como son las consecuencias socioeconómicas de la pandemia del COVID-19, de los flujos migratorios mixtos hacia fuera de Venezuela y de las problemáticas fronterizas relacionados a actividades ilícitas y conflictos de grupos armados que vive la población que reside en Venezuela, tales como desplazamientos y/o confinamientos masivos. Por medio de una intervención multisectorial, DRC brindará asistencia de emergencia con un enfoque de protección tanto para refugiados en Venezuela, venezolanos con la intención de migrar, venezolanos retornados, desplazados internos y a población de acogida afectada, aplicando de manera transversal un enfoque sensible a la edad, el género y la discapacidad para llegar a un total de 21,288 personas vulnerables. Los perfiles priorizados por DRC serán aquellos que presenten altos niveles de vulnerabilidad como lo son las personas con necesidades específicas de protección (NNA, mujeres, LGBTI, ancianos, etc.), personas con discapacidad, sobrevivientes o personas en riesgo de violencia basada en género, víctimas de desplazamiento masivo o confinamiento, grupos indígenas entre otros. Este proyecto será implementado en todas las regiones en las cuales DRC trabaja en Venezuela, que, al mismo tiempo, son zonas de mayor proporción de necesidades humanitarias severas de acuerdo con el HRP 2022/23: Zulia, Sucre y Apure. Esta acción tiene como objetivo ofrecer una intervención de protección integrada que combina la protección y asistencia de emergencia para mejorar las condiciones de las poblaciones vulnerables antes mencionadas. 
La acción propuesta incluye los siguientes sectores/actividades: Coordinación, Protección, Seguridad Alimentaria, Salud, Agua, saneamiento e higiene y Educación. El presente proyecto tendrá como línea de intervención principal, el abordaje de las necesidades de protección encontradas en una evaluación de campo llevada a cabo en noviembre del 2021 en los estados de Sucre (municipios de Arismendi, Cajigal, Mariño y Valdés), Zulia (municipios de Maracaibo, Rosario de Perijá, Machiques de Perijá, Páez) y Apure (municipio Páez) y como líneas complementarias a los sectores de salud, WASH, educación y seguridad alimentaria. Es por ello que DRC plantea una respuesta integral no solo a necesidades de  protección como son, el acceso a información, asistencia legal y acceso a documentación para población vulnerable, incluidas las personas sobrevivientes y en riesgo de VbG,  el acceso a asistencia individualizada y especifica de protección y prevención de trata sino también a cubrir necesidades básicas de seguridad alimentaria;  mediante distribuciones mensuales de kits familiares alimenticios por 10 meses en las zonas de intervención, salud; con la rehabilitación de centros médicos seleccionados y educación; proveyendo suministros escolares y de higiene personal y familiar, a través de una intervención multisectorial y previamente coordinada con autoridades y comunidades locales. Uno de los hallazgos de la evaluación de campo fue la falta de data relacionada a protección para poder producir análisis confiables, es por esto por lo que DRC plantea implementar un análisis de protección basado en evidencia a través de un monitoreo continuo de protección en las localidades de intervención, con la finalidad de tener información a tiempo para poder identificar riesgos y priorizar necesidades.

---- Irish Aid Provision of lifesaving GBV interventions for the crisis affected populations in Mayendit, Rubkona and Juba Counties IRC through the Women Protection and Empowerment program will provide specialized GBV response services and prevention interventions targeting the crisis affected populations in Mayendit, Rubkona and Juba counties.  This will be through the provision of life saving GBV case management services guided by the survivor centered approach.  IRC will ensure the service provision is in coordination with other service providers for a multisectoral approach which comprise of medical, legal, safety and psychosocial support services. A total of 472(325W, 123G, 12M, 12B) will be targeted for case management services across the proposed locations. IRC will continuously engage women and girls and the community at large to identify barriers in accessing the GBV services and collaboratively work together to address them through the existing community-based protection structures. In addition, quarterly reviews and updating of the referral pathways as well as continuous feedback sessions will be held to ensure that the pathways are functional across the proposed locations. The women and girls’ safe spaces (2 Rubkona, 2 Juba and 2 Mayendit) will serve as avenues of empowerment for women and girls with a major focus on provision of contextualized psychosocial support interventions which seek to support in the healing, recovery and building resilience of women and girls. The Women and Girls Safe Space toolkit will be instrumental in providing guidance on the operationalization of the safe spaces especially in ensuring accountability as well as encouraging the women-girls led processes and ownership. Tailored curriculums for the engagement of women and girls such as Girl Shine for the adolescent girls and their care givers as well as Women Rise a psychosocial support tool kits for the women will ensure each age group has appropriate and contextualized PSS intervention. 4,500(3,180W, 1,320G) will be targeted for the WGSS activities. On GBV prevention IRC will engage communities through SASA! Together and EMAP as the primary GBV prevention approaches. The two approaches seek to provoke discussions on power imbalance as the root cause of violence while analyzing negative social norms, beliefs, behavior, and practices that contribute to violence against women and girls. Additionally, IRC seeks to build the capacity of communities to respond and prevent GBV through training and community led dialogues which will equip them with knowledge and skills. For GBV risk mitigation measures, IRC will work closely with women and community led structures to carry out GBV safety audits where action points to address the identified risks and concerns will be tasked to the relevant actors. Findings from the safety audits will inform other interventions such as training on Fuel Efficient Stoves for the women as well as production of reusable sanitary materials with the locally available raw materials. In coordination with the GBV SC, IRC will distribute dignity kits to the women and girls of reproductive age at risk of GBV. The proposed interventions aim to target 54,715 (27,904 Women, 19,150 Girls, 4,924 Men and 2737 Boys) where 78% IDP will be targeted, 18% host communities and 4% returnees. Out of the total target, 10% will be people living with disabilities.  IRC currently has presence in Juba (Juba IPD camp 1 and 3, Don Bosco IPD camp, Mahad IPD camp, Juba way station and Juba Teaching Hospital), Rubkona (Bentiu IPD camp and in host communities) and Mayendit. In all these locations, IRC is providing GBV response services, GBV community engagement activities including EMAP, SASA! and awareness raising activities, psychosocial support activities including skills building activities and capacity building activities to community leadership structures and partners and community members.

HRP	Multi-Sector	Harmonised multi-purpose cash assistance to meet critical basic needs of flood and conflict affected communities in Jonglei and UnityStates, South Sudan Enhanced Access and Utilization of Quality Health Services in South Sudan (Kapoeta South, Rumbek East, Aweil East, Aweil South, Koch, Mayendit, Panyijar and Rubkona Counties) Health systems in South Sudan have been impacted by prolonged conflict, natural hazards, epidemics including COVID-19 pandemic. Reliance on humanitarian assistance due to inadequate health financing by the government (<1.9% allocation of the 2021 national budget allocation), inequitable distribution of functional health facility, human resources for health gaps and access constraints due to unprecedented flooding, frequent subnational conflict and runaway inflation contribute to challenges in meeting the health needs of underserved populations in Kapoeta South (Eastern Equatoria State), Rumbek East (Lakes State), Aweil East & Aweil South (Northern Bahr El Ghazal State), Koch, Mayendit, Panyijar & Rubkona Counties (Unity State).
The International Rescue Committee (IRC) proposes to respond to the immediate lifesaving health care needs of 340,728 people in need (71,579 Men, 79,095 Women, 93,220 Boys and 96,833 Girls with the inclusion of the elderly and persons living with disability. This project will provide essential outpatient care (communicable and non-communicable diseases), child health care, safe motherhood, Sexual and reproductive health, mental health care, gender-based violence response and emergency preparedness and response. The project will provide support to 12 static health facilities (2 PHCCs each in Aweil East, Rubkona, Panyijar, Koch; 1 PHCC each in Kapoeta South, Aweil South, Rumbek East, & Mayendit), 10 Rapid Response mobile (RRM) outreach posts (2 RRMs each in Panyijar, Mayendit, Koch, and Kapoeta South; 1 RRM each in Aweil South & Aweil East) and strengthen community health services by deploying 80 Boma Health Workers each in the 8 targeted Counties (39% of the BHI gap coverage).
Support to static health facilities will engage communities and County Health Departments (CHD) to map out underserved populations through assessments of intersectoral needs and prioritization of displaced populations without access to health services. The project will support the rehabilitation of structures, qualified staffing, pharmaceuticals supplies and commodities, health management information systems and reporting. Integration of services will be a priority of the project through multi-sector collaboration with food security and livelihoods, nutrition and protection mainstreaming. Providers will have capacity strengthening on provision of mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services, Clinical Management of Rape (CMR) and Infection prevention and control (IPC) measures. The flexible approach deployed by the RRMs including a rapid deployment approach ensures that these teams can provide immediate response within the first 72 hours of an emergency. The IRC will staff, resource, and facilitate early deployment of the RRM teams to locations pre-identified by the community and CHDs factoring the health priorities of affected populations.
Coordination through engagement with local duty bearers and partners, engagement with national and subnational coordination mechanisms will be an integral component of the response. The project will consider the perspective of the affected people through IRC’s Client Responsiveness Measurement Framework using evidence generated during implementation to amplify the voices of the affected people on services provision and decision making. Disability inclusive client responsiveness will be prioritized through engagement of organizations of persons with disability where these already exist and by direct data collection at health service points using the Washington Short Set of questions on disability. Joint support supervision will be an integral part of the intervention to provide mentorship and coaching to health staff. The project will mainstream COVID-19 risk mitigation measures across all service delivery channels to protect clients and the service providers.

The humanitarian situation in South Sudan continue to deteriorate due to the increase of vulnerability drivers including inter communal violence, climatic shock, severe flood leading to population displacement, commodity price fluctuations, and pre-existing vulnerabilities such as malnutrition. The 2022 Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) indicated that about 6.1 million  people’s living standards and their wellbeing will be impacted in 2022 as a result of inadequate or lack of access to safe water and improved sanitation. This intervention targets underserved and vulnerable population in Bentiu/Rubkona and Pariang County which is at catastrophic level according to the WASH cluster 2022 severity map and stressed severity stage in humanitarian conditions shown in 2022 HNO. 

Through this proposed intervention, the IRC seeks to improve access to safe water supply and sanitation for vulnerable communities across Bentiu/Rubkona as well as Pariang, and 2 static primary health care centers (PHCC) and 2 primary schools through the rehabilitation and maintenance of non-functional community water systems, provide safe access to household and or communal sanitation facilities and hand washing stations at strategic locations, provide hygiene promotion activities targeting diseases outbreak hotspots, and provide trainings to WASH committees.

The intervention will work closely with the County WASH department structure, community leadership, and WASH actors present in the targeted location for coordinated response as the custodian of water and sanitation services at the County level to foster coordination and collaboration with key actors in WASH and health in the targeted County. This will also support county led services mapping to ensure complementarity of interventions proposed by this project with other ongoing WASH services delivery partners.
The intervention will mainstream COVID-19 risk reduction measures across all service delivery channels to ensure reduction in transmission.
