Addressing humanitarian needs by providing information management support and distributing essential non-food items to displaced and vulnerable crisis-affected populations in Sudan. Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM): Mobility Tracking of IDPs, Returnees and Other Mobile Populations in Sudan Following the crises that has affected Sudan since February 2003 and, in response to the need for accurate information on displacement and the identification of beneficiaries for the delivery of humanitarian aid, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) began its Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) program in 2004 to support the Government of Sudan (GoS) and its humanitarian partners in establishing an accurate data collection system and providing data on displacement in areas most affected by the conflict and natural disaster. DTM is a system to track and monitor displacement and population mobility. It is designed to regularly and systematically capture, process and disseminate information to provide a better understanding of the movements and evolving needs of displaced populations, whether on site or en route.
Data collection strategies and tools are based on the DTM global methodology but have been adapted to reflect context and population movements specific to Sudan. IOM has been working in close collaboration with the Humanitarian Aid Commission (HAC) and partners in the field to establish a unified and systematic method to collect individual data on internally displaced persons (IDPs) and returnees in seven states. Up until 2018, the DTM program in Sudan focused on registration, including biometric registration (since 2010), of IDPs and returning IDPs. Registration was mostly carried out in response to requests from the government and humanitarian partners for the identification of beneficiaries and the delivery of humanitarian assistance (i.e. food vouchers by WFP), positioning DTM Sudan as the reference source of displacement data in the country.
While the emergency levels of the crisis in the country reduces and the situation stabilizes in most of the conflict affected areas, there remains a strong need to restructure the program and tailor the operation to better suit the current protracted displacement and return scenario, to in turn inform evidence-based programming by IOM and the wider humanitarian community in Sudan. Specifically, there is the need to further update displacement figures more frequently, comprehensively, systematically, and in regular intervals to ensure that data is continually collected, provides a meaningful resource and is available through IOM’s DTM system.

Improve food security and build resilience to seasonal climatic shocks for communities living in cattle camps Improved food security and livelihoods of IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host communities in South Sudan In line with the South Sudan 2022 Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP) and the FSL Cluster priorities, NPA will support vulnerable and food-insecure Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs), returnees and vulnerable host communities in IPC 4 locations in Canal/Pigi, Fangak, Pochalla & Bor South Counties of Jonglei State, Rumbek East, Rumbek Center, Cueibet, Yirol East, Yirol West and Awerial Counties of Lakes State, Terekeka County of Central Equatoria State and Kapoeta North County of Eastern Equatoria State. The targeted communities in the identified counties will be supported to improve their food security and livelihoods through provision of timely and appropriate main season and dry season inputs/kits (Crop, vegetable and fishing), training in improved agronomic and fishing practices. In addition, NPA will support food-insecure with cash transfers in Rumbek East and Rumbek Center Counties in Lakes State with cash transfers to address their food needs. NPA’s emergency assistance and livelihoods support aims at saving lives and averting total collapse of livelihoods in the target Counties. The provision of agricultural and fishing inputs/kits, training in agricultural production and fishing is expected to improve the food production and in turn the food security of the target households (HHs) thus supporting them to recover from crisis and placing them on an accelerated path to early recovery and resilience to acute shocks. NPA’s response will address the food security and livelihoods needs and priorities identified in the South Sudan 2022 Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO).

NPA seeks to support 105,056 HHs (630,338 individuals) in the targeted Counties with livelihood kits and cash transfers to address food insecurity. Some of the kits will be provided by FAO and some procured by NPA. Training on improved agronomic and fishing practices, marketing and group dynamics will be done through model farmers and fisher folk who will undergo a Training of Trainers (ToT) and subsequently cascade the knowledge and skills to the farmers and fisher folk in their communities. The knowledge gained from these trainings will improve the agricultural and fishing practices of the target HHs thus improving food production, addressing their immediate food security needs and building their resilience to future shocks. The provision of cash transfers and agricultural inputs and fishing kits and subsequent enhancement of food production and fishing is expected to contribute to improvement of the Household Diversity Score (HDDS) and Food Consumption Score (FCS) of the target HHs. COVID-19 preventive and mitigation measures will be mainstreamed throughout all activities to prevent spread and transmission of the virus. The proposed interventions are aligned to the FSL cluster objective 1: CO1: Provide food assistance to prevent famine and improve food consumption, dietary diversity and coping strategies for vulnerable populations (in IPC 5, 4 & some 3) in a way that prevents the spread & transmission of COVID 19 and Objective 2: Enhance and sustain emergency food production through complementary vegetable and crop livelihood inputs, fishing and livestock support in a way that prevents the spread & transmission of COVID 19.

NPA will employ a community-based beneficiary selection approach which will entail establishing Project Management Committees (PMC’s) to lead the selection of eligible beneficiaries based on the beneficiary selection criteria. Vulnerable HHs with severe food insecurity including female, child, disabled/chronically ill headed HHs; persons living with or at risk of HIV/AIDS and survivors of Gender-Based Violence (GBV) will be targeted in this project.

The target communities will be the prime movers of the implementation process through engagement in the project. Through various means, NPA will gather feedback from the target communities and stakeholders to improve project implementation.

Emergency aid in the areas of protection and health as well as cash transfers for those in particular need of protection Access to safe schools and quality education to crisis affected children in Northern Bahr El Ghazal State in South Sudan While every child has a right to education, access to safe schools and provision of quality education in government schools have been a standing challenge to most South Sudanese children. This has been influenced by different factors including cost of school fees and registration as well as education supplies, access to safe water and latrines with changing rooms has affected girls’ attendance in schools’ low incentive for teachers and limited number of in-service trainings for teachers largely impact the access and provision of quality education. According to the HNO 2022 an estimated 3.6 million people are in need of education services in South Sudan.
The proposed activities aim to ensure girls and boys can be enrolled to school and access safe and quality education while responding to strategic goal 2 and 3 and Education cluster goal 1,2 and 3 in Aweil East and Aweil South of the Northern Bahr el Ghazal as highlighted as second priority by education cluster. The project will reach a total of 5600 (3055G, 1874B, 312F and 359M). The project will ensure all groups are reached including girls, boys, men, and women as well as children with special needs.
To improve access and inclusion students will be provided with scholastic materials and recreational materials which will support retention of adolescent and pedagogical and protection trainings will be provided to teachers to improve their teaching practices and creating safe spaced for the students.  Improvement of WASH practices in school through latrines construction with safe water points and provision of hygiene material which not only will respond to hygiene practices in schools but also the prevention against COVID-19. The education administrator, school management committee and Parents teachers’ associations will be capacitated in school leadership and management and psychosocial social support as well as coaching technique training to school inspectors which will support in supervision and guidance for both educators and learners. During this HRP period, IRC will continue implementing the 15 months existing education project funded by LEGO Foundation ($1.4M), which is aims to contribute to improving children’s wellbeing and resilience  through Learning through Play (LtP) approaches in Aweil East and Aweil South.

Community based rural development project Improving short-term and long-term food security and livelihoods access in Jonglei, WBeG, Lakes, Upper Nile, through provision of unconditional food assistance, investment in food production assets, and utilization and strengthening of local capacities. In line with the FSL cluster strategy for 2022, ACTED will contribute towards improving food security of over 712,536 beneficiaries through provision of in-kind and cash food assistance, enhancing emergency food production though distribution of livelihood kits and reducing dependency on food and agricultural inputs through resilience building activities such as training and market support functionality. Millions of South Sudanese remain displaced across the country following years of violent conflict that resulted in one of the most devastating humanitarian crises in recent history. Based on the latest IPC analysis and projections until July 2021, 60% of the population living in South Sudan is critically food insecure with 7.2 million people estimated to face high levels of acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above). Specifically, 4.668 million people are facing crisis (IPC Phase 3), 2.413 million people are facing emergency (IPC Phase 4) and 108,000 people are facing catastrophic (IPC Phase 5) food insecurity  As such, the needs across South Sudan have severely increased, driven by flooding, insecurity, population displacements, declined crop production, diseases and pests, the economic crisis, the effects of COVID-19, limited access to basic services, and the cumulative effects of prolonged years of asset depletion and loss of livelihoods.  The project activity will be in line with the cluster Objectives “CO1: Provide food assistance to prevent famine and improve food consumption, dietary diversity and coping strategies for vulnerable populations (in IPC 5, 4 & some 3)

CO2: Enhance emergency food production through complementary vegetable and crop seeds and fishing and livestock support (in IPC 3, 4 & 5)

CO3: Reduce dependency on food and agricultural inputs to support and strengthen households’ ability to absorb shocks (implemented across all 78 counties)

Emergency food assistance Programa de seguridad alimentaria basado en la escuela  Con el objetivo de contribuir a la seguridad alimentaria de la población con mayores necesidades, el Programa Mundial de Alimentos de Naciones Unidas (WFP, por sus siglas en inglés) en Venezuela desarrolla un programa de asistencia humanitaria basado en la escuela para garantizar el acceso de los más vulnerables a una alimentación adecuada y nutritiva en el entorno escolar, familiar y comunitario. 
Este programa inició en 2021 con comidas escolares en emergencias priorizando escuelas iniciales y de educación especial.

WFP proporciona comidas escolares acompañado de un paquete integrado de intervenciones para mejorar el acceso a alimentos nutritivos y diversificados a través de las escuelas, contribuyendo al mismo tiempo a mejorar la salud y la nutrición de los niños en edad escolar, los estudiantes con discapacidad y el personal escolar, y apoyando a las comunidades a reducir la dependencia en estrategias de afrontamiento. De manera gradual, el WFP está realizando compras locales de alimentos, e incluyendo acciones para apoyar los mercados locales con compras a pequeños productores y apoyo técnico para acceso a mercados.

En este sentido, el programa de comidas escolares en emergencias tiene los siguientes componentes, para asegurar un enfoque integral que apoye al estudiante en el entorno escolar y familiar:

1. Entrega de comidas escolares nutritivas para estudiantes y personal escolar, promoviendo las compras locales y a pequeños productores.
2. Apoyo a la seguridad alimentaria del hogar a través de comida en especie o transferencias monetarias.
3. Rehabilitación de cocinas escolares para garantizar condiciones adecuadas de preparación de alimentos.
4. Comunicación para sensibilizar acerca de los principios humanitarios, la adecuada preparación de alimentos, nutrición, higiene y mantenimiento de cocinas escolares.
5. Fortalecimiento de capacidades de socios implementadores y personal escolar.
6. Acciones sensibles a la nutrición, que incluyen, tamizaje en las escuelas, educación nutricional, referencia a servicios especializados y entrega de alimento complementario fortificado (Supercereal Plus).

MC will work on improving access to basic Water and sanitation services through the delivery of water trucking, SWM, Desludging and the rehabilitation of water supply infrastructure in IDP locations and areas with a high number of IDPs and returnees, and areas we anticipate significant inward displacement (Ar-Raqqa and DEZ, Dana, Daret Azza and Atareb in Idleb and north Aleppo). Through ongoing Coordination with WASH cluster, working groups, local councils and other agencies, MC will be coordinating its response in relation to the gaps identified and associated needs. In 2021, a special focus will be given by MC to seek solutions for operation and maintenance (O&M), through support to local committees and water authorities directly after the completion of water supply rehabilitation. MC will work actively to identify and implement water trucking sustainable solutions and cost effi cient sanitation management in the targeted IDP locations. Internal water supply networks, water tanks and toilets will complement more comprehensive HH shelter activities, providing safe and dignified accommodation standards for displaced  and for those who have chosen to return. Assistance and Protection for Irregular Migrants and their Communities in Lebanon - PHASE I ​PROVISION OF PROTECTION AND HUMANITARIAN ASSISTANCE SERVICES TO MIGRANTS IN VULNERABLE SITUATIONS  The project’s aim is to provide a range of protection services to migrants in need, strengthen links between targeted community groups and partners, improve the quality of services available, and enhance knowledge on migrant population groups in Lebanon. Services will target both male and female migrants, with a higher caseload of the latter group due to their increased number in country. Beneficiaries will typically be working age, between 18 and 40 years old. The services that IOM will deliver, either directly or through partners, include legal assistance, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), safe and temporary shelters for vulnerable migrants, provision of non-food items, multipurpose cash assistance (MPCA), and voluntary humanitarian return. These services will be made accessible to migrants by scaling up IOM’s pre-existing case management services, supporting enhanced capacity of, and referral with partners, strengthening culturally appropriate outreach to large migrant groups, including translation and interpretation,, and expanding community-level networks to strengthen targeted communities’ awareness of and access to IOM and partner services, as well as wider issues of concern. Additionally, IOM will provide training to partner organizations in case management, identification of vulnerable migrants and victims of trafficking, and Psychological First Aid, as well as other important thematic areas such as migrants with diverse SOGIESC and rights of migrants with regards to detention. Finally, enhancing knowledge of migrant populations will involve nationwide data-collection efforts via key informant interviews. The project will be implemented by the IOM in partnership with civil society organizations (CSO) and community-based initiatives. Provision of or onward referral to multisector assistance such as food or health support will be mainstreamed across the project.

European Commission (DG-ECHO) Contribution to OCHA 2022 Renforcement des mécanismes de Coordination et de Plaidoyer pour la protection humanitaire et l’assistance aux populations les plus vulnérables au Mali En 2021, la crise humanitaire au Mali s'est aggravée en raison de l'augmentation et de l'expansion des de la violence intercommunautaire et des attaques des groupes armés non étatiques (GANE) dans les régions du centre, du sud et de l'ouest. Cette crise a été aggravée par les bouleversements politiques marqués par deux coups d'état en août 2020 et mai 2021, et l'incertitude persistante de la transition politique laisse l'État dans l'incapacité de répondre aux services sociaux de base des populations. 
Les déplacements internes de personnes ont augmenté de 100 000 en 2021, atteignant plus de 401 000 personnes soit quatre fois plus qu'il y a deux ans. Au total, 156 000 réfugiés maliens résident dans les pays voisins tandis que le Mali accueille 48 000 réfugiés et leur fournit protection et assistance. Les gains économiques du Mali se sont érodés, avec 900 000 personnes (0,04% de la population) qui sont retombées dans la pauvreté en raison de la crise socioéconomique de la COVID-19. la capacité des ménages est fragilisée à cause de la perte de revenus, de la réduction des transferts de fonds et à l'augmentation du coût de la vie. 
La Banque mondiale prévoit une augmentation du taux de pauvreté à 4,8 % en 2022. La crise de protection est également aggravée avec une augmentation des incidents de sécurité.  Les acteurs de la violence basée sur le genre (VBG) ont signalé 5 486 incidents de VBG, soit une augmentation de 41 % comparativement à la même période en 2020. Plus de 1 640 écoles sont fermées en raison de l'insécurité, affectant plus de 2,9 millions d'enfants dont 40 % se trouvent dans la région centrale de Mopti. Quatre districts centraux ont signalé que 40 % des écoles étaient fermées. Dans les régions du sud, 10 pour cent des écoles sont fermées à Koulikoro, Koutiala et Sikasso, privant 30 000 enfants de leur éducation. A ce jour, le Mali a rapporté plus de 15 800 cas de COVID-19.
En 2021, 1,3 million de personnes ont connu un niveau élevé d'insécurité alimentaire aiguë. le niveau le plus élevé depuis 2015, et 3 055 253 personnes ont été touchées par les mauvaises pluies et une saison de soudure prolongée. La situation humanitaire reste entravée par l'augmentation des besoins et la faiblesse des financements, avec 32 % des fonds mobilisés au 31 octobre 2021. Malgré les contraintes opérationnelles, les partenaires humanitaires ont aidé plus de 2,45 millions des 4,7 millions de personnes ciblées au 30 septembre 2021. 
Les capacités de réponse existantes au Mali représentent plus de 160 organisations humanitaires, acteurs du développement ainsi que des forces militaires (MINUSMA, Forces maliennes de défense et de sécurité, Barkhane, Mission européenne de formation, G5 Sahel). Le contexte susmentionné exigera une coordination efficace et la présence d’OCHA demeure très importante. OCHA maintiendra sa présence à Bamako, Mopti, Tombouctou, Gao et ouvrira une antenne à Ségou tout en couvrant à distance les régions de Taoudénit, Ménaka, Kidal et les régions du sud Est et Ouest. 

Sept clusters actifs (Éducation, Sécurité alimentaire, Santé, Nutrition, Protection, Abris/BNA et WASH), des sous-clusters et des groupes de travail spécialisés (Accès, CM-Coord, Redevabilité, Genre et Cash) sont en place au niveau national et local. Le Bureau d’OCHA au Mali continuera ainsi à jouer un rôle central dans la mobilisation, la coordination et le soutien des acteurs humanitaires dans les domaines de la coordination, la gestion de l’information, le financement humanitaire et le plaidoyer. 

OCHA continuera à jouer son rôle central dans la mobilisation des partenaires, l’utilisation des instruments et des mécanismes de financement tout en veillant à ce que les besoins humanitaires croissants soient prises en compte. OCHA assumera son rôle clé dans la coordination militaire au niveau national et régional de concert avec les forces militaires présentes dans le pays tout en renforçant les capacités des autorités nationales en matière de coordination

European Commission (DG-ECHO) Contribution to OCHA 2022 Renforcement de la coordination et du plaidoyer humanitaire au Tchad Le projet vise à renforcer le rôle de OCHA dans la mise en œuvre de son mandat et son rôle auprès des partenaires humanitaires et gouvernementaux au niveau des fonctions coordination, gestion de l’information et plaidoyer. Le bureau national d’OCHA à N’Djaména et ses trois sous-bureaux régionaux à l’Est (Abéché) au Sud (Goré) et la province du Lac (Baga Sola) mettent l’accent sur l’opérationnalisation de ses fonctions y compris en assurant un lien entre les activités humanitaires et de développement (nexus) en vue de promouvoir une solution durable visant à ne pas perpétuer une situation de dépendance humanitaire. Dans le cadre de cette nouvelle façon de travailler outre l’opérationnalisation du nexus, le lien avec les objectifs commun des programmes développement, paix et sécurité sera mis en avant. L’accent est aussi mis sur le renforcement de la coordination civilo-militaire afin de faciliter l’accès et la protection des civils.

Le projet a pour but de renforcer la coordination d’une réponse humanitaire rapide et efficace afin de sauver des vies et protéger les personnes affectées par les situations de crises au Tchad. Une coordination humanitaire rapide et correctement évaluée au niveau des besoins de la population affectée permettra aux acteurs humanitaires de mieux identifier et répondre aux besoins humanitaires, de renforcer la préparation de réponse aux urgences à travers le renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et plus spécifiquement l‘Equipe humanitaire pays, la coordination inter-clusters, la coordination civilo-militaire, les clusters et les mécanismes de coordination au niveau de terrain.
Le projet vise aussi à assurer le plaidoyer humanitaire à travers l’analyse des besoins faites par l’ensemble de la communauté humanitaire et ses partenaires en vue une compréhension commune des problématiques auxquels fait face le Tchad, ses causes profondes, l’impact sur les populations. OCHA jouera un rôle clé dans la création d'espaces de collection et d'analyse et gestion d’informations, pour assurer une stratégie de réponse coordonnée menant à des actions humanitaires répondant aux besoins les plus aigus et être mieux préparé face aux urgences soudaines. Le projet permettra également d’assurer conjointement avec la communauté humanitaire le plaidoyer en faveur du respect des principes humanitaires, de la protection des civils, de l'accès humanitaire et pour la mobilisation et l'allocation efficace de ressources humanitaires.

Un accent a été mis sur la mise en œuvre des plans d’action de la redevabilité envers les populations affectées (AAP), la PSEA et la préparation aux urgences en plus d'intégrer une attention au genre et de renforcer la centralité de la protection.
Un plaidoyer pour plus de visibilité des résultats tangibles au niveau de la réponse facilitant la mobilisation de ressources pour les différentes crises au Tchad (mouvement de population – crise du Bassin du Lac Tchad, insécurité alimentaire et malnutrition, urgences sanitaires) est aussi défini comme une priorité dans ce projet

OCHA continuera de jouer également un rôle moteur dans le renforcement du lien entre les acteurs humanitaires et de développement et la transformation de la réponse humanitaire, en lien avec les engagements pris au Sommet humanitaire mondial de 2016 et ceci à travers la nouvelle façon de travailler (NWOW) et le renforcement de l’utilisation de la modalité de transfert monétaire.

WASH II - Facilitating access to clean and safe drinking water to conflict-affected communities in Idleb 2022 Provide Lifesaving WASH Assistance to Vulnerable Populations in North West Syria  NGO X proposes to provide lifesaving safe water to approximately 851,935 vulnerable individuals in Idleb Governorate, North West Syria. This will be implemented via the provision of essential support to 51 Water Stations (WSs) and 4 Water Units (WUs). NGO X has extensive experience delivering water supply programming in Idleb since 2014. In 2021 NGO X provided clean safe water to the homes of over one million people in Idleb via 66 WS and 4 WU. The proposed project builds upon the experience of having successfully delivered several similar projects funded by OCHA, FCDO, ECHO and BHA.
The aim of the action is to ensure access to reliable, safe, and clean drinking water to vulnerable conflict-affected communities including host and displaced populations in high priority northern sub-districts of Idleb Governorate. Core activities will include procurement of electricity, fuel, minor infrastructure rehabilitation, training to water station operators, coaching to WUs, water quality monitoring and hygiene promotion.
The proposed action will enable people living in the targeted areas to access a sufficient quantity of clean and safe drinking water. Improving the access to safe water will reduce the time spent on collecting water, reduce protection risks and prevent the spread of waterborne diseases, often affecting children. Following WASH cluster standards, between 25 - 30 litres/person/day (LPD) will be piped directly to households (HH) to ensure equitable access for all community members. It should be noted that due to funding constraints and limited water network capacity, it may not be possible to go over 25 LPD.
In target areas, to complement the water supply activities, HHs—including school children, WU staff and vulnerable individuals benefiting from NGO X food or cash distributions will be reached with essential hygiene promotion sessions adapted to COVID-19 best working practices as outlined by the WASH cluster. Themes covered will include water safety, water conservation, COVID-19 and safe hygiene practices.
NGO X will also provide WASH services in camps and IDP sites. NGO X will install water supply infrastructure provide fuel, oil and other consumables to camp water stations. NGO X will extend sewage lines, construct communal latrines and undertake regular desludging services of septic tanks. To ensure adequate and appropriate solid waste collection, NGO X will also install solid waste bins and undertake solid waste collection.

Providing Lifesaving NFIs and Shelter Support in North of Syria The program provides life-sustaining shelter and NFI support and contributes towards the resilience and cohesion of communities and households by improving housing and related community/public infrastructure. Targeting both IDPs (70%) and host communities (30%) involves activities; 3,000 standard NFI kits distribution (3,000 HHs) and winterization components such as distributing (500,000 L) heating fuel to 1,667 HHs, and (2,000) stoves to 2,000 HHs and (25,000) winter clothes kits for 25,000 children both gender. As well as providing restricted cash for house rent services (1,000 units) for those IDP vulnerable groups and prioritizing female or child-headed households and elderly people and considering people with disabilities (1,000 HHs; 5,000 individuals).
This program includes 2,500 house rehabilitation activities which will target both IDPs and host communities (2,500 HHs; 12,500 individuals), this activity includes rehabilitating partially damaged units through ceiling repair, walls buildings and holes ﬁxing, doors and windows, infrastructure, electricity network, and solar panels, plastering, plumping and providing the water tank. This component will be guided by the shelter rehabilitation guidance published by the SNFI cluster in 2018 and ensuring that HLP documentations are well carried out in parallel with ﬁeld coordination with the relevant local councils

The program will seek feedback from both male and female beneﬁciaries and fully interact with both genders to ensure equitable access and equal opportunities.

Cameroon	Cameroon Humanitarian Response Plan 2023 Amélioration de la réponse multisectorielle en faveur des Réfugiés et demandeurs d’asile et mise en œuvre des solutions durables pour les réfugiés au Cameroun  Le projet a pour objectif l’amélioration de l’environnement de protection, l’accès aux solutions et voies complémentaires pour les réfugiés et demandeurs d’asile notamment en ce qui concerne  les activités d’enregistrement , de  la documentation, la protection de l’enfance, la prévention ,  la réponse aux violences sexuelles et sexistes, l’accès aux services sociaux de base (santé, éducation et eau), l’accès à un abri décent et aux biens domestiques essentiels ainsi que du  renforcement de la résilience.
Le projet cible en 2023, un total de 491,113 réfugiés au Cameroun notamment : 355,667 réfugiés RCA, 132,151 NIG, 2,533 des nationalités minoritaires, 9,239 demandeurs d’asile ainsi que 15% des populations autochtones par la présence des réfugiés dans les régions affectées.
Au cours de l’année 2021, en dépit du contexte sanitaire marquée par la survenue de la pandémie de la COVID19 qui a négativement affecté l’environnement socio-économiques des populations, la situation sécuritaire fragile en RCA et l’instabilité dans la région du bassin du Lac Chad, le HCR a initié des projets visant à améliorer l’environnement de protection des réfugiés et assurer l’accès aux solutions aux réfugiés.
Les projets déjà initiés requièrent une continuité dans la mise en œuvre afin renforcer la résilience et l’autonomisation des réfugiés de longue date, assurer leur inclusion effective dans les programmes de développement et donner accès aux solutions mais également apporter la réponse aux nouvelles situations d’urgences.
Au cours de 2023, il sera mis en œuvre par le HCR, les acteurs humanitaires et le gouvernement des activités qui garantissent l’accès équitable et la jouissance des droits humains fondamentaux aux femmes, aux hommes, aux filles et aux garçons de tout âge et ceux ayant diverses vulnérabilités.
L’UNHCR compte à travers ce projet :
-	Apporter la réponse aux besoins critiques de protection en assurant l’accès à l’asile, la documentation, la prévention et la réponse aux VBG, l’accès à l’éducation, l’accès durable aux infrastructures et services WASH, aux moyens d’existence et à l’inclusion socio-économique, ainsi que le renforcement de la cohésion sociale et de la coexistence pacifique entre les réfugiés et avec la communauté hôte.
-	Mettre en œuvre les solutions durables en renforçant la résilience des communautés affectées par les différentes crises et les moyens d’existence et explorer des opportunités viables par la mise en œuvre des alternatives aux camps notamment dans la région de l’extrême nord.
-	Le HCR continuera à faciliter le retour volontaire des réfugiés dans leur pays d’origine, à identifier les cas de réinstallation, d’importants besoins existent en termes de réfugiés pouvant potentiellement être considérés pour cette solution durable, cette dernière ne peut se réaliser que si les pays de réinstallations offrent des places. Par ailleurs, cette solution ne concerne qu’un pourcentage infime de la population réfugiée dans son ensemble. Le défi reste néanmoins la nécessité d’étendre le pool d’identification des réfugiés vers leurs zones d’installation mais avec des capacités très limitées et à faire le plaidoyer pour l’accès des réfugiés aux voies complémentaires.
-	Améliorer le bien-être socio-économique et environnemental des refugies par la promotion de l’agriculture, la pêche et l’élevage en milieu rural, par la promotion des programmes d’entrepreneuriat et de résilience à travers l’approche communautaire et par la promotion d’une approche sensible à l’environnement chez tous les acteurs et partenaires de la réponse ;
-	Améliorer la sécurité alimentaire des POCs et des communautés d’accueil à travers le Cash Based Intervention ;
-	Favoriser les partenariats, le partage de l'information et la planification conformément aux plans de développement nationaux et locaux ainsi que la stratégie régionale pour la stabilisation, le rétablissement et le développement des zones impactées par les activités de Boko Haram à l’Extrême

Au cours de l’année 2021, en dépit du contexte sanitaire marquée par la survenue de la pandémie de la COVID19 qui a négativement affecté l’environnement socio-économiques des populations, la situation sécuritaire fragile en RCA et l’instabilité dans la région du bassin du Lac Chad, le HCR a initié des projets visant à améliorer l’environnement de protection des réfugiés et assurer l’accès aux solutions aux réfugiés.
Les projets déjà initiés requièrent une continuité dans la mise en œuvre afin renforcer la résilience et l’autonomisation des réfugiés de longue date, assurer leur inclusion effective dans les programmes de développement et donner accès aux solutions mais également apporter la réponse aux nouvelles situations d’urgences.
Au cours de 2023, il sera mis en œuvre par le HCR, les acteurs humanitaires et le gouvernement des activités qui garantissent l’accès équitable et la jouissance des droits humains fondamentaux aux femmes, aux hommes, aux filles et aux garçons de tout âge et ceux ayant diverses vulnérabilités.
L’UNHCR compte à travers ce projet :
-	Apporter la réponse aux besoins critiques de protection en assurant l’accès à l’asile, la documentation, la prévention et la réponse aux VBG, l’accès à l’éducation, l’accès durable aux infrastructures et services WASH, aux moyens d’existence et à l’inclusion socio-économique, ainsi que le renforcement de la cohésion sociale et de la coexistence pacifique entre les réfugiés et avec la communauté hôte.
-	Mettre en œuvre les solutions durables en renforçant la résilience des communautés affectées par les différentes crises et les moyens d’existence et explorer des opportunités viables par la mise en œuvre des alternatives aux camps notamment dans la région de l’extrême nord.
-	Le HCR continuera à faciliter le retour volontaire des réfugiés dans leur pays d’origine, à identifier les cas de réinstallation, d’importants besoins existent en termes de réfugiés pouvant potentiellement être considérés pour cette solution durable, cette dernière ne peut se réaliser que si les pays de réinstallations offrent des places. Par ailleurs, cette solution ne concerne qu’un pourcentage infime de la population réfugiée dans son ensemble. Le défi reste néanmoins la nécessité d’étendre le pool d’identification des réfugiés vers leurs zones d’installation mais avec des capacités très limitées et à faire le plaidoyer pour l’accès des réfugiés aux voies complémentaires.
-	Améliorer le bien-être socio-économique et environnemental des refugies par la promotion de l’agriculture, la pêche et l’élevage en milieu rural, par la promotion des programmes d’entrepreneuriat et de résilience à travers l’approche communautaire et par la promotion d’une approche sensible à l’environnement chez tous les acteurs et partenaires de la réponse ;
-	Améliorer la sécurité alimentaire des POCs et des communautés d’accueil à travers le Cash Based Intervention ;
-	Favoriser les partenariats, le partage de l'information et la planification conformément aux plans de développement nationaux et locaux ainsi que la stratégie régionale pour la stabilisation, le rétablissement et le développement des zones impactées par les activités de Boko Haram à l’Extrême

Au cours de l’année 2021, en dépit du contexte sanitaire marquée par la survenue de la pandémie de la COVID19 qui a négativement affecté l’environnement socio-économiques des populations, la situation sécuritaire fragile en RCA et l’instabilité dans la région du bassin du Lac Chad, le HCR a initié des projets visant à améliorer l’environnement de protection des réfugiés et assurer l’accès aux solutions aux réfugiés.
Les projets déjà initiés requièrent une continuité dans la mise en œuvre afin renforcer la résilience et l’autonomisation des réfugiés de longue date, assurer leur inclusion effective dans les programmes de développement et donner accès aux solutions mais également apporter la réponse aux nouvelles situations d’urgences.
Au cours de 2023, il sera mis en œuvre par le HCR, les acteurs humanitaires et le gouvernement des activités qui garantissent l’accès équitable et la jouissance des droits humains fondamentaux aux femmes, aux hommes, aux filles et aux garçons de tout âge et ceux ayant diverses vulnérabilités.
L’UNHCR compte à travers ce projet :
-	Apporter la réponse aux besoins critiques de protection en assurant l’accès à l’asile, la documentation, la prévention et la réponse aux VBG, l’accès à l’éducation, l’accès durable aux infrastructures et services WASH, aux moyens d’existence et à l’inclusion socio-économique, ainsi que le renforcement de la cohésion sociale et de la coexistence pacifique entre les réfugiés et avec la communauté hôte.
-	Mettre en œuvre les solutions durables en renforçant la résilience des communautés affectées par les différentes crises et les moyens d’existence et explorer des opportunités viables par la mise en œuvre des alternatives aux camps notamment dans la région de l’extrême nord.
-	Le HCR continuera à faciliter le retour volontaire des réfugiés dans leur pays d’origine, à identifier les cas de réinstallation, d’importants besoins existent en termes de réfugiés pouvant potentiellement être considérés pour cette solution durable, cette dernière ne peut se réaliser que si les pays de réinstallations offrent des places. Par ailleurs, cette solution ne concerne qu’un pourcentage infime de la population réfugiée dans son ensemble. Le défi reste néanmoins la nécessité d’étendre le pool d’identification des réfugiés vers leurs zones d’installation mais avec des capacités très limitées et à faire le plaidoyer pour l’accès des réfugiés aux voies complémentaires.
-	Améliorer le bien-être socio-économique et environnemental des refugies par la promotion de l’agriculture, la pêche et l’élevage en milieu rural, par la promotion des programmes d’entrepreneuriat et de résilience à travers l’approche communautaire et par la promotion d’une approche sensible à l’environnement chez tous les acteurs et partenaires de la réponse ;
-	Améliorer la sécurité alimentaire des POCs et des communautés d’accueil à travers le Cash Based Intervention ;
-	Favoriser les partenariats, le partage de l'information et la planification conformément aux plans de développement nationaux et locaux ainsi que la stratégie régionale pour la stabilisation, le rétablissement et le développement des zones impactées par les activités de Boko Haram à l’Extrême

South Sudan. Humanitarian Response Quality Education for Emergency Affected Children and Youth in South Sudan. The overall objective of the intervention is to ensure that emergency affected girls and boys as well as youth continually access quality learning opportunities relevant for their psycho-social well-being, physical and cognitive development.  The project targets children and youth aged between 6 - 17  from IDP, returnees and host community families with age appropriate interventions that respond to their education needs. Primary focus for this project is displacement affected out-of-school children and youth affected by conflict and climate emergencies. NRC anticipates to reach 38,873 children (52% girls); 875 adults (400 men ; 475 women [375 teachers & 500 parents/caregivers and other non-teaching professionals) as direct beneficiaries. The project will focus on strengthening and improving quality and delivery of education in four strategic response areas which are 1) First Phase response - through NRC's mobile response operations and targeting newly displaced families, with short term education activities lasting from 6-9 months. 2) Formal education - conducted through NRC's static program operations across the country in prioritized counties where NRC has existing physical presence; 3) Non Formal education through ALP classes for over-aged children who missed years of schooling due to conflict and displacement and 4) Youth Education and training with an emphasis on vocational skills training, peace-building and life-skills training.  In close collaboration with parents, caregivers and local actors, NRC will construct and repair learning spaces/classrooms and gender segregated school WASH facilities; provide school hardware assets (desks/benches), essential learning materials, teacher aids, recreational & hygiene kits; girls dignity kits for MHM; support mgt of schools through teacher selection, recruitment, motivation, training on child centered pedagogical methods, curriculum planning, classroom mgt & conflict sensitive education; support teacher learning cycles (TLCs) for continuous professional dvpt; facilitate community engagement in education through establishment/strengthening of PTAs & SMCs through training in roles and responsibilities, school development planning and awarding school improvement grants; conduct awareness raising community dialogue sessions to mobilize enrollment, promote attendance and support retention especially for girls who face multiple barriers to education including harmful and social practices such as forced early marriages and boys who also face protection risks that include child labour and forced recruitment into armed groups; conduct life skills training & support structured recreational activities for physical and psycho-social development; provide technical and material support non-teaching professionals (county education directors,  supervisors) to effectively conduct their school supervision and support duties; training of teachers, facilitators, on Mental Health and psycho-social support (MHPSS), Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR), child protection, child safeguarding and PSEA; provide cash and vouchers assistance to the most vulnerable for examination registration. 
Key approaches that NRC will adopt in this project include integration, partnerships and community based programming.  NRC will collaborate local structures as well as with other clusters including protection, WASH, shelter, LFS, Nutrition and Health to deliver comprehensive package that addresses the holistic needs of targeted population. Furthermore, for durable solutions, NRC will work with local actors, parents and care-givers building their capacity for self reliance and also to increase coverage in hard to reach areas  with periodic access challenges and bureaucratic impediments. For effective and efficient use of resources and for learning purposes, NRC will continue to participate in coordination mechanisms at both the national and sub-national levels to avoid overlaps and duplication with other education players.

Niger Plan de Réponse Humanitaire 2023 Réponse aux Réfugiés Protection/solution et assistance multisectorielle en faveur des réfugiés au Niger et des communautés d’accueil  En 2023, l’intervention en faveur des réfugiés présents au Niger s’articule autour des objectifs suivants : 
-	Objectif 1 : Continuer de renforcer l’environnement de protection en ajustant de manière continue les dispositifs pour s’adapter aux dynamiques de mouvements.
-	Objectif 2 : Assurer une réponse d’urgence en faveur des réfugiés et demandeurs d’asile.
-	Objectif 3 : Maintenir les dynamiques d’inclusion et de recherches de solutions durables. 
L’intervention s’inscrit dans les principes du Pacte Mondial pour les Réfugiés et continue d’être guidée par la politique d’alternative aux camps de réfugiés soutenue avec constance par le Gouvernement du Niger et facilitant l’opérationnalisation du triple nexus Humanitaire-Développement-Paix. Aux régions de Niamey, Agadez, Tahoua, Tillaberi, Maradi et Diffa déjà ciblées en 2022 se greffe celle de Dosso par anticipation des répercussions de la situation prévalent au nord-ouest du Nigeria.

Accès à une Education de qualité, sûre et inclusive des enfants affectés par la crise sécuritaire dans la région de Tillabéri au Niger (AccED) Accès à une Education de qualité, sûre et inclusive des enfants affectés par la crise sécuritaire dans la région de Tillabéri au Niger (AccED) Le projet AccED contribuera à la réinsertion et la continuité de l’accès à une éducation inclusive, sûre et de qualité des filles, garçons et adolescent/es les plus vulnérables affectés par la crise humanitaire dans la région de Tillabéri en réduisant les obstacles à l’éducation. Dans les zones où l’accès à l’éducation est possible, l’action i) augmentera l’offre d’éducation dans les zones de forte présence de PDI et réfugiés à travers le renforcement de la capacité d’accueil et qualité de l’apprentissage et ii) promouvra des programmes d’éducation accélérés pour faciliter le rattrapage et passerelles avec le système formel d’éducation. Dans les zones de conflit où les écoles sont fermées, l’action prévoit des approches innovantes et/ou alternatives d’éducation à travers le transfert d’élèves du secondaire vers les écoles des zones sécurisées, éducation par la radio, Espaces d’apprentissage Communautaires Ouverts. La protection des enfants et la création d’environnements d’apprentissages sûrs et attractifs sera aussi un travail clé à travers des mécanismes de protection des enfants, l’appui psychosocial et l’apprentissage socio-émotionnel visant à favoriser la résilience et l’épanouissement des enfants en situation de grande vulnérabilité, notamment les filles, et de la communauté éducative. L’action renforcera la protection des écoles face aux risques sécuritaires par le plaidoyer et l’opérationnalisation de la Déclaration sur la Sécurité dans les Écoles. L’intégration du WASH en milieu scolaire face au risque C-19 et autres maladies infectieuses sera prise en compte. L’action, conforme aux normes de l'INEE et CPMS, touchera 8777 enfants de 6-17 ans, dont 60% filles,  88 enfants porteurs d’un handicap et 196 adultes

Protective Integrated Response for Conflict Affected Population (PIRCAP) in Northeast Nigeria
---- Protection Integrated Emergency, Recovery and Resilience Response for Crisis-affected Persons in MMC and Jere The aim of this intervention is: conflict-affected communities in MMC and Jere LGAs are sustainably protected from, and treated for, the main causes of morbidity and mortality; supported to meet immediate and long-term Shelter and Settlement, WASH and Protection needs, while being protected and provided with the legal assistance they need. To achieve this, the proposed project will be implemented by a consortium led by the International Rescue Committee (IRC), in partnership with the Danish Refugee Council (DRC) and Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC). The consortium will leverage the expertise of each partner to deliver a multi-sectoral, area-based response, providing integrated services across the following sectors: Health, WASH, Nutrition, Food Assistance, Multi-purpose Cash Assistance (MPCA), Nutrition, Economic Recovery and Market Systems (ERMS), Protection and Shelter and Settlements. The consortium aims to meet the most immediate and life-saving needs of IDPs, host communities and returnees in MMC and Jere, which will translate into reduced mortality and improved living conditions. The consortium will also address the ongoing, protracted needs, and supporting early recovery through capacity-building, the strengthening of existing health systems and community-based structures, and increasing the ownership of life-saving, life-sustaining, and life-building services by local authorities, service providers, and local communities to ensure sustainability. In order to build the resilience of individuals and communities, the unique humanitarian and development challenges in MMC and Jere LGAs (presence of service delivery actors against an ongoing flux of IDPs in and out of camps and host communities throughout the city) must be addressed simultaneously by increasing access to quality, sustainable basic services, building sustainable livelihoods, and strengthening local systems and structures.

Emergency Food Security and Livelihood assistance to vulnerable and conflict affected households in north east Nigeria Food insecurity and malnutrition remain prevalent across Nigeria, mainly driven by the ongoing protracted conflict in the Northeast, mass displacement and the resultant IDP return process, adverse climate change and variability, such as drought, long dry spells, and flood, land degradation increasing insecurity and banditry, natural resource-based conflicts and an unfavorable macroeconomic situation manifested in rising food price inflation, etc. Further, the disruption of food and agricultural input supply chains by the Russia-Ukrainian war has led to severe availability and access constraints especially for poor farming households because of high food and agricultural input prices, especially fertilizer.
Despite the efforts of humanitarian communities in addressing the manifestations of the emergency in the country, the situation of food security continues to be a challenge. According to the latest Cadre Harmonise (CH) analysis, an estimated 19.45 million people, nearly 63 percent of them in Northeast and Northwest Nigeria are projected to be at risk of severe food insecurity during the peak of the 2022 lean season. In addition, the latest IPC acute malnutrition analysis report released in June 2022 estimates that 1.4 million children and, nearly 152,000 pregnant and lactating women are likely to suffer acute malnutrition during this period. Therefore, the urgent need for an expanded humanitarian food security response cannot be overstated. While the humanitarian interventions have been playing vital and critical role in addressing the needs of affected populations, it is obvious more has to be done to support the resilience of the livelihoods and the households. Given that the majority of those in need are involved in agriculture related activities, it has become necessary and urgent to promote agriculture-based livelihoods to famers whose majority are smallholders.  
In 2021 FAO reached over 1 million people and is planning to scale up and reach 2 million people (approximately 285,715 households) in need of agricultural-based livelihoods assistance in Nigeria in 2023/2024 with a stronger focus on Northeast and Northwest Nigeria due to the high level of vulnerability in the two regions. Due to restrictions on target numbers submitted in the HRP and its limited coverage (only targeting the Northeast), 1.7 million people will be targeted through the HRP while the remaining 0.3 million will be planned outside the HRP framework. To achieve this target FAO Nigeria is requiring a total of USD 86 million. Notably, funding for agriculture livelihood had declined significantly, for example, in 2022 the livelihood and agriculture funding stand at 6%, while food assistance is 95% covered. This requires a strong coordinated advocacy strategy to shift the paradigm.  An estimated 1.7 million people will be targeted for emergency agricultural livelihoods assistance while 0.3 million will be targeted for resilience interventions including in agribusiness, skills development for the creation of decent employment and income such as stoves production, aquaculture, livestock, etc. that increase the resilience of the beneficiaries.  
The scale-up plan will target the most vulnerable groups including IDPs, returnees, and host communities, especially women, and girls.    FAO Nigeria provides various agricultural livelihood assistance packages based on the livelihoods of the targeted household and the related activity. This is including agricultural rainy and dry season inputs, livestock restocking goats and poultry, urban and peri-urban homestead gardening, aquaculture, agribusiness enterprise support, nutritional support, and SAFE kits. This intervention will be delivered through a combination of in-kind, cash, and cash+ assistance. The scale-up plan is aligned to the FAO Corporate Global strategy framework of achieving Better Production, Better Nutrition, Better environment and Better life.

Seguridad alimentaria - Programa de seguridad alimentaria basado en la escuela Programa de seguridad alimentaria basado en la escuela  Con el objetivo de contribuir a la seguridad alimentaria de la población con mayores necesidades, el Programa Mundial de Alimentos de Naciones Unidas (WFP, por sus siglas en inglés) en Venezuela desarrolla un programa de asistencia humanitaria basado en la escuela para garantizar el acceso de los más vulnerables a una alimentación adecuada y nutritiva en el entorno escolar, familiar y comunitario. 
Este programa inició en 2021 con comidas escolares en emergencias priorizando escuelas iniciales y de educación especial.

WFP proporciona comidas escolares acompañado de un paquete integrado de intervenciones para mejorar el acceso a alimentos nutritivos y diversificados a través de las escuelas, contribuyendo al mismo tiempo a mejorar la salud y la nutrición de los niños en edad escolar, los estudiantes con discapacidad y el personal escolar, y apoyando a las comunidades a reducir la dependencia en estrategias de afrontamiento. De manera gradual, el WFP está realizando compras locales de alimentos, e incluyendo acciones para apoyar los mercados locales con compras a pequeños productores y apoyo técnico para acceso a mercados.

En este sentido, el programa de comidas escolares en emergencias tiene los siguientes componentes, para asegurar un enfoque integral que apoye al estudiante en el entorno escolar y familiar:

1. Entrega de comidas escolares nutritivas para estudiantes y personal escolar, promoviendo las compras locales y a pequeños productores.
2. Apoyo a la seguridad alimentaria del hogar.
3. Rehabilitación de cocinas escolares para garantizar condiciones adecuadas de preparación de alimentos.
4. Comunicación para sensibilizar acerca de los principios humanitarios, la adecuada preparación de alimentos, nutrición, higiene y mantenimiento de cocinas escolares.
5. Fortalecimiento de capacidades de socios implementadores y personal escolar.
6. Acciones sensibles a la nutrición, que incluyen, tamizaje en las escuelas, educación nutricional, referencia a servicios especializados y entrega de alimento complementario fortificado (Super Cereal Plus).

UNICEF’s CP Strategy in 2022-2023 includes:
• Addressing behavioural, social, cultural and economic determinants of CP violations as a prevention approach.  
• Improving the reach and quality of specialized CP services
• Capacity development of CP responders
•  Monitoring, evidence generation and advocacy 

UNICEF will support the delivery of integrated programming that will encourage social transformation, prioritizing:
• Structured and sustained CP MHPSS and EORE programmes
• Specialized integrated CP services including case management for survivors of violence, exploitation, neglect and abuse (child labour, CAFAAG, child survivors of GBV, child marriages, justice for children, birth registration and unaccompanied or separated children amongst others) 
• Parenting programmes to promote positive child rearing skills and experience for caregivers
• Elimination of violence against children, including GBV prevention and empowerment for girls, boys and women, prevention of violence in schools, homes and communities.
• Awareness-raising on CP risks
• Capacity development of CP responders and social workers

UNICEF will generate evidence to inform the humanitarian response and advocacy including setting up an information management system for case management. UNICEF will embrace new delivery modalities and implement cash transfers aimed at child protection outcomes for vulnerable families. UNICEF will also continue to support the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism on grave violations against children.

CP services will be delivered by partners based on minimum standards and IASC guidelines. 7,200 CP and social workers will be trained on case management, MHPSS, EORE, advocacy, evidence generation and coordination across sectors for a comprehensive CP response.
 
UNICEF will support MHPSS for 364,000 children to benefit from improved mental health and social wellbeing. UNICEF will equip 61,500 parents and caregivers with skills to provide a stimulating and safe environment at home, including reduced violence.  

Violence prevention is a key priority. Family violence prevalence is high for girls 12-17 years (47%), boys 12-17 years (44%), boys below 12 (45%) and girls below 12 (44%) (UNICEF 2018). UNICEF will work to protect children from violence and abuse through prevention activities in schools, homes and communities and providing survivors of violence with child-friendly and gender sensitive services. Support will be provided for PSEA mechanisms to protect beneficiaries and build the capacity of humanitarian actors. PSEA programming will be implemented with the Protection Sector AORs.

Based on HNO 2021, one in three communities in Syria is reportedly contaminated by explosive ordnance. One in four victims is a child (Joint MA & CP Analysis, 2020). EORE messages will be provided to 1,460,000 children and adults through humanitarian actors and public service providers using static facilities and mobile teams. UNICEF will build the capacity of partners to provide quality EORE that is age, gender and disability appropriate and to provide child victims with assistance.
 
UNICEF will strengthen the justice system to ensure that children in contact with the law victims, offenders or witnesses are protected through child-friendly, gender-sensitive services, that are community-based and family focused.

As Lead Agency for the CP AOR, UNICEF will ensure coordination needs at Hub and WOS levels. Two UN-led and one INGO-led coordination hubs in Damascus, Gaziantep and NES, as well as a WOS overall coordination system, to ensure coherence across the CP response.

Distribution d'assistance vitale aux personnes fuyant le Soudan et aux communautés hôtes dans le Haut Nil et la région Nord-Ouest du Sud Soudan Provision of integrated, equitable, and timely WASH services to emergency affected populations in South Sudan Protracted crises in South Sudan, including climactic shocks and continued conflict, have resulted in 8.9 million people projected to be in need of humanitarian assistance in 2022. As a result of the shocks, such as flooding, inter-communal violence (ICV) and ongoing armed clashes, the majority of the population are facing increased food insecurity, lack of access to basic services, and protection risks. As per the Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) 2022, lack of or inadequate access to clean water and improved sanitation and hygiene practices in South Sudan will negatively impact an estimated 6.1 million people in 2022. 

Since 2006, Solidarites International has become a key WASH actor in South Sudan, implementing emergency lifesaving responses across the country and providing integrated WASH services to crisis-affected populations in areas of static presence in Upper Nile, Jonglei, and Western Bahr el Ghazal. Since 2012 SI has played a key role in the Emergency Preparedness and Response (EPR) strategy in South Sudan, implementing multi-sectoral assessments and delivering emergency responses to crisis-affected populations all over the country. 

In 2022, SI will continue to provide emergency live-saving  WASH responses across the South Sudan to restore basic access to safe water, hygiene, and sanitation while ensuring equitable access, safety, and accountability to supported populations. Through its roving Emergency Preparedness and Response (EPR) team, SI will deploy to emergency-affected locations to provide first phase and second phase responses including distribution of household water treatment items and soap, emergency provision of safe water, and rapid repair of emergency-affected infrastructure.

At the same time, SI will expand its presence in Upper Nile, Unity and Jonglei to provide basic integrated WASH services that target the most vulnerable, including those suffering malnutrition, food insecurity and protection threats (including GBV survivors). Static programs will focus on providing community-based solutions for sustainable WASH services that ensure that improvements in access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene are durable and can be maintained independently by communities. Engagement and joint programming with Protection and Nutrition actors will ensure that WASH services can be accessed by the most vulnerable and will have a tangible impact on reducing overall priority humanitarian needs. The increased integration of protection, inclusion, and conflict sensitivity analysis in all programming will ensure that WASH services and resources can be safely accessed by all in the community. Greater engagement of communities and local markets will support the design of long term and flood resistant WASH infrastructure and supply chains to ensure that interventions produce durable results for communities.

Delivering life-saving assistance and protection to people fleeing Sudan and assist the most vulnerable South Sudan returnees through integrated protection action Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2022, there are some 335,000 refugees and asylum seekers from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, primarily from Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic.
At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for longer term stability, hundreds of thousands of South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since the signing of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan, this spontaneous movement has prompted the development of an area-based approach, to support refugees, returnees and host communities, through enhanced engagement with development actors, to support greater access to services where possible.
Refugees largely reside in conflict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction in basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.
Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will benefit from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Specific protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identified at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with specific protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as verification exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the efficiency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to benefit from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

Integrated WASH and Nutrition Initiative (IWANI) to promote health, and optimum growth and development for the most vulnerable children and women in Lebanon Provision of emergency nutrition services and support optimum early childhood development to crisis affected pregnant and lactating women and children aged below 5 years among vulnerable Lebanese and migrants in Lebanon. With Growing triple burden of malnutrition (undernutrition, both stunting and wasting; deficiencies in vitamins and other micronutrients; and overweight and obesity) among women, children and adolescents which affects health, growth and development. 
70% of young children are not exclusively breastfed; 90% of children aged 6-23 months lack dietary diversity and meal frequency; over 40% of all women and children, including Lebanese, are affected by anaemia. In October 2021, 53% of children skipped a meal due to insufficient food in the house, up from 37% just 6 months before. 453,000 Lebanese women and children need urgent nutritional support.
Nutrition and child development should be prioritized as part of the emergency response plan, hence UNICEF will be working under the ERP appeal through a multi-system approach from food, health, social protection, education and water and sanitation systems to protect and promote adequate diets, practices and services to prevent all forms of malnutrition among children and women and support optimum early childhood development. In 2021, the percentage of childcare service providers encountering families with payment difficulties has doubled, reaching 41%.  Additionally, due to the local currency devaluation and the significant increase in fuel prices, the monthly fees per child are no longer sufficient to cover the operational expenses of childcare providers. Therefore, to remain affordable, childcare providers are often constrained to compromise on quality which can negatively affect the healthy development of children, while children in rural areas, camps or informal settlements have little access to ECD.
Building on this momentum of a strengthened enabling environment for nutrition and child development, UNICEF will work with the government and partners to reach the most vulnerable children and women with an essential service package for prevention, early detection, referral, and management of all forms of malnutrition and development delays. Maternal and child nutrition during the first 1,000 days coupled with a nurturing care framework – from conception to age 2 years – remains core to the response.
This will be done by strengthening national capacity across multiple sectors and systems through better evidence, policies, and facility and community-based solutions and programmes.

South Sudan	South Sudan Humanitarian Response Plan 2023	- CCCM services to assist affected populations through static, mobile, and area-based responses in Jonglei, Unity, Upper Nile, Warrap, Western Bahr el Ghazal, Northern Bahr el Ghazal, Western Equatoria and Central Equatoria States. Targeting 120,000 people in need living in IDP camps, settlements, collective sites and the increasing numbers living in urban areas, this project will focus on the provision of timely, well-coordinated, and integrated Camp Management services. With the aim of improving the well-being of displaced populations, strengthening their resilience and increasing their participation in decision-making processes, in Jonglei, Unity, Upper Nile, Warrap, Western Bahr el Ghazal, Northern Bahr el Ghazal, Western Equatoria and Central Equatoria, all states where UNHCR currently has a static presence through its field office operations, 
UNHCR and partners will put in place mechanisms to strengthen camp coordination and monitoring to enable the effective provision of cross-sectoral services. IDPs’ engagement in the delivery of services in an equal and needs-based manner will be possible through regular feedback and dissemination of information for example through community-based networks. In support of humanitarian interventions aimed at improving the well-being of displaced populations whilst providing some level of dignity and equitability by promoting AAP.
A key component of the project will be to support community-based structures to enhance participation in planning and decision-making, in particular seeking empowerment of communities. This will be done with a focus on vulnerable groups, PSNs and PWDs so that their views are received, and acknowledged and service delivery meets the specific needs of all groups. To this end, protection will be mainstreamed into all CCCM activities to respect and promote the rights of the most vulnerable. Site care and maintenance improvement projects will take place to minimize protection risks and determine the level of assistance required by PSNs.

Supporting the ability of vulnerable IDPs to recover from the external stresses they face, be it floods or conflict, this project will seek to promote capacity building and development of community self-management structures and practices. UNHCR and its partners will also ensure that communication channels with the concerned population are strengthened, diversified, and anchored on the views of the community. This will serve to facilitate timely and accurate information to respond to disasters and mitigate identified risks. CCCM will focus on capacity building, multi-sectoral assessments on a number of displaced persons affected by the flood, and conflict resolution services through CCCM monitoring, coordination meetings at the site level, care and maintenance activities conducted by the safety committee through cash for work initiatives and enhancing feedback and complaint mechanisms.
Finally, as CCCM Cluster Co-lead UNHCR will continue to strengthen and support CCCM partners through strategic guidance, advocacy with donors, and vitally step in as a provider of last resort in areas if partners have a low presence and limited capacity to respond.

Providing life-saving humanitarian protection and health care assistance to migrants and other vulnerable individuals in Lebanon Ensuring specialized services and protection for migrant children in vulnerable situations in Lebanon. Responding to the need for specialized child case management (including MHPSS) with this culturally sensitive approach, IOM seeks to enhance protection assistance for migrant and Lebanese children in need of protection, including victims of child labour, child marriage, and human trafficking. The project will aim to boost the capacity of local service providers, well positioned to provide the protection services needed. These include case management support, emergency cash assistance, psychosocial support, legal assistance for unaccompanied and/or undocumented children in line with their best interests and community-based child protection activities. Onward referral to multisector assistance such as food, education or health support will be mainstreamed across the project.

Niger Plan de Réponse Humanitaire 2023 Protection/solution et assistance multisectorielle en faveur des réfugiés au Niger et des communautés d’accueil  En 2023, l’intervention en faveur des réfugiés présents au Niger s’articule autour des objectifs suivants : 
-	Objectif 1 : Continuer de renforcer l’environnement de protection en ajustant de manière continue les dispositifs pour s’adapter aux dynamiques de mouvements.
-	Objectif 2 : Assurer une réponse d’urgence en faveur des réfugiés et demandeurs d’asile.
-	Objectif 3 : Maintenir les dynamiques d’inclusion et de recherches de solutions durables. 
L’intervention s’inscrit dans les principes du Pacte Mondial pour les Réfugiés et continue d’être guidée par la politique d’alternative aux camps de réfugiés soutenue avec constance par le Gouvernement du Niger et facilitant l’opérationnalisation du triple nexus Humanitaire-Développement-Paix. Aux régions de Niamey, Agadez, Tahoua, Tillaberi, Maradi et Diffa déjà ciblées en 2022 se greffe celle de Dosso par anticipation des répercussions de la situation prévalent au nord-ouest du Nigeria.

Syria Enhancement of protection of displaced persons, returnees and conflict affected host communities in Syria through integrated, community-based protection activities. The project aims to strengthen protection and resilience of Syrian IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host communities through advocacy, coordination, provision of community-based protection services and legal services. UNHCR Syria will continue to lead the Protection Sector to ensure coordinated protection interventions programming for IDPs and affected people as well as executing leadership roles in refugee return programmes in collaboration with the Government. UNHCR’s protection interventions will include provision of integrated protection services through a network of 120 centers in all 14 Governorates. The network of Community Centres, paired with some 120 mobile units and around 3,600 outreach volunteers of multifunctional thematic capacities, are fundamental to the implementation of UNHCR’s Protection and Solutions Strategy for Syria through outreach to affected populations, assessment of protection risks and vulnerabilities, consultation, identification and mobilization of community resources, strengthening of community self-help networks, and offering protection services and support to displaced persons, returnees and host communities in response to the priority needs expressed by the communities, while applying a highly participatory age, gender and diversity approach. The protection services extended at the UNHCR Community Centres include, but are not limited to, psycho-social support, GBV prevention, risk mitigation and response and child protection case management, legal awareness and legal aid, non-formal education programmes, services for persons with disabilities and older persons, provision of general and medical in-kind assistance, social and recreational activities, curriculum based awareness activities on various subjects targeting women, men, boys and girls, referrals and information sharing, social protection through livelihoods support to most vulnerable population.
As part of its commitment to Accountability to Affected Population (AAP), UNHCR will ensure meaningful participation of communities based on age, gender and diversity approach, structured focus group discussions and enhancement of the community-based feedback and complaint mechanisms. UNHCR will continue its capacity building efforts to ensure services are delivered according to the standards and that accountability to affected population and do no harm principles are respected.
UNHCR will continue co-leading the AAP Technical Working Group and the Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) In-Country Network and coordinate activities to strengthen AAP and SEA prevention, risk mitigation and response.
Monitoring and evaluation of the planned interventions is based on the reports and observations by the partners and on regular direct observation and ongoing assessment and consultations with the community by UNHCR and partners and the comparison of achievements and related financial expenditures with objectives. Evaluation is conducted through different channels, including post distribution monitoring to determine the effectiveness of/measure the satisfaction of people of concern with the service and the distribution process in addition to multiple satisfaction surveys and tracking tools related to different protection interventions. Monitoring and evaluation activities are carried out at various levels by partners and agencies implementing subprojects, UNHCR Country Office, Sub and Field Offices. Situation reports are submitted by all UNHCR Field Offices to their respective Supervising Office and Country Offices submit a corresponding report to Headquarters.
