---- USA / BPRM Amélioration de la réponse multisectorielle en faveur des Réfugiés et demandeurs d’asile et mise en œuvre des solutions durables pour les réfugiés au Cameroun  Le projet a pour objectif l’amélioration de l’environnement de protection, l’accès aux solutions et voies complémentaires pour les réfugiés et demandeurs d’asile notamment en ce qui concerne  les activités d’enregistrement , de  la documentation, la protection de l’enfance, la prévention ,  la réponse aux violences sexuelles et sexistes, l’accès aux services sociaux de base (santé, éducation et eau), l’accès à un abri décent et aux biens domestiques essentiels ainsi que du  renforcement de la résilience.
Le projet cible en 2023, un total de 491,113 réfugiés au Cameroun notamment : 355,667 réfugiés RCA, 132,151 NIG, 2,533 des nationalités minoritaires, 9,239 demandeurs d’asile ainsi que 15% des populations autochtones par la présence des réfugiés dans les régions affectées.
Au cours de l’année 2021, en dépit du contexte sanitaire marquée par la survenue de la pandémie de la COVID19 qui a négativement affecté l’environnement socio-économiques des populations, la situation sécuritaire fragile en RCA et l’instabilité dans la région du bassin du Lac Chad, le HCR a initié des projets visant à améliorer l’environnement de protection des réfugiés et assurer l’accès aux solutions aux réfugiés.
Les projets déjà initiés requièrent une continuité dans la mise en œuvre afin renforcer la résilience et l’autonomisation des réfugiés de longue date, assurer leur inclusion effective dans les programmes de développement et donner accès aux solutions mais également apporter la réponse aux nouvelles situations d’urgences.
Au cours de 2023, il sera mis en œuvre par le HCR, les acteurs humanitaires et le gouvernement des activités qui garantissent l’accès équitable et la jouissance des droits humains fondamentaux aux femmes, aux hommes, aux filles et aux garçons de tout âge et ceux ayant diverses vulnérabilités.
L’UNHCR compte à travers ce projet :
-	Apporter la réponse aux besoins critiques de protection en assurant l’accès à l’asile, la documentation, la prévention et la réponse aux VBG, l’accès à l’éducation, l’accès durable aux infrastructures et services WASH, aux moyens d’existence et à l’inclusion socio-économique, ainsi que le renforcement de la cohésion sociale et de la coexistence pacifique entre les réfugiés et avec la communauté hôte.
-	Mettre en œuvre les solutions durables en renforçant la résilience des communautés affectées par les différentes crises et les moyens d’existence et explorer des opportunités viables par la mise en œuvre des alternatives aux camps notamment dans la région de l’extrême nord.
-	Le HCR continuera à faciliter le retour volontaire des réfugiés dans leur pays d’origine, à identifier les cas de réinstallation, d’importants besoins existent en termes de réfugiés pouvant potentiellement être considérés pour cette solution durable, cette dernière ne peut se réaliser que si les pays de réinstallations offrent des places. Par ailleurs, cette solution ne concerne qu’un pourcentage infime de la population réfugiée dans son ensemble. Le défi reste néanmoins la nécessité d’étendre le pool d’identification des réfugiés vers leurs zones d’installation mais avec des capacités très limitées et à faire le plaidoyer pour l’accès des réfugiés aux voies complémentaires.
-	Améliorer le bien-être socio-économique et environnemental des refugies par la promotion de l’agriculture, la pêche et l’élevage en milieu rural, par la promotion des programmes d’entrepreneuriat et de résilience à travers l’approche communautaire et par la promotion d’une approche sensible à l’environnement chez tous les acteurs et partenaires de la réponse ;
-	Améliorer la sécurité alimentaire des POCs et des communautés d’accueil à travers le Cash Based Intervention ;

Famine Response 2023 Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM). WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.
Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (light resilience- building activities, peace/conflict resolution training also called GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness, training, or sensitisation on peaceful resolution of conflicts, mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace. 
Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities.

Syria Earthquake Response
-- CHILD PROTECTION Strengthening Child Protection interventions for girls and boys most at risk of violence, abuse, neglect and exploitation across whole of Syria In line with the CP Area of Responsibility (AOR) Strategy and the “No Lost Generation” framework, UNICEF will enhance equitable access to quality CP services with a resilience focus, including for Survivors of abuse, violence, neglect and exploitation as well as children with disabilities, targeting 117 high severity sub-districts (3 to 5) and 38 low severity ones.

UNICEF’s CP Strategy in 2022-2023 includes:
• Addressing behavioural, social, cultural and economic determinants of CP violations as a prevention approach.  
• Improving the reach and quality of specialized CP services
• Capacity development of CP responders
•  Monitoring, evidence generation and advocacy 

UNICEF will support the delivery of integrated programming that will encourage social transformation, prioritizing:
• Structured and sustained CP MHPSS and EORE programmes
• Specialized integrated CP services including case management for survivors of violence, exploitation, neglect and abuse (child labour, CAFAAG, child survivors of GBV, child marriages, justice for children, birth registration and unaccompanied or separated children amongst others) 
• Parenting programmes to promote positive child rearing skills and experience for caregivers
• Elimination of violence against children, including GBV prevention and empowerment for girls, boys and women, prevention of violence in schools, homes and communities.
• Awareness-raising on CP risks
• Capacity development of CP responders and social workers

UNICEF will generate evidence to inform the humanitarian response and advocacy including setting up an information management system for case management. UNICEF will embrace new delivery modalities and implement cash transfers aimed at child protection outcomes for vulnerable families. UNICEF will also continue to support the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism on grave violations against children.

CP services will be delivered by partners based on minimum standards and IASC guidelines. 7,200 CP and social workers will be trained on case management, MHPSS, EORE, advocacy, evidence generation and coordination across sectors for a comprehensive CP response.
 
UNICEF will support MHPSS for 364,000 children to benefit from improved mental health and social wellbeing. UNICEF will equip 61,500 parents and caregivers with skills to provide a stimulating and safe environment at home, including reduced violence.  

Violence prevention is a key priority. Family violence prevalence is high for girls 12-17 years (47%), boys 12-17 years (44%), boys below 12 (45%) and girls below 12 (44%) (UNICEF 2018). UNICEF will work to protect children from violence and abuse through prevention activities in schools, homes and communities and providing survivors of violence with child-friendly and gender sensitive services. Support will be provided for PSEA mechanisms to protect beneficiaries and build the capacity of humanitarian actors. PSEA programming will be implemented with the Protection Sector AORs.

Based on HNO 2021, one in three communities in Syria is reportedly contaminated by explosive ordnance. One in four victims is a child (Joint MA & CP Analysis, 2020). EORE messages will be provided to 1,460,000 children and adults through humanitarian actors and public service providers using static facilities and mobile teams. UNICEF will build the capacity of partners to provide quality EORE that is age, gender and disability appropriate and to provide child victims with assistance.
 
UNICEF will strengthen the justice system to ensure that children in contact with the law victims, offenders or witnesses are protected through child-friendly, gender-sensitive services, that are community-based and family focused.

As Lead Agency for the CP AOR, UNICEF will ensure coordination needs at Hub and WOS levels. Two UN-led and one INGO-led coordination hubs in Damascus, Gaziantep and NES, as well as a WOS overall coordination system, to ensure coherence across the CP response.

Camp Coordination / Management	Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM) Early Action intervention to expected floods in Unity and Upper Nile States CCCM Assistance to conflict and disaster-induced displaced persons in South Sudan According to Round 12 of IOM DTM’s monitoring of displacement and return movement, 2,229,657 people remain displaced in South Sudan, 78% of which are sheltering with already crisis-affected host communities. In a number of displacement sites and collective centers, including current and former PoCs, more than 440,000 individuals continue to live in situations of protracted displacement. Displacement figures have continued to increase despite the signing of the R-ARCSS in 2018 due to an increase of displacement-inducing incidents such as sub-national conflict and unprecedented climate-related disasters.

IOM CCCM aims to target 612,000 people of the total 1.4 million people targeted under the CCCM Cluster Response Plan. IOM will continue to provide displaced communities with basic and emergency camp management services, ensuring that the provision of protection and cross-sectoral humanitarian assistance is equitable, coordinated, monitored and adhering to standards. Of critical relevance to the current displacement environment in the country, IOM CCCM’s interventions will also integrate a robust, community-led disaster-mitigation lens in all care & maintenance interventions and capacity building exercises to enhance protective environments to increase resilience of infrastructure and communities to climate shocks. Further, fully committed to ensuring that AAP is streamlined in any and all activities, IOM will continue to develop and improve AAP mechanisms to ensure that the organization is accountable to the people that it serves and that programmes are informed by the voices of the displaced communities.

IOM intends to contribute to the sectoral objectives through the following interventions:

1)	Continued and adapted provision of critical CCCM activities to IDPs living in Bentiu, Naivasha and Hai Masna IDP Sites as well as critical care & maintenance activities in Malakal PoC.
2)	Deployment of emergency CCCM teams to deliver sustainable mobile responses promoting self-governance, community ownership and resilience in hard-to-reach locations following triggers at the ICCG-level.
3)	Co-lead the CCCM Cluster at national level and continue acting as SFP in WBeG, Jonglei and Upper Nile States in order to support national and state-level partner agencies in accountable CCCM responses and systems.
4)	Continue chairing the CCEWG in order to provide technical CCE support to partner organizations and to operationalize outputs under the 2021 South Sudan AAP Framework.

At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM). WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.
Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (light resilience- building activities, peace/conflict resolution training also called GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness, training, or sensitisation on peaceful resolution of conflicts, mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace. 
Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities.

Protection - Gender-Based Violence  South Sudan HRP 2023 Increasing safe, equitable and dignified access to essential basic protection services reducing exposure of affected vulnerable populations to protection risks, including GBV in Pibor (IPC 5), Nyirol (IPC 4) and Akobo (IPC 4) in Jonglei State The proposed HRP 2022 interventions will be implemented in Pibor, Nyirol and Akobo West which have been classified as IPC 4 and 5 facing deteriorating humanitarian conditions, worsened by endemic violence, conflict, access constraints and operational interference, public health challenges such as direct and indirect effects of COVID-19 and climatic shocks resulting in the dual phenomena of extraordinary flooding and localized drought, which have a severe impact on people’s livelihoods, hampers access to education and water, sanitation and hygiene and health services. Protection concerns remain high, with people impacted by violence having limited access to justice and the rule of law. The proposed intervention will contribute to the HRP 2022 Protection Cluster, General Protection Objectives: Prevent and mitigate protection risks through enhanced preparedness and resilience; Enhance protection assessment and monitoring to inform protection and overall humanitarian response; and Ensure the provision of critical protection related assistance and specialized services through an integrated approach to address the priority needs of targeted people among vulnerable women, men, girls and boys in hard-to-reach and priority geographical areas. The main objective of the proposed intervention is to increase safe, equitable and dignified access to essential basic protection services reducing exposure of affected vulnerable populations to protection risks, including GBV in Pibor, Nyirol and Akobo in Jonglei State. To achieve this, the proposed intervention has the following specific objectives: SO1 To undertake effective and timely protection assessments in targeted areas for timely and robust humanitarian and protection decisions, influence and actions; SO2 To strengthen community-based protection mechanisms for risk reduction and promotion of local peace and security for women and youths; SO3 To provide Individual Protection Assistance to address priority protection needs for vulnerable women, men, girls and boys in targeted areas; SO4 To support ‘safe programming’ (protection mainstreaming) including safeguarding in all interventions in all the targeted locations. Targeted population are Host Communities, Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) and Returnees consisting of women, girls, boys and men. The intervention will be contributing to the Protection Cluster target of 105,320 women, men, girls and boys provided with individual, group, specialized PSS and other related general protection services. This project will be implemented by Oxfam and its local partners. The expected number of people reached through Oxfam intervention is 6,600 (across all locations 60% women, 20% girls, 10% boys, 10% men): Pibor HC-1000, IDPs-800, Returnees-400; Akobo HC-1000, IDPs-800, Returnees-400 and Nyirol HC-1000, IDPs-800, Returnees-400.

Syria HRP 2023 Enhancement of protection of displaced persons, returnees and conflict affected host communities in Syria through integrated, community-based protection activities. The project aims to strengthen protection and resilience of Syrian IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host communities through advocacy, coordination, provision of community-based protection services and legal services. UNHCR Syria will continue to lead the Protection Sector to ensure coordinated protection interventions programming for IDPs and affected people as well as executing leadership roles in refugee return programmes in collaboration with the Government. UNHCR’s protection interventions will include provision of integrated protection services through a network of 120 centers in all 14 Governorates. The network of Community Centres, paired with some 120 mobile units and around 3,600 outreach volunteers of multifunctional thematic capacities, are fundamental to the implementation of UNHCR’s Protection and Solutions Strategy for Syria through outreach to affected populations, assessment of protection risks and vulnerabilities, consultation, identification and mobilization of community resources, strengthening of community self-help networks, and offering protection services and support to displaced persons, returnees and host communities in response to the priority needs expressed by the communities, while applying a highly participatory age, gender and diversity approach. The protection services extended at the UNHCR Community Centres include, but are not limited to, psycho-social support, GBV prevention, risk mitigation and response and child protection case management, legal awareness and legal aid, non-formal education programmes, services for persons with disabilities and older persons, provision of general and medical in-kind assistance, social and recreational activities, curriculum based awareness activities on various subjects targeting women, men, boys and girls, referrals and information sharing, social protection through livelihoods support to most vulnerable population.
As part of its commitment to Accountability to Affected Population (AAP), UNHCR will ensure meaningful participation of communities based on age, gender and diversity approach, structured focus group discussions and enhancement of the community-based feedback and complaint mechanisms. UNHCR will continue its capacity building efforts to ensure services are delivered according to the standards and that accountability to affected population and do no harm principles are respected.
UNHCR will continue co-leading the AAP Technical Working Group and the Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) In-Country Network and coordinate activities to strengthen AAP and SEA prevention, risk mitigation and response.
Monitoring and evaluation of the planned interventions is based on the reports and observations by the partners and on regular direct observation and ongoing assessment and consultations with the community by UNHCR and partners and the comparison of achievements and related financial expenditures with objectives. Evaluation is conducted through different channels, including post distribution monitoring to determine the effectiveness of/measure the satisfaction of people of concern with the service and the distribution process in addition to multiple satisfaction surveys and tracking tools related to different protection interventions. Monitoring and evaluation activities are carried out at various levels by partners and agencies implementing subprojects, UNHCR Country Office, Sub and Field Offices. Situation reports are submitted by all UNHCR Field Offices to their respective Supervising Office and Country Offices submit a corresponding report to Headquarters.

Niger HRP 2023	HNER23-WSH-197247-1	EHA (Water Sanitation Hygiene) RÉPONSE MULTISECTORIELLE D'URGENCE AUX POPULATIONS AFFECTÉES PAR L'INSÉCURITÉ ALIMENTAIRE ET LE CONFLIT DANS LES RÉGIONS DE TILLABÉRI ET DIFFA ET APPUI AUX SERVICES D'INFORMATION HUMANITAIRE AU NIGER Ce projet de 24 mois vise à appuyer les personnes déplacées, réfugiées et communautés hôtes des régions de Diffa et Tillabéri au Niger. L’objectif du projet est de fournir une aide d'urgence multisectorielle aux personnes en situation d'insécurité alimentaire et touchées par le conflit, par le biais d'une assistance alimentaire, d'activités de renforcement de la résilience des moyens de subsistance et du renforcement de l'environnement protecteur ; tout en renforçant l'action humanitaire avec des données multisectorielles et des outils d'information pour contribuer à une meilleure planification de la réponse humanitaire.
Bénéficiaires : un nombre estimé à 71 018 individus (en évitant le double comptage) bénéficiera du programme, dont 1 904 réfugiés. Les bénéficiaires seront sélectionnés parmi les personnes ayant les besoins les plus pressants, quel que soit leur statut (réfugiés, PDI, rhôtes). Les bénéficiaires directs de ce projet seront également les acteurs humanitaires ayant besoin de renforcer leurs capacités en matière de gestion de l'information (80 ONG).

Niger HRP 2023	HNER23-RR-197233-1	Camp Coordination / Management Réponse d'urgence multisectorielle aux populations affectées par l'insécurité alimentaire et le conflit dans les régions de Tillabéri et diffa, et soutien aux services d'information humanitaire au Niger L'intervention se concentrera sur les zones difficiles d'accès, souffrant d'une très faible couverture humanitaire, notamment le nord de Tillabéri et le nord-est de Diffa. Compte tenu de la continuité de la crise et de l'augmentation des besoins, le programme propose une approche intersectorielle à travers une réponse à 4 niveaux. 
Une assistance alimentaire d'urgence flexible, répondant aux besoins immédiats des communautés touchées par le déplacement et l'insécurité alimentaire, dans les zones difficiles à atteindre. Le programme adaptera l'aide au contexte et aux besoins, en combinant des actions soudaines et des actions en période de soudure. Une approche à deux piliers sera mise en œuvre chaque année en fournissant une assistance alimentaire d'urgence pendant la période de soudure pendant 3 mois et 3 autres mois pendant la période ordinaire. 
Complété par des activités multisectorielles, renforçant la capacité de production alimentaire, les moyens de subsistance et la cohésion sociale, par une intervention dans deux secteurs. Pour soutenir les capacités agricoles et les mécanismes d'adaptation, dans les zones où l'assistance alimentaire sera fournie, le programme soutiendra la production agricole et alimentaire au niveau des ménages, en intégrant les ménages les plus vulnérables dans les systèmes de résilience communautaires. En outre, la diversification des ressources économiques au-delà de l'agriculture est essentielle pour assurer un accès inclusif, en particulier pour les personnes déplacées et les femmes (non-agriculteurs), aux activités économiques et couvrir la sécurité alimentaire et les besoins nutritionnels. Les personnes vulnérables supplémentaires bénéficieront d'un soutien aux AGR et au bétail par le biais i) d'un soutien aux éleveurs, ii) de la vaccination du bétail et des moyens de subsistance, et iii) des AGR.  
Et en tenant compte de la nécessité de mesures de protection au niveau communautaire, en particulier en raison de la crise accrue de la protection et du déplacement ; pour améliorer la qualité, la responsabilité et l'efficacité de la réponse tout en assurant l'accès à la protection de base et aux services WASH pour les personnes les plus vulnérables touchées par le déplacement. A travers des activités de type CCCM en dehors du camp  , la troisième ligne de réponse vise à prendre en compte le lien intersectoriel entre le déplacement et la sécurité alimentaire et à fournir un cadre de protection amélioré pour la population affectée par le déplacement et les communautés d'accueil. 
Soutenir les acteurs humanitaires par la production de produits d'information pertinents et adaptés au contexte (multisectoriel, thématique et sectoriel, cartographie) et la mise en œuvre d'activités de renforcement des capacités techniques afin d'informer la réponse humanitaire : En tant que partenaires mondiaux, IMPACT et ACTED mettent en œuvre l'initiative conjointe REACH et coordonnent la mise en œuvre sur le terrain.  d'accueil). WASH PRGRAM IN MAYOM COUNTY Provision of Integrated Emergency WASH Services for IDPS,  returnees and Most Vulnerable Host community in Uror, Ayod counties of Jonglei, Panyijiar and Mayom counties of Unity and Juba Mangateen IDP Camp of Central Equatoria States. Panyijiar and Mayom Counties are two of the Nine Counties in Unity State currently grouped in WASH Severity Classification 3&4. while Uror and Ayod Counties of Jonglei state are classified under IPC4.The four counties have been beset by conflict and instability since the  2013 civil strife in South Sudan; characterized by localized violence, inadequate infrastructure development, and the situation even compounded by incessant floods for the last three years (HNO 2022). This has aggravated the WASH needs in the aforementioned Counties thus recording poor WASH indices; low access to clean water per person per day, the average distance to the nearest clean water source exceeding the standard 500m, and access to safe sanitation facilities are inadequate. In Uror, Ayod, Mayom and panyijiar Counties like the rest of South Sudan, 18 percent of households reported feeling unsafe while collecting water, of those, 12 percent of women and girls reported avoiding water points due to GBV concerns (FSNMS, 2021). The food insecurity in Unity State (75%) of the population is likely to face severe acute food insecurity, with the highest levels of severe acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 and worse) at the peak of the lean season 2023. The main drivers to face unprecedented levels of food insecurity. covariate climatic, conflict, and economic shocks (such as floods and dry spells, inflation and rising food prices, and the continued disruption of livelihoods due to conflict and insecurity); and household-level idiosyncratic stressors (such as the death of a breadwinner, gender-based violence, morbidity and mortality due to poor hygiene, and lack of access to essential basic services) which are greatly amplified by the compounded effect of shocks. Food insecurity is greatest when these shocks and stressors are compounded by the persistently high levels of vulnerability and poverty associated with the protracted crisis that has existed since December 2021 and progressively worsened over time reaching peaks in 2022 and it is continuing now in 2023.

This situation will be further exacerbated by the progressive reductions in funding against increasing humanitarian needs in recent years which has forced humanitarian agencies to reduce entitlements and prioritize the most vulnerable households. Given the high levels of severe acute food insecurity in the state, there is a need for an immediate scale-up of multi-sectoral humanitarian assistance to save lives and prevent the total collapse of livelihoods in the affected counties (Mayom, Koch, and Panyijar).  Based on the IPC findings, at least three-quarters of the population in the Mayom, Koch, and Panyijar counties are classified in IPC Phase 3 and above. The severe food insecurity situation pressed for calls for livelihood and food security support through the provision and distribution of Agriculture inputs of (crops seed, vegetable seeds, fishing kits, and agriculture hand tools. The intervention has to be supplemented by support training to target households in agriculture good agronomic practices, good fishing practices, i.e. seedbed and nursery preparation, all best agricultural practices, fishing, and fish postharvest handling, preservation, nutrition, and preservation techniques.  

Furthermore, there should be vaccination of livestock, and training in climate change adaptation. Humane Aid for Community Organization intends to target to support 13,033 Households (78,200 individuals) in Mayom, Koch, and Panyijar Counties/Unity State.

Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM). WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.
Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (light resilience- building activities, peace/conflict resolution training also called GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness, training, or sensitisation on peaceful resolution of conflicts, mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace. 
Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). Préparation et réponse humanitaire multi-secteurs aux vulnérabilités aigues des populations affectées par les conflits, catastrophes naturelles et épidémies au Niger (Rapid Response Mechanism - RRM)
---- Food Security Projet d ’appui à la Sécurité  Alimentaire et Nutritionnelle dans les départements de Tilia, Abalack  (Region de Tahoua),   N’Guiguimi, Mainé Soroa et Diffa  (Région de Diffa) et  Dakoro et Bermo (Région de Maradi). Le présent projet a pour but de contribuer à l'atténuation des souffrances des populations vulnérables (hommes, femmes, filles, garçons et des personnes à besoins spécifiques) des zones d'intervention d'Action contre la Faim à travers des activités d'assistance alimentaire et de renforcement de moyens d'existence pendant les périodes critiques pendant lesquelles elles font face à des situations de chocs notamment pendant les périodes de soudures agricoles et pastorales.  De façon spécifique le projet vise à : i) assurer une assistance alimentaire aux ménages vulnérables abritant des FEFA et des enfants de 6 à 23 mois au sein des communautés  hôtes et déplacées qui subissent de l'une ou de la combinaison des crises liées à l'insécurité et aux changements climatiques ; ii) apporter de la supplémentation alimentaire aux enfants âgés de 6 à 23 mois issus des ménages bénéficiaires ; iii) Appuyer le relèvement des populations victimes des crises sécuritaires.  Il touchera directement environ 37800 personnes réparties dans les régions de Tahoua (département de Tillia et Abalak) et Diffa (Département de Diffa, Mainé Soroa et N’Guigmi) et Maradi (  Mayahi, Bermo et Dakoro) où le besoin en assistance alimentaire se ferait sentir pour une frange importante de la population en période projetée (juin-septembre). Les principales activités qui seront menées à travers ce projet sont: i) le ciblages géographique et celui des ménages auxquelles seront impliquées toutes les parties prenantes (hommes, femmes, STD, autorités administratives et coutumières); ii) l'assistance alimentaire inconditionnelle en Cash ou en Vivre selon le contexte en prenant en compte les besoins des hommes, femmes, filles et garçons; iii) la distribution de suppléments alimentaires aux enfants de 6 à 23 mois issus des ménages bénéficiaires; iv) la mise en œuvre d'actions de relèvement au profit des populations bénéficiaires de l'assistance depuis un certain nombre d'années et qui ont des besoins spécifiques pour le relèvement (Reconstitution Sociale du Cheptel, Distribution d'aliments bétails, Distribution de semences, Renforcement de capacités tous azimuts, AGR etc.).

Préparation et réponse humanitaire multi-secteurs aux vulnérabilités aigues des populations affectées par les conflits, catastrophes naturelles et épidémies au Niger (Rapid Response Mechanism - RRM) Projet d’assistance d’urgence multisectorielle au profit des populations (hôtes, déplacées, retournées, agricoles et pastorales) affectées par les chocs climatiques, sécuritaires et sanitaires dans la région de Diffa L’action a pour objectif de contribuer à la réduction des impacts négatifs des chocs sécuritaires, climatiques et sanitaires sur les conditions de vie des populations vulnérables hôtes et déplacées au Niger dans la région de Diffa (Diffa, Maine-Soroa,  N’guigmi et Bosso)  à travers une approche multisectorielle adaptée aux pics de vulnérabilités. Afin de réduire d'une manière drastique et holistique ces impacts, Action contre la faim (ci-après ACF) propose un projet qui vise l'amélioration de l'accessibilité aux services de santé par la mise en oeuvre d'un mécanisme de réponse rapide (ci-après RRM santé) du paquet santé et nutrition et l'appui aux structures de santé fragilisées par les conflits, le renforcement de la sécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle notamment en période de soudure pour les populations vulnérables ycompris les populations pastorales, l'amélioration de l'accès à l'eau potable et des conditions d'assainissement et des bonnes
pratiques d'hygiène et de changement de comportement au niveau communautaire en prévention des épidémies dans ces zones sensibles.
ACF agira en synergie avec les acteurs humanitaires dans les deux zones en complémentarité à la mise en oeuvre du mécanisme de RRM santé. Ce projet sera renforcé en garantissant l’environnement protecteur des communautés à travers une réponse à leurs besoins et une coordination efficace pour un accès libre et durable aux services sociaux de base dans le respect des principes humanitaires. Action Contre la Faim propose donc une approche fondée sur un mécanisme de réponse rapide (RRM) pour assurer l'accès aux services de santé et de nutrition auprès des populations affectées par la crise du bassin du Lac Tchad dans la région de Diffa au Niger. Cette réponse viendra compléter et intégrer les interventions actuelles des autres mécanismes de RRM en cours par d’autres acteurs RRM dans la région. Le mécanisme proposé sera basé sur un système de surveillance et d'alerte construit sur des réseaux communautaires et les informations régulières recueillies directement auprès des centres de santé. Les structures sanitaires ciblées seront appuyées pour intégrer une surveillance de qualité des maladies à potentiel épidémique. Cet aspect sera assuré par l’amélioration des bases de données et métadonnées et de la promptitude de remontée des données épidémiques au Ministère de la Santé Publique, de la population et affaires sociales. Selon la nature de l'alerte, une évaluation rapide sera réalisée pour identifier la nature des obstacles à l'accès local aux services de santé et une réponse appropriée. Les évaluations rapides se feront selon les modalités d’évaluation mises en œuvre dans le RRM Santé et seront couplées dans la mesure du possible à celle d’autres secteurs dans les Zones affectées. Lors de l’évaluation, Action Contre la Faim fournira déjà dans la mesure du possible une première réponse en santé et nutrition avant la réponse multisectorielle conduite après l’analyse des besoins. 
Le paquet minimum d’activités Santé nutrition du RRM Santé reposera sur deux principales modalités de réponse (flexibles) : 
- L’implantation des Cliniques mobiles : des équipes mobiles capables de fournir le soutien nécessaire aux structures de santé affectées et / ou si nécessaire directement aux communautés par le biais de services mobiles équipes. La stratégie mobile sera composée de soins curatifs gratuits pour toute la population (soins de santé primaires, santé de la reproduction, prise en charge de la MAS), des soins préventifs (vaccination, CPN). L’appui psychosocial à base communautaire et une détection précoce des cas de protection des enfants et des femmes (composante GBV) suivi d’un référencement vers les autres acteurs pour une prise en charge plus globale. ACF accordera aussi , une attention particulière aux groupes spécifiques vulnérables et à besoin spécifiques pour les personnes âgées , les handicapées et tous  les influenceurs de soins de santé dans les communautés.

Duration From 200623 to 201223 (6 months) Fortalecimiento de la SAN y la resiliencia de las comunidades vulnerables, a través de un modelo de Alimentación Escolar saludable proveniente de la Agricultura Familiar local. La persistencia de la crisis económica y política en Venezuela durante los últimos años ha colocado a una parte importante de su población en situación de extrema precariedad. Las interrupciones de las actividades educativas y la cadena de suministro de alimentos locales debido a la pandemia COVID-19, ha afectado profundamente la oportunidad de la población vulnerable, incluidos niños en edad escolar y familias productoras, de acceder a alimentos esenciales y a insumos productivos que fortalezcan su SAN, respectivamente. 
En este sentido, durante el periodo 2020-2021, la cobertura del Programa de Alimentación Escolar (PAE) ha tenido deficiencia en frecuencia, ingesta nutricional y dieta equilibrada para no menos de 4.5 millones de niños y se estima que alrededor de 1.1 millones corren el riego de abandonar la Escuela. Al mismo tiempo, la disminución continua de la producción local de alimentos se agrava por el limitado acceso a insumos agrícolas esenciales -como semillas con calidad- por parte de los pequeños productores, agravando la inseguridad alimentaria y financiera preexistente en las comunidades.
Por lo anterior expuesto, la presente acción tiene como propósito principal el de mejorar la SAN de niños y niñas en edad escolar, además de los hogares rurales en situación de vulnerabilidad, esto, mediante el desarrollo de modelos de Alimentación Escolar basados en la producción local que FAO y UNICEF han pilotado y validad en cuatro estados del país. Complementariamente, la acción promoverá esquemas comunitarios de producción variada de semillas de forma artesanal, adaptadas climáticamente y que respetan la cultura y saberes locales productivos. 
Bajo este objetivo, se propone el desarrollo de los siguientes componentes:
PRODUCTO 1: Fortalecido el modelo de Alimentación Escolar basado en la producción local de la Agricultura Familiar (AF): A través de rehabilitar y/o mejorar las capacidades productivas de las Escuelas Técnicas Agrícolas (ETA) y Asociación Local de Productores (ALP) incrementando su productividad aplicando prácticas agroecológicas para producción de alimentos, huevos y semillas, además desarrollando acciones de asistencia técnica. Se espera que, con la disponibilidad de una producción local de huevos, hortalizas y frutas, se logre fomentar modelos alimentarios de circuito corto, saludables y sostenibles, en donde los niños y niñas de edad escolar en situación de vulnerabilidad - y de manera indirecta el de familias vulnerables de agricultores de pequeña escala - mejoran el consumo de alimentos diversificados, frescos y nutritivos.
PRODUCTO 2: Mejorado el acceso a semillas con calidad, por parte de los pequeños productores familiares locales; a través de una implementación de un modelo de producción de semillas comunitario, sostenibles y resilientes. En este modelo, las ETA jugarán un rol de motor de producción y difusión de conocimiento y los productores a través de las ALP, serán el factor de escalamiento de la capacidad de producción y accesibilidad de la semillas para los demás productores
Para la implementación del proyecto se han priorizado estados con población indígena y, cuando sea posible, se dará la prioridad de participación a agricultoras y agricultores indígenas y a mujeres líderes de hogar, en los estados Amazonas, Sucre, Monagas, Falcon, Zulia, Delta Amacuro, Bolívar y Apure. La acción espera dar cobertura a alrededor de 13 750 hogares de pequeños productores y productoras, aglutinando alrededor de 450 grupos productivos y/o Bancos de Semillas Comunitarios, que contribuyan a la protección y acumulación de sus medios de vida productivos esenciales y en conjunto con 50 ETAs y 25 escuelas de educación básica y primaria, puedan abastecer complementos alimentarios frescos y sanos para alrededor 27 000 niños y niñas en edad escolar.

Global Food Crisis – Humanitarian Assistance to People Affected by the Severe Food Insecurity Crisis in East and Southern Africa. Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM). WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.
Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (light resilience- building activities, peace/conflict resolution training also called GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness, training, or sensitisation on peaceful resolution of conflicts, mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace. 
Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities.

Multi-sectoral emergency aid for newly displaced populations while facilitating early and sustainable recovery Provision of integrated, equitable, and timely WASH services to emergency affected populations in South Sudan Protracted crises in South Sudan, including climactic shocks and continued conflict, have resulted in 8.9 million people projected to be in need of humanitarian assistance in 2022. As a result of the shocks, such as flooding, inter-communal violence (ICV) and ongoing armed clashes, the majority of the population are facing increased food insecurity, lack of access to basic services, and protection risks. As per the Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) 2022, lack of or inadequate access to clean water and improved sanitation and hygiene practices in South Sudan will negatively impact an estimated 6.1 million people in 2022. 

Since 2006, Solidarites International has become a key WASH actor in South Sudan, implementing emergency lifesaving responses across the country and providing integrated WASH services to crisis-affected populations in areas of static presence in Upper Nile, Jonglei, and Western Bahr el Ghazal. Since 2012 SI has played a key role in the Emergency Preparedness and Response (EPR) strategy in South Sudan, implementing multi-sectoral assessments and delivering emergency responses to crisis-affected populations all over the country. 

In 2022, SI will continue to provide emergency live-saving  WASH responses across the South Sudan to restore basic access to safe water, hygiene, and sanitation while ensuring equitable access, safety, and accountability to supported populations. Through its roving Emergency Preparedness and Response (EPR) team, SI will deploy to emergency-affected locations to provide first phase and second phase responses including distribution of household water treatment items and soap, emergency provision of safe water, and rapid repair of emergency-affected infrastructure.

At the same time, SI will expand its presence in Upper Nile, Unity and Jonglei to provide basic integrated WASH services that target the most vulnerable, including those suffering malnutrition, food insecurity and protection threats (including GBV survivors). Static programs will focus on providing community-based solutions for sustainable WASH services that ensure that improvements in access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene are durable and can be maintained independently by communities. Engagement and joint programming with Protection and Nutrition actors will ensure that WASH services can be accessed by the most vulnerable and will have a tangible impact on reducing overall priority humanitarian needs. The increased integration of protection, inclusion, and conflict sensitivity analysis in all programming will ensure that WASH services and resources can be safely accessed by all in the community. Greater engagement of communities and local markets will support the design of long term and flood resistant WASH infrastructure and supply chains to ensure that interventions produce durable results for communities.

Provision of integrated humanitarian assistance to the most vulnerable crisis-affected people through mobile teams in Sudan Facilitating the Creation of a Favourable Protection Environment in Sudan As a result of the clashes that erupted throughout the country between Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on 15 April 2023, the already fragile protection environment in Sudan has significantly deteriorated, with a multitude of protection risks that have further worsened access to services such as water, health care, electricity, and basic items and commodities such as food, cash, and fuel for millions of people. Several cities have faced heavy bombardments and clashes, and associated unexploded ordnance, causing hundreds of civilian deaths and casualties, as well as damage to critical water, health care and power infrastructure, increasing of criminal activities, with indiscriminate attacks on civilians and widespread looting. Furthermore, high insecurity and looting of humanitarian assets and offices have compromised humanitarian access to key locations. As of 21 May 2023 a total of 1,042,114 individuals (209,136 households) have been displaced across the country mostly from urban areas in affected states. Vulnerable groups are increasingly exposed to protection risks with significant harm to their physical and mental wellbeing. 
This project intends to contribute to promoting a favorable protection environment in communities particularly affected by the current crisis, while providing humanitarian assistance to individuals and groups. The proposed intervention intends to provide General, Child, and GBV related protection services in the areas of interventions with the cluster estimating 7.3 million people in need of these protection services. The project is in line with the Cluster and Sub-Cluster Objectives and will target localities across the target areas identified as “hotspots” by the Protection Cluster and partners.
IOM will improve access of vulnerable crisis-affected people, especially girls and women, to primary healthcare and protection services, including GBV response services. Also, IOM will assist conflict-affected population with the distribution of non-food items (NFIs), in coordination with the Emergency Shelter and Non-Food Items(ES/NFI) Cluster. IOM will also work towards strengthening the capacity and availability of GBV services through the training and deployment of social workers and psychologists, in addition to enhancing existing referral mechanism to address GBV and child protection issues and cases. To improve the crisis-affected people’s access to community-based dispute resolution mechanisms, IOM also will build the capacity of informal mediators and dispute resolvers. To achieve this aim, IOM will work with the existing community committees, community leaders, and representatives from other community-based organisations, including women and youth groups as well as those belonging to both farmers and herder groups. IOM staff will also contribute to “protection by presence” by collecting data on protection needs, gaps and trends for advocacy, IOM will coordinate with its other existing programming in the targeted states, such as the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) and humanitarian response and transition interventions including Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) and health activities, to leverage effective synergies between programme activities in view of delivering the best protection outcomes for affected populations. 
In coordination with the Civil Registry and UNHCR, IOM will support the local government to strengthen their capacity and resources to improve the birth registration of IDPs and service provision to persons with disabilities through the provision of office equipment, trainings, and facilitating regular visits of government staff to hard-to-reach areas to provide the services to rural communities. Finally, IOM will support the establishment and/or reactivation of women’s groups and centres in secure areas to ensure access to safe engagement platforms as well as to information on protection services.

Improving protection and safeguards of the most vulnerable conflict affected households and strengthening food security analysis and coordination in Northeast Nigeria Emergency Food Security and Livelihood assistance to vulnerable and conflict affected households in north east Nigeria Food insecurity and malnutrition remain prevalent across Nigeria, mainly driven by the ongoing protracted conflict in the Northeast, mass displacement and the resultant IDP return process, adverse climate change and variability, such as drought, long dry spells, and flood, land degradation increasing insecurity and banditry, natural resource-based conflicts and an unfavorable macroeconomic situation manifested in rising food price inflation, etc. Further, the disruption of food and agricultural input supply chains by the Russia-Ukrainian war has led to severe availability and access constraints especially for poor farming households because of high food and agricultural input prices, especially fertilizer.
Despite the efforts of humanitarian communities in addressing the manifestations of the emergency in the country, the situation of food security continues to be a challenge. According to the latest Cadre Harmonise (CH) analysis, an estimated 19.45 million people, nearly 63 percent of them in Northeast and Northwest Nigeria are projected to be at risk of severe food insecurity during the peak of the 2022 lean season. In addition, the latest IPC acute malnutrition analysis report released in June 2022 estimates that 1.4 million children and, nearly 152,000 pregnant and lactating women are likely to suffer acute malnutrition during this period. Therefore, the urgent need for an expanded humanitarian food security response cannot be overstated. While the humanitarian interventions have been playing vital and critical role in addressing the needs of affected populations, it is obvious more has to be done to support the resilience of the livelihoods and the households. Given that the majority of those in need are involved in agriculture related activities, it has become necessary and urgent to promote agriculture-based livelihoods to famers whose majority are smallholders.  
In 2021 FAO reached over 1 million people and is planning to scale up and reach 2 million people (approximately 285,715 households) in need of agricultural-based livelihoods assistance in Nigeria in 2023/2024 with a stronger focus on Northeast and Northwest Nigeria due to the high level of vulnerability in the two regions. Due to restrictions on target numbers submitted in the HRP and its limited coverage (only targeting the Northeast), 1.7 million people will be targeted through the HRP while the remaining 0.3 million will be planned outside the HRP framework. To achieve this target FAO Nigeria is requiring a total of USD 86 million. Notably, funding for agriculture livelihood had declined significantly, for example, in 2022 the livelihood and agriculture funding stand at 6%, while food assistance is 95% covered. This requires a strong coordinated advocacy strategy to shift the paradigm.  An estimated 1.7 million people will be targeted for emergency agricultural livelihoods assistance while 0.3 million will be targeted for resilience interventions including in agribusiness, skills development for the creation of decent employment and income such as stoves production, aquaculture, livestock, etc. that increase the resilience of the beneficiaries.  
The scale-up plan will target the most vulnerable groups including IDPs, returnees, and host communities, especially women, and girls.    FAO Nigeria provides various agricultural livelihood assistance packages based on the livelihoods of the targeted household and the related activity. This is including agricultural rainy and dry season inputs, livestock restocking goats and poultry, urban and peri-urban homestead gardening, aquaculture, agribusiness enterprise support, nutritional support, and SAFE kits. This intervention will be delivered through a combination of in-kind, cash, and cash+ assistance. The scale-up plan is aligned to the FAO Corporate Global strategy framework of achieving Better Production, Better Nutrition, Better environment and Better life.

With support from CRSF technical FSL team, a total of 1,000 households will be trained on modern agronomic practices and 100 Community Animal Health Workers (CAWHs) will be recruited and trained for the livestock support. Under CRSF supported farmers groups on seed multiplication project in Ibba County, CRSF will  use vouchers to support farmers in other locations during seed fair to access quality seed inputs for sustainable agriculture on food production. Protection and assistance of IDPs in South Sudan Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2022, there are some 335,000 refugees and asylum seekers from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, primarily from Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic.
At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for longer term stability, hundreds of thousands of South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since the signing of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan, this spontaneous movement has prompted the development of an area-based approach, to support refugees, returnees and host communities, through enhanced engagement with development actors, to support greater access to services where possible.
Refugees largely reside in conflict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction in basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.
Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will benefit from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Specific protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identified at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with specific protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as verification exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the efficiency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to benefit from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

To save lives and alleviate suffering Emergency Shelter and Non-Food Items Response to Assist IDPs, Returnees and Host Communities affected by conflict or natural disaster in Western Equatoria, Upper Nile, and Warrap States, South Sudan.  The 2022 Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) indicates that ‘’approximately 2.4 million people in South Sudan continue to be impacted by the destruction of housing and loss of essential goods caused by ongoing flooding and conflict. In addition, nearly 329,000 refugees and asylum seekers also require shelter and non-food item (NFI) support. At the end of 2021, nearly 1.9 million men, women, boys, girls, and older people live in inadequate shelter, while a total of 2.3 million require NFIs. The number of people in need increased in 2022 due to the increased displacement of approximately 300,000 people in 2021 and the returns of nearly 270,000 from neighboring countries. The top three shelter/NFI-related needs are access to emergency shelter, NFIs and housing, land and property (HLP) rights to ensure security of tenure’’. With the budget of $700,000, this project will enable World Vision International South Sudan to serve 55,000 (17,500 men, 17,500 women; 10,000 boys, 10,000 girls) IDPs, returnees and host communities with in-kind emergency shelter and non-food items in the counties of Tambura, Nagero and Yambio in Western Equatoria State, Tonj North, Tonj East, Tonj South, Gogrial East, Gogriel West and Aweil South counties in Warrap State, Laukpiny/Nasir, Ulang Melut and Baliet counties of Upper Nile State. In areas with existing functional markets, 18 % of the targeted beneficiaries will be supported through unconditional but restricted modality of cash-based interventions. Beneficiaries for both in-kind SNFI and cash interventions will be identified during needs assessments, where methodologies like Focused Group Discussions (FGD), Key informants (KI), Observation will be deployed to collect data for decision making and before beneficiary registration and distribution missions. Post distribution missions would also be effected to get feedback from affected population. In the course of the project, WVISS team will continuously conduct community awareness meetings and workshops on issues like climate change, AAP, Covid-19 etc. The project would contribute to the two Cluster objectives; (1). Percentage of the targeted population are able to access shelter material and non-food items in situations of emergency and transition, (2). Enhance the community’s dignity by increasing their ability to respond to new shocks and building on existing skills. World Vision International South Sudan will implement the project in adherence with the SNFI cluster standards where the cluster coordination team is closely consulted on operations at national and sub-national levels. The organization will also collaborate with men, women, boys, girls, persons with special needs, government authorities and partners like UNHAS, UNOCHA, IOM/pipeline, local and international organizations to realize durable solutions for emergency shelter and non-food items. The affected populations will be encouraged to actively participate in the project through the mainstreaming of AAP (accountability to affected populations) approach into project activities. Existing local community structures would be strengthened to support the project and where they are non-existent, WVISS will facilitate the formation to enhance full participation of affected populations in area. The CFM, (Complaint Feedback Mechanism) will be introduced in each project site and community members would be sensitized on how to use it throughout the project period. The awareness creation sessions will be tailored to complement efforts for conflict mitigation, long-term solutions for floods, Sexual Exploitation and Abuse, Housing, Land & Property, and COVID-19 pandemic. WVISS will continue to respond through the mobile response mechanism by deploying teams in hard to access locations or where there is urgent need of intervention across the country based on SNFI request.

-BHA Emergency Child Protection, GBV & Mine Action: Prevention, Mitigation & Response to assist IDPs, Returnees and Host Communities in conflict-affected & high risk areas of Warrap, Upper Nile, Western Equatoria and Central Equatoria States, South Sudan  The already high needs of critical child protection services in South Sudan has been exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic, protracted displacement, and limited access to basic services which continues to significantly affect the physical, mental, and social well-being of children, adolescents and caregivers. This situation has been worsened by the limited availability of mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services and the low level of core child protection services, including family tracing and reunification, case management, and reintegration services for children affected by armed forces and groups, leaving many children untreated and unable to access the needed services. The high contamination with landmines and explosive remnants of war (ERW), especially in the Greater Equatoria region, along major supply routes and areas for returnees from Uganda, and the increase in expected returns require to prevent, mitigate and respond to mine risk issues through enhanced preparedness and resilience.
This proposed integrated CP, GBV and EORE project is in line with the Protection Cluster Objectives and will ensure the provision of critical protection-related assistance and specialized services and the prevention and mitigation of Protection risks through enhanced preparedness. The project targets to reach an average of 60,000 (20,000 women, 20,000 men, 10,000 girls, 10,000 men) (CP), 50,000 (20,000 women, 10,000 men, 10,000 girls, 10,000 boys) (GBV) and 20,000 (5000 men, 5000 women, 5000 girls, 5000 boys) (MA) including people with disabilities.

Through the provision of specialized / lifesaving child protection and multi sectoral services WVI-SS seeks to reduce the suffering of boys, girls, women and men including children with disabilities who are at risk or experience violence, abuse, exploitation and neglect including GBV.
The proposed project will reduce the suffering of GBV survivors including women, men, girls, boys and people with disabilities by providing multi-sectoral specialized GBV response services. Furthermore, WVI-SS seeks to ensure that vulnerable women, men, girls, boys including people with disabilities have improved access to the provision of GBV prevention and risk mitigation interventions. Through protection monitoring, advocacy, awareness-raising and prevention and response services the project aims to reduce the vulnerability of women, men, girls and boys including people with disabilities at increased risk of mortality and morbidity and protection incidents/threats in priority areas.
In line with the Core Humanitarian Standards, WVI-SS will maintain its commitment to engage with affected communities at all phases of the project cycle, through focus group discussions with women, men, boys and girls. Establishing/strengthening local structures such as Project Management Committee is one example of how WVI-SS engages the community in a sustainable and accountable manner to determine and support appropriate need-based responses. WVI's Quality Assurance framework ensures that each project implemented is carried out effectively and continually reviewed in line with community needs and in line with other humanitarian frameworks.

Fostering Resilience through Early Recovery response for the most Crisis impacted Communities in Syria The Integrated Response for Resilience Programme aims at providing a comprehensive response through Early Recovery support in 80 communities impacted by the crisis. Communities, particularly  those most dramatically affected – and under additional stress because of IDPs returns and other displacements - need  assistance in reinforcing their resilience to address these shocks as well as the consequences of the protracted crisis, and to address their needs on seriously depleted infrastructures and service capacities.
The essence of the Programme is about providing Syrian communities with – still limited - support to regain  control  over their basic needs (livelihoods, access to essential services) and reduce their dependency on humanitarian assistance. Prioritization of locations, is the outcome of a context analysis and needs assessment conducted on more than  5,000
Syrian communities, based on the following three criteria:
1) Hard to Reach  Areas
2) Areas of major IDPs presence and IDPs returns
3) Highest scoring in the Severity Scale

---- Irish Aid Provision of lifesaving GBV interventions for the crisis affected populations in Mayendit, Rubkona, Koch and Panyijiar Counties IRC through the Women Protection and Empowerment program will provide specialized GBV response services and prevention interventions targeting the crisis affected populations in Mayendit, Rubkona, Koch and Panyijiar counties.  This will be through the provision of life saving GBV case management services guided by the survivor centered approach.  IRC will ensure the service provision is in coordination with other service providers for a multisectoral approach which comprise of medical, legal, safety and psychosocial support services. A total of 472(325W, 123G, 12M, 12B) will be targeted for case management services across the proposed locations. IRC will continuously engage women and girls and the community at large to identify barriers in accessing the GBV services and collaboratively work together to address them through the existing community-based protection structures. In addition, quarterly reviews and updating of the referral pathways as well as continuous feedback sessions will be held to ensure that the pathways are functional across the proposed locations. The women and girls’ safe spaces (2 Rubkona, 2 Koch, 2 Panyijiar and 2 Mayendit) will serve as avenues of empowerment for women and girls with a major focus on provision of contextualized psychosocial support interventions which seek to support in the healing, recovery and building resilience of women and girls. The Women and Girls Safe Space toolkit will be instrumental in providing guidance on the operationalization of the safe spaces especially in ensuring accountability as well as encouraging the women-girls led processes and ownership. Tailored curriculums for the engagement of women and girls such as Girl Shine for the adolescent girls and their care givers as well as Women Rise a psychosocial support tool kits for the women will ensure each age group has appropriate and contextualized PSS intervention. 4,500(3,180W, 1,320G) will be targeted for the WGSS activities. Additionally, IRC seeks to build the capacity of communities to respond and prevent GBV through training and community led dialogues which will equip them with knowledge and skills. In coordination with the GBV SC, IRC will distribute dignity kits to the women and girls of reproductive age at risk of GBV. The proposed interventions aim to target 54,715 (27,904 Women, 19,150 Girls, 4,924 Men and 2737 Boys) where 78% IDP will be targeted, 18% host communities and 4% returnees. HRP	Multi-Sector	Harmonised multi-purpose cash assistance to meet critical basic needs of flood and conflict affected communities in Jonglei and UnityStates, South Sudan Emergency Nutrition Response to mitigate the impact of malnutrition among the most vulnerable under five children and PLW living in, Aweil south, Panyjar , Rumbek east , Rumbek North and Yirol west counties of South Sudan. Malnutrition is one of the top causes of death in children under five years and has a long-term negative impact on the children’s abilities to live to their full potential. South Sudan (SS) has experienced continued crisis including floods, conflict, and food insecurity which have impacted on the key drivers of acute malnutrition and aggravated the nutrition situation within the country. The Food Security and Nutrition Monitoring System (FSNMS) Round 28 and 2022 SMART surveys report GAM prevalence at 16.0% (15.4 -16.7) in lean season.  This indicates no improvement since 2019, when the GAM prevalence was 16.2% (13.8-18.5) in lean season the rate of acute malnutrition remains above the emergency threshold of 15 percent (very high acute malnutrition level- WHO classification). The situation calls for strengthened multisector investment to address the impact of aggravating factors, and to maintain gains in tackling the nutrition situation in South Sudan.The objectives of the action will be; To increase equitable access and utilization of quality preventative nutrition specific service delivery for children, adolescents, and women .To increase equitable access and utilization of quality lifesaving nutrition services for early detection and treatment of acute malnutrition for girls and boys under five years of age and PLW affected by acute malnutrition .To increase equitable access to nutrition sensitive interventions from health, WASH, FSL, Education and Protection sectors through enhanced coordination and joint programming targeting vulnerable groups in Aweil South, Panyijar, Rumbek East, Rumbek North and Yirol West counties by the end of 2023.  The proposed intervention aims to increase coverage and access to the most vulnerable community by providing equitable and accessible nutrition prevention treatment services. The nutrition services will deliver by scaling up the emergency nutrition responses through 62 static OTP/TSFP (10 in Aweil south,10 in Panyijar, 23 in Rumbek east, 7 in Rumbek North, and 12 in Yirol west), 5 Stabilization center (1 in Panyijar, 1 Aweil south, 1 in Rumbek east, 1 in Rumbek north, and 1 in Yirol west) and through 4 RRM mobile tam (2 in Aweil south, 2 in Panyjar,). In addition, the IRC will implement integrated CMAM and MIYCN in all sites. Promotion of optimal nutrition and prevention of malnutrition among young children (0-23 months through the implementation of MIYCN to ensure vulnerable children have optimal growth. IRC will strengthen community participation using existing community structures and active engagements of the affected community. IRC will conduct meetings with MtMSG, regular community sensitization sessions and scaling up of the existing Nutrition response to ensure timely service availability. Scale up family MUAC to ensure early detection of acute malnutrition that contributes to early detection. An estimated 20,085 SAM children,37388 MAM, and 30131 PLW MAM will be reached through this action across all implementation areas in OTP and TSFP, respectively. Continue with the capacity building of CHD, primary health care service providers and nutrition staff. Train health and nutrition staff on CMAM and MIYCN to ensure timely nutrition services. A rapid response team will be deployed to the hard-to-reach area to provide nutrition services that are accessible and vulnerable groups have got timely treatment. Subsequently, the interventions will reduce mortality and morbidity associated with malnutrition. Integration of nutrition activities with other sectors will also be implemented, including integration of health and nutrition education messages, Malaria testing and treatment, promotion of hygiene and sanitation, training on GBV and CP for nutrition staff. Similarly, with food security, establish kitchen garden, cash programs for children discharged cured from SAM treatment, and cooking demonstrations to improve dietary diversification, conduct kitchen garden and cash programs.
