South Sudan/CE	South Sudan	Norwegian Refugee Council WASH static and emergency response for vulnerable IDPs, host communities and returnees in South Sudan. NRC’s planned and proposed Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) intervention for 2023 is continuation of 2022 and   is designed to address the emergency WASH needs through rapid response (RRT)  and  contribute to improve health,  nutrition, education , Livelihood and food security  and protection  outcomes through NRC static WASH response. The proposed interventions are  to reduce prevalence of malnutrition, contribute to reducing WASH-related morbidity and mortality, provide access to basic WASH services in underserved and hard to reach  locations affected by disaster, disability inclusion and mitigating GBV at WASH facility and durable access to WASH amongst 200, 000 IDPs, returnees and vulnerable host communities in in South Sudan.
The proposed WASH interventions will be implemented in close coordination with NRC’s Shelter, Education, Livelihood and Food security, ICLA and protection programming and teams, applying an integrated approach to uplift people’s lives and contributing to South Sudan HRP and WASH Cluster objectives and the 2022/2023 Humanitarian Response. Recognizing WASH services to be key drivers of health and malnutrition outcomes and women and girls to be the primary users of WASH services, the project aims to reduce GBV risk by ensuring adequate and needs based provision of WASH services that address key protection concerns. NRC’s integrated approach will further address high levels of malnutrition in targeted locations.
NRC will consult and engage communities in preliminary assessments and design process to ensure all NRC’s interventions are tailored to local context and to establish appropriated water and sanitation facilities at community, institutions and household level. To enhance and ensure sustainability and proper usage of the facilities comprehensive training will be provided to female and male members of Water User Committees (WUCs) , Schools and other institutional staff. Solid waste management training will also be provided to solid waste/hygiene committees to implement community-driven solid waste collection and disposal campaigns. 
To ensure durable and continues access to safe water ; NRC will establish / rehabilitate small scale solar powered water supply schemes , new boreholes through cost effective manual Borehole drilling. The proposed water supply interventions will increase the safe water access to schools, health, nutrition and protection centres, disability inclusion and mitigating GBV at WAH facilities and route to WASH facilities. NRC will construct own driven household / family shared latrines to ensure that immediate and long-term sanitation needs are adequately met and facilities are gender and culturally appropriate. The approach will enhance the ownership and sustainability of the facilities. NRC  will also promote good hygiene practices and  awareness through training of community hygiene promoters who then will be conducting hygiene promotion at their own communities , community hygiene campaigns, hygiene promotion campaigns and sessions at intuitional levels. NRC will also provide hygiene kits, WASH-NFIs and soaps to the vulnerable communities specially in hard to reach areas

Sudan Humanitarian Response Plan 2023  Entrepreneurship Support to Refugees and Host Communities in South Sudan Enhancing IDP Protection Services in South Sudan to facilitate and scale up protection monitoring, targeted Protection Assistance and Services (including GBV and CP), as well as HLP support to the most vulnerable IDPs and Returnees The projects seek to ensure that those most in need, most vulnerable or at risk, so-called Persons with Specific Needs (PSNs) in IDP, returnee and host communities are supported with tailored protection services and assistance, focused on lifesaving support, while also investing in people’s resilience to shocks. Restoration of housing, land and property rights, civil documentation, child protection and prevention and response services for GBV will be part of this general protection project. The activities will be implemented through UNHCR’s offices in Juba, Wau, Bentiu, Bor, Malakal, Yei, Yambio and prioritized respective counties in line with the Cluster’s prioritization.

The project will support the implementation of the Protection Monitoring System that was launched in October 2022 under the umbrella of the Protection Cluster aimed at informing the protection and wider humanitarian response with protection analysis and based on a harmonized methodology and tools. Protection concerns identified will be dealt with both on individual protection services/case management basis and through community-based protection responses tailored to the specific needs and considering the age, gender, diversity among the people served. Community based protection components of this project will involve community owned projects with social cohesion and peace benefits in areas with social tension as well as areas where durable solutions are pursued.  Particular attention is paid to segments of the community particular at risk or marginalized, including women and youth empowerment, tailored support to GBV survivors and children at risk as well as people with disabilities and older persons. 

Protection risks and social tensions will be prevented and mitigated through awareness and information campaigns, community sensitization using an AGD approach and community engagement, such as community action committees, peace dialogues, including by involving leaders of faith-based institutions. Quality procedures to identify those most in need, vulnerable and at risk will be implemented across all project locations, building on the protection monitoring reports and implemented through protection desks and protection outreach, including through static and mobile teams. Protection services and assistance will be multi-faceted and tailored to the specific assistance and protection needs identified, including to survivors of gender-based violence and children at risk amongst other at risk categories. Direct protection services and assistance includes identification of people at risk, counselling, social accompaniment, enabling access to safety, case management, psychosocial support, legal aid (including assistance and representation), as well as material support tailored to the individual, including in kind (e.g. mobility device, core relief) or cash, implemented through a cash plus approach. The project will also specifically address housing, land and property rights and implement individual assistance and community-based mechanisms, such as through community-based land committees, to restore access to housing, land and property as well as to related documentation, including HLP, identity and civil documentation. This is complemented by community services, including child friendly spaces, rehabilitation of community infrastructure or basic services through community-owned approaches. 

Overall, the project empowers communities affected by displacement, conflict and disasters, and invests in their own agency and resilience through the multi-faceted nature of the protection response provided under this project.

Sudan Humanitarian Response Plan 2023  Entrepreneurship Support to Refugees and Host Communities in South Sudan CCCM services to assist affected populations through static, mobile, and area-based responses in Jonglei, Unity, Upper Nile, Warrap, Western Bahr el Ghazal, Northern Bahr el Ghazal, Western Equatoria and Central Equatoria States. Targeting 120,000 people in need living in IDP camps, settlements, collective sites and the increasing numbers living in urban areas, this project will focus on the provision of timely, well-coordinated, and integrated Camp Management services. With the aim of improving the well-being of displaced populations, strengthening their resilience and increasing their participation in decision-making processes, in Jonglei, Unity, Upper Nile, Warrap, Western Bahr el Ghazal, Northern Bahr el Ghazal, Western Equatoria and Central Equatoria, all states where UNHCR currently has a static presence through its field office operations, 
UNHCR and partners will put in place mechanisms to strengthen camp coordination and monitoring to enable the effective provision of cross-sectoral services. IDPs’ engagement in the delivery of services in an equal and needs-based manner will be possible through regular feedback and dissemination of information for example through community-based networks. In support of humanitarian interventions aimed at improving the well-being of displaced populations whilst providing some level of dignity and equitability by promoting AAP.
A key component of the project will be to support community-based structures to enhance participation in planning and decision-making, in particular seeking empowerment of communities. This will be done with a focus on vulnerable groups, PSNs and PWDs so that their views are received, and acknowledged and service delivery meets the specific needs of all groups. To this end, protection will be mainstreamed into all CCCM activities to respect and promote the rights of the most vulnerable. Site care and maintenance improvement projects will take place to minimize protection risks and determine the level of assistance required by PSNs.

Supporting the ability of vulnerable IDPs to recover from the external stresses they face, be it floods or conflict, this project will seek to promote capacity building and development of community self-management structures and practices. UNHCR and its partners will also ensure that communication channels with the concerned population are strengthened, diversified, and anchored on the views of the community. This will serve to facilitate timely and accurate information to respond to disasters and mitigate identified risks. CCCM will focus on capacity building, multi-sectoral assessments on a number of displaced persons affected by the flood, and conflict resolution services through CCCM monitoring, coordination meetings at the site level, care and maintenance activities conducted by the safety committee through cash for work initiatives and enhancing feedback and complaint mechanisms.
Finally, as CCCM Cluster Co-lead UNHCR will continue to strengthen and support CCCM partners through strategic guidance, advocacy with donors, and vitally step in as a provider of last resort in areas if partners have a low presence and limited capacity to respond.

Sudan Humanitarian Response Plan 2023 Targeted support to persons with specific needs with lifesaving non-food items and emergency shelter to displaced population in hard-to-reach areas and IDP returnee families. In 2023, Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) continue to face multi-faceted crises which are worsened by conflict and protracted displacement from locations of their habitual residence that is further compounded by flooding. Displaced families often have inadequate shelter and household goods which expose them to heightened protection risks. Increased mobility, continued insecurity and protracted displacement has over the years eroded household coping mechanisms and livelihood options especially considering the poor nature of local markets without stocks for household goods and shelter materials.

UNHCR’s project will focus on responding to the humanitarian needs of IDPs and IDP and refugee returnees with targeted and protection focused core relief items (emergency shelter and non-food items – S/NFIs) prioritizing the most vulnerable households and persons with specific needs especially women and girls.

The project will contribute to the following sectoral objectives:

SO 1 – percentage of the targeted population that is able to access shelter material and non-food items in situations of emergency and transition.
The project will identify the most vulnerable IDPs and returnees through protection monitoring and assessments including through IRNAs and RRMs. The assessments and inter cluster discussions will inform the decisions regarding the specific response modalities between in kind and cash assistance. Unique contextual factors including market conditions will be considered.

SO 2 - Enhance community dignity and engagement in the provision of S/NFI services. The project will deliver timely lifesaving activities while streamlining protection-oriented initiatives including COVID – 19 preventive measures. The project will strengthen community-based protection through the involvement of community-based structures for self-management in response delivery, ensuring that their capacities to cope, recover, contribute to and achieve solutions are enhanced.

SO 3 - Community members’ exposure to environmental hazards is reduced through the construction of disaster-resistant structures.

In 2023, UNHCR will increase its active participation in humanitarian coordination forums, including the ES/NFI cluster, both at national level and in the field, strongly advocating for protection mainstreaming and joint vulnerability assessments, the results of which will be very useful in the optimization of the limited resources. UNHCR will endeavor to provide timely response to the most critical identified needs of vulnerable IDPs and returnees, among other affected populations. Protection risks remain high among women, girls, boys and persons with specific protection needs which may include transitional shelters and other material assistance.

Sudan Humanitarian Response Plan 2023 Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2022, there are some 335,000 refugees and asylum seekers from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, primarily from Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic.
At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for longer term stability, hundreds of thousands of South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since the signing of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan, this spontaneous movement has prompted the development of an area-based approach, to support refugees, returnees and host communities, through enhanced engagement with development actors, to support greater access to services where possible.
Refugees largely reside in conflict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction in basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.
Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will benefit from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Specific protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identified at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with specific protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as verification exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the efficiency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to benefit from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

Humanitarian initial allocation 2023 Integrated Food Security and Livelihoods Protection in Rubkona, Mayendit and Panyijiar Counties, Unity State, South Sudan  The project objective(s) is to enhance and sustain emergency food production through complementary vegetable and crop livelihood inputs, fishing, and livestock; reduce dependency on food and agricultural inputs to support and strengthen households’ ability to absorb shocks in floods and conflict-affected communities in Rubkon, Panyijiar and Mayendit counties, Unity state. The IRC proposes to provide a sequence of food production to support to most severe food-insecure and malnourished households in the main season farming of May to July and dry season of Nov to March. To strengthen households’ resilience, the project will mainstream gender, conflict sensitivity, disaster risks reduction to support at-risk households focused on improving vegetable, crop, livestock, and fisheries production and bolstering resilience towards recurrent shocks and stresses. In pursuit of the project objective(s), the following activities will be implemented: 
(a) The IRC together with the complaint and feedback mechanism (CFM/AAP) committee will mobilize, engage community members to inform the needs of the most vulnerable households and selection criteria for registration together with Nutrition partners. 
(b) Preposition and distribute emergency (short-term maturing) agricultural inputs (Cereal & Vegetable seeds, and tools) and fishing kits to 56,400 people. The IRC anticipates FAO will provide complimentary in-kind inputs to support the project.  
(c) To improve nutritional practices for pregnant women and caregivers of children under 5 years with MAM and SAM. Nutrient-dense vegetable seeds will be provided, establish demonstration gardens at nutrition facilities close to water points, provide basic training on vegetable production, harvest, and conservation techniques. The IRC Nutrition team will conduct nutrition-sensitive awareness, food cooking demonstrations showing how to enrich households’ meals with locally available foods.
(d) The IRC will identify 200 potential seed producers, provide foundation seeds, establish seeds multiplication centers and plots. The seed producers will receive at least 200 USD cash grants, training on quality seeds selection, quality seeds production techniques, and crop management practices. Seed producers will be supported to form VSLA to increase access to finance for seeds production and access to markets will be facilitated.  
(e) The IRC with the County Agriculture Department, State Ministry of Agriculture, and FAO will contribute to livestock disease surveillance and monitoring, facilitate vaccination campaigns, mass vaccination exercises and treatments to livestock to be led by CAHW.
(f) Facilitate capacity building to community-based extension agents (CAHWs, AEA’s), crop producers, pastoralists, and fisherfolks on sustainable production skills and provision of proximate extension services on production, post-harvest handling through demonstration gardens. Also, fisherfolks to receive basic training on fish preservation and kit repairs to enhance household nutrition and income.
Overall, the project will reach 5% (188,000 people) (i.e 56,400 people, 9,400 HHs) in emergency or severe (IPC 4 & 5 for 2023) in Rubkona, Mayendit, Panyijiar counties. In Particular, Rubkona (36,000 people, 6,00 HHs), Mayendit (9,600 people, 1,600 HHs) and Panyijiar (10,800 people, 1,800 HHs) equivalent to a total of 56,400 people (5,640 Male children, 8,460 Female children, 13,536 Adult male, 20,304 Adult female, 3,384 elderly Male, 5,076 elder Female) people. By program type: 56,400 livelihoods inputs distribution (Crop, Vegetable, Tools & fishing Kits), 9,400 individuals with production skills (Crop, Vegetables, fisheries skills (Fishing kits repairs, fish preservation etc) training, and 200 seeds growers/producers

Coordinated lifesaving multisectoral response to crisis affected populations in South Sudan Provision of timely, equitable and integrated food security and livelihood support to emergency affected populations in South Sudan Protracted crises in South Sudan, including climactic shocks and continued conflict, have resulted in 8.9 million people projected to be in need of humanitarian assistance in 2022. As a result of the shocks, such as flooding, intercommunal violence (ICV) and ongoing armed clashes, the majority of the population are facing increased food insecurity, lack of access to basic services, and protection risks. As per the IPC classification released in November 2022, 7.76 million people (62.7% of the population) are expected to experience severe food insecurity between April to July 2023.

Solidarites International has been operating in South Sudan since 2006, and currently provide assistance in Upper Nile, Jonglei and Unity states. In addition, SI has a fully roving Emergency Response and Preparedness (EPR) team based in Juba that implements frontline responses to new emergencies across the country. SI implements integrated programs in Food Security and Livelihoods (FSL) and Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH). 

In FSL, SI aims at supporting the most vulnerable households, who are suffering from severe food insecurity and/or struggling to restore their livelihoods. In previous years, SI’s FSL activities have included large-scale seed and tool distributions, fishing kit distributions, cash transfers for households affected by malnutrition, and training on agronomic and fishing good practices. In addition, SI provides Income Generating Activities (IGA) for vulnerable population in Greater Upper Nile within a 2 years project. Finally, SI currently provides  flood-adapted responses with, for instance, the development of ""agriculture in sacks"" solution in crowded settlements.

In 2023, SI will focus on providing rapid livelihoods support in emergency affected areas, while developing resilience and reduced dependency. 

SI will support for the most vulnerable emergency affected households (with a focus on households suffering from or at risk of malnutrition) with seeds, tools, and assets for fishing and vegetable production and follow up training. Flood adaptations to regular practices will be developed to reduce the impact of expected future flooding in 2023 (i.e floating garden etc.). Through its roving Emergency Preparedness and Response (EPR) team, SI will deploy to emergency-affected locations identified through the Clusters and Needs Analysis Working Group to provide emergency responses in IPC 4+ locations. SI will expand its EPR programs to include rapid response kits distribution (fishing kits/fast growing seeds) to affected households in new rapid onset emergencies. Activities ensuring access to basic WASH services will be integrated with FSL activities in priority locations to contribute to reductions in malnutrition and food insecurity. In parallel, SI will focus on developing livelihood resilience among communities and reducing dependency on humanitarian aid through programs on seed replication, and value chain addition, while ensuring basic needs for livelihoods inputs are met through main season seed, tool, and fishing kit distributions. Income Generating Activities (IGA) will also be implemented, mainly targeting youths and women, to boost local resilience. All programs will be integrated with nutrition services through beneficiary targeting and support to nutrition centres to develop and maintain kitchen gardens.

While the overall Global acute malnutrition (GAM) remains at 13.6%, the prevalence of GAM varies significantly across the localities with very high situation (GAM above 15% and above as per WHO classification) reported in 64 localities. The proposed nutrition project aim is to improve equitable access to quality life-saving curative and preventive services through the systematic provision of nutrition services in South Kordofan, North Kordofan, Central Darfur, North Darfur, West Darfur, Sennar, Blue Nile and Red Sea states in which 29 localities will be covered. Vulnerable children under-five and PLWs are the main target of the project. Through SC -Nutrition interventions, a total of 362,874 beneficiaries will benefit from the services provided, among them (87,131 boys, 90,680 girls, 184,383 women, 680 men). Save the children will implement lifesaving, preventative interventions, treatment of severe and moderate acute malnutrition among children under five years and Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLWs), referral of SAM children with medical complications and minor rehabilitation to nutrition sites. To reach the estimated targets and planned response scale up, the nutrition sector will deploy integrated response modalities with health sector, WASH, FSL, protection, education at facility and community levels. SC will deliver nutrition services through existing health facilities, mobile and outreach teams and at community such as mother-to mother support groups activities including IDPs and hard to reach areas, use of cash-based interventions to increase access and utilization of nutrition services through FSL will be used for most cases in need. In term of emergency response, rapid response mechanisms for timely delivery of nutrition interventions in the onset emergencies will applied.

-- NUTRITION Emergency Nutrition Response to mitigate the impact of malnutrition among the most vulnerable under five children and PLW living in, Aweil south, Panyjar , Rumbek east , Rumbek North and Yirol west counties of South Sudan. Malnutrition is one of the top causes of death in children under five years and has a long-term negative impact on the children’s abilities to live to their full potential. South Sudan (SS) has experienced continued crisis including floods, conflict, and food insecurity which have impacted on the key drivers of acute malnutrition and aggravated the nutrition situation within the country. The Food Security and Nutrition Monitoring System (FSNMS) Round 28 and 2022 SMART surveys report GAM prevalence at 16.0% (15.4 -16.7) in lean season.  This indicates no improvement since 2019, when the GAM prevalence was 16.2% (13.8-18.5) in lean season the rate of acute malnutrition remains above the emergency threshold of 15 percent (very high acute malnutrition level- WHO classification). The situation calls for strengthened multisector investment to address the impact of aggravating factors, and to maintain gains in tackling the nutrition situation in South Sudan.The objectives of the action will be; To increase equitable access and utilization of quality preventative nutrition specific service delivery for children, adolescents, and women .To increase equitable access and utilization of quality lifesaving nutrition services for early detection and treatment of acute malnutrition for girls and boys under five years of age and PLW affected by acute malnutrition .To increase equitable access to nutrition sensitive interventions from health, WASH, FSL, Education and Protection sectors through enhanced coordination and joint programming targeting vulnerable groups in Aweil South, Panyijar, Rumbek East, Rumbek North and Yirol West counties by the end of 2023.  The proposed intervention aims to increase coverage and access to the most vulnerable community by providing equitable and accessible nutrition prevention treatment services. The nutrition services will deliver by scaling up the emergency nutrition responses through 62 static OTP/TSFP (10 in Aweil south,10 in Panyijar, 23 in Rumbek east, 7 in Rumbek North, and 12 in Yirol west), 5 Stabilization center (1 in Panyijar, 1 Aweil south, 1 in Rumbek east, 1 in Rumbek north, and 1 in Yirol west) and through 4 RRM mobile tam (2 in Aweil south, 2 in Panyjar,). In addition, the IRC will implement integrated CMAM and MIYCN in all sites. Promotion of optimal nutrition and prevention of malnutrition among young children (0-23 months through the implementation of MIYCN to ensure vulnerable children have optimal growth. IRC will strengthen community participation using existing community structures and active engagements of the affected community. IRC will conduct meetings with MtMSG, regular community sensitization sessions and scaling up of the existing Nutrition response to ensure timely service availability. Scale up family MUAC to ensure early detection of acute malnutrition that contributes to early detection. An estimated 20,085 SAM children,37388 MAM, and 30131 PLW MAM will be reached through this action across all implementation areas in OTP and TSFP, respectively. Continue with the capacity building of CHD, primary health care service providers and nutrition staff. Train health and nutrition staff on CMAM and MIYCN to ensure timely nutrition services. A rapid response team will be deployed to the hard-to-reach area to provide nutrition services that are accessible and vulnerable groups have got timely treatment. Subsequently, the interventions will reduce mortality and morbidity associated with malnutrition. Integration of nutrition activities with other sectors will also be implemented, including integration of health and nutrition education messages, Malaria testing and treatment, promotion of hygiene and sanitation, training on GBV and CP for nutrition staff. Similarly, with food security, establish kitchen garden, cash programs for children discharged cured from SAM treatment, and cooking demonstrations to improve dietary diversification, conduct kitchen garden and cash programs.

Integrated response to emergency needs in Nutrition, WASH, Health and Protection for recently displaced populations and other disaster-affected people in West and Central Darfur provision of emergency lifesaving and resilience WASH, ES/NFI, Education FSL and child protection integrated services for IDPS, returnees and venerable host community of Sudan in CD, WD, BN, Aj Jazirah, Khartoum and SK state. Starting on 15 April 2023, fighting between the SAF and the RSF, the number of people in need (PiN) of humanitarian assistance has increased from 15.8 million, estimated in November 2022, to 24.7 million in May 2023, representing a 57 per cent increase. 
The primary objective of this project is to safe live through supporting the newly displaced individuals who are the most vulnerable and marginalized people at risk through multi-sectoral lifesaving intervention. This project will prioritize activities that ensure life-saving assistance and protection to people affected by recent crisis primely and also people at risk of epidemics and floods, and other vulnerable residents - in order to reduce mortality and morbidity in the targeted areas. The proposed action will address 350000 (IDPs-175000(F-85750, M-89250), Returnees- 105,000(F-51450, M-53550), Vulnerable community-70,000(F-34300, M-35700)) crisis affected peoples. The WASH component will respond to the most urgent needs through Operationalization of water treatment plants in Khartoum, Water trucking in areas where supply is disrupted including health facilities and the establishment of distribution points, including in gathering and transit points; Essential WASH supplies and NFI emergency sanitation and handwashing facilities will be provided in hotspot locations; Hygiene promotion and household water treatment practices will be promoted as an immediate alternative, especially for those reliant on surface/river water. Following the immediate lifesaving response (stabilization and restoration), Rehabilitate, operate and maintain water supply schemes, replenish supplies and strengthen technical and management capacity for sustained service delivery will continue. This component will be complemented by Education, Child Protection FSL and ES/NFI activities: it will include provision of NFI kits, establishment of rapid-response communal shelters, distribution of tents for swift deployment in mass displacement scenarios. Additionally, upon local market and banking functionality, cash assistance for rent, emergency shelter construction, shelter repair, distribution of Emergency Shelter Kits (ESKs) will be included based on local market availability; Identify acutely vulnerable boys and girls via using outreach methodologies, provided with specialized child protection response services, identification of specific sources of threat and/or vulnerabilities of children, provided with gender & age appropriate (structured) psychosocial support and life skill, and communities are mobilized to support children through activation of child protection networks and community volunteers. 
The FSL project will focus on Cash/Vouchers Based Transfer (Full Ration), Cash/Vouchers Based Transfer (Half Ration) related to food activity while the livelihood part will support on agricultural Support (Seeds, Tools), livestock Support (Distribution, Treatments, Kits), and livelihood Cash/Voucher Support. The Education project will supporting the most vulnerable and marginalized girls and boys at risk of exclusion from education.  TGH will also strategically responding in the hotspot zones (conflict zone – Khartoum, Darfur) through local NGO and CBOs who have strong partnership with TGH, including AORD, & AL Massar. The education response programme aims to prioritize immediate critical life-saving education needs. The response will include awareness session to children age between 5 to 18 years, provision of life skills in emergency training to teachers, ALP Facilitators and PTAs, distribution of Education in Emergency supplies to both schools and safe learning spaces, support for the facilitators in the learning centers, providing psychosocial support through counselling and support to equip children with the skills they need to cope with trauma. By focusing on the same area where the education sector is being targeted, the WASH and child protection response will be delivered and integrated with it.

THM HUMANITAR 2022-2025
---  CHILD PROTECTION Strengthening Child Protection interventions for girls and boys most at risk of violence, abuse, neglect and exploitation across whole of Syria In line with the CP Area of Responsibility (AOR) Strategy and the “No Lost Generation” framework, UNICEF will enhance equitable access to quality CP services with a resilience focus, including for Survivors of abuse, violence, neglect and exploitation as well as children with disabilities, targeting 117 high severity sub-districts (3 to 5) and 38 low severity ones.

UNICEF’s CP Strategy in 2022-2023 includes:
• Addressing behavioural, social, cultural and economic determinants of CP violations as a prevention approach.  
• Improving the reach and quality of specialized CP services
• Capacity development of CP responders
•  Monitoring, evidence generation and advocacy 

UNICEF will support the delivery of integrated programming that will encourage social transformation, prioritizing:
• Structured and sustained CP MHPSS and EORE programmes
• Specialized integrated CP services including case management for survivors of violence, exploitation, neglect and abuse (child labour, CAFAAG, child survivors of GBV, child marriages, justice for children, birth registration and unaccompanied or separated children amongst others) 
• Parenting programmes to promote positive child rearing skills and experience for caregivers
• Elimination of violence against children, including GBV prevention and empowerment for girls, boys and women, prevention of violence in schools, homes and communities.
• Awareness-raising on CP risks
• Capacity development of CP responders and social workers

UNICEF will generate evidence to inform the humanitarian response and advocacy including setting up an information management system for case management. UNICEF will embrace new delivery modalities and implement cash transfers aimed at child protection outcomes for vulnerable families. UNICEF will also continue to support the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism on grave violations against children.

CP services will be delivered by partners based on minimum standards and IASC guidelines. 7,200 CP and social workers will be trained on case management, MHPSS, EORE, advocacy, evidence generation and coordination across sectors for a comprehensive CP response.
 
UNICEF will support MHPSS for 364,000 children to benefit from improved mental health and social wellbeing. UNICEF will equip 61,500 parents and caregivers with skills to provide a stimulating and safe environment at home, including reduced violence.  

Violence prevention is a key priority. Family violence prevalence is high for girls 12-17 years (47%), boys 12-17 years (44%), boys below 12 (45%) and girls below 12 (44%) (UNICEF 2018). UNICEF will work to protect children from violence and abuse through prevention activities in schools, homes and communities and providing survivors of violence with child-friendly and gender sensitive services. Support will be provided for PSEA mechanisms to protect beneficiaries and build the capacity of humanitarian actors. PSEA programming will be implemented with the Protection Sector AORs.

Based on HNO 2021, one in three communities in Syria is reportedly contaminated by explosive ordnance. One in four victims is a child (Joint MA & CP Analysis, 2020). EORE messages will be provided to 1,460,000 children and adults through humanitarian actors and public service providers using static facilities and mobile teams. UNICEF will build the capacity of partners to provide quality EORE that is age, gender and disability appropriate and to provide child victims with assistance.
 
UNICEF will strengthen the justice system to ensure that children in contact with the law victims, offenders or witnesses are protected through child-friendly, gender-sensitive services, that are community-based and family focused.

As Lead Agency for the CP AOR, UNICEF will ensure coordination needs at Hub and WOS levels. Two UN-led and one INGO-led coordination hubs in Damascus, Gaziantep and NES, as well as a WOS overall coordination system, to ensure coherence across the CP response.

---- Livelihoods and vocational training Restoring Disrupted Livelihoods and Supporting Early Recovery Efforts for Palestine Refugees in Syria Over eleven years of crisis in Syria has drastically eroded the living conditions of Palestine refugees and Syrian nationals alike. The rapid depreciation of the Syrian pound accompanied by staggering inflation levels, the impact of Lebanon's financial and banking crisis, and the tightened trade restrictions imposed on the country since June 2020, have all contributed to a worsening of the socio-economic conditions. The COVID-19 pandemic has led to additional stress on basic services that has impacted the livelihoods of Palestine refugees and Syrians. 

To support Palestine refugee youth access to employment opportunities, the UNRWA TVET programme will continue to provide short-term courses to 800 students in Damascus, Dera’a, Homs, Aleppo, Latakia, and Hama offering a variety of specializations that respond to the needs of the local market. Short-term courses (three months on average) are designed to strengthen technical skills, with minimal financial costs to the refugee students, to improve their prospects of accessing the labour market. In addition to the courses offered in the Damascus Training Centre, UNRWA will continue to expand its provision of long-term courses in its vocational training centres (VTCs) in Aleppo, Homs, Latakia and Dera’a and will introduce these in Hama in 2023. This is in response to the increasing demand of refugee youth in these areas for similar courses to those offered in Damascus and to promote equal access for all young Palestine refugees to livelihood opportunities to support their resilience. 

UNRWA will also provide employability and soft skills sessions to TVET students to encourage their confidence and abilities in approaching companies and communicating with potential future employers during job interviews. The Agency will maintain the dormitory at the Damascus Training Centre to provide a limited number of students, who live in remote locations, with accommodation to support the continuation of their TVET training. Transportation of vulnerable students will also be subsidised to mitigate the impact of the fuel crisis and associated rising transportation costs on the ability of students to access VTCs.

The various components of UNRWA's interventions in 2022-2023 will also contribute to supporting refugees who have spontaneously returned to their places of residence either internally or from other countries. Where possible, UNRWA will aim at restarting services in camps that were heavily destroyed during the conflict (Dera’a, Yarmouk and Ein el Tal) through the rehabilitation of the Agency’s installations (including schools and clinics) in these camps.

Finally, depending on the availability of funds, UNRWA will explore the feasibility of conducting small-scale cash-for-work initiatives in 2023 mainly focusing on unskilled job placements supporting UNRWA works in camps and Palestine refugee gatherings.

Facilitating the Creation of a Favourable Protection Environment in Sudan As a result of the clashes that erupted throughout the country between Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on 15 April 2023, the already fragile protection environment in Sudan has significantly deteriorated, with a multitude of protection risks that have further worsened access to services such as water, health care, electricity, and basic items and commodities such as food, cash, and fuel for millions of people. Several cities have faced heavy bombardments and clashes, and associated unexploded ordnance, causing hundreds of civilian deaths and casualties, as well as damage to critical water, health care and power infrastructure, increasing of criminal activities, with indiscriminate attacks on civilians and widespread looting. Furthermore, high insecurity and looting of humanitarian assets and offices have compromised humanitarian access to key locations. As of 21 May 2023 a total of 1,042,114 individuals (209,136 households) have been displaced across the country mostly from urban areas in affected states. Vulnerable groups are increasingly exposed to protection risks with significant harm to their physical and mental wellbeing. 
This project intends to contribute to promoting a favorable protection environment in communities particularly affected by the current crisis, while providing humanitarian assistance to individuals and groups. The proposed intervention intends to provide General, Child, and GBV related protection services in the areas of interventions with the cluster estimating 7.3 million people in need of these protection services. The project is in line with the Cluster and Sub-Cluster Objectives and will target localities across the target areas identified as “hotspots” by the Protection Cluster and partners.
IOM will improve access of vulnerable crisis-affected people, especially girls and women, to primary healthcare and protection services, including GBV response services. Also, IOM will assist conflict-affected population with the distribution of non-food items (NFIs), in coordination with the Emergency Shelter and Non-Food Items(ES/NFI) Cluster. IOM will also work towards strengthening the capacity and availability of GBV services through the training and deployment of social workers and psychologists, in addition to enhancing existing referral mechanism to address GBV and child protection issues and cases. To improve the crisis-affected people’s access to community-based dispute resolution mechanisms, IOM also will build the capacity of informal mediators and dispute resolvers. To achieve this aim, IOM will work with the existing community committees, community leaders, and representatives from other community-based organisations, including women and youth groups as well as those belonging to both farmers and herder groups. IOM staff will also contribute to “protection by presence” by collecting data on protection needs, gaps and trends for advocacy, IOM will coordinate with its other existing programming in the targeted states, such as the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) and humanitarian response and transition interventions including Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) and health activities, to leverage effective synergies between programme activities in view of delivering the best protection outcomes for affected populations. 
In coordination with the Civil Registry and UNHCR, IOM will support the local government to strengthen their capacity and resources to improve the birth registration of IDPs and service provision to persons with disabilities through the provision of office equipment, trainings, and facilitating regular visits of government staff to hard-to-reach areas to provide the services to rural communities. Finally, IOM will support the establishment and/or reactivation of women’s groups and centres in secure areas to ensure access to safe engagement platforms as well as to information on protection services.

Displacement Tracking Matrix: Mobility Tracking of IDPs, Returnees, and Other Mobile Populations in Sudan Following the crises that has affected Sudan since February 2003 and, in response to the need for accurate information on displacement and the identification of beneficiaries for the delivery of humanitarian aid, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) began its Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) program in 2004 to support the Government of Sudan (GoS) and its humanitarian partners in establishing an accurate data collection system and providing data on displacement in areas most affected by the conflict and natural disaster. DTM is a system to track and monitor displacement and population mobility. It is designed to regularly and systematically capture, process and disseminate information to provide a better understanding of the movements and evolving needs of displaced populations, whether on site or en route.
Data collection strategies and tools are based on the DTM global methodology but have been adapted to reflect context and population movements specific to Sudan. IOM has been working in close collaboration with the Humanitarian Aid Commission (HAC) and partners in the field to establish a unified and systematic method to collect individual data on internally displaced persons (IDPs) and returnees in seven states. Up until 2018, the DTM program in Sudan focused on registration, including biometric registration (since 2010), of IDPs and returnees. Registration was mostly carried out in response to requests from the government and humanitarian partners for the identification of beneficiaries and the delivery of humanitarian assistance (i.e., food vouchers by WFP), positioning DTM Sudan as the reference source of displacement data in the country. There remains a strong need to restructure the program and tailor the operation to better suit the current protracted displacement and return scenario, to in turn inform evidence-based programming by IOM and the wider humanitarian community in Sudan. Specifically, there is the need to further update displacement figures more frequently, comprehensively, systematically, and in regular intervals to ensure that data is continually collected, provides a meaningful resource, and is available through IOM’s DTM system. Since 15 April 2023, military conflict has erupted between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) across Sudan. The fighting has been centralised in Khartoum, and has also broken out across the Darfur region (including cities such as Ag Geneina, El Fasher, and Nyala), as well as in the North (Merowe) and Kordofan (El Obeid). The conflict has led to rapidly increasing civilian vulnerability, significant losses and casualties across Sudan, the destruction of key infrastructure in affected areas (such as hospitals, warehouses, and markets), and the immediate suspension of humanitarian activities, widespread looting of UN facilities, and the evacuation of international staff and foreign nationals. Despite the notable limitations to DTM's logistical operations (given the deteriorating security and economic environments) and the connectivity and telecommunication challenges, DTM has been able to maintain key data collection operations, and has provided the UN community with preliminary estimates of displacement and return. These preliminary estimations have expanded from providing initial information on incidences and mobility (locations of origin to displacement), to capturing information on shelter typology, return intentions, and priority needs. In this way, data collection activities have adapted to the current context, establishing an operational framework for the resumption of Mobility Tracking Rounds. Given the pressing emergency context presented by this military conflict, DTM is best placed to provide essential and evidence-based information about the humanitarian context. DTM forms a core component of IOM’s ongoing response to the unfolding humanitarian crisis, among IOM’s other PC1 programming, in Sudan.

All agricultural and fisheries activities will be implemented in collaboration with the State Ministry of Agriculture in order to ensure that government extension workers benefit from and also contribute to the technical components that will be offered by the project by so doing building capacities that will continue to be utilized after project closure. Ce projet propose de répondre aux besoins des ménages sinistrés à travers les requêtes qui seront exprimées par le Gouvernement au travers du Ministère de l’Action Humanitaire et de la Gestion des Catastrophes (MAH/GC). Cette réponse s’adressera uniquement aux ménages vulnérables victimes d’inondations dont les abris ou cases auront été effondrées et/ou ceux dont les Biens non-alimentaires (BNA) auront été emportés par les eaux. Le présent projet poursuit comme objectif d’atteindre 10 000 ménages soit 70 000 personnes à travers tout le Niger prioritairement dans les régions de Zinder, Diffa, Maradi et Tahoua. En coordination avec le MAH/GC et la Direction Générale de la Protection Civile (DGPC), l’OIM mettra à disposition 10 000 kits abris et 10 000 kits Biens non-alimentaires qui seront distribués aux ménages sinistrés. En plus des kits, l’OIM couvrira les coûts liés à la logistique et à la distribution des kits. Ce projet ne couvrira pas une zone ou région donnée mais permettra d’intervenir là où les besoins se présentent et aussi de pouvoir compléter les activités des autres acteurs en cas de besoin en tant que prestataire de dernier recours pour la réponse humanitaire en abri d'urgence et BNA. L’OIM en tant que Co-Lead du Groupe de Travail Abri et Bien non-alimentaire (GTABNA) avec le MAH/GC s'assurera que les activités sont menées en étroite coordination avec les autres partenaires humanitaires membres du GTABNA pour la réponse en abri et Biens non-alimentaires pour les ménages sinistrés des inondations au Niger. Conformément à la logique de la stratégie du Secteur abris/BNA et en fonction de la faisabilité, les interventions pourront se faire en transferts monétaires conditionnels. Cela réduirait considérablement les coûts logistiques qui sont très élevés en période hivernale à cause du mauvais état des routes mais aussi et permettrait aussi de résoudre en partie le problème d’accès lié à l'insécurité qui souvent retarde les interventions. Enfin, la mise en œuvre du présent projet fera l’objet d’un suivi régulier de la qualité des interventions réalisées mais aussi de l’implication des bénéficiaires et autorités locales. Pour cela, les feedbacks de la communauté cible seront collectés à travers des évaluations post-distribution et des séances de discussion de groupe séparées par genre et âge avant et après l'assistance. Aussi, en tant qu’acteur humanitaire, l'OIM et ses partenaires de mise en œuvre s’assureront que ses actions n’induisent aucune tension ou problème dans la zone et n’exposent pas les bénéficiaires. A cet effet la phase d'évaluation de besoins sera réalisée de commun accord avec les populations dans les communes ciblées, les sessions d'information sur le projet seront organisées à l'attention de communauté bénéficiaires, le mecanisme de ciblage de bénéficiaires sera réalisé en étroite collabation avec les autorités au niveau local (do no harm). Une collaboration étroite faite avec les acteurs de protection pour un suivi de près de toutes questions de protection et de LTB. Le cout total du projet sera de 6.090.000 USD.

Improving access to prevention and response protection services for 15,440 people in Monguno LGA at high risk of GBV and other types of violence, especially women and girls Multi-sectoral life-saving assistance, including life-saving GBV prevention and response services, to conflict-affected population in Pulka, Monguno and Maiduguri, Borno State, Nigeria This project’s objective is to contribute to the reduction of mortality and morbidity of the most vulnerable, IDPs and host community, including children under 5, pregnant and lactating women, adolescent girls and women of reproductive age, the elderly, and people with disabilities, in the hard-to-reach areas of Pulka and Monguno (respectively Gwoza and Monguno LGA), and in Maiduguri Metropolitan Council (MMC). To meet the most vulnerable populations’ urgent and complex needs, and ensure a long-lasting impact, integrated multi-sectoral activities in health, nutrition, protection, psychosocial support (PSS), food security, and livelihoods, will be implemented. The response will also be based on a robust community-based approach, with community activities planned for all sectors to ensure beneficiaries' and communities' ownership of the project. This comprehensive approach and the proposed activities align with all the sectors’ and HRP's priorities, including targeting hard-to-reach areas in Northeast Nigeria’s Borno State, the state most affected by the large-scale humanitarian crisis.
Premiere Urgence Internationale will continue to provide free quality life-saving healthcare services to IDPs and host community in the 9 facilities the organization already supports in Maiduguri MC, Monguno, and Pulka. These services include free outpatient consultations to all age groups and comprehensive sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRH) services. SRH activities comprise ante/postnatal care, 24 hours skilled birth delivery services, including Basic Emergency Obstetric Care (BEmONC), and Gender-based Violence (GBV) treatment with CMR (Clinical Management of Rape). 
PUI will continue to provide life-saving treatment to children under 5 suffering from Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) by supporting 4 OTPS across all three locations (one in Maiduguri’s Bollori II, two in Monguno, and one in Pulka), for treatment of SAM without medical complications, and three Stabilization Centres (SCs), one in every three locations, to provide treatment to SAM with medical complications. In case further emergencies arise, PUI plans to increase its SCs' bed capacities in Monguno and Pulka, and to establish three more OTPs. The nutrition response will include systemic identification and referrals of children suffering from SAM to PUI-supported OTPs and SCs, and awareness-raising sessions and sensitization implemented at community level.
PUI will continue to implement a range of activities to contribute to strengthening targeted protection services to address the needs and vulnerability of persons at heightened risks of violence and exploitation, with tailored responses for GBV survivors, through internal/external referrals whenever needed (i.e legal assistance). To prevent GBV and violence, awareness sessions for women and girls on their rights, as well as for community members, boys, men will be conducted. Community knowledge on protection will be strengthened, with key community stakeholders receiving training on protection issues, including GBV, mental health, PSS, to in turn support identification of cases and concerns, and ensure referrals. PUI will continue to ensure protection monitoring in the intervention areas, to ensure risk identification, referrals, concerted and tailored interventions, as well as advocacies with partners at all levels.
To promote the targeted beneficiaries' self-reliance, and reduce their dependency on humanitarian assistance, PUI will provide food assistance to 5,390 vulnerable individual beneficiaries on a monthly basis for 12 months, as food e-vouchers or e-cash. PUI will identify 700 individuals among beneficiaries of PUI Nutrition services and survivors of GBV or persons exposed to Protection risks due to their economic vulnerability. These persons will receive a training on the management of small business, and a start capital to launch an Income Generating Activity (IGA) of their choice.

Emergency Food Assistance - Venezuela Programa de seguridad alimentaria basado en la escuela  Con el objetivo de contribuir a la seguridad alimentaria de la población con mayores necesidades, el Programa Mundial de Alimentos de Naciones Unidas (WFP, por sus siglas en inglés) en Venezuela desarrolla un programa de asistencia humanitaria basado en la escuela para garantizar el acceso de los más vulnerables a una alimentación adecuada y nutritiva en el entorno escolar, familiar y comunitario. 
Este programa inició en 2021 con comidas escolares en emergencias priorizando escuelas iniciales y de educación especial.

WFP proporciona comidas escolares acompañado de un paquete integrado de intervenciones para mejorar el acceso a alimentos nutritivos y diversificados a través de las escuelas, contribuyendo al mismo tiempo a mejorar la salud y la nutrición de los niños en edad escolar, los estudiantes con discapacidad y el personal escolar, y apoyando a las comunidades a reducir la dependencia en estrategias de afrontamiento. De manera gradual, el WFP está realizando compras locales de alimentos, e incluyendo acciones para apoyar los mercados locales con compras a pequeños productores y apoyo técnico para acceso a mercados.

En este sentido, el programa de comidas escolares en emergencias tiene los siguientes componentes, para asegurar un enfoque integral que apoye al estudiante en el entorno escolar y familiar:

1. Entrega de comidas escolares nutritivas para estudiantes y personal escolar, promoviendo las compras locales y a pequeños productores.
2. Apoyo a la seguridad alimentaria del hogar.
3. Rehabilitación de cocinas escolares para garantizar condiciones adecuadas de preparación de alimentos.
4. Comunicación para sensibilizar acerca de los principios humanitarios, la adecuada preparación de alimentos, nutrición, higiene y mantenimiento de cocinas escolares.
5. Fortalecimiento de capacidades de socios implementadores y personal escolar.
6. Acciones sensibles a la nutrición, que incluyen, tamizaje en las escuelas, educación nutricional, referencia a servicios especializados y entrega de alimento complementario fortificado (Super Cereal Plus).

Rohingya Humanitarian Crisis Joint Response Plan 2023		Early Recovery	Promoting Shelter Upgrade and Community Building in Bhasan Char and Cox's Bazar District IMPROVING SKILLS AND ECONOMIC OPPORTUNITIES FOR THE BANGLADESHI COMMUNITY AND ROHINGYA WOMEN & YOUTHS IN COX'S BAZAR 							 ""IOM will undertake wide variety of activities to create an enabling environment for the Rohingya refugees towards eventual sustainable voluntary return and reintegration in Myanmar in the future when conditions may permit. Such activities will help Rohingya beneficiaries increase self-reliance skills. The livelihoods activities will also focus on the host communities affected by the influx by integrating income-generating livelihoods through support to agricultue and other sectors.
IOM will implement skills development projects to promote the economic resilience of Rohingya refugees in the camps. This training will enhance their capacity and help them utilize their skills in the camps in Bangladesh as self-reliance opportunities and can be used as transferrable skills by them upon return to Myanmar. Rohingya beneficiaries will receive skills training related and applicable to the humanitarian sector (e.g. health, wash, sanitation, site development-construction, etc.) to enable them earning income in the camps. After the end of the training IOM will facilitate in-kind asset support materials to  Rohingya beneficiaries working outside the agricultural sector who are willing to gain basic skills or competencies but lack the physical assets to do so.
IOM will provide host communities with transferable and life skills training (e.g., computer skills, communication, negotiation, psychosocial) and vocational skills training including skills related to green businesses and green financing such as plumbing, ac repair, secretary, patient administration, catering to disaster resilient off-farming tools and methods, waste recycling, electronic refurbishment, financial literacy related to resilient investments and planning, etc. The trades will be identified by thorough skills and needs assessment exercises. This training will give scope to beneficiaries in the host community for income generation. Productive asset support will be given to women beneficiaries who have technical skills but lack inputs/opportunities/assets but are willing to earn a modest income. IOM will provide small business grants through Entrepreneurship Program to the existing Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) to help beneficiaries expand and strengthen their businesses. Support will be given for the establishment of women's cooperatives (such as livestock, handicrafts, etc.,). Cash for work activities will also be included as an income-generation activity in the host community.
To enhance the private sector engagement and promote market linkages, wage subsidy opportunities for beneficiaries will be implemented. To ensure sustainable income generation, emphasis will be given to activities like product fairs for/by the beneficiaries in the host community to sell and promote their products to individuals and wholesalers.  A labour market assessment will be conducted to identify the needs of the beneficiaries based on which suitable activities will be selected. All these activities in both host, as well as refugee community, will be carried out by either implementing partners or implemented directly by IOM. IOM will ensure integration of various cross-cutting issues in the project design by identifying and including the most vulnerable beneficiaries through gender and disability-sensitive beneficiary selection criteria. The selection criteria of vulnerable women will be based on eligibility criteria such as  female-headed households, income below the poverty line, widow, etc.  IOM will also focus on disability throughout the beneficiary selection criteria and assist livelihoods and self-reliance opportunities. Women empowerment, leadership, and decision-making will be promoted by incorporating income opportunities and entrepreneurship opportunities, business development training, financial literacy, etc., for women in the Host Community and self-reliance opportunities for women in the camps to ensure sustainable development and integration into the society.

Cameroon Humanitarian Response Plan 2023
---- USA / BPRM Amélioration de la réponse multisectorielle en faveur des Réfugiés et demandeurs d’asile et mise en œuvre des solutions durables pour les réfugiés au Cameroun  Le projet a pour objectif l’amélioration de l’environnement de protection, l’accès aux solutions et voies complémentaires pour les réfugiés et demandeurs d’asile notamment en ce qui concerne  les activités d’enregistrement , de  la documentation, la protection de l’enfance, la prévention ,  la réponse aux violences sexuelles et sexistes, l’accès aux services sociaux de base (santé, éducation et eau), l’accès à un abri décent et aux biens domestiques essentiels ainsi que du  renforcement de la résilience.
Le projet cible en 2023, un total de 491,113 réfugiés au Cameroun notamment : 355,667 réfugiés RCA, 132,151 NIG, 2,533 des nationalités minoritaires, 9,239 demandeurs d’asile ainsi que 15% des populations autochtones par la présence des réfugiés dans les régions affectées.
Au cours de l’année 2021, en dépit du contexte sanitaire marquée par la survenue de la pandémie de la COVID19 qui a négativement affecté l’environnement socio-économiques des populations, la situation sécuritaire fragile en RCA et l’instabilité dans la région du bassin du Lac Chad, le HCR a initié des projets visant à améliorer l’environnement de protection des réfugiés et assurer l’accès aux solutions aux réfugiés.
Les projets déjà initiés requièrent une continuité dans la mise en œuvre afin renforcer la résilience et l’autonomisation des réfugiés de longue date, assurer leur inclusion effective dans les programmes de développement et donner accès aux solutions mais également apporter la réponse aux nouvelles situations d’urgences.
Au cours de 2023, il sera mis en œuvre par le HCR, les acteurs humanitaires et le gouvernement des activités qui garantissent l’accès équitable et la jouissance des droits humains fondamentaux aux femmes, aux hommes, aux filles et aux garçons de tout âge et ceux ayant diverses vulnérabilités.
L’UNHCR compte à travers ce projet :
-	Apporter la réponse aux besoins critiques de protection en assurant l’accès à l’asile, la documentation, la prévention et la réponse aux VBG, l’accès à l’éducation, l’accès durable aux infrastructures et services WASH, aux moyens d’existence et à l’inclusion socio-économique, ainsi que le renforcement de la cohésion sociale et de la coexistence pacifique entre les réfugiés et avec la communauté hôte.
-	Mettre en œuvre les solutions durables en renforçant la résilience des communautés affectées par les différentes crises et les moyens d’existence et explorer des opportunités viables par la mise en œuvre des alternatives aux camps notamment dans la région de l’extrême nord.
-	Le HCR continuera à faciliter le retour volontaire des réfugiés dans leur pays d’origine, à identifier les cas de réinstallation, d’importants besoins existent en termes de réfugiés pouvant potentiellement être considérés pour cette solution durable, cette dernière ne peut se réaliser que si les pays de réinstallations offrent des places. Par ailleurs, cette solution ne concerne qu’un pourcentage infime de la population réfugiée dans son ensemble. Le défi reste néanmoins la nécessité d’étendre le pool d’identification des réfugiés vers leurs zones d’installation mais avec des capacités très limitées et à faire le plaidoyer pour l’accès des réfugiés aux voies complémentaires.
-	Améliorer le bien-être socio-économique et environnemental des refugies par la promotion de l’agriculture, la pêche et l’élevage en milieu rural, par la promotion des programmes d’entrepreneuriat et de résilience à travers l’approche communautaire et par la promotion d’une approche sensible à l’environnement chez tous les acteurs et partenaires de la réponse ;
-	Améliorer la sécurité alimentaire des POCs et des communautés d’accueil à travers le Cash Based Intervention ;
-	Favoriser les partenariats, le partage de l'information et la planification conformément aux plans de développement nationaux et locaux ainsi que la stratégie régionale pour la stabilisation, le rétablissement et le développement des zones impactées par les activités de Boko Haram à l’Extrême

-	Améliorer le bien-être socio-économique et environnemental des refugies par la promotion de l’agriculture, la pêche et l’élevage en milieu rural, par la promotion des programmes d’entrepreneuriat et de résilience à travers l’approche communautaire et par la promotion d’une approche sensible à l’environnement chez tous les acteurs et partenaires de la réponse ;
-	Améliorer la sécurité alimentaire des POCs et des communautés d’accueil à travers le Cash Based Intervention ;
-	Favoriser les partenariats, le partage de l'information et la planification conformément aux plans de développement nationaux et locaux ainsi que la stratégie régionale pour la stabilisation, le rétablissement et le développement des zones impactées par les activités de Boko Haram à l’Extrême

-- protection Protection and Legal Assistance for Displacement affected populations in South Sudan The NRC seeks to improve the overall protective environment in South Sudan by not only responding to people's most immediate material needs during a crisis, but also by promoting their safety and dignity, as well as preventing, reducing, or mitigating the protection risks they face. It is also to address the root causes of displacement and to contribute to the creation of conditions conducive to long-term solutions for displaced people. To achieve the project objective, NRC will focus on three key components i.e. 1) General Protection; Housing, Land and Property; 3) Gender Based Violence. 

NRC proposes a community-based approach to displaced and conflict-affected populations protection, including static, mobile, and emergency responses.  Protection context assessments will be done in all locations, as well as, where possible, community-based protection monitoring, in which community focal points will be trained to report on protection needs and risks. Protection incidents will be documented and analyzed in order to better understand trends and evolution in the protection context, and the findings will be disseminated to communities and relevant stakeholders. 

NRC will provide at-risk populations with both awareness-raising sessions and individualized assistance in obtaining national identity documentation. Foster improved ability to exercise HLP rights for individuals and groups affected by displacement with priority given to the most vulnerable, including female and child headed households, the elderly, individuals with physical and mental disabilities, and those who are extremely poor. NRC will target conflict-affected areas and areas of potential return.

NRC will also carry out GBV prevention and risk mitigation activities in 6 counties located in hard to reach areas. Activities will include awareness raising, referrals to response services, cash assistance to GBV survivors, distribution of dignity kits and training on GBV basic concepts among others.

To achieve the main objective, the will focus on the below key activities
1) Carrying out of information and awareness raising activities; awareness will focus on GBV (GBV risks, available response services, GBV referral pathways, timely reporting), HLP (social cohesion and collaborative dispute resolution mechanisms, land rights issues) and general protection (protection risks, available services)
2) Provision of cash assistance (individual protection assistance) to persons at GBV survivors and other persons at heightened risks including referral of GBV survivors for response services
3) Training frontline workers and community focal points on basic GBV concepts, GBV guiding principles and responses services.
4) Training of state-level authorities, community leaders and representative on HLP, alternative dispute resolution
5) Facilitating peaceful coexistence and inclusive resolutions of local conflict through training and mentoring the local community in collaborative dispute resolution (CDR) mechanisms
6) Distribute dignity kits to women and adolescent girls.
7) Provision of legal aid and counselling

South Sudan - Food and Nutrition Assistance to Crisis-Affected Populations - 2023
--- FOOD SECURITY Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM). WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.
Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (light resilience- building activities, peace/conflict resolution training also called GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness, training, or sensitisation on peaceful resolution of conflicts, mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace. 
Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities.

South Sudan Humanitarian Response Plan 2023 Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2022, there are some 335,000 refugees and asylum seekers from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, primarily from Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic.
At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for longer term stability, hundreds of thousands of South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since the signing of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan, this spontaneous movement has prompted the development of an area-based approach, to support refugees, returnees and host communities, through enhanced engagement with development actors, to support greater access to services where possible.
Refugees largely reside in conflict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction in basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.
Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will benefit from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Specific protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identified at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with specific protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as verification exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the efficiency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to benefit from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.
