Strengthening lifesaving nutrition services in Pulka, Gwoza LGA, Borno State, Northeast Nigeria Multi-sectoral life-saving assistance, including life-saving GBV prevention and response services, to conflict-affected population in Pulka, Monguno and Maiduguri, Borno State, Nigeria This project’s objective is to contribute to the reduction of mortality and morbidity of the most vulnerable, IDPs and host community, including children under 5, pregnant and lactating women, adolescent girls and women of reproductive age, the elderly, and people with disabilities, in the hard-to-reach areas of Pulka and Monguno (respectively Gwoza and Monguno LGA), and in Maiduguri Metropolitan Council (MMC). To meet the most vulnerable populations’ urgent and complex needs, and ensure a long-lasting impact, integrated multi-sectoral activities in health, nutrition, protection, psychosocial support (PSS), food security, and livelihoods, will be implemented. The response will also be based on a robust community-based approach, with community activities planned for all sectors to ensure beneficiaries' and communities' ownership of the project. This comprehensive approach and the proposed activities align with all the sectors’ and HRP's priorities, including targeting hard-to-reach areas in Northeast Nigeria’s Borno State, the state most affected by the large-scale humanitarian crisis.
Premiere Urgence Internationale will continue to provide free quality life-saving healthcare services to IDPs and host community in the 9 facilities the organization already supports in Maiduguri MC, Monguno, and Pulka. These services include free outpatient consultations to all age groups and comprehensive sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRH) services. SRH activities comprise ante/postnatal care, 24 hours skilled birth delivery services, including Basic Emergency Obstetric Care (BEmONC), and Gender-based Violence (GBV) treatment with CMR (Clinical Management of Rape). 
PUI will continue to provide life-saving treatment to children under 5 suffering from Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) by supporting 4 OTPS across all three locations (one in Maiduguri’s Bollori II, two in Monguno, and one in Pulka), for treatment of SAM without medical complications, and three Stabilization Centres (SCs), one in every three locations, to provide treatment to SAM with medical complications. In case further emergencies arise, PUI plans to increase its SCs' bed capacities in Monguno and Pulka, and to establish three more OTPs. The nutrition response will include systemic identification and referrals of children suffering from SAM to PUI-supported OTPs and SCs, and awareness-raising sessions and sensitization implemented at community level.
PUI will continue to implement a range of activities to contribute to strengthening targeted protection services to address the needs and vulnerability of persons at heightened risks of violence and exploitation, with tailored responses for GBV survivors, through internal/external referrals whenever needed (i.e legal assistance). To prevent GBV and violence, awareness sessions for women and girls on their rights, as well as for community members, boys, men will be conducted. Community knowledge on protection will be strengthened, with key community stakeholders receiving training on protection issues, including GBV, mental health, PSS, to in turn support identification of cases and concerns, and ensure referrals. PUI will continue to ensure protection monitoring in the intervention areas, to ensure risk identification, referrals, concerted and tailored interventions, as well as advocacies with partners at all levels.
To promote the targeted beneficiaries' self-reliance, and reduce their dependency on humanitarian assistance, PUI will provide food assistance to 5,390 vulnerable individual beneficiaries on a monthly basis for 12 months, as food e-vouchers or e-cash. PUI will identify 700 individuals among beneficiaries of PUI Nutrition services and survivors of GBV or persons exposed to Protection risks due to their economic vulnerability. These persons will receive a training on the management of small business, and a start capital to launch an Income Generating Activity (IGA) of their choice.

Humanitarian initial allocation 2023 Improving the nutrition security of Lebanese and migrant caregivers and young children through provision nutrition services that are both preventive and manage undernutrition This project aims to address the increasing nutrition insecurity conditions in the country, in particular those affecting the most vulnerable Lebanese and migrant communities. The response of Action Against Hunger (AAH under the Nutrition Sector Response is divided into interventions that cover both prevention and management of malnutrition. In order to ensure that services aiming to prevent and manage malnutrition complement each other, the response entails improving promotion, protect and support for appropriate infant and young child feeding (IYCF) practices to pregnant women and caregivers of children 0-2 years of age and improve timely detection of malnutrition and appropriate management of malnutrition, especially wasting, the most dangerous form of malnutrition. AAH will complement this support to the most vulnerable households, based on in-depth assessments, with multi-purpose cash assistance under its Food Security Response, especially households with women who are pregnant and breastfeeding and children under the age of 5 years. AAH will also dedicate efforts to ensure that multi-sectoral needs expressed by targeted communities are actively referred and followed up, especially that impact on nutrition outcomes are amplified when WASH, food security, protection, GBV, health, including mental health, are simultaneously addressed. Interventions under this program will target communities in Beirut, Bekaa, and South governorates, though it is important to note that not all interventions included here below will be implemented in all 3 governorates concomitantly, but depending on the needs, context, as well as AAH's capacity.

Overall, 2885 caregivers and 3875 children aged 0-59m will be targeted, inclusive of LHF activities. As AAH is mainly targeting migrants only in Beirut a maximum of 5% of the targets will be dedicated to support migrant communities.

To address malnutrition AAH implements interventions that it has experience with and are evidence-based, by prioritizing pregnant and lactating women (PLWs) and caregivers of young children with IYCF, health and hygiene promotion and counseling, both one-on-one and in groups, in health facilities and household level, including community mobilization. Another aspect of address malnutrition is timely detection of cases. For this reason, community mobilizers will be trained and supervised to conduct community level screening of wasting of children aged 6-59 months through MUAC (mid-upper arm circumference) screening. Caregivers with children aged 6-59 months will also be trained on the Family MUAC approach, so that they themselves can conduct screening on their own children on a regular basis. Included in this approach caregivers will also be supported to seek timely treatment in the nearest treatment center. Children aged 6-59 months will also receive micronutrient supplements to mitigate the risks associated with inadequate dietary intake. In parallel, AAH staff and stakeholders, including health facilities, will be supported to create and maintain enabling environments that protect, promote and support breastfeeding and optimal feeding practices. This includes training on the evidence based IYCF principles as recommended by WHO, MoPH, nutrition sector, IYCF committee etc. and oriented on the implementation of Law 47/2008 that adopts all the provisions of the International Code of Marketing of Breastmilk Substitutes. Health facilities will also be supported to create safe, private spaces to support breastfeeding. 
All interventions prioritized by AAH are in line with the ERP's Nutrition Sector's response.

Additionally, AAH plans to conduct a nutrition survey at governorate level, in line with the SMART methodology to be able to update the specific nutrition needs in AAH areas of interventions, especially in Baalbek-Hermel, where this project is targeted.

UNICEF’s CP Strategy in 2022-2023 includes:
• Addressing behavioural, social, cultural and economic determinants of CP violations as a prevention approach.  
• Improving the reach and quality of specialized CP services
• Capacity development of CP responders
•  Monitoring, evidence generation and advocacy 

UNICEF will support the delivery of integrated programming that will encourage social transformation, prioritizing:
• Structured and sustained CP MHPSS and EORE programmes
• Specialized integrated CP services including case management for survivors of violence, exploitation, neglect and abuse (child labour, CAFAAG, child survivors of GBV, child marriages, justice for children, birth registration and unaccompanied or separated children amongst others) 
• Parenting programmes to promote positive child rearing skills and experience for caregivers
• Elimination of violence against children, including GBV prevention and empowerment for girls, boys and women, prevention of violence in schools, homes and communities.
• Awareness-raising on CP risks
• Capacity development of CP responders and social workers

UNICEF will generate evidence to inform the humanitarian response and advocacy including setting up an information management system for case management. UNICEF will embrace new delivery modalities and implement cash transfers aimed at child protection outcomes for vulnerable families. UNICEF will also continue to support the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism on grave violations against children.

CP services will be delivered by partners based on minimum standards and IASC guidelines. 7,200 CP and social workers will be trained on case management, MHPSS, EORE, advocacy, evidence generation and coordination across sectors for a comprehensive CP response.

Improve food security and build resilience to seasonal climatic shocks for communities living in cattle camps Improved food security and livelihoods of IDPs, Returnees and Vulnerable host communities in South Sudan The purpose of the project is to improve food consumption, food security, dietary diversity and coping strategies and enhance emergency food production of vulnerable populations in the targeted counties. This will be achieved through provision of Cash-Based Transfers (CBT) to address food needs of vulnerable communities during the lean season and provision of timely and appropriate complementary vegetable and crop livelihood inputs and fishing kits coupled with training in improved agronomic and fishing practices.
In line with the South Sudan FSL cluster HRP objectives and priorities, NPA will support vulnerable populations in IPC 4 and 5 locations as well as some IPC 3 locations. Specifically, NPA will target Canal/Pigi, Fangak, Pochalla and Bor South Counties of Jonglei State, Rumbek East, Rumbek Centre, Cueibet, Yirol East, Yirol West and Awerial Counties of Lakes State, Terekeka County of Central Equatoria State and Kapoeta North County of Eastern Equatoria State.

NPA seeks to support 86,200 HHs (517,200 individuals) through provision of complementary vegetable and crop livelihood inputs and fishing kits across the target counties. Some of the kits will be provided by FAO (core pipeline) while the rest will be procured and distributed directly by NPA to enhance food production.  NPA will build the capacity of the HHs supported with the kits through training on improved agronomic and fishing practices, marketing and group dynamics. A Training of Trainers (ToT) approach will be utilized whereby lead farmers and fisher folk will be trained by NPA. They will then train/share the knowledge and skills with other farmers and fisher folk in their communities. The kits provided through this project and the knowledge gained from the trainings is expected to improve the agricultural and fishing practices of the target HHs thus enhancing and sustaining food production. CBT interventions will target 1,000 HHs (6,000 individuals ) in Rumbek East, Rumbek Centre and Cuiebet Counties in Lakes State to improve their access to food, diversify and improve their food consumption and dietary diversity scores and promote the adoption of positive coping strategies. The planned interventions are aligned to the FSL cluster objectives 1 and 2 and will provide emergency assistance and livelihoods support to save lives and avert total collapse of livelihoods in the target counties.

NPA will integrate development-oriented and conflict-sensitivity activities in this project to enhance the resilience of  vulnerable HHs in line with the Triple Nexus. Therefore, 1,200 vulnerable HHs will be supported with small-scale cash grants to establish IGAs. The target HHs will be mobilized and sensitized to transition to and establish VSLA’s to ease access to financial services and encourage the spirit of saving among the VSLA group members. The IGAs will contribute to increasing and diversifying income and building the resilience of the target HHs at the same time improving functionality of local markets and boosting the local value chains.

NPA will employ a community-based beneficiary selection approach which will entail establishing Project Management Committees (PMCs) to lead the selection of eligible beneficiaries based on the beneficiary selection criteria. Vulnerable HHs with severe food insecurity including female, child, disabled/chronically ill headed HHs; persons living with or at risk of HIV/AIDS and the elderly will be targeted in this project. 
NPA will ensure meaningful engagement of the target communities throughout the project life-cycle through holding regular meetings with the PMCs and community members and Post Distribution Monitoring (PDM) to get their feedback on the project. NPA will ensure that the feedback is incorporated in the implementation of this project and design of future projects. Further, NPA will use a community-based complaints and feedback mechanism to provide a platform for beneficiaries to voice any issues or concerns.

NPA will integrate development-oriented and conflict-sensitivity activities in this project to enhance the resilience of  vulnerable HHs in line with the Triple Nexus. The target HHs will be mobilized and sensitized to transition to and establish VSLA’s to ease access to financial services and encourage the spirit of saving among the VSLA group members. The IGAs will contribute to increasing and diversifying income and building the resilience of the target HHs at the same time improving functionality of local markets and boosting the local value chains.

NPA will employ a community-based beneficiary selection approach which will entail establishing Project Management Committees (PMCs) to lead the selection of eligible beneficiaries based on the beneficiary selection criteria. NPA will ensure that the feedback is incorporated in the implementation of this project and design of future projects. Further, NPA will use a community-based complaints and feedback mechanism to provide a platform for beneficiaries to voice any issues or concerns.

Protection	Pillar I - Provision of Gender-Based Violence (GBV) Prevention and Response Services, for Vulnerable Populations in Wadi Khaled and Jezzine. Protection Response for Vulnerable Lebanese and Other Resident Populations According to OCHA, approximately 393,000 people across 26 districts are in need of GBV services in 2022, a significant increase from 67,000 people in need in the 2021 ERP. Around a quarter of Lebanese households reported having safety and security concerns for women in their community (OCHA, 2022). The GBVIMS shows that in the last quarter of 2022, the most common types of GBV incidents were physical assault and emotional abuse mostly happening in the context of intimate partner violence, followed by forced marriage. Protection risks for all targeted populations remains high, with women and girls facing significant risks of multiple forms of GBV. The economic insecurity combined with different levels of crisis affecting the country as well as risks related to legal status, add to these vulnerabilities. Shortage in electricity and increased transportation and telecom prices all act as contributing factors to different forms of GBV in all locations. Sexual harassment through online platform and cyber abuse is an emerging GBV trend. Another alarming trend is the increased rates of sexual exploitation by landlords and employers especially affecting female heads of households with financial vulnerability.  Preventing, mitigating, and responding to GBV in emergencies is a lifesaving priority and an essential component of humanitarian action, especially in a country with extreme structural gender inequalities. 

The below proposed activities focus on survivor-centered care with case management teams working to meet the immediate, lifesaving needs of women and girls while laying the groundwork for survivors of GBV, their families and their communities to recover. Under the GBV prevention component, the project will be providing dignity kits to 3000 beneficiaries and awareness raising sessions to 2500 non-unique beneficiaries. There will be an overlap of beneficiaries attending awareness sessions and receiving dignity kits. Also, 120 men will receive men engagement activities (Cycle of Violence), and those are already counted under the awareness sessions target. The COV is composed of three sessions including: Life and daily stressors, Violence and How to deal with stressors. 
Aim of the sessions:
 During the dire economic situation in the country, the team will look at the effects of the family on this period, and its goal is the ability to mitigate its effects on both, society and family. 
 In the three sessions, the team will discuss together with the men about the stress and frustrations of the situation as well its effects on the family members and their reactions towards it in a positive or negative way.
Under the GBV response component, IMC will be providing focused PSS groups for 300 beneficiaries as well as GBV case management (including emergency cash assistance). IMC will also provide non-focused PSS for 500 unique beneficiaries (which overlap with the focused PSS activities as well as the dignity kits beneficiaries). IMC will provide the services in three safe spaces in Akkar, Beirut and South. GBV department is well established in these areas with well-trained case workers and social workers.

Based on IMC’s presence in the different areas proposed under this project, the objectives of the ERP directly address the needs of the communities especially vulnerable women and girls. IMC will organize empowerment activities for women and girls and will engage with men as allies to prevent GBV. IMC will coordinate with local actors, authorities, and other sectors to strengthen GBV prevention and response and will continue working with communities to shift social norms that contribute to GBV and threaten the protection and wellbeing of women and children.

Lebanon: Contribution to the implementation of the Lebanon Integrated Micronutri	Nutrition	UN TO UN WITH WFP Provision of emergency nutrition services and support optimum early childhood development to crisis affected pregnant and lactating women and children aged below 5 years among vulnerable Lebanese and migrants in Lebanon. With Growing triple burden of malnutrition (undernutrition, both stunting and wasting; deficiencies in vitamins and other micronutrients; and overweight and obesity) among women, children and adolescents which affects health, growth and development. 
70% of young children are not exclusively breastfed; 90% of children aged 6-23 months lack dietary diversity and meal frequency; over 40% of all women and children, including Lebanese, are affected by anaemia. In October 2021, 53% of children skipped a meal due to insufficient food in the house, up from 37% just 6 months before. 453,000 Lebanese women and children need urgent nutritional support.
Nutrition and child development should be prioritized as part of the emergency response plan, hence UNICEF will be working under the ERP appeal through a multi-system approach from food, health, social protection, education and water and sanitation systems to protect and promote adequate diets, practices and services to prevent all forms of malnutrition among children and women and support optimum early childhood development. In 2021, the percentage of childcare service providers encountering families with payment difficulties has doubled, reaching 41%.  Additionally, due to the local currency devaluation and the significant increase in fuel prices, the monthly fees per child are no longer sufficient to cover the operational expenses of childcare providers. Therefore, to remain affordable, childcare providers are often constrained to compromise on quality which can negatively affect the healthy development of children, while children in rural areas, camps or informal settlements have little access to ECD.
Building on this momentum of a strengthened enabling environment for nutrition and child development, UNICEF will work with the government and partners to reach the most vulnerable children and women with an essential service package for prevention, early detection, referral, and management of all forms of malnutrition and development delays. Maternal and child nutrition during the first 1,000 days coupled with a nurturing care framework – from conception to age 2 years – remains core to the response.
This will be done by strengthening national capacity across multiple sectors and systems through better evidence, policies, and facility and community-based solutions and programmes.

Niger:  Prevención y el tratamiento de la desnutrición infantil grave	Nutrition Renforcement de la prise en charge et la prévention de la malnutrition aiguë sévère chez les enfants âgés de 0 à 59 mois Les interventions de l’UNICEF dans le cadre de la réponse Humanitaire 2023 vont cibler les objectifs suivants :  1) le renforcement de la coordination au niveau central et décentralisé ; 2) le renforcement des capacités des acteurs à tous les niveaux pour la préparation et la réponse aux urgences, la dépistage précoce, le référencement et la prise en charge des enfants souffrant de la malnutrition aiguë sévère (y compris les approches simplifiées, les cliniques mobiles et l’approche Surge) et la promotion de l’ANJE dans le contexte d’urgence; 3) le renforcement de de la chaine d'approvisionnement en intrants nutritionnels (aliments thérapeutiques prêts à l'emploi (ATPE), laits thérapeutiques),  les médicaments pour le traitement systématique et spécifique, les équipements et le matériels anthropométriques ; 4) L’appui au fonctionnement du système d’information sanitaire (DHIS 2) ainsi que le suivi et la supervision de la mise en œuvre des interventions.
L’UNICEF dans le cadre de la multisectorialité travaillera en étroite collaboration avec les autres secteurs notamment la Santé, la Sécurité Alimentaire/Moyens d’Existence, la Protection, l’Eau/ L’Hygiène/l’Assainissement pour une meilleure synergie des interventions et un plus grand impact sur les bénéficiaires.  Cette synergie avec les autres secteurs visera à réduire la survenue des cas de malnutrition aiguë sévère dans les communautés avec un focus sur la prévention et une prise en charge adéquate des cas de malnutrition aiguë sévère.
L’engagement Communautaire sera la clé de voûte de la stratégie de prévention a travers l’implication de la communauté dans la préparation, la mise en œuvre et le suivi des interventions dans la communauté.
Les ménages seront impliqués dans la détection précoce des enfants malnutris à travers l’approche PB/Famille et seront sensibilisés pour la conduite à tenir en cas d’identification d’enfants malnutris aiguë. Les Agents de Sante communautaire seront egalement impliques dans la mises en oeuvre des activites de prevention pour le changement de comportement dans les communautés.

Annual Programme 2023 Renforcement de l'environnement protecteur des personnes vulnérables affectées par les conflits au Niger Afin de répondre aux besoins de protection des personnes vulnérables affectées par les conflits et de les renforcer dans leurs droits, DRC identifie des cas de protection et leur apporte une première assistance psychologique (Premiers Secours Psychologiques - PSP). Ces référencement sont effectués soit vers des structures externes (ex: services techniques déconcentrés, ONG locales, ONG internationales), soit en interne, vers d'autres départements d'intervention de DRC (par exemple, le département Sécurité Alimentaire et Relèvement Économique). DRC contribue par ailleurs aux renforcements des capacités des structures communautaires (conformément à l'approche de protection communautaire), et collabore avec elles afin de mieux connaitre en temps réels les tendances de protection (risques, besoins, etc.),  dans le cadre du monitoring de protection. 

La stratégie d'intervention de DRC dans le secteur de la protection se base sur l'approche vulnérabilité, en ce qu'elle vise à fournir une assistance adaptée à toutes les personnes vulnérables affectées par les conflits (PDI, communautés hôtes, réfugiés),  adaptée à leurs besoins spécifiques  liés à leur âge, leur genre et leurs vulnérabiltités propres (enfants,  personnes âgées, Femmes Enceintes et Femmes Allaitantes - FEFA, personnes en situation de handicap, etc.). Chad - OCHA Office [Donor:O543, Recipient:O270] Renforcement de la coordination et du plaidoyer humanitaire au Tchad Le projet vise à renforcer le rôle de OCHA dans la mise en œuvre de son mandat et son rôle auprès des partenaires humanitaires et gouvernementaux au niveau des fonctions coordination, gestion de l’information et plaidoyer. Le bureau national d’OCHA à N’Djaména et ses trois sous-bureaux régionaux à l’Est (Abéché) au Sud (Goré) et la province du Lac (Baga Sola) mettent l’accent sur l’opérationnalisation de ses fonctions y compris en assurant un lien entre les activités humanitaires et de développement (nexus) en vue de promouvoir une solution durable visant à ne pas perpétuer une situation de dépendance humanitaire. Dans le cadre de cette nouvelle façon de travailler outre l’opérationnalisation du nexus, le lien avec les objectifs commun des programmes développement, paix et sécurité sera mis en avant. L’accent est aussi mis sur le renforcement de la coordination civilo-militaire afin de faciliter l’accès et la protection des civils.
Le projet a pour but de renforcer la coordination d’une réponse humanitaire rapide et efficace afin de sauver des vies et protéger les personnes affectées par les situations de crises au Tchad. Une coordination humanitaire rapide et correctement évaluée au niveau des besoins de la population affectée permettra aux acteurs humanitaires de mieux identifier et répondre aux besoins humanitaires, de renforcer la préparation de réponse aux urgences à travers le renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et plus spécifiquement l‘Equipe humanitaire pays, la coordination inter-clusters, la coordination civilo-militaire, les clusters, des groupes de travail et les mécanismes de coordination au niveau de terrain.
Le projet vise aussi à assurer le plaidoyer humanitaire à travers l’analyse des besoins faites par l’ensemble de la communauté humanitaire et ses partenaires en vue une compréhension commune des problématiques auxquels fait face le Tchad, ses causes profondes, l’impact sur les populations. OCHA jouera un rôle clé dans la création d'espaces de collection et d'analyse et gestion d’informations, pour assurer une stratégie de réponse coordonnée menant à des actions humanitaires répondant aux besoins les plus aigus et être mieux préparé face aux urgences soudaines. Le projet permettra également d’assurer conjointement avec la communauté humanitaire le plaidoyer en faveur du respect des principes humanitaires, de la protection des civils, de l'accès humanitaire et pour la mobilisation et l'allocation efficace de ressources humanitaires.
Un accent a été mis sur la mise en œuvre des plans d’action de la redevabilité envers les populations affectées (AAP), la PSEA et la préparation aux urgences en plus d'intégrer une attention au genre et de renforcer la centralité de la protection.
Un plaidoyer pour plus de visibilité des résultats tangibles au niveau de la réponse facilitant la mobilisation de ressources pour les différentes crises au Tchad (mouvement de population – crise du Bassin du Lac Tchad, insécurité alimentaire et malnutrition, urgences sanitaires, catastrophes naturelles) est aussi défini comme une priorité dans ce projet.
OCHA continuera de jouer également un rôle moteur dans le renforcement du lien entre les acteurs humanitaires et de développement et la transformation de la réponse humanitaire, en lien avec les engagements pris au Sommet humanitaire mondial de 2016 et ceci à travers la nouvelle façon de travailler (NWOW) et le renforcement de l’utilisation de la modalité de transfert monétaire.

South Sudan. Humanitarian Response	Humanitarian response in South Sudan. Quality Education for Emergency Affected Children and Youth in South Sudan. The overall objective of the intervention is to ensure that emergency affected girls and boys as well as youth continually access quality learning opportunities relevant for their psycho-social well-being, physical and cognitive development.  The project targets children and youth aged between 6 - 17  from IDP, returnees and host community families with age appropriate interventions that respond to their education needs. Primary focus for this project is displacement affected out-of-school children and youth affected by conflict and climate emergencies. NRC anticipates to reach 38,873 children (52% girls); 875 adults (400 men ; 475 women [375 teachers & 500 parents/caregivers and other non-teaching professionals) as direct beneficiaries. The project will focus on strengthening and improving quality and delivery of education in four strategic response areas which are 1) First Phase response - through NRC's mobile response operations and targeting newly displaced families, with short term education activities lasting from 6-9 months. 2) Formal education - conducted through NRC's static program operations across the country in prioritized counties where NRC has existing physical presence; 3) Non Formal education through ALP classes for over-aged children who missed years of schooling due to conflict and displacement and 4) Youth Education and training with an emphasis on vocational skills training, peace-building and life-skills training.  In close collaboration with parents, caregivers and local actors, NRC will construct and repair learning spaces/classrooms and gender segregated school WASH facilities; provide school hardware assets (desks/benches), essential learning materials, teacher aids, recreational & hygiene kits; girls dignity kits for MHM; support mgt of schools through teacher selection, recruitment, motivation, training on child centered pedagogical methods, curriculum planning, classroom mgt & conflict sensitive education; support teacher learning cycles (TLCs) for continuous professional dvpt; facilitate community engagement in education through establishment/strengthening of PTAs & SMCs through training in roles and responsibilities, school development planning and awarding school improvement grants; conduct awareness raising community dialogue sessions to mobilize enrollment, promote attendance and support retention especially for girls who face multiple barriers to education including harmful and social practices such as forced early marriages and boys who also face protection risks that include child labour and forced recruitment into armed groups; conduct life skills training & support structured recreational activities for physical and psycho-social development; provide technical and material support non-teaching professionals (county education directors,  supervisors) to effectively conduct their school supervision and support duties; training of teachers, facilitators, on Mental Health and psycho-social support (MHPSS), Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR), child protection, child safeguarding and PSEA; provide cash and vouchers assistance to the most vulnerable for examination registration. 
Key approaches that NRC will adopt in this project include integration, partnerships and community based programming.  NRC will collaborate local structures as well as with other clusters including protection, WASH, shelter, LFS, Nutrition and Health to deliver comprehensive package that addresses the holistic needs of targeted population. Furthermore, for durable solutions, NRC will work with local actors, parents and care-givers building their capacity for self reliance and also to increase coverage in hard to reach areas  with periodic access challenges and bureaucratic impediments. For effective and efficient use of resources and for learning purposes, NRC will continue to participate in coordination mechanisms at both the national and sub-national levels to avoid overlaps and duplication with other education players.

Food Assistance Programme Programa de seguridad alimentaria basado en la escuela  Con el objetivo de contribuir a la seguridad alimentaria de la población con mayores necesidades, el Programa Mundial de Alimentos de Naciones Unidas (WFP, por sus siglas en inglés) en Venezuela desarrolla un programa de asistencia humanitaria basado en la escuela para garantizar el acceso de los más vulnerables a una alimentación adecuada y nutritiva en el entorno escolar, familiar y comunitario. 
Este programa inició en 2021 con comidas escolares en emergencias priorizando escuelas iniciales y de educación especial.

WFP proporciona comidas escolares acompañado de un paquete integrado de intervenciones para mejorar el acceso a alimentos nutritivos y diversificados a través de las escuelas, contribuyendo al mismo tiempo a mejorar la salud y la nutrición de los niños en edad escolar, los estudiantes con discapacidad y el personal escolar, y apoyando a las comunidades a reducir la dependencia en estrategias de afrontamiento. De manera gradual, el WFP está realizando compras locales de alimentos, e incluyendo acciones para apoyar los mercados locales con compras a pequeños productores y apoyo técnico para acceso a mercados.

En este sentido, el programa de comidas escolares en emergencias tiene los siguientes componentes, para asegurar un enfoque integral que apoye al estudiante en el entorno escolar y familiar:

1. Entrega de comidas escolares nutritivas para estudiantes y personal escolar, promoviendo las compras locales y a pequeños productores.
2. Apoyo a la seguridad alimentaria del hogar.
3. Rehabilitación de cocinas escolares para garantizar condiciones adecuadas de preparación de alimentos.
4. Comunicación para sensibilizar acerca de los principios humanitarios, la adecuada preparación de alimentos, nutrición, higiene y mantenimiento de cocinas escolares.
5. Fortalecimiento de capacidades de socios implementadores y personal escolar.
6. Acciones sensibles a la nutrición, que incluyen, tamizaje en las escuelas, educación nutricional, referencia a servicios especializados y entrega de alimento complementario fortificado (Super Cereal Plus).

Food Security and Livelihoods - Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM). WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.
Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (light resilience- building activities, peace/conflict resolution training also called GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness, training, or sensitisation on peaceful resolution of conflicts, mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace. 
Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities.

CP & GBV & PSEA Integrated psychosocial support and child protection services for the most affected boys and girls in the Gaza Strip Strip This project will support the delivery of quality, integrated child protection and psychosocial support (PSS) services to the most vulnerable boys and girls aged 6-18 in the Gaza Strip, especially those affected by the 2021/2022 escalations. The escalation has affected all aspects of life in the Gaza Strip, including child protection needs and services.

The project will ensure that 12 family centres and 30 outreach sites in Gaza are fully operational, responding to the pressing mental health and psychosocial and child protection needs of 11,900 children (50% girls) and 4,300 caregivers (20% males). Additionally, 9,900 children and adults will be reached with Explosive Remnants of War (ERW) awareness messages, while 300 non-child protection professionals and community members will benefit from training and coaching opportunities on child protection, detection, identification and referral. 

Service delivery will be directed to the most affected locations and the most vulnerable children through a coordinated continuum of services in Gaza. Each family centre will be connected to a community-based child protection committee that identify the child protection concerns and refer identified children to the family centre within that community. Family centres will operate through established Community-Based Organisations (CBOs) and outreach sites and will assess/screen and refer children for further specialised services through:
1) a case management approach for the most affected;
2) referral of severe and complicated child protection cases to child protection services (managed by relevant stakeholders and Civil Society Organizations (CSOs); and
3) referral of children with further psychosocial support needs to more specialized psychological support services.

Services will also strengthen outreach capacities to detect and link children in need with service providers while providing mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) through the family centres. A total of 11,900 children (50% girls) and 4,300 caregivers (20% males), as well as 300 community members will be reached through the project.

This project aligns with and contributes to the Protection Cluster Objective no. 2, which calls for putting in place protection response mechanisms to prevent and mitigate occupation and conflict-related violence.

Ensuring compliance with the Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) principles and procedures, project beneficiaries will be oriented on prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse. They will receive information on UNICEF and other interagency channels, including SAWA Free toll number, social media platforms, and WhatsApp to report on PSEA.

At least 70% of the project budget will support the two project implementing partners to ensure that timely services are provided to children with protection and MHPSS needs. The funds will be transferred in line with UNICEF Harmonised Approach to Cash Transfer (HACT), which ensures close follow-up on expenditures. Partners are normally micro-assessed and spot checks are regularly conducted to ensure compliance with UNICEF regulations.

Child Protection Strengthening Child Protection interventions for girls and boys most at risk of violence, abuse, neglect and exploitation across whole of Syria In line with the CP Area of Responsibility (AOR) Strategy and the “No Lost Generation” framework, UNICEF will enhance equitable access to quality CP services with a resilience focus, including for Survivors of abuse, violence, neglect and exploitation as well as children with disabilities, targeting 117 high severity sub-districts (3 to 5) and 38 low severity ones.

UNICEF’s CP Strategy in 2022-2023 includes:
• Addressing behavioural, social, cultural and economic determinants of CP violations as a prevention approach.  
• Improving the reach and quality of specialized CP services
• Capacity development of CP responders
•  Monitoring, evidence generation and advocacy 

UNICEF will support the delivery of integrated programming that will encourage social transformation, prioritizing:
• Structured and sustained CP MHPSS and EORE programmes
• Specialized integrated CP services including case management for survivors of violence, exploitation, neglect and abuse (child labour, CAFAAG, child survivors of GBV, child marriages, justice for children, birth registration and unaccompanied or separated children amongst others) 
• Parenting programmes to promote positive child rearing skills and experience for caregivers
• Elimination of violence against children, including GBV prevention and empowerment for girls, boys and women, prevention of violence in schools, homes and communities.
• Awareness-raising on CP risks
• Capacity development of CP responders and social workers

UNICEF will generate evidence to inform the humanitarian response and advocacy including setting up an information management system for case management. UNICEF will embrace new delivery modalities and implement cash transfers aimed at child protection outcomes for vulnerable families. UNICEF will also continue to support the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism on grave violations against children.

CP services will be delivered by partners based on minimum standards and IASC guidelines. 7,200 CP and social workers will be trained on case management, MHPSS, EORE, advocacy, evidence generation and coordination across sectors for a comprehensive CP response.
 
UNICEF will support MHPSS for 364,000 children to benefit from improved mental health and social wellbeing. UNICEF will equip 61,500 parents and caregivers with skills to provide a stimulating and safe environment at home, including reduced violence.  

Violence prevention is a key priority. Family violence prevalence is high for girls 12-17 years (47%), boys 12-17 years (44%), boys below 12 (45%) and girls below 12 (44%) (UNICEF 2018). UNICEF will work to protect children from violence and abuse through prevention activities in schools, homes and communities and providing survivors of violence with child-friendly and gender sensitive services. Support will be provided for PSEA mechanisms to protect beneficiaries and build the capacity of humanitarian actors. PSEA programming will be implemented with the Protection Sector AORs.

Based on HNO 2021, one in three communities in Syria is reportedly contaminated by explosive ordnance. One in four victims is a child (Joint MA & CP Analysis, 2020). EORE messages will be provided to 1,460,000 children and adults through humanitarian actors and public service providers using static facilities and mobile teams. UNICEF will build the capacity of partners to provide quality EORE that is age, gender and disability appropriate and to provide child victims with assistance.
 
UNICEF will strengthen the justice system to ensure that children in contact with the law victims, offenders or witnesses are protected through child-friendly, gender-sensitive services, that are community-based and family focused.

As Lead Agency for the CP AOR, UNICEF will ensure coordination needs at Hub and WOS levels. Two UN-led and one INGO-led coordination hubs in Damascus, Gaziantep and NES, as well as a WOS overall coordination system, to ensure coherence across the CP response.

United States (USAID-BHA) Contribution to OCHA 2023 Renforcement de la coordination et du plaidoyer humanitaire au Tchad Le projet vise à renforcer le rôle de OCHA dans la mise en œuvre de son mandat et son rôle auprès des partenaires humanitaires et gouvernementaux au niveau des fonctions coordination, gestion de l’information et plaidoyer. Le bureau national d’OCHA à N’Djaména et ses trois sous-bureaux régionaux à l’Est (Abéché) au Sud (Goré) et la province du Lac (Baga Sola) mettent l’accent sur l’opérationnalisation de ses fonctions y compris en assurant un lien entre les activités humanitaires et de développement (nexus) en vue de promouvoir une solution durable visant à ne pas perpétuer une situation de dépendance humanitaire. Dans le cadre de cette nouvelle façon de travailler outre l’opérationnalisation du nexus, le lien avec les objectifs commun des programmes développement, paix et sécurité sera mis en avant. L’accent est aussi mis sur le renforcement de la coordination civilo-militaire afin de faciliter l’accès et la protection des civils.
Le projet a pour but de renforcer la coordination d’une réponse humanitaire rapide et efficace afin de sauver des vies et protéger les personnes affectées par les situations de crises au Tchad. Une coordination humanitaire rapide et correctement évaluée au niveau des besoins de la population affectée permettra aux acteurs humanitaires de mieux identifier et répondre aux besoins humanitaires, de renforcer la préparation de réponse aux urgences à travers le renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et plus spécifiquement l‘Equipe humanitaire pays, la coordination inter-clusters, la coordination civilo-militaire, les clusters, des groupes de travail et les mécanismes de coordination au niveau de terrain.
Le projet vise aussi à assurer le plaidoyer humanitaire à travers l’analyse des besoins faites par l’ensemble de la communauté humanitaire et ses partenaires en vue une compréhension commune des problématiques auxquels fait face le Tchad, ses causes profondes, l’impact sur les populations. OCHA jouera un rôle clé dans la création d'espaces de collection et d'analyse et gestion d’informations, pour assurer une stratégie de réponse coordonnée menant à des actions humanitaires répondant aux besoins les plus aigus et être mieux préparé face aux urgences soudaines. Le projet permettra également d’assurer conjointement avec la communauté humanitaire le plaidoyer en faveur du respect des principes humanitaires, de la protection des civils, de l'accès humanitaire et pour la mobilisation et l'allocation efficace de ressources humanitaires.
Un accent a été mis sur la mise en œuvre des plans d’action de la redevabilité envers les populations affectées (AAP), la PSEA et la préparation aux urgences en plus d'intégrer une attention au genre et de renforcer la centralité de la protection.
Un plaidoyer pour plus de visibilité des résultats tangibles au niveau de la réponse facilitant la mobilisation de ressources pour les différentes crises au Tchad (mouvement de population – crise du Bassin du Lac Tchad, insécurité alimentaire et malnutrition, urgences sanitaires, catastrophes naturelles) est aussi défini comme une priorité dans ce projet.
OCHA continuera de jouer également un rôle moteur dans le renforcement du lien entre les acteurs humanitaires et de développement et la transformation de la réponse humanitaire, en lien avec les engagements pris au Sommet humanitaire mondial de 2016 et ceci à travers la nouvelle façon de travailler (NWOW) et le renforcement de l’utilisation de la modalité de transfert monétaire.

Top-up Sahel 2023 - Annual programme 2023 Projet Approvisionnement en Eau et Promotion d’Hygiène/Assainissement dans la région de Diffa La proposition de CARE vise à apporter une réponse adaptée et coordonnée aux besoins dans le l’Eau, Hygiène et Assainissement (EHA). Elle cherche à contribuer à des solutions adaptées pour atténuer les souffrances des communautés d’accueils, des retournés et des réfugiés dans la région de Diffa. En effet, en dépit des efforts importants de l’État du Niger et de la communauté humanitaire, d’importants gaps sont encore à combler en matière d’eau, hygiène et assainissement particulièrement sur les sites d’accueil des personnes déplacées et dans les villages de retour des populations déplacées internes. Pour répondre aux besoins croissants en matière d’ l’Eau, Hygiène et Assainissement, CARE procédera à la construction et/ou réhabilitation d’ouvrages d’approvisionnement en eau potable et d’assainissement, la mise en place, formation et équipement de Comités d’Hygiène et Assainissement (CHA), la fourniture de kits EHA (matériel de transport et de stockage de l'eau, des produits de traitement de l'eau et des kits d'hygiène intime pour les femmes), la création de dépotoirs publics et fosses à ordures et la sensibilisation sur le changement de comportement dans la pratique d’hygiène et assainissement. Aussi, là où l’approvisionnement en eau potable est payant, CARE organisera une opération « Voucher eau de consommation » au profit des ménages pauvres. 
Ainsi, le projet contribuera à l’amélioration des conditions de vie de 14000 personnes (dont au moins 60% de femmes) vivant dans les ménages vulnérables des déplacés et familles d’accueil.
CARE travaillera en collaboration avec les (i) les autorités, (ii) les services techniques déconcentrés, (iii) les leaders communautaires à tous les niveaux. Cette implication permettra une appropriation des activités et est gage d’une durabilité des actions. 
Dans la région de Diffa, CARE a conduit plusieurs Analyses Genre Rapides (RGA) jusqu’en 2020 qui ont ressorti les besoins spécifiques des hommes, des femmes, des filles et des garçons dans tous les secteurs, y compris le secteur EHA ; ainsi que la meilleure façon de les impliquer dans la mise en œuvre de la réponse humanitaire. Le présent projet proposé procédera à une mise à jour des analyses genre rapides. Ainsi, la réponse sera bâtie non seulement sur la base des besoins identifiés par les acteurs, mais également en se basent sur les besoins spécifiques ressortis par les l’analyse genre rapide. Dans sa mise en œuvre, le projet se basera sur les recommandations de la RGA pour assurer une pleine implication de toutes les composantes sociales et apporter une réponse de qualité dans le secteur de l’Eau, Hygiène et Assainissement, prenant en compte les besoins spécifiques des bénéficiaires.

- Provide timely equitable access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene for IDPs/host

Provision of integrated life saving Gender Based Violence services including Covid-19 prevention and protection to IDP's and host communities in NWest SWest, West and Littoral regions in Cameroon. Strengthening Gender Based Violence prevention & response services  to conflict-affected populations in the North West & South West regions of Cameroon Since 2016, the Northwest and Southwest regions of Cameroon have been involved in a crisis which started as a teacher-lawyer strike and degenerated into what has been dubbed an armed conflict. 
In North West and South West, 53% of women are exposed to risk of violence during travelling, 33% of the avoided sites by women and girls are water points and 32% are latrines. In terms of GBV, 18% of the protection issues in the accessed villages were identified to face GBV 29% exposed to sexual violence, 17% forced into marriages, 10% child marriages, 10% domestic violence and 19% unable to access services. 30% of accessed locations do not have women and girls safe space. 
Incidences of emotional violence, denial of resources, opportunities and services, physical violence, rape and sexual assault, and forced marriage continue to be reported mostly by women and girls, as intimate partner violence or committed by known or unknown persons including armed men. As per the GBV IMS data a total of 7,996 GBV survivors received specialized GBV services from January to September in North West, South West and the Far North. It includes 79% of IPV, 20% of sexual violence. More 90% of GBV survivors in NW and SW and 100% in FN are women. Reported incidents are a sign of response capacity but not of the prevalence, as many barriers including closure of services in most parts of the North West and South West (NW, SW), lack of access to services, lack of awareness about available services hamper survivors to report and seek services. Despite efforts deployed, GBV protection services and GBV prevention mechanisms are insufficient or totally absent in many localities. The limited funding allocated to the GBV sector in 2022 resulted in the suspension of services in some locations. Many GBV survivors did not have access to specialised services, risking infection of STI or HIV, mental distress and unwanted pregnancy. From 2021-2022 there was 35% decrease in GBV services delivery. In both NWSW and FN some health facilities are not functional, or don’t have resources to provide Clinical Management of Rape services.  In 2022 only 0,01% (as per FTS) of the requested GBV funding was granted. The situation in 2023 will get worse for 953,524 women and girls, the most exposed to GBV risks and 33,854 men and boys as well, if no attention and adequate support and resources are allocated to address GBV needs
The main activities will focus on sensitization and awareness raising for communities, emphasizing the participation of men and boys, strengthen referral and legal assistance mechanisms for internally displaced persons and host communities with legal protection needs (detention/documentation, GBV survivors etc.), provide basic vocational training and economic/Empowerment support to women and girls, Provide cash transfer assistance, build the capacity of operational organizations on the holistic response to GBV. UNFPA and partners will continue providing individualized case management and psychosocial support to survivors of GBV and other vulnerable people. Finally, UNFPA, in collaboration with the Ministry of Women Empowerment and the Family (MINPROFF), will also continue to reinforce close collaboration between actors and service providers involved in responding to the needs of women and girls. Ensure that safe and ethical systems for the transfer of data including confidential personal records of GBV survivors are put in place by organizations and authorities.

Syria, Arab Republic of: DFAT support to Syria HAC, specifically for activities	
-- CHILD PROTECTION Strengthening Child Protection interventions for girls and boys most at risk of violence, abuse, neglect and exploitation across whole of Syria In line with the CP Area of Responsibility (AOR) Strategy and the “No Lost Generation” framework, UNICEF will enhance equitable access to quality CP services with a resilience focus, including for Survivors of abuse, violence, neglect and exploitation as well as children with disabilities, targeting 117 high severity sub-districts (3 to 5) and 38 low severity ones.

UNICEF’s CP Strategy in 2022-2023 includes:
• Addressing behavioural, social, cultural and economic determinants of CP violations as a prevention approach.  
• Improving the reach and quality of specialized CP services
• Capacity development of CP responders
•  Monitoring, evidence generation and advocacy 

UNICEF will support the delivery of integrated programming that will encourage social transformation, prioritizing:
• Structured and sustained CP MHPSS and EORE programmes
• Specialized integrated CP services including case management for survivors of violence, exploitation, neglect and abuse (child labour, CAFAAG, child survivors of GBV, child marriages, justice for children, birth registration and unaccompanied or separated children amongst others) 
• Parenting programmes to promote positive child rearing skills and experience for caregivers
• Elimination of violence against children, including GBV prevention and empowerment for girls, boys and women, prevention of violence in schools, homes and communities.
• Awareness-raising on CP risks
• Capacity development of CP responders and social workers

UNICEF will generate evidence to inform the humanitarian response and advocacy including setting up an information management system for case management. UNICEF will embrace new delivery modalities and implement cash transfers aimed at child protection outcomes for vulnerable families. UNICEF will also continue to support the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism on grave violations against children.

CP services will be delivered by partners based on minimum standards and IASC guidelines. 7,200 CP and social workers will be trained on case management, MHPSS, EORE, advocacy, evidence generation and coordination across sectors for a comprehensive CP response.
 
UNICEF will support MHPSS for 364,000 children to benefit from improved mental health and social wellbeing. UNICEF will equip 61,500 parents and caregivers with skills to provide a stimulating and safe environment at home, including reduced violence.  

Violence prevention is a key priority. Family violence prevalence is high for girls 12-17 years (47%), boys 12-17 years (44%), boys below 12 (45%) and girls below 12 (44%) (UNICEF 2018). UNICEF will work to protect children from violence and abuse through prevention activities in schools, homes and communities and providing survivors of violence with child-friendly and gender sensitive services. Support will be provided for PSEA mechanisms to protect beneficiaries and build the capacity of humanitarian actors. PSEA programming will be implemented with the Protection Sector AORs.

Based on HNO 2021, one in three communities in Syria is reportedly contaminated by explosive ordnance. One in four victims is a child (Joint MA & CP Analysis, 2020). EORE messages will be provided to 1,460,000 children and adults through humanitarian actors and public service providers using static facilities and mobile teams. UNICEF will build the capacity of partners to provide quality EORE that is age, gender and disability appropriate and to provide child victims with assistance.
 
UNICEF will strengthen the justice system to ensure that children in contact with the law victims, offenders or witnesses are protected through child-friendly, gender-sensitive services, that are community-based and family focused.

7F-10721.01	Bangladesh	UN Women	BGD Refugee Participation (UN Women) Empowering women and adolescent girls in the Rohingya refugee camps and host community through livelihoods and skills development support This project aims to build the resilience of Rohingya and Host Community women, adolescent girls, women with a disability, and transgender (Hijra) through increased livelihood skills and access to livelihood opportunities, including start-up support and support to establishing market linkages. 
UN Women has five Multi-Purpose Women's Centers (MPWCs) in camps 3, 4, 4-Extension, 5, and 18; and three MPWCs in host communities in Ukhia, Teknaf, and Cox's Bazar Sadar. Through these centers, women and girls including gender diverse population can access tailored multi-sectoral services that consider their specific needs and challenges, with a focus on women’s empowerment to build resilience and strengthen women’s role and leadership in their communities. The project has a separate programme for the transgender (hijra) community in the camp.
Activities provided through these centers encompass 1) those that promote the empowerment of women and girls, building their resilience through livelihood and skills development activities; and 2) activities that respond to and mitigate risks of Gender-Based Violence (GBV), inclusive of psychosocial support, case management and referral services for GBV survivors, alongside 1st aid medical assistance, SRH services and awareness-raising sessions on women’s rights issues. The current project is focused on the former (1) activities, with specific attention placed on ensuring the inclusion of the most marginalized women and girls in the project’s activities, including women and girls from female-headed households, women with disabilities, and gender-diverse persons in the MPWCs. 
Through the project, skills development training ranging in length from one to six months will be provided in the MPWCs to Rohingya and host community women. The training will focus on handicrafts, beauty parlors, tailoring, production of masks and reusable sanitary napkins, as well as eco-friendly jute products. At the end of the training, the skills of the participants will be tested. Upon the successful completion of the test, the participants will receive certificates. If the participant is found unsuccessful, they will be provided the opportunity to continue attending the training. UN Women will also be liaising with the sector on the standard training modules and provision of the certificates. 
Following the training, beneficiaries will be supported to continue their own businesses through the provision of in-kind grants comprising specific materials from the training and other start-up kits, and support to set up shop and access the market through the Women's Market in Camp 5 as well as three dedicated women’s café and display corners set up in camp 4, 4-Ext. and in the Women's Market in camp 5, facilitating private sector engagement and contributing to social cohesion, as the women vendors will be from both Rohingya and the host community. UN Women will provide the shopkeepers with a monthly incentive in kind/cash for coming to the market and running their business, alongside which the women can collect orders from the community and do home delivery. Project activities will include basic entrepreneurship skills development training for the women for setting up their businesses. 
In Camp 5, the Women's Market will continue to serve as a hub for women producers supported by also other partners such as AAB, DCA, FAO, HIS, PRANTIC, SNKSS, UNDP, and WFP.
Linkages to the local and national market and private sector will be strengthened by the Women Entrepreneur Association of Bangladesh (WEAB), a Women Peace and Humanitarian Fund grantee. In addition, the implementing partners (Oxfam, ActionAid Bangladesh, and BRAC) will sell the products through their national-level outlets. Also, UN Women will explore opportunities for conducting a market assessment and will engage with the ISCG for the planned market survey.

Syrian Arab Republic Humanitarian Response Plan
Early Recovery	JSB 2022 Fostering Resilience through Early Recovery response for the most Crisis impacted Communities in Syria The Integrated Response for Resilience Programme aims at providing a comprehensive response through Early Recovery support in 80 communities impacted by the crisis. Communities, particularly  those most dramatically affected – and under additional stress because of IDPs returns and other displacements - need  assistance in reinforcing their resilience to address these shocks as well as the consequences of the protracted crisis, and to address their needs on seriously depleted infrastructures and service capacities.
The essence of the Programme is about providing Syrian communities with – still limited - support to regain  control  over their basic needs (livelihoods, access to essential services) and reduce their dependency on humanitarian assistance. Prioritization of locations, is the outcome of a context analysis and needs assessment conducted on more than  5,000
Syrian communities, based on the following three criteria:
1) Hard to Reach  Areas
2) Areas of major IDPs presence and IDPs returns
3) Highest scoring in the Severity Scale
The integrated response consists of the following components: strengthening of social services-related capacities (access and coverage), livelihoods creation and rural recovery, PWDs support, social cohesion/community safety, reducing gender inequality  and youth marginality, women empowerment, tensions reduction and rehabilitation of basic infrastructure and public services.
The program is built in a modular manner both in terms of geographical and sectoral/thematic interventions and foresees the allotment of average 1 Million US$ per community. Hence, donors willing to support this approach will be able to pre-select certain location(s) and/or area(s) of intervention of their preference, within the 200 prioritized  communities.
The programme relates directly to the sector objectives:
1. Living conditions
2. Livelihoods
3. Access to social services
4. Access to productive and market infrastructure
5.social protection
6. Strengthening of local public services delivery capacity
7. Reinforcing  opportunities and capacities for civic engagement

Zakat Fund :2023 Emergency Appeal for Food and Cash assistance in Gaza  and West Bank Emergency Food Assistance in Gaza The unique socio-economic conditions of blockade, with its movement restrictions and destruction of productive capacity, are further compounded by repeated cycles of conflict and political instability, undercutting employment and livelihood opportunities in the Gaza Strip. 

The humanitarian needs of its more than 2 million residents were further exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic, the Ukraine Crisis and the military escalation in August 2022 and May 2021, which negatively impacted livelihoods and access to essential services in Gaza. 

The HRP 2023 Strategic Objective 3 states that the capacity of vulnerable Palestinians to cope with and overcome protracted crisis, including from environmental threats, is supported, while solutions to violations and other root causes of threats and shocks are pursued.

2023 Syria, Lebanon, and Jordan Emergency Appeal	Multi-Population/Other	Syria	United Nations Relief and Works Agency Restoring Disrupted Livelihoods and Supporting Early Recovery Efforts for Palestine Refugees in Syria Over eleven years of crisis in Syria has drastically eroded the living conditions of Palestine refugees and Syrian nationals alike. The rapid depreciation of the Syrian pound accompanied by staggering inflation levels, the impact of Lebanon's financial and banking crisis, and the tightened trade restrictions imposed on the country since June 2020, have all contributed to a worsening of the socio-economic conditions. The COVID-19 pandemic has led to additional stress on basic services that has impacted the livelihoods of Palestine refugees and Syrians. 

To support Palestine refugee youth access to employment opportunities, the UNRWA TVET programme will continue to provide short-term courses to 800 students in Damascus, Dera’a, Homs, Aleppo, Latakia, and Hama offering a variety of specializations that respond to the needs of the local market. Short-term courses (three months on average) are designed to strengthen technical skills, with minimal financial costs to the refugee students, to improve their prospects of accessing the labour market. In addition to the courses offered in the Damascus Training Centre, UNRWA will continue to expand its provision of long-term courses in its vocational training centres (VTCs) in Aleppo, Homs, Latakia and Dera’a and will introduce these in Hama in 2023. This is in response to the increasing demand of refugee youth in these areas for similar courses to those offered in Damascus and to promote equal access for all young Palestine refugees to livelihood opportunities to support their resilience. 

UNRWA will also provide employability and soft skills sessions to TVET students to encourage their confidence and abilities in approaching companies and communicating with potential future employers during job interviews. The Agency will maintain the dormitory at the Damascus Training Centre to provide a limited number of students, who live in remote locations, with accommodation to support the continuation of their TVET training. Transportation of vulnerable students will also be subsidised to mitigate the impact of the fuel crisis and associated rising transportation costs on the ability of students to access VTCs.

The various components of UNRWA's interventions in 2022-2023 will also contribute to supporting refugees who have spontaneously returned to their places of residence either internally or from other countries. Where possible, UNRWA will aim at restarting services in camps that were heavily destroyed during the conflict (Dera’a, Yarmouk and Ein el Tal) through the rehabilitation of the Agency’s installations (including schools and clinics) in these camps.

Finally, depending on the availability of funds, UNRWA will explore the feasibility of conducting small-scale cash-for-work initiatives in 2023 mainly focusing on unskilled job placements supporting UNRWA works in camps and Palestine refugee gatherings.

THM HUMANITAR 2022-2025	Thematic Humanitarian funds for Syria
--- SOCIAL PROTECTION Expanding Social, Civic and Economic Engagement and Social Cohesion Interventions for Conﬂict-Affected Adolescents and Youth in the Syrian Arab Republic In support of the ERL Sector (Strengthened Communities and Participation), UNICEF, through this project in 2023, will further support its Generation Unlimited initiative and No Lost Generation Agenda by empowering vulnerable adolescents and youth (10-24 years), female and male and those with disabilities, to access social, civic and economic opportunities for skill development and engagement (including participation in social cohesion initiatives) with the objective of contributing to enhancing resilience and social cohesion. UNICEF will build on strategic partnerships, integration and at scale programming focusing on the most vulnerable adolescents to strengthen skills development, employability and meaningful engagement through friendly spaces and mobile teams. The proposed project will support young women and men to have better access to civic, social, and economic opportunities for skill development and engagement and to unleash their potentials and increase their learning, leadership, and employability opportunities. 
UNICEF will promote the active and meaningful participation of young people brought together from different ages, genders, abilities and cultural and educational backgrounds to be agents of positive change in their communities. UNICEF will work in the following three pillars and related interventions: (1) Provide access to services and skills-building for adolescents and youth for enhanced employability. (2) Strengthen social, civic and economic engagement of adolescents and youth and foster volunteerism and social cohesion-building. (3) Support young entrepreneurs to start their own project projects through seed funding. UNICEF will continue strengthening the capacity of local partners including services providers, youth workers and young volunteers to improve the quality of provided services and enhance the evidence generation. UNICEF will support the scalable and sustainable approaches with national partners including integrated centers & platforms.
In this project, UNICEF will give priority to adolescents and youth in the high severity areas such as Dara’a, Rural Damascus, Northern Homs, Southern Hama, East and Northeast of Aleppo, Deir-ez-Zor and Idleb. UNICEF will expand its support to young people in NES, focusing on returnees and displaced people in Raqqa and Hasakah, including those in camps, collective shelters and urban settings. UNICEF will focus on the most deprived areas in rural and urban areas. These will include camps (Hol, Roj, Newroz, Areesha, Mahmoudli) in Al-Hasakeh and Raqqa , the collective shelters in Al-Hasakeh city, and the rural areas in Qamishli, Malikia, Yaroubia, and Raqqa Governorate. Projects engaging young people will be essential needs for their effective integration in their communities. In addition, since 2014, many young people have been staying in camps and collective shelters. They do not enjoy the freedom of movement and face other risks, thus offering them activities that will enhance their skills and allow them to catch up to their peers in terms of skills and non-formal education.  The programme will coordinate with and support other UNICEF programmes to ensure interventions are tailored to the particular needs of young people. The programme will implement activities for young people affected by, or at high risk of, emergencies or the socio-economic situation, to acquire the right skills, become empowered and resilient community members who help their communities to cope with emergencies. Life-skills and citizenship education for these adolescents will equip and empower them to act as both participants and catalysts of change in their community as volunteers and peer influencers.

The proposed project will support young women and men to have better access to civic, social, and economic opportunities for skill development and engagement and to unleash their potentials and increase their learning, leadership, and employability opportunities. 
UNICEF will promote the active and meaningful participation of young people brought together from different ages, genders, abilities and cultural and educational backgrounds to be agents of positive change in their communities. UNICEF will work in the following three pillars and related interventions: (1) Provide access to services and skills-building for adolescents and youth for enhanced employability. (2) Strengthen social, civic and economic engagement of adolescents and youth and foster volunteerism and social cohesion-building. (3) Support young entrepreneurs to start their own project projects through seed funding. UNICEF will continue strengthening the capacity of local partners including services providers, youth workers and young volunteers to improve the quality of provided services and enhance the evidence generation. UNICEF will support the scalable and sustainable approaches with national partners including integrated centers & platforms.
In this project, UNICEF will give priority to adolescents and youth in the high severity areas such as Dara’a, Rural Damascus, Northern Homs, Southern Hama, East and Northeast of Aleppo, Deir-ez-Zor and Idleb. UNICEF will expand its support to young people in NES, focusing on returnees and displaced people in Raqqa and Hasakah, including those in camps, collective shelters and urban settings. UNICEF will focus on the most deprived areas in rural and urban areas. These will include camps (Hol, Roj, Newroz, Areesha, Mahmoudli) in Al-Hasakeh and Raqqa , the collective shelters in Al-Hasakeh city, and the rural areas in Qamishli, Malikia, Yaroubia, and Raqqa Governorate. Projects engaging young people will be essential needs for their effective integration in their communities. In addition, since 2014, many young people have been staying in camps and collective shelters. They do not enjoy the freedom of movement and face other risks, thus offering them activities that will enhance their skills and allow them to catch up to their peers in terms of skills and non-formal education.  The programme will coordinate with and support other UNICEF programmes to ensure interventions are tailored to the particular needs of young people. The programme will implement activities for young people affected by, or at high risk of, emergencies or the socio-economic situation, to acquire the right skills, become empowered and resilient community members who help their communities to cope with emergencies. Life-skills and citizenship education for these adolescents will equip and empower them to act as both participants and catalysts of change in their community as volunteers and peer influencers.

Multi-Sector Assistance for Sudanese Refugees in Ajuong Thok and Pamir Refugee Camps, and Child Protection  Intervention for the Host Community in Pariang County Child Protection response for the most vulnerable and at-risk children and their caregivers in South Sudan The IRC Child Protection program will continue to provide comprehensive protection response services and create a safe and protective environment for children who are at risk of or have experienced abuse, exploitation, neglect, and violence as a result of recurrent crisis and conflict, assisting them in healing, recovering, and feeling safe again while collaborating with their caregivers and the local government and community-level prevention mechanisms in accordance with the Minimum Standards for CP and national level SOPs, guidelines, and protocols. The IRC CP program will reach 66,201(32,3232M, 33869F) people through an integrated response of static and mobile response approaches in the CP AOR priority locations (severity 3 and 4) of Panyijiar, Mayendit, and Koch Counties in Unity State; Aweil East and Aweil South in Northern Bahr el Ghazal State, and Juba IDPs in Rajaf Counties in Central Equatoria State.
The proposed child protection responses are linked with the strategic objectives of the cluster and three domains of the CP AOR for HRP 2022. Case management services will be provided to children who have concerns about their safety. FTR services, alternative care arrangements for unaccompanied and separated children (UASC), and protection cash aid will also be provided to meet the basic needs of the children. The Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) service will be provided for children and caregivers with psychological distress using a combination of approaches such as Safe Healing and Learning Space (SHLS) and schools for Social and Emotional Learning, Families Make the Difference Curriculum for parenting skills of caregivers, Supporting Adolescents and their Families in Emergencies Curriculum (SAFE) for life skills of adolescents, and IRC’s Brighter Futures Model for malnourished under five years children with protection concerns.
