Danish contribution to regional Refugee and Resilience Plan for Syria 2023 Education Support to IDPs and Returnees The Syrian crisis has weakened intensely the capacity of the education system to address basic education needs. According to the Ministry of Education (MoE) over 120,000 teachers required capacity development, an estimated 180,000 educational personnel have left the education system and around 5,722 schools are either damaged or destroyed which has caused an acute need for additional safe learning spaces across the country affecting 2.45 million out of school. Education needs and  gaps are also compounded by the COVID-19 pandemic which resulted to children drop out and a setback in learning.  
The project aims to enhance equitably and quality access to education to crisis affected IDPs, returnees and vulnerable children aged between 5-17 years. Several barriers prohibit children from being in school. Schools are destroyed or unsafe, some children feel unsafe on the way to school or while in school due to lack of electricity especially for the second shift students, families have had to displace to areas where schools are no longer available; as a result schools in safe areas are overcrowded and tensions between host community and those who were displaced have increased, lack of documentation prevent children from accessing primary and/or secondary education in which case, children may be exposed to higher risks of child labour, early marriage and social protection. Beyond that, the socio-economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic combined with the currency depreciation has placed additional challenges for children in accessing education imposing children to work to support their families and families’ ability to afford school expenses such as school uniform, stationery, and transportation continue to be a key reason for children are not attending school.
UNHCR education intervention includes the provision of non-formal education in community centres. The non-formal education activities will enhance the school enrolment of out of school children and the retention of children with low school performance. School rehabilitation will be very limited as a last resort and part of a comprehensive intervention in priority return areas. UNHCR pays specific attention to the future adolescents and youth populations that can contribute to resilience and social cohesion in their communities through facilitating their access to education. In line to age gender and diversity, accountability to affected population and rights-based approaches, UNHCR will reach out to children and their parents during project monitoring activities and through focus group discussion seeking feedback including receipt of complaints regarding the project. Resources permit, UNHCR plans to provide non-formal education activities to over 185,000 children and rehabilitation of around 150 classrooms.

To save lives and alleviate suffering Improve food security through provision of emergency food and enhance food production of food insecure housholds in Aweil North, Aweil West, Aweil South, NBeG State, South Sudan  Given the high level of food insecurity, Concern will continue to provide FSL support to most vulnerable households in Aweil North, Aweil West and Aweil South Counties in Northern Bahr el Ghazal (NBeG) state while the nutrition sensitive agriculture support is integrated across all nutrition centres in Juba IDP camp in Central Equatoria and Guit County in Unity State.  Concern will provide access to food, agriculture inputs and improve agriculture production to prevent famine and support vegetable production to improve food consumption, dietary diversity and coping strategies for vulnerable populations. Concern will engage with the County Agriculture Department (CAD), extension workers and lead farmers for training on agriculture extension services and Climate Smart Agriculture practices, informal seeds systems, pest and post-harvest management. Concern will also support vegetable production across all targeted location to increase HHs dietary diversity and contributing to improved complementary feeding practices among children 6-23 months of age. Considering asset depletion, crop losses due to flooding, inflation and limited access to livelihood, hunger is expected to deepen due mainly to depleted food stocks and high food prices therefore Concern in partnership with WFP in NBeG continue to provide emergency food assistance through General Food Distribution, School Feeding Program and Cash/Food for Asset program.

To save lives and alleviate suffering Promouvoir la protection et la cohésion sociale entre les populations déplacées et les communautés hôtes de Ouallam,Tillabery GOAL est présente sur les 4 sites des déplacés de Ouallam à savoir Ouallam, Tondikiwindi, Diney et Mangaizé, sur financement de OCHA (FRHAOC) dans les secteurs de la santé (Cliniques mobiles), nutrition, Abris et biens non alimentaires. GOAL vise à travers ce nouveau projet à donner une réponse aux gaps en contribuant aux Objectifs Spécifiques  du cluster protection, en renforçant la cohésion sociale par une sensibilisation sur les thématiques de la protection et de la redevabilité ainsi que des actions d’accompagnement et d'assistance ABNA/CASH pour certains vulnérables, dans les sites IDPs des communes rurales de Tondikiwindi et Ouallam, dudit département. Le projet ciblera intentionnellement parmi les populations déplacées et les communautés hôtes les veuves, les ménages dirigés par les femmes ou les enfants, les personnes vivant avec handicap, les vieillards, les familles accueillant les enfants non accompagnés, les jeunes filles, les élèves déplacés. L’éveil des consciences général et le renforcement de l’autonomisation financière se feront à travers des formations, des sensibilisations sur les thématiques de protections et des remises des kits de protection ou de réhabilitation. Ainsi le projet contribuera en:

Ainsi, des points focaux genre sensible seront identifiés avec les communautés suivant le zonage existant sur chaque site (ou ajuste au besoin). Ces points focaux et les mobilisateurs communautaires seront formes et accompagnes sur l'équité genre et inclusion sociale, les droits des enfants et leurs protections, la protection transversale, la redevabilité, PSEA et le plaidoyer lobbying) pour mieux prendre en compte les intérêts des plus vulnérables. GN s'appuiera sur l'existant en termes de structuration tout en le renforçant. 
• mettant en relation les points focaux protection avec les autres acteurs clés de la  protection de leurs zones pour le référencement au besoin, renforcer le circuit de référencement et contre référencement dans la zone.
 • collaborant avec les autres partenaires intervenant dans les programmes pour une meilleure prise en compte des plus vulnérables dans leurs ciblages. 
• Organisant des conférences débats sur la cohésion sociale et/ou Organisation d'émissions radios sur la paix et la réconciliation. 
• Créant et diffuser des messages de sensibilisation via la plateforme de service Viamo et les ondes des radios communautaires.
 • Organisant des séances de sensibilisation sur la prévention au COVID-19.
 • Mettant en place un mécanisme d’Ecoute & de Gestion des Plaintes.

Compte tenu du contexte sécuritaire, toutes les formations se feront à Ouallam. To save lives and alleviate suffering Increasing safe, equitable and dignified access to essential basic protection services reducing exposure of affected vulnerable populations to protection risks, including GBV in Pibor (IPC 5), Nyirol (IPC 4) and Akobo (IPC 4) in Jonglei State The proposed HRP 2022 interventions will be implemented in Pibor, Nyirol and Akobo West which have been classified as IPC 4 and 5 facing deteriorating humanitarian conditions, worsened by endemic violence, conflict, access constraints and operational interference, public health challenges such as direct and indirect effects of COVID-19 and climatic shocks resulting in the dual phenomena of extraordinary flooding and localized drought, which have a severe impact on people’s livelihoods, hampers access to education and water, sanitation and hygiene and health services. Protection concerns remain high, with people impacted by violence having limited access to justice and the rule of law. The proposed intervention will contribute to the HRP 2022 Protection Cluster, General Protection Objectives: Prevent and mitigate protection risks through enhanced preparedness and resilience; Enhance protection assessment and monitoring to inform protection and overall humanitarian response; and Ensure the provision of critical protection related assistance and specialized services through an integrated approach to address the priority needs of targeted people among vulnerable women, men, girls and boys in hard-to-reach and priority geographical areas. The main objective of the proposed intervention is to increase safe, equitable and dignified access to essential basic protection services reducing exposure of affected vulnerable populations to protection risks, including GBV in Pibor, Nyirol and Akobo in Jonglei State. To achieve this, the proposed intervention has the following specific objectives: SO1 To undertake effective and timely protection assessments in targeted areas for timely and robust humanitarian and protection decisions, influence and actions; SO2 To strengthen community-based protection mechanisms for risk reduction and promotion of local peace and security for women and youths; SO3 To provide Individual Protection Assistance to address priority protection needs for vulnerable women, men, girls and boys in targeted areas; SO4 To support ‘safe programming’ (protection mainstreaming) including safeguarding in all interventions in all the targeted locations. Targeted population are Host Communities, Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) and Returnees consisting of women, girls, boys and men. The intervention will be contributing to the Protection Cluster target of 105,320 women, men, girls and boys provided with individual, group, specialized PSS and other related general protection services. This project will be implemented by Oxfam and its local partners. The expected number of people reached through Oxfam intervention is 6,600 (across all locations 60% women, 20% girls, 10% boys, 10% men): Pibor HC-1000, IDPs-800, Returnees-400; Akobo HC-1000, IDPs-800, Returnees-400 and Nyirol HC-1000, IDPs-800, Returnees-400.

Integrated health and nutrition prevention and treatment response in Lakes State (Rumbek East, Rumbek North and Yirol West), NBEG (Aweil South) and Unity, Panyijiar, South Sudan. Emergency Nutrition Response to mitigate the impact of malnutrition among the most vulnerable under five children and PLW living in, Aweil south, Panyjar , Rumbek east , Rumbek North and Yirol west counties of South Sudan. Malnutrition is one of the top causes of death in children under five years and has a long-term negative impact on the children’s abilities to live to their full potential. South Sudan (SS) has experienced continued crisis including floods, conflict, and food insecurity which have impacted on the key drivers of acute malnutrition and aggravated the nutrition situation within the country. The Food Security and Nutrition Monitoring System (FSNMS) Round 28 and 2022 SMART surveys report GAM prevalence at 16.0% (15.4 -16.7) in lean season.  This indicates no improvement since 2019, when the GAM prevalence was 16.2% (13.8-18.5) in lean season the rate of acute malnutrition remains above the emergency threshold of 15 percent (very high acute malnutrition level- WHO classification). The situation calls for strengthened multisector investment to address the impact of aggravating factors, and to maintain gains in tackling the nutrition situation in South Sudan.The objectives of the action will be; To increase equitable access and utilization of quality preventative nutrition specific service delivery for children, adolescents, and women .To increase equitable access and utilization of quality lifesaving nutrition services for early detection and treatment of acute malnutrition for girls and boys under five years of age and PLW affected by acute malnutrition .To increase equitable access to nutrition sensitive interventions from health, WASH, FSL, Education and Protection sectors through enhanced coordination and joint programming targeting vulnerable groups in Aweil South, Panyijar, Rumbek East, Rumbek North and Yirol West counties by the end of 2023.  The proposed intervention aims to increase coverage and access to the most vulnerable community by providing equitable and accessible nutrition prevention treatment services. The nutrition services will deliver by scaling up the emergency nutrition responses through 62 static OTP/TSFP (10 in Aweil south,10 in Panyijar, 23 in Rumbek east, 7 in Rumbek North, and 12 in Yirol west), 5 Stabilization center (1 in Panyijar, 1 Aweil south, 1 in Rumbek east, 1 in Rumbek north, and 1 in Yirol west) and through 4 RRM mobile tam (2 in Aweil south, 2 in Panyjar,). In addition, the IRC will implement integrated CMAM and MIYCN in all sites. Promotion of optimal nutrition and prevention of malnutrition among young children (0-23 months through the implementation of MIYCN to ensure vulnerable children have optimal growth. IRC will strengthen community participation using existing community structures and active engagements of the affected community. IRC will conduct meetings with MtMSG, regular community sensitization sessions and scaling up of the existing Nutrition response to ensure timely service availability. Scale up family MUAC to ensure early detection of acute malnutrition that contributes to early detection. An estimated 20,085 SAM children,37388 MAM, and 30131 PLW MAM will be reached through this action across all implementation areas in OTP and TSFP, respectively. Continue with the capacity building of CHD, primary health care service providers and nutrition staff. Train health and nutrition staff on CMAM and MIYCN to ensure timely nutrition services. A rapid response team will be deployed to the hard-to-reach area to provide nutrition services that are accessible and vulnerable groups have got timely treatment. Subsequently, the interventions will reduce mortality and morbidity associated with malnutrition. Integration of nutrition activities with other sectors will also be implemented, including integration of health and nutrition education messages, Malaria testing and treatment, promotion of hygiene and sanitation, training on GBV and CP for nutrition staff. Similarly, with food security, establish kitchen garden, cash programs for children discharged cured from SAM treatment, and cooking demonstrations to improve dietary diversification, conduct kitchen garden and cash programs.

Building the MHPSS-Gender-Peacebuilding nexus: Fostering wellbeing, non-violent, gender equitable masculinity, and social restoration with young people in West Darfur, Sudan Facilitating the Creation of a Favourable Protection Environment in Sudan As a result of the clashes that erupted throughout the country between Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on 15 April 2023, the already fragile protection environment in Sudan has significantly deteriorated, with a multitude of protection risks that have further worsened access to services such as water, health care, electricity, and basic items and commodities such as food, cash, and fuel for millions of people. Several cities have faced heavy bombardments and clashes, and associated unexploded ordnance, causing hundreds of civilian deaths and casualties, as well as damage to critical water, health care and power infrastructure, increasing of criminal activities, with indiscriminate attacks on civilians and widespread looting. Furthermore, high insecurity and looting of humanitarian assets and offices have compromised humanitarian access to key locations. As of 21 May 2023 a total of 1,042,114 individuals (209,136 households) have been displaced across the country mostly from urban areas in affected states. Vulnerable groups are increasingly exposed to protection risks with significant harm to their physical and mental wellbeing. 
This project intends to contribute to promoting a favorable protection environment in communities particularly affected by the current crisis, while providing humanitarian assistance to individuals and groups. The proposed intervention intends to provide General, Child, and GBV related protection services in the areas of interventions with the cluster estimating 7.3 million people in need of these protection services. The project is in line with the Cluster and Sub-Cluster Objectives and will target localities across the target areas identified as “hotspots” by the Protection Cluster and partners.
IOM will improve access of vulnerable crisis-affected people, especially girls and women, to primary healthcare and protection services, including GBV response services. Also, IOM will assist conflict-affected population with the distribution of non-food items (NFIs), in coordination with the Emergency Shelter and Non-Food Items(ES/NFI) Cluster. IOM will also work towards strengthening the capacity and availability of GBV services through the training and deployment of social workers and psychologists, in addition to enhancing existing referral mechanism to address GBV and child protection issues and cases. To improve the crisis-affected people’s access to community-based dispute resolution mechanisms, IOM also will build the capacity of informal mediators and dispute resolvers. To achieve this aim, IOM will work with the existing community committees, community leaders, and representatives from other community-based organisations, including women and youth groups as well as those belonging to both farmers and herder groups. IOM staff will also contribute to “protection by presence” by collecting data on protection needs, gaps and trends for advocacy, IOM will coordinate with its other existing programming in the targeted states, such as the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) and humanitarian response and transition interventions including Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) and health activities, to leverage effective synergies between programme activities in view of delivering the best protection outcomes for affected populations. 
In coordination with the Civil Registry and UNHCR, IOM will support the local government to strengthen their capacity and resources to improve the birth registration of IDPs and service provision to persons with disabilities through the provision of office equipment, trainings, and facilitating regular visits of government staff to hard-to-reach areas to provide the services to rural communities. Finally, IOM will support the establishment and/or reactivation of women’s groups and centres in secure areas to ensure access to safe engagement platforms as well as to information on protection services.

Multisectoral humanitarian emergency aid in the areas of nutrition, housing, WASH for refugees, internally displaced persons and host communities in Nigeria (2023 portion) WASH Response to Conflict Affected Population in North East Nigeria (Borno and Adamawa) The project aims to address the WASH needs of a targeted total of 117,000 conflict affected populations across Borno and Adamawa States. The overall project objective is to ensure that conflict affected have reduced exposure to WASH related illnesses through improved access to potable drinking water, appropriate/dignified sanitation facilities and strengthened hygiene practices. Prioritization of interventions will be based on the needs identified to and tailored to the needs for the disabled, elderly, different age groups and displacement status. The project will address the needs for the internally displaced persons (newly displaced and protracted crisis), returnees and extremely vulnerable host communities. The targeted communities will contribute to the implementation of the project through further needs assessments, contributing to the design, and participation during project monitoring and giving feedback during the project surveys and post distribution monitoring. The project will also be tailored to address the emerging and re-emerging epidemics, related to provision of adequate water, sanitation and hygiene services. This will include responding to such outbreaks such as cholera, the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic and other related epidemics. More specially, the project activities will include the following; Rehabilitation/upgrading and construction water points. This includes optimization, solarisation, replacing pumps to optimize the capacity of the boreholes, improvement of the water collection points, replacement of taps and old pipes. Water treatment and water quality monitoring. This includes introduction of inline water chlorination, monitoring of the free residual chlorine levels both at the point of collection and at the household level. Samples will be collected for bacteriological analysis from households that will have zero free residual chlorine levels. Emergency water distribution/treatment via water trucking (where all other water supply options are not available). This activity shall be limited to a period of not more than 3months. Establishment and capacity building of water management committees. Water committees will be equipped with tool boxes in order to undertake minor works Construction of new latrines and bathing shelters. Priority shall be given to communities who practice open defecation and do not have latrines. Operation and maintenance of latrines, including minor repairs and maintenance, desludging and minor rehabilitations such as replacement of broken doors, handles and some missing part of the super structure. Hygiene Promotion messages will be delivered through community based trained hygiene promoters and the information, education and communication materials will be adopted from the sector approved materials. Distribution of Hygiene Non-Food Items (NFIs), including the installation of hand washing stations. The distribution will be targeted, and will be done through both in kind and the use of vouchers (where markets are functioning). The NFIs will also be adopted from the sector approved kits, which includes family hygiene kits, latrine cleaning kits, cholera kits etc. Trainings and capacity building, this will be done for community based hygiene promoters, WASH committees, adolescent girls and other targeted trainings for water, sanitation and hygiene staff implementing the project.The project will target Monguno, Jere, MMC and Gwoza Local Government Areas (LGA) of Borno State and Yola North, Yola South and Mubi North LGAs.The implementation of this project shall be closely coordinated with the relevant government ministry (ministry of water resources), Rural Water and Sanitation agency(RUWASA), UN agencies (UNICEF, IOM), other WASH implementing partners and local Non-Governmental Organizations.

Strengthening climate-adapted production systems and local value creation Mitigate the worst effects of hunger through provision of emergency assistance in Unity State According to the IPC released in November 2022, there are over 6.6 million people in South Sudan experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above) between October and November 2022. Food insecurity in the country is highly driven by ongoing conflicts, and climatic shocks, citing from the Humanitarian Needs Overview published in February 2022 states that climate change continues to impact different sectors, particularly agriculture, which is one of the most climate-sensitive economic sectors. Above-normal rainfall for the third consecutive year in 2022 led to prolonged flooding, which impacted areas that had not flooded in previous years constituting a rise in food insecurity countrywide.

Unity state is one of the most food insecure states, that contributes to the estimated 7.8 million people (63% of the population) who likely will face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse acute food insecurity, with 43,000 people likely to be in Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5) in the lean season projection period of April to July 2023. Approximately three-quarters of the state's population is undergoing severe food insecurity, as well as acute malnutrition children attributed to several factors, but primarily because of conflict (including tribal and interclan fighting) and secondarily because of inaccessibility due to poor infrastructure and swampy nature of most of its land that makes it susceptible to floods, resulting to destruction of crops, properties which equates to hunger.

In response to the above problem, Welthungerhilfe (WHH) proposes a project aiming at mitigating the humanitarian crises in Unity State by ensuring the provision of needs-based emergency aid to prevent or decrease morbidities, mortality, and acute malnutrition, especially for vulnerable people in acute humanitarian crises triggered by flight and displacement, droughts, floods, and anticipated periods of hunger. 

The project approach will revolve around addressing issues of climate change through training of 20 DRR committees to develop vulnerability mappings for their specific context on boma (village level) or Payam level (sub-county level), depending on context. The committees will present a cross-section of the population since all ages and genders will be represented. The project will therefore target 56,000 beneficiaries in total in the form of IDPs, returnees and host communities. More specifically, the intervention will target, women and children-headed households, including women of reproductive age and pregnant and lactating women (PLWs), unaccompanied minors, people with disabilities, the elderly and chronically ill with various activities that include the distribution of NFI kits consisting of various household items, cash for work activities to help the most vulnerable households meet the food consumption gap while building household and community assets that reduce the risk of disaster, strengthen livelihoods and build resilience over time. They will also benefit from agriculture crop production training, distribution of ruminants and support to livestock health to help build their resilience to shocks. The project will seek to reduce the deterioration of people’s physical and mental well-being through coping mechanisms.  Target groups will additionally be linked to other ongoing interventions implemented by Welthungerhilfe and other agencies so that they can benefit from the services offered.

Emergency food aid for refugees, internally displaced persons and host communities in accordance with Strategic Objective 1 of the WFP country program (excluding UNHAS flights) Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM). WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.
Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (light resilience- building activities, peace/conflict resolution training also called GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness, training, or sensitisation on peaceful resolution of conflicts, mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace. 
Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities.

Coordinated Action for Multi-Sector Programming in Camp and Out-of-Camp Settings Humanitarian coordination and provision of CCCM-integrated responses to displacement-affected populations in Juba and Bor former PoC sites (semi-static) in hard-to-reach areas (mobile) In line with the CCCM cluster strategy, ACTED will continue to provide humanitarian coordination and CCCM integrated response to displacement affected population in Juba former PoC sites and will provide mobile support in hard-to-reach areas in response to displacement shocks.  Due to natural hazards, localized and state conflicts, displacement waves remain high in South Sudan with 1.64 million people currently being Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) in need of CCCM assistance according to the South Sudan HNO 2022. The trend has been increasing in 2022 following massive natural hazards such as floodings in Jonglei state, leading to the multiplication of displacement sites. 
As South Sudan has been subject to displacement waves since its creation, and particularly following the 2013 civil war, some IDP sites have existed for several years with residents not willing to return to their areas of origin and ongoing humanitarian aid. To address this issue, ACTED aims to provide a more sustainable solution and support these IDP communities to become more empowered and increase their integration into host communities settings. Following a strategy implemented since 2021 in agreement with CCCM cluster, ACTED handed over camp management responsibilities to the community representatives and local authorities, especially Relief and Rehabilitation Commission (RRC) in Bor and Juba former PoC camps in 2022. In 2023, ACTED will strengthen social cohesion between IDPs and host communities in Juba to foster peaceful coexistence and will provide ad-hoc support to community representatives if needed to ensure a smooth transition. 
In parallel, ACTED provides emergency CCCM assistance in response to displacement shocks across the country. Through a well-established coordination system with REACH, the Inter Cluster Coordination Group, the Needs Analysis Working Group and the clusters, ACTED has access to timely information on displacements, allowing for a rapid multi-sectoral intervention whose core is CCCM services. Within its CCCM rapid response, ACTED aims to provide life saving coordination activities among humanitarian actors and build local communities’ capacities to self manage the sites. 
Therefore, ACTED will continue implementing CCCM interventions in line with the following cluster objectives: CO1: Improve living condition of IDPs by facilitating safe, equitable and dignified access to cross-sectoral humanitarian services, including CCCM CO2: Enhance the protective environment, respond to vulnerable population with priority on addressing protection gaps and strengthen the predictability and effectiveness of multi sectorial interventions at site level CO3: Support vulnerable IDPs to recover from the crisis by strengthening community self-management, build resilience to promote solutions for displaced people in sites.

Aid and protection measures for refugees and internally displaced persons in the East Africa / Great Lakes region Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2022, there are some 335,000 refugees and asylum seekers from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, primarily from Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic.
At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for longer term stability, hundreds of thousands of South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since the signing of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan, this spontaneous movement has prompted the development of an area-based approach, to support refugees, returnees and host communities, through enhanced engagement with development actors, to support greater access to services where possible.
Refugees largely reside in conflict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction in basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.
Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will benefit from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Specific protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identified at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with specific protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as verification exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the efficiency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to benefit from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

WASH humanitarian emergency aid in South Sudan (2023 portion) Emergency WASH Response in South Sudan UNICEF will provide women, men, girls, and boys affected by multiple shocks and hazards
in South Sudan with critical water, sanitation, and hygiene services, items, and facilities.
The objective of this project is to provide lifesaving emergency water supply, sanitation
and hygiene promotion services for con􀂧ict affected people, vulnerable host communities
and people in disease prone (high GAM famine and outbreak related) areas including
protection related actions to mitigate GBV, strengthening of communities’ resilience to
cope with the impact of emergencies and recurrent shocks. This emergency WASH project
will comprise of situation assessments, preparedness, transitional programs, frontline
emergency WASH response, strengthening of partners’ capacity, and cluster coordination
including sector information management. UNICEF will deliver emergency lifesaving
support by providing access to WASH services as per Sphere and WASH Cluster
standards.
The project will focus on addressing the following:
- Effective Cluster coordination mechanism in the country
- Provide timely equitable access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene for IDPs/host
communities and returnees, including transitional programming
- WASH in Nutrition for famine prevention with a minimum package of interventions.
- WASH in Health for outbreak control at wider community level (i.e. Ebola, Cholera, etc.)
- While implementing projects a special attention will be given to mitigate WASH-related
GBV.
The project will also support expansion of partnerships with local and international NGOs
and CBOs in highly affected areas to ensure basic services are provided and long-term
capacity built. The activities will be implemented in complementarity with other sectors
such as Health, Nutrition, Protection and where possible Education projects including
disaster risk reduction (DRR) focusing on strengthening community coping mechanisms.

Multi-sector emergency aid for displaced persons and communities in counties in the states of Western Jonglei and Eastern Lakes affected by flooding (2023 portion) Sustainable Agriculture and Livelihoods Empowerment project and Unconditional Cash/Food voucher to the Host and IDPs in Yirol and Awerial Counties. South Sudan underwent series of humans suffering before and after the attainment of Independence all brought by civil wars, communal conflicts and natural calamities such as flooding and COVID-19 pandemic and these hampers people's sources of livelihood and deteriorate the economy. In 2022, the Humanitarian Nee community in South Sudan estimated that two third (2/3) of South Sudan population which is approximately 8.2 million are in need of humanitarian assistance. This includes the 2 million in which 55% of them are women and girls with an additional 2.3 million residing in the countries as refugees. All these negative factors will only aggravate humanitarian conditions in South Sudan. The lands for farming will be limited by flooding and drought and this increases the risk of vulnerability rates and increase in the number of IDPs in the Country. Yirol East recently hosted a huge number of IDPs with 9473 HHs registered and verified by WFP through according to Yirol East Relief and Rehabilitation Commission office in Yirol East County with another 160 HHs that later arrived after the verification, and this will only exacerbate the humanitarian situation Yirol East County as the resources of the host communities are shared and soon will be depleted. In Yirol East County of Lakes State, Help-Hilfe zur Selbsthilfe has been implementing Food security and Livelihood project alongside WASH and nutrition. Major support under this this sector falls under distribution of farm inputs (seeds, tools and implements) and training (Climate Smart Agriculture), conservation agriculture and distribution of fishing gears. Help is scaling up to promote the enterprise farming that will boost other sectors of livelihood such as agribusiness. So far, Help previously supported and trained several groups in Yirol East and West Counties and many of those groups had progressed expectedly. Under the project “Multisector emergency aid for displaced persons and host communities in Eastern Lakes State”, Help is currently implementing a three (3) years project that is targeting 10,000 Households in Lakes and part of Jonglei states to benefit from seeds and tools distribution and agronomic trainings such as kitchen gardening, perm gardening, aerial gardening especially in the flood affected population places. Another 9500 HHs to benefit for unconditional Cash/food voucher where 4000 HHs already distributed food items and other essential things like washing soaps and another 5000 HHs to benefit from fishing gears. The proposed intervention is designed to contribute to Help Interim Country Strategic Plans of 2022-2024. The combination of these interventions will contribute to its work in realizing Sustainable Development Goal 2 to “end hunger, achieve food security and improved nutrition, and promote sustainable agriculture” in South Sudan. As food insecurity problems in Lakes State are complex and interrelated, it requires multifaceted and integrated responses both at household and individual levels in addressing immediate and underlying causes of food insecurity and malnutrition to enhance their capacities and reduce vulnerabilities to disaster risks. The supplementary coping mechanism is acquired through consumption of wild fruits and greens. The IDPs and host community households prepare smaller portion of less nourishing food for survival and the number of meals per a day reduces to one. The project will also incorporate GBV, HIV/AIDS, accountability to affected populations, and gender equality during the implementation. In our intervention, Help implements hand in hand with the community stakeholders Chiefs, Women representatives, church leaders, youth representatives, and government representatives (boma and Payams administrators) during the identification of the most vulnerable households and the distribution of humanitarian assistance and agricultural inputs.  The targeting criteria include women headed HHs, Child headed HHs, destroyed HHs.

El programa ASH propone modalidades de (a) respuesta de emergencia, (b) respuesta con soluciones duraderas basada en un enfoque comunitario, y (c) una respuesta Integrada con otros programas de NRC tales como: Educación e ICLA. 

 

La respuesta ASH de NRC continuará incluyendo la provisión de un mínimo de servicios ASH durante la Respuesta de Emergencia (COVID-19 y crisis humanitaria venezolana). Por otro lado, durante la Respuesta con Soluciones Duraderas se pretende mejorar la resiliencia en comunidades meta, fomentando la participación de comunidades en el diseño e implementación del programa, desarrollando sus capacidades locales, y asegurando la sostenibilidad del programa. 

 

La componente de AGUA incluirá: (a) Provisión de agua segura (a nivel del hogar) a través de kits de tratamiento de agua para el hogar y/o kits de manejo de agua) y rehabilitación y sistema de tratamiento de agua a nivel comunitario; (b) Provisión de capacitación y sensibilización (tratamiento, calidad del agua y uso seguro). 

 

La componente de SANEAMIENTO incluirá: (a) Provisión de baterías de baños y duchas culturalmente apropiadas, desagregados por género y estaciones de lavado de manos. Las instalaciones se ubicarán en áreas públicas o institucionales en zonas clave de flujo migratorio; (b) Provisión de kits NFIs de saneamiento (mantenimiento / limpieza); (c)Provisión de contenedores de basura para gestión de residuos sólidos. 

 

La componente de HIGIENE incluirá: (a) Provisión de kits de dignidad e higiene, junto con sensibilizaciones sobre su uso apropiados; (b)Provisión de campañas de sensibilización sobre higiene personal, prevención de enfermedades, higiene menstrual y protección; (c) Creación, capacitación y sensibilización de comités ASH en colegios y comunidades que servirán como apoyo a la promoción de higiene. La respuesta ASH de NRC pretenden ser Integradas a otros programas como el de Educación que apunta a una mejora de la calidad de la educación, inclusivas e integradas con el programa ASH centrándose en la mejora de la infraestructura ASH, para garantizar las instalaciones satisfagan las necesidades de todos los grupos de NNAs, profesores y personas con discapacidad.

Multi year 2021 to 2023. 2023 portion total amount  USD 2,638,372 Improving short-term and long-term food security and livelihoods access in Central and Eastern Equatoria and WBeG through investment in food production assets and utilization and strengthening of local capacities. In line with the FSL cluster strategy for 2022, ACTED will contribute towards improving food security of over 22,754 beneficiaries (excluding beneficiaries reached through WFP funding) to enhance emergency food production and reduce dependency on food and agricultural inputs through resilience building activities such as training and market support functionality. Millions of South Sudanese remain displaced across the country following years of violent conflict that resulted in one of the most devastating humanitarian crises in recent history. Based on the latest IPC analysis and projections, in October 2022, 53.6% of the population living in South Sudan facing high levels of acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above). Specifically, 4.36 million people are facing crisis (IPC Phase 3), 2.22 million people are facing emergency (IPC Phase 4) and 61,000 people are facing catastrophic (IPC Phase 5) food insecurity.  As such, the needs across South Sudan have severely increased, driven by flooding, insecurity, population displacements, declined crop production, diseases and pests, the economic crisis, the effects of COVID-19, limited access to basic services, and the cumulative effects of prolonged years of asset depletion and loss of livelihoods.  The project activity will be in line with the cluster Objectives : 
CO1 : Provide food assistance to prevent famine and improve food consumption, dietary diversity and coping strategies for vulnerable populations (in IPC 5, 4 & some 3)
“CO2: Enhance emergency food production through complementary vegetable and crop seeds and fishing and livestock support (in IPC 3, 4 & 5)”

multisectoral response to meet the basic humanitarian needs of people affected by displacement and vulnerable host communities in East Africa Protection and Legal Assistance for Displacement affected populations in South Sudan The NRC seeks to improve the overall protective environment in South Sudan by not only responding to people's most immediate material needs during a crisis, but also by promoting their safety and dignity, as well as preventing, reducing, or mitigating the protection risks they face. It is also to address the root causes of displacement and to contribute to the creation of conditions conducive to long-term solutions for displaced people. To achieve the project objective, NRC will focus on three key components i.e. 1) General Protection; Housing, Land and Property; 3) Gender Based Violence. 

NRC proposes a community-based approach to displaced and conflict-affected populations protection, including static, mobile, and emergency responses.  Protection context assessments will be done in all locations, as well as, where possible, community-based protection monitoring, in which community focal points will be trained to report on protection needs and risks. Protection incidents will be documented and analyzed in order to better understand trends and evolution in the protection context, and the findings will be disseminated to communities and relevant stakeholders. 

NRC will provide at-risk populations with both awareness-raising sessions and individualized assistance in obtaining national identity documentation. Foster improved ability to exercise HLP rights for individuals and groups affected by displacement with priority given to the most vulnerable, including female and child headed households, the elderly, individuals with physical and mental disabilities, and those who are extremely poor. NRC will target conflict-affected areas and areas of potential return.

NRC will also carry out GBV prevention and risk mitigation activities in 6 counties located in hard to reach areas. Activities will include awareness raising, referrals to response services, cash assistance to GBV survivors, distribution of dignity kits and training on GBV basic concepts among others.

To achieve the main objective, the will focus on the below key activities
1) Carrying out of information and awareness raising activities; awareness will focus on GBV (GBV risks, available response services, GBV referral pathways, timely reporting), HLP (social cohesion and collaborative dispute resolution mechanisms, land rights issues) and general protection (protection risks, available services)
2) Provision of cash assistance (individual protection assistance) to persons at GBV survivors and other persons at heightened risks including referral of GBV survivors for response services
3) Training frontline workers and community focal points on basic GBV concepts, GBV guiding principles and responses services.
4) Training of state-level authorities, community leaders and representative on HLP, alternative dispute resolution
5) Facilitating peaceful coexistence and inclusive resolutions of local conflict through training and mentoring the local community in collaborative dispute resolution (CDR) mechanisms
6) Distribute dignity kits to women and adolescent girls.
7) Provision of legal aid and counselling

Syria HRP for UNICEF Protection Strengthening Child Protection interventions for girls and boys most at risk of violence, abuse, neglect and exploitation across whole of Syria In line with the CP Area of Responsibility (AOR) Strategy and the “No Lost Generation” framework, UNICEF will enhance equitable access to quality CP services with a resilience focus, including for Survivors of abuse, violence, neglect and exploitation as well as children with disabilities, targeting 117 high severity sub-districts (3 to 5) and 38 low severity ones.

UNICEF’s CP Strategy in 2022-2023 includes:
• Addressing behavioural, social, cultural and economic determinants of CP violations as a prevention approach.  
• Improving the reach and quality of specialized CP services
• Capacity development of CP responders
•  Monitoring, evidence generation and advocacy 

UNICEF will support the delivery of integrated programming that will encourage social transformation, prioritizing:
• Structured and sustained CP MHPSS and EORE programmes
• Specialized integrated CP services including case management for survivors of violence, exploitation, neglect and abuse (child labour, CAFAAG, child survivors of GBV, child marriages, justice for children, birth registration and unaccompanied or separated children amongst others) 
• Parenting programmes to promote positive child rearing skills and experience for caregivers
• Elimination of violence against children, including GBV prevention and empowerment for girls, boys and women, prevention of violence in schools, homes and communities.
• Awareness-raising on CP risks
• Capacity development of CP responders and social workers

UNICEF will generate evidence to inform the humanitarian response and advocacy including setting up an information management system for case management. UNICEF will embrace new delivery modalities and implement cash transfers aimed at child protection outcomes for vulnerable families. UNICEF will also continue to support the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism on grave violations against children.

CP services will be delivered by partners based on minimum standards and IASC guidelines. 7,200 CP and social workers will be trained on case management, MHPSS, EORE, advocacy, evidence generation and coordination across sectors for a comprehensive CP response.
 
UNICEF will support MHPSS for 364,000 children to benefit from improved mental health and social wellbeing. UNICEF will equip 61,500 parents and caregivers with skills to provide a stimulating and safe environment at home, including reduced violence.  

Violence prevention is a key priority. Family violence prevalence is high for girls 12-17 years (47%), boys 12-17 years (44%), boys below 12 (45%) and girls below 12 (44%) (UNICEF 2018). UNICEF will work to protect children from violence and abuse through prevention activities in schools, homes and communities and providing survivors of violence with child-friendly and gender sensitive services. Support will be provided for PSEA mechanisms to protect beneficiaries and build the capacity of humanitarian actors. PSEA programming will be implemented with the Protection Sector AORs.

Based on HNO 2021, one in three communities in Syria is reportedly contaminated by explosive ordnance. One in four victims is a child (Joint MA & CP Analysis, 2020). EORE messages will be provided to 1,460,000 children and adults through humanitarian actors and public service providers using static facilities and mobile teams. UNICEF will build the capacity of partners to provide quality EORE that is age, gender and disability appropriate and to provide child victims with assistance.
 
UNICEF will strengthen the justice system to ensure that children in contact with the law victims, offenders or witnesses are protected through child-friendly, gender-sensitive services, that are community-based and family focused.

As Lead Agency for the CP AOR, UNICEF will ensure coordination needs at Hub and WOS levels. Two UN-led and one INGO-led coordination hubs in Damascus, Gaziantep and NES, as well as a WOS overall coordination system, to ensure coherence across the CP response.

States, Improved food security and livelihoods of IDPs, Returnees and Vulnerable host communities in South Sudan The purpose of the project is to improve food consumption, food security, dietary diversity and coping strategies and enhance emergency food production of vulnerable populations in the targeted counties. This will be achieved through provision of Cash-Based Transfers (CBT) to address food needs of vulnerable communities during the lean season and provision of timely and appropriate complementary vegetable and crop livelihood inputs and fishing kits coupled with training in improved agronomic and fishing practices.
In line with the South Sudan FSL cluster HRP objectives and priorities, NPA will support vulnerable populations in IPC 4 and 5 locations as well as some IPC 3 locations. Specifically, NPA will target Canal/Pigi, Fangak, Pochalla and Bor South Counties of Jonglei State, Rumbek East, Rumbek Centre, Cueibet, Yirol East, Yirol West and Awerial Counties of Lakes State, Terekeka County of Central Equatoria State and Kapoeta North County of Eastern Equatoria State.

NPA seeks to support 86,200 HHs (517,200 individuals) through provision of complementary vegetable and crop livelihood inputs and fishing kits across the target counties. Some of the kits will be provided by FAO (core pipeline) while the rest will be procured and distributed directly by NPA to enhance food production.  NPA will build the capacity of the HHs supported with the kits through training on improved agronomic and fishing practices, marketing and group dynamics. A Training of Trainers (ToT) approach will be utilized whereby lead farmers and fisher folk will be trained by NPA. They will then train/share the knowledge and skills with other farmers and fisher folk in their communities. The kits provided through this project and the knowledge gained from the trainings is expected to improve the agricultural and fishing practices of the target HHs thus enhancing and sustaining food production. CBT interventions will target 1,000 HHs (6,000 individuals ) in Rumbek East, Rumbek Centre and Cuiebet Counties in Lakes State to improve their access to food, diversify and improve their food consumption and dietary diversity scores and promote the adoption of positive coping strategies. The planned interventions are aligned to the FSL cluster objectives 1 and 2 and will provide emergency assistance and livelihoods support to save lives and avert total collapse of livelihoods in the target counties.

NPA will integrate development-oriented and conflict-sensitivity activities in this project to enhance the resilience of  vulnerable HHs in line with the Triple Nexus. Therefore, 1,200 vulnerable HHs will be supported with small-scale cash grants to establish IGAs. The target HHs will be mobilized and sensitized to transition to and establish VSLA’s to ease access to financial services and encourage the spirit of saving among the VSLA group members. The IGAs will contribute to increasing and diversifying income and building the resilience of the target HHs at the same time improving functionality of local markets and boosting the local value chains.

NPA will employ a community-based beneficiary selection approach which will entail establishing Project Management Committees (PMCs) to lead the selection of eligible beneficiaries based on the beneficiary selection criteria. Vulnerable HHs with severe food insecurity including female, child, disabled/chronically ill headed HHs; persons living with or at risk of HIV/AIDS and the elderly will be targeted in this project. 
NPA will ensure meaningful engagement of the target communities throughout the project life-cycle through holding regular meetings with the PMCs and community members and Post Distribution Monitoring (PDM) to get their feedback on the project. NPA will ensure that the feedback is incorporated in the implementation of this project and design of future projects. Further, NPA will use a community-based complaints and feedback mechanism to provide a platform for beneficiaries to voice any issues or concerns.

The economic, financial, political, and pandemic crises in Lebanon, have affected every aspect of children’s lives, including education, nutrition, and mental health. According to the assessment “Children’s future on the line” conducted by UNICEF on June 2021, nine per cent of families sent their children to work, 15 per cent stopped their education, and 60 per cent had to buy their food on credit or borrow money.
The outlook of the future is grim. The World Bank says the economy looks likely to contract by a further 9.5 per cent in 2021 and has warned that there is “no clear turning point in the horizon” (Lebanon Economic Monitor, Spring 2021). The longer children in Lebanon are out of school, the higher the possibility that they will experience violence and exploitation, including child labor and child marriage. The increasing socio-economic pressure on families in Lebanon during the economic and COVID-19 crisis, increases this possibility. The increased pressure on children to support their families may lead to an increase in psychosocial distress and negative coping mechanisms.
•	Migration from Private to Public Schools
In the scholastic year 2020-2021, around 54,000 students transitioned from private to the public schools. MEHE estimates that another 50,000-60,000 Lebanese students will transfer from private to public schools during the SY 2021/2022, resulting in 100,00- 120,000 Lebanese students migrating to public schools. This will pause additional challenges to an already stressed system. A hiring freeze of teachers in public schools has been in place for around 2 years. With the rapid increase in number of students in public schools, human resources are required to match the demand. However, due to the unprecedented diminishing value of the LBP, teacher salaries in the public system are now valued at less than 1 USD per hour, which is pausing yet another serious risk of teachers leaving the schools or be on strike more often.
The purpose of this project would be to provide direct community support measures to most vulnerable Lebanese and migrant children to retain them in education and to ensure that students affected by the economic crisis are provided relevant, inclusive and quality education adhering to national and international standards on education in emergencies and child protection by ensuring that schools have maintained their basic educational resources, including adequate human resources. Ana Aqra is suggesting the “Safe Enabling Learning Environments: a Shared Responsibility” project as part of the Lebanon emergency response plan.
Aqra strives to make learning accessible to all children and works to support the education sector and the public school to respond to the specific needs of all children as well as empowering partnerships to partake in the responsibility for the safe and enabling learning of girls and boys.

Targeting criteria, intervention and mechanism:
This project will support 10,000 girls and boys and 75 public schools, including those receiving learners transferred from the private sector. The project activities will include provision of funds to ensure that students affected by the economic crisis are provided relevant, inclusive and quality education adhering to national and international standards on education in emergencies and child protection. The project will also ensure that schools will receive necessary stationery, books, and funds to cover operational costs and adequate human resources. It will also ensure school retention of most vulnerable girls and boys by providing them and their caregivers with direct community support program, including remote awareness sessions, remote PSS/SEL activities, responsive caregiving and remote basic and digital literacy to parents /caregivers, assistive technologies for children with disabilities, cash for education support and food parcels during the academic year 2022-2023.

Protection Response for Vulnerable Lebanese and Other Resident Populations According to OCHA, approximately 393,000 people across 26 districts are in need of GBV services in 2022, a significant increase from 67,000 people in need in the 2021 ERP. Around a quarter of Lebanese households reported having safety and security concerns for women in their community (OCHA, 2022). The GBVIMS shows that in the last quarter of 2022, the most common types of GBV incidents were physical assault and emotional abuse mostly happening in the context of intimate partner violence, followed by forced marriage. Protection risks for all targeted populations remains high, with women and girls facing significant risks of multiple forms of GBV. The economic insecurity combined with different levels of crisis affecting the country as well as risks related to legal status, add to these vulnerabilities. Shortage in electricity and increased transportation and telecom prices all act as contributing factors to different forms of GBV in all locations. Sexual harassment through online platform and cyber abuse is an emerging GBV trend. Another alarming trend is the increased rates of sexual exploitation by landlords and employers especially affecting female heads of households with financial vulnerability.  Preventing, mitigating, and responding to GBV in emergencies is a lifesaving priority and an essential component of humanitarian action, especially in a country with extreme structural gender inequalities.

 During the dire economic situation in the country, the team will look at the effects of the family on this period, and its goal is the ability to mitigate its effects on both, society and family.

project is focused towards  supporting conflict affected  households in BAY states to rebuild their resilient capacities to respond to shocks and stresses Emergency Food Security and Livelihood assistance to vulnerable and conflict affected households in north east Nigeria Food insecurity and malnutrition remain prevalent across Nigeria, mainly driven by the ongoing protracted conflict in the Northeast, mass displacement and the resultant IDP return process, adverse climate change and variability, such as drought, long dry spells, and flood, land degradation increasing insecurity and banditry, natural resource-based conflicts and an unfavorable macroeconomic situation manifested in rising food price inflation, etc. Further, the disruption of food and agricultural input supply chains by the Russia-Ukrainian war has led to severe availability and access constraints especially for poor farming households because of high food and agricultural input prices, especially fertilizer.
Despite the efforts of humanitarian communities in addressing the manifestations of the emergency in the country, the situation of food security continues to be a challenge. According to the latest Cadre Harmonise (CH) analysis, an estimated 19.45 million people, nearly 63 percent of them in Northeast and Northwest Nigeria are projected to be at risk of severe food insecurity during the peak of the 2022 lean season. In addition, the latest IPC acute malnutrition analysis report released in June 2022 estimates that 1.4 million children and, nearly 152,000 pregnant and lactating women are likely to suffer acute malnutrition during this period. Therefore, the urgent need for an expanded humanitarian food security response cannot be overstated. While the humanitarian interventions have been playing vital and critical role in addressing the needs of affected populations, it is obvious more has to be done to support the resilience of the livelihoods and the households. Given that the majority of those in need are involved in agriculture related activities, it has become necessary and urgent to promote agriculture-based livelihoods to famers whose majority are smallholders.  
In 2021 FAO reached over 1 million people and is planning to scale up and reach 2 million people (approximately 285,715 households) in need of agricultural-based livelihoods assistance in Nigeria in 2023/2024 with a stronger focus on Northeast and Northwest Nigeria due to the high level of vulnerability in the two regions. Due to restrictions on target numbers submitted in the HRP and its limited coverage (only targeting the Northeast), 1.7 million people will be targeted through the HRP while the remaining 0.3 million will be planned outside the HRP framework. To achieve this target FAO Nigeria is requiring a total of USD 86 million. Notably, funding for agriculture livelihood had declined significantly, for example, in 2022 the livelihood and agriculture funding stand at 6%, while food assistance is 95% covered. This requires a strong coordinated advocacy strategy to shift the paradigm.  An estimated 1.7 million people will be targeted for emergency agricultural livelihoods assistance while 0.3 million will be targeted for resilience interventions including in agribusiness, skills development for the creation of decent employment and income such as stoves production, aquaculture, livestock, etc. that increase the resilience of the beneficiaries.  
The scale-up plan will target the most vulnerable groups including IDPs, returnees, and host communities, especially women, and girls.    FAO Nigeria provides various agricultural livelihood assistance packages based on the livelihoods of the targeted household and the related activity. This is including agricultural rainy and dry season inputs, livestock restocking goats and poultry, urban and peri-urban homestead gardening, aquaculture, agribusiness enterprise support, nutritional support, and SAFE kits. This intervention will be delivered through a combination of in-kind, cash, and cash+ assistance. The scale-up plan is aligned to the FAO Corporate Global strategy framework of achieving Better Production, Better Nutrition, Better environment and Better life.

In 2021 FAO reached over 1 million people and is planning to scale up and reach 2 million people (approximately 285,715 households) in need of agricultural-based livelihoods assistance in Nigeria in 2023/2024 with a stronger focus on Northeast and Northwest Nigeria due to the high level of vulnerability in the two regions. Due to restrictions on target numbers submitted in the HRP and its limited coverage (only targeting the Northeast), 1.7 million people will be targeted through the HRP while the remaining 0.3 million will be planned outside the HRP framework. To achieve this target FAO Nigeria is requiring a total of USD 86 million. Notably, funding for agriculture livelihood had declined significantly, for example, in 2022 the livelihood and agriculture funding stand at 6%, while food assistance is 95% covered. This requires a strong coordinated advocacy strategy to shift the paradigm.  An estimated 1.7 million people will be targeted for emergency agricultural livelihoods assistance while 0.3 million will be targeted for resilience interventions including in agribusiness, skills development for the creation of decent employment and income such as stoves production, aquaculture, livestock, etc. that increase the resilience of the beneficiaries.  
The scale-up plan will target the most vulnerable groups including IDPs, returnees, and host communities, especially women, and girls.    FAO Nigeria provides various agricultural livelihood assistance packages based on the livelihoods of the targeted household and the related activity. This is including agricultural rainy and dry season inputs, livestock restocking goats and poultry, urban and peri-urban homestead gardening, aquaculture, agribusiness enterprise support, nutritional support, and SAFE kits. This intervention will be delivered through a combination of in-kind, cash, and cash+ assistance. The scale-up plan is aligned to the FAO Corporate Global strategy framework of achieving Better Production, Better Nutrition, Better environment and Better life.

WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM). WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.

WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace.

Renforcement de la protection des populations affectées par les conflits
(2023 portion of EUR 1.6 mio) Renforcement de l'environnement protecteur des personnes vulnérables affectées par les conflits au Niger Afin de répondre aux besoins de protection des personnes vulnérables affectées par les conflits et de les renforcer dans leurs droits, DRC identifie des cas de protection et leur apporte une première assistance psychologique (Premiers Secours Psychologiques - PSP). En fonction de leurs besoins de protection (vulnérabilités, risques auxquels ils sont exposés), DRC fournit des assistances de protection d'urgence (API, SNF) et/ou un appui psychosocial, et réfère les cas de protection auxquels ses services ne peuvent pas répondre directement. Ces référencement sont effectués soit vers des structures externes (ex: services techniques déconcentrés, ONG locales, ONG internationales), soit en interne, vers d'autres départements d'intervention de DRC (par exemple, le département Sécurité Alimentaire et Relèvement Économique). En tant que partenaire du RRM, DRC réalise des Évaluations Rapides de Protection (ERP) et adapte ses interventions de protection aux ménages enregistrés suite à des déplacements de populations, sur des cycles de  3 mois d'intervention. DRC contribue par ailleurs aux renforcements des capacités des structures communautaires (conformément à l'approche de protection communautaire), et collabore avec elles afin de mieux connaitre en temps réels les tendances de protection (risques, besoins, etc.),  dans le cadre du monitoring de protection. 

La stratégie d'intervention de DRC dans le secteur de la protection se base sur l'approche vulnérabilité, en ce qu'elle vise à fournir une assistance adaptée à toutes les personnes vulnérables affectées par les conflits (PDI, communautés hôtes),  adaptée à leurs besoins spécifiques  liés à leur âge, leur genre et leurs vulnérabiltités propres (enfants,  personnes âgées, Femmes Enceintes et Femmes Allaitantes - FEFA, personnes en situation de handicap, etc.). DRC s'assure que ses interventions de protection sont réalisées de manière sûre, accessible, redevable et participative pour l'ensemble de ses bénéficiaires.

Verbesserter Zugang zu lebensrettenden Dienstleistungen der sexuellen und reproduktiven Gesundheit und Schutz für Vertriebene und Aufnahmegemeinschaften in der Demokratischen Republik Kongo, im Südsudan und in Uganda Creating a Safe Environment for and Providing Life-Saving GBV Response Services as well as integrating child protection components to the Crisis-Affected Women, Girls and Children in South Sudan In line with the identified needs and gaps, CARE International in South Sudan aims to provide a comprehensive package of GBV response services, which will be complemented with the prevention activities that address the root causes of the GBV in Juba, Magwi, Ikotos, Torit, Kapoeta North, Budi, Wau, Jur River, Koch, Rubkona, Pariang, Bor South, Pibor, Twic East, Duk and Akobo.  The interventions will be provided through static centers and through mobile and outreach teams. Static Women Girls Safe Spaces (WGFS) will be used as entry points to reach out to the communities, while outreach sessions by mobile teams will also be used as means of engaging with communities. The WGFSs will serve as the centers where women and girls can come together and socialize while also improving their psychosocial wellbeing. In order to do that CARE will provide structured and unstructured PSS activities. The unstructured activities will take the form of recreational activities which will be determined in consultation with the women and girls, i.e.. knitting, baking, sewing, painting or handicrafts. The structured activities on the other hand will aim to promote overall life skills of women and girls. Similarly, CARE will train women and girls on usage and set up of Fuel Efficient Stoves as part of GBV risk mitigation measures. These efforts will be supported with experience sharing sessions among women on cooking or sharing recipes to promote cohesion and communication among women groups. CARE will also offer income generation activities to the women and girls who fit into the activity criteria, which will include vulnerable individuals, survivors, female-headed households and so on.

Through the WGFSs, CARE will provide GBV case management services to the survivors, while ensuring updating (or creating referral pathways) referral pathways and service mappings for these locations to provide safe referrals to the services. As part of the individual case management plans, CARE will also provide one-time cash assistance to support the GBV survivors, when deemed necessary according to the developed SOPs. Community members who need legal advice and/or need to attend legal information sessions will also be provided with legal support at the WGFSs. Women and girls of reproductive age, who fit into vulnerability criteria set up in line with UNFPA's guidance will also be provided with dignity kits to ensure they can maintain their dignity and mobility in a crisis context.

CARE will also additionally provide awareness raising sessions to raise awareness on key gender and protection topics, as well as gender equality through mobile teams and at the WGFSs. This will help to engage men and boys in the discussions. Similarly, CARE will lead on the primary prevention activities by engaging men and boys through structured curriculums such as EMAP and Program RA.

In order to ensure that the staff are well equipped to provide support to the communities, all frontline staff and community mobilizers will be trained in various topics including case management, PSS, GBV risk mitigation and GBV core concepts. CARE's previous and existing presence in the aforementioned locations, as well as GBV programming experience in these locations will help to ensure community buy-in and prevent backlash from the communities. 

CARE will partner with UNIDOR to implement CP activities to provide case management, PSS, referrals to support child GBV survivors.
