Renforcement des systèmes de préparation, d’alerte et de réponses aux chocs multirisques des autorités locales dans la région de Tillabéri
(2023 portion of EUR 400,000) Appui à l'amélioration de l'accès à l’eau potable, l’assainissement et l’hygiène dans les sites des déplacés et communautés hôtes dans les régions de Tillabéri, Maradi et Diffa La détérioration de la situation humanitaire au Niger est alarmante. Bien que les partenaires EHA s’efforcent de fournir une aide humanitaire de qualité dans les régions de Tillabéri , Maradi et Diffa, les besoins subsistent en raison de l’insécurité, de mouvements de populations et des aléas climatiques. L’aide humanitaire, principalement pour des raisons liées à l’accès et au manque de financements, est actuellement en quantité insuffisante pour avoir l’impact attendu sur les populations vulnérables. Dans 80% des 425 localités évaluées par REACH dans la région de Tillabéri, les personnes interrogées ont rapporté ne pas avoir bénéficié d’assistance. En conséquence, les conditions de vie des populations hôtes et déplacées continuent de se détériorer
Les services de base en EHA sont largement insuffisants dans ces départements; étant pourtant fortement exposés aux déplacements, inondations, épidémies et malnutrition. L’évaluation d’IRC a montré que les mouvements de population viennent amplifier des problèmes et déficits structurels d’accès à l’eau et aux infrastructures d’assainissement. Dans les villages hôtes, l’approvisionnement en eau se fait via des puits traditionnels, sans système d’exhaure approprié, qui mettent à risque les usagers.
A Tillabéri, depuis 2019, IRC mène également une intervention EHA visant à améliorer l’accès à l’eau pour plus de 30,000 bénéficiaires . IRC bénéficie donc d’une bonne acceptance de la part des acteurs locaux et a une forte capacité de déploiement pour conduire les activités proposées.
L’intervention proposée par IRC visera à contribuer à améliorer les conditions de vie des personnes vulnérables de l arégion de Tillabéri, MAradi et Diffa. En lien avec les objectifs du Cluster, elle permettra de cibler les personnes déplacées et communautés hôtes impactées et résidant dans des zones difficiles d’accès. IRC, en partenariat avec l’ONG ADKOUL, contribuera directement à améliorer l’accès des populations vulnérables de la région de Tillabéri aux services de base EHA, via (i) des constructions et réhabilitations d’ouvrages pérennes en conformité avec les standards SPHERE ; (ii) la construction de latrines familiales et (iii) un package complet d’activités de sensibilisations aux bonnes pratiques d’hygiène et gestion des conflits liés à l’accès aux ressources via des relais communautaires. Pour faciliter l’appropriation du projet et assurer sa durabilité, des comités des gestion des points d’eau seront mis en place.

Save the Children International Humanitarian Fund nonthematic, flexible Nutrition Provision of Integrated lifesaving Nutrition interventions to conflict affected populations in Jonglei, Eastern Equatoria states and Abyei administrative area in South Sudan. Through the proposed response, Save the Children International will provide integrated lifesaving nutrition service to the population in Akobo West, Budi , Bor, Kapoeta, Lopa Lafon, Magwi, Nyirol, Torit Counties, and Abyei administrative area. The aim of this is to reduce suffering, morbidity, and mortality related to malnutrition among vulnerable populations, SCI's proposed response will focus both treatment and preventative approaches, using community-based management of acute malnutrition (CMAM) and infant and young child feeding (IYCF) approaches. SCI Emergency nutrition programs will include. i) Community mobilization to increase access and coverage of CMAM services, ii) Treatment of children and PWLs with acute malnutrition through inpatient and Outpatient therapeutic programs. iii) blanket Supplementary feeding program. iv) Institutional feeding program (IFP), v) Maternal dietary supplementation, vi) Promotion of optimal IYCF through mother-to-mother support groups. vii) Improving Dietary Diversity through household kitchen gardening, viii) Strengthen nutrition information systems and operations research to ensure an evidence-based response, ix) Building capacity for frontline nutrition workers and institutions at all levels. SCI will work through communities to promote, protect and support recommended IYCF practices through one-on-one counselling and group message and counselling. Besides the CMAM and behaviour change interventions, SCI will implement cash transfer intervention in selected areas targeting families of severely malnourished children and SAM PLW to maximize the program's nutrition outcomes and reduce the relapse of acute malnutrition among under-five children and PLW. Through this response, SCI will support 104 static OTP/TSFPs and eight stabilization centres integrated with health facilities. The service will be delivered through static and outreach/mobile facilities for remote and hard-to-reach areas in the targeted project locations. SCI will work with MOH, UNICEF and WFP to secure timely provision of Nutrition supplies necessary for Nutrition Service Delivery. SCI will reach 73,683 under-five Children and 66,992 PLW. 
SCI will make deliberate efforts to enhance coordination and integration with the Health, WASH, FSL, Protection and Education clusters to address the causes of malnutrition through a multi-sectoral approach that aims to reduce vulnerabilities, prevent malnutrition and build resilience among the vulnerable people. Specific multi-sectoral activities are to increase access to safe water and sanitation, promote critical WASH messages, and integrate early childhood development strategies in nutrition treatment sites. Kitchen gardening, screening and treating of malaria, managing diarrhea, and mainstreaming child protection and gender-based violence risk mitigation will also be promoted at the nutrition sites.y. SCI will also support hygiene interventions to improve nutrition outcomes and reduce risk of hygiene-related morbidities
SCI will monitor the nutrition situation and the needs of the affected people through KAP survey, SMART surveys, monthly nutrition programme data collection and analysis, and joint field monitoring visits. Spot checks, supportive supervision and monitoring visits will monitor service delivery and engage with the community and other stakeholders to gauge evolving needs. Community nutrition volunteers will be supported to undertake household visits, conduct regular screening of malnourished children and women to ensure timely detection and treatment, and report on a monthly basis. Data collection tools and analysis will be strengthened to enhance monitoring of integrated services

Comprehensive life saving GBV services to affected women and girls in  the North West and South Regions of Cameroon Strengthening Gender Based Violence prevention & response services  to conflict-affected populations in the North West & South West regions of Cameroon Since 2016, the Northwest and Southwest regions of Cameroon have been involved in a crisis which started as a teacher-lawyer strike and degenerated into what has been dubbed an armed conflict. 
In North West and South West, 53% of women are exposed to risk of violence during travelling, 33% of the avoided sites by women and girls are water points and 32% are latrines. In terms of GBV, 18% of the protection issues in the accessed villages were identified to face GBV 29% exposed to sexual violence, 17% forced into marriages, 10% child marriages, 10% domestic violence and 19% unable to access services. 30% of accessed locations do not have women and girls safe space. 
Incidences of emotional violence, denial of resources, opportunities and services, physical violence, rape and sexual assault, and forced marriage continue to be reported mostly by women and girls, as intimate partner violence or committed by known or unknown persons including armed men. As per the GBV IMS data a total of 7,996 GBV survivors received specialized GBV services from January to September in North West, South West and the Far North. It includes 79% of IPV, 20% of sexual violence. More 90% of GBV survivors in NW and SW and 100% in FN are women. Reported incidents are a sign of response capacity but not of the prevalence, as many barriers including closure of services in most parts of the North West and South West (NW, SW), lack of access to services, lack of awareness about available services hamper survivors to report and seek services. Despite efforts deployed, GBV protection services and GBV prevention mechanisms are insufficient or totally absent in many localities. The limited funding allocated to the GBV sector in 2022 resulted in the suspension of services in some locations. Many GBV survivors did not have access to specialised services, risking infection of STI or HIV, mental distress and unwanted pregnancy. From 2021-2022 there was 35% decrease in GBV services delivery. In both NWSW and FN some health facilities are not functional, or don’t have resources to provide Clinical Management of Rape services.  In 2022 only 0,01% (as per FTS) of the requested GBV funding was granted. The situation in 2023 will get worse for 953,524 women and girls, the most exposed to GBV risks and 33,854 men and boys as well, if no attention and adequate support and resources are allocated to address GBV needs
The main activities will focus on sensitization and awareness raising for communities, emphasizing the participation of men and boys, strengthen referral and legal assistance mechanisms for internally displaced persons and host communities with legal protection needs (detention/documentation, GBV survivors etc.), provide basic vocational training and economic/Empowerment support to women and girls, Provide cash transfer assistance, build the capacity of operational organizations on the holistic response to GBV. UNFPA and partners will continue providing individualized case management and psychosocial support to survivors of GBV and other vulnerable people. Finally, UNFPA, in collaboration with the Ministry of Women Empowerment and the Family (MINPROFF), will also continue to reinforce close collaboration between actors and service providers involved in responding to the needs of women and girls. Ensure that safe and ethical systems for the transfer of data including confidential personal records of GBV survivors are put in place by organizations and authorities.

Fortalecimiento de la SAN y la resiliencia de las comunidades vulnerables, a través de un modelo de Alimentación Escolar saludable proveniente de la Agricultura Familiar local. La persistencia de la crisis económica y política en Venezuela durante los últimos años ha colocado a una parte importante de su población en situación de extrema precariedad. Las interrupciones de las actividades educativas y la cadena de suministro de alimentos locales debido a la pandemia COVID-19, ha afectado profundamente la oportunidad de la población vulnerable, incluidos niños en edad escolar y familias productoras, de acceder a alimentos esenciales y a insumos productivos que fortalezcan su SAN, respectivamente. 
En este sentido, durante el periodo 2020-2021, la cobertura del Programa de Alimentación Escolar (PAE) ha tenido deficiencia en frecuencia, ingesta nutricional y dieta equilibrada para no menos de 4.5 millones de niños y se estima que alrededor de 1.1 millones corren el riego de abandonar la Escuela. Al mismo tiempo, la disminución continua de la producción local de alimentos se agrava por el limitado acceso a insumos agrícolas esenciales -como semillas con calidad- por parte de los pequeños productores, agravando la inseguridad alimentaria y financiera preexistente en las comunidades.
Por lo anterior expuesto, la presente acción tiene como propósito principal el de mejorar la SAN de niños y niñas en edad escolar, además de los hogares rurales en situación de vulnerabilidad, esto, mediante el desarrollo de modelos de Alimentación Escolar basados en la producción local que FAO y UNICEF han pilotado y validad en cuatro estados del país. Complementariamente, la acción promoverá esquemas comunitarios de producción variada de semillas de forma artesanal, adaptadas climáticamente y que respetan la cultura y saberes locales productivos. 
Bajo este objetivo, se propone el desarrollo de los siguientes componentes:
PRODUCTO 1: Fortalecido el modelo de Alimentación Escolar basado en la producción local de la Agricultura Familiar (AF): A través de rehabilitar y/o mejorar las capacidades productivas de las Escuelas Técnicas Agrícolas (ETA) y Asociación Local de Productores (ALP) incrementando su productividad aplicando prácticas agroecológicas para producción de alimentos, huevos y semillas, además desarrollando acciones de asistencia técnica. Se espera que, con la disponibilidad de una producción local de huevos, hortalizas y frutas, se logre fomentar modelos alimentarios de circuito corto, saludables y sostenibles, en donde los niños y niñas de edad escolar en situación de vulnerabilidad - y de manera indirecta el de familias vulnerables de agricultores de pequeña escala - mejoran el consumo de alimentos diversificados, frescos y nutritivos.
PRODUCTO 2: Mejorado el acceso a semillas con calidad, por parte de los pequeños productores familiares locales; a través de una implementación de un modelo de producción de semillas comunitario, sostenibles y resilientes. En este modelo, las ETA jugarán un rol de motor de producción y difusión de conocimiento y los productores a través de las ALP, serán el factor de escalamiento de la capacidad de producción y accesibilidad de la semillas para los demás productores
Para la implementación del proyecto se han priorizado estados con población indígena y, cuando sea posible, se dará la prioridad de participación a agricultoras y agricultores indígenas y a mujeres líderes de hogar, en los estados Amazonas, Sucre, Monagas, Falcon, Zulia, Delta Amacuro, Bolívar y Apure. La acción espera dar cobertura a alrededor de 13 750 hogares de pequeños productores y productoras, aglutinando alrededor de 450 grupos productivos y/o Bancos de Semillas Comunitarios, que contribuyan a la protección y acumulación de sus medios de vida productivos esenciales y en conjunto con 50 ETAs y 25 escuelas de educación básica y primaria, puedan abastecer complementos alimentarios frescos y sanos para alrededor 27 000 niños y niñas en edad escolar.

Strengthening the Emergency Protection Response for internally displaced people (IDPs) in Upper Nile, Unity and Northern Jonglei states Enhancing IDP Protection Services in South Sudan to facilitate and scale up protection monitoring, targeted Protection Assistance and Services (including GBV and CP), as well as HLP support to the most vulnerable IDPs and Returnees The projects seek to ensure that those most in need, most vulnerable or at risk, so-called Persons with Specific Needs (PSNs) in IDP, returnee and host communities are supported with tailored protection services and assistance, focused on lifesaving support, while also investing in people’s resilience to shocks. Restoration of housing, land and property rights, civil documentation, child protection and prevention and response services for GBV will be part of this general protection project. The activities will be implemented through UNHCR’s offices in Juba, Wau, Bentiu, Bor, Malakal, Yei, Yambio and prioritized respective counties in line with the Cluster’s prioritization.

The project will support the implementation of the Protection Monitoring System that was launched in October 2022 under the umbrella of the Protection Cluster aimed at informing the protection and wider humanitarian response with protection analysis and based on a harmonized methodology and tools. Protection concerns identified will be dealt with both on individual protection services/case management basis and through community-based protection responses tailored to the specific needs and considering the age, gender, diversity among the people served. Community based protection components of this project will involve community owned projects with social cohesion and peace benefits in areas with social tension as well as areas where durable solutions are pursued.  Particular attention is paid to segments of the community particular at risk or marginalized, including women and youth empowerment, tailored support to GBV survivors and children at risk as well as people with disabilities and older persons. 

Protection risks and social tensions will be prevented and mitigated through awareness and information campaigns, community sensitization using an AGD approach and community engagement, such as community action committees, peace dialogues, including by involving leaders of faith-based institutions. Quality procedures to identify those most in need, vulnerable and at risk will be implemented across all project locations, building on the protection monitoring reports and implemented through protection desks and protection outreach, including through static and mobile teams. Protection services and assistance will be multi-faceted and tailored to the specific assistance and protection needs identified, including to survivors of gender-based violence and children at risk amongst other at risk categories. Direct protection services and assistance includes identification of people at risk, counselling, social accompaniment, enabling access to safety, case management, psychosocial support, legal aid (including assistance and representation), as well as material support tailored to the individual, including in kind (e.g. mobility device, core relief) or cash, implemented through a cash plus approach. The project will also specifically address housing, land and property rights and implement individual assistance and community-based mechanisms, such as through community-based land committees, to restore access to housing, land and property as well as to related documentation, including HLP, identity and civil documentation. This is complemented by community services, including child friendly spaces, rehabilitation of community infrastructure or basic services through community-owned approaches. 

Overall, the project empowers communities affected by displacement, conflict and disasters, and invests in their own agency and resilience through the multi-faceted nature of the protection response provided under this project.

South Sudan	South Sudan Humanitarian Response Plan 2023 Protection and Assistance for Refugees, Returnees and Asylum Seekers in South Sudan As of January 2022, there are some 335,000 refugees and asylum seekers from neighbouring countries sheltering in South Sudan. Despite enormous socio-economic, security and political challenges, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, South Sudan has maintained its open-door policy for people seeking international protection, the majority of whom are women and children, primarily from Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Central African Republic.
At the same time, against a backdrop of fragile peace and cautious optimism for longer term stability, hundreds of thousands of South Sudanese refugees have spontaneously returned to the country since the signing of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement. While UNHCR is not promoting or facilitating return to South Sudan, this spontaneous movement has prompted the development of an area-based approach, to support refugees, returnees and host communities, through enhanced engagement with development actors, to support greater access to services where possible.
Refugees largely reside in conflict-affected regions, challenged by an unpredictable security environment as well as at times fragile relations with host communities. Displaced communities will continue to rely on life-saving humanitarian assistance provided by UNHCR and its partners as a result of enduring economic hardship, weak rule of law, limited development support and a lack of social services and infrastructure in refugee-hosting areas as well as in areas of origin. A reduction in basic assistance, especially during a global pandemic, will immediately lead to the deterioration of the humanitarian situation to emergency levels, due to the absence of a safety net, including social services, community support networks and limited access to livelihoods in displacements sites hosting refugees and South Sudanese refugee returnees.
Under the refugee response, all refugees and asylum seekers registered with UNHCR will benefit from various forms of protection interventions, including individual registration and documentation, and multi-sector assistance. Specific protection services, such as SGBV response and child protection will focus on the identified at-risk groups. While water, health, nutrition and education services will continue to maintain indicators within global standards for refugees living in camps, provision of other assistance, including shelter, non-food items and livelihoods support, will be undertaken in a targeted manner, focusing on persons with specific protection needs and vulnerabilities. This will primarily be achieved through participatory assessments, surveys as well as verification exercise to identify vulnerable refugees and their needs. Impact monitoring will be used to gauge the efficiency of projects implemented and for the purposes of course-correction in terms of better targeting of assistance. The needs of persons with disabilities and the elderly will be further mainstreamed in various multi-sector response services. Vulnerable refugees in urban settings will also continue to benefit from targeted protection interventions and facilitation of their access to national services.

Food assistance and livelihoods support to vulnerable people in Amazonas, Apure and Sucre Programa de seguridad alimentaria basado en la escuela  Con el objetivo de contribuir a la seguridad alimentaria de la población con mayores necesidades, el Programa Mundial de Alimentos de Naciones Unidas (WFP, por sus siglas en inglés) en Venezuela desarrolla un programa de asistencia humanitaria basado en la escuela para garantizar el acceso de los más vulnerables a una alimentación adecuada y nutritiva en el entorno escolar, familiar y comunitario. 
Este programa inició en 2021 con comidas escolares en emergencias priorizando escuelas iniciales y de educación especial.

WFP proporciona comidas escolares acompañado de un paquete integrado de intervenciones para mejorar el acceso a alimentos nutritivos y diversificados a través de las escuelas, contribuyendo al mismo tiempo a mejorar la salud y la nutrición de los niños en edad escolar, los estudiantes con discapacidad y el personal escolar, y apoyando a las comunidades a reducir la dependencia en estrategias de afrontamiento. De manera gradual, el WFP está realizando compras locales de alimentos, e incluyendo acciones para apoyar los mercados locales con compras a pequeños productores y apoyo técnico para acceso a mercados.

En este sentido, el programa de comidas escolares en emergencias tiene los siguientes componentes, para asegurar un enfoque integral que apoye al estudiante en el entorno escolar y familiar:

1. Entrega de comidas escolares nutritivas para estudiantes y personal escolar, promoviendo las compras locales y a pequeños productores.
2. Apoyo a la seguridad alimentaria del hogar.
3. Rehabilitación de cocinas escolares para garantizar condiciones adecuadas de preparación de alimentos.
4. Comunicación para sensibilizar acerca de los principios humanitarios, la adecuada preparación de alimentos, nutrición, higiene y mantenimiento de cocinas escolares.
5. Fortalecimiento de capacidades de socios implementadores y personal escolar.
6. Acciones sensibles a la nutrición, que incluyen, tamizaje en las escuelas, educación nutricional, referencia a servicios especializados y entrega de alimento complementario fortificado (Super Cereal Plus).

Strengthening the Emergency Protection Response for internally displaced people (IDPs) in Upper Nile, Unity and Northern Jonglei states Enhancing IDP Protection Services in South Sudan to facilitate and scale up protection monitoring, targeted Protection Assistance and Services (including GBV and CP), as well as HLP support to the most vulnerable IDPs and Returnees The projects seek to ensure that those most in need, most vulnerable or at risk, so-called Persons with Specific Needs (PSNs) in IDP, returnee and host communities are supported with tailored protection services and assistance, focused on lifesaving support, while also investing in people’s resilience to shocks. Restoration of housing, land and property rights, civil documentation, child protection and prevention and response services for GBV will be part of this general protection project. The activities will be implemented through UNHCR’s offices in Juba, Wau, Bentiu, Bor, Malakal, Yei, Yambio and prioritized respective counties in line with the Cluster’s prioritization.

The project will support the implementation of the Protection Monitoring System that was launched in October 2022 under the umbrella of the Protection Cluster aimed at informing the protection and wider humanitarian response with protection analysis and based on a harmonized methodology and tools. Protection concerns identified will be dealt with both on individual protection services/case management basis and through community-based protection responses tailored to the specific needs and considering the age, gender, diversity among the people served. Community based protection components of this project will involve community owned projects with social cohesion and peace benefits in areas with social tension as well as areas where durable solutions are pursued.  Particular attention is paid to segments of the community particular at risk or marginalized, including women and youth empowerment, tailored support to GBV survivors and children at risk as well as people with disabilities and older persons. 

Protection risks and social tensions will be prevented and mitigated through awareness and information campaigns, community sensitization using an AGD approach and community engagement, such as community action committees, peace dialogues, including by involving leaders of faith-based institutions. Quality procedures to identify those most in need, vulnerable and at risk will be implemented across all project locations, building on the protection monitoring reports and implemented through protection desks and protection outreach, including through static and mobile teams. Protection services and assistance will be multi-faceted and tailored to the specific assistance and protection needs identified, including to survivors of gender-based violence and children at risk amongst other at risk categories. Direct protection services and assistance includes identification of people at risk, counselling, social accompaniment, enabling access to safety, case management, psychosocial support, legal aid (including assistance and representation), as well as material support tailored to the individual, including in kind (e.g. mobility device, core relief) or cash, implemented through a cash plus approach. The project will also specifically address housing, land and property rights and implement individual assistance and community-based mechanisms, such as through community-based land committees, to restore access to housing, land and property as well as to related documentation, including HLP, identity and civil documentation. This is complemented by community services, including child friendly spaces, rehabilitation of community infrastructure or basic services through community-owned approaches. 

Overall, the project empowers communities affected by displacement, conflict and disasters, and invests in their own agency and resilience through the multi-faceted nature of the protection response provided under this project.

Famine Response 2023 Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM). WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.
Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (light resilience- building activities, peace/conflict resolution training also called GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness, training, or sensitisation on peaceful resolution of conflicts, mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace. 
Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities.

Emergency aid in the areas of protection and health as well as cash transfers for those in particular need of protection Provision of lifesaving GBV interventions for the crisis affected populations in Mayendit, Rubkona, Koch and Panyijiar Counties IRC through the Women Protection and Empowerment program will provide specialized GBV response services and prevention interventions targeting the crisis affected populations in Mayendit, Rubkona, Koch and Panyijiar counties.  This will be through the provision of life saving GBV case management services guided by the survivor centered approach.  IRC will ensure the service provision is in coordination with other service providers for a multisectoral approach which comprise of medical, legal, safety and psychosocial support services. A total of 472(325W, 123G, 12M, 12B) will be targeted for case management services across the proposed locations. IRC will continuously engage women and girls and the community at large to identify barriers in accessing the GBV services and collaboratively work together to address them through the existing community-based protection structures. In addition, quarterly reviews and updating of the referral pathways as well as continuous feedback sessions will be held to ensure that the pathways are functional across the proposed locations. The women and girls’ safe spaces (2 Rubkona, 2 Koch, 2 Panyijiar and 2 Mayendit) will serve as avenues of empowerment for women and girls with a major focus on provision of contextualized psychosocial support interventions which seek to support in the healing, recovery and building resilience of women and girls. The Women and Girls Safe Space toolkit will be instrumental in providing guidance on the operationalization of the safe spaces especially in ensuring accountability as well as encouraging the women-girls led processes and ownership. Tailored curriculums for the engagement of women and girls such as Girl Shine for the adolescent girls and their care givers as well as Women Rise a psychosocial support tool kits for the women will ensure each age group has appropriate and contextualized PSS intervention. 4,500(3,180W, 1,320G) will be targeted for the WGSS activities. On GBV prevention IRC will engage communities through SASA! Together and EMAP as the primary GBV prevention approaches. The two approaches seek to provoke discussions on power imbalance as the root cause of violence while analyzing negative social norms, beliefs, behavior, and practices that contribute to violence against women and girls. Additionally, IRC seeks to build the capacity of communities to respond and prevent GBV through training and community led dialogues which will equip them with knowledge and skills. For GBV risk mitigation measures, IRC will work closely with women and community led structures to carry out GBV safety audits where action points to address the identified risks and concerns will be tasked to the relevant actors. Findings from the safety audits will inform other interventions such as training on Fuel Efficient Stoves for the women as well as production of reusable sanitary materials with the locally available raw materials. In coordination with the GBV SC, IRC will distribute dignity kits to the women and girls of reproductive age at risk of GBV. The proposed interventions aim to target 54,715 (27,904 Women, 19,150 Girls, 4,924 Men and 2737 Boys) where 78% IDP will be targeted, 18% host communities and 4% returnees. Out of the total target, 10% will be people living with disabilities.  IRC currently has presence in Koch, Rubkona (Bentiu IPD camp and in host communities) Panyijiar( Nyal and Ganyiel) and Mayendit. In all these locations, IRC is providing GBV response services, GBV community engagement activities including EMAP, SASA! and awareness raising activities, psychosocial support activities including skills building activities and capacity building activities to community leadership structures and partners and community members.

Securing the basic needs of vulnerable groups through cash assistance, primary care and psychosocial activities (2023 portion) Strengthening resilience of high at risk groups through Multi-AoR protection services in Jebel Saman, Aleppo The project contributes to increasing the resilience of the local community (46%), returnees (40%) and IDPs (14%) in the four neighbourhoods: Karm Jazmati, Seken Shebebi, Karm al Tarrab, and Dahret Awwad. The project will be held by Caritas Germany (CG), planned to be back-funded by the German Federal Foreign Ministry (GFFO) and implemented from 01.04.2023 -31.03.2025 by Caritas Syria (CS). The preparation of the proposal is still in process, therefore all of the numbers are only estimates.
The Outcome 1 aims in 2023 at meeting the basic needs of 10.000 individuals of 4 conflict-affected neighbourhoods, and they are empowered to better protect themselves. 1.1: Hybrid Food Package Distribution (Oil and Sugar; blanket approach); percentage of most vulnerable will receive additional items depending on family size; 1.2.: Hybrid Hygiene Basket Distributions (Shampoo and washing powder; blanket approach); percentage of most vulnerable will receive additional items depending on family size; 1.3: Distribution of winterization items (carpets, blankets, heaters, clothes). Output 2 aims in 2023 at the reduction of protection risks of 2.000 vulnerable families as well as 100 CS staff. The activities are implemented at the community center in Karm al Jazmati. 2.1.: Awareness Sessions for women, men, children and adolescent girls and boys. 2.2.: Training on and implementation of community initiatives for youth, men and women. 2.3.: Psychosocial Support Sessions for elderly, children, women and men. 2.4.: Literacy and life skill courses for women and adolescent girls; 2.5.: Tutoring sessions for schoolchildren and offering a summer club during school holidays. 2.6.: Capacity building and Protection Activities for the Project Staff; 2.7 Case management and referrals for protection cases
The NFI and Food Kits distribution will be coordinated with the respective sectors and alligned with their strategies. The exact modalities that make sense in this context are still being assessed. The protection activities are alligned to the protection sector strategy. The regular coordination with the Aleppo-based sub-sectors Protection, CP, GBV, and FSL, CS ensures avoiding duplication of efforts. The community center in Jazmati has been well received by the residents since its opening in 2019 and continues to be the central point for the provision of integrated community-based protection services, to women, adolescent girls and boys, children, men and elderly.
The Community center follows an open-door policy, ensuring the active engagement of the community, allowing real-time evaluations and timely adjustments of activities. Following a participatory approach, the needs will be regularly assessed, i.e., via PDMs applying a proportional piling method, and FDGs. Furthermore, a robust FCM will contribute to ensure the engagement and thus self-identification of the needs in the community. Hence, throughout the project lifetime, the engagement of all community members will be promoted, establishing a two-way communication with the community. This will ensure a timely incorporation of community feedback.

Comprehensive response addressing education needs, food insecurity and socio-economic vulnerabilities of affected populations in Venezuela and Colombia, with a focus on children, and vulnerable indigenous and migrant populations.
(2023 portion of EUR 5 mio -- Education) Programa de seguridad alimentaria basado en la escuela  Con el objetivo de contribuir a la seguridad alimentaria de la población con mayores necesidades, el Programa Mundial de Alimentos de Naciones Unidas (WFP, por sus siglas en inglés) en Venezuela desarrolla un programa de asistencia humanitaria basado en la escuela para garantizar el acceso de los más vulnerables a una alimentación adecuada y nutritiva en el entorno escolar, familiar y comunitario. 
Este programa inició en 2021 con comidas escolares en emergencias priorizando escuelas iniciales y de educación especial.

WFP proporciona comidas escolares acompañado de un paquete integrado de intervenciones para mejorar el acceso a alimentos nutritivos y diversificados a través de las escuelas, contribuyendo al mismo tiempo a mejorar la salud y la nutrición de los niños en edad escolar, los estudiantes con discapacidad y el personal escolar, y apoyando a las comunidades a reducir la dependencia en estrategias de afrontamiento. De manera gradual, el WFP está realizando compras locales de alimentos, e incluyendo acciones para apoyar los mercados locales con compras a pequeños productores y apoyo técnico para acceso a mercados.

En este sentido, el programa de comidas escolares en emergencias tiene los siguientes componentes, para asegurar un enfoque integral que apoye al estudiante en el entorno escolar y familiar:

Germany Contribution to OCHA 2023 Renforcement de la coordination et du plaidoyer humanitaire au Tchad Le projet vise à renforcer le rôle de OCHA dans la mise en œuvre de son mandat et son rôle auprès des partenaires humanitaires et gouvernementaux au niveau des fonctions coordination, gestion de l’information et plaidoyer. Le bureau national d’OCHA à N’Djaména et ses trois sous-bureaux régionaux à l’Est (Abéché) au Sud (Goré) et la province du Lac (Baga Sola) mettent l’accent sur l’opérationnalisation de ses fonctions y compris en assurant un lien entre les activités humanitaires et de développement (nexus) en vue de promouvoir une solution durable visant à ne pas perpétuer une situation de dépendance humanitaire. Dans le cadre de cette nouvelle façon de travailler outre l’opérationnalisation du nexus, le lien avec les objectifs commun des programmes développement, paix et sécurité sera mis en avant. L’accent est aussi mis sur le renforcement de la coordination civilo-militaire afin de faciliter l’accès et la protection des civils.
Le projet a pour but de renforcer la coordination d’une réponse humanitaire rapide et efficace afin de sauver des vies et protéger les personnes affectées par les situations de crises au Tchad. Une coordination humanitaire rapide et correctement évaluée au niveau des besoins de la population affectée permettra aux acteurs humanitaires de mieux identifier et répondre aux besoins humanitaires, de renforcer la préparation de réponse aux urgences à travers le renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et plus spécifiquement l‘Equipe humanitaire pays, la coordination inter-clusters, la coordination civilo-militaire, les clusters, des groupes de travail et les mécanismes de coordination au niveau de terrain.
Le projet vise aussi à assurer le plaidoyer humanitaire à travers l’analyse des besoins faites par l’ensemble de la communauté humanitaire et ses partenaires en vue une compréhension commune des problématiques auxquels fait face le Tchad, ses causes profondes, l’impact sur les populations. OCHA jouera un rôle clé dans la création d'espaces de collection et d'analyse et gestion d’informations, pour assurer une stratégie de réponse coordonnée menant à des actions humanitaires répondant aux besoins les plus aigus et être mieux préparé face aux urgences soudaines. Le projet permettra également d’assurer conjointement avec la communauté humanitaire le plaidoyer en faveur du respect des principes humanitaires, de la protection des civils, de l'accès humanitaire et pour la mobilisation et l'allocation efficace de ressources humanitaires.
Un accent a été mis sur la mise en œuvre des plans d’action de la redevabilité envers les populations affectées (AAP), la PSEA et la préparation aux urgences en plus d'intégrer une attention au genre et de renforcer la centralité de la protection.
Un plaidoyer pour plus de visibilité des résultats tangibles au niveau de la réponse facilitant la mobilisation de ressources pour les différentes crises au Tchad (mouvement de population – crise du Bassin du Lac Tchad, insécurité alimentaire et malnutrition, urgences sanitaires, catastrophes naturelles) est aussi défini comme une priorité dans ce projet.
OCHA continuera de jouer également un rôle moteur dans le renforcement du lien entre les acteurs humanitaires et de développement et la transformation de la réponse humanitaire, en lien avec les engagements pris au Sommet humanitaire mondial de 2016 et ceci à travers la nouvelle façon de travailler (NWOW) et le renforcement de l’utilisation de la modalité de transfert monétaire.

Mitigate the worst effects of water scarcity and hunger through access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene services and provision of emergency assistance to vulnerable communities in acute crises in Sub-Saharan Africa Mitigate the worst effects of hunger through provision of emergency assistance in Unity State According to the IPC released in November 2022, there are over 6.6 million people in South Sudan experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above) between October and November 2022. Food insecurity in the country is highly driven by ongoing conflicts, and climatic shocks, citing from the Humanitarian Needs Overview published in February 2022 states that climate change continues to impact different sectors, particularly agriculture, which is one of the most climate-sensitive economic sectors. Above-normal rainfall for the third consecutive year in 2022 led to prolonged flooding, which impacted areas that had not flooded in previous years constituting a rise in food insecurity countrywide.

Unity state is one of the most food insecure states, that contributes to the estimated 7.8 million people (63% of the population) who likely will face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse acute food insecurity, with 43,000 people likely to be in Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5) in the lean season projection period of April to July 2023. Approximately three-quarters of the state's population is undergoing severe food insecurity, as well as acute malnutrition children attributed to several factors, but primarily because of conflict (including tribal and interclan fighting) and secondarily because of inaccessibility due to poor infrastructure and swampy nature of most of its land that makes it susceptible to floods, resulting to destruction of crops, properties which equates to hunger.

In response to the above problem, Welthungerhilfe (WHH) proposes a project aiming at mitigating the humanitarian crises in Unity State by ensuring the provision of needs-based emergency aid to prevent or decrease morbidities, mortality, and acute malnutrition, especially for vulnerable people in acute humanitarian crises triggered by flight and displacement, droughts, floods, and anticipated periods of hunger. 

The project approach will revolve around addressing issues of climate change through training of 20 DRR committees to develop vulnerability mappings for their specific context on boma (village level) or Payam level (sub-county level), depending on context. The committees will present a cross-section of the population since all ages and genders will be represented. The project will therefore target 56,000 beneficiaries in total in the form of IDPs, returnees and host communities. More specifically, the intervention will target, women and children-headed households, including women of reproductive age and pregnant and lactating women (PLWs), unaccompanied minors, people with disabilities, the elderly and chronically ill with various activities that include the distribution of NFI kits consisting of various household items, cash for work activities to help the most vulnerable households meet the food consumption gap while building household and community assets that reduce the risk of disaster, strengthen livelihoods and build resilience over time. They will also benefit from agriculture crop production training, distribution of ruminants and support to livestock health to help build their resilience to shocks. The project will seek to reduce the deterioration of people’s physical and mental well-being through coping mechanisms.  Target groups will additionally be linked to other ongoing interventions implemented by Welthungerhilfe and other agencies so that they can benefit from the services offered.

Support to International Medical Corps (IMC) for the Gender Based Violence Prevention and Response for conflict- affected population in South Sudan
-- FCDO Gender-based Violence (GBV) Prevention and Response for Conflict-Affected Population in South Sudan The GBV prevention and response program of International Medical Corps (IMC) in South Sudan aims to empower communities and build resilience through promoting social and behavioral change to address the root causes of GBV in the country. The project targets key population to create a sustainable change in attitude and practices through male engagement, working with community leaders and building capacity of local stakeholders. Leveraging on the vast experiences, gains, and successes of IMC in implementing GBV prevention and response interventions through the FCDO-HARISS program, ECHO, SSHF and UNFPA . This project will be continued to implement in the states of Western Bahr el Ghazal (Wau IDP Camp and County), Upper Nile and Malakal PoC and County), Unity (Nyal County), and in Canal/Pigi County. This project  will directly benefit about 27495 vulnerable women and girls across the target locations. One of the project’s key priorities is to further strengthen core services to survivors of GBV and other vulnerable women and girls in the aforesaid intervention sites. These services include quality case management using a survivor-centered approach, along with psychosocial support to enhance healing and recovery. IMC UK works to ensure that survivors’ holistic needs are met by providing multi-sectoral services, referring to health centers for clinical management of rape, to legal justice services and to other kinds of support based on the needs of survivors. In addition to individual Psychososcia support (PSS ) for survivors, IMC UK will continue with PSS group activities for all vulnerable women and girls in the women girls’ safe spaces (WGSS). To ensure sustainability of the project and ownership by the community, especially of the WGSSs, in Wau, Nyal Malakal, and Canal Pigi . IMC already established, leadership committee comprise of 8 members from the community selected by their fellow women with the responsibility to give support, information, feedback, and suggestions that will foster empowerment and ownership of the space and the overall wellbeing of their members. The women committee members will be further empowered with knowledge and skills through hands-on management of the spaces and co-leading with them on the daily functioning of the WGSS. The women committee will be continuously mentored and trained on GBV basic concepts, safe referral, and referral pathways, and on leadership and conflict management and facilitation techniques and on various psychosocial support activities using IMC’s and IRC’s global WGSS toolkit. IMC UK will implement holistic community engagement strategies on the promotion of long-term positive change in the targeted communities. IMC will use the GBV community mobilization tool called SASA! - Phase-based strategy to help communities rethink about “power” and the positive use of power. “Preventing Violence against Women and Girls: Engaging Men in Accountable Practice (EMAP)” is also another tool that will be used to ensure men engagement with accountability to prevent GBV in the targeted community in Nyal, Wau and Malakal. In addition, IMC trains and collaborates with GBV Taskforce members in Wau, Malakal and Nyal. These will be supported by staff IMC UK staff to do awareness raising, and safe confidential referral of any survivors who disclose to them. IMC UK will provide emergency cash assistance for case management to the vulnerable women and girls. Cash assistance is one of the interagency minimum standards in GBV programming in emergency. Additionally, IMC UK opts to implement cash assistance based on lesson learnt and feedback from women and girls on importance of cash assistance as lifesaving. IMC will procure and distribute dignity for the conflict-affected women and girls. The dignity kits will include sanitary items, as well as other items explicitly tailored towards the local needs of women and girls of reproductive age affected by the conflict.

Support to reduce hunger gaps, improve long-term food security and mitigate conflict among the rural poor in three states of Northern Bahr El Ghazal, Western Bahr El Ghazal and Warrap, South Sudan
-- FCDO Food and livelihood assistance to the most vulnerable and crisis affected population in South Sudan  The proposed project aims to provide food assistance, livelihood and resilience support to 1,105,380 vulnerable populations in Upper Nile, Western Equatoria, Central Equatoria and Greater Bahr el Ghazal. The project will implement activities that will prevent famine and improve food consumption, dietary diversity and coping strategies of target beneficiaries in IPC 5, 4 and 3. The project will also seek to enhance emergency food production and contribute to the reduction of dependency to food and agricultural inputs. World Vision will adopt a mix of intervention approaches including but not limited to unconditional and General Food Distribution, cash transfers, complementary livelihood support, capacity building (e.g., modern agronomic practices, Integrated Pest Management, Natural Resource Management, etc.), and resilience building at the household level. The proposed project will also be implemented in synergy with other sectors implemented by World Vision in the targeted locations such as health, nutrition, WASH, gender and protection related programming while maintaining coordinating and complementarity with the efforts of other humanitarian actors and line ministries. In order to reach the target beneficiaries with prioritized cluster objectives, World Vision South Sudan proposed a total of $4,512,952 US project budget for 2023.

Brief project description: The project seek to support conflict affected vulnerable communities in northeast Nigeria to rebuild their livelihoods and resilience through the provision of agricultural based livelihoods support to communities to enable them produce their own food. Emergency Food Security and Livelihood assistance to vulnerable and conflict affected households in north east Nigeria Food insecurity and malnutrition remain prevalent across Nigeria, mainly driven by the ongoing protracted conflict in the Northeast, mass displacement and the resultant IDP return process, adverse climate change and variability, such as drought, long dry spells, and flood, land degradation increasing insecurity and banditry, natural resource-based conflicts and an unfavorable macroeconomic situation manifested in rising food price inflation, etc. Further, the disruption of food and agricultural input supply chains by the Russia-Ukrainian war has led to severe availability and access constraints especially for poor farming households because of high food and agricultural input prices, especially fertilizer.
Despite the efforts of humanitarian communities in addressing the manifestations of the emergency in the country, the situation of food security continues to be a challenge. According to the latest Cadre Harmonise (CH) analysis, an estimated 19.45 million people, nearly 63 percent of them in Northeast and Northwest Nigeria are projected to be at risk of severe food insecurity during the peak of the 2022 lean season. In addition, the latest IPC acute malnutrition analysis report released in June 2022 estimates that 1.4 million children and, nearly 152,000 pregnant and lactating women are likely to suffer acute malnutrition during this period. Therefore, the urgent need for an expanded humanitarian food security response cannot be overstated. While the humanitarian interventions have been playing vital and critical role in addressing the needs of affected populations, it is obvious more has to be done to support the resilience of the livelihoods and the households. Given that the majority of those in need are involved in agriculture related activities, it has become necessary and urgent to promote agriculture-based livelihoods to famers whose majority are smallholders.  
In 2021 FAO reached over 1 million people and is planning to scale up and reach 2 million people (approximately 285,715 households) in need of agricultural-based livelihoods assistance in Nigeria in 2023/2024 with a stronger focus on Northeast and Northwest Nigeria due to the high level of vulnerability in the two regions. Due to restrictions on target numbers submitted in the HRP and its limited coverage (only targeting the Northeast), 1.7 million people will be targeted through the HRP while the remaining 0.3 million will be planned outside the HRP framework. To achieve this target FAO Nigeria is requiring a total of USD 86 million. Notably, funding for agriculture livelihood had declined significantly, for example, in 2022 the livelihood and agriculture funding stand at 6%, while food assistance is 95% covered. This requires a strong coordinated advocacy strategy to shift the paradigm.  An estimated 1.7 million people will be targeted for emergency agricultural livelihoods assistance while 0.3 million will be targeted for resilience interventions including in agribusiness, skills development for the creation of decent employment and income such as stoves production, aquaculture, livestock, etc. that increase the resilience of the beneficiaries.  
The scale-up plan will target the most vulnerable groups including IDPs, returnees, and host communities, especially women, and girls.    FAO Nigeria provides various agricultural livelihood assistance packages based on the livelihoods of the targeted household and the related activity. This is including agricultural rainy and dry season inputs, livestock restocking goats and poultry, urban and peri-urban homestead gardening, aquaculture, agribusiness enterprise support, nutritional support, and SAFE kits. This intervention will be delivered through a combination of in-kind, cash, and cash+ assistance. The scale-up plan is aligned to the FAO Corporate Global strategy framework of achieving Better Production, Better Nutrition, Better environment and Better life.

Lukmef	Child Protection. 2022-2023. 2022 portion total amount CHF 123'200 (7F-11035.01) Comprehensive WASH response to affected children and displaced families in the South West and Littoral Regions of Cameroon The socio-political crisis in the NW and SW regions of Cameroon, now in its sixth year, characterized by continued fighting between State security forces (SSF) and non-State armed groups (NSAG, targeted attacks, destruction of property, arbitrary arrest, kidnappings for ransom, extortion of money and continued use of improvised explosive devices (IEDs) (OCHA, 2022), has left more than 1.08 million people from NW, SW, LIT and West region in need of humanitarian assistance (HNO, 2022). More especially, the insufficient investment of Cameroon Government in basic social services, poverty and limited response provided by Humanitarian actor in the Northwest and South west regions continue to exacerbate the water and sanitation need of affected population including neighboring regions (Littoral and West regions). The crisis has had serious negative effects on water, hygiene and sanitation with mostly children, women and girls highly affected, as they are the ones who often access WASH facilities. The situation further compounded with the public health crisis of COVID 19, cholera outbreak and monkey pox which have hit the already crisis affected communities. In September 2022 SitRep, Out of 12 517 cases and 254 deaths reported at national level, the South-West region represent 48% of cases (6017) and 36% (93) of deaths, marking 2022 as the second most affected year by cholera for the past 25 years with more than 13,000 cases and 284 deaths of cholera reported (HNO, 2023). The risk factors are still much evident in these affected regions such as lack safe of access to safe water, sanitation facilities (latrines) and poor hygiene practices that poses a thread to the lives of these vulnerable children and displaced families. It is therefore the responsibility of humanitarian actors and service providers to scale up humanitarian response and delivery of life saving humanitarian needs and services to the affected persons in most insecure and inaccessible locations. It is within this framework that this project in its response will prioritize the safety and dignity of the targeted children, women and girls, as well as affected host population and will reduce the risk and exposure to gender-based violence and other violence related to accessing WASH facilities. Our project will provide WASH humanitarian assistance through all modalities with specificity to 6500 individuals directly utilizing improve water supply service with systematic control of water quality at household level, 1750 households will directly utilize improve sanitation facilities through the support and construction of Eco-friendly boifil latrines, and the provision of latrine kits to displaced families and vulnerable host communities. 15,625 Individuals reached with community sensitization messaging on critical handwashing and good hygiene practices through information and communication materials, door-to-door and cholera tools to efficiently address cholera risk factors and other possible outbreaks associated to poor hygiene practices. 18750 individuals will benefits complete WASH kits through all modalities, 1875 vulnerable adolescent girls and women within reproductive age will be reached with menstrual hygiene kits. 600 beneficiaries will be trained on how to access humanitarian assistance as well as capacitated on how to provide feedback and complains to humanitarian actors. The adoption of community based approached will be the central response strategy through consultation and engagements of all relevant stakeholders and community groups for an impactful, dignify and sustainable WASH service delivery to the vulnerable affected population. For a more responsible intervention that respect the dignity of beneficiaries, the project will mainstream accountability to affected population (AAP) within the response from project inception to the exit strategy and ensure humanitarian principle are respected at all stage of the intervention.

Breaking the Silence Against SGBV in Torit and Ikwotos, Eastern Equatoria State Creating a Safe Environment for and Providing Life-Saving GBV Response Services as well as integrating child protection components to the Crisis-Affected Women, Girls and Children in South Sudan In line with the identified needs and gaps, CARE International in South Sudan aims to provide a comprehensive package of GBV response services, which will be complemented with the prevention activities that address the root causes of the GBV in Juba, Magwi, Ikotos, Torit, Kapoeta North, Budi, Wau, Jur River, Koch, Rubkona, Pariang, Bor South, Pibor, Twic East, Duk and Akobo.  The interventions will be provided through static centers and through mobile and outreach teams. Static Women Girls Safe Spaces (WGFS) will be used as entry points to reach out to the communities, while outreach sessions by mobile teams will also be used as means of engaging with communities. The WGFSs will serve as the centers where women and girls can come together and socialize while also improving their psychosocial wellbeing. In order to do that CARE will provide structured and unstructured PSS activities. The unstructured activities will take the form of recreational activities which will be determined in consultation with the women and girls, i.e.. knitting, baking, sewing, painting or handicrafts. The structured activities on the other hand will aim to promote overall life skills of women and girls. Similarly, CARE will train women and girls on usage and set up of Fuel Efficient Stoves as part of GBV risk mitigation measures. These efforts will be supported with experience sharing sessions among women on cooking or sharing recipes to promote cohesion and communication among women groups. CARE will also offer income generation activities to the women and girls who fit into the activity criteria, which will include vulnerable individuals, survivors, female-headed households and so on.

Through the WGFSs, CARE will provide GBV case management services to the survivors, while ensuring updating (or creating referral pathways) referral pathways and service mappings for these locations to provide safe referrals to the services. As part of the individual case management plans, CARE will also provide one-time cash assistance to support the GBV survivors, when deemed necessary according to the developed SOPs. Community members who need legal advice and/or need to attend legal information sessions will also be provided with legal support at the WGFSs. Women and girls of reproductive age, who fit into vulnerability criteria set up in line with UNFPA's guidance will also be provided with dignity kits to ensure they can maintain their dignity and mobility in a crisis context.

CARE will also additionally provide awareness raising sessions to raise awareness on key gender and protection topics, as well as gender equality through mobile teams and at the WGFSs. This will help to engage men and boys in the discussions. Similarly, CARE will lead on the primary prevention activities by engaging men and boys through structured curriculums such as EMAP and Program RA.

In order to ensure that the staff are well equipped to provide support to the communities, all frontline staff and community mobilizers will be trained in various topics including case management, PSS, GBV risk mitigation and GBV core concepts. CARE's previous and existing presence in the aforementioned locations, as well as GBV programming experience in these locations will help to ensure community buy-in and prevent backlash from the communities. 

CARE will partner with UNIDOR to implement CP activities to provide case management, PSS, referrals to support child GBV survivors.

Chad - OCHA Office [Donor:O533, Recipient:O270] Renforcement de la coordination et du plaidoyer humanitaire au Tchad Le projet vise à renforcer le rôle de OCHA dans la mise en œuvre de son mandat et son rôle auprès des partenaires humanitaires et gouvernementaux au niveau des fonctions coordination, gestion de l’information et plaidoyer. Le bureau national d’OCHA à N’Djaména et ses trois sous-bureaux régionaux à l’Est (Abéché) au Sud (Goré) et la province du Lac (Baga Sola) mettent l’accent sur l’opérationnalisation de ses fonctions y compris en assurant un lien entre les activités humanitaires et de développement (nexus) en vue de promouvoir une solution durable visant à ne pas perpétuer une situation de dépendance humanitaire. Dans le cadre de cette nouvelle façon de travailler outre l’opérationnalisation du nexus, le lien avec les objectifs commun des programmes développement, paix et sécurité sera mis en avant. L’accent est aussi mis sur le renforcement de la coordination civilo-militaire afin de faciliter l’accès et la protection des civils.
Le projet a pour but de renforcer la coordination d’une réponse humanitaire rapide et efficace afin de sauver des vies et protéger les personnes affectées par les situations de crises au Tchad. Une coordination humanitaire rapide et correctement évaluée au niveau des besoins de la population affectée permettra aux acteurs humanitaires de mieux identifier et répondre aux besoins humanitaires, de renforcer la préparation de réponse aux urgences à travers le renforcement des mécanismes de coordination et plus spécifiquement l‘Equipe humanitaire pays, la coordination inter-clusters, la coordination civilo-militaire, les clusters, des groupes de travail et les mécanismes de coordination au niveau de terrain.
Le projet vise aussi à assurer le plaidoyer humanitaire à travers l’analyse des besoins faites par l’ensemble de la communauté humanitaire et ses partenaires en vue une compréhension commune des problématiques auxquels fait face le Tchad, ses causes profondes, l’impact sur les populations. OCHA jouera un rôle clé dans la création d'espaces de collection et d'analyse et gestion d’informations, pour assurer une stratégie de réponse coordonnée menant à des actions humanitaires répondant aux besoins les plus aigus et être mieux préparé face aux urgences soudaines. Le projet permettra également d’assurer conjointement avec la communauté humanitaire le plaidoyer en faveur du respect des principes humanitaires, de la protection des civils, de l'accès humanitaire et pour la mobilisation et l'allocation efficace de ressources humanitaires.
Un accent a été mis sur la mise en œuvre des plans d’action de la redevabilité envers les populations affectées (AAP), la PSEA et la préparation aux urgences en plus d'intégrer une attention au genre et de renforcer la centralité de la protection.
Un plaidoyer pour plus de visibilité des résultats tangibles au niveau de la réponse facilitant la mobilisation de ressources pour les différentes crises au Tchad (mouvement de population – crise du Bassin du Lac Tchad, insécurité alimentaire et malnutrition, urgences sanitaires, catastrophes naturelles) est aussi défini comme une priorité dans ce projet.
OCHA continuera de jouer également un rôle moteur dans le renforcement du lien entre les acteurs humanitaires et de développement et la transformation de la réponse humanitaire, en lien avec les engagements pris au Sommet humanitaire mondial de 2016 et ceci à travers la nouvelle façon de travailler (NWOW) et le renforcement de l’utilisation de la modalité de transfert monétaire.

food aid Food assistance to address increasing levels of severe food insecurity in South Sudan Meet the lifesaving food requirements of people in South Sudan who are facing food security crises, including those living in (ex)-POCs and IDP and those otherwise affected by conflict, natural disaster and/or seasonal food insecurity. WFP will provide general food distributions (GFD) to the most food insecure people in South Sudan. At the field level, food assistance will be overseen by the WFP Field Offices and implemented by NGO partners or provided through the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM). WFP provides food assistance and common services through a comprehensive and collaborative humanitarian intervention by deploying mobile teams, supported by cooperating partners to reach populations facing the most urgent needs in the most inaccessible areas of the South Sudan, subject to the availability of resources.
Complementary to food distributions, WFP will seek to offer value-added solutions (light resilience- building activities, peace/conflict resolution training also called GFD+), in response to needs and priorities identified by the community. Through GFD+, WFP together with its cooperating partners and other stakeholders will provide unconditional opportunities, identified through a community-based, people-centric participatory approach to targeted beneficiaries. GFD+ adds value to emergency food assistance with a focus on solutions that address the root causes of food and nutrition insecurity and better equip beneficiaries to fight hunger. The GFD+ activity type, duration, frequency, and participation will be catered to specific local sites and may range from COVID-19 awareness, training, or sensitisation on peaceful resolution of conflicts, mitigation measures to nutrition education, dyke rehabilitation and communal asset management, income-generating activities which lead to women's economic empowerment and have positive impact on household food security, or other solutions. WFP will also implement resilience building activities including Food Assistance for Assets (FFA) to support communities to improve their food security, restore their livelihoods, strengthen their resilience to shocks and build self-reliance, while contributing to peace. 
Mitigation measures to reduce and prevent the potential the spread of COVID-19, including new variants, and other potential viral outbreaks have been incorporated into standard operating procedures for all interactions with beneficiaries, including training of partners and stakeholders, increasing general awareness among partners and beneficiaries, enforcing social distancing, promoting handwashing, disinfecting sites, reducing the frequency of distribution cycles, and mandating the utilization of personal protective equipment (PPE). These measures are mainstreamed into all WFP activities.

--- 2023 ---- Protection Fortalecer el sistema de protección de NNA con servicios de prevención y respuesta con enfoque en edad, genero y diversidad.  UNICEF mantendrá su enfoque en apoyar a los diferentes integrantes del sistema de Protección para que brinden servicios de prevención y respuestas de calidad con un enfoque en edad, género y diversidad para los NNA y familias más vulnerables y en riesgo. UNICEF mantendrá los esfuerzos en el desarrollo de los objetivos e indicadores sectoriales del Plan de Respuesta Humanitaria 2022-2023, a través de planes de trabajo con socios implementadores nacionales e internacionales. La Protección de la Infancia es la prevención y respuesta a la explotación, abuso, negligencia, prácticas nocivas y la violencia contra los niños, niñas y adolescentes (NNA). Está incorporada en la Convención sobre los Derechos del Niño y las Metas de Desarrollo Sostenible. Con un abordaje socio-ecológico, UNICEF y sus socios trabajaran con un enfoque en los NNA, las familias, las comunidades y el sistema de protección formal e informal para que acciones preventivas y de respuestas para temas de protección de NNA sean implementadas en los estados priorizados del país.  El enfoque principal de esta propuesta es la prevención que se realiza no solamente a través de los socios de protección, pero también con el apoyo de otros sectores como nutrición, salud y educación para cumplir resultados de protección infantil. Los principales temas cubiertos incluyen: VbG y trata, separación familiar/cuidado alternativo, violencia en general incluyendo la de género y crianza positiva. Además de nuestro enfoque central en la prevención, UNICEF Venezuela se enfoca en que ningún NNA se quede atrás: trabajaremos con socios para alcanzar a los NNA con mayor riesgo de protección que incluyen NNA con discapacidades, NNA separados y no acompañados, de poblaciones indígenas y afro-descendientes, en situacion de movilidad y NNA que sufren otras formas de discriminación y exclusión. 
Donde los NNA están sufriendo violaciones, UNICEF trabajará con socios gubernamentales y no-gubernamentales para fortalecer el acceso a los servicios de respuesta para prevenir reincidencia y brindar atención y vinculación segura a otros servicios. Los principales servicios brindados incluyen: apoyo en acceder a registro de nacimiento, salud mental y apoyo psicosocial, gestión de caso incluyendo a NNA sobreviviente de VbG. Una modalidad diferente para alcanzar objetivos de protección será la de las transferencias monetarias/incentivos, otra componente importante de todas las intervenciones es el enfoque en la calidad y en temas transversales como lo de género, AAP, PEAS, adolescencia y inclusión.

These action will be implemented in selected urban, peri-urban and rural remote areas of 8 prioritized states at nationwide and will reach 683,649 people, including 553,649 children and 150,000 pregnant women.

South Sudan/CE ,Nutrition  BHA/USAID Gender-based Violence (GBV) Prevention and Response for Conflict-Affected Population in South Sudan The GBV prevention and response program of International Medical Corps (IMC) in South Sudan aims to empower communities and build resilience through promoting social and behavioral change to address the root causes of GBV in the country. The project targets key population to create a sustainable change in attitude and practices through male engagement, working with community leaders and building capacity of local stakeholders. Leveraging on the vast experiences, gains, and successes of IMC in implementing GBV prevention and response interventions through the FCDO-HARISS program, ECHO, SSHF and UNFPA . This project will be continued to implement in the states of Western Bahr el Ghazal (Wau IDP Camp and County), Upper Nile and Malakal PoC and County), Unity (Nyal County), and in Canal/Pigi County. This project  will directly benefit about 27495 vulnerable women and girls across the target locations. One of the project’s key priorities is to further strengthen core services to survivors of GBV and other vulnerable women and girls in the aforesaid intervention sites. These services include quality case management using a survivor-centered approach, along with psychosocial support to enhance healing and recovery. IMC UK works to ensure that survivors’ holistic needs are met by providing multi-sectoral services, referring to health centers for clinical management of rape, to legal justice services and to other kinds of support based on the needs of survivors. In addition to individual Psychososcia support (PSS ) for survivors, IMC UK will continue with PSS group activities for all vulnerable women and girls in the women girls’ safe spaces (WGSS). To ensure sustainability of the project and ownership by the community, especially of the WGSSs, in Wau, Nyal Malakal, and Canal Pigi . IMC already established, leadership committee comprise of 8 members from the community selected by their fellow women with the responsibility to give support, information, feedback, and suggestions that will foster empowerment and ownership of the space and the overall wellbeing of their members. The women committee members will be further empowered with knowledge and skills through hands-on management of the spaces and co-leading with them on the daily functioning of the WGSS. The women committee will be continuously mentored and trained on GBV basic concepts, safe referral, and referral pathways, and on leadership and conflict management and facilitation techniques and on various psychosocial support activities using IMC’s and IRC’s global WGSS toolkit. IMC UK will implement holistic community engagement strategies on the promotion of long-term positive change in the targeted communities. IMC will use the GBV community mobilization tool called SASA! - Phase-based strategy to help communities rethink about “power” and the positive use of power. “Preventing Violence against Women and Girls: Engaging Men in Accountable Practice (EMAP)” is also another tool that will be used to ensure men engagement with accountability to prevent GBV in the targeted community in Nyal, Wau and Malakal. In addition, IMC trains and collaborates with GBV Taskforce members in Wau, Malakal and Nyal. These will be supported by staff IMC UK staff to do awareness raising, and safe confidential referral of any survivors who disclose to them. IMC UK will provide emergency cash assistance for case management to the vulnerable women and girls. Cash assistance is one of the interagency minimum standards in GBV programming in emergency. Additionally, IMC UK opts to implement cash assistance based on lesson learnt and feedback from women and girls on importance of cash assistance as lifesaving. IMC will procure and distribute dignity for the conflict-affected women and girls. The proposed interventions  will be implemented in 10 Counties  of Uror, Twic East, Pochalla, Morobo, Kajo Keji, Yei, Lainya, Aweil East, Aweil Centre, and Aweil South of the 4 states  Jonglei, Greater Pibor Administrative Area and Central Equatoria, Northern Bahr el Ghazal respectively.
